summary: Kleppmann explains the principles behind reliable, scalable and maintainable data systems: storage, replication, partitioning, transactions, distributed-systems trouble, and batch and stream processing.

unitSummaries.Chapter 1: Defines reliability, scalability and maintainability as the goals every data system is judged by, with the faults, load and change they must survive.
unitSummaries.Chapter 2: Compares relational, document and graph data models and the query languages that go with each, and what each makes easy or hard.
unitSummaries.Chapter 3: Explains how databases store and index data: log-structured and B-tree engines, plus transaction versus analytics storage and column stores.
unitSummaries.Chapter 4: Compares encoding formats such as JSON, Thrift, Protocol Buffers and Avro, and how each handles schema change, compatibility and dataflow between processes.
unitSummaries.Chapter 5: Covers keeping copies of data on several machines: leader-follower, multi-leader and leaderless designs, replication lag, and conflict handling.
unitSummaries.Chapter 6: Explains splitting data across nodes by key range or hash, secondary indexes, rebalancing and request routing.
unitSummaries.Chapter 7: Explains transactions, ACID, weak isolation levels and the anomalies they allow, and how serializability is achieved.
unitSummaries.Chapter 8: Shows what goes wrong in distributed systems: unreliable networks, clocks and process pauses, and how to reason about truth and system models.
unitSummaries.Chapter 9: Covers linearizability, ordering and causality, distributed transactions and consensus algorithms, and what each guarantee costs.
unitSummaries.Chapter 10: Explains batch processing from Unix tools to MapReduce and dataflow engines, joins and grouping, and how outputs are built from immutable inputs.
unitSummaries.Chapter 11: Covers event streams, message brokers and logs, databases as streams, stream joins, time reasoning and fault tolerance.
unitSummaries.Chapter 12: Argues for integrating specialised systems through derived data and dataflow, designing for correctness and auditability, and doing right by the people whose data it is.
unitSummaries.Whole book: Puts the book together: how reliability, scale, models, replication, transactions and derived data combine, and which design to reach for in a given situation.

concepts.title: Data-intensive, not compute-intensive
concepts.question: What makes an application data-intensive rather than compute-intensive?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Many applications are slowed down by their data, not by arithmetic. Treating every performance worry as a shortage of processor power sends effort to the wrong place.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Ask what limits the application. For a data-intensive one, raw CPU power is rarely the limit; the bigger problems are usually the amount of data, the complexity of the data, and the speed at which it changes.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The label says where the difficulty lies, not what to build. You still have to choose tools and approaches that fit the application's own requirements.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You are sizing up a new application and need to decide whether to spend design effort on data handling or on computation.

card.rule: Call an application data-intensive when the amount, complexity or speed of change of its data, not raw CPU power, is its main difficulty.
card.limits: The word is typical, not universal: an application whose time goes into heavy computation on little data is compute-intensive, and this lens fits it less well.

concepts.title: Standard building blocks
concepts.question: Which standard building blocks do data-intensive applications combine, and what does each one do?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Applications keep needing the same few data functions. Rebuilding each one inside every application wastes effort.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use standard blocks: databases store data to be found again later; caches remember an expensive result to speed up reads; search indexes let users search by keyword or filter; stream processing sends a message to another process to be handled asynchronously; batch processing periodically crunches accumulated data.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each block comes in many variants, so you must choose among them, and combining blocks for a job that no single tool can do alone is hard.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You are splitting an application's data needs into functions before you choose tools.

card.rule: Name the function each building block provides, then choose among its variants for your own requirements.
card.limits: The five blocks are examples, not a full list, and one tool can serve more than one role.

media.alt: A white silhouette of a leaping wild boar on a black background, used as title-page art.

concepts.title: Combining tools into one data system
concepts.question: What responsibility falls on you when you stitch several data tools together behind one service?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Tools no longer fit neat categories, and many applications need more than any one tool offers. A datastore may double as a message queue, and a message queue may offer database-like durability.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Split the work into tasks that each tool does well, stitch the tools together with application code, and hide them behind the service's API. Application code keeps a cache or search index in sync with the main database.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You have built a new special-purpose data system and now own its guarantees, such as a cache that is correctly invalidated or updated on writes so outside clients see consistent results.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: No single tool can meet the application's storage and processing needs.

card.rule: When you combine tools into one service, you are designing a new data system and must provide its guarantees yourself.
card.limits: The API hides the parts from clients, not from you. No composite design is right everywhere, because more than tools shapes it.

concepts.title: Reliability, scalability, maintainability
concepts.question: Which three concerns does the book use to judge a data system, and what does each demand?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A designer faces tricky questions, yet words like reliable and scalable are often used without a clear meaning.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Judge a system on three concerns. Reliability: keep working correctly, at the desired performance, in the face of adversity. Scalability: have reasonable ways to deal with growth in data, traffic or complexity. Maintainability: let many people, in engineering and operations, work on it productively over time.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: There are no easy fixes for any of the three. The chapter defines them and ways of thinking about them; later chapters give techniques.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need a shared vocabulary to judge or discuss a data system in most software.

card.rule: Judge a data system by whether it keeps working correctly under adversity, copes with growth, and stays productive for many people over time.
card.limits: These three are the book's focus, not the whole list: the chapter's summary also names security, compliance and compatibility.

media.alt: A back-cover page for the book: publisher name, description of the book, two endorsement quotes, a list of bullet points about the author, a barcode and a QR code.

concepts.title: What working correctly means
concepts.question: What do users typically expect from software they call reliable?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Everyone has an intuitive idea of reliable, but the word is too vague to design or test against.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Break working correctly into four expectations: the application performs the function the user expected; it tolerates users' mistakes or unexpected use; its performance is good enough for the use case, under the expected load and data volume; it prevents unauthorized access and abuse. Reliability is roughly continuing to work correctly even when things go wrong.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Correct is broad: performance and security count too, so a system can fail to be reliable without ever crashing.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Someone says make it reliable and you need checkable expectations.

card.rule: Reliability means continuing to work correctly, where correct covers the expected function, tolerance of mistakes, adequate performance and security, even when things go wrong.
card.limits: Good enough performance is tied to the use case and expected load and data volume, so no single threshold fits every system.

concepts.title: Fault versus failure
concepts.question: How does a fault differ from a failure, and why can we not tolerate every fault?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Things inside a system go wrong all the time, and a system cannot be made free of them.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Separate the two terms. A fault is one component deviating from its spec; a failure is the system as a whole ceasing to provide the required service. Design fault-tolerance mechanisms that stop faults from causing failures; systems that anticipate and cope with faults are fault-tolerant or resilient.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Fault-tolerant is slightly misleading, because tolerating every possible fault is not feasible. You must pick which types of faults to tolerate.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You decide what a design must survive and what it may reasonably give up.

card.example: A web service runs on three servers. One server's disk fails: that is a fault. Pages still load from the other two, so there is no failure. If all three were lost together, users would get nothing, and that is a failure.
card.rule: Aim to keep a component's fault from becoming a failure of the whole system, for the types of fault you choose to tolerate.
card.limits: Tolerance covers only certain types of fault, and some faults cannot be cured afterwards.

concepts.title: Inducing faults on purpose
concepts.question: Why might a fault-tolerant system deliberately cause faults, and when is prevention better than tolerance?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Fault-tolerance code runs rarely, so it may fail the first time a real fault arrives.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Trigger faults deliberately, for example by randomly killing individual processes without warning. The fault-tolerance machinery is exercised continually and tested, raising confidence that real faults will be handled. Netflix's Chaos Monkey is an example.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You raise the fault rate on purpose, which only makes sense in systems built to tolerate faults. For some faults there is no cure, such as an attacker gaining sensitive data, so prevention is better there.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You depend on fault tolerance and want proof that it works.

card.rule: In a fault-tolerant system, exercise the tolerance with deliberate faults; where a fault cannot be cured afterwards, prevent it instead.
card.limits: Inducing faults suits systems designed to tolerate them, and it does not apply to faults like leaked secrets that cannot be undone.

concepts.title: Hardware faults and redundancy
concepts.question: How common are hardware faults in large installations, and how are they usually handled?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Disks crash, RAM becomes faulty, the power grid has a blackout, someone unplugs the wrong cable. With many machines these things happen all the time.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Add redundancy to individual hardware components: disks in a RAID configuration, servers with dual power supplies and hot-swappable CPUs, datacenters with batteries and diesel generators. When one component dies, its twin takes over while it is replaced.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Redundancy cannot completely prevent hardware problems from causing failures, though it is well understood and can keep a machine running uninterrupted for years.

blocks.label: Numbers
blocks.text: Disks report a mean time to failure of about 10 to 50 years. On a storage cluster of 10,000 disks, expect on average about one disk to die per day.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You run on machines whose individual failures are random and rare enough for spares to cover them.

card.rule: Expect routine hardware faults in a large installation and add redundancy to components so a spare takes over.
card.limits: Redundancy cannot completely prevent hardware problems from causing failures.

concepts.title: Tolerating the loss of whole machines
concepts.question: Why is there a move toward software that tolerates the loss of entire machines?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Hardware redundancy inside one machine is not enough when whole machines vanish. In some cloud platforms such as AWS, virtual machine instances commonly become unavailable without warning, because those platforms prioritize flexibility and elasticity over single-machine reliability.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use software fault-tolerance techniques in preference to, or in addition to, hardware redundancy, so the system tolerates the loss of entire machines.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Tolerance becomes the software's job rather than the hardware's, so the system must be built that way from the start.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You run many machines, depend on cloud instances, or cannot afford downtime for routine maintenance.

card.rule: Build the software to survive the loss of whole machines, which also lets you maintain one node at a time.
card.limits: Hardware redundancy still helps; the book says software tolerance is used in preference or in addition, not as a replacement in every case.

concepts.title: Systematic software faults
concepts.question: How do software faults differ from hardware faults in how widely they strike?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Hardware faults are typically random and independent: one machine's failing disk does not imply that another will fail. Weak correlations exist, such as a hot server rack, but a large number of components rarely fail together.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat systematic errors as a separate class. They are harder to anticipate and are correlated across nodes, so they tend to cause many more system failures than uncorrelated hardware faults. Examples: a bug that crashes every server on a bad input, a runaway process that uses up a shared resource, a dependency that slows down or returns corrupted responses, and cascading failures.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Our reading: identical copies run identical code, so redundancy of the usual hardware kind does little against a bug they all share.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You judge which faults can take many nodes down at once.

card.rule: Plan for software faults as correlated and systematic, since they can hit every node together unlike random hardware faults.
card.limits: Hardware faults can also correlate weakly through a common cause, and not every software bug is systematic.

concepts.title: Coping with dormant software bugs
concepts.question: What can help with systematic software faults when there is no quick solution?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Software bugs often lie dormant for a long time. An unusual set of circumstances reveals that the software was making an assumption about its environment: usually true, but eventually it stops being true.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: No quick fix exists, but many small things help: think carefully about assumptions and interactions in the system, test thoroughly, isolate processes, allow processes to crash and restart, and measure, monitor and analyze behavior in production.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: No single measure removes the problem; each covers part of it, so effort is spread over several.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You design or operate software whose faults could hit many nodes at once.

card.rule: Combine many small measures, from checking assumptions to monitoring in production, because no single fix removes systematic faults.
card.limits: These measures reduce the risk; they do not make bugs impossible.

concepts.title: Designing against human error
concepts.question: What causes most outages according to the cited study, and how can design reduce human mistakes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Humans design, build and operate systems, and even with the best intentions they are unreliable. A study of large internet services found operator configuration errors to be the leading cause of outages, ahead of hardware faults.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Make it easy to do the right thing and discourage the wrong thing through well-designed abstractions, APIs and admin interfaces. Decouple the places where people make the most mistakes from the places where they can cause failures, with fully featured non-production sandboxes where people can experiment on real data without affecting real users.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: If interfaces are too restrictive, people work around them and the benefit is lost, so the balance is tricky.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: People change configuration, run commands or deploy on a system that matters.

card.rule: Make mistakes hard to make and keep them away from real users, without locking people into workarounds.
card.limits: Prevention alone is not enough; the best systems combine it with testing, recovery and monitoring.

concepts.title: Testing, recovery and monitoring
concepts.question: Beyond prevention, how do the best systems limit the damage of human mistakes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Mistakes still happen however good the interfaces are, and some reach production.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Test thoroughly at all levels, from unit tests to whole-system integration and manual tests. Allow quick, easy recovery: fast rollback of configuration changes, gradual rollout of new code so bugs affect few users, and tools to recompute data. Set up detailed monitoring such as performance metrics and error rates.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each practice costs effort, and none replaces the others. Management practices and training matter too but are beyond the book's scope.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You accept that some errors will reach production and want to limit their damage.

card.rule: Test at every level, make recovery quick and gradual, and monitor so a mistake is found and fixed early.
card.limits: These practices limit damage; they do not prevent mistakes from happening.

concepts.title: Why reliability matters everywhere
concepts.question: Why do even mundane applications need reliability, and when may it be sacrificed?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Reliability can seem a concern only for nuclear power stations and air traffic control.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Expect reliability in ordinary software too. Bugs in business applications cost productivity. Outages of ecommerce sites cost revenue and reputation. Even noncritical applications carry a responsibility to users: picture a parent whose only copies of their children's pictures sit in your photo application.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You may choose to sacrifice reliability to cut development cost, as in a prototype for an unproven market, or operational cost, as in a service with a very narrow profit margin.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You decide how much reliability to build, or whether to cut corners.

card.rule: Treat reliability as a duty to users in every application, and give it up only knowingly.
card.limits: Cutting corners is allowed only as a conscious choice for reasons such as an unproven prototype or razor-thin margins.

concepts.title: What scalability means
concepts.question: What does scalability mean, and why is it meaningless to call a system scalable without more detail?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A system that works reliably today may not work reliably tomorrow. A common reason is increased load: more concurrent users, or much larger volumes of data.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Define scalability as a system's ability to cope with increased load. It is not a one-dimensional label. Ask what the options are if the system grows in a particular way, and say which growth you mean.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You give up the comfort of a single verdict. A system may cope with one kind of growth and not another, so each claim needs a named kind of growth.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Someone says the system is scalable or does not scale and you need to turn that into a question you can answer.

card.rule: Never judge scalability in one word; name the growth and ask what options exist to cope with it.
card.limits: Scalability concerns growth only; a system can scale and still be unreliable or hard to maintain.

concepts.title: Describing load with load parameters
concepts.question: How do you describe a system's current load with a few numbers?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You cannot discuss growth, such as what happens if load doubles, until you can say succinctly what the load is now.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Describe load with a few numbers called load parameters. The best choice depends on the architecture: requests per second to a web server, the ratio of reads to writes in a database, the number of simultaneously active users in a chat room, or the hit rate on a cache.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: There is no universal parameter; the wrong one hides what limits the system.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You start any scalability discussion.

card.rule: Pick the few numbers that describe the load your architecture feels, then ask what happens when they grow.
card.limits: A parameter that suits one architecture can mislead for another.

concepts.title: Twitter's two timeline approaches
concepts.question: Why can shifting work from read time to write time make a system faster?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Twitter in 2012: posting a tweet averaged 4.6k requests a second, over 12k at peak; viewing a home timeline took 300k a second. The challenge was fan-out, since each user follows many people and is followed by many.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Approach 1: a post inserts the tweet into a global collection; a timeline read looks up whom the user follows, finds their tweets and merges them by time. Approach 2: keep a cached home timeline per user; a post inserts the tweet into each follower's cache, so a read is cheap.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Approach 2 does more work when a tweet is posted. Twitter switched to it because the first version struggled with timeline reads, and publishing was almost two orders of magnitude rarer than reads.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Reads far outnumber writes and you can afford to precompute the result.

card.example: A news site publishes 50 articles a minute but serves 100,000 page views a minute. Rebuilding the headline list on each view repeats the same work. Building it once at publish time makes each view cheap.
card.rule: When reads far outnumber writes, do more work at write time so each read is cheap.
card.limits: The trade only pays off if the write-time work stays affordable.

concepts.title: When the average hides the extremes
concepts.question: Why does the average follower count hide the real load, and how does a hybrid fix it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Under approach 2, a tweet reaches about 75 followers on average, so 4.6k tweets a second become 345k cache writes a second. But follower counts vary wildly, and some users have over 30 million followers.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat the distribution of followers per user, perhaps weighted by how often users tweet, as the key load parameter. Then use a hybrid: fan out most users' tweets at post time, except celebrities, whose tweets are fetched separately and merged into the timeline at read time, as in approach 1.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Our reading: the hybrid has two delivery paths to build and merge, in exchange for avoiding extreme write bursts.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The distribution of a load parameter has a long tail of extreme cases.

card.rule: Look at the distribution of the load parameter, and treat the extreme cases differently from the typical ones.
card.limits: A hybrid adds complexity and is worth it only when a few extreme cases drive the load.

concepts.title: Throughput and response time
concepts.question: Which performance measure suits a batch system, and which suits an online service?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: After describing load, you ask what happens when it rises: how performance changes with resources fixed, and how many resources you must add to keep performance unchanged.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Both questions need performance numbers. For a batch processing system such as Hadoop, the usual measure is throughput: records processed per second, or total time for a job on a dataset of a certain size. For an online system, the usual measure is response time: the time between a client sending a request and receiving a response.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Choosing the wrong measure points the effort at the wrong thing: a fast batch can still serve a slow page.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You must say how well a system performs under a given load.

card.rule: Measure batch systems by throughput and online systems by response time.
card.limits: The usual measure is not the only one; check which one the users of the system actually feel.

media.alt: A small blue silhouette of a perched bird with a long curved beak, inside a thin square outline; a decorative ornament.

concepts.title: Response time, service time and latency
concepts.question: How do response time, service time and latency differ, and why is response time a distribution?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Latency and response time are often used as synonyms, which hides where a client's waiting time goes. Even the same request repeated gives a slightly different time on every try.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Response time is what the client sees: the actual time to process the request (service time) plus network delays and queueing delays. Latency is the duration a request spends waiting to be handled, during which it is latent. Treat response time as a distribution of measured values, not a single number.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Using one word for both blurs which part of the wait you can fix.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You measure or discuss how long clients wait.

card.rule: Response time is everything the client waits for; latency is only the wait before handling begins.
card.limits: Many people still use the two words interchangeably, so check which meaning is intended.

concepts.title: Percentiles instead of averages
concepts.question: Why are percentiles a better description of response time than the average?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The mean response time of all requests response time is often reported, but it does not tell you how many users actually experienced that delay, so it is a poor guide to what is typical.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Sort the response times from fastest to slowest. The median response time of all requests, the 50th percentile or p50, is the halfway point: half of requests are faster and half slower. For outliers, use higher percentiles: p95, p99 and p999 are the thresholds that 95%, 99% or 99.9% of requests beat. High percentiles are also called tail latencies.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A percentile describes one request. A user who makes several requests faces a different chance of seeing a slow one.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You report or set targets for response times.

card.rule: Describe response time by percentiles: the median for the typical wait, high percentiles for the outliers.
card.limits: A percentile says nothing about the distribution above it; pick the percentiles that match what users feel.

media.alt: Bar chart of response time for about 100 requests along the horizontal axis, most bars short and a few tall. Dotted horizontal lines mark the median (p50) at the lowest level, the mean (average) slightly above it, then the 95th percentile and the 99th percentile near the top. Only a few bars reach above the 95th line.

concepts.title: Why tail latencies matter
concepts.question: Why do companies care about the slowest few requests, and how are percentiles used in service agreements?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The slowest requests are rare, so it is tempting to ignore them.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: High percentiles directly affect users' experience. Amazon states response time requirements for internal services at the 99.9th percentile, though that affects only 1 in 1,000 requests, because the customers with the slowest requests often have the most data and are the most valuable. Percentiles also appear in service level objectives and agreements (SLOs and SLAs), contracts that define expected performance and availability.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Chasing ever higher percentiles costs more and returns less. Amazon judged optimizing the 99.99th percentile too expensive for the benefit: it is easily affected by random events outside your control.

blocks.label: Numbers
blocks.text: Amazon observed that a 100 ms increase in response time reduces sales by 1%. An example SLA: up if the median is under 200 ms and the 99th percentile is under 1 s, and up at least 99.9% of the time.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You set performance targets or write a contract.

card.rule: Set targets at a high percentile where slow requests hurt valuable users, and stop where the cost outruns the benefit.
card.limits: There is no universal percentile; Amazon chose p99.9 for its situation and rejected p99.99.

concepts.title: Queueing delay and head-of-line blocking
concepts.question: Why do a few slow requests slow down fast ones, and what does that mean for measurement?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Queueing delays often account for a large part of the response time at high percentiles.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A server can process only a small number of things in parallel, so a small number of slow requests can hold up the ones behind them. This is head-of-line blocking. Subsequent requests may be fast to process, but the client still sees a slow response. So measure response times on the client side.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Client-side measurement includes everything the user waits for, at the price of needing the instrument at the client. When generating test load, the client must keep sending requests regardless of responses, or the queues stay artificially short.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You monitor response times or test how a system scales.

card.rule: Measure response times at the client, and send test load independently of the responses.
card.limits: A test client that waits for each response before sending the next skews the measurements.

concepts.title: Tail latency amplification and aggregating percentiles
concepts.question: Why do many backend calls make slow end-user requests more likely, and how should percentiles be combined?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A single end-user request often needs several backend calls. Even in parallel, it waits for the slowest. One slow call makes the whole request slow, and the more calls, the higher the chance of meeting a slow one. This is tail latency amplification.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: To put percentiles on a dashboard, keep a rolling window of recent response times, such as the last 10 minutes, and recompute the median and other percentiles every minute. Sorting the whole list works but may be inefficient; approximation algorithms give a good estimate at minimal CPU and memory cost.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Averaging percentiles, for example to combine machines or reduce time resolution, is mathematically meaningless. Combine response time data by adding the histograms.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A request fans out to many backend calls, or you aggregate latency data across machines.

card.rule: Expect more slow requests as calls multiply, and combine latency data by adding histograms, not averaging percentiles.
card.limits: Approximations trade a little accuracy for lower cost; averaging percentiles is wrong whatever the cost saving.

concepts.title: Scaling up versus scaling out
concepts.question: When load grows, how do scaling up and scaling out differ, and why is a mix usually best?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: An architecture that suits one level of load is unlikely to cope with ten times that load, so a fast-growing service is rethought at every order of magnitude of growth.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Scaling up (vertical scaling) moves to a more powerful machine. Scaling out (horizontal scaling) distributes the load across several smaller machines, a shared-nothing architecture. Good architectures usually mix the two: several fairly powerful machines can be simpler and cheaper than a large number of small virtual machines.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A single machine is often simpler, but high-end machines become very expensive, so very intensive workloads often cannot avoid scaling out.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Load is growing and you must decide how to add capacity.

card.rule: Scale up while it is simple and affordable, scale out when it is not, and expect to use a pragmatic mixture.
card.limits: The choice depends on the workload: very intensive workloads often cannot avoid scaling out, and the common wisdom about databases may change.

concepts.title: No generic scalable architecture
concepts.question: Why is there no one-size-fits-all scalable architecture?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: It is tempting to look for a generic recipe that makes any system scale.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Accept that the architecture of a large-scale system is highly specific to the application. The problem may be volume of reads, writes or stored data, complexity of the data, response time requirements, access patterns, or most often a mixture. Build around assumptions about which operations will be common and which rare, the load parameters.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: If those assumptions are wrong, the scaling effort is at best wasted and at worst counterproductive. In an early-stage startup, iterating quickly on product features is usually more important than scaling to a hypothetical load.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You are tempted to copy another company's scale architecture or to scale before you have the load.

card.rule: Design for the load your application actually has and expects, not for a generic notion of scale.
card.limits: Specific designs still use general-purpose building blocks in familiar patterns.

concepts.title: The three maintainability principles
concepts.question: Why is maintenance the larger cost of software, and which three principles reduce its pain?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Most of the cost of software is not in building it but in maintaining it: fixing bugs, keeping it running, investigating failures, adapting it to new platforms and uses, repaying technical debt, adding features. People dislike legacy systems, and every legacy system is unpleasant in its own way.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Design software to minimize pain in maintenance and avoid creating legacy software. Follow three principles. Operability: make it easy for operations teams to keep the system running smoothly. Simplicity: make it easy for new engineers to understand by removing as much complexity as possible. Evolvability: make it easy to change the system for unanticipated use cases.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: There are no easy solutions, so the principles guide thinking rather than give recipes.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You judge a design by how it will be to live with.

card.rule: Design for the long life of the software by keeping it easy to operate, understand and change.
card.limits: Simplicity here is about the system's internals for engineers, not the simplicity of the user interface.

concepts.section: Operability: Making Life Easy for Operations
concepts.title: Making life easy for operations
concepts.question: What can a data system do to make routine operations easy?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Good operations can often work around bad software, but good software cannot run reliably with bad operations. Even automation is set up by humans, who must check that it works.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Make routine tasks easy so the operations team can focus on high-value work. Give visibility into runtime behavior with good monitoring; support automation and standard tools; avoid dependency on individual machines; offer good documentation and a clear operational model (if I do X, Y will happen); provide good defaults with freedom to override; self-heal where appropriate with manual control as an option; behave predictably.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Automation and self-healing help, but administrators must keep manual control when needed.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You design or choose a data system that someone else will run.

card.rule: Make routine tasks easy and keep humans in control when automation is not enough.
card.limits: Automation does not remove people: humans set it up and check that it works.

concepts.title: Removing accidental complexity
concepts.question: What is accidental complexity, and how does abstraction help remove it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: As projects grow they often become complex and hard to understand, which slows everyone and raises maintenance cost. Symptoms include tangled dependencies, tight coupling, inconsistent naming, special-casing and performance hacks. Changes risk new bugs because hidden assumptions and unintended consequences are easily overlooked.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Make simplicity a key goal, which does not mean cutting functionality but removing accidental complexity: complexity not inherent in the problem as users see it, arising only from the implementation. Abstraction is one of the best tools: a clean façade hides much detail and can be reused across applications, so improvements to it benefit all of them.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Finding good abstractions is very hard. In distributed systems, many good algorithms exist, but it is much less clear how to package them into abstractions.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A system is getting harder to understand or change.

card.example: A high-level programming language hides machine code, CPU registers and system calls. We still run machine code, but we do not have to think about it directly, so the language abstraction removes complexity.
card.rule: Remove complexity that comes only from the implementation, and hide detail behind good, reusable abstractions.
card.limits: Some complexity is inherent in the problem and cannot be removed; abstractions help only if they are good ones.

concepts.title: Making change easy
concepts.question: Why must a system be built for change, and what makes it easier to modify?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A system's requirements will not stay unchanged. New facts are learned, unforeseen use cases arrive, business priorities shift, users ask for features, and new platforms replace old ones.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Agile working patterns give a framework for adapting to change, with technical tools such as test-driven development and refactoring. These usually operate on a small, local scale of a few source files. The book looks for agility at the level of a larger data system, which may span several applications or services, and calls it evolvability.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Evolvability cannot be bought separately. It is closely linked to simplicity and abstraction: simple, easy-to-understand systems are usually easier to modify.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You expect the system to outlive its first set of requirements.

card.rule: Keep a data system simple and well abstracted so that it can be modified as requirements change.
card.limits: Agile techniques such as test-driven development and refactoring address change at a smaller scale than a whole data system.

concepts.title: Functional and nonfunctional requirements
concepts.question: How does the chapter sort an application's requirements, and what is each concern in essence?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: An application must meet many requirements to be useful, and they are easy to lump together.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Separate functional requirements, what the application should do, such as storing, retrieving, searching and processing data, from nonfunctional ones: general properties like security, reliability, compliance, scalability, compatibility and maintainability. Reliability means working correctly despite faults in hardware, software and humans. Scalability means keeping performance good as load grows. Maintainability means making life better for engineering and operations.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: There is no easy fix for making applications reliable, scalable or maintainable, but certain patterns and techniques keep reappearing.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You review a system against the chapter's three concerns or write down its requirements.

card.rule: Write down both what the system must do and the general properties it must have.
card.limits: The list of nonfunctional properties is broader than the three the chapter develops.

concepts.title: Data models stack in layers
concepts.question: What does each layer of a data system do for the layer above it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Real-world things such as people, orders and sensors have to end up as bytes on hardware. Without structure, nobody could build or change such a system in pieces.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Build in layers, each answering how it represents the layer above in terms of the layer below. The application models the world as objects and APIs. It stores them in a general-purpose model: JSON or XML documents, relational tables or a graph. The database engine turns that model into bytes, and hardware turns bytes into physical signals.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each layer hides the complexity beneath it behind a clean model, so different teams can work together. The price is that the layer you pick constrains everything built on top of it.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Locating a design question. This chapter works on the second layer, the general-purpose model for storing and querying data. How engines implement that model comes in the next chapter.

card.rule: Each layer represents the layer above it in terms of the layer below, and hides the complexity underneath behind a clean data model.
card.limits: Hiding is not erasing: a choice made at a lower layer still shows through in what the layers above can do easily.

media.alt: A rotated engraved fantasy map of database regions: the Relational Empire, Document Data District, Column-Family District, Key-Value District, Graph Data Peaks, a NoSQL Danger Zone, with database names as towns and rivers between them.

concepts.title: Each model assumes a way of being used
concepts.question: Why does the choice of data model make some jobs easy and others awkward?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A data model is picked early, and mastering even one takes real effort. Whatever you pick will decide what the software above it can and cannot do.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat every model as carrying assumptions about its expected use. Some kinds of usage are easy and some are unsupported. Some operations are fast and some perform badly. Some data transformations feel natural and others awkward.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Depth in one model costs time that you cannot spend on others. A model that suits one workload will fit another one badly.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing storage for a new application: list the access patterns you expect and test each candidate model against them.

card.rule: Choose the data model whose assumed usage matches how your application will actually use the data.
card.limits: The principle says to compare models against your workload; it does not name a winner, and the rest of the chapter supplies the comparison.

concepts.title: The relational model hides representation
concepts.question: What was the relational model designed to hide from application developers?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: Relational ideas grew out of business data processing on 1960s and 1970s mainframes. That meant transaction processing, such as sales, banking, airline reservations and warehouse stock-keeping, and batch work such as invoicing, payroll and reporting. Earlier databases made developers think hard about how data was stored.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: Edgar Codd proposed the relational model in 1970. Data is organized into relations (tables in SQL), each an unordered collection of tuples (rows in SQL). It started as a theory, and many doubted it could be implemented efficiently.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: The goal was to hide the implementation detail behind a cleaner interface. By the mid-1980s relational database systems and SQL were the usual tools for stored data.

card.rule: The relational model organizes data as tables of rows and aims to hide how data is represented internally.
card.limits: A 1970 proposal was not guaranteed to succeed: it began as theory, and many people doubted it could be implemented efficiently.

concepts.title: Relational outlasted its rivals
concepts.question: What happened to the models that challenged the relational one, and why did it spread so far?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: In the 1970s and early 1980s the main alternatives were the network model and the hierarchical model. Each rival to the relational model attracted hype in its day.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: Computers grew far more powerful and networked, and were used for ever more varied purposes. Relational databases turned out to generalize well beyond business data processing, to online publishing, discussion, social networking, e-commerce, games and productivity software.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: The relational model came to dominate. Dominance lasted around 25 to 30 years, which the author calls an eternity in computing.

card.rule: Relational databases outlasted each rival and generalized far beyond their first use in business data processing.
card.limits: Past dominance does not show fit for every workload; the NoSQL movement, covered next, challenges it on particular needs.

concepts.title: NoSQL is a label, not a technology
concepts.question: What does the name NoSQL actually refer to?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: In the 2010s NoSQL appeared as the latest attempt to overthrow the relational model's dominance. A number of interesting database systems came to be associated with the name.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: The name began as a catchy Twitter hashtag for a 2009 meetup on open source, distributed, nonrelational databases. It struck a nerve and spread quickly through the web startup community and beyond.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: The author calls the name unfortunate, because it does not refer to any particular technology. It is a label that many different systems share.

card.rule: NoSQL is a loose label for many nonrelational systems, not the name of one technology.
card.limits: Because the label is loose, it says little about any single system; look at that system's actual data model.

concepts.title: Four forces behind NoSQL adoption
concepts.question: What pushed teams toward NoSQL databases in the 2010s?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Relational databases did not fit every need that teams had in the 2010s, and some teams went looking for alternatives.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The chapter names four driving forces. First, a need for greater scalability than relational databases can easily achieve. Second, a preference for free and open source software over commercial products. Third, specialized query operations that the relational model supports poorly. Fourth, frustration with relational schemas and a wish for a more dynamic, expressive model.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each force is a need that drove adoption, not proof that a nonrelational store wins. Some forces concern fit (scale, queries, schema), and one concerns licensing.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A team asks why it wants to leave its relational database: name which of the four forces applies, and check whether that force is really present.

card.rule: NoSQL adoption was driven by scalability needs, open-source preference, specialized queries and schema frustration.
card.limits: The forces explain why systems were adopted, not that one model beats another for every use.

concepts.title: Polyglot persistence: right store for the job
concepts.question: What does the author expect relational and nonrelational databases to do in future?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Different applications have different requirements, and the best technology for one use case may differ from the best for another.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use relational databases alongside a broad variety of nonrelational datastores, choosing each store for the job it fits. This idea is sometimes called polyglot persistence.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You give up the simplicity of a single system. Our reading: the book does not cost out the extra learning and operating effort.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Different parts of one application have clearly different needs, for example regular transactional records and heavily linked data.

card.rule: Expect to use relational databases alongside other stores, choosing each for the job it fits.
card.limits: This is the author's forecast, not a law; a single store is enough when one model fits the whole application.

concepts.title: The object-relational impedance mismatch
concepts.question: Why do ORM frameworks reduce the object-to-table gap without removing it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Most application development uses object-oriented languages. If data lives in relational tables, an awkward translation layer is needed between objects in code and tables, rows and columns in the database.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Object-relational mapping (ORM) frameworks such as ActiveRecord and Hibernate generate much of that translation code. They reduce the boilerplate a team must write.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: ORMs cannot completely hide the differences between the two models. The disconnect, called an impedance mismatch, remains.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Judging how much work an application spends on translating between its objects and its storage model, and whether a closer model is worth considering.

card.rule: The disconnect between objects in code and relational tables is an impedance mismatch; ORMs reduce its boilerplate but cannot remove it.
card.limits: An ORM is a mitigation, not a cure; the chapter does not say that any storage model removes the mismatch entirely.

concepts.title: Three ways to store one-to-many data in SQL
concepts.question: How can a relational database store a person's many jobs, schools and contact details?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A résumé has fields that appear once per user, such as first_name, so these can be columns. But a user can have many positions, many periods of education and many contacts. That is a one-to-many relationship.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The chapter lists three routes. In the traditional normalized model, positions, education and contacts go in separate tables with a foreign key to the users table. Later SQL versions added structured types, XML and JSON datatypes, so multi-valued data can sit in a single row and be queried and indexed. Or encode the data as JSON or XML text in a text column.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Separate tables spread one profile over several tables. Typed columns depend on product support. Text columns are simple, but the database usually cannot query inside them.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing a relational layout for nested data: decide whether you need to query inside the nested values and how self-contained the data is.

card.rule: A relational schema can hold one-to-many data as separate tables, as structured or JSON columns, or as encoded text.
card.limits: Support for structured types and JSON varies by database product, so check yours before relying on them.

media.alt: A LinkedIn profile for Bill Gates on the left and, on the right, its relational tables. The users table row 251 has region_id us:91 and industry_id 131 pointing to the regions and industries tables. The positions, education and contact_info tables each have several rows carrying user_id 251, one row per job, school or contact.

concepts.title: A self-contained document loads in one query
concepts.question: Why can one JSON document be easier to load than several joined tables?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: To show a profile stored over several tables you must run several queries (one per table, by user_id) or write a messy multi-way join.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Store the profile as one JSON document, with positions, education and contact info nested inside. All the relevant information sits in one place, so one query is sufficient. Document databases such as MongoDB, RethinkDB and CouchDB support this model.

blocks.label: Example document
Trade-off
blocks.text: JSON is much simpler than XML. Some developers feel it reduces the impedance mismatch, but the author notes problems with JSON as an encoding and takes up schema flexibility later.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The data is mostly a self-contained document that is usually loaded as a whole, such as a résumé.

card.rule: Nest one-to-many data inside a single document, so one query returns the whole tree.
card.limits: The advantage holds for self-contained data; relationships between documents are a separate problem.

media.alt: Tree diagram rooted at user 251. Branches carry first_name, last_name and summary directly, plus a positions node with job 1 to job 3 and an education node with edu 1 and edu 2. Each job leads to job_title and organization; each edu leads to school_name, start and end.

concepts.title: Store an ID or the text?
concepts.question: When is it better to store an ID for a value instead of its text?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A profile could store a region or industry as free text, such as a city-area name. Different users would then spell and style the same thing differently, and names can be ambiguous.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Offer standardized lists in a drop-down or autocompleter and store the ID. The chapter's advantages: consistent style and spelling, no ambiguity when several cities share a name, and easy updating, because the name is held in one place.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The ID is meaningless to humans, so the name must be looked up by following the ID.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The values come from a shared list that many records use and that might change.

card.rule: When many records share a value that may change, store an ID that points to one standardized entry.
card.limits: If the user interface has free-text fields for the value, storing plain-text strings makes sense.

concepts.title: Normalization removes duplicated meaning
concepts.question: What do you save yourself from by storing an ID instead of duplicating text?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: When human-meaningful text is stored in every record that uses it, any change has to be made in every copy. That costs write overhead and risks inconsistencies, where some copies are updated and others are not.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Store the meaningful text in one place and let everything refer to it by ID. An ID has no meaning to humans, so it never needs to change, even if the thing it identifies changes. Removing this duplication is the key idea behind normalization.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Reading a record with its name now needs a lookup through the reference. The author suspends judgment on normalization versus denormalization until Part III.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Values meaningful to humans, such as names, may change and appear in many records.

card.rule: Normalization means storing each human-meaningful value once and pointing to it by ID.
card.limits: The author calls distinctions between normal forms of little practical interest, and he does not yet judge normalization against denormalization.

concepts.title: Many-to-one references strain the document model
concepts.question: Why are many-to-one references awkward in a document database?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Normalizing means many-to-one relationships: many people live in one region and work in one industry. These do not fit nicely in the document model. In relational databases referring to rows by ID is normal because joins are easy. Document databases do not need joins for one-to-many trees, and join support is often weak.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: If the database cannot join, emulate the join in application code by making multiple queries.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The work of making the join moves from the database to the application code.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Judging a document store: list the many-to-one references the application needs, and count how many joins it must emulate.

card.rule: When a document store has no joins, many-to-one references must be resolved by extra queries in application code.
card.limits: The cost is small when the referenced lists are small and change slowly; it grows with the number of references you must resolve.

concepts.title: Data grows more interconnected over time
concepts.question: How can a join-free document design turn into a many-to-many design as features are added?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The first version of an application may fit a join-free document model well. But data has a tendency to become more interconnected as features are added.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Two feature changes show it. If organizations and schools become entities, each with its own page, logo and news feed, a résumé links to them rather than holding a string. If users can write recommendations of each other, a recommendation must reference its author's profile, so the author's current name and photo show.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: These changes create many-to-many relationships, so references to organizations, schools and users appear and need joins when queried.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing a model for a product that will keep gaining features, not only for its first version.

card.rule: Plan for features to turn strings into entities and references, which brings many-to-many relationships and joins.
card.limits: Not every application grows more connected; an analytics store of events may never need many-to-many links.

User 251 has a recommendation rec 1 pointing to user 467.

concepts.title: IMS and the hierarchical model
concepts.question: Why do document databases face problems like those of IBM's 1960s database?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: IBM's Information Management System (IMS) was the most popular database for business data processing in the 1970s. It used the hierarchical model, which represents all data as a tree of records nested within records, much like the JSON structure of a document.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: IMS handled one-to-many relationships well. It made many-to-many relationships difficult and did not support joins.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: Developers had to decide whether to duplicate (denormalize) data or to resolve references from one record to another by hand. The author says these 1960s and 1970s problems resemble those developers meet with document databases today.

card.rule: The hierarchical model resembles JSON documents and shares their weakness with many-to-many relationships and joins.
card.limits: Our reading: the parallel concerns relationships only; IMS is not a document database, and the two differ in other ways.

concepts.title: The network model and access paths
concepts.question: How did the network model go beyond the tree, and how were records reached?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In the hierarchical model every record has exactly one parent, so many-to-one and many-to-many relationships are hard to express.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The network model, standardized by the CODASYL committee, generalized the tree so that a record could have multiple parents. One record for the Greater Seattle Area could be linked from every user living there. The links were not foreign keys but more like pointers in a programming language, still stored on disk. The only way to reach a record was to follow a path from a root record along chains of links, called an access path.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Many-to-one and many-to-many relationships could now be modeled. But several different paths could lead to the same record, and the programmer had to keep track of them.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Reading older database designs: spot navigation by pointer chains, which the relational model was meant to replace.

card.rule: The network model let a record have several parents, but every record was reached by following an access path from a root.
card.limits: The model did solve many-to-one and many-to-many relationships; its cost lay in how programmers had to navigate them.

concepts.title: Hand-picked access paths made code rigid
concepts.question: What price did programmers pay for choosing access paths by hand?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: A CODASYL query moved a cursor through the database, iterating over lists of records and following access paths. If a record had multiple parents, the application code had to track all those relationships.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: Choosing paths by hand made the most efficient use of the very limited 1970s hardware, such as tape drives with extremely slow seeks. But the code for querying and updating became complicated and inflexible.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: If there was no path to the data you wanted, you were in a difficult spot. You could change the access paths, but then you had to rewrite a lot of handwritten query code, so changing an application's data model was difficult.

card.rule: Hand-chosen access paths bought speed on 1970s hardware at the price of complicated, inflexible code.
card.limits: The trade made sense on tape-era hardware; the criticism targets hand-chosen paths, not every kind of pointer-based design.

concepts.title: The relational model lays data out in the open
concepts.question: What did the relational model do instead of making programmers follow access paths?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With the hierarchical and network models, a missing path to the data you wanted left you in a difficult situation.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The relational model lays all data in the open. A relation is simply a collection of tuples, with no labyrinthine nested structures and no access paths to follow. You can read any or all rows of a table, selecting those that match an arbitrary condition, or read one row by matching on key columns. The query optimizer decides automatically which parts of a query run in which order and which indexes to use.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Those optimizer choices are effectively the access path, but they are made by the optimizer, not the developer, so we rarely need to think about them.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Comparing how a system lets you reach data: ask who chooses the path, the programmer or the engine.

card.rule: The relational model exposes plain tables and lets the query optimizer, not the programmer, choose the access path.
card.limits: Declaring useful indexes is still the developer's job; the optimizer only chooses among them.

concepts.title: Build the optimizer once
concepts.question: Why does a general-purpose query optimizer beat hand-coded access paths in the long run?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Choosing access paths by hand for every query is wasteful. If you declare a new index, you do not want to rewrite your queries to take advantage of it.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Build a general-purpose query optimizer into the database once, so that all applications that use the database benefit from it. When you declare a new index, queries automatically use whichever indexes suit best, with no change to the queries.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Without an optimizer, hand-coding the access path for one particular query is easier than writing a general optimizer. The author says the general solution wins in the long run.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Deciding where to put effort: in one shared engine used by many applications, or in code repeated in each.

card.rule: Put access-path choice in one general-purpose optimizer, so every application benefits and adding an index needs no query change.
card.limits: The payoff comes over the long run and across many applications; for a single query hand-coding is easier.

concepts.title: Documents borrow from two traditions
concepts.question: In which aspect do document databases revert to the hierarchical model?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: Document databases went back to the hierarchical model in one aspect: they store nested records, the one-to-many relationships such as positions, education and contact_info, inside their parent record instead of in a separate table.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: For many-to-one and many-to-many relationships, relational and document databases are not fundamentally different. In both, the related item is referenced by a unique identifier, called a foreign key in the relational model and a document reference in the document model.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: To date, document databases have not followed the path of CODASYL.

card.rule: Documents nest one-to-many data like the hierarchical model, but refer to shared records by identifier like relational databases.
card.limits: The comparison concerns relationships only; the two kinds of database still differ in join support, schemas and more.

concepts.title: Arguments for each side
concepts.question: What are the main arguments for the document model, and what does the relational model counter with?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Document and relational databases differ in many ways. This chapter compares only their data models.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The main arguments for the document model are schema flexibility, better performance due to locality, and, for some applications, a closer match to the data structures the application uses. The relational model counters with better support for joins and for many-to-one and many-to-many relationships.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Choosing the document model gives up join strength, and choosing the relational model gives up some flexibility and locality.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You start comparing the two for an application: list which of these arguments applies to your data.

card.rule: Documents argue schema flexibility, locality and closeness to application structures; relational argues joins and many-to-one and many-to-many support.
card.limits: This is a comparison of data models only, so it is not a complete verdict on which database to choose.

concepts.title: Document-like data and the cost of shredding
concepts.question: When does the document model give simpler application code?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Some data has a document-like structure: a tree of one-to-many relationships whose whole tree is typically loaded at once.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use the document model for such data. The relational technique of shredding splits a document-like structure into multiple tables, such as positions, education and contact_info, and can lead to cumbersome schemas and unnecessarily complicated application code.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You cannot refer directly to a nested item, so you need a path into the document. That is usually fine while documents are not too deeply nested.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The data is a tree, is usually loaded whole and is not deeply nested.

card.rule: If data is a tree normally loaded whole, a document model avoids the cumbersome schemas that shredding creates.
card.limits: Deep nesting makes the lack of direct references to nested items a growing problem.

concepts.title: When weak joins matter
concepts.question: When does weak join support hurt a document database, and when can you ignore it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Poor support for joins in document databases may or may not be a problem, depending on the application.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: If the application needs many-to-many relationships, you can reduce the need for joins by denormalizing, but then application code must do extra work to keep the copies consistent. Or you can emulate joins in application code with multiple requests to the database.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Emulated joins move complexity into the application and are usually slower than a join performed by specialized code inside the database. The result can be significantly more complex code and worse performance.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Before choosing a document store, ask whether the application will need many-to-many relationships.

card.rule: Weak join support matters when an application needs many-to-many relationships, and much less when it does not.
card.limits: Whether it is a problem depends on the relationships in the application, not on the database alone.

concepts.title: No model is simplest in general
concepts.question: Which data model leads to simpler application code, and what decides it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: It is tempting to ask which data model gives simpler application code, as though one answer fits all.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The chapter says it is not possible to say in general. It depends on the kinds of relationships between the data items. For highly interconnected data the document model is awkward, the relational model is acceptable and graph models are the most natural.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each model eases some relationships and strains others, so choosing means giving up the strengths of the others.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Before picking a model, classify your data's relationships: a tree, some links, or a web.

card.rule: Choose the model by the shape of your relationships: trees favor documents, and densely linked data favors graphs.
card.limits: The author gives no threshold for how interconnected is highly interconnected, so the classification takes judgment.

concepts.title: Schemaless is misleading: schema-on-read
concepts.question: Why is schemaless a misleading name for document databases?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Most document databases, and the JSON support in relational ones, do not enforce a schema on the data in documents. Arbitrary keys and values can be added, and readers get no guarantee about which fields a document holds.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Calling such databases schemaless misleads, because the code that reads the data usually assumes some structure. There is an implicit schema, but the database does not enforce it. A more accurate term is schema-on-read: the structure is implicit and only interpreted when the data is read. Its contrast is schema-on-write: the traditional relational approach, where the schema is explicit and the database ensures all written data conforms to it.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Schema-on-read lets writers add fields freely but gives readers no guarantees. Schema-on-write guarantees structure at the cost of agreeing on it up front.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Deciding who is responsible for the structure of the data: the database when writing, or your code when reading.

card.rule: Documents are not truly schemaless: the schema is implicit and applied on read, whereas relational databases enforce an explicit schema on write.
card.limits: The two terms say where structure is checked, not whether structure exists.

concepts.title: Schemas are like static versus dynamic typing
concepts.question: How does the schema debate compare with the debate about type checking in programming?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Whether a database should enforce a schema is a debated question, and arguing about it can feel endless.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Compare it to programming languages. Schema-on-read is similar to dynamic, run-time type checking. Schema-on-write is similar to static, compile-time type checking. Advocates of static and dynamic typing argue over their merits, and the same goes for enforcing schemas in databases.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each side gives up what the other offers, checks at the point of use versus checks before the data is accepted.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Explaining the choice to a team that already holds views on static versus dynamic typing.

card.rule: Treat schema-on-read like dynamic typing and schema-on-write like static typing: the debate is of the same kind.
card.limits: An analogy helps reasoning but does not prove which side wins for a given application.

concepts.title: Changing a data format in each approach
concepts.question: How do you split a stored name into first and last names in a document database and a relational one?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: An application stores each user's full name in one field and now wants first and last names stored separately.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In a document database, start writing documents with the new fields and have read code handle the old ones. In a relational database, run a migration that adds the column and fills it for every row.

blocks.label: Document approach
Relational migration
Trade-off
blocks.text: The UPDATE rewrites every row, so it is likely to be slow on a large table in any database. If that is unacceptable, leave first_name as NULL and fill it in at read time, as a document database would.

card.rule: A format change is either handled in read code (schema-on-read) or applied once to all rows by a migration (schema-on-write).
card.limits: The snippets use SQLite-style SQL; the book's PostgreSQL and MySQL versions use other string functions.

concepts.title: When a schema hurts more than it helps
concepts.question: When does schema-on-read beat a fixed schema, and when does a schema earn its keep?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Sometimes the items in a collection do not all have the same structure. That is called heterogeneous data.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Schema-on-read is advantageous in two cases. There are many different types of objects and it is not practical to give each type its own table. Or the structure is dictated by external systems that you do not control and that may change at any time. There a schema may hurt more than it helps.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Where all records are expected to share a structure, a schema is a useful way to document and enforce that structure.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Judging a new data source: ask whether its records really vary in shape, and who controls that shape.

card.rule: Prefer schema-on-read for genuinely varied or externally controlled data, and a schema where records share one structure.
card.limits: Do not read 'no schema' as 'no structure'; even then, your code still has expectations.

concepts.title: Locality pays only when you read whole documents
concepts.question: When does storing a document as one piece help performance, and when does it hurt?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A document is usually stored as one continuous string, encoded as JSON, XML or a binary variant such as MongoDB's BSON. Whether that layout helps depends on how the data is used.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: If the application often needs the entire document, for example to render it on a web page, there is a performance advantage in this storage locality. With data split across tables, multiple index lookups are needed, which may mean more disk seeks and more time.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The advantage holds only if you need large parts of the document at the same time. The database typically loads the entire document even when you need a small part, which wastes effort on large documents. On an update the entire document usually has to be rewritten.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Documents are fairly small and are mostly read whole. The chapter recommends keeping documents small and avoiding writes that increase their size.

card.rule: Locality helps when you read most of a document at once; it costs when you read little or rewrite it often.
card.limits: These limits narrow the situations where document databases are useful; the chapter says they significantly reduce them.

concepts.title: Locality is not only a document feature
concepts.question: Which other systems group related data for locality?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Grouping related data together for locality is easy to credit to the document model alone. That would suggest locality requires giving up relational features.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The idea is not limited to documents. Google's Spanner offers the same locality in a relational model: the schema can declare that a table's rows should be interleaved, or nested, within a parent table. Oracle allows this with multi-table index cluster tables.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Our reading: interleaving ties child rows to their parent, so it helps access that follows the parent. The chapter states no costs.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want document-style locality but also relational features such as joins.

card.rule: Locality is a storage property: relational systems such as Spanner and Oracle can group related rows too.
card.limits: The chapter only names these features; how they work is left to the storage chapter.

concepts.title: Relational and document databases converge
