concepts.question: Why does the author consider a hybrid of the relational and document models a good route?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: Most relational database systems, other than MySQL, have supported XML since the mid-2000s, including indexing and querying inside XML documents. PostgreSQL, MySQL and IBM DB2 later added a similar level of JSON support, and the author expects others to follow.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: On the document side, RethinkDB supports relational-style joins, and some MongoDB drivers resolve database references automatically. That is effectively a client-side join, likely slower than one in the database because it needs extra network round-trips and is less optimized.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: Relational and document databases are becoming more similar over time. According to the author that is good, because the models complement each other. A database that handles document-like data and relational queries lets applications combine the features that fit best.

card.rule: A database that handles both document-like data and relational queries lets applications use the mix that fits.
card.limits: The claim is the author's opinion, and the version numbers date from the time of writing.

concepts.title: Declarative versus imperative queries
concepts.question: What is the difference between telling a database how to find data and telling it what you want?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: IMS and CODASYL queried the database with imperative code. The relational model introduced a new way of querying: SQL, a declarative query language.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: An imperative language tells the computer to perform certain operations in a certain order, step by step, updating variables and looping. In a declarative language you specify the pattern of the data you want, meaning the conditions the results must meet and how to transform them, such as sorting, grouping and aggregating, but not how to achieve it.

blocks.label: Imperative version
Declarative version
blocks.code: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE dept = 'Sales';

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The query optimizer decides which indexes, join methods and order of execution to use. SQL is less powerful than general code, and that limit is what makes the choice possible.

card.rule: Declarative queries state the pattern of data wanted and leave the method to the database; imperative code spells out the steps.
card.limits: A declarative language is more limited than general code, so some jobs still need an imperative approach.

concepts.title: Declarative queries leave room to optimize
concepts.question: Why does a declarative query leave a database freer to improve itself?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A database wants to improve its internals without breaking applications. For example, it may reclaim unused disk space and move records around, changing the order in which they appear.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A declarative language hides implementation details, so the database can introduce performance improvements without any change to queries. SQL does not guarantee any particular ordering, so it does not mind if the order changes. With imperative code the database can never be sure whether the code relies on the ordering.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The fact that SQL is more limited in functionality gives the database much more room for automatic optimization.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Judging an interface: the less it promises about method and order, the more the engine can change underneath.

card.rule: A declarative language promises less about how, so the database may change its methods without breaking queries.
card.limits: Our reading: the freedom lasts only as long as the query avoids promises about order or method.

concepts.title: Declarative queries parallelize more easily
concepts.question: Why can a declarative query run in parallel more readily than imperative code?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: CPUs are getting faster mainly by adding cores, not by much higher clock speeds. Software must therefore run on many cores and machines to keep up.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Imperative code is very hard to parallelize across cores and machines, because it specifies instructions that must be performed in a particular order. Declarative languages specify only the pattern of the results, not the algorithm, so the database is free to use a parallel implementation where appropriate.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: As with optimization, the freedom is paid for by a more limited language.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A workload must scale over many cores or machines and the engine, not the programmer, should decide how to split the work.

card.rule: Declarative queries describe results, not steps, so a database can spread them over many cores.
card.limits: Declarative languages have a better chance of speeding up in parallel; this is a tendency, not a guarantee.

concepts.title: CSS versus imperative DOM code
concepts.question: What do CSS and XSL show about declarative languages outside databases?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A page has a navigation list, and the title of the currently selected item should get a highlight colour. The same job can be done declaratively or imperatively.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In CSS a selector declares the pattern of elements to style: here, every a element that is a direct child of an li with the class active. The browser finds the elements and applies the style. XSL does the same with an XPath expression. Both are declarative languages for specifying the styling of a document.

blocks.label: Declarative version
Imperative version
Trade-off
blocks.text: The imperative version is longer and harder to read. If the active class is later removed, the colour stays, even if the code is re-run, until the page reloads. With CSS the browser removes the style by itself.

card.rule: In a browser, declarative CSS selectors beat imperative DOM scripting, just as SQL beats imperative query APIs.
card.limits: CSS and XSL are not database query languages; the chapter uses them for their parallel to databases.

concepts.title: MapReduce: between declarative and imperative
concepts.question: Where does MapReduce sit between a declarative language and an imperative API?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Some jobs need bulk, read-only queries across very many documents or machines. A limited form of MapReduce, a model popularized by Google, is offered by some NoSQL stores, including MongoDB and CouchDB.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: MapReduce is neither declarative nor fully imperative, but in between. The query logic is written as snippets of code that the framework calls repeatedly. A map function is called once for each matching document and emits key-value pairs. The framework groups the pairs by key, then calls a reduce function once per key with all of its values.

blocks.label: Sketch in Python
Trade-off
blocks.text: You must write two carefully coordinated functions, which is often harder than writing one query, and a declarative language gives the optimizer more to work with.

card.rule: MapReduce splits a bulk query into a map function that emits key-value pairs and a reduce function that combines each key's values.
card.limits: The sketch imitates the model in plain Python; real MongoDB MapReduce uses JavaScript functions inside the database.

concepts.title: Pure functions let the database run MapReduce anywhere
concepts.question: Why must map and reduce functions be pure?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A database that runs query code on many machines wants to run it anywhere, in any order, and rerun it when something fails. Arbitrary code would make that unsafe.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Map and reduce must be pure functions. They use only the data passed to them as input, they cannot perform additional database queries, and they must not have side effects.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The restriction still leaves them powerful: they can parse strings, call library functions and perform calculations. The cost is that they cannot read anything beyond their input.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Writing query code for a distributed engine: keep each function dependent only on its inputs.

card.rule: Keep map and reduce pure, so the engine may run them anywhere, in any order, and rerun them on failure.
card.limits: Purity limits what a function may do; code that needs outside data or side effects does not fit.

concepts.title: The aggregation pipeline: reinventing SQL
concepts.question: Why did MongoDB add a declarative aggregation pipeline beside MapReduce?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: MapReduce makes you write two carefully coordinated functions, which is often harder than writing one query. A declarative language also gives a query optimizer more chances to improve performance.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: For these reasons MongoDB 2.2 added the aggregation pipeline, a declarative language with similar expressiveness to a subset of SQL. The chapter's moral is that a NoSQL system may find itself accidentally reinventing SQL, albeit in disguise.

blocks.label: Pipeline and SQL
Trade-off
blocks.text: MapReduce is a fairly low-level model. Higher-level languages like SQL can be built as a pipeline of MapReduce operations, but many distributed SQL systems do not use it.

card.rule: Declarative pipelines replaced hand-written MapReduce because one query is easier than two coordinated functions and is easier to optimize.
card.limits: The pipeline is similar in expressiveness to a subset of SQL, not to all of it.

concepts.title: Graphs for heavily connected data
concepts.question: When does it become natural to model data as a graph?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If an application has mostly one-to-many relationships or none, the document model is appropriate. But some data is full of many-to-many relationships. The relational model handles simple cases, and as the connections grow more complex a graph fits better.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A graph has two kinds of objects: vertices (also called nodes or entities) and edges (relationships or arcs). Social graphs have people as vertices and who-knows-whom as edges. The web graph has pages and links. Road or rail networks have junctions and the roads or lines between them.

blocks.label: Numbers
blocks.text: Well-known algorithms run on such graphs: car navigation systems search for the shortest path between two points in a road network, and PageRank on the web graph helps rank search results.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Many-to-many relationships are common and the connections matter to your queries.

card.rule: Model data as a graph of vertices and edges when many-to-many relationships are common and complex.
card.limits: For tree-shaped data or data with few links, a document or relational model is simpler.

concepts.title: The property graph model
concepts.question: What does a property graph store for each vertex and each edge?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Connected things need an exact structure for vertices, edges and the facts attached to them.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In the property graph model (Neo4j, Titan, InfiniteGraph), each vertex has a unique identifier, a set of outgoing edges, a set of incoming edges and a collection of key-value properties. Each edge has a unique identifier, the vertex where it starts (tail), the vertex where it ends (head), a label for the kind of relationship, and key-value properties.

blocks.label: Two-table sketch
Use it when
blocks.text: You can think of a graph store as these two relational tables, one for vertices and one for edges.

card.rule: A property graph has vertices with properties and edges that each have a tail, a head, a label and properties.
card.limits: The sketch stores properties as text; the book's version uses PostgreSQL's json datatype.

concepts.title: Why property graphs are flexible
concepts.question: What three properties make property graphs flexible for modeling data?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A traditional relational schema struggles when regions are structured differently in different countries, when one country sits inside another, or when facts are known at different levels of detail.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Three aspects of the model help. First, any vertex can have an edge connecting it with any other vertex; no schema restricts what can be associated. Second, given any vertex you can efficiently find both its incoming and its outgoing edges, so you can traverse the graph forward and backward. Third, different labels for different kinds of relationships let one graph store several kinds of information while keeping a clean data model.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: France has départements and régions whereas the US has counties and states; Lucy's birthplace may be given only at state level while her residence is a city. A graph holds these varying shapes without redesign.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Your data has uneven shapes and is likely to grow new kinds of facts.

card.rule: Property graphs allow any vertex to link to any other, traversal in both directions, and many relationship kinds in one clean model.
card.limits: Our reading: with no schema restricting links, nothing in the model stops meaningless connections.

media.alt: Graph of boxes with properties. Lucy and Alain, type person, are linked by married. Lucy is born_in Idaho (state) and lives_in London (city). Alain lives_in London and is born_in Beaune. Within arrows chain Idaho to United States to North America, London to England to United Kingdom to Europe, and Beaune to Cote-d'Or to Burgundy to France to Europe.

concepts.title: Cypher: patterns drawn with arrows
concepts.question: How does Cypher describe a pattern to create or find in a property graph?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A property graph needs a way to create vertices and edges and to ask for patterns, without spelling out how to search.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Cypher is a declarative query language for property graphs, created for Neo4j. Each vertex gets a symbolic name, and an arrow notation creates edges: (Idaho) -[:WITHIN]-> (USA) makes an edge labeled WITHIN with Idaho as tail and USA as head. The same arrow notation inside a MATCH clause finds patterns, and RETURN names what to give back.

blocks.label: Create and match
blocks.code:
CREATE
  (Paris:City {name:'Paris'}),
  (France:Country {name:'France'}),
  (Paris) -[:WITHIN]-> (France)

MATCH (c:City) -[:WITHIN]-> (:Country {name:'France'})
RETURN c.name

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Cypher is declarative, so you describe the pattern and leave the search strategy to the database.

card.rule: In Cypher, draw the pattern of vertices and labeled arrows you want, and the database finds the matches.
card.limits: The snippets are our own small example; they are written to Cypher's syntax but not run here.

concepts.title: Variable-length paths and free execution
concepts.question: How does Cypher follow a chain of edges of unknown length, and who picks the strategy?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Locations nest at different depths: a person might be linked to a street, a city or a region, each inside a larger place. A query cannot assume how many steps lead to the country.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In Cypher, :WITHIN*0.. means follow a WITHIN edge zero or more times, like the star in a regular expression. A query for people born in one place and living in another reads: find a person with a BORN_IN edge to some vertex, from which a chain of WITHIN edges reaches the first place, and a LIVES_IN edge reaching the second.

blocks.label: Query
blocks.code:
MATCH
  (p) -[:BORN_IN]-> () -[:WITHIN*0..]-> (:Location {name:'France'}),
  (p) -[:LIVES_IN]-> () -[:WITHIN*0..]-> (:Location {name:'Japan'})
RETURN p.name

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The query does not say how to run. The optimizer chooses the strategy it predicts to be most efficient, so you can get on with the rest of the application.

card.rule: Use *0.. to follow an edge zero or more times, and let the optimizer choose the search strategy.
card.limits: Declaring the pattern leaves speed to the optimizer; the pattern itself must still be correct.

concepts.title: Graph queries in SQL
concepts.question: Why is a variable-depth graph query harder to write in SQL than in Cypher?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Graph data can be stored in relational tables, but can it be queried with SQL? Yes, with difficulty. In a relational database you usually know in advance which joins a query needs. In a graph query the number of edges to traverse is variable, so the number of joins is not fixed in advance.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Since SQL:1999, variable-length traversal can be written with recursive common table expressions (WITH RECURSIVE). A recursive query starts from a seed row and keeps adding rows reached through the edges until nothing new is found.

blocks.label: Recursive query
blocks.code:
WITH RECURSIVE in_europe(vertex_id) AS (
  SELECT vertex_id FROM places WHERE name = 'Europe'
  UNION
  SELECT links.tail_vertex FROM links
  JOIN in_europe ON links.head_vertex = in_europe.vertex_id
  WHERE links.label = 'within'
)
SELECT vertex_id FROM in_europe;

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It works, but the syntax is clumsy compared with Cypher. The lesson drawn is that data models are designed for different use cases, so pick one suited to the application.

card.rule: SQL can follow variable-length paths with recursive common table expressions, but far more clumsily than a graph query language.
card.limits: The example assumes tables places(vertex_id, name) and links(tail_vertex, head_vertex, label); it ran correctly on SQLite.

concepts.title: The triple-store model
concepts.question: How does a triple-store represent graph data as three-part statements?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Graph data needs another description that some tools and languages use: the triple-store, which is mostly equivalent to the property graph model but uses different words.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: All information is stored as simple three-part statements (subject, predicate, object). The subject is equivalent to a vertex. The object is either a primitive value, in which case the predicate and object act as a property key and value on the subject, or another vertex, in which case the predicate is an edge from the subject (tail) to the object (head).

blocks.label: Example in Turtle
Use it when
blocks.text: The tools and languages for triple-stores are valuable additions to a toolbox, even if you prefer property graphs.

card.rule: A triple (subject, predicate, object) is either a property of a vertex or an edge between two vertices.
card.limits: The example is our own small Turtle sketch; it was written to the format but not run here.

concepts.title: The semantic web and RDF
concepts.question: What is the semantic web, and does using triples depend on it?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: Triple-stores are often tied to the semantic web, but the data model is completely independent of it; Datomic is a triple-store that claims nothing to do with it. The semantic web asks a simple question: websites publish text and pictures for humans, so why not also publish machine-readable data?

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: The Resource Description Framework (RDF) was meant to let different websites publish data in a consistent format and so be combined into a web of data, a kind of internet-wide database of everything. The idea was overhyped in the early 2000s and has shown no sign of being realized, which made many people cynical.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: Triples can still be a good internal data model without publishing RDF. Because RDF is for internet-wide exchange, subjects, predicates and objects are often URIs, so your within and someone else's within do not clash, as the two live in different namespaces.

card.rule: Triples are a sound internal data model whether or not the semantic web ever arrives.
card.limits: The author judges the semantic web overhyped so far; that is an opinion and could change.

concepts.title: SPARQL: the same patterns for triples
concepts.question: How does SPARQL express the same graph pattern as Cypher?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A triple-store using RDF needs its own query language for patterns.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: SPARQL is a query language for triple-stores using the RDF data model. It predates Cypher, and Cypher's pattern matching is borrowed from it, so the two look similar. Variables start with a question mark. Because RDF does not distinguish properties from edges and uses predicates for both, the same syntax matches both.

blocks.label: Example
Use it when
blocks.text: You query a triple-store, or read Cypher and want to see where its pattern notation came from.

card.rule: SPARQL matches patterns of triples with ?variables, and predicate paths such as :within* follow edges zero or more times.
card.limits: SPARQL and Cypher share structure, so skills carry over, but their syntax differs.

concepts.title: Graph databases are not CODASYL again
concepts.question: How do graph databases differ from the network model they resemble?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: At first glance CODASYL's network model looks like the graph model, so graph databases might be the second coming of CODASYL in disguise.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: They differ in several important ways. CODASYL had a schema saying which record type could nest within which; a graph allows an edge from any vertex to any other. In CODASYL the only way to reach a record was an access path; in a graph you can refer to any vertex by its unique ID or find it through an index. CODASYL kept the children of a record in an ordered set; graph vertices and edges are unordered, and you can only sort results in a query.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Graphs give more flexibility to adapt to changing requirements, since nothing fixes the shape in advance.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Someone dismisses graphs as old technology: compare them on schema, access and ordering.

card.rule: Graph databases drop CODASYL's rigid schema, access paths and ordered sets, so they are not the old network model again.
card.limits: The similarity is real at the level of linked records; the differences lie in how data is reached.

concepts.title: Datalog: facts and rules
concepts.question: How does Datalog build queries out of facts and reusable rules?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Cypher and SPARQL write a query in one go. For complex data we may want pieces that can be reused and combined.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Datalog is much older than SPARQL or Cypher, studied by academics in the 1980s, and provides the foundation later languages build on. It is used by Datomic, and Cascalog applies it to large Hadoop datasets. Its data model is the triple-store generalized: a triple is written predicate(subject, object). Rules define new predicates, derived from data or from other rules. A rule applies when every predicate on the right of :- can be matched; the left side is then added as if it were stored.

blocks.label: Facts and rules
blocks.code:
within(paris, france).
within(france, europe).

within_recursive(P, R) :- within(P, R).
within_recursive(P, R) :- within(P, V),
                          within_recursive(V, R).

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Variables start with an uppercase letter. Rules can call other rules, even themselves, so complex queries are built up a small piece at a time.

card.rule: Datalog states data as facts and queries as rules, which can be combined and call themselves.
card.limits: The facts and rules shown are our own sketch in Prolog-style syntax; the derived answers were checked by hand-simulating the rules.

media.alt: Three tables named within_recursive with columns Location and Name. After rule 1 there are three rows: namerica North America, usa United States, idaho Idaho. After rule 2 once, usa North America and idaho United States are added. After rule 2 twice, idaho North America is added. Dashed lines link rows between tables.

concepts.title: Three models, one choice
concepts.question: Which kinds of data does each model target, and what do document and graph databases share?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: Data began as one big tree, the hierarchical model, which was poor for many-to-many relationships. The relational model was invented to fix that. Later, some applications did not fit the relational model either, and NoSQL stores diverged in two directions.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: Document databases target self-contained documents where relationships between documents are rare. Graph databases go the opposite way, targeting data in which anything is potentially related to everything. All three models are widely used, each good in its own domain. Document and graph databases typically enforce no schema, though the application still assumes a structure, explicit and enforced on write, or implicit and handled on read.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: One model can be emulated in terms of another, but the result is often awkward, so we have different systems for different purposes rather than one size fits all. Each model comes with its own query language: SQL, MapReduce, the aggregation pipeline, Cypher, SPARQL and Datalog.

card.rule: Use documents for self-contained data, graphs when anything may relate to anything, and relational in between; the schema is only explicit or implicit.
card.limits: Many data models are not covered, such as genome databases, huge particle-physics data sets and full-text search.

concepts.section: Data Structures That Power Your Database
concepts.title: Why storage internals matter
concepts.question: Why should an application developer care how a database stores and finds data internally?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You will rarely write a storage engine, yet you must pick one from many and tune it for your workload.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Learn roughly what an engine does under the hood: how it writes data, how it finds it again, and whether it is built for transactions or for analytics.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The time buys better choices and tuning, but this chapter gives vocabulary and a feel for the effects, not expertise in tuning one product.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing a database, changing a tuning parameter, or reading a database's documentation.

card.rule: Choose and tune a storage engine by knowing what it does for your kind of workload.
card.limits: Internals knowledge guides choices and tuning; it does not replace testing with your own workload.

media.alt: A sideways old-style engraved map of an imaginary land named Storage and Retrieval, with regions such as log-structured storage, land of the B-trees, kingdom of analytics and Hadoop region, plus ships and sea.

concepts.section: Data Structures That Power Your Database
concepts.title: The append-only log and its lookup cost
concepts.question: What does an append-only log do well, and what does a lookup in it cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A store must keep key-value pairs and hand back the latest value for a key, with as little machinery as possible.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Append every write to the end of a file. Old versions are never overwritten, so a read scans the whole file and keeps the last occurrence of the key.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Appending is about the cheapest write there is, but a lookup costs O(n): double the records and the scan takes twice as long.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: As the mental model of a database's core, or when writes are plentiful and reads are rare or can scan.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: In this book a log means any append-only sequence of records. It may be binary and need not be readable by people.

card.rule: A log makes writes cheap and leaves reads scanning, which is why reads need an index.
card.limits: This is a teaching model: a real engine adds extra machinery around the same appending principle.

concepts.section: Data Structures That Power Your Database
concepts.title: Indexes: faster reads, slower writes
concepts.question: What do indexes give a database, and what do they cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Scanning every record for each lookup is too slow, and the same data may need searching in several ways.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Keep extra metadata on the side as a signpost to the data. An index is derived from the primary data, so adding or removing one changes performance, not contents.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Well-chosen indexes speed up reads, but every index slows writes, because it must be updated whenever data is written.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choose indexes by hand from the typical query patterns, since databases do not usually index everything by default.

card.rule: Index what your queries need and no more, because each index taxes every write.
card.limits: An index nobody queries is pure write overhead; and with no index, writes are cheapest but reads scan.

concepts.title: The in-memory hash index (Bitcask)
concepts.question: How can an in-memory hash map make lookups in an append-only file fast?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A lookup in an append-only log scans the whole file.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Keep a hash map in RAM from each key to a byte offset in the data file. Update it on every append; to read, look up the offset, seek there and read the value. Bitcask, Riak's default engine, works this way.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Reads and writes are fast, but every key must fit in RAM. Values may exceed RAM, because each is loaded with one disk seek.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The number of distinct keys is modest enough to hold in memory.

card.rule: Map each key to its newest offset in memory, so a lookup is one hash probe plus one seek.
card.limits: The map must fit in memory; once keys outgrow RAM the design stops working as described.

media.alt: Diagram: an in-memory hash map with two rows, key 123456 at byte offset 0 and key 42 at byte offset 64, each with an arrow down to a log-structured file on disk drawn as one box per byte. The file holds the text of two records, one per key: JSON documents for London and San Francisco, each ending in a newline. Arrows land on the first byte of each record.

concepts.title: When a hash index suits the workload
concepts.question: Which kind of workload suits a Bitcask-style engine, and why?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Choose an engine for a workload with many writes but a limited set of keys.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A Bitcask-style engine suits a workload with a large number of writes per key but not too many distinct keys, because keeping every key in RAM stays feasible. The book's example is a counter per cat video, incremented on each play.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It handles write-heavy updating well, but the same design is a poor fit once the number of distinct keys outgrows memory.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Few distinct keys, each updated very often, such as play counts or hit counters.

card.rule: Many writes per key and few keys fit a hash-indexed log.
card.limits: The fit rests on the key count; a workload with billions of distinct keys breaks it, however write-heavy.

concepts.title: Segments, compaction and merging
concepts.question: How does an append-only log avoid running out of disk space?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: An append-only file only grows, so it eventually fills the disk.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Break the log into segments: close a file at a certain size and write to a new one. Compact each segment by dropping duplicate keys and keeping the latest value, and merge several segments into a new file.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Space is reclaimed and files stay small, at the cost of background work. Segments are frozen, so the merged result goes to a new file.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A log-structured store must live a long time under continuing updates.

blocks.label: Switch-over
blocks.text: While merging runs on the old segments, reads and writes carry on as normal. When it finishes, reads move to the merged segment and the old files are deleted.

card.rule: Cut the log into segments, then compact and merge frozen ones in the background.
card.limits: Merging is background work, and frozen files are replaced by new ones, never edited.

media.alt: Diagram: a data file segment of twelve entries of the form word: number, such as mew: 1078, purr: 2103 and yawn: 511, with repeats of mew and purr. An arrow through a compaction process leads to a compacted segment of three entries only: yawn: 511, mew: 1082, purr: 2108.

Diagram: data file segment 1 (mew 1078 up to 1082, purr 2103 to 2108, yawn 511) and data file segment 2 (purr 2109 to 2114, mew 1083 to 1087, scratch 252) both feed arrows into a compaction and merging process. It outputs merged segments 1 and 2: yawn: 511, scratch: 252, mew: 1087, purr: 2114.

concepts.title: Looking up a key across segments
concepts.question: In what order does a read check the segments, and what keeps that cheap?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: After segmenting, the newest value of a key could be in any segment.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Give each segment its own in-memory hash table from key to file offset. A read checks the newest segment first, then the next-newest, and so on until the key is found.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Reads may probe several maps. Merging keeps the number of segments small, so few maps are checked.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A segmented log with per-segment hash indexes.

card.rule: Search segments from newest to oldest, and keep their number down by merging.
card.limits: If merging falls behind, the number of segments grows and so does the number of maps a read may probe.

concepts.title: Deleting with tombstones
concepts.question: How do you delete a key from a log whose segments are never edited?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Closed segments are frozen, yet a deleted key must stop being returned.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Append a special deletion record, a tombstone, for the key. When segments are merged, the tombstone tells the merge process to discard any earlier values for that key.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A delete costs one more appended record, and the old values keep taking space until a merge reaches them.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Any append-only or segment-based store that must support deletes.

card.rule: Delete by appending a marker and let the merge drop the earlier values.
card.limits: Until a merge runs, the older values still occupy disk, so a delete does not free space at once.

concepts.title: Crash recovery and concurrency in a hash-indexed log
concepts.question: How does a hash-indexed log recover after a restart or a crash mid-write?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A restart loses the in-memory hash maps, and a crash can happen halfway through appending a record.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Rebuild each map by reading its segment from start to end and noting the newest offset per key. To speed this up, store a snapshot of each map on disk, as Bitcask does. Add checksums so corrupted parts of the log can be detected and ignored.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Full rescans make restarts slow for big files, and snapshots add more files to maintain.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Any engine whose index lives in RAM and whose writes can be interrupted.

card.rule: Persist a snapshot of the index and checksum every record to make restarts fast and safe.
card.limits: A snapshot only speeds up recovery and does not replace checksums; each guards against a different problem.

concepts.title: Why appending beats overwriting
concepts.question: Why might a database choose to append instead of updating records in place?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: An append-only design looks wasteful, because old values pile up instead of being overwritten.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Append anyway. Appending and segment merging are sequential writes, which are generally much faster than random writes, especially on spinning disks. Immutable segment files also make concurrency and crash recovery simpler.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Stale values take space until compaction removes them, but writes become cheap and the failure cases easier to reason about.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Write-heavy loads on magnetic disks, or where simple recovery matters more than space.

card.rule: Sequential writes are fast, and files that are never edited are easy to make safe.
card.limits: On SSDs the advantage is smaller, and the space cost is real until segments are compacted.

concepts.title: Where hash indexes fall short
concepts.question: What two limits does a hash index on a log have?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A hash-indexed log is simple and fast, but it breaks down for some data sets and queries.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The hash map must fit in memory, so a very large number of keys is a problem; making a hash map on disk perform well is difficult. And range queries are not efficient: to scan keys between two bounds you must look up each key separately.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You get fast point lookups and writes, but give up large key sets and range scans.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Only when key count is modest and every query names an exact key.

card.rule: Hash-indexed logs serve exact-key lookups on a key set that fits in RAM and little else.
card.limits: These limits drove the move to sorted segments; they are not limits of every log design.

concepts.title: The SSTable format
concepts.question: What change to a log segment turns it into an SSTable?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Unsorted segments force a hash index and rule out range scans.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Require the key-value pairs in a segment to be sorted by key, and each key to appear only once in a merged segment. This format is called a Sorted String Table, or SSTable.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Sorting looks incompatible with sequential writes at first glance. How writes still stay sequential is shown in the next ideas.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: As the segment format for an engine that needs range scans, cheap merges and a small index.

card.rule: An SSTable is a segment sorted by key with one entry per key.
card.limits: Compaction already ensures one entry per key in a merged segment; a segment that is just written out is a different matter.

concepts.title: Merging SSTables like mergesort
concepts.question: How does merging sorted segments work, and why does it scale beyond memory?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Merging segments is a frequent job, and the files may be bigger than memory.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Read the input files side by side, look at the first key in each, copy the lowest to the output, and repeat. This is the approach of the mergesort algorithm. If a key appears in several inputs, keep the value from the most recent segment.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The inputs are read once, only sequentially, so the files can be bigger than memory.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Compacting sorted segments in the background.

card.rule: Merge sorted files by repeatedly copying the lowest current key, newest segment winning ties.
card.limits: The tie rule relies on recency of whole segments; the merge itself does not compare values.

media.alt: Diagram: three sorted segments of word: number entries (handbag, handcuffs, handful, handicap, handiwork, handkerchief and so on, with different numbers per segment) feed arrows into a compaction and merging process. Output merged segments 1, 2, 3 is one sorted list with one entry per word, using the value from the newest segment that has it.

concepts.title: The sparse in-memory index
concepts.question: Why does an SSTable need only a sparse in-memory index?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A hash index needs every key in memory, but sorted data should not.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Keep one key for every few kilobytes of segment file with its offset. To find a key, jump to the nearest known key before it and scan forward; sorting tells you the key lies between two indexed keys.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Lookups scan a few kilobytes, which is quick, in exchange for a much smaller index.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Sorted segment files with variable-length records.

card.rule: Index a few keys, jump near the target, and scan the short gap.
card.limits: A sparser index means longer scans; too sparse and the scan itself becomes costly.

media.alt: Diagram: a sparse in-memory index with rows hammock 100491, handbag 102134, handsome 104667 and hangout 106812, with arrows into a sorted segment file (SSTable) on disk. Between handbag and handsome lies a shaded compressible block of sorted entries from handbag to handprinted; handsome starts the next block.

concepts.title: Compressing blocks of an SSTable
concepts.question: Why does an SSTable group records into compressed blocks?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A read scans several key-value pairs in a range anyway, so work can be shared.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Group records into a block and compress it before writing it to disk. Each entry in the sparse index then points at the start of a compressed block.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Reading a block means decompressing it, but disk space shrinks.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Sorted segments with a sparse index, where reads touch a few neighbouring records.

card.rule: Compress per block and point each sparse index entry at a block start.
card.limits: Compression helps when records compress well; random data gains little.

concepts.title: Memtable and the LSM write path
concepts.question: How can an engine keep segments sorted when writes arrive in any order?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Incoming writes arrive in any order, yet SSTables must be sorted by key.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Sort in memory. Add each write to an in-memory balanced tree, the memtable. When it passes a threshold of a few megabytes, write it out as a new SSTable, the newest segment, while fresh writes go to a new memtable. A read checks the memtable, then segments from newest to oldest.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Writes reach disk sequentially and sorted, but recent writes live only in memory until flushed, and a read may check several structures.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Write-heavy key-value loads that also need sorted, range-scannable data.

card.rule: Sort in memory, flush sorted runs to disk, and merge them in the background.
card.limits: Reads must probe the memtable and every segment, so absent keys are costly; the next ideas patch that.

concepts.title: A recovery log for the memtable
concepts.question: How does an LSM engine avoid losing writes held only in the memtable?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If the database crashes, the recent writes in the memtable that are not yet on disk are lost.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Keep a separate append-only log on disk and append every write to it immediately. After a crash, read the log to rebuild the memtable. Each time the memtable is written out as an SSTable, the matching log can be discarded.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Every write is also appended to the log, adding a sequential write, but recent data survives crashes.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Any design where recent writes live in memory before reaching a sorted file.

card.rule: Log every write first, and drop the log once its memtable is flushed.
card.limits: The log protects only writes not yet flushed; it does not replace the SSTables as the main store.

concepts.title: The LSM family in real systems
concepts.question: Which well-known systems are built on merging and compacting sorted files?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You will meet this design under many product names, so it helps to recognise the family.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Engines based on merging and compacting sorted files are called LSM storage engines, after the Log-Structured Merge-Tree of O'Neil and colleagues. LevelDB and RocksDB are embedded key-value libraries; Cassandra and HBase were inspired by Google's Bigtable. Lucene uses a similar method for its term dictionary.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The family shares strengths and weaknesses, but products differ in details such as the compaction strategy.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Reading documentation or comparing engines.

card.rule: Recognise LSM engines by merged, compacted sorted files, whatever the product name.
card.limits: Sharing a design does not make two products behave identically; check the details of each.

concepts.title: Bloom filters for missing keys
concepts.question: How does an LSM engine avoid wasted disk reads for keys that do not exist?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A lookup for a key that is absent must check the memtable and every segment back to the oldest.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Put a Bloom filter in front: it can tell you that a key does not appear in the database, so the engine skips the memtable-to-oldest-segment walk and its disk reads for that key.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The filter takes memory, and it only rules keys out; it does not fetch values.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Workloads with many lookups of keys that may not exist.

card.rule: Check a Bloom filter first, so absent keys never trigger a walk through every segment.
card.limits: It helps only with missing keys; lookups for present keys still read segments.

concepts.title: Size-tiered versus leveled compaction
concepts.question: What are the two common ways to decide when and how SSTables are merged?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: An LSM engine must decide the order and timing of its merges.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In size-tiered compaction, newer and smaller SSTables are merged into older and larger ones. In leveled compaction, the key range is split into smaller SSTables and older data moves to separate levels, so compaction proceeds more incrementally and uses less disk space.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each strategy trades off different costs; the book does not say one is best.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing or tuning an LSM engine.

card.rule: Size-tiered merges small into large; leveled splits the key range into levels.
card.limits: Support varies: LevelDB and RocksDB use leveled, HBase uses size-tiered, and Cassandra supports both.

concepts.title: What LSM-trees do well
concepts.question: What are the main strengths of the LSM approach?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A storage engine should handle huge write rates and data bigger than memory.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Keep a cascade of SSTables merged in the background. Because data is stored in sorted order, range queries are efficient, and because disk writes are sequential, write throughput can be remarkably high. It keeps working well when the dataset is much bigger than memory.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Reads must consult several structures, and background merging competes with foreground work.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Write-heavy workloads, big datasets, or range scans over sorted keys.

card.rule: Sorted segments give range scans, and sequential writes give high write throughput.
card.limits: These strengths come with read and compaction costs, covered when LSM-trees are compared with B-trees.

concepts.title: B-trees: pages and the tree of pages
concepts.question: How does a B-tree organise a database, and how does it differ from log-structured segments?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: An index must keep keys sorted for lookups and ranges, and the most widely used design is not log-structured.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Break the database into fixed-size pages, traditionally 4 KB, and read or write one page at a time. Pages refer to each other by on-disk address, forming a tree: a root page, child pages each covering a continuous key range, and leaf pages holding keys with their values or references to them.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Sorted lookups and range queries work well, and pages match the disk's own blocks, but updates overwrite pages in place.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: General-purpose indexing: the standard in almost all relational databases and many nonrelational ones.

blocks.label: Branching factor
blocks.text: The number of references to child pages in one page is the branching factor. It depends on the space for references and range boundaries, and is typically several hundred.

card.rule: A B-tree is a tree of fixed-size pages, each owning a continuous key range.
card.limits: Page size is fixed, unlike variable-size log segments; the design assumes overwriting a page keeps its address valid.

media.alt: Diagram: a B-tree lookup for user_id = 251. A root page holds references separated by keys 100, 200, 300, 400, 500. The arrow for 200 to 300 goes to a child page with keys 210, 230, 250, 270, 290, whose arrow for 250 to 270 goes to a leaf page of keys 250 to 254 with values.

concepts.title: B-tree depth and capacity
concepts.question: Why do B-tree lookups follow only a handful of pages even in huge databases?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A lookup should touch very few pages, however many keys exist.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Because each page has a large branching factor, a tree with n keys has depth O(log n). With branching factor b, each extra level multiplies capacity by b, so a few levels cover a lot.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Depth stays tiny, but splitting pages keeps it balanced.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Estimating how many page reads a lookup needs.

blocks.label: Numbers
blocks.text: The book's example: a four-level tree of 4 KB pages with branching factor 500 holds up to about 250 TB, since 500 to the power 4 pages of 4 KB is roughly 250 TB.

card.rule: Capacity grows as the branching factor to the power of the depth, so depth stays small.
card.limits: The estimate assumes a large branching factor; short keys and small pages give a deeper tree.

concepts.title: Updating a B-tree and splitting pages
concepts.question: How does a B-tree take new keys while staying balanced?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: New keys must go into the right place in a sorted tree without letting it become lopsided.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: To update a key, find its leaf page, change the value and write the page back. To add a key, find the page whose range covers it. If the page is full, split it into two half-full pages and update the parent with the new boundary.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Writes overwrite pages in place and a split touches several pages, which makes crashes more dangerous.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A sorted index with frequent inserts and updates.

card.rule: Overwrite the leaf page; if it is full, split it and fix the parent.
card.limits: Splitting handles insertion; deleting while keeping the tree balanced is more involved.

media.alt: Diagram in two parts: a parent page with keys 310, 333, 345 and spare space, whose child leaf holds keys 333, 335, 337, 340, 342 with no room. After adding key 334, the leaf is split into two leaves, 333 to 335 and 337 to 342, and the parent gains boundary key 337 pointing to both.

concepts.title: Making B-trees crash-safe with a write-ahead log
concepts.question: Why do B-tree engines keep a write-ahead log?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Operations such as a split overwrite several pages; a crash midway can leave a corrupted index.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Keep an append-only write-ahead log (WAL, or redo log). Every modification is written to it before it is applied to the tree's pages. After a crash, the log restores the tree to a consistent state.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each change is written twice, once to the log and once to the page, but the index survives crashes.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Any page-oriented engine that updates pages in place.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Without it, a crash after only some pages of a split are written leaves an orphan page that no parent refers to.

card.rule: Write the intent to an append-only log first, then change the pages.
card.limits: A WAL protects consistency after a crash; it does not make the page writes themselves any cheaper.

concepts.title: Latches and concurrency in B-trees
concepts.question: Why is concurrency harder for B-trees than for log-structured engines?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: When pages are updated in place, another thread can read the tree while it is half changed.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Protect the tree's data structures with latches, which are lightweight locks, so a thread never sees a half-changed tree.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Latching adds care and overhead whenever pages are updated in place.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing between in-place and log-structured designs for concurrent workloads.

card.rule: Pages updated in place need latches so readers see a consistent tree.
card.limits: Latches handle concurrent access only; they do not protect against crashes, which the write-ahead log covers.

concepts.title: B-tree optimizations
concepts.question: What have designers done to improve on the basic B-tree?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A basic B-tree pays for a WAL, wide keys and scattered leaf pages.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Copy-on-write writes a changed page to a new location with new parent pages, with no WAL, as LMDB does. Abbreviated interior keys fit more per page, raising the branching factor. Leaf pages are laid out in sequence and carry sibling references to speed range scans.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: These tricks add complexity, and keeping leaves in sequence is hard as the tree grows.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Tuning or comparing B-tree-based engines.

card.rule: Improve B-trees by avoiding the WAL, packing more keys per page, and speeding range scans.
card.limits: Layout optimizations are hard to maintain over time; log-structured engines keep sequential keys together more easily.

concepts.title: LSM versus B-tree: rule of thumb and testing
concepts.question: Which engine should you pick, a B-tree or an LSM-tree, and how sure can you be?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You must choose between two mature index designs for a workload.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: As a rule of thumb, LSM-trees are typically faster for writes and B-trees are thought to be faster for reads, since LSM reads check several structures at different stages of compaction. Benchmarks are often inconclusive and sensitive to workload details, so test with your own workload.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The rule of thumb is a starting point, not an answer, and B-tree implementations are generally more mature.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing between engines when no quick rule decides it.

card.rule: Lean LSM for writes and B-tree for reads, then confirm by testing your workload.
card.limits: The rule is a tendency; configuration and workload can reverse it, and there is no quick rule for choosing.

concepts.title: Write amplification
concepts.question: What is write amplification and why does it matter?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Storage engines rewrite data, and each rewrite uses disk bandwidth.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Write amplification is one write to the database causing multiple writes to disk over its lifetime. A B-tree writes data at least twice, to the log and to the page, plus whole pages for small changes. An LSM-tree rewrites data in repeated compaction and merging.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: More disk writes mean fewer database writes per second within the disk bandwidth.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Comparing engines for write-heavy loads, where the disk write rate is the bottleneck.

card.rule: Count how many times the disk is written for each database write.
card.limits: LSM-trees sometimes have lower write amplification, but this depends on configuration and workload.

concepts.title: Compression and fragmentation: space efficiency
concepts.question: Why do LSM-trees often use less disk space than B-trees?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A storage engine should use disk space well, as well as writing and reading fast.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: LSM-trees can be compressed better, so their files are often smaller. B-trees leave space unused when pages split or rows do not fit; LSM-trees are not page-oriented and periodically rewrite SSTables, so they have lower overhead.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The saving comes from rewriting, which links back to write amplification.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Capacity-bound deployments, or where I/O bandwidth is tight.

card.rule: No pages to leave half-empty and regular rewriting mean smaller LSM files.
card.limits: On many SSDs the firmware itself uses a log-structured scheme, which softens the engine-level difference.

concepts.title: When compaction gets in the way
concepts.question: What can go wrong with compaction in an LSM engine?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Background compaction shares the disk with ongoing reads and writes.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Compaction can make a request wait while the disk finishes an expensive merge, so high-percentile response times can be high while averages stay fine. At high write rates, disk bandwidth must be shared between flushing and compaction; if compaction cannot keep up, unmerged segments pile up.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: SSTable engines typically do not throttle incoming writes, so you need explicit monitoring to catch it.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Capacity planning and monitoring of LSM deployments.

card.rule: Watch compaction: it can inflate tail latencies and fall behind a high write rate.
card.limits: The effect on throughput and average response time is usually small; the trouble shows at higher percentiles and at sustained peaks.

concepts.title: A key in exactly one place: B-trees and transactions
concepts.question: Why might a database that offers strong transactions prefer B-trees?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Strong transactional guarantees need to lock key ranges.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In a B-tree each key exists in exactly one place in the index, whereas a log-structured engine may hold several copies of a key in different segments. In many relational databases, isolation uses locks on ranges of keys, and in a B-tree index those locks can be attached directly to the tree.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: This favours B-trees for transactional semantics, but log-structured indexes are gaining popularity in new datastores.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A transactional database that locks key ranges.

card.rule: One place per key makes it easy to attach range locks to the index.
card.limits: This is a reason to prefer B-trees, not a proof they are always better; test your own use case.

concepts.title: Primary and secondary indexes
concepts.question: How does a secondary index differ from a primary key index, and how is one built?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Queries often search by something other than the primary key, and keys in such an index repeat.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A primary key uniquely identifies one row, document or vertex, and other records refer to it. A secondary index is built from a key-value index, but its keys are not unique. Either each value becomes a list of matching row IDs, or each key is made unique by appending the row ID.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each secondary index speeds up queries on another field, and adds write overhead.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Searching on fields other than the primary key.

card.rule: A secondary index is a key-value index whose keys may repeat.
card.limits: The two fixes for repeated keys work in both B-trees and log-structured indexes.

concepts.title: Index values: row or reference (heap file)
concepts.question: What can an index store as its value, and what is a heap file?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Several indexes over the same rows should not each hold a copy of the data.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The value in an index can be the row itself, or a reference to a row stored elsewhere. The place where rows are stored is a heap file, with data in no particular order. Each index just points to a location in the heap file, so the data is kept in one place.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Updates are cheap while the value fits in its old slot, but a larger value must move. Reads pay an extra hop from index to heap.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A table with several secondary indexes.

card.rule: Store rows once in a heap file and let every index point to them.
card.limits: The extra hop from index to heap can cost too much for reads, which motivates clustered indexes.

concepts.title: Clustered and covering indexes
concepts.question: When is it worth storing row data inside an index?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The extra hop from an index to the heap file can be too slow for reads.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A clustered index stores the row directly inside the index. A covering index stores some columns in the index so some queries can be answered from the index alone. A nonclustered index stores only references.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Reads get faster, but the data is duplicated, needing more storage, adding write overhead and extra effort to keep transactions consistent.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Read-heavy access paths where the extra hop dominates.

card.rule: Keep needed columns inside the index to save a hop, and pay for duplication.
card.limits: Duplicating data in indexes costs space and writes; do it only for hot read paths.

concepts.title: Concatenated indexes and field order
concepts.question: How does a concatenated index work, and which queries can it serve?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Queries often filter on several columns at once, but a plain index maps a single key.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A concatenated index joins several fields into one key by appending one column to another, in an order set by the index definition. It works like a phone book indexed by last name, then first name.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It serves lookups by the leading field or by both fields, but not by a later field alone.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Queries that filter on the first field, or on the first and second together.

card.rule: A concatenated index sorts by the first field, then by the next.
card.limits: The field order is fixed when the index is defined, so it must match your queries.

concepts.title: Multi-dimensional indexes
concepts.question: How can an index answer a range query on two columns at once?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A B-tree or LSM index gives a range on one key, not on two at once, as in a map-window search by latitude and longitude.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use a space-filling curve to turn two coordinates into one number and index that with a B-tree, or use a specialised spatial index such as an R-tree. PostGIS implements geospatial indexes as R-trees.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Specialised structures are more complex, and a standard index returns only one dimension's range.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Geographic search, or any pair of columns with range filters, such as (date, temperature).

card.rule: Index several dimensions together with an R-tree or a space-filling curve.
card.limits: A standard one-dimensional index leaves the second filter to a scan of its range.

concepts.title: Full-text and fuzzy indexes
concepts.question: How do search engines find words that are similar, not exact matches?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: All earlier indexes need exact keys or key ranges, so they cannot find misspelled or related words.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Full-text engines expand a search to synonyms, ignore grammatical variation, and find words near each other. Lucene copes with typos by searching for words within an edit distance, where distance 1 means one letter added, removed or replaced.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Fuzzy search needs linguistic analysis and more complex structures than key-value indexes.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Search boxes over text where users misspell or vary words.

card.rule: Fuzzy search matches words within an edit distance, not exact keys.
card.limits: These techniques go beyond the exact-value indexes of this chapter; machine learning methods exist too.

concepts.title: In-memory databases and durability
concepts.question: Why keep a whole database in memory, and how can it survive restarts?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Disks are awkward but durable and cheaper per gigabyte; as RAM gets cheaper, many datasets fit in memory.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In-memory databases keep data in RAM, possibly across machines. Some, such as Memcached, are for caching and may lose data on restart. Others aim for durability with battery-powered RAM, a log of changes on disk, periodic snapshots, or replicas.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Without durability measures a restart loses data; Redis and Couchbase provide only weak durability by writing asynchronously.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Datasets that fit in RAM, or caches where loss is acceptable.

card.rule: Trade disk's durability for RAM's convenience, and add a log, snapshots or replicas to survive restarts.
card.limits: A disk log for durability does not make it disk-based: reads are served from memory.

concepts.title: Why in-memory databases are fast
concepts.question: Is an in-memory database faster mainly because it avoids reading from disk?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Vendors claim big gains from in-memory databases; what is the actual source?

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The chapter calls it counterintuitive: the gain is not from skipping disk reads, because a disk-based engine may never read from disk if the operating system caches recently used blocks. In-memory databases are faster because they avoid the overhead of encoding in-memory structures into a form that can be written to disk.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The gain applies only where that encoding overhead dominates.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Judging vendor claims about in-memory speed.

card.rule: Speed comes from not encoding data for disk, not from avoiding disk reads.
card.limits: This claim comes from cited research; test your own workload before relying on it.

concepts.title: Anti-caching and datasets larger than memory
concepts.question: Can an in-memory design handle data bigger than memory?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Some datasets outgrow RAM, but disk-centric overhead is what the in-memory design avoided.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Anti-caching evicts the least recently used data from memory to disk when memory is short, and loads it back when accessed. This resembles operating-system virtual memory and swap files, but the database works on individual records instead of whole pages.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Indexes must still fit entirely in memory, as with the Bitcask example at the start of the chapter.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Datasets slightly beyond RAM where the hot set fits.

card.rule: Evict cold records, not pages, and keep the indexes in RAM.
card.limits: It remains research-stage; non-volatile memory may force further changes.

concepts.title: OLTP versus OLAP access patterns
concepts.question: How do transaction-processing and analytic workloads differ?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Applications look up a few records by key, while analysts scan huge numbers of records. One engine design cannot serve both well.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: OLTP (online transaction processing) reads a small number of records per query by key, with random-access low-latency writes, for end users. OLAP (online analytic processing) aggregates over a large number of records, with bulk or event-stream imports, for analysts.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Different patterns need different storage layouts; one design rarely wins at both.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Classifying a workload before choosing a storage engine.

card.rule: OLTP touches few records by key; OLAP scans many records for aggregates.
card.limits: The line is not always clear-cut; the table lists typical characteristics only.

concepts.title: What 'transaction' means here
concepts.question: Does transaction processing mean ACID guarantees?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The word transaction invites confusion with ACID and with money.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A transaction is a group of reads and writes that form a logical unit. Transaction processing here only means allowing clients to make low-latency reads and writes, as opposed to batch jobs that run periodically. It does not require ACID properties.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The loose meaning avoids confusion, but the ACID properties are a separate topic covered later.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Reading about OLTP without assuming guarantees.

card.rule: Transaction processing means low-latency reads and writes, not necessarily ACID.
card.limits: Do not infer strict guarantees from the word transaction.

concepts.title: Why a separate data warehouse, and ETL
concepts.question: Why do companies copy their data into a separate warehouse for analysis?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: OLTP databases must be highly available and fast, and analysts run expensive scans that could harm them.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A data warehouse is a separate, read-only copy of the data from the company's OLTP systems, which analysts can query freely. Data is extracted by periodic dump or stream of updates, transformed into an analysis-friendly schema, cleaned and loaded: Extract–Transform–Load (ETL).

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Analysts do not slow transactions and the warehouse is optimised for analytics, at the cost of an extra pipeline and copy.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Large enterprises with many OLTP systems and heavy analytic queries.

card.rule: Copy OLTP data through ETL into a warehouse built for scans.
card.limits: Small companies with little data may just query a normal SQL database or a spreadsheet.

media.alt: Diagram: three users (customer, warehouse worker, truck driver) each use an OLTP system (ecommerce site with Sales DB, stock-keeping app with Inventory DB, vehicle route planner with Geo DB). Each database goes through extract, a transform box and load into one data warehouse; a business analyst sends a query arrow to the warehouse only.

concepts.title: One SQL interface, two kinds of engine
concepts.question: If both use SQL, why are warehouses and OLTP databases different inside?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A warehouse and a relational OLTP database look alike from outside.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Both usually offer SQL and are relational, which suits analytic queries and graphical analysis tools. But internals are optimised for different query patterns. Many vendors focus on one workload, and products that offer both increasingly run two separate engines behind a common SQL interface.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The common interface hides that the engines differ, which can mislead you about performance.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing between OLTP and warehouse products.

card.rule: Same SQL surface, different engines underneath.
card.limits: Some products, such as SQL Server and SAP HANA, offer both in one product but as separate engines.

concepts.section: Stars and Snowflakes: Schemas for Analytics
concepts.title: The star schema: facts and dimensions
concepts.question: How is a typical data warehouse schema laid out around events?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Analytics data is mostly records of events plus the context in which they happened.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A star schema puts a fact table in the middle. Each row is an event, such as a purchase or a page view. Its columns are attributes such as sale price, or foreign keys to dimension tables that hold the who, what, where, when, how and why of the event. Even dates are often a dimension, so holidays can be encoded.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Recording facts as individual events keeps the most flexibility for later analysis, but makes the fact table extremely large.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A warehouse that analyses events such as sales, clicks or page views.

card.rule: Store each event as a fact row that points at dimension tables describing it.
card.limits: The fact table can reach tens of petabytes; the shape is a formulaic template, not the only possible model.

media.alt: Diagram of a star schema: a central fact_sales table (date_key, product_sk, store_sk, promotion_sk, customer_sk, quantity, net_price, discount_price) with arrows from its key columns to dim_product, dim_store, dim_date, dim_customer and dim_promotion tables. The first fact row is date 140102, product 31 (Fish food), store 3 (Palo Alto), NULL promotion, NULL customer, quantity 1, price 2.49.

concepts.section: Stars and Snowflakes: Schemas for Analytics
concepts.title: Snowflake schemas and very wide tables
concepts.question: How does a snowflake schema differ from a star, and why are warehouse tables so wide?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Dimensions can be stored flat or further broken down, and analysts want lots of metadata per event.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A snowflake schema breaks dimensions into subdimensions, such as separate brand and category tables referenced by a product row. It is more normalized than a star, yet stars are often preferred because analysts find them simpler. Fact tables often have over 100 columns, and dimension tables can be wide too.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Snowflakes remove repetition but cost simplicity; wide tables hold rich metadata but make every row large.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing a warehouse schema: choose a star unless normalization is worth the complexity.

card.rule: Star is flat and simple; snowflake is more normalized with subdimensions.
card.limits: Neither is required; the chapter notes only that stars are often preferred for their simplicity.

concepts.title: Column-oriented storage
concepts.question: Why store the values of each column together instead of each row?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A query over trillions of fact rows typically needs only 4 or 5 of 100 or more columns, yet a row store loads whole rows.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Store all the values of each column together, in its own file. A query then reads and parses only the columns it uses. Every column file holds the rows in the same order, so row 23 is rebuilt from the 23rd entry of each file.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Analytic scans read far less data, but fetching or writing whole rows becomes more work.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Analytic queries that read few columns of very wide tables with many rows.

card.rule: Store column values together so a query reads only the columns it needs.
card.limits: Column storage suits scan-heavy analytics; it gives little for queries that need whole rows.

media.alt: Table and lists: a fact_sales table of eight rows with columns date_key, product_sk, store_sk, promotion_sk, customer_sk, quantity, net_price, discount_price. Below it, the columnar layout lists each column's values as one file, for example date_key file contents 140102 four times then 140103 four times, in the same row order in every file.

concepts.title: Bitmap and run-length encoding of columns
concepts.question: How can a column with few distinct values be compressed and queried cheaply?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Column files are repetitive, and queries must still filter them quickly.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Turn a column with n distinct values into n bitmaps, one per value, with a bit per row: 1 if the row has that value. If n is small each bitmap can use one bit per row; if n is bigger the bitmaps are mostly zeros, so run-length encode them by storing the lengths of runs.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A column with many distinct values gets many bitmaps; the saving depends on repetitive data.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Warehouse columns with a small number of distinct values compared with the number of rows.

card.rule: One bitmap per distinct value, compressed by run lengths when sparse.
card.limits: Only worthwhile when distinct values are few compared with the rows.

media.alt: Diagram: a product_sk column of 18 values (69 69 69 69 74 31 31 31 31 29 30 30 31 31 31 68 69 69). Below, one row of 18 zero or one boxes per distinct value (29, 30, 31, 68, 69, 74), with ones where that value occurs, then run-length encodings such as 31 as 5, 4, 3, 3 and 69 as 0, 4, 12, 2.

concepts.title: Memory bandwidth and vectorized processing
concepts.question: Why do column stores also save CPU time, not only disk reads?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Scanning millions of rows is limited by disk bandwidth, but also by memory bandwidth and CPU efficiency.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A query engine can take a chunk of compressed column data that fits in the CPU's L1 cache and loop through it with no function calls. Compression fits more rows into the cache, and operators like bitwise AND and OR can work directly on the compressed chunks. This is called vectorized processing.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Tight loops run much faster than per-record code with many calls and conditions, but the engine must be written for it.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Analytic engines scanning large column chunks.

card.rule: Process compressed column chunks in tight cache-sized loops.
card.limits: The benefit depends on columnar layout and compression; row-at-a-time code with many calls cannot match it.

concepts.title: Column families are not column storage
concepts.question: Does a column family in Cassandra or HBase mean column-oriented storage?
