blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The name suggests column storage, so it is easy to assume column compression.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Cassandra and HBase inherited column families from Bigtable. Within each family they store all columns of a row together, along with a row key, and they do not use column compression. So the Bigtable model is still mostly row-oriented.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The name can lead you to expect scan and compression gains that these engines do not provide.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Reading product documentation that uses the term column family.

card.rule: Check how data is laid out, not what the feature is called.
card.limits: A product may offer real columnar engines separately; the point is only the name.

concepts.title: Choosing a sort order in a column store
concepts.question: How is a sort order chosen for a column store, and why sort whole rows?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Insertion order is easiest, yet a chosen order can work as an index.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The administrator chooses sort columns from knowledge of common queries, for example date_key first if queries target date ranges. A second column orders rows with equal first values. Sorting is by whole rows, even though the data is stored by column, because the kth item of each column must belong to the same row.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Sorting makes inserts harder than appending, but gives an index-like benefit for the chosen queries.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A warehouse with predictable query patterns, such as date ranges.

card.rule: Sort entire rows by keys that match the common queries.
card.limits: Only the leading sort keys help; a query that filters on an unsorted column gets no benefit.

concepts.title: Sorting helps column compression
concepts.question: Why does sorting make the first sort column compress so well?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Compression of columns depends on runs of repeated values.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: If the primary sort column has few distinct values, then after sorting it has long runs of the same value, and simple run-length encoding can shrink it to a few kilobytes even for billions of rows. The effect is strongest on the first sort key; later keys look more jumbled.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Later sort columns compress less, and columns far down the priority appear in nearly random order.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing sort keys that also have few distinct values.

card.rule: Sorting by a low-cardinality column turns it into a few long runs.
card.limits: The benefit fades down the sort order, so do not expect later columns to compress as well.

concepts.title: Several sort orders of the same data
concepts.question: Why store the same column data sorted in several different ways?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Different queries benefit from different sort orders.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Data is replicated to several machines anyway, so each replica can be sorted differently, and a query uses the version that fits it best. This idea came from C-Store and was adopted in the commercial warehouse Vertica.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Extra sort orders take effort and storage to keep in step.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Warehouses with several distinct query patterns.

card.rule: Keep redundant replicas in different sort orders and route each query to the best.
card.limits: It uses extra space and effort, and only the leading keys of each order benefit.

concepts.title: Writing to a column store with an LSM approach
concepts.question: How can a compressed, sorted column store accept writes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Inserting a row into the middle of sorted, compressed column files would require rewriting all of them.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use the LSM idea: send writes to a sorted in-memory store, and when enough accumulate, merge them with the column files and write new files in bulk. Queries read both disk and memory and combine them.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Writes become fast and bulk, but queries must merge two sources; the optimizer hides this from analysts.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Warehouses that must accept inserts, updates and deletes while keeping column storage.

card.rule: Buffer writes in sorted memory, then merge them into column files in bulk.
card.limits: Update in place, as B-trees do, is not possible with compressed columns.

concepts.section: Aggregation: Data Cubes and Materialized Views
concepts.title: Materialized views
concepts.question: How does a materialized view differ from a virtual view, and what does it cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If many queries use the same aggregates, crunching raw data each time is wasteful.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A materialized view is an actual copy of a query's results, written to disk. A virtual view is only a shortcut: the engine expands it into its query at read time. Since the copy is denormalized, it must be updated when the underlying data changes.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Reads can be faster, but every write gets more expensive, so materialized views are not often used in OLTP databases.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Read-heavy warehouses with repeated aggregates.

card.rule: Cache common aggregates as a stored copy of a query result.
card.limits: A materialized view is a denormalized copy, so it goes stale if it is not refreshed.

concepts.section: Aggregation: Data Cubes and Materialized Views
concepts.title: Data cubes
concepts.question: What does a data cube precompute, and what flexibility does it give up?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Queries often sum the same facts by date, product or store, and scanning millions of rows each time is slow.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A data cube (OLAP cube) is a grid of aggregates grouped by dimensions. With date and product, each cell holds the sum for that date-product pair, and sums along a row or column drop one dimension.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Certain queries become very fast, but you cannot answer questions on anything that is not a dimension, such as the share of sales from items costing over $100.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A few well-known aggregate queries over fixed dimensions.

card.rule: Precompute aggregates per dimension combination, and keep the raw data too.
card.limits: Cubes are a performance boost for certain queries, not a replacement for raw data.

media.alt: Diagram of a grid: rows are date_key (140101 to 140104), columns are product_sk (32 to 35), each cell holds a sum of net_price, for example 149.60 for 140101 and product 32. A right column totals each date (140101 is 40710.53) and a bottom row totals each product (32 is 14967.09). Three SQL SUM queries point at a cell, the right total and the bottom total.

concepts.title: Putting the chapter together
concepts.question: How do the chapter's storage engines map onto workloads?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You face a new workload and must pick between very different storage designs.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: First decide OLTP or analytics. For OLTP, choose between the log-structured school (Bitcask, SSTables, LSM-trees, LevelDB, Cassandra, HBase, Lucene), which only appends files, and the update-in-place school (B-trees), which overwrites fixed-size pages. For analytics, column-oriented storage is increasingly popular.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each choice trades something: write throughput, read predictability, transaction semantics or scan speed.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing and tuning an engine for a new workload.

card.rule: Pick by workload first, then by family, then test with your own data.
card.limits: The chapter gives no single best engine; testing your workload remains necessary.

concepts.title: Old and new versions coexist
concepts.question: Why do old and new versions of code and data formats exist in the same system at the same time?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A change to a data format needs matching code changes, but in a large application code cannot change everywhere at once.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: On the server side, a rolling upgrade (also called a staged rollout) puts the new version on a few nodes at a time and checks it before moving on. Client apps change only when each user installs the update.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Rolling upgrades avoid downtime, but for a while old and new code, and old and new data formats, run side by side.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You deploy server software that has to stay up, or ship client apps whose users decide when to update.

card.rule: Plan for old and new versions to coexist, because real upgrades are gradual.
card.limits: A system stopped and replaced in one step meets no mix of code versions, but it accepts downtime. The book treats gradual rollout as the normal case for large applications.
card.example: A shop moves its order service to version 2 on 2 of its 10 servers. For the next hour, servers on version 1 and version 2 both write order records that the other version may read.

media.alt: Antique-style engraved map of an imaginary coastline with named regions such as Gulf of Binary Encodings and Coast of Textual Encodings, with roads linking labelled formats like JSON, Avro, Thrift, XML and Protocol Buffers.

concepts.title: Backward and forward compatibility
concepts.question: Which direction of compatibility lets newer code read old data, and which lets older code read new data?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: When versions coexist, code written at different times must be able to read each other's data.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Backward compatibility: newer code can read data written by older code. Forward compatibility: older code can read data written by newer code.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Keeping both limits how a format may change, because every change must be checked in each direction.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You review a schema or format change that will roll out gradually or be stored and read later.

card.rule: Backward means new code reads old data; forward means old code reads new data.
card.limits: Each direction can hold while the other fails, so a change is safe only if the direction your deployment needs is covered.
card.example: Service v2 adds a field. v2 reading a stored v1 record is backward compatibility. v1 reading a v2 record is forward compatibility.

concepts.title: Why forward compatibility is trickier
concepts.question: Why does forward compatibility need more care than backward compatibility?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Old code cannot know about fields a newer version adds, yet it may receive them.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The author of newer code knows the older format and can handle it explicitly. For forward compatibility the older code must instead ignore additions it does not understand.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Ignoring unknown data has to be designed into the format and the reading code; it does not come free.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You judge whether a deployment can put old code in front of data from a newer version.

card.rule: Newer code can be taught the old format; old code must be built to ignore what it cannot know.
card.limits: This is the book's usual pattern, not a law. Our reading: a format with no way to skip unknown data can break old readers even on a small addition.

concepts.title: Encoding bytes and in-memory data
concepts.question: Why must a program translate between its in-memory data and a sequence of bytes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In memory, data sits in objects, lists and hash tables, tuned for fast CPU access and linked by pointers. A pointer means nothing to another process.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: To write to a file or send over a network, translate the data into a self-contained byte sequence. Going in-memory to bytes is encoding (also called serialization or marshalling); the reverse is decoding (parsing, deserialization, unmarshalling).

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The byte form differs from the efficient in-memory form, so every hand-off costs a translation step.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Data leaves your process: it is stored, sent, or shared with code that does not share your memory.

card.rule: Encode in-memory data into self-contained bytes before it leaves the process, and decode on arrival.
card.limits: Encoding is not encryption, and the book avoids the word serialization because transactions use it with a different meaning.

concepts.title: Language-specific encodings
concepts.question: What problems come with encoding data using your programming language's built-in library?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Built-in encoders such as Java Serializable, Ruby Marshal and Python pickle save and restore objects with almost no extra code.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use them only for very transient purposes. For anything lasting or shared, choose a standardised format that many languages can read.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Convenience costs lock-in to one language, security risk, weak versioning and often poor efficiency.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The data lives briefly inside one program or team, and no other system or version will ever read it.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: To restore objects of the same types, decoding must be able to create arbitrary classes. An attacker who controls the bytes may create classes that run code remotely.

card.rule: Do not rely on a language's built-in encoding for anything beyond transient use.
card.limits: For short-lived data that stays in one language and one version, the convenience can be a fair trade; the book's warning is about lasting or shared data.

concepts.title: Numbers in textual formats
concepts.question: What goes wrong with numbers in JSON, XML and CSV?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In XML and CSV a number looks like a string of digits. JSON separates strings from numbers but not integers from floating-point values, and fixes no precision.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat large numbers with care: integers above 2 to the power 53 cannot be held exactly in an IEEE 754 double, so a language that parses JSON numbers as doubles loses accuracy.
blocks.code:
big = 2**53 + 1
print(float(big) == big)
print(int(float(big)))

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Textual formats stay simple and readable, but meaning depends on an outside schema or hard-coded rules.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You send 64-bit identifiers or large integers through JSON to clients such as JavaScript.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Twitter's API returned each tweet ID twice, once as a JSON number and once as a decimal string, so JavaScript clients could use the string.

card.rule: Send large integers as strings (or in a typed format) when a reader may parse numbers as doubles.
card.limits: Numbers below 2 to the power 53 are safe in doubles. A schema or typed binary format can also settle the ambiguity.

concepts.title: Binary strings in text formats
concepts.question: How do you carry raw bytes in JSON or XML, and what does it cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: JSON and XML handle Unicode text well, but they have no binary string: a sequence of bytes with no character encoding.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Encode the bytes as text with Base64, and let the parties agree that the value is to be read as Base64.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It works but is somewhat hacky, and it increases the data size by 33%.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You must embed a small binary payload, such as a thumbnail, in a text document that other organisations can parse.

card.rule: Raw bytes in JSON or XML travel as Base64 text, at a cost of about a third more size.
card.limits: For large payloads or high volume, the extra third adds up; some binary encodings of JSON add a binary string type to avoid this.

concepts.title: Textual formats and optional schemas
concepts.question: Why do JSON, XML and CSV stay popular as exchange formats despite their flaws?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: XML and JSON have optional schema languages that are powerful but complicated; many JSON tools ignore them. CSV has no schema, and its handling of commas and newlines in values is vague.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Without a schema, the application must hard-code how to read numbers and binary strings, and must handle a new CSV row or column by hand.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Flexibility and easy adoption are paid for with manual interpretation work and subtle bugs.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You exchange data between organisations: as long as people agree on the format, its beauty or efficiency matters little.

card.rule: For exchange between organisations, an agreed textual format usually beats a better one that not everyone adopts.
card.limits: Inside one organisation there is less pressure to use a lowest-common-denominator format, and at terabyte scale the choice of format can matter a lot.

concepts.title: Binary encodings of JSON
concepts.question: How much do binary encodings of JSON, such as MessagePack, actually save?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: JSON and XML use a lot of space compared with binary formats, which led to MessagePack, BSON and many others.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: These formats keep the JSON data model. With no schema, they must include every field name inside each encoded record.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The saving is small: the example record takes 66 bytes in MessagePack against 81 bytes as compact JSON text, and human readability is lost.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A modest size or parsing gain justifies giving up readable data. The book itself doubts that it is worth it.

card.rule: Binary JSON variants keep field names in every record, so they save only a little.
card.limits: A real saving needs the field names removed, which needs a schema. Our reading: that is the step the next formats take.

media.alt: MessagePack encoding of the example record, 66 bytes. A hex byte sequence is shown, then a breakdown: an object marker with 3 entries, then the strings userName, favoriteNumber and interests each with a length byte and the field name spelled in characters, followed by values: Martin, 1337 as uint16 (05 39), and an array of 2 strings, daydreaming and hacking.

concepts.title: Schemas and code generation
concepts.question: How do Thrift and Protocol Buffers describe a record, and what do they produce from that description?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Binary JSON variants cannot drop field names because they have no schema. A compact format needs the structure known in advance.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: You write a schema in an interface definition language (IDL). A code generation tool turns it into classes in several languages that your code calls to encode and decode.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Protocol Buffers expresses the same record in a very similar schema.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Every encoded value needs a schema, and the data is not human-readable until it is decoded.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Several programs, possibly in different languages, share records that you control on both sides.

card.rule: Thrift and Protocol Buffers need a schema for any data they encode, and generate code from it.
card.limits: A schema adds a build step and a shared file to maintain. Data from outside your control, in an unknown format, cannot use it.

concepts.title: Field tags instead of field names
concepts.question: How do Thrift and Protocol Buffers identify fields in the bytes without storing names?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Storing every field name in every record wastes space.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The schema gives each field a number, a field tag. The encoded record holds the tag with a type annotation (and a length where needed) instead of the name. Thrift BinaryProtocol takes 59 bytes for the example record, because no names appear.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Tags work like aliases: the bytes are meaningless without the schema that maps tags to names and types.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You control the schema on both sides and want records without the repeated names.

card.rule: In Thrift and Protocol Buffers, field tags, not names, identify fields in the encoded bytes.
card.limits: Tags save space but add a duty: they must be chosen and tracked, and they make the schema essential to reading the data.

media.alt: Thrift BinaryProtocol encoding of the example record, 59 bytes. The breakdown lists each field as a type byte, a two-byte field tag (1, 2, 3), then the value: string Martin with a four-byte length 6, an i64 holding 1337 in eight bytes, and a list of 2 strings, daydreaming and hacking, each with a four-byte length. A final zero byte ends the struct.

concepts.title: Compact encodings and variable-length integers
concepts.question: How do CompactProtocol and Protocol Buffers shrink the record further than field tags alone?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Thrift BinaryProtocol still uses a full eight bytes for a number such as 1337 and separate bytes for the type and the tag.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: CompactProtocol packs the field type and tag number into a single byte and uses variable-length integers. The top bit of each byte says whether more bytes follow. 1337 fits in two bytes; the example record shrinks to 34 bytes.
blocks.code:
def size(n):
    z = (n << 1) ^ (n >> 63)
    c = 1
    while z >= 128:
        z >>= 7
        c += 1
    return c

print(size(1337), size(63), size(64))

blocks.label: Numbers
blocks.text: Numbers from -64 to 63 take one byte, from -8192 to 8191 take two, and bigger numbers take more.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Small numbers cost little, but large ones can take more bytes than a fixed width would.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Integers in your records are mostly small, and bandwidth or storage matters.

card.rule: Pack type and tag into one byte and use variable-length integers, so small numbers cost one or two bytes.
card.limits: Large values use more bytes, so the gain depends on the value mix. The code is a sketch consistent with the book's size ranges, not Thrift's own code.

media.alt: Thrift CompactProtocol encoding of the example record, 34 bytes. Each field starts with one byte whose bit pattern packs the field tag (shown as an increment from the previous one) beside the type. Martin has a one-byte length 6. The number 1337 is packed into two bytes by a variable-length integer with a sign bit. The list header byte holds 2 items and item type string. Strings carry one-byte lengths, and a zero byte ends the struct.

concepts.title: Evolving schemas through field tags
concepts.question: Why can old Thrift or Protocol Buffers code read records that contain fields it has never heard of?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Schemas must change over time, yet an encoded record identifies each field only by its tag number and type.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Rename fields freely, but do not change an existing tag. Add a new field under a new tag. Old code that meets an unknown tag uses the type annotation to learn how many bytes to skip, and ignores the field.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Tags become permanent commitments: every number you assign stays meaningful for as long as old data exists.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You add fields to a schema while older readers are still running.

card.rule: Keep tags fixed and give new fields new tags, so old code can skip what it does not know.
card.limits: Skipping works because every field carries a type annotation. Adding a field is only half the story: requirements on new fields come next.

concepts.title: Rules for adding and removing fields
concepts.question: Which additions and removals keep Thrift and Protocol Buffers schemas compatible?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: After the first deployment, old data and old code remain. A schema change must work for readers and writers of every version.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Any field added later must be optional or have a default value. Only an optional field can be removed. A removed field's tag number must not be used again.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Marking a field required enables a runtime check that can catch bugs, but nothing in the bytes records it, and it locks the field in.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: A new required field makes new code fail on old data, since old writers never wrote it. A reused tag gives old stored data a new meaning.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You review a pull request that changes a schema file.

card.rule: Add only optional or defaulted fields, remove only optional fields, and never recycle a tag.
card.limits: These rules are for Thrift and Protocol Buffers. Avro uses default values and unions instead of required and optional.

concepts.title: Changing a field's datatype
concepts.question: What can go wrong when a field's datatype changes in an existing schema?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A schema change may widen a number, for example from a 32-bit to a 64-bit integer.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: New code reads old data without trouble, since the parser fills any missing bits with zeros. Old code reading new data still holds a 32-bit variable.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: If a decoded 64-bit value does not fit in 32 bits, it is truncated, so values lose precision.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A datatype change may be allowed, but each format has its own rules.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You consider widening or changing a numeric field in a live schema.

card.rule: A wider type is safe for new code reading old data but can truncate when old code reads new data.
card.limits: Only values that no longer fit are damaged. Small values survive the change in either direction.

concepts.title: Repeated fields versus list types
concepts.question: How can Protocol Buffers turn a single-valued field into a multi-valued one without breaking compatibility?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A field that held one value must sometimes hold several.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Protocol Buffers has no list datatype. It marks a field repeated, a third option beside required and optional, and encodes it by writing the same tag several times. An optional field can become repeated.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: New code reading old data sees a list with zero or one elements; old code reading new data sees only the last element.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Thrift has a dedicated list datatype; the single-to-multi change is not available, but the type is parameterised by the element type.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You expect single values to grow into several, such as one owner turning into many.

card.rule: In Protocol Buffers, repeating the same tag encodes a list, which lets optional become repeated.
card.limits: Old code reading a list sees only the last element, so data can be silently lost. Thrift's list type cannot make this change.

media.alt: Protocol Buffers encoding of the example record, 33 bytes. Each entry is one byte holding the field tag and a wire type, then the value: tag 1 string Martin with length 6, tag 2 varint holding 1337 in two bytes (b9 0a), and then two separate entries both with tag 3, string, one for daydreaming (length 11) and one for hacking (length 7). No list marker or end-of-struct byte appears.

concepts.title: Avro: values without tags
concepts.question: How does Avro encode a record so compactly, and what must a reader have to decode it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Even field tags and type annotations cost bytes in every record.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Avro schemas have no tag numbers. The encoding is just the values concatenated: a string is a length prefix plus UTF-8 bytes, and an integer is a variable-length integer. The example record takes 32 bytes, the smallest so far. A reader walks the fields in schema order and takes each type from the schema.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Nothing in the bytes identifies fields or types, so the data cannot be read without the schema.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You can supply the right schema at read time and want the smallest records.

card.rule: Avro records are bare values in schema order, so decoding needs the schema.
card.limits: Compactness is bought by dependence: with the wrong schema the same bytes decode into wrong values without any warning.

media.alt: Avro encoding of the example record, 32 bytes. The breakdown shows only values, with no field tags and no type markers: length 6 then Martin, a union branch byte (1, long, not null) then 1337 in two bytes, an array count of 2, then daydreaming with length 11 and hacking with length 7, ending with a zero byte for the end of the array.

concepts.title: Writer's schema and reader's schema
concepts.question: How can Avro readers and writers use different schema versions and still understand each other?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Avro's bytes can be decoded correctly only with the schema that wrote them, but writers and readers are upgraded at different times.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The data is encoded with the writer's schema, the version the writing application knows. The reader expects its own reader's schema. The two need only be compatible. The Avro library compares them side by side and translates the data from the writer's schema to the reader's schema.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The reader must obtain the writer's schema as well, which costs a lookup or space in the data.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Different applications or versions read and write the same data over time.

card.rule: Avro resolves the writer's schema against the reader's schema; they need to be compatible, not identical.
card.limits: Resolution fails if the two schemas are not compatible, and it cannot work if the reader never obtains the writer's schema.

media.alt: Two tables side by side, writer's schema and reader's schema for a Person record, each with datatype and field name columns. Writer: string userName, union of null and long favoriteNumber, array of string interests, string photoURL. Reader: long userID, union of null and int favoriteNumber, string userName, array of string interests. Arrows join userName, favoriteNumber and interests across the two tables even though their row positions differ. photoURL and userID have no arrow.

concepts.title: Avro compatibility rules
concepts.question: Which fields may be added or removed from an Avro schema without breaking compatibility?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Schema resolution only works if changes follow rules.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Forward compatibility: new schema as writer, old schema as reader. Backward compatibility: new schema as reader, old schema as writer. To keep both, add or remove only fields that have a default value.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Adding a field without a default breaks backward compatibility, because new readers cannot fill it for old data. Removing a field without a default breaks forward compatibility.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Avro has no optional or required markers; it uses union types and default values instead.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You review an Avro schema change before rollout.

card.rule: In Avro, only add or remove fields that have a default value.
card.limits: Defaults for a field exist only where the schema declares them, so a field without one is a permanent commitment.

concepts.title: Renaming fields with aliases
concepts.question: How can an Avro reader cope with a field that the writer renamed?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Avro matches fields by name, so a renamed field no longer matches the name in older data.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The reader's schema can contain aliases for a field name, so the reader matches an old writer's field names against the aliases.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Renaming a field is backward compatible but not forward compatible: new readers know the old names, but old readers do not know the new ones.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You must rename a field and every reader of the old data will upgrade first.

card.rule: Aliases in the reader's schema make a rename backward compatible but not forward compatible.
card.limits: Rename only when old readers will not meet new data, or give up forward compatibility knowingly.

concepts.title: How a reader learns the writer's schema
concepts.question: How does a reader find out which schema wrote a given piece of Avro data?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Including the whole schema with every record would usually be larger than the record, wasting the saving from the binary encoding.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Pick by context. A big file of records written with one schema holds the writer's schema once at the start. A database stores a version number at the start of each record and keeps a list of schema versions. A network connection negotiates the schema version at setup and uses it for the connection's lifetime.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each choice adds something to maintain: a file header, a schema registry, or a handshake.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You use Avro for files, a database or RPC and need readers to find the writer's schema.

card.rule: Match the way you convey the writer's schema to the data's context: file header, per-record version number, or connection setup.
card.limits: A record version number works only if a trusted list of schema versions exists to look it up in.

concepts.title: Dynamically generated schemas
concepts.question: Why is Avro friendlier than Thrift or Protocol Buffers to schemas generated from another source?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Dumping a relational database to a binary file means building a schema from the table definitions, and those change.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: With Avro, generate a record schema per table, with each column as a field of the same name. When the database schema changes, generate a new schema and export again. Readers match fields by name.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Thrift and Protocol Buffers would need an administrator to update the mapping from columns to tags by hand, taking care never to reuse a tag.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The schema is derived from a changing source, such as a database or a configuration.

card.rule: Because Avro identifies fields by name, a schema can be regenerated whenever its source changes.
card.limits: Tags in Thrift and Protocol Buffers are an advantage when you hand-write one stable schema, since they give field identity that names cannot.

concepts.title: Code generation and dynamically typed languages
concepts.question: Does code generation help in dynamically typed languages, and how does Avro cope without it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Thrift and Protocol Buffers depend on generated code, but dynamically typed languages such as Python or Ruby have no compile-time type checker to satisfy.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In those languages there is little point generating code, and it is often frowned upon. Avro's code generation is optional. A container file embeds the writer's schema, so it can be opened with the library and looked at like a JSON file.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Without generated types you lose compile-time checks; you gain direct access to data that describes itself.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You work in a dynamically typed language, or the schema is generated and changes often.

card.rule: Generate code where a compiler can use it; elsewhere rely on self-describing files.
card.limits: Code generation stays useful in statically typed languages, which gain checking and efficient structures.

concepts.title: What schemas give you
concepts.question: Why choose a schema-based binary encoding over JSON or XML?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Textual formats are widespread, but they are bulky, loosely specified and offer little help with change.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Schema-based binary encodings can omit field names and so be much more compact than binary JSON variants. The schema doubles as documentation that cannot go stale, since it is needed for decoding. A database of schemas lets you check compatibility before deployment. Generated code gives compile-time type checking.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The data must be decoded before a person can read it.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You control both ends and need compactness, checked evolution and tooling.

card.rule: Schemas give compact data, trustworthy documentation, pre-deployment compatibility checks and typed code.
card.limits: For exchange with parties you do not control, an agreed textual format may matter more than these gains.

concepts.title: Simple schema languages and ASN.1
concepts.question: Why are the schema languages of Thrift, Protocol Buffers and Avro simpler than XML Schema, and what does ASN.1 teach?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: XML Schema and JSON Schema support detailed rules, such as a regular expression for a string or a range for an integer, but they are complex.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Protocol Buffers, Thrift and Avro offer far simpler schema languages, so they are easier to implement and use, and have spread to many programming languages.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Less validation power. The idea itself is old: ASN.1, standardised in 1984, supports tag-number evolution, but it is complex and badly documented.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You choose a schema language for a new application: favour a simple, widely implemented one.

card.rule: Simple schema languages spread widely; complex ones such as ASN.1 are a poor fit for new applications.
card.limits: If you need fine-grained validation rules, a simple schema language will not express them.

concepts.title: Three modes of dataflow
concepts.question: In which ways does encoded data flow between processes, and who encodes and decodes in each?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Compatibility is abstract until you ask who writes the data and who reads it.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The chapter looks at three modes: through databases, through service calls such as REST and RPC, and through asynchronous message passing. In each, ask which process encodes and which decodes.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each mode has its own timing and version mix, so one compatibility rule does not fit all.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You design a system boundary and must decide which direction of compatibility it needs.

card.rule: For any boundary, name the encoder and the decoder before judging compatibility.
card.limits: The three modes overlap: message passing sits somewhere between RPC and databases.

concepts.title: Databases need both directions
concepts.question: Which compatibility directions does a database need, and why?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In a database the writing process encodes and the reading process decodes, possibly much later and often by a different version.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Backward compatibility is necessary, since newer code must decode what older code wrote. Forward compatibility is also often required, because several applications or instances share the database and some run newer code than others.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Supporting both directions restricts every schema change for the life of the data.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: More than one process, or more than one version of a process, touches the same stored data.

card.rule: A database needs backward compatibility, and forward compatibility whenever old and new code share it.
card.limits: A database used by one process that is stopped before the next version starts has no old code reading new data.

concepts.title: Keeping fields that old code does not know
concepts.question: How can old code avoid destroying a field it cannot interpret?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: New code adds a field and stores it. Old code reads the record, updates it, and writes it back. The new field may vanish.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The encoding formats can keep unknown fields, but the application must not undo it. If you decode into model objects and re-encode those objects, the unknown field can be lost.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Preserving unknown fields takes some care in application code, though the book calls the problem not hard.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Code you run may read records written by a newer version and then write them back.

card.rule: When old code rewrites a record, keep the fields it does not understand.
card.limits: If old code only reads, or rewrites only the columns it changed, the loss does not arise.

media.alt: Data loss with an old application. A database holds a JSON record with userName, favoriteNumber, interests and photoURL, written by newer code. Old Java Person class code, which has no photoURL field, reads and decodes it into a model object, calls setFavoriteNumber(42), then re-encodes it to JSON and writes it back. The stored record now lacks photoURL, which the diagram labels as lost.

concepts.title: Data outlives code
concepts.question: Why do old encodings stay in a database long after the code that wrote them is gone?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A server-side application can be replaced within minutes, but a database holds values written five milliseconds ago and five years ago.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat it as data outlives code. Rewriting (migrating) data into a new schema is possible but expensive on a large dataset, so most databases avoid it. A simple change such as adding a column with a null default needs no rewrite: on reading an old row, the database fills in null for the missing column.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Avoiding migrations means old encodings remain, and the system must read every historical version.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You plan schema changes for stored data.

card.rule: Stored data keeps its original encoding, so schema evolution must let new code read all historical versions.
card.limits: A small dataset can be migrated cheaply, and a one-off rewrite is sometimes the right choice.

concepts.title: Archival snapshots
concepts.question: How should a database snapshot for backup or a data warehouse be encoded?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The live database holds a mixture of schema versions from different eras, but a snapshot is a copy.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Since you are copying the data anyway, encode the whole dump consistently in the latest schema. Because the dump is written in one go and is immutable, formats such as Avro object container files fit, and it is a chance to use an analytics-friendly column-oriented format such as Parquet.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The snapshot no longer shows the original encoding of each record.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You take backups or load data into a data warehouse.

card.rule: Encode a snapshot consistently in the latest schema, in a format suited to one-shot immutable files.
card.limits: If you need evidence of how a record was originally stored, a normalised snapshot hides it.

concepts.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
concepts.title: Services and independent evolution
concepts.question: Why does a service-oriented design require compatible encodings across versions?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A large application is hard to change if everything is one unit.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Split it into services, each exposing an application-specific API to clients; a server can itself be a client of another service. The aim of a service-oriented or microservices architecture is that each service is owned by one team and can be released often without coordinating with others.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Independent releases mean old and new versions of servers and clients run together, so the encodings of requests and responses must be compatible across versions.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Several teams build one product and want to deploy on their own schedules.

card.rule: Independent deployability means clients and servers of different versions coexist, so API encodings must stay compatible.
card.limits: Where one team releases all services together in one step, version mixing is smaller, but the aim of microservices is to avoid that.

concepts.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
concepts.title: REST and SOAP
concepts.question: How do REST and SOAP differ as approaches to web services?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: When HTTP carries calls between clients and services, you need a style for describing the API.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: REST is a design philosophy built on HTTP: simple data formats, URLs for identifying resources, and HTTP features for caching, authentication and content negotiation. SOAP is an XML-based protocol that avoids most HTTP features and brings the WS-* standards and a WSDL description.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: SOAP depends on tools and code generation and has had interoperability problems; REST favours simpler tooling and can be described with OpenAPI.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing an API style: REST suits public and cross-organisation integration, SOAP survives mainly in large enterprises.

card.rule: REST is a philosophy using HTTP as it is; SOAP is a separate XML protocol with heavy tooling.
card.limits: These are tendencies; each camp has internal arguments and the book describes the two as nearly opposed in philosophy.

concepts.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
concepts.title: Why a remote call is not a local call
concepts.question: Why can a network request fail in ways a local function call cannot?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: RPC tries to make a remote service look like a local function call, called location transparency. The two are fundamentally different.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Expect failure. A network request may lose its request or its response, or meet a slow or unavailable machine. On a timeout you do not know whether the request got through.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: If you retry after a lost response, the action may run twice, unless the protocol builds in deduplication (idempotence).

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Hiding these facts is convenient, but code that forgets them breaks.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You design or call any remote API, however local it looks.

card.rule: Treat every remote call as able to fail without telling you whether it worked.
card.limits: A failure with a clear error from the server is easier to handle; the hard case is the timeout with no answer.

concepts.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
concepts.title: More ways a remote call differs
concepts.question: Besides failure, how else does a network request differ from a local function call?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: RPC technologies have a long history of hype and trouble: Enterprise JavaBeans and Java RMI are limited to Java, DCOM to Microsoft platforms, and CORBA is excessively complex with no backward or forward compatibility.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Remember the other differences. Latency is wildly variable. You cannot pass a pointer into local memory, so every parameter must be encoded as bytes, which becomes a problem for larger objects.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: There is no point making a remote service look too much like a local object, so REST's openness about being a network protocol is part of its appeal.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You evaluate an RPC framework that promises a call just like any other.

card.rule: A remote call is slower, more variable and needs its arguments encoded, so do not disguise it as a local call.
card.limits: Primitive parameters such as numbers or strings are easy to send; the cost grows with larger objects.

concepts.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
concepts.title: Modern RPC versus REST
concepts.question: When should a team choose an RPC framework over a REST API?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Despite its problems RPC remains, and newer frameworks are built on the encodings of this chapter.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: gRPC uses Protocol Buffers, Finagle uses Thrift, Rest.li uses JSON over HTTP, and Thrift and Avro include their own RPC. Custom RPC with a binary encoding can beat generic JSON over REST on performance.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: REST is good for experimentation (a browser or curl is enough), is supported by all main languages, and has a vast tool ecosystem.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: RPC: requests between services of one organisation in one datacenter. REST: public APIs.

card.rule: Use RPC frameworks inside one organisation for performance; use REST for public APIs.
card.limits: These are tendencies in the book, not rules: performance needs or tooling can change the choice.

concepts.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
concepts.title: Evolving services over time
concepts.question: Which compatibility does a service API need, and how do providers cope when clients cannot be forced to upgrade?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Clients and servers deploy independently, so old and new versions meet.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A simplifying assumption is that servers are updated first and clients second. You then need only backward compatibility on requests and forward compatibility on responses. The properties come from the encoding: Thrift, gRPC and Avro RPC follow their formats' rules.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Across organisations the provider has no control over clients, so compatibility may need to hold for a long time, perhaps indefinitely.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You change a published API.

card.rule: For services, assume servers upgrade first: backward compatible requests, forward compatible responses.
card.limits: The assumption fails if clients can be newer than servers, such as when a server rolls back.

concepts.title: Message brokers
concepts.question: What does a message broker give you that a direct RPC call does not?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A direct call fails if the recipient is down or overloaded, and the sender must know the recipient's address.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A sender publishes to a named queue or topic on a broker, which stores the message temporarily and delivers it to one or more consumers. It buffers, redelivers to a crashed process, spares the sender the address, allows several recipients and decouples sender from recipient.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Communication is usually one-way and asynchronous: the sender does not wait for a reply.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Recipients may be unavailable, may be many, or may come and go, as in a cloud deployment.

card.rule: A broker decouples sender and recipient in time and place, at the price of a one-way, asynchronous flow.
card.limits: If you need an answer straight away, a direct request is the better fit.

concepts.title: Distributed actor frameworks
concepts.question: Why does location transparency work better with actors than with RPC?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Threads, locks and race conditions make concurrency hard in a single process.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In the actor model each actor holds local state and communicates only by asynchronous messages, processing one message at a time. A distributed framework uses the same mechanism across nodes: a message to a remote actor is transparently encoded, sent and decoded.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Delivery is not guaranteed, so messages can be lost; but because the model already assumes this, there is less mismatch between local and remote.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want to scale actor-style logic over several nodes and accept lost messages.

card.rule: Actors already assume lost messages, so remote messaging fits them better than RPC fits ordinary calls.
card.limits: Rolling upgrades still need compatible message encodings, since new and old nodes exchange messages.

concepts.title: Choosing formats by compatibility
concepts.question: What do the three families of formats offer for compatibility, and why does it matter for rolling upgrades?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Services are upgraded gradually, so nodes run different versions and all data in flight must be readable across them.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Language-specific encodings are restricted to one language and often lack compatibility. Textual formats such as JSON, XML and CSV are widespread; compatibility depends on how you use them, and they are vague about numbers and binary strings. Binary schema-driven formats such as Thrift, Protocol Buffers and Avro give compact encodings and clear compatibility rules.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The binary formats need decoding before a person can read the data.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Rolling upgrades are in use: the gradual rollout allows releases without downtime and makes them less risky.

card.rule: Choose the format by the compatibility you need, assuming mixed versions during every upgrade.
card.limits: The summary counts what holds with care: compatibility is achievable, but no format provides it without discipline.

concepts.title: Why keep copies, and where the difficulty lies
concepts.question: Why replicate data, and which part of replication is hard?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A single machine is far from some users, stops everything when it fails, and can serve only so many read queries.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Keep a copy of the same data on several machines connected by a network. Copies near users cut latency, surviving copies keep the system working when a part fails, and more machines can answer reads.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Copying unchanging data once is easy. All the difficulty lies in handling changes to replicated data, so every extra copy is one more place where a change must arrive.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need lower latency, higher availability or more read throughput, and each machine can hold the whole dataset.

card.rule: Replicate for latency, availability and read throughput, and expect the hard part to be propagating changes.
card.limits: If the data never changes there is no replication problem to solve.

media.alt: Engraved map of an island whose regions are labelled single-leader, multi-leader and leaderless replication, with database names along its coasts and two small sailing ships heading to other chapters.

Four boxes in two columns. The left column is Partition 1 with Replica 1 above Replica 2; the right is Partition 2 with Replica 1 above Replica 2. Partition 1 boxes each hold three documents keyed 136, 211 and 377; Partition 2 boxes hold 629, 696 and 858. A dashed double-headed arrow labelled copy of the same data joins the two replicas of each partition.

concepts.title: Three ways to replicate changes
concepts.question: Which three algorithms replicate changes, and what does each cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Every write must reach every replica, or the copies stop being the same. Something must decide where clients send writes.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Single-leader: all writes go to one node that streams changes to the others. Multi-leader: several nodes accept writes and forward them to each other. Leaderless: clients send writes to several replicas, and any replica accepts them.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Single-leader is popular because it is fairly easy to understand and has no conflict resolution to worry about.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You choose or operate a database and need to know how its write path behaves under faults.

card.rule: Almost every distributed database uses single-leader, multi-leader or leaderless replication.
card.limits: A database may also let you tune details such as synchronous versus asynchronous copying within one approach.

concepts.title: Leader-based replication
concepts.question: How do leader and followers split the work of writes and reads?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Every write must be processed by every replica, in an order that leaves all copies equal.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: One replica is the leader. Clients send writes only to it, and it stores them locally. It then sends each change to the followers in a replication log. Each follower applies the writes in the same order as on the leader. Reads can go to the leader or any follower.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Followers are read-only from the client's point of view, so all writes pass through one node.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want a simple model with one place that decides the order of writes.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: The same pattern is called active/passive or master-slave; leader is also called master or primary, and followers are called read replicas, slaves, secondaries or hot standbys.

card.rule: Writes go to the leader, which streams them in order to followers; reads can go anywhere.
card.limits: Only writes are restricted to the leader. Any one follower may be behind the leader when you read from it.

media.alt: Diagram of leader-based replication. User 1234, who configures a new profile picture, sends a read-write update query to a leader replica. Replication streams carrying a data change record (table, primary key, column, old value, new value, transaction number) flow from the leader to two follower replicas. User 2345 sends a read-only select query for user 1234 to one follower.

concepts.title: Synchronous versus asynchronous replication
concepts.question: When does the leader report success: before or after a follower has the write?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The leader must decide when to tell the client that a write succeeded, and the answer decides what is lost or blocked when something fails.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Synchronous: the leader waits until the follower confirms it received the write, then reports success. Asynchronous: the leader sends the change and does not wait for a response.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A synchronous follower is guaranteed to hold an up-to-date copy, so the data survives a sudden leader failure. But if that follower does not respond, the write cannot be processed and the leader must block all writes until it is back.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need a follower copy you can trust after a leader failure and can accept that an unresponsive follower stalls writes.

card.rule: Synchronous copying buys a guaranteed up-to-date follower at the price of blocking writes when it stops answering.
card.limits: Many relational databases let you choose per setup, while other systems hardcode one mode, so check what yours does.

concepts.title: One synchronous follower, the rest asynchronous
concepts.question: Why make only one follower synchronous instead of all of them?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If every follower were synchronous, any single node outage would bring the whole system to a halt.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Make one follower synchronous and keep the others asynchronous. If the synchronous follower becomes unavailable or slow, promote one of the asynchronous followers to synchronous.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You keep an up-to-date copy on at least two nodes, the leader and one follower, but the other followers can still lag behind.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want durability beyond a single node without letting one failed follower stop all writes.

card.rule: Enable synchronous replication on one follower at a time, so you hold two up-to-date copies without a halt-on-any-failure risk.
card.limits: It guarantees two current copies, not that every follower is current, so reads from asynchronous followers can be stale.

media.alt: Timeline with time running left to right and lanes for user 1234, leader, follower 1 and follower 2. The user sends an update to the leader, which sends a data change to both followers and waits. Follower 1 replies ok, and then the leader sends ok to the user. Follower 2's ok reaches the leader later, after the user already has its ok.

concepts.title: Asynchronous replication and lost writes
concepts.question: What is lost with fully asynchronous replication, and why is it still widely used?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With fully asynchronous replication, a confirmed write may exist only on the leader when it fails.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Accept that trade: the leader keeps accepting writes even if all followers have fallen behind, and reports success without waiting.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: If the leader fails and cannot be recovered, writes not yet replicated are lost, so a write is not guaranteed to be durable even after the client has been told it succeeded.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You run many followers or spread them across geographies, where waiting for them would be too slow or fragile.

card.rule: Asynchronous replication keeps the leader writing at the cost of durability for the latest confirmed writes.
card.limits: It is a poor fit when no confirmed write may be lost. In that case you need at least one synchronous follower or another method.

concepts.title: Adding a follower from a snapshot
concepts.question: How can you set up a new follower without stopping writes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: To add or replace a follower you need an accurate copy of the leader's data, but clients keep writing. A plain file copy sees different parts of the database at different times and may make no sense. Locking the database for the copy would make it unavailable for writes.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Take a consistent snapshot of the leader's database at one point in time, ideally without locking the whole database, then copy the snapshot to the new follower.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The snapshot is only a starting point; the follower still has to be brought up to date with what changed afterwards.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You increase the number of replicas or replace a failed one while the leader keeps serving.

card.rule: Copy a consistent snapshot, not live files, so a new follower can be set up without downtime.
card.limits: If your database lacks a lock-free snapshot, you may need a third-party tool or a manual multi-step workflow.

concepts.title: Catching up from a log position
concepts.question: What must a snapshot be tied to so a new follower can catch up?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A snapshot is out of date the moment it is taken, so the new follower must find out exactly which changes it is missing.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Associate the snapshot with an exact position in the leader's replication log. The follower connects to the leader and asks for all changes since that position, processes the backlog and is then caught up.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: This depends on the leader keeping its log from that position onward and on the position being exact.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You bring up a new follower, restore one from a backup or rebuild a failed one.

card.rule: A snapshot plus an exact log position lets a follower replay what it missed and join the stream.
card.limits: If the position is not exact, the follower may miss changes or apply some twice, so do not guess it. Setup steps differ widely by database.

concepts.title: Follower failure and catch-up recovery
concepts.question: How does a follower recover after a crash or a lost connection?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Any node can go down unexpectedly or for planned maintenance, and the system as a whole should keep running.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Each follower keeps on its local disk a log of the changes it received from the leader. After a restart or a network interruption it knows the last transaction it processed, asks the leader for everything since then and applies it.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Recovery is easy, but a follower that was away for long has a long backlog to replay and meanwhile serves stale data.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A follower reboots, crashes or loses its network link.

card.rule: A follower resumes from the last change in its own log and replays what it missed.
card.limits: This handles follower failure only. If the leader fails, the system needs failover, which is harder.

concepts.title: Failover when the leader fails
concepts.question: What three steps does automatic failover take when the leader fails?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: When the leader fails, writes stop until some other node takes over and everyone agrees who that is.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Failover has three steps. First, decide the leader has failed, usually with a timeout on missing replies. Second, choose a new leader, by election among the remaining replicas or by appointment through a controller node. Third, reconfigure clients to write to it and make the other followers consume from it.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: There is no foolproof way to tell what went wrong, so the decision rests on a guess, and getting nodes to agree on a new leader is a consensus problem.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The leader crashes, loses power or becomes unreachable and you need writes to continue.

card.rule: Failover means detect by timeout, choose the most up-to-date replica as leader, then reconfigure clients and followers.
card.limits: A planned shutdown of the leader is not detected by a timeout. Failover can be done by hand instead of automatically.

concepts.title: Failover and discarded writes
concepts.question: What goes wrong when an out-of-date follower is promoted?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With asynchronous replication, the new leader may lack writes the old leader had accepted. If the old leader later rejoins, those unreplicated writes conflict with what the new leader has accepted since.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The most common solution is to discard the old leader's unreplicated writes.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Discarding may break clients' durability expectations. It is especially dangerous when other systems must stay consistent with the database.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: At GitHub, an out-of-date MySQL follower became leader. Its autoincrement counter lagged, so it reused primary keys that were also used in a Redis store. The mismatch exposed some private data to the wrong users.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You plan automatic failover on an asynchronously replicated database.

card.rule: Promoting a lagging follower can lose confirmed writes and corrupt coordination with external systems.
card.limits: With a synchronous follower promoted as leader, a confirmed write is not lost this way.

concepts.title: Split brain
concepts.question: What is split brain and how do systems guard against it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In certain fault scenarios two nodes can both believe they are the leader, an outcome called split brain.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Some systems add a safety catch that shuts down one node when two leaders are detected.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: If both leaders accept writes and nothing resolves conflicts, data is likely to be lost or corrupted. The catch itself can go wrong: if it is not carefully designed, both nodes can be shut down.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You design or configure automatic failover, where an old leader may return unaware that it was replaced.

card.rule: Two believed leaders mean lost or corrupted writes, so detect them and make sure at most one survives.
card.limits: A shutdown mechanism is only as good as its design. A badly designed one can leave no leader at all.

concepts.title: Failover timeouts and manual failover
concepts.question: What is the cost of setting the failover timeout too long or too short?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The timeout that declares a leader dead is a guess. If it is wrong in either direction, availability suffers.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Choose the timeout between two risks. A longer timeout means a longer time to recovery when the leader really fails. A timeout that is too short triggers unnecessary failovers when a load spike or a network glitch delays a reply.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: If the system is already struggling with high load or network problems, an unnecessary failover is likely to make the situation worse.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You configure automatic failure detection, or decide whether to keep failover manual.

card.rule: Too long delays recovery, too short causes needless failovers, and neither has an easy solution.
card.limits: Because of these problems some operations teams prefer to perform failovers manually even when the software supports automatic failover.

concepts.title: Statement-based replication
concepts.question: Why does shipping SQL statements to followers tend to break?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The simplest replication log is the stream of write statements the leader executes: every INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE is forwarded and each follower executes it as if from a client.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Send the statements, and work around the breakage, for instance by replacing nondeterministic calls with fixed values when the statement is logged.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It is compact, but it breaks on nondeterministic functions such as NOW() or RAND(), on statements that depend on existing data or autoincrement unless run in the same order, and on side effects from triggers or stored procedures.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You can guarantee deterministic transactions. VoltDB does so by requiring them.

card.rule: Statement shipping is compact but fragile, so most systems now prefer other methods.
card.limits: MySQL before version 5.1 used it, and by default it now switches to row-based replication if a statement is nondeterministic.

concepts.title: Write-ahead log shipping
concepts.question: What does shipping the storage engine's own log cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Storage engines already append every write to a log, so the leader could reuse it rather than invent a replication format.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Send the exact same append-only log to followers, which build identical data structures from it. PostgreSQL and Oracle do this.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The log describes data at a very low level, which bytes changed in which disk blocks, so replication is tightly coupled to the storage engine. Different software versions on leader and follower are typically not possible, and upgrades then require downtime.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Leader and followers run the same version and storage format, and you want exact copies.

card.rule: WAL shipping gives exact replicas but ties replication to the storage engine and its version.
card.limits: If the protocol allowed a newer follower, you could upgrade followers first and then fail over.

concepts.title: Logical (row-based) logs
concepts.question: How does a row-level log decouple replication from the storage engine?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A physical log couples replication to the storage engine. Statement shipping is fragile.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use a separate, logical log for replication, at the granularity of a row. An inserted row logs the new column values. A deleted row logs enough to identify it, typically the primary key. An updated row logs its identity plus the new values. A transaction that changes several rows also logs a commit record.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You maintain a second log format, but leader and follower can run different versions or even different storage engines.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need replication that survives upgrades. MySQL's binlog with row-based replication works this way.

card.rule: A logical log describes row changes, so replication no longer depends on storage-engine internals.
card.limits: If a table has no primary key, deletes must log the old values of all columns to identify the row.

concepts.title: Logical logs for outside consumers
concepts.question: Why is a logical log useful beyond follower replicas?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You may want to send the contents of a database to an outside system, such as a data warehouse for offline analysis, or to build custom indexes and caches.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Read the logical log. Its row-level format is easy for external applications to parse. This technique is called change data capture.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You depend on the database exposing its log in a usable form.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Another system must track every change to the database without being a replica.

card.rule: A logical log doubles as a clean stream of changes for external systems.
card.limits: A physical log is hard for outsiders to parse because it describes bytes and blocks.

concepts.title: Trigger-based replication
concepts.question: When would you move replication up into application code?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Built-in replication works without application code, but sometimes you need more flexibility: replicate only a subset, replicate to another kind of database, or apply conflict resolution logic.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Move replication to the application layer. A trigger registers custom code that runs when a data change occurs. It can log the change into a separate table that an external process reads and replicates onward. Databus for Oracle and Bucardo for Postgres work like this.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Trigger-based replication has greater overhead and is more prone to bugs and limitations than built-in replication.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The flexibility is worth the cost.

card.rule: Use triggers when you need custom replication logic, accepting the overhead and the extra bugs.
card.limits: Built-in replication is what you want in most cases.

concepts.title: Read scaling with asynchronous followers
concepts.question: Why does read scaling work only with asynchronous replication?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Many web workloads are mostly reads with a small share of writes, yet all writes go through one leader.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Create many followers and spread read requests across them. This takes load off the leader and lets nearby replicas answer reads. Capacity for reads grows by adding followers.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It only realistically works with asynchronous replication. Making all followers synchronous would let a single node failure or network outage stop all writes, and the more nodes there are, the likelier one is down.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Reads far outnumber writes and slightly stale reads are tolerable.

card.rule: Add asynchronous followers to scale reads, and accept that followers can be behind the leader.
card.limits: It adds no capacity for writes, which still go to the leader, and reads from a lagging follower may be outdated.

concepts.title: Eventual consistency and replication lag
concepts.question: What does eventual consistency promise, and what does it leave open?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A read from an asynchronous follower can return outdated data, so the same query on leader and follower can differ.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The difference is temporary. If you stop writing and wait, followers catch up and match the leader. This effect is called eventual consistency. The delay between a write on the leader and its appearance on a follower is the replication lag.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The word eventually is deliberately vague: there is no limit on how far a replica can fall behind.

blocks.label: Numbers
blocks.text: Normally lag is a fraction of a second. Near capacity or during a network problem it can reach seconds or minutes.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You decide whether the application can tolerate stale reads when lag grows.

card.rule: Eventual consistency means replicas converge when writes stop, with no bound on how long that takes.
card.limits: It is a weak promise. When lag is large the effect becomes a real problem for the application.

concepts.title: Read-after-write consistency
concepts.question: What does read-after-write consistency promise a user?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A user submits data, which goes to the leader, and then views it from a follower that has not received it yet. It looks as if the submission was lost.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Provide read-after-write (read-your-writes) consistency: if the user reloads the page, they always see updates they submitted themselves.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The guarantee makes no promises about other users. Their updates may not be visible until later. It only reassures the user that their own input was saved.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Users submit data and then view it, for example a comment on a discussion thread or a record in a customer database.

card.rule: Make a user see their own writes even if other users' updates arrive later.
card.limits: It covers only the writer's own data and says nothing about when others see it.

media.alt: Timeline with lanes for user 1234, leader, follower 1 and follower 2. The user sends an insert of a comment to the leader and gets insert ok. The leader sends the insert to both followers, but the copy to follower 2 travels slowly. The user's select for that comment goes to follower 2 and returns no results before the insert arrives there.

concepts.title: Reading from the leader to get your writes
concepts.question: How can reads that may have been modified go to the leader?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You need read-after-write consistency on a leader-based system, but sending every read to the leader defeats read scaling.

blocks.label: Approach
