blocks.text: Read from the leader whatever the user may have modified, and read the rest from a follower. A simple rule is to read the user's own profile from the leader and other people's profiles from followers.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: This needs a way to know what the user may have modified without querying it. If most things are editable by the user, most reads go to the leader and read scaling is lost.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Only a small part of the data is editable by the person reading it, such as a profile editable only by its owner.

card.rule: Route reads of possibly user-modified data to the leader and everything else to followers.
card.limits: If almost everything is editable, use another criterion, such as time since the last update.

concepts.title: Remembering the timestamp of your last write
concepts.question: How can a client make sure a replica is up to date for it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You want read-your-writes without sending every read to the leader.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Let the client remember the timestamp of its most recent write. The system must serve that user's reads from a replica that reflects updates at least up to that timestamp. A replica that is behind either hands the read to another replica or makes the query wait.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You must track a timestamp per client and may delay or reroute reads.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Almost any data may be edited by the reader and a leader-reads rule is too broad.

card.rule: Carry the timestamp of your latest write and read only from replicas that have caught up to it.
card.limits: A clock-based timestamp makes clock synchronization critical, so a logical position is safer.

concepts.title: Cross-device read-after-write consistency
concepts.question: What makes read-your-writes harder when one user has several devices?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The same user may write on a desktop browser and read in a mobile app. Each device can know only its own last write, and their requests may be routed differently.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Provide cross-device read-after-write consistency: information entered on one device must be visible on another. Centralize the metadata about a user's last update, and if you need the leader, route requests from all of the user's devices to the same datacenter.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You need shared state across devices and constrained routing.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Users switch between devices and expect their data to follow them.

card.rule: Make a user's latest-write metadata shared, and route their devices consistently.
card.limits: There is no guarantee devices reach the same datacenter by default.

concepts.title: Seeing time go backward
concepts.question: How can a user see data appear and then disappear?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A user reads twice, and each request goes to a different follower. The first follower has little lag and returns a recently added comment. The second lags more and does not have it yet.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Recognize the anomaly: the second query observes the system at an earlier point in time than the first, so time appears to move backward.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It is likely when a page is refreshed and each request is routed to a random server. It is confusing only if the user already saw the data, because they would not miss what they never saw.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You read from several asynchronous followers on behalf of the same user.

card.rule: Reading different followers in turn can show newer data and then older data to the same user.
card.limits: If both followers are equally current, no anomaly appears. Lag differences cause it.

media.alt: Timeline with lanes for user 1234, leader, follower 1, follower 2 and user 2345. User 1234 inserts a comment on the leader, which sends the insert to both followers; the copy reaching follower 2 arrives late. User 2345 first runs a select against follower 1 and gets 1 result, then runs the same select against follower 2 and gets no results.

concepts.title: The monotonic reads guarantee
concepts.question: Where does monotonic reads sit between eventual and strong consistency?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Eventual consistency allows a user to see newer data and then older data, which confuses them.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Monotonic reads guarantees that one user making several reads in sequence will not read older data after having read newer data.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It is a lesser guarantee than strong consistency: a read may still return an old value. It is stronger than eventual consistency.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The same user reads repeatedly from replicas that may differ in lag.

card.rule: Monotonic reads means a user never sees time go backward, though what they see can still be stale.
card.limits: It does not promise freshness, only that successive reads for one user do not regress.

concepts.title: Pinning a user to one replica
concepts.question: How can routing alone provide monotonic reads?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You want monotonic reads without tracking each user's read history.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Make each user always read from the same replica. Different users can use different replicas. Choose the replica by a hash of the user ID rather than randomly.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: If that replica fails, the user's queries have to be rerouted to another replica, which may be further behind.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Users read repeatedly and you can route by user.

card.rule: Route each user to a fixed replica, chosen by hashing the user ID.
card.limits: A reroute after a failure can break the guarantee if the new replica is further behind.

concepts.title: Hearing the answer before the question
concepts.question: How can lag make an effect appear before its cause?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Two writes have a causal dependency: a question and its answer. An observer reads through followers with different lags.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: If the answer's follower has little lag and the question's follower has more, the observer sees the answer first, as if Mrs. Cake answered before Mr. Poons asked.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The outcome violates causality and is confusing for readers.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You replicate writes that depend on each other through paths with different delays.

card.rule: When causally related writes travel on paths with different lag, readers can see the effect before the cause.
card.limits: It matters only when writes depend on each other. Independent writes in any order cause no confusion.

media.alt: Timeline with lanes for Mr. Poons, partition 1 leader, partition 1 follower, Mrs. Cake, partition 2 leader, partition 2 follower and an observer. Mr. Poons's question goes to the partition 1 leader and to Mrs. Cake, whose answer goes to the partition 2 leader. The answer reaches the observer through partition 2's follower first; the question arrives later through partition 1's follower.

concepts.title: The consistent prefix reads guarantee
concepts.question: What does consistent prefix reads promise, and why can partitions break it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Readers can see causally related writes in the wrong order.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Consistent prefix reads guarantees that if a sequence of writes happens in a certain order, anyone reading those writes sees them appear in the same order.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: If the database applies all writes in one order, reads always see a consistent prefix. In many distributed databases partitions operate independently, so there is no global ordering and a reader may see some parts older and some newer.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Your data is partitioned and some writes depend on others.

card.rule: Readers must see writes in the order they happened, which a global ordering provides and independent partitions do not.
card.limits: Within a single partition applying writes in order, the anomaly cannot happen.

concepts.title: Keeping causally related writes together
concepts.question: How can a system keep a consistent prefix when partitions are independent?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Independent partitions cannot guarantee that readers see dependent writes in order.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Write causally related data to the same partition, so one log orders it. Alternatively, use algorithms that explicitly track causal dependencies.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: In some applications keeping related writes together cannot be done efficiently.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You can tell in advance which writes depend on each other, for example by a conversation ID.

card.rule: Co-locate causally related writes in one partition, or track causal dependencies explicitly.
card.limits: Tracking dependencies is more complex; the book returns to it with the happens-before relationship.

concepts.title: Designing for large replication lag
concepts.question: What should you ask about an eventually consistent system, and what do transactions offer?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: It is easy to pretend that asynchronous replication is synchronous, because lag is small most of the time.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Ask how the application behaves if the lag grows to minutes or hours. If the answer is no problem, fine. If users would have a bad experience, design for a stronger guarantee such as read-after-write.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Application code can provide stronger guarantees, for example by reading from the leader, but this is complex and easy to get wrong.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You design an application on an eventually consistent store.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Transactions let the database provide the stronger guarantees so that the application can be simpler.

card.rule: Plan for large lag, and prefer database-provided guarantees over fragile application workarounds.
card.limits: Not every application needs a stronger guarantee. If large lag is harmless, eventual consistency is fine.

concepts.title: Multi-leader replication
concepts.question: What is multi-leader replication and what single-leader weakness does it address?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With one leader, every write must pass through it. If a client cannot reach the leader, for example because of a network interruption, it cannot write at all.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Allow more than one node to accept writes. Each node that processes a write forwards the change to all the other nodes, and each leader acts as a follower of the others at the same time. This is also called master-master or active/active replication.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: More nodes can accept writes, but writes to the same data on different leaders can now conflict. The rest of this chapter returns to that cost.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A single write path is the bottleneck for availability, such as across datacenters or for offline devices.

card.rule: Multi-leader replication lets several nodes accept writes and forward them to each other.
card.limits: It is not a free upgrade of single-leader replication, since concurrent writes can conflict.

concepts.title: When multi-leader replication is justified
concepts.question: In which situations is a multi-leader setup reasonable, and where is it not?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Multi-leader replication brings conflict handling and subtle pitfalls, so it needs a strong reason.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The chapter names three situations where it is reasonable: replicas in several datacenters, clients that keep working offline, and real-time collaborative editing.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Inside a single datacenter the benefits rarely outweigh the added complexity, so it rarely makes sense there.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Local write availability matters more than avoiding conflicts, across datacenters, devices or editors.

card.rule: Reserve multi-leader replication for multi-datacenter, offline and collaborative cases, not for one datacenter.
card.limits: Even in those cases the conflict handling remains the main cost.

concepts.title: Multi-datacenter: performance
concepts.question: Why can multi-leader replication make writes faster across datacenters?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In a single-leader setup spread over datacenters, the leader sits in one of them, so every write from elsewhere crosses the internet to reach it. That adds significant latency and can defeat the purpose of having several datacenters.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Put a leader in each datacenter. Each write is handled in the local datacenter and replicated asynchronously to the others, so the delay between datacenters is hidden from users.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Writes in different datacenters can conflict, and that must be dealt with.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Users in several regions need fast writes.

card.rule: A local leader per datacenter hides inter-datacenter latency from writers.
card.limits: Reads of other regions' data stay behind by the asynchronous delay.

media.alt: Two dashed boxes, Datacenter 1 and Datacenter 2. Each holds a leader, a follower and a conflict resolution component. In each, the leader sends changes to its local follower, and a user's read-write queries go to that leader. Long curved arrows cross between the two leaders in both directions, passing through the conflict resolution components.

concepts.title: Multi-datacenter: outages and links
concepts.question: How does multi-leader handle datacenter outages and flaky links better than single-leader?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Datacenters fail, and the public internet between them is less reliable than the network inside one.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: With a single leader, an outage of the leader's datacenter needs failover to promote a follower elsewhere. With a leader in each datacenter, each datacenter keeps running independently and replication catches up when the failed one returns.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A single-leader setup is very sensitive to problems on the inter-datacenter link, because writes travel over it. Asynchronous multi-leader replication usually tolerates network problems better.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need continued writes through datacenter outages and unreliable links.

card.rule: Independent leaders per datacenter keep working through outages and link problems, then catch up.
card.limits: During an outage, work done on both sides may need conflict resolution afterward.

concepts.title: Pitfalls of retrofitted multi-leader
concepts.question: Why is multi-leader replication often called dangerous territory?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In many databases multi-leader replication is a somewhat retrofitted feature, added to a design built around one leader.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Expect subtle configuration pitfalls and surprising interactions with other database features. Autoincrementing keys, triggers and integrity constraints can all be problematic.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: For these reasons multi-leader replication is often considered dangerous territory that should be avoided if possible.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You have a clear need and have studied the documentation and tested your database.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Some databases support it by default, while it is often added with external tools such as Tungsten Replicator for MySQL, BDR for PostgreSQL and GoldenGate for Oracle.

card.rule: Treat retrofitted multi-leader replication as risky: check how keys, triggers and constraints behave first.
card.limits: Databases designed for it, such as CouchDB for offline operation, may fit better than a retrofitted feature.

concepts.title: Offline clients as leaders
concepts.question: Why does an offline-capable app look like multi-leader replication?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: An app such as a calendar must show meetings and accept new ones at any time, whether or not the device is online.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Give every device a local database that acts as a leader and accepts writes. An asynchronous multi-leader process syncs the replicas of the calendar across all devices.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Replication lag may be hours or even days, depending on when internet access is available. A rich history of broken calendar sync shows it is tricky to get right.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The application must keep working while disconnected.

card.rule: Each offline-capable device is a leader, and sync is asynchronous multi-leader replication.
card.limits: The longer devices stay offline, the larger the lag and the likelier conflicts become.

concepts.title: Collaborative editing
concepts.question: How do locks change real-time collaborative editing?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Tools like Etherpad and Google Docs let several people edit one document at the same time.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Apply each change instantly to the user's local replica and replicate it asynchronously to the server and other editors. To guarantee no conflicts, take a lock on the document first, so others wait until the editor commits and releases it.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Locking is equivalent to single-leader replication with transactions on the leader. For faster collaboration, make the unit of change tiny, such as a keystroke, and skip the lock; then all the challenges of multi-leader replication return, including conflict resolution.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You must choose between safe, slow turn-taking and fast simultaneous editing.

card.rule: Editing with locks avoids conflicts but serializes editors, while lock-free editing is fast but needs conflict resolution.
card.limits: Lock-free editing needs a merge algorithm, such as operational transformation, to be usable.

concepts.title: Write conflicts between leaders
concepts.question: How can two successful writes still conflict in a multi-leader system?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Two users edit the same wiki page title at the same time. User 1 changes it from A to B on one leader, and user 2 changes it from A to C on another. Each write succeeds locally.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: When the changes replicate asynchronously, each leader receives the other's write and a conflict is detected, so some conflict resolution is required.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: This problem does not occur in a single-leader database, and it is the biggest problem of multi-leader replication.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You assess whether your workload lets different users write the same record on different leaders.

card.rule: Concurrent writes to one record on different leaders both succeed locally and conflict when replicated.
card.limits: If writers never touch the same record concurrently, no conflict appears.

media.alt: Timeline with lanes for user 1, leader 1, leader 2 and user 2. A page with id 123 starts with title A. User 1 sets the title to B on leader 1 and user 2 sets it to C on leader 2; each gets ok. The leaders then send each other the change messages (old A, new B and old A, new C), and each reports a conflict on receiving the other's.

concepts.title: Why conflicts are detected late
concepts.question: Why can multi-leader replication not ask the user to settle a conflict?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In a single-leader database, the second writer waits for the first or has its transaction aborted, so the user can retry. In multi-leader both writes succeed, and the conflict surfaces only later.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Accept that conflicts are detected asynchronously. By then the user has moved on, so it may be too late to ask them.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You could make detection synchronous by waiting until the write has reached all replicas before reporting success. That would lose the main advantage of multi-leader replication, which is that each replica accepts writes independently.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You decide how conflicts should be handled in a multi-leader design.

card.rule: In multi-leader systems conflicts are found after both writes succeed, so resolution cannot wait for the user.
card.limits: If you need synchronous detection, you may as well use single-leader replication.

concepts.title: Avoiding conflicts
concepts.question: What is the simplest strategy against write conflicts, and when does it fail?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Many multi-leader implementations handle conflicts poorly.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Avoid them: ensure all writes for a particular record go through the same leader, so conflicts cannot occur. For example, route a user's requests to a home datacenter and use that datacenter's leader for reading and writing.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: From any one user's point of view the setup is essentially single-leader. Different users can have different home datacenters, perhaps chosen by geographic proximity.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Each record has a natural owner, such as the user who edits their own data.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: If you must change a record's designated leader, say because its datacenter failed or the user moved, avoidance breaks down and concurrent writes on different leaders become possible.

card.rule: Route all writes for a record through one leader, and keep a plan for when that assignment must change.
card.limits: It fails when ownership cannot be fixed, for instance with data edited by many users.

concepts.title: Converging on one value
concepts.question: Why must a multi-leader system resolve conflicts in a convergent way?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A single-leader database applies writes in sequence, so the last write sets the final value. Multi-leader has no defined order of writes, and neither order is more correct than the other.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Resolve conflicts convergently: when all changes have replicated, every replica must arrive at the same final value.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Applying writes in arrival order leaves replicas on different values, such as C at one leader and B at another, which is not acceptable.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You choose or design a conflict resolution rule.

card.rule: Whatever the rule, all replicas must end with the same value once all changes are replicated.
card.limits: Convergence says nothing about which value wins or whether data is lost.

concepts.title: Convergent conflict resolution methods
concepts.question: What four ways can replicas converge on one value, and which lose data?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Replicas need a rule that gives the same winner everywhere.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Four ways: give each write a unique ID and keep the highest; give each replica an ID and let higher-numbered replicas win; merge the values, for example alphabetically and concatenated as B/C; or record the conflict in a data structure that keeps everything and resolve it later with application code.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The first two discard the losing writes. When the ID is a timestamp, the method is last write wins (LWW), popular but dangerously prone to data loss.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You choose how your database settles concurrent writes.

card.rule: Choosing a winner by ID loses data; merging or keeping all versions loses nothing but needs more work.
card.limits: Merging only helps if the merge result is meaningful for the data, and keeping everything needs resolving code.

concepts.title: Custom resolution on write or on read
concepts.question: When does application code resolve conflicts, and at what granularity?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The best way to resolve a conflict depends on the application, so most multi-leader tools let you write conflict resolution code.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: On write: as soon as the database detects a conflict in the replicated log, it calls your handler. On read: the database stores all conflicting writes and returns the multiple versions the next time the data is read, and the application resolves them and writes back.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A write handler runs in a background process and must be quick, so it cannot prompt a user. Read-time resolution can ask the user.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A generic rule such as last write wins loses data you care about.

card.rule: Resolve conflicts with application code at write time for speed, or at read time to involve the user.
card.limits: Resolution applies per row or document, so the writes of one transaction are resolved separately.

concepts.title: When conflict resolution surprises users
concepts.question: What went wrong with the shopping cart conflict logic, and what does it teach?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Conflict resolution rules can quickly become complicated, and custom code is error-prone.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: For some time the conflict resolution logic on Amazon's shopping cart preserved items added to the cart but not items removed from it.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Customers sometimes saw items reappear in their carts after removing them.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You write or evaluate resolution code for data that supports both adds and removals.

card.rule: A resolution rule that remembers additions but forgets removals resurrects deleted items.
card.limits: The lesson is about rules that treat adding and removing differently; it does not say union is always wrong.

concepts.title: Automatic conflict resolution research
concepts.question: What approaches try to resolve conflicts automatically?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Hand-written resolution code is complicated and error-prone.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Research offers three lines. Conflict-free replicated datatypes (CRDTs) are data structures for sets, maps, ordered lists and counters that many users can edit concurrently and that resolve conflicts sensibly on their own. Mergeable persistent data structures track history like Git. Operational transformation resolves concurrent edits to an ordered list such as text.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Implementations in databases are still young, but they could make multi-leader synchronization much simpler for applications.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want conflicts resolved without writing custom merge code.

card.rule: CRDTs, mergeable persistent structures and operational transformation resolve concurrent edits automatically.
card.limits: They are young in databases, and they still define one specific meaning for merging.

concepts.title: What counts as a conflict
concepts.question: Which kinds of conflict are obvious and which are subtle?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Not every conflict is two writes to the same field.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: An obvious conflict: two writes set the same field of the same record to different values. A subtle one: a meeting room booking system must prevent overlapping bookings for a room, but two different bookings created at the same time on two leaders can overlap even though each leader checked availability first.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: There is no quick ready-made answer; later chapters build understanding of the problem.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You list the invariants of your application that concurrent writes on different leaders could break.

card.rule: A conflict is any set of concurrent writes that breaks what the application needs to be true.
card.limits: Detecting subtle conflicts needs more than comparing writes to one field.

concepts.title: Replication topologies
concepts.question: Which communication shapes can connect more than two leaders?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With more than two leaders, each write must still reach all of them, and there are several possible paths.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A replication topology is the set of communication paths along which writes propagate. All-to-all: every leader sends its writes to every other leader. Circular: each node receives writes from one node and forwards them, with its own, to one other node. Star: one root node forwards writes to all others, and a star generalizes to a tree.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Restricted shapes need fewer links, but a write may need to pass through several nodes before it reaches all replicas.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You operate more than two leaders and must know how writes flow between them.

card.rule: A topology names the paths along which writes travel between leaders: all-to-all, circular or star.
card.limits: With only two leaders there is just one plausible topology: each sends to the other.

media.alt: Three small sketches of database nodes joined by arrows. (a) Circular topology: four nodes in a ring with arrows pointing one way around. (b) Star topology: a central node with two-way arrows to three outer nodes. (c) All-to-all topology: four nodes with arrows in both directions between every pair.

concepts.title: Preventing infinite replication loops
concepts.question: How do nodes keep a forwarded write from circling forever?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In circular and star topologies a write passes through several nodes, and nodes forward changes they receive from others. A write could circle forever.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Give every node a unique identifier and tag each write in the replication log with the identifiers of all nodes it has passed through.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each write carries a list of node identifiers, and every node must check the tags.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Writes are forwarded across nodes rather than sent directly from the origin.

card.rule: Tag each write with the nodes it has visited and ignore any write that already carries your own ID.
card.limits: All-to-all topologies need no forwarding, so they do not need this device.

concepts.title: Topology and fault tolerance
concepts.question: Why are all-to-all topologies more fault tolerant than circular or star ones?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In circular and star topologies, if just one node fails, it can interrupt the flow of replication messages between other nodes.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use a more densely connected topology such as all-to-all, where messages can travel along different paths and so avoid a single point of failure.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The topology of a circular or star setup can be reconfigured around a failed node, but in most deployments this must be done manually.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A node outage must not stop replication between the remaining nodes.

card.rule: Denser topologies offer alternate paths, so a single failed node does not cut off the others.
card.limits: Dense topologies bring their own issue: messages can overtake each other.

concepts.title: Messages overtaking each other
concepts.question: How can a replica receive an update before the insert it depends on?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In an all-to-all topology, client A inserts a row on leader 1 and client B updates it on leader 3. Leader 2 may receive the update first, an update to a row it does not have, and the insert later.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat it as a causality problem like consistent prefix reads: the update depends on the insert, so every node must process the insert first. Attaching a timestamp to every write is not enough, because clocks cannot be trusted to be in sync well enough.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Correct ordering needs a technique such as version vectors, which the chapter covers later.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You run multi-leader replication and rely on updates following their inserts.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Verify the guarantees you assume by reading the documentation and testing the database thoroughly.

card.rule: Causally related writes can arrive out of order in all-to-all replication, and timestamps do not fix it.
card.limits: Systems differ: some provide no causal ordering or do not even try to detect conflicts.

media.alt: Timeline with client A, leaders 1, 2 and 3, and client B. Client A inserts key x with value 1 on leader 1 and gets ok; leader 1 sends the insert to leaders 2 and 3. Client B updates x to value plus one on leader 3, which sends update value 2 to leaders 1 and 2. At leader 2 a shaded box marks the update arriving before the insert.

concepts.title: Leaderless replication
concepts.question: What does leaderless replication change, and where did it come from?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Single-leader and multi-leader replication both send a write to one node that copies it to the rest. A leader fixes the order of writes.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Abandon the leader and let any replica accept writes directly from clients. In some implementations the client sends the write to several replicas itself, and in others a coordinator node does it on the client's behalf.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Unlike a leader, a coordinator does not enforce an ordering of writes, which has profound consequences for how the database is used.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want to keep accepting writes without failover and can live with weaker ordering.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Amazon's in-house Dynamo made the idea fashionable again. Riak, Cassandra and Voldemort are open source stores in this style, called Dynamo-style.

card.rule: Leaderless replication lets any replica accept writes and gives up a single ordering of writes.
card.limits: The coordinator in some designs does not impose order, so it is not a leader.

concepts.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
concepts.title: Writing when a node is down
concepts.question: How does a leaderless database keep accepting writes when a replica is down?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With three replicas and one down for maintenance, a leader-based system might need a failover to keep processing writes.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In a leaderless configuration there is no failover. The client sends the write to all three replicas in parallel, and two available ones accept it. If two of three acknowledgments suffice, the write is successful and the client ignores the missed replica.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: When the down node returns it lacks the writes made meanwhile, so a read from it may return stale values. For that reason reads are also sent to several nodes in parallel.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Replica outages are routine and write availability matters.

blocks.label: Numbers
blocks.text: Version numbers decide which of the differing read responses is newer.

card.rule: Leaderless writes succeed with enough acknowledgments, and reads from several nodes catch the stale replica.
card.limits: A write acknowledged by too few nodes fails, so availability still has a limit.

concepts.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
concepts.title: Read repair
concepts.question: How can a read fix a stale replica?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A replica that missed a write while it was down must eventually catch up.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: When a client reads from several nodes in parallel, it can detect stale responses. In the chapter's example, a client gets version 7 from two replicas and version 6 from the third, sees that the third is stale and writes the newer value back to it.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It works well for values that are frequently read, but a value that is rarely read may stay stale for a long time.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Reads often touch several replicas and values are read regularly.

card.rule: Detect stale replicas during reads and write the newer value back to them.
card.limits: It only repairs what is read. Rarely read values stay stale without another mechanism.

media.alt: Timeline with user 1234, replicas 1, 2 and 3, and user 2345. User 1234 sets a profile picture; replicas 1 and 2 answer ok, while replica 3 is marked node offline and the write to it is lost. User 2345 then reads all three: replicas 1 and 2 return me-new.jpg version 7, replica 3 returns me-old.jpg version 6. User 2345 then sends a set with version 7 to replica 3, which answers ok.

concepts.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
concepts.title: Anti-entropy process
concepts.question: What does a background anti-entropy process add to read repair?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Read repair misses values that are not read.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Run a background process that constantly looks for differences in the data between replicas and copies any missing data from one replica to another.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Unlike a replication log, it does not copy writes in any particular order, and there can be a significant delay before data is copied.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You must bound how long rarely read data can stay missing from a replica.

card.rule: Combine read repair with a background sweep so every replica eventually receives every value.
card.limits: Not every system has it. Voldemort, for example, has no anti-entropy process.

concepts.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
concepts.title: The quorum condition w + r > n
concepts.question: Why does w + r > n let a read see the latest write?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If a write is acknowledged by only some replicas, a read from other replicas may miss it.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: With n replicas, require w confirmations for a write to count and query at least r nodes for each read. If w + r > n, the nodes written and the nodes read must overlap, so at least one of the r nodes read has the latest value. Reads and writes obeying this are quorum reads and writes.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each operation must hear from enough nodes, so fewer nodes can be down or slow before operations fail.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Leaderless replication needs reads that are normally up to date despite missed writes.

blocks.label: Numbers
blocks.text: With n = 3, w = 2, r = 2 each read touches two nodes and at least one of them holds every acknowledged write.

card.rule: If w + r > n, any read set overlaps any acknowledged write set, so a read sees the newest value.
card.limits: Overlap guarantees that the latest value is among the responses, not that nothing can go wrong. Edge cases remain.

media.alt: Five replicas in a row with n = 5. A writer above reaches replicas 1, 2 and 3 (w = 3 successful writes, outlined) while the arrows to replicas 4 and 5 are crossed out. A reader below fails to reach replicas 1 and 2 (crossed out) but reads replicas 3, 4 and 5 (r = 3 successful reads, outlined). The two outlines overlap at replica 3.

concepts.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
concepts.title: Choosing n, w and r
concepts.question: How many node failures can common choices of n, w and r tolerate?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You must pick n, w and r so that reads and writes continue through failures.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A common choice is an odd n, typically 3 or 5, with w = r = (n + 1) / 2 rounded up. Reads and writes are sent to all n replicas in parallel; w and r only say how many replies to wait for. With n = 3, w = r = 2 you tolerate one unavailable node, and with n = 5, w = r = 3 you tolerate two.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Different settings shift cost between reads and writes. A read-heavy workload might use w = n and r = 1: reads are faster, but one failed node makes all writes fail.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You tune a Dynamo-style database for its failure and workload profile.

card.rule: Wait for w or r replies out of n; majorities tolerate the loss of a minority of nodes.
card.limits: If fewer than w or r nodes respond, the operation returns an error.

concepts.title: Smaller quorums trade freshness for availability
concepts.question: What do you gain and lose by choosing w + r ≤ n?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Strict quorums wait for many nodes, which costs latency and availability when many replicas are unreachable.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Set w and r so that w + r ≤ n. Operations still go to n nodes but need fewer successful responses.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You are more likely to read stale values, because your read may miss the node with the latest value. In return you get lower latency and higher availability, since the database stays usable until the reachable replicas fall below w or r.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The application can tolerate stale reads and values availability or speed more.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Quorums need not be majorities; it only matters that the read and write sets overlap in at least one node.

card.rule: Drop below the quorum condition to buy availability and speed, and accept stale reads.
card.limits: Do not drop below it where a read must see the latest write.

concepts.title: Edge cases where quorums return stale data
concepts.question: Even with w + r > n, when can a read still return stale data?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Quorums appear to guarantee that a read returns the latest write, but in practice the guarantee has holes.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Know the cases. With a sloppy quorum the w writes and r reads may land on different nodes. Concurrent writes have no clear order, and last write wins can lose writes to clock skew. A write concurrent with a read may be on only some replicas. A write that failed on fewer than w replicas is not rolled back where it succeeded. A node holding the new value may be restored from an older replica.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Even with everything working, timing can occasionally make you unlucky.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You rely on quorums for correctness and need to know where the guarantee ends.

card.rule: Quorums with w + r > n usually return the latest value, but they are not an absolute guarantee.
card.limits: Treat n, w and r as tuning the probability of stale reads, not as a promise.

concepts.title: Quorums and the lag guarantees
concepts.question: Do quorums give read-your-writes, monotonic reads or consistent prefix reads?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You might hope that choosing w + r > n removes the replication-lag anomalies.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: It does not. In a leaderless database you usually do not get read-your-writes, monotonic reads or consistent prefix reads, so those anomalies can occur.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Stronger guarantees generally require transactions or consensus.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You choose between a leaderless store and a system with stronger guarantees.

card.rule: Quorum settings do not buy you the replication-lag guarantees; stronger guarantees need transactions or consensus.
card.limits: Individual systems may add some guarantees on top, so check the documentation of your database.

concepts.title: Monitoring staleness
concepts.question: Why is monitoring replication health harder in leaderless systems?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Even if your application tolerates stale reads, you need to know whether replication is healthy; a significant lag may signal a network problem or an overloaded node.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: With leader-based replication, writes are applied in the same order on the leader and followers, and each node has a position in the log. Subtract a follower's position from the leader's to measure lag and feed it into monitoring.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: In leaderless systems there is no fixed order of writes, which makes monitoring harder. With read repair only, there is no limit on how old a stale value might be.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You operate a replicated database and need alerts on staleness.

card.rule: Measure lag as the difference of log positions in leader-based systems, and work harder to quantify staleness in leaderless ones.
card.limits: Research can predict the percentage of stale reads from n, w and r, but it is not common practice.

concepts.title: Sloppy quorums
concepts.question: What is a sloppy quorum and why is it not a real quorum?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A network interruption can cut a client off from the nodes it needs. Those nodes are alive, but the client cannot reach w or r of them, so a strict quorum fails.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In a large cluster the client can often still reach other nodes. A sloppy quorum accepts writes and reads on any w or r reachable nodes, even if they are not among the n home nodes for that value. It is like knocking on a neighbor's door and asking to stay on their couch when you are locked out.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It raises write availability, since writes are accepted as long as any w nodes are reachable. But even when w + r > n you cannot be sure to read the latest value, because it may sit on nodes outside the n home nodes. It is only an assurance of durability.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Write availability matters more than reading the latest value.

card.rule: A sloppy quorum trades the read guarantee of a strict quorum for write availability during network trouble.
card.limits: It is optional in Dynamo implementations and should be left off where reads must see the latest value.

concepts.title: Hinted handoff
concepts.question: How do temporarily stored writes get back to their home nodes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Under a sloppy quorum some writes live on nodes that are not their home, and they must eventually reach the right place.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Once the network interruption is fixed, any writes that one node temporarily accepted on behalf of another are sent to the appropriate home nodes. This is hinted handoff. In the couch analogy, the neighbor asks you to go home once you find your keys.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Until the handoff completes, a read may not see the write.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Your database accepts sloppy-quorum writes.

card.rule: Hinted handoff returns temporarily stored writes to their home nodes after the interruption ends.
card.limits: It repairs placement after the fact. It does not make reads during the interruption fresh.

concepts.title: Leaderless replication across datacenters
concepts.question: How do leaderless databases handle several datacenters?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You want data in several datacenters without a leader in one of them.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Leaderless replication tolerates conflicting concurrent writes, network interruptions and latency spikes, so it suits multiple datacenters. In Cassandra and Voldemort, n includes nodes in all datacenters and you configure how many replicas each datacenter holds. A write goes to all replicas, but the client waits only for a quorum in its local datacenter.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The slower writes to other datacenters are often asynchronous, though configuration offers some flexibility.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need cross-datacenter replication without a single write path.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Riak keeps client-to-node traffic local to one datacenter, so n counts the replicas in that datacenter. Replication between clusters runs asynchronously in the background, in a style similar to multi-leader replication.

card.rule: Wait for a local quorum and let the remote datacenters catch up asynchronously.
card.limits: Remote datacenters may lag, so cross-datacenter reads can be stale.

concepts.title: Concurrent writes in a leaderless database
concepts.question: Why can replicas permanently disagree after concurrent writes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Several clients may write the same key at once. Conflicts occur even with strict quorums, and also during read repair and hinted handoff. Events can arrive in different orders at different nodes because of variable network delays and partial failures.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Picture two clients A and B writing key X to three nodes. Node 1 receives A but misses B because of an outage. Node 2 receives A and then B. Node 3 receives B and then A.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: If each node simply overwrites on receipt, node 2 ends with B while the others hold A, and they stay inconsistent. To be eventually consistent, replicas must converge on one value.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Most implementations handle this poorly, so developers who want to avoid losing data need to know how their database handles conflicts.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You write to a Dynamo-style store from several clients.

card.rule: Overwriting on arrival leaves replicas permanently different, so a convergence rule is required.
card.limits: If a key is written by one client only, or once, these conflicts cannot arise.

media.alt: Timeline with client A, nodes 1, 2 and 3, and client B. Client A sends set X = A and client B sends set X = B to all three nodes, but node 1 is marked unresponsive and B's write to it is lost. Node 2 receives A then B; node 3 receives B then A. A later get X by client B returns A from node 1, B from node 2 and A from node 3.

concepts.title: Last write wins
concepts.question: What does last write wins achieve, and what does it cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Replicas need a way to converge after concurrent writes.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Each replica stores only the most recent value and lets older values be overwritten or discarded. Because concurrent writes have no natural order, an arbitrary one is forced: attach a timestamp to each write, keep the biggest, and discard earlier ones. This is last write wins (LWW).

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: LWW achieves eventual convergence at the cost of durability. Of several concurrent writes, all reported successful, only one survives and the others are silently discarded.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Lost writes are acceptable, as they can be for a cache.

card.rule: LWW converges replicas by silently discarding all but one of the concurrent writes.
card.limits: If losing data is not acceptable, LWW is a poor choice.

concepts.title: Using LWW safely
concepts.question: When is last write wins an acceptable choice?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: LWW silently drops writes, and the chapter notes it may even drop writes that are not concurrent.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use it where lost writes are acceptable, such as caching. Otherwise use it only if each key is written once and then treated as immutable, so there are no concurrent updates to the same key.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You give up updates in place. Cassandra's recommended pattern is to use a UUID as the key, giving each write operation a unique key.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The data is a cache or is append-only.

card.rule: Use LWW only for data you can afford to lose, or for keys that are written exactly once.
card.limits: For mutable data that must not lose updates, choose a conflict method that keeps or merges concurrent writes.

concepts.title: The happens-before relationship
concepts.question: How do you decide whether two operations are concurrent?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: To resolve conflicts you must first tell whether one write should overwrite another or whether they clash.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Operation A happens before B if B knows about A, depends on A, or builds on A. Two operations are concurrent if neither happens before the other, that is, neither knows about the other. For any two operations there are three possibilities: A before B, B before A, or concurrent.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: If one operation happened before the other, the later one should overwrite the earlier. If they are concurrent, there is a conflict that needs resolving.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You design or debug conflict handling in a multi-leader or leaderless system.

card.rule: Two operations are concurrent exactly when neither knew about the other; only then is there a conflict.
card.limits: Knowledge, not physical time, decides it, so a clock comparison cannot settle it.

concepts.title: Concurrency is not about clock time
concepts.question: Why does concurrency not depend on the time at which operations occur?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: It is tempting to call operations concurrent if they happen at the same time. But clocks in distributed systems make it hard to tell if two things happened at exactly the same time.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Call two operations concurrent if they are unaware of each other, regardless of the physical time at which they occurred.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Operations far apart in time can still be concurrent if a slow or interrupted network stopped one from learning of the other.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You reason about concurrency in a system with unreliable networks and clocks.

card.rule: Concurrency means mutual ignorance, not simultaneity.
card.limits: Two operations that overlap in time are not automatically concurrent in this sense if one knew of the other.

concepts.title: Version numbers detect concurrency
concepts.question: How do version numbers let a server tell overwrites from concurrent writes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You want to detect concurrent writes without silently dropping any, starting with a database that has one replica.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The server keeps a version number per key, increments it on every write and stores it with the value. A read returns all values not yet overwritten plus the latest version number, and the client must read before writing. A write carries the version number from the prior read and must merge all values from that read. The server overwrites values with that version or below and keeps higher ones.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: No data is silently dropped, but clients must clean up by merging.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Several clients write the same key and you want to detect concurrency.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: A write without a version number is concurrent with all other writes: it overwrites nothing and is returned as one of the values on later reads.

card.rule: A write overwrites exactly the versions the client had seen and leaves every other version as a sibling.
card.limits: The server compares versions without interpreting values, so the value may be any structure.

media.alt: Timeline with client 1, a database and client 2 building a shopping cart. Client 1 sets cart [milk], then [milk, flour] with version 1, then [milk, flour, eggs, bacon] with version 3. Client 2 sets [eggs] with no version, then [eggs, milk, ham] with version 2. Each reply gives a version number and the values held; from the second write onward replies list two values.

concepts.title: Merging siblings
concepts.question: How should concurrently written values be merged?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The version algorithm keeps concurrent values, which Riak calls siblings, and leaves the clients to merge them.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Merge in application code. For a shopping cart with additions only, take the union of the siblings.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Picking one sibling by version number or timestamp is last write wins and loses data. A union also fails if items can be removed, because an item removed in only one sibling reappears.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Concurrent values must all be preserved.

card.rule: Merge siblings with logic that fits the data, because choosing one sibling loses data and a naive union resurrects deletions.
card.limits: Merging in application code is complex and error-prone; automatic data structures can do it.

media.alt: Flow graph of cart edits (Figure 5-14, a separate diagram from the timeline). From empty, arrows lead to plus milk and plus eggs. Plus milk points to plus flour and plus ham; plus eggs points to plus ham and plus bacon; plus flour points to plus bacon. Labels [milk], [milk, flour], [eggs], [milk, flour, eggs, bacon] and [eggs, milk, ham] sit along the arrows.

concepts.title: Tombstones
concepts.question: How can a merge tell a removed item from one that was never there?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If an item is simply deleted from a sibling, a merge cannot tell the deletion from absence, and the item comes back.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Leave a marker with an appropriate version number to show that the item was removed. This deletion marker is called a tombstone.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The deleted item keeps taking some space as a marker.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Merging siblings of data that supports deletion.

card.rule: Record a deletion as a versioned marker so that merging can honour it.
card.limits: Markers must be kept long enough to be seen by all replicas.

concepts.title: Version vectors
concepts.question: How does the version number approach extend to many replicas?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: One version number per key is not enough when several replicas accept writes concurrently.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use a version number per replica as well as per key. Each replica increments its own number when processing a write and tracks the numbers it has seen from other replicas. The collection of version numbers from all replicas is a version vector.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The vector must travel with values: it is sent to clients on reads and sent back to the database on writes.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A leaderless database lets clients read from one replica and write to another.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: A common variant is the dotted version vector used in Riak 2.0, which encodes the vector as a string called the causal context.

card.rule: A version vector lets the database tell overwrites from concurrent writes across replicas.
card.limits: Applications may still need to merge siblings, but no data is lost if they merge correctly.

concepts.title: The four purposes of replication
concepts.question: What are the purposes of replication, and what must you handle?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Replication sounds simple: keep a copy of the same data on several machines.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: It serves high availability, disconnected operation, low latency and scalability of reads. High availability keeps the system running when machines or a datacenter fail. Disconnected operation lets an application work through a network interruption. Latency means placing data near users. Scalability means serving more reads than one machine can.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It is a remarkably tricky problem. It needs careful thinking about concurrency and everything that can go wrong, at a minimum unavailable nodes and network interruptions.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You list why you replicate before choosing an approach.

card.rule: Replicate for availability, disconnected work, latency or read scale, and design for concurrency and faults.
card.limits: Not all kinds of fault are covered; silent data corruption from software bugs is more insidious still.

concepts.title: Comparing the three approaches
concepts.question: Which approach suits which fault profile, and what does each cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Three approaches exist, and each has advantages and disadvantages.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Single-leader sends all writes to one node and streams changes to followers; reads can use any replica but followers may be stale. Multi-leader lets several leaders accept writes and stream changes to each other. Leaderless sends each write to several nodes and reads from several in parallel to detect and correct stale replicas.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Single-leader is popular because it is fairly easy to understand and has no conflict resolution. Multi-leader and leaderless are more robust to faulty nodes, network interruptions and latency spikes, at the cost of being harder to reason about and giving only very weak guarantees.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You pick a replication approach for a new system.

card.rule: Choose single-leader for simplicity and the others for fault tolerance and write availability, knowing the guarantees are weaker.
card.limits: Replication mode matters too. A promoted asynchronous follower can lose recently committed data.

concepts.title: The three lag guarantees and concurrency
concepts.question: Which guarantee answers which replication-lag anomaly?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Replication lag causes strange effects, and each needs a different promise.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Read-after-write consistency: users always see data they submitted themselves. Monotonic reads: after seeing data at one point in time, users do not later see data from an earlier point. Consistent prefix reads: users see data in a state that makes causal sense, such as a question before its reply.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Multi-leader and leaderless replication allow concurrent writes, so they must detect whether one operation happened before another or the two were concurrent, and resolve conflicts, for example by merging.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You name the anomaly in a bug report and pick the weakest guarantee that removes it.

card.rule: Pick the guarantee that matches the anomaly: own writes, no regress, or causal order.
card.limits: None of these guarantees alone resolves conflicts between concurrent writes.

concepts.title: Why split data into partitions
concepts.question: Why split a dataset into partitions when replication already puts copies of the data on several nodes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Replication keeps copies of the same data on different nodes. That does not help once the dataset, or the query load, is too big for one machine.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Break the data into partitions, also called sharding, so that each record, row or document belongs to exactly one partition. Partitions can sit on different nodes of a shared-nothing cluster, so the data spreads over many disks and the queries over many processors.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A query that touches a single partition can run on its own node, so adding nodes raises throughput. Large, complex queries can be parallelised over many nodes, but that gets significantly harder.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The data or the request rate is more than one machine can handle.

card.rule: Partition when one machine cannot store or serve the data, and give every record exactly one partition.
card.limits: While a single machine copes, partitioning adds effort for no gain, and queries that span many partitions are harder to run than single-partition queries.
card.example: A music streaming service keeps 600 million play records. Splitting them into 60 partitions on 20 nodes lets each node store about a twentieth of the data and answer requests for its own partitions.

media.alt: Engraved map of a ring-shaped atoll labelled Partitioning Atoll, its coast sections named hash partitioning, key range partitioning, secondary indexes, rebalancing and request routing, with sea creatures inside and a lighthouse.

concepts.title: Combining partitioning with replication
concepts.question: How do partitioning and replication fit together on one cluster, and can a node play both leader and follower?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A partition stored on a single node is lost for the time that node is down.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Combine the two: each record belongs to one partition, and copies of every partition are stored on several nodes. With leader-follower replication, each partition's leader is assigned to one node and its followers to others.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A node usually stores more than one partition, and can be the leader for some partitions and a follower for others. You pay for the extra copies in storage and write work, in return for fault tolerance.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need both scale and survival of node failures, which is the usual case.

card.rule: Each record has one partition, each partition has several copies, and a node can lead some partitions while following others.
card.limits: Replication copies a partition; it never splits one record across partitions, and a node's role for one partition says nothing about its role for another.
card.example: Eight partitions run on four nodes, with each partition kept on three nodes. Node A leads partitions 1 and 5 and follows partitions 2, 3, 6 and 8, so it stores six of the eight partitions.

media.alt: Four nodes, each holding three partition replicas. Node 1 holds partition 1 leader and partition 2 and 3 followers; node 2 holds partition 2 follower, 3 leader, 4 follower; node 3 holds partition 1 follower, 2 leader, 4 follower; node 4 holds partition 1 and 3 followers and partition 4 leader. Arrows show replication streams from each leader to its followers. A user writes to partition 4 at node 4.

concepts.title: Even spread, skew and hot spots
concepts.question: What does an unfair spread of data or load across partitions do to the benefit of adding nodes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The goal is to spread data and query load evenly. If every node takes a fair share, 10 nodes should handle about 10 times the data and the throughput of one node, ignoring replication.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: If the spread is unfair, the partitioning is skewed. A partition with disproportionately high load is a hot spot. Assigning records to nodes at random avoids hot spots and spreads data quite evenly.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: With random assignment you cannot tell which node holds a given item, so a read has to query all nodes in parallel. A good scheme must spread load and still let you locate a record from its key.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You judge any partitioning scheme: ask how evenly it spreads load, and how a reader finds a record.

card.rule: Good partitioning spreads data and load evenly while still letting a key lead to its record; skew wastes the added nodes.
card.limits: The tenfold figure ignores replication and assumes every node takes a fair share. Even spread alone is not enough, as random assignment shows.
card.example: A forum splits its threads over 10 nodes. If 8 nodes each hold 5 percent of the traffic and two hold 30 percent each, those two nodes limit the whole cluster.

concepts.title: Key range partitioning
concepts.question: How does key range partitioning tell which partition holds a key, and what does sorted order bring?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You want to find which node holds a record from its key alone, without asking every node.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Give each partition a continuous range of keys, from some minimum to some maximum, like the volumes of a paper encyclopedia. Knowing the range boundaries tells you the partition. Keys can be kept sorted inside each partition.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Sorted keys make range scans easy, and the key can work as a concatenated index to fetch related records in one query. Certain access patterns, such as many requests for neighbouring keys, can create hot spots.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Queries often read ranges of keys and the traffic spreads over the whole key space.

card.rule: Assign each partition a continuous key range and keep keys sorted, so any key is located by the boundaries and ranges are cheap to scan.
card.limits: Equal-width ranges give uneven partitions when keys are unevenly distributed, and hot spots appear when traffic concentrates on neighbouring keys.
card.example: Customer IDs 0 to 999,999 are split at 250,000, 500,000 and 750,000. ID 612,000 goes to the third partition, and a request for IDs 600,000 to 620,000 also stays on the third.

media.alt: A shelf of twelve encyclopedia volumes numbered 1 to 12, each spine labelled with an alphabetical key range, from A-ak to Bayes on volume 1 through to Trudeau to Zywiec on volume 12. The ranges follow alphabetical order and differ in how much of the alphabet they cover.

concepts.title: The timestamp key hot spot
concepts.question: Why does partitioning time-ordered data by timestamp overload one partition, and what key change helps?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With a timestamp as the key, partitions are ranges of time, such as one per day. Sensor readings are written as they happen, so all writes go to the partition for today, which can be overloaded while the others sit idle.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Put something other than the timestamp first in the key, for example the sensor name, so the data is partitioned by sensor name first and then by time. With many sensors active at once, the write load spreads across the partitions.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: To read several sensors over a time range you must run a separate range query for each sensor name.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Writes arrive in key order, as in time-ordered data, and many independent sources write at the same time.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: One partition saturates with writes while the others do nothing, so the cluster behaves like a single node.

card.rule: Do not lead a range-partitioned key with a value that grows with time; lead with something that spreads simultaneous writes.
card.limits: The fix assumes many sources are active at once, and it costs the cheap time-range query across all sources.
card.example: A smart-meter service stores readings under the key 2026-10-14-09-30 and writes every minute. All of today's writes hit the partition for 14 October, while the partitions for earlier days receive none.

concepts.title: Partitioning by hash of key
concepts.question: What does hashing the key do to the spread of load, and what does it cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Key range partitioning risks skew and hot spots when keys that sit close together are accessed together.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Apply a hash function to the key and give each partition a range of hash values rather than a range of keys. A good hash function takes skewed data and makes it uniformly distributed: even very similar strings get hashes spread over the whole range.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Keys that were adjacent are now scattered over all partitions, so their sort order is lost and range queries on the key become inefficient.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Even load matters more than ordered range scans, and records are looked up by exact key.

card.rule: Hash the key and give each partition a range of hashes: load spreads evenly, but ordered range scans on the key are lost.
card.limits: Hashing does not remove hot spots caused by many requests for one key, and range queries on the key lose their efficiency.
card.example: A chat service hashes each message ID to a 32-bit number and splits the number range into 16 equal pieces, one per partition. Consecutive message IDs land on unrelated partitions.

media.alt: Six consecutive one-second timestamps, 17:08:10 to 17:08:15, each hashed with the first two bytes of MD5 to a number between 0 and 65,535, drawn against eight equal partitions p0 to p7. Values 7,372, 18,805, 50,537, 31,579, 62,253 and 24,510 land in p0, p2, p6, p3, p7 and p2 respectively, so neighbouring timestamps end up in scattered partitions.

concepts.title: Why avoid the term consistent hashing
concepts.question: Why do the authors advise against the term consistent hashing, and what should we call it instead?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: Consistent hashing, as defined by Karger and colleagues, is a way of spreading load evenly over an internet-wide system of caches such as a content delivery network.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: The word consistent here has nothing to do with replica consistency or ACID consistency. It describes a particular approach to rebalancing. Database documentation still uses the term, often inaccurately.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: The authors suggest avoiding the term and saying hash partitioning instead.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You read or write about hash-partitioned stores: say hash partitioning, and check what a claim of consistent hashing really means.

card.rule: Call it hash partitioning: the word consistent in consistent hashing says nothing about data consistency.
card.limits: The term has a precise original meaning for caches; the advice is about avoiding confusion in database talk, not about the original idea being wrong.

concepts.title: Compound keys: hash first, sort within
concepts.question: How can one key give an even spread across partitions and efficient range scans within a group of records?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Hash partitioning loses range scans, and key range partitioning risks hot spots. Sometimes you want a bit of both.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Declare a compound primary key of several columns, as Cassandra allows. Only the first part is hashed to choose the partition. The other columns serve as a concatenated index that sorts the data inside it.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A query cannot search a range of values of the first column. If it fixes the first column to one value, it can scan the other columns efficiently.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You read many records that share a fixed first value, in order, and want different first values spread across the cluster.

card.rule: Hash the first key column to place the data and sort by the remaining columns to scan within it.
card.limits: Ranges over the first column are not supported, so the first column must be something every query fixes.
card.example: A chat app keys messages by (room_id, sent_at) and hashes only the room ID. One room's messages from last Tuesday come from a single partition in order, while other rooms live elsewhere.

concepts.section: Skewed Workloads and Relieving Hot Spots
concepts.title: Splitting a hot key
concepts.question: What can an application do when all requests aim at one key and hashing cannot spread them?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Hashing a key cannot help when all reads and writes are for the same key: identical keys have identical hashes, so every request goes to one partition. A single very busy key can cause this.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The application reduces the skew itself. If one key is known to be very hot, add a random number to the start or end of the key. A two-digit decimal random number splits the writes to that key evenly over 100 keys, which can be on different partitions.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Reads must now fetch the data from all 100 keys and combine it. You also need bookkeeping to track which keys are split.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A small number of keys take heavy write traffic. For the many keys with low write throughput it is unnecessary overhead.

card.rule: Split a known hot key with a random number, and accept costlier reads and extra bookkeeping.
card.limits: It pays only for the few hot keys; applied to every key it adds read work and bookkeeping for no gain.
card.example: A video site stores the view counter of one viral video under key video:42. The code writes to video:42:07 or video:42:93 and so on, and a reader adds up the 100 counters.

concepts.title: Document-partitioned (local) secondary indexes
concepts.question: In a document-partitioned index, where is each secondary index kept and which partitions does a write touch?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A secondary index searches for occurrences of a value, such as all red cars. Such an index does not map neatly onto partitions chosen by primary key.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Partition by document ID, and let each partition keep its own secondary index covering only its own documents. Adding a red car updates the color:red entry in the partition that stores it. This is a document-partitioned index, also called a local index.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A write deals only with the one partition holding the document. But documents with a given value may sit in any partition, so a read cannot be sent to just one.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Writes should stay simple and in one partition, and you can accept broad reads on the secondary index.

card.rule: A local index lives with its documents, so a write touches one partition, but a read on the indexed value must look at every partition.
card.limits: A read can stay in one partition only if the document IDs were chosen so that matching documents sit together.
card.example: A recipe site keeps recipes 0 to 499 in partition 0 and 500 to 999 in partition 1. Each partition has its own list of recipe IDs for cuisine:thai, covering only the recipes it stores.

media.alt: Two partitions, each with a primary key index of car records (id to colour, make, location) and its own secondary indexes on colour and make, covering only its own cars. Partition 0 lists colour:red as 191 and 306; partition 1 lists colour:red as 768. A user asking for a red car sends a scatter/gather read to both partitions.

concepts.title: Scatter/gather and tail latency
concepts.question: Why is reading a document-partitioned index expensive even when the partitions are queried in parallel?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Matching documents for a secondary index value can be in any partition. A read cannot be directed to one partition.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Send the query to all partitions and combine the results. This way of querying is called scatter/gather.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It makes secondary index reads quite expensive. Even when the partitions are queried in parallel, scatter/gather is prone to tail latency amplification: a few slow responses can delay the whole combined answer.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: A query that filters by two secondary indexes, such as colour and make, is especially unlikely to be served from a single partition.
