card.rule: Scatter/gather asks every partition and then merges, so a few slow partitions can slow every such read.
card.limits: It is widely used in practice despite its cost, and some queries cannot avoid it.
card.example: A listings site with 30 partitions searches for red bikes. Its request goes to all 30 and the user waits until the last of the 30 answers has arrived.

concepts.title: Term-partitioned (global) secondary indexes
concepts.question: How does a term-partitioned global index change the cost of reads and of writes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A local index makes every secondary index read a scatter/gather over all partitions.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Build one global index that covers the data of all partitions, and partition it too, because a single index node would become a bottleneck. Partition it by the term being looked up: entries for color:red from all partitions sit together, with colours a to r on one index partition and s to z on another.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A read goes to the one index partition that holds the term, so no scatter/gather is needed. A write is slower and more complicated, because one document's terms may sit on different index partitions on different nodes.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Secondary-index reads matter more than the extra cost of writes.

card.rule: A global index is partitioned by term, so a read hits one index partition while a write may hit several.
card.limits: A document with many terms can touch many index partitions on one write, so write-heavy workloads pay the most.
card.example: A used-car index puts colours a to r in index partition 0 and s to z in index partition 1. A search for color:red asks only index partition 0, whichever partition holds each car.

media.alt: Two partitions with primary key indexes of car records and secondary indexes partitioned by term. Partition 0 holds colour:black, colour:red, make:Audi, make:Dodge, make:Ford; partition 1 holds colour:silver, colour:yellow, make:Honda, make:Volvo. Colour:red in partition 0 lists 191, 306 and 768, though 768 is stored in partition 1. Dashed arrows show records pointing to index entries in the other partition. A red-car query goes to partition 0 only.

concepts.title: Why global index updates lag
concepts.question: Why are global index updates often asynchronous, and what might a reader see right after a write?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: One document write can change index entries on several partitions on different nodes. Keeping the index always up to date would need a distributed transaction across all of them, which not every database supports.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In practice, updates to global secondary indexes are often asynchronous: the write is acknowledged and the index entries follow.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Writes stay cheaper, but if you read the index shortly after a write, the change may not be reflected yet.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A short delay between a write and its appearance in the index is acceptable to readers.

card.rule: Global index updates usually lag the write, so a read of the index may be briefly out of date.
card.limits: Asynchronous updates do not guarantee a reader sees its own write in the index. An always-current index needs a cross-partition transaction.
card.example: A marketplace acknowledges a new listing and then updates the price index and the category index on two other nodes. For a moment, a buyer searching either index may not find the listing.

concepts.title: Why rebalance and what it must achieve
concepts.question: Why do clusters need rebalancing, and what three requirements should any rebalancing meet?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Over time the query throughput rises, the dataset grows, or a machine fails and others must take over its duties. Data and requests have to move between nodes.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Moving load from one node of the cluster to another is called rebalancing. It should leave the load (storage, reads and writes) shared fairly, keep the database accepting reads and writes while it runs, and move no more data than necessary.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Moving data uses network and disk I/O, so a good scheme ends fair while moving as little as it can.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Nodes are added or removed, whether to add capacity or to replace a failed machine.

card.rule: Rebalance so that load ends fair, service continues meanwhile, and only necessary data moves.
card.limits: These are minimum expectations; they do not say how often or how automatically to rebalance.

concepts.title: How not to do it: hash mod N
concepts.question: Why does assigning keys to nodes by hash mod the number of nodes make rebalancing so expensive?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Using hash(key) mod N, where N is the number of nodes, looks like an easy way to assign each key to a node.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Avoid it. Divide the possible hashes into ranges and assign each range to a partition, so that the assignment of keys does not depend on how many nodes there are.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Mod N is trivial to compute, but when N changes most keys have to move from one node to another, which makes rebalancing excessively expensive.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The number of nodes can change, which is the case for real clusters; use hash ranges instead.

card.rule: Do not place keys by hash mod N: changing N moves most keys.
card.limits: Our reading: if the node count never changed, mod N would never move keys, but real clusters grow, shrink and lose machines.

concepts.title: A fixed number of partitions
concepts.question: How does creating many more partitions than nodes make rebalancing cheap, and what must be chosen up front?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Rebalancing should move little data and should not change which partition a key belongs to.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Create many more partitions than nodes from the start, for example 1,000 partitions on 10 nodes with about 100 each. A new node steals a few partitions from every existing node until the spread is fair again; removing a node does the reverse. Only whole partitions move, and key-to-partition assignment never changes.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The number is usually fixed at setup and is the maximum number of nodes, so it must be high enough for future growth. Each partition has management overhead, so too high a number is counterproductive.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: If the dataset size varies a lot, no count is just right: huge partitions make rebalancing and recovery expensive, tiny ones carry too much overhead.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Data is hash partitioned and growth can be estimated well enough to pick a good count.

card.rule: Fix many partitions up front and rebalance by moving whole partitions between nodes.
card.limits: A fixed count suits neither a dataset whose size is highly variable nor a cluster that may need more nodes than partitions.
card.example: A cluster of 10 nodes starts with 1,000 partitions. When an 11th node joins, it takes about 90 partitions, a few from each old node, and no key changes partition.

media.alt: Before and after rebalancing. Four nodes (0 to 3) hold partitions p0 to p19, five each. After a fifth node is added, nodes 0 to 3 keep four partitions each and node 4 holds p4, p9, p14 and p19. Dashed lines mark partitions staying on the same node; four solid arrows show those partitions migrating, one from each old node, to node 4.

concepts.title: Dynamic partitioning: split and merge
concepts.question: How do key-range databases keep partitions at a sensible size, and what is the problem with an empty database?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With key range partitioning, a fixed number of partitions with fixed boundaries is inconvenient: wrong boundaries could put all data in one partition and leave the others empty, and redrawing them by hand is tedious.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Create partitions dynamically. When a partition grows past a configured size it is split into two, with about half of the data on each side. If lots of data is deleted, a partition that shrinks below a threshold can be merged with a neighbour. One half of a split can move to another node.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The number of partitions adapts to the volume of data, so overhead stays small for small datasets and partition size is capped for large ones. But an empty database starts with a single partition, so all writes go to one node until the first split.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Key-range data of unpredictable size and distribution.

card.rule: Split a partition when it outgrows a size limit and merge it when it shrinks, so the partition count follows the data volume.
card.limits: Splitting starts only once the first partition has outgrown its limit, so a brand-new database behaves like one node at first.
card.example: A key-range store splits a partition when it exceeds its configured size. A 12 GB partition with a 10 GB limit splits into two of about 6 GB, and one of them can move to an idle node.

concepts.title: Partitions proportional to the number of nodes
concepts.question: How does a fixed number of partitions per node keep partition sizes stable as nodes are added?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With a fixed number of partitions, each partition grows with the dataset. With dynamic partitioning the partition count follows the data. In both cases the number of partitions is independent of the number of nodes.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Make the number of partitions proportional to the number of nodes, a fixed number per node, as Cassandra and Ketama do. A new node randomly picks a fixed number of existing partitions to split and takes one half of each, leaving the other half in place.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Random splits can be unfair, but averaged over many partitions per node (256 by default in Cassandra) the new node takes a fair share. Partitions shrink when nodes are added and grow with the data when nodes stay the same.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Data is hash partitioned, because the random boundaries are picked from the range of numbers the hash function produces.

card.rule: Fix the number of partitions per node, so that adding nodes makes partitions smaller and keeps their size fairly stable.
card.limits: Random boundaries need hash partitioning, and a few partitions per node make unfair splits more likely.

concepts.title: Automatic or manual rebalancing
concepts.question: What does fully automatic rebalancing risk, and why might a human stay in the loop?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Rebalancing can be fully automatic, fully manual, or somewhere between. Automatic means less operational work, but rebalancing is expensive: it reroutes requests and moves a lot of data, and can overload the network or nodes and harm other requests.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Some systems, such as Couchbase, Riak and Voldemort, generate a suggested partition assignment automatically but need an administrator to commit it before it takes effect.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Automation is convenient but can be unpredictable. A human in the loop is slower, but helps prevent operational surprises.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: With automatic failure detection, a slow overloaded node may be judged dead; the cluster moves load off it, which adds load to it, the others and the network, and can cascade.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A rebalancing is expensive and a wrong decision could make an overload worse.

card.rule: Automatic rebalancing is convenient but can be dangerous, so a human approval step can be worth the delay.
card.limits: The authors say a human in the loop can be a good thing, not that it is required: the choice is a gradient from fully automatic to fully manual.
card.example: A cluster adds three nodes. The system proposes a plan to move 120 partitions, and an administrator reviews it and commits it at night when traffic is low.

concepts.title: Three ways to route a request
concepts.question: What are the three ways to get a request to the node that owns its partition?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Partitions move as the cluster is rebalanced, so someone must know which IP address and port to use for a given key.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: There are three options. Clients may contact any node, for example through a round-robin load balancer, and that node forwards the request if it does not own the partition. Or all requests go first to a routing tier, a partition-aware load balancer that handles no requests itself. Or clients know the partitioning and connect directly.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each moves the knowledge somewhere else: into every node, into a routing tier, or into every client. In all cases the component that decides must learn of changes, and all must agree, or requests go to the wrong nodes.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You choose where the complexity belongs: the nodes, a separate tier, or the clients.

card.rule: Pick where routing knowledge lives: any node, a routing tier, or the client, and keep it in step with partition moves.
card.limits: All three need the same up-to-date assignment; none removes the problem of keeping the deciding component informed.
card.example: A cluster has three nodes. A client sends a read for key foo to a load balancer, which picks node 2. Node 2 does not own foo's partition, so it asks node 3 and returns the reply to the client.

media.alt: Three numbered panels showing a client getting key foo, stored on node 2. In 1, the client contacts node 0 at random, which holds partition knowledge and forwards to node 2. In 2, the client asks a routing tier that holds the knowledge and sends the request to node 2. In 3, the client holds the knowledge and connects directly to node 2. A hatched fill marks where that knowledge lives.

concepts.title: Keeping routers informed: coordination service or gossip
concepts.question: How do systems keep routing components in agreement about which node owns which partition?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Every routing component must agree on the partition assignment. Consensus protocols exist, but they are hard to implement correctly.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Many systems use a separate coordination service such as ZooKeeper. Each node registers itself there, and ZooKeeper keeps the authoritative mapping of partitions to nodes. A routing tier or partition-aware client subscribes and is notified when a partition changes owner or a node joins or leaves.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Cassandra and Riak use a gossip protocol among the nodes to spread changes in cluster state. A request can go to any node, which forwards it to the right one.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A coordination service adds a dependency but takes on the agreement work. Gossip avoids the dependency but puts more complexity in the database nodes.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You are choosing between an external dependency and heavier nodes.

card.rule: Keep the authoritative partition map in one coordination service, or let the nodes gossip changes to each other.
card.limits: Both rely on timely updates: a router with a stale picture still sends requests to the wrong node.
card.example: A node joins and registers with ZooKeeper. ZooKeeper tells the routing tier, which then sends requests for the partitions moved to the new node to its address.

media.alt: A client requests Danube through a routing tier to one of three nodes. A ZooKeeper box with hatched fill, linked by dashed lines to the routing tier and to each node, holds the table: twelve key ranges (A-ak to Bayes up to Trudeau to Zywiec), their partitions 0 to 11, node (0, 1, 2) and IP addresses 10.20.30.100 to .102.

concepts.title: Parallel execution of complex queries
concepts.question: How do parallel databases run complex analytic queries over partitions, unlike single-key lookups?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Most NoSQL distributed datastores support simple reads and writes of a single key, plus scatter/gather over a secondary index. A data warehouse query combines joins, filtering, grouping and aggregation.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Massively parallel processing (MPP) relational databases, often used for analytics, have an optimizer that breaks a complex query into execution stages and partitions. Many of these run in parallel on different nodes of the cluster.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: These engines support much more sophisticated queries, but fast parallel execution is a specialised topic. Queries that scan large parts of the dataset benefit most.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Analytic queries that scan large parts of a partitioned dataset.

card.rule: Analytic databases split a complex query into stages that run in parallel over partitions on different nodes.
card.limits: Single-key access does not need this machinery, and parallelising complex queries is harder than single-partition work.

concepts.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
concepts.title: What can go wrong, and what a transaction is
concepts.question: What is a transaction, and which kinds of trouble is it meant to remove?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Data systems fail in many ways at once: the database or hardware can fail mid-write, an application can crash halfway through a series of operations, and the network can cut the application off. Handling every such case by hand takes careful thought and heavy testing.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A transaction groups several reads and writes into one logical unit that is conceptually executed as a single operation. It either succeeds in full (commit) or fails (abort, rollback), and after a failure the application can safely retry.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The application gives up worrying about partial failure, where some operations succeed and some fail. In return the database has to supply the guarantees, and that is not free.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Several writes must stand or fall together and you would rather handle one simple outcome, abort, than many half-done states.

card.example: A ride-booking service marks a driver as assigned, marks the rider as matched and records a deposit. If the deposit write fails, the whole group is aborted and tried again.
card.rule: Group related operations in a transaction so that any failure means abort and retry, never a half-done state.
card.limits: Transactions reduce error cases but do not remove every one; an application with very simple access patterns may do without them.

media.alt: Black-and-white engraved map of an island with two peninsulas, labelled with isolation levels and anomalies as landmarks, and a ship at the bottom heading toward distributed transactions.

concepts.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
concepts.title: Why transactions exist and what they cost
concepts.question: Why were transactions created, and how do you decide whether an application needs them?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Developers who have used transactions for years may find them obvious, as if they were a law of nature. They are not: without them each application must handle every error scenario and every concurrency issue itself.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Transactions were created to simplify the programming model for applications that use a database. The database takes certain error scenarios and concurrency issues on itself, so the application may ignore them. The book calls these promises safety guarantees.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The promises have costs. To judge a bargain you first need to know exactly which guarantees you get and what they cost.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You are deciding whether a new application needs transactions: list the guarantees and costs first, then compare with the application's needs.

card.rule: Treat transactions as a purposeful bargain: simpler application code in return for guarantees the database must pay for.
card.limits: Having a database does not settle the question. Some applications need transactions little, and some safety can come from elsewhere.

concepts.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
concepts.title: Transactions versus scalability: two overstatements
concepts.question: Must a large-scale system give up transactions, and are they essential for serious data?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In the late 2000s many NoSQL databases abandoned transactions or redefined the word to mean much weaker guarantees. A popular belief followed that transactions are the enemy of scalability and that large systems must drop them to stay fast and available.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The book rejects that belief and its mirror image, the vendor claim that serious applications with valuable data must have transactions. Both are called hyperbole. It treats transactions like any design choice, with advantages and limitations.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Avoiding slogans costs effort: you have to study what a given transaction mechanism guarantees before you can say whether the price is worth paying.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A vendor page or a team argument says transactions are always required or always unaffordable.

card.rule: Judge transactions by the concrete guarantees and costs of a mechanism, not by a slogan about scale or seriousness.
card.limits: The rejection of slogans does not make distribution free: the book defers distributed transactions to later chapters because they bring hard problems.

concepts.title: ACID as a label, not a guarantee
concepts.question: What can you infer from the claim that a database is ACID compliant?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: ACID (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability) was coined in 1983 to give precise terminology for fault tolerance. In practice one database's ACID does not equal another's, so the claim leaves it unclear which guarantees you really get.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat the letters as questions to ask of a specific system. The high-level idea is sound, but the details decide what you actually receive.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Asking per letter costs reading and testing time; trusting the label is cheap but ACID has become mostly a marketing term.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Systems that do not meet the ACID criteria are sometimes called BASE. That term is even vaguer; its only sensible reading is not ACID.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You are comparing products whose pages say ACID, or you meet BASE in a design discussion.

card.rule: Do not rely on the words ACID or BASE; ask what each property means in the specific system.
card.limits: The four letters are still a useful checklist. The book goes through each one to refine what a transaction should give.

concepts.title: Atomicity: all or nothing after a fault
concepts.question: What does atomicity promise in ACID, and which concern does it leave to isolation?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A client makes several writes and a fault hits after only some of them have been processed. Without a guarantee, nobody knows which writes took effect.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In ACID, atomicity means that when the writes are grouped in a transaction and it cannot be committed, the transaction aborts and the database discards or undoes every write made so far.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The database must be able to undo partial work; in return the application sees only two outcomes, all or nothing.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: One business operation changes several records that must stand or fall together.

card.rule: ACID atomicity means abort undoes every write of the transaction; it is about faults, not about concurrency.
card.limits: Atomicity says nothing about what other clients see while the transaction runs; that question belongs to isolation.

media.alt: Timeline with User 1 and Database. User 1 inserts an email row and gets ok. User 1 then sends an update of the mailbox unread counter, but the database shows an explosion mark and an error or timeout is returned to User 1, so the counter is not updated.

concepts.title: Why atomicity makes retry safe
concepts.question: Why does an abort make it safe to run the same operation again?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If an error strikes partway through several changes, it is hard to know which changes took effect. Trying again risks making the same change twice and so leaving duplicate or incorrect data.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: With atomicity, an aborted transaction changed nothing. The application can therefore be sure of the starting state and can retry safely.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The guarantee covers the database's own writes and needs undo machinery in the database.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Designing error handling for operations that write several records.

card.rule: An abort leaves no trace, so retrying is safe; atomicity turns partial failure into a retryable error.
card.limits: The guarantee covers the database's writes only; retries still need care in other respects.

concepts.title: Consistency: one word, four meanings
concepts.question: Which meaning of consistency does ACID use, and how does it differ from the others?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The word consistency carries at least four unrelated meanings in this book. Reading it without checking which one is meant lets a guarantee of one kind be mistaken for another.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Sort the senses: replica consistency, where copies agree under asynchronous replication (eventual consistency); consistent hashing, a partitioning term; consistency in the CAP theorem, a strong ordering property; and ACID consistency, the database being in a good state by the application's own definition.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Keeping four senses apart takes effort, but it stops you from applying a guarantee from one setting to another.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A document, vendor page or design review says consistent and you must decide which guarantee is meant.

card.rule: Name which of the four meanings is in play before reasoning with the word consistency.
card.limits: Context usually settles the meaning; ACID's C is about the application's idea of valid data, not about replicas agreeing.

concepts.title: ACID consistency belongs to the application
concepts.question: Why does the book say the C in ACID is a property of the application, not the database?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Some statements about your data must always hold, for example credits and debits across all accounts must balance. These statements are invariants.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: If a transaction starts from a valid state and its writes preserve validity, the invariants stay true. The application must define its transactions correctly; it relies on database atomicity and isolation to keep them whole.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The database can check only some kinds of invariants. If you write bad data that breaks the rest, it cannot stop you; in general it only stores what it is given.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Deciding where a business rule is enforced: in declared constraints where the database supports them, in correct transaction logic otherwise.

card.rule: Atomicity, isolation and durability are database properties; consistency in ACID is the application's job.
card.limits: The book concludes the C does not really belong in ACID, but declared constraints still let the database help.

concepts.title: Isolation and the race condition it prevents
concepts.question: What goes wrong when two clients touch the same record at once, and what does isolation promise?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Most databases serve several clients at once. If they use different parts of the data there is no trouble, but if they use the same records, race conditions can occur. Two clients each read a counter at 42, add 1 and write back: the counter should reach 44 but ends at 43.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Isolation in ACID means concurrently executing transactions are isolated from each other and cannot step on each other's toes.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Stronger isolation limits concurrency; how much is given up is the subject of the rest of the chapter.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Judging whether concurrent clients can corrupt shared data: check whether their read-then-write steps can interleave.

card.rule: Isolation exists to stop concurrent transactions from interfering; the lost counter increment shows what happens without it.
card.limits: Isolation protects transactions from one another; it does not make a single transaction's logic correct.

media.alt: Timeline with User 1, Database and User 2. Each user gets the counter, receives 42, computes 42 + 1 = 43, then sets counter = 43 and gets ok. The two get-and-set round trips overlap in time, so both read 42 before either writes.

concepts.title: Serializability, the textbook meaning of isolation
concepts.question: What does serializable isolation promise, and why do many databases not provide it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Isolation needs a precise definition so you can reason about concurrent transactions.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Textbooks define isolation as serializability: each transaction can pretend it is the only transaction on the whole database. After they commit, the result equals that of running them serially, one after another, even though they may really have overlapped.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Serializable isolation carries a performance penalty, so it is rarely used in practice.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Checking what a level named serializable really gives you: compare its behaviour with this definition.

card.rule: Serializable means the committed outcome equals some one-at-a-time order; weaker levels give up that promise for speed.
card.limits: Serializability is a promise about outcomes, not a rule that transactions must actually run one at a time.

concepts.title: Durability: committed data is not forgotten
concepts.question: What does durability promise, and what must a database do before it reports a commit?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A database is meant to be a safe place for data. Users need to know that once a transaction reports success, its data will not vanish if the hardware fails or the database crashes.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Durability is the promise that data written by a successfully committed transaction will not be forgotten. On one node this means the data reached nonvolatile storage such as a disk or SSD. In a replicated database it means the data was copied to some number of nodes.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: To give the promise, the database must wait until those writes or copies are complete before it reports the commit, so commits take longer.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Deciding when a commit may be acknowledged to the client.

card.rule: Do not report a commit until the data is safely stored on disk, on replicas, or both.
card.limits: Durability reduces risk; it does not make loss impossible.

concepts.title: Durability: disk versus replication
concepts.question: What does each way of making data durable still fail to protect against?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Durability has meant different things over time: once writing to an archive tape, then to a disk or SSD, and more recently replication. None of them is perfect.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Compare the weaknesses. A disk write survives a machine death, but the data is inaccessible until the machine is fixed or the disk moved. Replicas can stay available, but a correlated fault can hit them all at once.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each approach buys protection against one failure at the cost of exposure to another.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: In an asynchronously replicated system recent writes may be lost when the leader becomes unavailable. A power outage or a bug triggered by one input can crash every node together, losing anything held only in memory.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing where a commit must be stored before it is acknowledged.

card.rule: Judge each durability method by the failure it leaves open, then combine methods.
card.limits: Our reading: the lists of weaknesses are not a ranking; which gap matters depends on the faults you expect.

concepts.title: Why even disks cannot be trusted completely
concepts.question: What evidence does the chapter give that writing to disk does not guarantee durability?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: It is tempting to treat a completed disk write as the end of the story. The chapter lists many ways data can still be lost or corrupted.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Read the list as an argument: SSDs have been shown to violate their guarantees when power is cut suddenly, and even fsync is not guaranteed to work. Disk firmware can have bugs. Subtle storage-engine and filesystem interactions can corrupt files after a crash. Data can slowly corrupt without detection.

blocks.label: Numbers
blocks.text: One study found that between 30% and 80% of SSDs develop at least one bad block in four years. Magnetic drives have fewer bad sectors but fail completely more often. An SSD unpowered for a few weeks can start losing data.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: More copies and checks cost money and effort; the evidence shows why they are still needed.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Someone argues that a durable commit to a local disk is enough.

card.rule: Treat a disk write as strong evidence of durability, not a guarantee, because hardware and software below it can also fail.
card.limits: These faults are reasons to layer protections, not reasons to avoid disks.

concepts.title: Layering risk reduction instead of trusting guarantees
concepts.question: What should a team do, given that no technique provides absolute durability?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Every durability technique has gaps, so no single one gives an absolute guarantee. Perfect durability does not exist.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Combine risk-reduction techniques: write to disk, replicate to remote machines, and keep backups. They can and should be used together.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Layers cost money, effort and latency. Their value is that the gap of one technique is usually covered by another.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Designing a storage strategy, or when a vendor or paper states a theoretical guarantee.

card.rule: Combine disk writes, replication and backups, and read any promised guarantee with a grain of salt.
card.limits: Layering reduces risk but does not remove it, and each extra layer costs effort.

concepts.title: Atomicity and isolation side by side
concepts.question: Which problem does atomicity solve for multi-write transactions, and which does isolation solve?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: When one transaction makes several writes, two separate things can go wrong: a fault can strike partway through, or another client can look at or touch the data while the transaction is half done.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Atomicity handles the fault: if an error occurs halfway, the writes made so far are discarded, giving an all-or-nothing guarantee. Isolation handles the other client: it should see either all of a transaction's writes or none, not some subset.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Both guarantees assume you change several pieces of data at once, which is what makes a transaction multi-object. The more objects involved, the more they matter and the more they cost to provide.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Classifying a bug: was the data left half-done by a fault, or was a half-done state seen or overwritten by someone else?

card.rule: Atomicity answers partial failure; isolation answers partial visibility and interference.
card.limits: Single-object writes need both guarantees as well, in a simpler form.

concepts.title: The denormalized counter and the need for transactions
concepts.question: How do both atomicity and isolation protect an unread-message counter that is stored separately?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: An email app can count unread messages with a query, but that may be slow on big mailboxes, so it stores a separate unread counter. Every new message must now add a row and increase the counter.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Without isolation, another user can see the new message while the counter still reads zero because the increment has not yet happened. Without atomicity, if the counter update fails, the inserted message stays and the two disagree. A transaction avoids both: readers see both changes or neither, and a failure rolls the message back.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Storing the count speeds reads but creates a second copy of the truth that must be kept in sync.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Any derived or duplicated value is stored beside its source, such as counters, totals and balances.

card.rule: When a value is stored beside its source, change both in one transaction so neither readers nor failures can split them.
card.limits: The example is a mild failure; the same pattern with money is serious.

media.alt: Timeline with User 1, Database and User 2. User 1 inserts an email for recipient 2 and gets ok. User 2 then selects the email (returns Hello, true) and next selects the unread count, which returns 0. Only afterwards does User 1 send the update that adds 1 to the unread counter, and it gets ok.

concepts.title: How operations are grouped into a transaction
concepts.question: How does a relational database know which reads and writes belong to one transaction?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A multi-object transaction needs a way to tell which operations belong together.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Relational databases usually use the client's connection to the server. On a given connection, everything between a BEGIN TRANSACTION statement and a COMMIT statement belongs to the same transaction.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Binding a transaction to a connection is simple but not ideal. If the connection is interrupted, the transaction must be aborted.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Reasoning about where a transaction starts and ends in application code and what happens if a connection drops.

card.rule: In SQL databases a transaction is the set of operations between BEGIN and COMMIT on one connection.
card.limits: Not all datastores group operations this way; some offer no grouping at all.

concepts.title: A multi-key operation is not a transaction
concepts.question: Why does a database with a multi-put operation not automatically offer transaction guarantees?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Many nonrelational databases have no way of grouping operations into a transaction. Some do provide a multi-object API, such as a multi-put that updates several keys in one command.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Do not read a multi-key command as a transaction by default. The command may succeed for some keys and fail for others, leaving the database partially updated.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The multi-key command saves network round trips but gives no all-or-nothing outcome.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Reviewing a key-value store's API: ask what happens to the other keys when one write fails.

card.rule: A command touching several objects is a transaction only if failure undoes all of it.
card.limits: Some stores may well make a particular multi-key command all-or-nothing; the point is that you must check.

concepts.title: Atomicity and isolation for one object
concepts.question: Why do storage engines guarantee atomicity and isolation for a single object, and how?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Imagine writing a 20 KB JSON document. If the network drops after 10 KB, the database could keep an unparseable fragment. A crash during an overwrite could leave old and new values spliced. A reader could see a partly updated value.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Storage engines almost universally aim to provide atomicity and isolation for one object, such as a key-value pair, on one node. The document is then stored whole or not at all, and readers never see it half written.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: These protections are cheap but cover only one object on one node.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need to know what is safe in a store that does not offer multi-object transactions.

card.rule: Single-object writes are atomic and isolated by storage-engine design, but only per object on one node.
card.limits: The protection stops at the object boundary and the single node; it does not cover related objects.

concepts.title: Increment and compare-and-set are not transactions
concepts.question: Why does the book object to calling single-object operations lightweight transactions?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Some databases offer richer single-object operations, such as an increment or a compare-and-set that writes only if the value has not changed. Some vendors call these lightweight transactions or even ACID.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use them for what they do well: they can prevent lost updates when several clients write one object. But do not call them transactions in the usual sense, which means grouping several operations on several objects into one unit of execution.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: They are cheap and easy, but they cover one object and offer no all-or-nothing outcome across objects.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A vendor describes a single-object operation as a transaction or as ACID.

card.rule: A transaction groups multiple operations on multiple objects; single-object operations, however useful, are not that.
card.limits: Calling them transactions is a marketing choice; the operations themselves remain valuable.

concepts.title: Where multi-object transactions are needed
concepts.question: In which common situations must writes to several objects be coordinated?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Could an application run on only a key-value model with single-object operations? Sometimes, but often writes to several objects have to be coordinated.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Look for three patterns. First, references: a row with a foreign key, or a graph vertex with edges, must point at things that exist. Second, denormalization: a document store without joins pushes you to copy data, and all copies must change together. Third, secondary indexes: each index is a separate object that must change with the record.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Without transactions you can still build such applications, but error handling becomes much more complicated and missing isolation causes concurrency problems.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Auditing a design for places where several objects must move together.

card.rule: Whenever references, copies or indexes have to stay in step, you are coordinating multiple objects.
card.limits: A document model keeps fields that change together in one document, which counts as a single object and needs no multi-object transaction.

concepts.title: Why distributed stores dropped transactions
concepts.question: Why did many distributed datastores abandon multi-object transactions, and what does the book say about that?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Many distributed datastores gave up multi-object transactions. Their reasons: transactions are hard to implement across partitions, and they can get in the way where very high availability or performance is required.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Read the reasons as costs, not as impossibility. The book says nothing fundamentally prevents transactions in a distributed database, and it plans to discuss implementations in later chapters.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Without them, an application can still be built, but error handling becomes more complicated and lack of isolation causes concurrency problems.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Evaluating a distributed store whose docs say transactions cannot scale.

card.rule: Distributed transactions are hard and costly, not impossible; dropping them shifts work to the application.
card.limits: Costs are real: the book reserves distributed transactions for later chapters because they raise difficult challenges.

concepts.title: Abort and retry as a design philosophy
concepts.question: How does the ACID philosophy about errors differ from best-effort datastores?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Errors will happen, but many developers prefer to think only about the happy path.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: ACID databases follow a philosophy: if they are in danger of violating atomicity, isolation or durability, they abandon the transaction entirely rather than leave it half done. The application is meant to retry. Leaderless-replication stores work on best effort: they do as much as they can and do not undo what has been done when they hit an error.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Abort and retry gives clean semantics but needs retry logic; best effort gives flexibility but pushes recovery onto the application.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Popular ORM frameworks such as Rails ActiveRecord and Django do not retry aborted transactions. The exception bubbles up, user input is thrown away and the user sees an error.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Designing error handling around a database.

card.rule: A transaction can be aborted and safely retried; use that, rather than letting errors discard the user's work.
card.limits: Retrying is not free of problems; the next ideas list the cases where it misleads.

concepts.title: When a retry repeats work that already succeeded
concepts.question: How can retrying a transaction cause duplicate work, and how is that guarded against?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A transaction may actually commit while the network fails as the server tries to confirm. The client thinks it failed and retries, so the work is done twice.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Add an application-level deduplication mechanism, so that a repeated request with the same identity is recognised and not executed again.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Deduplication needs extra bookkeeping in the application; without it the retry is unsafe.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: If the client process itself fails while retrying, any data it was trying to write to the database is lost.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A retry is triggered by a timeout or lost reply rather than by a clear abort.

card.rule: A retry after an unclear failure needs deduplication, or it may run twice.
card.limits: A clear abort reported by the database is safe to retry; the ambiguity comes from lost replies.

concepts.title: Which errors to retry and how often
concepts.question: When is retrying a failed transaction useful, and when does it make things worse?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A retry loop can help or hurt. If the failure was caused by overload, retrying adds more load and makes things worse. If the failure was permanent, retrying cannot succeed.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Retry only after transient errors, such as deadlock, isolation violation, temporary network interruption or failover. Do not retry permanent errors such as a constraint violation. To avoid feedback cycles under overload, limit the number of retries, use exponential backoff and handle overload errors differently.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Selective retry needs the application to classify errors, but it avoids wasted work and feedback loops.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Writing the retry logic around a transaction.

card.rule: Retry transient errors with limits and backoff; do not retry permanent errors or blindly retry overload.
card.limits: Classification may be imperfect; an unfamiliar error should be treated cautiously.

concepts.title: Side effects outside the database
concepts.question: Why can a retried transaction repeat effects that the database cannot undo?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A transaction may also cause effects outside the database, such as sending an email. Those effects may happen even if the transaction is aborted.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Do not rely on the database to undo what happens elsewhere. Treat each outside effect as its own problem: decide whether it can be repeated safely, deduplicated, or delayed until the transaction has committed.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Handling outside effects separately adds design work compared with a purely local transaction.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A transaction triggers emails, messages or calls to other services.

card.rule: Database rollback does not undo effects in other systems; plan for them separately.
card.limits: Not every outside effect needs care; a rare duplicate notification may be acceptable.

concepts.title: Why concurrency bugs are so hard to find
concepts.question: Why can testing not be relied on to expose concurrency bugs?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Two transactions that touch different data can run side by side safely. Trouble starts only when one reads data another is changing, or both change the same data. Such bugs appear only when the timing is unlucky, so they are rare and hard to reproduce.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Do not rely on testing alone. Reason about what the database guarantees, because the guarantee, not luck, is what protects you. Databases try to hide concurrency from developers through transaction isolation.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Reasoning about every possible timing is hard work, especially in a large application, but it is the only way to be sure.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A bug appears once a month and nobody can make it happen on demand.

card.rule: Timing bugs hide from tests, so rely on the database's isolation guarantee rather than on hoping the tests passed.
card.limits: Passing tests are still worth having; they just cannot prove the absence of a race.

concepts.title: Why weak isolation is common and costly
concepts.question: Why do most databases offer weak isolation levels, and what has that cost real users?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In theory isolation lets you pretend there is no concurrency. But serializable isolation has a performance cost, and many databases do not want to pay it.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Weaker isolation levels are common. They protect against some concurrency problems but not all, are harder to understand, and can lead to subtle bugs.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You gain speed and give up protection against some race conditions.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: These bugs have caused substantial financial loss, investigation by auditors and corrupted customer data. The advice to use an ACID database for money misses the point, because many popular ACID databases use weak isolation too.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Someone tells you that picking a relational database is enough to be safe with money.

card.rule: Most databases ship weak isolation by default, so a database being ACID does not protect you from race conditions.
card.limits: Weak levels are not wrong; they are adequate when you know which anomalies you can tolerate.

concepts.title: Learn the anomalies, then pick the level
concepts.question: What should a developer learn so that the choice of isolation level is a decision rather than a guess?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Tool labels such as ACID or serializable do not tell you which race conditions you are exposed to.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Instead of relying blindly on tools, learn the kinds of concurrency problems that exist and how to prevent them. Then examine each weak isolation level for what race conditions it allows and does not allow, and choose the level your application needs.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: This takes study, and the book's treatment is informal, built on examples; rigorous definitions are in the research literature.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing an isolation level or reviewing code written against one.

card.rule: Know the anomalies each level allows; choose the level from the anomalies, not from its name.
card.limits: An informal, example-based understanding is enough to start but not to prove correctness.

concepts.title: Read committed: two promises
concepts.question: What are the two guarantees of read committed, and what do they stop?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Without any isolation, one transaction can see or overwrite another's unfinished work, which makes results unpredictable.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Read committed, the most basic level of isolation, makes two guarantees. When reading, you see only committed data (no dirty reads). When writing, you overwrite only committed data (no dirty writes).

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It is cheap and widely used, but it leaves other race conditions open.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need a baseline that stops transactions from reading or overwriting each other's uncommitted data.

card.rule: Read committed: read only committed data, and overwrite only committed data.
card.limits: It is a floor, not a ceiling; later ideas show race conditions it does not stop.

concepts.title: Dirty reads and why they must be prevented
concepts.question: What is a dirty read, and why is it harmful?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A transaction has written data but has not yet committed or aborted. If another transaction can read that data, it is a dirty read.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Read committed prevents dirty reads: a transaction's writes become visible to others only when it commits, and then all at once.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Readers may have to be given an older value while a write is in progress.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: If dirty reads were allowed, a reader could see some of a transaction's updates but not others. If the transaction aborted, the reader would have seen data that was never actually committed.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Judging the risk of a level that allows reading uncommitted data.

card.rule: Prevent dirty reads so that others never see partial or rolled-back work.
card.limits: Preventing dirty reads does not make successive reads agree; that is a separate problem.

media.alt: Timeline with User 1, Database and User 2. User 1 sets x = 3, then y = 3, each acknowledged ok, then commits. User 2 runs get x three times: the first two, made before the commit, return 2, and the third, made after the commit, returns 3.

concepts.title: Dirty writes and the car sale
concepts.question: What is a dirty write, and what harm does it do to multi-object updates?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Two transactions update the same object. If the earlier write belongs to a transaction that has not yet committed, and the later write overwrites it, that is a dirty write.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Read committed prevents dirty writes, usually by delaying the second write until the first transaction has committed or aborted.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The second writer waits.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Two people, Alice and Bob, try to buy the same used car. Buying needs two writes: the listing is updated to show the buyer and an invoice is sent to the buyer. With dirty writes the listing may go to Bob while the invoice goes to Alice.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A business action writes several objects and two clients may race on the same ones.

card.rule: No dirty writes: a later writer must wait until the earlier transaction commits or aborts.
card.limits: Preventing dirty writes does not protect against all conflicting writes, such as lost updates.

media.alt: Timeline with Alice, Listings, Invoices and Bob. Alice sets the listing buyer to Alice, then the invoice recipient to Alice. Bob updates the listing buyer to Bob between her two writes, then sets the invoice recipient to Bob. Annotations say the listing ends with buyer Bob and the invoice with recipient Alice.

concepts.title: What read committed does not stop
concepts.question: Which familiar race condition survives read committed, and why?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: It is easy to assume that a level preventing dirty reads and dirty writes prevents all write races.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Check the counter example. Two clients read 42, add one, and write 43. The second write comes after the first transaction has committed, so it is not a dirty write. The result is still wrong, but for a different reason.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Read committed is cheap because it does not track such conflicts.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Deciding whether read committed is enough for read-modify-write code.

card.rule: Read committed stops dirty reads and dirty writes but not lost updates from read-modify-write cycles.
card.limits: A different mechanism is needed for the lost update; later ideas supply it.

concepts.title: Row-level locks against dirty writes
concepts.question: How do databases usually prevent dirty writes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Two transactions may want to modify the same row at once, and the second must not overwrite the first's uncommitted value.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use row-level locks. A transaction that wants to modify an object (row or document) must first acquire a lock on it and must hold the lock until it commits or aborts. Only one transaction can hold the lock; another that wants to write waits.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Writers on the same object wait, but the locking is automatic in read committed mode or stronger.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Explaining how writers are kept apart.

card.rule: Take a row-level lock on first write and hold it until commit or abort.
card.limits: Locks stop write-write overlap only; they say nothing about readers.

concepts.title: How dirty reads are prevented without blocking readers
concepts.question: Why do most databases avoid read locks, and what do they do instead?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: To prevent dirty reads one could make readers briefly take the object's lock, so no read happens while an uncommitted value is there. But one long-running write transaction would then force many read-only transactions to wait.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Most databases remember both the old committed value and the new value set by the transaction holding the write lock. While that transaction is ongoing, readers are given the old value. When it commits, readers switch to the new one.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Keeping two versions costs storage, but readers never wait.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: With read locks, a slowdown in one part of an application can have a knock-on effect on a completely different part, which is bad for operability.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Weighing locking against versioning for reads.

card.rule: Keep the old committed value for readers while a write is pending, instead of making readers wait.
card.limits: The version approach needs extra storage and bookkeeping.

concepts.title: Read uncommitted and which databases default to read committed
concepts.question: How does read uncommitted differ from read committed, and how common is read committed?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Isolation levels are named, but the names hide what each prevents.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Read uncommitted is an even weaker level than read committed: it prevents dirty writes but does not prevent dirty reads. Read committed is a very popular level and the default in Oracle 11g, PostgreSQL, SQL Server 2012, MemSQL and many other databases.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Defaults suit most workloads but leave several race conditions open.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Checking what your database does when you do not configure isolation.

card.rule: Read uncommitted stops only dirty writes; read committed stops dirty writes and dirty reads and is a common default.
card.limits: A default can differ across versions and products; check your own.

concepts.title: Read skew: a consistent total that adds up wrongly
concepts.question: How can a reader see only committed data and still observe an impossible state?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Alice has $1,000 split over two accounts of $500 each. A transfer moves $100 from one to the other. If she looks at her balances while it runs, she can read one account before the incoming payment ($500) and the other after the outgoing transfer ($400), and conclude she has $900.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Name the anomaly: a nonrepeatable read, also called read skew. If Alice read the first account again at the end she would see $600, a different value than before. Read committed allows it, because each balance she saw was committed when she read it.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Read committed is cheap and good enough where a short-lived oddity heals itself; it does not give a single point-in-time view.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A reader looks at several objects that a concurrent transaction is changing together.

card.rule: Read skew: committed values from different moments combine into a state that never existed.
card.limits: Alice would see consistent balances if she reloaded a few seconds later, so the harm is temporary for her case.

media.alt: Timeline with Alice, Account 1, Account 2 and a Transfer. Both balances start at 500. Alice reads account 1 and gets 500. The transfer then adds 100 to account 1 (now 600), subtracts 100 from account 2 (now 400) and commits. Alice reads account 2 and gets 400.

concepts.title: Backups and analytics that cannot tolerate skew
concepts.question: Which operations cannot tolerate read skew, and why?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A backup copies the whole database over hours while writes continue, so some parts come from older data and others from newer. Analytic queries and integrity checks scan large parts of the database and may see parts at different times.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat these as the cases where temporary inconsistency becomes harmful: a restore from a skewed backup makes the inconsistency permanent, and a scan over mismatched parts returns nonsensical results.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Preventing the problem requires a stronger isolation level than read committed.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Planning backups, reports or integrity checks on a database taking writes.

card.rule: Long reads over changing data need a consistent point-in-time view, or their results are unreliable.
card.limits: For short interactive views, brief skew is tolerable.

concepts.title: Snapshot isolation: a frozen, consistent view
concepts.question: What does a transaction see under snapshot isolation, and who benefits most?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Backups, analytics and integrity checks need a consistent view of the database even while writes continue.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Under snapshot isolation each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot: it sees all the data committed in the database at the moment the transaction started. Changes made later by other transactions are not visible, even if they commit during the transaction.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The view may be stale by the time the transaction ends.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Long-running read-only queries need a stable, easy-to-understand view.

card.rule: Snapshot isolation: each transaction sees the database as it was committed at its start, and nothing later.
card.limits: A snapshot stops read skew in reading, but writes based on a stale snapshot can still conflict.

concepts.title: Readers never block writers
concepts.question: Which operations take locks under snapshot isolation, and what performance benefit does that give?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Locks that make readers wait for writers harm response times and spread slowness.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Snapshot implementations typically use write locks to prevent dirty writes, so a writer can block another writer to the same object. Reads need no locks. The principle is that readers never block writers, and writers never block readers.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Writers still wait for writers on the same object.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Mixing long-running read queries with normal writes on the same data.

card.rule: Under snapshot isolation only writes lock; reads take no locks, so long reads and writes run together.
card.limits: Write-write conflicts on the same object still block.

concepts.title: Multi-version concurrency control
concepts.question: How can a database give different transactions different views of the same object at the same time?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Several transactions may be running at once, each started at a different moment. Each needs the database as it was when it began, while writers keep changing the data.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Keep several committed versions of each object side by side. Each transaction is shown the version that was current at its snapshot. This technique is called multi-version concurrency control, or MVCC.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Old versions take space and must be cleaned up later, but readers need no locks.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Long-running reads must proceed alongside normal writes.

card.rule: MVCC keeps several committed versions of each object so that every transaction can read its own snapshot.
card.limits: Extra versions are only worth keeping while some running transaction may still need them.

concepts.title: How versions are tagged: transaction IDs
concepts.question: How does an MVCC database record which transaction created or deleted each row version?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: To pick the right version for a reader, the database must know which transaction wrote each version and when.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In the PostgreSQL-style design each transaction gets a unique, always-increasing transaction ID at the start. Each row has a created_by field holding the ID of the inserting transaction and a deleted_by field, empty at first. Deleting a row only sets deleted_by. An update is a delete plus a create, so changing a balance from $500 to $400 leaves two rows.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Nothing is updated in place, so snapshots are cheap, but dead rows pile up until cleaned.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Reading how an MVCC table looks after updates and deletes.

card.rule: Each row version carries created_by and deleted_by transaction IDs; an update is a delete plus a create.
card.limits: Dead versions use space until garbage collection can prove no transaction needs them.

media.alt: Transaction 12 reads two accounts while transaction 13 transfers 100 between them. Account 1 rows show created by 3 with balance 500, then a row deleted by 13 and a new row created by 13 with 600. Account 2 shows 500 deleted by 13 and a new 400 row created by 13. Transaction 12 reads 500 from both accounts.

concepts.title: Which versions a transaction can see
concepts.question: How do transaction IDs decide which row versions a reader sees?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A reader holding a snapshot must see exactly the writes committed when it started and nothing else, even though newer versions sit beside the old ones.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: At the start of each transaction the database lists all other transactions in progress. Then: ignore writes by those transactions even if they later commit; ignore writes by aborted transactions; ignore writes by transactions with a later ID; show all other writes. The rules apply to creation and to deletion.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Every read needs these checks, which is cheap compared with locking.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Predicting what a given transaction sees in an MVCC database.

card.rule: A version is visible if its creator had committed when the reader started and its deleter, if any, had not.
card.limits: The rules show a snapshot; they do not detect conflicts between writes.

concepts.title: Indexes in a multi-version database
concepts.question: How can an index work when each object has several versions?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: An index points to rows, but with MVCC a row can have many versions, and not all are visible to every reader.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: One option is to let the index point to all versions and filter out the ones the reader cannot see; when garbage collection removes old versions the entries go too. Another, used by CouchDB, Datomic and LMDB, is an append-only, copy-on-write B-tree that never overwrites pages but copies each changed page and its parents up to the root.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Filtering costs work per query. The copy-on-write tree gives each write a new root that is itself a consistent snapshot, but needs background compaction and garbage collection.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing a storage engine for snapshot reads.

card.rule: Either filter versions at the index, or make every write a new immutable tree root.
card.limits: Implementation details such as same-page version placement strongly affect real performance.

concepts.title: Snapshot isolation under many names
concepts.question: Why does one isolation guarantee carry different names, and what does repeatable read really mean?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Snapshot isolation is useful, but databases call it by different names. In Oracle it is called serializable, and in PostgreSQL and MySQL it is called repeatable read.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The SQL standard has no concept of snapshot isolation, because it follows System R's 1975 definitions and snapshot isolation had not been invented. It defines repeatable read, which looks similar. PostgreSQL and MySQL use that name for their snapshot level so they can claim compliance.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Standard names are easy to claim, but the standard's definitions are ambiguous and imprecise.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You compare isolation levels across products by name.

card.rule: Do not compare isolation levels by name alone: one behaviour has several names and one name has several behaviours.
card.limits: Inside one product a name is stable; the confusion arises when moving across products.

concepts.title: The lost update
concepts.question: What is a lost update, and which kind of code is exposed to it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Read committed and snapshot isolation mostly concern what a read-only transaction sees. Two transactions can also write concurrently, and dirty writes are only one kind of write-write conflict.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Look for the read-modify-write cycle: the application reads a value, computes a new one from it, and writes it back. If two transactions do this at the same time, the second write does not include the first change, so one modification is lost. The later write is said to clobber the earlier one.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Neither read committed nor snapshot isolation is designed to stop this, so protection needs extra mechanisms.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Reviewing code that reads a value and writes back a result derived from it.

card.rule: Whenever code reads a value, changes it and writes it back, concurrent copies of that code can lose updates.
card.limits: Code that writes values not derived from a prior read, such as setting a status flag, does not lose updates in this way.

concepts.title: Recognising read-modify-write in disguise
concepts.question: In which everyday forms does a read-modify-write cycle hide?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The pattern is not limited to counters, so it is easy to write without noticing it.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Watch for three forms. The first is incrementing a counter or updating an account balance, which needs the current value, a calculation and a write-back. The second is making a local change to a complex value, such as adding an element to a list inside a JSON document, which needs parsing, change and rewrite. The third is two users editing a wiki page, each saving the full contents.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Spotting these requires reading code for any write that depends on a prior read.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Auditing code for places where concurrency could lose changes.

card.rule: If a write depends on a value read earlier, treat it as a read-modify-write cycle.
card.limits: Not every update is of this kind; a write that stands on its own does not need protection.

concepts.title: Atomic write operations
concepts.question: How can a database apply a change without the application doing a read-modify-write?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Read-modify-write cycles in application code can lose updates.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use the database's atomic update operations, which remove the need for the cycle. A relational example is UPDATE counters SET value = value + 1 WHERE key = 'foo', which is safe under concurrency. Document databases such as MongoDB offer atomic changes to part of a JSON document, and Redis offers them for structures such as priority queues.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Not every update can be expressed this way; editing arbitrary text, for example, cannot.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The change can be expressed in the operations the database offers.

card.rule: Prefer an atomic update operation to a read-modify-write cycle whenever the change can be expressed with one.
card.limits: Where the logic is arbitrary, such as editing wiki text, atomic operations do not apply and other methods are needed.

concepts.title: How atomic operations work, and how ORMs undo them
concepts.question: How are atomic operations implemented, and why can they still be bypassed by accident?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: An atomic operation must not allow another transaction to interfere between its read and its write.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: One method is to take an exclusive lock on the object when it is read, so that no other transaction can read it until the update has been applied; this is sometimes called cursor stability. Another is to run all atomic operations on a single thread.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The lock makes other transactions wait for a short time.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Object-relational mapping frameworks make it easy to write an unsafe read-modify-write cycle in application code instead of using the database's atomic operation. This is easy to miss and hard to find by testing.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Code uses an ORM that hides the SQL it sends.

card.rule: Check what SQL your ORM sends; make sure increments use the database's atomic operation.
card.limits: A developer who knows what the framework generates has no problem; the risk is not knowing.

concepts.title: Explicit locking with SELECT FOR UPDATE
concepts.question: How can an application prevent lost updates when no single atomic operation fits its logic?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Sometimes the update logic cannot be expressed as one database operation. In a multiplayer game, for example, a move must obey the rules of the game, and that logic cannot sensibly be written as a database query.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Lock the objects explicitly. Inside a transaction, select the rows with FOR UPDATE, which takes a lock on every row returned. Then check the move is valid and update. Any other transaction that wants to read the same rows for update must wait until this cycle completes.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It works, but you must think carefully about the application logic. It is easy to forget a necessary lock somewhere in the code and so introduce a race condition.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Atomic operations are not enough and automatic detection is not available.

card.rule: Lock the rows you will update with FOR UPDATE before the read-modify-write, and hold the lock until the transaction ends.
card.limits: Every code path touching the data must take the lock; one that forgets reintroduces the race.

concepts.title: Detecting lost updates automatically
concepts.question: Which databases detect lost updates for you, and why is that safer than locks?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Locks and atomic operations rely on developers remembering to use them.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Let the read-modify-write cycles run in parallel. If the transaction manager detects a lost update, it aborts the offending transaction and it retries its cycle. The check works efficiently together with snapshot isolation. PostgreSQL's repeatable read, Oracle's serializable and SQL Server's snapshot isolation detect lost updates; MySQL with InnoDB, at repeatable read, does not.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Aborted transactions must be retried, but there is no way to forget the protection because it happens automatically.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Your database detects lost updates and you want protection without special code.

card.rule: Prefer a level that detects lost updates automatically; it removes the risk of forgetting a lock or an atomic operation.
card.limits: Not every database with snapshot-like isolation detects lost updates, so check yours.

concepts.title: Compare-and-set without transactions
concepts.question: How can a store without transactions avoid lost updates?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Databases without transactions still face lost updates from read-modify-write.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use compare-and-set: allow an update only if the value has not changed since you last read it. If the current value does not match what was read, the update has no effect and the cycle must be retried. For a wiki, UPDATE wiki_pages SET content = 'new' WHERE id = 1234 AND content = 'old' changes the page only if nobody changed it first.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The application must check whether the update took effect and retry if it did not.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need protection but the database offers neither transactions nor atomic operations that fit.
