card.rule: Make the write conditional on the old value, check that it took effect, and retry if it did not.
card.limits: It is only as safe as the database's handling of the condition; see the next idea.

concepts.title: When compare-and-set is not safe
concepts.question: Why might a compare-and-set condition pass even though another write is happening?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A WHERE clause that tests the old value looks like a safe check.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Look at where the condition reads from. If the database lets the WHERE clause read from an old snapshot, the condition may be true even though another concurrent write has already changed the value. The statement then may not prevent lost updates.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Relying on compare-and-set is cheap but ties correctness to the database's implementation.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Using conditional updates in a database that has snapshot isolation.

card.rule: Check that your database's compare-and-set condition reads current data, not an old snapshot, before relying on it.
card.limits: On databases where the WHERE clause sees the latest committed data, it is safe.

concepts.title: Lost updates across replicas
concepts.question: Why do locks and compare-and-set not work in multi-leader or leaderless replication, and what does?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With copies of data on several nodes that may be written concurrently, there is no single up-to-date copy. Locks and compare-and-set assume there is one.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Allow concurrent writes to create conflicting versions, called siblings, and resolve and merge them afterwards in application code or with special data structures. Atomic operations work well if they are commutative, such as incrementing a counter or adding an element to a set, because replicas can apply them in any order. Riak 2.0 datatypes merge concurrent updates so none are lost.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Conflict resolution moves complexity to the application or the data structure.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Last write wins (LWW) conflict resolution is prone to lost updates, and it is the default in many replicated databases.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing a store with multi-leader or leaderless replication.

card.rule: In replicated stores with concurrent writers, use commutative operations or merge siblings; do not rely on last write wins.
card.limits: Locks and compare-and-set still work in single-leader setups that have one up-to-date copy.

concepts.title: Write skew: the on-call doctors
concepts.question: How can two transactions that each look safe together break a rule about several records?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A hospital app must always keep at least one doctor on call per shift. Doctors may give up a shift provided a colleague remains on call. Alice and Bob are the two doctors on call, both feel unwell, and both click the button to go off call at about the same moment.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Under snapshot isolation each transaction first checks that two or more doctors are on call. Both checks return 2, so both proceed. Alice updates her own record and Bob updates his. Both transactions commit, and now no doctor is on call.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Snapshot isolation is cheap and gives consistent reads, but it does not notice that the two transactions together broke the rule.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A rule depends on several records, and different transactions might each change a different one.

card.rule: Write skew: each transaction is valid alone, but together, on stale snapshots, they break a rule over several records.
card.limits: Run one after the other, the second transaction would have found one doctor and refused; the harm arises only from overlap.

media.alt: Two columns of pseudo-code for Alice and Bob. Each begins a transaction, counts doctors with on_call true for shift 1234 (result 2), and if the count is at least 2 sets their own on_call to false, then commits. The doctors table starts with Alice and Bob true, Carol false, and ends with all three false.

concepts.title: What write skew is, and what it generalises
concepts.question: How does write skew relate to dirty writes and lost updates?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The anomaly in the on-call example is neither a dirty write nor a lost update, so it is less obvious that any conflict occurred.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Define write skew: two transactions read the same objects and then update some of those objects, with different transactions possibly updating different objects. It is a race condition, because serial execution would have prevented it. You can think of it as a generalisation of the lost update.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Because it hides in different objects, it is harder to see and to prevent than the simpler anomalies.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Classifying a concurrency bug by what the two transactions read and wrote.

card.rule: Write skew: same objects read, different objects written. If they wrote the same object, it is a dirty write or lost update.
card.limits: If the transactions never read what the other writes, there is no write skew.

concepts.title: Why the usual defences fail against write skew
concepts.question: Which protections that work against lost updates do not stop write skew?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Lost updates have several defences. It is tempting to assume they cover write skew too.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Check each. Atomic single-object operations do not help because several objects are involved. The automatic detection of lost updates found in some snapshot isolation implementations does not help either: write skew is not detected by PostgreSQL's repeatable read, MySQL InnoDB's repeatable read, Oracle's serializable or SQL Server's snapshot isolation.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Preventing it automatically needs true serializable isolation, which has a performance cost.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Reviewing a design that relies on those defences for a multi-record rule.

card.rule: Automatic protection against write skew needs serializable isolation; atomic operations and lost update detection do not cover it.
card.limits: If the rule can be expressed as a constraint, or a lock can be placed, weaker defences may work.

concepts.title: Constraints and explicit locks against write skew
concepts.question: What can protect a multi-record rule when serializable isolation is not available?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A rule such as at least one doctor on call involves several records.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Two options. First, a constraint the database enforces: most databases lack built-in support for constraints spanning several objects, but you may implement one with triggers or materialized views, depending on the database. Second, if you cannot use serializable isolation, the second-best option is probably to lock explicitly the rows the transaction depends on, with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the on-call doctors before updating.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Constraints need database features that may be missing. Explicit locks need careful placement in all code paths.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Serializable isolation is not available and the rule involves rows that exist.

card.rule: Without serializable isolation, enforce multi-record rules through triggers or views, or lock the rows the decision depends on.
card.limits: Locking helps only if the rows the decision depends on exist; it fails when the decision depends on absence.

concepts.title: Four more places write skew hides
concepts.question: Which everyday features have the same weakness as the on-call example?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Write skew can look esoteric, but once you know it you start to see it in many designs.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Four examples, each a check followed by a write. A room booking checks for overlapping bookings, then inserts. A game lock stops two moves of one figure but not two figures to one square. A site checks a username is free, then creates the account. A spending service checks the sum keeps the balance positive, then adds a spending item.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Recognising the pattern costs attention; ignoring it risks double bookings, duplicate names and negative balances.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Auditing booking, reservation, uniqueness and balance logic.

card.rule: Any check followed by a write based on its result can suffer write skew under snapshot isolation.
card.limits: Some of these can be fixed with a database constraint, such as uniqueness; others need serializable isolation.

concepts.title: When a uniqueness constraint settles the race
concepts.question: Which write skew cases can a database constraint solve, and which still need serializable isolation?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Several check-then-write designs are unsafe under snapshot isolation, but not all need heavy protection.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: For claiming a username, a unique constraint is a simple fix: the second transaction that tries to register the name is aborted for violating the constraint. In the game, a unique constraint on position may enforce the rule if it fits. A room booking, in contrast, again needs serializable isolation.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A constraint is cheap and automatic, but only for rules it can express: equal keys, not overlapping ranges or sums.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The rule is equality of a key rather than a range or a total.

card.rule: Use a unique constraint when the rule is that two rows may not share a key; use serializable isolation for ranges and totals.
card.limits: Whether a constraint suffices depends on the rule; overlapping times and spending totals are beyond a simple unique key.

concepts.title: The check-then-write pattern
concepts.question: What common pattern do all write skew examples follow?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The doctors, bookings, game, usernames and spending look different but share a structure.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Spot three steps. A SELECT checks whether a requirement holds by searching rows that match a condition. The application decides, from the result, whether to go on or abort. If it goes on, it writes with INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE and commits. The write changes the precondition of the decision: repeating the SELECT after the commit would give a different result.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The pattern is natural to code but fragile under concurrency.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: The order may vary: you can write first, then run the SELECT, and decide whether to abort or commit based on its result.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You review code for race conditions that involve a decision based on a query.

card.rule: Whenever a decision rests on a query and the decision's own write changes that query's result, suspect write skew.
card.limits: Checks whose result the write cannot change, such as reading a fixed setting, do not form this pattern.

concepts.title: Phantoms, and why locking rows cannot stop them
concepts.question: What is a phantom, and why can SELECT FOR UPDATE not protect against it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In four of the five examples the check looks for the absence of rows: no booking in this time slot, no figure on this square, no user with this name, no overspending. The write adds a row matching the same condition.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Name the effect: a write in one transaction changes the result of a search query in another transaction. This is a phantom. SELECT FOR UPDATE attaches locks to the rows a query returns; if the query returns no rows, there is nothing to lock.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Row-level locks are precise, but they cannot cover rows that do not exist yet.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A decision depends on nothing existing.

card.rule: A phantom is a row that appears in a search result because of a concurrent write; row locks cannot lock what is not there.
card.limits: In the doctors case the rows exist, so locking them does work; phantoms matter when the check is about absence.

concepts.title: Snapshot isolation, read-only queries and phantoms
concepts.question: Does snapshot isolation protect against phantoms, and where does it fail?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Snapshot isolation hides concurrent changes from a transaction. Does that mean phantoms are no problem?

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: For read-only queries it does: a snapshot sees a fixed set of rows. In read-write transactions, however, a phantom can lead to particularly tricky write skew, because the decision is based on a snapshot while a concurrent insert is already changing the truth.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Snapshot isolation is cheap and good for reads, but it gives no protection for decisions that must hold at commit time.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Judging whether a read-only report or a read-write decision is exposed.

card.rule: Snapshot isolation stops phantoms in read-only queries but not in decisions that write based on what they read.
card.limits: A transaction that only reads can safely rely on its snapshot.

concepts.title: Materializing conflicts as a last resort
concepts.question: How can you create something to lock when the problem is a row that does not exist yet?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A phantom has no object to which a lock can attach.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Introduce a lock object artificially. For room bookings, create a table with a row for every room and 15-minute slot for the next six months. A transaction first locks the rows for its room and time with SELECT FOR UPDATE, then checks for overlaps and inserts. The table holds no booking data; it only holds locks. This turns a phantom into a lock conflict and is called materializing conflicts.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It can be hard and error-prone to design, and it leaks a concurrency mechanism into the application data model.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Only as a last resort if no alternative is possible; serializable isolation is much preferable in most cases.

card.rule: Materialize conflicts only when nothing better exists: create rows to lock, and prefer serializable isolation.
card.limits: The approach works only if every code path locks the same prepared rows, and the rows must exist before they are needed.

concepts.title: The sad situation with weak isolation
concepts.question: Why are weak isolation levels hard to rely on in real applications?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Read committed and snapshot isolation stop some races but not others, so developers must know which ones remain.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Name the three complaints. Levels are hard to understand and inconsistently implemented: the meaning of repeatable read varies. From application code it is hard to tell whether a level is safe, especially in a large application. And there are no good tools to detect race conditions.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Weak levels give speed and simplicity inside the database, but push the reasoning burden onto the application developer.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Testing rarely exposes the bugs, because they are nondeterministic and appear only when the timing is unlucky.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Deciding whether a weak level is enough for a given piece of application code.

card.rule: A weak level is only as safe as your ability to prove which races your code can still meet.
card.limits: The complaints concern weak levels; they do not claim that every application suffers from every anomaly.

concepts.title: Serializable isolation
concepts.question: What does serializable isolation guarantee, and what does it spare you from reasoning about?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Weak levels leave races that application code must reason about case by case.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use serializable isolation, usually regarded as the strongest level. It guarantees that although transactions may execute in parallel, the end result is the same as if they had run one at a time, serially, without any concurrency. The database therefore prevents all possible race conditions.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You get the strongest guarantee, but the cost depends on how the database implements it, and some implementations are slow.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Correctness depends on invariants across several objects, and you cannot list every race your code could meet.

card.rule: Serializable means the outcome equals some one-at-a-time order, not that transactions literally run one at a time.
card.limits: The guarantee concerns transactions that are correct when run alone; it does not repair a transaction with faulty logic.

concepts.title: Three ways to get serializability
concepts.question: How do databases implement serializable isolation, and why is it not used everywhere?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If serializable isolation is better than weak levels, adoption should be universal. The cost of the implementations explains why it is not.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Most databases that offer serializability use one of three techniques. Literally execute transactions in a serial order. Use two-phase locking, which for several decades was the only viable option. Use optimistic concurrency control such as serializable snapshot isolation.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each technique gives the same guarantee at a different performance price and with different limits.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing or evaluating a database for transactions with strict correctness needs.

card.rule: Serializability has three families of implementation: serial execution, two-phase locking and optimistic techniques such as SSI.
card.limits: The chapter first discusses them on single-node databases; extending them across nodes comes in a later chapter.

concepts.title: Why single-threaded execution became viable
concepts.question: What changed around 2007 to make one transaction at a time feasible?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: For 30 years, multi-threaded concurrency was regarded as essential for good performance.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Remove concurrency entirely and run one transaction at a time on a single thread. The isolation is then serializable by definition. Two developments made this feasible: cheap RAM lets the active dataset sit in memory, and OLTP transactions are short with few reads and writes. Long analytic queries are read-only and can use a snapshot outside the loop.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You avoid the coordination overhead of locking, but throughput is limited to a single CPU core.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Transactions are small and fast and the working set fits in memory.

card.rule: Single-threaded execution works when data is in memory and transactions are short; analytics run on snapshots elsewhere.
card.limits: If a transaction must wait for disk, user input or the network, the one thread stalls.

concepts.title: Interactive transactions versus stored procedures
concepts.question: Why do single-threaded systems require stored procedures instead of interactive transactions?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If a transaction goes back and forth with the application, the single thread idles during network round trips.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Submit the entire transaction code to the database ahead of time as a stored procedure. With all data in memory, the procedure executes fast, without waiting for network or disk I/O. Systems with serial execution therefore do not allow interactive multi-statement transactions.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The application gives up the flexibility of deciding the next query from the previous result in client code.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Humans are slow to decide, so a transaction waiting for user input would hold the thread, or force many idle concurrent transactions.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Throughput matters under serial execution and the logic can be shipped to the database.

card.rule: With one transaction at a time, ship the whole transaction as a stored procedure instead of talking statement by statement.
card.limits: Stored procedures help only if the data they need is in memory; otherwise disk waits stall the thread again.

media.alt: Two timelines. Interactive transaction: Application sends a select count query across a network hop to query processor and storage, gets 2, evaluates an if in its own code, then sends a separate update and gets ok. Stored procedure: Application sends one call to run the procedure, whose select, if and update run inside the database, and gets one ok.

concepts.title: Stored procedures: reputation and modern fixes
concepts.question: Why do stored procedures have a bad reputation, and which problems have been overcome?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Stored procedures are needed for serial execution, yet they have a bad reputation.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Know the three complaints. Each vendor has its own archaic language, such as PL/SQL, T-SQL or PL/pgSQL, with a weak library ecosystem. Code in the database is harder to debug, version, deploy, test and monitor. And a database is shared by many application servers, so a badly written procedure hurts more. Modern systems use general-purpose languages: Java, Groovy, Clojure or Lua.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You gain fast, round-trip-free transactions but take on operational risk inside a shared, performance-sensitive component.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The data store runs transactions serially and the team can test and deploy database code.

card.rule: Stored procedures are the price of serial execution; modern ones use general-purpose languages to soften the old complaints.
card.limits: Using a general-purpose language fixes the ecosystem complaint, not the risk of a slow procedure harming every client.

concepts.title: Determinism and replication by re-execution
concepts.question: How can a database replicate by running the same procedure on every node?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Copying every write of a transaction to other nodes costs bandwidth, and replicas must end in the same state.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Run the same stored procedure on each replica instead of shipping its writes. This requires that procedures be deterministic: when run on different nodes, they must produce the same result. A procedure that needs the current date and time must use special deterministic APIs.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Replication becomes simple, but every procedure must be written with determinism constraints.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: A procedure reading the local clock or a random value would give different results on different nodes, and replicas diverge.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Transactions are stored procedures and you can control all sources of nondeterminism.

card.rule: To replicate by re-execution, procedures must be deterministic: same inputs on any node, same result.
card.limits: Re-execution works for procedures; it does not apply to interactive transactions whose logic lives in the client.

concepts.title: Partitioning to scale serial execution
concepts.question: How can single-threaded execution scale past one CPU core?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Serial execution limits write throughput to one core on one machine; high-write applications hit a bottleneck.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Partition the data so that each transaction touches only one partition. Each partition then has its own transaction processing thread running independently. Give each CPU core its own partition, and throughput scales linearly with the number of cores. VoltDB supports this. Read-only transactions can run elsewhere on snapshots.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Scaling depends on the data model: single-partition transactions scale, cross-partition ones need coordination.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Most transactions can be confined to one partition, as with simple key-value data.

card.rule: One thread per partition scales serial execution, provided each transaction stays within a single partition.
card.limits: The structure of the data decides whether this works; secondary indexes and cross-entity transactions can defeat it.

concepts.title: The cost of cross-partition transactions
concepts.question: Why are cross-partition transactions so much slower under serial execution?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A transaction that needs several partitions cannot run on one thread.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The database must coordinate the transaction across all partitions it touches. The stored procedure runs in lock-step across all of them to ensure serializability for the whole system. This extra coordination makes cross-partition transactions vastly slower.

blocks.label: Numbers
blocks.text: VoltDB reports about 1,000 cross-partition writes per second, orders of magnitude below its single-partition throughput.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Adding machines does not raise the cross-partition rate, so there is a hard limit on how much of the workload can be cross-partition.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Estimating whether a data model can tolerate multi-partition transactions.

card.rule: Cross-partition transactions run in lock-step across partitions, which makes them far slower and not scalable by adding machines.
card.limits: The 1,000 per second figure is VoltDB's report; other systems and versions will differ.

concepts.title: When serial execution is viable
concepts.question: Under what constraints is serial execution a good way to get serializability?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Serial execution is simple, but only within limits that must be checked before adopting it.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Check four constraints. Every transaction must be small and fast, since one slow transaction stalls everything. The active dataset must fit in memory. Write throughput must be low enough for one core, or transactions must be partitioned without cross-partition coordination. Cross-partition transactions are possible, with a hard limit.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Accessing data that is not in memory in a single-threaded transaction makes the system very slow.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Anti-caching: abort the transaction, fetch the data asynchronously while processing others, then restart the transaction once it is loaded.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: All four constraints hold; otherwise prefer two-phase locking or SSI.

card.rule: Serial execution fits small, fast transactions on in-memory data with write rates one core can handle or partitions that do not interact.
card.limits: Anti-caching is a mitigation for rarely used data, not a license for frequent disk access inside the loop.

concepts.title: Two-phase locking: readers and writers block each other
concepts.question: How does two-phase locking differ from locks that only prevent dirty writes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: For about 30 years, 2PL was the only widely used serializability algorithm; its strong locking rules explain both its safety and its cost.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Several transactions can read the same object while nobody writes it. As soon as anyone wants to write, exclusive access is needed. If A has read an object, B must wait before writing it. If A has written it, B must wait before reading it. Writers block readers and vice versa.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It protects against lost updates, write skew and the other races, but readers and writers wait for each other.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Snapshot isolation follows the mantra that readers never block writers and writers never block readers.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need serializability and can tolerate blocking.

card.rule: Under 2PL, writers block readers and readers block writers; that blocking gives serializability.
card.limits: Two-phase locking (2PL) is not two-phase commit (2PC); the two are completely different things.

concepts.title: Shared and exclusive locks, and why 2PL has two phases
concepts.question: How are shared and exclusive locks used, and where does the name two-phase come from?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Blocking readers and writers needs a concrete lock protocol.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Every object has a lock in shared or exclusive mode. To read, take it shared; several transactions can hold it together unless someone has it exclusively. To write, take it exclusive; no other lock may exist. A transaction that reads then writes may upgrade shared to exclusive. Hold every lock until commit or abort.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Holding locks to the end gives serializability but lengthens waits.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Reasoning about which operations can run together under a lock-based serializable level.

card.rule: Acquire locks while executing (phase one), release all at the end (phase two); shared for reads, exclusive for writes.
card.limits: Several shared holders can coexist; an exclusive lock admits no other holder.

concepts.title: Deadlock under 2PL
concepts.question: What is a deadlock, and what does the database do about it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With so many locks in use, transaction A can wait for B's lock while B waits for A's.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Name the situation deadlock. The database automatically detects deadlocks between transactions and aborts one of them so that the others can make progress. The application must retry the aborted transaction.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Automatic detection resolves the stall, but the aborted transaction redoes all its work.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Deadlocks are much more frequent under 2PL serializable isolation than under lock-based read committed, wasting effort when they are frequent.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Designing retry logic and judging the cost of serializable 2PL.

card.rule: A deadlock is a cycle of lock waits; the database aborts one victim and the application retries it.
card.limits: Deadlocks can occur under read committed too, but far less often than under 2PL serializable.

concepts.title: Why 2PL performs poorly
concepts.question: What makes 2PL slow, and why are its latencies unstable?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: 2PL gives serializability, but transaction throughput and query response times are significantly worse than under weak isolation.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Two causes: the overhead of acquiring and releasing locks, and, more important, reduced concurrency. If two concurrent transactions try anything that could cause a race, one waits for the other. Traditional databases do not limit transaction duration, so waits have no upper bound, and queues form on popular objects.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Latencies become unstable and high percentiles slow under contention. One slow transaction, or one acquiring many locks, can bring the whole system to a halt.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Strong safety against all races in exchange for throughput and tail latency.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need serializability, contention is low, and tail latency is not critical.

card.rule: 2PL trades reduced concurrency and unstable tail latency for serializability.
card.limits: Short transactions and low contention reduce, but do not remove, the instability.

concepts.title: Predicate locks stop phantoms
concepts.question: How does a predicate lock prevent phantoms in 2PL?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A serializable level must prevent phantoms, but row locks cannot cover rows that do not exist yet.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use a predicate lock. It works like a shared or exclusive lock, but it belongs to all objects matching a search condition, not to one row. A reader takes a shared predicate lock on its query conditions and waits if another transaction holds an exclusive lock on any matching object. A writer checks whether the old or new value matches an existing predicate lock and waits if so.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It is precise and stops all phantoms, but checking for matches is expensive.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Specifying what a serializable lock-based database must protect.

card.rule: A predicate lock covers every object, existing or future, that matches a search condition.
card.limits: Predicate locks are a conceptual model; real databases mostly approximate them with index-range locks.

concepts.title: Index-range locks: a cheaper approximation
concepts.question: Why do most databases use index-range locks instead of predicate locks?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Checking many predicate locks is time-consuming, so predicate locking performs badly.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use index-range locking, or next-key locking. Make the predicate match a greater set of objects: lock room 123 at any time, or all rooms between noon and 1 p.m. Any write matching the original predicate also matches the approximation. Attach a shared lock to an index entry or range; a writer that must update that part of the index meets the lock and waits.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It is less precise and may lock more than necessary, but its overhead is much lower.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: With no suitable index, the database falls back to a shared lock on the whole table, which is safe but stops all writes.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need phantom protection under 2PL at acceptable cost.

card.rule: Approximate a predicate with a larger lock on an index range; safe, cheaper and slightly over-protective.
card.limits: The fallback to a whole-table lock is safe but damages write concurrency.

concepts.title: Pessimistic versus optimistic concurrency control
concepts.question: What separates pessimistic from optimistic concurrency control?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Serial execution and 2PL are slow or limited, so is serializability fundamentally at odds with performance?

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Two-phase locking is pessimistic: if anything might go wrong, wait until it is safe. Serial execution is pessimistic to the extreme, like an exclusive lock on the whole database. Serializable snapshot isolation is optimistic: transactions continue anyway, and at commit the database checks whether isolation was violated, aborting and retrying if so.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Optimistic control performs badly under high contention, since many aborts and retries add load. With spare capacity and low contention it tends to beat pessimistic control.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Commutative atomic operations, such as counter increments, reduce contention.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Contention is low and there is spare capacity.

card.rule: Pessimistic waits before acting; optimistic acts and checks at commit; contention decides which wins.
card.limits: Optimistic control is an old idea; its pros and cons have long been debated.

concepts.title: Serializable snapshot isolation in brief
concepts.question: What does SSI offer that serial execution and 2PL do not?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Serial execution does not scale and 2PL does not perform well; weak levels are fast but racy.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Serializable snapshot isolation adds to snapshot isolation an algorithm that detects serialization conflicts among writes and decides which transactions to abort. All reads come from a consistent snapshot. The result is full serializability with only a small performance penalty compared with snapshot isolation.

blocks.label: Numbers
blocks.text: SSI was first described in 2008. PostgreSQL has offered it as the serializable level since version 9.1, and FoundationDB uses a similar algorithm.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It is young, so its performance is still being proven in practice.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want serializability without the blocking of 2PL or the single-core limit of serial execution.

card.rule: SSI is snapshot isolation plus conflict detection: full serializability at a small cost over snapshot isolation.
card.limits: The chapter treats SSI as promising and still proving itself, not as settled for every workload.

concepts.title: Decisions based on an outdated premise
concepts.question: What must a database detect to make snapshot isolation serializable?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Under snapshot isolation, the result of a query may no longer be current when the transaction commits.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat a read as a premise: a fact true at the start, such as there being two doctors on call. The database does not know how the application uses the result, so it must assume any change in that result may invalidate the writes. It must detect when a transaction may have acted on an outdated premise and abort it.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Assuming a causal dependency between reads and writes is safe but can abort transactions that did not truly depend on the read.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Understanding why SSI tracks reads, not just writes.

card.rule: A transaction's writes may depend on what it read; if that premise changes before commit, abort.
card.limits: The database cannot see the application's logic, so it must treat every change in a read result as possibly harmful.

concepts.title: Detecting stale MVCC reads
concepts.question: How does SSI detect that a transaction read a stale version?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A snapshot ignores writes by transactions that had not committed when it was taken, but those may commit before this transaction does.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Track when a transaction ignores another transaction's writes because of MVCC visibility rules. At commit, check whether any ignored writes have now been committed. If so, abort.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Waiting until commit avoids needless aborts: a read-only transaction needs no abort, and the ignoring writer might still abort.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Explaining why SSI does not abort at the moment of the stale read.

card.rule: Record ignored writes during the transaction; at commit, abort if any have become committed.
card.limits: Deferring the check preserves long-running reads from a consistent snapshot.

media.alt: Timeline with Transaction 42, Database and Transaction 43. Both count on-call doctors for shift 1234 and get 2. Transaction 42 sets Alice off call and commits. Transaction 43 then reads again, sees Alice still on call, updates Bob and commits, but is aborted. A table shows Alice's old row created by 1 and deleted by 42, new row created by 42.

concepts.title: Detecting writes that affect prior reads
concepts.question: How does SSI notice a write that invalidates a read made earlier?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Another transaction may modify data after it has been read, making the reader's premise stale.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use index-range style records, but without blocking. If there is an index on shift_id, record on index entry 1234 that transactions 42 and 43 read this data; without an index, track at table level. When a transaction writes, it checks the indexes for recent readers of the affected data and notifies them. The record acts as a tripwire, not a lock.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Information about reads must be kept until concurrent transactions finish, which costs memory and time.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Explaining how SSI differs from 2PL in handling the same range of data.

card.rule: Readers leave tripwires on the data they read; a later writer notifies them, and the reader aborts if the writer committed first.
card.limits: A notified transaction aborts only if the conflicting write commits before it does.

media.alt: Same timeline of transactions 42 and 43 as the previous figure, each reading doctors for shift 1234, then updating, 42 committing first and 43 aborted. A table of index-range locks lists key range 1234 as read by transaction 42 and read by transaction 43, with a note that 42's update affects 43's read.

concepts.title: Performance of SSI
concepts.question: How does SSI compare with 2PL and serial execution in performance?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Engineering details, such as tracking granularity and abort rates, decide how well an algorithm works.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Compare with 2PL: transactions do not block waiting for locks, so writers do not block readers and latency is more predictable, and read-only queries run on a snapshot without locks. Compare with serial execution: not limited to one core, since FoundationDB distributes conflict detection across machines. Tracking detail trades precision against overhead; PostgreSQL can prove some overwritten reads harmless.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: The abort rate matters: a transaction that reads and writes over a long time tends to conflict and abort, so read-write transactions must be fairly short.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: SSI is probably less sensitive to slow transactions than 2PL or serial execution.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Read-heavy workloads that need serializability.

card.rule: SSI avoids lock waits and the one-core limit; its cost is aborts, so keep read-write transactions short.
card.limits: Long read-only queries may be fine; long read-write transactions are likely to abort.

concepts.title: Transactions as an abstraction
concepts.question: What does a transaction let an application pretend, and when can it be skipped?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Applications face crashes, network interruptions, power outages, full disks and unexpected concurrency.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use transactions as an abstraction layer that lets an application pretend certain concurrency problems and hardware and software faults do not exist. A large class of errors reduces to a transaction abort, and the application tries again.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Simple access patterns, such as reading and writing a single record, can manage without them; complex patterns benefit enormously.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Without transactions, denormalized data can easily go out of sync with its source.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Access patterns involve multiple objects or interacting accesses.

card.rule: Transactions turn many fault and race cases into a simple abort and retry.
card.limits: The benefit is concentrated in complex access patterns; a single-record workload may not need them.

concepts.title: The catalogue of race conditions
concepts.question: Which race conditions did the chapter name, and what does each look like?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Choosing an isolation level requires knowing which anomalies it allows.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Know five. Dirty reads: reading uncommitted writes. Dirty writes: overwriting uncommitted data. Read skew: seeing different parts of the database at different times. Lost updates: a read-modify-write cycle overwritten. Write skew: a decision on a stale premise. Phantom reads: another write changes a search result.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each defence handles some anomalies at some cost, so match the defence to the anomaly.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Reviewing a design to see which of these a given isolation level leaves open.

card.rule: Six anomalies, from dirty reads to phantoms; each has a distinct trigger and a distinct defence.
card.limits: Names for the anomalies are clearer than names for levels; the same level can vary by database.

concepts.title: Which defence handles which anomaly
concepts.question: Which isolation levels and tools prevent each anomaly?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Weak levels protect against some anomalies and leave the rest to the developer.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Map each anomaly to its defence. Read committed and stronger prevent dirty reads; almost all implementations prevent dirty writes. Snapshot isolation prevents read skew, usually via MVCC. Lost updates are prevented automatically by some snapshot implementations, others need SELECT FOR UPDATE. Write skew needs serializable isolation. Phantoms in write skew need index-range locks or similar.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Manual protections such as explicit locking put the burden on developers.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing between a weak level plus manual defences and a serializable level.

card.rule: Only serializable isolation protects against all anomalies; weaker levels leave some to explicit locking and constraints.
card.limits: Check what your database means by each level before depending on it.

concepts.title: Choosing a serializable implementation
concepts.question: When does each serializable technique fit best?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Three implementations each fit different workloads.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Serial execution: each transaction very fast and throughput low enough for one core. Two-phase locking: the standard for decades, but many applications avoid it for its performance. SSI: a fairly new optimistic algorithm that avoids most downsides, letting transactions proceed without blocking and checking at commit, aborting if the execution was not serializable.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each technique trades something: single-core ceiling, blocking and instability, or aborts under contention.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Picking a database or isolation level for a workload with strict correctness needs.

card.rule: Pick serial execution for tiny fast transactions, 2PL when blocking is tolerable, SSI for read-heavy low-contention loads.
card.limits: The chapter discusses single-node databases; distributed transactions raise further challenges, treated in later chapters.

concepts.title: One computer: working or broken
concepts.question: Why does a single computer behave so predictably compared with a group of networked computers?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: On one computer the same operation gives the same result, and a hardware fault usually means a total crash rather than a half-working state.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Designers chose to make a computer crash completely when an internal fault occurs, because wrong results are hard and confusing to deal with. Software then sees an idealized model that works with mathematical perfection.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You give up partial service on a faulty machine in return for never receiving silently wrong answers.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You reason about code on a single node, and you need the baseline that distributed systems then lose.

card.rule: A single computer is deterministic and either fully works or fully breaks, because designers prefer a crash to a wrong result.
card.limits: Buggy software can still look flaky on one machine, and the guarantee ends once several machines talk over a network.

media.alt: Engraved drawing of a huge sea monster with long tentacles wrapped around a sailing ship, with a stormy wind-cloud blowing from the left; the picture is turned sideways.

concepts.title: Partial failure is nondeterministic
concepts.question: What makes a failure in a distributed system harder to handle than a crash of one computer?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Some parts of a distributed system can break in unpredictable ways while other parts work fine. This is called a partial failure.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat partial failure as normal. An operation that involves several nodes and the network may work one time and fail unpredictably the next.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You lose the clear working-or-broken state of one machine, so every multi-node step needs code for uncertain outcomes.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You design or operate anything that spans several nodes connected by a network.

card.rule: Partial failures are nondeterministic, and that nondeterminism is what makes distributed systems hard to work with.
card.limits: A fault that stops everything at once is a total failure, the kind a single machine shows, not a partial one.

concepts.title: Plan for faults, even rare ones
concepts.question: How should software treat faults that look unlikely, even in a system with only a few nodes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Faults feel rare in a small system, so teams hope for the best, and then a fault arrives with no planned behavior.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Make fault handling part of the software design. Consider a wide range of faults, even fairly unlikely ones, and create them on purpose in a test environment to see what happens.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You spend design and test effort on cases that seldom happen.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Your software works with other nodes, even if there are only a few. Operators also need to know what behavior to expect during a fault.

card.rule: Assume faults will occur, build handling into the design, and provoke them in testing.
card.limits: Handling does not mean surviving everything: perfect reliability does not exist, so you also need to know the limits of what you can promise.

concepts.title: A reliable system on unreliable parts
concepts.question: How can a more reliable system be built on parts that sometimes fail?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: It seems a system can only be as reliable as its weakest component.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Add a layer that hides low-level faults. Error-correcting codes repair flipped bits on a noisy channel. TCP sits on top of IP, which may drop, delay, duplicate or reorder packets, and retransmits missing ones, removes duplicates and restores order.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The upper layer is more reliable, but not perfect: some faults remain, though they are easier to reason about.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A lower layer has faults of a known kind that a higher layer can mask.

card.rule: A layer on top can hide low-level faults, so the whole can be more reliable than its parts, up to a limit.
card.limits: There is always a limit to how much more reliable the upper layer can be.

concepts.title: Supercomputers versus cloud services
concepts.question: How do supercomputers and cloud services differ in design philosophy, and why does that matter for faults?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Large-scale computing has opposite philosophies, so fault-handling lessons from one end do not carry over to the other.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: High-performance computing (HPC) uses supercomputers with thousands of CPUs for computation-heavy science such as weather forecasting. Cloud computing, a loosely defined term, uses multi-tenant datacenters, commodity computers on IP networks, on-demand allocation and metered billing.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each end optimizes for something different, so they accept different amounts of fault risk and cost.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You decide which fault-handling lessons apply to your system. Traditional enterprise datacenters lie between the two ends.

card.rule: Internet services sit at the cloud end, so plan for cloud-style faults rather than supercomputer-style reliability.
card.limits: Cloud is not a well-defined term, so real systems fall on a spectrum rather than at two clean ends.

concepts.title: Supercomputers escalate partial failure
concepts.question: How does a supercomputer deal with a failed node, and what does that make it resemble?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A computation spread over thousands of nodes cannot carry on in a confusing half-broken state when one node dies.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The job saves its state to durable storage from time to time, a checkpoint. When a node fails, the whole cluster workload stops, the node is repaired, and the job restarts from the last checkpoint.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Partial failure becomes total failure. This is simple to reason about, like a kernel panic on one machine, but all progress since the last checkpoint is redone.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Stopping and restarting the whole job is affordable and the nodes are reliable.

card.rule: A supercomputer behaves like a single machine: if any part fails, let everything crash.
card.limits: This only suits work that can pause and restart cheaply; a service that must answer users continuously cannot stop.

concepts.title: At scale, something is always broken
concepts.question: Why must internet services tolerate failed nodes instead of stopping when one fails?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In a system with thousands of nodes something is always broken, so a give-up-on-failure strategy would spend its time recovering, not working.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Tolerate failed nodes and keep the whole service running. This allows rolling upgrades that restart one node at a time, and a poorly performing virtual machine can simply be killed and replaced by a new one.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Commodity machines give equivalent performance at lower cost but fail more often, so tolerance must be built into the software.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The service is online and must answer users at any time, with many commodity nodes.

card.rule: At scale, design the whole to keep working while individual nodes are broken, repaired or replaced.
card.limits: Tolerance at node level does not cover faults shared by all nodes: a bad configuration change rolled out everywhere still brings the system to its knees.

concepts.title: Shared-nothing systems
concepts.question: What does shared-nothing mean, and why do internet services mostly use it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Machines must cooperate, yet none can reach into another machine's memory or disk.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In a shared-nothing system each machine has its own memory and disk, and the network is the only way machines communicate. One machine can read another's data only by making requests to a service over the network.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Everything one machine learns about another arrives as a message that can be lost or late.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You build internet services out of ordinary machines connected by a network.

card.rule: In a shared-nothing system the network is the only channel between machines.
card.limits: Shared-nothing is not the only way to build systems; it is the dominant one for internet services.

concepts.title: Asynchronous packet networks
concepts.question: What does an asynchronous packet network promise about when, or whether, a packet arrives?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A node sends a message across the network and needs to know when it will arrive, or whether it will arrive.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In an asynchronous packet network a node can send a packet to another node, but the network gives no guarantee about when it arrives, or whether it arrives at all. Timing and delivery are your software's problem.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Such networks are general and cheap to run, but you cannot count on delivery or on a delay limit.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You reason about the timing and failure assumptions of any message exchange between nodes.

card.rule: An asynchronous packet network guarantees neither when a packet arrives nor that it arrives.
card.limits: Special networks can offer bounded delay, but they are not what the internet or ordinary datacenters give you.

concepts.title: What can go wrong with a request
concepts.question: After sending a request and waiting for a response, what different things could have gone wrong?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You sent a request and expect a response, but none arrives, and the cause could lie on any side of the network.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Know the six causes. Request side: the request was lost, or it waits in a queue and arrives later. Node side: the node crashed, or it paused temporarily, for example in a long garbage collection pause, and will respond again. Response side: the node processed the request but the response was lost, or it is delayed.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each cause calls for a different reaction, yet from the sender's side they look the same.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You design request handling, retries and failure detection.

card.rule: A missing response can come from the request, from the node, or from the response on its way back.
card.limits: The list names common causes; it does not give you a way to tell them apart.

media.alt: Three timelines with Client, Network and Service, each ending in question marks as the client waits. (a) The request is lost in the network, shown as an X. (b) The request reaches a service marked node unresponsive and is lost. (c) The service replies ok, but the response is lost in the network.

concepts.title: Silence cannot be explained
concepts.question: If no response arrives, can the sender tell whether the request, the node or the response failed?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The only thing a sender knows is that it has not received a response yet.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Accept that in an asynchronous network a lost request, a dead remote node and a lost response are indistinguishable. The sender cannot even tell whether the packet was delivered: only a response from the recipient could say, and that response may itself be lost or delayed.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Using a reply as evidence of delivery pushes the uncertainty one step back rather than removing it.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You design request handling or reason about what a client may infer from silence.

card.rule: Without a response it is impossible to tell why: request lost, node down and response lost look identical.
card.limits: A positive response does settle one thing, namely that something happened; only the absence of one is ambiguous.

concepts.title: Timeouts leave things unknown
concepts.question: What does a timeout tell you, and what does it leave unknown?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You cannot wait forever for a reply that may never come.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use a timeout: after some time, give up waiting and assume the response will not arrive.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: When the timeout fires you still do not know whether the remote node received your request or what it did with it.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A reply is missing and you need to stop waiting and decide what to do next.

card.rule: A timeout ends the wait; it does not reveal what happened to the request.
card.limits: A timeout is a guess about the response, not a fact about the request.

concepts.title: Network faults are common
concepts.question: How common are network faults, and does redundant hardware remove them?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: After decades of building networks one might hope they are reliable by now, yet they are not.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Expect network faults even in controlled environments such as a datacenter run by one company, and plan the software for them.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Redundant networking gear reduces faults less than hoped, because it does not guard against human error such as misconfigured switches, a major cause of outages.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You estimate how often your software will meet network trouble.

blocks.label: Numbers
blocks.text: One study of a medium-sized datacenter found about 12 network faults per month: half disconnected a single machine and half disconnected a whole rack.

card.rule: Network faults are surprisingly common, and redundant hardware does not remove human error.
card.limits: Well-managed private datacenters can be stabler than public clouds, so rates differ by environment, but nobody is immune.

concepts.title: A link may fail in one direction
concepts.question: If a network link works in one direction, does that mean it works in the opposite direction?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: People assume connectivity is symmetric: if I hear you, you must hear me.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat each direction as its own path. A network interface can drop all inbound packets while sending outbound ones successfully.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Checking both directions means more to monitor and more to reason about.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You work out why two nodes disagree about whether the other is alive.

card.rule: A link that works in one direction may fail in the other.
card.limits: Many faults cut both directions at once, so one-way failure is a special case to remember, not the default.

concepts.title: Network partition and netsplit
concepts.question: What do network partition and netsplit mean, and why does the book prefer network fault?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The word partition is used for two different things in this field, which invites confusion.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A network partition (or netsplit) is the case where one part of the network is cut off from the rest by a network fault. The book mostly says network fault to avoid mixing it up with partitions (shards) of a storage system, covered in Chapter 6.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A broader term covers every kind of network trouble but says less about the specific shape of the failure.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You read documentation or papers where the word partition could mean either thing.

card.rule: A network partition means part of the network is cut off, and it is a different thing from a shard.
card.limits: The word is a convention: other sources may use it more loosely, so check the context.

concepts.title: Handling and testing network faults
concepts.question: Does handling network faults mean tolerating them, and how can the handling be tested?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If the reaction to network faults is not defined and tested, arbitrarily bad things can happen.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Decide how the software reacts and make sure it recovers. If the network is normally fairly reliable, showing users an error message during trouble can be a valid approach. Test by deliberately triggering network problems, the idea behind Chaos Monkey.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Showing an error costs little but gives users a worse experience than full tolerance, which costs more to build.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Your network is mostly reliable, or you need higher availability and can afford more engineering.

card.rule: Handle network faults by defining, and testing, what the software does, even if that means only an error message.
card.limits: A defined error message is acceptable only if the system also recovers once the network returns.

concepts.title: Why systems must detect faulty nodes
concepts.question: Which parts of a system must detect faulty nodes automatically, and why is that hard?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Several mechanisms depend on knowing whether a node is working, but network uncertainty hides the answer.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Detect faulty nodes automatically. A load balancer stops sending requests to a node that is dead, taking it out of rotation. Replicated databases that rely on a leader must replace a failed one.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Acting early on a suspicion risks a wrong judgment; waiting for certainty means slower reaction.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You use load balancers, replicas or any mechanism that must route around dead nodes.

card.rule: Systems need automatic failure detection, but network uncertainty makes it hard to tell whether a node is working.
card.limits: Explicit feedback sometimes exists, so detection is not always pure guesswork, but you cannot depend on it.

concepts.title: Explicit signals that a node is down
concepts.question: Which explicit signals can tell you a node is down, and when are they unavailable?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Waiting for a timeout is slow, so it helps to use any direct feedback the environment offers.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use what is available. If the machine is reachable but no process listens on the port, the operating system refuses or closes the TCP connection with an RST or FIN packet. If you can query the network switches, you can detect link failures. A router that is sure an address is unreachable may reply with an ICMP Destination Unreachable packet.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each signal exists only in some setups: switch interfaces are off limits over the internet or in a shared datacenter, and a router has the same limits as other participants.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You control or can see the machines, operating systems or switches involved.

card.rule: Use explicit feedback about a down node when it is available, but treat it as a bonus, not a guarantee.
card.limits: Rapid feedback is useful, but you cannot count on it being there.

concepts.title: Delivery is not handling
concepts.question: If TCP says a packet was delivered, can you be sure the application handled the request?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Lower layers give quick feedback, but they speak for the packet, not for the program that should act on it.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: To be sure a request succeeded, wait for a positive response from the application itself. A TCP acknowledgment shows only that the packet reached the machine.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You need the application to produce and send a reply, which costs an extra message and its own timeout.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: The success of the request matters, such as a payment or booking.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: The application may crash after TCP acknowledges the packet but before it processes the request.

card.rule: Only a response from the application itself proves the application handled the request.
card.limits: A positive application response settles that the work was handled; the lack of any response still proves nothing.

concepts.title: Retry, wait, then declare dead
concepts.question: With no explicit signal, what steps lead a client to declare a node dead?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In general there is no feedback at all, yet a client must eventually decide what to do.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Retry a few times, since TCP retries transparently and the application may also retry. Wait for a timeout to elapse. If nothing comes back within the timeout, declare the node dead.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The declaration is a decision based on silence, so it can be wrong, and the waiting delays the reaction.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: No explicit signal about the node is available, which is the usual situation.

card.rule: Without explicit feedback, retry, wait for the timeout and then declare the node dead.
card.limits: Declaring a node dead is a judgment from missing news, not knowledge, and it can be mistaken.

concepts.title: Choosing a timeout length
concepts.question: How long should a timeout be, and what does each choice cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A timeout is the only sure way to detect a fault, yet there is no simple answer for how long it should be.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Weigh two costs. A long timeout means a long wait until a node is declared dead, during which users may wait or see errors. A short timeout detects faults sooner but risks declaring a node dead when it only suffered a temporary slowdown, such as a load spike.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Fast detection against few false alarms: you cannot maximize both.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You pick or tune a failure-detection timeout.

card.rule: Short timeouts detect faults sooner but misjudge slow nodes as dead; long timeouts do the reverse.
card.limits: There is no universally right value: it depends on the system and the cost of each kind of error.

concepts.title: Premature death declarations
concepts.question: What goes wrong when a live node is declared dead too early?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A node that is alive but slow may be mid-action when the others give up on it.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Remember that declaring a node dead too early is itself a fault: if the node is actually alive and in the middle of an action, and another node takes over, the action may be performed twice.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Waiting longer avoids the duplicate but delays real takeovers.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You design takeover, failover or retry logic where actions have side effects.

card.rule: Declaring a live node dead can make its work run twice.
card.limits: If actions are safe to repeat, a premature takeover does little harm.

concepts.title: Cascading failure from false alarms
concepts.question: How can declaring nodes dead make an already overloaded system worse?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: When a node is declared dead its work moves to other nodes, adding load to them and to the network.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Be wary of declaring nodes dead during overload: a node that was only slow because of overload is removed, its load is moved to the others, they slow down too, and more of them get declared dead.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Quick failure detection under load can turn a slowdown into an outage.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You tune failure detection for a system that may run near capacity.

card.rule: False death declarations under overload shift work onto others and can cascade.
card.limits: When the system has spare capacity, a takeover can be absorbed without trouble.

concepts.title: The timeout that would be exact
concepts.question: If delays were bounded, what would a correct timeout be?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Choosing a timeout is guesswork, but a thought experiment shows what an exact one would look like.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Imagine a network where each packet arrives within a time d or is lost, and a non-failed node always handles a request within time r. Then every successful request gets its response within 2d + r, and silence beyond that means the network or the node is not working.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The exact timeout is a luxury of a fictitious system; real systems must live with guesses.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want a reference point for what a perfect timeout would take.

card.rule: With max packet delay d and max handling time r, a timeout of 2d + r detects failure without false alarms.
card.limits: Most real systems offer neither guarantee, so the formula is a thought experiment.

concepts.title: Where network delay comes from
concepts.question: What most often causes packet delays to vary on a computer network?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Packet delays vary a lot, and most of that variation comes from waiting in queues rather than from the wire.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Look for queues at four places. A switch queues packets when several senders target one destination. The destination operating system queues requests while all cores are busy. A virtual machine paused for tens of milliseconds buffers incoming data. TCP flow control queues data at the sender.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Sharing links and CPUs dynamically gives good utilization but produces waits.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You diagnose latency spikes or reason about why a timeout fired.

card.rule: Variable packet delay is mostly queueing: at switches, at busy receivers, at paused virtual machines, and at senders.
card.limits: A full switch queue drops packets, so some delay shows up as retransmission rather than waiting.

media.alt: A network switch with four input ports on the left, each carrying a steady stream of packets in a different shade. Inside, lines cross the switch fabric to output queues. Output port 3 shows a long mixed queue of all shades, while ports 1, 2 and 4 carry few packets.

concepts.title: TCP versus UDP for delay-sensitive traffic
concepts.question: Why do videoconferencing and voice calls use UDP rather than TCP?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: TCP's retransmission and flow control make delays vary, which hurts traffic where late data is useless.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Latency-sensitive applications such as videoconferencing and Voice over IP use UDP. UDP does not perform flow control and does not retransmit lost packets. In a call, a missing packet's slot is filled with silence and the stream moves on.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You trade reliability for steadier delays: some audio is simply lost.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Delayed data is worthless, as in a live call where a late packet cannot be played.

card.rule: Choose UDP when delayed data is worthless; choose TCP when every byte must arrive.
card.limits: UDP is wrong for data that must arrive intact, such as a file or a web page.

concepts.title: Measuring timeouts instead of guessing
concepts.question: How should timeouts be chosen when delays cannot be guaranteed?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In shared clouds, network delays can be highly variable because other customers use the same links, switches and CPUs.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Choose timeouts experimentally. Measure the distribution of round-trip times over a long time and many machines, then pick a trade-off between detection delay and premature timeouts. Better, let the system keep measuring response times and jitter and adjust timeouts itself, as the Phi Accrual failure detector does.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Adaptive detection is more complex than a constant but follows real conditions.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You run in shared infrastructure with no control over, or insight into, neighbors' usage.

card.rule: With no delay guarantees, set timeouts from measured round-trip times, ideally adjusting them automatically.
card.limits: Measurement describes past behavior, so an unprecedented spike can still exceed any chosen timeout.

concepts.title: Telephone circuits give bounded delay
concepts.question: How does a traditional telephone network guarantee a fixed maximum delay?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A phone call needs constantly low latency and enough bandwidth, which computer networks do not promise.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Set up a circuit when the call starts: a fixed, guaranteed amount of bandwidth is allocated along the entire route and held until the call ends. Because space is already reserved at each hop, there is no queueing and the maximum end-to-end latency is fixed. This is a synchronous network with bounded delay.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The reserved bandwidth is held for the whole call even if nobody is speaking.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Traffic needs a constant rate for a known duration, such as an audio or video call.

card.rule: A circuit reserves bandwidth along the whole route, which removes queueing and bounds the delay.
card.limits: The guarantee comes from reservation; it vanishes if bandwidth is shared dynamically.

concepts.title: A circuit is not a TCP connection
concepts.question: How does a telephone circuit differ from a TCP connection?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Both are called connections, but they treat bandwidth in opposite ways.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A circuit is a fixed amount of reserved bandwidth that nobody else can use while it exists. A TCP connection's packets opportunistically use whatever bandwidth is available, and you can hand TCP a block of any size and it tries to move it as fast as it can. An idle TCP connection uses no bandwidth.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Circuits give predictable delay but reserve idle capacity; TCP uses capacity flexibly but its delay is unbounded.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You classify a network or protocol as circuit-switched or packet-switched.

card.rule: A circuit reserves bandwidth; TCP takes whatever bandwidth is free.
card.limits: The two words connection and circuit overlap in casual speech, but only the circuit gives a delay guarantee.

concepts.title: Why the internet uses packets
concepts.question: Why do datacenter networks and the internet use packet switching, given that it causes unbounded delays?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Circuits would give guaranteed round-trip times, yet Ethernet and IP do not use them.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: They are optimized for bursty traffic. Requesting a web page, sending an email or transferring a file has no particular bandwidth need; we want it done as fast as possible. A circuit suits traffic with a fairly constant rate.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Packet switching gives up bounded delay in exchange for not wasting capacity on bursty transfers.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Traffic is bursty and variable-sized, not constant.

card.rule: Packet switching suits bursty traffic, circuits suit constant-rate traffic.
card.limits: If the traffic had a steady known rate, a circuit would give it a guarantee that packets cannot.

concepts.title: Sharing resources: utilization versus latency
concepts.question: What do you gain and lose by sharing a resource dynamically rather than reserving fixed shares?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Variable delays are a consequence of how a shared resource is divided between users.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A telephone wire carrying up to 10,000 calls divides its capacity statically: your call keeps its slot even if the other 9,999 are idle. The internet shares bandwidth dynamically: senders compete and switches decide moment by moment, which queues packets but keeps the wire busy.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Static division gives guaranteed latency but lower utilization and higher cost per byte; dynamic sharing gives better utilization and lower cost but variable delay.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You choose between predictable latency and cheaper, better-used hardware.

card.rule: Dynamic sharing raises utilization and lowers cost but causes variable delay; static division does the reverse.
