card.limits: Neither is better in general; the right one depends on whether guaranteed latency is worth the cost.

concepts.title: Variable delay is a cost choice
concepts.question: Are unbounded network delays a law of nature, and what follows for timeouts?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: It is tempting to treat unreliable timing as inevitable, but that is not what the book says.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Variable delays are not a law of nature but the result of a cost/benefit trade-off. Latency guarantees are achievable in some environments with static partitioning, at lower utilization and higher cost. In multi-tenant datacenters, public clouds and across the internet no such guarantee is on offer, so assume congestion, queueing and unbounded delays.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Guarantees can be bought, but most systems that are not safety-critical choose cheap over expensive.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You decide whether the cost of guaranteed latency is worth it, or how to set timeouts in an environment without guarantees.

card.rule: Unbounded delays result from a cost choice, and where guarantees are not offered there is no correct timeout, only measured ones.
card.limits: Do not read the trade-off as a promise: in the cloud, on the internet and in shared datacenters you simply do not get the guarantee.

concepts.title: Durations and points in time
concepts.question: What two kinds of questions do applications ask of clocks?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Applications use clocks for many purposes, and the purposes are not all the same kind.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Separate durations from points in time. Durations measure an interval: has a request timed out, what is the 99th percentile response time, how many queries per second, how long did a user stay. Points in time are events on a date and time: when was an article published, when to send a reminder email, when does a cache entry expire, the timestamp on a log line.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Mixing the two leads to using the wrong kind of clock, which the next section distinguishes.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You design anything that reads a clock and must pick which clock to read.

card.rule: Before reading a clock, decide whether you need a duration or a point in time.
card.limits: Some questions combine both, such as expiry: the stored point in time is compared with an elapsed time.

concepts.title: Delay makes ordering uncertain
concepts.question: Why is it hard to order events that happen on different machines?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A message takes time to cross the network, and you do not know how long.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Remember that the receive time of a message is always later than its send time, but variable network delay means you do not know how much later. That makes it hard to decide the order of events when several machines are involved.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You cannot place events from different machines on one timeline just by reading each machine's clock.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You reason about causality or ordering across nodes.

card.rule: A message arrives later than it was sent, but by an unknown amount, so cross-machine ordering is uncertain.
card.limits: On one machine, events can be ordered by a single clock without this uncertainty.

concepts.title: Each machine has its own clock
concepts.question: Why does every machine have its own notion of time, and how is it adjusted?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Machines on a network do not share one clock, so each tells time slightly differently.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Each machine has its own hardware clock, usually a quartz crystal oscillator. These devices are not perfectly accurate, so each clock may run a little faster or slower than another. Clocks can be synchronized to some degree using the Network Time Protocol, NTP, which adjusts the computer clock according to a group of servers.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Synchronization narrows the differences but cannot remove them.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You rely on clocks in several machines and need to know how far they agree.

card.rule: Every machine has an imperfect clock of its own; NTP brings clocks closer together.
card.limits: NTP depends on its servers and the network path to them, so it reduces but never eliminates the differences.

concepts.title: Time-of-day clocks
concepts.question: What does a time-of-day clock return, and how can timestamps from two machines be compared?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You need a clock that gives the current date and time in a form that other machines can interpret.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A time-of-day clock, also called wall-clock time, returns the current date and time according to a calendar. For example, Java's System.currentTimeMillis returns milliseconds since the epoch, midnight UTC on January 1, 1970, not counting leap seconds. Usually synchronized with NTP, so a timestamp from one machine ideally means the same as one from another.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Meaning across machines depends on synchronization, which is imperfect.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need a calendar time that other machines can interpret.

card.rule: A time-of-day clock gives calendar time since the epoch, comparable across machines only to the accuracy of NTP.
card.limits: Time-of-day clocks have oddities, such as jumps, that make them poor for measuring elapsed time.

concepts.title: Why time-of-day clocks mislead on durations
concepts.question: Why is a time-of-day clock a poor choice for measuring how much time has passed?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A clock meant for calendar time can behave oddly when read twice to compute elapsed time.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Do not use it for elapsed time. If the local clock is too far ahead of the NTP server it may be forcibly reset and appear to jump back in time. Time-of-day clocks also often ignore leap seconds. Subtracting two readings can then give a wrong, even negative, duration.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You must use a different clock for durations, which a second clock type provides.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You compute durations such as timeouts or response times.

card.rule: Time-of-day clocks can jump, so never use them to measure elapsed time.
card.limits: For calendar timestamps the jumps are an accepted risk; only the duration use is the mistake.

concepts.title: Monotonic clocks measure durations
concepts.question: Which clock should measure a timeout or response time, and what does its value mean?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You need a clock that never jumps backward so that subtracting two readings gives the elapsed time.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use a monotonic clock, such as Java's System.nanoTime. It is guaranteed always to move forward. Read it before and after an operation and subtract: the difference is the elapsed time. The absolute value is meaningless, perhaps nanoseconds since boot.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You cannot use monotonic readings as timestamps, nor compare them between computers.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You measure durations such as timeouts and service response times.

card.rule: Measure durations with a monotonic clock: only the difference between two readings means anything.
card.limits: A monotonic clock cannot tell you the date or time of day.

concepts.title: Limits of the monotonic guarantee
concepts.question: What can NTP do to a monotonic clock, and how far can the guarantee be trusted?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A clock that cannot jump can still run a bit fast or slow, and its guarantee has soft spots.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: NTP may adjust the frequency at which the monotonic clock moves forward, called slewing, if the local quartz runs faster or slower than the NTP server. By default NTP allows a speed-up or slow-down of up to 0.05 percent, but it cannot make the monotonic clock jump forward or backward. Comparing values from two computers makes no sense.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You get steady forward time at the cost of a small rate error.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You depend on a monotonic clock for timeouts and can tolerate a rate error of 0.05 percent.

card.rule: NTP can slew a monotonic clock by up to 0.05 percent but cannot make it jump, so differences remain usable.
card.limits: Treat the monotonicity guarantee with a pinch of salt on multi-socket servers, where separate per-CPU timers may differ.

concepts.title: Quartz clocks drift
concepts.question: How far can a quartz clock drift between synchronizations?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A quartz clock runs slightly fast or slow, so its error grows between synchronizations even when everything works.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Estimate the worst-case error as drift rate times the time since the last synchronization. Google assumes 200 parts per million (ppm) for its servers. Shortening the sync interval shrinks the error.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Synchronizing more often costs more traffic and leans harder on the network for each sync.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You size how often to synchronize, or judge how precise a timestamp can be.

blocks.label: Numbers
blocks.text: At 200 ppm, a clock resynchronized every 30 seconds can be 6 ms off, and one resynchronized once a day about 17 seconds off.

card.rule: Clock drift limits the best possible accuracy: the error grows in proportion to the time since the last sync.
card.limits: The 200 ppm figure is Google's assumption for its servers; other hardware may drift differently.

concepts.title: NTP accuracy is limited by the network
concepts.question: What limits how accurate NTP synchronization can be?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Synchronizing a clock over a network inherits the network's unpredictable delay.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Expect NTP to be only as good as the network delay. One experiment found a minimum error of 35 ms when synchronizing over the internet, with occasional spikes to around a second. Large delays can make the client give up. A clock that differs too much from the server may be refused or forcibly reset.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Better accuracy needs a better time source or a calmer network, and both cost more.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You decide how far to trust timestamps from NTP-synchronized machines.

card.rule: NTP accuracy is bounded by the network round-trip delay and its variation, not only by clock quality.
card.limits: On a quiet local network accuracy can be much better, so the figures describe synchronizing over the internet.

concepts.title: Leap seconds, virtual machines and untrusted devices
concepts.question: Which other causes make clocks misbehave: leap seconds, virtual machines and devices you do not control?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Even a well-synchronized clock can break software assumptions through the calendar, virtualization or users.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Plan for each. A leap second makes a minute 59 or 61 seconds long; smearing spreads the adjustment over a day. On a virtual machine, a pause of tens of milliseconds looks to the application like the clock jumping forward. On mobile or embedded devices you do not control, users may set the clock wrongly.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Smearing needs NTP servers that deliberately lie by small amounts.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Your software runs across a leap second, on shared virtual machines, or on user devices.

card.rule: Do not trust a clock blindly: leap seconds, VM pauses and user settings all produce wrong readings.
card.limits: Smearing practice varies between NTP servers, so what is documented as the best way may differ from what happens.

concepts.title: Very accurate clocks are possible but costly
concepts.question: Can clocks be synchronized very accurately, and what does it take?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Some applications, such as finance, need much better clock accuracy than ordinary NTP delivers.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Invest in it. The MiFID II draft regulation requires high-frequency trading funds to synchronize clocks to within 100 microseconds of UTC. This is achieved with GPS receivers, the Precision Time Protocol (PTP), and careful deployment and monitoring.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It takes significant effort and expertise, and there are plenty of ways for it to go wrong.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A regulation or the correctness of your system requires accuracy far beyond ordinary NTP.

card.rule: Accurate clocks are possible with dedicated hardware and careful operation, but they cost significant effort.
card.limits: A misconfigured NTP daemon or a firewall blocking NTP traffic lets drift error grow large again quickly.

concepts.title: Clock errors fail silently
concepts.question: Why are wrong clocks more dangerous than a defective CPU or network?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A defective CPU or misconfigured network soon stops working and gets fixed, but a wrong clock often looks fine.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Assume clocks can be wrong, and watch for it. If software relies on accurate synchronization, a bad clock more likely causes silent, subtle data loss than a dramatic crash. Monitor the clock offsets between all machines, and declare any node that drifts too far from the others dead and remove it.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Monitoring and removing drifting nodes costs effort and capacity.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Your software requires synchronized clocks.

card.rule: Wrong clocks go unnoticed, so monitor offsets and remove nodes whose clocks drift too far.
card.limits: Monitoring finds drift only once it has begun; it does not make a clock correct.

concepts.title: Last write wins can drop a later write
concepts.question: How can timestamps from time-of-day clocks make a database drop the newer of two writes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Replicas that resolve conflicts by timestamp trust clocks that may disagree about which write came last.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Last write wins (LWW) keeps the value with the highest time-of-day timestamp. Client A writes x = 1 on node 1 at 42.004 s; it replicates to node 3. Client B then increments x there to 2 at 42.003 s, because node 3's clock lags. Node 2 receives both, takes 42.004 as later, and drops the increment.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: LWW is simple and widely used, but a later write can be lost without any error.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Only when silently losing some writes is acceptable.

card.rule: LWW trusts timestamps, so a node with a lagging clock can lose writes that really happened later.
card.limits: Clock skew in the example is under 3 ms, better than you can expect in practice, and it still misorders the writes.

media.alt: Timeline with Client A, Nodes 1, 2, 3 and Client B, each node showing clock readings. Client A sets x = 1 on node 1 (clock 42.004). Client B then increments x on node 3 (clock 42.003). Node 1's write is replicated with ts 42.004, node 3's x = 2 with ts 42.003, and both arrive at node 2.

concepts.title: Three more problems of LWW
concepts.question: Besides misordering, what other problems does last write wins have?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A lost write is only the first problem with resolving conflicts by clock time.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Know three problems. A node with a lagging clock cannot overwrite values from a node with a fast clock until the skew has elapsed, so data vanishes silently. LWW cannot tell writes in quick succession from truly concurrent ones. Two nodes can produce equal timestamps, so a tiebreaker, such as a large random number, is needed.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Fixing these needs extra mechanisms, such as version vectors for tracking causality.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You evaluate a database that resolves conflicts by timestamp.

card.rule: LWW can silently drop data, cannot separate sequential from concurrent writes, and needs tiebreakers for equal timestamps.
card.limits: If the application tolerates losing writes, LWW can still be acceptable.

concepts.title: Better NTP cannot fix event ordering
concepts.question: Could NTP be made accurate enough that timestamps order events correctly?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If clocks were a little more accurate, perhaps timestamps could order events safely.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Do not count on it. NTP accuracy is limited by network round-trip time, plus other errors such as quartz drift. To order events correctly you need a clock source significantly more accurate than the thing you are measuring, namely network delay.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A real fix needs far better clock sources; otherwise events inside the error margin stay ambiguous.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You consider using timestamps to order events from different machines.

card.rule: Timestamps order events only when clock error is much smaller than the gaps between events.
card.limits: If events are far apart compared with the clock error, timestamps do order them correctly.

concepts.title: Logical clocks order without time
concepts.question: What is a logical clock, and what is it good for?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Physical clocks cannot order events safely, but ordering is what many systems actually need.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use logical clocks. They are based on incrementing counters rather than an oscillating quartz crystal. They measure neither the time of day nor elapsed seconds, only the relative order of events: whether one happened before another. Time-of-day and monotonic clocks, which measure real elapsed time, are called physical clocks.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You lose any connection to real time: a counter cannot say when something happened.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need event ordering or causality more than a calendar time.

card.rule: Logical clocks count events to give a safe ordering; physical clocks measure time.
card.limits: If you need to know the actual time an event occurred, a logical clock cannot tell you.

concepts.title: A clock reading is a range
concepts.question: Why is a clock reading better understood as a range than a point?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A clock can show microseconds, but it is not accurate to that precision.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat a reading as a confidence interval. A system may be 95 percent confident that the time is between 10.3 and 10.5 seconds past the minute, and know no more precisely than that. If the time is only known to plus or minus 100 ms, the microsecond digits are meaningless. Most systems do not expose this uncertainty.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Working with intervals costs more complexity than reading a single number.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You compare timestamps from different machines or rely on their order.

card.rule: Think of a clock reading as a range of possible times, not a point.
card.limits: A GPS receiver or atomic clock attached to the machine reports its own error range, but most clock calls give no error bound.

concepts.title: Snapshot isolation needs causal transaction IDs
concepts.question: Why is a global, causality-respecting transaction ID hard to generate in a distributed database?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Snapshot isolation lets read-only transactions see a consistent state, but it needs monotonically increasing transaction IDs.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Understand the constraint. A write with an ID greater than the snapshot's ID is invisible to that snapshot. On one node a counter is enough. Across machines and datacenters a global monotonic ID needs coordination, and with many small rapid transactions that becomes a bottleneck.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Coordination gives correct IDs but limits throughput; uncoordinated generators scale but can break causality.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You design snapshot isolation for a database spread over several machines.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: If B reads a value written by A but gets a lower ID than A, the snapshot would not be consistent.

card.rule: A distributed snapshot ID must increase and respect causality, which a simple local counter cannot give without coordination.
card.limits: Generators such as Snowflake scale well but cannot guarantee an order consistent with causality.

concepts.title: Spanner waits out the uncertainty
concepts.question: How does Spanner use clock uncertainty to give transactions reliable timestamps?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Timestamps from clocks could serve as transaction IDs, but only if the doubt about order is removed.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use non-overlapping confidence intervals: if A's interval ends before B's begins, B definitely happened after A. Spanner deliberately waits for the length of the confidence interval before committing a read-write transaction, so that later readers have non-overlapping intervals.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Every read-write commit is delayed by the interval length, so smaller uncertainty means faster commits.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need snapshot isolation across datacenters and can invest in precise clocks.

card.rule: Wait out the confidence interval before committing, so timestamps reflect causality.
card.limits: The approach is active research and has not been implemented in mainstream databases outside Google.

concepts.title: A lease check that can be wrong
concepts.question: What is wrong with a leader that checks its lease and then processes a request?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A leader must know it still holds leadership before accepting writes, but a check can be stale by the time the work happens.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A lease works like a lock with a timeout: one node holds it at a time and must renew it before it expires. The sample loop renews the lease if less than 10 seconds remain, then processes the request if the lease is valid.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Leases let a failed leader be replaced after expiry, but a leader that cannot notice its own lapse is unsafe.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You build leader election or locking on timeouts and must decide what a check really proves.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Flaw one: the expiry was set by another machine yet is compared with the local clock. Flaw two: even with a local monotonic clock, the code assumes almost no time passes between the check and the work.

card.rule: A check proves the lease was valid at that moment, not when the request is processed.
card.limits: If the gap between check and action were bounded by the system model, the check would be safe; the loop fails because the gap is not bounded.

concepts.title: Why a process can stop without warning
concepts.question: What can pause a running program for a long time without it noticing?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A program might assume it runs continuously, but many layers can suspend it at any instruction.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Know the sources. Stop-the-world garbage collection can last minutes. A virtual machine can be suspended and resumed or live-migrated. A laptop lid can close. The operating system or hypervisor can switch threads. Synchronous disk access can block, and so can paging. A SIGSTOP, as from Ctrl-Z, halts a Unix process.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Tuning can shorten some pauses, but robust guarantees must assume the worst.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You reason about locks, leases or timeouts and wonder how steadily code really runs.

card.rule: A process can be paused for an unbounded time at any point by GC, virtualization, scheduling, I/O, paging or signals.
card.limits: Pauses can be reduced by tuning and design, but they cannot be ruled out.

concepts.title: A paused node does not know it was paused
concepts.question: What must a node assume about its own execution in a distributed system?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The usual tools for thread safety assume shared memory and cannot guard against a long unnoticed pause.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Assume the node can be paused for a significant time at any point, even mid-function. While it sleeps the rest of the world moves on and may declare it dead. On waking it learns that time passed only when it next checks a clock.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You must design so that a stale node cannot do damage.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You write code whose safety depends on timing, such as locks and leadership.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Single-machine tools such as mutexes, semaphores and lock-free structures do not translate directly, because they rely on shared memory.

card.rule: A node must assume it can be paused at any point, and others may declare it dead meanwhile.
card.limits: On one machine, mutexes and atomic counters remain valid; a distributed system has no shared memory, only messages over an unreliable network.

concepts.title: Hard real-time systems
concepts.question: What does it take to guarantee a response within a deadline?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Some systems, such as airbag controllers, cause serious harm if they respond late, so pauses must be eliminated.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Build a hard real-time system with support at every level. A real-time operating system schedules processes with guaranteed CPU time. Library functions document their worst-case execution times. Extensive testing and measurement confirm the guarantees.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It is a large amount of extra work and severely limits the languages, libraries and tools you can use.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A missed deadline can cause the failure of an entire system, as in aircraft, rockets, cars and robots.

card.rule: Hard real-time means specified deadlines are met in all circumstances, achieved by design and testing across the whole stack.
card.limits: On the web, real-time often only means pushing data to clients, without hard response-time constraints.

concepts.title: Why servers do not run in real time
concepts.question: Why do most server-side data systems not use real-time guarantees?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Eliminating pauses is possible, but the price is high compared with the benefit for ordinary services.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Accept the pauses. Developing real-time systems is very expensive, so they are mostly used in safety-critical embedded devices. Real-time is not the same as high performance: it may mean lower throughput, since timely responses come first.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Servers accept pauses and clock instability in return for lower cost and a wider choice of tools.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You decide whether your service needs guaranteed deadlines or can tolerate occasional delays.

card.rule: Real-time guarantees are costly and can lower throughput, so ordinary servers do without them.
card.limits: If missing a deadline can harm people or equipment, the economics change and real time is justified.

concepts.title: Treating GC pauses as planned outages
concepts.question: How can the impact of garbage collection pauses be reduced without real-time guarantees?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: GC pauses cannot be removed, but their effect on clients can be hidden by routing around them.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat a pause as a brief planned outage of a node. If the runtime warns that a collection is due, stop sending that node new requests, let outstanding ones finish, collect, then resume. A variant uses the collector only for short-lived objects and restarts processes periodically, one node at a time.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It needs runtime warnings and spare capacity on other nodes, and it only reduces pauses.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: High percentiles of response time matter, as in some latency-sensitive financial trading systems.

card.rule: Hide GC pauses from clients by draining a node before it collects, or restart it before a full collection is needed.
card.limits: These measures cannot fully prevent GC pauses, only reduce their impact.

concepts.title: A node can only guess
concepts.question: What can a node in a distributed system actually know about other nodes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Everything so far leaves a node unsure about the state of the rest of the system.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Accept that a node cannot know anything for sure; it can only guess from the messages it receives, or does not receive. It learns another node's state, such as its stored data or whether it works, only by exchanging messages. If a remote node is silent, you cannot tell its state, because network problems cannot reliably be distinguished from node problems.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Knowledge costs messages, and even then it can be stale.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You reason about what a component can safely conclude.

card.rule: A node knows only what messages tell it, and silence is ambiguous.
card.limits: Within one process the node does know its own state; the uncertainty concerns other nodes.

concepts.title: Stating assumptions as a system model
concepts.question: How can we build reliable systems when little can be known for sure?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A system that must guess cannot be reliable unless its guesses rest on stated assumptions.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: State the assumptions about behavior, the system model, and design the actual system to meet them. Algorithms can be proved to work correctly within a given model. That makes reliable behavior achievable even when the underlying system provides very few guarantees.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It is not straightforward to make software well behaved in an unreliable model.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You choose or design distributed algorithms and need to know when they are safe.

card.rule: Write down what you assume, then design and prove against those assumptions.
card.limits: A proof holds only inside the model; reality may break the assumptions.

concepts.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
concepts.title: A node cannot trust its own judgment
concepts.question: Why can a node not rely on its own opinion that it is alive and in charge?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Peers decide from silence, and a node that is fine from its own view can still be treated as dead.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Take the moral of the stories: a node cannot necessarily trust its own judgment, and a system cannot rely exclusively on one node. A node can be working yet unheard, or paused for a minute in a stop-the-world GC and then wake, healthy but unaware that a minute passed, to find others have declared it dead.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Depending on peers' verdicts means a healthy node can be removed.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You design decisions about who is alive and who is in charge.

card.rule: A node may be wrongly declared dead and cannot dispute it, so its self-view is not authoritative.
card.limits: A node's own observations still matter as input; they are just not final.

concepts.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
concepts.title: Quorums: decisions by vote
concepts.question: How do many distributed algorithms decide, for example whether a node is dead?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A decision made by one node can be wrong, and a system needs decisions that survive failures.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use a quorum: voting among nodes, with decisions needing a minimum number of votes. Usually the quorum is an absolute majority, more than half the nodes. If a quorum declares a node dead, it must be considered dead and must step down, even if it still feels alive.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You need more nodes to vote, and a majority must stay reachable to decide.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Decisions such as declaring a node dead or choosing a leader must be safe.

blocks.label: Numbers
blocks.text: With three nodes, one failure can be tolerated; with five nodes, two. Only one majority can exist, so two majorities cannot make conflicting decisions.

card.rule: Decide by majority vote: a majority declaration binds even the node it concerns.
card.limits: Other kinds of quorums exist, but a majority is the most common.

concepts.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
concepts.title: Only one leader, lock holder or user
concepts.question: Why does a node's belief that it is the chosen one not make it so?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Systems often need exactly one of something, and a node can wrongly believe it is that one.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Remember three common cases: one leader per database partition to avoid split brain, one holder of a lock on a resource, one registered user per username. A node believing it is the chosen one needs the agreement of a quorum. It may have been demoted after being declared dead, and a new leader may already be elected.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Agreement costs a vote, which takes time and needs a reachable majority.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You design leader election, locks or uniqueness checks.

card.rule: Being the chosen one is decided by a quorum, not by the node's own belief.
card.limits: A node acting as chosen after a quorum has moved on can mislead other nodes into incorrect actions.

concepts.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
concepts.title: A paused lock holder corrupts a file
concepts.question: How can a client that holds an expired lease still damage a shared file?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A lock or lease protects a file only while its holder knows it is still valid, and a paused client does not.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Trace the failure. Client 1 gets a lease from a lock service to write a file, then pauses for too long. The lease expires. Client 2 obtains the lease and starts writing. Client 1 wakes, still believes its lease is valid, and also writes. The writes clash and corrupt the file.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A lease alone protects only clients that check it at the right moment.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A storage service must allow one client at a time, and clients may pause.

card.rule: A lease check inside the client is not enough, because the client can be paused after checking.
card.limits: The bug is not theoretical: HBase used to have this problem.

media.alt: Timeline with Lock service, Client 1, Client 2 and Storage. Client 1 gets a lease and a long stop-the-world GC pause begins. The lease expires, client 2 gets the lease and writes data to storage, which returns ok. Client 1 wakes up and writes data, and the write ends in an explosion mark at storage.

concepts.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
concepts.title: Fencing tokens
concepts.question: How can storage protect itself from a client that wrongly believes it holds a lease?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A client with a false belief of being the chosen one must not be able to disrupt the rest of the system.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use fencing. Each time the lock server grants a lock or lease, it also returns a fencing token, a number that increases with every grant. Clients include their token with every write. The storage service remembers the highest token it has processed and rejects writes with a lower one.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The resource itself must check tokens, so the storage needs support for them.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A lock or lease protects a shared resource and clients may pause or be wrongly confident.

blocks.label: Numbers
blocks.text: Client 1 gets token 33 and pauses. Client 2 gets token 34 and writes. When client 1 wakes and sends token 33, the storage rejects it.

card.rule: Make the resource reject writes whose fencing token is older than one it has already seen.
card.limits: Fencing stops mistaken nodes; a node that deliberately sends a fake token is a different problem.

media.alt: Same lock service timeline, now with fencing tokens. Client 1 gets lease with token 33 and pauses in GC. Client 2 gets token 34 and writes data with token 34, which storage accepts. Client 1 wakes and writes with token 33, and storage rejects it as an old token.

concepts.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
concepts.title: The resource must check the tokens
concepts.question: Why must the protected resource, not the client, enforce fencing?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A client cannot be trusted to police itself, because its picture of its own lock may be stale.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Require the resource to take an active role: it rejects any write with an older token than one already processed. If a resource has no support, you may work around it, for example by including the fencing token in a file name. Some check is necessary to avoid processing requests outside the lock's protection.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The service does extra work on each request, and clients must carry and send tokens.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You offer a resource to many clients whose priorities and behavior you do not control.

card.rule: Make the service protect itself, because it is unwise to assume clients are always well behaved.
card.limits: Server-side checks stop accidents; they do not stop a client that deliberately fakes a token.

concepts.title: Unreliable but honest nodes
concepts.question: What does the book assume about whether nodes tell the truth, and what is a Byzantine fault?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Fencing tokens block a node that errs by accident, but a node that wants to cheat could fake a token.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Assume nodes are unreliable but honest. They may be slow or never respond, and their state may be out of date after a GC pause or network delay, but when they respond they tell the truth as far as they know. A Byzantine fault is a node that lies, sending arbitrary faulty or corrupted responses.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The honest assumption keeps algorithms simpler; allowing lies makes the problems much harder.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You work inside one organization's datacenter where nodes run your own software.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: A node might claim to have received a message it never got; reaching agreement among nodes that may lie is called the Byzantine Generals Problem.

card.rule: Assume nodes may be slow, silent or out of date, but not lying, unless you have reason to expect lies.
card.limits: The assumption fails when nodes can be corrupted or controlled by parties with their own interests.

concepts.title: The Byzantine Generals Problem
concepts.question: What is the Byzantine Generals Problem, and when is a system Byzantine fault-tolerant?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Agreement is hard enough when messages are lost; it is harder when some participants lie.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Picture the Two Generals Problem first: two generals in separate camps agree on a battle plan by messengers that may be delayed or lost. In the Byzantine version, n generals must agree, but some are traitors who send fake messages, and nobody knows in advance who. A system is Byzantine fault-tolerant if it keeps operating correctly even when some nodes do not obey the protocol or attackers interfere.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Tolerating traitors needs more complicated protocols than tolerating mere crashes.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You must reach agreement among parties some of whom may be hostile or corrupted.

card.rule: Byzantine fault tolerance means correct operation despite nodes that deviate from the protocol or attackers on the network.
card.limits: The name comes from Byzantine meaning devious and over-complicated, not from any historical evidence about Byzantine generals.

concepts.title: When Byzantine fault tolerance is worth it
concepts.question: In which systems does Byzantine fault tolerance matter, and why do ordinary data systems usually skip it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Protocols that tolerate lying nodes are complicated and expensive, so they need a reason to be used.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use Byzantine fault tolerance where the risk justifies the cost. In aerospace, radiation can corrupt memory or CPU registers so that a node responds unpredictably, and a failure may be fatal. In systems with several participating organizations, some may try to cheat; peer-to-peer networks such as Bitcoin get untrusting parties to agree without a central authority.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The protocols are quite complicated, and in most server-side data systems the cost makes them impractical.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Nodes may be corrupted by physical effects or controlled by mutually distrusting parties.

card.rule: Pay for Byzantine tolerance when nodes can be corrupted or cannot be trusted; in your own datacenter you can usually assume they are not.
card.limits: Your datacenter nodes are controlled by one organization and radiation is low enough that memory corruption is not a major problem.

concepts.title: What Byzantine tolerance cannot fix
concepts.question: Why can Byzantine fault tolerance not protect against software bugs or most attacks?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: It is tempting to think a protocol that tolerates traitors would also cover bugs and security breaches.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Look at the conditions. Most Byzantine protocols need more than two-thirds of the nodes to work correctly: with four nodes, at most one may malfunction. If every node runs the same software, a bug hits all of them. An attacker who compromises one node probably compromises all, since they run the same software.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Using the idea against bugs would need four independent implementations, which is costly.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You consider whether to buy security or bug tolerance through a Byzantine protocol.

card.rule: Byzantine protocols do not help when all nodes share the same bug or vulnerability; use traditional security mechanisms.
card.limits: If implementations were truly independent, a bug in one could be outvoted, but that assumes it appears in at most one.

concepts.title: Cheap guards against weak forms of lying
concepts.question: What simple, pragmatic steps protect against weak forms of lying without full Byzantine tolerance?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Nodes are assumed honest, yet hardware faults, bugs and misconfiguration can produce invalid messages.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Add simple guards. Use checksums in the application-level protocol to catch corrupted packets that slip past TCP and UDP checksums. Sanitize inputs by checking ranges and limiting string sizes, and do basic sanity checks even behind a firewall. Configure NTP clients with several servers and accept a time range agreed by a majority.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: These measures do not withstand a determined adversary, but they cost little.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Your system trusts its nodes but must survive invalid messages from faults, bugs or misconfiguration.

card.rule: Use cheap checks like checksums, input sanity checks and multiple time servers, which catch accidental lies though not deliberate ones.
card.limits: A determined adversary defeats these measures, so they are not full Byzantine fault tolerance.

concepts.title: Three timing models
concepts.question: What are the three common system models for timing, and which fits real systems?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Algorithms must not depend on the details of particular hardware, so we describe the timing they may assume.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Define a system model: an abstraction of what an algorithm may assume. For timing there are three. The synchronous model assumes bounded network delay, pauses and clock error. The partially synchronous model behaves synchronously most of the time but sometimes exceeds the bounds. The asynchronous model allows no timing assumptions and has no clock.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The synchronous model is simplest but unrealistic; the asynchronous model is realistic but very restrictive.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You choose which algorithm fits your environment.

card.rule: Partial synchrony is a realistic model: well behaved most of the time, with occasionally shattered timing assumptions.
card.limits: The synchronous model does not imply exactly synchronized clocks or zero delay; it just says the bounds exist.

concepts.title: Three node failure models
concepts.question: What are the three common models for node failures?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Besides timing, an algorithm has to say how nodes are allowed to fail.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Choose a node failure model. In crash-stop, a node can fail only by crashing and then is gone forever. In crash-recovery, a node may crash and perhaps respond again later; disk contents survive but in-memory state is lost. In Byzantine (arbitrary) faults, nodes may do anything, including deceive others.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Richer fault models make an algorithm more realistic but harder to design and prove.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You pick the weakest fault model that matches how your nodes really fail.

card.rule: For real systems, the partially synchronous timing model with crash-recovery faults is generally the most useful.
card.limits: Crash-stop is simpler than reality, because real nodes often restart and rejoin.

concepts.title: Correctness as properties
concepts.question: How do we define what it means for a distributed algorithm to be correct?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Saying an algorithm works is vague unless we state exactly what it must guarantee.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Describe correctness by properties. A sorting algorithm's property is that, for any two distinct output elements, the left one is smaller. For fencing tokens we might require uniqueness (no two requests return the same value), a monotonic sequence (if x completed before y began, then token x is less than token y) and availability (a requesting node that does not crash eventually gets a response).

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Listing properties forces precision, but it does not by itself show the algorithm achieves them.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You specify or verify an algorithm.

card.rule: An algorithm is correct in a system model if it always satisfies its properties in every situation that model allows.
card.limits: If every node crashes or all delays become infinite, no algorithm achieves anything, so correctness is always relative to the model.

concepts.title: Safety and liveness
concepts.question: What is the difference between safety and liveness properties?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Some properties must hold even in disaster, while others can only be promised when things go reasonably well.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Tell them apart. Safety is informally nothing bad happens; liveness is something good eventually happens. If a safety property is violated, you can point to the moment it broke and the damage cannot be undone. A liveness property may not hold now, but there is always hope it will be satisfied later.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Informal words like good and bad are subjective, so use the precise definitions.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You classify properties of an algorithm before deciding what to guarantee.

card.rule: A violated safety property has a definite moment and is irreversible; a liveness property can still come true later.
card.limits: Do not rely on the informal slogans alone, because the actual definitions are precise and mathematical.

concepts.title: Safety always, liveness with caveats
concepts.question: Which properties must an algorithm guarantee in all situations, and which may carry caveats?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In a hostile model such as total network failure, no algorithm can be responsive, but it must not be wrong.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Require safety properties to hold in all possible situations of the system model. Even if all nodes crash or the whole network fails, the algorithm must not return a wrong result. Liveness may have caveats: a request needs a response only if a majority of nodes have not crashed, and only if the network eventually recovers.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Safety under all conditions may mean refusing to answer rather than risking a wrong answer.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You decide what to promise when parts of the system fail.

card.rule: Guarantee safety always; promise liveness only under stated conditions such as a majority being up and the network recovering.
card.limits: Liveness caveats must be clear and not so weak that the algorithm never does anything.

concepts.title: When reality breaks the model
concepts.question: What happens when the real world violates a system model's assumptions?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A model is a simplified abstraction, and real machines do things the model said were impossible.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Expect it. Crash-recovery algorithms assume disk data survives crashes, yet data may be corrupted or wiped by hardware error or misconfiguration, or a firmware bug may stop a server recognizing its drives. Quorum algorithms rely on nodes remembering what they stored; a node with amnesia breaks the quorum condition and the correctness.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A model that admits sometimes-lost storage is closer to reality but harder to reason about.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You implement a proven algorithm on real machines.

card.rule: An implementation should still handle cases the model calls impossible, even if only by stopping and letting a human clean up.
card.limits: Handling the impossible is a matter of engineering, not of the proof, and it cannot cover everything.

concepts.title: Why models are still worth it
concepts.question: If models are simplifications, why are they still valuable?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: After seeing models fail, one might conclude that formal analysis is pointless.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Keep using models, but treat them as a first step. Abstract models distill the complexity of real systems to a manageable set of faults, so the problem can be understood and tackled systematically. Algorithms can be proved correct by showing their properties always hold in a model. Such analysis can uncover problems that would stay hidden for a long time in a real system.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A proof of an algorithm does not prove its implementation will always behave correctly.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You design or select a distributed algorithm and plan how to verify it.

card.rule: Use theoretical analysis and empirical testing together; each catches problems the other misses.
card.limits: Proofs only cover situations inside the model; unusual circumstances can still defeat the assumptions.

concepts.title: Limping nodes and false suspicion
concepts.question: Why can a node that is slow but not dead be harder to handle than one that failed cleanly?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Failure detection relies on timeouts, which cannot separate network failure from node failure.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Recognize the degraded state. Timeouts cannot tell a network failure from a node failure, and variable delay can make a healthy node falsely suspected of crashing. A node can also limp: for example, a gigabit network interface can drop to 1 Kb/s because of a driver bug.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A limping node produces no clean signal, so it can drag a system down for a long time.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You design monitoring or failure detection and must handle partial degradation.

card.rule: A node that limps without dying can be harder to deal with than one that fails cleanly.
card.limits: Treat the limping node like a failed one only if you can detect the degradation, which needs more than a liveness check.

concepts.title: No shared state, so decisions need a quorum
concepts.question: Why can no single node make major decisions in a distributed system?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Once a fault is detected, tolerating it is hard too, because nodes have nothing in common but messages.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Accept that there is no global variable, no shared memory, no common knowledge or other shared state. Nodes cannot even agree on what time it is. Information flows only by sending messages over an unreliable network. Major decisions therefore cannot safely be made by a single node, so protocols enlist other nodes and try to get a quorum to agree.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Quorum protocols need extra messages and a reachable majority.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A decision must remain valid even when some nodes are unreachable or wrong.

card.rule: With no shared state, important decisions need a quorum of nodes to agree.
card.limits: Quorum agreement removes dependence on one node but not the uncertainty of the network.

concepts.title: Keep it on one machine if you can
concepts.question: When is it better to avoid a distributed system, and when is it unavoidable?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: After a chapter of problems, the obvious question is whether to avoid distribution altogether.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: If you can avoid opening Pandora's box and keep things on a single machine, it is generally worth doing so. A single computer can do a lot nowadays, and distributed systems engineers regard a problem as trivial if it can be solved on one computer.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Staying on one machine gives up fault tolerance and low latency by placing data near users, which a single node cannot provide.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Scale, fault tolerance or geographic latency requirements go beyond what one machine can offer.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Unreliable networks, clocks and processes are not a law of nature: hard real-time responses and bounded network delays are possible, but they are very expensive and lower hardware utilization.

card.rule: Use one machine when it suffices; distribute when you need scale, fault tolerance or low latency near users.
card.limits: Scalability is not the only reason for distribution, so a small workload can still need several nodes.

concepts.title: Guarantees implemented once
concepts.question: Why build fault tolerance as a shared abstraction instead of handling each fault in every application?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Lost, delayed or duplicated packets, approximate clocks and paused or crashed nodes can all occur. Handling each of them inside every application is error-prone.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Find general-purpose abstractions with useful guarantees, implement them once, and let applications rely on the guarantees. A transaction is the model: the application can pretend that there are no crashes, no concurrent access and perfectly reliable storage.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The application must know exactly what the guarantee promises. Anything the abstraction does not cover is still the application's problem.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Many applications need protection from the same faults, for example when several nodes must agree on one leader.

card.rule: Implement a guarantee once, below the applications, and let them rely on it instead of coping with faults one by one.
card.limits: A guarantee hides only the faults it covers. In some situations a system can tolerate faults and keep working, and in others that is impossible, so the limits must be known.

media.alt: Pen-and-ink map of an island, drawn sideways, titled Wrecks of Homegrown Consensus Algorithms. A smoking volcano, Mount Consensus, sits in the middle, surrounded by regions labelled linearizability, total order broadcast, distributed transactions and global constraints.

concepts.title: Eventual consistency is convergence
concepts.question: What does an eventually consistent database promise, and what does it leave unsaid?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Replicas of a database receive writes at different times, so two nodes read at the same moment can show different data, whichever replication method is used.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Eventual consistency: if writes stop and you wait for an unspecified time, all reads return the same value. The inconsistency is temporary, and convergence is a better name for it.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The guarantee names no time limit. Until replicas converge, reads could return anything or nothing.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Temporary disagreement between replicas is acceptable and a stronger, slower guarantee is not worth its cost.

card.rule: Eventual consistency promises only that replicas converge once writes stop, not when.
card.limits: The promise assumes that writing stops and any network faults are eventually repaired. It says nothing about what a read returns before convergence.

concepts.title: Why weak guarantees are hard to use
concepts.question: Why is eventual consistency hard for application developers, and when do its bugs show up?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A database looks like a variable you can read and write, but its semantics are much more complicated. A single-threaded program never reads back an old value right after assigning a new one.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: With weak guarantees, stay constantly aware of the limits and do not assume too much. Stronger consistency models are easier to use correctly.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Stronger guarantees may give worse performance or less fault tolerance. Weaker ones are cheaper, but the bugs they allow are subtle.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Applications work well most of the time, so testing rarely finds the bugs. The edge cases appear with a network interruption or at high concurrency.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You are choosing a consistency model and need to weigh ease of use against performance and fault tolerance.

card.rule: A weak guarantee moves the burden of correctness to the developer, and the resulting bugs hide until a fault or heavy concurrency.
card.limits: Strong guarantees are not free: they can cost performance or fault tolerance, so the stronger model is not always the better choice.

concepts.title: Consistency versus isolation
concepts.question: How do distributed consistency models differ from transaction isolation levels?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Consistency models and isolation levels look alike, as both form a hierarchy of weaker and stronger guarantees. They are easily taken for one thing.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat them as mostly independent concerns. Transaction isolation is about avoiding race conditions between concurrently executing transactions. Distributed consistency is about coordinating the state of replicas in the face of delays and faults.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Some overlap exists, so a guarantee from one area can resemble one from the other, yet one cannot be used in place of the other.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You must decide whether a problem is a race between transactions or a question of what replicas show.

card.rule: Isolation concerns concurrent transactions; consistency concerns replicas under delay and faults.
card.limits: The two areas overlap somewhat. The distinction is a rule of thumb about the main purpose, not a wall between them.

concepts.title: Linearizability: one copy of the data
concepts.question: What does linearizability make a replicated system look like, and what does that spare the application?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In an eventually consistent database, two replicas asked the same question at the same time may give different answers, which is confusing.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Linearizability gives the illusion that there is only one copy of the data and that every operation on it is atomic. Even though there are several replicas, the application does not need to worry about them.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The illusion has to be paid for with coordination, so it can be slow, especially where network delays are large.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want the database to behave like a variable in a single-threaded program and no application code should deal with replication lag.

card.rule: A linearizable system behaves as if there is a single copy of the data and every operation on it is atomic.
card.limits: The illusion lasts only as long as the system keeps it; the cost of keeping it grows with network delay and failures.

concepts.title: Linearizability is a recency guarantee
concepts.question: What exactly must a read return in a linearizable system after a write finishes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A client reading from a replica or stale cache might get an old value even though another client's write has already succeeded.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: As soon as one client successfully completes a write, all clients reading from the database must be able to see the value just written. The value read must be the most recent, up-to-date value.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Every read has to be checked against the newest state, so reads cannot just use whichever replica is nearby.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Readers must never act on data that is older than a write they could have heard about.

card.rule: After a write completes, every read must return that value or a newer one, never one from a stale cache or replica.
card.limits: The guarantee is about reads and writes of a single object. It does not group several operations together the way a transaction does.

concepts.title: The stale read after the news
concepts.question: Why does Bob's stale result break linearizability when it would be unremarkable if he and Alice reloaded together?

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: Alice and Bob sit together watching the 2014 World Cup final. Alice refreshes after the final score is announced, sees the winner and tells Bob. Bob reloads, but his request goes to a lagging replica and shows the game still going.

blocks.label: Why it is a violation
blocks.text: Bob started his query after hearing Alice, so he expects a result at least as recent as hers. A stale result is a violation of linearizability.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: If they had reloaded at exactly the same time, different answers would be less surprising, because neither knows when the server processed each request.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Judging whether a request that began after another one finished may return an older state.

card.rule: A request that starts after another has finished must see at least as recent a state as the first one did.
card.limits: Truly simultaneous requests carry no such expectation; the guarantee binds requests that are ordered in real time.

media.alt: Timeline with six rows: Referee, Leader, Follower 1, Follower 2, Alice, Bob. Referee sends an insert of the final score (Germany 1, Argentina 0) to Leader, which replies ok and forwards the insert to Follower 1 (arrives early) and Follower 2 (arrives late). Alice's select reads Follower 1 and returns the score, and she says Germany has won. Bob's select starts after Alice's finishes, reads Follower 2 before the insert arrives there, and he says the website shows the match still playing.

concepts.title: Registers, operations and the client's view
concepts.question: What can a client know about when its request was processed, and which operations does the model use?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: To say precisely what linearizable means, we need a simple model of what a client sees.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Model the data as a register: one key in a key-value store, one row or one document. Each operation is a bar from the moment the request is sent to the moment the response arrives. The database processed it at some point inside that bar. Operations are read(x), write(x, v) and cas.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Because of variable network delay, a client only knows the request was processed somewhere between sending and receiving, not exactly when.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Reasoning about whether a result is allowed in a linearizable system.

card.rule: A request is processed at some unknown point between being sent and its response arriving.
card.limits: The diagrams assume a global clock for analysis. Real systems lack accurate clocks, but the algorithm just cannot use one.

concepts.title: Three cases for a read near a write
concepts.question: Which value may a read return when it finishes before, overlaps, or starts after a write?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The client does not know exactly when the database processed each request, so it is unclear what a read may return while a write is in progress.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Take a register holding 0 while one client writes 1. A read that completes before the write begins must return 0. A read that begins after the write has completed must return 1. A read that overlaps the write may return either 0 or 1.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Allowing either value for overlapping reads is not sufficient on its own to describe linearizability fully.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Deciding whether a particular read result is allowed, given where its interval sits relative to a write.

card.rule: A read that ends before a write starts sees the old value, one that starts after the write ends sees the new value, and an overlapping read may see either.
card.limits: These three cases alone permit the value to flip between old and new during a write, which a single copy would not do.

media.alt: Timeline for clients A, B and C on a register x. C has one long bar, write(x, 1), ending with ok. A makes three reads: the first, before the write, returns 0; the second, overlapping the write, returns 0 or 1; the third starts after the write ends, with an arrow from the write's end, and returns 1. B makes two reads, both overlapping the write, each labelled returns 0 or 1.

concepts.title: After a new value is read, it stays
concepts.question: What must every later read return once any read has returned the new value?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If reads that overlap a write may return old or new, a reader could see a value flip back and forth while the write is going on. A single copy of the data would not behave like that.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Add a constraint: after any one read has returned the new value, all following reads, on the same client or on other clients, must also return the new value.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Replicas cannot answer independently. Once any client has seen the new value, no later read may be served from a replica that still holds the old one.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Checking an execution for a read that returns an older value than a read that finished before it started.

card.rule: Once a read has returned the new value, every read that starts after it must return the new value too.
card.limits: The constraint binds reads ordered in real time. Two reads that overlap each other are still free to differ.

media.alt: Timeline for clients A, B and C on register x, with C's long write(x, 1) ending in ok. A reads three times, returning 0, then 1, then 1. B reads twice: the first returns 0 and ends before A's second read begins; the second returns 1. An arrow runs from A's second read, which returned 1, to B's second read, which starts after A's second read ended.

concepts.title: Operations take effect at one point in time
concepts.question: How can we check an execution by giving each operation a single point at which it took effect?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Overlapping requests make it hard to say whether a set of results is allowed.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Mark each operation with a point inside its bar at which it seems to have taken effect, and join the points in time order. A linearizable execution is one where such markers can be chosen so that the joined line always moves forward in time, never backward.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The markers are a reasoning device. Real systems do not record them, so they must be inferred from request and response times.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need to decide if a recorded execution could come from a single copy of the data.

card.rule: An execution is linearizable if each operation can be given one point inside its interval so that the points form a valid sequence moving forward in time.
card.limits: The markers only exist in the analysis. The database does not tell clients when each operation took effect.

media.alt: Timeline for clients A, B, C, D and a Database line with marker points x=0, x=1, x=2, x=4. Operations: D write(x,0) ok; A write(x,1) ok; B read returns 1; C reads 1 then 2; B cas(x,1,2) ok; C cas(x,2,4) ok; D cas(x,0,3) returns error; A read returns 4. Grey lines join each operation to a database marker. B's last read, shaded with a warning sign, starts after A's read of 4 ended and returns 2.

concepts.title: Processing order need not match sending order
concepts.question: Why can a database legitimately process concurrent requests in a different order from the one they were sent?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A reader may send its request first and still see a write that was sent after it. That looks like reading the future.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Look at the intervals. If requests overlap, they are concurrent, and any order consistent with their results is acceptable. The read may simply have reached the database late because of a network delay.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Clients cannot infer the processing order from send order. They learn it only from the results, and only when intervals do not overlap.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A result looks impossible because of the order in which requests were sent.

card.rule: Concurrent requests may be processed in any order that gives valid results, not necessarily the order in which they were sent.
card.limits: This freedom applies only to overlapping requests. A request that begins after another has finished cannot be moved in front of it.

concepts.title: Compare-and-set in the model
concepts.question: What does compare-and-set add to the register model, and what does the model leave unprotected?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The model does not assume any transaction isolation. Another client may change a value at any time, so a client that reads and then writes may overwrite a change it never saw.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use an atomic compare-and-set, cas(x, old, new). If the current value of x equals old, it is atomically set to new. Otherwise the register is left unchanged and an error is returned.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A failed cas tells the client that the value changed concurrently, so the client must retry with fresh information.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A client must update a value only if no one else has changed it since it last looked.

card.rule: Compare-and-set updates a register only if its current value equals the expected one, so a concurrent change is detected.
card.limits: The model itself provides no transactions. One cas protects a single register and not a group of them.

concepts.title: Checking a recorded execution
concepts.question: How can one test whether a system's behaviour was linearizable, and why is that costly?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Linearizability is subtle, so it is hard to be sure that a system really provides it.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Record the timings of all requests and responses, then check whether they can be arranged into a valid sequential order.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The test works on a recorded run, so it can reveal a violation but cannot prove that no later run will violate it.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You doubt a system's claim and have a log with a send time and a response time for every request.

card.rule: Record every request and response with its timing, then check that some valid sequential order explains them all.
card.limits: Passing a test shows only that the recorded run was explicable. It does not prove the system is linearizable in other runs.

concepts.title: Linearizability is not serializability
concepts.question: How do linearizability and serializability differ, although both suggest a sequential order?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Both words mean something like can be arranged in a sequential order, so they are easily confused.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Serializability is an isolation property of transactions that may read and write several objects. It guarantees they behave as if executed in some serial order. Linearizability is a recency guarantee on reads and writes of a single object, a register.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Linearizability does not group operations into transactions, so it does not prevent problems such as write skew. Serializability does not promise recency.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A requirement mentions an order: decide whether it concerns whole transactions or the freshness of one object.

card.rule: Serializability is about transactions behaving as if run one at a time; linearizability is about recency of reads and writes on one object.
card.limits: A database can offer both, one, or neither. The names are close, but the guarantees are independent.

concepts.title: Both guarantees together, and a case with only one
concepts.question: What is the combination of serializability and linearizability called, and which serializable design lacks the second?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Serializability and linearizability can be combined, but it is not obvious which serializable designs give both.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A database that provides both is said to give strict serializability, also called strong one-copy serializability. Serializable snapshot isolation does not: it reads from a consistent snapshot, which excludes writes more recent than the snapshot.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Snapshot reads avoid lock contention between readers and writers, but they are not guaranteed to see the latest data.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing a serializable implementation for data that must also be read up to date.

card.rule: Strict serializability is serializability plus linearizability, and serializable snapshot isolation gives up the second part.
card.limits: The label names the combination only. It does not tell which implementations achieve it.

concepts.title: Locks and leader election need linearizability
concepts.question: Why must a lock used for electing a leader be linearizable?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A system with single-leader replication must ensure that there is exactly one leader, not several. Two leaders cause split brain.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Elect the leader with a lock. Every node that starts up tries to acquire the lock, and the one that succeeds becomes the leader. The lock must be linearizable, whatever its implementation, so that all nodes agree which node owns it.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A linearizable lock needs coordination between replicas, so it is slower and less available than an unsynchronised one.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Only one node may act as leader, primary or scheduler at a time.

card.rule: A lock that picks a leader must be linearizable, or nodes may disagree about who owns it and the lock is useless.
card.limits: Linearizability gives agreement on who holds the lock, but correct locking has further subtleties, such as fencing.

concepts.title: Coordination services provide the linearizable base
concepts.question: How do ZooKeeper and etcd give applications linearizable locks, and what is stale by default?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Implementing a fault-tolerant, linearizable lock inside each application is hard.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use a coordination service such as Apache ZooKeeper or etcd. They use consensus algorithms to implement linearizable operations in a fault-tolerant way, and they are often used for distributed locks and leader election.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Strictly speaking they provide linearizable writes, but reads may be stale, because by default they can be served by any one replica.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Several nodes need to agree on a lock owner or on a leader and the service must survive node failures.

card.rule: Coordination services use consensus to give linearizable operations, which is the foundation for distributed locks and leader election.
card.limits: Reads from them may be stale unless you ask for a linearizable read, so check how a read is served.

concepts.title: Uniqueness enforced at write time
concepts.question: Why does enforcing a uniqueness rule while data is written call for linearizability?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A username or email address must identify one user. If two people try to create the same one at the same time, one of them must get an error.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Enforce the rule as the data is written, using a linearizable store. All nodes then agree on one up-to-date answer to the question: is this name taken?

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Every registration must be checked against the single agreed state, so it cannot be answered by a nearby stale replica.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A hard uniqueness rule must hold at the moment a write is accepted.

card.rule: To reject a duplicate at write time, all nodes must agree on one up-to-date record of which names are taken, which needs linearizability.
card.limits: A duplicate that is only detected and repaired afterwards does not need this guarantee, but then the conflict is visible for a while.

concepts.title: A username claim as compare-and-set
