concepts.question: How can a username claim be expressed as one atomic operation that only one claimant wins?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A registration must be accepted for one user and refused for any other who asks at the same time.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat the claim as an atomic compare-and-set: set the name to the ID of the user who claims it, provided that the name is not already taken.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The compare-and-set must be linearizable, so every claim is decided against one agreed state.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A key may be claimed once, such as a name, a seat or a lock.

card.rule: Claim a unique key by compare-and-set: it succeeds only if the key is still unclaimed.
card.limits: The compare-and-set only protects a single key. Rules over several keys need more than one register.

concepts.title: Balances, stock and seats
concepts.question: Which constraints on money, stock and seats need one up-to-date value that all nodes agree on?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A bank balance must not go negative, a warehouse must not sell more items than it has, and two people must not book the same seat on a flight or in a theater.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Each of these rules reads and changes one value: the balance, the stock level or the seat occupancy. All nodes need to agree on a single up-to-date copy of it.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Agreement on the latest value slows every update and makes it harder to keep working during network problems.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Overshooting the limit is not acceptable and cannot be repaired later.

card.rule: A hard limit on a balance, stock level or seat needs all nodes to agree on one up-to-date value.
card.limits: Many real businesses tolerate small violations and repair them afterwards, in which case this strict agreement is not needed.

concepts.title: Hard constraints versus other kinds
concepts.question: Which constraints require linearizability, and which can be implemented without it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Not every rule in a database needs the expensive guarantee, but it is hard to tell which ones do.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A hard uniqueness constraint requires linearizability. Other kinds of constraints, such as foreign key or attribute constraints, can be implemented without requiring it.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Choosing the weaker route for the constraints that allow it saves coordination, but you must be sure each one really allows it.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Reviewing the rules of an application to find the few that justify linearizability.

card.rule: Only some constraints, such as hard uniqueness, force linearizability; foreign key and attribute constraints do not.
card.limits: Whether a rule is hard or loose is a business judgement. The book gives the reasoning but does not give a complete list.

concepts.title: Cross-channel timing dependencies
concepts.question: Why does a second communication channel turn a stale read into a visible race?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If Alice had not announced the score, Bob would not have known his result was stale. He would have refreshed again and seen the final score.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The violation was noticed only because there was an additional communication channel: Alice's voice to Bob's ears. The same pattern arises in computer systems when two components talk to each other both through the database and through some other path.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Without the recency guarantee, a race between the two channels is possible. With it, the race cannot occur, but you pay for the guarantee.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A component learns something through one path and then reads the data through another.

card.rule: A stale read becomes a bug when information about the write travels faster through another channel than through the data store.
card.limits: Without a second channel, a stale read is only a delay. The guarantee matters for the paths that carry timing information.

concepts.title: The image resizer race
concepts.question: How can a message queue beat the file store and leave full-size and resized images inconsistent?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A website lets users upload photos and a background resizer makes thumbnails. The web server does not put the multi-megabyte photo on the queue, because message brokers are built for small messages.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The web server first writes the photo to a file storage service, and only when that write completes does it queue the instruction to the resizer. The resizer then fetches the photo from storage.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: If the storage service is not linearizable, the queue may be faster than its internal replication. The resizer may see an old version or nothing.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Reasoning about any pipeline in which one step writes data and another is told to read it.

card.rule: If the store is not linearizable, the message to the worker can arrive before the data it points to.
card.limits: A linearizable store removes the race, but only the two channels in this flow are covered; other paths need their own check.

media.alt: Diagram with a user, Web server, File storage, Message queue and Image resizer. Numbered arrows: 1 user uploads image to web server; 2 web server stores full-size image in file storage; 3 web server sends message to the queue; 4 queue delivers message to image resizer; 5 resizer fetches full-size image from file storage; 6 resizer stores resized image in file storage.

concepts.title: When you control the extra channel
concepts.question: What can you do about a cross-channel race if linearizability is too costly?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A cross-channel race can be removed with a linearizable store, but that guarantee has costs.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: If you control the additional channel, as with a message queue but not with Alice and Bob, use approaches similar to those for reading your own writes. Our reading: for instance, let the message carry the version of the write, so that the reader fetches data at least that recent.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: These techniques add complexity, and each pipeline needs its own design.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You own both channels and a linearizable store is too slow or unavailable.

card.rule: Linearizability is the simplest cure for cross-channel races, not the only one; when you control the channel, you can design around it.
card.limits: The idea assumes you can change the second channel. If you cannot, as with people talking to each other, only a recency guarantee on the store helps.

concepts.title: One copy is simple but fragile
concepts.question: Why is the obvious way to get linearizability unusable on its own?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Linearizability means behaving as though there is a single copy of the data with atomic operations. The simplest answer is to really use only one copy.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Keep the one copy on a single node, and give up on tolerating faults, or add replication and work out which methods can still behave as one copy.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: With one copy, if the node holding it fails, the data is lost, or at least inaccessible until the node is brought up again.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Weighing a single node against replicated designs for something that must act as one copy.

card.rule: A single copy is trivially linearizable but cannot tolerate faults, so real systems replicate and have to work for the guarantee.
card.limits: Replication is the most common approach to fault tolerance, but not every replication method can provide linearizability.

concepts.title: Single-leader replication: potentially linearizable
concepts.question: When can reads from a single-leader database be linearizable, and what can still spoil it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A single-leader database keeps the primary copy on the leader and backup copies on followers. Which reads can behave as one copy?

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Reads from the leader, or from synchronously updated followers, have the potential to be linearizable.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Not every single-leader database is actually linearizable, either by design, for example because it uses snapshot isolation, or because of concurrency bugs.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Planning reads in a leader-based database that must see the latest write.

card.rule: A leader, or a synchronous follower, can serve linearizable reads, but being leader-based does not guarantee it.
card.limits: Potentially is the key word: the design makes linearizability possible and does not provide it by itself.

concepts.title: When the leader is not what it thinks
concepts.question: How can a leader-based database lose linearizability even though reads come from the leader?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Reading from the leader relies on the assumption that you know for sure who the leader is. A node can think it is the leader when it is not, and then it is a delusional leader.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat leader-based linearizability as conditional: it holds only while there is exactly one real leader and acknowledged writes survive a failover.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Closing these gaps needs more than single-leader replication, namely agreement among nodes about who leads.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Judging whether a leader-based design can honestly be called linearizable.

card.rule: Leader-based linearizability depends on the leader really being the leader and on acknowledged writes surviving a failover.
card.limits: These are failure cases. While one genuine leader serves reads and no failover occurs, its reads can be linearizable.

concepts.title: Consensus algorithms make storage linearizable safely
concepts.question: What do consensus algorithms add to single-leader replication that makes linearizable storage safe?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Single-leader replication can be fooled by a delusional leader or by stale replicas, so it cannot promise linearizability.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Some consensus algorithms resemble single-leader replication, but they contain measures that rule out the two failure cases. Thanks to these, consensus algorithms can implement linearizable storage safely.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The extra measures cost coordination: the nodes must agree before an operation counts, and the later sections explain what this costs.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A store must be linearizable and survive node failures, for example one that holds locks.

card.rule: A consensus algorithm is like single-leader replication plus protection against split brain and stale replicas, so it can be linearizable.
card.limits: The protection depends on a majority of nodes being reachable. Without one, the system stops instead of giving up the guarantee.

concepts.title: Multi-leader replication is not linearizable
concepts.question: Why can multi-leader replication not behave as a single copy?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A multi-leader system takes writes at several nodes at once and copies them to the others later.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat it as generally not linearizable. It processes writes concurrently on multiple nodes and replicates them asynchronously.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The design can produce conflicting writes that need resolution. Such conflicts are an artifact of not having a single copy of the data.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You choose multi-leader replication for another benefit, such as working across datacenters, and accept giving up linearizability.

card.rule: Multi-leader systems accept concurrent writes on several nodes and replicate asynchronously, so they are generally not linearizable.
card.limits: Generally is not absolutely: the point is that the design has no single timeline of writes, not that a given read is always stale.

concepts.title: Leaderless replication: probably not linearizable
concepts.question: Why is the claim that quorum reads and writes give strong consistency only roughly true?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: People sometimes claim that Dynamo-style leaderless systems obtain strong consistency by requiring quorum reads and writes, with w + r > n.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat the claim as not quite true. Whether it holds depends on the exact configuration of the quorums and on how strong consistency is defined.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Leaderless designs favour availability, and the simple quorum arithmetic does not buy the single-copy illusion.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A product page says it provides strong consistency through quorums, and you must decide whether to trust it for locks or uniqueness.

card.rule: Do not assume that w + r > n makes a leaderless system linearizable; it probably does not.
card.limits: The wording is probably not: some configurations can be made linearizable at a cost, as a later idea shows.

concepts.title: A strict quorum that is not linearizable
concepts.question: How can reads with w + r > n still return an old value after another read returned the new one?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With variable network delays, strict quorum reads and writes can suffer race conditions.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Take n = 3 and w = 3. A writer sends x = 1 to all three replicas. While the write is in flight, client A reads from two replicas and sees 1 on one of them. Client B then reads from a different pair and gets the old value 0 from both.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: The quorum condition w + r > n is met, yet the execution is not linearizable: B's request begins after A's request completes, but B returns an older value than A.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Checking claims that quorums alone give strong consistency.

card.rule: Quorum overlap does not stop a later read from returning an older value than an earlier read, because the write reaches replicas at different times.
card.limits: The race needs a write in progress and variable delays. Between writes, with every replica updated, the quorum reads agree.

media.alt: Timeline with Writer, Replica 1, 2 and 3, Reader A and Reader B. Writer sends set x = 1 to all three replicas; Replica 3 receives it first and replies ok, Replicas 1 and 2 receive it later. Reader A's get x queries Replica 3, which returns 1, and Replica 2, which returns 0; A gets 1 and 0. Reader B's get x starts after A finishes, queries Replicas 1 and 2 before the write arrives; both return 0.

concepts.title: Paying to make quorums linearizable
concepts.question: What would a Dynamo-style system have to do to make quorum reads and writes linearizable, and what does it cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Strict quorums leave a window in which a later read can return older data than an earlier read.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A reader performs read repair synchronously, before returning results to the application. A writer reads the latest state of a quorum of nodes before sending its writes.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Both steps add work to every operation, so performance is reduced.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You use a leaderless store and need linearizable reads and writes, and can pay for the extra round trips.

card.rule: Quorum reads and writes can be made linearizable by synchronous read repair and by writers reading the latest quorum state first, at the price of speed.
card.limits: This handles reads and writes only. Compare-and-set and last-write-wins resolution still break it.

concepts.title: A network cut between two datacenters
concepts.question: What happens to clients in each datacenter when a network interruption separates them, for single-leader and multi-leader setups?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Two datacenters cannot reach each other, though the network inside each works and clients can reach their datacenter.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: With multi-leader replication, each datacenter carries on, and writes are queued for the other and exchanged once the link is restored. With single-leader replication, the leader sits in one datacenter, so clients elsewhere cannot write or do linearizable reads.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Multi-leader stays available but is not linearizable. Single-leader requires linearizable operations to go to the leader, so clients cut off from it are unavailable.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Comparing replication designs for a multi-datacenter service.

card.rule: During a datacenter split, multi-leader keeps working but may be stale, while single-leader makes cut-off clients wait or fail if they need linearizable operations.
card.limits: The loss is only for clients cut off from the leader and who need linearizable operations. Clients in the leader's datacenter carry on.

media.alt: Two boxes, Datacenter 1 on the left and Datacenter 2 on the right, each holding an Application with an arrow to its DB. A curved replication connection between the two DBs is broken by a mark labelled network interruption (network partition). Below, client figures send arrows to the application in their own datacenter: four on the left, three on the right.

concepts.title: Linearizable or available when disconnected
concepts.question: When replicas are cut off from each other, what must a system that needs linearizability do?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Some replicas are disconnected from the others by a network problem, in a single datacenter or across several.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: If the application requires linearizability, the cut-off replicas cannot process requests: they must wait until the network is fixed or return an error, so they become unavailable. If it does not, each replica can process requests independently, as in multi-leader replication.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Linearizability gives the single-copy illusion but gives up availability under network problems. Dropping it keeps the service up, with non-linearizable behaviour.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Deciding how a service should behave when parts of it cannot talk to each other.

card.rule: When replicas are disconnected, an application that needs linearizability must make some of them unavailable, and one that does not can stay available.
card.limits: The trade applies only during a network problem. When the network works, a system can be both linearizable and available.

concepts.title: The CAP theorem as a trade-off
concepts.question: What trade-off does the CAP theorem describe, and what was it originally for?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A linearizable database becomes unavailable on the disconnected side of a network problem. Systems that do not need linearizability can stay available.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: This insight is popularly known as the CAP theorem. It started as a rule of thumb, without precise definitions, to open a discussion about trade-offs in databases.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The rule says that tolerance of network problems and linearizability pull in opposite directions.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Explaining why a database that stays available during a network cut cannot also be linearizable.

card.rule: CAP says applications that do not need linearizability can tolerate network problems better; it began as a rule of thumb.
card.limits: The popular form has no precise definitions, and later ideas show why it is of limited practical help.

concepts.title: Why pick two out of three misleads
concepts.question: Why is the slogan consistency, availability, partition tolerance, pick two, misleading?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: CAP is sometimes presented as Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance: pick two out of three.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Network partitions are a kind of fault, so they are not something about which you have a choice: they will happen whether you like it or not. When the network works, a system can have both linearizability and total availability. When a fault occurs, you must choose. A better phrasing is either Consistent or Available when Partitioned.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The choice is forced only during a network fault. A more reliable network faces it less often.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Someone describes a database as CP or AP, and you want to restate what it does during a fault.

card.rule: You do not choose partitions; you choose, when one happens, between linearizability and availability.
card.limits: The choice cannot be avoided entirely. A better network makes it less frequent but does not remove it.

concepts.title: How narrow CAP is
concepts.question: Why does the book say CAP has little practical value for designing systems?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: CAP is widely quoted, yet there are several contradictory definitions of availability, and the formal theorem does not match the usual meaning.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Read the theorem as narrow. It considers only one consistency model, linearizability, and one kind of fault, a network partition: nodes that are alive but disconnected from each other.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It says nothing about network delays, dead nodes or other trade-offs, so it cannot guide most design questions.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Judging whether a CAP argument actually answers a question about a real system.

card.rule: CAP covers only linearizability and network partitions, so it is of limited use; more precise results have superseded it.
card.limits: It deserves credit for its influence on database design. The criticism is that it does not help us understand systems better today.

concepts.title: Even RAM is not linearizable
concepts.question: Why is memory on a multi-core CPU not linearizable, and what does that show?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A thread on one core writes to a memory address, and a thread on another core reads the same address shortly afterwards. It is not guaranteed to read the written value.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Every core has its own memory cache and store buffer. Memory access goes to the cache first, and changes are written to main memory asynchronously. This leaves several copies of the data that are updated asynchronously.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The caches make access much faster, which is essential for performance on modern CPUs, but linearizability is lost.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Someone assumes that all fast systems must be linearizable, or that only distributed systems give up the guarantee.

card.rule: Multi-core memory gives up linearizability because per-core caches and store buffers create several asynchronously updated copies.
card.limits: Within one computer the cause is not faults. The guarantee is traded away for speed.

concepts.title: Linearizability is slow all the time
concepts.question: Why do many systems give up linearizability for performance rather than for fault tolerance?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Because of CAP, it is tempting to explain every non-linearizable system by network faults.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In multi-core memory, the reason is performance, not fault tolerance. The same holds for many distributed databases that choose not to provide linearizable guarantees: they do so primarily for speed.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Linearizability is slow, and this is true all the time, not only during a network fault. Dropping it buys speed in normal operation.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Deciding whether a service needs linearizability when its network is usually healthy.

card.rule: Systems usually drop linearizability to be faster, not to survive faults, because linearizability costs time on every operation.
card.limits: Some systems do drop it for availability. The point is that speed alone is often enough reason.

concepts.title: No faster linearizable algorithm exists
concepts.question: Why can no cleverer algorithm make linearizable reads and writes fast on a network with variable delays?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Linearizable storage seems like it might be implemented more efficiently, if only someone found a cleverer algorithm.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Attiya and Welch prove that if you want linearizability, the response time of reads and writes is at least proportional to the uncertainty of delays in the network. In a network with highly variable delays, like most computer networks, the response time is inevitably high.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A faster algorithm for linearizability does not exist. Weaker consistency models can be much faster.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A latency-sensitive system must decide whether to accept weaker guarantees.

card.rule: Linearizable reads and writes cannot be faster than the uncertainty of network delays allows, so weaker models are the only way to be faster.
card.limits: The bound concerns response time on networks with variable delays. It does not say weaker models give up correctness.

concepts.title: Ordering as a recurring theme
concepts.question: Why does ordering keep coming back in this book, and where has it appeared?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A linearizable register behaves as if it has one copy and each operation takes effect at one point in time, which implies operations run in a well-defined order.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Ordering has been a recurring theme: the leader in single-leader replication determines the order of writes in the replication log; serializability makes transactions behave as if executed in some sequential order; and timestamps and clocks are an attempt to introduce order, for example to decide which of two writes happened later.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each context buys order at a different cost: a leader, locks or aborts, or clocks that are only approximately right.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Looking for the common thread behind replication logs, isolation levels and timestamps.

card.rule: Ordering of operations is the thread that links leaders, serializability and timestamps, and it leads to linearizability and consensus.
card.limits: The chapter calls this notion more theoretical and abstract than the rest of the book. Treat it as a way to clarify what systems can and cannot do.

concepts.title: Causality puts cause before effect
concepts.question: What ordering does causality impose on events, and why does it keep coming up?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Some orderings in a system are not optional: an effect must not be seen before its cause.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Causality imposes an ordering on events. Cause comes before effect, a message is sent before it is received, and a question comes before its answer.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Preserving causality takes extra work in a distributed system, where events reach different nodes at different times.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Reasoning about which anomalies a system must prevent for users to find it sensible.

card.rule: Causality orders events so that causes come before effects, and a system should not show an effect without its cause.
card.limits: Causality orders only events that are related as cause and effect. Unrelated events have no causal order between them.

concepts.title: Where causality violations showed up before
concepts.question: Which earlier anomalies in this book were really violations of causality?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Several anomalies met earlier look unrelated, such as odd conversations in a replicated database or rows that seem to be updated before they exist.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: They share one cause. In a conversation, an observer sees the answer before the question, though the person who answered must have seen the question. In multi-leader replication, one replica sees an update to a row that does not exist yet, though a row must be created before it is updated.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Preventing them means keeping track of what depends on what, which costs coordination.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A reported bug shows an effect without its cause and you want to name the guarantee that is missing.

card.rule: Answers seen before questions and updates seen before creations are both causal dependencies that were violated.
card.limits: Not every odd-looking sequence is a causality violation. Concurrent events have no causal link, so either order is fine.

concepts.title: Happened before, and concurrent
concepts.question: How is the happened-before relationship related to concurrency and to causality?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Given two operations A and B, we need a precise way to say whether one of them could have influenced the other.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: There are three possibilities: A happened before B, B happened before A, or A and B are concurrent. The happened-before relationship is another expression of causality.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Concurrency is not a measure of simultaneous clock time. It means that neither operation was in a position to know about the other.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Deciding whether two operations may be applied in any order or must be kept in a fixed order.

card.rule: Two operations are causally ordered if one happened before the other, and concurrent if neither could have known about the other.
card.limits: Concurrent means no causal link, not at the same instant. Operations far apart in clock time can still be concurrent.

concepts.title: Snapshots and skew as causality
concepts.question: In what sense is a consistent snapshot consistent with causality, and how do read skew and write skew relate?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A snapshot of a database is called consistent, but it is not obvious what the word refers to.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Consistent means consistent with causality: if the snapshot contains an answer, it must also contain the question being answered. Observing the entire database at a single point in time makes it consistent with causality, because the effects of all operations that happened causally before that point are visible, and none that happened causally afterwards.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A snapshot avoids causality violations but shows an older state, and it is not the latest one.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Read skew, or non-repeatable reads, means reading data in a state that violates causality.

card.rule: A consistent snapshot shows every effect together with its causes and none of the operations that came causally after it.
card.limits: Consistency with causality does not mean up to date. A snapshot may be old and still be causally consistent.

concepts.title: Causal consistency defined
concepts.question: What does it mean for a system to be causally consistent?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A system needs a name for the guarantee that effects are not seen without their causes.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: If a system obeys the ordering imposed by causality, it is causally consistent. When you read from the database and see some piece of data, you must also be able to see any data that causally precedes it.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The system has to track or enforce the causal order, which costs some bookkeeping.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Users must never see replies without their posts, or results without their inputs.

card.rule: A causally consistent system obeys the ordering that causality imposes, so anything you see comes with what it depended on.
card.limits: Causal consistency says nothing about recency. A reader may be well behind and still be causally consistent.

concepts.title: Total order versus partial order
concepts.question: What is the difference between a total order and a partial order?

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: A total order allows any two elements to be compared, so you can always say which is greater and which is smaller. Natural numbers are totally ordered: of 5 and 13, 13 is greater.

blocks.label: Contrast
blocks.text: Mathematical sets are only partially ordered. Is {a, b} greater than {b, c}? You cannot say, because neither is a subset of the other. They are incomparable.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: Different consistency models impose different kinds of order on operations, so the difference decides what a system can promise.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Asking if every pair of operations in a system must have a defined order.

card.rule: In a total order every pair can be compared; in a partial order some pairs are incomparable.
card.limits: The comparison is about the definition of order. A partial order can still order many pairs, just not all.

concepts.title: A single timeline has no concurrency
concepts.question: Why are there no concurrent operations in a linearizable datastore?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Linearizability and causality both talk about order. They give different orders.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In a linearizable system there is a total order of operations: for any two operations we can say which happened first. There must be a single timeline along which all operations are totally ordered.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Concurrency would mean the timeline branches and merges again, and operations on different branches are incomparable. A linearizable store forbids that.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Telling apart a system with one timeline from one whose history branches and merges.

card.rule: A linearizable datastore has one timeline, so every pair of operations is ordered and nothing is concurrent.
card.limits: Requests may wait together to be handled. They are still handled atomically at one point each, so the timeline has no branches.

concepts.title: Linearizability is stronger than causal consistency
concepts.question: How are linearizability and causality related, and what do linearizable systems gain from that?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Systems with several communication channels need causality to be preserved across them.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Linearizability implies causality: any system that is linearizable preserves causality correctly. With several channels, such as a message queue and a file storage service, causality is preserved automatically.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Linearizability can harm performance and availability, especially where network delays are significant, for instance in a geographically distributed system.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want causality preserved without passing extra information between components, and can pay for linearizability.

card.rule: Every linearizable system preserves causality, which is why it is simple to reason about, but it is stronger than causal consistency requires.
card.limits: The implication runs one way. A system can be causally consistent without being linearizable.

concepts.title: Causal consistency as a middle ground
concepts.question: Is there a guarantee weaker than linearizability that still preserves causality without the cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Linearizability preserves causality but costs performance and availability.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Linearizability is not the only way of preserving causality. A system can be causally consistent without the performance hit of linearizability. Causal consistency is the strongest consistency model that does not slow down due to network delays and remains available in the face of network failures.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It gives up the total order. Some operations are concurrent, so some questions that linearizability answers are left open.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A system needs cause and effect respected but cannot afford to wait for coordination across a slow or unreliable network.

card.rule: Causal consistency is the strongest model that stays fast and available under network delays and failures.
card.limits: It cannot give what a total order gives, such as a uniqueness check that must succeed or fail right now.

concepts.title: Tracking what happened before what
concepts.question: What does a replica need to know, and do, in order to preserve causal order?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A nonlinearizable system can be causally consistent only if it knows which operation happened before which other operation.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Concurrent operations may be processed in any order, but if one operation happened before another, it must be processed first on every replica. A replica that receives an operation must check that all causally preceding operations have been processed. If a preceding operation is missing, the later one waits.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: To tell what an operation depended on, the system must describe the knowledge of a node: whether it had already seen value X when it issued the write Y.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Designing a replicated store that wants causal consistency without a global total order.

card.rule: To keep causal order, delay each operation until everything it causally depends on has been processed.
card.limits: Tracking can be costly. Dependencies across many reads are often unclear, which motivates sequence numbers.

concepts.title: Sequence numbers instead of dependency tracking
concepts.question: Why use sequence numbers or timestamps to order events rather than tracking every causal dependency?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Keeping track of all causal dependencies can become impractical, because the system rarely knows which of a client's earlier reads a new write really depends on.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Order events by sequence numbers or timestamps instead. A timestamp need not come from a time-of-day clock. It can come from a logical clock: an algorithm that generates a sequence of numbers to identify operations, typically with counters that are incremented for every operation.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A single number cannot tell a dependency from coincidence, so the order it gives can be stricter than causality needs.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Causal tracking is too costly and a cheap, comparable label for each operation will do.

card.rule: A logical clock labels each operation with a counter-based number, which orders events more cheaply than tracking every dependency.
card.limits: The numbers order events only as well as the generator allows. Ones that ignore causality are no help, as the next ideas show.

concepts.title: A total order consistent with causality
concepts.question: What promise must sequence numbers keep to be consistent with causality?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Any total order can be defined, but most of them are useless for reasoning about cause and effect.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Create sequence numbers in a total order that is consistent with causality. We promise that if operation A causally happened before B, A occurs before B in the total order, so A has a lower sequence number. Concurrent operations may be ordered arbitrarily.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Such an order captures all the causality information but imposes more ordering than causality strictly requires.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need a single sequence for all operations that never contradicts cause and effect.

card.rule: A causally consistent total order gives a cause a lower number than its effect and may order concurrent operations either way.
card.limits: The extra order between concurrent operations is arbitrary, so the numbers cannot be used to detect concurrency.

concepts.title: The replication log as a sequence
concepts.question: How does single-leader replication already give a total order consistent with causality?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A causally consistent total order needs a source of numbers that follow cause and effect.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In single-leader replication, the replication log defines a total order of write operations consistent with causality. The leader increments a counter for each operation and assigns a monotonically increasing sequence number to each operation in the log.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: All operations pass through one node, which limits throughput and is a single point of failure for ordering.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A single node can sequence all writes, and followers need only apply them in log order.

card.rule: A single leader can number the log with an incrementing counter, which is a total order consistent with causality.
card.limits: It works because one node sees every write. With several leaders, or with partitions, the number source is no longer unique.

concepts.title: Practical number generators that ignore causality
concepts.question: Which common ways of generating sequence numbers are cheap, and what do they have in common?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Without a single leader, nodes still need unique, roughly increasing numbers for their operations.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Three methods are used in practice. Each node generates its own set of numbers, for example one node only odd numbers and another only even numbers. Each operation gets a timestamp from a time-of-day clock, as in last write wins. Nodes preallocate blocks of numbers, say node A takes 1 to 1,000 and node B takes 1,001 to 2,000.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: All three perform better and scale better than pushing every operation through one leader's counter, but the numbers they give are not consistent with causality.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Uniqueness and rough ordering matter more than exact cause and effect.

card.rule: Per-node counters, clock timestamps and preallocated blocks are cheap and scalable, but none is consistent with causality.
card.limits: They give a unique, approximately increasing number. Their weakness is the order across nodes, as the next idea explains.

concepts.title: Why they are inconsistent with causality
concepts.question: How can each cheap number generator give a causally later operation a lower number?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The three cheap generators do not correctly capture the ordering of operations across different nodes.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Odd and even counters: nodes process different numbers of operations per second, so one counter lags the other. Time-of-day timestamps: clock skew can give a causally later operation a lower timestamp. Block allocation: an operation may get a number from 1,001 to 2,000 while a causally later one gets a number from 1 to 1,000.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each has speed and scale, but each can place an effect before its cause.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Checking if a numbering scheme can be relied on to respect cause and effect.

card.rule: Counters at different rates, skewed clocks and separate blocks can each give a later operation a lower number.
card.limits: A scheme that ignores communication between nodes cannot respect causality, whatever its other merits.

concepts.title: A Lamport timestamp is a pair
concepts.question: What is a Lamport timestamp, and how are two of them compared?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The cheap generators are inconsistent with causality, yet a simple method exists that is consistent.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A Lamport timestamp is a pair: (counter, node ID). Each node has a unique identifier and keeps a counter of the operations it has processed. To compare two timestamps, the greater counter wins. Because the node ID is included, every timestamp is unique.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It has no relationship to a physical time-of-day clock, so it cannot be used to answer how long ago something happened.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need a cheap total order of operations across nodes that never contradicts causality.

card.rule: A Lamport timestamp is a (counter, node ID) pair ordered by counter first, so it gives a unique total order that is not tied to physical time.
card.limits: The ordering is consistent with causality only if the counter is carried and updated as the next idea describes.

concepts.title: Carrying the maximum counter
concepts.question: What extra rule makes Lamport timestamps consistent with causality?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Counters alone resemble the odd and even counters, which drift apart and ignore causality.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Every node and every client keeps track of the maximum counter value it has seen so far and includes that maximum on every request. When a node receives a request or response with a maximum greater than its own counter, it immediately increases its counter to that maximum.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Every message carries an extra number, and every node must update its counter when it sees a larger one.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need a cheap order that never puts an effect before its cause, and each operation can carry a counter.

card.rule: Pass the highest counter you have seen along with every request, and move a node's counter forward when it sees a larger one.
card.limits: The rule gives causal order only when the counter travels with every operation. Operations that leave the system without it break the guarantee.

media.alt: Timeline with Client A, Node 1, Node 2, Client B. A writes with max = 0 to Node 1 (counter c = 1) and receives (1, 1). B writes to Node 2 four times with max = 0, 1, 2, 3, counters c = 1 to 4, replies (1, 2), (2, 2), (3, 2), (4, 2). A writes max = 1 to Node 2 (c = 5), gets (5, 2); then writes max = 5 to Node 1 (c = 6), gets (6, 1). B writes max = 4 to Node 2 (c = 6), gets (6, 2).

concepts.title: Lamport timestamps versus version vectors
concepts.question: What can version vectors tell you that Lamport timestamps cannot, and what do Lamport timestamps offer instead?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Lamport timestamps and version vectors look alike, so they are sometimes confused.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: They have different purposes. Version vectors can distinguish whether two operations are concurrent or whether one is causally dependent on the other. Lamport timestamps always enforce a total ordering.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: From the total ordering of Lamport timestamps you cannot tell whether two operations are concurrent or causally dependent. The advantage of Lamport timestamps is that they are more compact.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing between detecting concurrency exactly and labelling operations cheaply.

card.rule: Version vectors reveal concurrency; Lamport timestamps give a compact total order that hides it.
card.limits: Neither replaces the other. Use version vectors when concurrency itself matters, such as detecting conflicts.

concepts.title: A total order is not enough for uniqueness
concepts.question: Why can a node not decide right now on a username using only Lamport timestamps?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Two users concurrently try to create an account with the same username. One should succeed and the other fail.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: With Lamport timestamps you can pick the claim with the lower timestamp after the fact, once all the username operations are collected. But a node that has just received a request must decide right now. It does not know whether another node is concurrently creating the same username, or what timestamp it will assign.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: To be sure, the node would have to check with every other node. If one has failed or cannot be reached, the system grinds to a halt.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Judging whether a timestamp order alone can enforce a constraint that needs an immediate answer.

card.rule: A total order of operations decides the winner only after all operations are known; a node must answer now, before it can know them all.
card.limits: The method does work for deciding winners after the fact. It fails only when an immediate, fault-tolerant answer is needed.

concepts.title: Knowing when the order is final
concepts.question: What do you need besides a total order to implement a uniqueness constraint?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A total order of operations is not enough to enforce uniqueness, as the next ones may still be inserted ahead.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: You also need to know when the order is finalized. If you have an operation to create a username, and you are sure no other node can insert a claim for the same name ahead of yours in the total order, you can declare it successful.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Establishing finality needs coordination between nodes, which is exactly what the cheap numbering schemes avoid.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: An operation must be answered once and for all, such as a username claim, a lock or a seat.

card.rule: To enforce a uniqueness constraint you need a total order plus knowledge of when that order is final.
card.limits: Finality has a cost in coordination and fault tolerance, which the following topic, total order broadcast, addresses.

concepts.title: Total order broadcast
concepts.question: What problem does total order broadcast solve that a single leader and timestamps do not?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Single-leader replication gives a total order by sequencing all operations on one CPU core of the leader. Timestamp ordering is less powerful, since it cannot tolerate faults when used for uniqueness.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Total order broadcast, also called atomic broadcast, is the protocol that gets all nodes to agree on the same total order of operations. It is described as a protocol for exchanging messages between nodes.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The hard parts are scaling when throughput exceeds what a single leader can handle, and handling failover when the leader fails.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Every node must see the same operations in the same order, even when nodes or the network fail.

card.rule: Total order broadcast gets every node to agree on one sequence of messages, without depending on a single fragile leader.
card.limits: It does not say when a message is delivered, only in what order, as a later idea explains.

concepts.title: Two safety properties
concepts.question: Which two properties must a correct total order broadcast always satisfy?

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: Reliable delivery: no messages are lost, so if a message is delivered to one node, it is delivered to all nodes. Totally ordered delivery: messages are delivered to every node in the same order.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: Together these let any node replay the same sequence and reach the same state.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: The properties are safety properties: they must be met even if a node or the network is faulty.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Checking whether a messaging scheme really offers total order broadcast.

card.rule: Total order broadcast promises that every message reaches all nodes and that all nodes see them in the same order.
card.limits: These promises are about safety, not timing. A message may be late, but it may not be lost or delivered out of order.

concepts.title: Ordering per partition versus across partitions
concepts.question: Why does a per-partition leader not give consistency guarantees across partitions?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Partitioned databases often have a single leader per partition, and each leader orders only the writes in its own partition.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Such a database maintains ordering only per partition. It cannot offer consistency guarantees that span partitions.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Total ordering across all partitions is possible, but it requires additional coordination.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A design needs guarantees across partitions and must decide whether it can pay for that coordination.

card.rule: A per-partition order does not give guarantees across partitions; a global order needs extra coordination.
card.limits: Within one partition the order is complete. The gap is only for operations that touch several partitions.

concepts.title: Using total order broadcast for replication
concepts.question: How does total order broadcast keep replicas consistent, and what else can it implement?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Replicas must end up in the same state even though writes arrive at different nodes.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: If every message represents a write to the database, and every replica processes the same writes in the same order, the replicas remain consistent with each other, aside from temporary replication lag.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Writes must be sequenced through the broadcast, so each write waits for its place in the order.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need replicas of a database to be consistent without a single fixed leader.

card.rule: If every replica applies the same writes in the same order, the replicas stay consistent.
card.limits: Replicas may lag, but the lag is temporary. The scheme does not say how fresh a read is.

concepts.title: The order is fixed when delivered
concepts.question: Why is total order broadcast stronger than timestamp ordering?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With timestamps, a message with a lower timestamp may show up after later ones have been processed.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In total order broadcast the order is fixed at the time the messages are delivered. A node is not allowed to retroactively insert a message into an earlier position if subsequent messages have already been delivered.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The broadcast must delay delivery until it is sure no earlier message can still appear, which costs time.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A decision, such as a username claim, must be final as soon as a message is delivered.

card.rule: Once a message is delivered, nothing can be inserted ahead of it, which is what makes the order final.
card.limits: Final does not mean immediate. Delivery can be late, but never reordered.

concepts.title: Total order broadcast as a log
concepts.question: What does it mean to view total order broadcast as a log, and what does a lock service gain from it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Systems keep several kinds of log: replication log, transaction log and write-ahead log.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Total order broadcast can be seen as creating a log: delivering a message is like appending to the log. Since all nodes deliver the same messages in the same order, all nodes can read the log and see the same sequence of messages.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The log grows, and every reader must follow it in order.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want to build services such as replication or locks on a shared, ordered history.

card.rule: Delivering a message is appending to a shared log that every node reads in the same order.
card.limits: The log view says nothing about timing. A node may read it later than another does.

concepts.title: Total order broadcast versus linearizability
concepts.question: In what way are total order broadcast and linearizability close but different?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Both put operations in a total order, so they are easily taken for the same thing.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Total order broadcast is asynchronous: messages are guaranteed to be delivered reliably in a fixed order, but there is no guarantee about when a message is delivered. Linearizability is a recency guarantee: a read is guaranteed to see the latest value written.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Total order broadcast gives order without recency. Linearizability gives recency, which costs coordination on every read and write.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A requirement needs agreement on order, and you must decide whether it also needs freshness.

card.rule: Total order broadcast fixes the order but not the timing; linearizability promises the latest value.
card.limits: They are closely linked. Each can be built from the other, as the next ideas show.

concepts.title: Compare-and-set on a total order log
concepts.question: How can an append-only log with total order broadcast decide which of several competing claims wins?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You need a linearizable compare-and-set, such as claiming a unique username, but the only primitive you have is total order broadcast used as an append-only log.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Append a message tentatively claiming the name. Read the log until your message is delivered back to you. If yours is the first claim for that name, commit and acknowledge it; if another user's claim is first, abort.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The client has to wait for its own message to come back around before it learns the outcome, which adds delay to every claim.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Several nodes may concurrently claim the same value and every node must agree on the single winner.

card.rule: Append the claim, wait for it to be delivered back, and the first claim for that name in the log wins.
card.limits: The winner is whichever claim sits first in the log, which every node sees identically, not whichever was sent first.

concepts.title: Linearizable writes, stale reads
concepts.question: The log gives linearizable writes. Why can reads still be stale, and how do you fix that?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The log-based procedure makes writes linearizable, but a read from a store that is updated asynchronously from the log may return a stale value.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: What the procedure provides is sequential consistency, also called timeline consistency, slightly weaker than linearizability. To make reads linearizable you can sequence the read through the log, wait for the log's latest position to be delivered, or read from a synchronously updated replica.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each fix costs something: an extra log round trip, a wait for the replica to catch up, or reliance on a synchronous replica.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Readers must see the latest write, not merely a consistent order of events.

card.rule: Log-ordered writes are linearizable, but reads need one of three extra steps to become linearizable too.
card.limits: Without the extra steps everyone agrees on the order of writes, yet a read can still lag behind the latest one.

concepts.title: Total order broadcast from a linearizable register
concepts.question: Given linearizable storage, how can you build total order broadcast from it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You have linearizable storage and want total order broadcast on top of it, the reverse of the previous construction.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Keep an integer in a linearizable register with an atomic increment-and-get. For each message, increment-and-get, attach the result as its sequence number, send it to all nodes and resend lost ones. Recipients deliver messages consecutively by sequence number.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Making the counter itself fault tolerant is the hard part, since a single node's variable fails when the node does.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want to see how recency and ordering guarantees relate, or you need gap-free numbering.

card.rule: Gap-free numbers from a linearizable counter become a total order when recipients deliver them in sequence.
card.limits: The scheme is easy only if nothing fails; keeping the counter alive through crashes and network breaks is the real problem.

concepts.title: Equivalent to consensus
concepts.question: What do a linearizable compare-and-set register and total order broadcast have in common?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: One construction builds compare-and-set from total order broadcast, and the other builds total order broadcast from an increment-and-get register. What does that say about how hard each is?

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Each can be transformed into the other, and both are equivalent to consensus. If you can solve one of them, you can turn it into a solution for the others.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: None of them is easier than the rest, so building any fault-tolerantly means solving consensus.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You are judging which parts of a design secretly need a consensus algorithm.

card.rule: A linearizable compare-and-set register and total order broadcast are both equivalent to consensus.
card.limits: The equivalence concerns registers with atomic operations; be clear which kind of register is meant.

concepts.title: Where nodes must agree
concepts.question: In which situations must nodes agree, and what goes wrong if they do not?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Informally consensus is just getting several nodes to agree on something, but without it nodes diverge or disagree on an outcome.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Two classic cases. In leader election all nodes must agree on which node leads, to avoid split brain. In atomic commit all nodes must agree to commit or all must abort a transaction that spans nodes.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The goal sounds easy, but the topic is subtle and builds on replication, transactions, system models and ordering.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A design needs every node to settle on one outcome even when some nodes cannot talk to others.

card.rule: Leader election and atomic commit are both situations where all nodes must agree on a single outcome.
card.limits: Agreement must hold even when a network fault cuts some nodes off from the rest.

concepts.title: The FLP impossibility result
concepts.question: If consensus is provably impossible when nodes may crash, why do real systems reach it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The FLP result proves no algorithm can always reach consensus if a node may crash, and nodes may crash in any distributed system. Yet consensus algorithms exist.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The proof is in the asynchronous system model, a restrictive model with a deterministic algorithm that cannot use clocks or timeouts. Let the algorithm use timeouts, or any way of suspecting crashed nodes even if sometimes wrong, and consensus becomes solvable.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Suspicion can be wrong, so practical algorithms accept some false alarms and wasted effort.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You read an impossibility result: check which model it assumes before applying it to your system.

card.rule: FLP forbids consensus only in a restrictive model with no clocks or timeouts, not in practice.
card.limits: FLP is of great theoretical importance, but it is not a verdict that real systems cannot agree.

concepts.title: Atomic commit and consensus compared
concepts.question: How does atomic commit differ in its rules from consensus, and are they really the same problem?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Atomic commit and consensus are stated slightly differently, so it is not obvious they are the same problem.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In atomic commit, a transaction can commit only if all participants vote to commit and must abort if any participant needs to abort. Consensus may decide any value proposed by one of the participants. Even so, each is reducible to the other.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Nonblocking atomic commit is harder than consensus, so the equivalence covers only the ordinary, blocking form.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want to treat two-phase commit as a consensus algorithm and judge its quality that way.

card.rule: Atomic commit and consensus are formulated differently but reduce to each other.
card.limits: The equivalence does not extend to the nonblocking form, which is harder than consensus.

concepts.title: Atomic commit on a single node
concepts.question: How does one database node make a commit atomic across a crash?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A node can crash in the middle of committing, and the transaction must end up either fully committed or fully rolled back.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The storage engine makes the transaction's writes durable, typically in a write-ahead log, and then appends a commit record to the log on disk. On restart, a transaction whose commit record reached disk is committed; otherwise its writes are rolled back.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Everything depends on the order of durable writes, so the engine must never write the commit record before the data.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want to see what a distributed commit has to replace once several nodes are involved.

card.rule: On one node, commit depends on the order of durable writes: first the data, then the commit record.
card.limits: This relies on one log on one node; it does not extend by itself to a transaction spanning several nodes.

concepts.title: Why independent commits fail
concepts.question: Why is sending a commit request to each node and letting each commit on its own not enough?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A transaction spans several nodes, such as partitions or a secondary index on another node, and each would commit independently.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Three things can split the outcome. Some nodes detect a conflict and must abort while others commit. Some commit requests are lost and time out while others arrive. Some nodes crash before the commit record is written and roll back while others commit.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Avoiding the split needs extra coordination, which means more messages and waiting.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You are explaining why a distributed commit needs a protocol rather than a broadcast.

card.rule: Independent commits let nodes disagree, so one round of commit requests cannot give atomicity.
card.limits: Any one of conflict, message loss or crash is enough to split the outcome.

concepts.title: Commits are irrevocable
concepts.question: Can a committed transaction be taken back, and what can you do instead?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A node that has committed may later learn that another node aborted, and would like to take its commit back.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A commit must be irrevocable: you may not change your mind and retroactively abort. The effects of a committed transaction can later be undone by another, compensating transaction.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A compensating transaction is a separate transaction to the database, so correctness across the pair is the application's problem.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You must decide whether an undo belongs inside atomic commit or in application logic.

card.rule: A commit is irrevocable; the only undo is a separate compensating transaction.
card.limits: The database offers no guarantee across the original and the compensating transaction.

concepts.title: Two-phase commit
concepts.question: How does two-phase commit get all nodes to commit or all to abort?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A transaction spanning several nodes must end with all nodes committing or all aborting, even though messages can be lost.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Split commit into two phases. In phase 1 a coordinator sends a prepare request to each node asking whether it can commit. If all reply yes, the coordinator sends commit in phase 2. If any replies no, it sends abort to all.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It adds round trips and a new component, the coordinator, on which every transaction depends.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A transaction spans several database nodes that must reach the same outcome.

card.rule: Phase 1 asks every node whether it can commit, and phase 2 commits only if all said yes.
card.limits: The coordinator's decision, once taken, is what phase 2 carries out; it is not a fresh vote.

media.alt: Timeline with Coordinator, Database 1 and Database 2. Coordinator sends write data to each database, each replying ok. In phase 1 it sends prepare to both and each replies yes. In phase 2 it sends commit to both and each replies ok. A grey bar on each database, running from its write data until after commit is processed, marks locks held by the transaction.

concepts.title: The coordinator, and 2PC versus 2PL
concepts.question: What is the coordinator, and how do two-phase commit and two-phase locking differ?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The names sound alike, and 2PC brings a component that single-node transactions do not have.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: 2PC provides atomic commit in a distributed database, while two-phase locking provides serializable isolation. Treat them as entirely separate concepts. 2PC also uses a coordinator, which is also known as the transaction manager.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The coordinator is an extra moving part, and its failure matters to every transaction it handles.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You read a design that mentions two phases and must say which problem it solves.

card.rule: 2PC gives atomic commit across nodes and 2PL gives serializable isolation; they are unrelated.
card.limits: Do not carry intuitions about locks over to commit, or the reverse.

concepts.title: A yes vote is a promise
concepts.question: Prepare and commit messages can be lost in 2PC too, so why does 2PC still give atomicity?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Prepare and commit requests can be lost in the two-phase case just as in the one-phase case, so something else must make 2PC different.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: On a prepare request, a participant makes sure it can definitely commit under all circumstances: it writes all transaction data to disk and checks for conflicts and constraint violations. By replying yes it promises to commit without error if requested, surrendering the right to abort.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: After voting yes, the participant no longer controls the outcome and depends on the coordinator.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need to explain why a yes vote can be relied on by the coordinator.

card.rule: A yes vote is a promise to commit if asked, and the participant gives up the right to abort.
card.limits: Voting yes does not commit the transaction; the coordinator may still decide to abort.

concepts.title: The commit point and endless retries
concepts.question: Once all votes are in, what must the coordinator do before telling anyone, and what if messages fail?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: After collecting votes, the coordinator makes a decision that it must never forget, even if it crashes immediately.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: With all responses in, the coordinator decides to commit only if every participant voted yes. It writes the decision to its transaction log on disk; that write is the commit point. Only then does it send commit or abort, retrying until it succeeds.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Retrying forever means a participant that is down keeps being chased until it comes back.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need to explain why a coordinator persists its decision before sending it.

card.rule: The coordinator logs its decision to disk first, then sends it, retrying until every participant has it.
card.limits: The log write has to come before any commit or abort message; swapping them loses the decision on a crash.

concepts.title: Two points of no return
concepts.question: Which two events make 2PC atomic?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Messages and nodes can fail, so you need to know what exactly stops the protocol from drifting into a split outcome.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: There are two crucial points of no return. When a participant votes yes, it promises it will definitely be able to commit later, although the coordinator may still abort. When the coordinator decides, that decision is irrevocable.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Both promises remove flexibility: others can rely on them, but nobody can back out afterwards.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You check any commit protocol by finding where each party can no longer change its mind.

card.rule: A yes vote and the coordinator's decision are the two points of no return that ensure atomicity.
card.limits: Before each point, the party may still abort; after it, it cannot.

concepts.title: In doubt after coordinator failure
concepts.question: What happens to a participant that voted yes when the coordinator disappears?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If the coordinator crashes after participants have voted yes, they cannot decide the outcome themselves.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A participant that voted yes and has not heard the result is in doubt, also called uncertain. It cannot abort on its own, because another participant may have committed, and cannot commit on its own, because another may have aborted. It has to wait to hear the outcome from the coordinator.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The participant is stuck until the coordinator recovers, and a timeout does not help.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You predict where a 2PC system stalls after a coordinator crash.

card.rule: An in-doubt participant must wait, because neither committing nor aborting alone is safe.
card.limits: Waiting is the only safe action; any guess risks disagreeing with another participant.

media.alt: Timeline with Coordinator, Database 1 and Database 2. Coordinator sends write data (both ok), then prepare in phase 1 (both reply yes). In phase 2 the coordinator crashes, shown by an explosion and a grey crashed bar. The commit request reaches Database 2, which replies ok; the commit to Database 1 never arrives, and its line is labelled stuck in prepared state.

concepts.title: Blocking commit and three-phase commit
concepts.question: Can an atomic commit protocol avoid blocking, and why is 2PC still used?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: 2PC can get stuck waiting for the coordinator to recover, so it is called a blocking atomic commit protocol.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In theory an atomic commit protocol can be nonblocking, so that it does not get stuck when a node fails. Three-phase commit is an alternative, but it assumes bounded network delay and bounded response times.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Real systems have unbounded network delay and process pauses, so 3PC cannot guarantee atomicity there.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You explain why 2PC remains in use despite its known coordinator-failure problem.

card.rule: 2PC blocks on coordinator failure, and 3PC avoids blocking only under timing bounds that practice cannot promise.
card.limits: Process pauses and unbounded delay are what undermine the bounded-timing assumptions of 3PC.

concepts.title: The mixed reputation of distributed transactions
concepts.question: Why are distributed transactions both valued and criticized, and where does the cost come from?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Distributed transactions give an important safety guarantee that is hard to get otherwise, yet they are criticized for operational problems, poor performance and promising more than they deliver.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Rather than dismiss them, look at the cost. Much of the performance cost of two-phase commit comes from the additional disk forcing (fsync) needed for crash recovery and from the additional network round trips.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The extra safety is paid for in speed and in operational burden.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You weigh the safety guarantee against the cost in your own system.

card.rule: Two-phase commit trades performance and operability for a safety guarantee that is hard to get otherwise.
card.limits: The cost differs between implementations, so examine the specific kind of distributed transaction.

concepts.title: Internal versus heterogeneous transactions
concepts.question: What are the two kinds of distributed transaction, and which is harder?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Two quite different kinds of distributed transaction are often conflated, though they behave very differently.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Database-internal transactions run among the nodes of one distributed database, all running the same software. Heterogeneous transactions span two or more different technologies, such as databases from different vendors or non-database systems like message brokers.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A heterogeneous transaction must still reach atomic commit even though the systems differ underneath.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You judge whether a planned distributed transaction is likely to be practical.

card.rule: Internal distributed transactions often work quite well, while heterogeneous ones are a lot more challenging.
card.limits: Both need atomic commit; the difference is how much one vendor controls the protocol.

concepts.title: Exactly-once message processing
concepts.question: How can atomic commit across a broker and a database make message processing effectively exactly once?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A consumer processes a message and writes results to a database. A failure halfway can leave the message processed twice or lost.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Commit the message acknowledgment and the database writes in a single distributed transaction. If either the message delivery or the database transaction fails, both abort, so the broker may redeliver the message later.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Every system touched by the processing has to take part in the same atomic commit protocol.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A broker and a database, possibly on different machines, must stay consistent.

card.rule: Atomically committing the acknowledgment with the processing writes makes handling effectively exactly once.
card.limits: It protects only the side effects that take part in the transaction.

concepts.title: XA transactions
concepts.question: How does XA let different systems take part in one two-phase commit?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Heterogeneous systems need a common way to take part in the same two-phase commit.

blocks.label: Approach
