blocks.text: X/Open XA, introduced in 1991, is a standard for 2PC across heterogeneous technologies. It is not a network protocol but a C API for interfacing with a transaction coordinator, with bindings in other languages, such as the Java Transaction API.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Participants must be reached through XA-capable drivers, and the driver has to expose callbacks for prepare, commit and abort.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Databases and message brokers from different vendors need one atomic commit.

card.rule: XA is a standard C API, not a network protocol, through which drivers let a coordinator run 2PC.
card.limits: It only works where the client driver or library for each system supports XA.

concepts.title: Locks held while in doubt
concepts.question: Why does an in-doubt transaction hurt the rest of the system?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: It is tempting to ignore a transaction stuck in doubt and let the rest of the system carry on.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Transactions take row-level exclusive locks on rows they modify, to prevent dirty writes, and cannot release them until they commit or abort. So an in-doubt transaction keeps its locks the whole time, and others that touch those rows must wait.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: 2PC's safety is paid for with locks held for as long as the coordinator is unavailable.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You estimate the blast radius of a coordinator outage.

card.rule: An in-doubt transaction keeps its locks, so anyone needing those rows is blocked until the doubt ends.
card.limits: Large parts of an application can become unavailable until the in-doubt transaction is resolved.

concepts.title: Orphaned transactions and heuristic decisions
concepts.question: What if the coordinator can never decide an in-doubt transaction?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A coordinator may be unable to decide the outcome of an in-doubt transaction, for example because its log was lost or corrupted by a software bug. Such transactions are orphaned.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Orphans cannot be resolved automatically, so they sit holding locks and blocking others. Even restarting the database servers does not clear them. An administrator must check each participant for an existing commit or abort and apply the same outcome to the others.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Resolution is manual, slow, and likely done under stress during a serious outage.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You plan operations and runbooks for a 2PC deployment.

card.rule: An orphaned in-doubt transaction needs a human to apply one outcome to every participant.
card.limits: In theory the coordinator recovers cleanly from its log; in practice orphans do occur.

concepts.title: Limitations of XA transactions
concepts.question: What makes XA transactions troublesome in operation?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: XA solves the real problem of keeping several data systems consistent, but it brings major operational issues.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The coordinator is itself a kind of database, storing transaction outcomes, so it needs the care of any important database. XA must suit many data systems, so it is a lowest common denominator. And for 2PC to commit, every participant must respond.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A broken part anywhere makes the transaction fail, so distributed transactions amplify failures.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You choose between XA and other ways of keeping systems consistent.

card.rule: The coordinator needs database-grade care, XA is a lowest common denominator, and failures get amplified.
card.limits: Database-internal transactions escape some of these limits; heterogeneous XA does not.

concepts.title: Consensus defined as propose and decide
concepts.question: How is consensus stated precisely, in terms of proposing and deciding?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Informally consensus means getting nodes to agree, but to design and judge an algorithm you need a precise statement of the problem.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: One or more nodes may propose values, and the consensus algorithm decides on one of those values. In a seat-booking example, each node handling a customer proposes that customer's ID, and the decision says who got the seat.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A precise definition must also say what holds when nodes fail, which is where the properties come in.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You map a real choice, such as who wins the last seat, onto propose and decide.

card.rule: Consensus means some nodes propose values and the algorithm decides on one of the proposed values.
card.limits: Four properties constrain the decision; the following cards cover them.

concepts.title: Agreement, integrity and validity
concepts.question: What do the first three consensus properties guarantee, and what do they rule out?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A definition of consensus must capture a shared, final outcome while ruling out trivial cheats.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Uniform agreement: no two nodes decide differently. Integrity: no node decides twice. Validity: if a node decides value v, then v was proposed by some node.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: These three alone are easy to satisfy by cheating, so they cannot be the whole definition.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You check whether a protocol really solves consensus or only looks as if it does.

card.rule: Agreement means no two nodes decide differently, integrity means no node decides twice, validity means the value was proposed.
card.limits: They say what must not happen; they do not say that anything must happen.

concepts.title: Termination as fault tolerance
concepts.question: Which property makes consensus fault tolerant, and what does it demand?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A dictator satisfies the first three properties, but if it fails nobody can decide anything, so the definition must demand fault tolerance.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Termination: every node that does not crash eventually decides some value. The algorithm cannot sit idle forever; even when some nodes fail, the others must still reach a decision. Termination is a liveness property, and the other three are safety properties.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Demanding progress rules out any design that waits for a failed node to come back.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You test whether a design is genuinely fault tolerant or just has a single point of decision.

card.rule: Termination requires that nodes which do not crash eventually decide, even when other nodes fail.
card.limits: In this model a crashed node disappears and does not come back.

concepts.title: A majority is needed for termination
concepts.question: How many nodes must work for consensus to make progress, and what stays true when they do not?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If all nodes crash and none is running, no algorithm can decide anything, so fault tolerance has a limit.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: It can be proved that any consensus algorithm requires at least a majority of nodes to be functioning correctly to assure termination. That majority can safely form a quorum.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A large outage can stop the system from handling requests.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You size a consensus cluster for the failures you want to survive.

card.rule: Termination holds only while a majority of the nodes are working.
card.limits: Progress needs the majority; the safety properties are a separate matter.

concepts.title: Consensus and Byzantine faults
concepts.question: Do standard consensus algorithms tolerate nodes that misbehave?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Consensus algorithms usually assume nodes either follow the protocol or crash, but a node might misbehave.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Most consensus algorithms assume there are no Byzantine faults. A node that does not correctly follow the protocol can break the safety properties. Consensus can be made robust against Byzantine faults, but those algorithms are beyond this chapter.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Byzantine tolerance needs more complex algorithms and more nodes than crash tolerance.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You decide whether your threat model needs only crash tolerance or Byzantine tolerance as well.

card.rule: Typical consensus tolerates crashing nodes, not nodes that deliberately or accidentally misbehave.
card.limits: A misbehaving node can break safety even when a majority of nodes is healthy.

concepts.title: Consensus algorithms are total order broadcast
concepts.question: How are real consensus algorithms related to total order broadcast?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The formal model decides a single value, but real systems need an ordered stream of decisions.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The best-known fault-tolerant algorithms, Viewstamped Replication, Paxos, Raft and Zab, decide on a sequence of values, which makes them total order broadcast algorithms. Total order broadcast is equivalent to repeated rounds of consensus, one decision per message delivered.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The algorithms are similar but not the same, and implementing one yourself is hard and probably not advisable.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You read about or choose a consensus system and expect a log rather than a single decision.

card.rule: Real consensus algorithms decide a sequence of values, so they are total order broadcast algorithms.
card.limits: The shared high-level ideas matter more than the full detail of each algorithm.

concepts.title: A manually chosen leader
concepts.question: Single-leader replication looks like total order broadcast, so why did Chapter 5 not need consensus?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Single-leader replication applies writes in the same order on followers, much like total order broadcast, yet no consensus was needed there.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: It depends on how the leader is chosen. If humans on the operations team choose and configure the leader, you have a dictatorial kind of consensus: only one node accepts writes, and if it fails writes stop until operators configure another.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It can work well in practice, but progress needs human intervention, so termination is not satisfied.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You judge a failover design by asking who or what picks the next leader.

card.rule: A manually chosen leader is consensus of the dictatorial variety, and it fails the termination property.
card.limits: It is a fine operational choice, but it is not a consensus algorithm in the full sense.

concepts.title: To elect a leader you first need a leader
concepts.question: Why does leader election seem to be a circular problem?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Consensus algorithms are total order broadcast algorithms, total order broadcast is like single-leader replication, and single-leader replication needs a leader.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: To elect a leader we seem to need a leader first, and to solve consensus we must first solve consensus. The circle is broken by weakening what the leader promises, which the next idea explains.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Without breaking the circle, every design needs an outside tie-breaker such as a human.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You wonder why consensus protocols never rely on one permanent leader.

card.rule: Electing a leader needs consensus, and consensus seems to need a leader first.
card.limits: The loop is only apparent; it assumes that the leader must be unique at all times.

concepts.title: Epoch numbers and leader uniqueness
concepts.question: How can a protocol live without a globally unique leader and still avoid conflicting decisions?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Protocols cannot promise a single leader at all times, yet two leaders deciding at once would be disastrous.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: They define an epoch number and guarantee that within each epoch the leader is unique. When the leader is thought dead, a vote starts with an incremented epoch number. If leaders from two epochs conflict, the one with the higher epoch number prevails.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A deposed leader may not know it has been replaced, so it has to check before it decides.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You explain how consensus avoids split brain without a permanent leader.

card.rule: Epoch numbers are totally ordered, each epoch has one leader, and the higher epoch wins.
card.limits: Uniqueness holds within one epoch, not across all time.

concepts.title: Two overlapping quorum votes
concepts.question: How does a leader know it has not been ousted before it decides?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A node cannot trust its own belief that it leads, so a leader needs proof that no higher epoch exists.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The leader collects votes from a quorum for every decision. There are two rounds of voting: one to choose a leader, and one on the leader's proposal. A node votes for a proposal only if it knows of no leader with a higher epoch. The two quorums must overlap.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Every decision costs a round of messages to a quorum.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You explain why a decision approved by a quorum is safe.

card.rule: The quorum voting on a proposal overlaps the quorum that elected the leader, so a higher epoch would be noticed.
card.limits: A successful vote on a proposal includes at least one node that took part in the latest election.

concepts.title: Why consensus differs from 2PC
concepts.question: The voting in consensus looks like two-phase commit. What makes one fault tolerant and the other blocking?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The voting in fault-tolerant consensus looks superficially like two-phase commit, yet 2PC blocks on a coordinator failure and consensus does not.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In 2PC the coordinator is not elected and needs a yes vote from every participant. Fault-tolerant consensus elects its leader and needs votes from only a majority of nodes.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Consensus needs more machinery than 2PC: elections, epochs and quorum rules.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You argue why 2PC is not a good consensus algorithm.

card.rule: Consensus elects its leader and needs only a majority, which is why it tolerates faults that stop 2PC.
card.limits: These differences are what make consensus correct and fault tolerant; the surface similarity misleads.

concepts.title: The cost of consensus
concepts.question: Why is consensus not used everywhere?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Consensus is a breakthrough, but its benefits come at a cost, so it is not used everywhere.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Voting on proposals before they are decided is a kind of synchronous replication. Consensus also requires a strict majority. After a network failure only the majority side can make progress, and the rest is blocked.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You pay in write latency and in a blocked minority, in return for strong safety.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You choose between consensus and cheaper replication that accepts weaker guarantees.

card.rule: Consensus buys safety with synchronous voting and a strict majority requirement.
card.limits: The blocked minority is the same price that linearizability pays under network partitions.

concepts.title: Where consensus is fragile
concepts.question: What practical weak spots do consensus algorithms have besides their cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Beyond cost, consensus algorithms have practical weak points that show up in real networks.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Most assume a fixed set of nodes, so adding or removing nodes is not free. They rely on timeouts to detect failed leaders, so a transient network issue can trigger a needless election. Some are particularly sensitive to specific network problems.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: False suspicion does not harm safety, but frequent elections can leave the system choosing a leader more than doing useful work.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You plan a deployment across regions with variable network delays.

card.rule: Consensus stays safe under false suspicion, but repeated elections can make it useless.
card.limits: More robust algorithms for unreliable networks are still an open research problem.

concepts.title: ZooKeeper holds small data and outsources coordination
concepts.question: If ZooKeeper and etcd look like key-value stores, why do they implement consensus, and what are they for?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: ZooKeeper and etcd have an API much like a database, yet they implement a consensus algorithm, which an ordinary database does not.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: They hold small amounts of data that fit entirely in memory, still written to disk for durability, and replicate it to all nodes using a fault-tolerant total order broadcast algorithm. Applications outsource coordination to them.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: They are not suited as a general-purpose database, so you would not store all of your application's data there.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A cluster that may grow large needs agreement on a few facts, such as who leads which partition.

card.rule: ZooKeeper and etcd replicate a small amount of data with total order broadcast so that applications can outsource coordination.
card.limits: They suit slow-changing information, not data that changes constantly.

concepts.title: Locks and fencing tokens from a coordination service
concepts.question: Which ZooKeeper features let nodes take locks safely?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Nodes racing for a resource need a lock that only one can win, and the resource needs protection from a client that paused.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Linearizable atomic operations, such as compare-and-set, implement a lock: if several nodes try at once, only one succeeds. A distributed lock is usually a lease with an expiry time. Total ordering of operations gives every operation a monotonically increasing ID that can serve as a fencing token.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Without expiry a failed holder would block the lock forever, and without fencing a paused holder could still corrupt the resource.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A shared resource must be accessed by only one client at a time.

card.rule: Atomic compare-and-set gives locks, and the total ordering of operations gives fencing tokens.
card.limits: A lock alone does not stop a paused client; the fencing token does.

concepts.title: Failure detection and change notifications
concepts.question: How does a coordination service detect failed clients and tell others, without polling?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Clients need to learn when other clients join or fail, and locks held by dead clients must be freed.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Clients keep a long-lived session and exchange heartbeats with the servers. If heartbeats stop for longer than the session timeout, the session is declared dead, and locks held by it can be released automatically as ephemeral nodes. Clients can watch values and get notifications of changes.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A slow but healthy client can be declared dead if its heartbeats are delayed.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need to notice joins and failures without frequent polling.

card.rule: Sessions with heartbeats detect failures, ephemeral nodes free locks, and watches avoid polling.
card.limits: The service is useful because of the combination of these features, not any one alone.

concepts.title: Allocating work to nodes
concepts.question: How can a coordination service pick leaders and assign partitions as nodes come and go?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A service with several instances needs one chosen as leader, or partitions of a resource need assigning to nodes as nodes join and fail.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Combine atomic operations, ephemeral nodes and notifications. One instance claims leadership and another takes over if it fails. As nodes join, some partitions move to them to rebalance load, and as nodes leave, others take over their work.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Doing this correctly is hard, but much easier than building the consensus yourself.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need automatic recovery from faults without human intervention.

card.rule: Atomic operations, ephemeral nodes and notifications let a cluster recover from faults without humans.
card.limits: It automates recovery only when it is implemented correctly.

concepts.title: Service discovery does not need consensus
concepts.question: Does finding the address of a service require consensus?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In cloud datacenters virtual machines come and go, so services do not know each other's IP addresses ahead of time.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Services register their network endpoints in a service registry when they start, and others look them up. ZooKeeper, etcd and Consul are often used for this. But DNS, the traditional lookup, uses multiple layers of caching for performance and availability, and its reads are not linearizable.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Slightly stale results are usually not considered a problem; reliable availability matters more.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You decide whether lookups need linearizable reads or only available ones.

card.rule: Service discovery does not require consensus, although leader election does.
card.limits: Stale lookups are tolerable only if clients can retry or recover from a wrong address.

concepts.title: Membership services
concepts.question: How can nodes agree on who is alive when failure detection is unreliable?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Because of unbounded network delays, you cannot reliably tell whether another node has failed, yet a cluster needs a shared view of who is in it.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A membership service determines which nodes are currently active, live members of a cluster. Couple failure detection with consensus, and nodes can agree on which nodes should be considered alive.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A node can still be wrongly declared dead even though it is alive.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Group decisions depend on who is currently in the cluster.

card.rule: Failure detection plus consensus gives the cluster agreement on membership, even if the detector is sometimes wrong.
card.limits: Agreement on a possibly wrong membership is still more useful than disagreement.

concepts.title: Six problems that reduce to consensus
concepts.question: Which seemingly different problems are really the same problem as consensus?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Many parts of a system look unrelated, yet each requires the system to decide one thing so that everyone agrees and the decision is irrevocable.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A wide range of problems reduce to consensus and are equivalent: a linearizable compare-and-set register, atomic transaction commit, total order broadcast, locks and leases, a membership or coordination service, and a uniqueness constraint.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Solving one of them fault-tolerantly means paying the cost of consensus for all of them.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You list requirements for a design and want to see which of them secretly need consensus.

card.rule: Six problems are equivalent to consensus: solving one lets you transform it into a solution for the others.
card.limits: On a single node each is easy; the difficulty is tolerating failures of the decision-maker.

concepts.title: Decision power vested in one leader
concepts.question: Why do single-leader databases get strong guarantees so cheaply?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Consensus-hard problems become easy if one node is allowed to make every decision.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In a single-leader database all the power to make decisions is vested in the leader, so it can order operations and settle conflicts by itself, with no vote.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: If the single leader fails or becomes unreachable, the system cannot make progress.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You explain what a single-leader database gets for free and what it risks.

card.rule: Giving one node all the decision power makes everything easy until that node fails.
card.limits: The weakness lies in the leader's failure, not in the quality of its decisions.

concepts.title: Three ways to handle a failed leader
concepts.question: What can a single-leader system do when its leader fails or is unreachable?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: When the single leader fails or a network interruption makes it unreachable, the system cannot make progress.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Three options. Wait for the leader to recover, and accept being blocked meanwhile. Fail over manually, with humans choosing and configuring a new leader. Or use an algorithm to choose a new leader automatically, which requires a consensus algorithm.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Waiting may block forever, manual failover is slow, and automatic election demands a consensus algorithm.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You place a system, such as a transaction coordinator or a database, among the three options.

card.rule: Wait, fail over by hand, or elect automatically with consensus; only the last satisfies termination.
card.limits: The right option depends on how long the system can afford to stall.

concepts.title: A leader kicks the can down the road
concepts.question: Does having a leader mean the system avoids consensus?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A single-leader database provides linearizability without running a consensus algorithm on every write, so it seems consensus is avoided.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: It still needs consensus to maintain its leadership and for leadership changes. Having a leader only kicks the can down the road: consensus is still required, only in a different place and less frequently.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The per-write cost drops, but leader changes remain the hard case.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You evaluate a claim that a design avoids consensus because it has a leader.

card.rule: A leader moves consensus to leadership changes, where it is needed less often.
card.limits: Fault-tolerant consensus systems exist, so the hard case can be handled rather than avoided.

concepts.title: Not every system needs consensus
concepts.question: When can a system do without consensus?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Consensus is costly and adds fragility, so it is worth asking whether every system really needs it.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Not necessarily. Leaderless and multi-leader replication typically do not use global consensus. Maybe we can cope without linearizability and learn to work better with data that has branching and merging version histories.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You give up linearizability and must deal with divergent versions and their merging.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A system favours availability and low latency and can merge conflicting writes.

card.rule: Leaderless and multi-leader systems skip global consensus and accept branching and merging version histories.
card.limits: If you need uniqueness, locks or atomic commit that survive failures, you need consensus after all.

concepts.title: What the theory is good for
concepts.question: Why does the book lean on theoretical papers and proofs?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The chapter relied on research whose papers and proofs can be hard to read and sometimes assume unrealistic things.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The theory is still valuable: it helps us reason about what can and cannot be done, and helps us find the counterintuitive ways in which distributed systems are often flawed.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It takes time to read, and its assumptions must be checked against your own system.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You decide whether the references are worth your time.

card.rule: Read theory to learn what is possible, and check its assumptions against your own system.
card.limits: An impossibility result holds inside its model; always ask whether your system matches that model.

concepts.title: Services, batch jobs and stream jobs
concepts.question: Which kind of system fits a workload where no user waits and the size of the input matters most?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Systems differ in who is waiting and in what counts as good performance. Judge a nightly data job by the standard of a web page, or a checkout API by the standard of a nightly job, and you aim at the wrong goal.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Sort a system by how it interacts. A service (online system) waits for a request from a client, answers as fast as it can, and is judged mainly by response time. A batch system (offline system) takes a large input, runs a job and produces output data; its main measure is throughput. A stream system (near-real-time) consumes events and produces outputs.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A service must reply quickly, so it cannot spend long on one request. A batch job is allowed to run long, so no person can sit and wait for its answer. Each type pays for its strength with the other's convenience.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Pick a service when a person or caller is waiting for a reply, a batch job when a large body of data needs crunching with nobody waiting, and a stream job when results are wanted soon after events happen.

card.rule: Match the design to who is waiting: services answer fast, batch jobs maximise throughput, stream jobs sit in between.
card.limits: The three types are points on a range, not sealed boxes: the author places stream processing between online and offline, and one system can contain all three.

media.alt: Pen-and-ink map of an island in the Sea of Derived Data, with regions labelled distributed filesystems, dataflow engines, MPP databases, iterative processing and search indexes. Ships head toward other chapters.

concepts.title: Where MapReduce stands
concepts.question: Why does the chapter still teach MapReduce even though its importance is declining?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Readers either treat MapReduce as the algorithm that explains all scale, or drop it because newer tools exist. Both views hide what it is good for.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: MapReduce, a batch algorithm published in 2004, is a fairly low-level programming model compared to the parallel processing systems built earlier for data warehouses. Its big step was the scale of processing possible on commodity hardware. It was implemented in Hadoop, CouchDB and MongoDB.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The model is low-level, so the user does more work than with the older warehouse systems. In return it ran on cheap machines at very large scale.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Study MapReduce as a clear picture of why and how batch processing is useful; the author says its importance is declining, so treat it as a teaching model rather than a default choice.

card.rule: MapReduce matters as a clear teaching model of batch processing, not as today's default tool.
card.limits: Old does not mean obsolete: the ideas it shows, such as partitioning and fault tolerance, return in later engines in the chapter.

concepts.title: Reading a web server log line
concepts.question: How do you know which field of an access log line holds the requested URL?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A web server appends one line to a log file for every request it serves. Each line packs in many facts, but nothing in the line tells you which piece is which.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Look up the log format definition. In the nginx default format a line holds the client address, the user, the time, the request, the status, the bytes sent, the referrer and the user agent. Splitting by whitespace puts the requested URL in field 7.
blocks.code:
203.0.113.9 - - [14/Oct/2026:09:30:02 +0000] "GET /pricing.html HTTP/1.1" 200 5120 "https://example.com/" "Mozilla/5.0"
# format: $remote_addr - $remote_user [$time_local] "$request" $status $body_bytes_sent "$http_referer" "$http_user_agent"

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Counting fields by position is quick, but the number 7 says nothing about meaning. The author notes that a named field would read better than a bare position.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it before any log analysis: find the format, then match each question you want answered to the field that holds it.

card.rule: Read the log format first, then pick the field that answers your question.
card.limits: Positions only mean something under one format and one way of splitting lines; another server or another separator moves the fields.

concepts.title: Top pages from a chain of small tools
concepts.question: How can a chain of small commands find the most popular pages of a website?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You want the five most requested pages from a web server log, and you do not want to set up a reporting product to get them.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Chain small tools, each doing one step: read the file, print only the URL field, sort the URLs so equal ones sit together, count each run of equal lines, sort the counts largest first, and keep five lines.
blocks.code:
cat /var/log/nginx/access.log |
  awk '{print $7}' |
  sort |
  uniq -c |
  sort -r -n |
  head -n 5

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each stage is tiny and replaceable, but the chain reads as obscure to a newcomer, and the stages depend on each other: counting before sorting would give wrong numbers.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it for quick one-off analysis of large text logs, where you want to change the question by editing one stage and run it again.

card.rule: Build the analysis as a chain of small steps: extract, sort, count, rank, cut.
card.limits: A chain of text tools is a quick answer for one question; it is not a report product, and it handles one machine's files.

concepts.title: Why sorting comes before counting
concepts.question: Why does the counting step in the pipeline need its input sorted first?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: To count how often each URL appears, a tool must find every occurrence of the same URL. Scanning a file of millions of lines for matches would need all counts kept somewhere.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The uniq command only compares two neighbouring lines. If a line equals the one before it, it is a repeat; with -c it also prints a counter. So the input is sorted first: a URL requested n times then appears n times in a row.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Neighbour comparison keeps almost nothing in memory, but it forces a full sort of the input first, and unsorted input gives wrong counts.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use the sort-then-count pattern whenever you need a count per key and the keys are too many to hold in a table.

card.rule: Sort first so equal items are neighbours; then counting needs only a glance at the previous line.
card.limits: Counting runs only works if equal items are adjacent; unsorted data produces a count for each run, not for each value.

concepts.title: Counting with an in-memory hash table
concepts.question: How does a short program count requests per URL without sorting?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The same top-pages question can be answered by a custom program instead of a chain of commands. The two differ in how they run once the log gets large.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Keep a hash table that maps each URL to a counter. Read the log one line at a time, take the URL field and add one to its counter, then sort the table by counter and print the top five. Counters start at zero.
blocks.code:
from collections import Counter
counts = Counter()
with open('access.log') as f:
    for line in f:
        counts[line.split()[6]] += 1
for url, n in counts.most_common(5):
    print(n, url)

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: One pass and no sorting of the whole log, but the table lives in memory. The pipeline is more concise, the program is fairly readable, and the choice is partly taste.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when you can keep one entry per distinct URL in memory and want the counting logic inside a program you can extend.

card.rule: A hash table counts in one pass by keeping one counter per distinct key in memory.
card.limits: The table is only as good as the memory it fits in; a very large set of distinct keys needs another approach.

concepts.title: The working set decides the approach
concepts.question: What decides whether counting with an in-memory table will fit in memory?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A job that works on a small test file can fail on the real one if its memory needs grow with the data. You need a way to predict that before you run.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Measure the working set: the amount of memory a job needs random access to. For counting URLs it depends only on the number of distinct URLs, not on how many log entries there are. A million entries for one URL need one URL and one counter.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: An in-memory table is the simple route while the working set is small. If the working set grows past memory, the table approach stops working and another method has to take over.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it before picking a method: estimate the distinct keys, multiply by the entry size, and compare with the memory you have.

card.rule: Estimate memory from the number of distinct keys, not from the size of the input.
card.limits: The working set follows the job: sums per key need one value per key, while a job that must keep every record has a much bigger working set.

concepts.title: Sorting when memory is too small
concepts.question: How can a sort-based approach handle data larger than memory?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: When the working set is bigger than the available memory, a table of counts cannot be held in memory, and random access to disk would be slow.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Sort in chunks. Chunks that fit in memory are sorted there and written to disk as sorted segment files; the sorted segments are then merged into a larger sorted file. This is mergesort, the same principle as SSTables and LSM-trees in Chapter 3.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Memory stops being the limit, because mergesort reads and writes sequentially, which disks do well. The cost is that the data goes through disk and through a merge rather than a quick table lookup.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when the distinct keys exceed memory, so that the table approach is out of reach.

card.rule: When memory is short, sort chunks, spill sorted segments to disk, and merge them.
card.limits: If everything fits in memory, a hash table avoids the extra disk work; sorting wins only once the working set outgrows memory.

concepts.title: The Unix philosophy in four rules
concepts.question: Which design rules let small Unix programs be joined into larger data jobs?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A big data job is hard to build as one huge program. Unix answered by letting many small programs be joined together, an idea Doug McIlroy described in 1964 as connecting programs like a garden hose.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The 1978 statement of the philosophy has four parts. First, make each program do one thing well, and for a new job build a new program rather than adding features to an old one. Second, expect every program's output to become the input of another, unknown program: keep output free of extra information, avoid fixed-column or binary formats, and do not insist on interactive input.

blocks.label: Other rules
blocks.text: Third, design software to be tried early, within weeks if possible, and be ready to throw away clumsy parts and rebuild them. Fourth, prefer tools to unskilled help when lightening a programming task, even if you must detour to build the tools and discard some of them afterwards.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Small single-purpose tools are easy to understand and replace, but each is of little use alone and gains its power only in combination with others.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when you need flexible data processing out of parts written by different people, and expect to change the job often.

card.rule: Build small programs that do one thing well and emit output that any later program can read.
card.limits: The rules suit pipelines of text tools on one machine; they do not by themselves say how to spread the work over many machines.

concepts.title: A uniform interface: the file
concepts.question: What common interface lets any Unix program connect to any other?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If the output of one program is to feed any other program, all programs must share one input and output interface. Without it, every pair of programs needs a custom adapter.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In Unix the interface is the file, or more precisely a file descriptor: an ordered sequence of bytes. Many different things share it: a real file, a channel to another process such as stdin and stdout, a device driver, and a socket for a TCP connection.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A very simple interface makes it easy to plug things together, but it says nothing about what the bytes mean, so the programs must also agree on conventions.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when many independently written tools must interoperate: fix one simple interface, and let each tool be written without knowing its neighbours.

card.rule: Give every component the same simple interface and any two can be plugged together.
card.limits: A shared byte interface connects tools only if they also agree on how to read the bytes; the interface alone does not give meaning.

concepts.title: Text lines as the shared record format
concepts.question: What do awk, sort, uniq and head agree on that lets them work together?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A byte sequence has no marked boundaries. Tools that use it must agree on where one record ends and how to read its pieces.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: By convention many Unix programs treat the bytes as ASCII text, a list of records separated by the newline character. The tools in the log example all share that choice. How a record is cut into fields is less settled: whitespace or tabs are common, and CSV and pipe-separated forms exist too.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Plain text mostly works and keeps everything compatible, but it is not beautiful: the field in the log example is fetched as the seventh one rather than by a readable name.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when tools must interoperate without a schema: agree on one record separator, and document how fields are split.

card.rule: Agree on a record separator, and treat the splitting of fields as a separate, looser convention.
card.limits: Text conventions give compatibility, not meaning; a line format can change between systems and silently shift field positions.

concepts.title: Why Unix-style composition is rare
concepts.question: Why can you not pipe your email and shopping history through one tool into a spreadsheet?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Programs from different makers usually cannot work together. Getting data from one system into another takes custom work, and the work repeats for every pair.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The author notes that few pieces of software compose as well as Unix tools do. You cannot easily send your email account and your shopping history through a custom analysis tool, put the result into a spreadsheet and post it to a wiki. Even databases with the same data model often make it hard to move data from one to another.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Giving up a common interface lets each product choose its own model, but the cost is isolated pools of data that cannot be joined, called Balkanization of data.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when judging a design: ask whether its data can leave the system through a simple shared interface.

card.rule: Without a shared interface, data ends up in separate pools that are hard to combine.
card.limits: The argument shows a cost of isolation; it does not say every system must expose raw bytes, only that integration should be easy.

concepts.title: Separating logic from wiring
concepts.question: How does using stdin and stdout make small programs easy to combine?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A program that opens its own input and output files decides for itself where data comes from and goes. That makes it hard to reuse in a different arrangement.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Let the program read standard input (stdin) and write standard output (stdout). The shell wires them up: keyboard and screen by default, or redirected to files, or joined to other processes by pipes. A pipe uses a small in-memory buffer and does not write the whole intermediate stream to disk. The program does not know or care where its data comes from.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The program gains reusability, but gives up control of its own sources and sinks, and anything that needs several inputs or outputs fits the model badly.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when you write a data tool: read stdin, write stdout, and leave the wiring to whoever runs the program.

card.rule: Keep the logic in the program and let the shell decide where its input and output go.
card.limits: The model fits one input and one output; programs that must open several files or connections do their own wiring.

concepts.title: Where stdin and stdout stop being enough
concepts.question: What kinds of programs cannot be wired freely with pipes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The pipe model shines for one stream in and one stream out. Real programs sometimes need more.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Programs that need multiple inputs or multiple outputs are possible but tricky. You cannot pipe a program's output into a network connection directly. If a program itself opens files, starts a subprocess or opens a network connection, that input and output is wired by the program, not by the shell.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A program can still make this I/O configurable, for example through command-line options, but the shell user then has less flexibility in wiring.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it as a check on a design: keep the I/O of a tool on stdin and stdout wherever possible, and wire the rest explicitly.

card.rule: Pipes handle one stream in and one out; anything beyond that is wired by the program.
card.limits: This is a limit of the model, not a flaw to avoid at all costs: some tools must open several files or connections.

concepts.title: Immutable inputs make experiments safe
concepts.question: What makes Unix pipelines easy to inspect and rerun while you experiment?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: When you explore data, you try commands many times and want to see what each stage does. A tool that changes its input, or hides its steps, makes this risky.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Unix commands treat their input files as immutable, so you can rerun them with different options without damaging the input. You can end a pipeline at any point and pipe the output into less to check its form. You can write one stage's output to a file and use that file as the input of the next stage, restarting only the later stage.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: These tools are blunt and simple compared with the query optimizer of a relational database, but their transparency makes them very useful for experimentation.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when exploring: keep inputs read-only, and save intermediate results so a mistake in a later stage does not force a rerun of everything.

card.rule: Leave inputs unchanged and make every stage inspectable, so you can experiment freely.
card.limits: Intermediate files help when stages are slow; for a quick pipeline, rerunning the whole chain may be simpler.

concepts.title: MapReduce as Unix across many machines
concepts.question: How is a MapReduce job like a Unix process spread across thousands of machines?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Unix tools keep inputs unchanged and compose well, but they run on one machine. A dataset larger than one machine needs the same discipline spread out.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: MapReduce is a bit like Unix tools distributed across potentially thousands of machines. A single job is comparable to a single Unix process: it takes one or more inputs and produces one or more outputs, does not modify the input and has no side effects other than its output. Where Unix tools use stdin and stdout, MapReduce jobs read and write files on a distributed filesystem.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Like most Unix tools it is blunt and brute-force, but it is surprisingly effective: you trade finesse for the ability to process data far beyond one machine.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when the input is too big for one machine and the work can be expressed as jobs that read files and write new files.

card.rule: A MapReduce job is a Unix-style process: read immutable input files, write new output files, change nothing else.
card.limits: The Unix comparison is about discipline, not mechanics: a MapReduce job needs a distributed filesystem and a framework that moves data between machines.

concepts.title: Shared nothing instead of shared disk
concepts.question: Why does HDFS need no special storage hardware?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A very large filesystem needs a lot of storage and a way for many machines to reach it. One answer, a central appliance, is expensive and has special requirements.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: HDFS follows the shared-nothing principle: it needs no special hardware, only computers connected by a conventional datacenter network. This contrasts with the shared-disk approach of NAS and SAN architectures, where a centralized storage appliance, often with custom hardware and special network infrastructure such as Fibre Channel, holds the data.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Plain machines and a plain network keep costs down. The price is that file access and copying go over the ordinary datacenter network.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when you want large, cheap storage that grows by adding ordinary machines.

card.rule: Shared nothing: ordinary machines and an ordinary network replace a central storage appliance.
card.limits: The contrast is about where data lives; it does not make a shared-disk system wrong for workloads that need its special hardware.

concepts.title: HDFS daemons and the NameNode
concepts.question: How does HDFS make the disks of many machines look like one filesystem?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Files are spread across many machines, so a reader has to know where each piece is. Someone has to keep that map.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: HDFS runs a daemon process on every machine, exposing a network service that lets other nodes access the files stored on that machine. A central server, the NameNode, keeps track of which file blocks are stored on which machine. Together they create one big filesystem using the space on the disks of all machines running the daemon.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A central record of block locations makes lookups simple, at the price of depending on one server for the map of where things are.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use this picture when reasoning about how a job finds its input: ask the NameNode where each block is, then read from the machine that has it.

card.rule: A daemon on every machine serves its disks; the NameNode knows which blocks are where.
card.limits: This is a conceptual description; real deployments add many details such as how the NameNode itself is protected.

concepts.title: Replication and erasure coding
concepts.question: How does HDFS survive machine and disk failures, and what does each method cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Machines and disks fail. A file block that lives on one disk is lost when that disk dies.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: File blocks are replicated on multiple machines: either several copies of the same data, or an erasure coding scheme such as Reed-Solomon codes, which lets lost data be recovered with lower storage overhead than full replication. The techniques resemble RAID, which spreads redundancy across disks in one machine.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Full copies are simple but take a lot of storage; erasure coding takes less storage for the same protection.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use full copies when simplicity matters, and consider erasure coding when the cost of storage dominates.

card.rule: Protect blocks by storing redundancy on other machines: copies for simplicity, erasure codes for space.
card.limits: Neither method protects against a mistake in the data itself; both only guard against lost machines and disks.

concepts.title: The four steps of a MapReduce job
concepts.question: Which four steps does a MapReduce job follow, and which of them do you write yourself?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A framework that spreads work over many machines needs a fixed pattern, or no one could predict what it does with the data.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The pattern mirrors the log pipeline. One: read the input files and break them into records. Two: call the mapper to extract a key and a value from each record. Three: sort all key-value pairs by key. Four: call the reducer to go over the sorted pairs. In the log example, the mapper is the awk step and the reducer is uniq -c.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You write only two pieces of code, the mapper and the reducer; the sorting is implicit and always happens, which costs time even when your job could do without it.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it to translate a Unix pipeline or an aggregation idea into a job: decide the key, write what to emit per record, and write what to do per key.

card.rule: Read records, map them to keys and values, sort by key, reduce each key's values.
card.limits: One job covers one round of grouping; questions that need a second round of sorting need a second job.

concepts.title: What mappers and reducers may do
concepts.question: What does the framework promise each mapper call and each reducer call?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The framework can only spread work over machines safely if the two callbacks follow strict rules about what they see and remember.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The mapper is called once for every input record and extracts a key and value; it may emit any number of pairs, including none, and keeps no state from one record to the next. The framework collects all values for the same key and calls the reducer once with that key and an iterator over the values; the reducer may emit any number of output records.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Because each mapper call is independent, the framework can run them anywhere; the price is that a mapper cannot compare one record with another.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it to check a design: anything that needs memory across records belongs in the reducer, grouped by key, not in the mapper.

card.rule: A mapper handles one record at a time with no memory; a reducer handles one key with all its values.
card.limits: The no-state rule is what the framework relies on for retries and parallelism; code that cheats breaks those guarantees.

concepts.title: The implicit sort and the second job
concepts.question: Why does a second sorting stage need a second MapReduce job?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The log example sorted twice: first by URL, then by count. A single job has one sort, between map and reduce, and you cannot add another.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The sort is implicit, since the mapper output is always sorted before it is given to the reducer. If you need a second sorting stage, as when ranking URLs by request count, write a second MapReduce job and use the first job's output as its input.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The built-in sort saves you code, but a job can only group on one key; extra rounds of sorting cost a whole additional job.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when planning a computation: count the distinct groupings and rankings you need, and expect one job for each.

card.rule: One job has one sort; a second ordering needs a second job fed by the first.
card.limits: Some orderings can be had inside one job, for example through a secondary sort within a key, but a new grouping still needs a new job.

concepts.title: Map tasks follow input blocks
concepts.question: How does MapReduce decide how many map tasks to run?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: To use many machines, a job must cut its work into pieces that can run on their own.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Parallelization is based on partitioning. The input of a job is typically a directory in HDFS, and each file or file block within it is a separate partition that can be processed by its own map task. The number of map tasks is therefore decided by the number of input file blocks.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Cutting by file blocks needs no coordination between tasks, but it leaves the job with no say in how many map tasks there are.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it to estimate how a job will spread: count the blocks in the input directory and expect about that many map tasks running in parallel.

card.rule: One map task per input file block: the input's layout sets the map parallelism.
card.limits: This covers the map side only; the reduce side is partitioned differently and its task count is chosen by the job author.

concepts.title: Moving the computation to the data
concepts.question: Why does the scheduler run each mapper where its input already is?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Copying hundreds of megabytes of input to each task over the network adds load and slows the job.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The MapReduce scheduler tries to run each mapper on one of the machines that stores a replica of its input file, provided that machine has enough spare RAM and CPU. This is called putting the computation near the data; it saves copying the input over the network, reducing network load and increasing locality. The framework first copies the code, for example JAR files, to the machine.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Moving a small program is cheaper than moving a large file, but a machine that holds the data may be busy, in which case the benefit is lost.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when data is big and code is small: ship the code, not the data.

card.rule: Ship the small code to the machine that holds the large data.
card.limits: Locality needs a replica on a machine with spare resources; with object stores or erasure coding the benefit disappears.

concepts.title: Choosing the reducer by hashing the key
concepts.question: How does the framework make sure every pair with the same key reaches the same reducer?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: All values for one key must meet in a single reducer call, but they are produced by many different mappers.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The reduce side is partitioned too. The job author configures the number of reduce tasks, which may differ from the number of map tasks. The framework uses a hash of the key to decide which reduce task receives each pair, so that all pairs with the same key reach the same reducer.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Hashing spreads keys evenly in the typical case without any coordination, but a key with a huge number of records still lands wholly on one reducer.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it to reason about reducers: same key, same hash, same reducer; the number of reducers is your choice.

card.rule: Hash the key to pick the reduce task, so equal keys always meet.
card.limits: Hashing balances keys, not records: one very frequent key still goes to a single reducer.

concepts.title: The shuffle between map and reduce
concepts.question: How does a big dataset get sorted and delivered to reducers without sorting it on one machine?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The key-value pairs must be sorted, but the whole dataset is likely too big to sort with an ordinary algorithm on one machine.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Sorting is done in stages. Each map task partitions its output by reducer, using the hash of the key, and writes each partition to a sorted file on its local disk, in a way similar to SSTables and LSM-trees. When a mapper finishes, the scheduler tells the reducers, which connect to each mapper and download the sorted file for their partition.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Staged sorting scales, but it needs local disk writes and a network copy of every partition; the reducer then merges the files, keeping the order.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when explaining where a job spends its time: the partitioning, sorting and copying between mappers and reducers is called the shuffle.

card.rule: The shuffle: mappers write sorted partitions to local disk, reducers download theirs and merge.
card.limits: Despite the name there is no randomness in the shuffle; and the work it costs is the reason map-side joins and dataflow engines try to avoid it.

media.alt: Three map tasks on the left, each with an input file (m1, m2, m3 from the HDFS input directory), a Mapper and three sorted output files named by map and reduce number, such as m1,r1 m1,r2 m1,r3. Arrows carry each file to the reduce task with its r number. Each of three reduce tasks gets three files, merges them, runs a Reducer and writes r1, r2 or r3 to the HDFS output directory.

concepts.title: Chaining jobs through directories
concepts.question: How are MapReduce jobs chained, and how is that unlike a Unix pipe?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A single job can do only so much, so real computations need several jobs one after another.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Jobs are chained into workflows in which one job's output is the next one's input. The framework has no workflow support, so the chain is made by directory name: the first job writes to a designated directory and the second reads that same directory. To the framework they are two independent jobs.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: This is like a sequence of commands where each writes a temporary file for the next to read, not like a Unix pipe with a small in-memory buffer. It has advantages and disadvantages, discussed later.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it to understand how a multi-step computation is wired: by names in the filesystem, not by a connection between running jobs.

card.rule: Chained jobs share a directory name and nothing else; each job is independent.
card.limits: A workflow is only as tidy as the people who agree on the directory names; the framework itself does not know the jobs belong together.

concepts.title: Schedulers and valid output
concepts.question: Why do large batch workflows need schedulers, and when is a job's output valid?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With dozens of chained jobs, written by different teams, someone must start each job at the right time and make sure it reads good data.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A batch job's output is considered valid only if the job completed successfully; MapReduce discards the partial output of a failed job. So a job may start only after the jobs that produce its input directories have completed successfully. Workflow schedulers for Hadoop, such as Oozie, Azkaban, Luigi, Airflow and Pinball, manage these dependencies.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Waiting for whole jobs keeps data clean but delays downstream work; schedulers add one more system to run.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use a scheduler once a workflow has many jobs or many teams, where tool support for the dataflow becomes important.

card.rule: Start a job only after its input jobs succeeded; let a scheduler track the dependencies.
card.limits: Schedulers order whole jobs; they do not make an individual job faster or fix a failed job's output.

concepts.title: Joins in a batch job read everything
concepts.question: What does a join mean in a batch job that has no indexes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Records often point to other records: a foreign key, a document reference or a graph edge. Any code that needs both sides of such a link needs a join.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A database uses an index to find a few records quickly. MapReduce has no indexes in the usual sense: a job reads the entire content of its input files, which a database would call a full table scan. In a batch job, a join means resolving all occurrences of an association in a dataset, for all users at once.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A full scan is outrageously expensive if you want only a few records. For analytic queries that aggregate over many records, scanning everything is reasonable, especially when the work is spread over machines.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use a batch join when the question is about all records or a large share of them; use an index lookup when it is about one record.

card.rule: A batch join resolves a link for every record at once, by scanning the whole input.
card.limits: For a handful of records a full scan is wasteful; an index lookup in a database is the better tool.

concepts.title: Why not ask the user database per event
concepts.question: Why is looking up the user database for every event a poor way to run a join in a batch job?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A log of user activity events holds only user IDs, but the analysis needs each user's profile, such as date of birth. Embedding the profile in every event would be wasteful.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The simplest join goes over the events one by one and queries the user database on a remote server for every ID. It works but performs very poorly: throughput is limited by the round-trip time to the database server, a local cache helps only as much as the data distribution allows, and running many queries in parallel could easily overwhelm the database.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It is easy to write, but a batch job gets good throughput only if its computation is as local as it can be to one machine. Random-access requests over the network for every record are too slow.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Avoid it for large batch jobs; consider it only for a small number of lookups, where a few round trips cost little.

card.rule: Per-record network lookups cap a batch job at the speed of round trips; bring the data to the job instead.
card.limits: For a handful of records a remote lookup is fine; the argument bites when the number of lookups matches the size of a big dataset.

media.alt: Two lists with arrows. Left, User activity events: lines such as user 105 clicked button, user 296 viewed a profile, user 101 posted a response. Right, User database, a table with columns user_id, email, date_of_birth and rows 100 to 105. Arrows link the user 105 event and the user 101 event to the matching table rows.

concepts.title: Put a copy of the user data beside the events
concepts.question: What is the better approach when a batch job must join events with a database?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The events are in files on the distributed filesystem, but the user profiles live in a database. A direct join would have to cross the network for every record.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Take a copy of the user database and put it in the same distributed filesystem as the log of activity events. You then have the user data in one set of files in HDFS and the events in another, and you can use MapReduce to bring together all the relevant records in the same place and process them efficiently.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You pay for an extra copy and an extraction step, but the job runs on local files at full throughput and no longer depends on a live database.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when a large batch join needs data that normally sits in an operational database.

card.rule: Copy the other side of the join into the filesystem, then join inside the batch framework.
card.limits: The copy is a snapshot: it does not show changes made in the database after the copy was taken.

concepts.title: The reduce-side sort-merge join
concepts.question: How does a MapReduce job join two datasets on a shared key?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The activity events and the user records sit in different files. The join needs each event next to the profile of its user.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: One set of mappers reads the activity events and emits the user ID as key and the event as value; another reads the user database and emits the user ID as key and the date of birth as value. Partitioning and sorting then put each user record next to that user's events in the reducer input, and the reducer, called once per user ID, joins them.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The reducer needs only one user record in memory at a time and never makes a network request, but all the sorting, copying and merging is expensive.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when you know nothing about the layout of the inputs: the mappers can prepare any data for joining, so no assumptions are needed.

card.rule: Key both inputs by the join key; the shuffle puts matching records in the same reducer call.
card.limits: The cost of sorting and moving everything is what map-side joins try to avoid when the inputs have a known layout.

media.alt: Two mapper pipelines feed two reducer partitions. The user activity mapper reads events (user 104 loaded /x, user 173 loaded /y, user 104 loaded /z) and emits 104 with url /x, 104 with url /z, 173 with url /y. The user database mapper reads records of users 103 and 104 and emits 104 with dob 1989 and 103 with dob 1947. Reducer partition 1 (even-numbered user IDs) receives the 104 records and outputs url and dob pairs; partition 2 (odd-numbered IDs) takes 173 and 103.

concepts.title: Secondary sort: profile first, events after
concepts.question: How can the reducer be sure it sees the user record before the user's events?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In the join, the reducer needs the date of birth before it handles the events, so that it can keep one value and stream the rest. Plain sorting by user ID does not fix the order of values within a key.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The MapReduce job can arrange the records so that the reducer always sees the record from the user database first, followed by the activity events. This technique is known as a secondary sort.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You get a reducer that is a simple loop over the values, in exchange for designing the sort order of the values inside each key.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when a reducer must see one record before the others of the same key, for example a reference record before its events.

card.rule: Arrange the sort so one kind of record comes first within each key.
card.limits: A secondary sort orders the values for a key; it does not change which reducer a key goes to.

concepts.title: Keys act like addresses
concepts.question: In what sense do mappers send messages to reducers?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Joins need related data to meet in one place. In ordinary application code, fetching related data is a call from deep inside the program to a database.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Think of the mappers as sending messages to the reducers. When a mapper emits a key-value pair, the key acts like the address to which the value should be delivered. It is just an arbitrary string, not an IP address and port, yet all pairs with the same key are delivered to the same destination: one call to the reducer.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The model separates the physical network communication from the application logic, which is clean, but you must express your task as keys and values.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when designing a job: decide which records must meet, and make their key the same.

card.rule: A key is a destination: equal keys meet in the same reducer call.
card.limits: The address picture explains where records meet; it says nothing about how many records one key may have.

concepts.title: Grouping uses the same pattern as joining
concepts.question: How is a GROUP BY done in MapReduce, and why does it look like a join?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Besides joins, analyses often group records by a key and aggregate within each group, as with the GROUP BY clause of SQL.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Set up the mappers so that the key-value pairs they produce use the desired grouping key. The partitioning and sorting bring all records with the same key to the same reducer. Within each group the reducer performs an aggregation, such as counting records, adding up one field, or picking the top k records by a ranking function.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The pattern is simple, but a single group always lands on one reducer, so it relies on groups being of reasonable size.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it for any per-key summary: counts per URL, sums per customer, best items per category.

card.rule: To group, make the grouping field the mapper's key and aggregate in the reducer.
card.limits: The pattern assumes each group can be handled by one reducer; very large groups need special treatment.

concepts.title: Sessionization: gathering a user's events
concepts.question: How do you collect all the events of a user session that are scattered over several web servers?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With several web servers handling requests, the activity events for one user are scattered across the log files of different servers. To see the sequence of actions you must bring them together.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use a session cookie, a user ID or a similar identifier as the grouping key. All the activity events of one user reach the same reducer, while different users' events are spread across different partitions.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It gives complete sessions and parallelism over users, but one user's events must fit through one reducer call.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when you need the sequence of a user's actions, for example to compare whether users shown a new site version buy more than users shown the old one.

card.rule: Key the events by session or user ID so each user's actions arrive together.
card.limits: The result is as good as the identifier: events without a session cookie or user ID cannot be grouped.

concepts.title: Hot keys and skew
concepts.question: What happens when one key has far more records than the others?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Bringing all records with one key to one place breaks down when a single key has a very large amount of data.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In a social network most users have a few hundred connections, but a few celebrities have millions of followers. Such disproportionately active records are called linchpin objects or hot keys. Collecting all activity about a celebrity in one reducer produces skew, also called hot spots: one reducer that must process far more records than the others.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Grouping by key keeps related data together, but it hands the busiest key to a single reducer.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Check for skew whenever a job groups or joins on a key whose frequency is very uneven, such as followers, popular products or one big customer.

card.rule: One reducer with a hot key can hold up the whole job.
card.limits: Skew matters only when some key is far bigger than the rest; evenly spread keys need no special treatment.

concepts.title: Spreading a hot key over several reducers
concepts.question: How does a skewed join spread the work for a hot key?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Joining on a hot key sends all its records to one reducer, which becomes the bottleneck.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The skewed join method in Pig first runs a sampling job to find out which keys are hot. In the real join, the mappers send records relating to a hot key to one of several reducers chosen at random, instead of the single reducer that a hash would pick. The records of the other input for the hot key are replicated to all the reducers handling that key.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The work for the hot key is spread over several reducers and so parallelized better, at the cost of replicating the other join input to several reducers.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when a join input has a few very hot keys and the other side's records for those keys are few.

card.rule: Split the hot key over several reducers at random, and copy the other side's matching records to each.
card.limits: It costs a sampling job and extra copies; for evenly spread keys the ordinary join is cheaper.

concepts.title: Hive's alternative for hot keys
concepts.question: How does Hive's skewed join optimization treat hot keys differently from Pig and Crunch?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Pig finds hot keys by sampling and spreads them over random reducers. Is there another way to deal with them?

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Hive's skewed join optimization requires the hot keys to be specified explicitly in the table metadata. It stores the records for those keys in separate files from the rest. When joining on that table, it uses a map-side join for the hot keys.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Telling Hive the hot keys in advance saves a sampling job and avoids reduce-side work for them, but someone must know and maintain the list of hot keys.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when the hot keys are known in advance and stable, and the data can be stored as separate files.

card.rule: Hive stores known hot keys in separate files and joins them on the map side.
card.limits: The method depends on knowing the hot keys; when they change often, sampling is the more flexible approach.
