concepts.title: Grouping hot keys in two stages
concepts.question: How can you aggregate a hot key without overloading one reducer?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A hot key sends all its records to one reducer when you group and aggregate.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Do the grouping in two stages. The first MapReduce stage sends records to a random reducer, so each reducer groups only a subset of the records for the hot key and outputs a more compact aggregated value per key. A second job then finishes the aggregation.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The load is spread, but you pay for a second job and the aggregation must be of a kind that partial results can be combined.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when grouping on a hot key with an aggregation such as a count or sum.

card.rule: Aggregate hot keys in two rounds: partial aggregates at random reducers, then combine them.
card.limits: It suits aggregations whose partial results can be combined; it does not help joins, which need records of both sides together.

concepts.title: Reduce-side versus map-side joins
concepts.question: When is it worth giving up the general reduce-side join for a map-side join?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The reduce-side join works on any input, but all of the data must be sorted, copied to reducers and merged. This can be quite expensive.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A map-side join makes assumptions about the input so as to skip that work. It is a cut-down MapReduce job with no reducers and no sorting: each mapper reads one input file block from the distributed filesystem and writes one output file, and that is all.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Reduce-side joins need no assumptions about the data, but they are expensive. Map-side joins are faster but only work when the input has the right size, sorting or partitioning.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Pick a map-side join when you know something about the layout or size of the inputs; otherwise use the reduce-side join.

card.rule: Reduce-side joins are general and costly; map-side joins are cheap and need inputs of a known shape.
card.limits: A map-side join is not an upgrade for all data; if the assumptions fail, it gives wrong or failed results.

concepts.title: Broadcast hash join
concepts.question: How does a mapper join a big input with a small one without any reducer?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Joining a large dataset with a small one by sorting both through reducers moves the large data for the sake of the small one.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Load the small input entirely into memory in each mapper, as a hash table. Then scan the large input one record at a time and look up each key in the table. Each mapper for a block of the large input loads the small input entirely, so it is broadcast to all partitions, and a hash table does the lookups.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: No sorting and no reducers, but the small input must fit in memory of every mapper, and each mapper reads the whole small input.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when one side of the join is small enough to hold in memory: a user table, a product list, a lookup of country codes.

card.rule: Copy the small input into every mapper's memory and stream the large input past it.
card.limits: The method fails when the small side outgrows the memory of a mapper; then use partitioned or sort-based joins.

concepts.title: A read-only index instead of memory
concepts.question: How can a map-side join work when the small input is too big for memory?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A broadcast hash join needs the small input in memory in every mapper. A table slightly too large for memory seems to rule it out.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Instead of an in-memory hash table, store the small join input in a read-only index on the local disk. The frequently used parts of the index stay in the operating system's page cache.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You gain the ability to join larger small inputs; you pay in somewhat slower lookups for parts of the index that are not in the cache.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when the small side is too large for memory but queries concentrate on a hot subset that the page cache can hold.

card.rule: A read-only index on local disk gives nearly memory-speed lookups through the page cache.
card.limits: If lookups are spread evenly over a huge index, the page cache cannot hold the working set and lookups become slow.

concepts.title: Partitioned hash join
concepts.question: How do matching partitions make a map-side join work for larger inputs?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: When neither input is small enough to broadcast, each mapper still needs a way to load only the data it can match.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: If both join inputs are partitioned in the same way, the hash join can be applied to each partition independently. For example, partition both the activity events and the user database by the last decimal digit of the user ID. Mapper 3 then loads only users whose ID ends in 3 into a hash table and scans only the events for those users. Hive calls this a bucketed map join.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each mapper loads a smaller part of the data, but the method works only if both inputs have the same number of partitions, with records assigned by the same key and the same hash function.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when the inputs were produced by earlier MapReduce jobs that already grouped them the same way.

card.rule: If both inputs are partitioned alike, join each pair of partitions on its own with a hash table.
card.limits: It fails if the inputs differ in the number of partitions, the partitioning key or the hash function.

concepts.title: Map-side merge join
concepts.question: What lets a mapper do the merge that a reducer normally does?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Partitioned hash joins still need each partition to fit into a hash table. Larger partitions call for a different method.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: If the inputs are partitioned in the same way and also sorted by the same key, a mapper can do what a reducer does in a sort-merge join. It reads both input files incrementally in ascending key order and matches the records with the same key.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It does not matter whether the inputs fit in memory, but the inputs must already have been brought to this partitioned and sorted form, which usually means earlier jobs did that work.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when co-partitioned, sorted datasets already exist.

card.rule: Co-partitioned, sorted inputs can be merged by a mapper without any reducer.
card.limits: If the data is not sorted and partitioned alike, a map-side merge join gives wrong results; the sort has to be paid for elsewhere.

concepts.title: How the join type shapes the output
concepts.question: How does the choice of join affect the layout of the output that later jobs read?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A join's output is often read by downstream jobs. Its layout decides which later joins are cheap.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The output of a reduce-side join is partitioned and sorted by the join key. The output of a map-side join is partitioned and sorted in the same way as the large input.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Map-side joins preserve the layout of the large input and cost less, but they make more assumptions about the size, sorting and partitioning of their inputs.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use this when planning a chain of jobs: choose each join with the layout the next job needs in mind.

card.rule: Reduce-side output is partitioned and sorted by join key; map-side output follows the large input.
card.limits: The layout rules apply to MapReduce joins as described; other engines may arrange output differently.

concepts.title: Knowing the physical layout of datasets
concepts.question: What must you know about a dataset besides its format and its directory to join it cleverly?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Map-side joins make more assumptions about the size, sorting and partitioning of the inputs. A wrong assumption gives wrong results or a failed job.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Knowing the physical layout of the datasets in the distributed filesystem becomes important. It is not enough to know the encoding format and the directory name; you must also know the number of partitions and the keys by which the data is partitioned and sorted.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Layout metadata unlocks cheaper joins, but someone has to record it and keep it correct.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it whenever you plan a map-side join or a chain of joins across datasets owned by different teams.

card.rule: To pick a join, know each dataset's partition count and its partitioning and sorting keys.
card.limits: Metadata that drifts from the real layout is worse than none; check it before trusting it.

concepts.title: Where batch processing sits
concepts.question: Is a batch workflow transaction processing, analytics, or something else?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: After all the join and grouping machinery, a question is left over: what is the result of all that processing, and why run the jobs at all?

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: OLTP queries look up a few records by key, using indexes, to show them to a user. Analytic queries scan many records, group and aggregate them, and often produce a report. Batch processing is neither of the two. A workflow of MapReduce jobs is not the same as an analytic SQL query, and its output is often some other kind of structure.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Calling batch work analytics helps you reason about scans and aggregates, but it hides that the product may be an index or a database, not a chart.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it to decide what to expect from a job: ask who consumes the output and in what form.

card.rule: Batch is closest to analytics because it scans large inputs, but its output is often a data structure, not a report.
card.limits: The comparison is a rough guide; a batch job can also produce reports, and some analytics run as SQL on batch engines.

concepts.title: Building a search index in a batch job
concepts.question: How does a batch job build a full-text search index?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A search engine must find the documents containing a keyword quickly. For a fixed set of documents, someone has to build that index in bulk.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A full-text index such as Lucene's is a term dictionary in which a keyword is looked up to find the postings list of all document IDs containing it. With a batch job, the mappers partition the set of documents as needed, each reducer builds the index for its partition, and the index files are written to the distributed filesystem. Such document-partitioned indexes parallelize very well.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Batch is very effective for a fixed document set. Because querying by keyword only reads, the index files are immutable once created, so the index cannot take in changes.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when the documents are known in advance and the index can be rebuilt as a whole.

card.rule: Partition the documents, let each reducer build one partition's index, and write immutable index files.
card.limits: The view of an index here is simplified; real indexes add ranking data, spelling correction and synonyms.

concepts.title: Rebuild the index or update it step by step
concepts.question: When documents change, should you rebuild the whole index or update it incrementally?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A fixed document set is easy to index. But documents get added, changed and removed, and the index must follow.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: One option is to rerun the entire indexing workflow periodically for the entire set of documents, and replace the previous index files wholesale. The other is to build the index incrementally: Lucene writes out new segment files for added, removed or updated documents and merges and compacts segment files in the background.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Rebuilding is expensive when only a few documents have changed, but it is easy to reason about: documents in, indexes out. Incremental updates cost less work per change but need more machinery.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Rebuild when changes are few and simplicity matters most, or when the full rebuild fits your time budget; go incremental when rebuilds are too slow or the data changes constantly.

card.rule: Rebuild wholesale for simplicity; update incrementally to save work when changes are small.
card.limits: How often the set changes decides the choice; in the extreme of constant changes, streaming (the next chapter) fits better.

concepts.title: Batch output that is queried by a web app
concepts.question: Why does the output of a recommendation job end up in a database?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Another common use of batch processing is building machine learning systems: classifiers such as spam filters, anomaly detection and image recognition, and recommendation systems such as people you may know, products you may like and related searches.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The output is often a database: one that can be queried by user ID to get suggested friends, or by product ID to get related products. These databases are queried by the web application that handles user requests, which is usually separate from the Hadoop infrastructure.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The batch job computes expensive results offline, so requests are cheap; but the result must travel from the batch system to a database, and the answers are only as fresh as the last run.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when predictions can be computed ahead of time for every key and served by lookup.

card.rule: Compute recommendations offline for every key, then serve them by lookup from a database.
card.limits: Precomputing suits stable, frequent keys; a request that needs fresh, personalized work per click cannot be served this way.

concepts.title: Why tasks should not write to the live database
concepts.question: Why is writing batch output record by record into a production database a bad idea?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The most obvious way to deliver batch results is to use your favorite database's client library inside a mapper or reducer and write each record straight to the database server. It works, if the firewall allows it, but it is a bad idea.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Keep tasks free of side effects: let them write only to the job's output files, and deliver results to the database in a separate step.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Three costs. A network request per record is orders of magnitude slower than batch throughput, even with client-side batching. Many parallel tasks can overwhelm the database, hurting its queries and other systems. The all-or-nothing output guarantee is lost: external writes are visible side effects, so partial results can be seen, and task attempts and speculative execution add complexity.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Direct writes are the easiest thing to code, but you pay with speed, with database health and with the clean job semantics.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Do not use it for large outputs; keep tasks free of side effects other than their output files.

card.rule: Do not write from batch tasks into a live database: it is slow, floods the database and breaks all-or-nothing output.
card.limits: For a tiny output, a direct write may be fine; the reasons here are about volume and parallel tasks.

concepts.title: Build the database inside the job
concepts.question: What is the better way to get batch output into a serving database?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Batch results must reach a database that serves queries, without the problems of record-by-record writes.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Build a brand-new database inside the batch job and write it as files to the job's output directory in the distributed filesystem, as for the search indexes. The files are immutable once written and can be loaded in bulk into servers that handle read-only queries. Voldemort, Terrapin, ElephantDB and HBase bulk loading support building database files in MapReduce.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You get fast, side-effect-free jobs and simple read-only data structures, but the serving data is only as fresh as the last job.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when a batch job produces a lookup database that applications read but do not write.

card.rule: Write the database as immutable files in the job's output directory, then bulk-load it into read-only servers.
card.limits: It suits read-only serving data; a database that applications must update continuously cannot be a batch-built file set.

concepts.title: Switching to the new files atomically
concepts.question: How does a server swap in a freshly built database without downtime or risk?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A server holds yesterday's data files and must start serving today's without interrupting queries or ending up half-way between.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Voldemort keeps serving requests from the old data files while the new files are copied from the distributed filesystem to the server's local disk. When the copy is complete, the server atomically switches over to the new files.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It needs enough disk for both sets of files for a while, but there is no downtime and no mixed state.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when loading a new version of read-only data into a server that must stay available.

card.rule: Serve the old files while copying the new ones, then switch over in one step.
card.limits: The pattern relies on files being immutable; with in-place updates there is no clean old version to fall back on.

concepts.title: Human fault tolerance: roll back and rerun
concepts.question: Why can a buggy batch job be repaired by rerunning it, while a buggy database writer cannot?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Developers ship bugs. When buggy code has written bad data into a read-write database, rolling back the code does nothing to fix that data.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat inputs as immutable and avoid side effects such as writes to external databases. If a bug makes the output wrong or corrupted, roll back to a previous version of the code and rerun the job, and the output is correct again. Or keep the old output in a different directory and switch back to it. The idea of recovering from buggy code is called human fault tolerance.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You pay for storage of old outputs and the time to rerun, and you give up in-place updates.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when mistakes in code are likely and the cost of irreversible damage is high.

card.rule: Immutable inputs and replaceable outputs let you undo a code bug by rerunning.
card.limits: Rerunning cures wrong derived data, not decisions already made on it, such as emails sent or payments made.

concepts.title: Why automatic retries are safe
concepts.question: Why can MapReduce rerun a failed task on the same input without harm?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Tasks fail: a machine dies, a process is preempted or a bug crashes the code. The framework must decide whether to rerun a task.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: If a map or reduce task fails, the framework automatically reschedules it and runs it again on the same input. If the cause is a bug, it keeps crashing and after a few attempts the job fails; if the cause is a transient problem, the fault is tolerated.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Retrying is only safe because inputs are immutable and the outputs of failed tasks are discarded by the framework; this restricts what tasks may do.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Rely on retries when a job's tasks are stateless and have no side effects other than their designated output.

card.rule: Retrying is safe because inputs do not change and failed output is thrown away.
card.limits: A task with external side effects breaks the guarantee, because retries repeat those effects.

concepts.title: Many jobs can read the same files
concepts.question: What do immutable files and separate wiring let different teams do with the same data?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Data written by one job is valuable to others. If jobs depended on each other's internals, reuse would be hard.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Because inputs are immutable, the same set of files can be used as input for various different jobs, including monitoring jobs. Like Unix tools, MapReduce jobs also separate logic from wiring, that is, the configuration of input and output directories.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Loose coupling through files makes reuse easy, but nothing in the filesystem tells a reader what the files mean or who depends on them.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when several teams build on a shared dataset: one team writes a job that does one thing well, and others decide where and when to run it.

card.rule: Read-only files and configurable directories let many jobs and teams share the same data.
card.limits: Sharing needs agreements on layout and meaning; the model gives the mechanism, not the agreement.

concepts.title: Structured file formats instead of raw text
concepts.question: How does Hadoop reduce the parsing work that Unix text tools need?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Most Unix tools assume untyped text files, so they spend a lot of effort parsing input; the log example needed a field position just to extract the URL.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: On Hadoop, some of those low-value syntactic conversions are removed by using more structured file formats. Avro and Parquet are often used because they provide efficient schema-based encoding.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Structured formats remove parsing and add types and schema evolution, but they need tools that understand the format and give up Unix's plain-text universality.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it for data shared between jobs and teams, where agreed field names and types are worth the extra tooling.

card.rule: Schema-based formats such as Avro and Parquet replace error-prone text parsing between jobs.
card.limits: Plain text remains the simplest interface for quick work; structured formats pay off at scale and with many consumers.

concepts.title: MapReduce was not new: MPP databases came first
concepts.question: How does MapReduce on a distributed filesystem differ from the parallel databases that preceded it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The join and grouping algorithms in this chapter sound like new inventions of the Hadoop world. That would be a wrong picture of where they came from.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: When the MapReduce paper was published it was not at all new: the parallel join algorithms had been implemented in massively parallel processing (MPP) databases more than a decade earlier.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: MPP databases focus on parallel execution of analytic SQL queries on a cluster. The combination of MapReduce and a distributed filesystem is much more like a general-purpose operating system that can run arbitrary programs.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use this comparison when judging a new batch tool: ask what it does that MPP databases already did, and what it adds.

card.rule: Parallel joins came from MPP databases; MapReduce plus a filesystem added general-purpose programs.
card.limits: The comparison simplifies: the two families have since moved toward each other, and neither is a strict superset of the other.

concepts.title: Dump the data first, model it later
concepts.question: Why can collecting raw data in a distributed filesystem beat careful up-front modeling?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Databases require you to structure data by a particular model, such as relational or documents. MPP databases typically need careful up-front modeling of the data and query patterns before import into the database's own storage format.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Files in a distributed filesystem are just byte sequences, in any data model and encoding: text, images, videos, sensor readings, feature vectors and more. Hadoop made it possible to dump data into HDFS and figure out later how to process it. The author finds that making data available quickly, even in a raw form, is often more valuable than choosing the ideal model first.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Careful modeling gives better-quality data to users, from a purist's view, but it slows central collection. Raw collection is fast, and gathering data from across an organization in one place enables joins across datasets that were disparate.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when data from many sources must be brought together quickly and its uses are not yet known.

card.rule: Collect first, in raw form; decide the model later, when you know the use.
card.limits: Raw dumping defers work, it does not remove it: someone still has to clean and model the data before a downstream user can rely on it.

concepts.title: Who pays for interpreting raw data
concepts.question: When data is dumped raw, who has to make sense of it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If a dataset is dumped without being forced into a standard format, someone must still interpret it. The question is who.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Indiscriminate data dumping shifts the burden of interpretation: instead of forcing the producer to bring the data into a standardized format, interpretation becomes the consumer's problem. This is the schema-on-read approach. It can be an advantage when producer and consumers are different teams with different priorities.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Producers are freed from agreeing on a format, but every consumer must work out the data's meaning, and the same work may be repeated by many teams.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when there may be no single ideal data model, only different views of the data for different purposes.

card.rule: Schema-on-read moves interpretation from the producer to each consumer.
card.limits: It works best when consumers differ; if everyone needs the same view, one cleaned copy saves repeated work.

concepts.title: Hadoop as the ETL step before the warehouse
concepts.question: How can raw dumping and careful modeling both be used in one pipeline?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Raw collection is fast but hard to use, while a relational warehouse is easy to use but needs clean, modeled data.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Dump data from transaction processing systems into the distributed filesystem in some raw form. Then write MapReduce jobs to clean up the data, transform it into a relational form and import it into an MPP data warehouse for analytic purposes.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You add a processing stage, but data modeling still happens in a separate step, decoupled from the data collection.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when you want both: quick collection from many systems and a clean relational warehouse for analysts.

card.rule: Collect raw into the filesystem, clean and model with batch jobs, then load the warehouse.
card.limits: The extra stage adds delay and operational cost; for a single clean source, loading the warehouse directly may be enough.

concepts.title: Not all processing is SQL
concepts.question: Why was MapReduce needed when MPP databases already offered SQL?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: MPP databases are monolithic, tightly integrated systems: storage layout, query planning, scheduling and execution are tuned together. They perform well on the queries they were built for, and SQL is expressive and accessible to graphical tools such as Tableau.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: But not all processing can sensibly be expressed as SQL. Machine learning and recommendation systems, full-text search indexes with relevance ranking, and image analysis need a more general model, and such processing is specific to an application, so it needs code and not just queries. MapReduce let engineers easily run their own code over large datasets.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: SQL engines give optimization and accessibility; running your own code gives generality but leaves optimization to you.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use SQL for queries it expresses naturally, and general programs where application-specific logic is needed.

card.rule: SQL covers queries; machine learning, search ranking and image analysis need arbitrary code.
card.limits: The line is not fixed: Hive built a SQL engine on top of HDFS and MapReduce, so one platform can offer both.

concepts.title: Many processing models on one cluster
concepts.question: What does a shared cluster over one filesystem give you that separate specialized systems do not?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If each kind of processing lives in its own specialized system, data must be imported into each one before it can be used.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In the Hadoop approach, the various processing models can all run on a single shared-use cluster, all accessing the same files on the distributed filesystem. There is no need to import the data into several specialized systems, because the system supports a diverse set of workloads in one cluster.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The data stays where it is, which is simple; the price is a shared platform that has to serve many different workloads.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when several teams or tools want different views of the same large datasets.

card.rule: One cluster and one filesystem can host many processing models on the same files.
card.limits: A shared cluster needs scheduling and isolation between workloads, which this chapter touches on only later.

concepts.title: Faults and memory: MPP versus MapReduce
concepts.question: Why does MapReduce retry single tasks and write to disk eagerly while MPP databases abort queries?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Batch processes are less sensitive to faults than online systems: a failure does not immediately affect users, and a job can always be run again. Still, systems differ in how they react to a crashed node.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: If a node crashes during a query, most MPP databases abort the entire query, which is acceptable because queries run for seconds or minutes, and they keep as much as possible in memory. MapReduce instead retries a single task and writes data to disk eagerly, partly for fault tolerance.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Task-level recovery makes fault-free processing slower, but it is a reasonable trade-off if tasks fail often enough, and it is more appropriate for large jobs.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Pick query-level restart for short queries; pick task-level retry for jobs so large and long that one task failure is likely along the way.

card.rule: Short jobs can restart whole; long jobs should recover task by task, at the price of writing to disk.
card.limits: The argument depends on how often tasks fail; where failures are rare, the overhead of task-level recovery may not pay off.

concepts.title: Preemption: where MapReduce's design comes from
concepts.question: What makes task termination so frequent in the environment MapReduce was designed for?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If machine failures are rare, why would MapReduce pay for task-level recovery? The answer lies in the environment it was built for.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Google runs mixed-use datacenters where online production services and offline batch jobs share machines. Every task has a resource allocation, enforced with containers, and a priority; if a higher-priority task needs resources, lower-priority tasks on the machine can be terminated (preempted). MapReduce jobs run at low priority, so they pick up the scraps under the table and risk preemption at any time.

blocks.label: Numbers
blocks.text: A MapReduce task running for an hour has roughly a 5 percent risk of being terminated to make room for a higher-priority process, more than an order of magnitude above the rate of hardware failures.
blocks.code:
p_hour = 0.05
per_10_min = 1 - (1 - p_hour) ** (1 / 6)
at_least_one = 1 - (1 - per_10_min) ** 100
print(round(at_least_one, 2))

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Preemption lets low-priority resources be overcommitted, which improves machine utilization, at the price of frequent task termination.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it as a worked example of why a design that looks over-cautious can be right for its environment.

card.rule: Frequent preemption by higher-priority work, not weak hardware, explains task-level recovery.
card.limits: The numbers describe Google's environment, not every cluster; with less preemption the case is weaker.

concepts.title: A design fits its environment
concepts.question: When do MapReduce's design decisions stop making sense?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Choices that were right in one environment can be costly in another. MapReduce's sparing use of memory and its task-level recovery came from Google's mixed-use datacenters.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: MapReduce tolerates frequent unexpected task termination not because the hardware is particularly unreliable, but because the freedom to terminate processes arbitrarily allows better resource utilization. Among open source cluster schedulers, preemption is less widely used.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: In an environment where tasks are not often terminated, the design decisions of MapReduce make less sense, since its recovery costs buy little.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Before adopting a system's trade-offs, ask which environment they were made for and whether yours matches.

card.rule: Check whether the environment that justified a design is the environment you have.
card.limits: Fewer preemptions weaken the case for MapReduce's design but do not prove an alternative is better.

concepts.title: MapReduce: a clear model that is hard to use and slow for some jobs
concepts.question: Why did people build tools on top of MapReduce and then look for alternatives to it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: MapReduce received a lot of hype in the late 2000s, but it is just one of many programming models for distributed systems. Depending on the volume and structure of the data and the kind of processing, other tools may fit better.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The chapter dwells on MapReduce because it is a clear and simple abstraction on top of a distributed filesystem, simple in the sense of being understandable, not easy to use. Writing a complex job with the raw APIs is laborious, since you would implement join algorithms from scratch. So higher-level models such as Pig, Hive, Cascading and Crunch were built on top of it.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Some problems lie in the execution model itself, which a further layer of abstraction does not fix; they show up as poor performance for some kinds of processing.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: MapReduce is very robust: it gets the job done on an unreliable multi-tenant system with frequent task terminations, albeit slowly. Other tools can be orders of magnitude faster for some kinds of processing.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use MapReduce as a learning tool and for very robust processing; reach for higher-level tools and other engines for productivity and speed.

card.rule: MapReduce is understandable and robust, but laborious to program directly and slow for some work.
card.limits: Higher-level languages ease the effort, yet they inherit the performance limits of the engine beneath them.

concepts.title: Materialization versus pipes
concepts.question: What does it mean to materialize intermediate state, and how is it unlike a Unix pipe?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: In a MapReduce workflow the only contact point between jobs is the output and input directory on the distributed filesystem. That raises the question of when this is the right way to pass data along.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The process of writing intermediate state out to files is called materialization. A Unix pipe does not fully materialize: it streams output to input incrementally through a small in-memory buffer.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Materialized files can be named, published and reused by other teams, which gives loose coupling. If the output is only the input of one other job of the same team, the files are just intermediate state, and writing them is a cost.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Materialize when the output is a dataset to publish widely in the organization; avoid it for temporary data passed between two stages of one team's workflow.

card.rule: Materialize data you want to publish and reuse; pass temporary data between stages without writing it all out.
card.limits: The cost of materializing depends on the size of the data and on how much replication the filesystem adds.

concepts.title: Three costs of materializing everything
concepts.question: Why can fully materializing intermediate state make a workflow slower than a Unix pipe?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: MapReduce fully materializes the intermediate state between jobs. Compared with Unix pipes, that choice has downsides.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: A job can start only when all tasks in the preceding jobs have finished, whereas processes joined by a pipe start together and consume output as it is produced. Skew or uneven load creates straggler tasks that take much longer than the rest, and waiting for them slows the whole workflow.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Mappers are often redundant: they only read back the file a reducer has just written and prepare it for the next partitioning and sorting. Where the reducer output is partitioned and sorted as mapper output would be, reducers could be chained directly.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Intermediate files in the distributed filesystem carry a storage cost for temporary data. Materialization buys durability and reuse, at a cost in storage and writes.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use these three costs as a checklist when judging a multi-stage workflow: waiting, redundant reading and over-replication.

card.rule: Full materialization makes jobs wait for stragglers, adds redundant mappers and replicates temporary data.
card.limits: The costs matter for chained internal steps; for published datasets, materialization is the point.

concepts.title: Dataflow engines and operators
concepts.question: What do Spark, Tez and Flink do differently from chained MapReduce jobs?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The problems of materializing every step called for new execution engines for distributed batch computations.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Spark, Tez and Flink handle an entire workflow as one job, instead of breaking it into independent subjobs. Because they explicitly model the flow of data through several processing stages, they are called dataflow engines. Like MapReduce they call a user-defined function on one record at a time, partition inputs to parallelize work, and copy the output of one function over the network as input to another.

blocks.label: Operators
blocks.text: Unlike MapReduce, the functions, called operators, need not alternate as map and reduce but can be assembled flexibly. The engine offers several ways to connect operators: repartition and sort by key as in the shuffle, partition several inputs the same way but skip sorting, or send one operator's output to all partitions of a join operator.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Flexible operators give the engine more freedom to optimize; the price is a more complex framework than a fixed map and reduce pair.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use a dataflow engine for multi-stage workflows, where passing intermediate state between jobs through a filesystem is costly.

card.rule: A dataflow engine runs a whole workflow as one job built from flexible operators.
card.limits: Dataflow engines still partition data and call per-record functions; they change the wiring, not the basic model.

concepts.title: What dataflow engines gain over MapReduce
concepts.question: Which optimizations become possible when the engine sees the whole workflow?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: MapReduce sorts between every map and reduce stage, starts a mapper for every step, and writes everything to HDFS. Much of this effort is wasted in a multi-stage workflow.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Dataflow engines sort only where it is actually required; they need no extra map tasks, since a mapper's work can be folded into the preceding reduce operator; and because all joins and data dependencies are explicitly declared, the scheduler has an overview of what data is required where, so it can make locality optimizations, such as running a consumer on the same machine as its producer.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: These engines need to keep intermediate state in memory or on local disk, which requires less I/O than writing it to HDFS, but state in memory or on a local disk is lost if the machine fails.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use a dataflow engine when a workflow has many stages, so that skipping sorts, extra mappers and HDFS writes pays off.

card.rule: With the whole workflow in view, the engine sorts less, writes less and places tasks near their data.
card.limits: The gains depend on the workflow: a single-stage job gains little from these optimizations.

concepts.title: Recovering by recomputing lost data
concepts.question: How do engines that skip HDFS for intermediate state survive a lost machine?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: MapReduce is easy to make fault tolerant because intermediate state is durable in the distributed filesystem: a failed task restarts and reads the same input again. Dataflow engines avoid that write, so they need another way.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: If a machine fails and the intermediate state on it is lost, Spark, Flink and Tez recompute it from other data that is still available, going back as far as needed. To make that possible, the framework must keep track of how a piece of data was computed, that is, which input partitions it used and which operators were applied.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Recomputation avoids the write cost in the normal case, but a failure means redoing work, so recovery is slower than reading durable intermediate files.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use recomputation when failures are rare enough that redoing work occasionally costs less than materializing everything.

card.rule: Lost intermediate data is rebuilt from its ancestors, so the engine must record how data was computed.
card.limits: Recomputation is only as good as the data it can start from; if ancestors are lost too, it has to go back to the original input.

concepts.title: Why deterministic operators matter
concepts.question: Why does recomputation work best when operators are deterministic?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: When lost data is recomputed, some of the lost output may already have been sent to downstream operators. If the recomputed data differs, the downstream operators have contradictory versions.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Ask whether a computation is deterministic: given the same input data, do the operators always produce the same output? If an operator is nondeterministic, recovery needs extra work further downstream. To avoid that, it is better to make operators deterministic.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Nondeterminism creeps in easily: many programming languages give no guarantee on the order of iteration over a hash table, probabilistic algorithms rely on random numbers, and any use of the system clock or an external data source is nondeterministic.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Removing nondeterminism takes care, for example by generating pseudorandom numbers from a fixed seed, but it makes recovery reliable.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use deterministic operators in any workflow that recovers by recomputation.

card.rule: Make operators deterministic so that recomputed data matches what downstream operators already received.
card.limits: Determinism is a property to engineer, not to assume; a single clock read can break it.

concepts.title: Recompute or write it down?
concepts.question: When is it cheaper to materialize intermediate data than to recompute it after a fault?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Recovering by recomputation avoids writing intermediate data, but it is not free.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Compare the cost of recomputing with the cost of writing the data out. Two signals, one about data size and one about computation, can tip the balance toward writing it.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Materializing buys cheap recovery at the price of write cost on every run; recomputing saves that cost but pays when a fault strikes.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it as a rule of thumb for each stage: small outputs or expensive computation point to materializing.

card.rule: Materialize small or expensive intermediate results; recompute large cheap ones.
card.limits: This is a rule of thumb from the cost comparison; actual choices depend on failure rates and measured costs.

concepts.title: Pipelined execution and the sort that must wait
concepts.question: Which parts of a workflow can be pipelined, and which operator must wait for all its input?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Dataflow engines look much more like Unix pipes than like MapReduce's temporary files, but some operators cannot start producing output until they have seen everything.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Flink in particular is built around pipelined execution: incrementally passing the output of an operator to other operators, without waiting for the input to be complete before processing it. A sorting operation cannot do this, because the very last input record might be the one with the lowest key and so be the first output record. Any operator that requires sorting must accumulate state, at least temporarily.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Pipelining reduces waiting and intermediate writes, but operators such as sorting still need their full input before they can emit anything.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it when reasoning about latency in a dataflow job: find the operators that block, and expect the rest to stream.

card.rule: Most operators can stream their output onward; a sort has to see all of its input first.
card.limits: Pipelining speeds up the flow, but a blocking operator still sets the pace for everything after it.

concepts.title: Graphs in batch processing, and the DAG naming trap
concepts.question: What is graph processing in batch, and how does it differ from a dataflow engine's DAG?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Chapter 2 treated graphs in OLTP style: quickly find a small number of vertices matching some criteria. Machine learning and ranking systems need offline analysis of an entire graph.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: PageRank is the famous example: it estimates the popularity of a web page from what other pages link to it, and feeds the order of search results. Many graph algorithms traverse one edge at a time, joining a vertex with its neighbour to pass information on, and repeat until a condition is met.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Dataflow engines arrange their operators as a directed acyclic graph, but that is the shape of the data flow, while the data itself is relational-style tuples. In graph processing the data itself has the form of a graph. Two different things share one word.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use the term graph processing only when the data is a graph; call the operator layout a dataflow DAG.

card.rule: Graph processing means the data is a graph; a dataflow DAG is only the shape of the job.
card.limits: The two can meet: a graph job may itself run on a dataflow engine whose operators form a DAG.

concepts.title: Why iterating on graphs with MapReduce is wasteful
concepts.question: How is a repeat-until-done algorithm run on MapReduce, and what does that cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Repeating until done cannot be expressed in plain MapReduce, since it only performs a single pass over the data.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Run it in an iterative style. An external scheduler runs a batch process for one step, checks the completion condition when it ends, and starts another round if not finished. The condition may be that no edges remain to follow or that the change from the last round is below a threshold.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: MapReduce does not account for the iterative nature of the algorithm. Each round repeats the full work on the whole graph, however little has changed since the last round.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: It works and reuses the same simple model, but the cost per round is proportional to the whole graph and not to the change.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Judge by how much changes each round: a small changing fraction makes whole-dataset rewrites a poor fit.

card.rule: Iterating with MapReduce rereads and rewrites the whole graph each round, however little changed.
card.limits: Cost grows with the number of rounds times the size of the full dataset, not with the amount of change.

concepts.title: The Pregel model: vertices that pass messages
concepts.question: How does Pregel (bulk synchronous parallel) process a graph one round at a time?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Iterating with MapReduce rewrites the whole graph each round. A model that remembers state between rounds would do far less work.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The bulk synchronous parallel (BSP) model, also known as Pregel, is implemented by Apache Giraph, Spark's GraphX API and Flink's Gelly API. In each iteration a function is called for each vertex, passing it all messages sent to it, much like a reducer call. Messages typically travel along the edges.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A vertex remembers its state in memory from one iteration to the next, so it only needs to process new incoming messages. Where no messages flow, no work is done. The price is that all messages of one iteration must be delivered before the next starts.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: The actor model is similar if each vertex is an actor, but Pregel communicates in fixed rounds and keeps vertex state and messages durable, which actors normally do not.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use it for iterative algorithms where each step touches only part of the graph.

card.rule: Pregel calls a function per vertex per round with that vertex's messages, keeping vertex state in memory.
card.limits: Vertices communicate by message passing only, and a round cannot start until the previous one is complete.

concepts.title: Exactly-once messages and checkpoints in Pregel
concepts.question: How does Pregel survive lost machines and unreliable networks?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The network can drop, duplicate or arbitrarily delay messages, and a node failure loses in-memory vertex state. The programming model should not expose this.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Implementations guarantee that each message is processed exactly once at its destination vertex in the following iteration. To get this, the state of all vertices is periodically checkpointed at the end of an iteration, that is, written in full to durable storage.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The simplest recovery rolls back the entire computation to the last checkpoint and restarts. If the algorithm is deterministic and messages are logged, only the lost partition can be recovered, as with dataflow engines.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Pick the simple rollback unless restart cost is high and the algorithm is deterministic with logged messages.

card.rule: Pregel checkpoints all vertex state at iteration ends and rolls back to the last checkpoint after a failure.
card.limits: Selective recovery of one partition needs deterministic code and logged messages.

concepts.title: Graph partitioning cost and when one machine wins
concepts.question: Why can a single machine beat a Pregel cluster on a graph job?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A vertex does not know which machine it runs on; it sends messages to vertex IDs. The framework decides where each vertex runs and how messages are routed.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Because the model handles one vertex at a time, the framework may partition the graph in arbitrary ways. Ideally vertices that talk a lot are on the same machine, but finding such a partitioning is hard, so in practice the graph is often partitioned by an arbitrarily assigned vertex ID.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Graph algorithms then have a lot of cross-machine communication overhead, and the intermediate state (messages between nodes) is often bigger than the original graph. Sending messages over the network can significantly slow down the algorithm.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: If the graph fits in memory on one computer, a single-machine, maybe even single-threaded, algorithm will quite likely outperform a distributed batch process. If it fits only on disk, a framework such as GraphChi is viable.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Go distributed only if the graph is too big for one machine; then Pregel is unavoidable.

card.rule: Arbitrary partitioning makes cross-machine messages costly, so a graph that fits on one machine is faster there.
card.limits: Efficient parallelization of graph algorithms is described as an area of ongoing research.

concepts.title: High-level dataflow APIs and interactive use
concepts.question: Why did high-level APIs on top of batch engines catch on, beyond saving code?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Once running batch jobs at the scale of petabytes and clusters of over 10,000 machines was considered more or less solved, attention turned to the programming model, to efficiency, and to the set of problems the technology can solve.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Spark and Flink include their own high-level dataflow APIs, often inspired by FlumeJava. They express a computation with relational-style building blocks: joining datasets on a field, grouping tuples by key, filtering by a condition, and aggregating by counting or summing. Internally these use the join and grouping algorithms covered earlier in the chapter.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Besides needing less code, these interfaces allow interactive use: you write analysis code incrementally in a shell and run it often to see what it does. That helps when exploring a dataset, and it echoes the Unix philosophy.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use a high-level API for exploration and day-to-day jobs; drop to hand-written callbacks only for what the building blocks cannot express.

card.rule: High-level APIs use relational building blocks, need less code, and allow interactive exploration.
card.limits: They also let the engine run more efficiently, which the next ideas explain.

concepts.title: Declarative joins and the cost-based optimizer
concepts.question: What do you gain by stating which join you need, instead of coding how to do it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The choice of join algorithm can make a big difference to the performance of a batch job, and remembering all the algorithms is a burden.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Specify joins as relational operators in a declarative way: the application states which joins are required and the query optimizer decides how to execute them. The framework can analyze the properties of the join inputs and automatically pick the most suitable algorithm.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Hive, Spark and Flink have cost-based query optimizers that can also change the order of joins to minimize the amount of intermediate state. You give up direct control of the algorithm.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use declarative joins by default; spell out the join code yourself only when the optimizer cannot know something about your data.

card.rule: State which joins you need and let a cost-based optimizer choose the algorithm and the join order.
card.limits: The optimizer can only use what it can analyze; it knows nothing beyond the input properties it can see.

concepts.title: Callbacks give freedom, declarative gives speed
concepts.question: How does MapReduce's callback style differ from SQL's declarative model, and why does it matter?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: MapReduce and its dataflow successors differ from the fully declarative query model of SQL in other ways.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: MapReduce is built around function callbacks: for each record or group of records a user-defined function (the mapper or reducer) is called, and it is free to call arbitrary code to decide what to output. That lets you draw on a large ecosystem of existing libraries for parsing, natural language analysis, image analysis and numerical or statistical algorithms.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: This freedom is what long distinguished batch systems of MapReduce heritage from MPP databases. Databases have user-defined functions, but they are often cumbersome and not well integrated with package managers and dependency management such as Maven, npm and Rubygems.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choose callbacks when you need arbitrary code or existing libraries; choose declarative operators when the optimizer can do the work for you.

card.rule: Callbacks run arbitrary code and libraries, which MPP user-defined functions handle poorly.
card.limits: Opaque callbacks give the optimizer nothing to analyze, which is the cost of that freedom.

concepts.title: Declarative filters, column reads and vectorized execution
concepts.question: Why do dataflow engines want even simple filters and field selections to be declarative?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If a callback only holds a simple filtering condition, or only selects some fields from a record, there is significant CPU overhead in calling the function for every record.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Express such simple filtering and mapping in a declarative way, so the query optimizer can use column-oriented storage layouts and read only the required columns from disk. Hive, Spark DataFrames and Impala also use vectorized execution: iterating over data in a tight inner loop that is friendly to CPU caches and avoids function calls.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The framework can optimize what it can see; a callback stays opaque. Adding declarative features helps performance, while arbitrary code remains possible.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use declarative filters and projections for simple per-record work, and keep callbacks for logic the operators cannot express.

card.rule: Declarative filters let the engine read only needed columns and run tight, vectorized loops.
card.limits: Callbacks that do real work still pay a per-record call, so the gain is for simple conditions and field selections.

concepts.title: Reusable building blocks for different domains
concepts.question: Why do batch engines grow domain libraries, and what does that say about batch and MPP systems?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Running arbitrary code is useful, but standard processing patterns keep recurring, so reusable implementations of common building blocks are worth having. MPP databases traditionally served business intelligence and reporting, which is just one of many domains.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Statistical and numerical algorithms for machine learning, such as classification and recommendation, are one growing domain. Mahout implements machine learning algorithms on top of MapReduce, Spark and Flink, while MADlib implements similar functionality inside a relational MPP database (Apache HAWQ).

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Spatial algorithms such as k-nearest neighbors search for items close to a given item in some multi-dimensional space, a kind of similarity search. Approximate search is also important for genome analysis, which must find strings that are similar but not identical.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Each side gains features of the other, so the choice between them is less clear-cut.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Check for a reusable library in your domain before writing the algorithm yourself.

card.rule: Domain libraries package recurring algorithms, and batch and MPP systems converge toward each other.
card.limits: The chapter lists examples and does not claim the two families become identical.

concepts.title: The two problems batch frameworks solve
concepts.question: Which two problems must a distributed batch framework solve, and how do the engines differ?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A distributed batch framework has to bring related data together across many machines, and it has to survive failures along the way.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Partitioning: mappers are partitioned by input file blocks, and their output is repartitioned, sorted and merged into a configurable number of reducer partitions. Post-MapReduce dataflow engines avoid sorting unless required, but partition in a broadly similar way.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Fault tolerance: MapReduce writes to disk often, which makes recovery of a failed task easy but slows the failure-free case. Dataflow engines materialize less and keep more in memory, so they must recompute more after a node fails, and deterministic operators reduce what must be recomputed.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use this pair as a lens on any batch engine: ask how it partitions and how it recovers.

card.rule: Batch frameworks solve partitioning and fault tolerance; MapReduce favours easy recovery, dataflow engines favour speed.
card.limits: The summary compares engines by two questions; it does not cover every difference between them.

concepts.title: A deliberately restricted model buys reliability
concepts.question: What does the restricted batch programming model give up, and what does it buy?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Fault tolerance in a distributed system is hard to get right in application code, especially with crashes and network issues.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Distributed batch engines have a deliberately restricted programming model: callback functions such as mappers and reducers are assumed to be stateless and to have no externally visible side effects besides their designated output. This lets the framework hide hard distributed systems problems behind its abstraction.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Tasks can be retried safely, and the output of failed tasks is discarded. If several tasks for a partition succeed, only one of them makes its output visible. The cost is that your code cannot rely on state or side effects.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Rely on this guarantee when writing batch jobs; keep side effects out of the callbacks.

card.rule: Stateless callbacks with no side effects let the framework retry tasks safely and publish one result per partition.
card.limits: A callback that writes to an external system breaks the guarantee, since retries would repeat that write.

concepts.title: Bounded input: a batch job knows when it is done
concepts.question: What distinguishes a batch job, and why does bounded input matter?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You need to tell batch processing apart from other styles of processing, such as the streams in the next chapter.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A batch job reads some input data and produces some output data without modifying the input, so the output is derived from the input. Crucially, the input is bounded: it has a known, fixed size, such as a set of log files at some point in time or a snapshot of a database.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Bounded input gives a clear point at which the job is complete. Many real data sets do not end that way, which is the subject of the next chapter.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use batch when the input can be cut off at a point in time; look at streams when data keeps arriving.

card.rule: A batch job reads bounded input, writes derived output, and finishes once the input is consumed.
card.limits: Bounded means known and fixed in size; unbounded data never reaches such a finishing point.

concepts.title: Unbounded input and why streams exist
concepts.question: Why does a daily batch job show a user's action in its output only a day later?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Batch jobs assume the input is bounded: of known, finite size, so the job knows when it has finished reading. Real data arrives gradually and never ends, so a batch job has to cut it into fixed slices, such as one day's data processed at the end of each day.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Stream processing gives up the fixed slices and handles every event as it happens. A stream is data that is made available incrementally over time.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Slicing is simple but delays the output: with daily slices, a change shows up a day later. Running the slices more often shortens the delay, and continuous processing removes the slices, but then the job can no longer rely on its input ending.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Users cannot wait for the next slice to finish, for example when a dashboard or alert should reflect events within seconds.

card.rule: Unbounded input forces a choice between artificial time slices (batch) and continuous processing of each event (streams).
card.limits: Our reading: where a day's delay is acceptable, a daily batch can remain the simpler choice; streams are not automatically better.

media.alt: Engraved fantasy map of a land of stream processing: message queues and sensors in the northeast, a forest of logs, mountains of state, a sands of time region, and a great event stream river, with a ship sailing toward batch processing.

concepts.title: Events, producers, consumers and topics
concepts.question: What is an event, and how do producers, consumers and topics fit around it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A streaming system needs a unit of data to hand from one place to another, the counterpart of a record in a batch file.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The unit is an event: a small, self-contained, immutable object that records something that happened at a point in time, usually with a timestamp. A producer generates it once, and several consumers may process it. Related events are grouped into a topic.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: An event's timestamp comes from a time-of-day clock, so it says when something happened, not when the event reaches a consumer.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want to process things such as page views, purchases, sensor readings or web server log lines as they occur.

card.rule: An event is generated once by a producer, and any number of consumers can then process it.
card.limits: A topic only groups related events; it is not by itself a guarantee about delivery or ordering.

concepts.title: Why polling a datastore does not scale
concepts.question: Why is it better for consumers to be notified of new events than to poll a datastore?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A file or database is enough to connect producers and consumers in principle: the producer writes each event, and consumers check for new ones since they last ran. A daily batch job works this way.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: For low-delay processing, let consumers be notified when new events appear. Specialised tools exist for delivering event notifications.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The more often you poll, the lower the share of requests that return anything new, so overhead rises as delay falls. Database triggers can react to changes, but they are limited and were an afterthought in database design.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Delays must be low enough that frequent polling would cost more than a dedicated notification mechanism.

card.rule: Frequent polling mostly returns nothing new, so low-delay processing wants notification instead.
card.limits: For a slow, occasional job such as a nightly batch, polling the datastore is perfectly adequate.

concepts.title: When producers outpace consumers
concepts.question: What can a messaging system do when producers send messages faster than consumers can process them?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Producers and consumers run at different speeds. If producers send faster than consumers can process, something has to give.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: There are three options: drop messages, buffer them in a queue, or apply backpressure (also called flow control), which blocks the producer from sending more. Unix pipes and TCP use backpressure with a small fixed-size buffer.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Dropping loses data, buffering needs to be sized and may slow down as it spills from memory to disk, and backpressure slows the producer.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing or comparing a messaging system: ask first which of the three it does, and what happens when its queue grows.

card.rule: Ask what the system does when consumers are slower than producers: drop, buffer or block.
card.limits: The three options are a map for a system's default; many systems let configuration choose between them.

concepts.title: Durability and acceptable message loss
concepts.question: What happens to messages when nodes crash, and how do you decide whether losing some is acceptable?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Nodes crash or go offline. The system must decide whether messages are lost.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: As with databases, durability may need writing to disk and/or replication, which has a cost. If you can afford to sometimes lose messages, you can probably get higher throughput and lower latency on the same hardware.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Whether loss is acceptable depends on the application. Periodic sensor readings can lose a point, since an updated value comes soon, though many dropped messages may not be visible. Counting events needs reliable delivery, as every lost message means a wrong counter.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Deciding how much durability to pay for: ask what a lost message would cost the application.

card.rule: Pay for durability only where a lost message would make results wrong.
card.limits: Occasional loss may be invisible: if many messages are dropped, it may not be immediately apparent that the metrics are incorrect.

concepts.title: Direct messaging between producers and consumers
concepts.question: How do systems that message directly between producers and consumers handle lost messages and offline consumers?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The simplest way to deliver messages is directly from producer to consumer, with no intermediary node.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Examples include UDP multicast for stock market feeds, where low latency matters, brokerless libraries such as ZeroMQ, StatsD and Brubeck for metrics over UDP, and webhooks, where a callback URL registered with one service receives a request whenever an event occurs.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Application code must be aware of possible message loss. A consumer that is offline misses messages, and a producer that crashes may lose its buffer of messages to retry.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Latency matters most and both sides are constantly online, or occasional loss is tolerable.

card.rule: Direct messaging is fast and simple but assumes producers and consumers are always online.
card.limits: Protocols can retransmit lost packets, but they cannot help if the producer's retry buffer disappears when it crashes.

concepts.title: Message brokers
concepts.question: What does a message broker add, and what does it take over from producers and consumers?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Direct messaging breaks when a consumer is offline or a producer crashes with unsent messages in memory.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Send messages through a message broker (also called a message queue): a kind of database optimised for message streams, running as a server. Producers write to it and consumers read from it, and durability moves to the broker, which may keep messages in memory or write them to disk.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Consumers become asynchronous: the producer waits only until the broker has buffered the message, not until it is processed. Delivery happens at some undetermined later time, often within a fraction of a second but later if a backlog builds.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Clients connect, disconnect and crash, and messages should not be lost with them.

card.rule: A broker centralises the data, so clients can come and go and durability is the broker's job.
card.limits: A broker makes consumers asynchronous: confirmation of sending is not confirmation of processing.

concepts.title: Message brokers compared with databases
concepts.question: How do traditional message brokers differ from databases, even when brokers support two-phase commit?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Some brokers can take part in two-phase commit with XA or JTA, which makes them look like databases.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Four differences remain. Databases keep data until it is explicitly deleted, while most brokers delete a message once delivered. Brokers assume a small working set with short queues. Databases offer secondary indexes and searches, while brokers let clients subscribe to topics matching a pattern. A query returns a point-in-time snapshot, while a broker notifies clients of new data.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A broker that must buffer a lot, because consumers are slow, makes each message take longer and may lower throughput.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Deciding whether a broker can replace a store: traditional brokers are not suitable for long-term data storage.

card.rule: A traditional broker forgets messages after delivery and pushes changes to clients; a database remembers and answers queries.
card.limits: This is the traditional view, expressed in JMS and AMQP; log-based brokers, covered next, change several of these points.

concepts.title: Load balancing and fan-out
concepts.question: When several consumers read one topic, how do load balancing and fan-out differ?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: More than one consumer may read the same topic, and the broker must decide who gets which message.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Load balancing delivers each message to one of the consumers, so they share the work. Fan-out delivers each message to all consumers, so several independent consumers can tune in to the same broadcast without affecting each other.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Load balancing parallelises expensive work but each consumer sees only part of the stream. Fan-out gives each consumer everything, but adds no parallelism on its own.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use load balancing when messages are expensive to process and you want to add consumers. Use fan-out when several independent systems each need every message.

card.rule: Load balancing splits the messages among consumers; fan-out gives every message to every consumer.
card.limits: Fan-out gives every consumer the whole stream, so it adds no parallelism; load balancing hides part of the stream from each consumer.

media.alt: Two timelines, (a) load balancing and (b) fan-out, with lanes Producer 1, Producer 2, Broker, Consumer 1 and Consumer 2. In both, producers send messages m1 to m5 to the broker. In (a) m1 and m3 go to Consumer 2 while m2 and m4 go to Consumer 1. In (b) every message m1 to m4 goes to both consumers.

concepts.title: Acknowledgments and redelivery
concepts.question: How does a broker avoid losing a message when a consumer crashes while processing it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A consumer may crash after the broker delivers a message but before it processes it, or after processing only part of it.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The broker uses acknowledgments: a client must explicitly tell the broker when it has finished processing a message, so the broker can remove it from the queue. If the connection closes or times out without an acknowledgment, the broker assumes the message was not processed and delivers it again to another consumer.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The message may in fact have been fully processed, with only the acknowledgment lost in the network, so it can be processed twice. Handling this case needs an atomic commit protocol.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Messages must not be lost when consumers crash, and you can handle or tolerate a message being processed more than once.

card.rule: Delete a message only after the consumer acknowledges it, and redeliver it if no acknowledgment arrives.
card.limits: Acknowledgments prevent lost messages but not duplicate processing; the lost-acknowledgment case needs more machinery.

concepts.title: Load balancing plus redelivery reorders messages
concepts.question: Why can load balancing combined with redelivery make consumers see messages in a different order from the one sent?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Consumers generally process messages in the order producers sent them. Order matters when messages depend on each other.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Suppose consumer 2 crashes while processing message m3 and consumer 1 is processing m4. The unacknowledged m3 is redelivered to consumer 1, which now processes m4, m3, m5. Even a broker that tries to preserve order, as JMS and AMQP require, cannot avoid this.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: To avoid reordering, use a separate queue per consumer, which means giving up load balancing.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Messages depend on one another, so their order matters and you can accept less parallelism in return.

card.rule: Load balancing together with redelivery inevitably reorders messages; use a queue per consumer if order matters.
card.limits: A separate queue per consumer avoids the problem but gives up the parallel consumption that load balancing was for.
