media.alt: Timeline with lanes Producer 1, Producer 2, Broker, Consumer 1 and Consumer 2. Consumer 1 processes m2 and returns an ack, then m4. Consumer 2 processes m1 with an ack, receives m3 and crashes, shown as a burst followed by a grey crashed bar. The broker redelivers m3 to Consumer 1 after m4, and m5 follows.

concepts.title: Transient messaging versus durable storage
concepts.question: Why can you not rerun a consumer of a traditional broker and expect the same result?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Traditional brokers are built around a transient mindset: a message is deleted once it has been delivered and acknowledged. Databases and filesystems keep what is written until someone explicitly deletes it.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Ask for a hybrid: the durable storage of databases combined with the low-latency notification of messaging. Log-based message brokers are built on exactly this idea.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: With deletion on acknowledgment, receiving a message is destructive, so a consumer cannot be run again to get the same result. Batch jobs lack this problem because their input is read-only.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want to experiment with the processing steps behind derived data, without risking the input.

card.rule: If receiving a message deletes it, you cannot replay it; keeping the data durable is what allows repeated processing.
card.limits: Deleting is the right choice when messages are meant to be transient and nobody will need to read them again.

concepts.title: Log-based message brokers
concepts.question: How does a partitioned append-only log serve as a message broker?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You want durable storage that is also a low-latency notification channel, with throughput beyond what one disk can offer.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use a log, an append-only sequence of records on disk. A producer appends a message to the end, and a consumer reads sequentially and waits for a notification at the end, much as tail -f does. To scale, split the log into partitions on different machines; a topic is a group of partitions carrying the same type of message.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Within a partition the broker gives every message a monotonically increasing offset, so messages there are totally ordered. There is no ordering guarantee across different partitions.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need durable messaging with high throughput and ordering within a stream of related messages, as in Apache Kafka, Amazon Kinesis Streams or Twitter's DistributedLog.

card.rule: A log-based broker is a partitioned append-only log: order holds inside a partition, not across partitions.
card.limits: A single partition is bounded by what one machine can handle, which is why the log is partitioned in the first place.

media.alt: Two topics drawn as rows of numbered boxes. Topic A has partition 0 (1 to 10) and partition 1 (1 to 8); topic B has partition 0 (1 to 4), partition 1 (1 to 7) and partition 2 (1 to 12). Two producer clients append at dashed empty slots at partition ends. A consumer group has two clients: one reads B partitions 0 and 1 with offsets B.0 = 4 and B.1 = 5, the other reads B partition 2 with offset B.2 = 9.

concepts.title: Fan-out and load balancing in a log
concepts.question: How does a log-based broker give fan-out, and what does it cost to share work by partition?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The same two patterns are needed as before, fan-out and load balancing, but messages are not deleted when they are read.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Fan-out comes free, because consumers read the log independently and reading does not delete. For load balancing, the broker assigns whole partitions, not single messages, to consumer nodes. Each node consumes every message in its partitions, usually sequentially in a single thread.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: At most as many nodes can share a topic as it has partitions. One slow message holds up all later messages in its partition, a form of head-of-line blocking.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Messages are fast to process and their order matters, rather than when single messages are expensive.

card.rule: Log-based load balancing assigns partitions to consumers, so parallelism is capped by the partition count.
card.limits: If messages are expensive and order matters little, per-message distribution suits better; see the next idea.

concepts.title: Choosing between an AMQP/JMS-style and a log-based broker
concepts.question: Which kind of broker suits a task queue, and which suits high-throughput ordered streams?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Two broker styles exist and each makes different assumptions about processing cost, order and rereading.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The AMQP/JMS style assigns individual messages to consumers, who acknowledge each one, and deletes messages once acknowledged. The log-based style assigns all messages of a partition to the same consumer and delivers them in the same order, and consumers record the offset of the last message they have processed.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The first suits expensive messages and per-message parallelism where order matters little and there is no need to reread. The second suits high throughput, fast messages and important ordering, and keeps messages on disk so you can reread.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A task queue calls for the AMQP/JMS style, like an asynchronous form of RPC. Stream processing that builds derived state or derived streams calls for the log-based style.

card.rule: Pick per-message acknowledgment for work queues, and a partitioned log for ordered high-throughput streams that may be reread.
card.limits: The choice follows the workload; neither style is better for every purpose.

concepts.title: Consumer offsets
concepts.question: How can a log-based broker track which messages a consumer has processed without per-message acknowledgments?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A broker has to know where each consumer is, so that a restart neither skips nor repeats messages.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Because a partition is read sequentially, every message with an offset below the consumer's current offset is processed and every message above has not been seen. The broker only needs to record the consumer offset periodically.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Less bookkeeping and the chance to batch and pipeline raise throughput. But if a consumer processed messages and failed before its offset was recorded, those messages are processed a second time after restart.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Consuming a partition sequentially, so one position number describes all progress.

card.rule: A single recorded offset replaces per-message acknowledgments, at the price of possible reprocessing after a crash.
card.limits: Reprocessing after a crash means consumers should expect some messages twice; later ideas deal with this.

concepts.title: Segments, the disk as a ring buffer, and retention
concepts.question: If a log only ever appends, how does it avoid running out of disk space, and how much history does it keep?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A log that only appends will eventually fill the disk.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The log is divided into segments, and from time to time old segments are deleted or moved to archive storage. The log is effectively a bounded-size buffer that discards old messages when full, also called a circular or ring buffer.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A consumer that falls so far behind that its offset points to a deleted segment misses messages.

blocks.label: Numbers
blocks.text: A 6 TB drive written at 150 MB/s fills in about 11 hours. Real deployments rarely use the full write bandwidth, so the buffer typically holds several days or weeks.

card.rule: A log is a large ring buffer: how far back it reaches depends on disk size and write rate.
card.limits: The 11-hour figure is the worst case of writing at the disk's full speed; it was a typical large drive at the time of writing.

concepts.title: When consumers cannot keep up with a log
concepts.question: What does a log do when a consumer falls behind, and how do other consumers fare?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A consumer may fall behind the rate at which producers write.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Of the three options for a fast producer, the log is buffering with a large but fixed-size buffer. If a consumer lags beyond what is retained, the broker effectively drops the old messages it needs. You can monitor how far a consumer is behind the head of the log and alert when it falls far behind.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Because the buffer is large, a human operator has time to fix the slow consumer before it misses messages.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want consumers isolated from each other: only the lagging consumer is affected.

card.rule: A log turns a slow consumer into a monitored lag, and only that consumer suffers if it falls off the end.
card.limits: The protection relies on the buffer being large and someone watching the lag; it does not remove the loss.

concepts.title: Replaying old messages
concepts.question: Why can you reprocess yesterday's events from a log but not from an AMQP-style broker?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: To fix a bug or try a new processing step, you need to run the same processing over past events and compare.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In a log, consuming is a read-only operation: the only side effect besides the consumer's output is that the consumer offset moves forward, and the consumer controls the offset. Start a copy of a consumer from yesterday's offset, write its output to a different location, and repeat as often as you like with different code.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Replaying is limited by retention, and the output location must be kept separate to avoid mixing results.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want to experiment, recover from bugs or integrate dataflows across an organisation, treating the log as the input and the output as derived data.

card.rule: In a log, reading does not change the data, so moving the offset back lets you rerun processing any number of times.
card.limits: Replay only reaches as far back as the log retains messages.

concepts.title: A replication log is a stream of write events
concepts.question: In what sense is a database's replication log already an event stream?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Message brokers and databases are usually seen as separate tools, but an event can also be a write to a database.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A replication log is a stream of database write events, produced by the leader as it processes transactions. Followers apply that stream to their own copy and end up with the same data. State machine replication states the principle: if every event is a write and every replica processes the same events in the same order, all replicas end in the same state.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The principle needs processing of an event to be a deterministic operation.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want to treat database changes like any other stream, so the same tools and ideas for streams can be applied to databases.

card.rule: Replicas that apply the same deterministic writes in the same order end in the same state.
card.limits: The principle covers one leader whose order every replica follows; independent systems with no shared order can still diverge.

media.alt: Diagram: Client 1 sets X = A and Client 2 sets X = B on a system of record database. Change data capture appends these changes to a log of data changes shown as boxes with X = A then X = B. Two log consumers, a search index and a data warehouse, each read the log and apply the changes in order.

concepts.title: Keeping several data systems in sync
concepts.question: Why must an application's database, cache, search index and warehouse be kept in sync, and how is it usually done?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Most non-trivial applications combine technologies: an OLTP database for requests, a cache, a full-text index for search, and a data warehouse for analytics. Each holds its own copy of the data in a form suited to it, and all must reflect an update.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Warehouses are usually synchronised by ETL: a full copy of a database is transformed and bulk-loaded, which is a batch process. If full dumps are too slow, applications may use dual writes, explicitly writing to each system in turn.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Batch loads are slow to reflect changes. Dual writes are faster but have serious problems, shown next.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: More than one system holds a copy of the same or related data.

card.rule: Every derived copy of data needs a mechanism that carries each change to it.
card.limits: Periodic full dumps are acceptable when the delay is tolerable, since they are simple.

concepts.title: Dual writes: the race condition
concepts.question: How can dual writes leave two systems permanently inconsistent even though no error occurred?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Two clients write item X at the same time: client 1 sets A, client 2 sets B. Each writes first to the database and then to the search index.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: With unlucky timing the requests interleave. The database sees A then B, so its final value is B. The search index sees B then A, so its final value is A.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The two systems are now permanently inconsistent with each other, and nothing failed. Without a concurrency detection mechanism such as version vectors you will not even notice: one value silently overwrites another.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.text: Each system is internally correct; the disagreement exists only between them.

card.rule: Dual writes can apply two updates in different orders in two systems, leaving them different for good.
card.limits: A single leader that fixes the order of writes avoids this, but two independent systems each with a leader do not follow one another.

media.alt: Timeline with lanes Client 1, Database, Search index and Client 2. Client 1 sends set X = A and Client 2 sends set X = B to each store, each getting ok. The database receives A first and then B, ending with final value X = B. The search index receives B first and then A, ending with final value X = A.

concepts.title: Dual writes: partial failure and the single-leader fix
concepts.question: What other problem do dual writes have, and what would be a better arrangement?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: One of the two writes may succeed while the other fails. This is a fault-tolerance problem, not a concurrency problem, and the systems become inconsistent just the same.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Making both succeed or both fail is the atomic commit problem, which is expensive to solve. A better arrangement is a single leader: if the database were the only leader and the search index its follower, the leader would fix the order of writes.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: State machine replication works within one replicated database with a single leader. With a database and an index that each may have a leader and neither follows the other, conflicts can occur.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Deciding whether to write to several systems from application code: prefer making one system the leader of the others.

card.rule: Dual writes risk partial failure as well as reordering; one leader that others follow avoids both.
card.limits: This is the goal, not yet a mechanism: the next ideas show how databases can act as the leader.

concepts.title: Change data capture
concepts.question: What is change data capture, and how does it turn other systems into followers of a database?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Replication logs were long treated as an internal detail of a database, not a public API, so it was hard to get all the changes out to a search index, cache or warehouse.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Change data capture (CDC) observes all data changes written to a database and extracts them in a form that can be replicated to other systems, ideally as a stream right as they are written. Apply them in the same order and the search index matches the database. It makes one database the leader and the others followers.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The captured log must be transported with its order intact. A log-based message broker suits, since it preserves message order and avoids the reordering issue seen earlier.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A system of record feeds derived data systems such as search indexes, caches and warehouses.

card.rule: CDC makes the system of record the leader and every derived data system a follower consuming its ordered change stream.
card.limits: CDC depends on the database exposing its changes, which was historically poor.

concepts.title: Implementing CDC: triggers or log parsing
concepts.question: How can CDC be implemented, and why are database triggers a weaker choice than parsing the replication log?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A database must hand over its changes in order, without the application having to know.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Triggers can watch all changes to data tables and add entries to a changelog table. Alternatively, parse the database's replication log, as Debezium and Maxwell do for MySQL's binlog, Bottled Water does for PostgreSQL and GoldenGate for Oracle.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Triggers tend to be fragile and add significant performance overhead. Parsing the replication log is more robust but has its own challenges, such as handling schema changes.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You need CDC from a database that has no built-in change stream, and the application should not need to be aware.

card.rule: Prefer reading the replication log to triggers: it is more robust and cheaper, though schema changes need handling.
card.limits: No option is free: log parsing depends on what the database exposes and on tool support.

concepts.title: CDC is asynchronous: the benefit and the lag
concepts.question: What does it mean that CDC is asynchronous, and what follows for the system of record and its consumers?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The database that is the source of truth should not be slowed or blocked by the systems that consume its changes.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Like message brokers, CDC is usually asynchronous: the system of record commits a change without waiting for it to be applied to consumers.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Adding a slow consumer does not affect the system of record much. But all the issues of replication lag apply: a derived system may show data that is behind the database.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You can tolerate derived systems being slightly behind, in exchange for keeping the source fast.

card.rule: Asynchronous CDC protects the source from slow consumers, and in return derived data can lag.
card.limits: If a reader must see its own write in a derived view at once, asynchrony needs extra care.

concepts.title: The initial snapshot
concepts.question: Why does a new derived system need a consistent snapshot, and how is it tied to the change log?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: If you keep the whole history of changes, replaying it rebuilds the database. But keeping all changes forever takes too much disk space, and replaying takes too long, so the log is truncated.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: To build a new derived system, such as a full-text index, start with a consistent snapshot of the database, because recent changes alone would miss items not recently updated. The snapshot must correspond to a known position or offset in the change log.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The position tells you where to start applying changes after the snapshot is processed. Some CDC tools integrate snapshots, while others leave them as a manual operation.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You add a new derived data system but only a limited tail of the log is kept.

card.rule: With a truncated log, a new consumer needs a snapshot taken at a known log position, then applies changes from there.
card.limits: If you keep the full log, or compact it so that it holds the latest value of each key, the snapshot step can be skipped.

concepts.title: Log compaction
concepts.question: How can a log keep a full copy of a database without growing without bound?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Snapshots are needed every time a new derived system is added if only a limited history is kept.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Log compaction periodically finds log records with the same key, discards duplicates and keeps only the most recent update for each key. A tombstone, a null value, marks a key as deleted and causes its removal.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The log's size depends on the current contents of the database, not on the number of writes ever made. Compaction only works if every change has a primary key and replaces the previous value for that key.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A new consumer must rebuild a derived system: start from offset 0 of the compacted topic and scan sequentially, with no new snapshot of the source.

card.rule: A compacted log keeps the latest value of every key, so reading it from the start yields a full copy of the data.
card.limits: Compaction suits updates that replace the whole value for a key; when later events do not override earlier ones, it does not work.

concepts.title: Databases with built-in change streams
concepts.question: What does it mean for a database to offer change streams as a first-class interface?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Most CDC today is retrofitted and reverse-engineered from logs that were never meant as an interface.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Some databases offer change streams directly: RethinkDB lets a query subscribe to notifications when its results change; Firebase and CouchDB synchronise data through a change feed exposed to applications; Meteor uses the MongoDB oplog to update the user interface; VoltDB exports data as a stream.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: In VoltDB the stream is a table that transactions can insert into but that cannot be queried; the stream is the log of tuples committed transactions wrote to it, in commit order.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want consumers to follow data changes without parsing the database's internal log; Kafka Connect integrates CDC tools for many databases with Kafka.

card.rule: A first-class change stream exposes data changes as an interface instead of leaving consumers to reverse-engineer the log.
card.limits: Such interfaces are database-specific; their design differs, as the examples show.

concepts.title: Event sourcing compared with CDC
concepts.question: At what level of abstraction do change data capture and event sourcing each record changes?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Both CDC and event sourcing store all changes to application state as a log of change events, so they are easy to confuse.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In CDC the application uses the database in a mutable way, updating and deleting at will, and the change log is extracted at a low level, for example by parsing the replication log. The application need not know. In event sourcing the application logic is built on immutable events written to an append-only event log, where updates and deletes are discouraged or prohibited.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: CDC's low-level extraction guarantees the order of writes matches the real one, but events say how rows changed. Event sourcing events reflect things that happened at the application level, which requires building the application that way.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use CDC to add streams to an existing mutable database. Use event sourcing when you design the application around immutable events.

card.rule: CDC records low-level state changes taken from a mutable database; event sourcing records application-level events as the primary data.
card.limits: A conventional database or a log-based broker can hold an event-sourced log; the approach does not depend on a particular tool.

concepts.title: Why store intent as events
concepts.question: Why is recording what users did more useful than recording how the database changed?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Recording only the effect of an action, such as a deleted row, embeds assumptions about how the data will be used later.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Record the user's action as an immutable event. 'Student cancelled their course enrolment' expresses the intent of one action neutrally, while the side effects, one row deleted and one cancellation reason added elsewhere, assume a particular later use.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Event sourcing eases evolving an application, helps debugging by making it easier to see afterwards why something happened, and guards against application bugs.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: New features will need to react to existing actions: a new feature such as offering the place to the next person on the waiting list can be chained off the existing event.

card.rule: An event that states what happened lets new side effects be added later without changing what was recorded.
card.limits: It is a modelling choice with a cost: you must design events and derive current state from them.

concepts.title: Deriving current state from the event log
concepts.question: How does an application that stores only events show users their current state?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: An event log by itself is not very useful, because users expect to see the current state of a system, such as the contents of a cart, not the history of every change.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Transform the log of events (the write side) into application state suited to showing users (the read side). The transformation can use arbitrary logic, but it should be deterministic so a rerun derives the same state.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Reprocessing the full log each time is slow, so applications keep snapshots of the derived state. Snapshots are only a performance optimisation to speed up reads and crash recovery.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You store events as the system of record: the intention is that all raw events can be kept forever and reprocessed when required.

card.rule: Current state is a deterministic function of the event log; snapshots only speed it up.
card.limits: Keeping all events forever has limits, discussed under the limits of immutability.

concepts.title: Why log compaction works for CDC but not for event sourcing
concepts.question: Why can a CDC log be compacted by key while an event-sourced log generally cannot?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Both reconstruct current state by replaying a log, but they differ in whether older entries can be thrown away.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A CDC event for a record update typically holds the entire new version of the record, so the latest event for a primary key fully determines the current value, and compaction can discard earlier events for that key.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: An event-sourced event typically expresses the intent of a user action, not the mechanics of the state update, so later events do not override earlier ones and the full history is needed. Compaction is not possible in the same way.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choose compaction only where each entry replaces the previous state for its key.

card.rule: Compaction works when the newest entry for a key replaces everything before it; event-sourced events do not.
card.limits: Our reading: the rule depends on what an entry means, not on the log technology.

concepts.title: Commands and events
concepts.question: What is the difference between a command and an event, and when does a request become a fact?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A user's request may be invalid. Recording it as an immutable fact before checking it would make a rejected request part of the log.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A request first arrives as a command, which may still fail, for instance because an integrity condition is violated. The application validates it first. If it is accepted, it becomes an event, which is durable and immutable.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Once generated, an event is a fact. If the customer later cancels a reservation, the fact that they once held it remains true, and the cancellation is a separate later event.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A request needs a check, such as whether a username or seat is already taken, before it counts as something that happened.

card.rule: A command can be rejected; once validated and accepted it becomes an immutable event, a fact.
card.limits: Our reading: the distinction is a discipline of the event sourcing style, not a feature of every messaging system.

concepts.title: Validating a command before it becomes an event
concepts.question: How can the check on a command be made safe when the log is append-only?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Validation must finish before the event exists, since consumers cannot reject it afterwards.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Validate synchronously: use a serialisable transaction that atomically validates the command and publishes the event. Or split the request into two events: a tentative reservation, then a separate confirmation event once the reservation has been validated.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Synchronous validation blocks the request until the check succeeds. The two-event version leaves a tentative state in place until the confirmation event arrives.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use synchronous checks where a request must be accepted or refused at once; use tentative-then-confirm where validation can wait.

card.rule: Validate atomically before publishing, or publish a tentative event and confirm it later.
card.limits: The confirmation approach relies on a way to order or serialise the requests behind the scenes.

concepts.title: State and the changelog are two sides of one coin
concepts.question: How are mutable state and an append-only log of immutable events related?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Databases store the current state and support updates and deletes, yet event sourcing and CDC rest on immutability. How do these fit together?

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: State is the result of the events that changed it over time: seats available come from the reservations processed, a balance from credits and debits. The log of all changes, the changelog, represents the evolution of state over time. Mutable state and an append-only log of immutable events do not contradict each other.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Treat the log as the system of record and mutable state as derived from it: the database is then a cache of the latest values in the log. Storing the changelog durably makes the state reproducible.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want to reason about the flow of data through a system.

card.rule: Application state is what you get by integrating an event stream over time; the change stream is the derivative of the state.
card.limits: The integration analogy has limits: for instance the second derivative of state does not seem to be meaningful.

media.alt: Two mathematical formulas side by side. On the left, state(now) equals the integral from t = 0 to now of stream(t) dt. On the right, stream(t) equals the derivative d state(t) over dt.

concepts.title: Immutable events: ledgers, audit and extra information
concepts.question: Why do accountants never erase a wrong transaction, and what do other systems gain from the same habit?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Mistakes happen. If wrong data can be erased or overwritten, you lose the evidence of what went wrong.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Accountants record every transaction in an append-only ledger and derive the accounts from it. If a mistake is made, they add a compensating transaction, such as a refund, and the incorrect one stays for ever for auditing. Published figures that were wrong are corrected in the next period.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: An append-only log makes it easier to diagnose bugs and recover from them. Immutable events also capture more than the current state, for example an item that was added to a cart and then removed.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Audit matters, or buggy code might otherwise destructively overwrite data.

card.rule: Correct mistakes by appending compensating events, so the history shows what happened and why.
card.limits: Immutability has a cost, discussed in the limits of immutability.

concepts.title: Several read views and CQRS
concepts.question: What do you gain by deriving several read-optimised views from one event log?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Storing data is easy if you ignore how it will be queried; most complexity of schema design, indexing and storage engines comes from supporting certain access patterns.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Separate the mutable read state from the immutable event log and derive several read-oriented representations from the same log, just as a stream can have multiple consumers. Examples include Druid ingesting from Kafka, Pistachio using Kafka as a commit log, and Kafka Connect sinks exporting to databases and indexes.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: An explicit translation step from log to database makes it easy to add a new feature with a new view and run it beside the old system, which is often easier than a complicated schema migration. The old system can be shut down when no longer needed. The extra step makes read views lag.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want to change how data is presented or queried without altering the system of record. The idea is known as command query responsibility segregation (CQRS).

card.rule: Keep one write-optimised event log and derive as many read-optimised views from it as you need.
card.limits: Each view is another asynchronous consumer, so views can lag behind the log.

concepts.title: Writing in one form and reading in another
concepts.question: Why does the chapter call it a fallacy that data must be written in the same form as it will be queried?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Traditional schema design assumes the form in which data is written must also be the form in which it is queried. This drives debates over normalisation and denormalisation.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: If you translate data from a write-optimised event log into read-optimised state, the debates become largely irrelevant. It is reasonable to denormalise the read views, since the translation keeps them consistent with the log.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Denormalised copies need maintaining, and a process must keep them in sync. In the Twitter home timeline example, tweets are duplicated in every follower's timeline, and the fan-out service keeps the duplicated state in sync with new tweets and follows.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Read patterns need data in shapes that differ from how it is naturally written.

card.rule: With a translation step from log to views, you can denormalise reading without compromising how data is written.
card.limits: Denormalised views only stay manageable because something explicitly keeps them consistent with the log.

concepts.title: The cost of asynchronous read views
concepts.question: What goes wrong for a user who writes to the log and immediately reads from a derived view?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Consumers of an event log are usually asynchronous, so a user may append a write and then read from a log-derived view that does not show it yet.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: One remedy is to update the read view synchronously with appending the event. This needs a transaction combining the writes into an atomic unit: either keep the log and the read view in one storage system, or use a distributed transaction. Another is the approach for implementing linearizable storage using total order broadcast.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Synchronous updates give read-your-writes, but cost the transaction machinery and tie the view to the log.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Users must see their own writes at once in the view.

card.rule: Asynchronous views can lag behind the log, so reading your own write needs synchronous updates or a stronger ordering mechanism.
card.limits: If the view may lag without harm, asynchronous consumers are simpler and avoid the transaction cost.

concepts.title: A serial log simplifies concurrency control
concepts.question: How can deriving state from an event log reduce the need for transactions and concurrency control?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Much of the need for multi-object transactions comes from a single user action requiring changes in several places.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In event sourcing, design an event as a self-contained description of a user action. The action then needs one write, appending the event to the log, which is easy to make atomic. If the event log and the application state are partitioned the same way, a single-threaded log consumer needs no concurrency control for writes: it processes one event at a time.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The log defines a serial order of events within a partition, removing nondeterminism. If an event touches several state partitions, more work is needed, which the book covers in the next chapter.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Events map cleanly onto partitions, for instance by customer.

card.rule: A self-contained event plus a partitioned single-threaded consumer gives atomicity and serial order without locks.
card.limits: Events that span several state partitions bring back the need for coordination.

concepts.title: How far immutability can go
concepts.question: When is it impractical to keep an immutable history of all changes for ever?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Keeping the full history of every change is attractive, but how feasible it is depends on the amount of churn in the dataset.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Workloads that mostly add data and rarely update or delete are easy to make immutable. Many systems that are not event sourced still rely on immutability: databases use immutable structures or multi-version data for point-in-time snapshots, and Git, Mercurial and Fossil keep version history.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Workloads with a high rate of updates and deletes on a comparatively small dataset see the immutable history grow prohibitively large, with fragmentation, so the performance of compaction and garbage collection becomes crucial.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Churn is low, or you can afford the history and its garbage collection.

card.rule: Immutability suits add-mostly workloads; heavy update and delete churn on a small dataset makes the history grow too large.
card.limits: Churn is the decisive factor, not the total data size.

concepts.title: When data really must be deleted
concepts.question: Why is appending a deletion event not enough when data must truly be removed, and why is real deletion hard?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Sometimes data must be deleted despite immutability: privacy rules may require deleting a user's personal data after they close their account, protection law may require removing erroneous data, or a leak of sensitive data must be contained.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Appending an event that says the data should be considered deleted is not enough; you want to rewrite history as if the data was never written. Datomic calls this excision, and the Fossil version control system calls it shunning.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Truly deleting data is surprisingly hard. Copies can live in many places: storage engines, filesystems and SSDs often write to a new location instead of overwriting, and backups are often deliberately immutable.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Law or incident response requires removal; accept that deletion often means making the data harder to retrieve rather than impossible.

card.rule: A deletion event hides data without removing it; real deletion rewrites history and is hard because copies spread.
card.limits: Deletion is more a matter of making retrieval harder than making it impossible.

concepts.title: Three things to do with a stream
concepts.question: Once you have a stream of events, what can you do with it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A stream carries events from user activity, sensors and database writes. Transporting it is only half of the job: something must consume it.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: There are three options. Write the events to a database, cache, search index or similar store that other clients can query; this is the streaming counterpart of batch workflow output. Push the events to people through email alerts, push notifications or a real-time dashboard. Process one or more input streams to produce output streams.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The first two end the stream at a storage system or a human. The third keeps the data flowing through a pipeline of stages before it reaches an output of the first or second kind.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choose by where the result is needed: in a queryable store, in front of a person, or as another stream that more jobs can consume.

card.rule: A stream can end in a store, end with a person, or feed another stream-processing stage.
card.limits: The rest of the chapter concentrates on the third option, processing streams into derived streams.

concepts.title: Stream jobs versus batch jobs
concepts.question: What do stream processors share with batch jobs, and what changes because a stream never ends?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Stream processing looks like batch processing, so it is tempting to expect the same techniques to work unchanged.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A piece of code that processes streams is called an operator or a job. Like a Unix process or a MapReduce job, it reads its input in a read-only fashion and writes its output to a different place in an append-only fashion. Partitioning and parallelisation patterns are very similar, and mapping and filtering work the same.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The crucial difference is that a stream never ends. Sorting makes no sense on an unbounded dataset, so sort-merge joins cannot be used. Fault tolerance must change: a failed batch task can restart from the beginning, but a stream job running for years cannot.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Moving a batch design to streams: keep what is shared, and redesign anything that relied on the input ending.

card.rule: Stream jobs share batch jobs' dataflow patterns, but anything that needs the whole input, such as sorting, must be rethought.
card.limits: The shared parts help only so far; the rest of the chapter deals with what the missing end changes.

concepts.title: Monitoring as a long-standing use of streams
concepts.question: What kinds of monitoring have long used stream processing, and what do they need?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Organisations want to be alerted when certain things happen, not hear about them in a later report.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Stream processing has long been used for monitoring: fraud detection that blocks a card whose usage pattern has unexpectedly changed, trading systems that execute trades by rules when prices move, manufacturing systems that spot machine malfunctions quickly, and military systems that raise the alarm on signs of an attack.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: These applications need quite sophisticated pattern matching and correlations, not just counting.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A late answer loses most of its value, so the event must trigger action as it happens.

card.rule: Monitoring uses streams to act on patterns in events as they happen.
card.limits: Other uses of stream processing, such as analytics and view maintenance, have emerged over time.

concepts.title: Complex event processing
concepts.question: How do complex event processing systems turn the usual relationship between queries and data upside down?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You want to find certain patterns of events in a stream, much as a regular expression finds patterns of characters in a string.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Complex event processing (CEP), developed in the 1990s, lets you specify rules for event patterns, often in a high-level declarative language like SQL or through a graphical interface. A processing engine consumes the streams and internally keeps a state machine that does the matching. On a match it emits a complex event describing the pattern found.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The usual roles are reversed. A database stores data and treats queries as transient; a CEP engine stores queries long-term and lets events flow past them.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You search for specific sequences of events, not aggregate statistics. Implementations include Esper and IBM InfoSphere Streams, and Samza is gaining SQL support.

card.rule: CEP stores the queries and streams the data past them, emitting a complex event on each match.
card.limits: The boundary with stream analytics is blurry; CEP is more about specific event sequences.

concepts.title: Stream analytics and windows
concepts.question: How does stream analytics differ from CEP, and what is a window?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Often you do not want a particular event sequence but a statistic over many events: how fast something is happening, or whether it differs from usual.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Stream analytics computes aggregations and statistical metrics: the rate of an event type, a rolling average of a value, or a comparison with earlier intervals, such as the same time last week. The statistics are usually computed over fixed time intervals, called windows.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Averaging over a few minutes smooths out irrelevant second-to-second fluctuation while still giving a timely picture. Longer windows are smoother but slower to show change.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want rates, averages or percentiles for a service, for instance queries per second over the last five minutes and their 99th percentile response time.

card.rule: Analytics aggregates many events over a window of time; CEP looks for specific event patterns.
card.limits: The line between CEP and analytics is blurry, so treat the difference as a tendency.

concepts.title: Approximation is an optimisation, not a property of streams
concepts.question: Are stream processing systems inherently approximate, and why do some use probabilistic algorithms?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Stream processing is often assumed to be lossy and inexact.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Some stream analytics systems use probabilistic algorithms: Bloom filters for set membership, HyperLogLog for cardinality estimation, and several percentile estimation algorithms. Their results are approximate but they need significantly less memory than exact algorithms.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Memory is saved at the price of exactness, and you must accept an approximate answer.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: State is too big to hold exactly and an approximate answer suffices. The belief that streams are inherently inexact is wrong: probabilistic algorithms are an optimisation.

card.rule: Stream processing can be exact; probabilistic algorithms are an optional way to save memory.
card.limits: Approximate algorithms suit questions where a small error is acceptable; they do not suit exact accounting.

concepts.title: Maintaining materialised views
concepts.question: How does keeping derived data up to date count as maintaining a materialised view, and why does it need a very long window?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Caches, search indexes and warehouses derived from a database all need to follow changes in the source.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat them as materialised views: an alternative view of a dataset that you can query efficiently and update whenever the underlying data changes. Event-sourced application state is also a kind of materialised view.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Unlike analytics, you usually cannot consider only a window of recent events. Building the view may need all events over an arbitrary period, apart from obsolete ones discarded by log compaction. You need a window stretching back to the beginning of time.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Derived state must track a source. Samza and Kafka Streams support this, building on Kafka's log compaction, whereas some analytics frameworks assume windows of limited duration.

card.rule: A materialised view over a stream needs a window reaching back to the beginning of time, not a short one.
card.limits: A framework built around short windows may be a poor fit for view maintenance.

concepts.title: Searching on streams
concepts.question: How does searching a stream differ from searching an indexed collection of documents?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Sometimes you want to find individual events that match complex criteria such as a full-text query, as they arrive.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Formulate the search query in advance and continually match the stream against it. Media monitoring services do this with news feeds, and real estate sites notify users of new properties matching their search. Elasticsearch's percolator feature is one way to implement it.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A conventional search engine indexes the documents first and then runs queries over the index. Stream search turns this around: the queries are stored and the documents run past them. Testing every document against every query gets slow with many queries.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Many saved searches must be matched against new items. To speed up, index the queries as well as the documents, to narrow the set of queries that may match.

card.rule: In stream search, saved queries are fixed and each new document is matched against them.
card.limits: With few queries, brute force is enough; with many, indexing the queries becomes important.

concepts.title: Message passing, actors and stream processing
concepts.question: How do actor frameworks and RPC-like systems differ from stream processors, and where do they overlap?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Actor frameworks and stream processors both send messages, which blurs the line between them.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Three differences: actor frameworks mainly manage concurrency and distributed execution of communicating modules, while stream processing is mainly a data management technique. Actor communication is often ephemeral and one-to-one, while event logs are durable and multi-subscriber. Actors can communicate in arbitrary ways, including cyclic request/response, while stream processors are usually acyclic pipelines where each stream derives from a well-defined set of inputs.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Some crossover exists: Apache Storm's distributed RPC farms user queries out to nodes that also process event streams. Actor frameworks used for stream processing often do not guarantee delivery after a crash, so you must add retry logic.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Pick actors for concurrency of communicating modules and streams for managing data flows.

card.rule: Actors manage concurrency with ephemeral, arbitrary messaging; stream processors manage data with durable, acyclic pipelines.
card.limits: The boundary is fuzzy where systems mix RPC-style queries with event processing.

concepts.title: Which clock to use for time windows
concepts.question: Why does a batch job ignore the machine's clock when breaking data down by time, while many stream processors use it?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Windows such as the average over the last five minutes sound clear, but the meaning of last five minutes turns out to be tricky.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A batch job processes a large collection of historical events quickly, so it uses the timestamp embedded in each event: the time the job runs has nothing to do with when the events happened. This also makes the processing deterministic, so a rerun gives the same result.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Many stream frameworks instead use the local system clock of the processing machine, called processing time. That is simple and reasonable if the delay between creating and processing an event is negligible, but breaks down with significant processing lag.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Windows must reflect when things happened, not when they were processed.

card.rule: Window by the timestamp inside the event when the processing may lag behind real time.
card.limits: Processing time is acceptable when events are processed almost as soon as they occur.

concepts.title: Event time versus processing time
concepts.question: What goes wrong if a stream processor confuses the time an event occurred with the time it was processed?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Processing can lag: queueing, network faults, contention in the broker or processor, a consumer restart, or reprocessing of old events. Delays can also reorder events: a user's request to server A and then to server B may reach the broker as B's event first.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Treat the time at which an event occurred (event time) separately from the time it is processed (processing time), and window by event time when ordering matters. Stream algorithms must be written to accommodate these timing and ordering issues.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Confusing them gives bad data. A request-rate counter by processing time will show a spike while it works through a backlog after a redeploy, when the real rate was steady.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Events can arrive late or out of order, or you reprocess old events.

card.rule: Event time says when something happened, processing time says when it was handled; mixing them produces artefacts such as false spikes.
card.limits: Windowing by event time brings its own problem: you cannot be sure when a window is complete.

media.alt: Four stacked panels over time. A web server row of request boxes feeds a stream processor row, which has a grey restarting gap followed by a dense burst of boxes. The processing-time rate graph falls from 10 to 0 during the restart then jumps above 10 and decays. The actual request rate line stays flat at 10 throughout.

concepts.title: Knowing when a window is complete
concepts.question: When windowing by event time, how do you decide a window is ready, and what do you do with late events?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: With event-time windows you can never be sure you have all events for a window. Events may be buffered elsewhere, delayed by a network interruption.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: You can time out and declare a window ready after no new events for a while. Events that arrive after that are stragglers, and there are two ways to treat them: ignore them, tracking the dropped count as a metric and alerting if it grows, or publish a correction, an updated value for the window, possibly retracting the earlier output.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Ignoring is simple but loses data; corrections are accurate but force consumers to handle updates and retractions.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Late data is rare and small, ignore it; when accuracy matters, publish corrections.

card.rule: Declare windows complete with a timeout, then either drop stragglers while counting them or publish corrections.
card.limits: Our reading: the threshold between dropping and correcting is a judgement about how much late data you can afford to lose.

concepts.title: Whose clock timestamps an event
concepts.question: How can an event from an offline mobile device be given a trustworthy time of occurrence?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A mobile app may buffer usage events while offline and send them hours or days later, so to the consumers they look like extremely delayed stragglers.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The right timestamp is when the interaction occurred by the device's clock, but a user-controlled device clock cannot be trusted. The server's clock is accurate, but says when the event arrived, not when it occurred. Log three timestamps: when the event occurred (device clock), when it was sent (device clock), and when it was received (server clock).

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Subtracting the second timestamp from the third estimates the offset between device and server clocks, assuming negligible network delay. You then apply the offset to the event timestamp. This assumes the offset did not change in between.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Events are buffered in places whose clock you do not control.

card.rule: Log three timestamps and use the device-to-server offset to estimate the true time an event occurred.
card.limits: The estimate rests on two assumptions: network delay is negligible, and the device clock offset did not change.

concepts.title: Tumbling and hopping windows
concepts.question: How do tumbling and hopping windows divide time, and how are they implemented?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Once you know an event's timestamp, you must decide how windows over time are defined before aggregating.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A tumbling window has fixed length and every event belongs to exactly one window. A 1-minute tumbling window groups events with timestamps from 10:03:00 to 10:03:59, then 10:04:00 to 10:04:59. Implement it by rounding each timestamp down to the nearest minute.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A hopping window has fixed length but windows overlap, which gives some smoothing. A 5-minute window with a 1-minute hop covers 10:03:00 to 10:07:59, then 10:04:00 to 10:08:59. Each event now belongs to several windows.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use tumbling windows for simple per-interval counts. Use hopping windows for smoothed rolling statistics. Hopping can be built by first computing 1-minute tumbling windows and aggregating adjacent ones.

card.rule: A tumbling window puts each event in one fixed window; a hopping window overlaps fixed windows for smoothing.
card.limits: Both have fixed boundaries, so two events close in time can still fall in different windows.

concepts.title: Sliding and session windows
concepts.question: How do sliding and session windows differ from windows with fixed boundaries?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Fixed-boundary windows can split events that are close together, and some analyses need windows defined by the events themselves.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: A sliding window holds all events that occur within some interval of each other. A 5-minute sliding window covers events at 10:03:39 and 10:08:12, since they are under 5 minutes apart, though tumbling or hopping 5-minute windows would not. Implement it with a buffer of events sorted by time, removing old ones as they expire.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A session window has no fixed duration. It groups all events for one user that occur close together in time, and ends when the user has been inactive for a while, such as 30 minutes. Sessionization is a common website analytics need.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Use sliding windows for within-interval proximity. Use session windows for per-user activity bursts.

card.rule: Sliding windows group events within an interval of each other; session windows group a user's activity until an inactivity gap.
card.limits: Sliding windows need a time-sorted buffer, so their cost grows with how many events fall in the interval.

concepts.title: Three kinds of stream join
concepts.question: Which three kinds of join exist on streams, and why are they harder than batch joins?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Batch jobs join datasets by key, and such joins are an important part of data pipelines. Since stream processing generalises pipelines to incremental processing of unbounded data, the same need arises on streams.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Distinguish three types: stream-stream joins, stream-table joins and table-table joins. They differ in what each input is: events, or the changelog of a database table.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: New events can appear on a stream at any time, which makes joins on streams more challenging than in batch jobs, where both inputs are complete.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Planning a join: first name what each side is, an event stream or a table, since that decides the technique.

card.rule: Name each join input as a stream of events or a table's changelog, and that tells you which of the three joins you need.
card.limits: All three share one pattern: keep state from one input and look it up when events arrive on the other.

concepts.title: Stream-stream (window) joins
concepts.question: How do you join two event streams, such as searches and clicks, when events may arrive late or never?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: To compute click-through rates you must bring together search events and click events with the same session ID. The click may never come, the gap may be seconds or weeks, and the click event may even arrive before the search event.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Choose a window for the join, for example a click joins a search if they are at most one hour apart. The processor keeps state: all events from the last hour, indexed by session ID. Each new event is added and the other index is checked for a match.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: On a match you emit an event saying which result was clicked. If a search expires without a click, you emit an event saying which results were not clicked. Putting search details inside the click event is not equivalent: it would miss the searches with no click.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Related events in two streams must be paired within a time bound.

card.rule: A stream-stream join keeps recent events from both sides indexed by key, emits matches, and emits no-match results when events expire.
card.limits: Events outside the window are never paired, so the window length is a modelling decision.

concepts.title: Stream-table joins (stream enrichment)
concepts.question: How does a stream processor add database information to each event without querying the database every time?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Activity events carry a user ID, and each should be enriched with profile information from a database. Querying a remote database for every event is likely to be slow and risks overloading the database.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Load a copy of the database into the stream processor, such as an in-memory hash table or an index on local disk, and look up locally without a network round trip. This is like the hash join used in batch map-side joins.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A batch job uses a point-in-time snapshot, but a stream processor is long-running and the data changes. Keep the local copy current with change data capture: subscribe to the profile changelog and update the copy when a profile is created or modified.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Each event needs lookups into slowly changing reference data. The join is then between two streams, the activity events and the profile updates.

card.rule: Keep a local copy of the table in the processor, updated from its changelog, and join events against it.
card.limits: The local copy needs memory or disk, and processing order between the two inputs affects which version an event sees.

concepts.title: Table-table joins (materialised view maintenance)
concepts.question: How can a stream processor maintain a timeline cache that equals the result of a join between tweets and follows?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Reading a home timeline by looking up everyone a user follows, finding their recent tweets and merging them is too expensive. A timeline cache, an inbox written to as tweets are sent, makes the read a single lookup.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Process events: a new tweet is added to the timeline of every follower, a deleted tweet is removed from all timelines, a follow adds the followee's recent tweets, an unfollow removes them. The processor needs streams for tweets and for follow relationships, and a database of followers per user.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Seen another way, it maintains a materialised view of a query joining the tweets and follows tables. The timelines are a cache of that query's result, updated whenever either table changes.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: A costly join is read often, so you maintain its result incrementally. Both inputs are database changelogs.

card.rule: A table-table join joins every change on one side with the latest state of the other, producing a stream of changes to the joined view.
card.limits: The cache holds duplicated data per user and costs work on each write; it pays off when reads dominate.

concepts.title: Time-dependence of joins
concepts.question: If state changes over time and you join with that state, which point in time do you join with?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: The order of the events that maintain join state matters: following then unfollowing differs from the reverse. In a partitioned log, order is kept within a partition, but there is typically no ordering guarantee across different streams or partitions.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Ask which point in time applies: if a user updates their profile, which activity events are joined with the old profile and which with the new one? For sales, you usually want the tax rate at the time of the sale, which can differ from the current rate when reprocessing historical data.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: If the order of events across streams is undetermined, the join is nondeterministic: you cannot rerun the same job on the same input and necessarily get the same result, as the inputs may interleave differently.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Joining with reference data that changes, especially when you may reprocess history.

card.rule: If events on different streams have no fixed order, the join result can differ between runs.
card.limits: Within one partition order is preserved, so the problem comes from combining separate streams or partitions.

concepts.title: Slowly changing dimensions and versioned identifiers
concepts.question: How can a join with changing reference data be made deterministic, and what does it cost?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A join with state that changes over time, such as a tax rate table, can produce different results on a rerun.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: In data warehouses this issue is called a slowly changing dimension (SCD). The usual remedy is a unique identifier for each version of the joined record: every time a tax rate changes, it gets a new identifier, and the invoice stores the identifier of the rate in force at the time of sale.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The join becomes deterministic, but log compaction is no longer possible, because all versions of the records in the table must be retained.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You must reproduce historical results exactly, for instance for audit or tax purposes.

card.rule: Store the version identifier of the reference record with each fact, so the join always uses the same version.
card.limits: The cost is that every version of the reference data has to be kept, so compaction cannot reclaim space.

concepts.title: Exactly-once semantics
concepts.question: What does exactly-once processing promise, and why is it harder for streams than for batch?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A failed task in a batch job can simply be restarted, and the output of the failed task is discarded. This works because input files are immutable, each task writes to a separate file, and output becomes visible only when the task completes.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The result is the same as if nothing had gone wrong, as if every record had been processed exactly once. Tasks may in fact be run several times, but the visible effect is as if once. This principle is called exactly-once semantics, though effectively-once would be a more descriptive term.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Streams make this harder: waiting until a task is finished before making its output visible is not an option, because a stream is infinite and never finishes.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Failures must not skip records or count them twice, as with counters and money.

card.rule: Exactly-once means the visible effect is as if each record were processed once, even if tasks are retried.
card.limits: The term is about visible effects, not about records being physically handled only once.

concepts.title: Microbatching
concepts.question: How does microbatching bring batch-style fault tolerance to a stream, and what does batch size trade off?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A stream never finishes, so output cannot wait for completion. Yet failed work must still be discardable.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Break the stream into small blocks and treat each as a miniature batch process, as Spark Streaming does. The batch size is typically around one second.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Smaller batches incur more scheduling and coordination overhead; larger batches delay the results. About a second is a performance compromise.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want batch-style retries on streams and can accept about a second of delay. Microbatching implicitly gives a tumbling window equal to the batch size, by processing time.

card.rule: Cut the stream into tiny batches so each can be retried and discarded like a batch task.
card.limits: Windows longer than a batch must carry state from one microbatch to the next.

concepts.title: Rolling checkpoints
concepts.question: How does checkpointing let a stream operator recover without forcing a fixed window size?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: A crashed operator needs to restart from a known good point, and output produced after that point must not count twice.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Periodically generate rolling checkpoints of state and write them to durable storage, as Apache Flink does. If an operator crashes, it restarts from its most recent checkpoint and discards output produced between that checkpoint and the crash.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Checkpoints are triggered by barriers in the message stream, similar to the boundaries between microbatches, but without forcing a particular window size.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You want batch-like recovery without tying windows to the batch size.

card.rule: Checkpoint operator state periodically; after a crash, restore the latest checkpoint and discard later output.
card.limits: Within the framework this gives exactly-once semantics, but not for outputs that have left it.

concepts.title: Side effects that leave the framework
concepts.question: Why are microbatching and checkpointing not enough once output leaves the stream processor?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Inside the framework, microbatching and checkpointing give the same exactly-once semantics as batch processing.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: The guarantee stops at the framework boundary. When output leaves the processor, for example writing to a database, sending messages to an external broker or sending emails, the framework can no longer discard the output of a failed batch.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Restarting a failed task then causes the external side effect to happen twice, so microbatching or checkpointing alone is not sufficient.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Any step has side effects outside the framework: add a way to make them happen once, such as the atomic commit and idempotence ideas that follow.

card.rule: Exactly-once inside the framework does not undo emails sent or rows written outside it.
card.limits: The next two ideas, atomic commit and idempotence, are the remedies.

concepts.title: Atomic commit for exactly-once processing
concepts.question: What must happen atomically for processing of an event to look exactly-once, and where is this practical?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: To appear exactly-once despite faults, all outputs and side effects of processing an event must take effect if and only if processing succeeds.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Those effects include messages to downstream operators or external systems, database writes, changes to operator state, and acknowledging the input, including moving the consumer offset in a log-based broker. They must all happen or none, together. This is the earlier exactly-once message processing problem from distributed transactions.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Traditional distributed transactions such as XA have problems, but in more restricted environments atomic commit can be efficient. Google Cloud Dataflow and VoltDB do this, and Kafka plans to. They do not span heterogeneous technologies; they keep state changes and messaging inside the framework.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: You control state and messaging in one framework. The overhead of the protocol can be amortised by processing several input messages in one transaction.

card.rule: Make outputs, state changes and input acknowledgments commit together or not at all, inside one framework.
card.limits: This is not a general solution for effects in external systems built on different technologies.

concepts.title: Idempotent operations
concepts.question: What makes an operation idempotent, and how can a non-idempotent write be made safe to retry?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: You want to retry a failed task without its effects taking place twice, and transactions are not the only way.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: An idempotent operation has the same effect when performed several times as when performed once. Setting a key to a fixed value is idempotent; incrementing a counter is not. A non-idempotent operation can often be made idempotent with metadata: when consuming from Kafka, write the offset of the message that triggered the write together with the value.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: You can then tell whether an update has already been applied and skip it. This costs storing an offset with the data and relies on assumptions covered next.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Writing to an external store where you cannot use a distributed transaction but each message has a persistent, increasing offset.

card.rule: Make writes safe to repeat, for example by storing the source offset with the value and skipping updates already applied.
card.limits: Idempotence holds only under assumptions about replay order and concurrency, covered in the next idea.

concepts.title: What idempotent recovery assumes
concepts.question: Which conditions must hold for idempotent retries to give exactly-once results?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Idempotence looks free, but it only works if retries do the same thing as the original attempt.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Three assumptions: restarting a failed task must replay the same messages in the same order, as a log-based broker does; the processing must be deterministic; and no other node may concurrently update the same value.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: When failing over from one node to another, fencing may be needed to stop a node that is thought dead but is actually alive from interfering.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: All three assumptions can be guaranteed. Otherwise a retry may write a different value.

card.rule: Idempotent recovery needs replay in the same order, deterministic processing, and a single writer per value.
card.limits: If any assumption fails, repeating a write may not reproduce the first one.

concepts.title: Rebuilding state after a failure
concepts.question: How can a stream processor recover the state it needs after a failure?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Windowed aggregations such as counters, averages and histograms, and tables and indexes used for joins, all hold state that must survive a failure.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Keep the state in a remote datastore and replicate it, or keep it local to the processor and replicate it periodically. A new task can then read the replicated state and resume without loss. Flink writes snapshots of operator state to durable storage such as HDFS; Samza and Kafka Streams send state changes to a dedicated Kafka topic with log compaction; VoltDB processes each input redundantly on several nodes.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: A remote database costs a query for each message. Local state avoids that but needs replication.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Sometimes no replication is needed: rebuild from the input. A short-window aggregate can be recomputed by replaying the window's events, and a local database replica can be rebuilt from the log-compacted change stream.

card.rule: Recover state from a replica, a snapshot, or a replay of the input, whichever is cheapest for that state.
card.limits: Each method has costs that depend on the infrastructure.

concepts.title: Local versus remote state is a trade-off
concepts.question: Why does the chapter say there is no universally ideal choice between local and remote state?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: State can live in a remote datastore or locally in the processor, and replication choices differ.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Weigh the costs of each option against the infrastructure: remote queries add network round trips per message, while local state needs periodic replication and recovery.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The balance depends on the performance of the underlying infrastructure. In some systems network delay is lower than disk access latency, and network bandwidth may be comparable to disk bandwidth.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Choosing where stream state lives: measure your own network and disk before copying someone else's design.

card.rule: There is no universally ideal trade-off; the best place for state depends on your network, disks and workload.
card.limits: Technology changes over time, so the merits of local versus remote state may shift.

concepts.title: Brokers and logs as the streaming filesystem
