concepts.question: How do the batch concepts of file and job map onto the streaming concepts of this chapter?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Stream processing resembles batch processing but continuous and on unbounded input. The two worlds use different words for similar things.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Message brokers and event logs serve as the streaming equivalent of a filesystem. An event is a record, a topic groups related events like a file name groups records, and a stream job reads inputs read-only and writes appended outputs like a batch job.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Two broker types stand out: the AMQP/JMS style assigns individual messages and deletes them once acknowledged, and the log-based style assigns whole partitions and retains messages on disk, so you can jump back and reread.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Translating a batch design to streams, or explaining stream processing to someone who knows batch.

card.rule: Think of brokers and logs as the filesystem of streaming, with the log-based type letting you reread like a file.
card.limits: The analogy fails where the input never ends: sort-based steps and run-to-completion recovery have no counterpart.

concepts.title: Treating a database as a stream to integrate systems
concepts.question: What does it buy you to treat database writes as a stream, and how is it done?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Naturally stream-shaped data such as user activity, sensor readings and market feeds is easy to process. Database contents seem to be a different kind of thing.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Think of the writes to a database as a stream too: the changelog, the history of all changes, captured implicitly with change data capture or explicitly with event sourcing. Log compaction lets the stream hold a full copy of the database.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Consuming the log of changes keeps derived data systems such as search indexes, caches and analytics systems continually up to date. You can also build fresh views by consuming the log from the beginning to the present.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Integrating several systems that hold copies of the same data.

card.rule: A database's changelog, captured implicitly or explicitly, lets every derived system follow it and be rebuilt from the log.
card.limits: Both CDC and event sourcing carry asynchrony, so derived systems lag behind the source.

concepts.title: Choosing among CEP, analytics and view maintenance
concepts.question: Which of the three main purposes of stream processing fits a given problem?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Stream processing serves several purposes, and picking the wrong frame leads to the wrong tool and window.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: For searching specific event patterns, use complex event processing. For aggregates and statistics over windows, use stream analytics. For keeping derived data systems up to date, use materialised view maintenance.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: The boundary between CEP and analytics is blurry. View maintenance often needs a window back to the beginning of time, which clashes with analytics-oriented frameworks built for limited windows.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Starting a stream processing design: write down whether you need patterns, statistics, or a maintained copy of data.

card.rule: Patterns of events mean CEP, statistics over windows mean analytics, and a maintained copy of data means a materialised view.
card.limits: Real systems often combine purposes, so use the labels to pick the dominant requirement.

concepts.title: Choosing the right stream join
concepts.question: Given two inputs, how do you decide between a stream-stream, stream-table or table-table join?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Three joins look alike but differ in their inputs and in what they produce.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Stream-stream: both inputs are streams of activity events, and the join finds related events within a window, for example two actions by the same user within 30 minutes; the two inputs may be the same stream in a self-join. Stream-table: one input is activity events and the other a database changelog that keeps a local copy of the database current; each event is enriched. Table-table: both inputs are changelogs, every change on one side is joined with the latest state of the other, producing a stream of changes to a materialised view of the join.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Stream-stream joins need windows; the table sides need history back to the beginning of time.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Pick by asking what each input is and what the output should represent.

card.rule: Decide by input types: two event streams, an event stream and a changelog, or two changelogs.
card.limits: All three depend on the order of events across inputs, which is not guaranteed across streams.

concepts.title: Fault tolerance techniques compared
concepts.question: Which finer-grained recovery techniques let a long-running stream processor tolerate faults?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: As in batch processing, partial output of failed tasks must be discarded. But a stream job is long-running and produces output continuously, so you cannot discard all output.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Use a finer-grained recovery mechanism based on microbatching, checkpointing, transactions, or idempotent writes.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Microbatching and checkpointing give exactly-once inside the framework; effects outside it need transactions or idempotent writes. Transactions cover restricted environments efficiently; idempotence needs replay in order, deterministic processing and a single writer.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Decide per output: framework state, an external database, or an external message such as an email.

card.rule: Pair each kind of output with a recovery technique that undoes or repeats it safely.
card.limits: No technique covers everything: the assumptions of each must hold for your system.

concepts.title: Time problems in stream processors
concepts.question: What are the main difficulties with time that every stream processor must handle?

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Windows such as the last five minutes depend on a clock, and the right clock is not obvious.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Distinguish processing time from the event timestamps: processing time is when the processor handles an event, event time is when it happened. Windowing by event time needs a plan for straggler events that arrive after the window was thought complete.

blocks.label: Trade-off
blocks.text: Event time gives correct windows but needs timeouts, corrections or special messages to decide when a window is done. Processing time is simple but distorted by lag and backlogs.

blocks.label: Use it when
blocks.text: Any time-based aggregation or join where events may be delayed, buffered, or reprocessed.

card.rule: Choose event time when lag is possible, then plan for stragglers and untrusted device clocks.
card.limits: Processing time is acceptable when lag is negligible.

concepts.title: No single tool fits every use of data
concepts.question: Why does a data-intensive application usually end up combining several tools instead of relying on one?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Every problem has several solutions with different trade-offs, such as log-structured storage, B-trees and column storage. A piece of software has to pick one approach, and trying to do everything in one program almost guarantees a poor implementation. Even a so-called general-purpose database is designed for a particular usage pattern.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Match each tool to the circumstances where it fits. Because complex applications use the same data in several ways, no single product suits all of them, so the application is assembled from several pieces of software.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The best tool depends on the circumstances, not on reputation. The price is an integration problem: the pieces must be kept in step with one another.

card.rule: Pick each tool for the access pattern it was built for, and expect to combine several when one dataset serves different uses.
card.limits: If one product covers every requirement you have, the chapter says to use it rather than compose your own. Combination is a response to a real gap, not a goal.

media.alt: Engraved fantasy map of a coastline on the Sea of Derived Data with the Realm of Dataflow, data integration mountains, two dragons marked security and privacy, and ships heading to chapters 10 and 11.

concepts.title: Many copies of the same data make integration harder
concepts.question: What makes keeping a database, a search index and other copies of the same data in step a growing problem?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: An OLTP database is a good system of record, but a search index is generally not suitable as a durable one, and specialist search needs tools beyond what some databases build in. So applications keep the same data in both.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: List every representation: search index, analytics copies, caches, denormalised objects, machine learning and recommendation inputs, notification triggers. Each is a derived copy that must be fed from the data.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: As the number of representations increases, the integration problem becomes harder. The need often only becomes visible when you zoom out and look at dataflows across the whole organisation.

card.rule: Every extra representation of the data is one more place that must be kept in step, so count them across the whole organisation.
card.limits: Copies only become a serious problem when needs go beyond what one product offers. A system with a single representation has no integration problem to solve.

concepts.title: Treat claims that nobody needs a feature with caution
concepts.question: What does a statement like 99 percent of people only need X tell you about the person who says it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Engineers often say that 99 percent of people only need X, or do not need X. But the range of things people want to do with data is dizzyingly wide, and what one person finds obscure may be central to someone else.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Read such a sentence as a statement about the speaker's experience, not about how useful the technology is.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: You avoid dismissing tools or features whose use case you have not met. The chapter gives this as the author's own view.

card.rule: A claim that almost nobody needs a feature says more about the speaker's experience than about the feature's usefulness.
card.limits: The remark is about sweeping percentages, not about all judgement. It does not mean every feature deserves adoption; you still match a tool to your own circumstances.

concepts.title: One system of record, everything else derived in order
concepts.question: How can a search index be made entirely derived from, and consistent with, the database it copies?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Copies of the same data serve different access patterns. You need to know where data is written first and which representations derive from which sources.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Write first to a system of record database. Capture the changes made to it (change data capture, CDC) and apply them to the search index in the same order. If CDC is the only way the index is updated, the index is entirely derived from the system of record. Writing to the database is the only way to supply new input.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: You can be confident the index is consistent with the system of record. All new data enters through one door, so the origin of every copy is clear.

card.rule: Let one system of record take all writes and feed every other copy only from its captured changes, in the same order.
card.limits: The confidence holds only when there are no bugs in the software doing the capture and apply. It also does not make the index instantly current: it is updated after the record.

concepts.title: Writing to two stores directly can make them differ for good
concepts.question: What goes wrong when an application writes directly to both a database and a search index?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Two clients may send conflicting writes at the same time. Each storage system receives them over its own path and may process them in a different order.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The application writes directly to the database and also to the search index. Neither system is in charge of deciding the order of writes.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The two systems can make contradictory decisions and become permanently inconsistent with each other. The difference does not heal by waiting.

card.example: Client A sets a product title to Alpha while client B sets it to Beta. The database applies Alpha then Beta. The index applies Beta then Alpha. The two now disagree for good.
card.rule: If two stores each decide write order for themselves, concurrent conflicting writes can leave them permanently different.
card.limits: With no conflicting concurrent writes, the two copies may still agree, so the harm shows up only under concurrency. The chapter also treats it as a problem of ordering, not of any one fault.

concepts.title: Decide a total order of writes
concepts.question: What principle matters more than the choice between change data capture and event sourcing?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Derived copies stay consistent only if they apply writes in the same order. Something has to decide that order for every write.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Funnel input through one system that decides a total order for all writes, and derive each other representation by processing the writes in that order. This is state machine replication, the idea behind total order broadcast.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Whether the order is exposed through CDC or an event sourcing log matters less than the principle of deciding on a total order.

card.rule: Choose one authority that fixes a single order of writes, and make everything else follow it.
card.limits: The approach needs the ordering to be feasible. At larger scale, or with several datacenters, services or offline clients, a single total order becomes hard to build, as later ideas show.

concepts.title: Make derivation from the log deterministic and idempotent
concepts.question: Why does deriving data from an event log make recovery from faults quite easy?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Updates to a derived data system can fail or be repeated after a fault. A repeat must not corrupt the derived copy.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Update the derived system from an event log so that the update is deterministic (same input gives the same result) and idempotent (same effect whether run once or many times).

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: After a fault you can retry or replay the log safely, so recovery is often quite easy.

card.rule: Derive from the log with deterministic, idempotent updates so that retrying is always safe.
card.limits: Idempotence is not free: an operation that is not naturally idempotent needs extra metadata or care before a retry is safe, as a later idea shows.

concepts.title: Log-based derived data versus distributed transactions
concepts.question: How do derived data systems and distributed transactions pursue the same goal by different means?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Different data systems must be kept consistent with each other. The classic tool is a distributed transaction using two-phase commit.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Distributed transactions order writes with locks for mutual exclusion and ensure effect exactly once with atomic commit. CDC and event sourcing order writes with a log and rely on deterministic retry and idempotence.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Transactions usually give linearizability, including reading your own writes. Derived data is often updated asynchronously, so it does not by default offer the same timing guarantees.

card.rule: Both routes keep systems consistent, but locks plus atomic commit buy timing guarantees while log plus idempotence buys asynchrony.
card.limits: This is a comparison of means, not a verdict. The chapter's own preference for logs comes in a later idea, and stronger guarantees on top of derived data are covered later.

concepts.title: The author's case for log-based integration
concepts.question: According to the author, what is the most promising way to integrate data systems, and what caution does he add?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The author thinks XA, the standard for distributed transactions across systems, has poor fault tolerance and performance, which severely limits its usefulness. There is no widely supported alternative protocol.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: In the author's opinion, log-based derived data is the most promising approach for integrating different data systems when no good distributed transaction protocol is widely supported.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Guarantees such as reading your own writes are still useful. The author does not think it productive to tell everyone eventual consistency is inevitable without good guidance on how to deal with it.

card.rule: According to the author, prefer log-based derived data over XA for integration today, but do not wave away stronger guarantees.
card.limits: This is the author's opinion in a chapter he labels as personal. Within limited environments willing to pay the cost, distributed transactions have been used successfully.

concepts.title: Why a total order stops scaling
concepts.question: Which two scale-related situations make a single totally ordered log hard to build?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In most cases a totally ordered log requires every event to pass through one leader node that decides the order. Small systems can do this, as single-leader replication shows.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: When event throughput exceeds one machine, the log is partitioned, and the order of events in two different partitions is ambiguous. When servers sit in several geographically distributed datacenters, each datacenter typically has its own leader, so events from two datacenters have no defined order.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Past a certain scale you either accept ambiguity between parts of the log or pay for coordination that network delays make inefficient.

card.rule: One leader gives a total order only while its throughput and location suffice; partitions and multiple datacenters leave the order undefined.
card.limits: The limits come with scale. For systems small enough, a totally ordered log is entirely feasible, as the popularity of single-leader databases demonstrates.

concepts.title: Services and offline clients have no shared order
concepts.question: Why do microservices and offline-capable clients also lack a single order of events?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Microservices commonly keep each service's durable state as an independent unit, with none shared between services. Some applications keep client-side state that updates at once on user input and keep working offline.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Where two events originate in different services, no order between them is defined. Clients that act without waiting for a server are a third case.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A total order cannot be assumed across such boundaries. Where events have no causal link, concurrent events can be ordered arbitrarily, so the missing order is not always a problem.

card.rule: Wherever state is held independently, such as in separate services or on offline clients, expect events to be seen in different orders.
card.limits: Lack of a total order matters only when events are causally related. Updates to the same object can still be ordered by routing them all to the same partition.

concepts.title: Causality can be lost without a total order
concepts.question: How can an unfriend event and a later message be processed in the wrong order?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Some events are causally related even when no total order exists. In a social network, a user removes an ex-partner as a friend and then posts a message complaining about them, intending that the ex does not see it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Friendship status is stored in one place and messages in another. The notification service effectively joins messages with the friend list.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: If the causal dependency between the unfriend event and the message event is not captured, the service may process the message first and wrongly notify the ex-partner. The chapter says there does not seem to be a simple answer.

card.rule: When a join depends on the order of two events kept in different places, losing their causal order produces wrong external effects.
card.limits: The example matters because the effect is external, a notification. If events do not depend on each other, the missing order does not cause harm.

concepts.title: Starting points for capturing causal order
concepts.question: What are three starting points the chapter offers for capturing causal dependencies without a total order?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A total order for every event is costly, but the unfriend example shows that dependencies can matter. The chapter says there is no simple answer.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Three starting points: logical timestamps, which give a total ordering without coordination but need extra metadata and out-of-order handling; logging an event for the state the user saw before deciding, with a unique id that later events reference; and conflict resolution algorithms for events delivered in an unexpected order.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Conflict resolution helps maintain state but does not help when actions have external side effects, such as sending a notification.

card.rule: Capture a causal link by tagging or referencing an earlier event, and remember that reordering fixes only state, not outside actions.
card.limits: None of the three is a complete answer. The author hopes patterns will emerge that capture causality without forcing all events through the bottleneck of total order broadcast.

concepts.title: Batch and stream processors as integration tools
concepts.question: What is the main difference between batch and stream processing, and why is it blurring?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The goal of data integration is to get data into the right form in all the right places. That means consuming inputs, transforming, joining, filtering, aggregating, training models, evaluating, and writing to outputs.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Batch and stream processors do this work. Their outputs are derived datasets such as search indexes, materialized views, recommendations and aggregate metrics. The fundamental difference is that stream processors work on unbounded datasets while batch inputs have a known, finite size.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Many details differ between engines, but the distinctions are beginning to blur. Spark runs stream processing on a batch engine using microbatches, and Apache Flink runs batch processing on a stream engine.

card.rule: Use batch and stream processors to derive datasets; the real difference is bounded versus unbounded input, and engines increasingly emulate each other.
card.limits: One kind of processing can be emulated on the other in principle, yet performance differs, so the blur does not make them interchangeable for every workload.

concepts.title: Derived state is easiest as pure functions over immutable input
concepts.question: Why does a functional style help when maintaining derived data?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Derived data must be recomputable after faults, and a whole organisation's dataflows must be understandable.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Batch processing has a strong functional flavour: deterministic, pure functions whose output depends only on the input, with no side effects other than explicit outputs. Inputs are treated as immutable and outputs as append-only.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The principle helps fault tolerance and simplifies reasoning about dataflows. Whether the derived data is a search index, a model or a cache, think of pipelines that derive one thing from another.

card.rule: Treat derivations as pure functions from immutable inputs to append-only outputs, whatever the derived system.
card.limits: Real systems have state. Stream processing extends the idea with managed, fault-tolerant state, so purity is a guiding principle rather than a ban on state.

concepts.title: Asynchronous derivation contains faults
concepts.question: Why are asynchronously maintained derived systems more robust than synchronous or transactional ones?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In principle derived data could be updated synchronously, in step with the write to the source.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Event-log based systems update derived data asynchronously. A fault in one part of the system stays contained locally. Distributed transactions abort if any participant fails, so they tend to spread failures to the rest of the system.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Asynchrony makes event-log systems robust but gives up synchronous timing guarantees.

card.rule: Asynchronous maintenance keeps one component's fault local, while distributed transactions amplify it.
card.limits: Synchronous index maintenance inside a single database is fine. The advantage applies to derived data crossing system boundaries and, in particular, partitions.

concepts.title: Reprocessing lets applications evolve
concepts.question: What does reprocessing existing data allow that schema changes alone cannot?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Applications gain new features and changed requirements over time. Stream processing reflects input changes in derived views with low delay.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Batch processing can reprocess large amounts of accumulated historical data to derive new views onto an existing dataset.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Without reprocessing, schema evolution is limited to simple changes such as adding a new optional field or a new type of record. With it, a dataset can be restructured into a completely different model.

card.rule: Keep the input and rerun new derivation code over it, so a changed requirement means a new view, not a risky in-place change.
card.limits: Reprocessing everything can be expensive on large datasets, so it is used when a restructuring justifies it. Simple additions may not need it.

concepts.title: Migrate gradually with two derived views side by side
concepts.question: How do derived views let you change a dataset's structure without a sudden switch?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Restructuring a dataset by a sudden switch is risky. A railway faced the same problem when changing gauge: it converted track to carry both gauges by adding a third rail.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Maintain the old and new schemas side by side as two independently derived views onto the same data. Shift a small number of users to the new view to test performance and find bugs. Gradually raise the share and eventually drop the old view.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Every stage is easily reversible, since there is always a working system to go back to.

card.rule: Run old and new derived views together, move users over in steps, and keep the old view until you trust the new one.
card.limits: Two views cost extra storage and processing while they coexist. The railway example shows such conversion can be expensive.

concepts.title: The lambda architecture: two systems side by side
concepts.question: How does the lambda architecture combine batch and stream processing to produce a view?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Batch processing reprocesses historical data and stream processing handles recent updates, so something must combine them.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Record incoming data as immutable events appended to an always-growing dataset, as in event sourcing, and derive read-optimised views from them. Run a batch system and a separate stream system in parallel. The stream processor quickly produces an approximate update to the view. The batch processor later reads the same events and produces a corrected version.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: It was an influential idea that popularised deriving views onto streams of immutable events and reprocessing events when needed.

card.rule: Lambda runs a fast, approximate stream path and a slower, corrective batch path over the same immutable events.
card.limits: The author also lists practical problems with the design, covered in the next idea, so the architecture is shown here as a proposal, not a recommendation.

concepts.title: Practical problems of the lambda architecture
concepts.question: What three practical problems does the author see in the lambda architecture?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Lambda was influential, but running two pipelines over the same events creates burdens.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: First, the same logic must be maintained in both a batch and a stream framework, which is significant additional effort. Second, the two pipelines produce separate outputs that must be merged to answer requests. Third, reprocessing everything is expensive on large datasets, so the batch pipeline is often set to process incremental batches.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Merging is fairly easy for a simple aggregation over a tumbling window but much harder for joins, sessionization or output that is not a time series. Incremental batches bring problems such as stragglers and windows crossing batch boundaries.

card.rule: Two codebases, a merge step and incremental batches are the costs that make lambda hard to run.
card.limits: These are the author's critique, not proof the design is unusable. A simple aggregation over a tumbling window keeps the merge easy.

concepts.title: Unify batch and stream in one system
concepts.question: What three features let one system do both batch reprocessing and stream processing?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Lambda's two systems and duplicated logic are costly. More recent work enables its benefits without its downsides by implementing both kinds of computation in one system.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Three features are needed. First, replay historical events through the same engine that handles the stream of recent events. Second, exactly-once semantics for stream processors: the output is the same as if no faults had occurred, which like batch processing means discarding the partial output of failed tasks. Third, windowing by event time rather than processing time.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: These features are becoming increasingly widely available. Processing time is meaningless when you reprocess historical events, which is why event time matters.

card.rule: Replay history through the same engine, give exactly-once output, and window by event time, and one system can do both jobs.
card.limits: The features are becoming widely available, not universal. A system missing one of them, such as replay, cannot reprocess history the same way.

concepts.title: Two philosophies: Unix and relational databases
concepts.question: How do Unix and relational databases differ in their approach to managing information?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Databases, Hadoop and operating systems all store data and let you process and query it. Both Unix and the relational model emerged in the early 1970s and the tension between them is still not resolved.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Unix presents programmers with a logical but fairly low-level hardware abstraction: pipes and files as sequences of bytes. Relational databases give a high-level abstraction that hides data structures on disk, concurrency and crash recovery: SQL and transactions.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Each is simpler in its own sense: Unix is a thin wrapper around hardware, while a short declarative query draws on powerful infrastructure.

card.rule: Unix offers thin low-level building blocks while relational databases offer a high-level hiding layer, and neither is better in every case.
card.limits: The author says which is better depends on what you want, and there are practical differences, such as a filesystem coping poorly with millions of small files.

concepts.title: Creating an index is reprocessing the data
concepts.question: What does a database do when you run CREATE INDEX, and what other task does that resemble?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Databases have features such as secondary indexes, materialized views, replication logs and full-text indexes, and batch and stream systems build similar derived data.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: CREATE INDEX scans a consistent snapshot of the table, picks out the values being indexed, sorts them and writes out the index. It then processes the backlog of writes made since the snapshot and keeps the index up to date for every later write.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The process is similar to setting up a new follower replica and to bootstrapping change data capture with an initial snapshot. In effect the database reprocesses the existing dataset and derives the index as a new view onto it.

card.rule: Building an index means snapshotting, deriving, catching up on the backlog, then staying current, the same shape as other derived-data setups.
card.limits: The existing data may be a snapshot of state rather than a log of all changes, though the two are closely related.

concepts.title: The dataflow of an organisation as one huge database
concepts.question: In what sense does the dataflow across an organisation look like one huge database?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Batch, stream and ETL processes move data from one place and form to another. Databases do the same inside themselves when they keep indexes and materialized views up to date.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Seen this way, the dataflow across an entire organisation starts to look like one huge database. Batch and stream processors are like elaborate implementations of triggers, stored procedures and materialized view maintenance routines. The derived data systems they maintain are like different index types.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A relational database supports B-tree, hash and spatial indexes in one product. In the emerging architecture these facilities come from different pieces of software, running on different machines, administered by different teams.

card.rule: Treat processors as the index-maintenance machinery and derived systems as index types of one organisation-wide database.
card.limits: This is an analogy the author uses to reason about design, not a claim that the pieces share one engine or one team.

concepts.title: Federated databases unify reads
concepts.question: How does a federated database combine different storage engines, and what does it leave unsolved?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: No single data model suits every access pattern, yet users want to combine data from different places easily.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A federated database, or polystore, provides a unified query interface over a wide variety of underlying storage engines and processing methods. PostgreSQL's foreign data wrapper fits this pattern.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: It follows the relational tradition of one integrated system with a high-level query language and elegant semantics, but with a complicated implementation. It addresses read-only querying across systems and has no good answer for synchronising writes.

card.rule: A federated interface unifies reads across engines but does not keep their writes in step.
card.limits: Federated reads mean mapping one data model into another, which the author calls a manageable problem. The harder write side needs a different approach.

concepts.title: Unbundled databases unify writes
concepts.question: How does unbundling a database's index maintenance synchronise writes across different technologies?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Within one database, creating a consistent index is built in. When several storage systems are composed, all data changes still need to reach all the right places, even in the face of faults.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Make it easy to plug storage systems together reliably, for example through change data capture and event logs. This is like unbundling a database's index-maintenance features so that writes are synchronised across disparate technologies. It follows the Unix tradition of small tools that do one thing well, communicate through a uniform low-level API (pipes) and are composed with a higher-level language (the shell).

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Federation and unbundling are two sides of the same coin for composing a reliable, scalable and maintainable system from diverse components.

card.rule: Unbundling synchronises writes by having change streams carry every change to every derived store.
card.limits: Unbundling does not replace databases and does not address the read-side mapping that federation handles.

concepts.title: Across technologies, prefer an async log to distributed transactions
concepts.question: Why does the author prefer an asynchronous event log with idempotent writes over distributed transactions across different technologies?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The traditional way to synchronise writes across heterogeneous storage systems is a distributed transaction. The author thinks this is the wrong solution. Transactions inside one storage or stream processing system are feasible.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: When data crosses the boundary between different technologies, use an asynchronous event log with idempotent writes. Consumers of an ordered log apply each event so that repeats do no harm.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: An ordered log with idempotent consumers is a much simpler abstraction and so much more feasible to implement across heterogeneous systems.

card.rule: Use transactions within one system, and use an ordered log with idempotent consumers when data crosses between systems built by different groups.
card.limits: This is the author's judgement (he writes I think and I believe), and he notes distributed transactions can work well within a single stream processor.

concepts.title: Log-based integration gives loose coupling at two levels
concepts.question: In which two ways does log-based integration loosen the coupling between components?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Synchronous interaction, as in distributed transactions, tends to escalate local faults into large-scale failures. Separate teams also need to work without constant coordination.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: At the system level, asynchronous event streams make the whole more robust to outages or slow components: if a consumer runs slow or fails, the log buffers messages, the producer and other consumers carry on, and the faulty consumer catches up later without missing data. At the human level, different teams can develop, improve and maintain components independently, each focusing on doing one thing well behind a well-defined interface.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Faults stay contained and teams gain independence. The price is giving up synchronous guarantees.

card.rule: A buffering log lets components fail and evolve independently, in the system and in the organisation.
card.limits: Loose coupling does not give timeliness by itself. The consumer that catches up later is behind until it does.

concepts.title: Unbundling does not replace databases or integrated products
concepts.question: When does the author say a single integrated product beats composing many tools?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Each extra piece of infrastructure has a learning curve, configuration issues and operational quirks. Building for scale you do not need is wasted effort and may lock you into an inflexible design.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: If a single technology does everything you need, use it rather than reimplementing it from lower-level components. The advantages of unbundling and composition come into the picture only when no single piece of software satisfies all your requirements.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Databases are still needed to maintain state in stream processors and to serve queries on the output of batch and stream processors. The goal of unbundling is breadth, not depth: to combine databases so you get good performance across a wider range of workloads than one piece of software allows.

card.rule: Deploy as few moving parts as possible, and compose tools only when no single product meets every requirement.
card.limits: Unbundling is not meant to compete with a specialised database on its own workload, so it does not remove the need for specialised engines.

concepts.title: What is still missing: a shell for unbundled data systems
concepts.question: What does the author say is missing from the tools for composing data systems?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Tools for composing data systems are getting better, but one major part is missing: the unbundled-database equivalent of the Unix shell, a high-level language to compose storage and processing systems simply and declaratively.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: By analogy with Unix pipes, the author would like to declare mysql | elasticsearch, the unbundled equivalent of CREATE INDEX. It would take all documents in a MySQL database, index them in an Elasticsearch cluster, then continually capture changes and apply them to the index without custom application code.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The same idea could precompute and update caches by declaring materialized views, including recursive queries on graphs and application logic. Early-stage research such as differential dataflow points this way.

card.rule: A declarative way to connect one system to another, with initial copy and continuing updates built in, would make unbundling easy to use.
card.limits: This is a wish and a research direction, not an available product. The chapter calls the work early stage and says the integration should be possible with almost any storage or indexing system.

concepts.title: The database inside-out idea and the spreadsheet
concepts.question: What does the author mean by the database inside-out approach, and how do spreadsheets relate to it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Data systems should refresh dependent results automatically when inputs change, so that you do not need to worry how the refresh happens. A spreadsheet does exactly this: change a cell and the formula results are recalculated.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Compose specialised storage and processing systems with application code so that a change to a record automatically updates indexes, cached views and aggregations that depend on it. This is also called database inside-out, after a conference talk the author gave in 2014.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Unlike a spreadsheet, today's data systems must be fault-tolerant, scalable and durable, and integrate disparate technologies written by different groups. The author calls it a design pattern, not a grand new architecture, built from other people's ideas.

card.rule: Aim for spreadsheet-like automatic recalculation of derived data, but with fault tolerance, scale and durability.
card.limits: The author stresses the ideas are not his own and calls the new architecture label too grandiose. It is a starting point for discussion.

concepts.title: Application code as a derivation function
concepts.question: What transformation functions turn a base dataset into a secondary index, a search index, a model or a cache?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Every derived dataset comes from another through some transformation function. Some derivations are so common that databases build them in, while others depend on the application.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A secondary index picks out the indexed values from each row or document and sorts by them. A full-text index applies language processing such as language detection, word segmentation, stemming, spelling correction and synonym identification, then builds a structure like an inverted index. A machine learning model is derived from training data by feature extraction and statistical analysis, and its output is derived from new input and the model. A cache holds an aggregation in the form the user interface displays.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The index derivation is common enough to invoke with CREATE INDEX. When the function is not cookie-cutter, custom code is needed, and that is where many databases struggle.

card.rule: Describe every derived dataset as a function of its source, and expect custom code wherever the function is not a standard one.
card.limits: Databases do support triggers, stored procedures and user-defined functions, but the author calls them somewhat of an afterthought, so their existence does not remove the problem.

concepts.title: Keep application code and state in separate systems
concepts.question: Why does the author prefer running application code outside the database rather than inside it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In theory a database could host arbitrary application code like an operating system. In practice databases fit poorly with modern development needs: dependency and package management, version control, rolling upgrades, evolvability, monitoring, metrics, calls to network services, and integration with external systems.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Let some parts of a system specialise in durable data storage and other parts in running application code, interacting while remaining independent. Deployment and cluster tools such as Kubernetes and Docker are designed specifically for running code. Most web applications are stateless services: any request can go to any server, which forgets it once it has replied.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Servers can be added or removed at will, but the state has to go somewhere, typically a database. The trend is to keep stateless application logic apart from state management.

card.rule: Run code on platforms built for running code, and keep durable state in databases built for storing it.
card.limits: The argument is about arbitrary application code. Databases still run their own built-in derivations such as index maintenance.

concepts.title: A database is a passive variable you must poll
concepts.question: What does the typical web application model leave out that a spreadsheet provides?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In the typical model the database acts as a mutable shared variable accessed synchronously over the network. The application reads and updates it, and the database makes it durable, with some concurrency control and fault tolerance.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: In most programming languages you cannot subscribe to changes in a mutable variable and can only read it periodically. Readers are not notified when the value changes, unlike in a spreadsheet. Databases inherited this passive approach: to find out whether content changed, often your only option is to poll by repeating the query.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Applications must ask repeatedly instead of being told. Subscribing to changes is only just beginning to emerge as a database feature.

card.rule: A plain database tells you nothing when data changes, so unless it supports change subscriptions you must keep asking.
card.limits: You can build notifications yourself with the observer pattern, but most languages do not include it as a built-in feature, and some databases now offer change streams.

concepts.title: Derived data needs order and fault tolerance, not just messaging
concepts.question: Why is maintaining derived data not the same as asynchronous job execution?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Thinking in dataflow means treating state changes and the code that reacts to them as collaborators, instead of treating the database as a passive variable. Application code responds to a state change in one place by causing a state change in another.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Maintaining derived data differs from the asynchronous job execution that messaging systems are traditionally designed for. First, order often matters: views derived from one log must process events in the same order to stay consistent, and many brokers lose order when redelivering unacknowledged messages. Dual writes are also ruled out. Second, fault tolerance is key: losing one message leaves the derived dataset permanently out of sync.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Stable ordering and fault-tolerant processing are stringent demands, but much less expensive and more operationally robust than distributed transactions. Stream operators can then run application code and be composed like Unix tools.

card.rule: Use a messaging layer that keeps order and loses nothing when it feeds derived data, because a lost or reordered message corrupts the copy for good.
card.limits: For ordinary background jobs where order and the occasional loss do not matter, a traditional message queue can be enough. The demands come from keeping derived data exact.

concepts.title: Stream operators compared with microservices
concepts.question: How do chains of stream operators resemble microservices, and how do they differ?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Service-oriented architecture breaks functionality into services that call each other by synchronous requests such as REST. Its main advantage over a monolith is organisational scalability through loose coupling, because teams can deploy and update services independently.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Composing stream operators into a dataflow system has many similar characteristics. The difference is the communication mechanism: one-directional, asynchronous message streams instead of synchronous request and response.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Dataflow systems can add better fault tolerance and, as the next idea shows, better performance than synchronous calls.

card.rule: Stream operators give the independence of services but communicate through one-way asynchronous streams instead of request and response.
card.limits: Services remain a good fit when a caller needs an immediate answer. The comparison concerns how derived state is kept current.

concepts.title: Subscribe to a stream instead of calling a service
concepts.question: How does a dataflow approach avoid a network request when converting currency in a purchase?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A purchase priced in one currency and paid in another needs the current exchange rate.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: In the microservices approach the purchase code queries an exchange-rate service or database when it needs the rate. In the dataflow approach it subscribes to a stream of exchange-rate updates ahead of time, records the current rate in a local database whenever it changes, and queries only that local database when processing a purchase.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A synchronous network request becomes a query to a local database, possibly in the same process. It is faster and more robust to the failure of another service. The fastest and most reliable network request is no network request at all.

card.example: A ticket shop prices tickets in euros but charges in pounds. Instead of asking a rates service on every sale, it keeps the latest rate in a local table updated from a stream of rate changes.
card.rule: Replace a per-request call to another service by a local copy kept fresh from a change stream.
card.limits: You can also avoid the request in the service style by caching the rate, but keeping that cache fresh needs polling or a subscription, which is exactly the dataflow approach.

concepts.title: Stream joins depend on time
concepts.question: Why must a reprocessed purchase use the exchange rate from the time of purchase?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In the dataflow approach the purchase handler joins purchase events with exchange-rate updates. The join depends on time: the rate keeps changing.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: If purchase events are reprocessed later, the current rate has changed. To reconstruct the original output you must obtain the historical exchange rate at the original time of purchase.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: This holds whether you query a service or subscribe to a stream of rate updates. Either way you need to handle the time dependence. The author sees time-dependent joins as one of several open questions in this direction.

card.rule: When a join involves data that changes, reprocessing needs the value as it was at the original event time.
card.limits: The problem arises only for reprocessing or replay. If outputs are never recomputed from old events, the current value may be all you need.

concepts.title: The write path and the read path meet in the derived dataset
concepts.question: What are the write path and the read path, and where do they meet?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Dataflow systems create derived datasets and keep them up to date. Those datasets exist because someone will query them later.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The write path is the journey from the moment data enters the system through batch and stream stages until every derived dataset has absorbed it. It is the part that is precomputed, done eagerly as soon as data arrives, whether or not anyone asks to see it. The read path is the part that happens only when someone asks: reading the derived dataset, doing more processing and building the response.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The derived dataset is where the two paths meet, and it sets the trade-off between work done at write time and work done at read time. In programming terms the write path resembles eager evaluation and the read path lazy evaluation.

card.rule: Every derived dataset marks a boundary: work before it is done on write, work after it is done on read.
card.limits: The boundary is a design choice, not a law. Where it sits can differ by use, as the next idea shows.

media.alt: Left-to-right flow. A user sends update document to an application server, then new document version goes to linguistic analysis, then terms appearing in document go to the search index; this is bracketed as the write path. The user's search query goes to an application server, a search query executor with expanded query, and back and forth with the search index via search terms and posting lists; bracketed as the read path.

concepts.title: Indexes, caches and materialized views move the boundary
concepts.question: How do an index, a cache and a materialized view each shift work between writing and reading?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A full-text search needs some work on both paths: the write path updates index entries for every term in a document, and the read path searches each query word and applies AND or OR logic.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: With no index, writes do nothing but each query scans all documents, like grep: cheap writes, expensive reads. Precomputing results for every possible query makes reads trivial but needs infinite time and space on the write path. Precomputing results for only the most common queries is a cache, or a materialized view, which must be updated when new documents affect those queries.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Index, cache and materialized view are all places where the boundary between write path and read path can be drawn: they do more work on the write path to save effort on the read path.

card.rule: Choose how much to precompute on write to save work on read, from nothing, through an index, to a cache of common answers.
card.limits: Precomputing everything is impossible when the space of queries is unbounded. Scanning without an index is acceptable only for a small number of documents.

concepts.title: Stateful, offline-capable clients
concepts.question: How does the offline-first view change what a client device is?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The client/server model, with stateless clients and servers holding authority over data, is so common that we almost forget alternatives. Traditional browsers were stateless and useful only with a connection. Mobile networks are often slow and unreliable.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Single-page JavaScript apps and mobile apps can now store a lot of state on the device, so offline-first applications use a local database on the device and sync with remote servers in the background when a network is available. The on-device state can be treated as a cache of server state.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Users gain a user interface that does not wait for synchronous network requests and mostly works offline. In the author's picture the pixels on the screen are a materialized view onto model objects in the app, and the model objects are a local replica of state in a remote datacenter.

card.rule: Treat on-device state as a replica and cache of server state, so the interface can work without waiting on the network.
card.limits: Offline-first needs sync logic and brings its own ordering problems, as seen earlier. The stateless client model remains common and simpler.

concepts.title: Push state changes all the way to the client
concepts.question: What does pushing state changes to clients extend, and how do offline devices catch up?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In an ordinary web page the browser reads data once and assumes it static. The state on the device is a stale cache unless you poll. RSS and similar feed protocols are only a basic form of polling.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Server-sent events and WebSockets let a browser keep an open TCP connection so the server can push messages as long as it stays connected. This extends the write path all the way to the end user. A client first uses a read path for its initial state and then relies on a stream of changes.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Devices will be offline some of the time. The consumer-offset technique of log-based brokers applies: a reconnecting device resumes after the last message it saw, so each device is a small subscriber to a small stream of events.

card.rule: Keep client state fresh by subscribing it to a stream of changes, and let a reconnecting device resume from its last position.
card.limits: Push channels exist only while the connection holds. Between connections the client depends on the offset-based catch-up.

concepts.title: End-to-end event streams from device to device
concepts.question: What would an end-to-end write path look like, and why do few applications work this way?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Tools such as the Elm language and the React, Flux and Redux toolchain already manage client-side state by subscribing to a stream of events for user input or server responses, structured like event sourcing.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Extend this model so a server can also push state-change events into the client pipeline. A state change then flows from the interaction on one device through event logs, derived data systems and stream processors to the screen of a person observing on another device, with low delay such as under one second.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Instant messaging and online games already work like this. Most applications do not, because the stateless client and request/response assumption is deeply ingrained in databases, libraries, frameworks and protocols, and few datastores can answer a request with a stream of responses.

card.rule: Move from request/response toward publish/subscribe so that one change reaches other users' screens end to end.
card.limits: The author asks for the option of subscribing to changes to be kept in mind, not for every query to be replaced. It requires rethinking many systems.

concepts.title: Reads can be events too
concepts.question: What happens when read requests are treated as events and joined with the data?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Usually writes go through an event log while reads are transient network requests sent directly to the nodes that hold the data. Stream processors also keep state for aggregations and joins, and some frameworks let outside clients query it, making the processor a simple database.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Represent read requests as streams of events and send both reads and writes through a stream processor. The processor answers a read event by emitting the result to an output stream. That is a stream-table join between the stream of read queries and the database, and the read event must reach the partition that holds the data.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Serving requests and performing joins correspond closely. A one-off read passes through the join operator and is forgotten, while a subscribe request is a persistent join with past and future events on the other side.

card.rule: Treat reads as events so that serving a query becomes a join between the query stream and the stored data.
card.limits: It is one possible design, not the only one. The author calls the usual write-via-log, read-via-request design reasonable.

concepts.title: Logging reads helps track causal dependencies
concepts.question: What benefit and cost come from recording read events durably?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: To understand why a user made a decision you need to know what they saw. In an online shop, the predicted shipping date and inventory status shown to a customer are likely to affect whether they buy.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Record the result of the user's query of shipping and inventory status as an event. Logging read events can help track causal dependencies and data provenance across the system and allows you to reconstruct what the user saw before a particular decision.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Writing read events to durable storage improves tracking of causal dependencies but costs extra storage and I/O. Reducing this overhead is still an open research problem.

card.rule: Record what users were shown when you need to explain their later decisions, and weigh the storage and I/O cost.
card.limits: If you already log read requests for operational reasons, making the log the source of requests is not a great change. Without such a need, the overhead may not be worth it.

concepts.title: Queries as streams across partitions
concepts.question: When is treating queries as streams useful for multi-partition processing?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: For a query that touches one partition, sending it through a stream and collecting a stream of responses is probably overkill.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The idea opens up distributed execution of complex queries that combine data from several partitions, using the message routing, partitioning and joining infrastructure of stream processors. Storm's distributed RPC computed the number of people who saw a URL on Twitter, the union of the follower sets of everyone who tweeted it. Fraud scoring looks up reputation scores for the IP, email, billing and shipping addresses, each in a partitioned database, as a sequence of joins.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: It gives an option for large applications that run against the limits of off-the-shelf solutions. If a database already offers multi-partition joins, as MPP databases do, it is probably simpler to use that.

card.rule: Use query-as-stream processing for multi-partition queries only when conventional solutions run out of capacity.
card.limits: For single-partition queries it is overkill, and where an MPP database offers the feature, it is simpler.

concepts.title: Stateful systems make correctness hard and costly to get wrong
concepts.question: Why does correctness matter more for stateful systems than for stateless services?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: With a stateless service that only reads data, a bug can be fixed and the service restarted. A database is designed to remember things more or less forever, so the effects of a mistake can last forever too.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: For about four decades, the transaction properties of atomicity, isolation and durability have been the tool of choice for correct applications. Yet they are weaker than they seem, as the confusion over weak isolation levels shows. Some areas have dropped transactions for models with better performance and scalability but messier semantics, and consistency is talked about without a clear definition.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: It is very difficult to tell whether an application is safe at a given isolation level or replication setup. Simple solutions often appear to work at low concurrency with no faults, then reveal subtle bugs under harder conditions.

card.rule: Treat correctness of stateful systems as a design problem, because mistakes in state persist and the usual guarantees are hard to reason about.
card.limits: Stateless read-only services are forgiving, since restarting fixes them. The concern applies to systems that remember.

concepts.title: Strong correctness costs scale and fault tolerance
concepts.question: What do serializability and atomic commit give up in exchange for correctness?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: If your application can tolerate occasionally corrupting or losing data in unpredictable ways, life is simpler and you might get away with crossing your fingers. If you need stronger assurance, you need a stronger approach.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Serializability and atomic commit are established approaches for strong correctness.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: They typically work only in a single datacenter, which rules out geographically distributed architectures, and they limit the scale and fault-tolerance properties you can achieve. The author believes the traditional transaction approach is not going away, but is not the last word either.

card.rule: Strong transactional guarantees buy correctness at the cost of scale, geography and fault tolerance.
card.limits: The cost matters only when you need the scale or geographic spread. A single-datacenter application can use these tools well.

concepts.title: Strong database guarantees do not protect against application bugs
concepts.question: Why can an application with serializable transactions still lose or corrupt data?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: An application using a data system with comparatively strong safety properties, such as serializable transactions, is not guaranteed to be free from data loss or corruption. An application bug that writes incorrect data or deletes data cannot be stopped by serializable transactions.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Application bugs occur and people make mistakes, so take this example seriously. The author used it earlier to argue for immutable and append-only data, because recovery is easier when faulty code cannot destroy good data.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Immutability is useful but not a cure-all by itself. There are more subtle ways for data corruption to arise.

card.rule: Design for bugs in your own code, since the database's guarantees cover only what the database sees.
card.limits: The example may look frivolous, but the chapter says it is worth taking seriously. Immutability reduces the harm without removing every failure.

concepts.title: Exactly-once means the effect is the same as with no faults
concepts.question: How can a retried operation have the same effect as if it had run once?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: When something goes wrong in processing a message you can drop it, which loses data, or try again. A retry may repeat an operation that already succeeded unnoticed, so it is processed twice, charging a customer twice or incrementing a counter twice.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Exactly-once (or effectively-once) means arranging the computation so the final effect is the same as if no faults had occurred, even if the operation was retried. One of the most effective ways is to make the operation idempotent: it has the same effect whether executed once or many times.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Making an operation that is not naturally idempotent into one takes effort and care. You may need extra metadata, such as the set of operation IDs that have updated a value, and fencing when failing over from one node to another.

card.rule: Make operations idempotent, with metadata such as operation ids where needed, so a retry cannot change the result.
card.limits: Naturally idempotent operations, such as setting a value, need no extra work. Operations like incrementing need the added bookkeeping.

concepts.title: TCP removes duplicates only within one connection
concepts.question: What happens when a client retries a database transaction after a connection timeout?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: TCP numbers packets, so it can reorder them, notice losses and drop duplicates before handing data to the application. But this works only inside a single TCP connection. In many databases a transaction is tied to a client connection.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: If the connection drops after the client sent COMMIT but before it heard back, the client does not know whether the transaction committed or aborted. Reconnecting and retrying is outside TCP's duplicate suppression.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A transfer that adds and subtracts the same amount is not idempotent, so a retry could move twice the amount. The chapter notes that this standard textbook example of atomicity is not correct as written, and real banks do not work like this.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Running this script twice moves 50, not 25.

card.rule: Do not assume the database connection's duplicate suppression covers a retry after a timeout.
card.limits: Within one connection TCP does suppress duplicates. The problem begins once the client opens a new connection and resends the work.

concepts.title: Every hop between user and database can duplicate a request
concepts.question: Why does making the database layer reliable still leave duplicate requests possible?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Even if duplicates are suppressed between the database client and server, there is still the network between the end-user device and the application server.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A browser submits a POST. On a weak cellular connection the user may send it but lose the signal before the response arrives, see an error, and retry. Browsers ask Are you sure you want to submit this form again, and the user says yes. From the web server's point of view the retry is a separate request, and from the database's point of view it is a separate transaction.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The usual deduplication mechanisms do not help. Post/Redirect/Get avoids the warning in normal operation but does not help if the POST itself times out.

card.rule: A retry can enter at any hop, so duplicates must be caught by something that spans the whole request path.
card.limits: Two-phase commit lets a coordinator reconnect to a database and resolve an in-doubt transaction, which fixes only the database hop.

concepts.title: Pass a unique operation id from the client to the database
concepts.question: How does a request id plus a uniqueness constraint make an operation safe to retry end to end?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A transaction mechanism in the database alone cannot make an operation idempotent across several hops. You need to consider the whole flow of the request.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Generate a unique id for the operation, such as a UUID in a hidden form field, or a hash of the form fields, and pass it all the way to the database. In the same transaction as the update, insert a row with that id into a table that has a uniqueness constraint on the id. A second attempt fails the insert, so the transaction aborts and has no effect.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Relational databases can generally maintain a uniqueness constraint correctly even at weak isolation levels, whereas an application-level check then insert may fail under nonserializable isolation.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The unique transfer id makes a repeat harmless.

card.rule: Carry one client-generated id through every hop and let a uniqueness constraint reject the second attempt.
card.limits: It works only if the id stays the same across retries. Generating a fresh id per attempt defeats the protection.

concepts.title: The end-to-end argument
concepts.question: What does the end-to-end argument say about where a function such as duplicate suppression can be implemented?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: TCP suppresses duplicate packets within a connection, and some stream processors give exactly-once semantics at the level of message processing. Neither stops a user from submitting a duplicate request when the first one timed out.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The end-to-end argument, put forward by Saltzer, Reed and Clark in 1984, says a function of this kind can be implemented completely and correctly only with the knowledge and help of the applications at the endpoints of the communication. Providing it as a feature of the communication system itself is not possible.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: TCP, database transactions and stream processors cannot by themselves entirely rule out duplicates. The problem needs an end-to-end solution: a transaction identifier passed all the way from the end-user client to the database.

card.rule: A function that must be right across a whole path can only be completed at the endpoints, so lower layers cannot fully provide it.
card.limits: The argument does not make lower layers useless. The authors allow that an incomplete version provided by the communication system may help as a performance enhancement.

concepts.title: End-to-end checks for integrity and encryption
concepts.question: Which other safeguards, such as checksums and encryption, are only partly effective unless applied end to end?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The same argument applies beyond duplicates. Checksums built into Ethernet, TCP and TLS detect packet corruption in the network but not corruption caused by bugs in the software at either end or on the disks where data is stored.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: To catch all possible sources of corruption you also need end-to-end checksums. A similar argument holds for encryption: a home WiFi password protects against people snooping on your WiFi traffic but not against attackers elsewhere on the internet; TLS between client and server protects against network attackers but not against a compromised server.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Only end-to-end encryption and authentication protect against all of these. Each lower-level feature closes part of the gap.

card.rule: A check or protection applied at one layer covers only that layer, so use the check at the endpoints to cover everything between them.
card.limits: End-to-end protection does not make lower layers pointless: they reduce the chance of problems reaching the higher levels.

concepts.title: Applying end-to-end thinking in data systems
concepts.question: Why does using a strong database not remove the need for application-level fault tolerance?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Using a data system with strong safety properties, such as serializable transactions, does not guarantee freedom from data loss or corruption. The application itself needs end-to-end measures such as duplicate suppression.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Low-level reliability mechanisms work quite well, so the remaining high-level faults occur fairly rarely, but fault-tolerance machinery is hard to get right. Transactions are a good abstraction, collapsing concurrent writes, constraint violations, crashes, network interruptions and disk failures to two outcomes: commit or abort.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The author fears this is not enough. Transactions are expensive, especially across heterogeneous storage. When we refuse distributed transactions as too costly, we must reimplement fault tolerance in application code, and the author suspects most such mechanisms do not work correctly, which means lost or corrupted data.

card.rule: Provide end-to-end correctness properties in the application, and look for better fault-tolerance abstractions than plain transactions.
card.limits: This is the author's opinion and open challenge: he says we have not yet found the right abstraction.

concepts.title: Many constraints are like uniqueness constraints
concepts.question: Which kinds of requirement can be handled with techniques used for uniqueness?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Request-id duplicate suppression is one kind of uniqueness constraint. Other features also need uniqueness: a username or email address must identify one user, a file store cannot hold two files of the same name, and two people cannot book the same seat.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Similar constraints include an account balance that never goes negative, not selling more items than are in stock, and a meeting room with no overlapping bookings. Techniques that enforce uniqueness can often be used for these kinds of constraints as well.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Studying uniqueness gives tools for a wider family of constraints.

card.rule: Learn how to enforce uniqueness, since the same techniques often apply to balances, stock levels and booking overlaps.
card.limits: Not every constraint reduces to uniqueness. The chapter says only that the techniques can often be used.

concepts.title: Enforcing uniqueness requires consensus
concepts.question: Why does enforcing a uniqueness constraint across a distributed system require consensus?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: If several concurrent requests carry the same value, the system must decide which one wins and reject the others as violations. That is a consensus problem.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The usual way is to make one node the leader and put it in charge of all decisions. That works if you accept funnelling all requests through one node and it does not fail. To tolerate its failure you are back at consensus. Uniqueness checking can scale out by partitioning on the value that must be unique, such as hashing the username.

blocks.label: Consequences
