blocks.text: Asynchronous multi-master replication is ruled out, because different masters might accept conflicting writes concurrently and the values would no longer be unique. To reject a violating write immediately, synchronous coordination is unavoidable.

card.rule: To reject duplicates at once you need one decider per value, found by partitioning on the unique value, with synchronous coordination.
card.limits: This describes immediate, strict enforcement. Looser forms of uniqueness, covered later, can avoid the coordination.

concepts.title: Uniqueness via a partitioned log and a stream processor
concepts.question: How does a partitioned log with one stream processor decide who claims a username?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A log delivers messages to all consumers in the same order, which is total order broadcast and equivalent to consensus. A stream processor reads each log partition sequentially on a single thread.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Encode each username request as a message appended to the partition chosen by the hash of the username. A stream processor reads the requests in order and uses a local database to track taken names. It emits a success message for an available name and a rejection for a taken one. The requesting client watches the output stream for its answer.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The algorithm is basically the same as implementing linearizable storage with total order broadcast. It scales with the number of partitions, since each is processed independently.

card.rule: Route all requests for one value to one log partition and let a single-threaded processor accept the first and reject the rest.
card.limits: The client has to wait for the output stream to learn the result. Correctness of the check does not depend on that waiting.

concepts.title: Route conflicting writes to the same partition
concepts.question: What general principle lies behind the username algorithm?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The username example generalises: many other constraints can be checked the same way.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Any writes that may conflict are routed to the same partition and processed sequentially. What counts as a conflict may depend on the application, and the stream processor can use arbitrary logic to validate a request.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: This is similar to the approach pioneered by Bayou in the 1990s. See also the earlier discussions of what a conflict is and of write skew and phantoms.

card.rule: Make conflicting operations meet in one place and process them in order.
card.limits: You must know in advance which writes can conflict, so you can choose the partition key. Writes that touch several partitions need further steps.

concepts.title: A money transfer across partitions without atomic commit
concepts.question: How can a transfer touching three partitions be applied exactly once without an atomic commit?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A transfer may involve three partitions: the one holding the request id, the payee account and the payer account. Nothing says they belong together. The traditional approach is an atomic commit across all three, which forces the transfer into a total order with other transactions on those partitions, so throughput suffers.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Step 1: the client gives the request a unique id and appends it to a log partition chosen by the request id. Step 2: a stream processor reads the request log and emits a debit instruction for the payer account, partitioned by payer, and a credit instruction for the payee, partitioned by payee, both carrying the original request id. Step 3: further processors consume the debit and credit streams, deduplicate by request id and apply the changes.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Every request is applied exactly once to both accounts even in the face of faults, with equivalent correctness and no atomic commit. The idea of several differently partitioned stages is similar to the multi-partition data processing seen earlier.

card.rule: Log the request once, then derive the debit and credit as separate streams deduplicated by the request id.
card.limits: It relies on the request id surviving to every stage. Without that id, the final stage cannot deduplicate.

concepts.title: Crashes, duplicates and overdrafts in the log-based transfer
concepts.question: What happens in the log-based transfer if the stream processor crashes, and how is an overdraft prevented?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: If the processor that turns requests into debit and credit instructions crashes, it resumes from its last checkpoint. It does not skip any request, but it may process some twice and produce duplicate instructions.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Because the processor is deterministic, it produces the same instructions again, and the processors in step 3 deduplicate them using the end-to-end request id. To stop the payer being overdrawn, add a stream processor partitioned by payer account that maintains balances and validates transactions, and place only valid transactions in the request log.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Splitting the transaction into differently partitioned stages and carrying the request id gives the same correctness property as an atomic commit protocol, even with faults.

card.rule: Replay is safe because derivation is deterministic and the request id lets the last stage drop repeats.
card.limits: The overdraft check sits before the log, so only requests that passed validation enter it. Without that stage, nothing prevents overdraft.

concepts.title: Timeliness and integrity: two parts of consistency
concepts.question: What are timeliness and integrity, and how do they differ from each other?

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: Timeliness means users observe the system in an up-to-date state. A stale read is inconsistent only temporarily: waiting and trying again resolves it. Integrity means absence of corruption: no data loss and no contradictory or false data, and any derived view must be derived correctly.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: The author thinks the word consistency conflates the two, so they are worth considering separately. If integrity is violated the inconsistency is permanent and needs explicit checking and repair. The slogan: violations of timeliness are eventual consistency, violations of integrity are perpetual inconsistency.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: The CAP theorem uses consistency as linearizability, a strong way of achieving timeliness. In ACID, consistency is usually some application-specific idea of integrity, supported by atomicity and durability.

card.rule: Separate how fresh data is (timeliness) from how correct it is (integrity), because they fail differently.
card.limits: In ACID transactions both usually come together, so the distinction matters most when you leave transactions behind.

concepts.title: In most applications integrity matters more than timeliness
concepts.question: Why does the author say integrity is usually more important than timeliness?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The author asserts that in most applications integrity is much more important than timeliness. Violations of timeliness can be annoying and confusing, but violations of integrity can be catastrophic.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: On a credit card statement it is normal that a purchase from the last 24 hours does not yet appear, because banks reconcile and settle asynchronously. A statement whose balance differs from the previous balance plus the transactions (an error in the sums), or a charge that is never paid to the merchant (disappearing money), would be integrity failures.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Systems can often accept a lag of timeliness while treating integrity as non-negotiable.

card.rule: Accept some lag in what users see, but never accept corrupt, lost or contradictory data.
card.limits: This is the author's assertion about most applications. Where freshness is itself critical, timeliness may weigh more.

concepts.title: Waiting for the outcome is separate from enforcing it
concepts.question: Why does the correctness of the uniqueness check not depend on the client waiting for the result?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Transactions are typically linearizable: a writer waits until the transaction is committed, and afterwards its writes are visible to all readers. Unbundled processing across stages is asynchronous by design, so the sender does not wait for consumers to process its message.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A client can still wait for a message to appear on an output stream, as in the username example. The waiting only serves to tell the sender synchronously whether the check succeeded.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The correctness of the uniqueness check does not depend on whether the sender waits. The notification of the outcome can be decoupled from the effects of processing the message.

card.rule: Let the system enforce the rule asynchronously, and let the client wait for the answer only if it needs to know.
card.limits: If the user must see the outcome at once, the client does need to wait. Waiting adds latency but not correctness.

concepts.title: Dataflow systems decouple timeliness from integrity
concepts.question: What do event-based dataflow systems separate that ACID transactions usually provide together?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: ACID transactions usually provide both timeliness (for example linearizability) and integrity (for example atomic commit), so the distinction between them is fairly inconsequential from that point of view.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Event-based dataflow systems decouple the two. Processing event streams asynchronously gives no timeliness guarantee unless you build consumers that wait for a message. But integrity is central to streaming systems.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Exactly-once or effectively-once semantics is a mechanism for preserving integrity, since a lost event or an event taking effect twice could violate it. Fault-tolerant message delivery and duplicate suppression, such as idempotent operations, are important for integrity in the face of faults.

card.rule: In dataflow systems you choose timeliness separately, and you make integrity the first-class guarantee.
card.limits: Integrity in a dataflow system depends on the mechanisms in the next idea. Without them, asynchrony does not preserve it.

concepts.title: Four mechanisms that preserve integrity in dataflow
concepts.question: Which four mechanisms together preserve integrity without distributed transactions?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Reliable stream processing can preserve integrity without distributed transactions and atomic commit, and so with much better performance and operational robustness, through a combination of mechanisms.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: One: represent the content of a write as a single message, which is easily written atomically and fits event sourcing. Two: derive all other state updates from that message with deterministic derivation functions, like stored procedures. Three: pass a client-generated request id through all levels of processing for end-to-end duplicate suppression and idempotence. Four: make messages immutable and allow derived data to be reprocessed from time to time, easing recovery from bugs.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The author sees this combination as a very promising direction for building fault-tolerant applications.

card.rule: One atomic message, deterministic derivations, an end-to-end request id and immutable reprocessable messages preserve integrity.
card.limits: The combination preserves integrity, not timeliness. It also depends on all four holding together.

concepts.title: Many applications can interpret constraints loosely
concepts.question: Which real-world business examples show that a constraint can be violated and then compensated?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Enforcing a strict uniqueness constraint requires consensus, and stream processing cannot avoid that. But many real applications can get away with much weaker notions of uniqueness.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: If two people concurrently register the same username or book the same seat, send one an apology and ask them to choose another: a compensating transaction. If customers order more than the warehouse holds, order more stock, apologise for the delay and offer a discount. Airlines and hotels deliberately overbook and use refunds, upgrades or a room elsewhere. A bank lets someone overdraw, charges an overdraft fee and limits total daily withdrawals to bound its risk.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The apology processes already exist for other reasons, such as a forklift damaging stock or a cancelled flight, so a linearizable constraint is often unnecessary.

card.rule: Where an apology process already exists, a constraint can be checked after the fact instead of before the write.
card.limits: This works only when the cost of the apology is acceptable. Some actions, like paying out cash, cannot be taken back.

concepts.title: Whether an apology is affordable is a business decision
concepts.question: When is it acceptable to write first and check a constraint afterwards?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: It is often acceptable to violate a constraint temporarily and fix it later by apologising. The cost in money or reputation varies. You cannot unsend an email, but you can send a correction. A double charge can be refunded for the cost of processing fees and perhaps a complaint. Cash paid out by an ATM cannot be directly recovered.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Whether the cost of the apology is acceptable is a business decision. If it is, checking all constraints before even writing the data is unnecessarily restrictive, and a linearizable constraint is not needed. It may be reasonable to write optimistically and check afterwards, while still validating before doing things that are expensive to recover from.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: These applications still need integrity: you would not want to lose a reservation or have money vanish from mismatched credits and debits. They do not need timeliness of the enforcement.

card.rule: Weigh the cost of an apology against the cost of strict checking, and validate first only before actions that are costly to reverse.
card.limits: Some actions, such as paying out cash or sending an email, cannot be unsent. For those the check must come first.

concepts.title: Coordination-avoiding data systems
concepts.question: What do the two observations about integrity and constraints add up to?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Two observations: first, dataflow systems can maintain integrity guarantees on derived data without atomic commit, linearizability or synchronous cross-partition coordination. Second, strict uniqueness needs timeliness and coordination, but many applications are fine with loose constraints that are temporarily violated and fixed later, as long as integrity is preserved.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Together they mean dataflow systems can provide data management for many applications without coordination while keeping strong integrity. Such coordination-avoiding systems can have better performance and fault tolerance. One could run multi-leader across datacenters and replicate asynchronously, with each datacenter operating independently.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Such a system has weak timeliness, since it cannot be linearizable without coordination, but strong integrity. Serializable transactions remain useful at a small scope, and synchronous coordination can be added only where needed.

card.rule: Avoid coordination where a fixable violation is acceptable, and keep it only where an unrecoverable action needs it.
card.limits: You cannot reduce the number of apologies to zero. The aim is the trade-off between inconsistency apologies and outage apologies.

concepts.title: System models are really about probabilities
concepts.question: Should a system model treat unlikely faults as impossible, or as improbable but real?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Correctness arguments rest on a system model: processes can crash, machines can lose power and the network can delay or drop messages, but data written after fsync is not lost, memory is not corrupted and the CPU multiplies correctly. These assumptions are true most of the time, and it would be hard to get anything done without them.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Traditionally the model is binary: some things can happen and others can never happen. In reality it is a question of probabilities, with some faults more likely and others less likely. What matters is whether violations occur often enough that we may meet them in practice.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Data can become corrupted while sitting untouched on disk, and corruption on the network can sometimes evade the TCP checksums. Such cases deserve some attention, even though they are rare.

card.rule: Ask how often an assumption is violated, not only whether it is written into the model.
card.limits: Random bit-flips are still very rare on modern hardware, so this argues for attention, not for panic.

concepts.title: Software bugs can corrupt data that checksums never catch
concepts.question: Why can checksums on the network, memory and filesystem not protect against software bugs?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Lower-level checksums on network, memory or filesystem do not catch software bugs. Even widely used databases have bugs: MySQL has failed to maintain a uniqueness constraint and PostgreSQL's serializable isolation level has exhibited write skew anomalies.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Despite careful design, testing and review, bugs creep in, and during the period before they are found they can corrupt data. Application code gets far less review and testing than database code, so many more bugs must be assumed. Many applications do not even use the integrity features databases offer, such as foreign key or uniqueness constraints.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: ACID consistency starts from a consistent state and moves to another one, which only makes sense if the transaction is free from bugs. Using a weak isolation level unsafely means integrity cannot be guaranteed.

card.rule: Assume bugs exist at every layer, and application code has the most.
card.limits: The examples are drawn from the author's own experience of robust, battle-tested databases.

concepts.title: Auditing: check that data is still correct instead of trusting it
concepts.question: How can a system find out whether its data has been corrupted?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: With hardware and software both imperfect, data corruption is inevitable sooner or later. We need a way to find out about it so that it can be fixed and its source tracked down.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Checking the integrity of data is known as auditing. Large storage systems such as HDFS and Amazon S3 do not fully trust disks: background processes continually read back files, compare them to other replicas and move files between disks. Restoring from backups from time to time checks that the backups work.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Data you never read back may be gone without your knowledge. Finding out sooner is much better than finding out when it is too late.

card.rule: To be sure data is still there, read it and check it.
card.limits: Auditing is worth most where mistakes are costly, as in finance, but the author says it is not only for financial applications.

concepts.title: A culture of trust, but verify
concepts.question: What has the culture of ACID databases done to attitudes toward checking data?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: HDFS and S3 still assume disks work correctly most of the time, which is reasonable but not the same as assuming they always work. Few systems continually audit themselves, and many assume correctness guarantees are absolute.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The author fears that the culture of ACID databases led developers to build on blind trust in technology such as the transaction mechanism, and to neglect auditability.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Then weaker consistency became normal under the banner of NoSQL, and less mature storage became widely used. Applications still relied on blind trust, which had become more dangerous. The author hopes for self-validating systems that continually check their own integrity.

card.rule: Trust the technology, but verify the data it holds.
card.limits: This is the author's opinion and fear about the industry, not a measured survey.

concepts.title: Event sourcing makes the system easier to audit
concepts.question: Why are event-based systems easier to audit than ones that only record the effects of transactions?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: If a transaction changes several objects, it is hard to tell afterwards what it meant. Even with the transaction log, the inserts, updates and deletes in various tables do not give a clear picture of why they were made, and the application logic that decided on them is transient and cannot be reproduced.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: In event sourcing, user input is one immutable event, and any state updates are derived from it. The derivation can be deterministic and repeatable, so the same log through the same code version gives the same state. Being explicit about dataflow makes provenance clearer. Hashes can check that the event storage is not corrupted, and derived state can be checked by rerunning the processors, or by a redundant derivation in parallel.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A deterministic, well-defined dataflow also makes it easier to debug and trace why the system did something. It gives a kind of time-travel debugging.

card.rule: Record the input as an immutable event so every derived state can be recomputed and compared.
card.limits: It helps only if the derivation really is deterministic and the event log itself is trustworthy.

concepts.title: Check integrity end to end, and check it continuously
concepts.question: Why is it best to check data integrity across the whole pipeline instead of one component at a time?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: If we cannot trust every component to be free of corruption, we must at least periodically check the data. Without checks, corruption is found only after downstream damage, when the problem is much harder and more expensive to track down.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Integrity checking is best done end to end: the more systems an integrity check includes, the fewer opportunities for corruption to go unnoticed at some stage. If an entire derived-data pipeline is checked end to end, the disks, networks, services and algorithms along the path are implicitly included.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Continuous end-to-end checks give more confidence in correctness. Like automated testing, auditing increases the chance that bugs are found quickly, which reduces the risk of a change or a new storage technology doing damage.

card.rule: Wrap the whole pipeline in one check and run it all the time.
card.limits: An end-to-end check shows that something went wrong, not necessarily where, so tracing the source still takes work.

concepts.title: Cryptographic tools may make data systems auditable
concepts.question: Which cryptographic ideas could help prove that a data system's integrity has not been broken?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Few data systems make auditability a top-level concern. Some applications log all changes to a separate audit table, but guaranteeing the integrity of both the audit log and the database state is hard. Signing a transaction log with a hardware security module makes it tamper-proof, but does not prove that the right transactions went into it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Cryptocurrencies, blockchains and distributed ledgers are essentially distributed databases whose replicas may be hosted by mutually untrusting organisations. The replicas continually check each other's integrity and use a consensus protocol to agree on transactions. Merkle trees, trees of hashes, can efficiently prove that a record appears in a dataset.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The author could imagine such algorithms becoming more widely used in data systems, if they can be made as scalable as systems without cryptographic auditing.

card.rule: Borrow the integrity-checking ideas of ledgers and Merkle trees, not necessarily their currency or mining.
card.limits: The author is skeptical about the Byzantine fault tolerance aspects, finds proof of work extraordinarily wasteful, and says Bitcoin's throughput is low.

concepts.title: Engineers share responsibility for what their systems do
concepts.question: Do software engineers bear ethical responsibility for the consequences of the systems they build?

paragraphs: The author claims that engineers must consider the consequences of their systems and consciously decide what kind of world they want to live in. His first reason is that every system has a purpose, and every action has intended and unintended consequences that may reach far beyond the original purpose.

A second reason is that many datasets are about people: their behaviour, interests and identity. Such data must be treated with humanity and respect, because users are humans too and human dignity is paramount.
A third reason is that a technology is not good or bad in itself. What matters is how it is used, which holds for a search engine as much as for a gun.
card.rule: Focusing only on the technology and ignoring its consequences is not enough, because the ethical responsibility is the engineers' to bear.
card.limits: Reasoning about ethics is difficult, and the author offers no complete method here, only the claim that it is too important to ignore.

concepts.title: Predictions about individuals can exclude people from society
concepts.question: Why is predicting a person's default or reoffending different from predicting the weather?

paragraphs: The author claims that predicting the weather or disease spread differs from predicting whether a convict will reoffend, a borrower will default or an insured customer will claim. The reason is that the latter have a direct effect on individual lives.
Organisations see a low cost in a missed opportunity and a high cost in a bad loan or an untrustworthy hire, so it is natural for them to be cautious. If in doubt, they say no.

The consequence is that a person labelled risky, accurately or falsely, may suffer many such no decisions. Being systematically excluded from jobs, travel, insurance, rental and finance is such a constraint on freedom that it has been called algorithmic prison.
card.rule: When predictions decide things about people, caution on the organisation's side turns into exclusion on the person's side.
card.limits: The argument concerns predictions with a direct effect on individuals, not every use of data analysis.

concepts.title: Data-driven decisions can launder and amplify bias
concepts.question: Does basing decisions on data automatically make them fair?

paragraphs: The author argues that algorithmic decisions are not necessarily better or worse than human ones. People are biased, and there is hope that data could give a fairer chance to those overlooked in the traditional system.

But the rules of a predictive system are inferred from data, and the learned patterns are opaque: even with a correlation, we may not know why. If the input has a systematic bias, the system will most likely learn and amplify it.
Features such as a postal code can be a strong predictor of race in segregated neighbourhoods, so analysing apparently neutral features can still end in discrimination.
card.rule: Predictive systems extrapolate from the past, so a discriminatory past is codified, and only humans can supply the moral imagination for a better future.
card.limits: The author grants that data might improve on human judgement; his point is that fairness is not guaranteed.

concepts.title: Automated decisions need accountability, and opaque models resist it
concepts.question: Who is accountable when an algorithm makes a wrong decision about a person?

paragraphs: The author claims that automated decision-making opens a question of responsibility. A human who errs can be held accountable and the affected person can appeal, but when an algorithm goes wrong it is unclear who is accountable, as with a self-driving car accident or a discriminatory credit scoring algorithm.

A traditional credit score is based on relevant facts of a person's actual borrowing history, and errors in the record can be corrected, although not easily. Machine-learning scoring uses a wider range of inputs and is much more opaque.
That opacity makes it harder to understand how a decision came about and whether a person is treated unfairly. It also raises the question of whether the system could be explained to a judge.
card.rule: A decision that cannot be explained or appealed has no real accountability.
card.limits: The author poses these as open questions, and does not claim that any current law settles them.

concepts.title: Predictions are probabilistic, and data can help or harm
concepts.question: Why can a correct prediction about a group still be wrong about one person?

paragraphs: The author claims that much data is statistical in nature. Even if the probability distribution is right overall, individual cases may be wrong. If average life expectancy is 80, it does not mean you will die on your 80th birthday.

Therefore the output of a prediction system is probabilistic and may be wrong in individual cases. Treating it as certain is a blind belief in the supremacy of data, which he calls not only delusional but positively dangerous.
He adds that data can be used to do good, such as focusing aid on those who most need it, or to do harm, when predatory businesses use it to find vulnerable people.
card.rule: Treat a prediction as a probability about a population, not a fact about a person.
card.limits: Statistical output remains useful in aggregate; the warning is about individual decisions based on it alone.

concepts.title: Self-reinforcing feedback loops make predictions harm people
concepts.question: How can a prediction system worsen the very situation it predicts?

paragraphs: The author claims that even less obviously far-reaching predictors, such as recommendation systems, raise difficult issues. When a service gets good at predicting what users want to see, it may show only opinions they already agree with, leading to echo chambers in which stereotypes, misinformation and polarisation breed.

He also claims that predictions affecting lives can create self-reinforcing loops. Suppose employers use credit scores to evaluate hires. A good worker hit by misfortune misses payments, the score drops and finding work gets harder. Joblessness deepens poverty and worsens the score further.
The result is a downward spiral built on poisonous assumptions, hidden behind a camouflage of mathematical rigour.
card.rule: Consider the entire system, including the people interacting with it, to foresee loops before they harm.
card.limits: We cannot always predict when feedback loops happen, and good intentions do not prevent unintended consequences.

concepts.title: Tracking turns a service for the user into one with interests of its own
concepts.question: When does storing user data stop being a service to the user?

paragraphs: The author claims that the relationship between a data collector and the person depends on how data arrives. When a system stores only what a user explicitly entered because they want it stored and processed, it performs a service for the user, who is the customer.

When activity is instead tracked as a side effect of other things the user does, the service takes on interests of its own that may conflict with the user's. Some tracking helps users, such as improving search ranking, recommending items or guiding interface changes through A/B tests.
In an advertising-funded service the advertisers are the real customers. Data becomes more detailed, analyses further-reaching and retention longer, to build profiles for marketing.
card.rule: Ask whose interests the data collection serves: the user's, or the paying advertiser's.
card.limits: Tracking is not bad in itself; the concern is tracking that goes beyond what features for users require.

concepts.title: Much data collection amounts to mass surveillance
concepts.question: What changes if we replace the word data with surveillance in common phrases?

paragraphs: The author claims we have built the greatest mass surveillance infrastructure the world has seen. His thought experiment replaces data with surveillance in phrases such as surveillance warehouse and surveillance scientists, to test whether they still sound good.

His reasons are that smartphones, smart TVs, voice assistants, baby monitors and toys put an internet-connected microphone in nearly every inhabited space, many with terrible security. Even repressive regimes could only dream of microphones in every room and a tracker carried by everyone, yet we embrace it, because corporations collect the data rather than government agencies.

Benign purposes become less benign once surveillance feeds insurance premiums or employment decisions, and analysis can reveal intrusive facts, such as passwords typed, from a smartwatch's motion sensor.
card.rule: Examining data collection as surveillance helps expose what relationship we have with the collector.
card.limits: Not all data collection qualifies as surveillance, and the author calls the thought experiment unusually polemic for this book.

concepts.title: Consent to tracking is not meaningful, and opting out is not free
concepts.question: Can users meaningfully consent to data collection by accepting a privacy policy?

paragraphs: The author considers the argument that users choose a tracking service, agree to its terms and receive value. He answers that users know little about what data they feed in or how it is processed, and most privacy policies obscure more than they illuminate. Without understanding, consent cannot be meaningful.

Data from one user also says things about non-users who never agreed. Derived datasets combining the whole user base with behavioural tracking and external sources are precisely what users cannot understand.

Extraction is one-way, not reciprocal: the service sets the terms, with no dialogue or negotiation. The alternative of not using the service is not free if it is essential for social participation, and only the privileged can afford it.
card.rule: Choice requires understanding and a real alternative; without both, agreeing to the terms is not consent.
card.limits: The author accepts that free online services are valuable to users; his objection is to the consent argument, not the value.

concepts.title: Privacy is a decision right, and surveillance transfers it to companies
concepts.question: What does the right to privacy actually protect?

paragraphs: The author rejects the claim that privacy is dead because people post personal things online. It rests on a misunderstanding. Privacy does not mean keeping everything secret; it means the freedom to choose what to reveal to whom, what to make public and what to keep secret.
So privacy is a decision right, letting each person pick a point between secrecy and transparency in each situation. It is part of freedom and autonomy.

When surveillance extracts data, the right is not eroded but transferred to the collector, who says trust us to do the right thing. Companies keep much of the outcome secret, revealing it indirectly, for example through ad targeting at groups such as people with an illness.
card.rule: Whoever decides what is revealed and to whom holds the privacy right.
card.limits: Privacy settings return some control but leave the service itself with unfettered access, constrained only by its own policy.

concepts.title: Personal data is a core asset, a hazard and a source of power
concepts.question: Is behavioural data worthless exhaust, or the most valuable thing a service holds?

paragraphs: The author claims behavioural data is not waste but the core asset of a service paid for by targeted advertising, and the app is a means to lure users into feeding more personal information to the surveillance infrastructure. Data brokers, who buy, aggregate, infer and resell personal data, and startups valued by eyeballs, support that claim.
Because data is valuable many want it, including governments, by secret deals, coercion, legal compulsion or theft. Bankrupt companies sell it, and breaches occur often.

So critics call data a toxic asset or hazardous material. Collection must weigh benefits against the risk of criminals, insiders, bad management or a future regime obtaining it, and knowledge is power.
card.rule: Before collecting data, weigh the benefit against the risk of it reaching the wrong hands, now or under any future government.
card.limits: The author notes that today's technology companies are not overtly seeking political power.

concepts.title: Data is the pollution problem of the information age
concepts.question: What can the Industrial Revolution teach us about managing data collection?

paragraphs: The author argues by analogy. The Industrial Revolution brought sustained growth and better living standards in the long run, but also dreadful air and water pollution, workers in poor housing and harsh conditions, and child labour.

It took a long time before safeguards such as environmental rules, workplace safety, a ban on child labour and food inspections were established. They raised the cost of doing business, yet society benefited hugely, and few would return to the time before them.

In the same way, the information age has a dark side that must be managed. Quoting Bruce Schneier, he calls data the pollution problem of the information age and protecting privacy the environmental challenge.
card.rule: Expect the benefits of a technological revolution to come with harms that need deliberate safeguards.
card.limits: An analogy suggests a path rather than proving it; the safeguards for data are still being worked out.

concepts.title: Data protection law helps but conflicts with the Big Data approach
concepts.question: Can data protection legislation alone preserve individuals' rights over their data?

paragraphs: The author says data protection law might help. The 1995 European Data Protection Directive requires that personal data be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not processed in an incompatible way, and be adequate, relevant and not excessive.

He doubts that this is effective in the internet context. The rules run counter to the philosophy of Big Data: maximise collection, combine datasets and explore for new insights. Exploration means unforeseen purposes, the opposite of specified and explicit purposes agreed in consent.

Companies that collect much data oppose regulation as a burden, and he grants some of that is justified. Sharing medical data carries privacy risks but could prevent deaths through better diagnosis, so over-regulation may block breakthroughs.
card.rule: Regulation is needed, but it must balance potential opportunities against the risks, which is difficult.
card.limits: Updated regulations were being developed when the book was written, so the doubt applies to the 1995 rules.

concepts.title: A culture shift, data purging and cryptographic access control
concepts.question: What does the author propose to protect people's control over their data?

paragraphs: The author argues that we need a culture shift in the tech industry. We should stop regarding users as metrics to be optimised and remember that they are humans who deserve respect, dignity and agency. We should self-regulate data collection and processing to keep the trust of those who depend on our software, and educate users about how their data is used.
He compares an individual's right to control their data to a national park: if not explicitly protected it will be destroyed, a tragedy of the commons. Ubiquitous surveillance is not inevitable.

How to achieve this is open, but two ideas are given. Data should not be kept forever, but purged when no longer needed. And access control can be enforced through cryptographic protocols instead of policy alone.
card.rule: Collect less, keep it shorter, and enforce access technically rather than by promise.
card.limits: The author calls the method an open question, and admits that purging runs counter to the idea of immutability.

concepts.title: Summary: derived data, dataflow and unbundled databases
concepts.question: How does the chapter's architecture for integrating data systems fit together?

paragraphs: No single tool serves all use cases efficiently, so applications compose several pieces of software. Batch processing and event streams let data changes flow between them, with certain systems designated systems of record and other data derived through transformations such as indexes, materialised views, machine learning models and statistical summaries.

Asynchronous, loosely coupled derivation stops a problem in one area from spreading, increasing robustness and fault tolerance. It also helps evolution: to change an index or cache, rerun the new code over the whole input, and to recover from a fault, fix the code and reprocess.

This recasts dataflow as unbundling database components and composing them. Derived state can be observed by downstream consumers, all the way to end-user devices that update dynamically and work offline.
card.rule: Designate systems of record, derive everything else through asynchronous loosely coupled transformations.
card.limits: This summarises the author's opinions and speculations about the future, not settled practice.

concepts.title: Summary: correctness without coordination, and the engineer's responsibility
concepts.question: What does the chapter conclude about correctness, auditing and ethics?

paragraphs: Strong integrity guarantees can be implemented scalably with asynchronous event processing, using end-to-end operation identifiers to make operations idempotent and checking constraints asynchronously. Clients can wait until the check passes, or go ahead and risk having to apologise. This is more scalable and robust than distributed transactions and fits how business processes work.

Structuring applications around dataflow and checking constraints asynchronously avoids most coordination, so systems keep integrity and perform well, even across geographies and faults. Audits verify the integrity of data and detect corruption.

Finally, data can do good but also significant harm, through hard-to-appeal decisions, discrimination, exploitation, normalised surveillance and exposure of intimate information. Engineers carry a responsibility to work toward a world that treats people with humanity and respect.
card.rule: Get integrity through idempotent operations and asynchronous checks, verify it by auditing, and own the human consequences.
card.limits: Avoiding coordination is a design stance, not a promise that no application will ever need a distributed transaction.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Three goals as a lens on every technique
concepts.question: Which of reliability, scalability or maintainability does each technique in the book serve, and what does it cost the others?

paragraphs: The book opens with three goals for a data system: reliability (keep working correctly despite faults), scalability (stay fast as load grows) and maintainability (stay easy for people to operate, understand and change). Reading the later parts as one book means asking of every technique which goal it serves and which goal it taxes.

Replication shows how one technique serves several goals: copies tolerate machine loss, let reads spread over more machines, and can sit near users. Partitioning serves scale. Compatible encodings serve maintainability, because old and new code can then run side by side during a rolling upgrade, so releases can be small and frequent.

Each gain has a price elsewhere. Replica lag weakens freshness, partitioning makes writes across partitions hard to reason about, and strong guarantees slow everything down. A technique is judged by the goal it buys and the goal it taxes.
card.example: A team adds a read replica in another region to speed up reads for European users. The goal served is latency and read scale. The price is that a user may read a copy that has not yet received their own latest write.
card.rule: For each technique, name the goal it serves and the cost it places on another goal.
card.limits: The goals can pull against each other, and which one matters most depends on your own requirements and load.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Fault tolerance as stacked layers
concepts.question: How do replication, transactions, quorums and consensus stack so that faults in parts do not become failures of the whole?

paragraphs: Chapter 1 asks that a fault in one component not become a failure of the whole system. The book answers in layers. Replication and partitioning spread data over machines that fail independently, and transactions give all-or-nothing writes so a crash leaves no half-finished state.

Chapter 8 shows what those layers stand on: networks that lose or delay messages, clocks that disagree, and processes that pause unseen. A node cannot trust its own view, so decisions that must be right are made by a quorum, a vote among a majority of nodes. A paused lock holder is stopped by fencing tokens, numbers that rise with each grant and that the resource checks.
Chapter 9 packages these decisions as reusable abstractions such as consensus. Each layer hides only the faults it was designed for.
card.example: A bank app retries a transfer after a timeout. Atomicity makes the retry safe if the first attempt aborted, but the timeout alone cannot say whether it committed, so a higher layer must also guard against a duplicate.
card.rule: Build correctness on abstractions that tolerate the faults below them, and state which faults each layer assumes away.
card.limits: A guarantee holds only for the fault model it was designed for; faults outside that model, such as bugs that silently corrupt data, pass through every layer.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Fitting data model and storage engine to the workload
concepts.question: How should the shape of your data and its access pattern guide the choice of data model and storage engine?

paragraphs: The early chapters teach one habit: start from how the data is used. Self-contained documents with few links between records suit a document store, heavily interlinked data suits a graph, and data with many-to-many relationships suits relational tables. No model is simplest in general, and one can imitate another, though often awkwardly.

The same habit selects the engine. User-facing work that fetches a few records by key (OLTP, online transaction processing) is served by an index, either in a log-structured engine tuned for write throughput or in a B-tree that updates pages in place. Analytic work that scans millions of rows is limited by disk bandwidth and favours a warehouse with column-oriented storage.
Quick rules, such as log-structured engines writing faster and B-trees reading faster, are rules of thumb only; the book advises testing with your own workload.
card.example: A shop fetches orders by order id thousands of times a second and also runs a nightly report over three years of orders. The first need points to an indexed OLTP store; the second to a warehouse with column storage.
card.rule: Choose the data model and storage engine from the shape of the data and the access pattern, and test with your own workload.
card.limits: The book gives no scoring method, the engine rule of thumb can fail on a real workload, and one application may need several stores rather than one best choice.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Replication and partitioning combined
concepts.question: How do replication and partitioning combine in one system, and what does each scheme choice cost?

paragraphs: Replication keeps copies of the same data on several nodes; partitioning splits a dataset so each node holds only part of it. Large systems use both: every partition is replicated, so one node can lead some partitions and follow others. The two are separate choices.

Each choice has a price. Single-leader replication is easy to reason about but sends all writes through one node. Multi-leader and leaderless replication cope better with faults and delays but accept concurrent writes, so conflicts arise and guarantees are weak. Key-range partitioning allows range scans but can create hot spots; hash partitioning spreads load but loses key order.

Partitioning also reshapes other features. A secondary index must itself be partitioned: a local (document-partitioned) index keeps writes cheap but makes reads scatter across every partition, while a global (term-partitioned) index does the reverse. A transaction touching several partitions needs coordination that single-partition work avoids.
card.example: A catalogue is hashed by product id into 64 partitions, each with three replicas. Fetching one product is a single-partition read, but searching by colour needs either a scatter/gather over all partitions or a global colour index that every write must update.
card.rule: Pick the replication scheme for your fault and consistency needs, the partitioning scheme for your load and queries, and then price the cross-partition work.
card.limits: The book presents trade-offs, not a ranking: single-leader is not best everywhere, and hashing is a poor fit when the workload depends on range scans.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: A ladder of consistency guarantees
concepts.question: What ladder of consistency and isolation guarantees does the book describe, and what does each rung cost?

paragraphs: The word consistency covers a ladder of different promises. Eventual consistency promises only that replicas converge once writes stop. Read-after-write, monotonic reads and consistent prefix reads rule out specific odd views under replication lag. Causal consistency keeps cause before effect. Linearizability makes replicated data behave as if there were one copy.

A second ladder is about transactions: read committed stops dirty reads and writes, snapshot isolation also stops read skew, and serializable isolation stops write skew and phantoms as well. Do not merge the ladders. Linearizability is a recency guarantee on a single object; serializability concerns transactions over several objects.

Higher rungs cost more: coordination between nodes, speed and availability when the network fails. Causal consistency needs no per-operation coordination across nodes and copes better with network problems than linearizability.
card.example: A chat app shows a reply before the question it answers. That is a consistent-prefix problem, fixed by keeping causally related writes together, not by making every read linearizable.
card.rule: Name the exact guarantee you need and pay only for that rung; do not use consistency, isolation and linearizability as synonyms.
card.limits: The ladders are not one line: causal consistency and snapshot isolation guard different things, and a stronger rung is not better if its coordination cost breaks availability.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Many jobs, one agreement problem
concepts.question: Why do leader election, locks, uniqueness, atomic commit and message ordering all reduce to the same agreement problem?

paragraphs: Several jobs that look unrelated turn out to be one: getting nodes to agree on a decision that cannot be undone. Electing a leader, granting a lock, enforcing a uniqueness constraint, committing a transaction across nodes, fixing the order of messages and running a compare-and-set register are all consensus problems. A solution to one can be turned into a solution to the others.

With one node, or one node given all the decision power, each is easy. A single leader gives ordering and uniqueness, but if it fails the system needs a way to pick a new one, and that choice itself needs consensus. A proven algorithm, usually reached through a service such as ZooKeeper, is safer than one you write.
Consensus costs coordination, so ask which problems you really have. Multi-leader and leaderless systems skip global consensus and accept branching version histories.
card.example: Two users register the same username on different nodes at the same moment. Only a decision all nodes agree on can reject one of them; timestamps alone cannot, because neither node knows the other is mid-registration.
card.rule: When a requirement says exactly one winner, one order or one decision across nodes, treat it as consensus and use a proven implementation.
card.limits: Not every system needs consensus; leaderless and multi-leader systems do without it, at the price of weaker guarantees such as uniqueness.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: The log as the book's recurring spine
concepts.question: Why does the append-only log recur through the book, and how does it keep several systems in step?

paragraphs: An append-only sequence of records turns up in almost every part of the book. Storage engines append to log segments, a leader's replication log is the stream of writes followers apply in order, and a log-based message broker keeps events on disk so consumers can track an offset (their position) and replay.

Because a log fixes one order, it keeps several systems consistent. If every write goes to one log, a search index, a cache and a warehouse that consume it in order become derived views of one history, with none of the races of writing to two stores directly. Total order broadcast, which is equivalent to consensus, is the theory behind such a log.
That is why the book ends by naming one system of record and deriving everything else from its log, through change data capture or event sourcing. A derived view can be rebuilt by replaying the log.
card.example: A retailer writes orders only to its database and publishes the change log. A search index and a reporting store consume it. If the index has a bug, the team fixes the code and replays the log to rebuild it.
card.rule: To keep several systems in step, put writes in one ordered log and make every other system a view derived from it.
card.limits: Order is guaranteed only within one log partition, so scale is limited, and services or offline clients with no shared log have no shared order, so causality can be lost.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Batch and stream as one derivation
concepts.question: How are batch and stream processing the same idea, where do they differ, and how might one system do both?

paragraphs: Batch and stream processing share one pattern: read input, derive output without changing the input, and pass the output to another stage. The difference is the input. Batch input is bounded, so a job knows when it has finished; stream input is unbounded, so a job never completes and must keep producing output.

That difference changes other things. A batch job can discard a failed task's output and rerun it, and the final result matches a fault-free run. A long-running stream job cannot discard everything, so it recovers with microbatches, checkpoints or idempotent writes. Time windows must use event time, since processing time is meaningless when old events are replayed.
The lambda architecture ran a batch system and a stream system side by side over the same events. Later work runs history and fresh events through one engine.
card.example: A team counts page views per hour. Run nightly over yesterday's logs, that is a batch job; run continuously, emitting each hour's count as its window closes, it is a stream job over the same events.
card.rule: Treat batch and stream as one derivation over immutable events, then choose by whether the input is bounded and how fresh the output must be.
card.limits: Running both in one engine needs replayable input, exactly-once semantics and event-time windows; an engine without them cannot give a stream job the simple recovery of a batch job.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Integrity first: questions for choosing a design
concepts.question: What sequence of questions does the book leave for choosing a design, and when is integrity worth more than timeliness?

paragraphs: The book offers no universal design, but it leaves questions to ask in order. What are the requirements and the load? What is the data's shape and how is it read? Which copies are systems of record and which are derived? Which failures must be survived? Which guarantees does the application truly need?

The last question splits consistency in two. Timeliness means users see an up-to-date state; a violation is temporary. Integrity means no corruption, loss or contradiction; a violation is permanent unless repaired. According to the author, most applications need integrity far more than timeliness, and integrity can be protected without coordination when a client passes a unique operation id through every stage, so retries become harmless.

Where a constraint is loose, such as overbooked seats, checking afterwards and apologising may cost less than synchronous coordination. Whether an apology is affordable is a business decision; strict constraints still need coordination.
card.example: A hotel site books rooms in two regions that sync asynchronously. It may briefly sell the last room twice and apologise, but it must not lose a confirmed booking or charge a guest who has no booking.
card.rule: Guard integrity with idempotent end-to-end operations, and pay for timeliness and coordination only where an apology would cost more.
card.limits: These are the author's opinions, drawn mainly from the last chapter; an action that cannot be undone, such as paying out money, may justify checking before acting.

questions.q: A photo-sharing app slows down as people upload more albums and edit them constantly. What is the likeliest main difficulty?
options: Too little raw CPU power on each server
A lack of compute-heavy algorithms in the application code itself
The growing amount of data and the speed at which it changes
Users having screens that are too small
optionExplain: A common first guess, but raw CPU power is rarely the limiting factor for these applications.
Data-intensive applications are defined by what limits them, not by how clever their algorithms are.
Right: volume and rate of change of data are what usually limit such applications.
A display issue has nothing to do with a slowdown that grows with uploads.
questions.explain: Such an app mostly struggles with how much data it holds and how fast it changes. The card next names this idea.
questions.rule: Call an application data-intensive when the amount, complexity or speed of change of its data, not raw CPU power, is its main difficulty.

questions.q: Raw ____ power is rarely a limiting factor for a data-intensive application.
questions.explain: The book says the bigger problems are usually the amount of data, its complexity, and the speed at which it changes.
questions.rule: Look at the data before the processor.

questions.q: Which application fits the book's description of data-intensive?
options: A messaging service whose stored conversations grow and change constantly
A tool that renders one huge animated film, limited only by processor speed
A solver that spends hours of CPU time on one small equation system
A screensaver that animates shapes on the user's own computer
optionExplain: Right: the load comes from the amount of data and the rate at which it changes.
Its limit is computation, so it is compute-intensive rather than data-intensive.
Heavy arithmetic on little data is the compute-intensive pattern.
It has almost no data to store or change, and no data problem to solve.
questions.explain: A messaging service is limited by data volume and change, not by arithmetic.
questions.rule: Call an application data-intensive when the amount, complexity or speed of change of its data, not raw CPU power, is its main difficulty.

questions.q: Which are the three data-side difficulties the book names? Select all that apply.
options: The amount of data
The complexity of the data
The clock speed of the processors
The speed at which the data is changing
The number of programming languages used
optionExplain: Right: volume is the first difficulty named.
Right: how tangled the data is counts as its own difficulty.
This is the raw CPU power the book says is rarely the limit.
Right: a fast rate of change is the third difficulty.
This is not among the difficulties the book names for data-intensive applications.
questions.explain: The book names amount, complexity and rate of change of data as the usual bigger problems.
questions.rule: Call an application data-intensive when the amount, complexity or speed of change of its data, not raw CPU power, is its main difficulty.

questions.q: A hospital app keeps the same number of records, but they become far more tangled across departments. Which difficulty has grown?
options: The amount of data
The speed at which the data changes
Raw CPU power needed
The complexity of the data
optionExplain: The number of records stayed the same, so volume did not grow.
Nothing in the case says updates became faster.
The book says CPU power is rarely the limit, and nothing here points to it.
Right: the amount is unchanged, so the added difficulty is complexity.
questions.explain: Each difficulty can grow alone: here only complexity did.
questions.hint: Which of the three changed in the story?
questions.rule: Call an application data-intensive when the amount, complexity or speed of change of its data, not raw CPU power, is its main difficulty.

questions.q: Why do most engineers not write a new data storage engine from scratch for each application?
options: Storage engines can only be written by the vendors who sell database products
Databases are a successful abstraction, a good tool used without much thought
Data-intensive applications need no storage at all
Every application has exactly the same storage needs
optionExplain: Nothing in the text says writing one is forbidden or impossible.
Right: the book says these systems are such a successful abstraction that we use them all the time without thinking too much.
They are defined by their data, so they certainly store it.
The book stresses that different applications have different requirements.
questions.explain: Reuse of a trusted tool beats rebuilding it for each application.
questions.teaches: Data systems are such a successful abstraction that engineers use them constantly without much thought, and most would not dream of writing a new storage engine from scratch.
questions.rule: Call an application data-intensive when the amount, complexity or speed of change of its data, not raw CPU power, is its main difficulty.

questions.q: A ride-booking app's CPUs sit idle while driver locations stream in every second. Having called it data-intensive, what is the next job?
options: Buy faster CPUs, because a high data rate proves that the processors are too slow
Work out which tools and approaches suit its requirements, as databases differ
Pick any database, because the database systems are interchangeable
Wait until the data volume forces a new storage engine to be written
optionExplain: Idle CPUs show the opposite; raw CPU power is not the limit.
Right: the label points at data, but the choice of tools still depends on the application's requirements.
The book says there are many database systems because requirements differ.
The book notes that engineers rarely write their own engines.
questions.explain: Naming the difficulty is the start; matching tools to requirements is the work.
questions.teaches: There are many database systems with different characteristics because different applications have different requirements, so tools must be chosen for the task at hand.
questions.rule: Call an application data-intensive when the amount, complexity or speed of change of its data, not raw CPU power, is its main difficulty.

questions.q: An app must answer repeated requests faster by remembering the result of an expensive operation. Which kind of block does that?
options: A batch processing job
A search index
A stream processor
A cache
optionExplain: Batch jobs crunch accumulated data periodically; they do not serve repeated reads.
An index helps find data by keyword or filter, not to reuse a computed result.
Stream processing passes messages for asynchronous handling.
Right: a cache keeps the result of an expensive operation so later reads are fast.
questions.explain: Remembering an expensive result to speed up reads is the job of a cache. The card lists the other blocks.
questions.rule: Name the function each building block provides, then choose among its variants for your own requirements.

questions.q: Match each building block to the function the book gives it.
pairs: Store data so it can be found again later
Remember the result of an expensive operation to speed up reads
Let users search data by keyword or filter it
Periodically crunch a large amount of accumulated data
questions.explain: Each block is defined by the function it serves, not by a product name.
questions.rule: Name the function each building block provides, then choose among its variants for your own requirements.

questions.q: An online shop wants customers to find products by typing words and narrowing by price. Which block serves that?
options: A search index
A batch processing job
A stream processor
A cache of last week's pages
optionExplain: Right: search indexes allow searching by keyword and filtering in various ways.
A batch job could prepare data, but it does not answer a customer's typed query.
It hands messages to other processes; it does not look things up.
Remembering results speeds repeats but cannot search or filter new queries.
questions.explain: Keyword search and filtering is the search index's function.
questions.rule: Name the function each building block provides, then choose among its variants for your own requirements.

questions.q: A nightly job totals the day's sales; another part hands each new order to the warehouse process to deal with later. Which blocks are these?
options: Stream processing for the totals, batch processing for the order handoff
A search index for the totals, a cache for the order handoff
Batch processing for the totals, stream processing for the order handoff
A cache for the totals, a database for the order handoff
optionExplain: This swaps the two: the periodic crunch of accumulated data is batch.
Neither of these does periodic crunching or asynchronous messaging.
Right: batch crunches accumulated data periodically; stream processing sends a message to be handled asynchronously.
A cache only remembers results, and a database stores data rather than passing a message.
questions.explain: Periodic work on accumulated data is batch; message handoff for later handling is stream processing.
questions.rule: Name the function each building block provides, then choose among its variants for your own requirements.

questions.q: A design note assigns functions to blocks. Which assignments are wrong? Select all that apply.
options: Database: store articles so they can be found again later
Cache: let readers search articles by keyword
Batch processing: hand each new comment to a moderation process to be handled asynchronously
Search index: let readers filter articles by category
optionExplain: This matches the database's function.
Wrong: keyword search belongs to a search index.
Wrong: handing a message to another process for asynchronous handling is stream processing.
This matches the search index's function.
questions.explain: Two assignments mix up the functions: search belongs to the index, asynchronous handoff to stream processing.
questions.rule: Name the function each building block provides, then choose among its variants for your own requirements.

questions.q: Two teams both need caching, one for login sessions and one for rendered pages. Why might they choose different caching approaches?
options: A cache can only hold one kind of data per company
One of the two teams must be using a database instead
Caches are suited only to session data, so the page team must use a search index instead of caching
Caching has various approaches, and the best fit depends on each team's requirements
optionExplain: Nothing in the text limits a cache this way.
Both teams said they need caching; the choice is between caching approaches.
A search index serves a different function, not the page team's caching need.
Right: the variants differ in characteristics, and requirements decide among them.
questions.explain: Even within one block, the right variant depends on the application.
questions.teaches: There are various approaches to caching and several ways of building search indexes, so even one building block needs a choice that depends on the task at hand.
questions.rule: Name the function each building block provides, then choose among its variants for your own requirements.

questions.q: A team runs a separate search server and a cache beside its main database. Who has to keep them in step with the database?
options: The application code the team writes
The search server, which watches the database on its own
The clients, who re-check the database on each request
The operations team, through a nightly manual comparison
optionExplain: Right: keeping caches and indexes in sync is normally the application code's job.
Separate tools do not automatically follow each other's data.
Clients only see the service's interface.
Operations may monitor, but keeping the copies in step is the application's responsibility.
questions.explain: The stitching is done in application code. The card next shows what that implies.
questions.rule: When you combine tools into one service, you are designing a new data system and must provide its guarantees yourself.

questions.q: True or false: According to the book, the boundaries between categories such as datastores and message queues are becoming blurred.
questions.explain: Examples are Redis, a datastore also used as a message queue, and Kafka, a message queue with database-like durability.

questions.q: Put these steps in order for a price change in a shop that keeps a database and a cache.
items: The shop writes the new price to the database
The application code invalidates or updates the cache entry
A client requests the price
The client sees the new price, consistent with the database
questions.explain: In a composite system the application code must make the write reach the cache, so outside clients see consistent results.
questions.rule: Somebody must make writes reach the cache; in a composite system, that is the application.

questions.q: A team replaces its search server with another product, and the service's API stays the same. What are clients likely to notice?
options: They must change their code, because the search component is visible to them
Every cached result becomes invalid, because the API reaches through to the cache
Little or nothing, because the API hides the implementation details
They notice that the service has become a different kind of system
optionExplain: The API hides implementation details from clients.
Nothing links a changed search product to cache validity at the API.
Right: a service's interface usually hides how it is built from components.
The API still presents the same service.
questions.explain: The interface isolates clients from the parts.
questions.hint: What does the API hide?
questions.rule: When you combine tools into one service, you are designing a new data system and must provide its guarantees yourself.

questions.q: Dana says: we bought a database, a cache and a search server, so we are only application developers; the combined service's guarantees are the products' business. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, because each product separately provides its own guarantee to clients
Combining them created a new data system, so she is also a data system designer
Only that products need an API, which she has forgotten to publish
Only that databases cannot be combined with caches
optionExplain: Guarantees of the combination, like cache consistency, do not belong to any one product.
Right: the book says exactly this once several tools are combined.
The book already says the service's API hides the parts; the issue is who owns the guarantees.
The book describes such combinations as common.
questions.explain: The composite's guarantees belong to whoever built the composite.
questions.rule: When you combine tools into one service, you are designing a new data system and must provide its guarantees yourself.

questions.q: Two companies build the same photo service from several tools, one a bank under regulation, one a small startup. Why might their designs differ?
options: A regulated company is required to use exactly one tool, while a startup is free to stitch several together
The bank's cache has a different API contract with its clients
Design depends on the situation: skills, legacy systems, deadlines, risk tolerance, regulation
Photo services need a different set of building blocks in each country
optionExplain: Nothing in the text ties regulation to a number of tools.
An API is a design output, not a reason the designs differ.
Right: these are the factors the book lists as influencing a data system's design.
The factors listed are about the organization, not geography.
questions.explain: The same requirements can lead to different designs.
questions.teaches: Many factors influence a data system's design, including the skills and experience of the people involved, legacy dependencies, delivery timescale, tolerance of different kinds of risk, and regulatory constraints.
questions.rule: When you combine tools into one service, you are designing a new data system and must provide its guarantees yourself.

questions.q: A system keeps giving correct answers while a disk dies. Which quality is that?
options: Reliability
Scalability
Maintainability
Compatibility
optionExplain: Right: continuing to work correctly despite faults is reliability.
Scalability concerns coping with growth, not faults.
Maintainability is about people working on the system over time.
It is not one of the three concerns the book focuses on here.
questions.explain: Surviving a fault while staying correct is reliability. The card next sets all three side by side.
questions.rule: Judge a data system by whether it keeps working correctly under adversity, copes with growth, and stays productive for many people over time.

questions.q: Match each concern to what it asks of the system.
pairs: Keep working correctly even in the face of adversity
Have reasonable ways of dealing with growth
Let many different people work on it productively
questions.explain: Each concern is a different demand: surviving trouble, growing, and being workable over time.
questions.rule: Judge a data system by whether it keeps working correctly under adversity, copes with growth, and stays productive for many people over time.

questions.q: A bank's app doubles its customers every year, and the team asks how to add machines. Which concern are they working on?
options: Reliability
Maintainability
None of the three, because growth is a business matter
Scalability
optionExplain: Reliability is about staying correct despite faults, not about growth.
Maintainability is about people changing and running the system.
The book names growth in data volume, traffic or complexity as exactly what scalability covers.
Right: dealing reasonably with growth in traffic or data is scalability.
questions.explain: Growth is the trigger for scalability questions.
questions.rule: Judge a data system by whether it keeps working correctly under adversity, copes with growth, and stays productive for many people over time.

questions.q: A service handles its peak traffic well but corrupts data after a power cut. Which concern is failing, and why not scalability?
options: Scalability: corrupting data after a power cut means that the incoming load was too large for it
Reliability: it does not keep working correctly under a fault, and traffic is fine
Maintainability: data corruption means engineers cannot work on it
Scalability: any problem that appears over time is a scaling problem
optionExplain: The load was fine; the trigger was a power cut.
Right: the failure is a fault, not growth.
Nothing here is about people working on the system.
Scalability is specifically about growth, not any problem.
questions.explain: Match the trigger to the concern: a fault points to reliability.
questions.rule: Judge a data system by whether it keeps working correctly under adversity, copes with growth, and stays productive for many people over time.

questions.q: True or false: Reliability and scalability are the same concern, since both are about coping when conditions get worse.
questions.explain: They are different: reliability is about adversity such as faults, scalability about growth in load or data. A system can have one without the other.

questions.q: A ride-booking designer asks four questions. Which one falls outside the three concerns the book focuses on?
options: How do we keep data correct and complete when things go wrong internally?
What does a good API for the service look like?
How do we scale to handle an increase in load?
How do we let many engineers work on the system productively over time?
optionExplain: This is the reliability concern.
Right: it is one of the designer's tricky questions, but it is not one of the three concerns.
This is the scalability concern.
This is the maintainability concern.
questions.explain: The book's designer questions also include API design, which is not one of the three concerns.
questions.teaches: A data system designer faces tricky questions: how to keep data correct and complete when things go wrong, how to give consistently good performance when parts are degraded, how to scale with load, and what a good API looks like.
questions.rule: Judge a data system by whether it keeps working correctly under adversity, copes with growth, and stays productive for many people over time.

questions.q: Which would the book count among typical expectations of reliable software? Select all that apply.
options: It does the function the user expected
It tolerates the user making mistakes
It has a modern, fashionable look
It keeps unauthorized people out
It never needs any update at all
optionExplain: Right: working correctly starts with doing what users expect.
Right: unexpected use or mistakes should not break it.
Appearance is not in the book's list.
Right: preventing unauthorized access and abuse is on the list.
