The book lists no such expectation.
questions.explain: Three of the four listed expectations appear here. The card next gives the full list.
questions.rule: Reliability means continuing to work correctly, where correct covers the expected function, tolerance of mistakes, adequate performance and security, even when things go wrong.

questions.q: We can understand reliability as, roughly, continuing to work ____, even when things go wrong.
questions.explain: That sentence defines reliability by combining working correctly with surviving trouble.
questions.rule: Reliable = keeps working correctly through trouble.

questions.q: A payment page takes 40 seconds to load at normal traffic. Which expectation does it fail?
options: Tolerating the user making mistakes
Preventing unauthorized access and abuse
Performing the function the user expected, since the page does eventually appear
Performance that is good enough for the use case under the expected load
optionExplain: No user mistake is involved in the slowness.
Nothing here concerns security.
The page eventually works, but the book lists performance as a separate expectation.
Right: slow performance at expected load breaks the third expectation.
questions.explain: A correct but unusably slow system still fails the performance expectation.
questions.rule: Reliability means continuing to work correctly, where correct covers the expected function, tolerance of mistakes, adequate performance and security, even when things go wrong.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it is among the book's expectations of reliable software.

items.t: The app copes when a user types text into a number field
The app keeps unauthorized people out
The app does what the user expected it to do
The app responds fast enough at the expected load and data volume
The interface wins a design award
The code is written in a fashionable language

questions.explain: The list is about function, tolerance of mistakes, performance at expected load, and security, not looks or tooling.
questions.rule: Reliability means continuing to work correctly, where correct covers the expected function, tolerance of mistakes, adequate performance and security, even when things go wrong.

questions.q: An app is fast with 10,000 records. The same use case grows to 10 million records. What does the book's expectation imply?
options: Its performance must be judged against the new data volume and may no longer be good enough
It stays reliable, since its past performance is the only measure that counts for reliability
Reliability does not concern speed, so nothing changes
It is now a different system and must be rebuilt
optionExplain: Right: good enough is defined under the expected load and data volume.
The expectation refers to the expected load and volume, not the past.
Performance is part of the book's list of expectations.
The text says nothing like this; it only ties performance to expected volume.
questions.explain: Change the volume and the same performance may stop being good enough.
questions.hint: Where does the book tie performance to a condition?
questions.rule: Reliability means continuing to work correctly, where correct covers the expected function, tolerance of mistakes, adequate performance and security, even when things go wrong.

questions.q: A file-sync service must keep working correctly under adversity. Which set of adversities does the book name?
options: Competitors' price cuts, regulation changes and fashion shifts
Hardware faults only, because software always behaves as written
Hardware or software faults, and even human error
User mistakes only, because machines and code are dependable
optionExplain: These are business pressures, not the faults the chapter examines.
The next sections show software errors are an important class.
Right: these are the three sources of trouble the chapter examines.
Hardware and software faults are both covered.
questions.explain: Reliability is examined against hardware, software and human trouble.
questions.teaches: The adversity a reliable system must survive is hardware or software faults, and even human error.
questions.rule: Reliability means continuing to work correctly, where correct covers the expected function, tolerance of mistakes, adequate performance and security, even when things go wrong.

questions.q: One of five servers in a cluster crashes, yet users notice nothing. In the book's terms, what happened?
options: A failure occurred, but a small one
Nothing occurred, since users noticed no change
A failure occurred in the cluster but not for the users
A fault occurred but did not become a failure
optionExplain: A failure means the system as a whole stops providing the service.
The crash is a real fault even when hidden.
The book defines failure as the service stopping for users.
Right: a component deviated from its spec, but the service as a whole kept working.
questions.explain: A component fault that users never see is a fault without a failure. The card next gives both terms.
questions.rule: Aim to keep a component's fault from becoming a failure of the whole system, for the types of fault you choose to tolerate.

questions.q: A ____ is when the system as a whole stops providing the required service to the user.
questions.explain: A fault is one component deviating from its spec; a failure is the whole system failing the user.
questions.rule: Fault is a part; failure is the whole.

questions.q: A disk in a storage cluster dies, and reads are served from a replica. Which description fits?
options: The dead disk is a fault, and service continued, so there was no failure
The dead disk is a failure, since a component that stops working has failed
Both a fault and a failure occurred, since a disk died
Neither occurred, since the replica hid the problem
optionExplain: Right: a component failed, but the system as a whole kept serving.
Failure is about the whole system's service, not a component.
The service continued, so only a fault occurred.
The disk deviated from its spec; hiding the effect does not erase the fault.
questions.explain: Use fault for a part and failure for the service.
questions.rule: Aim to keep a component's fault from becoming a failure of the whole system, for the types of fault you choose to tolerate.

questions.q: True or false: Tolerating every possible kind of fault is not feasible, so it only makes sense to talk about tolerating certain types of fault.
questions.explain: The book calls the term fault-tolerant slightly misleading for this reason: no design survives every possible fault.
questions.rule: Tolerate named types of fault, not all faults.

questions.q: A team tolerates single-server faults. A blackout then takes down the whole datacenter. What does the book's reasoning suggest?
options: The system was never fault-tolerant, so the earlier design had no value
A properly fault-tolerant system would have survived any fault
That fault type was outside what the design tolerated, so the service may fail
Nothing happens, because redundancy automatically covers a blackout of any size
optionExplain: It still protected against the faults it was built for.
The book says tolerating every fault is not feasible.
Right: tolerance covers chosen types of fault, and this type was not covered.
Redundancy covers only what it was designed for.
questions.explain: Change the fault type and the tolerance may not apply.
questions.hint: Which types did the team choose to tolerate?
questions.rule: Aim to keep a component's fault from becoming a failure of the whole system, for the types of fault you choose to tolerate.

questions.q: A payments team proposes buying premium servers to remove all faults instead of building fault tolerance. Why does the book prefer tolerance mechanisms?
options: Premium servers are not allowed under the book's definitions
Fault probability cannot be reduced to zero, so faults must be kept from causing failures
Faults occur only in software, which better servers cannot affect, so tolerance is needed
Tolerance mechanisms never cost more than better hardware
optionExplain: The book sets no such rule.
Right: since faults cannot be eliminated, the aim is to stop them from causing failures.
The book describes hardware faults as well.
The book makes no cost comparison here.
questions.explain: Prevention alone cannot reach zero faults, so tolerance is the main tool.
questions.teaches: It is impossible to reduce the probability of a fault to zero, which is why it is usually best to design mechanisms that prevent faults from causing failures.
questions.rule: Aim to keep a component's fault from becoming a failure of the whole system, for the types of fault you choose to tolerate.

questions.q: True or false: A mature fault-tolerant system should avoid ever triggering faults itself.
questions.explain: In fault-tolerant systems it can make sense to cause faults deliberately so the machinery is tested. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: In a fault-tolerant system, exercise the tolerance with deliberate faults; where a fault cannot be cured afterwards, prevent it instead.

questions.q: Netflix's ____ Monkey is the book's example of deliberately inducing faults.
questions.explain: It randomly kills individual processes without warning to exercise fault tolerance.

questions.q: A team's failover to a standby database has not run in two years. Which action fits the book's idea?
options: Leave failover alone, since any change to it could only cause new faults
Remove failover and rely on a second power supply
Randomly kill processes without warning so failover is exercised often
Test it once before launch and treat it as proven
optionExplain: Untested failover may fail when needed.
That replaces software tolerance with a hardware measure.
Right: regular deliberate faults keep the machinery tested.
The book wants the machinery exercised continually.
questions.explain: Untested recovery paths cannot be trusted; use them regularly.
questions.rule: In a fault-tolerant system, exercise the tolerance with deliberate faults; where a fault cannot be cured afterwards, prevent it instead.

questions.q: Which fault is better prevented than tolerated, according to the book?
options: An attacker gaining access to sensitive data
A single disk dying in a large storage cluster
A process crashing and being restarted
A virtual machine disappearing without warning
optionExplain: Right: such an event cannot be undone, so no cure exists.
Redundancy can cure this.
Restart and failover can cure this.
A fault-tolerant system can replace the machine.
questions.explain: Prevention wins where no cure exists.
questions.hint: Which of these cannot be reversed?
questions.rule: In a fault-tolerant system, exercise the tolerance with deliberate faults; where a fault cannot be cured afterwards, prevent it instead.

questions.q: True or false: According to the book, tolerating faults is better than preventing them for every kind of fault.
questions.explain: The book says it generally prefers tolerance, but for security, where a leak cannot be undone, prevention is better.
questions.rule: Tolerance is the general preference, not a law.

questions.q: A system is not designed to tolerate any faults. What would randomly killing its processes most likely cause?
options: More confidence that faults will be handled
A better test of its error handling, with no harm
No effect, because killed processes restart on their own
Failures, because nothing is built to absorb the faults
optionExplain: That benefit appears only when tolerance machinery exists to be tested.
Without tolerance, the faults reach users.
Restarting needs designed machinery that this system lacks.
Right: the practice makes sense only in fault-tolerant systems.
questions.explain: The technique depends on the tolerance already being there.
questions.rule: In a fault-tolerant system, exercise the tolerance with deliberate faults; where a fault cannot be cured afterwards, prevent it instead.

questions.q: A team's error-handling code has not run in production. Which fact from the book makes that risky?
options: Error handling is slower than normal code, so it times out
Many critical bugs are actually due to poor error handling
Error handling is written by a different team in most companies
Poor error handling affects only prototypes, not production
optionExplain: The book does not make this claim.
Right: error-handling code is where many serious bugs hide.
No such claim appears in the book.
The book ties it to critical bugs in real systems.
questions.explain: Untested error paths are where critical bugs are found.
questions.teaches: Many critical bugs are actually due to poor error handling.
questions.rule: In a fault-tolerant system, exercise the tolerance with deliberate faults; where a fault cannot be cured afterwards, prevent it instead.

questions.q: A cluster has 10,000 disks, each reported to fail once in 10 to 50 years. How often should one disk death be expected?
options: About once a month
About once a day on average
About once a year
Almost never, since each disk lasts decades
optionExplain: Too rare; the scale of 10,000 disks makes failures much more frequent.
Right: many disks make even rare failures routine.
That would be true for a few disks, not thousands.
A disk's long lifetime does not carry over to a large fleet.
questions.explain: Scale turns rare events into daily ones. The card next gives the numbers.
questions.rule: Expect routine hardware faults in a large installation and add redundancy to components so a spare takes over.

questions.q: Hard disks are reported as having a mean time to failure of about 10 to 50 ____.
questions.explain: On a cluster of 10,000 disks this means about one disk dying per day.

questions.q: Disks have a mean time to failure of 20 years (about 7,300 days). In a cluster of 3,650 disks, how many deaths per day on average?
options: About 2 per day
About 5 per day
About 0.05 per day
About 0.5 per day
optionExplain: This inverts the ratio; dividing disks by days gives 0.5.
That would need many more disks or a far shorter lifetime.
That is ten times too small.
Right: 3,650 divided by 7,300 gives 0.5 deaths per day.
questions.explain: Expected deaths per day equal disks divided by days of lifetime.
questions.rule: Expect routine hardware faults in a large installation and add redundancy to components so a spare takes over.

questions.q: Which are forms of hardware redundancy named by the book? Select all that apply.
options: Disks set up in a RAID configuration
Servers with dual power supplies
Unit tests for the application code
Batteries and diesel generators for backup power
Rolling upgrades of servers one at a time
optionExplain: Right: disk redundancy is the first example.
Right: a second supply covers a failed one.
Testing is a software and human measure, not hardware redundancy.
Right: they cover a power outage.
A rolling upgrade is a software-level technique.
questions.explain: Redundancy duplicates the physical parts that can fail.
questions.rule: Expect routine hardware faults in a large installation and add redundancy to components so a spare takes over.

questions.q: Disk makers improve their disks from a mean time to failure of 10 years to 50 years. What happens to expected deaths in a fixed-size cluster?
options: They fall to about a fifth of the earlier rate
They fall to a tenth, since 50 is much greater than 10
They stay equal, since redundancy sets the failure rate
They rise five times, since longer life means more use
optionExplain: Right: expected deaths are inversely proportional to the lifetime.
The ratio is 10 to 50, which is a factor of five.
Redundancy hides failures; it does not change the disk failure rate.
A longer mean time to failure means fewer failures.
questions.explain: Five times the lifetime gives one-fifth the failures.
questions.rule: Expect routine hardware faults in a large installation and add redundancy to components so a spare takes over.

questions.q: True or false: With redundant disks, power and CPUs in place, hardware problems can no longer cause failures.
questions.explain: The book says redundancy cannot completely prevent hardware problems from causing failures, though it is well understood and works well in practice.
questions.rule: Redundancy lowers the risk but does not remove it.

questions.q: A small internal wiki runs on one server with nightly backups. By the book's reasoning, why has this long been acceptable?
options: Single servers cannot fail, since their redundant parts take over before any outage can occur at all
Backups prevent hardware faults from occurring
A single machine rarely fails completely, and a quick backup restore keeps downtime tolerable
Wikis are exempt from reliability expectations
optionExplain: Redundancy lowers but does not remove failures.
Backups help recovery; they do not stop faults.
Right: for most applications that downtime was not catastrophic.
The book says even mundane applications are expected to work reliably.
questions.explain: Rare failures plus fast restore made single-machine designs adequate.
questions.teaches: Until recently, hardware redundancy was enough for most applications because total failure of a single machine is fairly rare and a backup restored quickly makes downtime not catastrophic; multi-machine redundancy was needed only where high availability was absolutely essential.
questions.rule: Expect routine hardware faults in a large installation and add redundancy to components so a spare takes over.

questions.q: A cloud provider may make a virtual machine vanish without warning. Which design response seems most fitting?
options: Add a second power supply to each virtual machine
Ask the provider to guarantee each VM
Keep one VM and restore a backup by hand each time it vanishes
Build the software to tolerate losing whole machines
optionExplain: Hardware redundancy inside one VM cannot stop the instance from vanishing.
Cloud platforms of this kind favor flexibility over single-machine reliability.
That leaves downtime on every loss.
Right: that is the response the book describes.
questions.explain: The loss happens outside your hardware's control. The card next explains the shift.
questions.rule: Build the software to survive the loss of whole machines, which also lets you maintain one node at a time.

questions.q: True or false: In some cloud platforms such as AWS it is fairly common for virtual machine instances to become unavailable without warning.
questions.explain: The book gives this as a reason for tolerating whole-machine loss in software.

questions.q: A team reboots its servers one at a time to apply operating system security patches while the service keeps running. What property allows that?
options: The system tolerates machine loss, so one node can be patched at a time
Each server has dual power supplies, so one can be rebooted while it keeps running
The disks are arranged in a RAID configuration
The patches are small enough to need no reboot
optionExplain: Right: this is the rolling upgrade the book describes.
Power supplies cover power faults, not planned reboots.
RAID protects data against a disk failing, not against a machine reboot.
The case says servers are rebooted.
questions.explain: Tolerance of machine loss also gives planned maintenance without downtime.
questions.rule: Build the software to survive the loss of whole machines, which also lets you maintain one node at a time.

questions.q: A team runs a single-server system and must apply a patch that needs a reboot. The reboot requires planned ____ of the whole system.
questions.explain: With one server there is no other node to carry the load, so a reboot stops the service. A system that tolerates machine loss can be patched one node at a time.
questions.rule: Without spare machines, maintenance means downtime.

questions.q: Mira argues: cloud platforms make single machines more reliable, so hardware redundancy is all we need. What is wrong?
options: Cloud platforms have no machines, only software
Hardware redundancy is not possible in the cloud
These platforms favor flexibility and elasticity over single-machine reliability
Redundancy protects only against software errors and so cannot help in the cloud
optionExplain: They run on machines, and virtual machine instances can disappear.
The point is that it is not sufficient, not that it is impossible.
Right: instances can become unavailable without warning.
Redundancy is a hardware measure.
questions.explain: The platform's design goal explains why machine loss is common.
questions.rule: Build the software to survive the loss of whole machines, which also lets you maintain one node at a time.

questions.q: A startup's analytics grows from 5 machines to 500. Which consequence does the book point to?
options: Each machine becomes less reliable as the cluster grows, so single machines must be replaced more often
The rate of hardware faults rises in proportion, which favors tolerating machine loss in software
Hardware faults become correlated across all machines
Redundancy inside each machine is no longer helpful
optionExplain: The rate per machine stays the same; the total rate rises.
Right: more machines means proportionally more hardware faults.
The book describes hardware faults as mostly independent.
It remains helpful, though no longer sufficient alone.
questions.explain: More machines means more faults per day overall.
questions.teaches: As data volumes and computing demands grow, more applications use larger numbers of machines, which proportionally increases the rate of hardware faults.
questions.rule: Build the software to survive the loss of whole machines, which also lets you maintain one node at a time.

questions.q: Which event is most likely to take down many servers at the same moment?
options: A disk wearing out in one server of a large storage cluster in a single rack
A power supply failing in one machine
A software bug triggered by one input that every server receives
Someone unplugging one network cable
optionExplain: That is a single-machine, independent fault.
Also limited to one machine.
Right: the same code on every node fails together.
This affects the machine at the end of that cable.
questions.explain: Shared causes make failures simultaneous. The card next names this class.
questions.rule: Plan for software faults as correlated and systematic, since they can hit every node together unlike random hardware faults.

questions.q: True or false: Hardware faults are typically random and independent: one machine's disk failing does not imply another machine's disk will fail.
questions.explain: There may be weak correlations from a common cause, such as rack temperature, but otherwise large numbers of components rarely fail together.

questions.q: Every instance of a chat server crashes when it receives a message with an unusual date format. Which class of fault is this?
options: A systematic error that is correlated across nodes
A random hardware fault that happens to repeat on each node
A weak correlation due to rack temperature
A human error by an operator
optionExplain: Right: the same bug is in every instance.
Hardware faults are random and independent, not triggered by an input.
Temperature is a hardware common cause and has nothing to do with message formats.
The trigger is a message, not an operator's action.
questions.explain: A bug triggered by input hits all copies together.
questions.rule: Plan for software faults as correlated and systematic, since they can hit every node together unlike random hardware faults.

questions.q: Sort each fault by whether it is typically random and independent or systematic and correlated.

items.t: A disk wears out in one server
A power supply fails in one machine
Someone unplugs a network cable
A bug crashes every instance on one bad input
A runaway process uses up a shared resource
A dependency returns corrupted responses to all callers

questions.explain: Single-component physical faults are independent; shared code or shared dependencies correlate failures.
questions.rule: Plan for software faults as correlated and systematic, since they can hit every node together unlike random hardware faults.

questions.q: Many replicas all receive the same unusual input at once, and the code mishandles it. What follows?
options: Only one replica fails, since faults are independent of one another across nodes
None fail, because replicas hide each other's faults
They fail one at a time over the following days
Many nodes fail together, since the fault is correlated across them
optionExplain: That holds for hardware faults, not for a shared bug.
They run the same code, so none is spared.
A shared trigger acts on all replicas at the same moment.
Right: a shared bug acts on every node.
questions.explain: Correlation turns one bug into many failures.
questions.hint: Do the replicas share the same bug?
questions.rule: Plan for software faults as correlated and systematic, since they can hit every node together unlike random hardware faults.

questions.q: Priya claims hardware faults are completely uncorrelated. What does the book say?
options: They are strongly correlated, since all hardware in a datacenter shares one supplier
There may be weak correlations from a common cause such as rack temperature
They correlate exactly as software bugs do
They are always caused by software
optionExplain: The book calls the correlation weak and cites temperature.
Right: independence is the typical case, not an absolute.
Software faults are described as the strongly correlated kind.
Hardware faults are a separate class from software errors.
questions.explain: Independence is typical for hardware, with weak exceptions.
questions.rule: Plan for software faults as correlated and systematic, since they can hit every node together unlike random hardware faults.

questions.q: Which event in the book shows one systematic bug hitting many applications at the same time?
options: Netflix's Chaos Monkey killing individual processes on purpose, without warning, in production
The leap second of June 30, 2012, which made many applications hang
A disk dying in a storage cluster of 10,000 disks over the course of one day
Amazon's observation that 100 ms more response time cut sales
optionExplain: That is deliberate fault induction, not a shared bug.
Right: it is the book's example of a correlated software fault.
That is a hardware fault.
That is about response time and sales.
questions.explain: A shared kernel bug hit many applications on the same day.
questions.teaches: On June 30, 2012, a leap second caused many applications to hang simultaneously because of a bug in the Linux kernel.
questions.rule: Plan for software faults as correlated and systematic, since they can hit every node together unlike random hardware faults.

questions.q: A bug has lain dormant for two years, then crashes the service on a new kind of input. What is the likeliest underlying cause?
options: A hard disk reached the end of its mean time to failure after many years of service
The code slowly degraded while it was unused
The operators changed the logging format
An assumption about the environment that was usually true stopped holding
optionExplain: A disk failure is random hardware, not a dormant software bug.
Code does not decay on its own.
Nothing links logging to a crash on new input.
Right: that is the book's explanation of dormant bugs.
questions.explain: Dormant bugs rest on an assumption. The card next lists remedies.
questions.rule: Combine many small measures, from checking assumptions to monitoring in production, because no single fix removes systematic faults.

questions.q: Systematic software bugs often lie ____ for a long time until an unusual set of circumstances triggers them.
questions.explain: When triggered, they reveal an assumption about the environment that stopped being true.

questions.q: A runaway process keeps using up shared CPU and memory and drags down other services. Which measure best targets that?
options: Process isolation
Adding more RAID disks
Adding dual power supplies
Making bigger nightly backups
optionExplain: Right: isolating processes limits what one can take from the others.
Disk redundancy does not limit CPU and memory use.
Power supplies guard against power faults.
Backups restore data; they do not stop resource hogging.
questions.explain: Isolation contains a process that misbehaves.
questions.rule: Combine many small measures, from checking assumptions to monitoring in production, because no single fix removes systematic faults.

questions.q: Which are among the small things the book says can help with systematic faults? Select all that apply.
options: Carefully thinking about assumptions and interactions in the system
Thorough testing
Allowing processes to crash and restart
Ignoring errors so processes keep running
Waiting for hardware redundancy to cover them
optionExplain: Right: dormant bugs rest on assumptions.
Right: it is on the list.
Right: crash-and-restart is listed.
Not listed; ignoring errors hides faults.
Hardware redundancy does little against a bug all nodes share.
questions.explain: The list favors understanding, testing, isolation, restart and observation.
questions.rule: Combine many small measures, from checking assumptions to monitoring in production, because no single fix removes systematic faults.

questions.q: A team tests only in staging and has no production monitoring. What does the book's list suggest is missing?
options: Hardware redundancy for the staging environment, in addition to testing
More frequent leap seconds
Measuring, monitoring and analyzing system behavior in production
Fewer building blocks in the architecture
optionExplain: That addresses hardware faults, not this gap.
A leap second is an event, not a practice.
Right: this is the listed practice for catching what testing missed.
The book's list names no such step.
questions.explain: Production behavior is observed only in production.
questions.rule: Combine many small measures, from checking assumptions to monitoring in production, because no single fix removes systematic faults.

questions.q: True or false: Thorough testing alone solves the problem of systematic faults in software.
questions.explain: The book says there is no quick solution; lots of small things help, testing among them.

questions.q: A message queue is meant to deliver as many messages as it receives. Which technique can detect a silent breach of that guarantee?
options: Wait for users to report missing messages
Restart the queue every night and hope that any problem clears itself by morning
Add a second power supply to the queue server
Have the system check itself while running and raise an alert on a mismatch
optionExplain: That finds the problem late, through users.
A restart does not detect or explain a discrepancy.
Power supplies protect against power faults, not lost messages.
Right: a running self-check turns a silent fault into an alert.
questions.explain: Guarantees can be monitored from inside the system.
questions.teaches: If a system is expected to provide a guarantee, such as the number of incoming messages equalling the number of outgoing messages, it can constantly check itself while running and raise an alert if a discrepancy is found.
questions.rule: Combine many small measures, from checking assumptions to monitoring in production, because no single fix removes systematic faults.

questions.q: A study of large internet services looked for the leading cause of outages. What is the likeliest finding?
options: Configuration errors by operators
Hard disk crashes in the servers
Power grid blackouts at the datacenter
Network cable faults between racks
optionExplain: Right: the cited study found this the leading cause.
Hardware faults played a smaller role in that study.
Hardware and environment causes were less common than configuration errors.
Network faults fall under hardware faults, which were not the leading cause.
questions.explain: People, not parts, topped the list. The card next draws the consequence.
questions.rule: Make mistakes hard to make and keep them away from real users, without locking people into workarounds.

questions.q: A study found that configuration errors by ____ were the leading cause of outages.
questions.explain: Hardware faults played a role in a smaller share of outages.

questions.q: A deploy tool lets anyone delete production data with one mistyped command. Which approach from the book applies?
options: Give operators more training in how to use the tool, and leave the tool itself unchanged
Add a second power supply to the database server
Design the admin interface to make the right thing easy and discourage the wrong thing
Move the delete command into the sandbox only
optionExplain: The book treats training as important but beyond its scope; here the tool invites error.
That addresses power faults, not mistyped commands.
Right: good interface design minimizes opportunities for error.
Removing it from production without replacement would remove a needed capability.
questions.explain: Design the tool so mistakes are hard.
questions.rule: Make mistakes hard to make and keep them away from real users, without locking people into workarounds.

questions.q: Sort each measure by the approach to human error it belongs to.

items.t: The admin interface makes the right thing the easy thing
APIs and abstractions discourage the wrong action
A non-production environment uses real data
Experiments cannot affect real users

questions.explain: Interface design makes mistakes less likely; a sandbox keeps the mistakes that do happen away from users.
questions.rule: Make mistakes hard to make and keep them away from real users, without locking people into workarounds.

questions.q: A team locks its admin interface down so tightly that routine tasks become hard. What does the book predict?
options: Mistakes fall to zero since nothing risky can be done with the interface any more
People work around the restrictions, which negates the benefit
Operators stop making configuration errors altogether
The interface becomes a sandbox automatically
optionExplain: People will still need to do their work.
Right: restriction beyond a point drives workarounds.
Workarounds bring the errors back.
Nothing in the text links the two.
questions.explain: Too much restriction defeats itself.
questions.hint: What do people do when a tool blocks their work?
questions.rule: Make mistakes hard to make and keep them away from real users, without locking people into workarounds.

questions.q: Lena reads the study and invests in more hardware redundancy as the best way to cut outages. What is the flaw?
options: Hardware redundancy is impossible to build in the kind of large internet services the study covered
The study found software bugs were the leading cause
Operator configuration errors were the leading cause, so it targets the smaller share
Redundancy increases the number of human errors
optionExplain: It is common in large installations.
The study named operators' configuration errors.
Right: the investment aims at the less common cause.
The text makes no such claim.
questions.explain: Aim the remedy at the biggest cause.
questions.rule: Make mistakes hard to make and keep them away from real users, without locking people into workarounds.

questions.q: In the cited study, hardware faults played a role in 10 to 25 percent of outages. Of 200 outages, about how many involved hardware?
options: About 20 to 50
About 100 to 150
About 2 to 5
About 150 to 190
optionExplain: Right: 10 percent of 200 is 20 and 25 percent is 50.
That would be 50 to 75 percent.
That is 1 to 2.5 percent.
That would be most outages.
questions.explain: Hardware was a minority cause in that study.
questions.teaches: In that study, hardware faults (servers or network) played a role in only 10 to 25 percent of outages.
questions.rule: Make mistakes hard to make and keep them away from real users, without locking people into workarounds.

questions.q: A new release contains a bug. Which practice most limits the number of users affected?
options: Releasing to every user at once to learn faster
Adding a second power supply to the servers
Rebooting the servers more often
Rolling out the new code gradually
optionExplain: That exposes all users to the bug.
Power supplies do not limit software bugs.
Reboots do not limit the reach of a bug.
Right: a gradual rollout exposes only a small subset of users.
questions.explain: Spread a release slowly. The card next gives the other practices.
questions.rule: Test at every level, make recovery quick and gradual, and monitor so a mistake is found and fixed early.

questions.q: Match each practice to what it achieves.
pairs: Unexpected bugs affect only a small subset of users
Recovers if the old computation was wrong
Gives early warning and helps diagnosis
questions.explain: Each practice shrinks a different part of the damage.
questions.rule: Test at every level, make recovery quick and gradual, and monitor so a mistake is found and fixed early.

questions.q: A job computed wrong invoice totals for a week. Which provision from the book helps most?
options: A second power supply for the billing server
Tools to recompute the data
A larger number of disks in a RAID configuration
A sandbox where nobody can touch real data
optionExplain: That protects against power faults, not wrong calculations.
Right: recomputation corrects data after a faulty computation.
RAID protects against disk loss, not wrong totals.
A sandbox prevents damage; this damage has happened.
questions.explain: Plan to recompute data when computations prove wrong.
questions.rule: Test at every level, make recovery quick and gradual, and monitor so a mistake is found and fixed early.

questions.q: Which kind of testing does the book call especially valuable for corner cases that rarely arise in normal operation?
options: Manual testing only
Automated testing
Waiting for production to reveal them
Hardware burn-in
optionExplain: Manual tests are part of the mix but are not the one the book singles out for corner cases.
Right: it is widely used, well understood and good at corner cases.
That is the opposite of testing.
The text does not mention it.
questions.explain: Automation covers the rare cases humans skip.
questions.rule: Test at every level, make recovery quick and gradual, and monitor so a mistake is found and fixed early.

questions.q: True or false: Deploying to all users at once, with no quick rollback of configuration, lets a bad change reach everyone and last longer.
questions.explain: Gradual rollout limits who is affected, and fast rollback limits how long. Without both, the damage is wide and slow to undo.
questions.rule: Without limits on scope and time, mistakes cost more.

questions.q: A team writes only unit tests and declares the system thoroughly tested. What does the book's advice say?
options: Unit tests are unnecessary once the team has monitoring that watches the error rates
Only manual tests are thorough
Integration tests should replace unit tests
Thorough testing spans all levels, from unit tests to integration and manual tests
optionExplain: The book lists testing and monitoring as separate practices.
Manual testing is one of several levels.
The book wants all levels.
Right: unit tests alone cover one level.
questions.explain: Cover every level.
questions.rule: Test at every level, make recovery quick and gradual, and monitor so a mistake is found and fixed early.

questions.q: Why does the book borrow the word telemetry from rocketry for monitoring?
options: Once a rocket is airborne, telemetry is essential for tracking events and understanding failures
Rockets and data systems use the same kinds of sensors, and monitoring was first invented for rockets
Telemetry is the term for rolling back configuration
Rocket engineers invented monitoring dashboards
optionExplain: Right: running systems, like rockets, can be understood only from the data they send back.
The book makes no such claim.
Rollback is a different practice.
The text does not say this.
questions.explain: You cannot reach into a running system; you read its signals.
questions.teaches: In other engineering disciplines monitoring is called telemetry; once a rocket has left the ground, telemetry is essential for tracking what is happening and for understanding failures.
questions.rule: Test at every level, make recovery quick and gradual, and monitor so a mistake is found and fixed early.

questions.q: True or false: Reliability matters for ordinary business applications too, not only for safety-critical software such as air traffic control.
questions.explain: More mundane applications are also expected to work reliably. The card next gives the reasons.
questions.rule: Treat reliability as a duty to users in every application, and give it up only knowingly.

questions.q: Outages of ecommerce sites can have huge costs in lost revenue and damage to ____.
questions.explain: Business applications also lose productivity when they have bugs.

questions.q: A photo app stores a parent's only copies of their children's pictures, and its database corrupts. What does the book say about such noncritical applications?
options: Noncritical applications owe their users nothing beyond a refund of any fees that were paid
Corruption is acceptable when the app is free
Even they carry a responsibility to users, who may not know how to restore a backup
Photo apps are safety-critical software
optionExplain: The book argues for a responsibility to users.
The text says no such thing.
Right: the book's own example makes this point.
The book calls such applications noncritical, yet still responsible.
questions.explain: Importance depends on what users stand to lose.
questions.rule: Treat reliability as a duty to users in every application, and give it up only knowingly.

questions.q: Which reasons does the book give for possibly sacrificing reliability? Select all that apply.
options: To reduce development cost for a prototype of an unproven market
To reduce operational cost for a service with a very narrow profit margin
Because users are unlikely to notice small outages
Because monitoring is beyond the team's budget
optionExplain: Right: this is the book's first example.
Right: this is the second example.
The book does not offer this reason.
No such reason appears in the book.
questions.explain: The book gives two cost-based examples and asks for a conscious choice.
questions.rule: Treat reliability as a duty to users in every application, and give it up only knowingly.

questions.q: A prototype that skipped backups becomes a real product storing family photos. How should the team's stance change?
options: Nothing, since prototype choices stay valid
Reliability stops mattering once the product is popular
Backups become the users' own responsibility, because they chose to use the unfinished product
Data loss now hurts real users, so the earlier corner-cutting needs conscious review
optionExplain: The justification was the unproven market, which has now changed.
The book argues the opposite.
The book places responsibility on the builders.
Our reading: the book's advice to be conscious of corner-cutting applies more strongly once real users depend on the data.
questions.explain: A changed situation can remove the reason for a shortcut.
questions.hint: Why was the shortcut acceptable before?
questions.rule: Treat reliability as a duty to users in every application, and give it up only knowingly.

questions.q: A small accounting tool reports wrong figures after a bug. Which cost, beyond lost productivity, does the book mention?
options: Legal risks if figures are reported incorrectly
Higher electricity bills for the servers in the datacenter
The loss of the building lease
Hardware faults rising in the cluster
optionExplain: Right: the book names legal risk for business applications.
The text does not mention this.
No such cost is mentioned.
Wrong figures are not a hardware matter.
questions.explain: Business software errors can carry legal consequences.
questions.teaches: Bugs in business applications cause lost productivity, and legal risks if figures are reported incorrectly.
questions.rule: Treat reliability as a duty to users in every application, and give it up only knowingly.

questions.q: A colleague says our system is scalable. Which follow-up question gets closest to a useful answer?
options: Is it scalable in every possible situation that might ever arise, now or in future?
How many engineers built it?
Scalable under which kind of growth, and with what options for coping?
Does it use the newest database?
optionExplain: No system can be shown to cope with every possible growth.
Team size does not say how the system copes with growth.
Right: the claim means little until the growth is named.
Newness is unrelated to coping with a given growth.
questions.explain: Scalability is always about a particular growth. The card next shows how to ask.
questions.rule: Never judge scalability in one word; name the growth and ask what options exist to cope with it.

questions.q: Scalability is the term for a system's ability to cope with increased ____.
questions.explain: It is not a one-dimensional label that can be attached to a system.
questions.rule: Scalability is relative to a growth in load.

questions.q: A forum grows from 10,000 to 100,000 concurrent users. Which question frames this as a scalability question?
options: Is the forum scalable, yes or no, answered in a single word that we can put on a slide?
If users grow tenfold, what are our options for coping?
Will the forum ever fail?
Who will write the next feature?
optionExplain: A yes-or-no label is what the book calls meaningless.
Right: it names the growth and asks for options.
That is a reliability question.
That is a maintainability question.
questions.explain: State the growth and ask about options.
questions.rule: Never judge scalability in one word; name the growth and ask what options exist to cope with it.

questions.q: True or false: It is meaningless to say that a system does not scale without saying how it is expected to grow.
questions.explain: The book says it is meaningless to say X is scalable or Y does not scale; the discussion must name the growth.

questions.q: A system copes well with ten times more reads but not with ten times more writes. How should its scalability be described?
options: It is scalable, because it handled the reads
It does not scale, because it fails on writes
It scales for one kind of growth and not another, so each growth needs its own answer
Its scalability cannot be known until it actually fails under some growth in production
optionExplain: That ignores the growth in writes.
A single verdict hides the case it handles.
Right: scalability is judged per kind of growth.
Named growth cases can be analyzed beforehand.
questions.explain: Each growth path needs its own answer.
questions.hint: Is scalability one label or many?
questions.rule: Never judge scalability in one word; name the growth and ask what options exist to cope with it.

questions.q: In a capacity meeting, which question asks about the means rather than the target of scaling?
options: How can we add computing resources to handle the additional load?
What is the largest load that we have ever seen on the system in production?
Is the system reliable today?
Which team owns the system?
optionExplain: Right: it asks how resources can be added.
It describes load, not the means of coping.
It concerns reliability.
Ownership says nothing about adding resources.
questions.explain: Scalability talks about both the growth and the resources that meet it.
questions.teaches: Discussing scalability means asking not only what happens if the system grows in a particular way but also how computing resources can be added to handle the additional load.
questions.rule: Never judge scalability in one word; name the growth and ask what options exist to cope with it.

questions.q: Which number best describes the load on a chat service?
options: The number of lines of code in the chat service's source repository
The monthly marketing spend
The average temperature of the datacenter
The number of simultaneously active users in a chat room
optionExplain: Code size is not load.
Spending does not describe the work the system does.
It is environment, not load.
Right: it is one of the book's examples.
questions.explain: Load is the work the system receives. The card next lists more examples.
questions.rule: Pick the few numbers that describe the load your architecture feels, then ask what happens when they grow.

questions.q: Match each system to a load parameter the book lists for it.
questions.explain: The best parameter depends on the architecture.
questions.rule: Pick the few numbers that describe the load your architecture feels, then ask what happens when they grow.

questions.q: A support chat tool slows down when many agents are active in the same room. Which load parameter fits best?
options: The hit rate on a cache
The number of simultaneously active users in a chat room
The ratio of reads to writes in a database
The requests per second arriving at the company's web server
optionExplain: Nothing in the case concerns a cache.
Right: the slowdown follows that count.
The case is about how many people share a room.
A web server count may rise too, but it does not capture the room-size effect.
questions.explain: Choose the parameter that matches what slows the system.
questions.rule: Pick the few numbers that describe the load your architecture feels, then ask what happens when they grow.

questions.q: Which are load parameters the book lists? Select all that apply.
options: Requests per second to a web server
Ratio of reads to writes in a database
Number of engineers on the team
Hit rate on a cache
Number of features shipped last year
optionExplain: Right: it is the first example.
Right: it is listed.
That describes the team, not the load.
Right: it is listed.
That is product progress, not load.
questions.explain: Load parameters count the work arriving at the system.
questions.rule: Pick the few numbers that describe the load your architecture feels, then ask what happens when they grow.

questions.q: The same website changes from mostly reads to mostly writes. Which parameter shows the change?
options: The hit rate on a cache
The ratio of reads to writes
The number of chat rooms
The requests per second to the web server
optionExplain: A cache may be affected, but the ratio is the direct measure.
Right: it captures the shift in the mix of work.
Nothing concerns chat.
Total requests per second could stay the same while the mix changes.
questions.explain: Changing the mix of work changes the right parameter.
questions.hint: What mix changed?
questions.rule: Pick the few numbers that describe the load your architecture feels, then ask what happens when they grow.

questions.q: True or false: There is one best load parameter that works for every system.
questions.explain: The best choice depends on the architecture of the system.

questions.q: A video platform is slowed mainly by a handful of channels with millions of followers, though the typical channel is small. What is the point?
options: Average load is the right description for every system
Small channels should be ignored in all load planning, since only the big ones matter
Load parameters apply only to databases
The bottleneck may be dominated by a few extreme cases, not by the average case
optionExplain: The book says the average may or may not matter.
The book says nothing of the sort.
The book lists parameters for several systems.
Right: sometimes extremes matter more than averages.
questions.explain: Ask whether averages or extremes limit the system.
questions.teaches: Perhaps the average case is what matters for you, or perhaps your bottleneck is dominated by a small number of extreme cases.
questions.rule: Pick the few numbers that describe the load your architecture feels, then ask what happens when they grow.

questions.q: A service gets 300,000 reads per second but only 4,600 writes per second. Which split of work is likely to serve it best?
options: More work when writing, so each read is cheap
More work when reading, so each write is cheap
An equal split between reading and writing
More hardware instead of any change of design
optionExplain: Right: with reads so much more common, precomputing pays.
That multiplies the heavier side.
The split should follow the imbalance.
The point is to shift work where it is cheaper.
questions.explain: Put the work on the rarer operation. The card next shows how Twitter did it.
questions.rule: When reads far outnumber writes, do more work at write time so each read is cheap.

questions.q: Twitter's scaling challenge was not primarily tweet volume but ____: each user follows many people and is followed by many.
questions.explain: Fan-out is what multiplies the work of delivering a tweet.

questions.q: A podcast app shows each user the latest episodes from their subscriptions, read far more often than episodes are published. Which design resembles Twitter's approach 2?
options: Build each user's list from scratch from all of their subscriptions every time they open the app
Ask every show's server for its latest episode at every open
Add each new episode to every subscriber's prepared list when it is published
Store nothing and let the user search by show name
optionExplain: That repeats the heavy work on the common operation, as approach 1 does.
This also does the work at read time.
Right: the work moves to publish time and reading is cheap.
That removes the feature rather than serving it.
questions.explain: Precompute for the common read.
questions.rule: When reads far outnumber writes, do more work at write time so each read is cheap.

questions.q: Sort each step by the approach it belongs to.

items.t: Posting a tweet is a single insert into a global collection
Reading the timeline merges tweets from everyone the user follows
Posting a tweet inserts it into every follower's timeline cache
Reading the timeline returns a precomputed result

questions.explain: Approach 1 is cheap to write and costly to read; approach 2 is the reverse.
questions.rule: When reads far outnumber writes, do more work at write time so each read is cheap.

questions.q: What if the number of tweets published rose until it matched the number of timeline reads?
options: Approach 2 would become even better, since there would be more tweets to spread the work across
Approach 1 would stop working entirely
Both approaches would cost exactly the same
Approach 2's advantage would shrink, since its extra write-time work buys a smaller saving
optionExplain: Its case depended on reads outnumbering writes.
Nothing in the text says it would stop working.
The costs would be closer but not equal.
Our reading: the book's case for approach 2 rests on writes being far rarer than reads.
questions.explain: The balance of reads and writes drives the choice.
questions.hint: What made approach 2 pay off?
questions.rule: When reads far outnumber writes, do more work at write time so each read is cheap.

questions.q: A blog post says Twitter switched to approach 2 because posting 12,000 tweets per second was too heavy. What is wrong?
options: The first version struggled with timeline reads; 12,000 writes per second is fairly easy
Twitter never switched approaches
The switch was made because of users' complaints about the privacy of their timelines in the cache
Twitter kept both approaches unchanged
optionExplain: Right: reading was the problem, not posting.
The book says it did switch.
The book gives a load reason.
The company moved to approach 2 first and later to a hybrid.
questions.explain: Check which operation was the bottleneck.
questions.rule: When reads far outnumber writes, do more work at write time so each read is cheap.

questions.q: A checkout request triggers six requests to other services. In transaction processing, how is this number described?
options: As the throughput of the checkout
As the latency of the checkout
As the fan-out of that request
As the hit rate of the checkout
optionExplain: Throughput counts completed work per second.
Latency is the waiting time.
Right: fan-out counts the requests needed to serve one incoming request.
Hit rate belongs to caches.
questions.explain: The term comes from electronics and was carried over to services.
questions.teaches: Fan-out is a term borrowed from electronic engineering; in transaction processing it describes the number of requests to other services needed to serve one incoming request.
questions.rule: When reads far outnumber writes, do more work at write time so each read is cheap.

questions.q: On average a tweet reaches 75 followers. Why can that average mislead a designer?
options: Averages stay close to every individual value in the distribution
Follower counts vary wildly, so some tweets cause enormous work
Followers do not affect the work done per tweet
A tweet is delivered to exactly one follower
optionExplain: Averages can be far from extremes.
Right: the extremes hide inside the average.
Each follower adds work in approach 2.
Tweets reach many followers.
questions.explain: Extreme cases can dominate. The card next shows how Twitter responded.
questions.rule: Look at the distribution of the load parameter, and treat the extreme cases differently from the typical ones.

questions.q: 4.6k tweets per second, each delivered to about 75 followers, become about ____ thousand writes per second to timeline caches.
questions.explain: Multiply 4.6k by 75 to get about 345k.

questions.q: A podcast app delivers each new episode into every subscriber's inbox when it is published. Most shows have about 800 subscribers; one has 2 million. What is the main risk?
options: The average subscriber count, which is the only figure that matters when planning for load
The total number of shows, regardless of subscribers
The distribution of subscribers per show, since the big show causes a burst of writes
The ratio of reads to writes, which is fixed by definition
optionExplain: The extreme show is the problem.
The count of shows does not capture the burst.
Right: the extreme case sets the load.
That ratio is not what changes with a very large show.
questions.explain: Plan for the tail of the distribution.
questions.rule: Look at the distribution of the load parameter, and treat the extreme cases differently from the typical ones.

questions.q: True or false: In the hybrid approach, a celebrity's tweet is written into every follower's timeline cache at the moment it is posted.
questions.explain: Celebrity tweets are excepted from fan-out: they are fetched separately and merged when the timeline is read.
questions.rule: Celebrities take the read path; everyone else the write path.

questions.q: What if no user had more than a few hundred followers?
options: Plain approach 2 would likely suffice, as fan-out would be uniform
The hybrid would become more necessary, since there are fewer extremes
Approach 1 would become the better choice again
Timeline reads would become impossible
optionExplain: Our reading: the hybrid exists to handle the extreme follower counts.
Its reason would disappear.
Reads would still outnumber writes.
Nothing in the text suggests this.
questions.explain: Remove the extremes and the special case goes away.
questions.hint: Why did the hybrid arise?
questions.rule: Look at the distribution of the load parameter, and treat the extreme cases differently from the typical ones.

questions.q: Why is a single tweet causing over 30 million writes a significant challenge for Twitter?
options: Twitter must store each tweet for a decade
The follower caches can hold only 75 tweets
Celebrities are charged by the number of writes their tweets cause
Twitter tries to deliver tweets to followers within five seconds
optionExplain: The text gives no such rule.
The text gives no such limit.
The text says nothing about charging.
Right: the delivery target makes the burst hard.
questions.explain: A time target turns a large fan-out into a hard problem.
questions.teaches: Twitter tries to deliver tweets to followers within five seconds, which makes a fan-out to over 30 million timelines a significant challenge.
questions.rule: Look at the distribution of the load parameter, and treat the extreme cases differently from the typical ones.

questions.q: A photo site precomputes feeds for followers, but a few accounts have 20 million followers. Applying the Twitter lesson, what should it do?
options: Precompute every account's feed in the same way and add more servers as needed
Exempt those accounts from fan-out and merge their posts at read time
Stop the large accounts from posting more than once a day
Compute all feeds at read time for everyone
optionExplain: The hybrid avoids the burst by treating extremes differently.
Right: the hybrid keeps normal accounts cheap and avoids bursts.
That limits the product instead of fixing the design.
That repeats the approach 1 problem for every user.
questions.explain: Mix the two approaches by account type.
questions.teaches: Twitter's hybrid approach is able to deliver consistently good performance, and the book returns to the example in Chapter 12.
questions.rule: Look at the distribution of the load parameter, and treat the extreme cases differently from the typical ones.

questions.q: A nightly batch job processes records. Which measure is usually most important for it?
options: The time between a client's request and the reply it receives
Throughput, the records processed per second or the job time
The hit rate on a cache
The number of engineers on call
optionExplain: That is response time, the online measure.
Right: batch cares about volume per time.
A cache measure does not describe batch work.
That is staffing, not performance.
questions.explain: Match the measure to the system. The card next gives the pairing.
questions.rule: Measure batch systems by throughput and online systems by response time.

questions.q: Match each system to the performance measure it usually cares about.
pairs: Batch processing system such as Hadoop
questions.explain: Batch asks how much per second; online asks how long a client waits.
questions.rule: Measure batch systems by throughput and online systems by response time.

questions.q: A website team measures how many pages it can render per second in a test. Another team watches how long a visitor waits. Which is the online measure?
options: Pages rendered per second, the response time
Both are response time, since they involve pages
Neither, since online systems have no measure
How long a visitor waits, the response time
optionExplain: That is throughput.
They measure different things.
Online systems care about response time.
Right: the online measure is the client's wait.
questions.explain: Throughput is how much; response time is how long.
questions.rule: Measure batch systems by throughput and online systems by response time.

questions.q: True or false: A batch job's running time is usually less than the dataset size divided by throughput.
questions.explain: In an ideal world the running time equals dataset size divided by throughput; in practice it is often longer.
questions.rule: Real jobs take longer than the ideal.

questions.q: A site's traffic doubles. The team wants response times to stay the same. Which of the book's two questions does it ask?
options: How much do we need to increase resources to keep performance unchanged?
How is performance affected if the resources stay unchanged as load grows?
How reliable is the system under faults?
How many engineers can work on it productively?
optionExplain: Right: this is the second question, with performance fixed.
That is the first question, with resources fixed.
That is a reliability question.
That is a maintainability question.
questions.explain: Fix resources to ask about performance; fix performance to ask about resources.
questions.hint: Which quantity is held fixed here?
questions.rule: Measure batch systems by throughput and online systems by response time.

questions.q: A batch job's ideal running time on a 1 TB dataset is one hour, but it takes two. One worker received far more data than the rest. What explains the gap?
options: Throughput rose, so the job processed more than the dataset
Response time was measured on the client side
Skew, with the job waiting for the slowest task to complete
The dataset size divided by throughput is an underestimate by exactly half
optionExplain: Higher throughput would shorten the job.
Client-side measurement does not change batch job length.
Right: unevenly spread data leaves one task running long.
No fixed ratio exists; the gap comes from skew and waiting.
questions.explain: The slowest task sets the pace.
questions.teaches: A batch job often runs longer than dataset size divided by throughput because of skew, meaning data not spread evenly across workers, and the need to wait for the slowest task.
questions.rule: Measure batch systems by throughput and online systems by response time.

questions.q: Which time does a client actually experience while waiting for a reply?
options: The service time only
The throughput
The hit rate
The response time
optionExplain: That excludes network and queueing delays.
Throughput counts work per second, not a wait.
Hit rate belongs to caches.
Right: it is what the client sees from sending to receiving.
questions.explain: The client sees everything. The card next splits it into parts.
questions.rule: Response time is everything the client waits for; latency is only the wait before handling begins.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning in the book.
pairs: What the client sees, including delays
The actual time to process the request
The duration a request waits to be handled
Waiting behind other requests, part of response time
questions.explain: Response time is the sum of several parts.
questions.rule: Response time is everything the client waits for; latency is only the wait before handling begins.

questions.q: A request waits 20 ms in a queue, takes 50 ms to process and spends 30 ms on the network in total. What is its response time?
options: 100 ms
50 ms
70 ms
80 ms
optionExplain: Right: 20 plus 50 plus 30 gives 100.
That is the service time only.
This leaves out the queueing delay.
This leaves out the network delay.
questions.explain: Add service time, network delays and queueing delays.
questions.rule: Response time is everything the client waits for; latency is only the wait before handling begins.

questions.q: A request waits 15 ms before a worker picks it up, then takes 40 ms to process. In the book's strict sense, what is the 15 ms?
options: Service time
Response time
Latency
Throughput
optionExplain: Service time is the 40 ms of processing.
Response time here would be the whole wait including processing.
Right: the time spent waiting to be handled is latency.
Throughput is a rate, not a duration.
questions.explain: Latency is the waiting before service.
questions.rule: Response time is everything the client waits for; latency is only the wait before handling begins.

questions.q: The same request is sent a thousand times to a lightly loaded service. What should you expect?
options: Exactly the same response time every time
Slightly different response times on each try
A response time that falls steadily as the test goes on
Failures on about one request in ten
optionExplain: Variation exists even without load.
Right: even identical requests vary.
No steady drop is described.
Nothing in the text suggests failures.
questions.explain: Think of response time as a distribution.
questions.rule: Response time is everything the client waits for; latency is only the wait before handling begins.

questions.q: A dashboard labels the time requests spend in a queue as the response time. What is wrong?
options: Queues do not exist in online systems, only in batch processing systems of the Hadoop kind
The queue wait is a throughput figure
Response time also includes service time and network delays; queue wait is latency
Response time excludes the waiting before service
optionExplain: Queueing delays are part of response time.
Throughput is a rate.
Right: the label covers only one part.
Response time includes queueing delays.
questions.explain: Do not equate one part with the whole.
questions.rule: Response time is everything the client waits for; latency is only the wait before handling begins.

questions.q: Two identical requests take 40 ms and 60 ms. Which could explain the gap? Select all that apply.
options: A context switch to a background process
The loss of a network packet and TCP retransmission
A garbage collection pause
The client choosing a different font
A request that was deliberately made larger
optionExplain: Right: it adds random delay.
Right: retransmission adds delay.
Right: pauses delay processing.
Not related to server response time.
The requests were stated to be identical.
questions.explain: Many random causes add variation even to identical requests.
questions.teaches: Even where all requests should take the same time, random extra latency can come from a context switch to a background process, packet loss with TCP retransmission, a garbage collection pause, a page fault forcing a read from disk, or even vibrations in the server rack.
questions.rule: Response time is everything the client waits for; latency is only the wait before handling begins.

questions.q: Of 100 requests, 99 take 100 ms and one takes 10 seconds. Which number best shows how long a typical user waits?
options: The median, 100 ms
The mean, about 199 ms
The maximum, 10 seconds
The total, nearly 20 seconds
optionExplain: Right: half the requests are at or below it, and it is not distorted by the outlier.
The single outlier drags the mean upward; almost nobody waited that long.
It describes one request, not the typical one.
A sum is not a wait.
questions.explain: The mean can mislead. The card next gives percentiles.
questions.rule: Describe response time by percentiles: the median for the typical wait, high percentiles for the outliers.

questions.q: If your median response time is 200 ms, then half your requests return in less than ____ ms.
questions.explain: The median is the halfway point of the sorted response times.

questions.q: A service's 95th percentile response time is 1.5 seconds. Of 2,000 requests, about how many take 1.5 seconds or longer?
options: About 1,900
About 20
About 1,500
About 100
optionExplain: That is the number faster than 1.5 s.
That would be the 99th percentile case.
This mixes up seconds and requests.
Right: 5 percent of 2,000 is 100.
questions.explain: p95 leaves 5 percent of requests at or above the threshold.
questions.rule: Describe response time by percentiles: the median for the typical wait, high percentiles for the outliers.

questions.q: Which measure best shows how bad your outliers are?
options: The median
Higher percentiles such as p99 and p999
The mean
The fastest request in the sample
optionExplain: It describes the typical request.
Right: they show the slow end of the distribution.
It blends outliers into the typical values.
It shows the best case, not the worst.
questions.explain: Look at the tail to see outliers.
questions.rule: Describe response time by percentiles: the median for the typical wait, high percentiles for the outliers.

questions.q: True or false: A service's median response time stays steady while its 99th percentile doubles. Typical requests have therefore become slower.
questions.explain: The change sits in the tail: the slowest one in a hundred requests got slower, while the typical request did not.
questions.rule: The tail can move while the middle stays still.

questions.q: A report states that the mean response time is 200 ms and concludes that typical users wait 200 ms. What is wrong?
options: The mean can never be computed from a list of measured response times at all
The mean does not tell how many users actually experienced that delay
200 ms is too fast to be a real response time
The mean is the same as the 99th percentile
optionExplain: It can be computed; it just misleads here.
Right: it is a poor guide to typical experience.
The text sets no such rule.
These are different things.
questions.explain: Prefer the median for the typical wait.
questions.rule: Describe response time by percentiles: the median for the typical wait, high percentiles for the outliers.

questions.q: A page needs several requests to load. How does the chance that at least one is slower than the median compare with 50%?
options: It is exactly 50 percent
It is much less than 50 percent, since more requests dilute it
It cannot be compared
It is much greater than 50 percent
optionExplain: The median describes a single request.
More requests give more chances for a slow one.
The book states the comparison.
Right: each extra request is another chance to be slow.
questions.explain: Several requests multiply the chance of meeting a slow one.
questions.teaches: The median refers to a single request; if a user makes several requests, over a session or because a page includes several resources, the probability that at least one is slower than the median is much greater than 50 percent.
questions.rule: Describe response time by percentiles: the median for the typical wait, high percentiles for the outliers.

questions.q: A retailer sets internal response-time targets at the 99.9th percentile, though that affects only 1 in 1,000 requests. What is the likeliest reason?
options: The slowest requests often come from the most valuable customers
The slowest requests are the cheapest to fix
Averages cannot be computed for internal services
Slow requests are caused by hardware faults alone, which internal services rarely have
optionExplain: Right: customers with the most data are often those who have bought the most.
The book says very high percentiles are hard and costly to improve.
Averages can be computed; they are just misleading.
Many random events cause them.
questions.explain: A rare request can matter a lot. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Set targets at a high percentile where slow requests hurt valuable users, and stop where the cost outruns the benefit.

questions.q: Amazon observed that a 100 ms increase in response time reduces sales by ____ percent.
questions.explain: Small slowdowns carry measurable costs.
questions.rule: Speed has a price in sales.

questions.q: An SLA says the service is up if the median is under 200 ms and the 99th percentile under 1 s. In one period the median was 150 ms and the p99 was 1.4 s. Is the service considered up?
options: Yes, because the median is under 200 ms
Yes, because the average of the two figures is under 1 s
No, because the 99th percentile is over 1 s
It cannot be told without the 99.9th percentile
optionExplain: The p99 condition also applies.
Percentiles are not averaged.
Right: both conditions must hold, and if the response is too slow it might as well be down.
The stated conditions are enough to decide.
questions.explain: Check every condition in the SLA.
questions.rule: Set targets at a high percentile where slow requests hurt valuable users, and stop where the cost outruns the benefit.

questions.q: Why did Amazon not optimize the 99.99th percentile?
options: The 99.99th percentile cannot be measured
Customers at that percentile are the least valuable customers that the company serves
Hardware faults make it identical to the median
It was too expensive, easily upset by random events, and the benefit was small
optionExplain: The book says it was deemed too expensive, not impossible.
The book says the slowest customers are valuable at p99.9.
No such claim appears.
Right: the book gives diminishing benefits and outside influence as the reasons.
questions.explain: There is a point past which tail work does not pay.
questions.rule: Set targets at a high percentile where slow requests hurt valuable users, and stop where the cost outruns the benefit.

questions.q: A service fails its SLA this month. The SLA lets customers demand a ____.
questions.explain: SLAs set expectations and let customers demand a refund if the targets are not met.

questions.q: True or false: Setting targets only on the median is safe, because the slowest requests come from the least valuable customers.
questions.explain: The book's example runs the other way: the customers with the slowest requests often have the most data and are the most valuable, and tail latencies directly affect experience.
questions.rule: Tails matter because of who is in them.

questions.q: A product manager says a one-second slowdown does not matter to users. Which evidence cited in the book speaks against this?
options: Reports that a 1-second slowdown reduces a customer satisfaction metric by 16%
Amazon's decision to state requirements for internal services at the 99.99th percentile
The fact that the median is also called p50
The ratio of reads to writes at Twitter
optionExplain: Right: the book cites this as an example of the cost of slowness.
The book says Amazon did not optimize that percentile.
That is a naming point.
That is about load.
questions.explain: Slowness has measurable costs.
questions.teaches: Others report that a 1-second slowdown reduces a customer satisfaction metric by 16 percent.
questions.rule: Set targets at a high percentile where slow requests hurt valuable users, and stop where the cost outruns the benefit.

questions.q: A server handles four requests at a time. Four very slow requests arrive, followed by 100 fast ones. What do the fast ones experience?
options: Fast service, since they are fast to process
A fault in the server
Waiting in a queue behind the slow requests
A faster response than usual
optionExplain: Their processing is fast; their wait is not.
Nothing is broken; the server is busy.
Right: they cannot start until a slot frees.
They wait longer, not less.
questions.explain: Queues turn slow requests into slow neighbours. The card next names the effect.
questions.rule: Measure response times at the client, and send test load independently of the responses.

questions.q: A few slow requests holding up later requests is called ____-of-line blocking.
questions.explain: The fast requests behind a slow one wait for it.
questions.rule: A slow request at the front blocks the rest.

questions.q: A server logs 5 ms per request, but customers report waits of several seconds. What is the likeliest explanation?
options: Customers overstate waiting times
The server timer starts after queueing, so it misses the delay clients see
The server logs response time and latency are identical
Throughput is too high for the server logs to record each request accurately
optionExplain: The case points to queueing, not exaggeration.
Right: clients also wait in the queue.
They are not identical.
Throughput does not explain missing queue time.
questions.explain: Measure where the user waits.
questions.rule: Measure response times at the client, and send test load independently of the responses.

questions.q: Which test client gives a realistic picture of queueing?
options: One that waits for each response to arrive before sending the next request
One that sends a single request and stops
One that keeps sending requests independently of the response times
One that sends requests only when the server is idle
optionExplain: That keeps queues shorter than reality.
That tests no load.
Right: real users do not wait for others' responses.
That also hides queueing.
