questions.explain: Load must arrive on its own schedule.
questions.rule: Measure response times at the client, and send test load independently of the responses.

questions.q: A load-test client waits for each response before sending the next. The server slows down. What happens to the measured queues?
options: They stay shorter than in reality, so results look better than they would
They grow longer than in reality, because waiting clients add extra load to the queue
They are measured exactly
They vanish since the clients send nothing
optionExplain: Right: waiting clients automatically slow the load.
The slowed load reduces queues.
The book says this behavior skews the results.
They still send requests, just slower.
questions.explain: A polite test client under-reports queueing.
questions.hint: What happens to the arrival rate when the server slows?
questions.rule: Measure response times at the client, and send test load independently of the responses.

questions.q: True or false: Slow requests are rare, so fast requests are not affected by them, because fast requests bypass the queue.
questions.explain: Fast requests wait in the same queue. With only a small number of things processed in parallel, a few slow requests can hold up the ones behind them.
questions.rule: Rare slow requests can have wide effects.

questions.q: A new four-core server receives a few very slow requests. Why can this affect many fast requests?
options: Slow requests enlarge the number of CPU cores
Fast requests are routed to a different server from the slow ones, so they cannot be affected at all
The cores cannot work on different requests
The server processes only a small number of things in parallel, limited for example by CPU cores
optionExplain: Core counts are fixed.
The case describes one server.
They can; the limit is how many.
Right: the limited parallelism is what makes a few slow requests block others.
questions.explain: Parallelism is limited, so delays chain.
questions.teaches: A server can only process a small number of things in parallel, limited for example by its number of CPU cores.
questions.rule: Measure response times at the client, and send test load independently of the responses.

questions.q: A page makes 20 parallel backend calls, and each is slow 1% of the time. How likely is a slow page?
options: Exactly 1%, as in each call
Much more likely than 1%, since any slow call slows the page
Less than 1%, because parallel calls hide each other's slowness from the page
Impossible to say anything about
optionExplain: The page is slow if any call is slow.
Right: each call is another chance to be slow.
Parallelism does not hide the slowest call.
The direction is clear even without exact numbers.
questions.explain: The slowest call decides. The card next names the effect.
questions.rule: Expect more slow requests as calls multiply, and combine latency data by adding histograms, not averaging percentiles.

questions.q: More backend calls per request make slow end-user requests more likely, an effect called tail latency ____.
questions.explain: A small share of slow calls turns into a larger share of slow requests.

questions.q: Assume each of 10 independent backend calls is slow with probability 1%. About what share of end-user requests that make all 10 calls will include a slow call?
options: About 1 percent
About 10 percent
About 50 percent
About 0.1 percent
optionExplain: That is the chance for a single call.
Right: one minus 0.99 to the tenth power is about 0.096.
That would need many more calls.
The chance goes up, not down, with more calls.
questions.explain: Compute the chance that none is slow, then subtract from one.
questions.rule: Expect more slow requests as calls multiply, and combine latency data by adding histograms, not averaging percentiles.

questions.q: Two servers report 99th percentile response times of 200 ms and 400 ms. How should the service-wide figure be found?
options: Average the two percentiles and report 300 ms as the service-wide 99th percentile figure
Take the median of the two percentiles
Choose whichever server has more requests
Add the underlying histograms together and compute the percentile from the sum
optionExplain: Averaging percentiles is mathematically meaningless.
This is still not a valid aggregation.
That discards data.
Right: that is the right way to aggregate.
questions.explain: Aggregate data, not summaries.
questions.rule: Expect more slow requests as calls multiply, and combine latency data by adding histograms, not averaging percentiles.

questions.q: True or false: Sorting every response time in the rolling window each minute is the only way to compute percentiles for a dashboard.
questions.explain: Sorting works but can be inefficient; approximation algorithms give a good estimate at minimal CPU and memory cost.
questions.rule: Scale makes the naive method expensive.

questions.q: A team averages the p99 figures of eight machines to get a service-wide p99. What is wrong?
options: Averaging percentiles is mathematically meaningless; add the histograms instead
Nothing, since the average of the eight p99 figures is the p99 of the whole service
They should have used p50 for everything
Eight is too few machines for percentiles
optionExplain: Right: the book states this directly.
It is not.
The issue is aggregation, not the chosen percentile.
The number of machines is not the issue.
questions.explain: Percentiles do not average.
questions.rule: Expect more slow requests as calls multiply, and combine latency data by adding histograms, not averaging percentiles.

questions.q: Which are named in the book as algorithms that approximate percentiles cheaply for a dashboard?
options: RAID, Chaos Monkey and TCP
Median, mean and mode
Forward decay, t-digest, HdrHistogram
Fan-out, shared-nothing and elasticity
optionExplain: These are unrelated to percentile estimation.
These are statistics, not approximation algorithms.
Right: these are the three the book names.
These are scaling terms.
questions.explain: Approximations make continuous percentile monitoring affordable.
questions.teaches: Algorithms that calculate a good approximation of percentiles at minimal CPU and memory cost include forward decay, t-digest and HdrHistogram.
questions.rule: Expect more slow requests as calls multiply, and combine latency data by adding histograms, not averaging percentiles.

questions.q: A service's database needs more capacity. Which option keeps the architecture on one machine?
options: Spreading the data across several smaller machines
Adding a second power supply
Averaging the percentiles
Moving to a more powerful machine
optionExplain: That distributes the load, which is scaling out.
That adds redundancy, not capacity.
That is a measurement matter, not a way to add capacity.
Right: that is scaling up.
questions.explain: One bigger machine versus many smaller ones. The card next names both.
questions.rule: Scale up while it is simple and affordable, scale out when it is not, and expect to use a pragmatic mixture.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Moving to a more powerful machine
Distributing load across several smaller machines
questions.explain: Vertical is one big machine; horizontal is many.
questions.rule: Scale up while it is simple and affordable, scale out when it is not, and expect to use a pragmatic mixture.

questions.q: A site's biggest server costs twenty times a mid-range one, and load may double again. What does the book's reasoning favor?
options: A pragmatic mixture, such as several fairly powerful machines
Only the single largest machine available on the market, whatever it costs
Hundreds of the smallest virtual machines
No change, as architectures keep working at any load
optionExplain: Right: the book says this can be simpler and cheaper than many small machines.
High-end machines become very expensive.
The book says a few fairly powerful machines can be simpler and cheaper.
An architecture is unlikely to cope with ten times its load.
questions.explain: Mix the approaches pragmatically.
questions.rule: Scale up while it is simple and affordable, scale out when it is not, and expect to use a pragmatic mixture.

questions.q: A service's load grows tenfold. What does the book say about its current architecture?
options: It will cope, since architectures scale automatically with the load
It will cope if the team adds more power supplies
It is unlikely to cope, so the design should be rethought
Only the user interface needs to change
optionExplain: The book says otherwise.
Power supplies do not raise capacity.
Right: each order of magnitude may require a rethink.
The architecture itself is unlikely to cope.
questions.explain: Growth by orders of magnitude breaks designs.
questions.hint: Look at the first sentence of the approach.
questions.rule: Scale up while it is simple and affordable, scale out when it is not, and expect to use a pragmatic mixture.

questions.q: True or false: Good architectures usually involve a pragmatic mixture of scaling up and scaling out rather than a strict choice of one.
questions.explain: Several fairly powerful machines can be simpler and cheaper than a large number of small virtual machines.

questions.q: A shop has highly unpredictable traffic spikes. Which kind of system helps most, and what does it cost?
options: A manually scaled system, because a human can react instantly to each sudden spike
An elastic system that adds resources itself, though manual scaling is simpler
A single machine, because spikes do not matter
A cache, because caches are elastic
optionExplain: The book says elasticity helps with unpredictable load.
Right: elasticity suits unpredictable load, with simplicity as the trade-off.
Spikes are the reason elasticity exists.
The book defines elastic systems differently.
questions.explain: Choose elasticity for unpredictable load and manual scaling for simplicity.
questions.teaches: Some systems are elastic and add computing resources automatically when they detect a load increase; manually scaled systems, where a human decides, are simpler and may have fewer operational surprises.
questions.rule: Scale up while it is simple and affordable, scale out when it is not, and expect to use a pragmatic mixture.

questions.q: A team spreads a stateless web tier and a stateful database across many machines. Which part adds more complexity, and what was the common wisdom?
options: The stateless web tier; keep it on a single node until cost or availability forces distribution
Both equally, so the order does not matter
The stateful database; keep it on one node until cost or availability forces distribution
Neither, because distribution is free
optionExplain: Stateless services are fairly straightforward to distribute.
The book contrasts the two.
Right: distributing stateful data systems adds a lot of complexity.
The book describes the added complexity.
questions.explain: State is what makes distribution hard.
questions.teaches: Distributing stateless services is fairly straightforward, but moving a stateful data system from a single node to a distributed setup adds much complexity, so the common wisdom was to keep the database on one node until scaling cost or high-availability needs forced distribution.
questions.rule: Scale up while it is simple and affordable, scale out when it is not, and expect to use a pragmatic mixture.

questions.q: Is there a generic architecture that makes any application scale well?
options: No; it depends on which operations are common and which are rare for that application
Yes, if the team follows a well-known recipe that other large companies have published
Yes, but only for databases
Yes, if enough servers are added
optionExplain: Right: scalable architectures are application-specific.
The book says there is no such recipe.
No generic architecture exists even for databases.
More servers do not make a design fit.
questions.explain: Scale is specific. The card next gives the reasons.
questions.rule: Design for the load your application actually has and expects, not for a generic notion of scale.

questions.q: There is no generic, one-size-fits-all scalable architecture, informally known as magic scaling ____.
questions.explain: Each large-scale system is built around its own load parameters.

questions.q: A system handles 2,000 requests per second of 50 kB each. Which other system has the same data throughput?
options: One request per second of 1 MB
100 requests per second of 100 kB
2,000 requests per minute of 500 kB
One request per second of 100 MB
optionExplain: That is 1 MB per second, one hundredth as much.
That is 10 MB per second.
That is about 17 MB per second.
Right: 2,000 times 50 kB is 100 MB per second, as is 1 times 100 MB.
questions.explain: Equal throughput does not mean equal design: the two systems look very different.
questions.rule: Design for the load your application actually has and expects, not for a generic notion of scale.

questions.q: Which could be the scaling problem for an application? Select all that apply.
options: The volume of reads
The response time requirements
The access patterns
The colour of the logo
The office location of the team
optionExplain: Right: the book lists it.
Right: the book lists it.
Right: the book lists it.
Not a load issue.
Not a load issue.
questions.explain: The problem may be one or a mixture of several of these.
questions.rule: Design for the load your application actually has and expects, not for a generic notion of scale.

questions.q: A team builds for ten million users, assuming mostly reads, but real usage turns out to be mostly writes. What does the book predict?
options: The design will adapt automatically as usage turns out to differ from the plan
The scaling effort is at best wasted and at worst counterproductive
The design will be better, since writes are cheaper
Only the monitoring needs to change
optionExplain: Nothing adapts without redesign.
Right: wrong assumptions about common operations undermine the design.
The design was built for reads.
The architecture itself rests on the wrong assumption.
questions.explain: A scaling design is only as good as its assumptions.
questions.hint: Which assumption failed?
questions.rule: Design for the load your application actually has and expects, not for a generic notion of scale.

questions.q: A seed-stage startup spends months building for a hypothetical hundred times its current load. What does the book say?
options: It is correct, since scaling must come first, before any further product features are built
In an early-stage startup, iterating quickly on product features usually matters more
It is wrong only because the servers are expensive
It is fine, provided percentiles are monitored
optionExplain: The book says otherwise.
Right: premature scaling may be wasted.
The reason is priorities, not just cost.
The book's point is about priorities.
questions.explain: Do not scale to load you do not have.
questions.rule: Design for the load your application actually has and expects, not for a generic notion of scale.

questions.q: If each large architecture is application-specific, what can engineers still learn and reuse?
options: A single template that fits every system
Nothing, since every large design is unique and shares no parts at all with any other design
Only the numbers of servers other companies use
The general-purpose building blocks and familiar patterns of scalable architectures
optionExplain: The book says no such template exists.
The designs share building blocks.
Numbers do not transfer.
Right: the book promises to discuss those building blocks and patterns.
questions.explain: Specific designs reuse general parts.
questions.teaches: Scalable architectures, though specific to an application, are nevertheless usually built from general-purpose building blocks arranged in familiar patterns.
questions.rule: Design for the load your application actually has and expects, not for a generic notion of scale.

questions.q: True or false: Most of the cost of software lies in its ongoing maintenance rather than in its initial development.
questions.explain: The majority of the cost lies in ongoing maintenance. The card next lists what that includes.
questions.rule: Design for the long life of the software by keeping it easy to operate, understand and change.

questions.q: Match each principle to what it asks.
pairs: Make it easy for operations teams to keep the system running smoothly
Make it easy for new engineers to understand the system
Make it easy to change the system for new use cases
questions.explain: Operate, understand, change.
questions.rule: Design for the long life of the software by keeping it easy to operate, understand and change.

questions.q: A new hire needs two months to understand a service whose modules depend on one another in tangled ways. Which principle is lacking?
options: Simplicity
Operability
Evolvability
Scalability
optionExplain: Right: understandability for new engineers is the aim of simplicity.
That concerns running the system day to day.
That concerns making changes.
That concerns growth in load.
questions.explain: Hard to understand means not simple.
questions.rule: Design for the long life of the software by keeping it easy to operate, understand and change.

questions.q: On-call engineers cannot see why a service is slow because the system offers no insight into its runtime behavior. Which principle is lacking?
options: Simplicity
Evolvability
Operability
Reliability
optionExplain: The issue is operational visibility, not understandability for new engineers.
No change is being attempted here.
Right: operations teams need visibility to keep systems running smoothly.
The case concerns running the system, not surviving faults.
questions.explain: Match the symptom to the principle.
questions.rule: Design for the long life of the software by keeping it easy to operate, understand and change.

questions.q: True or false: In the book, simplicity as a design principle means having a simple user interface.
questions.explain: The book notes it is not the same as simplicity of the user interface; it is about the system's internals being easy to understand.

questions.q: A team skips maintainability concerns to ship faster. Where does the book say most of the cost will eventually fall?
options: On the initial development of the first version of the system
On the hardware
On marketing
On ongoing maintenance, such as fixing bugs and adapting
optionExplain: The book says most cost is not there.
The book makes no such claim.
The book does not mention it.
Right: that is where the majority of the cost lies.
questions.explain: Skipping maintainability delays the bill rather than cancelling it.
questions.rule: Design for the long life of the software by keeping it easy to operate, understand and change.

questions.q: A colleague says the system lacks modifiability and plasticity. Which of the book's principles are they describing?
options: Evolvability, also known as extensibility, modifiability or plasticity
Operability, which is also known as modifiability and as extensibility in the book
Simplicity, which is also known as plasticity
Reliability, which is also known as extensibility
optionExplain: Right: these are alternative names for it.
Operability is a different principle.
Simplicity is a different principle.
Reliability is not one of the three maintainability principles.
questions.explain: Evolvability has several names.
questions.teaches: Evolvability is also known as extensibility, modifiability or plasticity.
questions.rule: Design for the long life of the software by keeping it easy to operate, understand and change.

questions.section: Operability: Making Life Easy for Operations
questions.q: True or false: Even when routine tasks are automated, humans still have to set up the automation and check that it works.
questions.explain: Automation is created and supervised by people. The card next lists what good operability involves.
questions.rule: Make routine tasks easy and keep humans in control when automation is not enough.

questions.section: Operability: Making Life Easy for Operations
questions.q: Good operability means making ____ tasks easy, so the team can focus on high-value activities.
questions.explain: This lets the operations team spend time on higher-value work.

questions.section: Operability: Making Life Easy for Operations
questions.q: A database lets admins take one machine out for maintenance while the cluster keeps running. Which operability feature is that?
options: Providing visibility into runtime behavior
Providing good documentation
Avoiding dependency on individual machines
Exhibiting predictable behavior
optionExplain: That concerns monitoring.
That concerns written guidance.
Right: machines can be taken down while the system as a whole continues.
That concerns surprises, not machine independence.
questions.explain: No single machine is essential.
questions.rule: Make routine tasks easy and keep humans in control when automation is not enough.

questions.section: Operability: Making Life Easy for Operations
questions.q: Which are operability features named by the book? Select all that apply.
options: Visibility into runtime behavior through good monitoring
Good default behavior with freedom to override
Self-healing with manual control over system state
Hiding internals so operators cannot interfere
Requiring a restart for every configuration change
optionExplain: Right: it is the first feature.
Right: defaults plus control.
Right: both together.
The opposite of visibility.
Not listed; it makes routine tasks harder.
questions.explain: Operability favors visibility, sensible defaults and control.
questions.rule: Make routine tasks easy and keep humans in control when automation is not enough.

questions.section: Operability: Making Life Easy for Operations
questions.q: A system heals itself automatically but gives administrators no way to take control. What does the book say is missing?
options: A guarantee that nothing in the system ever fails
Manual control over the system state when needed
More documentation about the user interface
Less monitoring
optionExplain: The book does not ask for that.
Right: self-healing should come with manual control.
The gap is control, not UI documentation.
Monitoring is itself an operability feature.
questions.explain: Automation needs an override.
questions.rule: Make routine tasks easy and keep humans in control when automation is not enough.

questions.section: Operability: Making Life Easy for Operations
questions.q: A product's docs say its behavior is complicated but usually fine. Which operability property is missing?
options: Self-healing
Dependence on individual machines
An understandable operational model: if I do X, Y will happen
Defaults that are hidden from administrators until something goes wrong
optionExplain: The docs do not concern healing.
That is something to avoid, not to add.
Right: operators need to predict effects.
Defaults are good, hidden ones are not the issue.
questions.explain: Operators need a model they can rely on.
questions.rule: Make routine tasks easy and keep humans in control when automation is not enough.

questions.section: Operability: Making Life Easy for Operations
questions.q: A company wants to cut its operations team because everything is automated. Which responsibility will still need people?
options: Preserving the organization's knowledge about the system as people come and go
Eliminating every hardware fault from all of the machines in the datacenter for good
Deciding how the user interface looks
Writing the first prototype
optionExplain: Right: it is one of the responsibilities the book lists for operations teams.
That is not listed, and faults cannot be eliminated.
Not listed as an operations task.
Not listed as an operations task.
questions.explain: Operations work includes knowledge and planning, not just button pushing.
questions.teaches: Operations teams also track down causes of problems, keep software and platforms up to date, do capacity planning, set up deployment and configuration practices, perform complex maintenance such as moving between platforms, and preserve the organization's knowledge.
questions.rule: Make routine tasks easy and keep humans in control when automation is not enough.

questions.q: Which makes a large codebase harder to change safely?
options: Having a large number of explanatory comments in the code of the application
A large number of users
Faster hardware
Hidden assumptions and unintended interactions that are easy to overlook
optionExplain: Comments are not named as a symptom.
Users do not make code harder to understand.
Hardware speed is unrelated to understandability.
Right: complexity hides risk.
questions.explain: Complexity breeds overlooked consequences. The card next names the cure.
questions.rule: Remove complexity that comes only from the implementation, and hide detail behind good, reusable abstractions.

questions.q: Complexity is ____ if it is not inherent in the problem the software solves but arises only from the implementation.
questions.explain: Moseley and Marks define it this way.

questions.q: A billing system needs five special cases because two modules disagree on date formats. How should this be classified?
options: Inherent complexity, since billing is a complicated domain with a lot of special rules
Accidental complexity, since it comes from the implementation, not the users' problem
Not complexity at all, since the code works
A hardware fault
optionExplain: Date-format disagreement is not part of billing itself.
Right: unifying the formats would remove it.
Working code can still be needlessly complex.
It is a design matter.
questions.explain: Ask whether the problem or the implementation causes it.
questions.rule: Remove complexity that comes only from the implementation, and hide detail behind good, reusable abstractions.

questions.q: Which counts as inherent rather than accidental complexity for a tax product?
options: Two modules using inconsistent names for the same thing in the codebase
Tax rules that differ by country, which the product must support
A hack added to speed up one slow query
Special cases added to work around a bug elsewhere
optionExplain: Inconsistent naming comes from the implementation.
Right: the users' problem includes the rules.
A performance hack is an implementation symptom.
These are implementation workarounds.
questions.explain: Inherent complexity belongs to the problem as users see it.
questions.rule: Remove complexity that comes only from the implementation, and hide detail behind good, reusable abstractions.

questions.q: True or false: Making a system simpler necessarily means reducing its functionality.
questions.explain: The book says simpler can also mean removing accidental complexity while keeping functionality.

questions.q: A team replaces five apps' own storage code with one well-designed shared library. What follows?
options: Each application becomes more complex than before, because it now depends on a shared library
Nothing changes, since the code does the same thing
The library's bugs can no longer affect anyone
Less repeated effort, and improvements to the library benefit every application using it
optionExplain: A good abstraction hides detail.
Reuse brings real gains.
Shared components share both gains and bugs.
Right: this is the benefit the book gives for good abstractions.
questions.explain: Reuse of a good abstraction multiplies improvements.
questions.hint: What happens when the shared part gets better?
questions.rule: Remove complexity that comes only from the implementation, and hide detail behind good, reusable abstractions.

questions.q: What does SQL, as an abstraction, hide from the application programmer?
options: On-disk and in-memory data structures, concurrent requests, and inconsistencies after crashes
The queries that the programmer writes, which the database rewrites before anyone sees them
The existence of any database at all
The hardware faults the datacenter cannot cope with
optionExplain: Right: these are the details the book lists.
Programmers write queries.
A database is the thing SQL addresses.
SQL does not hide such faults.
questions.explain: A good abstraction frees the programmer from lower-level concerns.
questions.teaches: SQL is an abstraction that hides complex on-disk and in-memory data structures, concurrent requests from other clients, and inconsistencies after crashes.
questions.rule: Remove complexity that comes only from the implementation, and hide detail behind good, reusable abstractions.

questions.q: True or false: A system's requirements are likely to be in constant flux over its life.
questions.explain: New facts, new use cases and changing priorities keep arriving. The card next lists what changes them.
questions.rule: Keep a data system simple and well abstracted so that it can be modified as requirements change.

questions.q: The book uses the word ____ for the ease of modifying a data system and adapting it to changing requirements.
questions.explain: It means agility at the level of a larger data system.

questions.q: A new law forces a company to keep customer data in another region. What determines how painful this is?
options: The hit rate of the company's cache when it serves customer data from the new region
The system's mean time to failure
How easily the system can be modified for changing requirements, its evolvability
The number of users in a chat room
optionExplain: The cache hit rate does not decide how easy a change is.
That concerns hardware faults.
Right: regulatory change is one of the listed causes of change.
That is a load measure.
questions.explain: Changing rules test evolvability.
questions.rule: Keep a data system simple and well abstracted so that it can be modified as requirements change.

questions.q: Which pair are technical tools from the Agile community named by the book?
options: RAID configurations and rolling upgrades of servers
Percentiles and SLAs
Fan-out and elasticity
Test-driven development and refactoring
optionExplain: These are hardware and deployment techniques.
These are performance measures.
These are scaling terms.
Right: both are named.
questions.explain: Agile tools for code-level change.
questions.rule: Keep a data system simple and well abstracted so that it can be modified as requirements change.

questions.q: Two systems do the same job: one is tangled and hard to follow, the other simple and well abstracted. Which is usually easier to modify?
options: The simple, well-abstracted one
The tangled one, since it has more code paths
Neither, since modifiability is random
The tangled one, since it was written first
optionExplain: Right: simple and easy-to-understand systems are usually easier to modify.
More paths make change riskier.
It is closely linked to simplicity.
Age does not make a system easier to change.
questions.explain: Simplicity and abstraction serve evolvability.
questions.hint: What does the book link evolvability to?
questions.rule: Keep a data system simple and well abstracted so that it can be modified as requirements change.

questions.q: True or false: The book says Agile techniques such as test-driven development and refactoring mainly address the architecture of a whole multi-service data system.
questions.explain: The book says most discussions of them focus on a small, local scale, such as a few source files in one application.

questions.q: Which change does the book give as an example of system-level agility?
options: Renaming a variable in one source file of a single application, then rerunning its unit tests
Replacing one failed disk
Refactoring Twitter's home timeline assembly from read-time computation to timeline caches
Adding a power supply to a server
optionExplain: That is a local refactoring.
That is a hardware repair.
Right: the book asks how you would refactor Twitter's architecture from approach 1 to approach 2.
That is hardware redundancy.
questions.explain: Evolvability concerns large changes too.
questions.teaches: The book asks how you would refactor Twitter's architecture for assembling home timelines from approach 1 to approach 2, as an example of agility at the level of a data system.
questions.rule: Keep a data system simple and well abstracted so that it can be modified as requirements change.

questions.q: Which of these is a functional requirement of an application?
options: Compliance with the regulations that apply to the application
Allowing data to be stored, retrieved and searched
Compatibility with older systems
Security against abuse
optionExplain: That is a general property, a nonfunctional requirement.
Right: it describes what the application should do.
That is also nonfunctional.
Security is a nonfunctional requirement.
questions.explain: Functional means what it does. The card next contrasts it.
questions.rule: Write down both what the system must do and the general properties it must have.

questions.q: Sort each requirement as functional or nonfunctional, as the chapter's summary does.

items.t: Search data by keyword
Store and retrieve data
Compliance
Compatibility
Security
Scalability

questions.explain: Functional is what it does; nonfunctional is general properties.
questions.rule: Write down both what the system must do and the general properties it must have.

questions.q: A new requirement says the product must pass an audit by regulators. Which category is it?
options: Functional, since it concerns what the application does
Neither, since audits are outside engineering
Nonfunctional, as a compliance requirement
A load parameter
optionExplain: Compliance is a general property.
Compliance is named among the requirements.
Right: compliance is listed as a nonfunctional property.
It does not describe load.
questions.explain: General properties such as compliance are nonfunctional.
questions.rule: Write down both what the system must do and the general properties it must have.

questions.q: Match each kind of fault to how the summary characterizes it.
pairs: Bugs are typically systematic and hard to deal with
People inevitably make mistakes from time to time
questions.explain: Each source of fault behaves differently.
questions.rule: Write down both what the system must do and the general properties it must have.

questions.q: A team writes down only the features its application offers and nothing about security or compatibility. What is missing?
options: The nonfunctional requirements
The functional requirements that were written down
The load parameters of the system
The faults of the system
optionExplain: Right: they are the general properties beyond the features.
The features are the functional ones.
Those describe load, not requirements.
Faults are not requirements.
questions.explain: Lists of requirements need both kinds.
questions.rule: Write down both what the system must do and the general properties it must have.

questions.q: A report says fault-tolerance techniques remove faults from a system. What does the summary say instead?
options: They prevent every possible fault from occurring in the system
They matter only for hardware
They increase the number of failures
They can hide certain types of faults from the end user
optionExplain: Tolerating every fault is not feasible.
The summary covers hardware, software and human faults.
They are meant to reduce failures.
Right: faults still occur but need not reach users.
questions.explain: Tolerance hides faults; it does not delete them.
questions.rule: Write down both what the system must do and the general properties it must have.

questions.q: A shop's scalable system adds machines during a holiday sale. Which concern does the added capacity support?
options: Compliance with regulation
Reliability under high load
Readability of the code
Compatibility with old browsers
optionExplain: Capacity does not address regulation.
Right: in a scalable system you can add capacity to remain reliable under high load.
Capacity does not change readability.
Capacity does not address compatibility.
questions.explain: Scalability serves reliability at peaks.
questions.teaches: In a scalable system you can add processing capacity in order to remain reliable under high load.
questions.rule: Write down both what the system must do and the general properties it must have.

questions.q: Which of these is a general-purpose data model for storing application data?
options: A Java class describing an order in the shop's code
A set of tables in a relational database
The magnetic pattern a disk uses to hold one bit
The byte layout of a database's index file on disk
optionExplain: That is an application-level structure, one layer above the storage model.
Right: tables, JSON documents and graphs are the general-purpose models the chapter compares.
That is a hardware representation, several layers below.
That is how the engine represents the model in bytes, one layer below it.
questions.explain: Application objects sit above the storage model, and bytes and signals sit below it. The card shows the full stack.
questions.rule: Tables, documents and graphs are storage-level data models.

questions.q: Each layer of a data system hides the complexity of the layers ____ it behind a clean data model.
questions.explain: A layer is built from the one under it, and exposes a clean model so the layers above need not know the details.
questions.rule: Layers hide what lies beneath them.

questions.q: A ride-booking team stores each trip as a row in a table. At which layer did they make that choice?
options: The application's own objects and the APIs around them
The engine's way of writing bytes to disk
The hardware's way of encoding bits as signals
The general-purpose model used to store data
optionExplain: The trip objects in code are a layer above; the row layout is a separate decision.
The vendor chose that; the team only chose the model the engine exposes.
Hardware engineers decided that long before the team's design.
Right: choosing tables over documents or a graph is the second layer.
questions.explain: Picking tables, documents or a graph is the second layer from the top: the model used to store and query data.
questions.rule: Tables, documents and graphs are choices at the storage-model layer.

questions.q: True or false: A vendor changes its on-disk byte layout but keeps the same tables and queries. Applications must then rewrite their queries.
questions.explain: The clean model layer hides the change, which is what lets vendor and application teams work apart.
questions.rule: A clean model lets lower layers change without breaking upper ones.

questions.q: A developer says: tables and documents are only storage details, so the data model can be chosen last. What is wrong with this?
options: The model shapes how code is written and how the problem is framed
Storage details have to be fixed before any application code exists
A model cannot be changed once the first row has been stored
Hardware limits decide the model, so there is no real choice left
optionExplain: Right: the author says the data model has a profound effect on both.
Order of work is not the book's point; the point is the effect of the model.
The chapter never claims that; it claims models influence what is easy.
The model is chosen above the hardware layer, and the choice is real.
questions.explain: The book calls data models perhaps the most important part of developing software because they affect both how software is written and how we frame the problem.
questions.rule: The data model affects code and thinking, so choose it early.

questions.q: A payments firm has a public REST API built on an internal service API that sits on a database. What do all three levels share?
options: Each must use the very same data model as the others
Only the lowest level needs to offer a clean model
Each offers a clean model hiding the level below it
Adding extra levels breaks the principle of layering
optionExplain: Layers may differ; each only needs to be expressed in terms of the one below.
Every layer exposes a clean model to the one above it.
Right: stacking APIs on APIs adds layers, but each still hides what is beneath it.
The book says extra levels leave the basic idea unchanged.
questions.explain: The book notes that a complex application may have more intermediary levels, such as APIs built upon APIs, and the basic idea stays the same.
questions.rule: More layers follow the same rule: hide what is below.
questions.teaches: A complex application may add intermediary layers, such as APIs built upon APIs, and each still hides the layer below behind a clean model.

questions.q: True or false: A data model only affects how data is stored on disk, not how application code is written.
questions.explain: The choice reaches into application code and into how the problem is framed. The card shows how.
questions.rule: A data model shapes the code above it.

questions.q: Which effects of a data model does the chapter name? Select all that apply.
options: Some kinds of usage are easy and others unsupported
Some operations are fast and others perform badly
The licence price of the database software
Some data transformations feel natural and others awkward
The programming language the application must use
optionExplain: Right: models differ in what they let you do.
Right: performance depends on the model.
Cost is a real concern elsewhere, but the book does not list it as a model effect.
Right: the fit of a transformation depends on the model.
The model constrains what is easy, not which language you write in.
questions.explain: The chapter lists three effects: what usage is supported, which operations are fast, and which transformations are natural.
questions.rule: Models differ in what is easy, fast and natural.

questions.q: A photo-sharing startup must pick a storage model. According to this chapter's reasoning, what should drive the choice?
options: Which model has the most learning material around it
Which model the company's competitors already chose
How the application will use its data
Which model is oldest, since age shows that it works
optionExplain: Learning effort matters, but fit decides what the software can and cannot do.
Different applications have different needs, so copying does not ensure fit.
Right: models embody assumptions about use, so fit to use is the test.
Age says nothing about whether the model matches this workload.
questions.explain: The book says the model should be appropriate to the application, and each model assumes particular uses.
questions.rule: Match the model to the workload, not to fashion.

questions.q: True or false: A model handles lookups across many links awkwardly. Such lookups will then be awkward or slow, though the rest works.
questions.explain: Awkward or unsupported usage is the price of a model's assumptions, whatever else works well.
questions.rule: A misfit shows up as awkward or slow operations.

questions.q: A reviewer says: this principle tells us which model to pick for any workload. What is the flaw in that reading?
options: It gives a test for fit; the comparison comes later
It says that every workload fits the relational model best
It applies to hardware choices only, not to software ones
It forbids comparing more than one model for a workload
optionExplain: Right (our reading): the rule is a method, and later sections do the comparing.
The chapter makes no such claim; it compares several models.
It is about data models, which are software choices.
Comparing is what the chapter does next.
questions.explain: The principle gives a criterion but not an answer; we need to know each model's strengths, which the chapter goes on to describe.
questions.rule: A criterion is not an answer: compare models on your workload.

questions.q: A lab must match one very long DNA string against a large database of similar, not identical, strings. What does the chapter conclude?
options: Any relational database handles it, because tables can hold strings
A document database handles it, because DNA records are self-contained
A graph database handles it, because DNA strands are linked
None of the described models fits, so specialized software was written
optionExplain: Strings fit in tables, but similarity search is not what these models support.
Self-contained records do not give similarity matching.
The book says none of the databases described can handle this usage.
Right: the book gives genome sequence-similarity search as a usage none of these models supports.
questions.explain: The chapter's closing section lists genome sequence-similarity search as a usage none of the described models supports, which is why specialized software such as GenBank exists.
questions.rule: Some jobs fit none of the general models.
questions.teaches: Genome sequence-similarity searches fit none of the described models, so researchers wrote specialized genome database software such as GenBank.

questions.q: What was the main aim of the relational model when it was proposed in 1970?
options: To make data storage cheaper than tape storage
To hide how data is stored behind a cleaner interface
To let any computer on a network share the same data
To replace the SQL language with a much simpler one
optionExplain: Cost was not the stated aim; the aim was a cleaner interface.
Right: earlier systems made developers think about internal storage.
Networking came later; the model concerns how data is organized and queried.
SQL grew out of the relational model, not the other way around.
questions.explain: The card shows what was being hidden and why it mattered.
questions.rule: The point was a cleaner interface over storage detail.

questions.q: Match each relational term to its SQL name or meaning.
questions.explain: A relation is a table, a tuple is a row, and Codd made the 1970 proposal.
questions.rule: A relation is a table of tuples (rows).

questions.q: Which of these jobs matches the use cases that relational databases originally grew out of?
options: Ranking web pages by how many pages link to them
Matching a long DNA string against similar strings
Storing data from a particle collider at huge scale
Recording seat bookings for an airline
optionExplain: That is a graph-algorithm job from the later graph section.
The chapter says none of the described models handle it.
Collider-scale analysis needs custom solutions, per the chapter.
Right: transaction processing, such as airline reservations, was a founding use case.
questions.explain: The first uses were mundane by today's standards: sales and bank transactions, reservations, stock-keeping, invoicing, payroll and reporting.
questions.rule: Relational databases began in business data processing.

questions.q: True or false: Developers in 1970 would have accepted that a relational system could be implemented efficiently, so adoption was immediate.
questions.explain: Many people doubted that the model could be implemented efficiently, and it took until the mid-1980s for it to become the usual choice.
questions.rule: A good idea is not always trusted at once.

questions.q: A student writes: relational databases won because they were designed in the 2000s for the web. What is the main error?
options: They were designed for the web, but in the 1990s not the 2000s
They date from 1970 and grew from business data processing
Only SQL was made for the web, while the model was older
They were built for tape drives, which the web later replaced
optionExplain: The web was not the design target at all.
Right: the roots are the 1960s and 1970s, and dominance began by the mid-1980s.
SQL followed the model closely and was not made for the web.
Tape speed is mentioned in a different context, about the network model.
questions.explain: The chapter dates the model to Codd in 1970 and ties it to mainframe business processing.
questions.rule: Check the date and the original use before claiming a cause.

questions.q: A warehouse keeps stock records in a fixed layout: item code, bin, quantity, reorder level. Which chapter claim applies?
options: Relational systems suit only data that has no regular structure
Relational systems cannot store stock-keeping data of any kind
Relational systems became the usual tool for regularly structured data
Only a network-model system can query fixed record layouts
optionExplain: The reverse is what the book says.
Stock-keeping is one of the founding use cases.
Right: from the mid-1980s most people storing and querying such data used them.
The network model lost out to the relational one.
questions.explain: The tool of choice for most people who needed to store and query data with some kind of regular structure was the relational database, from the mid-1980s.
questions.rule: Regular structure is where relational systems took hold.
questions.teaches: By the mid-1980s relational systems and SQL had become the tools of choice for people storing and querying data with some kind of regular structure.

questions.q: True or false: Relational databases have only ever been used for business data processing.
questions.explain: They generalized to many other uses. The card shows how far.
questions.rule: Relational systems spread well beyond their first use.

questions.q: In the 1970s and early 1980s the main alternatives to the relational model were the network model and the ____ model.
questions.explain: Those two were the chief alternatives; the relational model came to dominate them.
questions.rule: Network and hierarchical models were the early rivals.

questions.q: In 2005 a startup builds an online discussion forum. Judging by the chapter, which store was a reasonable mainstream choice?
options: A relational database, already used for discussion sites
An XML database, because it was the newest model then
An object database, because forum posts are objects
A hierarchical database, because replies form a tree
optionExplain: Right: the book lists online discussion among the uses relational systems powered.
The book says XML databases had only niche adoption.
Object databases had come and gone by the early 1990s.
The hierarchical model was an old alternative that the relational model displaced.
questions.explain: Much of the web, including publishing, discussion and social networking, still runs on relational databases.
questions.rule: Relational systems already served web workloads.
questions.hint: Which uses does the chapter list for relational systems on the web?

questions.q: A team in 1988 adopts an object database because it matches their code. By the chapter's account, what happened to such databases?
options: They came and went again by the early 1990s
They displaced relational databases by about 1995
They were absorbed into the network model by then
They stayed popular, but only for mainframe sites
optionExplain: Right: object databases appeared in the late 1980s and faded again.
The relational model kept its dominance.
The chapter does not say that; the network model faded on its own.
No such niche is mentioned.
questions.explain: Object databases came and went again in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

questions.q: True or false: Relational databases won because no alternative model had ever been tried against them.
questions.explain: Network and hierarchical models were the main alternatives in the 1970s and early 1980s, and the relational model came to dominate them.
questions.rule: Check whether the claimed absence of rivals is true.

questions.q: A consultant claims that each decade a new data model fully replaces the old one. How does the chapter's history bear on this?
options: Each model replaced the previous one, so relational lasted a few years
Only the hierarchical model ever challenged relational databases
Object and XML databases challenged it and neither replaced it
The history gives no examples of any competing models
optionExplain: The author says its dominance lasted 25 to 30 years and was not ended by those rivals.
Several others did, including object and XML databases.
Right: both appeared as rivals and neither displaced the relational model.
It lists network, hierarchical, object and XML models.
questions.explain: Object databases came and went in the late 1980s and early 1990s, and XML databases, which appeared in the early 2000s, have seen only niche adoption.
questions.rule: Look at the record before accepting a replacement story.
questions.teaches: Object databases came and went in the late 1980s and early 1990s, and XML databases of the early 2000s saw only niche adoption.

questions.q: Where did the term NoSQL come from?
options: A standard written by a database committee in the 1980s
A hashtag for a 2009 meetup on nonrelational databases
The product name of the first nonrelational database
A research paper that defined a new data model
optionExplain: The CODASYL committee standardized a different model; NoSQL has no such standard.
Right: it began as a catchy tag rather than a technical definition.
No single product carries the name; it labels many systems.
The term was never a research definition of a model.
questions.explain: It began as a catchy tag. The card tells more.
questions.rule: A catchy name is not a definition.

questions.q: NoSQL began as a catchy Twitter ____ for a meetup on open source, distributed, nonrelational databases in 2009.
questions.explain: The name was chosen to be catchy, which is why it names no technology.

questions.q: A vendor brochure says: our product is NoSQL. What can you safely conclude about its data model?
options: It stores self-contained documents, like a JSON store
It models data as vertices and edges, like a graph database
It rejects every form of schema and every query language
Nothing specific, because many systems share the label
optionExplain: Some NoSQL systems are document stores, but the label does not require it.
Some are graph databases, but the label does not imply it.
The label says nothing of the kind; several such systems have query languages.
Right: the label is not tied to any particular technology.
questions.explain: The name covers a mix of systems, so you must ask what model the product actually uses.
questions.rule: Ask for the data model, not the label.

questions.q: Which statement about the term NoSQL fits the chapter?
options: It was defined by a standards body as a family of data models
It started as a catchy hashtag and names no particular technology
It means that databases carrying it never support any query language
It names the technology that replaced the network model
optionExplain: No standards body defined it; it began as a hashtag.
Right: the author calls it unfortunate for that reason.
Systems with this label have their own query languages.
The relational model, not NoSQL, displaced the network model.
questions.explain: The term spread because it struck a nerve, not because it pinned down a technology.
questions.rule: The term is a label, not a definition.

questions.q: True or false: NoSQL began as a hashtag and does not refer to any particular technology.
questions.explain: The name was a catchy hashtag for a 2009 meetup, and it later came to label many different systems.
questions.rule: NoSQL is a label, not one technology.

questions.q: A colleague insists NoSQL means databases that reject SQL entirely. Which reading of the name does the chapter report?
options: It was always meant to be read as No Structured Query
It abbreviates New Open Source Query Language
It was coined by Codd to describe relations without SQL
It was later reinterpreted as Not Only SQL
optionExplain: The name began as a hashtag, with no hidden expansion.
The book gives no such expansion.
Codd proposed the relational model in 1970; the term dates from 2009.
Right: the reinterpretation came after the hashtag had spread.
questions.explain: The name has been retroactively reinterpreted as Not Only SQL, which fits the expectation that relational databases will stay in use alongside other stores.
questions.teaches: The hashtag was retroactively reinterpreted as Not Only SQL.

questions.q: Which of these was a driving force behind adopting NoSQL databases?
options: A need for scale beyond what relational systems offered
A ban on joins in most company data policies
Withdrawal of the SQL standard by its committee
A shortage of disk drives for relational servers
optionExplain: Right: scale was one of the four named forces.
No such ban is mentioned; join support differs by product.
SQL was not withdrawn; the forces were needs of the users.
Hardware supply is not among the named forces.
questions.explain: Several forces are possible. The card lists the four the author names.
questions.rule: Each force is a need, not a verdict on relational databases.

questions.q: Which of these were named as driving forces behind NoSQL? Select all that apply.
options: Frustration with the restrictiveness of relational schemas
A wish to encrypt all data by default
A preference for free and open source software
A need for greater scalability than relational systems easily give
A wish to replace SQL with a single global standard
optionExplain: Right: a wish for a more dynamic and expressive model.
Encryption is not one of the four forces.
Right: a preference over commercial database products.
Right: scalability was the first force.
No such wish is listed.
questions.explain: The chapter names scalability, open source preference, specialized queries and schema frustration.
questions.rule: Learn the four forces by name.

questions.q: Match each team's situation to the driving force behind NoSQL it illustrates.
pairs: Writes arrive faster than one relational server can absorb
A startup wants to avoid commercial database licences
Preference for free, open source software
Queries that SQL expresses badly are central to the product
Rigid column definitions keep blocking varied data
questions.explain: Each situation maps to one of the four forces the chapter names.
questions.rule: Tie a motive to one of the four forces.

questions.q: A team's workload is modest: small data and a low write rate. Which force is least likely to justify NoSQL for them?
options: Frustration with restrictive schemas
A preference for free and open source software
The need for scalability beyond relational systems
A need for specialized query operations
optionExplain: That could still apply if they dislike schemas, though data regularity weakens it.
Preference for open source does not depend on workload size.
Right: modest load and regular data give them no scale or schema problem.
That depends on the queries, not the size of the workload.
questions.explain: Scalability pressure comes from very large data or very high write rates, which a modest workload lacks.
questions.rule: Check whether the force is really present.

questions.q: A blog says: given the forces behind NoSQL, nonrelational databases suit every use case better. Which line corrects this?
options: The forces apply only to companies with mainframes
The forces are myths that no real team ever felt
Needs differ, so the best technology may differ too
The forces make every relational database obsolete
optionExplain: Nothing about mainframes is said of NoSQL's forces.
The author presents them as real driving forces.
Right: the author says the best choice for one use case may differ from another.
The author expects relational databases to remain in use.
questions.explain: The forces explain why people adopted these systems, not that one choice wins everywhere.

questions.q: A video platform's write rate has outgrown one relational server. Which force is this, and what does it cover?
options: Scalability: very large datasets or very high write throughput
Schema flexibility, which covers adding fields without a migration
Open source preference, which covers lowering licence costs
Query specialization, which covers operations SQL does not support
optionExplain: Right: greater scalability includes very large datasets or very high write throughput.
That is a different force, about schemas.
That is a licensing motive, not a load problem.
That concerns query features, not write volume.
questions.explain: The scalability force is about either very large datasets or very high write throughput.
questions.rule: Scalability means large data or heavy writes.
questions.teaches: The scalability force means very large datasets or very high write throughput, beyond what relational databases can easily achieve.

questions.q: What does the chapter expect about relational databases in the foreseeable future?
options: They will be replaced entirely by NoSQL systems
They will vanish as object databases return
They will be limited to mainframe batch processing
Used alongside many kinds of nonrelational datastores
optionExplain: The author expects relational databases to remain in use.
Object databases came and went in the 1980s and 1990s.
They already generalized well beyond that.
Right: the author expects coexistence, not replacement.
questions.explain: The next card gives the idea and its name.

questions.q: Using relational databases alongside nonrelational datastores, each for the job it fits, is sometimes called ____ persistence.
questions.explain: Polyglot means speaking many languages; here it means using many kinds of store.
questions.rule: Polyglot persistence mixes stores by need.

questions.q: An online shop keeps orders in a relational database and adds a graph store for recommendations. Which term fits this setup?
options: Schema-on-read
Polyglot persistence
Impedance mismatch
Normalization
optionExplain: That concerns when structure is interpreted, not how many stores are used.
Right: different stores for different needs in one application.
That concerns objects versus tables, not mixing stores.
That concerns removing duplicated data, not using several stores.
questions.explain: Using relational tables for orders and a graph store for recommendations is polyglot persistence.
questions.rule: Mixing stores by need is polyglot persistence.

questions.q: Suppose one data model fit every workload equally well. What would happen to the case for polyglot persistence?
options: It would grow stronger, since every store would then be needed
It would be unchanged, because it concerns hardware
It would apply only to relational databases
It would lose its basis, which is differing requirements
optionExplain: If one model fit everything, extra stores would add little.
It concerns requirements for data models, not hardware.
It is about mixing relational and nonrelational stores.
Right: the case depends on different applications needing different things.
questions.explain: The idea rests on the claim that different applications have different requirements.
questions.rule: Mixed stores exist because requirements differ.

questions.q: True or false: Polyglot persistence means that every service must use a different database.
questions.explain: Our reading: the principle is to choose each store by fit to its need. Two services whose needs match can share one store.

questions.q: A team stores a road network in relational tables and asks why anyone would add a graph store. Which point does the chapter make?
options: Relational tables cannot hold graph data at all
One model can emulate another, but awkwardly
Graph stores can only ever be used on their own
A single store always wins on operating cost
optionExplain: The chapter says graph data can be represented in a relational database.
Right: that is why different systems serve different purposes.
Nothing prevents using them alongside relational stores.
The chapter makes no such claim and favors fit.
questions.explain: The summary says one model can be emulated in terms of another, but the result is often awkward, so we have different systems for different purposes.
questions.rule: Emulation works but is often awkward.
questions.teaches: One data model can be emulated in terms of another, as graph data in a relational database, but the result is often awkward.

questions.q: Why do object-oriented applications on a relational database need a translation layer?
options: SQL can only be called from non-object-oriented languages
Relational databases cannot store strings and numbers
Objects and tables are different models of data
Objects are too large to be sent to a database
optionExplain: SQL is called from many languages, including object-oriented ones.
They store both; the issue is how structure maps.
Right: the two models do not line up one for one.
Size is not the issue; the models differ in shape.
questions.explain: Objects in memory and rows in tables are shaped differently. The card gives the term for that gap.

questions.q: The disconnect between objects in application code and the relational model is sometimes called an impedance ____.
questions.explain: The name borrows from electronics, where mismatched circuits lose efficiency at their connection.
questions.rule: The gap is called an impedance mismatch.

questions.q: A team uses Hibernate to map classes to tables. Which statement about what it does is accurate?
options: It trims translation boilerplate but leaves the differences
It removes the need for a relational schema in the database
It eliminates the impedance mismatch between the models
It moves all translation work into the database engine
optionExplain: Right: the book says ORMs cannot completely hide the differences.
The database still holds tables; the ORM sits in application code.
It reduces boilerplate but cannot completely hide the differences.
ORMs work in the application, not in the engine.
questions.explain: ORMs generate boilerplate, but the two models still differ.
questions.rule: ORMs reduce, not remove, the mismatch.

questions.q: A team drops its ORM and writes the mapping code by hand. What should it expect compared with using the ORM?
options: More boilerplate code, with the same underlying mismatch
No mismatch at all, because no framework hides anything
Faster queries, because tables will match objects exactly
A switch of the database to a document model
optionExplain: Right: the mismatch comes from the models, so it does not go away either way.
The mismatch lies between the models, not in the framework.
Hand-written mapping does not make tables and objects match.
Dropping an ORM does not change the data model of the store.
questions.explain: The ORM only trims boilerplate. Without it the same gap is bridged by hand.

questions.q: True or false: The impedance mismatch is a disconnect between two data models, not a flaw in the syntax of SQL.
questions.explain: The term describes objects in application code versus tables in the database, which are different models.
questions.rule: The mismatch is between models, not syntax.

questions.q: In electronics, joining circuits with mismatched impedances wastes power and can cause signal reflections. Which situation is the closest everyday analogy?
options: Storing the same file twice for safety
Running one program on two machines at once
Two parts with mismatched interfaces joined by an adapter
Compressing a file so that it takes less space
optionExplain: Redundancy is a different concern.
That concerns parallelism, not interface fit.
Right: a clumsy adapter between non-matching interfaces loses efficiency and causes trouble.
Compression is unrelated to interface mismatch.
questions.explain: The footnote explains the borrowed term: mismatched circuits transfer power poorly and can reflect signals.
questions.rule: The term is borrowed from electronics.
questions.teaches: The term comes from electronics: when one circuit feeds another with a mismatched impedance, power transfer suffers and signals can reflect.

questions.q: A user has one first name but any number of jobs. How is the jobs relationship described, from user to jobs?
options: Many-to-one
One-to-many
One-to-one
Many-to-many
optionExplain: That would mean many users point to one job entry.
Right: one user, many positions.
A user can have more than one position, so it is not one-to-one.
That would need jobs shared by many users and users with many jobs, which this case does not require.
questions.explain: One user has many positions. The card shows how a relational schema can hold that.
questions.rule: One user, many items is one-to-many.

questions.q: Match each relational way of storing a profile's jobs to its description.
pairs: Multi-valued data inside one row, queryable
JSON text in a text column
questions.explain: Three options: normalized tables, typed columns that the database can query, and opaque text interpreted by the application.

questions.q: A team stores each customer's phone numbers as a JSON string in a plain text column. What can they typically not do?
options: Fetch all of a customer's phone numbers with the row
Store more than one phone number per customer
Index the customer's identifier column
Use the database to query for values inside that column
optionExplain: They can, since the text arrives with the row.
A JSON string can hold many numbers.
Ordinary columns can still be indexed.
Right: with an opaque text column the database cannot see the structure.
questions.explain: The application interprets the text, so the database cannot query values inside it.
questions.rule: Opaque text cannot be queried inside.

questions.q: A team's database has no JSON or XML datatype. Which of the three options remain open to it?
options: Only a JSON datatype column
Separate tables, or encoded text in a text column
Only a structured type inside one row
No option, since nested data cannot be stored in SQL
optionExplain: That is the option the database lacks.
Right: typed columns need datatype support that this database lacks.
That also needs datatype support.
Tables and text columns still work.
questions.explain: Separate tables and text columns need no special datatype support.
questions.rule: Typed columns depend on the product.

questions.q: True or false: A relational database cannot represent a user with several jobs unless a document store is added.
questions.explain: Relational databases have three routes: separate tables, structured or JSON columns, and encoded text.
questions.rule: Relational systems have more than one way to hold nested data.

questions.q: A team on MySQL wants multi-valued data in one row that it can still query. Which option may be open?
options: A text column holding XML that SQL queries directly
A graph vertex table with one row per edge
A hierarchical record chain with pointers
A JSON datatype column
optionExplain: A plain text column cannot be queried inside.
That is a graph layout, not a way to nest values in one row.
That is the old hierarchical model, not a relational option.
Right: JSON datatypes are supported by several databases, including MySQL.
questions.explain: A JSON datatype is supported by several databases, including IBM DB2, MySQL and PostgreSQL.
questions.rule: Check the product before choosing a typed column.
questions.teaches: A JSON datatype is supported by several databases, including IBM DB2, MySQL and PostgreSQL.

questions.q: A profile is spread over a users table and three subordinate tables. Which is typically needed to display it?
options: Several queries, or a multi-way join
A single query on the users table alone
A full rewrite of the profile into one text column
Nothing, since foreign keys fetch rows automatically
optionExplain: Right: the data must be gathered from every table.
That returns only the users row, not the subordinate rows.
That is a redesign, not a way to fetch the existing rows.
Foreign keys only link rows; the fetching still takes queries or a join.
questions.explain: Data split over tables must be gathered. The card shows a document alternative.
questions.rule: Split data costs several queries or a join.

questions.q: Nesting a user's jobs inside one document gives better ____ than splitting them across several tables.
questions.explain: All the relevant information is in one place, so a single query is sufficient.
questions.rule: One document keeps related data together.

questions.q: Which data is the best candidate for storing as one nested document?
options: A catalogue that thousands of order records each point into
A road network where any junction can link to many others
A recipe with its ingredients and steps, always shown together
A price list that every order must reference and share
optionExplain: Many records referencing one catalogue is a many-to-one pattern.
Heavily linked data does not form a tree.
Right: it is self-contained and loaded as a whole.
Shared data referenced by many records is better kept in one place by ID.
questions.explain: Self-contained data that is mostly loaded together suits a document.
questions.rule: Self-contained, loaded whole: use a document.

questions.q: A profile sits in a users table plus three subordinate tables. How many queries does fetching it take without a join?
options: One, because user_id links all tables
Two, the user and then everything else together
Four, one per table
Three, one for each subordinate table only
optionExplain: The key links rows, but each table still needs its own query.
Each subordinate table needs its own query.
Right: the users table plus the positions, education and contact tables.
The users table needs a query as well.
questions.explain: Without a join, each table is queried by user_id: users plus three more makes four. A single document needs one.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says some developers feel the JSON model reduces the impedance mismatch.
questions.explain: It reports this feeling, while also pointing out problems with JSON as a data encoding.
questions.rule: Reduces is not the same as eliminates.

questions.q: A recipe holds many steps and each step holds many photos. What shape do these one-to-many links form inside a document?
options: A tree, with the recipe at the root
A flat list with no nesting at all
A cycle that returns to the recipe
A grid with the same number of photos per step
optionExplain: Right: one-to-many relationships imply a tree that nested JSON makes explicit.
Nesting steps and photos inside the recipe is a hierarchy, not a flat list.
Nothing in these relationships loops back.
Counts can vary; the link structure is a tree.
questions.explain: The chapter says one-to-many relationships imply a tree structure, and the JSON representation makes it explicit.
questions.teaches: One-to-many relationships imply a tree structure in the data, and nested JSON makes that tree structure explicit.

questions.q: A profile stores a region as an ID instead of the text of its name. What is a likely reason?
options: IDs always take less space than any text
Documents cannot hold text strings
Text strings cannot be searched in a database
The name sits in one place, so updating is easy
optionExplain: Space is not the stated reason; maintenance is.
Documents hold text fine.
Text can be searched; the issue is duplication and consistency.
Right: change it once and every record follows.
questions.explain: The name lives in one entry. The card lists the advantages.
questions.rule: Store the name once, point to it by ID.

questions.q: Which advantages of standardized lists does the chapter name? Select all that apply.
options: Consistent style and spelling across profiles
Automatic encryption of every name
Avoiding ambiguity between cities with the same name
Smaller database backups in every case
Easy updating, since the name is stored in only one place
optionExplain: Right: everyone picks the same entry.
Encryption is not an advantage of lists.
Right: the ID picks out one specific entry.
Backup size is not the stated reason.
Right: one change reaches every profile.
questions.explain: The card names consistent spelling, no ambiguity and easy updating.
questions.rule: Standardized entries give consistency and one place to update.

questions.q: A site lets users pick their country from a drop-down fed by one standard list. What does storing a country ID make easy?
options: Letting users spell the country any way they like
Renaming a country once for every profile
Keeping a different spelling in every profile
Avoiding the need to ever look up the name
optionExplain: A standardized list prevents free spelling.
Right: the name is in one place, so one change updates all profiles.
That is what the ID approach avoids.
The name must still be looked up through the ID.
questions.explain: Because the name lives in one entry, a change to it is made once.

questions.q: A region list records that Seattle is in Washington. A recruiter searches for people in Washington. What happens to a profile whose region is Seattle?
options: It cannot match, because the search sees only the ID number
It matches only if the user typed Washington
It matches every profile in the state at random
It matches, since the list encodes Seattle is in Washington
optionExplain: The search uses the list's data, not just the number.
With a standardized list the profile needs no extra typing.
Matching follows the list's structure, not chance.
Right: structured entries can carry such facts.
questions.explain: A free-text Greater Seattle Area string tells a search nothing about Washington, whereas a list entry can encode that Seattle lies in it.
questions.rule: Structured entries can carry facts a string cannot.

questions.q: True or false: Every field of a profile, even a free-text about-me box, should be stored as an ID.
questions.explain: IDs suit standardized lists that many records share. Where the interface has free-text fields, plain-text strings make sense.
questions.rule: Use IDs for shared values, strings for free text.

questions.q: A travel site is translated into French. How does storing region IDs help it show each region in the viewer's language?
options: Each profile stores the region name in every language
One localized list entry serves every language
The ID itself is printed in the viewer's language
The database translates free text automatically
optionExplain: That duplicates the name across records, which the ID avoids.
Right: localization works on the list rather than on each profile.
The ID has no meaning to humans.
No such automatic translation is described.
questions.explain: When the site is translated, the standardized lists can be localized and the region shown in the viewer's language.
questions.rule: Localize the list, not each record.
questions.teaches: Standardized lists can be localized, so a region or industry can be shown in the viewer's language.

questions.q: A city is renamed. Which storage choice makes the change easiest?
options: The name is copied into each record that mentions the city
The name is stored in each record with a version number
The name sits in one table and records point to it by ID
The name is stored only in the application's source code
optionExplain: Every copy would need editing.
Versions do not remove the many copies.
Right: one edit updates everything.
That hides it from the database and from other applications.
questions.explain: One copy means one edit. The card names the idea.

questions.q: Removing duplicated human-meaningful information is the key idea behind ____ in databases.
questions.explain: Normalization removes redundancy so each fact is stored in one place.

questions.q: A shop copies the delivery service's name into 200,000 order rows, and the service is renamed. What risk does the chapter flag?
options: Some copies get updated while others are missed
The IDs of the orders will change
The orders will become impossible to read
The database will refuse every later write
