optionExplain: Right: duplicated data creates write overhead and inconsistency risk.
IDs do not change when names do; that is the point of IDs.
They stay readable; the risk is inconsistency.
No such refusal follows from duplication.
questions.explain: Every redundant copy must be updated, which costs writes and risks inconsistent results.
questions.rule: More copies, more chances to disagree.

questions.q: A job renames the service in 150,000 of 200,000 order rows, then fails. What does the chapter's reasoning predict?
options: Some rows show the new name and some the old one
All rows show the old name until the next restart
All rows show a new ID assigned to the service
The remaining rows get the new name by themselves
optionExplain: Right: that is the inconsistency risk of duplicated text.
The 150,000 updated rows already show the new name.
Renaming does not change an ID.
Nothing propagates the change to the duplicated copies.
questions.explain: With duplicated copies, a partial update leaves a mix of old and new values.

questions.q: True or false: An ID rarely needs to change because it has no meaning to humans.
questions.explain: Only information meaningful to humans may need changing, so a meaningless ID can stay the same.

questions.q: A reviewer sees the same supplier address repeated in every purchase row. By the author's rule of thumb, what is the schema's status?
options: Normalized, because every row is complete on its own
Normalized, because addresses are text and not numbers
Not normalized, since one value is stored many times
Impossible to judge without learning every normal form
optionExplain: Self-contained rows can still be duplicating values.
Type does not decide normalization.
Right: that is the rule of thumb for spotting a schema that is not normalized.
The author gives a quick rule because the differences between forms matter little in practice.
questions.explain: The footnote gives a rule of thumb: duplicating values that could be stored in just one place means the schema is not normalized.
questions.rule: Duplicated values signal a schema that is not normalized.
questions.teaches: As a rule of thumb, if you duplicate values that could be stored in just one place, the schema is not normalized.

questions.q: Many users share one region entry. Which relationship is that, from users to region?
options: One-to-many
Many-to-one
One-to-one
Many-to-many
optionExplain: That would be one user with many regions.
Right: many users point to one region.
Each region is shared by many users, so it is not one-to-one.
That would also need each user to have many regions.
questions.explain: Many people, one region: many-to-one. The card covers the document model's trouble with this.
questions.rule: Many records pointing at one entry is many-to-one.

questions.q: If a document database lacks joins, the join must be emulated in ____ code by making multiple queries.
questions.explain: The join work moves out of the database and into the program that uses it.
questions.rule: No joins means joining in application code.

questions.q: A document store has no joins. A page needs a user and the name of the user's region. How is that page built?
options: Ask the database for a join that it does not offer
Copy the whole region table into every user document
Drop the region from the page, since documents cannot reference it
Query the user, then the region by ID, and combine in code
optionExplain: The scenario states there is no join.
That duplicates data and goes against normalization.
Documents can hold the ID; the application resolves it.
Right: two queries joined by application code.
questions.explain: Without a database join, the application makes the follow-up query itself.
questions.rule: Emulate the join with a second query.

questions.q: A team's referenced list grows large and changes constantly. How does the cost of emulating the join in application code change?
options: It falls, because larger lists are cheaper to join
It rises, since in-memory lookups stop being practical
It disappears, since documents always contain the lists
It stays flat, whatever the list size
optionExplain: Larger, faster-changing lists make the application's job harder.
Right (our reading): the shortcut depends on small, slow-changing lists.
Documents hold IDs, not the lists.
Emulated joins cost more as lookups grow.
questions.explain: The chapter's cheap case is small, slow-changing lists; a large moving list loses that advantage.
questions.rule: Emulated joins get costly as lookups grow.

questions.q: True or false: Document databases do not need joins for one-to-many trees such as positions inside a profile.
questions.explain: A nested document holds the tree, so joins matter for many-to-one and many-to-many references instead.
questions.rule: Joins matter for references, not for trees.

questions.q: A news app stores articles with a category ID. About 40 categories exist and rarely change. What is the cheapest way to show category names?
options: Run a database join per article on every page view
Store the full category name text in each article forever
Store categories as separate documents fetched per article
Keep the category list in memory and look names up there
optionExplain: The scenario's database has no join, and the lists are small.
That duplicates names and brings back update problems.
That adds a query per article for a tiny list.
Right: small, slow-changing lists make an emulated join cheap.
questions.explain: The lists of regions and industries are small and slow-changing enough that the application can keep them in memory.
questions.rule: Keep small, stable lists in memory.
questions.teaches: Small, slow-changing lists such as regions or industries can be kept in application memory, making the emulated join cheap.

questions.q: A profile stores each employer as a string. Product wants every company to get its own page. What must the string become?
options: A reference to a company entity
A longer string that includes the company description
A number that counts how many users work there
Nothing, because a page can be built from the string
optionExplain: Right: the résumé should link to the company's own record.
That keeps the data duplicated and unlinked.
A count does not link to the company's page.
Different users could spell the same company differently.
questions.explain: A company with its own page is an entity, so profiles must refer to it. The card shows more.

questions.q: Match each feature change to why it needs references.
pairs: Each gets its own page that résumés link to
The author's current name and photo must show
Many profiles share one standardized entry
questions.explain: Each change turns a plain string or copy into a link to a shared record.
questions.rule: New features turn values into references.

questions.q: A recipe app adds comments that show each commenter's current avatar. What does the chapter's reasoning say this calls for?
options: Each comment should copy the avatar image into its own record
The avatar should be removed from comments
Each comment should reference the commenter's profile
The comment should store only the commenter's first name
optionExplain: Copies would go stale when the avatar changes.
That drops the feature rather than designing for it.
Right: then an updated avatar shows everywhere.
That would not carry the current avatar.
questions.explain: As with recommendations, the item must refer to its author's profile.

questions.q: A user changes their photo. If each recommendation stored its own copy of the author's photo, what would the recommended résumé show?
options: The new photo immediately, as all copies share one source
No photo, since copies are deleted on update
The old photo until every copy is updated
A random photo from the author's history
optionExplain: Copies do not share a source.
Nothing deletes the copies.
Right: copies go stale unless all are updated.
Stored copies keep what they had.
questions.explain: A reference keeps the photo current; a copy keeps what it held.

questions.q: True or false: If a first version fits a join-free document model well, the model will keep fitting as features are added.
questions.explain: Data tends to become more interconnected as features are added, so references and joins may appear later.
questions.rule: A good first fit may not last.

questions.q: In a school app, each student document holds that student's grades. Teachers are shared by many students. What should stay inside the document?
options: The grades stay nested, and the teacher is a reference
The teacher's full record is nested in every student
The grades are moved out into a reference, but the teacher stays nested
Nothing can be nested, because teachers are shared
optionExplain: Right: private data nests, shared entities are referenced.
That duplicates the shared teacher record.
That reverses what is private and what is shared.
Grades belong to one student and nest fine.
questions.explain: The chapter says data within each boundary can be grouped into one document, while references to shared entities need joins.
questions.rule: Nest what is private, reference what is shared.
questions.teaches: Even in a many-to-many design, the data within each boundary can still be grouped into one document; only the references between them need joins.

questions.q: Which structure did IBM's IMS use to represent its data?
options: A set of unordered tables joined by foreign keys
A flat file of text lines read in sequence
A graph where any record may link to any other
A tree of records nested within records
optionExplain: That is the relational model, which was proposed as a solution to IMS's limits.
IMS organized records into a tree, not a flat file.
That is closer to the graph model, which came much later.
Right: this was the hierarchical model.
questions.explain: IMS stored a tree of nested records. The card shows what that meant for relationships.
questions.rule: A tree of nested records is the hierarchical model.

questions.q: IMS represented all data as a tree of records nested within other ____.
questions.explain: Each record sat inside a parent record, much like nested JSON.
questions.rule: A tree of nested records is the hierarchical model.

questions.q: Using IMS, which of these relationships was easy to represent?
options: Many students each linked to many courses, without copying
A customer with many orders nested inside the customer record
A product shared by thousands of orders through a join
A record that has several parents in the hierarchy
optionExplain: Many-to-many relationships were difficult in IMS.
Right: a one-to-many relationship nests naturally in a tree.
IMS did not support joins.
In a tree every record has exactly one parent.
questions.explain: One-to-many fits a tree because each child has one parent.

questions.q: An IMS developer needs one employer record shared by thousands of employee records. What choice did the chapter say developers faced?
options: Declare a foreign key and let a join combine them
Add a second parent to each employee record
Wait for the optimizer to pick a better layout
Duplicate the data, or chase references by hand
optionExplain: IMS had no joins.
A record had exactly one parent in the hierarchical model.
No automatic optimizer was available to them.
Right: denormalize or resolve references manually.
questions.explain: Without joins or multiple parents, sharing a record forced a choice between copying and manual references.
questions.rule: No joins means copy or chase references by hand.

questions.q: True or false: IMS did not support joins, which made many-to-many relationships difficult.
questions.explain: Without joins or multiple parents, developers had to duplicate data or resolve references by hand.

questions.q: A manager says hierarchical databases died out in the 1970s. What does the chapter say about IMS?
options: It was withdrawn once the relational model arrived in 1970
It is still in use and maintained today, on IBM mainframes
It now runs only as an open source research project
It was replaced everywhere by CODASYL systems
optionExplain: The book says it is still maintained.
Right: it was first released in 1968 and survives.
The chapter ties it to IBM mainframes.
CODASYL systems faded into obscurity too.
questions.explain: IMS was developed for stock-keeping in the Apollo space program, first commercially released in 1968, and is still in use and maintained today.
questions.teaches: IMS was originally developed for stock-keeping in the Apollo space program, first released commercially in 1968, and is still in use and maintained today.

questions.q: In the hierarchical model each record has exactly one parent. What did the network model change?
options: Records were stored as unordered rows in tables
Records could no longer be linked to each other
A record could have multiple parents
Records were identified only by their text content
optionExplain: That describes the relational model.
Linking grew richer, not weaker.
Right: that generalization allowed many-to-one and many-to-many links.
Records were linked by pointer-like references.
questions.explain: Allowing more than one parent is the key change. The card shows the cost.

questions.q: Match each network-model term to what it means.
pairs: The committee that standardized the network model
A chain of links followed from a root to reach a record
More like pointers than foreign keys
questions.explain: CODASYL standardized it, links acted like pointers, and an access path was the route to a record.

questions.q: In a network database, one region record is linked from every user who lives there. How does a program find all those users?
options: Follow the links along an access path from a root record
Select every row that matches an arbitrary condition
Declare an index and let an optimizer choose a plan
Join the tables on a foreign key at query time
optionExplain: Right: that was the only way to reach records.
That describes the relational model.
Optimizers belong to the relational model.
Network links were pointers, not foreign keys.
questions.explain: Records were reached by following chains of links, called access paths.

questions.q: Several different access paths lead to the same record. What must the programmer do?
options: Keep track of those different paths in their head
Nothing, since the database picks the path automatically
Delete all but one path from the database
Store a copy of the record at the end of each path
optionExplain: Right: the book says programmers had to do this.
Selection was manual, not automatic.
Removing paths would cut off needed ways to reach the record.
The chapter does not describe copying records for this.
questions.explain: In a world of many-to-many relationships, several paths reach one record and the programmer had to track them.

questions.q: True or false: In the network model, the links between records were foreign keys that the database resolved at query time.
questions.explain: They were more like pointers in a programming language, although still stored on disk.
questions.rule: Network links were pointers, not foreign keys.

questions.q: A team compares pointer links with foreign keys. At what moment was the join effectively done in CODASYL versus the relational model?
options: At query time in CODASYL, and at insert time with foreign keys
At insert time in both models
At insert time in CODASYL, and at query time with foreign keys
At query time in both models
optionExplain: This reverses the contrast.
Foreign key joins happen at query time.
Right: that is the footnote's contrast.
In CODASYL the link was effectively made when the record was inserted.
questions.explain: Even with constraints, joins on foreign keys are performed at query time, whereas in CODASYL the join was effectively done at insert time.
questions.rule: When the link is fixed matters.
questions.teaches: Joins on foreign keys are performed at query time, whereas in CODASYL the join was effectively done at insert time.

questions.q: A program can reach data only along fixed paths its author wrote. What is the main risk when requirements change?
options: The database will refuse to store new records
Query code may have to be rewritten for the new paths
The old data will be silently deleted
The hardware will need replacing at once
optionExplain: Storing is not blocked by fixed paths.
Right: code and paths are tied together.
Nothing deletes data when requirements change.
The risk is in the code, not the hardware.
questions.explain: Fixed paths tie code to a layout. The card shows what that cost.
questions.rule: Fixed paths tie code to layout.

questions.q: A CODASYL query moved a ____ through the database, iterating over lists of records and following access paths.
questions.explain: Queries were written as imperative navigation, one record at a time.
questions.rule: CODASYL queries navigated with a cursor.

questions.q: A 1970s team hand-picks access paths to keep tape seeks few. Which pair describes what it gained and what it risked?
options: Flexibility for new queries, and slower runs on weak hardware
Automatic tuning, and a complex optimizer to maintain
Simple code, and wasted tape seeks
Efficiency on weak hardware, and complicated, inflexible code
optionExplain: It was the other way round: efficient but rigid.
No optimizer chose paths for them.
Hand paths were efficient and the code was complicated.
Right: those are the benefit and the cost the chapter names.
questions.explain: Manual selection used the limited hardware well, but made querying and updating code hard to change.

questions.q: A new report needs data that no existing access path reaches. What follows in a CODASYL system?
options: The query runs unchanged using a path the database invents
Paths must change, and handwritten query code be rewritten
The report is built from a join on foreign keys
The database adds an index and the old code is left alone
optionExplain: No automatic path selection existed.
Right: code that relied on the old paths must be updated.
CODASYL had no query-time joins on foreign keys.
Index-driven change without rewrites came with the relational model.
questions.explain: Without a path to the data, you changed the access paths and rewrote the code that used them.

questions.q: True or false: Hand-picked access paths were pointless because they did not run faster than other approaches.
questions.explain: Manual access path selection made the most efficient use of very limited hardware, though at the cost of complicated code.
questions.rule: The paths were efficient but rigid.

questions.q: An intranet lets staff reach a document only by following a fixed chain of links from the home page. Which CODASYL problem does this resemble?
options: Data is duplicated into every page by an optimizer
Pages must be joined at query time with foreign keys
Every page is reachable directly by a unique ID
New needs mean tracking paths and rewriting navigation
optionExplain: No optimizer duplicates data in the analogy.
The analogy is about fixed paths, not foreign keys.
Direct reach is what the intranet lacks.
Right: reaching data only along fixed paths makes change costly.
questions.explain: Even CODASYL committee members admitted that tracking multiple parents was like navigating around an n-dimensional data space.
questions.rule: Fixed navigation paths make change costly.
questions.teaches: Even CODASYL committee members admitted that keeping track of multiple parents was like navigating around an n-dimensional data space.

questions.q: In a relational database, who decides in what order a query touches tables and which indexes it uses?
options: The query optimizer
The developer, who writes each path by hand
The hardware, which picks the fastest disk first
The user, who chooses a path while the query runs
optionExplain: Right: it chooses automatically.
That was the network model's way.
Hardware does not plan queries.
Paths are chosen before the query runs, by the optimizer.
questions.explain: The optimizer plans the query. The card explains what that replaced.
questions.rule: The optimizer chooses the access path.

questions.q: Which things can you do in a relational database without following access paths? Select all that apply.
options: Read all rows that match an arbitrary condition
Walk a chain of links from a root record
Read a particular row by matching on key columns
Hand-write the order in which indexes are used
Read any or all of the rows of a table
optionExplain: Right: a table can be searched by any condition.
That is how the network model worked.
Right: designate columns as a key and match on them.
The optimizer chooses this automatically.
Right: a relation is simply a collection of tuples.
questions.explain: In the relational model data is laid out in the open, and you select rows by condition or key.
questions.rule: Rows are reached by condition or key, not by path.

questions.q: A program needs every order over 500 pounds from a database. In a relational database and in a CODASYL database, what is the difference?
options: Relational: follow pointers. CODASYL: state the condition
Both: state the condition and let an optimizer plan it
Relational: state the condition. CODASYL: follow access paths
Both: iterate along access paths with a cursor
optionExplain: This swaps the two models.
CODASYL had no optimizer choosing paths.
Right: relational queries describe what is wanted.
Relational databases do not require this.
questions.explain: The relational query states the condition; the optimizer decides how to evaluate it.
questions.rule: State the condition, not the route.

questions.q: Suppose a relational database had no query optimizer. Who would have to choose the access paths for each query?
options: The users, who would pick paths while browsing
The tables, which would reorder themselves
The application developer, by hand-coding them
No one, because relational data needs no paths
optionExplain: Users do not plan queries.
Tables do not plan how they are read.
Right: that is what the optimizer saves developers from.
Some strategy must still be chosen.
questions.explain: The access path still exists in a relational system; the big difference is that the optimizer makes the choice.

questions.q: True or false: In the relational model the access path still exists, but the query optimizer chooses it automatically.
questions.explain: Execution choices are effectively the access path, made by the optimizer and not by the application developer.
questions.rule: The path exists; the engine picks it.

questions.q: A DBA removes every foreign key constraint from a schema. By the chapter, is the schema still relational?
options: Yes, since the relational model does not require them
No, because foreign keys define the relational model
No, because tables without constraints become hierarchical
Yes, but only if every join is rewritten as a pointer
optionExplain: Right: constraints may restrict modifications but are optional.
The footnote says constraints are not required.
Tables stay relational without constraints.
Pointers belong to CODASYL, not here.
questions.explain: Foreign key constraints allow you to restrict modifications, but such constraints are not required by the relational model.
questions.rule: Constraints are optional in the relational model.
questions.teaches: Foreign key constraints can restrict modifications, but they are not required by the relational model.

questions.q: A team adds a new index to a relational database. What must they do to existing queries to use it?
options: Rewrite each query to name the new index
Restart every application with new connection settings
Convert the table into a hierarchical structure
Nothing, because the optimizer uses the index when it suits
optionExplain: That was the cost with hand-chosen paths.
No restart is part of the argument.
Indexes do not change the data model.
Right: queries pick it up automatically.
questions.explain: Queries state what is wanted, not how. The card explains the payoff.

questions.q: You only need to build a query ____ once, and then all applications that use the database can benefit from it.
questions.explain: One shared optimizer serves every application on the database.

questions.q: Ten applications use one relational database, and an upgrade ships a better optimizer. What does the chapter's reasoning predict?
options: Only the application that requested the upgrade benefits
All ten can benefit, with no changes to their queries
Each application must rewrite its queries before benefiting
Nothing changes, since optimizers affect only indexes
optionExplain: A shared optimizer helps everyone using the database.
Right: the optimizer is shared by all applications.
Queries state what is wanted, not how.
Optimizers choose among execution strategies as well as indexes.
questions.explain: Because the optimizer is built once into the database, all applications benefit.
questions.rule: A shared engine spreads the benefit.

questions.q: A single fixed query must run in one small program, and no optimizer exists. By the chapter, which approach is easier for that query?
options: Building a general-purpose optimizer first
Redesigning the data as a graph
Waiting for a standard that covers it
Hand-coding its access path
optionExplain: The chapter says this is harder for one query.
Nothing in the argument points to graphs.
No standard is mentioned.
Right: for one query it is easier than writing a general optimizer.
questions.explain: If you do not have a query optimizer, it is easier to hand-code the access paths for a particular query, but the general-purpose solution wins in the long run.
questions.rule: Hand-coding wins small; generality wins long.

questions.q: True or false: For a single query, hand-coding the access path is easier than writing a general-purpose optimizer.
questions.explain: The general-purpose solution wins only in the long run, across many queries and applications.

questions.q: A firm builds one shared search service instead of coding search into each of twelve apps. What cost does the optimizer argument warn about?
options: Each app must still repeat the search logic by hand
The general service is complex and takes years to build
The service can help only the first app that uses it
The apps lose the ability to change how they search
optionExplain: Sharing removes that repetition.
Right: query optimizers consumed many years of research and development.
A shared service helps all its users.
Sharing does not remove flexibility; the cost is building it.
questions.explain: Query optimizers for relational databases are complicated beasts that have consumed many years of research and development effort.
questions.rule: A shared engine costs effort once.
questions.teaches: Query optimizers for relational databases are complicated and have consumed many years of research and development effort.

questions.q: How does a document database usually store positions that belong to one user profile?
options: In a separate table linked by a foreign key
As pointers on disk that form an access path
Nested inside the profile's own record
Spread across several machines, one position each
optionExplain: That is the traditional relational layout.
That describes the network model.
Right: nesting within the parent is the hierarchical idea.
Distribution is a different matter from nesting.
questions.explain: Nesting inside the parent is the old hierarchical idea. The card shows what else documents borrow.

questions.q: Match each term to its place in the comparison.
pairs: How the relational model references another row
How the document model references another document
Stored inside the parent, as in the hierarchical model
questions.explain: Foreign keys and document references both refer to something by identifier, and nesting echoes the hierarchical model.
questions.rule: Nest the children, reference the shared.

questions.q: A team nests each user's addresses in the user document but stores an employer_id for each user's employer. Which design idea does each choice follow?
options: Nesting echoes the hierarchical model, and employer_id acts like a foreign key
Nesting follows CODASYL, and employer_id follows the hierarchical model
Both choices follow the hierarchical model alone
Both choices follow the relational model alone
optionExplain: Right: nested children plus references by identifier.
CODASYL used pointer-like links, not nesting.
Hierarchical data has no references by identifier.
Nested children are not a relational idea.
questions.explain: Nested records echo the hierarchical model; the identifier is resolved like a relational foreign key.

questions.q: True or false: Document databases, to date, have followed the path of CODASYL's pointer-like access paths.
questions.explain: To date, document databases have not followed the path of CODASYL.

questions.q: A talk claims that for many-to-one relationships, document and relational databases differ fundamentally. What is wrong?
options: In both, the related item is referenced by a unique identifier
Document databases cannot represent many-to-one relationships
Relational databases cannot represent many-to-one relationships
Both use CODASYL-style pointer chains for this
optionExplain: Right: foreign key in one, document reference in the other.
They can, using references.
They do so with foreign keys.
Neither does; that was the network model.
questions.explain: Both store an identifier and look the item up when needed.
questions.rule: Both models reference shared items by identifier.

questions.q: A document store keeps a customer_id in each order. When is the customer record fetched?
options: At insert time, by following a stored pointer
At design time, when the schema is declared
At read time, by a join or a follow-up query
Never, because documents hold the whole customer inside
optionExplain: That describes CODASYL, where the join was effectively done at insert.
Schemas do not fetch records.
Right: the identifier is resolved when the data is read.
Here the order holds only an ID.
questions.explain: That identifier is resolved at read time by using a join or follow-up queries.
questions.rule: References are resolved at read time.
questions.teaches: A document reference or foreign key is an identifier that is resolved at read time, by a join or follow-up queries.

questions.q: Which is an argument for the document model rather than the relational model?
options: Stronger support for joins across records
Better performance from keeping related data together
Easier handling of many-to-many relationships
A fixed schema enforced by the database on write
optionExplain: Join support is the relational counter-argument.
Right: locality is a document-model argument.
That is also the relational side.
That is the relational approach.
questions.explain: Keeping related data together is called locality. The card lists the other arguments.

questions.q: Sort each argument by the model it supports.

items.t: Schema flexibility
Locality for whole-document reads
Closer to application data structures
Better support for joins
Better many-to-one relationships
Better many-to-many relationships

questions.explain: Documents bring flexibility, locality and closeness to application structures; relational brings joins and richer relationships.
questions.rule: Match each argument to its model.

questions.q: A site renders each article together with its nested comments in one page load. Which argument applies?
options: Joins: comments must be combined from several tables
Many-to-many support: articles and readers form a web
Enforced schemas: every article needs identical columns
Locality: the whole document is read together
optionExplain: That is how the relational approach would build it.
The scenario is a single tree loaded whole.
That is a relational strength, not a locality argument.
Right: related data kept together serves whole-document reads.
questions.explain: The whole article is loaded together, which is the locality advantage.

questions.q: A product adds many-to-many links between users that queries must follow in several directions. Which side's argument gains weight?
options: The document model's schema flexibility
The relational model's better support for joins and relationships
The document model's locality for whole documents
The document model's closeness to application objects
optionExplain: Flexibility does not help follow links.
Right: this is what the relational counter-argument covers.
Links between users cut across documents.
Closeness to objects is not about links.
questions.explain: Many-to-many relationships are where the relational model counters the document model.

questions.q: True or false: Because the data model comparison favors one side for a given workload, it settles every difference between the two kinds of database.
questions.explain: The chapter looks only at data models; fault tolerance and concurrency are other differences to consider.
questions.rule: A data-model comparison is not a full verdict.

questions.q: A team compared document and relational databases on data model alone and chose one. What else does the chapter say to consider?
options: Only the licence price of each database
Nothing, since data model decides everything
The age of each database's query language
Fault-tolerance properties and handling of concurrency
optionExplain: The chapter names other technical differences.
The chapter says there are many differences.
That is not among the differences named.
Right: these are treated in later chapters.
questions.explain: Many differences matter, including fault-tolerance properties (see Chapter 5) and handling of concurrency (see Chapter 7).
questions.rule: A data model is one factor among several.
questions.teaches: Beyond the data model, the databases differ in fault-tolerance properties (Chapter 5) and in handling of concurrency (Chapter 7).

questions.q: In relational terms, what does shredding a document-like structure mean?
options: Splitting it into multiple tables
Compressing it into one text column
Deleting the nested items that are rarely read
Encrypting each field separately
optionExplain: Right: positions, education and contacts each get a table.
That is a different technique; shredding means splitting.
Nothing is deleted when shredding.
Shredding concerns structure, not security.
questions.explain: Shredding spreads a tree over tables. The card shows when that hurts.
questions.rule: Shredding spreads a tree over tables.

questions.q: Splitting a document-like structure into multiple tables is called ____.
questions.explain: The relational technique of shredding gives positions, education and contact info their own tables.
questions.rule: Shredding splits a tree across tables.

questions.q: Which data suits the document model best?
options: A catalogue where thousands of orders refer to each product
A friendship network where anyone may link to anyone
An invoice with its line items, usually loaded and shown whole
A set of tables joined on three different foreign keys
optionExplain: Many-to-one links across records strain the document model.
Highly interconnected data is awkward in documents.
Right: a tree loaded at once.
Joins across many tables are where relational shines.
questions.explain: Document-like structure is a tree of one-to-many relationships loaded at once.

questions.q: An email thread is stored as a document nested twelve levels deep, and a program must update one reply. What difficulty should it expect?
options: The reply cannot be updated in any document database
The database will automatically add an index for every level
No direct reference to the reply, only a path into the nesting
The thread will be shredded into tables without being asked
optionExplain: Updating nested items is possible, just awkward to address.
Nothing in the chapter suggests so.
Right: you must name a path into the document.
Shredding is a manual relational technique.
questions.explain: As long as documents are not too deeply nested, the lack of direct references is not usually a problem; deep nesting makes it one.

questions.q: True or false: Shredding a resume-like tree is the best way to store it, because it avoids nesting.
questions.explain: For a tree that is loaded whole, shredding can lead to cumbersome schemas and unnecessarily complicated application code.
questions.rule: Do not shred data you load whole.

questions.q: A chat app nests messages in a conversation. A developer refers to the third message of conversation 88. Which older idea does this resemble?
options: An access path in the hierarchical model
A foreign key resolved by a join
A query optimizer choosing among indexes
A graph traversal over labeled edges
optionExplain: Right: reaching a nested item by following a path from the top.
A nested item is not reached through a foreign key.
Nothing is being chosen automatically here.
The reference runs down a tree, not across labeled edges.
questions.explain: Referring to the second item in a list of positions for user 251 is much like an access path in the hierarchical model.
questions.rule: Nested references act like access paths.
questions.teaches: Referring to a nested item by position, such as the second item in the list of positions for user 251, is much like an access path in the hierarchical model.

questions.q: An application's data does not need many-to-many relationships. How much does weak join support matter to it?
options: A lot, because every document store needs joins to run
A lot, because joins are required for any query
Not at all, because joins are impossible in any database
Little, since joins are rarely needed
optionExplain: Joins are not needed for simple trees.
Many queries need no join.
Relational databases do joins routinely.
Right: the problem depends on the relationships present.
questions.explain: Joins matter for relationships between items. The card names the cases.
questions.rule: Joins matter when relationships need them.

questions.q: You can reduce the need for joins by ____, but then application code must keep the copies consistent.
questions.explain: Denormalizing means keeping copies of data, which must be kept consistent by hand.
questions.rule: Denormalized copies must be kept consistent.

questions.q: A document-store application now needs many-to-many relationships. Which two workarounds does the chapter name?
options: Shred every document, or build a CODASYL layer
Denormalize the data, or emulate joins with multiple requests
Drop all references, or store every item twice by design
Convert documents to XML, or add a second parent
optionExplain: Neither is the chapter's workaround for document stores.
Right: each shifts work into the application.
Dropping references is not a workaround for the need to relate items.
Neither addresses the join problem as described.
questions.explain: Denormalizing reduces joins but burdens consistency; emulating joins burdens the application and is slower.
questions.rule: Both workarounds push work into the application.

questions.q: A team replaces a database join with several requests made by its application. Compared with a join in the database, what should it expect?
options: Less code in the application, and faster results
The same speed, since both fetch the same rows
Faster results, since requests run in parallel for free
More code in the application, and usually slower results
optionExplain: Joins done in specialized code inside the database are usually faster.
The extra round trips usually slow it down.
No such advantage is described.
Right: complexity shifts to the application and specialized join code is faster.
questions.explain: Emulated joins move complexity into the application and are usually slower than a join performed inside the database.
questions.rule: Emulated joins cost code and speed.

questions.q: True or false: Poor join support may or may not be a problem, depending on the application.
questions.explain: It matters when an application needs many-to-many relationships and little when it does not.
questions.rule: Fit decides whether weak joins hurt.

questions.q: A metrics service records which sensor reported which value at what time. Would weak join support hurt?
options: Yes, because event data always needs many-to-many links
Probably not, since many-to-many relationships may never be needed
Yes, because every sensor reading must be joined to a table
No, because analytics databases cannot use documents
optionExplain: The chapter says it may never need them.
Right: event-recording analytics is the chapter's example.
Not every record needs a join.
The chapter gives analytics as a document database use.
questions.explain: Many-to-many relationships may never be needed in an analytics application that uses a document database to record which events occurred at which time.
questions.teaches: Many-to-many relationships may never be needed in an analytics application that uses a document database to record which events occurred at which time.

questions.q: Which data model leads to simpler application code in general?
options: The relational model, because SQL is the most widely known
The document model, because JSON is simpler than XML
It depends on the relationships between the data items
The graph model, because it holds the most information
optionExplain: Familiarity is not the chapter's test.
Simplicity of an encoding is not the point.
Right: no model wins in general.
Holding more is not the same as simpler code.
questions.explain: The answer turns on the shape of the data. The card gives the criterion.

questions.q: For highly interconnected data, order the models from most awkward to most natural.
items: Document model
Relational model
Graph model
questions.explain: The chapter calls the document model awkward, the relational model acceptable and graph models the most natural for such data.
questions.rule: Graphs fit highly linked data best.

questions.q: A genealogy app links people to parents, spouses and birthplaces in many directions. Which model does the chapter find most natural for that data?
options: A graph model
A document model with every family nested in one document
A relational model chosen because it is acceptable for all data
An imperative CODASYL-style network of records
optionExplain: Right: highly interconnected data is where graph models fit best.
Many cross-links make nesting awkward.
Acceptable is not the most natural.
The chapter finds graph models natural, not the old pointer network.
questions.explain: For highly interconnected data graph models are the most natural.

questions.q: True or false: An app stores orders with line items and loads each order whole. A document model is likely to suit it.
questions.explain: Document-like data, a tree of one-to-many relationships loaded at once, is a good fit for a document model.

questions.q: A lead says: relational databases produce the simplest application code, since SQL is the best known. What does the chapter say?
options: It cannot be said in general; it depends on the relationships
The claim holds only when data is stored as XML
The claim is correct for every application with joins
The claim is correct, but graphs are always simpler still
optionExplain: Right: the author declines to name a universal winner.
The data format is not the deciding factor.
The chapter denies a universal answer.
The chapter makes neither universal claim.
questions.explain: It is not possible to say in general which data model leads to simpler application code.

questions.q: A team's many-to-many links are few and simple. Which model can the chapter say handles such cases, with graphs preferred as links grow complex?
options: The hierarchical model, which links any record to many parents
The document model, since it avoids joins altogether
The relational model
None, since simple links need a graph database
optionExplain: A record has exactly one parent in that model.
Documents are weak with many-to-many links.
Right: it can handle simple cases of many-to-many relationships.
The relational model handles simple cases.
questions.explain: The relational model can handle simple cases of many-to-many relationships, but as connections within your data become more complex it becomes more natural to model data as a graph.
questions.rule: Simple links: relational. Complex links: graph.
questions.teaches: The relational model can handle simple cases of many-to-many relationships, but as connections get more complex it becomes more natural to model the data as a graph.

questions.q: A document database accepts any JSON you send it. Where does the expected structure of the data usually live?
options: In the database, which rejects documents of the wrong shape
In the application code that reads the data
Nowhere, because documents have no structure of any kind
In the storage hardware that holds the documents
optionExplain: That describes schema-on-write, not most document databases.
Right: the code assumes a structure the database does not enforce.
Reading code still assumes some structure.
Hardware holds bytes, not meaning.
questions.explain: The reading code assumes a shape the database never checks. The card gives the name.
questions.rule: The structure lives where it is checked.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Structure is implicit and interpreted when data is read
Explicit schema that the database enforces on written data
Misleading, since reading code assumes an implicit schema
questions.explain: Schema-on-read and schema-on-write say where structure is applied, and schemaless hides the implicit schema.
questions.rule: Name where the schema is enforced.

questions.q: A relational database rejects an insert that lacks a required column. Which approach is this?
options: Schema-on-read
Schemaless storage with no assumed structure
Shredding of a nested document
Schema-on-write
optionExplain: In schema-on-read nothing rejects data at write time.
Rejecting an insert shows an enforced structure.
Shredding splits documents across tables and is unrelated to rejection.
Right: the database ensures written data conforms to the schema.
questions.explain: Rejecting nonconforming data at write time is the mark of schema-on-write.
questions.rule: Enforcement at write time is schema-on-write.

questions.q: A document store holds two documents, and one lacks a field the reading code expects. When does the problem appear?
options: When the document is written, because the store rejects it
When the code reads the document and finds the field missing
Never, because documents always contain every field
When the store is first installed, before any data exists
optionExplain: Document stores usually do not enforce a schema on write.
Right: structure is only interpreted on read.
Documents can differ; readers get no guarantee.
The mismatch only shows once data is read.
questions.explain: With no enforcement, a missing field is discovered by the reader.
questions.rule: Schema-on-read finds problems at read time.

questions.q: True or false: A document database has no schema of any kind, so application code makes no assumptions about structure.
questions.explain: The code that reads the data usually assumes some structure; the schema is implicit and not enforced by the database.

questions.q: A team stores XML in a column of a relational database. What does the chapter say about validating it?
options: XML columns are always checked against a schema on insert
XML cannot be validated in a relational database at all
Validation is possible only after exporting the XML
Optional schema validation usually comes with the XML support
optionExplain: Validation is optional there, not automatic.
The chapter says validation is usually available.
The validation is part of the database's XML support.
Right: relational XML support usually offers optional validation.
questions.explain: No schema means arbitrary keys can be added, while XML support in relational databases usually comes with optional schema validation.
questions.rule: Enforcement can be optional in relational systems too.
questions.teaches: XML support in relational databases usually comes with optional schema validation, whereas most document databases and JSON support enforce no schema.

questions.q: Which programming concept is schema-on-write most similar to?
options: Static, compile-time type checking
Dynamic, run-time type checking
Garbage collection of unused values
Operator overloading in a library
optionExplain: Right: structure is checked before the data is accepted.
That resembles schema-on-read.
Memory management is a different matter.
That is unrelated to enforcing structure.
questions.explain: Checks before use are static; checks during use are dynamic. The card pairs them.

questions.q: Match each database approach to its programming counterpart.
pairs: Like the debate between static and dynamic typing
questions.explain: Each database approach has a typing counterpart, and the debates match.
questions.rule: Map the schema choice to a typing choice.

questions.q: A team that prefers compile-time checking in its code is choosing a database. By the analogy, which approach will feel familiar?
options: Schema-on-read, where code interprets the structure
Shredding, where documents are split into tables
Schema-on-write, where the database enforces the structure
Polyglot persistence, where several stores are mixed
optionExplain: That matches dynamic checking at the point of use.
Shredding is a layout technique, not a checking style.
Right: static checking before use matches write-time enforcement.
That concerns mixing stores, not checking structure.
questions.explain: Compile-time checking corresponds to schema-on-write.

questions.q: True or false: A team happy to find type errors at run time in its code will find schema-on-read familiar.
questions.explain: Schema-on-read is similar to dynamic type checking, where structure is interpreted when the data is used.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter proves that enforcing schemas in the database is the right approach.
questions.explain: The author calls schema enforcement a contentious topic and says there is no right or wrong answer in general.

questions.q: Two teams argue over which schema approach is correct for their company. What position does the chapter take?
options: Schema-on-write is correct and the other is a mistake
Schema-on-read is correct and the other is a mistake
There is, in general, no right or wrong answer
The choice should be settled by flipping a coin
optionExplain: The author does not take that side.
The author does not take that side either.
Right: the topic is contentious, as with typing.
The choice depends on the application, not on chance.
questions.explain: Enforcement of schema in a database is a contentious topic, and in general there is no right or wrong answer.
questions.rule: Decide by the application, not by doctrine.
questions.teaches: Enforcement of schemas in databases is a contentious topic, and in general there is no right or wrong answer.

questions.q: An app stored one name field and now needs a first name too. How is the change typically handled in a document database?
options: New documents get the new field and read code copes with old ones
A migration rewrites every stored document before any new write
The database refuses the new field until its schema changes
Old documents are deleted and users re-enter their names
optionExplain: Right: no migration step is needed.
That is the relational style of migration.
Document databases usually enforce no schema.
Nothing so drastic is suggested.
questions.explain: Readers adapt to older documents. The card shows the code.
questions.rule: Document stores can evolve on read.

questions.q: Match each approach to how it handles the format change.
pairs: New documents carry the field and read code handles old ones
ALTER TABLE adds the column and UPDATE fills it
Copies the whole table, risking long downtime
questions.explain: Documents adapt on read, relational schemas migrate, and MySQL's table copy is the slow exception.
questions.rule: Know both routes and the MySQL exception.

questions.q: What does firstName return for an old document that has no first_name field?
options: Mary Ann
Lee
undefined
Mary
optionExplain: The split keeps only the first part, index zero.
Index zero is the first word, not the last.
The function returns a value when first_name is absent.
Right: it falls back to the first word of name.
questions.explain: The function returns user.first_name if it exists, else the first word of user.name.
questions.rule: Fall back to the old field on read.

questions.q: A table of 500 million rows needs a new filled column, and the UPDATE would be too slow. What can the team do instead?
options: Drop the old column so every row rewrites faster
Leave the column NULL and fill it in on read, as documents do
Switch the table to schema-on-write, which skips rewriting
Run the UPDATE twice so that it finishes sooner
optionExplain: Dropping data does not speed up the migration.
Right: this avoids rewriting every row.
The table is already schema-on-write.
Repeating it only doubles the work.
questions.explain: Running UPDATE on a large table is likely to be slow on any database because every row is rewritten, but the application can fill the value in at read time.
questions.rule: Defer the fill to read time when rewriting is too costly.

questions.q: True or false: Most relational databases run ALTER TABLE in a few milliseconds.
questions.explain: The reputation for slow schema changes is not entirely deserved; MySQL is the notable exception.
questions.rule: The bad reputation is only partly deserved.

questions.q: A team plans an ALTER TABLE on a huge MySQL table. What risk does the chapter warn about?
options: The table will lose all its existing rows
The change will complete in milliseconds, so nothing is tested
The new column must be filled by application code only
MySQL copies the whole table, risking minutes or hours of downtime
optionExplain: Nothing in the chapter suggests data loss.
That describes most other relational systems.
The risk is the table copy, not the filling.
Right: though tools exist to work around the limitation.
questions.explain: Most relational databases run ALTER TABLE in a few milliseconds, but MySQL copies the entire table, and various tools exist to work around this.
questions.rule: Check how your database runs ALTER TABLE.
questions.teaches: Most relational databases run ALTER TABLE in a few milliseconds, but MySQL copies the entire table, which can mean minutes or hours of downtime.

questions.q: Which data most favors schema-on-read?
options: Payroll rows that must always have the same fields
Records whose shape is set by an outside system
Invoice lines that all follow one fixed layout
Tax records whose fields are defined by your own team
optionExplain: A schema documents and enforces such uniform structure.
Right: you cannot enforce what you do not control.
Fixed layouts are where schemas help.
You control that structure, so a schema is affordable.
questions.explain: Control over structure decides it. The card lists the cases.

questions.q: Which situations does the chapter say favor schema-on-read? Select all that apply.
options: Many object types, and one table per type is not practical
All records are expected to have the same structure
Structure is decided by external systems that may change
You need the database to document and enforce structure
Every document is stored in a single continuous string
optionExplain: Right: heterogeneous types.
That is where a schema is useful.
Right: you cannot control it.
That is a case for schema-on-write.
That describes document storage, not a reason for schema-on-read.
questions.explain: Heterogeneous types and externally controlled structure favor schema-on-read.
questions.rule: Variety and lack of control favor schema-on-read.

questions.q: A pipeline ingests webhooks from partners who add new fields whenever they like. Which approach fits?
options: Schema-on-write, so the database refuses unknown fields
Shredding, so each partner gets its own set of tables
Schema-on-read, since the structure is set by outside systems
A fixed schema, since uniformity is always safer
optionExplain: Rejecting data would break ingestion when partners add fields.
Shredding does not address changing shapes.
Right: the shape changes at the partners' will.
Uniformity cannot be imposed on outside systems.
questions.explain: A schema may hurt more than it helps when you do not control the data's structure.
questions.rule: Do not enforce what you do not control.

questions.q: A payroll table where every row must carry the same fields is stored schema-on-read. What does the chapter suggest it gives up?
options: A schema's way of documenting and enforcing shared structure
The ability to store any text in the rows
The option to ever add a column later
The need for any application code at all
optionExplain: Right: uniform records are where a schema is useful.
Text is storable either way.
Columns can be added in either approach.
Schema-on-read relies on application code.
questions.explain: Where all records have the same structure, schemas are a useful mechanism for documenting and enforcing it.
questions.rule: Uniform records benefit from a schema.

questions.q: True or false: A schema may hurt more than it helps for data where every record has the same fixed structure.
questions.explain: For uniform records a schema documents and enforces the structure; the harm comes with heterogeneous or externally controlled data.

questions.q: A team adopts a graph database that enforces no schema. Does that mean its application assumes no structure?
options: No, the application still assumes an implicit structure, handled on read
Yes, because without enforcement there is nothing to assume
Yes, because graph databases cannot store properties
No, because graph databases always enforce a strict schema
optionExplain: Right: document and graph databases typically enforce none, yet code expects a shape.
The code still expects some shape.
Graphs store properties on vertices and edges.
The chapter says they typically do not.
questions.explain: Document and graph databases typically do not enforce a schema, which makes it easier to adapt to change, but the application most likely still assumes structure.
questions.rule: Implicit schema is still a schema.
questions.teaches: Document and graph databases typically enforce no schema, which eases adapting to changing requirements, but the application still assumes a structure that is implicit and handled on read.

questions.q: A page needs only the first name from a very large profile document. What does the database typically do?
options: Loads only the first name field and ignores the rest
Splits the document into tables on the fly
Loads the entire document
Refuses the request because the document is too large
optionExplain: Document databases typically load the whole document.
That would be shredding, done by a person.
Right: it usually cannot fetch only a small part.
It loads the whole document, which is wasteful rather than refused.
questions.explain: Large documents loaded whole waste effort when you need a small part. The card gives the details.

questions.q: On updates to a document, the ____ document usually needs to be rewritten.
questions.explain: Only modifications that do not change the encoded size can easily be performed in place.
questions.rule: Updates usually rewrite the whole document.

questions.q: Which access pattern gains most from storing a profile as one document?
options: Reading a single field from millions of profiles
Rendering the whole profile on a web page
Appending a small log entry to every profile daily
Joining profiles to a shared company table
optionExplain: Loading entire documents for one field wastes effort.
Right: the entire document is needed at once.
Growing documents forces rewrites.
Cross-record references are a different matter.
questions.explain: Locality helps when the application often needs the entire document.

questions.q: A feature adds a new comment to a large document on every page view. What does the chapter predict about those writes?
options: Each write touches only the new comment, however large the document
Writes become faster as the document grows
The database automatically splits the document into tables
Each write rewrites the whole document; growth blocks in-place edits
optionExplain: The whole document is usually rewritten.
Larger documents mean more rewriting.
Document databases do not shred documents for you.
Right: the document usually has to be rewritten and the size change prevents in-place edits.
questions.explain: That is why the chapter recommends avoiding writes that increase the size of a document.

questions.q: True or false: The locality advantage of a document applies only if you need large parts of it at the same time.
questions.explain: If you need a small part, the database still loads the entire document, which wastes effort.
questions.rule: Locality helps only some access patterns.

questions.q: In a document store, which update can most easily be done in place?
options: Adding a long new field to the document
Changing a stored count from 41 to 42
Appending a new element to a long list inside it
Replacing a short name with a much longer one
optionExplain: That increases the encoded size.
Right: the encoded size stays the same.
Appending grows the document.
A longer value changes the encoded size.
questions.explain: Only modifications that do not change the encoded size of a document can easily be performed in place.
questions.rule: Same-size edits can be made in place.
questions.teaches: Only modifications that do not change the encoded size of a document can easily be performed in place.

questions.q: True or false: Only document databases can keep related data physically together for locality.
questions.explain: Some relational systems can too. The card names examples.
questions.rule: Locality is a storage choice, not owned by one model.

questions.q: Match each system to its locality feature.
pairs: Rows interleaved within a parent table
A similar purpose of managing locality
questions.explain: Spanner interleaves tables, Oracle clusters them, and Bigtable-style column families manage locality too.

questions.q: A team wants each customer's orders stored next to the customer row in a relational database. Which Spanner feature fits?
options: Storing each order as a JSON string in a text column
Adding a foreign key from orders to customers
Moving orders into a separate database entirely
Declaring order rows interleaved within the parent table
optionExplain: That is a document-style layout, not Spanner's feature.
A foreign key links rows but does not co-locate them.
That separates data rather than grouping it.
Right: that gives relational data document-style locality.
questions.explain: Spanner lets the schema declare that a table's rows should be interleaved within a parent table.

questions.q: A team moves from a document database to Spanner to keep locality. Which data model do they use after the move?
options: The relational model, with interleaved tables
The document model, with nested JSON
The graph model, with vertices and edges
The network model, with pointer chains
optionExplain: Right: Spanner offers locality in a relational model.
Spanner is relational.
Spanner is not described as a graph store.
The network model is a historical one.
questions.explain: Spanner offers the same locality properties in a relational data model.
questions.rule: Locality does not require a document model.

questions.q: True or false: Spanner offers locality properties within a relational data model.
questions.explain: It lets the schema declare that a table's rows should be interleaved within a parent table.

questions.q: A team compares Cassandra with a document store for locality. What does the chapter say about Cassandra?
options: It stores nested JSON like MongoDB does
It offers no way to group related data
Its Bigtable-style column families manage locality similarly
It depends on interleaved tables as Spanner does
optionExplain: The chapter ties it to column families, not to nested JSON.
The column-family concept serves that purpose.
Right: Bigtable's column families, used in Cassandra and HBase, have a similar purpose.
Interleaving is Spanner's feature.
questions.explain: The column-family concept in the Bigtable data model, used in Cassandra and HBase, has a similar purpose of managing locality.
questions.teaches: The column-family concept in the Bigtable data model, used in Cassandra and HBase, has a similar purpose of managing locality.

questions.q: In which direction do relational and document databases appear to be moving over time?
options: Splitting into two incompatible camps
Merging into a single standard query language
Becoming more similar to one another
Dropping their different data models entirely
optionExplain: The chapter reports the opposite trend.
No single standard is claimed.
Right: each adds features of the other.
The models stay; features cross over.
questions.explain: Each side borrows from the other. The card gives the examples.

questions.q: Which developments does the chapter cite as convergence? Select all that apply.
options: Relational databases adding XML and JSON support
Document databases adding relational-style joins
Document databases dropping all references between records
Relational databases removing the SQL language
Relational databases giving up all schemas
optionExplain: Right: they can index and query inside documents.
Right: RethinkDB supports joins in its query language.
Nothing like this is cited.
SQL stays.
Not cited.
questions.explain: Convergence runs both ways: JSON and XML support in relational systems, and joins in document systems.

questions.q: A team has mostly regular records plus one document-like profile per user. According to the author, what is a good route?
options: Use a database that handles documents and relational queries
Insist on a pure document store for everything
Insist on a pure relational store with no JSON at all
Run two separate stores and join them in the browser
optionExplain: Right: the combination of features that best fits their needs.
The author favors a hybrid.
The author favors a hybrid.
That adds complexity the hybrid avoids.
questions.explain: If a database handles document-like data and also performs relational queries on it, applications can use the combination that best fits.
questions.rule: Use the mix that fits your data.

questions.q: A MongoDB driver resolves a reference automatically. Compared with a join inside the database, what does the chapter expect?
options: It is faster, because the driver bypasses the database
It is identical, because the driver runs the same code
It fails, because documents cannot hold references
Likely slower, from extra network round-trips and less optimization
optionExplain: The extra round-trips make it slower.
The chapter says it is likely slower.
Documents can hold references.
Right: it is effectively a client-side join.
questions.explain: Resolving references in the driver is effectively a client-side join, likely slower than a join performed in the database.

questions.q: True or false: The author regrets that relational and document databases are converging, because it blurs their strengths.
questions.explain: The author says the convergence is a good thing, because the models complement each other, and he calls a hybrid a good route.

questions.q: A newcomer says storing nested data in a row breaks the relational model. What does the chapter note about Codd's original description?
options: It banned any value that was not a number or a string
It allowed nested relations as values, called nonsimple domains
It required every value to be a pointer to another row
It did not mention nested values of any kind
optionExplain: The footnote says the opposite.
Right: much like later JSON or XML support.
Pointers belong to CODASYL.
The footnote says it did allow them.
questions.explain: Codd's original description allowed something quite similar to JSON documents within a relational schema, which he called nonsimple domains.
questions.teaches: Codd's original relational description allowed nested relations as values, called nonsimple domains, much like the JSON and XML support added to SQL over 30 years later.

questions.q: Which style of query specifies the pattern of the results wanted but not the algorithm to compute them?
options: Imperative
Pointer-chasing
Sequential scanning
Declarative
optionExplain: That style lists the steps and their order.
That describes navigating links by hand.
That is an execution method, not a style of asking.
Right: you state what, not how.
questions.explain: State the pattern and leave the rest to the database. The card names it.

questions.q: Match each term to its description.
pairs: Tells the computer which operations to run, in which order
States the pattern of data wanted, not how to get it
Chooses indexes, join methods and execution order
questions.explain: Imperative code gives steps, declarative code gives a pattern, and the optimizer decides the method.

questions.q: Which of these is a declarative way to get all rows of a table named orders where status is paid?
options: Loop over all rows, and append each paid one to a list
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid';
Move a cursor along a chain of links, testing each record
Read the rows in file order, then filter them in memory
optionExplain: That spells out the steps, which is the imperative style.
Right: it states the condition and leaves the method to the database.
That is navigation by hand.
That is an execution plan, written step by step.
questions.explain: A SELECT with a WHERE clause states the wanted pattern, not the steps.
questions.rule: State the condition, not the loop.

questions.q: What does the function print for this list of employees?
options: ['Ann', 'Bo', 'Cy']
['Ann', 'Cy']
optionExplain: Bo is in Ops, so the test excludes Bo.
The filter removes Bo.
Right: only the two employees in Sales are kept, in their original order.
Two employees match the test.
questions.explain: The loop appends each employee whose dept equals Sales, so Ann and Cy remain.
questions.rule: Trace the loop to predict its result.

questions.q: True or false: A SELECT statement tells the database to scan the table row by row and in what order to test the rows.
questions.explain: SQL states only the pattern of the result. The optimizer decides how to evaluate it.

questions.q: A spreadsheet filter says: show the rows where region is West, without saying how to scan the sheet. How does the chapter classify this style?
options: Declarative, since it gives a pattern rather than steps
Imperative, since it names a condition
Imperative, since it filters a list
Neither, since only databases can be declarative
optionExplain: Right: the same what-not-how idea as SQL.
Naming a condition is how declarative queries work.
Filtering is not what makes code imperative; stating steps is.
The chapter extends the idea beyond databases.
questions.explain: When SQL was defined, it followed the structure of relational algebra fairly closely, and relational algebra is itself declarative.
questions.teaches: When SQL was defined it followed the structure of relational algebra fairly closely, where a selection operator returns only the rows that match a condition.

questions.q: A database reclaims space and moves records, changing their order. Which query can safely survive this?
options: A SQL query that makes no promise about order
A loop that assumes the third record is always the same
A cursor walk that expects records in a fixed order
Any query written as imperative code
optionExplain: Right: it does not rely on the order.
That code relies on position.
That is order-dependent.
Imperative code may or may not rely on order, and the database cannot tell.
questions.explain: The database may reorder records freely only if no query depends on the order. The card explains.
questions.rule: No promise about order, freedom to change it.

questions.q: Because SQL is more limited in functionality than imperative code, the database has more room for automatic ____.
questions.explain: A limited language promises less, leaving the engine free to choose methods.
questions.rule: Less promised, more room to optimize.

questions.q: A vendor ships a faster index structure. Why can declarative queries benefit without being rewritten?
options: They name the old index, which the database then swaps
They store their own copies of the data in the index
They state what is wanted, so the database can switch methods
They are recompiled by the application on every call
optionExplain: A declarative query names no index.
Queries do not store data.
Right: queries do not name a method to be broken.
Recompiling is not part of the argument.
questions.explain: Hiding implementation details allows performance improvements without changes to queries.

questions.q: Imperative code relies on the order of records in a list, and the database moves records to reclaim space. What can happen?
options: The database detects the dependence and stops moving records
The code may give different or wrong results
The code gets faster because order no longer matters
Nothing, because order cannot change in a database
optionExplain: It can never be sure whether code relies on ordering.
Right: the database cannot know the code depends on order.
If order matters to it, a change can break it.
Reclaiming space may change the order.
questions.explain: If the database can never be sure about order dependence, imperative code ties its hands.

questions.q: True or false: Declarative languages are preferred only because their queries are shorter than imperative code.
questions.explain: Conciseness is one attraction, but more importantly a declarative language hides implementation details, which lets the database improve performance without changes to queries.
questions.rule: Hiding details is the larger benefit.

questions.q: A tool offers either a loop-based scripting interface or a pattern-based filter. Besides optimization room, which benefit does the chapter credit to the pattern-based one?
options: It always executes faster than any loop
It can express any computation a program could
It needs no engine to interpret it
It is typically more concise and easier to work with
optionExplain: The chapter promises room to optimize, not guaranteed speed.
It is more limited in functionality.
An engine still evaluates the pattern.
Right: that is the chapter's stated attraction.
questions.explain: A declarative query language is attractive because it is typically more concise and easier to work with than an imperative API.
questions.rule: Declarative is also easier to write.
questions.teaches: A declarative query language is typically more concise and easier to work with than an imperative API.

questions.q: Why is a loop that must run step by step hard to spread over many cores?
options: Cores cannot run loops at all
Its instructions must be performed in a particular order
Loops use too much memory to be shared
Loops are not allowed in database software
optionExplain: Cores run loops; the issue is order dependence.
Right: the order blocks parallel execution.
Memory use is not the stated problem.
That is not the problem the chapter names.
questions.explain: Strict order limits parallelism. The card shows how declarative queries avoid it.

questions.q: Today CPUs get faster by adding more ____ rather than by running at much higher clock speeds.
questions.explain: That makes parallel execution matter more.

questions.q: On a 32-core machine, which can the database parallelize by itself: a hand-coded loop, or the same report as a SQL GROUP BY query?
options: The loop, because loops always parallelize
Both equally, since the results are the same
Neither, since databases are single-threaded
The SQL query, which states only the result pattern
optionExplain: Imperative code is hard to parallelize.
The loop fixes an order of steps; the query does not.
The chapter says a database is free to use a parallel implementation.
Right: the database may choose a parallel implementation.
questions.explain: Declarative languages specify only the pattern of the results, so the database is free to use a parallel implementation.

questions.q: Next year a vendor doubles the cores of its servers. Which code has the better chance of speeding up without being rewritten?
options: A declarative query
A loop that updates variables in order
A hand-written cursor walk over linked records
Any code, since more cores always help equally
optionExplain: Right: the database can use the extra cores.
Its fixed order limits parallelism.
Hand-coded navigation is order dependent.
Order-bound code gains little.
questions.explain: Declarative languages have a better chance of getting faster in parallel execution.
questions.rule: Declarative code can ride extra cores.

questions.q: True or false: Imperative code is hard to parallelize because its steps must be performed in a particular order.
questions.explain: Declarative code states only the pattern of results, which leaves the database free to run it in parallel.

questions.q: Someone claims SQL queries can only run on one machine. What does the chapter say?
options: The claim is correct, which is why MapReduce was needed
The claim is correct, but only for declarative queries
Nothing in SQL confines it to one machine; distributed SQL exists
The claim is correct for relational databases only
optionExplain: MapReduce does not have a monopoly on distributed execution.
Declarative languages parallelize more readily.
Right: many distributed implementations do not use MapReduce.
The language does not limit the number of machines.
questions.explain: There is nothing in SQL that constrains it to running on a single machine, and there are many distributed implementations of SQL that do not use MapReduce.
questions.rule: SQL is not tied to one machine.
questions.teaches: Nothing in SQL constrains it to a single machine, and many distributed SQL implementations do not use MapReduce.

questions.q: A rule says: nav li.current > a { color: red; }. What does it specify?
options: A loop that visits every list item and tests its class
A function the browser calls once for each link in turn
The pattern of elements to style, without the steps for finding them
An index that speeds up searches through the page
optionExplain: A CSS rule has no loop; the browser does the matching.
No function is called by the page author.
Right: it is a declarative pattern.
A selector is not an index.
questions.explain: A selector states which elements to style. The card names the style.

questions.q: CSS and XSL are both ____ languages for specifying the styling of a document.
questions.explain: They state which elements get which style, not how to find them.

questions.q: Which elements does this CSS rule style?
options: Links that are direct children of an active item directly inside the menu list
Every link anywhere on the page whose text is menu
Every list item inside the menu, whatever its class
The menu list itself and all of its descendants
optionExplain: Right: the rule chains two direct-child steps.
The selector tests structure and classes, not link text.
Only items with the class active qualify.
The rule styles links, not the list.
