questions.explain: ul.menu > li.active > a matches an a that is a direct child of li.active, which is a direct child of ul.menu.
questions.rule: Read a selector as a structural pattern.

questions.q: The class active moves from one menu item to another. What happens to the bold styling under CSS?
options: Both items stay bold until the page is reloaded
Neither item is bold, because the rule ran only once
The old item stays bold unless the author clears it by hand
The browser removes it from the old item and applies it to the new one
optionExplain: That is the imperative script's flaw.
A CSS rule is not a one-off run.
That is what the imperative script needs.
Right: it re-evaluates the rule when the class changes.
questions.explain: With CSS the browser automatically detects when the rule no longer applies and removes the style.
questions.rule: Declarative rules stay true as the page changes.

questions.q: True or false: With the imperative script, the colour disappears by itself once the selected class is removed.
questions.explain: The colour stays, even if the code is re-run, until the whole page is reloaded.
questions.rule: The script only sets; it never unsets.

questions.q: A colleague uses XSL with the XPath expression li[@class='selected']/p to style the same list. How does it relate to the CSS rule?
options: It is an imperative loop written in XML syntax
It is an equivalent pattern in another declarative language
It styles different elements, since XPath ignores classes
It replaces the browser's own style engine
optionExplain: XSL is declarative.
Right: an XPath expression plays the role of the CSS selector.
The expression tests the class attribute.
XSL is used alongside, not as a replacement.
questions.explain: The XPath expression li[@class='selected']/p is equivalent to the CSS selector li.selected > p.
questions.rule: Different syntaxes can state the same pattern.
questions.teaches: In XSL, the XPath expression li[@class='selected']/p is equivalent to the CSS selector li.selected > p.

questions.q: Where does MapReduce sit between declarative query languages and imperative query APIs?
options: Fully declarative, like SQL
Fully imperative, like a cursor over records
Outside both, as a storage format
Somewhere in between, using code snippets the framework calls
optionExplain: Query logic is written as code, so it is not purely declarative.
The framework, not the author, controls how the functions are called.
It is a programming model for querying.
Right: neither purely declarative nor fully imperative.
questions.explain: The logic is code, but the framework decides how it is called. The card explains.

questions.q: Match each MapReduce part to its job.
pairs: Called per document, emits key-value pairs
Gathers the emitted pairs that share a key
Called once per key to combine its values
questions.explain: Map emits pairs, the framework groups them, and reduce combines each group.

questions.q: What does this code print?
optionExplain: The January group holds both 3 and 4.
Right: the two January values 3 and 4 add up to 7.
The reduce step sums the group, not takes its last value.
The months stay separate groups.
questions.explain: Map emits (2024-01, 3), (2024-01, 4) and (2024-02, 5); the sums per key are 7 and 5.

questions.q: February has one document with n equal to 5. A new February document with n equal to 2 is added. What is the February total?
optionExplain: The new value joins the group; it does not replace it.
The new document adds to the total.
Right: 5 plus 2.
The group holds 5 and 2 only, which sum to 7.
questions.explain: The February group becomes 5 and 2, and reduce sums them to 7.
questions.rule: New documents join their key's group.

questions.q: True or false: MapReduce is neither a declarative query language nor a fully imperative query API.
questions.explain: The query logic is code, but the framework calls it repeatedly, so MapReduce sits in between.

questions.q: A developer knows fold from functional programming. Which MapReduce function is its counterpart?
options: Reduce, which is also known as fold or inject
Map, which is also known as fold or inject
Emit, which is also known as fold or inject
Group, which is also known as fold or inject
optionExplain: Right: map is also known as collect.
Map corresponds to collect.
Emit passes pairs to the framework; it is not fold.
Grouping is done by the framework, not a named function.
questions.explain: MapReduce is based on the map (also known as collect) and reduce (also known as fold or inject) functions that exist in many functional programming languages.
questions.teaches: MapReduce is based on map (also known as collect) and reduce (also known as fold or inject) functions that exist in many functional programming languages.

questions.q: A function used inside a distributed query may be rerun after a machine fails. Which property keeps that rerun safe?
options: It has no side effects and uses only its inputs
It prints a message every time it starts
It counts calls in a shared global variable
It reads the latest rows from the database each time
optionExplain: Right: rerunning gives the same result and changes nothing.
Printing is a side effect.
Counting calls is a side effect that rerunning would double.
Extra queries break the pure-function rule.
questions.explain: Purity makes reruns harmless. The card lists the rules.

questions.q: Which restrictions apply to map and reduce functions? Select all that apply.
options: They use only the data passed to them as input
They must be written in SQL
They cannot perform additional database queries
They run on a single machine only
They must not have side effects
optionExplain: Right: no outside state.
MongoDB's MapReduce uses JavaScript functions.
Right: extra queries are not allowed.
They may run anywhere.
Right: no changes outside the return value.
questions.explain: A pure function reads only its input, queries nothing else and has no side effects.
questions.rule: Pure means input in, value out.

questions.q: A map function increments a global counter on each call. Why is that a problem?
options: It makes the function return a string instead of a number
It forces the database to run the function on one machine
It is a side effect, and a rerun after failure would count twice
It makes the function too slow to call on large documents
optionExplain: The return type is not the issue.
The problem is rerun safety.
Right: the database must be able to rerun functions safely.
Speed is not the stated reason.
questions.explain: A rerun would increment the counter again, so the function is not pure and cannot be safely rerun.
questions.rule: A side effect makes a rerun unsafe.

questions.q: A machine fails halfway through a MapReduce job. What can the database do if the functions are pure?
options: Abandon the job, because reruns cannot be trusted
Rerun the functions elsewhere and still get a correct result
Ask the programmer which calls had finished
Merge the partial output of both runs by hand
optionExplain: Pure functions make reruns safe.
Right: that is why the restrictions exist.
The database can decide on its own.
No manual merge is needed.
questions.explain: The restrictions allow the database to run the functions anywhere, in any order, and rerun them on failure.

questions.q: True or false: A map function may perform extra database queries because it receives its documents from the database.
questions.explain: The functions must be pure, so they cannot perform additional database queries.
questions.rule: No extra queries inside map or reduce.

questions.q: A team wants custom JavaScript inside a SQL query. Does the chapter say that only MapReduce allows this?
options: Yes, since SQL cannot call any programming language
Yes, since JavaScript can run only inside document stores
No, but only because SQL is itself written in JavaScript
No, some SQL databases can be extended with JavaScript functions too
optionExplain: Some SQL databases can.
The chapter mentions SQL databases with JavaScript functions.
SQL is not written in JavaScript.
Right: it is not limited to MapReduce.
questions.explain: Being able to use JavaScript code in the middle of a query is a great feature for advanced queries, but it is not limited to MapReduce.
questions.rule: Code inside queries is not unique to MapReduce.
questions.teaches: Using JavaScript code in the middle of a query is not limited to MapReduce, because some SQL databases can be extended with JavaScript functions too.

questions.q: Which MongoDB feature expresses a query declaratively as a pipeline of stages?
options: The mapReduce function
The aggregation pipeline
The emit function
The BSON encoder
optionExplain: That takes code snippets and is not declarative.
Right: added in MongoDB 2.2.
Emit is called inside map.
BSON is a storage encoding.
questions.explain: Stages such as match and group describe the result. The card gives the name.
questions.rule: A pipeline of stages is declarative.

questions.q: MongoDB 2.2 added a declarative query language called the aggregation ____.
questions.explain: It was added because MapReduce needs two coordinated functions and gives the optimizer less to work with.

questions.q: Which SQL query matches this aggregation pipeline?
options: SELECT customer, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY status
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer = 'paid' ORDER BY amount
SELECT status, COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer = amount
SELECT customer, SUM(amount) FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY customer
optionExplain: That groups by status, not by customer.
That filters on the wrong column and does not aggregate.
That counts rows and compares unrelated columns.
Right: match is the WHERE filter and group is the GROUP BY with a sum.
questions.explain: The match stage filters paid orders, and the group stage sums amount per customer.
questions.rule: Match is WHERE; group is GROUP BY.

questions.q: A NoSQL store grows popular for reporting and users ask for easier queries. By the chapter's moral, what may its query language turn into?
options: A disguised version of SQL
A purely imperative cursor API
A navigation scheme based on access paths
A language with no declarative features
optionExplain: Right: a NoSQL system may accidentally reinvent SQL.
Users asked for easier queries, which points away from that.
That was the network model's way.
MongoDB moved toward a declarative one.
questions.explain: The chapter's moral is that a NoSQL system may find itself accidentally reinventing SQL, albeit in disguise.
questions.rule: Query needs pull systems toward SQL.

questions.q: True or false: MapReduce is easier to write than a single declarative query.
questions.explain: The chapter calls the need to write two carefully coordinated functions a usability problem, often harder than writing a single query.
questions.rule: Two coordinated functions are harder than one query.

questions.q: A team debates a JSON-style syntax against SQL's English-sentence style for a new query language of equal power. What does the chapter say?
options: JSON syntax is more powerful than SQL syntax
Only the English-sentence style can be optimized
The difference is perhaps a matter of taste
JSON syntax forbids the use of aggregation
optionExplain: It is similar to a subset of SQL.
Both are declarative and can be optimized.
Right: the pipeline is similarly expressive and only the syntax differs.
Aggregation is what the pipeline does.
questions.explain: The aggregation pipeline language is similar in expressiveness to a subset of SQL, but uses JSON-based syntax; the difference is perhaps a matter of taste.
questions.rule: Syntax style is a matter of taste.
questions.teaches: Using a JSON-based syntax rather than SQL's English-sentence style is perhaps a matter of taste, since the pipeline is similar in expressiveness to a subset of SQL.

questions.q: Which data model fits best when many-to-many relationships are very common and complex?
options: A document model with one record per entity
A hierarchical model with one parent per record
A graph model
A plain list of unrelated rows
optionExplain: Documents are weak with many-to-many links.
A single parent cannot express many-to-many links.
Right: vertices and edges express connections directly.
Unrelated rows lose the connections.
questions.explain: Heavily linked data suits vertices and edges. The card gives the terms.

questions.q: Match each graph example to what its vertices and edges are.
pairs: People linked by who knows whom
Junctions linked by roads or rail lines
questions.explain: Each example names what the vertices are and what the edges mean.
questions.rule: Name what the vertices and edges are.

questions.q: Which data set is best modeled as a graph?
options: Airline routes between airports and the connections they allow
A stack of invoices, each with its own line items
A log of sensor readings ordered by time
A catalogue of product descriptions with no links
optionExplain: Right: airports are vertices and flights are edges.
That is a tree loaded as a whole.
A time-ordered log has no web of connections.
No relationships means no graph is needed.
questions.explain: Routes and connections between places are many-to-many relationships between like objects.
questions.rule: Connected places and routes are graph data.

questions.q: A navigation app models roads as a graph. What kind of question can well-known algorithms answer for it?
options: Which junction has the oldest tarmac
How many invoices a driver has issued
Which roads were named after cities
The shortest path between two points
optionExplain: That needs properties and not an algorithm on the graph.
That is not a graph question.
Names are properties, not path questions.
Right: car navigation systems do this.
questions.explain: Shortest-path search in a road network is the chapter's example.

questions.q: True or false: A graph can store completely different types of objects in one datastore.
questions.explain: Graphs are not limited to homogeneous data; different vertex and edge types can share one graph.
questions.rule: Vertices can be of many types.

questions.q: A fitness app wants users, workouts, gyms and comments in one datastore. What does the chapter say a graph can do for this?
options: Hold only objects of the same type in each graph
Store completely different types of objects consistently in one datastore
Replace the need for any identifiers or labels
Force each type into its own separate database
optionExplain: The chapter says graphs are not limited to homogeneous data.
Right: Facebook keeps people, places, events, check-ins and comments in a single graph.
Vertices and edges carry identifiers and labels.
A single graph can hold all the types.
questions.explain: Facebook maintains a single graph with vertices for people, locations, events, check-ins and comments, and edges for friendships, check-in locations, comments and attendance.
questions.rule: One graph can hold many kinds of things.
questions.teaches: Facebook keeps people, locations, events, check-ins and comments as different vertex types in a single graph, with edges such as friendship, check-in location and attendance.

questions.q: In a property graph, what does an edge's label describe?
options: The number of properties held by the tail vertex
The order in which the edge was created
The size of the graph that contains the edge
The kind of relationship between its two vertices
optionExplain: Labels name relationship kinds, not counts.
Creation order is not what a label records.
Labels do not describe the graph as a whole.
Right: for example BORN_IN or LIVES_IN.
questions.explain: A label names the relationship. The card lists all the parts of vertices and edges.

questions.q: In a property graph, the vertex at which an edge starts is called the ____ vertex.
questions.explain: The vertex where it ends is the head vertex.
questions.rule: Edges run from tail to head.

questions.q: An edge labeled WORKS_AT runs from vertex Dana to vertex Acme. Which vertex is the tail?
options: Acme, where the edge ends
Dana, where the edge starts
Both, because the edge connects them
Neither, because the label names the direction
optionExplain: The end of the edge is the head.
Right: the tail is the start of the edge.
Each edge has one tail and one head.
Direction comes from the tail and head fields.
questions.explain: The tail vertex is where the edge starts, so for an edge from Dana to Acme it is Dana.
questions.rule: Tail starts the edge; head ends it.

questions.q: Lucy was born in Idaho and lives in London. How many edges does a property graph use for those two facts about her?
options: One, labeled with both facts
None, since these facts are vertex properties only
Two, each with its own identifier and label
Three, adding a third for her name
optionExplain: An edge has a single label for one kind of relationship.
Places are better modeled as vertices linked by edges.
Right: BORN_IN and LIVES_IN are separate edges.
A name is a property, not an edge.
questions.explain: Each relationship is its own edge with its own label.

questions.q: True or false: In a property graph only vertices carry properties, while edges have only a label.
questions.explain: Edges carry a collection of key-value properties too, as well as an identifier, a tail, a head and a label.

questions.q: A road network is stored in vertices and edges tables with tail_vertex and head_vertex columns. Which column finds roads leaving junction 7?
options: tail_vertex, where the edge starts
head_vertex, where the edge ends
label, where the edge is named
edge_id, where the edge is numbered
optionExplain: Right: outgoing edges are found by tail_vertex.
head_vertex finds incoming edges.
A label names the kind of relationship, not the direction.
An edge identifier does not point at a vertex.
questions.explain: If you want the set of incoming or outgoing edges for a vertex, you can query the edges table by head_vertex or tail_vertex, respectively.
questions.rule: Tail gives outgoing; head gives incoming.
questions.teaches: Incoming edges of a vertex are found by querying the edges table by head_vertex, and outgoing edges by tail_vertex.

questions.q: Which feature of property graphs does a fixed relational schema lack?
options: Any vertex may connect to any other, with no schema restricting links
Rows that are unordered collections of tuples
A query optimizer that picks an execution plan
Primary keys that identify each record uniquely
optionExplain: Right: that is the first aspect the chapter lists.
Relational tables already work this way.
Relational systems have optimizers.
Relational tables have primary keys.
questions.explain: Free linking between any two vertices is a key difference. The card lists three aspects.

questions.q: Which aspects of property graphs does the chapter list? Select all that apply.
options: Any vertex can have an edge to any other vertex
Edges must be stored in a separate table for each label
Incoming and outgoing edges can both be found efficiently
Different labels let one graph hold several kinds of information
Every vertex must have the same fixed set of properties
optionExplain: Right: no schema restricts associations.
Labels share one edges structure.
Right: traversal works forward and backward.
Right: with a clean data model.
Properties are a free-form collection.
questions.explain: The three aspects are unrestricted links, two-way traversal and labels for several kinds of relationships.

questions.q: A geography data set has US states and counties but French départements and régions. Why does a graph suit it?
options: Graphs require every country to use identical region names
Graphs store each country in a separate database file
No schema forces one regional structure on every country
Graphs convert regions into a single flat table
optionExplain: Graphs impose no such rule.
One graph holds all of them.
Right: each country can have its own kinds of regions.
Graphs keep the shapes as they are.
questions.explain: The figure shows different regional structures in different countries as the kind of thing difficult to express in a traditional relational schema.

questions.q: Lucy's birthplace is known only as a state, while her residence is a city. How does a graph represent this?
options: Her birthplace must be refined to a city before storing
Her edges point to vertices of different granularity
Her residence must be reduced to a state to match
Both facts must be dropped until fully known
optionExplain: The graph stores what is known.
Right: varying granularity is easy in a graph.
No such matching is required.
Partial detail is fine.
questions.explain: Varying granularity of data, such as a city for one fact and a state for another, is one of the cases the graph holds easily.

questions.q: True or false: In a property graph, given any vertex you can efficiently find both its incoming and outgoing edges.
questions.explain: That is why the edges table is indexed on both tail_vertex and head_vertex and traversal works both ways.

questions.q: A school canteen app wants to know what each pupil can safely eat. By the chapter's pattern, what would you add to the graph?
options: A new column in a pupils table for every allergen
A separate graph database for each pupil
A free-text note that is read by staff only
A vertex per allergen, edges from pupils to allergens, and links to foods containing them
optionExplain: That is a schema change, which graphs avoid.
One graph can hold everyone.
Text notes cannot be queried through the graph.
Right: then a query can find what is safe for each person.
questions.explain: You could indicate food allergies by introducing a vertex for each allergen and an edge between a person and an allergen, and link allergens to the foods that contain them; graphs are good for evolvability.
questions.rule: Graphs extend as features are added.
questions.teaches: A graph can be extended with new kinds of facts, such as a vertex per allergen with edges from people and to foods, so a query can find what is safe to eat; graphs are good for evolvability.

questions.q: Cypher was created for which kind of database?
options: The MongoDB document database
The Neo4j graph database
The IMS hierarchical database
The Datomic triple-store
optionExplain: MongoDB uses its own query language.
Right: it is a declarative language for property graphs.
IMS used imperative code.
Datomic uses Datalog.
questions.explain: Cypher belongs to property graphs. The card gives its notation.

questions.q: In Cypher, the pattern (Idaho) -[:WITHIN]-> (USA) creates an edge labeled ____.
questions.explain: The label sits inside the square brackets after the colon.

questions.q: Which Cypher pattern creates an edge labeled WORKS_AT from vertex Dana to vertex Acme?
options: (Acme) -[:WORKS_AT]-> (Dana)
(Dana) -[WORKS_AT]- (Acme)
[Dana] -(:WORKS_AT)-> [Acme]
(Dana) -[:WORKS_AT]-> (Acme)
optionExplain: That arrow points from Acme to Dana.
That omits the colon and the arrowhead.
Parentheses and brackets are swapped.
Right: the arrow points from tail Dana to head Acme.
questions.explain: Parentheses hold vertices and square brackets hold the edge label; the arrow gives the direction.
questions.rule: Parentheses are vertices; brackets are edges.

questions.q: In this Cypher example, what does the MATCH query return?
options: Paris, the only city within France
France, the country that contains it
Nothing, because MATCH cannot read created vertices
Both Paris and France
optionExplain: Right: only the Paris vertex fits the pattern.
RETURN gives c.name, the city's name.
MATCH reads the data that CREATE added.
Only the city variable c is returned.
questions.code:
CREATE
  (Paris:City {name:'Paris'}),
  (France:Country {name:'France'}),
  (Paris) -[:WITHIN]-> (France)

MATCH (c:City) -[:WITHIN]-> (:Country {name:'France'})
RETURN c.name
questions.explain: The pattern matches City vertices with a WITHIN edge to the Country named France, and c.name is Paris.

questions.q: True or false: In Cypher you must write out the steps for scanning the graph, as in an imperative language.
questions.explain: Cypher is declarative: you describe the pattern, and the query optimizer chooses the execution strategy.

questions.q: In the MATCH pattern shown, what do the empty parentheses mean?
options: A vertex that must have no properties at all
A comment that the database ignores when matching
A vertex that is matched but not given a name
The tail vertex of the whole pattern, always named d
optionExplain: Empty parentheses do not mean empty properties.
The parentheses stand for a vertex in the path.
Right: the pattern needs it to exist but does not bind a variable to it.
The variable d is already the tail vertex.
questions.code:
MATCH (d) -[:SERVED_AT]-> () -[:WITHIN]-> (:City {name:'Lyon'})
RETURN d.name
questions.explain: In the chapter's example the head vertex of a BORN_IN edge is left unnamed, while the tail vertex is bound to the variable person.
questions.rule: Name a vertex only if you need it later.
questions.teaches: In a MATCH pattern a vertex can be bound to a variable, such as person, or left unnamed with empty parentheses when only its existence matters.

questions.q: People may be linked to a street, city or region, each inside a larger place. What lets a query reach the country in every case?
options: A pattern with exactly three steps from every person
A pattern that lists every possible place by name
A pattern that follows a containment edge zero or more times
A pattern that copies the country onto every person
optionExplain: A fixed depth fails when places nest differently.
That does not follow the nesting.
Right: the number of steps is left open.
Copying is not a path pattern.
questions.explain: The depth of nesting varies. The card shows the notation.
questions.rule: Open-ended paths need a repeat notation.

questions.q: In Cypher, :WITHIN*0.. means follow a WITHIN edge zero or ____ times.
questions.explain: It is like the star operator in a regular expression.

questions.q: In this query, what does the first MATCH line say about p?
options: p has a BORN_IN edge, then a chain of WITHIN edges reaching France
p is directly within France, with no intermediate steps
p lives in Japan and was born in a vertex named p
p is the name of the country, which is then returned
optionExplain: Right: the chain may have zero or more WITHIN steps.
The *0.. allows any number of WITHIN steps.
That mixes the two lines.
p stands for a person vertex.
questions.code:
MATCH
  (p) -[:BORN_IN]-> () -[:WITHIN*0..]-> (:Location {name:'France'}),
  (p) -[:LIVES_IN]-> () -[:WITHIN*0..]-> (:Location {name:'Japan'})
RETURN p.name
questions.explain: The first line pins down the place of birth, anywhere within France.
questions.rule: Read each line as a chain of steps.

questions.q: A new level, a district, is added between city and region in the data. Must the query change?
options: Yes, one more WITHIN step must be added to each line
Yes, the query must be rewritten as imperative code
No, but only if the district is removed again
No, because *0.. already follows however many WITHIN steps exist
optionExplain: A fixed number of steps would be needed only without *0..
Cypher stays declarative.
The query handles the new level as it is.
Right: the depth is not fixed in the query.
questions.explain: The star means any number of steps, so extra levels need no change to the query.

questions.q: True or false: A Cypher query for people born in one place and living in another must begin by scanning every person in the database.
questions.explain: That is only one possible strategy. The optimizer may instead start from the two location vertices and work backward.
questions.rule: Declarative queries leave the strategy open.

questions.q: Besides scanning all people, how could the database run the emigrants query, if an index exists on the name property?
options: Find the people by name, then sort every location
Find the two location vertices by name, follow incoming WITHIN edges, then look for people
Build an access path by hand for each person
Copy all locations into every person vertex
optionExplain: The query is not about people's names.
Right: work backward from the places.
Hand-built paths are what declarative queries avoid.
Nothing in the chapter proposes copying.
questions.explain: You could start with the two Location vertices, use the index to find the US and Europe, follow incoming WITHIN edges to all their locations, and then find people through incoming BORN_IN or LIVES_IN edges; the optimizer picks the strategy.
questions.rule: Different plans give the same answer.
questions.teaches: The database could start from the two location vertices found through an index on name, follow incoming WITHIN edges to all contained locations, then find people through incoming BORN_IN or LIVES_IN edges, instead of scanning all people.

questions.q: A relational query usually has a fixed set of joins. What differs in a graph query that follows chains of edges?
options: The query never needs to join anything at all
The query must always touch every row of every table
The query can be answered from a single row
The number of edges to traverse can vary, so the joins are not fixed
optionExplain: Following edges is a kind of join.
Indexes still let it start from chosen vertices.
A chain of edges spans many rows.
Right: depth is not known in advance.
questions.explain: How far to follow is data-dependent. The card shows SQL's answer.

questions.q: Since SQL:1999, variable-length traversal can be written with recursive common table expressions, using the keyword WITH ____.
questions.explain: The recursive part repeats until no new rows are added.
questions.rule: WITH RECURSIVE follows paths of any length.

questions.q: The tables hold Europe, France and Paris, with Paris within France and France within Europe. How many rows does the query return?
options: One: only Europe
Three: Europe, France and Paris
Two: France and Paris
Zero, because no row has the label within
optionExplain: The recursive part adds the places within it.
Right: the seed row plus everything reached by following within edges inward.
The seed row Europe is part of the result.
Two links carry the label within.
questions.code:
-- places: (1,'Europe'), (2,'France'), (3,'Paris')
-- links (tail, head, label): (2,1,'within'), (3,2,'within')
WITH RECURSIVE in_europe(vertex_id) AS (
  SELECT vertex_id FROM places WHERE name = 'Europe'
  UNION
  SELECT links.tail_vertex FROM links
  JOIN in_europe ON links.head_vertex = in_europe.vertex_id
  WHERE links.label = 'within'
)
SELECT vertex_id FROM in_europe;
questions.explain: The seed gives Europe; the first round adds France; the next adds Paris; then nothing new appears.
questions.rule: Recursion repeats until nothing new is found.

questions.q: A district, Montmartre, is added as within Paris. Does the recursive SQL need to change to include it?
options: Yes, one more JOIN is needed for each new level
Yes, the table must be recreated first
No, the recursion follows however many levels exist
No, but only because Montmartre is skipped
optionExplain: A fixed chain of joins would need that, but recursion does not.
The tables are unchanged apart from one row.
Right: it repeats until no new rows appear.
It is included by the recursion.
questions.explain: This is the advantage of recursion over a fixed number of joins.

questions.q: True or false: Graph data stored in relational tables can be queried with SQL, though with some difficulty.
questions.explain: Recursive common table expressions make variable-length traversal possible, but the syntax is clumsy.

questions.q: A team finds that the same query is 4 lines in one language and 29 in another. What does the chapter conclude?
options: Different data models suit different use cases, so choose one that fits
The shorter language is always better for every task
The longer language is more precise, so it should be used
Line counts say nothing, so the languages are equal
optionExplain: Right: that is the moral drawn from Cypher versus SQL.
The chapter draws a conclusion about fit, not about the shorter language.
Length does not show precision.
The chapter reads the difference as a sign of different purposes.
questions.explain: The same query takes 4 lines in Cypher and 29 in SQL, which just shows that different data models are designed to satisfy different use cases.
questions.rule: Match the model to the use case.
questions.teaches: The same query takes 4 lines in Cypher but 29 in SQL, which shows that different data models are designed for different use cases.

questions.q: In the triple (Jim, likes, bananas), which part is the predicate?
options: likes
Jim
bananas
The whole triple
optionExplain: Right: the verb is the predicate.
Jim is the subject.
Bananas is the object.
The predicate is one of the three parts.
questions.explain: A triple has subject, predicate and object. The card shows how they map to a graph.

questions.q: Match each triple part to what it can be in graph terms.
pairs: A property key or an edge label
A primitive value or another vertex
questions.explain: The subject is a vertex, the predicate names a property or edge, and the object is a value or a vertex.
questions.rule: Subject vertex, predicate key or label, object value or vertex.

questions.q: How should the triple (lucy, age, 33) be read as a graph?
options: An edge named age from vertex lucy to vertex 33
A vertex age with a property lucy equal to 33
A vertex lucy with the property age equal to 33
Two vertices, lucy and 33, with no connection
optionExplain: 33 is a primitive value, not a vertex.
The subject is lucy.
Right: the object is a plain value.
The triple states a single fact about lucy.
questions.explain: When the object is a primitive value, the predicate and object are a property key and value on the subject.
questions.rule: A plain value makes a property.

questions.q: In (lucy, marriedTo, alain), both lucy and alain are vertices. What is marriedTo?
options: A property of the vertex alain
The label of the edge from lucy to alain
A third vertex that links the two
The unique identifier of lucy
optionExplain: A property would need a plain value as its object.
Right: the predicate becomes the edge.
Triples have no extra vertex here.
Identifiers are not predicates.
questions.explain: When the object is another vertex, the predicate is an edge with the subject as tail and the object as head.
questions.rule: A vertex object makes an edge.

questions.q: True or false: In a triple-store an edge is expressed as a triple whose object is another vertex.
questions.explain: The predicate is then the edge label, with the subject as tail and the object as head.
questions.rule: A vertex object makes an edge.

questions.q: Datomic is described as a triple-store, yet it stores five fields per fact. What are the two additional fields for?
options: Pointers into a CODASYL access path
Pointers for a second parent of the subject
A schema declaration for the object
Metadata for versioning
optionExplain: Datomic is not a network model database.
Triples have no parent concept.
The extra fields are not a schema.
Right: technically Datomic uses 5-tuples.
questions.explain: Technically, Datomic uses 5-tuples rather than triples; the two additional fields are metadata for versioning.
questions.rule: Triples can be extended with metadata.
questions.teaches: Technically Datomic uses 5-tuples rather than triples, and the two additional fields are metadata for versioning.

questions.q: What problem was RDF meant to solve for websites?
options: Making pages load faster over slow networks
Publishing data in one consistent format so different sites' data could be combined
Replacing HTML as the markup for page layout
Enforcing one schema on every relational database
optionExplain: Speed was not its purpose.
Right: a web of data.
RDF concerns data exchange, not layout.
RDF is for data on the web.
questions.explain: RDF was for machine-readable data exchange. The card tells the story.
questions.rule: RDF aimed at combinable web data.

questions.q: True or false: A triple-store depends on the semantic web to work.
questions.explain: The triple-store data model is completely independent of the semantic web. Datomic is a triple-store that claims no relation to it.

questions.q: A team wants triples as an internal data model and has no plan to publish RDF. According to the author, is that reasonable?
options: No, triples work only when the data is published as RDF
No, because the semantic web was fully realized and replaced them
Yes, but only if the triples are written as XML
Yes, triples can be a good internal data model without the semantic web
optionExplain: The author says the model is independent.
The semantic web has not been realized.
The format is not the issue.
Right: the semantic web is optional.
questions.explain: Triples can be a good internal data model for applications, even if you have no interest in publishing RDF data on the semantic web.
questions.rule: Use triples internally if they fit.

questions.q: Two sites use a predicate named within with different meanings. RDF avoids a clash because predicates are often written as ____.
questions.explain: Each URI sits in its own namespace, so you can combine your data with someone else's even if they attach a different meaning to the word.

questions.q: Claim: the semantic web delivered an internet-wide database of everything, so triple-stores are essential. What is wrong?
options: It has shown no sign of being realized, and triple-stores are independent of it
It was realized, but triple-stores cannot use it
It was never an idea that anyone proposed
It was realized, and triple-stores are only a minor part
optionExplain: Right: neither part of the claim holds.
The author says it was not realized.
It was proposed and overhyped.
The first part is wrong too.
questions.explain: The semantic web was overhyped in the early 2000s but so far has shown no sign of being realized, and the triple-store model is independent of it.

questions.q: A developer sets a predicate to http://my-company.com/namespace#within and finds that the URL gives a 404 error. Is that a problem?
options: Yes, an unresolvable URL makes the triple invalid
Yes, the site must be restored before the data is used
No, from RDF's point of view it is a namespace and nothing more
No, but only if the URL is changed to start with https
optionExplain: Resolution is not required.
No site is needed.
Right: it need not resolve to anything.
The scheme is not the point.
questions.explain: The URL does not necessarily need to resolve to anything; from RDF's point of view it is simply a namespace, and examples use non-resolvable URIs such as urn:example:within.
questions.rule: A URI can be just a name.
questions.teaches: An RDF namespace URL does not need to resolve to anything; from RDF's point of view it is simply a namespace.

questions.q: Which query language is used with RDF triple-stores?
options: Cypher
MapReduce
SPARQL
XPath
optionExplain: Cypher is for property graphs such as Neo4j.
MapReduce is a bulk processing model.
Right: it is the query language for the RDF data model.
XPath selects parts of XML documents.
questions.explain: RDF has its own language. The card names it.

questions.q: Match each SPARQL idea to its meaning.
pairs: Variable with a leading question mark
Binds to a value in the data
Follow within edges zero or more times
questions.explain: Variables start with ?, a star repeats a step, and Cypher copied SPARQL's pattern idea.

questions.q: Which Cypher pattern is equivalent to the SPARQL expression shown here?
options: (x) -[:WORKS_AT]-> () -[:PART_OF*0..]-> (org)
(x) -[:PART_OF]-> () -[:WORKS_AT*0..]-> (org)
(x) -[:WORKS_AT*0..]-> (org) only
(org) -[:WORKS_AT]-> (x)
optionExplain: Right: the star becomes *0.. and the path becomes arrows.
The two steps are in the wrong order.
The second step is missing.
The direction and the repeated step are lost.
questions.code: ?x :worksAt / :partOf* ?org.
questions.explain: The chapter pairs ?person :bornIn / :within* ?location with (person) -[:BORN_IN]-> () -[:WITHIN*0..]-> (location).

questions.q: In SPARQL, does matching a property such as :name use different syntax from matching an edge such as :within?
options: Yes, properties need curly braces and edges need arrows
Yes, edges need a URI but properties do not
No, but only when the object is a number
No, both are predicates and use the same syntax
optionExplain: That is closer to Cypher's notation.
Both use predicates.
The same syntax holds for any object.
Right: RDF does not distinguish them.
questions.explain: Because RDF does not distinguish between properties and edges but just uses predicates for both, you can use the same syntax for matching properties.

questions.q: True or false: Cypher's pattern matching is borrowed from SPARQL.
questions.explain: SPARQL predates Cypher, which is why the two look similar.

questions.q: A team has no plan to publish RDF data. Does the author consider SPARQL still worth using?
options: No, since SPARQL works only on published RDF
Yes, it can be a powerful tool for applications to use internally
No, since Cypher replaced it completely
Yes, but only for data in an XML format
optionExplain: The author says it can be used internally.
Right: even if the semantic web never happens.
SPARQL predates Cypher and is still useful.
The format is not the point.
questions.explain: SPARQL is a nice query language, and even if the semantic web never happens it can be a powerful tool for applications to use internally.
questions.teaches: SPARQL can be a powerful tool for applications to use internally even if the semantic web never happens.

questions.q: Are graph databases the old CODASYL network model in disguise?
options: Yes, they use exactly the same access paths
Yes, but only their query languages differ
No, because they are older than CODASYL
No, they differ from it in several important ways
optionExplain: Graphs can reach a vertex directly by ID or index.
The data model differs too.
Graph databases are the newer idea.
Right: schema, access and ordering all differ.
questions.explain: The resemblance is superficial. The card lists the differences.

questions.q: Sort each feature by the model it describes.

items.t: Reach a record only by following an access path
Refer to a vertex directly by its unique ID
Children of a record kept in an ordered set
Vertices and edges are not ordered
Any vertex may have an edge to any other vertex
A schema says which record type nests in which

questions.explain: CODASYL fixed the schema, the paths and the order; graph databases leave those open.
questions.rule: Fixed paths and order are CODASYL.

questions.q: A programmer inserting new records must worry about where they sit in an ordered set of children. Which model is this?
options: A graph database
CODASYL's network model
A relational database
A triple-store
optionExplain: Graph vertices and edges are unordered.
Right: it kept ordered sets that the database had to maintain.
Rows in a table are an unordered collection.
Triples have no ordered children.
questions.explain: In CODASYL the children of a record were an ordered set, with consequences for storage and for inserting applications.

questions.q: A graph database user wants results in a particular order. When can that order be imposed?
options: When storing, because edges are kept in order
Never, since graph results have no defined order
When making a query, by sorting the results
Only when the database is created
optionExplain: Edges are not ordered in storage.
Results can be sorted in a query.
Right: the data itself is unordered.
Order is not fixed at creation.
questions.explain: In a graph database, vertices and edges are not ordered; you can only sort the results when making a query.
questions.rule: Sort in the query, not the storage.

questions.q: True or false: In a graph database you can refer directly to a vertex by its unique ID.
questions.explain: CODASYL required an access path, but a graph also lets you use an index to find vertices with a given value.

questions.q: A team wants to write graph traversals as imperative code. Is that possible in a graph database?
options: Yes, though most also offer declarative languages such as Cypher or SPARQL
No, graph databases accept only declarative queries
No, because imperative queries were banned after CODASYL
Yes, but only through the SQL language
optionExplain: Right: imperative traversal is allowed but not required.
The chapter says you can write imperative traversals.
No such ban exists.
Graph traversal need not use SQL.
questions.explain: In a graph database, you can write your traversal in imperative code if you want to, but most graph databases also support high-level, declarative query languages such as Cypher or SPARQL.
questions.teaches: In a graph database you can write a traversal in imperative code if you want, but most graph databases also support high-level declarative query languages such as Cypher or SPARQL.

questions.q: Which query language is much older than SPARQL and Cypher and underlies them?
options: Datalog
MapReduce
XPath
The aggregation pipeline
optionExplain: Right: studied in the 1980s.
MapReduce is a processing model popularized by Google.
XPath selects parts of XML documents.
That is a recent MongoDB feature.
questions.explain: Datalog dates from the 1980s. The card says what it provides.

questions.q: In Datalog a triple (subject, predicate, object) is written predicate(subject, ____).
questions.explain: Datalog's data model is the triple-store model, generalized a bit.

questions.q: How is the fact that Idaho is within the USA written in Datalog?
options: idaho(within, usa).
(idaho, within, usa)
within(idaho, usa).
Within(Idaho, USA).
optionExplain: The predicate comes first, not the subject.
That is the triple form, not Datalog.
Right: predicate(subject, object).
Capitalized names would be variables.
questions.explain: A Datalog fact is the predicate followed by subject and object in parentheses.

questions.q: Given the facts and rules, which places does within_recursive(paris, R) return?
options: france only
france and europe
europe only
paris, france and europe
optionExplain: Rule 2 applies again and reaches europe.
Right: rule 1 gives france, and rule 2 follows france to europe.
Rule 1 also gives france.
Paris is not within itself in these facts.
questions.code:
within(paris, france).
within(france, europe).

within_recursive(P, R) :- within(P, R).
within_recursive(P, R) :- within(P, V),
                          within_recursive(V, R).

?- within_recursive(paris, R).
questions.explain: Rule 1 derives within_recursive(paris, france). Rule 2 uses within(paris, france) with within_recursive(france, europe) to derive within_recursive(paris, europe).
questions.rule: Rules derive new facts step by step.

questions.q: True or false: A Datalog rule applies if any one of the predicates on its right-hand side can be matched.
questions.explain: A rule applies only if the system can find a match for all the predicates on the right-hand side of the :- operator.

questions.q: A team has simple one-off lookups and complex reusable queries on complex data. Where does Datalog pay off most?
options: Simple one-off lookups, where it is quicker than SQL
Queries on data that has no relationships at all
Only queries that never repeat any logic
Reusable rules for complex queries, more than simple one-off lookups
optionExplain: The chapter says it is less convenient for those.
Rules matter when relationships are complex.
Reuse is what it offers.
Right: it is less convenient for simple one-offs.
questions.explain: It requires a different kind of thinking, but rules can be combined and reused in different queries; it is less convenient for simple one-off queries but can cope better if your data is complex.
questions.teaches: Datalog is less convenient for simple one-off queries, but it can cope better if the data is complex, because rules can be combined and reused in different queries.

questions.q: For which kind of application are document databases a good target?
options: Data where anything may be related to anything else
Self-contained documents with rare relationships between documents
Data that needs enforced schemas on every write
Data that must be navigated only by access paths
optionExplain: That is the graph direction.
Right: nested trees loaded whole.
That is the relational approach.
That was the network model.
questions.explain: Documents suit self-contained data. The card shows the other directions.

questions.q: Match each model to the data it targets or why it arose.
pairs: Self-contained documents, rare relationships between them
Anything is potentially related to everything
Invented to fix the many-to-many weakness of one big tree
questions.explain: Documents handle rare links, graphs handle dense links, and the relational model arose to fix trees.

questions.q: A contract-management app keeps each contract as a self-contained record that rarely refers to others. Which direction does the chapter's summary favor?
options: A graph database, since contracts are linked to people
A hierarchical database from the 1960s
A triple-store published as RDF on the web
A document database
optionExplain: Rare links do not need a graph.
That is a historical model.
Nothing in the app calls for RDF.
Right: self-contained records with rare cross-references.
questions.explain: Document databases target use cases where data comes in self-contained documents and relationships between documents are rare.

questions.q: An app starts with self-contained documents, then every feature links everything to everything. Which direction does the summary point to?
options: Toward a graph database, where anything may be related to anything
Toward duplicating each record into every document
Toward storing everything in one text file
Toward staying with documents and ignoring the links
optionExplain: Right: dense links are the graph direction.
Duplication brings consistency trouble.
That ignores the relationships.
Documents are poor with dense links.
questions.explain: Graph databases go in the opposite direction from documents, targeting use cases where anything is potentially related to everything.

questions.q: True or false: Document and graph databases enforce no schema, so their applications assume no structure in the data.
questions.explain: The application most likely still assumes a structure; it is only a question of whether the schema is explicit (enforced on write) or implicit (handled on read).

questions.q: A physics experiment produces hundreds of petabytes of data. What does the chapter say about handling data at that scale?
options: Any relational database scales to it with enough indexes
A document database stores it cheaply as nested JSON
Custom solutions are required to keep hardware cost from spiraling
The data should be stored as a graph of observations
optionExplain: The chapter says custom solutions are needed.
No such claim is made.
Right: the Large Hadron Collider is the example.
Graph storage is not offered as a fix.
questions.explain: Particle physicists have been doing Big Data-style large-scale data analysis for decades, and projects like the Large Hadron Collider now work with hundreds of petabytes; at such a scale custom solutions are required to stop the hardware cost from spiraling out of control.
questions.teaches: Particle-physics projects such as the Large Hadron Collider work with hundreds of petabytes, and at that scale custom solutions are required to stop hardware cost from spiraling out of control.

questions.section: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.q: A team must choose a database for a new app. Which knowledge helps most with that choice?
options: Only the query language, since storage details stay hidden behind it
How engines store and look up data, and which workload each one suits
Only the price per gigabyte, since engines perform alike at equal size
Only the data model, since engines for one model behave alike
optionExplain: Tempting because SQL looks the same everywhere, but the same interface can sit on very different engines.
Right: engines differ in how they write and find data, so fit to the workload decides.
Cost matters, but engines can differ a lot in speed for a given workload.
The model narrows the field, but engines for one model still differ in their write and read costs.
questions.explain: Engines differ in how they write and find data, so the best choice depends on the workload. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Choose and tune a storage engine by knowing what it does for your kind of workload.

questions.section: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.q: The two broad workload categories that storage engines are optimized for are transaction processing and ____.
questions.explain: The chapter separates engines tuned for transactions (OLTP) from engines tuned for analytics (OLAP).
questions.rule: Two workloads, two kinds of engine.

questions.section: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.q: A write-heavy app slows down after a data growth spurt. Which first step fits the chapter's advice on tuning?
options: Switch to a database with a different query language
Raise every numeric parameter to its maximum, then keep whichever setting tests best
Reason about what the engine does on each write, then judge which parameter changes that work
Rewrite the application's own storage engine from scratch
optionExplain: The query language is not where write cost lives, so this changes the wrong thing.
This guesses blindly; the chapter's point is to predict a setting's effect from what the engine does inside.
Right: a rough picture of the internals lets you imagine what a higher or lower value does.
The chapter says you will probably not implement an engine, but choose and tune one.
questions.explain: The chapter argues that knowing the internals lets you imagine the effect of a higher or lower setting.
questions.rule: Tune with a model of the engine in your head.

questions.section: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.q: True or false: Because most databases offer SQL or a similar interface, the engine's internals do not matter to the application developer.
questions.explain: The chapter argues the opposite: you must select an engine for your application and tune it for your workload, which needs a picture of what it does inside.
questions.rule: The interface hides the engine; it does not make engines equal.

questions.section: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.q: You meet an unfamiliar database engine. Which question best sorts it into one of the chapter's two OLTP families?
options: Does it only append to files, or does it overwrite fixed-size pages in place?
Does it expose SQL or a document API?
Is the data stored on a magnetic disk or on an SSD, since the family depends on the hardware?
Is it open source or commercial?
optionExplain: Right: log-structured engines only append, while page-oriented engines such as B-trees overwrite pages.
The interface does not tell the family; both families can sit behind either.
Both families run on both kinds of disk, so the hardware does not tell you the family.
Licensing says nothing about how data is laid out on disk.
questions.explain: The chapter examines two families: log-structured engines that only append, and page-oriented engines such as B-trees.
questions.teaches: Storage engines behind familiar relational and most NoSQL databases fall into two families: log-structured engines and page-oriented engines such as B-trees.

questions.section: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.q: A file stores one key-value pair per line, and every update is added at the end. Reading a key must look at...
options: Only the first line that mentions the key, because the first match is the one that counts
Only the last line of the file
Nothing; the file is rewritten so each key sits on one line
Possibly every line, to find the most recent occurrence of that key
optionExplain: The first match is the oldest version, so reading it would return stale data.
The last line holds whichever key was written last, not necessarily yours.
Appending leaves old versions in place, so repeats of a key remain.
Right: the newest value is the last occurrence, and nothing says where it is.
questions.explain: With appends only, old versions stay and the latest is the last match, which may need a full scan. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A log makes writes cheap and leaves reads scanning, which is why reads need an index.

questions.section: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.q: In this book, a log is an ____ sequence of records.
questions.explain: A log here is any append-only sequence of records, readable or binary.

questions.section: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.q: A lookup in a plain log file scans 1,000,000 records in 2 seconds. For 4,000,000 records it should take about ____ seconds.
questions.explain: A full scan is O(n), so four times the records takes four times as long: 8 seconds. A tree-style index would add only a little, and a quadratic cost would give 32.
questions.rule: O(n) means cost grows in step with records.

questions.section: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.q: Calls: db_set 42 A, then db_set 7 C, then db_set 42 B. What does the file hold, and what does db_get 42 return?
options: Two lines, because the second write to 42 overwrote the first; returns B
Three lines; db_get 42 returns A because it appears first
Three lines; db_get 42 returns B
Three lines; db_get 42 returns A and B together
optionExplain: Writes append, so the first line for 42 is still there.
The lookup takes the last occurrence, not the first.
Right: all three writes are kept, and the last occurrence of 42 wins.
The function returns only the most recent value.
questions.explain: The file keeps every write, and the lookup returns the value from the last matching line.

questions.section: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.q: True or false: Because db_set only appends, db_get can stop at the first line that matches the key, reading from the top of the file.
questions.explain: The first match is the oldest version. Since updates are appended, the latest value is the last occurrence, so the scan must go on to the end.

questions.section: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.q: A sensor system writes millions of readings a day and rarely reads them. What is the main risk of using only an append-only file?
options: Each append is slower than updating in place
The file keeps growing unless disk space is reclaimed
Old readings are overwritten and lost
Lookups return the oldest value instead of the newest
optionExplain: Appending is generally the cheapest write, so this reverses the cost.
Right: old versions stay, so space must be reclaimed or the log grows forever.
Appends never overwrite earlier records, so nothing is lost this way.
A lookup can return the newest value by taking the last occurrence.
questions.explain: Real databases must deal with reclaiming disk space so the log does not grow forever, along with concurrency control and partly written records.
questions.teaches: Real engines built on a log must also handle concurrency control, reclaiming disk space so the log does not grow forever, and partially written records.

questions.section: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.q: A table gets a second index on a column that queries often filter on. What will most likely happen?
options: Queries on that column speed up and writes get somewhat slower
Both queries and writes speed up, since the index lets the database touch less data
Writes speed up and queries stay the same
Nothing changes, because indexes sit beside the data
optionExplain: Right: the index helps reads, and each write must also update the index.
Reads gain, but each write now has one more structure to update, so writes slow down.
This reverses the effect; extra structures cost work at write time.
Sitting beside the data does not make them free to maintain.
questions.explain: Extra structures must be kept in step with the data, so reads and writes move in opposite directions. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Index what your queries need and no more, because each index taxes every write.

questions.section: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.q: True or false: An index is an additional structure derived from the primary data.
questions.explain: An index is derived data kept on the side; dropping it would not change what the database contains.

questions.section: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.q: A log table takes heavy writes and one report a month on a rarely used field. What does the chapter's trade-off suggest?
options: Index every field, since any index only helps queries
Index it, because indexes do not affect write speed if built once
Skip it, because an index would alter the report's results as well as its speed
Probably skip the index: it would slow every write to speed one rare read
optionExplain: Indexes help reads but slow writes, so more is not free.
Every later write still has to update the index.
An index changes how fast a query runs, never what it returns, so this is not a reason to skip it.
Right: the write cost is paid constantly, the read benefit rarely.
questions.explain: Every index adds write overhead, so it should earn its place from the query patterns.
questions.rule: Weigh read gain against write cost.

questions.section: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.q: A team drops an index that one nightly query used. Which effects follow? Select all that apply.
options: That nightly query gets slower
Writes get a little cheaper
Query results change
The data the index covered is deleted
optionExplain: Right: it lost its signpost and must scan more.
Right: there is one fewer structure to update on each write.
An index changes speed, not results.
The index is derived, so the primary data remains.
questions.explain: Removing an index affects performance only: the covered queries slow down and writes speed up.
questions.rule: Dropping an index never changes contents.

questions.section: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.q: A pipeline only appends events and a weekly batch job scans all of them. Which design matches the chapter's reasoning?
options: Index every field, so the weekly job can skip the records it does not need to read
Index one field, because an index makes appends cheaper
Rewrite records in sorted order on every append
No index: appending is the cheapest write and a weekly full scan is tolerable
optionExplain: The job reads everything, so the indexes help nothing and still cost something on every write.
Appending to a file is already the simplest write, and an index makes it slower.
That is far more work per write than the pipeline needs.
Right: an index would only add write overhead for no gain here.
questions.explain: For writes it is hard to beat simply appending to a file, the simplest possible write, and any index adds work on top.
questions.teaches: Appending to a file is the simplest possible write and hard to beat; any kind of index usually slows it down.

questions.q: To speed up key lookups in an append-only file, what could an index remember for each key?
options: A copy of every older version of the value
Where in the file its newest value starts
The key's rank among all keys in sorted order
A count of how many times it was written
optionExplain: Older versions are not needed to answer a lookup.
Right: with a location you can seek straight to the value.
A hash map does not keep keys sorted.
A count says nothing about where to read.
questions.explain: A pointer to the newest value is enough to turn a scan into a seek. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Map each key to its newest offset in memory, so a lookup is one hash probe plus one seek.

questions.q: In a Bitcask-style index, each key maps to a byte ____ in the data file.
questions.explain: The map stores where the newest value for each key begins, as a byte offset.

questions.q: A server has 16 GB of RAM, 10 million keys and 2 TB of values. Does a Bitcask-style engine fit?
options: Yes: only the keys and offsets need RAM, and values are read from disk
No, because all values must also fit in memory
No, because a hash map must be larger than the data it indexes, so the values would not fit
Yes, but only if the whole data file is in the filesystem cache
optionExplain: Right: the hash map holds keys, not values.
Values are loaded from disk by a single seek.
The map holds only keys and offsets, which are small next to the values it points to.
The cache helps speed but is not required for it to work.
questions.explain: Memory must hold the keys; values can be far larger.
questions.rule: Size RAM by keys, not by values.

questions.q: A key is updated, and the new record lands at offset 9000. What must the engine do to its hash map?
options: Nothing, since reads take the last occurrence anyway
Add a second entry and keep the old offset too
Point that key's entry at offset 9000
Erase the old record so the offset stays valid
optionExplain: That is how a scan works; the map only knows what it was told.
One entry per key keeps the lookup unambiguous and small.
Right: the map always holds the newest offset for each key.
Segments are never edited after writing; the old record just becomes stale.
questions.explain: Each append updates the map, for new keys and updated ones alike.
questions.rule: Update the map on every append.

questions.q: True or false: In a Bitcask-style store only the keys have to fit in memory, while the values can use more space than there is memory.
questions.explain: The hash map holds keys and offsets; each value is loaded from disk with one seek.
questions.rule: Keys in RAM, values on disk.

questions.q: A hot key in a Bitcask-style store is read repeatedly and its region of the file sits in the filesystem cache. How many disk reads does a read need?
options: One disk seek every time, since values live on disk
Two, one for the map and one for the value
None: the offset lookup is in memory and the data comes from the cache
One scan of the segment, to confirm the offset is still current before reading
optionExplain: One seek is the worst case; a cached region needs none.
The map lives in memory, so it needs no disk read.
Right: no disk I/O is needed when the region is already cached.
The map already holds the newest offset, so no confirming scan is needed.
questions.explain: If that part of the data file is already in the filesystem cache, a read does not need disk I/O at all.
questions.rule: Cached regions cost no disk I/O.
questions.teaches: If the needed part of the data file is already in the filesystem cache, a Bitcask-style read needs no disk I/O at all.

questions.q: Which workload would a store keeping all keys in RAM and appending updates to disk handle most comfortably?
options: A hundred billion distinct keys, each written only once and never read again
A million counters, each incremented thousands of times a day
Wide range scans over consecutive keys
Rare writes with huge numbers of distinct keys
optionExplain: Far too many keys for memory, and no repeated writes for the design to exploit.
Right: many writes per key, but few distinct keys.
A hash map does not order keys, so ranges are costly.
Rare writes and a key count beyond RAM fit it poorly.
questions.explain: The design rewards repeated writes to a limited key set. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Many writes per key and few keys fit a hash-indexed log.

questions.q: True or false: The book's example of a good fit for a Bitcask-style engine is a counter of plays for each video, updated on every play.
questions.explain: Many writes per key and not too many distinct keys make it feasible to keep every key in memory.

questions.q: A shop wants page-view counts for 50,000 products, incremented on every view. Which engine fits the chapter's reasoning?
options: A design that needs the whole key set sorted on disk
A full-text index, because the counts are searchable
None of them; 50,000 keys is too many for any index that lives in memory
A hash-indexed log, as keys are few and each is updated very often
optionExplain: Sorting is not needed to count views and costs more per write.
Counting views is not a text search problem.
50,000 keys take very little memory, so this fear is misplaced.
Right: 50,000 keys fit easily in RAM and every write is a cheap append.
questions.explain: Few keys and heavy rewrites suit a hash-indexed log.
questions.rule: Match the engine to keys per write.

questions.q: Your key count grows a thousandfold while writes per key stay the same. What is the first constraint to fail?
options: The hash map no longer fits in available memory
Appends become random writes
Compaction stops being possible
Lookups need a disk seek per segment file
optionExplain: Right: the design requires all keys in RAM.
Appends stay sequential however many keys exist.
Compaction depends on segments, not on the key count.
Segment lookups use in-memory maps, so seeks do not multiply with keys.
questions.explain: The key count sets the memory the index needs.

questions.q: Sort each workload by whether a hash-indexed log suits it.

items.t: Video play counters, updated on every play
Session tokens updated on each request, a few thousand live
Scanning all keys between kitty00000 and kitty99999
Trillions of distinct keys each written once
Per-user last-seen timestamp for 200,000 users

questions.explain: It suits few keys with many writes each. Range scans and key counts beyond RAM are where it fails.
questions.rule: Fit follows key count and access pattern.

questions.q: A service keeps one record per active chat room, updated with every message, 100,000 rooms open at a time. Which statement is right?
options: Fits only if rooms are queried in sorted name order
Does not fit, because updates must overwrite records in place
Does not fit, because 100,000 keys exceed what memory holds
Fits: few keys, each updated often, so all keys fit in RAM
optionExplain: Sorted order is a weakness of hash maps, not a need here.
The design appends; it never overwrites in place.
100,000 keys are tiny next to typical RAM.
Right: this matches the write-heavy, few-keys profile.
questions.explain: Update-heavy loads on a limited key set are the sweet spot: the index grows with distinct keys, not with the number of writes.
questions.teaches: The memory a hash-indexed log needs depends on the number of distinct keys, not on how many writes arrive, so a high write rate alone does not break it.

questions.q: An append-only file keeps growing as keys are updated. Which idea reclaims space without stopping the system?
options: Cut the log into pieces and keep only the newest value per key in the background
Overwrite the old value in place as each update arrives, so that the file never grows at all
Stop writes until the file has been rewritten
Delete the oldest lines of the file regularly
optionExplain: Right: closing old pieces and compacting them frees space while serving requests.
That abandons the append-only design rather than managing its growth.
Pausing writes is not needed; merging can run in the background.
Old lines may still hold the only value of a key.
questions.explain: Compaction discards stale versions while the system keeps serving.
questions.rule: Cut the log into segments, then compact and merge frozen ones in the background.

questions.q: Throwing away duplicate keys in the log and keeping only the most recent update for each key is called ____.
questions.explain: That is the definition of compaction.
questions.rule: Compaction keeps the latest per key.

questions.q: A segment holds 1,000 writes to 10 distinct keys. After compaction, how many records remain?
options: 1,000, since compaction only rewrites the file
10, one latest value per key
1, the single newest write overall
500, as compaction keeps every second write
optionExplain: Compaction removes duplicates, so the count falls.
Right: compaction keeps only the most recent update per key.
One value is kept per key, not per segment.
It keeps the latest per key, not a fixed fraction.
questions.explain: One latest record per distinct key remains.

questions.q: Put the steps of merging frozen segments in order.
items: Merge and compact the old segments in a background thread, into a new file
Keep serving reads and writes from the old segment files meanwhile
Switch read requests to the merged segment when it is done
Delete the old segment files
questions.explain: Merging runs in the background while old files serve requests; only afterwards do reads switch and old files go.
questions.rule: Serve from old files until the new one is ready.

questions.q: True or false: During a merge, the engine writes the merged result to a new file and leaves the old segments unchanged until the switch-over.
questions.explain: Segments are never modified after being written; reads switch to the merged segment when it is ready, and then the old files are deleted.
questions.rule: Write a new file; switch over; delete the old.

questions.q: A log is split into 100 MB segments. Which change makes compaction pay off least?
options: A key being overwritten several times within one segment
Merging several small segments together into one
Writes touch mostly distinct keys, each only once
Running the merge in a background thread
optionExplain: That is where compaction shrinks segments the most.
Merging fewer, larger files is what keeps lookups short.
Right: with few overwrites, compaction finds little to remove.
Where it runs affects interference, not how much space it frees.
questions.explain: Compaction often makes segments much smaller, assuming a key is overwritten several times on average within one segment.
questions.teaches: Compaction shrinks segments a lot only if a key is overwritten several times on average within a segment, so its payoff depends on the overwrite rate.

questions.q: A key has been written in several segment files over time. Where should a read look first to get the current value?
options: The oldest segment, since it holds the key's first value
All segments at once, taking the largest value
The most recent segment
Any segment, since they all agree after compaction
optionExplain: The first value may be stale by now.
Values are not ordered by size.
Right: the newest segment holds the newest value.
Compaction works within segments; different segments can disagree.
questions.explain: Newer segments hold newer values, so start there. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Search segments from newest to oldest, and keep their number down by merging.

questions.q: True or false: Each segment has its own in-memory hash table mapping keys to file offsets.
questions.explain: Each frozen segment keeps its own map, and a read checks them from newest to oldest.

questions.q: Segments S1 (oldest), S2 and S3 (newest) exist. Key k is in S1 and S2 only. A read for k is answered by segment ____.
questions.explain: The search goes from newest to oldest and stops at the first hit; S3 lacks k, so S2 answers and the older copy in S1 is stale.

questions.q: Merging stops, and segments pile up from 10 to 400. What happens to lookups for keys that are rarely written?
options: They get faster, since each segment is smaller
They may check many more maps before finding the key
They stay equal, since every segment's map is held in memory and probes are instant
They fail, because old segments are deleted
optionExplain: More files means more maps to check, not fewer.
Right: with more segments, a read may probe many hash maps.
In-memory probes are cheap, but each extra segment still adds one more probe.
Nothing is deleted without a merge.
questions.explain: Merging keeps the number of segments small so lookups check few maps.

questions.q: True or false: A read must check every segment's hash map, because any of them could hold a newer value than the others.
questions.explain: Newer segments hold newer values, so the read stops at the first (newest) segment that has the key.

questions.q: A store merges only adjacent segments. Why does that keep a key's newest value in the right place?
options: All values in one segment are newer than all values in an adjacent older one
Adjacent segments never share keys
The merge keeps the larger value, so recency does not matter between adjacent segments
Old segments are deleted before merging starts
optionExplain: Right: so the newer segment's value wins when a key appears in both.
They can, and merging resolves those duplicates.
Merging goes by recency, not by the size of a value.
Old segments are deleted only after the merge completes.
questions.explain: Each segment holds the writes of a period, so within adjacent segments one is entirely newer than the other.
questions.rule: Merge adjacent segments, keep the newer value.
questions.teaches: Each segment contains all the values written during some period, so when merging adjacent segments, all values in one are more recent than all in the other.

questions.q: In an append-only log, how can a key be deleted?
options: Erase its lines from the segment files straight away
Append a special record that marks the key as deleted
Drop it from the in-memory hash map and rely on that alone
Rewrite the whole log without the key before returning
optionExplain: Segments are written once and left unchanged.
Right: nothing is erased in place, so the delete is itself a new record.
The map is lost on restart and rebuilt from the files, which would bring the key back.
That is a heavy rewrite for a single delete, and the design avoids it.
questions.explain: Deletion is recorded as one more append, like every other change. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Delete by appending a marker and let the merge drop the earlier values.

questions.q: A special deletion record appended to a log is sometimes called a ____.
questions.explain: The tombstone tells the merge process to discard earlier values for the key.
questions.rule: A delete is a tombstone record.

questions.q: Segment S1 holds key k with value 5. A newer segment holds a tombstone for k. What happens to the old value when they merge?
options: It is kept, since S1 is frozen and cannot change
It is kept in the new file but marked inactive
It is discarded, as the tombstone tells the merge to drop earlier values
It overwrites the tombstone, since in a merge the older record of a key wins ties
optionExplain: S1 is not changed, but the merge writes a new file without the value.
The merge discards earlier values for the key.
Right: that is the tombstone's job during merging.
Newer records win, so the tombstone beats the older value, not the other way round.
questions.explain: A merge applies the tombstone by dropping earlier values for the key.

questions.q: Suppose a delete only removed a key from the in-memory hash map. What could happen after a restart? (our reading of the design)
options: The map is rebuilt from the segment files, so the deleted key could reappear
Nothing, since the segments forget keys that were deleted from the map on their own
All other keys would be lost as well
The restart would fail, because the map and files disagree
optionExplain: Right: the files still hold its value, and rebuilding reads them.
Segments hold whatever was appended and forget nothing, so the old value is still there.
