Only the unrecorded delete is lost, not the other keys.
The engine would simply rebuild the map from the files.
questions.explain: Recording the delete in the log makes it durable; the map is only a cache of the log.
questions.rule: Make deletes durable in the log.

questions.q: True or false: To delete a key in a segmented log, the engine appends a deletion record instead of editing the closed segments.
questions.explain: Segments are never modified after being written, so the delete is recorded as a new tombstone record, and merging later drops the old values.
questions.rule: Append a marker; do not edit.

questions.q: Why might a log engine prefer length-prefixed binary records to CSV-like text lines?
options: Binary records are always smaller than text
Text lines cannot be appended to a file
Binary records let the engine keep the keys sorted without a separate sort step
The length comes first, then raw bytes, so no escaping is needed
optionExplain: Binary can be smaller, but the book's reason is simplicity and speed without escaping.
Text lines append fine; the earlier examples did exactly that.
The record format has no bearing on key order, which a log does not maintain.
Right: this is faster and simpler than escaping commas and newlines in text.
questions.explain: CSV is not the best log format; a binary format encodes the length of a string in bytes and then the raw string, avoiding escaping.
questions.teaches: A log's file format is better binary than CSV: first the length of a string in bytes, then the raw string, with no need for escaping.

questions.q: After a restart, the in-memory hash maps of a log store are gone. How can they be rebuilt?
options: Load them from the application's cache
Replay only the newest segment, since it holds all the current keys and offsets
Read each segment from start to end, noting the newest offset of every key
They cannot be rebuilt; data must be reimported
optionExplain: The application cache is not part of the storage engine.
Older segments may hold keys that were never rewritten, so skipping them loses keys.
Right: the files still hold everything, and the last occurrence wins.
The log files contain all that is needed.
questions.explain: The log is the source of truth, so the maps can be rebuilt by reading it. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Persist a snapshot of the index and checksum every record to make restarts fast and safe.

questions.q: Bitcask speeds up recovery by storing a ____ of each segment's hash map on disk.
questions.explain: Loading a snapshot into memory is faster than reading the whole segment again.

questions.q: A store with 400 GB of segments takes hours to restart. Which change targets that delay?
options: Add a checksum to every record so that corruption is detected on restart
Save a snapshot of each segment's map and load it on restart
Use a single writer thread
Merge all segments into one file
optionExplain: Checksums detect damaged records but do not shorten the rescan of the segment files.
Right: the map loads from the snapshot instead of rescanning the data.
The writer count affects concurrency, not restart time.
A merge shrinks files but still needs the map rebuilt.
questions.explain: A snapshot saves rescanning the segments on every restart.

questions.q: The server crashes halfway through appending a record. What lets the engine cope after restart?
options: A checksum on the record exposes the corrupted tail so it can be ignored
The hash map snapshot, since it contains the partial record
The single writer thread, which prevents half-written appends
Compaction, which rewrites the broken record on the next merge
optionExplain: Right: Bitcask files include checksums for this purpose.
A snapshot is a copy of the map and cannot repair a broken record.
One writer avoids concurrent writers, not a crash mid-append.
Compaction would copy the broken bytes if nothing flagged them.
questions.explain: Checksums let the engine detect and ignore corrupted parts of the log.

questions.q: True or false: Storing a snapshot of the hash map removes the need for checksums on records.
questions.explain: They solve different problems: the snapshot speeds recovery of the index, while checksums detect records that were only partly written.
questions.rule: Snapshot is speed; checksum is safety.

questions.q: Why can a Bitcask-style store use one writer thread and still serve many concurrent readers?
options: Readers lock the entire log while writing
A hash map cannot be read while it is being updated
The single writer thread also serves every read request, handling them one after another
Writes are sequential appends and segment files are immutable, so reads can overlap
optionExplain: Readers do not lock the log; immutability is what removes the need.
The point is that the data files are safe to read at once.
Reads run on multiple threads, in parallel with the writer.
Right: immutable files can be read concurrently by several threads.
questions.explain: Because writes arrive in a strictly sequential order, one writer thread is a common choice, and append-only segments can be read by many threads at once.
questions.rule: Single writer, many readers on immutable files.
questions.teaches: As writes are appended in strict sequence, a common choice is a single writer thread, while the immutable segment files can be read concurrently by multiple threads.

questions.q: Appending new values instead of overwriting old ones seems wasteful. What is a real advantage of appending?
options: It uses less disk space than updating in place
It makes reads faster because the data stays in order on disk, so no index is needed
Writes go to the end of a file in sequence, generally faster than random writes
It removes the need for any background work
optionExplain: It uses more, until stale values are compacted away.
Reads need an index; appending alone gives no read speedup.
Right: sequential writes beat random ones, especially on spinning disks.
Merging and compaction are still needed to reclaim space.
questions.explain: The advantage is in how the disk is written, not in space or reads. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Sequential writes are fast, and files that are never edited are easy to make safe.

questions.q: Appending and segment merging are ____ writes, generally much faster than random writes on spinning disks.
questions.explain: Sequential writes avoid moving the disk head around for each update.

questions.q: A crash happens while a value is being overwritten in place. Which risk does an append-only design avoid?
options: Losing every record written before the crash
Having to read the whole file to find any key, since overwriting scatters old values
Running out of memory for the index
A file holding part of the old value spliced with part of the new
optionExplain: Earlier data is intact; the worry is a single value half-written.
That is a lookup cost and does not come from overwriting in place.
Memory use is unrelated to how values are written.
Right: immutable segments leave no half-updated records among old data.
questions.explain: Crash recovery is simpler when segment files are append-only or immutable.
questions.rule: No in-place edits, no spliced values.

questions.q: The log moves from a spinning disk to an SSD. How does the book expect the benefit of sequential writes to change?
options: It disappears completely, as SSDs have no seek time
It shrinks, but sequential writes are still to some extent preferable
It grows, as SSDs punish random writes even more
It reverses, so overwriting in place becomes faster because flash needs no seeks
optionExplain: The book says sequential writes remain somewhat preferable on SSDs.
Right: the book says this holds to some extent on SSDs.
The effect is stronger on spinning disks.
Nothing in the book says in-place updates win on SSDs.
questions.explain: Sequential writes are preferred mostly on magnetic disks and to some extent on SSDs.
questions.rule: The gain is biggest on spinning disks.

questions.q: True or false: The main reason for an append-only design is that it uses less disk space than overwriting values in place.
questions.explain: Appending uses more space until compaction. The reasons given are fast sequential writes and simpler concurrency and crash recovery.
questions.rule: Appending trades space for speed and simplicity.

questions.q: After years of merging, will a segment-merging store's data files be fragmented?
options: No: merging old segments avoids data files getting fragmented over time
Yes, since each append leaves a gap in the file that is never filled in again
Yes, since overwritten values leave holes
Only on SSDs, where merges cannot run
optionExplain: Right: merging rewrites the surviving records into fresh compact segments.
Appends are written contiguously at the end, so they leave no gaps.
Nothing is overwritten in place, so overwriting leaves no holes in the segment files.
Merging works the same on both kinds of disk.
questions.explain: A third reason for the design: merging old segments avoids fragmentation.
questions.teaches: Merging old segments avoids the problem of data files getting fragmented over time.

questions.q: Which query is hardest for an index that maps each key to a file offset in a hash table?
options: Fetch the record for one exact key
Update the value of one exact key, since every update has to be appended first
Count how many writes have occurred
Fetch all records with keys between two bounds
optionExplain: That is exactly what a hash lookup does well.
An update is an append plus a map update, which a hash index handles easily.
This does not depend on key order.
Right: a hash map does not keep neighbouring keys together.
questions.explain: Hash tables answer exact lookups; they do not order keys. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Hash-indexed logs serve exact-key lookups on a key set that fits in RAM and little else.

questions.q: True or false: Range queries over a hash-indexed log are not efficient.
questions.explain: You cannot easily scan a key range, so you would look up each key individually.

questions.q: To scan every key from kitty00000 to kitty99999 with a hash index, you must make ____ individual lookups, if every key exists.
questions.explain: The range holds 100,000 keys, and the hash maps cannot return them as a range, so each is looked up on its own.

questions.q: Your keys outgrow RAM. Why not move the hash map to disk?
options: A hash map cannot be stored on disk at all
It is difficult to make an on-disk hash map perform well
Disk reads are slower than RAM reads, so any map kept on disk would be unusable
The data file would stop being append-only
optionExplain: It can be, but performance suffers.
Right: the book says so, and gives reasons.
Disk is slower, but the book names specific problems: random I/O, costly growth and collisions.
The data file stays append-only; the map is the problem.
questions.explain: An on-disk hash map needs lots of random access I/O.
questions.rule: Do not just spill the map to disk.

questions.q: True or false: A hash-indexed log is a good fit for a reporting query that sums values over a date range of consecutive keys.
questions.explain: That is a range query, which a hash index does not serve efficiently.

questions.q: A team proposes keeping the hash map on disk. Which problems does the book name? Select all that apply.
options: Lots of random access I/O
Values can no longer be larger than memory
Growing the map is expensive once it is full
Hash collisions need fiddly logic
optionExplain: Right: this is the first cost named.
Values are already read from disk, so this is not one of them.
Right: growing a full on-disk hash map is one of the problems the book names.
Right: collisions need fiddly logic, which the book also names.
questions.explain: On-disk hash maps need a lot of random I/O, are expensive to grow when full, and need fiddly collision handling.
questions.teaches: An on-disk hash map requires a lot of random access I/O, is expensive to grow when it becomes full, and needs fiddly logic for hash collisions.

questions.q: What change to the format of log segments could make later merges and lookups easier?
options: Require the key-value pairs to be sorted by key
Store each key's value in a separate file so that every lookup opens exactly one file
Sort pairs by the time they were written
Pad every record to the same length
optionExplain: Right: this is the SSTable idea.
That multiplies files without ordering anything.
Time order is how a plain log already works.
Fixed length could help binary search but does not give key order.
questions.explain: Key order is what the later techniques build on. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: An SSTable is a segment sorted by key with one entry per key.

questions.q: SSTable stands for Sorted String ____.
questions.explain: An SSTable is a segment file sorted by key.

questions.q: Which sequence of key-value pairs could be a merged SSTable segment?
options: apple 1, cherry 3, banana 2
apple 1, apple 2, banana 3
apple 1, banana 2, cherry 3
cherry 3, apple 1, banana 2
optionExplain: The keys are out of order.
A merged SSTable has each key only once.
Right: sorted by key, each key once.
Written in arrival order, not sorted by key.
questions.explain: A merged SSTable is sorted by key and each key appears once.

questions.q: A segment is rewritten as a sorted-by-key SSTable. Which capability does that layout now make efficient?
options: Keeping all keys in memory for faster lookups, as the old hash index did
Duplicate keys inside one segment
Sorting by value, so top results come first
Efficient range queries, since neighbouring keys sit together
optionExplain: Sorted segments reduce the need for a full in-memory index rather than rely on one.
A merged SSTable keeps each key only once.
The segments are sorted by key, not by value, so top values do not come first.
Right: sorted data keeps a key range contiguous.
questions.explain: Sorted order enables range scans and simpler merges.

questions.q: True or false: In a merged SSTable segment, each key appears only once.
questions.explain: The compaction process already ensures that each key appears only once within a merged segment.

questions.q: In a plain log segment with a hash index, what does the order of pairs in the file affect?
options: Which value wins for a repeated key, because later values take precedence
Whether binary search can find a key
Whether range queries are efficient
How fast two segments can be merged, since merging needs an ordered scan of both
optionExplain: Right: apart from that, the order does not matter.
Plain segments are not sorted, so binary search is unavailable.
Order of writing does not group keys by range.
Without sorting, merging has no ordered scan to use, and arrival order does not provide one.
questions.explain: In a plain segment, later values take precedence over earlier ones for the same key; apart from that, order does not matter.
questions.rule: Order only decides who wins ties.
questions.teaches: In a plain log segment, values later in the log take precedence over earlier values for the same key, and apart from that the order of the pairs does not matter.

questions.q: Two sorted files must be combined into one sorted file without loading both into memory. What approach fits?
options: Load the larger file into memory and insert the keys of the smaller file into it
Read both from the start, repeatedly copy the smaller front key to the output
Concatenate them and sort the result in memory
Pick one file and discard the other
optionExplain: This needs the larger file in memory, which the question rules out.
Right: this is how mergesort merges, using only sequential reads.
This too needs everything in memory.
Discarding one file loses all of its data, so the output would not be a merge.
questions.explain: Sorted inputs let you merge with a single pass over each. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Merge sorted files by repeatedly copying the lowest current key, newest segment winning ties.

questions.q: Merging SSTables is like the approach used in the ____ algorithm.
questions.explain: You read the inputs side by side and copy the lowest key each time.

questions.q: Older segment: apple 1, cat 4, dog 7. Newer segment: cat 9, eel 2. What is the merged output, in order?
options: apple 1, cat 4, dog 7, eel 2
apple 1, cat 4, cat 9, dog 7, eel 2
apple 1, cat 9, dog 7, eel 2
cat 9, eel 2, apple 1, dog 7
optionExplain: This keeps the older cat value.
A key appears once in the output.
Right: sorted by key, and the newer cat value wins.
This is not in key order.
questions.explain: Copy the lowest key each step; for a repeated key, take the newer segment's value.

questions.q: Each input file is five times larger than the machine's memory. What happens to the merge?
options: It fails, since both input files must be held in memory while their keys are compared
It works only if one file is smaller than memory
It still works: inputs are read sequentially and only the current keys are held
It needs a hash map for every key in both files
optionExplain: The merge reads the files side by side, not all at once.
Neither file needs to fit in memory, since the merge reads them side by side.
Right: it does not need the files in memory.
Sorting removes the need for a hash map here.
questions.explain: The merge reads sequentially, so size is not limited by memory.
questions.rule: Merging streams; it does not load.

questions.q: True or false: When the same key appears in two input segments of a merge, the engine keeps whichever value is larger.
questions.explain: It keeps the value from the most recent segment, discarding values in older segments.

questions.q: The merged output of several SSTable segments is a new file. What property does that new file have?
options: It is unsorted, since inputs were interleaved
It is also sorted by key, so it can itself be merged again
It keeps all older versions of each key, so that no data from the inputs is lost
It must be small enough to fit in memory
optionExplain: The merge writes keys in sorted order.
Right: the output is a valid sorted segment.
Only the most recent value of each key is retained.
The merge writes sequentially, so size is not bounded by memory.
questions.explain: The merge produces a new merged segment file, also sorted by key.
questions.rule: Output of a merge is again an SSTable.
questions.teaches: The result of merging SSTables is itself a segment sorted by key, so merges can be repeated on their own output.

questions.q: A file is sorted by key. You know the offsets of keys handbag and handsome. How can you find handiwork?
options: Jump to handbag and scan forward, since handiwork lies between the two
Scan from the start of the file
Look in the hash map for its exact offset, then read the record directly
Look up handiwork in a hash table holding every key
optionExplain: Right: sorting guarantees it sits between them.
This ignores what the sorting tells you.
There is no per-key map in this design; the sorting is what narrows the search.
The design avoids a per-key table; sorting makes it unnecessary.
questions.explain: Sorting narrows the key to the gap between two indexed keys. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Index a few keys, jump near the target, and scan the short gap.

questions.q: True or false: An SSTable's in-memory index may be sparse, with only one key for every few kilobytes of segment file.
questions.explain: A few kilobytes can be scanned very quickly, so denser indexes are not needed.

questions.q: Index entries: handbag at offset 4000 and handsome at offset 8000. A lookup for handiwork starts scanning at offset ____.
questions.explain: Handiwork sorts between the two indexed keys, so the scan starts at the earlier one, offset 4000, and ends before 8000.
questions.rule: Jump to the nearest indexed key before the target.

questions.q: You make the index ten times sparser. What is the main effect?
options: Lookups get faster, because there is less index to search
The segment must now be unsorted
Writes get slower, since the index must be rebuilt per write
The index shrinks, but each lookup has more data to scan
optionExplain: Fewer entries mean longer gaps to scan.
Sorting is what makes any sparse index work.
The index is built when the segment is written.
Right: fewer index entries mean longer gaps.
questions.explain: Sparseness trades memory for scan length.

questions.q: True or false: A sparse index can only work if the segment holds one key for every record in the index.
questions.explain: The point of sparseness is that most keys are not in the index; sorting lets you find them by scanning the gap.

questions.q: When could an SSTable skip the in-memory index entirely and use binary search on the file?
options: If all keys and values had a fixed size
If the file were smaller than the filesystem cache
If keys were hashed first
If every key were unique
optionExplain: Right: then you can compute where any record starts.
Cache size does not help locate record boundaries.
Hashing would break the sort order.
Uniqueness holds anyway and does not give record boundaries.
questions.explain: Variable-length records make it hard to tell where one record ends and the next starts without an index.
questions.teaches: If all keys and values had a fixed size, you could binary-search the segment file and need no in-memory index, but real records are variable-length, which makes record boundaries hard to find.

questions.q: A lookup scans a few neighbouring key-value pairs after jumping to the index. What could reduce disk use for them?
options: Compress the whole segment as one stream
Store each record in its own separate file so that each can be compressed alone
Remove the sparse index
Compress each block of neighbouring records and index the block start
optionExplain: Then the sparse index could not jump into the middle.
This adds overhead and shrinks nothing useful.
Then every lookup needs a full scan.
Right: the scan reads the whole block anyway.
questions.explain: Grouping makes compression fit the access pattern. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Compress per block and point each sparse index entry at a block start.

questions.q: Each entry of the sparse in-memory index points at the start of a ____ block.
questions.explain: The index points at the start of a compressed block, not a single record.

questions.q: A block holds 200 records and compresses to a third of its size. A lookup needs one record. What does it read?
options: Only the one record, as the index knows its offset
The whole compressed block, then decompresses to find the record
The entire segment file, since the index only says which segment holds the key
Only the first record in the block
optionExplain: The sparse index points to blocks, not single records.
Right: the index points to the block start.
The sparse index points to a block start, so only that block is read.
The needed record may be elsewhere in the block.
questions.explain: A read decompresses the block it lands in and scans inside it.

questions.q: Block size grows from 4 KB to 4 MB. What happens to a single-key lookup?
options: It gets faster, because there are fewer index entries to keep in memory and search
It stays the same, since compression is free
It decompresses and scans far more data, so lookups get slower
It fails, since blocks cannot exceed 64 KB
optionExplain: The index shrinks, but each read now decompresses and scans far more data.
Decompression has a cost per block.
Right: bigger blocks mean more work per read.
The book gives no such limit.
questions.explain: Block size trades index size against per-read work.

questions.q: True or false: Compressing blocks in an SSTable saves disk space but cannot reduce I/O bandwidth use.
questions.explain: Compressed blocks are smaller on disk, so reading them also uses less I/O bandwidth.

questions.q: Besides saving disk space, what else does compressing SSTable blocks help with?
options: It removes the need for a sparse index
It keeps the keys in sorted order
It reduces the use of I/O bandwidth
It makes merging unnecessary
optionExplain: The index is still needed to find the block.
Order comes from the sort, not compression.
Right: less data moves between disk and memory.
Merging is still needed to reclaim space.
questions.explain: Besides saving disk space, compression also reduces the I/O bandwidth use.
questions.teaches: Besides saving disk space, compressing blocks also reduces the use of I/O bandwidth.

questions.q: Writes arrive in random key order, but the files on disk must be sorted. Where can sorting be done cheaply?
options: On disk, by reordering the sorted file again after every single write
In memory, in a balanced tree, before data is written out
In the application, before the write is sent
At read time, by sorting the segments for each query
optionExplain: Rewriting a sorted file per write is very costly.
Right: sorted structures are easy to maintain in memory.
The engine cannot rely on clients to order keys.
That moves the work to every read.
questions.explain: Sorting is easy in memory and awkward on disk. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Sort in memory, flush sorted runs to disk, and merge them in the background.

questions.q: Put the LSM write path in order.
items: A write is added to the in-memory balanced tree
The tree grows past a threshold of a few megabytes
The tree is written out as a new SSTable, the newest segment
Background merging later combines segments
questions.explain: Writes land in the memtable, a full memtable is flushed as the newest SSTable, and merges follow in the background.

questions.q: A read arrives for key k. In which order does the engine look?
options: Oldest segment first, then newer ones, then the memtable
Newest segment, then the memtable, then older segments
Memtable, then the newest segment, then older segments
All segments in parallel, then the memtable
optionExplain: Looking at the oldest segment first would find stale values before the newest ones.
The memtable holds the newest writes and comes first.
Right: newest data is checked first.
The order matters because newer values override older ones.
questions.explain: The memtable holds the newest values, so it goes first.

questions.q: While a full memtable is being written out as an SSTable, new writes keep arriving. Where do they go?
options: Into a new memtable instance
Into the memtable being written out, which is reopened
They wait until the SSTable is finished
Straight to the newest SSTable on disk
optionExplain: Right: writes continue without waiting for the flush.
The one being flushed must stay unchanged.
The design lets writes continue into a new memtable, so they never wait for the flush.
SSTables are not edited after writing.
questions.explain: A fresh memtable takes new writes during the flush.
questions.rule: Flush one tree while filling another.

questions.q: True or false: To serve a read, the engine checks the oldest on-disk segment first and works towards the newest.
questions.explain: It checks the memtable, then the most recent segment, then older ones, because newer values take precedence.

questions.q: Why can a full memtable be written out as an SSTable efficiently?
options: The memtable is stored on disk already
SSTables need not be sorted when first written, because merging sorts them later
A hash map in the memtable orders the keys on the way out
The tree already keeps the pairs sorted, so one sequential pass writes them out
optionExplain: The memtable lives in memory; the flush is what writes it out to disk.
Sorted order is the defining property of an SSTable; merging relies on it and does not create it.
A balanced tree, not a hash map, keeps the order.
Right: no extra sorting step is needed.
questions.explain: The tree already maintains the key-value pairs sorted by key.
questions.rule: The tree keeps order, so a flush is one pass.
questions.teaches: A full memtable can be written out as an SSTable efficiently because the balanced tree already keeps its key-value pairs sorted by key.

questions.q: A key-value engine holds recent writes only in memory. After a crash, what is at risk?
options: Every segment already on disk
Only the oldest segments, because merges were running
Writes in memory that have not yet been written to disk
Nothing, since memory is restored by the operating system
optionExplain: Flushed segments are on disk and survive.
Merges work on files and do not cause this loss.
Right: flushed data is safe, but memory is lost on a crash.
Memory contents do not survive a crash.
questions.explain: Whatever was never written to disk is gone. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Log every write first, and drop the log once its memtable is flushed.

questions.q: Once the memtable is written out as an SSTable, the corresponding log can be ____.
questions.explain: Its job is done once the data is safe in an SSTable.

questions.q: After a crash, how does the engine restore the memtable?
options: By reading the newest SSTable back into memory
By reading the separate log of writes
By asking a client to resend its writes
By merging all segments
optionExplain: The newest SSTable lacks the writes that were still in memory.
Right: that log exists for this purpose.
The engine cannot depend on clients.
Merging cannot recover writes that never reached a segment.
questions.explain: The log is replayed to rebuild the memtable.

questions.q: A team skips the log to save a sequential write per update. What does a crash now cost them?
options: Every write since the last flush
Every write ever made
Only the most recent single write
Nothing, as the SSTables can rebuild it
optionExplain: Right: those writes were only in the memtable.
Flushed SSTables persist on disk, so only the unflushed writes are at risk.
All unflushed writes are lost, not just one.
SSTables hold only the flushed data, so they cannot rebuild the lost memtable contents.
questions.explain: Without the log, the memtable's contents die with the process.
questions.rule: The log buys durability for unflushed writes.

questions.q: True or false: The recovery log can be discarded each time its memtable has been written out as an SSTable.
questions.explain: Once the data is safe in an SSTable, the log has done its job, and SSTables stand alone.
questions.rule: Discard the log after a flush.

questions.q: Why does the memtable's recovery log not need to be sorted by key?
options: Sorted logs cannot be appended to
Reads consult the log before the memtable
The log is merged into the SSTables afterwards, so it must already be in key order
Its only purpose is to restore the memtable after a crash
optionExplain: They can; they are just awkward to build.
Reads do not use the log.
The log is discarded after a flush, not merged.
Right: the memtable does the sorting when it is rebuilt.
questions.explain: That log is not in sorted order, but that does not matter because its only purpose is to restore the memtable.
questions.rule: Unsorted is fine for a replay log.
questions.teaches: The recovery log is not in sorted order, which does not matter because its only purpose is to restore the memtable after a crash.

questions.q: Which description fits a Log-Structured Merge-Tree storage engine?
options: It overwrites fixed-size pages in place
It keeps one hash table of every key on disk
It merges and compacts sorted files written from an in-memory structure
It stores each column of a table in a separate file
optionExplain: That describes page-oriented engines such as B-trees.
The design avoids on-disk hash tables.
Right: that is the shared principle.
Storing each column in its own file describes column-oriented storage, not an LSM-tree.
questions.explain: Merging and compacting sorted files is the defining pattern. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Recognise LSM engines by merged, compacted sorted files, whatever the product name.

questions.q: Match each system to what the chapter says about it.
pairs: Key-value storage engine libraries embedded into other applications
Keeps its term dictionary in SSTable-like sorted files
Introduced the terms SSTable and memtable
questions.explain: Each system uses the sorted-files-plus-merging idea in its own setting.

questions.q: A search engine stores, for each word, the IDs of documents containing it. How does the chapter describe this in key-value terms?
options: The key is the document ID and the value is the list of words in that document
The key is the query and the value is the document text
There is no key; each document is a row
The key is the word and the value is the list of document IDs
optionExplain: This is the reverse of the term-to-postings-list mapping the chapter describes.
Queries are not stored as keys.
A full-text index does use a key-value structure.
Right: this mapping from term to postings list is kept in SSTable-like files.
questions.explain: A full-text index maps each term to a postings list.

questions.q: A team knows LevelDB well and is moving to RocksDB. What should they expect?
options: A page-based B-tree engine, so a different design
The same basic merged-SSTable design, with details to check
A column store, so data layout changes
An in-memory only store that loses all its data whenever the server restarts
optionExplain: Both are on the log-structured side.
Right: both are LSM engine libraries.
Neither LevelDB nor RocksDB is a column store, so the data layout idea stays the same.
Neither engine is described that way.
questions.explain: The family resemblance carries over; product details do not automatically.

questions.q: True or false: LevelDB and RocksDB are standalone database servers rather than libraries embedded into other applications.
questions.explain: The chapter calls them key-value storage engine libraries designed to be embedded into other applications.

questions.q: In a full-text index, what is a postings list?
options: The list of IDs of all documents that contain a given word
The list of words found in one document, in the order in which they appear
The queue of queries waiting to run
The sorted list of all indexed words
optionExplain: Right: it is the value stored under the term.
That is the reverse mapping, from a document to its words.
The term has nothing to do with query queues.
The sorted list of all indexed words is the term dictionary, not a postings list.
questions.explain: Given a word, the postings list holds the IDs of all documents mentioning it.
questions.rule: Postings list: the documents for one term.
questions.teaches: In a full-text index the key is a word (a term) and the value is the postings list: the IDs of all documents that contain the word.

questions.q: Why can an LSM engine be slow at looking up a key that is not in the database?
options: Absent keys force a full compaction first
The hash map has no entry, so it scans the log
Missing keys cannot be cached by the operating system, so each check goes to disk
It must check the memtable and then every segment back to the oldest
optionExplain: Lookups do not trigger a compaction; the cost is checking many places for the key.
LSM engines use sorted segments, not a hash map of all keys.
Caching is not the issue; the engine must check many places to prove the key is absent.
Right: only after all of those can it be sure the key is absent.
questions.explain: To prove a key is missing, every place it could be must be checked. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Check a Bloom filter first, so absent keys never trigger a walk through every segment.

questions.q: True or false: A Bloom filter can tell you that a key does not appear in the database.
questions.explain: That is what it is for: it saves many unnecessary disk reads for nonexistent keys.

questions.q: An engine has a memtable and 6 SSTables and no Bloom filter. A lookup of an absent key checks ____ structures.
questions.explain: It checks the memtable and each of the 6 segments, which is 7 structures.
questions.rule: Absent keys cost a full walk.

questions.q: With a Bloom filter in place, a lookup for an absent key arrives. What most likely happens?
options: The engine reads the newest segment first, then stops when it finds nothing there
The filter reports it is absent and the engine skips the segment reads
The filter fetches the key from disk
The memtable is rebuilt from the log
optionExplain: If the filter rules the key out, no segment needs reading at all.
Right: the negative answer lets the engine skip the segment reads for that key.
A Bloom filter only answers whether a key is absent; it holds no values to fetch.
The log is for crash recovery.
questions.explain: A negative answer from the filter ends the lookup.

questions.q: True or false: A Bloom filter helps lookups of keys that do not exist, not lookups of keys that do.
questions.explain: It can only tell you that a key does not appear, which saves unnecessary disk reads for nonexistent keys; present keys are still found by checking the memtable and segments.

questions.q: What is a Bloom filter?
options: A memory-efficient data structure for approximating the contents of a set
A sorted index of every key in the database together with its offset on disk
A compression scheme for blocks of records
A log that records which keys were deleted
optionExplain: Right: that is how the chapter describes it.
That would be a full index; a Bloom filter only approximates a set.
Compression of blocks is a separate technique and says nothing about absent keys.
Recording deleted keys is the job of tombstones, not of a Bloom filter.
questions.explain: It is a memory-efficient data structure for approximating the contents of a set.
questions.teaches: A Bloom filter is a memory-efficient data structure for approximating the contents of a set.

questions.q: An engine can merge its sorted files in different ways. Which is a genuine choice?
options: Merging only at restart, or only at shutdown, depending on how the process is run
Sorting by value, or sorting by key
Merging small new files into big old ones, or splitting key ranges into levels
Compressing blocks, or storing them raw
optionExplain: The two common options differ in how files are merged, not in when the process starts or stops.
Segments are always sorted by key, so sorting by value is not a compaction choice.
Right: these are the two common options.
That is a separate decision from the compaction order.
questions.explain: Order and timing of merges can vary. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Size-tiered merges small into large; leveled splits the key range into levels.

questions.q: Match each engine to the compaction strategy named in the chapter.
questions.explain: The chapter names these three engines and their strategies.

questions.q: You want compaction to proceed incrementally and use less disk space. Which strategy does the chapter point to?
options: Size-tiered compaction
No compaction
Leveled compaction
Compaction only at restart
optionExplain: It merges newer, smaller files into older, larger ones.
Without compaction, space is not reclaimed.
Right: it splits the key range into smaller SSTables across levels.
The chapter describes background strategies, not restart-time merges.
questions.explain: Leveled compaction is more incremental and uses less disk space.

questions.q: Under size-tiered compaction, what is merged into what?
options: Older, larger SSTables into newer, smaller ones as they age
Newer and smaller SSTables into older and larger ones
Whole levels into the memtable
Tombstones into the hash map
optionExplain: The direction is reversed: small new tables are folded into the large old ones.
Right: size-tiered compaction folds newer, smaller SSTables into older, larger ones.
Levels belong to the leveled strategy.
LSM engines have no such step.
questions.explain: Small new files are folded into the large old ones.

questions.q: True or false: In leveled compaction, the key range is kept in one large SSTable that is rewritten as a whole.
questions.explain: Leveled compaction splits the key range into smaller SSTables and moves older data into separate levels.

questions.q: What does the chapter say the different compaction strategies determine?
options: Whether keys are sorted
Whether a memtable is used
Whether range queries are possible, which depends on how the files are merged
The order and timing of how SSTables are compacted and merged
optionExplain: Sorting is a property of SSTables, not of the strategy.
The memtable comes before any compaction.
Range queries come from the sorted order of the data, not from the compaction strategy.
Right: the strategies differ in these two things.
questions.explain: Different strategies determine the order and timing of how SSTables are compacted and merged.
questions.teaches: Different strategies determine the order and timing of how SSTables are compacted and merged.

questions.q: Which pair of properties explains why an LSM-tree can offer both range queries and high write throughput?
options: Sorted data on disk and sequential disk writes
A hash index in memory and in-place overwrites
Fixed-size pages and a write-ahead log
Column files and bitmap indexes
optionExplain: Right: sorting enables ranges and sequential writes enable throughput.
A hash map does not give ranges, and overwrites are not sequential.
Fixed-size pages with a write-ahead log are features of B-trees.
Column files and bitmap indexes belong to column-oriented storage for analytics.
questions.explain: Order and sequential writes are the two ingredients. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Sorted segments give range scans, and sequential writes give high write throughput.

questions.q: Because LSM data is stored in sorted order, ____ queries over a key range are efficient.
questions.explain: Sorted order keeps neighbouring keys together.

questions.q: An app ingests events at a very high rate, queries by time range, and holds ten times more data than memory. What does the chapter's reasoning suggest?
options: A hash-indexed log, as all data must be in memory
An engine that overwrites each record in place
An in-memory store only, since a disk cannot keep up with a very high write rate
An LSM-style engine: sequential writes, sorted ranges, works beyond memory
optionExplain: Only the keys need memory there, and ranges are inefficient.
In-place random writes cost more at high write rates.
Sequential writes let a disk sustain high rates, and the dataset exceeds memory anyway.
Right: all three needs match its strengths.
questions.explain: High writes, ranges and large data all match LSM strengths.

questions.q: The dataset grows to ten times memory. What happens to an LSM engine?
options: It continues to work well
It stops working until the memtable is enlarged
Range queries become impossible
Writes turn into random writes
optionExplain: Right: the design does not rely on the data fitting in memory.
The memtable stays a few megabytes.
The data stays sorted however large it grows, so range queries remain possible.
Writes remain sequential however large the dataset is.
questions.explain: Even when the dataset is much bigger than memory, LSM-trees keep working well.

questions.q: True or false: An LSM-tree stops working well once the dataset becomes larger than the available memory.
questions.explain: The cascade of merged SSTables keeps working well even then.

questions.q: What is the key idea behind log-structured engines, in the chapter's summary?
options: Overwrite pages in place so that duplicate copies of a key never build up
Turn random-access writes into sequential writes on disk
Keep all data in memory and drop the disk
Store each column in its own file
optionExplain: That is the update-in-place school, not the log-structured one.
Right: that enables higher write throughput.
Keeping all data in memory describes in-memory databases, not log-structured engines.
Storing each column in its own file is column-oriented storage.
questions.explain: They systematically turn random-access writes into sequential writes on disk.
questions.teaches: The key idea of log-structured engines is that they systematically turn random-access writes into sequential writes on disk, which enables higher write throughput on both hard drives and SSDs.

questions.q: An index breaks the database into fixed-size blocks that refer to each other, starting from a root. How does it find key 251?
options: Scan the pages from the first to the last
Start at the root and follow the reference whose range encloses 251, level by level
Hash 251 and read the page stored at that address, since hashing finds any key fast
Merge all the pages and search the result
optionExplain: That is a full scan and ignores the tree.
Right: each reference covers a continuous key range.
Hashing would scatter neighbouring keys and a tree has no hash addresses.
Merging is a log-structured idea, not a lookup step.
questions.explain: Boundaries between references tell you which child to follow. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A B-tree is a tree of fixed-size pages, each owning a continuous key range.

questions.q: The number of references to child pages in one B-tree page is called the ____ factor.
questions.explain: It decides how many ranges a page splits into, typically several hundred.
questions.rule: Branching factor equals child references per page.

questions.q: A root page holds boundary keys 100, 200, 300, 400 between its child references. Which child do you follow for key 251?
options: The reference before 100
The reference between 300 and 400, since 251 lies closest to the boundary 300
The reference between the boundaries 200 and 300
All references between 200 and 400
optionExplain: The reference before 100 covers only keys below 100, and 251 is larger.
A key follows the range that contains it, not the nearest boundary; 251 is above 200 and below 300.
Right: 251 lies in that continuous range.
Only one child owns a given key.
questions.explain: Each child covers the range between the boundaries beside its reference.

questions.q: A leaf page is reached for key 251. What might it contain?
options: The value inline, or a reference to the page where the value is stored
Only a hash of the value
A list of every key in the database
Only boundary keys and child references to pages that cover smaller key ranges
optionExplain: Right: a leaf either holds the value inline or points to the page that does.
Leaf pages hold values or references, not hashes.
A leaf holds only its own range.
That describes interior pages, not leaves.
questions.explain: A leaf either holds values inline or points to where they live.

questions.q: True or false: B-trees break the database into variable-size segments, typically several megabytes, written out sequentially.
questions.explain: That describes log-structured indexes. B-trees use fixed-size pages, traditionally 4 KB, read and written one at a time.

questions.q: Why does the page-based design suit the underlying hardware?
options: Disks can only store tree structures, so any index on disk has to be a tree
Pages make all writes sequential
Pages avoid any need for an index in memory
Disks are also arranged in fixed-size blocks
optionExplain: Disks store bytes in blocks and know nothing of trees.
B-tree writes overwrite pages at arbitrary places.
Pages are the index, and they still must be read.
Right: pages mirror the hardware layout.
questions.explain: This design corresponds more closely to the hardware, as disks are also arranged in fixed-size blocks.
questions.teaches: The B-tree's fixed-size pages correspond closely to the underlying hardware, because disks are also arranged in fixed-size blocks.

questions.q: A database holds hundreds of gigabytes. About how many page references does a B-tree lookup follow?
options: Hundreds, one per page of the file
One per key in the database
A few, perhaps three or four
Thousands, since each page holds only a few keys
optionExplain: The tree avoids visiting every page.
Depth grows with the logarithm of keys, not linearly.
Right: with hundreds of references per page, few levels suffice.
Pages hold several hundred references each, so thousands of hops are never needed.
questions.explain: A large branching factor keeps trees shallow. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Capacity grows as the branching factor to the power of the depth, so depth stays small.

questions.q: A B-tree with n keys has a depth of O(____).
questions.explain: The tree stays balanced, so depth grows with the logarithm of the number of keys.

questions.q: Pages are 4 KB and the branching factor is 500. Roughly how much data can a four-level tree hold?
options: About 500 GB
About 250 TB
About 2 TB
About 8 PB
optionExplain: That is three levels: 500 cubed pages of 4 KB.
Right: 500 to the power 4 is 62.5 billion pages, times 4 KB.
This multiplies 500 by 4 KB, then by the number of levels.
This assumes far more pages than 500 to the power 4.
questions.explain: Each level multiplies capacity by the branching factor.
questions.rule: Capacity is branching factor to the depth, times page size.

questions.q: The branching factor falls from 500 to 250, with four levels and 4 KB pages. How does capacity change?
options: It falls about sixteenfold, to roughly 16 TB
It halves, as the branching factor halved
It falls fourfold, since two levels are affected
It stays the same, because depth is unchanged
optionExplain: Right: 250 to the power 4 is 16 times smaller than 500 to the power 4.
Capacity depends on the factor to the fourth power.
All four levels shrink, not two.
Depth fixed, capacity still falls with the factor.
questions.explain: Halving b cuts a four-level capacity by 2 to the power 4.
questions.rule: Capacity falls with b to the depth.

questions.q: True or false: B-tree depth grows in proportion to the number of keys, so large tables need very deep trees.
questions.explain: Depth grows with the logarithm of the number of keys, and most databases fit in three or four levels.

questions.q: A 2 TB database uses 4 KB pages and a branching factor of 500. About how many levels deep should its B-tree be?
options: Two levels
Three levels
Thirty levels
Four levels
optionExplain: Two levels hold only about 1 GB.
Three levels hold about 500 GB, short of 2 TB.
Depth is logarithmic and stays small.
Right: three levels hold about 500 GB, four hold about 250 TB.
questions.explain: Most databases can fit into a B-tree that is three or four levels deep.
questions.rule: Three or four levels cover most databases.
questions.teaches: Most databases can fit into a B-tree that is three or four levels deep, so you do not need to follow many page references to find a page.

questions.q: A B-tree leaf page is full and a new key belongs in it. What would you expect to happen?
options: The new key goes into a separate overflow file that is merged back later on
The oldest key is deleted to make room
The page is split into two, and the parent records the new boundary
The tree grows one level deeper along that path only
optionExplain: B-trees keep their keys inside the tree's pages.
Data is not dropped to make space.
Right: this keeps the tree balanced.
Splitting keeps all leaves at the same depth.
questions.explain: A full page divides in two. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Overwrite the leaf page; if it is full, split it and fix the parent.

questions.q: When a B-tree page has no room for a new key, it is ____ into two half-full pages.
questions.explain: The parent page is then updated for the new subdivision of key ranges.

questions.q: You update the value of an existing key in a B-tree. What is written to disk?
options: A new copy of the whole tree
A new record appended at the end of a log
The page and all its ancestors, since each parent must be rewritten too
The leaf page containing the key, overwritten in place
optionExplain: Only the leaf page changes, so there is no reason to copy the whole tree.
That is what log-structured engines do.
Only the leaf page is rewritten when a value changes, because references to it stay valid.
Right: the references to the page stay valid.
questions.explain: The page is changed and written back to its same location.

questions.q: A split page was written, but the parent page was not updated before a crash. What state is the index in?
options: Fine: the tree rebuilds the missing parent entry itself when the server restarts
Corrupted: for example an orphan page that no parent refers to
Fine: the old page remains valid
Slow but correct, as lookups scan all pages
optionExplain: Without a log, the engine has no record of what was intended, so nothing rebuilds it.
Right: a split touches several pages.
Part of the split is already written.
Lookups follow references, so orphan pages are lost.
questions.explain: Multi-page operations are dangerous when interrupted.

questions.q: True or false: After a page split, some leaves of the B-tree sit deeper than others, so lookups differ in cost.
questions.explain: The algorithm keeps the tree balanced, so a B-tree with n keys always has a depth of O(log n).

questions.q: A team wants to know how hard deleting a key is in a B-tree. What does the chapter say?
options: Deleting while keeping the tree balanced is more involved than inserting
Deletion is a single page overwrite with no extra steps, the same as an update
Deletion is impossible in B-trees
Deletion is easier than insertion in B-trees
optionExplain: Right: the book flags it in a footnote.
It is more involved than insertion, because the tree must stay balanced.
Deletion is possible; it is only more involved than insertion.
The chapter says it is more involved.
questions.explain: Inserting is reasonably intuitive, but deleting a key while keeping the tree balanced is more involved.
questions.teaches: Inserting a new key into a B-tree is reasonably intuitive, but deleting one while keeping the tree balanced is somewhat more involved.

questions.q: A page split needs three page writes. How can an engine make a crash between them harmless?
options: Write the three pages in a random order
Skip the parent update and fix it up later, when a read first notices the gap
Make the pages smaller so fewer are touched
Record the planned change in an append-only file first, then apply it
optionExplain: Order does not remove the dangerous gap.
That leaves an index that is wrong until someone fixes it.
Smaller pages do not make a multi-page change atomic.
Right: replaying that file restores consistency.
questions.explain: Log the intention before touching the pages. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Write the intent to an append-only log first, then change the pages.

questions.q: A B-tree's write-ahead log is also known as a ____ log.
questions.explain: It is an append-only file to which every modification is written before it is applied to the pages.

questions.q: After a crash, the database restarts. How is the B-tree returned to a consistent state?
options: By scanning every page for an orphan
By using the write-ahead log to restore it
By discarding the log and the half-applied changes
By merging the pages like SSTables
optionExplain: The log tells the engine what was intended.
Right: replaying the write-ahead log restores the tree to a consistent state.
That would leave the corrupted tree as it was.
B-trees do not have SSTable segments to merge; the log is what repairs them.
questions.explain: The WAL is replayed to restore consistency.

questions.q: An engine disables its WAL to speed up writes. What risk returns?
options: A crash during a multi-page change can corrupt the index
Reads can no longer find keys by range, since ranges rely on the log
Pages stop being fixed-size
Compaction can no longer run
optionExplain: Right: a split may be only partly written.
Range queries depend on sorted order, not on the log.
The log does not affect page size.
B-trees do not compact segments, so that is not what returns without the log.
questions.explain: Without the log, partial writes are not repaired.

questions.q: True or false: A B-tree needs a write-ahead log because it does not modify pages in place.
questions.explain: It is the other way round: pages are overwritten in place, which is why a crash can leave the index inconsistent.

questions.q: What does overwriting a page on disk involve at the hardware level?
options: Appending the page at the end of the file in both cases, which is why in-place updates are cheap
Writing only the changed bytes, on any device
On a hard drive, moving the head and waiting for the platter; on an SSD, erasing large blocks
Nothing, since the write goes only to memory
optionExplain: That is how log-structured engines write; an overwrite changes the page where it already is.
An SSD must erase and rewrite fairly large blocks.
Right: these are the costs described.
The write reaches the storage device.
questions.explain: On a hard drive the head moves and waits for the platter; an SSD must erase and rewrite large blocks of a chip.
questions.teaches: Overwriting a page is a hardware operation: on a magnetic drive the head moves and waits for the right position on the platter, and on an SSD fairly large blocks must be erased and rewritten.

questions.q: Several threads read and update a tree of pages in place. What must the engine guard against?
options: Pages being too small to hold keys
The index growing deeper than log n, which would slow every lookup that follows
A thread seeing the tree in an inconsistent state during an update
Reads being slower than writes
optionExplain: Page size is unrelated to thread safety.
Balanced splits keep depth small, so this is not the threat.
Right: this is why careful concurrency control is needed.
This is a performance matter, not safety.
questions.explain: In-place changes expose half-updated states. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Pages updated in place need latches so readers see a consistent tree.

questions.q: A B-tree typically protects its data structures with ____, which are lightweight locks.
questions.explain: Latches guard the pages while they are being changed.

questions.q: One thread splits a page while another thread wants to read the same page. What protects the reader?
options: The write-ahead log, which locks pages during replay
A latch on the page or tree structure
The page's checksum, which the reader verifies
Nothing, since fixed-size pages are always read atomically
optionExplain: The log helps after a crash; it does not coordinate threads.
Right: latches keep readers from seeing a half-changed tree.
A checksum detects damaged bytes but does not stop a reader seeing a mid-split tree.
A split touches several pages, so a reader could see them out of step.
questions.explain: Careful concurrency control is required when multiple threads access the B-tree, typically via latches.

questions.q: A B-tree implementation drops its latches to go faster. What is the likely result?
options: Nothing changes, since the write-ahead log already covers concurrent access
The tree stops being sorted
Pages become variable-size
Readers may see the tree in an inconsistent state mid-update
optionExplain: The WAL covers crashes, not concurrent readers.
Sorting is not governed by latches.
Page size is fixed by the design and has nothing to do with latches.
Right: latches are what prevent this.
questions.explain: Latches and the WAL guard against different problems.

questions.q: True or false: Latches protect a B-tree from corruption after a crash in the middle of a page split.
questions.explain: Latches coordinate threads working on the tree at the same time. Crash safety comes from the write-ahead log.
questions.rule: Latches for threads, WAL for crashes.

questions.q: A colleague says B-trees are unsafe because they need latches. How does the chapter frame it?
options: Latches are the price of updating in place; log-structured designs are simpler here
B-trees cannot be used by more than one thread, so they never serve concurrent users
Latches are needed only by log-structured engines
Concurrency is not a concern for either design
optionExplain: Right: the chapter presents it as a simplicity difference, not a safety verdict.
They can, with careful concurrency control.
The reverse holds: latches are the B-tree's cost of in-place updates.
The book discusses it as a real complication.
questions.explain: Careful concurrency control is required when pages are updated in place.
questions.rule: Latches are the cost of in-place updates.
questions.teaches: Log-structured approaches are simpler for concurrency control because all merging happens in the background, without interfering with incoming queries.

questions.q: Interior pages of a B-tree need only enough of each key to mark range boundaries. What could be done with that?
options: Store full keys twice in each page for safety, as a defence against corruption
Drop the boundaries and use a hash
Store keys in leaf pages only
Store abbreviated keys, so more fit in a page and the branching factor rises
optionExplain: That would lower the branching factor.
Boundaries are what route a lookup.
Interior pages need boundaries to route.
Right: a higher branching factor means fewer levels.
questions.explain: Shorter boundary keys pack more references per page. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Improve B-trees by avoiding the WAL, packing more keys per page, and speeding range scans.

questions.q: Match each B-tree optimization to its benefit.
pairs: Avoids overwriting pages and maintaining a WAL
Higher branching factor, so fewer levels
Scan keys in order without going back to parents
Leaf pages laid out in sequence on disk
Fewer disk seeks on long key-range scans
questions.explain: Each trick targets one cost of the basic design.
questions.rule: Know which problem each trick fixes.

questions.q: A database wants fewer levels in its B-tree without changing the page size. Which optimization applies?
options: Abbreviate keys in interior pages to raise the branching factor
Add sibling pointers between leaf pages so scans need not return to parents
Switch to a larger write-ahead log
Sort leaf pages by value
optionExplain: Right: more references per page means fewer levels.
These speed up scans, not depth.
The WAL does not affect depth.
Leaf pages are ordered by key, and reordering them by value would not reduce depth.
questions.explain: A higher branching factor means a shallower tree.

questions.q: A B-tree grows over years with many splits. What happens to the on-disk order of its leaf pages?
options: They stay in key order on disk, since pages never move once they are written
Nearby key ranges end up far apart on disk, so range scans need more seeks
They become sorted by write time
They are merged into one file
optionExplain: Splits put new pages anywhere there is room.
Right: the layout is hard to keep sequential as the tree grows.
Nothing orders pages by write time; they sit wherever space was available.
B-trees keep many pages, and nothing merges them into one file.
questions.explain: Pages can be positioned anywhere on disk.
questions.rule: Layout drifts as the tree grows.

questions.q: True or false: Copy-on-write B-trees overwrite pages in place and rely on a write-ahead log for crash recovery.
questions.explain: Copy-on-write writes the modified page to a different location and creates new parent pages, which avoids the WAL.

questions.q: What is a B+ tree, in this chapter's footnote?
options: A tree that keeps all of its pages in memory only, which makes every lookup faster
A B-tree with a second write-ahead log
The variant that abbreviates interior keys, so common it often is not distinguished from other B-tree variants
A log-structured tree of SSTables
optionExplain: A B+ tree is still stored on disk.
The footnote ties the name to key abbreviation.
Right: the footnote ties the B+ tree name to the key-abbreviation optimization.
A tree of merged SSTables is an LSM-tree, which is a different structure.
questions.explain: The name B+ tree is sometimes used for the key-abbreviation variant, though it is so common that it often is not distinguished.
questions.teaches: The key-abbreviation optimization is sometimes known as a B+ tree, though it is so common that it often is not distinguished from other B-tree variants.

questions.q: A team must choose between a B-tree engine and an LSM-tree engine for a write-heavy app. What is a sensible starting guess?
options: B-tree, since it is always faster, whatever the workload turns out to be
Either, as benchmarks are decisive
LSM, typically faster for writes, then test with their workload
Neither, as both are obsolete
optionExplain: No engine is faster on every workload.
Benchmarks are often inconclusive and sensitive to workload details, so they are not decisive.
Right: a rule of thumb, then verify.
B-trees remain the standard index in most relational databases.
questions.explain: Use the rule of thumb to start and tests to decide. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Lean LSM for writes and B-tree for reads, then confirm by testing your workload.

questions.q: As a rule of thumb, LSM-trees are typically faster for ____, whereas B-trees are thought to be faster for reads.
questions.explain: LSM reads must check several data structures and SSTables at different stages of compaction.

questions.q: Vendor benchmarks show engine A beating engine B on a workload unlike yours. What does the chapter advise?
options: Trust the vendor result and choose A
Test both with your own workload before comparing
Choose B, because vendor results are biased towards the vendor's own product
Choose the oldest engine
optionExplain: The benchmark used a workload unlike yours, so its winner may not win on yours.
Right: benchmarks are sensitive to the details of the workload.
The advice is to measure your own workload, not to guess the opposite.
Maturity is not the same as fit.
questions.explain: You need to test systems with your particular workload.

questions.q: A read-mostly service with few writes is considering an LSM engine. What does the rule of thumb suggest about its reads?
options: They may be slower, as reads check several structures
They will be faster, since the data is stored sorted and range scans are cheap
They are unaffected by compaction
They cannot be served
optionExplain: Right: reads must look at the memtable and SSTables.
Sorting helps ranges, but a point read still touches several files.
LSM reads depend on how files are compacted.
Reads work; they just cost more.
questions.explain: Reads are typically slower on LSM-trees because several structures are checked.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter gives a quick, reliable rule that tells you which type of storage engine is better for any use case.
questions.explain: It says there is no quick and easy rule, so it is worth testing empirically.

questions.q: According to the chapter, how mature are B-tree implementations compared with LSM-tree implementations?
options: LSM implementations are more mature
They are equally mature
Maturity is irrelevant to the comparison, since only speed counts
B-tree implementations are generally more mature
optionExplain: The chapter says the reverse: B-tree implementations are generally the more mature.
The chapter does not say that.
The chapter mentions it as one factor.
Right: that is a point in their favour.
questions.explain: Even though B-tree implementations are generally more mature, LSM-trees are interesting for their performance characteristics.
questions.teaches: B-tree implementations are generally more mature than LSM-tree implementations, even though LSM-trees are interesting for their performance characteristics.

questions.q: One update to the database ends up as several writes to the disk over time. What is this effect called?
options: Write amplification
Write skew, where two transactions make conflicting changes
Compaction
Replication lag
optionExplain: Right: one database write, many disk writes.
Write skew is a different concept entirely.
Compaction is one cause, not the name for the effect.
Lag concerns copies on other machines.
questions.explain: The effect is named after the multiplication of writes. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Count how many times the disk is written for each database write.

questions.q: True or false: A B-tree index writes every piece of data at least twice: once to the write-ahead log and once to the tree page.
questions.explain: It may write again as pages split, and writes a whole page even if few bytes changed.

questions.q: A record is written to the log, flushed to an SSTable, and then rewritten in 3 compactions. One database write caused ____ disk writes.
questions.explain: 1 for the log, 1 for the flush and 3 for the compactions makes 5.

questions.q: A write-heavy app is limited by disk bandwidth. If the engine doubles its write amplification, what happens?
options: Nothing changes, as the disk is the bottleneck and cannot go any faster
Throughput doubles, as there are more writes
Reads become sequential
The writes per second it can handle fall, about by half
optionExplain: The bottleneck is exactly why it matters.
More disk writes do not mean more database writes served.
Write amplification concerns writes and has no effect on whether reads are sequential.
Right: more disk writes per database write use up bandwidth.
questions.explain: The more a storage engine writes, the fewer writes per second it handles.

questions.q: True or false: Both B-tree engines and LSM-tree engines can suffer from write amplification.
questions.explain: B-trees write to the log and the page, and LSM-trees rewrite data in repeated compaction and merging.

questions.q: Why is write amplification of particular concern on SSDs?
options: SSDs cannot do sequential writes
They can overwrite blocks only a limited number of times before wearing out
SSDs lose data without a write-ahead log, so every update must be written twice
SSDs need larger pages than hard drives
optionExplain: They can, and benefit from them.
Right: more writes shorten their life.
Wear is the issue, not data loss without a log.
Page size is not the point.
questions.explain: Write amplification is of particular concern on SSDs, which can only overwrite blocks a limited number of times.
questions.teaches: Write amplification is of particular concern on SSDs, which can only overwrite blocks a limited number of times before wearing out.

questions.q: A page-oriented index splits pages when they fill. What does that do to disk space use?
options: It uses less space than other designs
It has no effect on space
It leaves some space in pages unused
It fills gaps by moving rows
optionExplain: Splitting leaves half-full pages, so it wastes space instead of saving it.
Half-full pages hold less data per page, so space use is affected.
Right: split pages are half-full, so fragmentation results.
Rows stay in their pages when a page is split, so gaps are not filled by moving them.
questions.explain: Splits leave free space inside pages. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: No pages to leave half-empty and regular rewriting mean smaller LSM files.

questions.q: B-tree engines leave some disk space unused when a page is split, a cost called ____.
questions.explain: That unused space is a cost LSM-trees largely avoid.

questions.q: Two engines hold the same data. One is an LSM-tree with leveled compaction, the other a B-tree. Which usually uses less disk?
options: The B-tree, since it overwrites in place
Both the same, as the data is the same
The LSM-tree, thanks to compression and removal of fragmentation
It depends only on the page size
optionExplain: Overwriting in place does not remove fragmentation, so the B-tree does not come out smaller.
Layout overheads differ between the two designs, so the same data takes different space.
Right: compression and removal of fragmentation give the LSM-tree lower storage overheads.
Compression and periodic rewriting matter as well as page size.
questions.explain: LSM files are better compressed and less fragmented.

questions.q: On an SSD whose firmware turns random writes into sequential ones, what happens to the LSM advantage?
options: It shrinks for writes, but lower amplification and compactness still help
It vanishes entirely
It grows, since SSD firmware favours random writes and makes B-trees cheaper still
It reverses, so B-trees win outright
optionExplain: Right: more compact data fits more requests in the bandwidth.
Lower write amplification and compact data still help on SSDs, so the advantage does not vanish.
The firmware makes random writes cheaper, which reduces the gap.
The book does not claim that.
questions.explain: Representing data compactly allows more read and write requests within the I/O bandwidth.

questions.q: True or false: Because SSD firmware often uses a log-structured algorithm, lower write amplification brings no benefit on SSDs.
questions.explain: Lower write amplification and reduced fragmentation remain advantageous on SSDs.

questions.q: Which compaction strategy does the chapter name as giving especially low storage overhead?
options: Size-tiered compaction
No compaction
Compaction at restart only
Leveled compaction
optionExplain: It was not singled out for overhead.
Without compaction, stale and duplicate data accumulates, so storage overhead rises.
The book does not discuss that.
Right: lower overheads, especially when using it.
questions.explain: LSM-trees have lower storage overheads, especially when using leveled compaction.
questions.teaches: LSM-trees have lower storage overheads especially when using leveled compaction, because they periodically rewrite SSTables to remove fragmentation.

questions.q: An LSM engine is fast on average, yet a few requests are very slow. What might explain it?
options: The hash map is too large
A request waiting while the disk finishes an expensive compaction
The write-ahead log is sorted
Pages have split too many times
optionExplain: LSM engines do not rely on one.
Right: a request that waits for an expensive compaction shows up at high percentiles.
The log's order does not matter.
Page splits are a B-tree behaviour and do not explain slow requests in an LSM engine.
questions.explain: Averages can hide waits caused by compaction. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Watch compaction: it can inflate tail latencies and fall behind a high write rate.

questions.q: Compaction usually barely changes average response time, but at higher ____ queries to log-structured engines can be quite slow.
questions.explain: B-trees can be more predictable here.

questions.q: A write-heavy LSM deployment sees segments piling up and disk use growing. What is the likely cause?
options: Bloom filters are too small, which makes reads of absent keys slower
The memtable is sorted
Compaction cannot keep up with the rate of incoming writes
Too many tombstones
optionExplain: They affect reads of absent keys, not segment growth.
The memtable is sorted by design, and that does not make segments pile up.
Right: when compaction cannot keep up, unmerged segments keep accumulating on disk.
Tombstones are removed by merging, which is the stuck step.
questions.explain: When compaction falls behind, the number of unmerged segments grows.

questions.q: Compaction is falling behind. What also happens to reads?
options: They slow down, because they must check more segment files
They speed up, since data is spread across more files that are read in parallel
They are unaffected
They are redirected to the log
optionExplain: Right: reads must probe more segment files, so they slow down.
More segments make reads slower, since each must be checked.
Reads depend on the number of segments.
Reads do not use the log.
questions.explain: Reads need to check more segments, so they slow down.

questions.q: True or false: When compaction cannot keep up, SSTable-based storage engines typically throttle incoming writes automatically.
questions.explain: They typically do not throttle writes, so explicit monitoring is needed to detect the situation.

questions.q: Why does compaction need more disk bandwidth as the database grows, at high write rates?
options: Larger databases need larger memtables, and larger memtables must be flushed more often
Disk write bandwidth is shared between the initial writes and background compaction
Compaction stops using sequential writes
Bloom filters rewrite themselves
optionExplain: Memtable size is separate from the sharing of bandwidth.
Right: bigger databases need more compaction work.
Compaction stays sequential; the issue is how much bandwidth it takes.
The filters are not the cause.
questions.explain: The bigger the database gets, the more disk bandwidth is required for compaction.
questions.teaches: When writing to an empty database the full disk bandwidth goes to the initial write, but the bigger the database gets, the more bandwidth compaction needs.

questions.q: A relational database locks ranges of keys to isolate transactions. Which index layout makes attaching those locks easiest?
options: One where several copies of each key sit in different files
A hash map with no key order
An unsorted log
One where each key exists in exactly one place
optionExplain: Copies make it unclear where a lock belongs.
A hash map keeps no key order, so ranges of keys cannot be locked on it.
There is no range structure to attach to.
Right: the lock can sit on the tree.
questions.explain: Locks need a single home for each key. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: One place per key makes it easy to attach range locks to the index.

questions.q: In a B-tree each key exists in exactly ____ place in the index.
questions.explain: A log-structured engine may have several copies of the same key in different segments.

questions.q: A new database promises strong transactional isolation using range locks. Which family fits the book's reasoning?
options: Log-structured, because merging segments in the background gives isolation
B-tree-based, as locks attach directly to the tree
Hash-indexed log, because keys are unique
Neither; locks do not need an index
optionExplain: Merging is background maintenance, not locking.
Right: that is the book's reason.
Hash indexes do not support range locks.
The book ties locks to key ranges in the index.
questions.explain: In a B-tree, range locks can be attached to the tree directly.

questions.q: A log-structured store has copies of key k in three segments. Why does that complicate locking?
options: Locks cannot be taken on files, so a store with many files cannot lock a key
The copies disagree after a merge
A lock on k would have to account for several copies spread over files
The copies are encrypted
optionExplain: Files can be locked, but this is not the issue.
Merges resolve duplicate copies, so the copies do not disagree afterwards.
Right: there is no single place to attach it.
Nothing about encryption is involved; the issue is multiple copies of the key.
questions.explain: Multiple copies mean no single spot for the lock.

questions.q: True or false: Since B-trees fit transactional semantics, the chapter concludes log-structured indexes will not be used in new datastores.
questions.explain: It says log-structured indexes are becoming increasingly popular in new datastores.

questions.q: What does the chapter say about B-trees going away?
options: They will be replaced by LSM-trees within a few years, since new datastores adopt them
They already vanished from relational databases
They are used only in legacy systems
