They are so ingrained and perform so consistently that they are unlikely to go away
optionExplain: The chapter says nothing of the sort.
B-trees remain the standard index in almost all relational databases.
They are the standard index in almost all relational databases.
Right: that is the chapter's view.
questions.explain: B-trees are very ingrained in database architecture and provide consistently good performance, so they are unlikely to go away anytime soon.
questions.teaches: B-trees are so ingrained in database architecture and so consistently good that they are unlikely to go away, while log-structured indexes are becoming increasingly popular in new datastores.

questions.q: Many rows share the same value in a column you want to index. What is the central difficulty?
options: The column cannot be sorted
Keys in the index are no longer unique
The index cannot be stored on disk, because disks only hold unique keys
Only hash indexes can handle it
optionExplain: Non-unique values sort without difficulty; the trouble is that one key matches many rows.
Right: one key may match many rows.
Where an index is stored is unrelated to key uniqueness.
B-trees and log-structured indexes can also serve as secondary indexes.
questions.explain: Repeated values break the one-key-one-row assumption. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A secondary index is a key-value index whose keys may repeat.

questions.q: A primary key ____ identifies one row, document or vertex.
questions.explain: Other records refer to a row by its primary key, and the index resolves such references.

questions.q: An index on city must return all rows in a given city. Which approach is one of the two named in the chapter?
options: Keep only the newest row per city
Require cities to be unique in the table, one row for each city name
Make each index value a list of matching row identifiers
Index only the first matching row
optionExplain: Keeping only the newest row per city would drop the other matching rows.
That changes the data to suit the index.
Right: like a postings list in a full-text index.
Indexing only the first matching row would miss all the others, but the query needs every match.
questions.explain: A list of row IDs per key, or a key made unique by appending the row ID.

questions.q: Each key is made unique by appending the row ID. What does a lookup of one city now become?
options: A range scan over all keys beginning with that city
A single point lookup of one key
A full scan of the whole index, since the row IDs break the sort order
A join with the primary index
optionExplain: Right: the matching keys sit together in sorted order.
The key now has many variants.
Sorted keys let it scan only the range of that city.
Nothing in the approach requires a join.
questions.explain: Appending the row ID keeps equal values adjacent.
questions.rule: Unique suffix turns lookups into ranges.

questions.q: True or false: Both B-trees and log-structured indexes can be used as secondary indexes.
questions.explain: The difference from a primary key index is only that keys are not unique, which can be solved in two ways that work with either family.

questions.q: Why would a relational database add a secondary index on a user_id column of several tables?
options: To make user_id unique across tables
To replace the primary key
To avoid writing the rows to disk
To find all of one user's rows in each table and make joins efficient
optionExplain: A secondary index is for values that repeat, so making them unique is the opposite of its point.
Secondary indexes do not replace primary keys.
Rows still have to be stored.
Right: secondary indexes are often crucial for joins.
questions.explain: Secondary indexes are often crucial for performing joins efficiently.
questions.teaches: In relational databases, secondary indexes created with CREATE INDEX are often crucial for performing joins efficiently, for example on a user_id column.

questions.q: A table has five secondary indexes. Where should the actual row data live?
options: Copied into each of the five indexes so each can answer queries alone
In the first index only, with the other four pointing at that index
In one place, with each index holding a reference to it
In memory only, since five indexes need fast access to the rows
optionExplain: That duplicates the data five times and multiplies the work of every update.
The other indexes would still need references to the rows' real home.
Right: this avoids duplicating data five times.
Rows must be durable, and memory alone does not survive a restart.
questions.explain: One home for the data, many pointers. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Store rows once in a heap file and let every index point to them.

questions.q: The place where rows are stored, in no particular order, when indexes hold references is called a ____ file.
questions.explain: Heap files may be append-only, or may track deleted rows so they can be overwritten later.

questions.q: A row in a heap file is updated to a value larger than its old slot. What must the engine do?
options: Overwrite it in place, whatever the size of the new value
Move it, then update all indexes or leave a forwarding pointer behind
Delete the row and its indexes, then rebuild them from the log later
Convert the heap file into an SSTable, which can hold larger values
optionExplain: In-place overwrite works only if the new value is not larger than the old one.
Right: the old location can no longer hold it.
Nothing requires deleting the indexes; they can be updated or can follow a forwarding pointer.
A heap file is unordered, and converting it is not how larger values are handled.
questions.explain: A larger value must go to a new location.

questions.q: A value is updated and is not larger than the old one. How efficient is the update?
options: Quite efficient: the record can be overwritten in place and no index changes
Slow: every index must be rebuilt, because any update changes the record
Impossible without a forwarding pointer left at the old location
Slow: the heap file must be sorted again after every single update
optionExplain: Right: the location stays the same.
The indexes need changing only when the record moves to a new location.
Forwarding pointers are for rows that must move, not for rows that still fit.
The heap file keeps data in no particular order, so no re-sorting arises.
questions.explain: If the row stays put, the references stay valid.

questions.q: True or false: Heap files keep rows sorted by primary key, which is why indexes can point into them.
questions.explain: A heap file stores data in no particular order.

questions.q: What are the two ways to handle a heap row that must move to a new location?
options: Delete the index entry, or make the row read-only so that it never has to move
Compress the row until it fits, or split it into two smaller rows in the heap
Wait for the next compaction, or restart the database to rebuild the heap
Update all indexes to the new location, or leave a forwarding pointer at the old one
optionExplain: Neither is described; the chapter names updating the indexes or leaving a pointer.
Nothing like that is suggested for moved rows.
These are not options for a heap file; the move is handled immediately.
Right: both are named in the chapter.
questions.explain: Either all indexes are updated to the record's new heap location, or a forwarding pointer is left in the old location.
questions.teaches: When a heap record must move, either all indexes are updated to point to its new location, or a forwarding pointer is left behind at the old location.

questions.q: Reads through an index are slow because each needs an extra hop to the stored row. What is a possible remedy?
options: Add a second heap file, so that rows are found in two different places
Make the index unsorted, so that lookups no longer have to follow its order
Store the row, or some of its columns, inside the index itself
Drop the primary key, so that the rows no longer need an identity at all
optionExplain: More heaps add hops instead of removing them.
Order is not the problem; the extra hop to the row is.
Right: keeping the row or some columns in the index removes the extra hop.
Rows still need an identity for other records to refer to them.
questions.explain: Moving data into the index trades space for speed. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Keep needed columns inside the index to save a hop, and pay for duplication.

questions.q: Match each index kind to what it stores.
pairs: The whole row inside the index
Some of a table's columns inside the index
Only a reference to the row elsewhere
questions.explain: They sit on a spectrum from references only to everything.
questions.rule: Spectrum of how much the index holds.

questions.q: A query needs only two columns that an index already stores as included columns. What is the index said to do?
options: It clusters the query, because the included columns sit in the index
It splits the query into pages, one for each included column
It becomes a hash index, because it answers without visiting the table
It covers the query, so the heap is never visited
optionExplain: Clustering describes storing the whole row; this index stores only some columns.
That is not how the term is used; the index is said to cover the query.
The index type is unchanged; only where the answer comes from differs.
Right: the index alone answers it.
questions.explain: A covering index lets some queries be answered by the index alone.

questions.q: A table gets a covering index with many included columns. What happens to writes?
options: They get cheaper, as less data has to be read
They get more expensive, as duplicated columns must be kept consistent
They are unaffected, because the index sits beside the table and not in it
They become append-only, since the index holds copies of the columns
optionExplain: Reads get cheaper; writes pay to keep the duplicated columns in step.
Right: the duplicated columns must be kept consistent, which adds write overhead.
Duplicated data must be updated on every write that changes it.
Nothing about a covering index changes the write pattern to append-only.
questions.explain: Clustered and covering indexes speed reads but need more storage and add write overhead.

questions.q: True or false: Duplicating data inside indexes is free, since the database keeps copies consistent automatically.
questions.explain: It costs storage and write overhead, and the database must work to enforce transactional guarantees so applications do not see inconsistencies.

questions.q: In MySQL's InnoDB engine, what do secondary indexes refer to?
options: The primary key, which is a clustered index
A heap file location, as in most databases that keep a heap file
A hash of the row, which is recomputed on every lookup
The memtable, which holds the newest version of the row
optionExplain: Right: not a heap file location.
InnoDB's secondary indexes refer to the primary key instead of a heap location.
No hash of the row is used; the reference is the primary key.
InnoDB is page-based and has no memtable for rows.
questions.explain: InnoDB's primary key is always a clustered index, and secondary indexes refer to the primary key.
questions.teaches: In MySQL's InnoDB the primary key is always a clustered index and secondary indexes refer to the primary key rather than to a heap file location, while SQL Server lets you specify one clustered index per table.

questions.q: A phone book is sorted by last name, then first name. Which search can it answer efficiently?
options: All people with a particular first name
All people whose first name is longer than their last
All people listed on a given page number
All people with a particular last name
optionExplain: First names are scattered through a book sorted by last name, so this is not efficient.
Neither ordering helps with comparing the length of names.
That is unrelated to the index's key.
Right: people with the same last name are adjacent in the sorted order.
questions.explain: Sorting by last name groups last names, not first names. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A concatenated index sorts by the first field, then by the next.

questions.q: A concatenated index combines several fields into one key by ____ one column to another.
questions.explain: The index definition says in which order the fields are put together.
questions.rule: Fields are joined in a set order.

questions.q: An index is defined on (country, city). Which query can use it fully?
options: Find customers in city Y in any country
Find customers in country X and city Y
Find customers whose city starts with Z
Find customers sorted by city only
optionExplain: The leading field is not constrained.
Right: both fields are used, and the leading one is country.
City alone is not the leading field.
The index is ordered by country first.
questions.explain: The index is useful from the first field onwards.

questions.q: A team reverses the field order of the index from (last, first) to (first, last). What changes?
options: Queries by first name become fast; queries by last name alone no longer are
Nothing changes, since both fields remain indexed and the same rows are found
All queries become slower, because the index must be searched in a new way
Queries by last name alone become faster, since last name is now second
optionExplain: Right: the leading field decides which queries the index can serve quickly.
Order decides which queries benefit, so the change matters.
Queries by first name get faster; only some queries lose out.
A field in second place cannot be used alone; it lost its leading position.
questions.explain: Field order decides which searches are cheap.

questions.q: True or false: A concatenated index on (lastname, firstname) is equally good for finding every person called Anna and every Smith.
questions.explain: It is useless for searching by first name alone because it is sorted by last name first.

questions.q: What does the chapter say about the paper phone book analogy's limit?
options: It works equally well for any single field, since the book is sorted
It cannot find people by last name, since it is sorted by first name
The index is useless for finding all people with a particular first name
It works only on SSDs, because a paper book has no seek time
optionExplain: A phone book helps only with its leading field, so this ignores the limit.
It is sorted by last name first, so last name lookups work well.
Right: that is its stated limit.
The analogy is about sort order, not hardware.
questions.explain: The index can find all people with a particular last name, or a last name and first name, but is useless for a first name.
questions.rule: Skip the first field, lose the index.
questions.teaches: A concatenated index on (lastname, firstname) is useless if you want all the people with a particular first name.

questions.q: A map shows restaurants within a rectangle of latitude and longitude. Why can a normal index not answer this well?
options: It cannot store decimal numbers such as latitudes and longitudes
It needs the data to be in memory before it can answer a range query
It can give a range on latitude or on longitude, but not both at once
It can only return a single row, never a group of rows in a range
optionExplain: Numbers are stored and sorted fine; the issue is combining two ranges.
Range queries on a B-tree work from disk, so memory is not required.
Right: a one-dimensional ordering can narrow only one of the two ranges.
An index can return many rows, but only for a range on its one sort order.
questions.explain: A single sort order serves one dimension. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Index several dimensions together with an R-tree or a space-filling curve.

questions.q: PostGIS implements geospatial indexes as ____-trees.
questions.explain: R-trees are specialised spatial indexes.

questions.q: Weather observations need all readings in 2013 with temperature between 25 and 30. Which index narrows both at once?
options: A one-dimensional index on date only, followed by a filter on temperature
A two-dimensional index on (date, temperature)
A hash index on temperature, which finds all readings between 25 and 30
No index at all; a column store alone narrows both conditions together
optionExplain: You would scan the whole year and then filter, so it does not narrow both at once.
Right: a two-dimensional index can narrow by date and temperature together.
Hash indexes find exact keys, not ranges.
A column store reduces the data read, but the chapter's answer here is a two-dimensional index.
questions.explain: Multi-dimensional indexes are not just for geography.

questions.q: A one-dimensional index on date serves the weather query above. What does the engine do?
options: Read only the matching records, since date narrows both conditions
Fail, since two filters need two separate queries to be answered
Switch to a hash index, which handles the second filter automatically
Scan all 2013 records and filter by temperature, or the reverse
optionExplain: One dimension cannot narrow the other, so records outside the temperature range are read too.
It can run; it just reads more records than needed.
There is no such automatic switch, and hash indexes do not handle ranges.
Right: one dimension cannot narrow both.
questions.explain: With one dimension you either scan by date then filter, or by temperature then filter.

questions.q: True or false: Multi-dimensional indexes can also serve data that is not geographic, such as colours or date and temperature.
questions.explain: The chapter gives examples such as (red, green, blue) colours and (date, temperature) observations.

questions.q: An online shop wants products within a range of colours. Which index idea from the chapter fits?
options: A three-dimensional index on (red, green, blue)
A concatenated index on red only, with green and blue filtered afterwards
A full-text index on colour names, so shoppers can search by word
A Bloom filter on colours, which lists every product in the range
optionExplain: Right: it is the chapter's example.
One channel alone cannot narrow the other two, so most products are still scanned.
Names are not numeric ranges in three dimensions.
A Bloom filter only rules keys out; it cannot return a range.
questions.explain: On an ecommerce website you could use a three-dimensional index on (red, green, blue) to search for products in a range of colors.
questions.teaches: A three-dimensional index on (red, green, blue) can search products in a certain range of colors, and HyperDex uses a two-dimensional index on (date, temperature) for weather observations.

questions.q: A user types a misspelled word into a search box. What does an exact-key index do?
options: Finds the closest word automatically, as it does for any search
Corrects the typo using a hash, then looks up the corrected word
Returns all keys in a range around the word, as a range query would
Fails to find similar words, since it matches only exact keys
optionExplain: Exact-key indexes match only exact values, so near-misses are not found.
A hash gives no notion of similarity, so it cannot correct a typo.
A sorted range does not contain misspellings; they may sit anywhere in the order.
Right: fuzzy querying needs different techniques.
questions.explain: Exact indexes treat near-misses as nothing. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Fuzzy search matches words within an edit distance, not exact keys.

questions.q: Lucene can search for words within a certain edit ____.
questions.explain: An edit distance of 1 means one letter added, removed, or replaced.

questions.q: Which of these words is NOT within edit distance 1 of color?
options: collar
colour
colon
colors
optionExplain: Right: turning color into collar needs two edits, so it is outside distance 1.
Adding one letter (u) gives colour, which is within distance 1.
Replacing one letter (r by n) gives colon, which is within distance 1.
Adding one letter (s) gives colors, which is within distance 1.
questions.explain: Count single-letter additions, removals, replacements.

questions.q: A user searches for wrunning while the index holds running. Within edit distance 1, is it a match?
options: No, since two letters differ between wrunning and running
Yes, removing one letter turns it into running
No, since fuzzy search only finds synonyms and not typing mistakes
Only if the capital letters of both words match exactly
optionExplain: Only one letter differs: removing the extra w gives running.
Right: removing the extra w turns wrunning into running, which is one edit.
Fuzzy search copes with typos through edit distance as well.
Case is not what edit distance counts here.
questions.explain: One extra letter is distance 1.

questions.q: True or false: Lucene's in-memory index for its term dictionary is a sparse list of some keys, as in LevelDB.
questions.explain: In Lucene it is a finite state automaton over the characters in the keys, similar to a trie.

questions.q: How does Lucene support efficient search for words within a given edit distance?
options: It adds a hash map of all possible misspellings of every word
It scans every document on each query and compares each word
It turns its automaton into a Levenshtein automaton
It uses a Bloom filter for typos, which approximates similar words
optionExplain: No such table is described; it would be enormous.
That would be far too slow, and it is not what is described.
Right: a Levenshtein automaton supports efficient search within an edit distance.
A Bloom filter rules out absent keys; it does not find similar words.
questions.explain: Lucene's in-memory index is a finite state automaton over the characters in the keys, similar to a trie, which can be transformed into a Levenshtein automaton.
questions.teaches: Lucene's in-memory index is a finite state automaton over the characters of the keys, similar to a trie, which can be transformed into a Levenshtein automaton to support efficient search for words within a given edit distance.

questions.q: A dataset fits comfortably in RAM. What would a design that keeps it all in memory have to solve to survive a restart?
options: Sorting, since memory cannot hold data that is sorted by key
Concurrency, which a disk-based design avoids but memory introduces
Durability, since memory contents vanish when power is lost
Compression, because RAM is too small to hold the dataset
optionExplain: Memory holds sorted structures very well; sorting is not the problem.
Disk-based engines face concurrency problems too, so it is not the new issue.
Right: it needs a log, snapshots or replicas.
The premise is that the dataset fits comfortably in RAM.
questions.explain: Memory is fast but forgets. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Trade disk's durability for RAM's convenience, and add a log, snapshots or replicas to survive restarts.

questions.q: Match each in-memory system to its durability approach.
pairs: Caching only; data may be lost on restart
Weak durability, writing to disk asynchronously
Durable, with a log-structured approach in memory and on disk
questions.explain: Systems differ in how much durability they promise.

questions.q: A team needs an in-memory store whose data survives a machine restart. Which is a way listed in the chapter?
options: Rely on the operating system's file cache alone to keep the data safe
Write a log of changes to disk, or replicate the state to other machines
Sort the data before storing it so that it can be found again
Use a larger memtable so that fewer writes are lost on a restart
optionExplain: The file cache is not a durability mechanism; it can be lost on a crash.
Right: a log of changes on disk and replication to other machines are both named.
Order does not make memory contents survive a restart.
Memtables belong to LSM-trees, and a larger one would lose more on a crash.
questions.explain: Durability options: special hardware, a log, snapshots, replication.

questions.q: An in-memory database writes a log to disk. Does that make it a disk-based database?
options: No: the disk is used only as an append-only log and reads are served from memory
Yes, because the data is on disk after the log is written there
Yes, because it needs to read the log from disk on every query
No, because the log is never read back from disk at all
optionExplain: Right: that is the chapter's view.
Reads are still served from memory, so the disk is only a log.
The log is read only on restart, to reload the state.
It is read after a restart to reload the state into memory.
questions.explain: Despite writing to disk, it is still in-memory.

questions.q: True or false: An in-memory database that writes a log to disk still serves its reads entirely from memory.
questions.explain: The disk is used only as an append-only log for durability, so it is still an in-memory database.

questions.q: Beyond durability, why is writing the log to disk useful for an in-memory database?
options: It makes reads faster, since the log can be searched before memory
It removes the need for restarts, since the log keeps the server alive
It sorts the data, so that memory lookups can use binary search
Files on disk can be easily backed up, inspected and analyzed by external utilities
optionExplain: Reads are already served from memory, so the log does not speed them up.
It does not; after a restart the log is used to reload the state.
Sorting is not the purpose of the log; it records changes in order.
Right: files on disk are an operational advantage, easy to back up and inspect.
questions.explain: Writing to disk also has operational advantages.
questions.teaches: Writing an in-memory database's changes to disk also has operational advantages: files on disk can easily be backed up, inspected and analyzed by external utilities.

questions.q: A vendor says its in-memory database is fast because it does not read from disk. How does the chapter respond?
options: It calls that counterintuitive: the gain is mostly avoiding encoding overhead
It agrees: the gain is the absence of reads from disk
It says in-memory databases are slower than disk engines in practice
It says the gain comes from compression of the stored data
optionExplain: Right: disk engines may never read from disk either.
The chapter says the OS cache means disk engines may also avoid reads.
No such claim is made; the point is where the gain comes from.
Compression is not given as the reason.
questions.explain: The OS cache also hides disk reads. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Speed comes from not encoding data for disk, not from avoiding disk reads.

questions.q: A disk-based engine may rarely read from disk, because the operating system ____ recently used disk blocks in memory.
questions.explain: That is why avoiding disk reads is not the main source of the advantage.

questions.q: A benchmark shows an in-memory database winning even when a disk database has everything in the OS cache. What explains it?
options: Disk databases must read from disk on every query, even when data is cached
In-memory databases do not need indexes or other data structures at all
The disk database lacks a log, so every write pays an extra cost
The in-memory one avoids encoding data structures into a disk format
optionExplain: The OS cache removes those reads, which is the premise of the benchmark.
They still use data structures; they avoid encoding them for disk.
A log is irrelevant to the read-side speed difference.
Right: avoiding the encoding of structures into a disk format removes real overhead.
questions.explain: The advantage is overhead of encoding.

questions.q: Is the advantage of an in-memory database likely to disappear for a disk-based engine given far more RAM than data?
options: Yes, completely, since the disk engine would never need to read from disk
Not entirely: the encoding overhead for disk structures remains
It grows, since extra RAM makes the in-memory engine faster still
It reverses, so that the disk engine becomes faster than the in-memory one
optionExplain: Encoding overhead for disk structures remains even when everything is cached.
Right: caching removes reads but not encoding.
The chapter does not say that; the advantage comes from avoiding encoding.
There is no evidence for that in the chapter.
questions.explain: Caching helps reads but not encoding.
questions.rule: Cache is not the same as in-memory.

questions.q: True or false: In-memory databases are useful only for speed and cannot offer any data model that disk-based indexes find hard.
questions.explain: Redis offers priority queues and sets, which are comparatively simple to implement because all data is in memory.

questions.q: Which data structures does Redis offer as a database interface because all data is in memory?
options: Column files and bitmaps
R-trees and tries
Priority queues and sets
Heap files and clustered indexes
optionExplain: Column files and bitmaps belong to column-oriented storage, not to Redis.
R-trees and tries are not what the chapter names for Redis.
Right: Redis offers priority queues and sets, which are simple to build in memory.
Heap files and clustered indexes are disk-based concepts, so they do not fit an in-memory store.
questions.explain: Redis offers a database-like interface to data structures such as priority queues and sets.
questions.teaches: Because Redis keeps all data in memory, it can offer a database-like interface to structures such as priority queues and sets with comparatively simple implementation.

questions.q: An in-memory database runs out of memory. What could it do without becoming a disk-based database?
options: Delete the oldest records until the rest fit in memory
Rewrite itself as a B-tree with pages that can be moved to disk
Move the least recently used data to disk and load it back when needed
Stop accepting reads until enough memory is free again
optionExplain: That loses data instead of managing it.
That would bring back the disk-oriented overhead the design avoids.
Right: evicting least recently used data to disk and reloading it is anti-caching.
That makes the database unavailable; it is not a solution.
questions.explain: Cold data can be evicted. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Evict cold records, not pages, and keep the indexes in RAM.

questions.q: Anti-caching evicts the ____ recently used data from memory to disk.
questions.explain: It loads the data back when it is accessed again.

questions.q: How does anti-caching differ from the operating system's virtual memory and swap files?
options: The database works at the granularity of individual records, not whole pages
It never writes anything to disk, unlike swapping by the operating system
It evicts the most recently used data first, while the OS keeps the oldest
It works at page granularity, exactly like the operating system does
optionExplain: Right: working with individual records lets the database use memory more efficiently than the OS.
It does write evicted data to disk and reloads it when needed.
It evicts the least recently used data.
The database can work at the level of individual records instead.
questions.explain: Record-level eviction is a finer unit.

questions.q: A dataset grows beyond memory with anti-caching. What must still fit in memory?
options: The whole data set
Nothing
Only the log
All the indexes
optionExplain: Cold data goes to disk, so the whole data set does not need to fit.
The indexes must still fit entirely in memory, so something does need to fit.
The log is not what must fit; the indexes are.
Right: the indexes must fit entirely in memory, as with the Bitcask keys.
questions.explain: Indexes must fit entirely in memory.

questions.q: True or false: Anti-caching removes the requirement that indexes fit entirely in memory.
questions.explain: The approach still requires indexes to fit entirely in memory, as in the Bitcask example.

questions.q: What does the chapter say about non-volatile memory (NVM)?
options: It makes B-trees obsolete, since pages need no longer be overwritten
Further changes to storage design will probably be needed if it spreads
It is already the standard, so storage engines no longer need disks
It removes the need for logs, since memory is no longer lost
optionExplain: The chapter does not claim this.
Right: it is a research area to watch.
It is described as a new area of research, not as the standard.
The chapter does not claim this either.
questions.explain: At present this is a new area of research, but worth keeping an eye on.
questions.teaches: If non-volatile memory technologies become more widely adopted, further changes to storage engine design will probably be needed.

questions.q: A query computes the total revenue of each store in January. Which workload is it?
options: Transaction processing: it handles money, as transactions do
Neither: it is a join, and joins belong to a separate kind of workload
Analytics: it aggregates over a large number of records
Transaction processing: it is written in SQL, like transactional queries
optionExplain: The topic does not decide it; the access pattern does.
Joins appear in both kinds of workload.
Right: aggregating over many records is the mark of an analytic (OLAP) query.
Both kinds of workload use SQL.
questions.explain: Pattern decides, not the topic. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: OLTP touches few records by key; OLAP scans many records for aggregates.

questions.q: Sort each characteristic: typical of OLTP or of OLAP?

items.t: Fetches a small number of records per query by key
Random-access, low-latency writes from user input
Primarily used by the end user via a web application
Aggregates over a large number of records
Bulk import or event stream writes
Dataset of terabytes to petabytes

questions.explain: OLTP is interactive and small; OLAP is bulk and large.

questions.q: Which query is OLAP?
options: How many more bananas than usual did we sell during our latest promotion?
Show the order status for customer 42 on the order tracking page
Add item X to the basket of user 7 when the button is pressed
Update the delivery address stored for order 99 after a customer edits it
optionExplain: Right: an aggregate over many records.
A single key lookup for an end user is OLTP.
A small low-latency write from user input is OLTP.
A small write driven by user input is OLTP.
questions.explain: Aggregates over many records mark OLAP.

questions.q: What is usually the bottleneck for OLTP storage, and for analytic storage?
options: Disk bandwidth for OLTP; disk seek time for analytics
Disk seek time for OLTP; disk bandwidth for analytics
CPU for both
Network for both
optionExplain: This reverses them: seeks dominate small lookups, and bandwidth dominates scans.
Right: OLTP is limited by seek time, and analytics by disk bandwidth.
The chapter names disk seek time and disk bandwidth, not CPU, for these workloads.
The chapter names disk costs, not the network, as the bottlenecks here.
questions.explain: Seeks dominate small lookups; bandwidth dominates scans.

questions.q: True or false: OLAP systems handle a much lower volume of queries than OLTP systems, though each query is demanding.
questions.explain: Each analytic query typically requires many millions of records to be scanned in a short time.

questions.q: How do OLTP and OLAP typically differ in what the data represents?
options: OLTP holds history over time; OLAP holds the latest state of data
Both hold only the latest state of the data at one point in time
Neither stores events; both store only summary figures about sales
OLTP holds the latest state; OLAP holds the history of events over time
optionExplain: This reverses them: OLTP holds the latest state, OLAP the history.
OLAP systems hold the history of events that happened over time.
OLAP systems typically store the individual events.
Right: OLTP holds the current state, while OLAP keeps the history of events.
questions.explain: From the comparison table.
questions.teaches: OLTP data represents the latest state (a current point in time) while analytic data represents the history of events over time, and dataset sizes run gigabytes to terabytes versus terabytes to petabytes.

questions.q: What does 'transaction processing' mean in this chapter?
options: Systems that guarantee the ACID properties for every group of operations
Allowing clients to make low-latency reads and writes
Only systems that handle money, such as sales and salary payments
Any query written in SQL, whatever it reads or writes
optionExplain: The chapter says transaction processing need not have ACID properties.
Right: as opposed to batch jobs.
That was the origin of the word, but the term has long since spread.
SQL is used for batch and analytic work as well, so it does not define it.
questions.explain: Low latency, not guarantees. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Transaction processing means low-latency reads and writes, not necessarily ACID.

questions.q: Transaction processing allows low-latency reads and writes, as opposed to ____ processing jobs that run periodically.
questions.explain: For example, once per day.

questions.q: A game stores each action instantly as players click. Is that transaction processing in the chapter's sense?
options: No: transactions involve money, and a game does not
No: transaction processing needs ACID guarantees, which a game lacks
Yes: low-latency reads and writes, even without money
No: transaction processing runs once per day, like a report
optionExplain: The term stuck even where no money changes hands.
ACID is not required; low latency is what counts here.
Right: low-latency reads and writes make it transaction processing, with or without money.
Periodic runs are batch processing, the opposite of low latency.
questions.explain: Low latency decides.

questions.q: A database offers low-latency writes but no ACID guarantees. Does it support transaction processing?
options: No, it needs ACID
No, it needs SQL
Only if it is a data warehouse
Yes, in the chapter's sense
optionExplain: ACID is not required for transaction processing in the chapter's sense.
SQL is not required either; low latency is the defining feature.
Being a data warehouse would make it analytic, not transactional.
Right: low-latency reads and writes are what the term means here.
questions.explain: Transaction processing is about latency.

questions.q: True or false: In this chapter, a database must provide ACID properties to count as supporting transaction processing.
questions.explain: Transaction processing just means allowing clients to make low-latency reads and writes.

questions.q: Why did the term 'transaction' stick for databases beyond business data?
options: The access pattern stayed similar to processing business transactions
Because all databases moved to ACID guarantees as they spread
Because of regulation
Because data warehouses adopted the term for their bulk loads
optionExplain: Right: the pattern of small reads and writes by key stayed like business transactions.
The chapter says transaction processing does not require ACID.
The chapter says nothing about regulation; the reason is the similar access pattern.
Warehouses came later and are the contrast, not the origin.
questions.explain: A transaction came to mean a group of reads and writes forming a logical unit.
questions.teaches: Even as databases were used for comments, game actions and contacts, the access pattern stayed similar to processing business transactions, so the term transaction stuck.

questions.q: Analysts want to run big ad hoc queries on live transaction data. Why do database administrators resist?
options: Analysts are not allowed to see sales data in the live systems
SQL cannot express analytic queries over large amounts of data
The queries scan large parts of the dataset and can harm concurrent transactions
The data is too small for analytic queries to be worth running
optionExplain: The reason given is performance, not permission.
SQL works well for analytic queries too.
Right: expensive scans over large parts of the dataset can harm concurrent transactions.
The scans are costly precisely because the dataset is large.
questions.explain: Expensive scans hurt latency-critical systems. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Copy OLTP data through ETL into a warehouse built for scans.

questions.q: The process of getting data into a warehouse is known as ____ (Extract–Transform–Load).
questions.explain: Data is extracted, transformed into an analysis-friendly schema, cleaned up and loaded.
questions.rule: ETL moves data into the warehouse.

questions.q: Put the ETL steps in order.
items: Extract data from the OLTP databases (dump or update stream)
Transform it into an analysis-friendly schema and clean it up
Load it into the data warehouse
questions.explain: ETL is extract, transform, load.

questions.q: A company with one small database and a few thousand rows considers a data warehouse. What does the chapter suggest?
options: Probably unnecessary; a conventional SQL database or spreadsheet can do
Essential for any company, however small its data volumes may be
Required by law for every company that stores customer records
Impossible to build, since a warehouse needs several OLTP systems
optionExplain: Right: a small company can use a conventional SQL database or even a spreadsheet.
Small companies usually have few OLTP systems and little data, so it is rarely needed.
Nothing about legal requirements is mentioned.
It can be built, but the chapter suggests a simpler route for small data.
questions.explain: Small companies have fewer OLTP systems and less data.

questions.q: True or false: A data warehouse is a writable replica that applications update directly alongside the OLTP systems.
questions.explain: It contains a read-only copy of the data in the various OLTP systems.

questions.q: What big advantage does a separate warehouse have besides protecting OLTP performance?
options: It avoids needing SQL, since analysts use their own languages
It can be optimized for analytic access patterns, unlike the OLTP systems
It removes the need for any indexes or sorted data in its tables
It needs no ETL, because analysts read the live OLTP tables directly
optionExplain: Warehouses typically use SQL, which suits analytic queries.
Right: the index structures that suit OLTP are not good at analytic queries, so the warehouse is built differently.
Indexes become less relevant for big scans, but sort order and compact encoding still matter.
Data still has to be extracted, transformed and loaded into the warehouse.
questions.explain: The indexing algorithms of the first half work well for OLTP but not for analytic queries.
questions.teaches: Indexing algorithms that work well for OLTP are not very good at answering analytic queries, which is why the warehouse is optimized for analytic access patterns.

questions.q: A data warehouse and an OLTP database both accept SQL. Does that mean they store data the same way?
options: Yes: SQL dictates the storage format, so the internals match
Yes: only the hardware differs between the two kinds of system
No, because warehouses are not relational and do not accept SQL
No: the internals are optimized for very different query patterns
optionExplain: A query language does not fix how data is laid out underneath.
The internals differ, not just the hardware they run on.
Warehouses are most commonly relational and accept SQL.
Right: the same SQL surface can sit on engines tuned for transactions or for analytics.
questions.explain: Interface does not decide internals. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Same SQL surface, different engines underneath.

questions.q: The data model of a data warehouse is most commonly ____, because SQL is generally a good fit for analytic queries.
questions.explain: Many graphical analysis tools generate SQL queries.

questions.q: A product offers transaction processing and warehousing under one SQL interface. How does the chapter say it is increasingly built?
options: As one engine that serves both workloads equally well
As a single B-tree storage engine with an analytic query layer
As two separate storage and query engines behind a common SQL interface
As an in-memory cache in front of a single OLTP database
optionExplain: Increasingly the products run two separate engines instead.
The chapter describes separate engines, not one B-tree for both.
Right: they are increasingly two engines that happen to share an interface.
Nothing like this is described for products offering both.
questions.explain: Examples are SQL Server and SAP HANA.

questions.q: A team assumes warehouses and OLTP stores perform alike because of identical SQL. What goes wrong?
options: SQL dialects will differ so much that no query can be shared between them
The warehouse refuses to accept SQL from tools built for OLTP databases
Nothing goes wrong, since identical SQL means identical performance
The same query can behave very differently, as the internals suit different patterns
optionExplain: Dialect differences are not the point; the layouts underneath differ.
Warehouses accept SQL; the surprises are in performance.
Performance depends on the internals, which suit different query patterns.
Right: a common interface does not make the engines perform alike.
questions.explain: Performance depends on internals.

questions.q: True or false: Open source SQL-on-Hadoop projects are old and mature competitors to commercial warehouses.
questions.explain: The chapter calls them young but aiming to compete.

questions.q: What do vendors of data warehouses such as Teradata and Vertica typically do?
options: Give them away free, funded by consultancy and support
Sell their systems under expensive commercial licenses
Offer only open source versions of their systems to attract users
Sell hosted versions only, since warehouses cannot be installed
optionExplain: Vendors such as Teradata typically sell them under expensive licences.
Right: the open source SQL-on-Hadoop projects are the younger alternative.
The open source projects are separate, younger competitors.
Amazon RedShift is a hosted ParAccel, but vendors also sell licensed systems.
questions.explain: Amazon RedShift is a hosted version of ParAccel.
questions.teaches: Data warehouse vendors such as Teradata, Vertica, SAP HANA and ParAccel typically sell under expensive commercial licenses, while open source SQL-on-Hadoop projects are young but aim to compete.

questions.section: Stars and Snowflakes: Schemas for Analytics
questions.q: A warehouse table has one row per customer purchase. Which other tables would make the data useful for analysis?
options: A second copy of the purchase table sorted by price
Tables describing the product, store, date and customer involved
A table of the hardware servers that stored the rows
A table of the SQL queries that analysts have run on the data
optionExplain: A copy adds no description of who, what or where.
Right: these describe each event's context.
Servers are not part of the event's context.
Query history does not describe the purchases themselves.
questions.explain: Events need context to be analysed. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Store each event as a fact row that points at dimension tables describing it.

questions.section: Stars and Snowflakes: Schemas for Analytics
questions.q: Match each star-schema part to its role.
pairs: One event, such as a purchase
Describes who, what, where or when
Foreign key column in a fact table
Points at a row in a dimension table
Attribute column in a fact table
A measured value such as the sale price
questions.explain: The fact table sits in the middle and the dimensions surround it.
questions.rule: Facts are events; dimensions are context.

questions.section: Stars and Snowflakes: Schemas for Analytics
questions.q: Sort each fact_sales column: stored as an attribute in the fact row, or a foreign key to a dimension?

items.t: Price at which the product was sold
Cost of buying the product from the supplier
product_sk, identifying which product
store_sk, identifying which store
date_key, identifying the day

questions.explain: Prices and costs are measured values; keys identify the who, what, where and when held in dimension tables.
questions.rule: Measures stay in the fact; context is referenced.

questions.section: Stars and Snowflakes: Schemas for Analytics
questions.q: An analyst wants to compare sales on public holidays with other days. Which design supports that?
options: Storing a text date in each fact row and guessing holidays in the query
Dropping dates from the fact table to save space
A date dimension table that records which days are public holidays
A separate fact table for each day of the year
optionExplain: The fact row would then have no holiday information to query.
Without dates, there is no way to pick holiday sales.
Right: dimension rows can carry extra information about dates.
That multiplies tables without adding holiday knowledge.
questions.explain: Even date and time are often represented using dimension tables.

questions.section: Stars and Snowflakes: Schemas for Analytics
questions.q: True or false: In a star schema, each row of the fact table represents one type of product available for sale.
questions.explain: Each fact row represents an event that occurred at a particular time. Product types are rows of a dimension table.

questions.section: Stars and Snowflakes: Schemas for Analytics
questions.q: A customer buys three different products in one checkout. How does the chapter's simplified fact table store that?
options: As three separate rows, one per product
As one row with three product columns
As one row holding a list of products
As one row, with the extra products in a dimension table
optionExplain: Right: each product purchased is its own row.
The chapter describes one product per row.
Facts are single events with simple keys.
Dimensions describe products, not the purchase event itself.
questions.explain: If the customer buys several different products at once, they are represented as separate rows in the fact table.
questions.teaches: When a customer buys several different products at once, the simplified fact table represents them as separate rows, one per product.

questions.section: Stars and Snowflakes: Schemas for Analytics
questions.q: A product dimension stores brand and category as text on every row. How could it be normalized?
options: Copy the product table into each fact row, so no joins are needed
Delete the brand column, so that only the category remains as text
Sort the product table by brand, so repeated names sit together
Move brand and category into their own tables referenced by foreign keys
optionExplain: That adds repetition, the opposite of normalization.
That loses information instead of organizing it.
Sorting does not remove the repeated text from each row.
Right: breaking a dimension into subdimensions is a snowflake schema.
questions.explain: Normalizing means referencing, not repeating. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Star is flat and simple; snowflake is more normalized with subdimensions.

questions.section: Stars and Snowflakes: Schemas for Analytics
questions.q: In a ____ schema, dimensions are further broken down into subdimensions.
questions.explain: A star keeps each dimension as a single table.

questions.section: Stars and Snowflakes: Schemas for Analytics
questions.q: A team values analyst simplicity over minimizing repeated brand names. Which does the chapter say is often preferred?
options: A snowflake schema, since it is more normalized and so cleaner
Neither: analysts should query the OLTP tables directly
A star schema, since it is simpler for analysts to work with
A single flat table with no dimensions at all, for easy querying
optionExplain: The chapter says star schemas are often preferred for simplicity.
Warehouses exist so that analytic queries stay off the OLTP databases.
Right: it is less normalized, but simplicity usually wins.
The chapter does not describe that; dimensions keep context in separate tables.
questions.explain: Snowflake schemas are more normalized than star schemas, but stars are often preferred for simplicity.

questions.section: Stars and Snowflakes: Schemas for Analytics
questions.q: A fact table has 120 columns and a typical query touches 5. In a row-oriented engine, what does it still have to do per matching row?
options: Read only the five columns it needs, skipping the other 115
Load and parse the whole row with all of its columns
Read only the dimension tables, since they hold the descriptions
Skip the row entirely, since a query can use an index instead
optionExplain: A row store keeps a row's values together, so it cannot skip inside a row.
Right: the layout stores whole rows together, so the unused columns are loaded too.
The fact rows still have to be read to answer the query.
The row matched the filter and still has to be fetched.
questions.explain: Wide tables make row-by-row reading costly.

questions.section: Stars and Snowflakes: Schemas for Analytics
questions.q: True or false: Snowflake schemas are more normalized than star schemas.
questions.explain: Snowflake schemas break dimensions into subdimensions and are therefore more normalized, yet stars are often preferred for simplicity.

questions.section: Stars and Snowflakes: Schemas for Analytics
questions.q: Why can a dim_store dimension table be very wide?
options: It holds all the metadata that may matter for analysis, such as bakery or square footage
It stores every sale made in that store, so each sale adds columns
It repeats all of the fact table's columns for each store listed
Dimension tables are always wider than the fact tables they describe
optionExplain: Right: it describes the store in rich detail.
Sales belong to rows of the fact table, not to the store dimension.
It describes the store, not the facts.
The chapter says that fact tables often have over 100 columns themselves.
questions.explain: Dimension tables include all the metadata that may be relevant for analysis.
questions.teaches: Dimension tables can be very wide because they hold all the metadata that may be relevant for analysis, for example which services a store offers, its square footage and its distance from the nearest highway.

questions.q: A query sums one column of a table with 100 columns and a billion rows. Which layout reads less data?
options: Storing each row's values together, as in a row store
Neither: both layouts have to read the same amount of data
Storing rows in a document format with one block per row
Storing each column's values together in its own file
optionExplain: It must load all 100 columns of every row.
A row layout cannot skip columns inside a row, so it reads more.
A document is also one contiguous block, so every field is read.
Right: only the column the query needs is read.
questions.explain: Skipping unneeded columns saves most of the work. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Store column values together so a query reads only the columns it needs.

questions.q: To rebuild the 23rd row from column files, take the ____ entry from each file.
questions.explain: Every column file holds the rows in the same order.

questions.q: A fact table has 100 equally wide columns and a query reads 4 of them. About what share of the data does a column store read, compared with a row store reading everything?
options: About 40 percent
About 25 percent
About 4 percent
About 100 percent
optionExplain: This miscounts four columns as forty.
This takes one quarter, ignoring the 100 columns.
Right: reading 4 of 100 equally wide columns means about 4 percent of the data.
This is what a row store reads.
questions.explain: Only the used columns are read: 4/100.
questions.rule: Read only the columns in the query.

questions.q: Suppose two column files stored the same rows in different orders. What would break?
options: Nothing, since each column file is self-contained and sorted alone
Only compression would stop working, while reads stay correct
Only writes would be slower, because appends need extra work
Rebuilding a row from the same position in each file would give wrong combinations
optionExplain: Position is the only link between columns, so mismatched order breaks it.
Reassembling rows itself would fail, not just compression.
Reads would also return wrong combinations of values.
Right: the kth entries would no longer belong to one row.
questions.explain: Rows are identified by position within a column.
questions.rule: Keep one row order in all columns.

questions.q: True or false: Column-oriented storage works only for relational data and not for document models.
questions.explain: It applies equally to nonrelational data; the layout idea does not depend on the relational model.

questions.q: How does a document database typically store each document?
options: With each field in its own file, as in columnar storage
As one contiguous sequence of bytes, much like row-oriented storage
As a hash of its fields, which is expanded when it is read
As a heap of pointers only, with each field stored elsewhere
optionExplain: That describes a column store, not a typical document database.
Right: the whole document is stored together.
Documents are stored whole, not as hashes.
The document itself is stored contiguously, not scattered.
questions.explain: Document databases are similar to row-oriented ones: an entire document is typically stored as one contiguous sequence of bytes.
questions.teaches: Document databases are row-oriented in this sense: an entire document is typically stored as one contiguous sequence of bytes.

questions.q: A column with a billion rows holds about 200 distinct country codes. Which encoding exploits that?
options: One bit sequence per country with a bit for each row
A separate file for each row, so each row can be read alone
A hash of each country code, which is shorter than the code
Repeating each code 200 times so every code is easy to find
optionExplain: Right: one bitmap per distinct value, with one bit for each row, exploits the few distinct values.
That multiplies files without compressing the column.
Hashing does not reduce a column of repeated values to a smaller form.
That makes the column larger, not smaller.
questions.explain: Few distinct values mean few bitmaps. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: One bitmap per distinct value, compressed by run lengths when sparse.

questions.q: A column with n distinct values becomes ____ bitmaps.
questions.explain: There is one bitmap per distinct value, with one bit per row.

questions.q: Column values by row are 3,3,3,2,3,2,2,3. The bitmap for value 3 is ____.
questions.explain: Write 1 where the row holds 3 and 0 elsewhere: 1,1,1,0,1,0,0,1.
questions.rule: 1 means the row has that value.

questions.q: A column has 100,000 distinct values over billions of rows. How do its bitmaps look, and what helps?
options: They are mostly ones, so they can be stored exactly as they are
They look random, so no compression can shrink them
They are too small to need storing on disk at all
They are mostly zeros, so run-length encoding makes them compact
optionExplain: Each value occurs in few rows, so the bitmaps are mostly zeros.
Long runs of zeros are very compressible by run-length encoding.
Each bitmap still has one bit per row, billions of bits long.
Right: with many distinct values the bitmaps are sparse, and run-length encoding compacts them.
questions.explain: The bigger n is, the sparser each bitmap.

questions.q: True or false: To combine the bitmaps of two different columns with a bitwise AND, the columns must hold rows in different orders.
questions.explain: It works because the columns hold the rows in the same order, so the kth bit of one bitmap matches the kth bit of the other.

questions.q: For WHERE product_sk IN (30, 68, 69), how does a bitmap-encoded column answer it?
options: Load the three bitmaps and compute their bitwise AND
Load the three bitmaps and compute their bitwise OR
Scan the column and compare each row
Load only the bitmap for 30
optionExplain: AND would select rows matching all three values at once.
Right: rows matching any of the values.
Scanning and comparing each row ignores the bitmaps, which exist to avoid exactly that.
The other values would be missed.
questions.explain: Bitmap indexes suit warehouse queries: OR for IN lists, AND for conditions on different columns.
questions.rule: IN means OR; combined conditions mean AND.
questions.teaches: For IN queries the engine loads the bitmaps of each value and computes a bitwise OR, and for conditions on two columns it computes a bitwise AND, which works because the columns hold rows in the same order.

questions.q: A column scan is limited by more than disk speed. What else might developers of analytic databases worry about?
options: Getting data from main memory into the CPU cache efficiently
The colour scheme of the user interface that shows the results
The number of dimension tables, which sets the speed of the CPU
Whether the keys in the table are unique, which sets cache use
optionExplain: Right: memory bandwidth is another bottleneck.
That has nothing to do with scan speed.
Schema choices do not set CPU speed.
Uniqueness of keys does not decide how a scan uses the cache.
questions.explain: The bottleneck moves as the first one is removed. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Process compressed column chunks in tight cache-sized loops.

questions.q: Operating on chunks of compressed column data in a tight loop, without function calls, is called ____ processing.
questions.explain: Operators such as bitwise AND and OR can work directly on compressed chunks.

questions.q: Which choice helps more rows of a column fit in the CPU's L1 cache?
options: Storing whole rows together
Adding more function calls per record
Compressing the column
Using wider data types
optionExplain: Whole rows carry unneeded columns, so fewer useful values fit in the cache.
Function calls slow the tight loop that vectorized processing depends on.
Right: more compressed rows fit in the same space.
Wider values fill the cache faster.
questions.explain: Column compression allows more rows to fit in the same amount of L1 cache.

questions.q: A query engine switches from row-at-a-time processing with many function calls to tight loops over column chunks. What changes?
options: Disk reads double, since the data is now processed in chunks
Column order must be randomized so the loop can skip checks
The CPU runs the loop much faster
Results become approximate, because chunks are processed together
optionExplain: Disk reads are unchanged; the change is in how the CPU handles the data.
The order is unchanged; the loop simply avoids per-record calls.
Right: no calls or per-record conditions.
Results stay exact; only the speed changes.
questions.explain: A CPU executes a tight loop much faster than code requiring function calls and conditions per record.

questions.q: True or false: Disk bandwidth is the only bottleneck that developers of analytical databases worry about.
questions.explain: They also worry about memory bandwidth into the CPU cache, branch mispredictions and SIMD use.

questions.q: Which CPU features do analytic database developers try to use efficiently, per the chapter?
options: Hyper-threading only, with everything else left to the operating system
SIMD instructions, while avoiding branch mispredictions and pipeline bubbles
GPU memory, which holds the compressed columns in a cache
Disk controllers, which decide how columns are laid out
optionExplain: The chapter names SIMD, branch prediction and pipeline use instead.
Right: these are the CPU features the chapter names.
GPUs are not discussed in the chapter.
Disks are a separate bottleneck from the CPU.
questions.explain: They worry about avoiding branch mispredictions and bubbles in the pipeline, and making use of SIMD instructions.
questions.teaches: Developers of analytical databases also worry about avoiding branch mispredictions and bubbles in the CPU instruction pipeline, and about making use of single-instruction-multi-data (SIMD) instructions.

questions.q: A database advertises column families. What should you check before assuming column-oriented performance?
options: Whether it has a SQL interface, which signals analytic design
Whether it uses a write-ahead log, which signals columnar design
Whether it is open source, which signals columnar design
Whether values of each column are stored together and compressed
optionExplain: SQL says nothing about how data is laid out.
A write-ahead log concerns crash recovery, not storage layout.
Licensing does not set the layout.
Right: that is what makes storage columnar.
questions.explain: Layout decides the performance. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Check how data is laid out, not what the feature is called.

questions.q: Cassandra and HBase inherited the concept of column ____ from Bigtable.
questions.explain: But it is misleading to call them column-oriented.

questions.q: Within one Cassandra column family, how is a row stored?
options: All its columns together with a row key
Each column in a separate compressed file
As one bitmap per value
As a sorted SSTable of columns only
optionExplain: Right: so it is mostly row-oriented.
Separate compressed column files would be column-oriented, which column families are not.
Bitmaps are used by column stores.
A sorted SSTable of columns only is not how column families are described.
questions.explain: They store all columns from a row together, along with a row key.

questions.q: An analyst expects column compression from a Bigtable-style store. What will they find?
options: Bitmap compression of every column, as in warehouse column stores
Compression of whole rows only, and only on SSDs
Run-length encoding of the first column, as in sorted column stores
None: column families do not use column compression
optionExplain: Column families do not use column compression.
Nothing like that is described; there is no column compression.
Run-length encoding is not part of the column family model.
Right: they store a row's columns together, so there is no column compression.
questions.explain: They do not use column compression.
questions.rule: No compression gain from the name.

questions.q: True or false: Because of column families, the Bigtable model is column-oriented.
questions.explain: The Bigtable model is still mostly row-oriented.

questions.q: Parquet stores a document data model. Can it still be a column-oriented format?
options: Yes: Parquet is a columnar storage format that supports a document data model
No, because document models need each whole document stored together
No, because only relational data has columns
Yes, but only because it uses column families like Bigtable
optionExplain: Right: column orientation does not depend on the relational model.
A columnar format can still support a document model; Parquet does.
Nonrelational data has fields that can be stored column by column.
Column families are the misleading case, not the reason Parquet is columnar.
questions.explain: Column storage is easiest to understand in a relational model but applies equally to nonrelational data.
questions.rule: Layout, not data model, makes storage columnar.
questions.teaches: Column-oriented storage applies to nonrelational data too: Parquet is a columnar storage format that supports a document data model, based on Google's Dremel.

questions.q: A column store's queries usually cover the last month. Which sort key helps most?
options: A random order, so that the load is spread evenly across files
Date, so the engine scans only the rows from the last month
Product name, because strings sort and compress well
The insertion order of the primary key, which tracks time
optionExplain: A random order helps no query that filters by date.
Right: the sort key matches the common filter.
The queries filter on dates, so the product name does not narrow the scan.
It may not match the date order, so it does not reliably narrow the scan.
questions.explain: The sort key should match the common filter. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Sort entire rows by keys that match the common queries.

questions.q: In a column store the data is sorted an entire ____ at a time, even though it is stored by column.
questions.explain: Otherwise the kth items would no longer belong to the same row.

questions.q: Queries group sales by product within a date range. Which sort keys fit?
options: product_sk first, date_key second
quantity first, date_key second
date_key first, product_sk second
No sort order
optionExplain: Putting product first would scatter the date ranges across the file.
The queries do not filter on quantity.
Right: same-product sales on the same day sit together.
Sorting can speed up these queries, so having no sort order forgoes that benefit.
questions.explain: A second sort key orders rows with equal first values.
questions.rule: Sort by the filter then the grouping.

questions.q: A column store sorted each column independently. What would break?
options: Nothing, since each column is read faster when sorted alone
Only the first column would work, and the rest would be unusable
The kth items of different columns would no longer belong to the same row
The queries would run twice as fast, but the answers would be wrong
optionExplain: Rows could no longer be rebuilt, so results would be wrong.
Every column is affected, not only the first.
Right: rows could not be reconstructed.
Speed is not the issue; the point is that rows could not be rebuilt.
questions.explain: Row identity depends on position.

questions.q: True or false: A column store should sort each column independently to compress each as well as possible.
questions.explain: That would stop you knowing which items belong to the same row, so the whole row must be sorted together.

questions.q: If insertion order is used and no sort is imposed, how easily are new rows added?
options: By rewriting every column file to make room in the right place
By appending to each column file
By rebuilding all of the bitmaps from scratch for each new row
They cannot be added without sorting the table first
optionExplain: That is needed only when rows must be kept in sorted order.
Right: the new row goes at the end of every column.
Nothing requires rebuilding bitmaps for an append.
Rows can be added in insertion order by appending.
questions.explain: It is easiest to store rows in insertion order since inserting a row means appending to each column file.
questions.teaches: In a column store it is easiest to store rows in the order of insertion, because inserting a new row then just means appending to each of the column files.

questions.q: A column has 365 distinct dates over billions of rows, and the table is sorted by it. How will it compress?
options: Very well: long runs of equal dates compress to a few kilobytes
Poorly: sorting scatters equal values and breaks up runs
The same as when unsorted, since compression ignores row order
Only if each date is hashed before storing it in the column
optionExplain: Right: after sorting, equal dates form long runs that run-length encoding shrinks to kilobytes.
Sorting groups equal values together, which is what makes runs.
Run lengths depend on row order, so sorting changes the result.
Hashing is not the method; long runs are what compress.
questions.explain: Equal values together mean long runs. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Sorting by a low-cardinality column turns it into a few long runs.

questions.q: Long runs of repeated values compress well with ____-length encoding.
questions.explain: It stores run lengths rather than every value.

questions.q: A table has 2 billion rows and 365 distinct dates, sorted by date. Roughly how many runs does the date column hold?
options: 2 billion
optionExplain: One run per row means no compression.
There is a run per date value.
Each date is one run, not two.
Right: one run per distinct date.
questions.explain: After sorting, equal values are adjacent.

questions.q: What happens to compression gain for the second and third sort keys?
options: It weakens, as they appear more jumbled
It strengthens, because they follow a sorted key
It is identical to the first key
It disappears entirely
optionExplain: Right: later sort keys are more jumbled, so they compress less well.
Their order is jumbled across first-key groups.
The effect is strongest on the first.
Some benefit remains for the second and third keys, so it does not disappear entirely.
questions.explain: The compression effect is strongest on the first sort key.

questions.q: True or false: After sorting by one column, every other column compresses as well as the sorted one.
questions.explain: Columns further down the sorting priority appear in essentially random order, so they probably do not compress as well.

questions.q: Is sorting only by the first few columns still worthwhile?
options: No: only the very first sort column ever matters
No: sorting never helps compression of other columns
Only for numeric columns, which compress better than text
Yes: having the first few columns sorted is still a win overall
optionExplain: The chapter says that having the first few columns sorted is still a win.
Sorted leading columns do compress better.
The chapter does not restrict this to numeric columns.
Right: the benefit fades down the order but does not vanish.
questions.explain: The second and third sort keys will be more jumbled up, but having the first few columns sorted is still a win overall.
questions.teaches: Even though the second and third sort keys are more jumbled and compress less, having the first few columns sorted is still a win overall.

questions.q: Two common queries filter on different columns. A column store is sorted by only one. What could help?
options: Sort each column independently, each in its own best order
Keep another copy of the data sorted by the second column
Delete the second query's column to keep one order for everything
Convert the table to row storage so each row stays together
optionExplain: Rows could no longer be reconstructed from the columns.
Right: the replica can be used for the second query.
This removes data that the query needs.
That gives up the scan benefits of column storage.
questions.explain: Different orders serve different queries. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Keep redundant replicas in different sort orders and route each query to the best.

questions.q: The idea of storing data in several sort orders came from C-Store and was adopted by the commercial data warehouse ____.
questions.explain: It builds on the fact that data is replicated anyway.

questions.q: A warehouse already keeps three replicas for fault tolerance. How might it add sort orders at low extra cost?
options: Add a fourth replica for each new query that needs a different sort
Sort all replicas the same way so that they can serve any query
Sort each replica differently and pick the best one per query
Drop two of the replicas so that one can be re-sorted for each query
optionExplain: The point is to reuse the existing copies instead of adding more.
That gives no extra choices of sort order.
Right: the redundancy is already paid for.
Replicas exist to protect against failure, so dropping them removes that.
questions.explain: Data needs to be replicated anyway, so store it sorted in different ways.

questions.q: A column store keeps replicas sorted by date and by product. A query filters on one product. Which replica should it use?
options: The replica sorted by date, since dates are always present
Either; the sort order has no effect on filtering
The replica sorted by product
Neither; a query must use the first replica created
optionExplain: Date order scatters one product's rows through the replica.
Sort order is exactly what makes a filter cheap.
Right: matching rows sit together there.
Queries can use whichever version fits best.
questions.explain: A query can use the version that best fits its pattern.
questions.rule: Pick the replica sorted for your filter.

questions.q: True or false: A column store with several sort orders must use the same sort order for every query.
questions.explain: The point of several orders is that each query can use the version that best fits its pattern.

questions.q: How does a multi-sort-order column store differ from a row store with several secondary indexes?
options: A row store keeps each row in one place and indexes point to it; a column store holds only values, with no pointers
Secondary indexes in a row store hold full copies of the data, as sorted replicas do
Both rely on pointers into a shared heap file
A column store keeps one row in one place, like a heap file
optionExplain: Right: each sorted copy holds the actual column values.
Row-store indexes normally hold pointers to the heap or clustered index.
A column store normally has no pointers to data elsewhere.
Rows are split across the column files.
questions.explain: Having multiple sort orders is similar to having multiple secondary indexes, but the row store keeps every row in one place and indexes point to it.
questions.rule: Sorted copies hold values, not pointers.
questions.teaches: In a column store there normally are not any pointers to data elsewhere, only columns containing values, unlike the secondary indexes of a row store which point into the heap file or clustered index.

questions.q: Rows must be inserted into a table whose columns are compressed and sorted. What is a problem with inserting in the middle?
options: Only one column file would change, since the insert touches one value
The insert cannot happen on SSDs because compressed files are read-only
Nothing: an insert in the middle is always instant in a sorted table
All the column files would likely need rewriting
optionExplain: Every column file must stay consistent, because rows are identified by position.
The storage medium is not the issue; position-based rows are.
Sorting and compression are what make it expensive.
Right: rows are identified by position in each column.
questions.explain: Position links the columns. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Buffer writes in sorted memory, then merge them into column files in bulk.

questions.q: An update-in-place approach, like B-trees use, is not possible with ____ columns.
questions.explain: Insertion would require rewriting the column files.

questions.q: Put the column-store write path in order.
items: Writes go to an in-memory sorted store
Enough writes accumulate
They are merged with the column files on disk
New files are written in bulk
questions.explain: This mirrors the LSM approach.

questions.q: An analyst queries rows inserted a moment ago. What does the query see?
options: Only the old data on disk, until the next merge happens
The new data, as the optimizer combines disk and memory
An error, until the pending writes have been merged into the files
A random sample of the new rows, since they are not yet merged
optionExplain: The query optimizer also consults the in-memory store.
Right: the optimizer combines the data on disk with recent writes in memory.
Queries are not blocked; they combine both sources.
Results are exact, including recent writes.
questions.explain: Data modified with inserts, updates or deletes is immediately reflected in subsequent queries.

questions.q: True or false: For writing to column storage, it does not matter whether the in-memory store is row-oriented or column-oriented.
