questions.explain: Writes are added to a sorted structure in memory and later merged into the column files in bulk.

questions.q: Which system does the chapter name as doing this?
options: Memcached
Lucene
Vertica
Bitcask
optionExplain: Memcached is an in-memory cache, not a column store with this write path.
Lucene is a text search library, not described as doing this.
Right: Vertica sends writes to an in-memory store and merges them into column files.
Bitcask is a hash-indexed log, not a column store.
questions.explain: All writes first go to an in-memory store; merged in bulk. This is essentially what Vertica does.
questions.teaches: Vertica handles writes by sending them to an in-memory sorted store and merging them with the column files on disk in bulk, in an LSM-tree fashion.

questions.section: Aggregation: Data Cubes and Materialized Views
questions.q: Many queries repeatedly compute the same sums over raw data. What could save the work?
options: Store the results of those sums and keep them updated
Delete the raw data and keep only the final answers
Re-run each query more slowly so that it uses less memory
Add a bitmap index for each query that is run repeatedly
optionExplain: Right: a materialized aggregate stores the result so that it is not recomputed each time.
The raw data is the source and cannot be dropped.
That repeats the same work instead of saving it.
Bitmaps compress columns; they do not store aggregate results.
questions.explain: Precompute what is used often. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Cache common aggregates as a stored copy of a query result.

questions.section: Aggregation: Data Cubes and Materialized Views
questions.q: A ____ view is an actual copy of the query results, written to disk.
questions.explain: A virtual view is just a shortcut for writing queries.

questions.section: Aggregation: Data Cubes and Materialized Views
questions.q: When you read from a virtual view, what happens?
options: It returns a stored copy of the results that was written to disk
The engine expands it into its underlying query on the fly
It reads a data cube that was built when the view was created
It reads the write-ahead log to find the latest query results
optionExplain: That describes a materialized view.
Right: a virtual view is expanded into its underlying query on the fly.
A cube is a special case of a materialized view, not a virtual one.
The log plays no part in expanding a view.
questions.explain: A virtual view is a shortcut for writing queries.

questions.section: Aggregation: Data Cubes and Materialized Views
questions.q: A materialized view sits over a table with heavy writes. What is the effect?
options: Writes get cheaper, since the view helps the database avoid work
Nothing changes, because the view is only a stored shortcut
Reads slow down, because the view must be consulted first
Writes get more expensive as the view is updated too
optionExplain: The view must be updated on each write, which adds cost.
It is a denormalized copy that must be kept in step with the data.
Reads are what the view speeds up.
Right: the view is a copy that must be updated on writes, so writes get more expensive.
questions.explain: Updates make writes more expensive.

questions.section: Aggregation: Data Cubes and Materialized Views
questions.q: True or false: Materialized views make more sense in read-heavy data warehouses than in OLTP databases.
questions.explain: They make writes more expensive, which is why they are not often used in OLTP databases.

questions.section: Aggregation: Data Cubes and Materialized Views
questions.q: Why must a materialized view be updated when the underlying data changes?
options: It is a virtual view, so it expands into its query on each read
It is a denormalized copy of the data
It holds the write-ahead log
It is sorted, so every change reshuffles its rows
optionExplain: A virtual view is not a copy and needs no refreshing.
Right: it is a denormalized copy, so it goes stale unless it is refreshed.
A write-ahead log has nothing to do with why a materialized view needs updating.
Sorting is not the reason; being a copy is.
questions.explain: Because it is a denormalized copy of the data.
questions.teaches: The database can update a materialized view automatically, but whether it actually improves read performance depends on the individual case.

questions.section: Aggregation: Data Cubes and Materialized Views
questions.q: A grid stores the sum of sales for every date-product pair. Which query is quick?
options: Sales from items priced above $100 only, since price is stored in each cell
The sales of one specific customer's first order, found in its cell
Total sales per product, summed along the date axis
A free-text search of the product notes, using the cell contents
optionExplain: Price is not a dimension, so the cube cannot filter by it.
A cube holds aggregates, not individual orders.
Right: totals along an axis of the grid are precomputed, so they are quick.
Free-text search is unrelated to precomputed aggregates.
questions.explain: A cube answers questions along its dimensions. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Precompute aggregates per dimension combination, and keep the raw data too.

questions.section: Aggregation: Data Cubes and Materialized Views
questions.q: A data cube is a grid of ____ grouped by different dimensions.
questions.explain: Each cell holds an aggregate such as a sum.

questions.section: Aggregation: Data Cubes and Materialized Views
questions.q: You need total sales per store yesterday and have a cube with a store dimension. What does it take?
options: Scan the raw fact table and add up the rows for each store
Rebuild the cube first so that the totals are up to date
Join all the dimension tables and aggregate the result
Look at the totals along the store dimension
optionExplain: That is the work the cube exists to avoid.
Nothing needs rebuilding; the totals are already there.
The totals are precomputed, so no join is needed.
Right: no scan of millions of rows.
questions.explain: Precomputed values mean no scan.

questions.section: Aggregation: Data Cubes and Materialized Views
questions.q: An analyst asks what share of sales comes from items costing more than $100, but price is not a dimension of the cube. What happens?
options: The cube cannot answer; the raw data is needed
It answers using the cell totals, since they contain every detail
It rebuilds itself automatically
It estimates the share from the sizes of the cells
optionExplain: Right: a cube is less flexible than the raw data and cannot answer on price.
Cells hold sums, so price information cannot be recovered.
Nothing like that is described; a cube has only the dimensions it was built with.
The cube has no such feature, and the answer would be a guess.
questions.explain: A data cube does not have the same flexibility as raw data.

questions.section: Aggregation: Data Cubes and Materialized Views
questions.q: True or false: Most data warehouses keep as much raw data as possible and use cubes only as a performance boost.
questions.explain: A cube lacks the flexibility of raw data, so aggregates supplement the raw data and do not replace it.

questions.section: Aggregation: Data Cubes and Materialized Views
questions.q: With five dimensions (date, product, store, promotion, customer), what does each cell of the cube hold?
options: A single raw row from the fact table for that combination
The total of all facts, which is the same in every cell
The aggregate for one date-product-store-promotion-customer combination
A pointer to a bitmap that selects the matching facts
optionExplain: Cells hold aggregates, not raw rows.
That is one overall total, not a per-combination value.
Right: each cell holds the aggregate for one combination of the five dimensions.
Cube cells contain aggregates, not pointers to bitmaps.
questions.explain: The principle remains the same; values can be summarized along each dimension.
questions.teaches: With five dimensions (date, product, store, promotion, customer) a cube cell holds the sales for one date-product-store-promotion-customer combination, and those values can be repeatedly summarized along each dimension.

questions.q: Which storage design fits a workload of big scans over a few columns of billions of rows?
options: Column-oriented storage
A hash-indexed log
A B-tree on every column
An in-memory cache
optionExplain: Right: column-oriented storage reads only the few columns that big scans need.
A hash-indexed log is built for exact key lookups, not for big scans.
Indexes matter less for big scans.
An in-memory cache does not solve the problem of scanning billions of rows.
questions.explain: Scans need compact column reads. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Pick by workload first, then by family, then test with your own data.

questions.q: Sort each system by school: log-structured or update-in-place?

items.t: Bitcask
LevelDB
Cassandra
Lucene
B-tree indexes in relational databases
Fixed-size pages overwritten in place

questions.explain: The log-structured school only appends; the other overwrites pages.

questions.q: A user-facing app serves millions of small key lookups. What does the chapter say the bottleneck often is?
options: Disk bandwidth, since each lookup reads a large amount of data
Disk seek time, with an index finding the data
Network latency only, since lookups are small and numerous
CPU instruction pipelines, which limit each tiny lookup
optionExplain: That is the usual bottleneck for analytics, not for small lookups.
Right: for many small lookups, seek time is often the bottleneck, and an index finds the data.
The chapter names disk seek time here, not network latency.
That concern belongs to scans in analytic databases.
questions.explain: OLTP: seek time; analytics: bandwidth.

questions.q: Queries scan a large number of rows sequentially. What becomes less relevant, and what more important?
options: Compact encoding becomes less relevant, and indexes more important
Indexes and compact encoding stay equally relevant for scans
Neither matters, since a scan always reads everything at the same speed
Indexes less relevant; compact encoding more important
optionExplain: This reverses the effect for scans.
The chapter says indexes become much less relevant.
Encoding decides how much data must be read, so it matters.
Right: indexes matter less for big scans, while compact encoding reduces what must be read.
questions.explain: Less data read means faster scans.

questions.q: True or false: Log-structured engines such as Bitcask and LSM-trees update files in place.
questions.explain: They only permit appending to files and deleting obsolete files, never updating a file that has been written.

questions.q: What does the chapter hope you can do after reading it?
options: Tune any storage engine like an expert
Design a new storage engine from scratch for any workload
Make sense of the documentation of the database of your choice
Avoid testing, because the internals predict every result
optionExplain: The chapter says it will not make you an expert in tuning one engine.
It says you will probably not implement an engine yourself.
Right: the chapter hopes you can make sense of your database's documentation.
It advises testing with your own workload.
questions.explain: It hopes to equip you with enough vocabulary and ideas.
questions.teaches: When queries must sequentially scan a large number of rows, indexes are much less relevant and it becomes important to encode data compactly to minimize the amount that has to be read from disk.

questions.q: A team must release a server update without any downtime. How do large applications usually do it?
options: Deploy to a few nodes at a time, checking each step before continuing
Release only to new customers and leave existing customers on old code
Switch every server to the new version at the same moment, overnight
Keep two full copies of the data and swap them when users log out
optionExplain: Right: a staged rollout keeps the service up and lets the team check the new version as it spreads.
This keeps versions apart for customers, but servers still change gradually and mix.
That is possible but needs downtime or a perfectly synchronised switch, which large systems rarely get.
Duplicating the data is a different, costly technique and does not describe an upgrade of code.
questions.explain: A gradual rollout keeps the service running and limits risk. The card next shows what it implies for data formats.
questions.rule: Upgrade a few nodes at a time.

questions.q: Deploying a new version to a few nodes at a time, checking each step, is called a ____ upgrade.
questions.explain: A rolling upgrade, also called a staged rollout, moves through the nodes gradually.
questions.rule: Rolling upgrade means a few nodes at a time.

questions.q: A ride-booking backend has 20 servers and adds a field to trip records during a rolling upgrade. What must the system tolerate?
options: Phones showing the new field instantly, because mobile apps update at the same moment as the servers do
Servers with old code and servers with new code reading and writing trip records at once
Only new servers touching trip records, because old servers are drained from the pool before the upgrade starts
No mixing of versions, because the new field is optional
optionExplain: Client apps update only when users install them, so phones lag behind.
Right: during the rollout both versions are live and share the same records.
Draining first would be a stop-and-replace upgrade, not a rolling one.
Optional fields make a mix easier to handle, but the mix still exists.
questions.explain: While the upgrade runs, some nodes run old code and some run new code against the same data.

questions.q: Why are mixed versions more likely for client apps than for servers you control?
options: Clients cache responses and replay them after an update
Operators stage client rollouts more slowly than server rollouts
Client code is compiled and server code is interpreted
Users may not install the update for some time
optionExplain: Caching may keep old data, but it is not the reason versions mix.
Operators do not control when a client updates, so there is no staging to slow down.
Compilation style does not decide how long old versions stay in use.
Right: the user, not the operator, decides when a client updates.
questions.explain: With client apps you are at the mercy of the user, so old versions can stay in use for a long time.

questions.q: True or false: A rolling upgrade is only useful for avoiding downtime.
questions.explain: According to the book it also makes deployments less risky: a faulty release can be detected and rolled back before it affects many users.
questions.rule: Gradual rollout also limits the damage of a bad release.
questions.teaches: Rolling upgrades make releases less risky because a faulty version is caught and rolled back while few users are affected.

questions.q: A clinic updates a device fleet by stopping all devices and replacing the software together. What still outlasts the old software version?
options: Only the client apps, which cannot be stopped together with the devices
Nothing, because every device now runs the new code and no old records remain anywhere
Data that the old version wrote earlier and that is still stored
Only the old network protocol, which is replaced during the stop
optionExplain: Clients are not part of this stop-and-replace scenario.
The code is uniform, but stored data keeps the format it was written in.
Right: data written by old code stays in its original encoding unless rewritten, so old formats persist.
Messages in flight may differ, yet the lasting item is stored data.
questions.explain: Even a perfectly synchronised upgrade leaves old data behind in its original encoding.
questions.rule: Stored data outlives the code that wrote it.
questions.teaches: Data outlives code: records written by an old version stay in their original encoding after the code is replaced.

questions.q: True or false: If newer code can read old data, then older code can also read new data.
questions.explain: The two directions are separate properties; one does not imply the other. The card next names them.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Newer code reads data written by older code
Older code reads data written by newer code
New version deployed to a few nodes at a time
questions.explain: Backward looks to the past: new code, old data. Forward looks ahead: old code, new data.
questions.rule: Backward: new reads old. Forward: old reads new.

questions.q: A phone app on release 5 reads responses from a server already on release 6. Which property must the format give?
options: Forward compatibility, because older code reads data from newer code
Both directions, because every response involves two different versions of the software
Neither, because JSON text has no versions that could ever differ
Backward compatibility, because the server is the newer side and the app must understand it
optionExplain: Right: the reader is old and the writer is new, which is forward compatibility.
This one response flows one way, so one direction is what it needs.
Text formats still change over time and still need rules about change.
The reading side is the old app, so newer code is not the reader.
questions.explain: Judge direction by who reads: here old code reads new data.
questions.rule: Ask who reads and who wrote.

questions.q: Version 2 of a service adds a field. Version 1 clients start failing on version 2 responses. Which property is missing?
options: Both, because any failure between two versions means both directions are missing
Neither, because adding a field to a record does not change what any reader must handle
Forward compatibility, because version 1 cannot read version 2 output
Backward compatibility, because version 2 cannot read version 1
optionExplain: One reader failing shows one missing direction, not both.
Adding a field can break old readers if they cannot cope with it.
Right: older code is failing on data written by newer code.
Version 2 is not the one failing; the failing reader is version 1.
questions.explain: The failing reader is old and the data is new, so forward compatibility is missing.
questions.rule: A failing old reader means forward compatibility is missing.

questions.q: True or false: Whether a change is compatible depends only on the format, not on which versions of the code meet.
questions.explain: Compatibility is judged for a pair: the process that encodes the data and the one that decodes it. A format with rules still gives different answers for different version pairs.
questions.rule: Compatibility is a relationship between encoder and decoder.
questions.teaches: Compatibility is a relationship between one process that encodes data and another that decodes it.

questions.q: A billing team and an invoicing team want to deploy on their own schedules, in either order. What makes that possible?
options: A single database that both services read and write directly without any messages
Messages that are readable by both old and new versions of each side
A rule that only one team may change the message at a time
A shared deployment calendar that fixes which team releases first and which waits
optionExplain: Sharing a database does not remove the version mismatch.
Right: with compatibility in both directions, either side can upgrade first.
Taking turns still ties the teams together.
Coordination can work but is the lockstep this aims to avoid.
questions.explain: The book ties compatibility to evolvability: parts can be upgraded independently instead of all at once.
questions.teaches: Backward and forward compatibility let parts of a system be upgraded independently instead of changing everything at once.

questions.q: A version 1 reader meets a record with an extra field from version 2. What is the main risk?
options: The database refuses to store a record that has a field it has not seen
The new field is encrypted by the writer so that no reader can open it
The extra field causes the same record to be delivered to the reader twice
The reader fails or misreads because it does not know the field
optionExplain: Storage is not the issue; reading is.
Encryption is unrelated to adding a field.
A field does not cause a record to be read twice.
Right: code written before the field existed has no plan for it.
questions.explain: Old code has to cope with something it was never told about. The card next shows why this is the harder direction.

questions.q: Forward compatibility requires older code to ____ additions made by a newer version.
questions.explain: Old code must be able to skip over what it does not understand.

questions.q: A chat app released last year must still work after the server adds a reaction field. What must the old app do?
options: Ask the server to resend the message in the old format
Reject the message as malformed until the user updates
Ignore the reaction field and show the rest of the message
Guess the meaning of the field from its name
optionExplain: A server cannot be asked for a format it may no longer produce.
Rejecting breaks chat for every user who has not updated.
Right: ignoring unknown additions is the behaviour forward compatibility asks for.
Guessing risks wrong behaviour on data the code never defined.
questions.explain: The old app has no knowledge of the new field, so the safe behaviour is to skip it.
questions.rule: Skip what you do not know.

questions.q: A teammate says: forward compatibility is easy because we know the old format. Where is the error?
options: The old format is rarely documented well enough for newer code to rely on it in practice
Knowing the old format helps newer code read old data, which is backward compatibility
Old code is rewritten and redeployed everywhere before it ever meets data from a newer version
Forward compatibility is harder only for languages with static types, where decoders are generated
optionExplain: Documentation quality is not the book's point.
Right: that knowledge belongs to the author of the newer code, who must read old data.
Old code often keeps running, which is the whole difficulty.
The difficulty comes from old code facing the unknown, whatever the typing.
questions.explain: The author of newer code knows the older format; the older code cannot know the future.
questions.rule: New authors know the past; old code does not know the future.

questions.q: True or false: Backward compatibility can be reached, if needed, by keeping the old code around to read the old data.
questions.explain: The book notes that, as author of the newer code, you know the old format and can handle it explicitly, if necessary by keeping the old code.
questions.rule: Backward compatibility is under your control.
questions.teaches: Backward compatibility can be met, if necessary, by keeping the old code to read old data.

questions.q: A weather service adds a field to its JSON responses; thousands of third-party clients are not updated. What do the clients need to do?
options: Reject any response that holds a field the client was not written to expect, to be safe
Update before the field appears, or the service has to roll back its change for them
Ask the weather service for the full list of fields before each request is parsed
Nothing about the new field, if they ignore fields they do not recognise
optionExplain: Rejecting would break every client at the moment of the change.
Waiting for every client to update is the lockstep that compatibility avoids.
Asking first adds work and a dependency without solving unknown fields.
Right: forward compatibility holds when clients skip unknown fields.
questions.explain: Third-party clients cannot be forced to update, so adding a field is safe only if they ignore it. The book calls new fields in response objects a change usually considered compatible.
questions.rule: Clients that ignore unknown fields tolerate additions.
questions.teaches: For REST APIs, adding new fields to response objects is usually considered a change that maintains compatibility.

questions.q: A program wants to save a hash table to disk and have another program read it. What must happen first?
options: The table is translated into a self-contained sequence of bytes
The second program is started from the first one's memory, sharing its objects
The table is converted to a sorted array in memory
The table's memory addresses are copied into the file along with the values
optionExplain: Right: the file needs a form that makes sense without the original process.
Separate processes do not share memory this way.
Sorting in memory does not make the data portable.
Addresses only mean something inside the process that created them.
questions.explain: Memory pointers cannot leave the process. The card next names this translation.
questions.rule: Bytes, not pointers, leave a process.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Another word for encoding in this chapter
questions.explain: The book uses encoding and treats serialization and marshalling as other names for it.

questions.q: A service writes a user object to a message queue and a second service reads it. Which describes each step?
options: The writer decodes the object and the reader encodes it
Neither, because both use the same language objects
The writer encodes the object and the reader decodes it
Both encode, because queues store only bytes
optionExplain: That is reversed: the writer turns memory into bytes.
Even with the same language, memory structures cannot be passed between processes directly.
Right: the sender encodes into bytes and the receiver decodes them.
Only the sender turns memory into bytes; the receiver turns them back.
questions.explain: Encoding happens on the sending side and decoding on the receiving side.

questions.q: True or false: Encoding data in this chapter means the same as encrypting it.
questions.explain: The book notes that encoding has nothing to do with encryption and that it does not cover encryption.

questions.q: Why does the book prefer the word encoding to serialization?
options: Serialization is also used for transactions, with a different meaning
Serialization means storing records on disk in sorted order by their key values
Serialization only applies to text formats such as JSON and is therefore too narrow
Serialization was dropped from modern programming languages and their library names
optionExplain: Right: the book avoids overloading a word that Chapter 7 uses for transactions.
Sorted order is an unrelated idea.
Serialization applies to binary formats too.
The term has not been removed from languages.
questions.explain: The same word means different things in different parts of the book, so it chose one term.
questions.teaches: Serialization is also used for transactions with a completely different meaning, so the book says encoding.

questions.q: A game saves player state to a file. Which structure is a poor candidate to save by copying its raw memory?
options: A list of integers stored in a flat array with no references between its items
A tree whose nodes point to each other by memory address
A string that holds ASCII text only and has no references to other objects
A pair of numbers for the player's position, stored one after another
optionExplain: Plain integers have no addresses to break.
Right: pointers refer to addresses that mean nothing in a later run or another process.
Characters carry no address.
Plain numbers do not depend on memory addresses.
questions.explain: Copying raw memory keeps pointers that are only valid inside the original process, so a self-contained encoding is needed.
questions.teaches: A byte-for-byte copy of memory keeps pointer values that mean nothing after the process ends.

questions.q: A team plans to store customer data using their language's built-in object saver. What would you worry about?
options: It cannot save objects that have more than one field, so records must be flattened first
It requires a separate schema file that must be shipped to every reader
It produces larger files than any text format would for the same objects
It ties the data to one language and risks security and version problems
optionExplain: These tools save complex objects easily; that is their appeal.
Built-in encoders usually need no schema, which is part of the risk.
Size can be poor, but this is not a universal rule and not the main worry.
Right: lock-in, security and weak versioning are the book's concerns.
questions.explain: Convenience hides costs that appear later. The card next lists them.

questions.q: Which are problems the book lists for language-specific encodings? Select all that apply.
options: Versioning and efficiency are often an afterthought
Decoding can instantiate arbitrary classes, a security risk
They always require a code generation step
Reading the data from another language is very difficult
They cannot store numbers larger than 2 to the power 53
optionExplain: Right: forward and backward compatibility and speed are often neglected.
Right: arbitrary class creation opens remote code execution.
Code generation belongs to Thrift and Protocol Buffers.
Right: the encoding is tied to a language.
That is a JSON number problem, not a language-specific one.
questions.explain: Lock-in, security, versioning and efficiency are the listed problems.

questions.q: A startup stores user sessions for months using pickle-like objects. Another team now wants them in a different language. What is the problem?
options: Sessions have no version, so they can never be read
The other language can read it, but only after a conversion step
Reading the data in another language is very difficult
The data must first be encrypted with a shared key
optionExplain: Versioning is weak, but that is a different issue from cross-language reading.
The book says reading in another language is very difficult, not a quick conversion.
Right: the encoding is often tied to one language, which locks the data in.
Encoding has nothing to do with encryption.
questions.explain: The data has become hostage to the original language, which also blocks integrating with other organisations.
questions.rule: Language-specific data traps you in the language.

questions.q: True or false: An attacker who can feed bytes to your decoder can do no harm, since decoding only reads data.
questions.explain: Decoding often must instantiate arbitrary classes, which can let an attacker execute code remotely.
questions.rule: Decoding untrusted bytes can run code.
questions.hint: Think about what restoring the same object types demands.

questions.q: According to the book, when is a language's built-in encoding acceptable?
options: For data exchanged between organisations
For anything, if the team only uses one language
For long-term archives, since they are compact
For very transient purposes only
optionExplain: Exchange between organisations is where lock-in hurts most.
Even a single language today may grow into many; the book still advises against it for lasting use.
The book warns the opposite: poor performance and weak versioning.
Right: the book says it is generally a bad idea except for very transient purposes.
questions.explain: The book's verdict is that built-in encodings suit only very short-lived data.
questions.rule: Use built-in encoders only for transient data.
questions.teaches: It is generally a bad idea to use your language's built-in encoding for anything other than very transient purposes.

questions.q: A cache stores computed results in memory for a few seconds and is restarted with each deploy. Which choice fits the book's reasoning best?
options: A shared database, so that the cache survives restarts
A built-in language encoding, as the data is transient and local
A binary format with schema, to guard compatibility for years
A textual format, so that other organisations can read the cache
optionExplain: Surviving restarts contradicts the requirement stated here.
Right: short-lived data that never crosses a version or language boundary is the narrow case where the convenience pays.
Years of compatibility is not needed for data discarded at each deploy.
No other organisation reads the cache, so that need is absent.
questions.explain: The book's exception is very transient use, which this cache is. Our reading: the cost shows up only when data lasts or crosses boundaries.
questions.rule: Transient and local is where built-in encoding is least harmful.
questions.teaches: Java's built-in serialization is notorious for bad performance and bloated encoding.

questions.q: A JSON API returns a 64-bit ID as a number. A JavaScript client parses it. What might happen?
options: The ID may become inaccurate if it is larger than 2 to the power 53
The ID is rounded to the nearest 100 whatever its size, which breaks lookups
The ID is turned into a decimal string automatically by the JSON parser
The client rejects any number that needs more than 32 bits to be stored
optionExplain: Right: doubles cannot represent every integer above 2 to the power 53.
There is no rounding to hundreds; the loss is at the level of a few units for large values.
JSON numbers are not automatically converted to strings.
JavaScript accepts the number; it just may not keep it exact.
questions.explain: A double has limited exact integer range. The card next gives the details.
questions.rule: Doubles lose exactness for large integers.

questions.q: Integers larger than 2 to the power ____ cannot be exactly represented in an IEEE 754 double-precision number.
questions.explain: A double holds integers exactly only up to 2 to the power 53.
questions.rule: Beyond 2 to the power 53 doubles lose exactness.

questions.q: An order service sends invoice numbers around 9,007,199,254,740,993 as JSON numbers to a browser app. What is the safest fix?
options: Compress the JSON body before sending it so that fewer digits are lost
Switch the XML schema language to one that supports larger integers
Send each number as a decimal string as well, like Twitter's API
Send the numbers with more decimal places so that extra digits are kept
optionExplain: Compression does not change how numbers are parsed.
Schema language does not change how a client parses a number.
Right: a string preserves every digit.
Decimal places concern fractions, not integer precision.
questions.explain: A string avoids the double conversion, as the tweet ID example shows.

questions.q: True or false: JSON can distinguish integers from floating-point numbers and specifies their precision.
questions.explain: JSON distinguishes strings and numbers but not integers and floating-point numbers, and it specifies no precision.
questions.rule: JSON does not separate integers from floats.

questions.q: In XML and CSV, how can a reader tell the number 42 from the text made of the characters 4 and 2?
options: By the first character
By the length of the value
By the quotation marks around the value
Only by reference to an external schema
optionExplain: The first character does not mark a type.
Length does not distinguish them.
Quotes do not decide meaning in these formats.
Right: without a schema the two look the same.
questions.explain: The meaning of digits depends on information outside the data.
questions.rule: Types live in the schema, not the data.
questions.teaches: In XML and CSV you cannot distinguish a number from a string of digits except by referring to an external schema.

questions.q: An RPC framework joins a Python client to a JavaScript server. Which datatype problem can its translation of types surface?
options: Lists arriving in random order because the two languages sort arrays differently
Integers above 2 to the power 53 turning inexact in JavaScript
Booleans gaining a third value in the other language
Strings losing their length when they cross the network connection
optionExplain: Order is preserved by the encoding; the issue is number types.
Right: JavaScript numbers are doubles, so large integers can lose accuracy.
Booleans have no third value in either language.
Length handling is part of encoding and is not what differs between the languages here.
questions.explain: Not all languages share the same types, so a framework that translates between them inherits the same number problem. A single-language process does not have it.
questions.teaches: An RPC framework must translate datatypes between languages, and JavaScript's trouble with numbers above 2 to the power 53 shows how this can end up ugly.

questions.q: A JSON API must carry an image thumbnail inside a text field. What do people usually do?
options: Convert the bytes to text with Base64 and mark the field accordingly
Store the image in a second JSON file with the same name
Split the bytes into an array of decimal numbers and a checksum
Paste the raw bytes straight into the JSON string
optionExplain: Right: Base64 turns bytes into safe text.
A second file does not solve how to carry bytes inside the document.
Arrays of numbers work but are a different, less common trick than the standard text encoding.
Raw bytes may not form valid text, so a string cannot hold them safely.
questions.explain: The format has no byte type, so bytes must be dressed up as text. The card next shows the price.
questions.rule: Bytes in text formats become text.

questions.q: Base64 makes binary data about ____ percent larger.
questions.explain: Base64 increases the data size by 33%, because each 3 bytes become 4 text characters.

questions.q: An app sends 300 KB images in JSON using Base64. About how large is each image on the wire?
options: About 310 KB, a 3% overhead
About 600 KB, double the original
About 100 KB, since text compresses well
About 400 KB
optionExplain: That would be a 3% overhead, not the 33% the book gives.
Doubling is far more than Base64 adds.
Compression is a separate step and is not what the encoding does.
Right: 300 KB with a third added is about 400 KB.
questions.explain: 300 KB plus 33% is about 400 KB, before any other compression.

questions.q: True or false: Because JSON strings support Unicode, a JSON string can hold any sequence of bytes directly.
questions.explain: JSON strings hold Unicode text; a binary string is bytes without a character encoding, which JSON does not support.
questions.rule: JSON strings are text, not bytes.

questions.q: How does the reader of a JSON document know a given string is Base64?
options: A schema is used to indicate that the value should be read as Base64
The parser detects the encoding by checking the characters
The JSON syntax marks Base64 values with a special prefix
Every JSON string is Base64 by default, so no marking is needed at all
optionExplain: Right: the schema tells the reader how to interpret the value.
Base64 looks like ordinary text, so detection would be unreliable.
JSON has no such marker.
Most strings are plain text.
questions.explain: The meaning of such a value depends on information outside the data itself.
questions.rule: Meaning of the value comes from the schema.
questions.teaches: The schema is used to indicate that the value should be interpreted as Base64-encoded.

questions.q: A sensor network uploads many small binary readings in JSON and the extra size now strains its link. What fits the book's reasoning?
options: Switch to CSV, which stores binary values natively without any overhead
Apply Base64 twice, which shrinks the data because the text is repeated
Use a binary encoding of JSON that adds a binary string type
Convert every reading to a floating-point number
optionExplain: CSV has no schema and no binary type either.
A second pass makes the data larger, not smaller.
Right: some binary JSON encodings extend the data types, for example with binary strings.
That changes the data rather than how it is carried.
questions.explain: Some binary variants extend the set of datatypes, for example with support for binary strings, while keeping the JSON data model.
questions.rule: Binary variants can add a byte type.
questions.teaches: Some binary encodings of JSON extend the set of datatypes, for example by adding support for binary strings.

questions.q: Two companies must exchange data. Which concern usually outweighs a format's efficiency?
options: Whether the format minimises bytes on the wire
Whether both sides can agree on the format
Whether the format is the newest available
Whether the format supports the most datatypes
optionExplain: Compactness helps but is not the main obstacle between organisations.
Right: getting different organisations to agree is the hard part.
Novelty has no bearing on interchange.
Richness may help, but only if both sides adopt it.
questions.explain: Agreement is the scarce resource. The card next gives the book's reasoning.

questions.q: True or false: CSV has no schema, so the application defines what each row and column means.
questions.explain: Right: CSV leaves meaning to the application, so a new column must be handled manually.
questions.rule: CSV meaning lives in the application.

questions.q: A retailer ingests supplier price lists as CSV. One supplier adds a column. What is the likely effect?
options: The extra column is ignored by the format itself, so no code change is needed
The CSV format rejects the file automatically because the header has changed
Older rows are rewritten by the CSV schema to include the new column
The retailer's code must be changed to handle the new column
optionExplain: Whether it is ignored depends on the application, not on CSV.
CSV has no schema to enforce anything.
No schema exists to rewrite rows.
Right: with no schema, a new column is the application's problem.
questions.explain: Without a schema, handling change falls to the application.

questions.q: Two CSV parsers read a field containing a comma and return different columns. What explains this?
options: CSV defines no escaping at all, so every parser invents its own handling
Escaping rules are formally specified, but not every parser implements them correctly
CSV forbids commas inside values, so such files are invalid and parsers disagree
One parser is faster and so drops the characters that it cannot buffer in time
optionExplain: Escaping rules have been formally specified.
Right: the rules exist yet some parsers do not follow them.
CSV allows commas with escaping.
Speed is not the cause.
questions.explain: Vague handling of commas and newlines leads to parser differences even though rules exist.
questions.rule: Specified is not the same as implemented.

questions.q: JSON's popularity owes much to built-in browser support, since it is a subset of ____.
questions.explain: Browser support for JavaScript carries over to JSON, and JSON is also simpler than XML.
questions.rule: JSON won on browser support and simplicity.
questions.teaches: JSON's popularity is mainly due to built-in support in web browsers, as a subset of JavaScript, and its simplicity relative to XML.

questions.q: A data team moves terabytes of internal logs between its own systems every day. How does the book's reasoning change?
options: A compact or fast format is worth considering, since only your organisation reads it
CSV is best, since it has no schema to maintain and every language reads it
Agreement matters most, so keep a textual format even for purely internal data
Textual formats are required by the HTTP standard for anything sent over a network
optionExplain: Right: for internal data there is less pressure for the lowest common denominator, and gains grow at terabyte scale.
Lack of a schema is a cost, not a benefit, at this scale.
Agreement between organisations is not the constraint for internal data.
HTTP does not require textual payloads.
questions.explain: The advice for exchange between organisations does not carry over to purely internal data.
questions.rule: Internal data can use more compact formats.
questions.teaches: For data used only inside your organisation you can choose a more compact or faster format, and at terabytes the choice can have a big impact.

questions.q: A team swaps JSON for MessagePack for an example record of about 81 bytes. What size do you expect?
options: About 40 bytes, half the size
About 8 bytes
About 66 bytes, a modest saving
Larger than JSON, because binary adds headers
optionExplain: Half would need field names removed.
That would need the names and punctuation to vanish.
Right: field names remain, so the saving is small.
It is a little smaller, not larger.
questions.explain: Names are still stored in every record. The card next explains why.

questions.q: Because binary JSON variants have no schema, they must include all object ____ names in the encoded data.
questions.explain: Without a schema the reader cannot know the names, so every record carries them.
questions.rule: Without a schema, names travel with data.

questions.q: A log pipeline writes 81-byte JSON records and tests MessagePack at 66 bytes per record. What saving does that show?
options: About 2%
About 50%
About 19%
About 60%
optionExplain: 2% would be about 1 byte per record.
That would mean 40 bytes per record.
Right: 15 bytes saved out of 81 is about 19%.
That would mean about 32 bytes per record.
questions.explain: 81 minus 66 is 15 bytes, about 19% of the original.

questions.q: True or false: A binary JSON encoding with no schema can leave the field names out of each record.
questions.explain: Without a schema the reader has nothing to supply the names, so they must be included in the encoded data.
questions.rule: No schema, so names stay in the data.

questions.q: How does MessagePack handle an object that has more than 15 fields?
options: It raises an error and refuses to encode any object with more than fifteen fields
It uses a different type indicator, with the count stored in two or four bytes
It stops encoding after the fifteenth field and drops the remaining fields from the output
It splits the object into several smaller objects, each holding at most fifteen fields
optionExplain: No error is described.
Right: the field count then no longer fits in four bits, so more bytes carry it.
Nothing in the text says it truncates.
Splitting is not described.
questions.explain: The first byte holds the type in its top four bits and a small count in its bottom four, so larger counts need extra bytes.
questions.rule: Small counts fit in four bits; larger ones need more bytes.
questions.teaches: If an object has more than 15 fields, it gets a different type indicator and the number of fields is encoded in two or four bytes.

questions.q: An API provider is choosing between plain JSON and a binary JSON variant for outside developers. What does the book's account suggest?
options: Pick plain JSON, as no binary JSON variant is as widely adopted as the textual one
Pick XML, as it has fewer variants and is less verbose than JSON
Pick the variant that allows the most fields per object, since outside developers need many
Pick the binary variant, as all of them are now more widely adopted than the textual versions
optionExplain: Right: none is as widely adopted as textual JSON and XML.
XML is not a smaller or more adopted choice here.
Field count is not a selection criterion.
The book says they are adopted only in niches.
questions.explain: Wide adoption among outside developers favours the textual format.
questions.teaches: Binary encodings of JSON and XML have been adopted in niches, but none are as widely adopted as the textual versions.

questions.q: A binary format wants to leave field names out of each record. Where must it get the structure instead?
options: From a table in the first record only
From the order of fields in memory
From guessing the types of values
From a schema known to both sides
optionExplain: Records are encoded independently, so the first cannot serve all.
Memory order is not available to another process.
Guessing would not be reliable.
Right: the shared schema supplies structure so records can omit names.
questions.explain: Something outside the record must say what the bytes mean. The card next names it.
questions.rule: Leave names out only if a schema supplies them.

questions.q: Match each item to its description.
pairs: Binary encoding library originally developed at Facebook
Binary encoding library originally developed at Google
Language used to write the schema
questions.explain: Both libraries came from big companies and both pair a schema with generated code.

questions.q: A team uses Go, Java and Swift services and writes one Thrift IDL file. What do they get from the generator?
options: A runtime check that blocks any old client from connecting to the services
A shared database with one table per struct in the IDL file
Classes in each language that encode and decode the records
A JSON copy of the data for each language, written to disk beside the code
optionExplain: Runtime checks of old clients are not what the generator provides.
The generator produces code, not a database.
Right: generated classes implement the schema in several languages.
JSON is not produced.
questions.explain: Application code calls generated classes to encode and decode records of the schema.
questions.rule: Call generated classes to encode and decode.

questions.q: True or false: Thrift and Protocol Buffers require a schema for any data that is encoded, whereas MessagePack does not.
questions.explain: Right: MessagePack carries field names instead of using a schema.

questions.q: True or false: One Thrift schema can be encoded in more than one binary format.
questions.explain: Thrift has BinaryProtocol and CompactProtocol, and the same schema works with either.
questions.teaches: Thrift has two different binary encoding formats, BinaryProtocol and CompactProtocol, for the same schema.

questions.q: A team writes services in Java and C#. Which benefit of generated code applies to them?
options: Automatic translation of the data into JSON for browsers and mobile clients
Efficient in-memory structures, type checking and IDE autocompletion
A guarantee that old clients can read new records without any further rules
Dynamic typing removes the need for compile-time checks in these languages entirely
optionExplain: JSON conversion is not described as a benefit here.
Right: generated code helps statically typed languages with efficient structures and type checking.
Compatibility comes from tag rules, not code generation.
Java and C# are statically typed, so this is the wrong direction.
questions.explain: In statically typed languages such as Java, C++ or C#, generated code allows efficient in-memory structures and type checking and autocompletion in IDEs.
questions.rule: Generated types help statically typed languages.
questions.teaches: In statically typed languages, generated code allows efficient in-memory structures for decoded data and type checking and autocompletion in IDEs.

questions.q: A binary record has no field names. How could a reader tell which value is which?
options: By tags, numbers the schema assigned to each field
By asking the writer at read time
By the length of each value
By the position of the value in the file only
optionExplain: Right: numbered tags stand in for names.
The writer is not available when a file is read later.
Equal lengths would make fields indistinguishable.
Position alone breaks when a field is missing.
questions.explain: Short numbers can stand in for long names. The card next shows the design.

questions.q: Numbers in the schema that act as compact aliases for field names are called field ____.
questions.explain: Field tags appear in the encoded data in place of field names.
questions.rule: Field tags replace names in the bytes.

questions.q: In the Ticket schema, field 2 is priority. Which detail identifies priority inside a raw Thrift-encoded record?
options: A hash of the schema file
The position of the third value
The text priority stored before the value
The tag number 2 with a type annotation
optionExplain: A hash is not part of the record.
Position is not used, since unset fields are omitted.
Field names are not stored in the encoded data.
Right: tag plus type tell the reader what the field is.
questions.explain: Each field is stored with its tag number and type annotation.
questions.rule: Tag and type identify the field.

questions.q: True or false: A Thrift BinaryProtocol record contains the strings userName and favoriteNumber, as JSON does.
questions.explain: The encoded data has tags 1, 2 and 3 instead of field names; only the string values appear.
questions.rule: Names stay in the schema, not in the bytes.

questions.q: A team renames the field title to subject in the schema and keeps tag 1. What happens to data already encoded?
options: Nothing breaks, since the encoded data never refers to field names
All old data becomes invalid because the stored names no longer match the schema
Old data must be rewritten with a new tag before it can be read again
Only new records can be read, since old ones carry the old name
optionExplain: Right: the bytes hold tag 1, whose meaning is unchanged.
Invalidity would follow from changing a tag, not a name.
Changing the tag is the dangerous step.
Old records are still readable by tag.
questions.explain: Names are only labels in the schema, so renaming a field is safe; changing a tag is not.
questions.teaches: You can change the name of a field in the schema, since the encoded data never refers to field names.

questions.q: A designer compares BinaryProtocol at 59 bytes with a compact format at 34 for the same record. What does BinaryProtocol still spend bytes on?
options: Field names, as in JSON, repeated in front of each value
A type annotation and, where needed, a length for each field
A copy of the schema at the start of each record, for self-description
A checksum for each value, so that corrupted fields can be detected
optionExplain: Names were removed, which is why 59 is below 66.
Right: each field still carries a type annotation and a length when required.
The schema is not stored in the record.
No checksum is described.
questions.explain: BinaryProtocol still spends a type annotation, and where required a length indication, on every field, which the compact format trims further.
questions.rule: Tags save names but fixed headers still cost.
questions.teaches: Each field has a type annotation and, where required, a length indication, such as the length of a string or the number of items in a list.

questions.q: An integer field usually holds small values, yet is stored in eight bytes. What could save space?
options: Store the number as text, since digits take less room than binary
Keep only the first byte of the number and drop the remaining bytes
Round all values to multiples of 8 so that fewer bits need storing
Use fewer bytes when the value is small, and more when it is large
optionExplain: Text is usually larger than binary for numbers.
Dropping bytes loses information.
Rounding changes the data.
Right: a length that adapts to the value saves space for small values.
questions.explain: A fixed width wastes space for small values. The card next shows one scheme.
questions.rule: Let small numbers use few bytes.

questions.q: In a variable-length integer, the top ____ of each byte signals whether more bytes follow.
questions.explain: The top bit of each byte is the continuation flag.
questions.rule: Top bit means more bytes follow.

questions.q: Using the book's ranges, how many bytes do the values 50 and 5000 take in a variable-length integer?
options: 1 byte each
2 bytes each
1 byte and 2 bytes
8 bytes each
optionExplain: 5000 is outside -64 to 63, so it needs more than one.
50 is within the one-byte range of -64 to 63.
Right: 50 fits in one byte, and 5000 falls in the two-byte range up to 8191.
Variable-length encoding avoids the fixed eight bytes.
questions.explain: 50 is between -64 and 63, so it takes one byte; 5000 is between -8192 and 8191, so it takes two.
questions.rule: Check the ranges: one byte, then two.

questions.q: True or false: A variable-length integer takes the same number of bytes whatever its value.
questions.explain: Bigger numbers use more bytes: the byte count follows the size of the value.

questions.q: How does Protocol Buffers compare with Thrift's CompactProtocol on the example record?
options: Much smaller, because it needs no tags and packs the type into the length
Identical byte for byte, since both formats use the same bit packing
Twice as large, since it keeps field names as Thrift's BinaryProtocol does
Very similar, with slightly different bit packing, at 33 bytes against 34
optionExplain: It uses tags like Thrift.
The bit packing differs slightly, giving a different size.
Protocol Buffers uses tags and not names.
Right: it does the bit packing slightly differently but is otherwise very similar.
questions.explain: The two formats are close cousins; Protocol Buffers is one byte shorter on the example.
questions.teaches: Protocol Buffers does the bit packing slightly differently but is otherwise very similar to Thrift's CompactProtocol, fitting the record in 33 bytes.

questions.q: A team using BinaryProtocol wants smaller messages and asks whether switching to CompactProtocol means rewriting the schema. What is the answer?
options: Yes, tags must be renumbered so that they fit into the packed header byte
No, the encoding is semantically equivalent and only the byte layout changes
No, but all stored data must first be converted to JSON before the switch is made
Yes, optional fields must become required so that their tags can be left out
optionExplain: Tags keep their meaning across the two encodings.
Right: CompactProtocol packs the same information into fewer bytes.
JSON conversion is not needed.
Field requirement markers are unrelated.
questions.explain: CompactProtocol is semantically equivalent to BinaryProtocol, so the schema stays; only the packing differs.
questions.teaches: The Thrift CompactProtocol encoding is semantically equivalent to BinaryProtocol, but packs the same information into fewer bytes.

questions.q: Old code reads a record that contains a tag number it does not know. How could it still parse the fields after it?
options: It asks the writer for the new schema first and waits until the schema has arrived
It stops reading at that field and returns only the fields found before it was met
It uses the type information stored with the field to skip the right number of bytes
It guesses where the field ends by looking for the position of the next tag number
optionExplain: The writer is not available when data is read.
Stopping early would lose the fields that follow.
Right: the type annotation tells the parser how much to skip.
Guessing from the next tag is not how the format works.
questions.explain: The encoded data carries enough type information to skip. The card next shows how this supports evolution.
questions.rule: Type information lets old code skip.

questions.q: In a Thrift or Protocol Buffers schema you may change a field's ____ but not its tag.
questions.explain: Encoded data never refers to field names, so renaming is safe.

questions.q: Ticket has tags 1 title, 2 priority, 3 labels. A team adds an assignee field. Which tag fits the book's rules?
options: Tag 4, a number never used before
Tag 3, shared with labels to save space
Tag 0, so it sorts first
Tag 2, replacing priority because it is rarely used
optionExplain: Right: a new field needs a new tag.
Sharing a tag would mix two meanings.
Tag 0 gains nothing and is not a rule in the book.
Reusing a tag gives old data a new meaning.
questions.explain: A new tag number keeps every old record meaning what it meant.

questions.q: A version 1 service reads a version 2 record that includes assignee, tag 4. What does it do with tag 4?
options: Stores it as a title, because tag 1 is the first free tag
Shifts all the later fields by one place to make room for tag 4
Skips it using the type annotation, and reads the rest
Fails with an error, since it cannot map the tag
optionExplain: Tags carry fixed meaning and are not remapped.
Records are not positional.
Right: the field is ignored and the rest decodes normally, which is forward compatibility.
That would be the behaviour of a format without type annotations.
questions.explain: Unknown tag, known type: old code skips and carries on.

questions.q: True or false: In an encoded record, a field whose value is not set is left out of the record.
questions.explain: Right: an encoded record is the concatenation of the fields that are present, each with its tag and type.
questions.teaches: If a field value is not set, it is simply omitted from the encoded record.

questions.q: An events team wants to renumber the tags of its schema so they run 1, 2, 3 without gaps. What does the book's reasoning say?
options: Safe, as long as the field names stay the same, since names are what the data holds
Safe, if the new numbers are all larger than the old ones, so nothing overlaps
Unsafe only for required fields, since optional fields are skipped when absent
Unsafe, because changing a tag makes existing encoded data invalid
optionExplain: Names are not in the data; tags are.
Size of the number does not help.
Every field is identified by its tag, whatever its marker.
Right: old records use the old tags, so they would be misread or invalid.
questions.explain: Encoded data refers to tags, so a changed tag no longer matches the stored bytes.
questions.teaches: You cannot change a field's tag, since that would make all existing encoded data invalid.

questions.q: A team adds a required field to a schema already in production. What fails?
options: New code reading old data, because old writers did not write the field
Nothing, since required fields are checked only at compile time
The tag numbers of existing fields
Old code reading new data, because it cannot ignore anything
optionExplain: Right: the required check fails when the field is missing from old data.
The check happens at runtime when decoding.
Existing tags are not affected.
Old code can skip an unknown field, so this direction survives.
questions.explain: Old data lacks the new field. The card next gives the rule.

questions.q: Which schema changes keep compatibility after deployment? Select all that apply.
options: Add a required field
Give a removed field's tag to a new field
Remove a required field
Add an optional field under a new tag
Remove an optional field
optionExplain: A required field fails on old data.
Old data may still carry the old tag with a different meaning.
Old writers may still need to supply it.
Right: new tag and optional means old data still reads.
Right: old code can ignore it and new code does not need it.
questions.explain: Only optional or defaulted additions and removals of optional fields are safe.
questions.rule: Optional in, optional out, no tag reuse.

questions.q: A ticketing service adds a required dueDate field. New servers read old tickets. What happens?
options: They skip dueDate for old tickets and ignore the required-field check there
The required-field check fails because the old tickets lack dueDate
They rewrite the old tickets in place with a default dueDate before reading them
They read them with dueDate set to zero, as an unset number defaults to zero
optionExplain: The check does not skip.
Right: old data never contained the field.
Decoding does not rewrite stored data.
No default exists for a required field.
questions.explain: Backward compatibility breaks because old data does not hold the new field.
questions.rule: Required fields cannot be added later.

questions.q: True or false: Marking a field required changes how it is encoded in the bytes.
questions.explain: Nothing in the binary data indicates whether a field was required. The difference is a runtime check that fails if the field is not set.
questions.rule: Required is a check, not an encoding.

questions.q: Why must a removed field's tag number not be reused?
options: The compiler refuses duplicate tags across versions, so the schema would not build
Old data written elsewhere may still hold that tag, which new code must ignore
Tags are limited to 255 in the format, and a retired tag would waste one of them
Reused tags change the name of the field for every reader of the older data
optionExplain: Old schemas are not compared by the compiler.
Right: the old tag may still appear in stored data.
No such limit is described.
Names are not stored in the data.
questions.explain: Data written earlier may still contain that tag, and new code must be able to ignore it rather than misread it.
questions.teaches: You can never use the same tag number again, because data written somewhere may still include the old tag number, which must be ignored by new code.

questions.q: A payments schema has changed. Sort each change by whether it keeps compatibility.

items.t: Add optional memo under a new tag
Add a field that has a default value
Remove an optional field
Add a required field
Remove a required field
Reuse a removed field's tag for a different type

questions.explain: Removing a field is like adding one with the compatibility directions reversed: a required field can never be removed, and tags are never recycled.
questions.teaches: Removing a field is just like adding a field, with backward and forward compatibility concerns reversed.

questions.q: A field changes from a 32-bit to a 64-bit integer. Who is at risk of reading a wrong value?
options: Old code reading new data that has large values
Neither, because a 64-bit field is larger than a 32-bit one so nothing is lost
Both old and new code, whatever the value that is stored
New code reading old data written with the narrower type
optionExplain: Right: old code has only 32 bits to hold what the new writer stored.
The larger writer can send values that the smaller reader cannot hold.
Small values are safe in both directions.
New code gets a smaller value and has room for it.
questions.explain: The smaller container is the risk. The card next gives details.

questions.q: If a decoded 64-bit value does not fit in 32 bits, old code ____ it.
questions.explain: Old code truncates the value, losing the high bits.

questions.q: Order totals in cents change from 32-bit to 64-bit. An old service reads a new order worth 5,000,000,000 cents. What happens?
options: It reads the value correctly because the stored value is still valid
It rounds the value up to the next billion to fit in 32 bits
The value is truncated because it does not fit in 32 bits
It refuses to read any further records from the whole database
optionExplain: 32 bits hold at most about 4.29 billion unsigned, less when signed.
Truncation drops bits and does not round.
Right: 5,000,000,000 does not fit, so it loses bits.
No refusal is described.
questions.explain: The value is larger than a 32-bit integer can hold.
questions.rule: Check the value against the old width.

questions.q: True or false: After widening a field from 32 to 64 bits, old code reading new data is the safe direction.
questions.explain: The safe direction is new code reading old data, where missing bits are filled with zeros. Old code can truncate what new code wrote.
questions.rule: Wider reader safe, narrower reader not.

questions.q: In Avro, when is a field datatype change possible?
options: Only for strings
Only with an alias
Never, because types are fixed by the schema
When Avro can convert the type
optionExplain: The rule is not limited to strings.
Aliases relate to names.
Changing a type is possible in some cases.
Right: the book says it is possible provided Avro can convert the type.
questions.explain: Avro resolves differences between writer and reader schemas and can convert some types.
questions.teaches: Changing the datatype of a field is possible in Avro, provided that Avro can convert the type.

questions.q: A metrics team widens a counter from 16-bit to 32-bit in a schema. Old dashboards still run. Which risk follows the book's reasoning?
options: Old dashboards truncate values larger than they can hold
Old dashboards stop receiving data because the schema no longer matches
New dashboards cannot read old counters, since they lack the high bits
The tag numbers of the other fields change to make room for the bigger type
optionExplain: Right: the same pattern as 32 to 64 bits applies.
Delivery is not part of the schema.
New readers fill missing bits with zeros.
Tags are unaffected by a type change.
questions.explain: Our reading: the book's 32 to 64 bit case generalises to any widening, where the old reader's smaller variable truncates.
questions.teaches: A datatype change may lose precision or values may get truncated, so check the format's documentation.

questions.q: A schema field holds a single phone number. You need several numbers. Which format lets you change this in place?
options: No format supports it without rewriting all stored data
Protocol Buffers, using a repeated marker
Only a format that has no schema and so no fixed field types
Any format that offers a dedicated list datatype for fields
optionExplain: Protocol Buffers supports it.
Right: it encodes a repeated field by repeating the tag.
Schemaless formats avoid the issue differently.
A dedicated list type changes the encoding of the field.
questions.explain: The card next shows the trick.
questions.rule: Repeating the tag makes a list.

questions.q: True or false: Protocol Buffers has no list datatype; it uses a repeated marker for fields.
questions.explain: A repeated field is encoded by writing the same tag more than once.

questions.q: A tags field is optional in an old schema and becomes repeated. New code reads an old record with no tags. What does it see?
options: An error, since the field is missing
A list with one empty element
The last value of the previous record
A list with zero elements
optionExplain: A missing optional field is allowed.
No value was written, so no element exists.
Records are independent.
Right: zero occurrences of the tag give an empty list.
questions.explain: Zero or one occurrence translates to a list of zero or one element.
questions.rule: Old data reads as a short list.

questions.q: Old code reading a record with three values for a field that became repeated sees only the ____ element.
questions.explain: The old single-valued reader keeps the last value seen.
questions.rule: Old reader keeps the last one.

questions.q: What advantage does the Thrift list type have over a repeated marker?
options: It uses fewer bytes for lists
It needs no schema
It supports nested lists
It can be evolved from single-valued to multi-valued
optionExplain: The book does not claim smaller lists.
Thrift still uses a schema.
Right: a list type parameterised by element type can nest.
That is the repeated marker's advantage.
questions.explain: A list parameterised by its element type can itself contain lists.
questions.teaches: Thrift's dedicated list datatype, parameterised with the element type, supports nested lists.

questions.q: A team stores a grid as a list of rows, each row a list of numbers. Which feature of the book's formats helps?
options: A repeated marker, since tags can repeat
A dedicated list datatype that can hold lists
Optional markers on every row
Variable-length integers
optionExplain: Repeating a tag makes one flat list.
Right: nesting needs a list type that takes element types.
Optional markers do not nest values.
Integer encoding does not structure data.
questions.explain: A flat repeated field cannot represent lists of lists, while a typed list can.
questions.rule: Nested data needs a typed list.
questions.teaches: Thrift's list datatype supports nested lists.

questions.q: A binary record contains no names, no tags and no type markers, only values. What does a reader need?
options: The IDL file only for strings
A copy of the previous record
The schema, to give each value its position and type
Nothing, since values can be recognised by their size
optionExplain: All types depend on the schema.
Records are independent.
Right: the schema tells what each value is.
Sizes alone cannot show type.
questions.explain: Structure must come from outside the bytes. The card next shows Avro's design.

questions.q: The Avro example record takes ____ bytes, the most compact encoding in the chapter.
questions.explain: Avro encodes the example in 32 bytes.
questions.rule: Avro is the most compact here.

questions.q: A reader's schema lists title, priority, labels. Given the bytes of a record written in that order, how does it find priority?
options: By searching the bytes for a tag number 2 followed by the type
By checking for the text priority in the bytes before the value starts
By asking the writer which field comes next in each record
By reading title first, then taking the next value as priority per the schema
optionExplain: There are no tag numbers in Avro.
Names are not stored.
The writer is not available.
Right: decoding follows the schema field by field.
questions.explain: The schema's field order drives decoding.

questions.q: True or false: The bytes of an Avro-encoded string tell the reader that the value is a string.
questions.explain: Nothing in the encoded data says it is a string; it could just as well be an integer, so only the schema identifies the type.

questions.q: How does Avro encode an integer?
options: As a variable-length integer, the same as Thrift CompactProtocol
As a fixed eight bytes whatever the value is
As a tag followed by four bytes holding the value in binary
As text digits, one character for each decimal digit
optionExplain: Right: Avro uses the same variable-length integer encoding as CompactProtocol.
Fixed width is what Avro avoids.
Avro has no tags.
Binary formats do not use text digits.
questions.explain: Avro borrows the compact integer scheme but drops tags.
questions.teaches: An integer is encoded using a variable-length encoding, the same as Thrift's CompactProtocol.

questions.q: An analyst opens Avro bytes with a schema that differs from the writer's. What is the likely result?
options: The library reports a clean error every time
Only extra fields are dropped
The bytes are converted to JSON automatically
Data is decoded incorrectly
optionExplain: With only values in the bytes, a mismatch often cannot be noticed.
Dropping is the behaviour of schema resolution, which needs both schemas.
No conversion happens.
Right: any mismatch would mean incorrectly decoded data.
questions.explain: With no markers in the data, a wrong schema cannot be detected from the bytes.
questions.teaches: The binary data can only be decoded correctly if the code reading the data is using the exact same schema as the code that wrote the data.

questions.q: Two programs use slightly different versions of a schema for the same data. How could a format cope?
options: Ignore the difference and read the bytes with whichever schema is at hand
Require both programs to upgrade together at the same moment
Compare the two schemas when reading and translate between them
Convert all data to text first so that the versions no longer matter
optionExplain: Ignoring differences gives wrong data.
Lockstep upgrading is what evolution tries to avoid.
Right: this is the idea of schema resolution.
Text conversion does not solve schema differences.
questions.explain: The card next describes the approach.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: The schema version the encoding application knows
The schema the decoding application expects
The library translating writer data into reader form
questions.explain: Both schemas are used side by side; the library does the translation.
questions.rule: Two schemas in, one reading out.

questions.q: A writer lists fields id, name, email. A reader lists name, id. How are the fields matched?
options: By type only, pairing the first string with the first string
By field name, so the different order is fine
By position in each schema, first field with first field
By tag number, as in Thrift and Protocol Buffers
optionExplain: Several fields share a type.
Right: resolution matches fields by name.
Position would pair id with name incorrectly.
Avro has no tags.
questions.explain: Different field order is no problem because resolution uses the names.

questions.q: The writer has field email; the reader's schema lacks it. The reader expects phone, which the writer lacks, and declares a default. What happens?
options: email is ignored and phone is filled with the reader's default
phone is left empty without a default, whatever the reader declares
Reading fails on both fields because neither schema matches the other
email is moved into phone because both are strings
optionExplain: Right: extra writer fields are ignored, and missing reader fields get the reader's default.
The default comes from the reader's schema.
Neither case forces failure when a default is declared.
Fields are not renamed this way.
questions.explain: A field in the writer's schema but not the reader's is ignored. A field the reader expects but the writer lacks takes the default declared in the reader's schema.
questions.teaches: Fields that appear in the writer's schema but not the reader's are ignored; missing ones are filled with a default from the reader's schema.

questions.q: True or false: Reordering the fields of the reader's schema relative to the writer's schema makes Avro misread the data.
questions.explain: Resolution matches fields by name, so the order in the two schemas does not need to agree.

questions.q: A fleet of devices compiles a schema into firmware. The cloud reader is newer. Where does the writer's schema come from?
options: It is chosen by the reader when the data arrives, from any version it likes
It is rebuilt from the data bytes by inspecting the lengths and the types
It is the schema each device compiled in, which may differ from the cloud's
It is the newest schema in the company, which every writer must have fetched
optionExplain: The reader does not choose; it must find out.
The bytes do not contain enough to rebuild it.
Right: the writer encodes with the schema version it knows, perhaps compiled into the application.
Writers use what they know, not always the newest.
questions.explain: A writer encodes with whichever schema version it knows, such as one compiled in.
questions.rule: Writers use the version they have.
questions.teaches: The application encodes the data using whatever version of the schema it knows about, for example one compiled into the application.

questions.q: A team adds a field with no default to a schema. Which readers can no longer read old data?
options: The old readers, which do not know the field and so cannot interpret the data
The new readers, which expect a value the old data lacks
Both new and old readers, since neither one has a default to fall back on
None, because absent fields are ignored by schema resolution in every case
optionExplain: Old readers ignore it when reading new data.
Right: new readers have no value to fill.
Only one direction fails.
Ignoring applies to extra fields, not missing ones.
questions.explain: No default means nothing to fill in. The card next gives the rule.
questions.rule: Missing and no default means failure.

questions.q: In Avro you may only add or remove a field that has a ____ value.
questions.explain: A default value lets resolution fill in missing data.

questions.q: A user schema adds nickname without a default. Which compatibility breaks?
options: Neither, since the name is unique
Both equally
Forward, since old readers cannot read data from new writers
Backward, since new readers cannot read data from old writers
optionExplain: Uniqueness does not matter.
