Only one side lacks the value.
Old readers ignore unknown fields.
Right: old writers never wrote nickname.
questions.explain: Old data lacks the field and the reader has no default.

questions.q: Match each Avro change to its effect.
pairs: Add a field without a default
Remove a field without a default
Add or remove a field with a default
questions.explain: Defaults protect the reader that would otherwise have nothing to fill in.

questions.q: How do you let an Avro field be null?
options: Declare a union type that includes null
Use an empty string
Mark the field optional
Nothing is needed, since null is allowed everywhere
optionExplain: Right: a union such as null or long makes null explicit.
An empty string is a different value.
Avro has no optional marker.
In Avro, null is not an acceptable default for any variable.
questions.explain: Avro makes nullability explicit through unions, which the book says helps prevent bugs.
questions.teaches: If you want a field to allow null in Avro you have to use a union type, which helps prevent bugs by being explicit.

questions.q: A warehouse team moves from Protocol Buffers to Avro and asks how to mark an optional colour field. What fits?
options: Use a union with null and a default of null
Use a new tag number for the colour field, as in Thrift
Use a required marker with a value of zero for every record
Use an optional marker as before, as Avro keeps the same markers
optionExplain: Right: a union with null and a null default does the job.
Avro has no tag numbers.
Required markers do not exist in Avro.
Avro has no optional marker.
questions.explain: Avro has no optional and required markers; it has union types and default values instead.
questions.teaches: Avro does not have optional and required markers in the same way as Protocol Buffers and Thrift.

questions.q: A team renames userName to name in the schema. Old stored data still says userName. What would help new code?
options: Deleting all old data so that only the new name remains in storage
Reading with an alias that maps the old name to the new
Keeping both fields in the schema so that every reader finds one
Converting field names to numbers so that renames no longer matter
optionExplain: Deleting is extreme and unnecessary.
Right: an alias lets the reader match the old name.
Duplicating fields wastes space and confuses readers.
Avro does not use numbers for fields.
questions.explain: The new reader needs to know the old name. The card next gives the mechanism.

questions.q: A reader's schema can contain ____ for field names to match against an old writer's names.
questions.explain: Aliases let the reader recognise the old field name.

questions.q: A reader schema renames customerName to client and lists customerName as an alias. It reads data written by the old writer. What happens?
options: The field is ignored and the reader fills in its default value
The alias creates a second field next to client in the record
Reading fails, as the writer's name differs from the reader's name
The data decodes, with customerName values going into client
optionExplain: Ignoring happens for unmatched writer fields.
An alias maps names, not new fields.
The alias exists to prevent failure.
Right: the alias matches the writer's old name.
questions.explain: The alias is the bridge from the old name to the new one.

questions.q: True or false: An old reader with no alias for the new name still matches the renamed field in new data.
questions.explain: The old reader does not know the new name, so it cannot match the field; renaming is backward compatible but not forward compatible.
questions.rule: Old readers do not know new names.

questions.q: What is true about adding a branch to an Avro union type?
options: It is neither
It is forward compatible but not backward compatible
It is backward compatible but not forward compatible
It is both
optionExplain: New readers can still read old data.
Old readers cannot handle a branch they do not know.
Right: new readers cope with old data, but old readers cannot cope with the new branch.
Only one direction works.
questions.explain: A reader that knows the extra branch still understands data without it; a reader without the branch cannot understand data that uses it.
questions.teaches: Adding a branch to a union type is backward compatible but not forward compatible.

questions.q: A schema needs a nullable string with default null. Which union lets that default work in Avro?
options: Either order
A union listing string first and null second
A union listing null first and string second
No union; null is allowed on any field
optionExplain: Order matters for the default.
The default must match the first branch's type.
Right: the default must be of the type of the first branch of the union.
Null is not allowed on every field in Avro.
questions.explain: A footnote says the default must be of the type of the union's first branch, a specific limitation of Avro.
questions.teaches: The default value must be of the type of the first branch of the union.

questions.q: A file holds millions of records all written with the same schema. Where should the writer's schema go?
options: In a separate email to readers
Nowhere, as readers will guess
Inside every record
Once, at the start of the file
optionExplain: Readers need it in the data's own context.
Guessing risks misdecoding.
Copying it into each record wastes space.
Right: one copy serves every record.
questions.explain: One schema serves many records. The card next lists the three contexts.

questions.q: Match each context to how the writer's schema is conveyed.
pairs: Writer's schema stored once at the start
Version number at the start of each record
questions.explain: The scheme depends on whether records share a schema and on how long the parties stay in touch.

questions.q: A gateway and a cloud service keep one long bidirectional connection open for hours. How should they agree on the schema?
options: Negotiate the version when the connection starts and use it for its lifetime
Send the full schema with every message so that nothing is negotiated at all
Store a version number in each message and look it up in a schema list
Give each message a randomly chosen schema from the list of old versions
optionExplain: Right: the Avro RPC protocol does it this way.
That wastes space.
Per-record version numbers are for databases.
Random schemas break decoding.
questions.explain: A long-lived connection can settle the schema once.

questions.q: True or false: A per-record version number is needed when every record in a file was written with the same schema.
questions.explain: A file with one schema needs it only once at the start; per-record numbers suit databases where records come from different eras.

questions.q: What does a database of schema versions give besides decoding?
options: Encryption of old data using the schema as the key
Documentation and a chance to check schema compatibility
Automatic code generation for every language the team uses
Faster network transfers through a smaller schema header
optionExplain: Encoding is not encryption.
Right: a list of schema versions is useful documentation and allows compatibility checks.
Generation is not claimed here.
Speed is not described.
questions.explain: A list of versions is documentation and also a place to check compatibility.
questions.rule: Keep a list of schema versions.
questions.teaches: A database of schema versions acts as documentation and gives you a chance to check schema compatibility.

questions.q: An event bus carries independent messages that different services read months later. What could identify the writer's schema?
options: The producer's IP address, which maps to a schema in the registry
A version number such as an incrementing integer or a hash of the schema
The consumer's own latest schema, since the consumer is the one decoding
The order in which messages arrive on the bus, oldest first
optionExplain: Addresses do not identify schemas.
Right: the version number can be a simple counter or a hash of the schema.
The reader's schema is not the writer's.
Order does not identify schemas.
questions.explain: Our reading: messages kept for months resemble database records, so a per-message version fits. The book names an incrementing integer or a hash as version numbers.
questions.rule: Number or hash as version id.
questions.teaches: As the version number, you could use a simple incrementing integer, or you could use a hash of the schema.

questions.q: A nightly job exports a database whose columns change often. What makes tag-numbered schemas awkward?
options: Tags must be assigned and tracked, and reused tags are dangerous
Tags cannot be used for string columns, only for number columns
Tags prevent the exported file from being compressed afterwards
Tags need the database to be offline while the tag mapping is rebuilt
optionExplain: Right: someone has to keep column-to-tag mappings.
Tags work for all types.
Compression is unrelated.
Availability is not the issue.
questions.explain: Each column change touches the tag mapping. The card next shows Avro's alternative.

questions.q: When Avro exports a database table, each column becomes a ____ in the record schema.
questions.explain: Each table becomes a record and each column a field of the same name.
questions.rule: Table is record, column is field.

questions.q: A table gains one column and loses another, and the Avro export is regenerated from the new table. What do old readers see?
options: The old columns restored in the files for the sake of old readers
The export fails until every reader has upgraded to the new schema
New files whose fields match old reader schemas by name
Tags renumbered by the generator for each changed column
optionExplain: Dropped columns are not restored.
Name matching lets resolution cope.
Right: the updated writer's schema still matches an old reader's by name.
Avro has no tags.
questions.explain: Fields identified by name let the schemas be matched up automatically.

questions.q: True or false: Automatically generating a Thrift schema from a database is impossible.
questions.explain: It might be possible to automate, but the generator would have to be very careful not to assign previously used field tags.

questions.q: Was dynamically generated schema support a design goal of Thrift and Protocol Buffers?
options: Yes, it was the main goal of both formats from the start
Yes, but only for Thrift and not for Protocol Buffers
No, it was not a goal of any format, Avro included
No, it was a design goal for Avro instead
optionExplain: The book says it was not.
Neither Thrift nor Protocol Buffers had it as a goal.
Avro had it as a goal.
Right: it was a goal for Avro and not for the others.
questions.explain: The formats reflect different origins and goals.
questions.rule: Avro was built for generated schemas.
questions.teaches: This kind of dynamically generated schema simply was not a design goal of Thrift or Protocol Buffers, whereas it was for Avro.

questions.q: A SaaS exports each customer's custom fields to files, with different columns per customer. Which choice fits the reasoning?
options: A single fixed schema for all customers, with every possible column in it
A schema generated per export, with fields identified by name
Hand-numbered tags for every custom field, assigned by an administrator
Plain CSV so that no schema is needed and every customer's file can differ
optionExplain: A fixed schema cannot hold varying columns.
Right: the schema is generated each time and matched by name.
Hand-numbering invites errors.
CSV loses types and needs manual handling.
questions.explain: Anyone reading new files sees that the fields changed, yet the writer's schema can still be matched with a reader's by name.
questions.teaches: Anyone who reads the new data files will see the fields have changed, but since fields are identified by name, the updated writer's schema can still be matched up with the old reader's schema.

questions.q: A Python team receives a binary file with a schema. Is generating classes from the schema likely to help?
options: Yes, because generated code is faster in all languages that read the file
Yes, because Python requires generated classes for every record it reads
Not much, because there is no compile-time type checker to satisfy
No, because Python cannot read binary files without a conversion step
optionExplain: Speed is not the book's argument.
Python does not require this.
Right: the main benefit of generated types is lost.
Python can read binary files.
questions.explain: The payoff of code generation depends on the language. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Value of generation depends on typing.

questions.q: True or false: In dynamically typed languages there is not much point in generating code, as there is no compile-time type checker.
questions.explain: That is the book's view; code generation is often frowned upon there.
questions.rule: Dynamic languages seldom need generated types.

questions.q: A Ruby analyst receives an Avro object container file. What is the easiest route to the data?
options: Generate classes first from a separate schema file and then load the data
Convert the file to CSV by hand, column by column, before analysing it
Ask the author to resend the file as XML, which Ruby reads directly
Open the file with the Avro library, which finds the embedded writer's schema
optionExplain: That is the unnecessary obstacle the book describes.
Conversion by hand is slower and loses types.
XML is not needed.
Right: the file is self-describing and can be read like a JSON file.
questions.explain: A container file embeds the writer's schema, so the data can be examined directly.

questions.q: Generated classes pay off most in ____ typed languages such as Java, C++ or C#.
questions.explain: Statically typed languages gain compile-time type checking, efficient in-memory structures and IDE autocompletion.

questions.q: How can Apache Pig users work with Avro files?
options: By opening the files, analysing them and writing derived Avro datasets without schema work
After writing a separate schema file for each Avro file that is to be analysed
Only on a cluster of statically typed machines that compile the schema code
Only after converting the files to JSON so that Pig can parse their fields
optionExplain: Right: the embedded schema removes the schema work.
That is the step the self-describing file avoids.
The book says nothing about this restriction.
Conversion is not needed.
questions.explain: A self-describing file lets Pig users skip the schema chores.
questions.teaches: In Pig you can open Avro files, analyse them and write derived datasets in Avro without even thinking about schemas.

questions.q: A Java team reads Avro files whose schema is regenerated nightly. What does the book's reasoning say about code generation?
options: It is required for every Avro file, since the library cannot read data without it
It is optional, and for a generated schema it can be an unnecessary obstacle to the data
It is forbidden by Avro whenever the schema is produced by another program
It is only needed for string fields, as other types need no generated classes
optionExplain: Avro's code generation is optional.
Right: for dynamically generated schemas it gets in the way.
Nothing forbids it.
No such limit to strings.
questions.explain: With a schema that changes nightly, regenerating classes each time adds work for little gain.
questions.teaches: In the case of a dynamically generated schema, code generation is an unnecessary obstacle to getting to the data.

questions.q: Why might a required schema make documentation more trustworthy than a wiki page?
options: It is written and reviewed by lawyers, which keeps it accurate over time
It is reviewed monthly by the team, so that it is corrected when it drifts
It must be correct for decoding to work, so it cannot drift from reality
It is stored in the cloud, where it is backed up and cannot be edited
optionExplain: Authorship is not the reason.
Review cadence is not the reason.
Right: a wrong schema breaks decoding, so errors show up.
Storage place is not the reason.
questions.explain: A document nobody executes can diverge. The card next lists the merits.

questions.q: Which merits does the book list for schema-based binary encodings? Select all that apply.
options: The schema is documentation that is known to be current
The bytes can be read by people without any tools
They can be more compact since field names are omitted
A database of schemas lets you check compatibility before deployment
They avoid needing any schema language
optionExplain: Right: decoding requires the schema, so it stays up to date.
Binary data must be decoded first.
Right: no field names in the data.
Right: compatibility can be checked beforehand.
They rely on schema languages.
questions.explain: Compactness, current documentation, and early compatibility checks are three of the four listed merits.

questions.q: A team's wiki describes message fields, but producers have changed them. Which benefit of schemas fixes this?
options: Smaller messages, which means fewer chances for drift
Better colours and highlighting in the IDE for field names
Faster network transfers, which keep the documents in step
The schema, needed for decoding, must match reality
optionExplain: Size does not fix stale documentation.
Irrelevant.
Speed does not fix documentation.
Right: the schema cannot diverge or decoding fails.
questions.explain: The schema is both specification and working code.

questions.q: True or false: Manually maintained documentation is as reliable as a schema, since both describe the format.
questions.explain: Manual documentation may easily diverge from reality; the schema is required for decoding, so it is known to be up to date.

questions.q: How does schema evolution compare with schema-on-read JSON databases?
options: It gives the same flexibility with better guarantees and tooling
It gives less flexibility than schemaless databases but is faster to read
It is identical in every respect, including guarantees and tooling
It is only possible with relational databases that have a fixed schema in force
optionExplain: Right: that is the book's summary.
The comparison is on flexibility, not speed.
Guarantees and tooling differ.
Schema evolution is not limited to relational databases.
questions.explain: Evolution rules allow change without giving up guarantees.
questions.teaches: Schema evolution allows the same kind of flexibility as schemaless JSON databases provide, while also providing better guarantees about your data and better tooling.

questions.q: An engineer wants to inspect production bytes with a text viewer. What does the book list as the downside here?
options: Records cannot be extended once the first one has been written
The bytes are encrypted, so a viewer needs the key to read them
Field names are repeated in every record, which makes them hard to scan
Data needs to be decoded before it is human-readable
optionExplain: Records can be extended within the rules.
Encoding is not encryption.
Repeated names are a trait of binary JSON.
Right: binary schema-driven formats are not readable as they are.
questions.explain: The summary notes the downside that data needs decoding before it is human-readable.
questions.teaches: Binary schema-driven formats have the downside that data needs to be decoded before it is human-readable.

questions.q: Which kind of rule can XML Schema or JSON Schema state that Thrift, Protocol Buffers and Avro schemas cannot?
options: That a string must match a regular expression
That a field is a string of text, not a number
That a field has a tag number that identifies it
That a record has several fields of different types
optionExplain: Right: detailed validation rules are available only in the heavier schema languages.
All formats can state a field type.
Tags are part of Thrift and Protocol Buffers.
All schema languages describe records.
questions.explain: Detailed validation is the heavier languages' strength. The card next gives the trade.

questions.q: Match each item to its description.
pairs: Schema language standardised in 1984 with tag-number evolution
Binary encoding of ASN.1 used for SSL certificates
questions.explain: Schema-based binary encoding is an old idea.

questions.q: A team needs the schema itself to require an age between 0 and 100. Which fits?
options: An Avro schema
A Thrift IDL
A JSON Schema
A Protocol Buffers schema
optionExplain: Avro schemas do not state ranges.
Thrift IDL does not either.
Right: JSON Schema can state a numeric range.
It does not support range validation.
questions.explain: Range rules belong to the more powerful schema languages.
questions.rule: Validation rules need richer schema languages.

questions.q: True or false: ASN.1 is a recent idea invented along with Protocol Buffers.
questions.explain: ASN.1 was first standardised in 1984, and its binary encoding is still used for SSL certificates.

questions.q: What does the book conclude about ASN.1 for a new application?
options: It is simpler than Avro and better documented than Protocol Buffers
It is probably not a good choice because it is complex and badly documented
It is required for SSL, since certificates are encoded with it
It is the best choice for new applications, thanks to its long history and standard
optionExplain: It is described as complex.
Right: that is the stated conclusion.
Only its binary encoding appears in certificates.
History alone is not the book's argument.
questions.explain: Complexity and poor documentation count against it.
questions.rule: Complex and badly documented means avoid.
questions.teaches: ASN.1 is very complex and badly documented, so it is probably not a good choice for new applications.

questions.q: A client library talks to a vendor's relational database. What turns the database's network responses into in-memory structures?
options: A schema file shared by every database vendor, so that no driver is needed
Nothing; responses are already in memory structures when they arrive
A driver for the vendor protocol, such as one using ODBC or JDBC
A JSON converter in the browser that reads the vendor's responses
optionExplain: Each vendor protocol is specific.
Memory structures cannot cross the network.
Right: such protocols are proprietary, and the vendor provides a driver.
Browsers are not involved.
questions.explain: Many data systems use their own binary protocols, decoded by vendor drivers.
questions.teaches: Most relational databases have a network protocol specific to a particular database, and the vendor provides a driver that decodes responses into in-memory data structures.

questions.q: A producer sends an event to a queue; a consumer reads it later. Who decodes the data?
options: The queue's disk
The producer
Nobody, since the queue is shared memory
The consumer
optionExplain: A disk does not decode.
The producer encoded it.
Processes do not share memory.
Right: the process that reads decodes.
questions.explain: Whoever reads decodes. The card next names the three modes.

questions.q: Match each mode to who encodes and decodes.
pairs: The writing process encodes, a reading process decodes later
The client encodes a request and the server decodes it, and the reverse for the response
The sender encodes and the recipient decodes, via a broker or actors
questions.explain: In every mode, someone encodes and someone decodes.
questions.rule: Encoder and decoder define the flow.

questions.q: A nightly job writes rows that a report job reads a month later. Which mode is this?
options: Dataflow through a database
Dataflow through a service call
Dataflow through message passing
None of the three
optionExplain: Right: written once and read later from storage.
No request waits for a reply.
No broker sits between them.
It fits the first mode.
questions.explain: Data written to storage and read later is dataflow through a database.
questions.rule: Storage read later means database mode.

questions.q: True or false: A client that waits for an immediate reply from another service is using asynchronous message passing.
questions.explain: Waiting for a quick reply is a service call. In message passing the sender usually sends and forgets.
questions.rule: Waiting for a reply means a service call.

questions.q: Where does asynchronous message passing sit among the modes?
options: It is the same as RPC with a different name
Somewhere between RPC and databases
It replaces REST entirely for public interfaces
It is a kind of database with a query language
optionExplain: RPC expects a quick response; messaging does not.
Right: low-latency delivery like RPC, but through an intermediary that stores like a database.
It does not replace REST.
Brokers store messages only temporarily.
questions.explain: Messaging delivers with low latency like RPC and uses a store-and-forward broker like a database.
questions.teaches: Asynchronous message-passing systems are somewhere between RPC and databases.

questions.q: A food-ordering app asks the payment service for an authorisation and cannot proceed without it. Which mode fits?
options: Archival storage, as the authorisation is kept for the records
A service call, as the client expects a response as quickly as possible
Message passing, as the client sends the request and forgets about it afterwards
A database, as the authorisation result is stored for later reading
optionExplain: Archival storage is a database mode.
Right: the request is expected to be answered quickly.
Message passing is typically one-way.
The result is needed immediately, not read later.
questions.explain: REST and RPC send a request over the network and expect a response as quickly as possible.
questions.rule: Needs an answer now, so call it.
questions.teaches: In REST and RPC, one process sends a request over the network to another process and expects a response as quickly as possible.

questions.q: One program writes records to a database; next month a newer version of that program reads them. Which compatibility is needed?
options: Both, but only when the data is stored in a text format such as JSON
Forward: the older code must read data written by the newer code later
Backward: the newer code must read data written by older code
Neither, since it is the same program writing and reading its data
optionExplain: Format type does not decide this.
No old code is reading new data here.
Right: the later version reads what the earlier version wrote.
Versions differ over time even in one program.
questions.explain: The reader is the later version. The card next widens the picture.

questions.q: Storing something in a database can be thought of as sending a message to your ____ self.
questions.explain: The later version of the process is the reader of what today's version writes.
questions.rule: Writing to a database is a message to the future.

questions.q: During a rolling upgrade, a new booking-service instance writes a row and an old instance reads it. What is needed?
options: Forward compatibility, since old code reads data written by new code
No compatibility, because the row is in the same table as the others it reads
Backward compatibility only, since new code reads the old rows
Compatibility only after the upgrade finishes and all instances run new code
optionExplain: Right: old code meets new data during the rollout.
A shared table does not remove the version difference.
Backward covers new reading old, the opposite flow.
The mix exists during the upgrade.
questions.explain: Mixed instances mean old code can read rows from new code.
questions.rule: Rolling upgrades make forward compatibility necessary.

questions.q: True or false: A team that ensures only backward compatibility is safe during a rolling upgrade where old and new instances share rows.
questions.explain: Old instances can still read rows written by new instances, so forward compatibility is also needed.

questions.q: A single process accesses a database and is replaced by a newer version. What is the reader in this case?
options: A message broker between the database and the process
A web browser that displays the stored records
A different application that shares the database
The same process at a later version
optionExplain: No broker is involved.
No browser is involved.
No other application is involved.
Right: it is the process itself, in a later version.
questions.explain: With one process, the reader is simply a later version of the writer.
questions.rule: One process: reader is a later version.
questions.teaches: There may be just a single process accessing the database, in which case the reader is simply a later version of the same process.

questions.q: A note-taking desktop app keeps a local database file. Users only upgrade, and one copy of the app runs. Which direction must the format support?
options: Neither, since the file is local
Both, because the file is a database
Backward compatibility, because newer versions read older files
Forward compatibility, because older versions read newer files
optionExplain: Local files still outlive versions.
Both are needed when old and new code share data.
Right: the later version reads what the earlier wrote.
No old code will meet new files under these conditions.
questions.explain: Our reading: with one process and upgrades only, only the backward direction is exercised. The book says backward compatibility is necessary here, since your future self must decode what you wrote earlier.
questions.teaches: Backward compatibility is necessary for a database read by a later version, otherwise your future self cannot decode what you previously wrote.

questions.q: Old code reads a record with an unknown field, changes one value and saves it. What may happen to that field?
options: It is kept by the database because the stored record is never changed
It is lost if the code rebuilds the record from its own model
It is encrypted by the database when the record is saved
It is duplicated into a second record next to the first
optionExplain: The database stores what it is given; a rewrite can omit the field.
Right: a model without the field cannot write it back.
Nothing encrypts it.
Nothing duplicates it.
questions.explain: Re-encoding what you decoded loses what you did not model. The card next states the issue.
questions.rule: When old code rewrites a record, keep the fields it does not understand.

questions.q: True or false: The encoding formats support keeping unknown fields, but an application can still lose them.
questions.explain: Application-level handling, for example mapping to model objects, can drop fields the format could have preserved.

questions.q: A profile service maps database rows to a model class that lacks the new avatarStyle field, then saves the whole object. What is the effect?
options: avatarStyle is lost for users whose rows are saved this way
avatarStyle is kept, since the database remembers it
The model class is updated automatically to include the new field
All rows are rejected because the model lacks one of their fields
optionExplain: Right: the saved object has no avatarStyle.
The save replaces the row's contents.
Nothing updates the class.
Nothing rejects the write.
questions.explain: A full rewrite from an incomplete model drops the field.
questions.rule: Rewrite from an incomplete model drops fields.

questions.q: True or false: Because Protocol Buffers can preserve unknown fields, application code does not need to take any care.
questions.explain: The format helps, but translating data into model objects and back can still lose fields, so you must be aware of it.

questions.q: The desirable behaviour is for old code to keep a field it cannot interpret ____ when it updates the record.
questions.explain: The new field should survive the update even though the old code could not interpret it.
questions.teaches: The desirable behavior is usually for the old code to keep the new field intact, even though it couldn't be interpreted.

questions.q: A consumer reads messages from one topic, adds data, and republishes to another topic. Which risk does the book warn about?
options: Republishing changes the sender's address so replies go to the wrong place
Consumers cannot decode any messages that were written by another version
Topics cannot hold more than one message at a time, so republishing is lossy
Unknown fields in messages may be lost when it republishes
optionExplain: Addresses are not the issue.
Decoding works when formats are compatible.
Topics hold many messages.
Right: the same loss as with databases applies.
questions.explain: Republishing re-encodes the message, so it needs care to preserve unknown fields.
questions.teaches: If a consumer republishes messages to another topic, you may need to be careful to preserve unknown fields.

questions.q: A team replaces its application servers within minutes. What happens to the five-year-old rows in the database?
options: They are deleted by the upgrade because the old code no longer exists
They become unreadable as soon as the code that wrote them is gone
They are converted automatically to the newest format
They remain in their original encoding unless explicitly rewritten
optionExplain: Upgrades do not delete data.
They stay readable if the format evolves compatibly.
No automatic conversion happens.
Right: stored data does not change with the code.
questions.explain: Code changes fast, data does not. The card next names the effect.
questions.rule: Stored data keeps its original encoding, so schema evolution must let new code read all historical versions.

questions.q: The observation that stored data stays while code is replaced is summed up as data ____ code.
questions.explain: Data outlives code.

questions.q: A team adds a nullable column to a 2-billion-row table. What do most relational databases do?
options: Leave existing rows alone and return null for the missing column
Refuse the change until the table has been emptied of all its rows
Rewrite every row at once so the new column is physically stored
Delete the rows that do not yet have the column, then reload them
optionExplain: Right: the database fills in null when it reads an old row.
Adding a column is a simple change.
That would be the expensive migration most databases avoid.
No deletion occurs.
questions.explain: Simple changes need no rewriting; the database fills in the null on read.
questions.rule: Fill defaults on read, skip the rewrite.

questions.q: A row written five years ago is read after three schema changes. What must hold for it to work?
options: The row must have been rewritten each year so that it uses the current encoding
The old encoding must remain readable under the current schema's evolution rules
The reader must use the oldest schema that was ever applied to the table
The row must be converted to text before the new code can interpret it
optionExplain: Rewriting is what the database avoids.
Right: schema evolution makes the database look as if it used one schema.
Readers use the current schema.
Text conversion is not required.
questions.explain: Evolution rules let the entire database appear as if encoded with a single schema.

questions.q: True or false: Every relational database avoids rewriting the table when a column is added.
questions.explain: MySQL often rewrites an entire table even though it is not strictly necessary.
questions.teaches: MySQL often rewrites an entire table when a column is added, even though it is not strictly necessary.

questions.q: A company has 20 TB of rows in four old encodings. What fits the book's reasoning?
options: Migrate everything in one weekend so all rows share the newest encoding
Switch to language-specific serialization, which handles versions for you
Rely on schema evolution to read old rows, and migrate rarely if at all
Delete rows older than a year so that only the newest encoding remains
optionExplain: That is the expensive migration most databases avoid.
That adds lock-in and weak versioning.
Right: evolution rules let new code read all versions.
Deleting loses data.
questions.explain: LinkedIn's Espresso database stores data in Avro, which lets it use Avro's schema evolution rules instead of migrating.
questions.teaches: LinkedIn's document database Espresso uses Avro for storage, allowing it to use Avro's schema evolution rules.

questions.q: A snapshot is taken of a database whose rows were written under several schemas. Which encoding is sensible for the copy?
options: Only the rows from the newest schema, leaving older rows out of the copy
One consistent encoding, using the latest schema
Each row in the original schema it was written with, to stay faithful
Plain text for all rows, so that any tool can open the copy
optionExplain: Skipping rows loses data.
Right: encode the copy consistently.
Mixed encodings complicate every reader.
Text is not required.
questions.explain: A copy is a chance to tidy up. The card next states the advice.
questions.rule: Encode a snapshot consistently in the latest schema, in a format suited to one-shot immutable files.

questions.q: A data dump is typically encoded using the ____ schema.
questions.explain: The dump is written in the latest schema even if the source mixes versions.

questions.q: A retailer backs up its orders table monthly. Rows come from five schema eras. What should the backup do?
options: Skip the old rows that use outdated schemas
Convert the rows to CSV so that no schema is needed
Keep five different encodings, one for each schema era
Write every row in the current schema
optionExplain: Old rows would be lost.
CSV is loosely specified and has no schema.
That is needless complexity.
Right: copying lets you normalise.
questions.explain: Encoding the copy consistently makes it easy to read later.

questions.q: True or false: An archive must keep each record in the schema version it was originally written in.
questions.explain: Since you are copying the data anyway, you might as well encode the copy consistently.

questions.q: Why do Avro object container files fit a data dump?
options: The dump is written in one go and is immutable
They need no schema because the records describe themselves
They are editable in place, which suits changing data
They are human-readable, so the dump can be checked by hand
optionExplain: Right: one-shot, immutable files suit them.
They embed a schema.
They are not edited in place.
They are binary.
questions.explain: A dump written once and never changed matches the container file model.
questions.teaches: As the data dump is written in one go and is thereafter immutable, formats like Avro object container files are a good fit.

questions.q: An analytics team loads the snapshot into a warehouse and mostly reads a few columns of many rows. Which format does the book suggest?
options: A language-specific format that can restore objects of the same types
A row-by-row text log that can be scanned by any tool
A column-oriented format such as Parquet
A key-value store dump that keeps the original record layout
optionExplain: Lock-in and weak versioning rule it out.
Row text is slow for column scans.
Right: column-oriented formats suit analytics.
The book names Parquet.
questions.explain: A snapshot is an opportunity to use an analytics-friendly column-oriented format such as Parquet.
questions.teaches: This is also a good opportunity to encode the data in an analytics-friendly column-oriented format such as Parquet.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: Why must microservice teams worry about data encodings between services?
options: Teams release independently, so old and new versions meet
Clients are newer than servers, so only forward compatibility matters
Services use only binary formats, which cannot be changed over time
Databases require it, since services always store data in them
optionExplain: Right: independent releases create mixed versions.
Neither side is always newer.
Services can use any format.
Databases are not the reason.
questions.explain: Independent releases mean version mixing. The card next sets this out.
questions.rule: Independent deployability means clients and servers of different versions coexist, so API encodings must stay compatible.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: The API that a server exposes over the network is known as a ____.
questions.explain: A service is the API exposed by a server.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: An inventory team releases weekly and does not notify other teams. What must their API encoding allow?
options: Only new clients to call it, once every team has upgraded
Old clients to keep working against new releases
Direct access to the database tables for any client that needs them
Clients to upgrade within the same hour as each release
optionExplain: Old clients exist.
Right: other teams cannot be forced to follow.
Services expose predetermined APIs.
That is the lockstep the design avoids.
questions.explain: Without coordination, clients lag behind and must still work.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: A service ships a change that breaks version 1 clients. What follows for teams that do not coordinate?
options: Clients upgrade by themselves as soon as the service changes
Nothing, since the old and new versions never run together
Those clients break until their teams catch up
The service rolls back automatically when a client reports an error
optionExplain: Clients do not self-update.
Versions do mix.
Right: uncoordinated clients fail.
Nothing rolls back automatically.
questions.explain: The aim of independence is defeated if a release breaks clients.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: True or false: A server can itself be a client of another service.
questions.explain: A typical web app server acts as a client to a database, and microservices call one another.
questions.teaches: A server can itself be a client to another service, for example a web app server acting as client to a database.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: A partner asks for direct read access to your database tables. What does the book say about a service instead?
options: It allows arbitrary queries like a database, which suits an outside partner
It exposes the storage engine, so the partner sees how data is kept
It removes versioning, because partners always call the latest release
It restricts clients to predetermined inputs and outputs, giving encapsulation
optionExplain: That is what databases allow.
Services hide internals.
Versioning remains.
Right: services impose fine-grained restrictions on what clients can do.
questions.explain: Unlike databases, services offer only application-specific operations.
questions.teaches: Services expose an application-specific API that only allows inputs and outputs predetermined by the business logic, giving a degree of encapsulation.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: Which description fits REST?
options: A message broker
An XML-based wire protocol independent of HTTP
A schema language for binary data
A design philosophy built on HTTP principles
optionExplain: Not a broker.
That describes SOAP.
Not a schema language.
Right: REST is not a protocol.
questions.explain: REST is a style, SOAP a protocol. The card next compares them.
questions.rule: REST is a philosophy using HTTP as it is; SOAP is a separate XML protocol with heavy tooling.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: Match each term to its description.
pairs: Design philosophy that builds on HTTP
XML-based protocol for network API requests
XML language that describes a SOAP service
Definition format for describing RESTful APIs
questions.explain: Each term has its place in the web service world.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: A small team using Python and curl for debugging must integrate with an outside partner's API quickly. Which style fits better?
options: CORBA, which gives full backward and forward compatibility
REST, with simple formats and little tooling
Java RMI, which keeps everything in one language and so is simple
SOAP, with generated classes and a WSDL description of the service
optionExplain: CORBA is complex.
Right: REST needs little code generation.
Java RMI is limited to Java.
SOAP relies on tooling that suits statically typed languages.
questions.explain: Simple tooling and debugging with curl favour REST.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: Which statement separates SOAP from REST?
options: SOAP aims to be independent of HTTP and avoids most of its features
SOAP uses URLs to identify resources and relies on HTTP caching
SOAP is a design philosophy that builds on the principles of HTTP
SOAP has no schema language of its own and is described informally
optionExplain: Right: it carries its own standards instead.
That is REST.
SOAP is a protocol.
SOAP has WSDL.
questions.explain: SOAP is usually over HTTP but does not use its features.
questions.rule: REST is a philosophy using HTTP as it is; SOAP is a separate XML protocol with heavy tooling.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: True or false: SOAP is a required part of service-oriented architecture.
questions.explain: SOAP is a particular technology, whereas service-oriented architecture is a general approach to building systems.
questions.teaches: Despite the similarity of acronyms, SOAP is not a requirement for SOA; SOAP is a technology and SOA is a general approach.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: A bank's cross-organisation integration team weighs the trends. What does the book report about REST and SOAP?
options: SOAP has overtaken REST everywhere because its WS-* standards make it interoperable
SOAP is the standard choice in smaller companies, which value its tooling
REST has gained on SOAP in cross-organisation integration, while SOAP persists in large enterprises
Both have vanished, replaced by the RPC frameworks built on binary encodings
optionExplain: The opposite is described.
SOAP has fallen out of favour in smaller companies.
Right: that is the book's observation.
Neither has vanished.
questions.explain: Interoperability problems between vendors pushed smaller companies away from SOAP.
questions.rule: REST gains, SOAP lingers in enterprises.
questions.teaches: REST has been gaining popularity compared to SOAP, at least in the context of cross-organizational service integration.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: A call to another service times out. What do you know?
options: That the server crashed before it could answer
That the request did not arrive at the remote machine
Nothing about whether the request got through
That the request succeeded and only the reply is late
optionExplain: The server may be fine.
It may have arrived.
Right: you cannot tell loss of the request from loss of the response.
No answer arrived to say so.
questions.explain: A timeout hides what happened. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Treat every remote call as able to fail without telling you whether it worked.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: Making a remote call look like a local call is called location ____.
questions.explain: The RPC abstraction is called location transparency.
questions.rule: RPC pretends location does not matter.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: A payment RPC times out and the client retries. What may go wrong?
options: The charge may be made twice, if the first request got through
The response is cached and returned for every later call
The retry is rejected by TCP as a duplicate connection
The client switches to REST, which cannot repeat requests
optionExplain: Right: only the response may have been lost.
Caching is unrelated.
Nothing rejects retries.
Nothing switches style.
questions.explain: Without deduplication a retry can duplicate the action.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: True or false: If an RPC times out, you can conclude the request did not reach the server.
questions.explain: The request may have arrived with only the response lost, so you do not know what happened.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: Besides returning a result, throwing an exception or hanging forever, what outcome does a network request add?
options: Returning a result before the request has been sent
Returning without a result because of a timeout
Returning two results, one from each retry
Returning the caller's own request as a copy
optionExplain: Not possible.
Right: a fourth outcome with unknown state.
No such outcome.
No such outcome.
questions.explain: A local call has three outcomes; a network request has a fourth.
questions.rule: Network calls add the timeout outcome.
questions.teaches: A network request has another possible outcome: it may return without a result, due to a timeout.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: A smart-heater API offers a toggle call and a set-to-on call. Retries after timeouts are likely. Which is safer under the book's advice?
options: Either, since retries are rare on a healthy network
Toggle, since a single short call means fewer messages
Neither; the book advises avoiding networks for such calls
Set-to-on, since repeating it gives the same result
optionExplain: Network problems are common.
Toggle flips back on a duplicate.
Avoiding networks is not the book's advice.
Right: a repeatable action is idempotent, so a duplicate does no harm.
questions.explain: Our reading: the book asks for a deduplication mechanism, idempotence, in the protocol so retries are safe.
questions.teaches: Retrying will cause the action to be performed multiple times, unless you build a mechanism for deduplication (idempotence) into the protocol.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: Why can a program not pass a memory pointer to a remote service?
options: Pointers are too long to fit in a network packet header
Services do not accept numbers, only text, so pointers fail
The pointer refers to local memory that the remote process cannot see
Pointers are encrypted by the operating system for safety
optionExplain: Length is not the issue.
Services accept numbers.
Right: the other process has its own memory.
Encryption is unrelated.
questions.explain: Memory is private to a process. The card next lists the consequences.
questions.rule: A remote call is slower, more variable and needs its arguments encoded, so do not disguise it as a local call.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: The latency of a network request is wildly ____, from under a millisecond to many seconds.
questions.explain: Latency varies with congestion and load.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: A developer plans to pass a 500 MB in-memory object graph as an RPC parameter. What is the issue?
options: Graphs cannot contain numbers, so the encoding would lose values
Remote services reject big messages as a rule of the HTTP standard
The pointers are sent for free, so only the data is copied
The whole graph must be encoded into bytes, which is problematic for large objects
optionExplain: Graphs can hold numbers.
No law applies.
Pointers do not travel.
Right: parameters must be encoded to travel.
questions.explain: Local calls pass references efficiently; remote calls pass encoded copies.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: Match each older RPC technology to the limit the book names.
pairs: Excessively complex, with no backward or forward compatibility
questions.explain: Each past technology failed in its own way.
questions.rule: A remote call is slower, more variable and needs its arguments encoded, so do not disguise it as a local call.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: What does the book say about REST and hiding the network?
options: REST avoids HTTP and uses its own transport protocol
REST does not try to hide that it is a network protocol
REST requires location transparency, like any RPC scheme
REST hides the network better than RPC does, with simple URLs
optionExplain: REST builds on HTTP.
Right: part of its appeal.
Location transparency is RPC's aim.
The reverse is true.
questions.explain: Being open about the network is an advantage.
questions.rule: REST is honest about the network.
questions.teaches: Part of the appeal of REST is that it does not try to hide the fact that it is a network protocol.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: A mobile UI calls getFeed(), a generated RPC stub that looks local, on its main thread. What may happen when the network is congested?
options: The call may take many seconds, freezing the interface
The call fails immediately with a compiler error
The call returns the pointer to the feed
The call always takes under a millisecond
optionExplain: Right: latency at bad times can reach many seconds.
Compile-time errors are unrelated.
Pointers do not cross the network.
That holds only at good times.
questions.explain: At good times a request may finish in under a millisecond; when the network is congested or the service overloaded it may take many seconds.
questions.teaches: A network request is much slower than a function call, and its latency is wildly variable: less than a millisecond at good times, many seconds when congested.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: A company offers an API to thousands of unknown developers. Which style is the book's predominant choice?
options: Java RMI
CORBA
A custom binary RPC
REST
optionExplain: RMI is limited to Java.
CORBA is complex.
Custom RPC suits internal use.
Right: REST seems predominant for public APIs.
questions.explain: Unknown clients prefer common tooling. The card next gives the reasoning.
questions.rule: Use RPC frameworks inside one organisation for performance; use REST for public APIs.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: Match each framework to what it builds on.
pairs: Schema version negotiated at connection setup
questions.explain: The new generation reuses the encodings of this chapter.
questions.rule: Use RPC frameworks inside one organisation for performance; use REST for public APIs.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: Two services of one company in one datacenter exchange millions of small calls a second. What does the book suggest?
options: An RPC framework with a binary encoding
SOAP, with its WS-* standards for reliability
Email between the services' mailboxes
REST with XML, readable by every tool
optionExplain: Right: RPC suits internal, performance-sensitive calls.
SOAP is rarely chosen for new work.
Email is not a service protocol.
REST with XML is heavy.
questions.explain: Same organisation, same datacenter, performance matters: RPC.
questions.rule: Use RPC frameworks inside one organisation for performance; use REST for public APIs.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: True or false: A public API provider who wants developers to try it with curl and a browser fits REST well.
questions.explain: REST supports experimentation and debugging without code generation or software installation.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: What do futures, as used in Finagle and Rest.li, add to RPC?
options: They hide the network completely so calls look local
They make failure and asynchrony explicit and ease parallel requests
They encrypt messages between the services in transit
They remove timeouts by making every call wait until done
optionExplain: They make the difference more explicit.
Right: a promise can fail, and results from several requests can be combined.
Encryption is unrelated.
Timeouts remain.
questions.explain: The new frameworks are more explicit that a remote call differs from a local one.
questions.teaches: Finagle and Rest.li use futures (promises) to encapsulate asynchronous actions that may fail, and futures simplify parallel requests.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: A driver app sends a series of position updates in one long call while the server replies over time. Which feature fits?
options: A Base64 string
An actor timeout
gRPC streams
A single REST GET
optionExplain: Base64 is an encoding.
Not what streaming means.
Right: a call can consist of a series of requests and responses over time.
GET is one request and one response.
questions.explain: gRPC supports streams, where a call is a series of requests and responses over time.
questions.teaches: gRPC supports streams, where a call consists of not just one request and one response, but a series of requests and responses over time.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: Servers are updated before clients. A new server receives a request from an old client. Which compatibility does this need?
options: Compatibility on responses only
Backward compatibility on requests
Forward compatibility on requests
Neither
optionExplain: The request itself needs it too.
Right: the new server reads a request written by older code.
Old code is not reading the request.
Both directions occur somewhere.
questions.explain: The new reader needs to understand the old writer. The card next sets this out.
questions.rule: For services, assume servers upgrade first: backward compatible requests, forward compatible responses.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: With servers updated first, you need backward compatibility on ____ and forward compatibility on responses.
questions.explain: New servers read old requests; old clients read new responses.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: A new server version adds a field to its responses. Old clients do not know it. Which property do they rely on?
options: Backward compatibility on requests
Deduplication
Neither
Forward compatibility on responses
optionExplain: That concerns requests.
Deduplication is a retry matter.
They rely on one.
Right: old code reads data written by newer code.
questions.explain: The old client reads a response written by new code.
questions.rule: For services, assume servers upgrade first: backward compatible requests, forward compatible responses.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: True or false: If a new server removes a response field that old clients depend on, forward compatibility on responses breaks.
questions.explain: Old clients read responses written by newer code, so a removed field they depend on breaks that direction.
questions.rule: Old readers depend on old fields.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: How do RESTful APIs commonly version themselves?
options: With a schema hash placed in the TCP header of each packet
They do not version, because REST forbids multiple versions
With a version number in the URL or in the HTTP Accept header
With a version number repeated in every byte of the body
optionExplain: Not described.
There is no agreed approach, but they do.
Right: both are common approaches.
No such practice.
questions.explain: There is no agreement on how API versioning should work; common approaches include the URL and the Accept header, and storing the version a client requests on the server for clients with API keys.
questions.rule: Version in URL or Accept header.
questions.teaches: For RESTful APIs, common approaches are to use a version number in the URL or in the HTTP Accept header.

questions.section: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
questions.q: A payments API serves thousands of partner companies. A breaking change is needed. What often happens?
options: The provider maintains multiple API versions side by side
The change ships silently and clients find out when they break
The old version is deleted at once to keep a single codebase
All partners are forced to upgrade the same day
optionExplain: Right: the provider cannot force clients to upgrade.
Silent breakage defeats compatibility.
Deleting breaks clients.
Providers lack that control.
questions.explain: If a compatibility-breaking change is required, the provider often ends up maintaining multiple versions side by side.
questions.rule: Run old and new side by side.
questions.teaches: If a compatibility-breaking change is required, the service provider often ends up maintaining multiple versions of the service API side by side.

questions.q: A consumer crashes while a message is on its way. What could a broker do that a direct call cannot?
options: Cancel the sender's request and report an error
Change the topic name so the message is routed again
Encrypt the payload so that the consumer can rely on it
Redeliver the message to the restarted process
optionExplain: Senders are unaffected.
Names do not change.
Encryption is unrelated.
Right: it stores messages and redelivers.
questions.explain: A broker holds the message. The card next lists the advantages.
questions.rule: A broker decouples sender and recipient in time and place, at the price of a one-way, asynchronous flow.

questions.q: Which advantages of a message broker over direct RPC does the book list? Select all that apply.
options: It forces every message into one data model
It lets one message reach several recipients
It gives the sender an immediate reply
It can redeliver messages to a crashed process
It can buffer if the recipient is unavailable or overloaded
optionExplain: Brokers do not enforce a data model.
Right: one message, many recipients.
Messaging is usually one-way.
Right: messages are not lost.
Right: buffering improves reliability.
questions.explain: Buffering, redelivery and fan-out are listed among the advantages.
questions.rule: A broker decouples sender and recipient in time and place, at the price of a one-way, asynchronous flow.

questions.q: After a photo upload, the thumbnail service, the search index and a notification service must each be told. What fits?
options: Publish one message to a topic with three consumers
Email the three services a link to the photo
Write the photo into three databases, one for each service
Make three blocking RPC calls in a row, waiting for each answer
optionExplain: Right: one message can go to several recipients.
Email is not a message broker.
That duplicates data.
Blocking calls couple the upload to all three.
questions.explain: A topic can have many consumers.
questions.rule: A broker decouples sender and recipient in time and place, at the price of a one-way, asynchronous flow.

questions.q: True or false: In message passing, the sender normally waits for a reply to each message.
questions.explain: Message passing is usually one-way and asynchronous: the sender sends and then forgets, unlike RPC.

questions.q: What do brokers typically require of message contents?
options: Only one schema per broker, which every message must follow
Nothing beyond bytes with metadata, so any encoding can be used
Only JSON, since brokers parse the message body
Only text, so that messages can be routed by content
optionExplain: No schema is enforced.
Right: brokers do not enforce a data model.
No such limit.
Messages can be binary.
questions.explain: With a compatible encoding, publishers and consumers can change independently and deploy in any order.
questions.teaches: Message brokers typically do not enforce any particular data model; a message is just a sequence of bytes with some metadata.

questions.q: A service needs an answer to a request it sent through a broker. How can that be done?
options: The broker returns the answer in the same call that sent the message
The sender polls the broker's database for the original message
The consumer publishes the answer to a reply queue the sender reads
Not possible with brokers, since messaging is strictly one-way
optionExplain: The call is asynchronous.
Polling is not described.
Right: a reply queue gives a request/response flow like RPC.
It is possible.
questions.explain: A consumer may publish to another topic or to a reply queue consumed by the sender, giving request/response like RPC.
questions.teaches: A consumer may publish messages to a reply queue that is consumed by the sender of the original message, allowing a request/response dataflow.

questions.q: Why might hiding the network be less harmful in an actor framework?
options: Actors never fail, so lost messages are not a concern
The model already assumes messages can be lost, even in one process
Messages are always delivered, even across several nodes
Networks are faster than memory access inside one process
optionExplain: Actors can fail.
Right: remote loss is not a new surprise.
Delivery is not guaranteed.
Memory is faster.
questions.explain: The assumption of loss is built in. The card next shows the model.
questions.rule: Actors already assume lost messages, so remote messaging fits them better than RPC fits ordinary calls.

questions.q: In the actor model, each actor processes only ____ message at a time.
questions.explain: That removes the need to worry about threads.

questions.q: A game has one actor per player on several nodes. Player A messages player B on another node. What happens?
options: The message is encoded, sent over the network and decoded on the other node
The message is copied by pointer to the memory of the other node
The nodes share an actor's state through a common memory region
The message is held until the other node is restarted and reachable
optionExplain: Right: the framework does it transparently.
Pointers cannot cross nodes.
State is not shared.
No such wait.
questions.explain: The same mechanism is used on one node or several.
questions.rule: Actors already assume lost messages, so remote messaging fits them better than RPC fits ordinary calls.

questions.q: True or false: In an actor-based system, rolling upgrades need no thought about compatibility because actors share no state.
questions.explain: Messages can flow between nodes running different versions, so forward and backward compatibility still matter.

questions.q: How does Akka handle message encoding by default, and how can it support rolling upgrades?
options: It uses Avro with a schema registry, which gives rolling upgrades by default
It cannot be changed, so rolling upgrades are impossible
It uses JSON with schemas, which gives full compatibility by default
Java serialization by default, which lacks compatibility; replace it, for example with Protocol Buffers
optionExplain: That is not the default.
It can be replaced.
That is not the default.
Right: by default no forward or backward compatibility.
questions.explain: Replacing the default with a format that offers compatibility gains the ability to do rolling upgrades.
questions.rule: Swap the encoding to gain upgrades.
questions.teaches: Akka uses Java's built-in serialization by default, which does not provide forward or backward compatibility; you can replace it with something like Protocol Buffers.

questions.q: A framework's default encoding does not support rolling upgrades, as with Orleans. How is a new version deployed?
options: Upgrade one node at a time while the others keep serving
Rewrite the actors in Erlang, where schema changes are easy
Set up a new cluster, move traffic across and shut down the old one
Restart every node together and accept the loss of in-flight data
optionExplain: That needs compatible encodings.
Erlang also needs planning.
Right: that is what the book describes for Orleans.
Nothing says data is lost.
questions.explain: By default Orleans uses a custom encoding without rolling upgrades, so a new cluster takes over.
questions.rule: No rolling upgrade means a new cluster.
questions.teaches: To deploy a new version you need to set up a new cluster, move traffic from the old cluster to the new one, and shut down the old one.

questions.q: A company runs rolling upgrades of many internal services. Which kind of format fits best?
options: Free-form text agreed on by the teams, with no schema
Whatever format the first team happens to pick for its service
Each language's built-in encoding, which is quick to use
A binary schema-driven format with clear compatibility rules
optionExplain: Vague about meaning.
Ad hoc choices break later.
Lock-in and weak versioning.
Right: clear rules and compactness.
questions.explain: Rolling upgrades need clear compatibility. The card next sums up.
questions.rule: Choose the format by the compatibility you need, assuming mixed versions during every upgrade.

questions.q: Match each family to its compatibility trait.
pairs: Tied to one language and often lacking compatibility
Compatibility depends on how you use them
Clearly defined forward and backward compatibility
questions.explain: The families differ in how much compatibility they promise.
questions.rule: Choose the format by the compatibility you need, assuming mixed versions during every upgrade.

questions.q: Two companies exchange data with no common tooling. Which format fits the book's reasoning?
options: A language-specific format that is easy for both to use
An agreed textual format such as JSON
A private binary format designed for the two companies
Avro with a private schema registry run by one company
optionExplain: Lock-in hurts across organisations.
Right: agreement matters more than elegance.
Private formats need agreement.
A private registry needs shared infrastructure.
questions.explain: For exchange between organisations, agreement outweighs other concerns.
questions.rule: Choose the format by the compatibility you need, assuming mixed versions during every upgrade.

questions.q: Sort each trait by the family of formats it describes.

items.t: Vague about numbers and binary strings
Compatibility depends on how you use them
Optional schema languages that are sometimes a hindrance
Clearly defined compatibility semantics
Compact and efficient encoding
Data must be decoded before it is human-readable

questions.explain: Each trait is from the chapter's summary.
questions.rule: Choose the format by the compatibility you need, assuming mixed versions during every upgrade.

questions.q: What does the book say matters more than efficiency about encoding details?
options: The architecture of applications and the options for deploying them
The speed at which engineers can type the schema files
The colour scheme used by the logging tools
The number of bytes in the header of each record
optionExplain: Right: the effects go beyond efficiency.
Irrelevant.
Irrelevant.
Efficiency is the smaller concern.
questions.explain: Encodings shape architecture and deployment options.
questions.teaches: The details of these encodings affect not only their efficiency, but more importantly also the architecture of applications and your options for deploying them.

questions.q: A service using a database, other services and a broker will get rolling upgrades. What must the team assume, and what must it ensure?
questions.a: Assume that different nodes run different versions of the code at the same time. Therefore all data flowing through the database, service calls and messages must be encoded so that newer code can read older data (backward compatibility) and older code can read newer data (forward compatibility).
questions.teaches: During rolling upgrades, or for various other reasons, we must assume that different nodes are running different versions of our application's code.
questions.rule: Choose the format by the compatibility you need, assuming mixed versions during every upgrade.

questions.q: Which are reasons to keep copies of the same data on several machines?
options: Lower latency for users who are far from one machine
Keeping the system running when some machines fail
Serving more read queries than one machine can
Making every machine store a smaller share of the data
Avoiding the need to handle changes to the data
optionExplain: Right: nearby copies reduce latency.
Right: other copies keep serving if one fails.
Right: reads can be spread over replicas.
That is partitioning, where each machine holds part of the data; replication keeps full copies.
Changes are exactly what makes replication hard.
questions.explain: Replication serves latency, availability and read throughput. The card next explains where the difficulty comes from.
questions.rule: Replication copies everything; partitioning splits it.

questions.q: If replicated data does not change over time, copying it once is enough; the difficulty lies in handling ____ to the data.
questions.explain: A static dataset needs one copy operation. Every ongoing change must reach every replica.
questions.rule: Static data is easy; changes are hard.

questions.q: A shop keeps its database in Dublin, and customers in Sydney report slow reads. Which purpose of replication answers this directly?
options: Scale out the number of machines serving read queries, so that the shop handles more page views
Keep data geographically close to users, which cuts the latency of each read they make
Keep serving customers if the Dublin machine should fail, so that an outage does not stop sales
Reduce the amount of data stored on each machine, so that every server holds a smaller share
optionExplain: More read capacity helps when servers are overloaded, but the complaint is about distance, not load.
Right: a copy in or near Sydney shortens the distance each read travels, which is the latency purpose.
Availability is a real benefit of copies, but nobody reported an outage; the symptom is slowness.
That describes partitioning. Replication keeps full copies, so each machine still holds the whole dataset.
questions.explain: The stated symptom is slow reads from far away, which is the latency purpose.
questions.rule: Match the purpose to the symptom: slow from afar means latency.

questions.q: Match each replication purpose to the goal it serves.
pairs: Copies kept geographically close to users
Other copies take over when a node fails
questions.explain: The same technique of copying data serves three different goals, and each goal points to a different placement of copies.

questions.q: According to the chapter, why have the principles of replication changed little since the 1970s?
options: Database vendors agreed on one standard replication algorithm long ago, so later work only refined it
Storage hardware has stayed almost unchanged since then, so the same disk limits still apply
Developers have always assumed a database is a single node, so no new ideas were needed
The fundamental constraints of networks have remained the same since that early research
optionExplain: The chapter names three different algorithms in use, so there is no single standard that settled things.
Hardware has changed a lot; the book credits the network, not disks, for the stability.
Many developers did assume one node, but the book says that assumption caused misunderstanding, not stability.
Right: the book ties the stable principles to network constraints, which have not changed.
questions.explain: Networks still delay and drop messages, so the same problems keep appearing.
questions.rule: Old principles last because network constraints last.
questions.teaches: Replication principles were studied in the 1970s and have changed little because the fundamental constraints of networks have stayed the same.

questions.q: A video archive is 400 TB, and each server holds 50 TB. Why can plain replication to every server not work?
options: Replication as described assumes each machine can hold the whole dataset
Replication needs all servers to sit in one single datacenter, which a 400 TB archive cannot satisfy
Replication only works after the data has stopped changing completely, and an archive keeps growing
Replication copies only the newest writes and never the older data, so the archive could not be rebuilt
optionExplain: Right: the chapter assumes a full copy fits on each machine and defers bigger datasets to partitioning.
Location is not the obstacle. Replicas can be in many datacenters; the size of the data is the problem.
Replication exists to handle changing data, so growth does not stop it; size per machine does.
Replicas hold the full dataset, so they are not limited to recent writes; that is why the size matters.
questions.explain: When the data is too big for one machine, it has to be split, which is partitioning (sharding).
questions.rule: Too big for one machine means partition, not only replicate.
questions.teaches: A dataset too big for one machine is split by partitioning (sharding), the subject of the next chapter, so replication alone does not fit it.

questions.q: A database lets any of its replicas accept a write straight from a client. Which approach is it using?
options: Single-leader replication, in which every client sends its writes to one designated node
Multi-leader replication, in which a few designated nodes each accept writes from clients
Leaderless replication, in which any replica accepts writes directly from clients
Statement-based replication, in which the leader ships the SQL text of each write to followers
optionExplain: Single-leader sends all writes through one node, so a replica that takes writes on its own does not fit.
Multi-leader has a few designated leaders, not every replica, and they forward writes to each other.
Right: when any replica accepts writes directly from clients there is no leader at all.
Statement-based describes how a log is shipped, not who accepts writes, so it does not answer the question.
questions.explain: Who accepts writes defines the approach. The card next lists the three.
questions.rule: The approach is defined by who accepts writes.

questions.q: Match each approach to who accepts client writes.
questions.explain: Each approach answers the question of where writes go differently.
questions.rule: Who takes the writes defines the approach.

questions.q: An internal admin tool has modest traffic from one office, and the team wants no conflict handling. Which approach suits?
options: Multi-leader replication, so each admin writes to a local leader and sees changes at once
Leaderless replication, so that no single node is responsible for ordering the admins' writes
Single-leader replication, which has no conflict resolution to manage
Any of them equally, because all three approaches give the same guarantees for such a tool
optionExplain: Multi-leader allows concurrent writes on different leaders, which creates conflicts to resolve.
Leaderless also allows concurrent writes, and the coordinator does not enforce an order.
Right: one node orders every write, so there are no conflicts to resolve for a small single-office tool.
The approaches differ in robustness and in how strong their guarantees are, so they are not equal.
questions.explain: The team wants simplicity, and single-leader is the one with no conflicts to resolve.

questions.q: True or false: Multi-leader and leaderless replication give stronger consistency guarantees than single-leader replication in return for being harder to operate.
