questions.explain: They tolerate faulty nodes and network problems better, but they are harder to reason about and give weaker guarantees.
questions.rule: More robust does not mean more consistent.

questions.q: Besides choosing among the three approaches, what does the chapter say is often a configuration option in databases?
options: Whether replication is synchronous or asynchronous, and how failed replicas are handled
Whether the database stores its data as rows or as documents, which the chapter treats as part of replication
Whether replicas are placed on the same machine as the leader, which the chapter offers as a setting
Whether clients are allowed to read from followers at all, which the chapter gives as the example
optionExplain: Right: the chapter calls synchronous versus asynchronous copying and failed-replica handling common options.
The data model is a separate subject covered in Chapter 2, not a replication option.
Keeping replicas on the leader's machine would defeat their purpose, and the chapter does not list it.
Reading from followers is discussed as a design choice with consequences, not as the configuration example.
questions.explain: Within one approach, details such as synchronous or asynchronous copying and failed-replica handling are often set by configuration, and their consequences are the chapter's next topic.
questions.rule: Details differ by database, but principles are similar.
questions.teaches: Whether replication is synchronous or asynchronous, and how failed replicas are handled, are often configuration options whose general principles are similar across databases.

questions.q: A vendor says its database tolerates network interruptions and latency spikes better than single-leader systems. What should you ask about?
options: Whether it can copy a dataset once to every node at startup, which is how replication mainly works
Whether it avoids needing any network between its replicas, since the network is the source of the problems
Whether it removes write conflicts by sending all writes to one node, which is what makes it robust
How hard it is to reason about and how weak its consistency guarantees are
optionExplain: Copying static data once is easy; the difficulty the chapter describes is handling changes.
Replication by definition needs a network between machines, so a design without one is not replication.
Sending all writes to one node would make it single-leader, the design the vendor is comparing against.
Right: the chapter says the robust approaches pay with harder reasoning and very weak consistency guarantees.
questions.explain: The robustness claim points to multi-leader or leaderless designs, which pay with weaker guarantees.
questions.rule: Robustness is bought with weaker guarantees.
questions.teaches: Multi-leader and leaderless replication can be more robust against faulty nodes, network interruptions and latency spikes, but are harder to reason about and give only very weak consistency guarantees.

questions.q: A database has one primary and several read replicas. Where must a client send a write?
options: To any read replica, since replicas hold the same data as the primary and so can accept new data
To the primary only, since followers are read-only from the client's point of view
To all replicas in parallel, so that each of them stores the new data straight away
To a replica chosen at random, because a read replica forwards the write to the primary
optionExplain: Read replicas are read-only for clients, so a write sent there is refused rather than stored.
Right: only the leader accepts writes; followers are read-only from the client's point of view.
Writing to all replicas in parallel is how leaderless databases work, not leader-based ones.
Random choice would send most writes to nodes that refuse them, and the chapter describes no forwarding.
questions.explain: The primary is the leader and replicas are followers. The card next walks through the flow.
questions.rule: Writes to the leader, reads anywhere.

questions.q: A follower updates its copy by applying the writes from the leader in the same ____ in which the leader processed them.
questions.explain: Order matters because later writes can depend on earlier ones.
questions.rule: Followers apply writes in the leader's order.

questions.q: A blog has a primary database and two secondaries. Where should the comment-posting code and the page-rendering code connect?
options: Posting to the primary, rendering from either the primary or a secondary
Posting to a secondary and rendering from the primary, so that the busy node only has to show pages
Posting to either node and rendering from the secondary that was written to, so a user sees their post
Posting and rendering both on the primary, because secondaries cannot be read by the application
optionExplain: Right: writes only on the leader, while reads may use the leader or any follower.
Secondaries are read-only for clients, so posting there fails; the roles are reversed.
Posting to a follower is not allowed, so there is no secondary that was written to.
Followers can be read; serving reads is one of the reasons for having them.
questions.explain: The leader takes writes and followers serve reads, so each code path has an obvious target.
questions.rule: Route writes to the leader and reads to any replica.

questions.q: Sort each statement into what leader-based replication allows and what it does not.

items.t: A client reads from a follower
A client reads from the leader
The leader sends changes to followers
A follower applies the leader's writes in order
A client writes directly to a follower
A follower applies writes in a different order

questions.explain: Reads may use any replica, but only the leader accepts client writes, and all replicas apply writes in the same order.
questions.rule: Only the leader takes client writes.

questions.q: Which of these systems besides relational databases also use leader-based replication, according to the chapter?
options: Content delivery networks that cache static files near users, spreading copies from one origin
Any system that uses leaderless replication, because it also sends changes to other nodes
Distributed message brokers such as Kafka and highly available RabbitMQ queues
Only relational databases such as PostgreSQL, because the pattern needs SQL tables to work
optionExplain: The chapter does not mention content delivery networks here; caching is a different pattern.
Leaderless replication is a different approach by definition: it has no leader.
Right: the chapter names Kafka and highly available RabbitMQ queues as other users of the pattern.
The chapter also lists nonrelational databases, brokers and some filesystems, so the pattern is not limited to SQL.
questions.explain: Leader-based replication is not restricted to databases; message brokers and some network filesystems and block devices use it as well.
questions.teaches: Distributed message brokers such as Kafka and RabbitMQ highly available queues, plus some network filesystems and replicated block devices, also use leader-based replication.

questions.q: A team keeps a standby that applies every change from the primary but answers no client queries. Is it a follower?
options: No, a follower must also serve reads, so a standby that answers no queries is only a backup copy
Yes, it receives the replication log; PostgreSQL calls it a warm standby
Yes, but only if clients can also write to it directly, otherwise it cannot count as a replica
No, followers are defined as replicas that do not apply the log, so this standby is something else
optionExplain: The book treats standbys as followers; serving reads is not what defines a follower.
Right: it consumes the leader's log, and PostgreSQL calls the no-queries kind a warm standby.
Followers do not take client writes, so that condition would exclude every follower.
Applying the leader's log is exactly what a follower does, so the definition is reversed.
questions.explain: A follower is defined by consuming the leader's changes; whether it also serves reads varies by naming.
questions.rule: Following means applying the log, not serving reads.
questions.teaches: In PostgreSQL, a hot standby accepts reads from clients, whereas a warm standby processes changes from the leader but does not process any queries.

questions.q: A leader waits for a follower to confirm each write before telling the client it succeeded. What is the main risk?
options: Confirmed writes can disappear if the leader fails, because the follower had not yet received them
Writes stall if the follower stops responding, because the leader must keep waiting for it
The follower may apply writes in a different order from the leader, so the copies diverge
Clients can no longer read from the leader at all while it waits for the follower
optionExplain: That risk belongs to asynchronous copying, where success is reported before the follower has the write.
Right: the leader must wait, so an unresponsive follower blocks writes.
The order is fixed by the leader's log in both modes, so waiting does not reorder writes.
Reads from the leader are unaffected by waiting for a follower to confirm a write.
questions.explain: Waiting for a follower trades availability of writes for safety. The card next details both sides.

questions.q: With synchronous replication the leader waits for the follower's ____ before reporting success to the user.
questions.explain: The leader needs the follower's confirmation that it received the write.
questions.rule: Synchronous means wait for the follower.

questions.q: After a sudden leader crash, a service must still find each confirmed write on a second machine. What provides that?
options: A follower that receives writes in the background without being waited on, which is usually very fast
Hourly snapshots copied to the follower from the leader, which gives a second copy of the data
More followers, all fed asynchronously from the same leader, so that some copy is likely to be current
A follower that confirms each write before success is reported to the client
optionExplain: A background copy may not have arrived when the leader dies, so a confirmed write can be missing.
Snapshots leave a gap of up to an hour of confirmed writes that exist only on the dead leader.
Extra asynchronous followers add copies that may still lag behind, so none is guaranteed current.
Right: waiting for the follower's confirmation means a copy exists before the client hears success.
questions.explain: Only waiting for the follower guarantees the copy exists when success is reported.

questions.q: True or false: If the only synchronous follower crashes and nothing is reconfigured, the leader keeps accepting writes and reporting success.
questions.explain: The leader must wait for the confirmation, so it blocks all writes until the follower is available again.
questions.rule: A dead synchronous follower stops writes.

questions.q: Under synchronous replication, besides reporting success to the client, what else waits for the follower's confirmation?
options: Making the write visible to other clients, which also waits for the follower's confirmation
Writing the change to the leader's own local storage, which must happen before anyone is told
Sending the same change to the other followers, which the leader holds back until the first one replies
Starting the next write request from a different client, which queues behind the current one
optionExplain: Right: the leader also holds the write back from other clients until the follower confirms.
The leader writes to its local storage first, before the follower hears of the change.
The change goes to the other followers regardless; they are not part of this wait.
The chapter does not describe other clients' writes waiting behind this one.
questions.explain: The chapter says the leader waits both before reporting success and before making the write visible to other clients.
questions.teaches: The leader waits for the synchronous follower before reporting success and also before making the write visible to other clients.

questions.q: An asynchronous follower is four minutes behind after a weekend restart. Which circumstance does the chapter list for such lag?
options: The leader sent the change in the wrong format, so the follower had to wait for a resend
The follower is configured as synchronous, so the leader waits for it before moving on
The follower is recovering from a failure, one of three circumstances the chapter lists
The client asked for an older version of the data, which delays the follower's copy
optionExplain: The chapter does not list format errors as a cause of lag.
A synchronous follower is waited for by the leader, so it would not fall behind like this.
Right: recovery after a failure is one of the listed causes, along with heavy load and network problems.
Lag concerns how fast changes reach the follower, not what a client asks for.
questions.explain: Replication is normally under a second, but nothing guarantees it; followers can fall behind by minutes or more when recovering, when the system runs near capacity or when the network has problems.
questions.teaches: Most systems apply changes to followers in under a second, but nothing guarantees it; lag can reach minutes during recovery, near maximum capacity, or with network problems.

questions.q: True or false: If you want every follower to hold every write before success is reported, a single node outage will not affect writes.
questions.explain: Waiting on every follower means any one of them being down blocks writes. The card next shows the usual compromise.
questions.rule: All-synchronous makes every follower a point of failure for writes.

questions.q: A setup with one synchronous follower and the rest asynchronous is sometimes called ____-synchronous.
questions.explain: Semi-synchronous describes the mixed configuration.

questions.q: A leader has four followers and writes must survive losing the leader. Which configuration balances durability and availability?
options: All four followers synchronous, so that every copy is current whenever the leader is lost
All four followers asynchronous, so that writes stay as fast as possible during normal operation
One synchronous follower and three asynchronous ones, which keeps two current copies
No followers at all, with the leader writing every change to two local disks
optionExplain: Four synchronous followers would stall every write whenever any one of them is down.
Fully asynchronous can lose the latest confirmed writes if the leader is lost.
Right: two current copies, and one follower outage does not halt writes.
Two disks in one machine do not protect against losing that machine, and there is no replication.
questions.explain: Semi-synchronous gives the leader plus one follower as current copies while tolerating outages of the others.
questions.rule: One synchronous follower is the usual balance.

questions.q: In a semi-synchronous setup, the synchronous follower becomes slow. What does the system do to keep writes moving?
options: Makes one of the asynchronous followers synchronous, so that two current copies remain
Switches every follower to synchronous mode at once, so that no write depends on a single node
Accepts writes without any synchronous follower permanently, which keeps the leader fast
Stops reads on the other followers until the slow one recovers, to keep the copies equal
optionExplain: Right: another follower takes over the synchronous role so two copies stay current.
Making all followers synchronous would recreate the halt-on-any-failure problem.
Dropping the synchronous follower for good would lose the guarantee of a second current copy.
Reads on other followers are not stopped by this; only the synchronous role is reassigned.
questions.explain: Swapping roles preserves the guarantee of two current copies.
questions.rule: A slow synchronous follower is replaced, not left blocking.

questions.q: Sort each property into the fully synchronous or the semi-synchronous setup.

items.t: Any single follower outage blocks writes
Every follower holds each acknowledged write
One follower is chosen to be synchronous
Another follower can be promoted to synchronous
Up-to-date copies are guaranteed on two nodes
Impractical because the whole system could grind to a halt

questions.explain: Full synchrony gives every follower current data but makes each one a write blocker; semi-synchrony guarantees two current copies and tolerates other outages.
questions.rule: All-sync is fragile; semi-sync is the practical compromise.

questions.q: A cache service has leader and twenty followers in five regions. Only the leader accepts writes. Which choice is the most realistic for durability?
options: Twenty synchronous followers, so that no region lags behind the leader at any time
Pure synchronous replication within each region only, so that regional readers see current data
No durability measures at all, because twenty copies already exist somewhere in the system
One synchronous follower with the others asynchronous, which keeps two current copies at low risk
optionExplain: The more nodes, the likelier one is down, so full synchrony would be very unreliable.
The chapter does not offer per-region synchronous replication as the answer to this case.
Copies that lag do not protect a write the leader just confirmed and then lost.
Right: with many followers, a single synchronous follower keeps two current copies without a stall.
questions.explain: The more followers there are, the likelier it is that one is down, which makes full synchrony less practical as the cluster grows.
questions.rule: Bigger clusters make all-synchronous less viable.
questions.teaches: The more nodes you have, the likelier it is that one of them is down, so a fully synchronous configuration becomes very unreliable at scale.

questions.q: A leader confirms a write to the client and then its disk is destroyed before any follower received the change. What happened?
options: The followers will replay it from the client's retry, so the write comes back by itself
An asynchronously replicated write was lost, because only the leader held it when it failed
The synchronous follower rolls the write back safely, so the state stays consistent
Nothing was lost, since the followers hold identical data to the leader at all times
optionExplain: The client was told the write succeeded, so it does not retry.
Right: only the leader had the write, so it is gone with the disk.
In this scenario no follower had the change, so there is nothing to roll back.
Followers had not received the change yet, so they do not hold the leader's latest data.
questions.explain: Asynchronous replication confirms before copying. The card next explains why it is still used.
questions.rule: Confirmed is not durable under async.

questions.q: True or false: With fully asynchronous replication, a write the client was told succeeded can still be lost if the leader fails unrecoverably.
questions.explain: Success is reported without waiting for any follower, so unreplicated writes die with the leader.

questions.q: A global leaderboard service has followers in eight regions. Brief loss of the newest scores is acceptable. Which mode is justified?
options: Asynchronous replication, which keeps the leader writing despite lagging followers
Synchronous replication to all eight regions, so that no region ever lags behind the leader
No replication at all, to avoid the chance of lost writes when a follower falls behind
Synchronous replication to one follower in each region, so every region holds a current copy
optionExplain: Right: with many distant followers, not waiting keeps the leader writing, and the loss is acceptable.
Waiting on eight distant regions would make writes slow and fragile.
Removing replication loses the latency and availability benefits for no gain here.
Eight synchronous followers multiply the chance that one is down and blocks writes.
questions.explain: The stated tolerance for some loss and the many geographically distributed followers point to asynchronous replication.

questions.q: The leader is fully asynchronous and all followers are minutes behind. The leader is healthy. What can it still do?
options: Only process reads until the followers catch up, because it must not run ahead of them
Process writes but hold back the success message to clients until a follower confirms
Keep processing writes without waiting for the followers, since asynchronous mode never waits
Refuse writes until at least one follower is current, to protect the durability of data
optionExplain: Writes continue; the leader is not limited to reads when followers lag.
Success is reported at once in asynchronous mode; that is why confirmed writes can be lost.
Right: asynchronous mode never waits for followers, so writes continue.
That describes synchronous behaviour, where the leader waits for a follower.
questions.explain: This is the advantage of a fully asynchronous setup: followers falling behind do not stop the leader.
questions.rule: Async decouples the leader from lagging followers.

questions.q: A variant of synchronous replication called ____ replication has been implemented in systems such as Microsoft Azure Storage.
questions.explain: Researchers keep looking for methods that lose no data yet perform well, and chain replication is one such variant.
questions.rule: Research tries to keep durability without the stall.
questions.teaches: Chain replication is a variant of synchronous replication that has been successfully implemented in a few systems such as Microsoft Azure Storage.

questions.q: A team says: our followers are asynchronous but replication is under a second, so confirmed writes are safe. What is the flaw?
options: Under-a-second delays are too slow for any replication system, so confirmed writes are never safe
Nothing guarantees the delay, and a leader failure can still lose unreplicated writes
Asynchronous followers do not receive the leader's writes at all, so they only hold old data
Safe writes would require clients to confirm each write twice before the leader accepts it
optionExplain: Under a second is fast, not slow; the issue is that nothing bounds the delay.
Right: typical speed is no guarantee, and a leader that dies first still loses unreplicated writes.
Asynchronous followers do receive the writes, only without the leader waiting.
No double confirmation is described in the chapter.
questions.explain: A fast average does not close the window in which only the leader holds a write.
questions.rule: Fast is not the same as guaranteed.
questions.teaches: There is no guarantee how long asynchronous replication takes, so even usually fast replication leaves a window in which a leader failure loses confirmed writes.

questions.q: You must add a follower to a busy leader. Why is copying the leader's data files over a network a poor plan?
options: Data files cannot be copied between machines at all, because the database holds them open
Followers must be built from empty disks only, so any existing files would be refused
Copying makes the leader permanently read-only, so clients could no longer write
The files change during the copy, so the result may be inconsistent
optionExplain: Files can be copied; the point is that a copy of live files may not be consistent.
A follower is built from a copy plus the log of later changes, not only from empty disks.
A copy does not lock the leader permanently; locking is a separate choice the chapter rejects for availability.
Right: the files change during the copy, so the result may mix different points in time.
questions.explain: The data is always in flux while the copy runs. The card next shows the standard remedy.
questions.rule: Live files are not a consistent view.

questions.q: To get a consistent starting copy for a new follower, you take a ____ of the leader's database at some point in time.
questions.explain: A snapshot freezes one consistent point in time.

questions.q: An online store must replace a failed follower without any outage for customers. Which first step fits?
options: Lock the leader for writes until the copy finishes, so that the files stop changing during the copy
Copy the leader's files while it is running and use them as they are, since they are close enough
Restart the leader so that the files stop changing, then copy them from the stopped machine
Take a consistent snapshot of the leader without locking the whole database
optionExplain: Locking makes the database unavailable for writes, which goes against high availability.
Live files may be inconsistent, so the follower could start from a state that never existed.
A restart is itself an outage and is unnecessary when a snapshot is available.
Right: a snapshot gives a consistent copy without taking the database offline for writes.
questions.explain: A snapshot avoids both the inconsistency of a live copy and the downtime of a lock.
questions.rule: Snapshot, not lock or live copy.

questions.q: True or false: Locking the leader against writes is the usual way to make its files consistent for copying, and it is compatible with high availability.
questions.explain: A lock makes the database unavailable for writes, which goes against high availability; a snapshot avoids that.
questions.rule: Do not trade availability for a copy.

questions.q: Why do many databases already offer consistent snapshots, according to the chapter?
options: Clients ask to read old versions of each row, so databases keep snapshots for them
Backups also need a consistent point-in-time copy, so most databases already provide it
Followers cannot apply a log without them, so every follower starts from a snapshot taken at write time
Leaders must snapshot before every write so that a failed write can be undone
optionExplain: The chapter does not tie snapshots to clients reading old versions of rows.
Right: backups need a consistent point-in-time copy, so most databases already have the feature.
A follower can apply a log; the snapshot only provides the starting point for it.
Snapshots are taken when needed, not before every write.
questions.explain: Because backups need a consistent point-in-time copy too, most databases have the feature, though some need third-party tools such as innobackupex for MySQL.
questions.rule: The same feature serves backups and new followers.
questions.teaches: Most databases have consistent snapshots because backups also require them; in some cases third-party tools such as innobackupex for MySQL are needed.

questions.q: A document store copies its files to a new replica while a nightly import runs. Which problem would a snapshot avoid?
options: Copying too slowly to finish before the next morning, since the import adds so much extra data
Needing a second network for the copy, because the import saturates the existing one
Copying half of the import, which would give a state that never existed on the leader
Losing the import after the leader's next restart, because the import is held only in memory
optionExplain: A snapshot does not make copying faster; it makes the copy consistent.
Network needs are not part of the argument for snapshots.
Right: a live copy can capture half of the import, giving a state that never existed on the leader.
The import persists on the leader either way; the issue is the follower's starting state.
questions.explain: A live copy can capture part of a multi-write job, producing contents that make no sense together.
questions.rule: A snapshot is a single point in time.
questions.teaches: Copying live files means different parts of the database are captured at different times, so the result might not make any sense.

questions.q: A new follower has a snapshot taken at noon. What does it need to catch up with the leader?
options: All the changes made on the leader since the snapshot was taken, replayed in order
A second full copy of the whole database, taken after the noon snapshot, to replace it
Only the changes made in the last minute, since earlier changes are already in the snapshot
The names of all clients that wrote since noon, so that it can ask each one for its writes
optionExplain: Right: it replays all the changes made since the snapshot, then continues with the live stream.
A second full copy would repeat the problem, because the data keeps changing during that copy too.
Changes between noon and the last minute would be missing, leaving gaps.
Followers get changes from the leader's log, not from clients, so client names are irrelevant.
questions.explain: A snapshot is a past state; the log carries what happened afterwards. The card next gives the exact mechanism.

questions.q: When a follower has processed the backlog of changes since the snapshot, we say it has ____ up.
questions.explain: Caught up means it is current and can follow the stream live.
questions.rule: Catching up ends when the backlog is processed.

questions.q: You restore a follower from a backup. It must join without gaps. What do you need to know about the backup?
options: The time of day when the backup started, roughly, so that it can ask for the next hour of changes
The exact position in the leader's log that matches the backup, so no change is missed
How many tables the backup contained, so that the follower can check it received them all
Which client wrote the most rows in it, so that those writes can be skipped on replay
optionExplain: A rough time can leave a gap or an overlap in the replay.
Right: only an exact log position tells the follower where to resume without gaps or repeats.
The number of tables says nothing about where in the log to resume.
Authorship of rows does not locate a resume point in the log.
questions.explain: Only an exact log position tells the follower where to resume.
questions.rule: Resume at an exact log position.

questions.q: True or false: If the leader has already discarded its log from the snapshot position onward, a new follower can still catch up fully from that log.
questions.explain: The backlog needed to bridge the gap no longer exists, so a fresh snapshot is needed. This is our reading of the requirement that the position be in the leader's log.

questions.q: What do PostgreSQL and MySQL call the exact position in the replication log that a snapshot is associated with?
options: Checkpoint ID and page address respectively, because both name a place on disk
Snapshot token and cursor respectively, because both mark a read position for a client
Both call it the commit timestamp of the snapshot, because it records when the copy was taken
Log sequence number in PostgreSQL and binlog coordinates in MySQL, respectively
optionExplain: Those names describe storage-engine internals; the chapter does not use them for the log position.
These names do not appear in the chapter.
The position is a place in the log, not a wall-clock time.
Right: PostgreSQL says log sequence number and MySQL says binlog coordinates.
questions.explain: The idea has different names in different databases, though it is the same exact log position.
questions.rule: Know the vendor term for the log position.
questions.teaches: PostgreSQL calls the log position the log sequence number, and MySQL calls it the binlog coordinates.

questions.q: A team builds a copy of a leader into a data warehouse and wants it to keep following changes without a gap. Which design fits?
options: A consistent snapshot tied to a log position, then streaming changes from that position
A nightly full export that overwrites the warehouse, so every morning it matches the leader
A snapshot with no position, then comparing row counts to find which changes are missing
Streaming only the changes from the last hour after the snapshot, since older ones are in the copy
optionExplain: Right: the same snapshot-plus-position pattern works for any consumer that must follow the log without gaps.
A nightly export leaves up to a day of changes missing rather than following the stream.
Row counts cannot show which individual changes are missing.
Changes between the snapshot and the last hour would be lost.
questions.explain: The pattern is general: start at a known state and then follow the log from the same point.
questions.teaches: A logical (row-based) replication log is decoupled from storage engine internals, so external applications such as a data warehouse can parse it more easily; this technique is called change data capture.

questions.q: A follower restarts after a ten-minute outage. What is the simplest way for it to recover?
options: Copy the entire database again from the leader, since a restart may have damaged the local data
Promote itself to leader and ignore the old one, so that clients can continue to write
Ask the leader for the changes since its last processed transaction
Wait until the leader sends a snapshot to all followers, since followers cannot ask for data
optionExplain: A full re-copy is unnecessary when the follower knows its last processed transaction.
Promotion is for leader failure, not follower recovery.
Right: its own log tells it where it stopped, so it can request just the missing changes.
Followers can request changes themselves from the leader, as the chapter describes.
questions.explain: A follower keeps a local log of what it has received. The card next explains how it uses it.
questions.rule: The follower knows where it stopped.

questions.q: A recovering follower looks at its own log to find the last ____ it processed before the fault.
questions.explain: It uses that point to request the missing changes.
questions.rule: The follower's log marks where it stopped.

questions.q: A server hosting a follower is rebooted to install a kernel security patch. What happens to the follower once it is back?
options: It is discarded and rebuilt from a fresh snapshot of the leader, as a rebooted node cannot be trusted
It must be promoted so that it is no longer behind the leader after the outage
It requests missed changes from the leader and then resumes the stream
It stays read-only until an administrator resets it and gives it a new position
optionExplain: A rebuild is not needed when the follower still has its log of received changes.
Promotion is a failover step for a failed leader, not a way to catch up.
Right: catch-up recovery works for planned reboots just as for crashes.
No manual reset is described; the follower resumes by itself.
questions.explain: Planned maintenance is handled the same way as a crash.

questions.q: True or false: Recovering a failed follower is harder than handling a failed leader, because the leader holds the only copy of the log.
questions.explain: Follower recovery is easy; leader failure is trickier because a follower must be promoted, clients reconfigured and the others redirected.
questions.rule: Follower failure is the easy case.

questions.q: According to the chapter, what is a big operational advantage of being able to reboot individual nodes without downtime?
options: Maintenance such as security patching can happen without taking the system down
Followers no longer need to keep a log on disk, because they can always rebuild from the leader
The leader never needs to be replaced, because maintenance only ever affects followers
Replication lag disappears while a node reboots, because it is not receiving changes
optionExplain: Right: patches and reboots can be done node by node while the system as a whole keeps running.
The log on disk is what makes quick recovery possible.
Leaders can still fail or need maintenance, so failover remains necessary.
Lag does not vanish; a rebooting follower falls behind and must catch up.
questions.explain: Nodes go down just as likely for planned maintenance as for a fault, so reboot-without-downtime is a big gain.
questions.teaches: Nodes go down as often for planned maintenance, such as rebooting to install a kernel security patch, as for faults, and rebooting without downtime is a big operational advantage.

questions.q: A reporting replica is rebooted nightly for patches and usually catches up quickly. Which condition would make catch-up slow?
options: The replica holding an exact copy of the dataset, because exact copies take longest to compare
The replica using a log on its local disk, because reading a log is slower than reading memory
The leader being in a different rack, because the network path then adds a long delay
A long outage during which the leader accepted many writes that now form a backlog
optionExplain: An exact copy is the goal, not a source of delay.
The local log is what makes recovery quick, not slow.
Rack placement does not by itself create a backlog of changes.
Right: the backlog grows with outage length and write rate, so catch-up takes longer.
questions.explain: Catch-up time depends on how many changes accumulated, which grows with outage length and write volume.
questions.teaches: Followers can fall behind the leader by several minutes or more, for example when recovering from a failure, when the system runs near maximum capacity, or when the network between nodes has problems.

questions.q: A leader stops responding. Which three jobs must a failover complete?
options: Copy the dataset, shut down all followers, and restart the leader from the copy
Detect the failure, pick a new leader, redirect clients and followers
Lock the database, take a snapshot, and delete the old leader's data from disk
Ask clients to retry, drop the failed writes, and rebuild the index on every node
optionExplain: Shutting down all followers is the opposite of keeping the system running.
Right: failover detects the failure, chooses a new leader and reconfigures clients and followers.
Locking and deleting the old leader's data are not failover steps.
Retrying writes and rebuilding indexes are not part of failover.
questions.explain: Failover is the process of handing leadership to another node. The card next lists the steps in order.

questions.q: Put the steps of automatic failover in order.
items: Determine that the leader has failed
Choose a new leader
Reconfigure clients and followers to use the new leader
questions.explain: A node must first be judged dead, then replaced, then everyone redirected.

questions.q: After a leader failure, the remaining replicas are A with 4,100 changes applied, B with 4,087 and C with 3,950. Whom do you choose?
options: Replica C, to give the slowest replica time to catch up before it takes over as leader
Replica B, because the middle value balances the other two and avoids extremes
Any replica, because a new leader recopies everything from the others after the election
Replica A, the most up-to-date one, because it keeps the most of the old leader's changes
optionExplain: Choosing a lagging replica discards more of the old leader's changes.
There is no benefit in picking the middle replica; the aim is to minimize data loss.
The new leader does not recopy from others; changes it lacks are lost or discarded.
Right: the most up-to-date replica loses the fewest changes from the old leader.
questions.explain: The new leader's log sets what survives, so the most current replica loses the fewest writes.

questions.q: True or false: An old leader that returns after a new leader was chosen may still believe it is the leader, so the system must demote it.
questions.explain: The returning node might not know it was replaced, so reconfiguration includes making it a follower of the new leader.
questions.teaches: If the old leader comes back, it might still believe that it is the leader, so the system must ensure it becomes a follower and recognizes the new leader.

questions.q: How do most systems decide that a leader is dead, given there is no foolproof way to know what went wrong?
options: A timeout: if a node does not respond for some period, it is assumed dead
A vote among clients, who each report whether they could reach the leader
A hardware sensor that signals that the leader's machine has crashed
A comparison of disk checksums across all replicas to find the one that stopped changing
optionExplain: Right: nodes expect regular replies, and silence beyond a timeout, say thirty seconds, means presumed dead.
The chapter describes nodes, not clients, judging a failure.
Crashes, power outages and network faults all look alike from outside, so no sensor helps.
Checksums do not detect a missing leader.
questions.explain: Crashes, power outages and network issues all look like silence, so a timeout is the common detector.
questions.rule: Silence for too long means presumed dead.
questions.teaches: Nodes bounce messages back and forth, and if a node does not respond for some period, such as 30 seconds, it is assumed to be dead; this does not apply to a leader taken down deliberately for maintenance.

questions.q: A team wants to avoid failover during a planned leader upgrade. Why would a timeout detector not apply?
options: Timeouts only work for follower nodes, not leaders, so a leader needs a different detector
Planned shutdowns cause data loss, so operators must disable failure detection beforehand
The leader is stopped on purpose, so the operators already know it is down
The upgrade makes replication synchronous during the window, so no timeout is needed
optionExplain: Timeouts apply to any node, leaders included.
Planned shutdowns do not inherently lose data.
Right: the timeout exists to discover unplanned failures; a deliberate shutdown is already known.
Nothing in the chapter ties upgrades to synchronous mode.
questions.explain: Failure detection exists for unplanned outages; deliberate maintenance is already known to the operators.
questions.rule: Do not rely on guessing when you already know.
questions.teaches: If the leader is deliberately taken down for planned maintenance, the timeout detection does not apply.

questions.q: An asynchronous follower that missed the last few writes is promoted. What happens to those writes if the old leader later rejoins?
options: They are merged into the new leader automatically, so no information is lost
They are sent back to the clients as errors, so that the clients can resubmit them
They are usually discarded, which may violate clients' expectations of durability
They are replayed first on the new leader, so that history stays in its original order
optionExplain: Automatic merging is not the common solution described; the new leader may hold conflicting writes.
Clients were already told the writes succeeded, so no errors are sent later.
Right: the most common solution is simply to discard them.
Replaying them would conflict with newer writes the new leader has accepted.
questions.explain: The new leader never saw them and has accepted other writes since. The card next explains the damage.

questions.q: True or false: After failover from an asynchronously replicated leader, the new leader may not have received every write the old leader accepted.
questions.explain: Asynchronous copying reports success before followers have the write, so some can be missing.
questions.rule: Async plus failover can lose writes.

questions.q: A shop database fails over to a follower. Order IDs come from an autoincrement counter, also used as keys in a cache. What is the risk?
options: The lagging counter on the new leader may reuse IDs that the cache already links to other orders
The cache will refuse every key lower than the new leader's counter, so new orders fail
The counter on the new leader jumps far ahead and wastes IDs, so the cache fills with gaps
IDs in the cache are rewritten automatically to match the database, so nothing is inconsistent
optionExplain: Right: a lagging counter may reuse IDs that the cache already links to other orders.
A cache does not enforce such a rule; the real danger is reuse.
A lagging counter is behind the old leader's, not ahead of it.
External stores are not updated by the database; that is why the mismatch arises.
questions.explain: Coordination with an outside store breaks when keys are reissued.
questions.rule: Discarded writes can leave outside systems inconsistent.

questions.q: After failover from an asynchronous leader, the most common solution is for the old leader's unreplicated writes to be ____.
questions.explain: Confirmation before replication is what makes loss possible: writes the new leader never saw are typically thrown away.
questions.rule: Confirmed does not mean surviving failover.

questions.q: In the GitHub incident, what made private data reach the wrong users?
options: A replication log was copied to the wrong datacenter, so the data was sent to other people
A synchronous follower returned stale reads, so users saw each other's earlier data
Clients wrote to two leaders and merged their results, so records were mixed up
Reused primary keys led MySQL and Redis to disagree about what each key meant
optionExplain: The chapter does not describe a datacenter mix-up.
The promoted follower was out of date, not synchronous.
The incident is a single promoted follower, not two leaders.
Right: reused primary keys made MySQL and Redis disagree about what each key meant.
questions.explain: The promoted follower's counter lagged, so it reused primary keys that were also used in a Redis store.
questions.teaches: An out-of-date MySQL follower was promoted; its autoincrement counter lagged, so it reused primary keys that were also used in a Redis store, and some private data went to the wrong users.

questions.q: A payments platform keeps ledger rows in a database and a fraud model in another store, both keyed by transaction ID. How should failover be viewed?
options: As harmless, since the second store is only read by the fraud model and never written
As risky if it discards writes, since the other store keeps the old key assignments
As safe, since transaction IDs are random and can never clash between the two stores
As irrelevant, since failover affects only the database engine and not other stores
optionExplain: Reading with stale or reused keys still returns the wrong record.
Right: discarded writes can leave the stores disagreeing about key assignments.
Randomness does not remove the risk; the case is about discarded writes and reissued keys.
The incident shows failover reaching beyond the database into coordinated systems.
questions.explain: Any outside system tied to database state inherits the inconsistency when writes are discarded.
questions.rule: Failover risk reaches into coordinated systems.
questions.teaches: Discarding writes is especially dangerous when other storage systems outside the database need to be coordinated with its contents.

questions.q: Two nodes both accept client writes because each thinks it is the leader. What is likely, with no conflict resolution?
options: Data is lost or corrupted, because both leaders accept writes that nobody reconciles
The nodes combine writes automatically and correctly, since both followed the same rules
Clients are routed to the faster node only, which keeps one copy of the data
Replication becomes synchronous on both nodes, which keeps their data equal
optionExplain: Right: independent writes diverge without a process to resolve them, so data is likely lost or corrupted.
Automatic correct merging needs conflict resolution that is absent in this question.
The chapter describes no routing that removes the second leader.
Mode does not change by itself when two leaders appear.
questions.explain: Two leaders with no conflict handling is the dangerous case named split brain. The card next covers it.
questions.rule: Two leaders without resolution is dangerous.

questions.q: When two nodes both believe they are the leader, the situation is called split ____.
questions.explain: The cluster's single decision-maker has become two.
questions.rule: Two believed leaders is split brain.

questions.q: After a network glitch, nodes N1 and N2 both accept writes as leader. What is the sensible response?
options: Let both continue and compare their data a year later, since both are leaders in their own right
Move all clients to the follower with the oldest data, since it is the safest
Shut down one node, with a mechanism designed carefully enough not to stop both
Switch every follower to read-only for good, so that no more writes are accepted
optionExplain: Long divergence makes lost or corrupted data worse.
Choosing the oldest data would lose the most writes.
Right: only one leader should survive, and the shutdown mechanism must be designed so it cannot stop both.
This makes the cluster unusable for writes.
questions.explain: Fencing off one leader limits the damage, and the mechanism needs careful design.
questions.rule: At most one leader should survive.

questions.q: True or false: A safety catch that shuts down one of two detected leaders cannot itself cause trouble.
questions.explain: If the mechanism is not carefully designed, both nodes can end up shut down.
questions.rule: A fence can cut both ways.

questions.q: What are the names given to the safety mechanism that shuts down the other node?
options: Quorum read, or more emphatically a sloppy quorum, which tells nodes which side holds the majority
Fencing, or more emphatically Shoot The Other Node In The Head (STONITH)
Failover, or more emphatically a hinted handoff, which moves control to a standby node
Read repair, or more emphatically an anti-entropy sweep, which resets nodes that disagree
optionExplain: Quorums concern leaderless reads and writes, not shutting down a rival leader.
Right: fencing, also called STONITH, shuts down the other node.
Failover and hinted handoff are different concepts.
Those repair stale replicas; they do not stop a second leader.
questions.explain: The footnote names the technique fencing, with the blunt acronym STONITH.
questions.rule: Fencing is the term for shutting down the rival.
questions.teaches: Shutting down one node when two leaders are detected is known as fencing or, more emphatically, Shoot The Other Node In The Head (STONITH).

questions.q: A scheduler has a primary and a hot spare. The spare sometimes starts a job run when the primary is only slow. What could go wrong?
options: The spare refuses to take over when the primary is slow, so no run happens in that window
The primary silently becomes read-only whenever the spare starts, so work is lost
The job runs once but with stale inputs, because the spare copied its inputs earlier
Both run the job, like two leaders each acting on its own belief
optionExplain: The question says the spare does start a run, so it does not refuse.
Nothing in the setup changes the primary's role.
Stale inputs are a different failure from duplication.
Right: both act on their own belief that they are in charge, so the job runs twice.
questions.explain: The failure pattern is the same as split brain: a slow node is mistaken for a dead one.
questions.teaches: There is no foolproof way of detecting what has gone wrong with a node, so most systems simply use a timeout: a node that does not respond for some period, say 30 seconds, is assumed dead.

questions.q: A failover timeout is set to two seconds. A brief load spike delays the leader's reply by three seconds. What is likely?
options: A faster recovery from a real failure, because the short timeout notices problems sooner
No effect, since the leader answered eventually and so was never declared dead
A switch to synchronous replication, because the system tries to protect its data
An unnecessary failover, because the leader is alive but is declared dead too early
optionExplain: There was no real failure to recover from, only a delay.
The reply came after the deadline, so the detector has already fired.
Replication mode does not change because of a timeout.
Right: the leader is alive but is declared dead, so the failover is unnecessary.
questions.explain: A short timeout mistakes delay for death. The card next shows the trade-off.

questions.q: True or false: A longer failover timeout means a longer time to recovery when the leader has really failed.
questions.explain: The system waits longer before acting, so writes stay unavailable for longer.

questions.q: A service has traffic spikes that sometimes slow the leader for twenty seconds. Which timeout reduces needless failovers?
options: A timeout of one second, so that failures are caught as fast as possible
A timeout comfortably above the twenty-second spikes, at the price of slower real recoveries
No timeout at all, so that failover never happens unless an operator asks for it
A timeout equal to the average response time, so it matches normal behaviour
optionExplain: One second would trigger on every twenty-second spike.
Right: waiting past normal spikes avoids false alarms, at the price of slower recovery in real failures.
Without a timeout a real failure is never detected automatically.
The average is far below the spikes and would fire constantly.
questions.explain: The timeout has to exceed ordinary delays, and the cost is a longer wait during real failures.
questions.rule: Set the timeout above normal delays.

questions.q: An unnecessary failover on a system that is already struggling with high load is likely to make the situation ____.
questions.explain: The takeover adds disruption exactly when the system can least afford it.
questions.rule: Do not fail over from overload.

questions.q: Why do some operations teams prefer to perform failovers by hand, according to the chapter?
options: Because manual failover is faster than a timeout, since a person decides at once
Because software cannot elect a new leader at all, so a person must do it
Because the problems of automatic failover have no easy solutions
Because replication logs are unusable after an automatic failover, so a person must rebuild them
optionExplain: A person has to be notified and act, so manual failover is not described as faster.
Software can elect leaders, as the election process in the chapter shows.
Right: automatic failover has no easy solutions to its problems, so some teams prefer human judgment.
The logs are not described as unusable.
questions.explain: Failover is fraught with problems: lost writes, split brain, bad timeouts. Hence manual failover is a considered choice.
questions.rule: Manual failover is a legitimate choice.
questions.teaches: There are no easy solutions to the problems of failover, so some operations teams prefer to perform failovers manually even if the software supports automatic failover.

questions.q: A team runs a database whose leader has a history of slow replies during backups. They choose manual failover. Which argument fits the book?
options: An unnecessary automatic failover during a slow backup could do more harm than a short wait
Manual failover removes the possibility of split brain completely, since a person decides
Humans can detect network glitches without any timeout, so a person never mistakes a slow node
Manual failover makes asynchronous replication lossless, because a person waits for followers
optionExplain: Right: a false positive can worsen things, so a human can judge whether the slowness is a failure.
A person can also promote a node while the old one still runs.
People also judge from observed silence, so they can be wrong too.
Replication mode, and with it the loss window, is unchanged by who triggers failover.
questions.explain: A person can judge whether a slowdown is a failure before disrupting the cluster.
questions.rule: Judgment can replace a blunt timeout.
questions.teaches: With asynchronous replication a newly promoted leader may not have received all writes from the old leader; the most common solution is to discard the old leader's unreplicated writes, which may violate clients' durability expectations.

questions.q: A leader logs the statement UPDATE users SET seen = NOW() and ships it to a follower. What is likely?
options: The follower stores the same timestamp as the leader, because the statement text is identical
The follower stores a different timestamp from the leader, since each replica reads its own clock
The follower rejects the statement as invalid, because the function is not allowed on followers
The follower converts the statement into a row change, so the timestamp is copied from the leader
optionExplain: The text is the same but the clock reading is not.
Right: each replica evaluates NOW() when it executes the statement, so values differ.
The statement is valid SQL, so there is nothing to reject.
Converting to a row change is what row-based replication does, not statement shipping.
questions.explain: Functions evaluated at each replica give different results. The card next lists the problem cases.

questions.q: Which statements are likely to cause replicas to diverge under statement-based replication?
options: A statement that calls RAND()
A statement with a trigger that has side effects
An INSERT of fixed literal values into a table with no triggers
UPDATE ... WHERE that depends on existing data, executed in a different order
A DELETE that names a primary key
optionExplain: Right: a random value differs per replica.
Right: the side effects may differ unless deterministic.
Literal values with no triggers produce the same result on each replica.
Right: order changes the effect.
A deterministic delete by key gives the same result everywhere.
questions.explain: Anything that depends on time, randomness, execution order or side effects can differ between replicas.
questions.rule: Nondeterminism and order break statement shipping.

questions.q: A team must keep statement-based replication. What is the book's workaround for NOW() and RAND()?
options: Each follower asks the leader for its clock before running the statement
Followers run the statement twice and compare the resulting values for agreement
Clients pass their own server time with every statement so all replicas share it
The leader replaces such calls with fixed return values when the statement is logged
optionExplain: The chapter describes no clock query between nodes.
Running twice does not make two replicas produce the same value.
Client clocks are not mentioned as the fix.
Right: the leader replaces nondeterministic calls with fixed values when it logs the statement.
questions.explain: The leader fixes the value once, so every follower sees the same literal.

questions.q: True or false: Two order-dependent UPDATE statements applied in opposite order on a follower can leave it with a different result than the leader.
questions.explain: Statements that depend on existing data must run in exactly the same order on each replica.
questions.rule: Same statements, different order, different state.

questions.q: How does VoltDB make statement-based replication safe, according to the chapter?
options: By requiring transactions to be deterministic, so every replica computes the same result
By switching to row-based replication whenever a statement looks risky
By shipping every statement to a single follower that checks it for the others
By forbidding transactions that touch more than one row, so order cannot matter
optionExplain: Right: VoltDB requires transactions to be deterministic, so every replica reaches the same result.
Switching to row-based is MySQL's default behaviour, not VoltDB's.
The chapter does not say VoltDB uses a single checking follower.
The chapter describes no such restriction on multi-row transactions.
questions.explain: VoltDB uses statement-based replication and makes it safe by requiring transactions to be deterministic.
questions.teaches: VoltDB uses statement-based replication and makes it safe by requiring transactions to be deterministic.

questions.q: A team replicates a job queue table by sending SQL. Jobs get random UUIDs from a database function. What change do you suggest?
options: Increase the timeout between leader and follower so that the follower has time to agree
Add more followers to outvote the replicas that generated different UUIDs
Log the generated UUIDs as literal values, or use another replication method
Disable triggers on the leader only so that side effects stay in one place
optionExplain: A timeout does not make results identical across replicas.
Replicas do not vote on values in leader-based replication.
Right: fix the generated values in the log, or choose a replication method that avoids the problem.
Disabling triggers on one node does not fix the nondeterministic function.
questions.explain: A random function is nondeterministic, so the same remedies apply as for RAND().
questions.teaches: Because there are so many edge cases, other replication methods are now generally preferred over statement-based replication.

questions.q: A leader sends its low-level disk log to followers. What problem is likely during a software upgrade?
options: Followers cannot read the log in any version, because it is written in a private binary form
The upgrade deletes data on the leader, because the log is replayed backwards
Leader and followers may be unable to run different versions
The log becomes synchronous, because both sides must agree on the format
optionExplain: Followers can read the log when versions match; the issue is mixing versions.
Upgrades do not delete data by themselves.
Right: the log is tied to the storage format, so mixed versions are typically not possible.
Shipping a log does not change whether replication is synchronous.
questions.explain: A log that names bytes in disk blocks depends on the engine's format. The card next explains the consequences.

questions.q: A write-ahead log describes which bytes were changed in which disk ____.
questions.explain: That low level is the cause of the coupling to the storage engine.

questions.q: A PostgreSQL cluster uses WAL shipping. The new release changes the storage format. What can the team usually not do?
options: Upgrade followers first and then promote one without downtime
Take backups from the leader during the upgrade, since backups need the storage format
Read from followers before the upgrade starts, since reads need the same version
Add a follower that runs the same old version, since mixed versions are the problem
optionExplain: Right: a newer follower typically cannot follow an older leader, so rolling upgrades are blocked.
Backups are unrelated to mixing versions in the log.
Reading before the upgrade starts is unaffected by the log format.
Same-version followers work fine with WAL shipping.
questions.explain: The zero-downtime rolling upgrade needs follower and leader to differ in version, which WAL shipping typically forbids.

questions.q: Sort each property into write-ahead log shipping or statement-based replication.

items.t: Ships the storage engine's byte-level log
Ties replicas to the same storage format
Ships SQL INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE text
Breaks on RAND() and NOW()
Builds identical data structures on the follower
Needs triggers and side effects to be deterministic

questions.explain: WAL shipping copies physical changes, so replicas match exactly but are coupled to the engine; statement replication ships logical text and breaks on nondeterminism.
questions.rule: WAL is physical; statements are logical text.

questions.q: Why does the version mismatch matter for operations, according to the chapter?
options: Version mismatch helps detect failed leaders earlier, because a changed version shows a restart
Followers always need to be older than the leader to receive the log, so mismatch is normal
Version mismatch lets replicas hold different data on purpose, such as a trial version
If the follower could be newer, you could upgrade followers first and fail over for a zero-downtime upgrade
optionExplain: Failure detection has nothing to do with software versions.
The chapter says allowing a newer follower would help upgrades; it does not say older ones are required.
The goal is identical data on all replicas, not intended differences.
Right: with a newer follower allowed, you could upgrade followers first and fail over to one with no downtime.
questions.explain: With WAL shipping this path is typically closed and upgrades need downtime.
questions.rule: Allow version mismatch to enable rolling upgrades.
questions.teaches: If the replication protocol allows the follower to use a newer software version, you can upgrade the followers first and then fail over to one of them for a zero-downtime upgrade.

questions.q: Your database engine switches from B-trees to LSM-trees in the next release and ships its own on-disk log to followers. What is the likely effect?
options: Only the followers need the new engine, because the leader keeps its old files
Old-format leaders and new-format followers cannot interoperate during the change
The log keeps working unchanged because it is append-only, whatever the format
Replication becomes asynchronous and stays so, because the formats cannot be compared
optionExplain: Both ends handle the same physical format, so one side changing breaks it.
Right: a log tied to the engine's format cannot connect old-format and new-format nodes.
Append-only does not protect against a change in what the bytes mean.
Mode is a separate choice and does not change because of a format change.
questions.explain: Changing the storage format changes what the physical log means.
questions.rule: Physical logs follow the engine's format.
questions.teaches: If the database changes its storage format from one version to another, it is typically not possible to run different versions of the software on the leader and the followers.

questions.q: A replication log describes each change as a row inserted, deleted or updated, not as bytes in blocks. What is the main benefit?
options: Leader and follower can use different software versions or storage engines
Writes become synchronous automatically, since row changes are small enough to wait for
Followers no longer need to apply changes in order, since rows are independent
Clients can write to any follower, since followers can interpret row changes
optionExplain: Right: the format does not depend on engine internals, so versions and engines can differ.
Mode is unrelated to the log format.
Order still matters, because changes to the same row must be applied in sequence.
Writes still go to the leader.
questions.explain: Row-level descriptions do not depend on disk layout. The card next explains the format.
questions.rule: Logical logs decouple from the engine.

questions.q: Match each row change to what a logical log records.
pairs: Enough to identify it, usually the primary key
Its identity plus the new values
questions.explain: The log lists row-level facts and marks commit points.

questions.q: A table has no primary key. A row is deleted. What must the logical log contain to identify the row?
options: Only the table name, because the log records which table changed
The new values of all columns, because the follower writes them after the deletion
The old values of all columns, which together identify the deleted row
A hash of the leader's disk block address, because it points to the row
optionExplain: A table name cannot tell which row was deleted.
A deleted row has no new values to log.
Right: without a key, the old values of all columns identify the deleted row.
Block addresses are physical details, which a logical log avoids.
questions.explain: The primary key is the usual identifier; without one, the old column values play that role.
questions.rule: Identify by key, else by old values.

questions.q: True or false: Because a logical log is decoupled from the storage engine, leader and follower can run different versions of the database software.
questions.explain: A logical log can more easily be kept backward compatible, unlike a physical log.

questions.q: What does a transaction touching several rows add to the logical log besides one record per row?
options: A copy of the whole table, so that the follower can compare before and after
A record indicating that the transaction was committed
A statement describing the SQL text used, so the follower can double-check
A list of other leaders, so that the follower knows where the transaction came from
optionExplain: Tables are not copied into the log.
Right: the commit record tells the follower where the transaction ends.
Logical logs describe rows, not statement text.
Other leaders are irrelevant in single-leader row-based logs.
questions.explain: Several log records, then a commit record, tell the follower where the transaction ends.
questions.teaches: A transaction that modifies several rows generates several log records, followed by a record indicating that the transaction was committed.

questions.q: A team wants to upgrade a PostgreSQL-like cluster with no downtime and consider two log formats. Which supports the plan?
options: A physical log that records byte changes in disk blocks, since it is exact
A statement log that contains RAND() calls, since it is compact and easy to read
Any log, since upgrades do not involve replication at all
A logical row-based log that tolerates different versions on leader and followers
optionExplain: Physical logs typically require equal versions on leader and followers.
RAND() statements produce different values on each replica.
The log format decides whether rolling upgrades are possible.
Right: a logical log tolerates different versions or engines, so followers can be upgraded first.
questions.explain: The decoupling is what makes a rolling upgrade possible.
questions.teaches: Since a logical log is decoupled from storage engine internals, it can more easily be kept backward compatible, allowing different versions or even different storage engines on leader and follower.

questions.q: A company wants a data warehouse to receive every change made in its main database. Which log format is easiest to parse?
options: A byte-level disk log, because it records every change exactly
A log of SQL statements that contain RAND() calls, because it is easy to read
No log, only nightly screenshots of the data files
A row-level logical log, whose records name rows and values that outsiders can read
optionExplain: Byte-level logs describe disk layout, which outsiders cannot easily interpret.
Nondeterministic statements produce ambiguous results outside the database.
Screenshots miss all changes in between.
Right: row records are easy for external applications to parse.
questions.explain: Logical logs are easier for external applications to parse. The card next names the technique.
questions.rule: Rows are easier to parse than bytes.

questions.q: Capturing the changes of a database as a stream for an outside system is called change data ____.
questions.explain: The technique reads the logical log to export changes.
questions.rule: Change data capture reads the log.

questions.q: A search index must follow a products database row by row. How should it get its updates?
options: By querying every table every minute and comparing it with the last copy
By reading the database's logical log, using change data capture
By copying the data files while the database runs and rereading them
By asking customers to resubmit their changes to the search service
optionExplain: Polling is heavy and misses intermediate states between polls.
Right: the logical log carries each row change in order, so it can feed the index.
Live files are inconsistent when copied while running.
Customers cannot be asked to resubmit changes.
questions.explain: The log is already an ordered record of changes.
questions.rule: Follow the log, not the tables.

questions.q: True or false: A byte-level physical log is as easy for an external application to parse as a row-based logical log.
questions.explain: Physical logs describe bytes in disk blocks, so outsiders need engine internals; logical logs describe rows.

questions.q: Where does the chapter say it will return to change data capture?
options: In Chapter 3, with storage engines and indexes
In Chapter 6, with partitioning of large datasets
In Chapter 11, in the material on stream processing
In the preface, with the overview of the book
optionExplain: Chapter 3 covers storage engines, not the use of logs for outside consumers.
Chapter 6 covers partitioning.
Right: Chapter 11, on stream processing, returns to change data capture.
The preface is not mentioned as a place for this.
questions.explain: Change data capture is developed later, in the stream-processing material.
questions.rule: CDC appears again later in the book.
questions.teaches: The chapter says this technique is called change data capture and that it will return to it in Chapter 11.

questions.q: A cache must stay in line with a database. The team triggers cache updates from application code on each write. What does the book suggest as an alternative?
options: Building the cache from the database's logical log using change data capture
Making the cache a synchronous follower of the database, so it is always current
Copying the database's data files to the cache host at regular intervals
Rebuilding the cache only when users complain about missing data
optionExplain: Right: reading the logical log through change data capture feeds caches and indexes with every change.
A cache is not a database follower, and synchronous replication would slow writes.
Live files are inconsistent and miss changes between copies.
Waiting for complaints is not a design.
questions.explain: The chapter lists building caches among the uses of the logical log.
questions.rule: Use the log to keep derived data in sync.
questions.teaches: A logical log format is useful for building custom indexes and caches, as well as warehouse feeds.

questions.q: You must replicate only some tables, and into a different kind of database. What is the typical approach?
options: Use write-ahead log shipping, because it copies every change exactly
Use triggers or other application-layer replication, which allow custom logic
Copy the data files, because they contain all tables
Synchronize the clocks of both databases, so that rows can be selected by time
optionExplain: WAL shipping copies everything and needs the same engine.
Right: custom logic such as subsets and cross-database copying needs application-layer replication.
Files carry the whole database and need the same engine.
Clocks do not select data.
questions.explain: Built-in methods copy everything in the same engine. The card next explains the alternative.

questions.q: A ____ lets you register custom application code that runs automatically when a data change occurs.
questions.explain: Triggers can log a change into a table for an external process.

questions.q: A team must replicate a customer table to an analytics database of a different vendor but only the non-sensitive columns. What fits?
options: WAL shipping of the whole database, then filtering columns in the target
Statement-based replication of every query, then dropping the sensitive ones
A synchronous follower of the same vendor, with views hiding the sensitive columns
A trigger that logs the permitted columns, read by an external process
optionExplain: WAL shipping copies everything and needs the same engine.
Statement shipping sends every statement, including sensitive ones.
A same-vendor follower does not reach another vendor.
Right: a trigger can log only the permitted columns for an external process to deliver.
questions.explain: Subset and cross-vendor replication are the book's reasons for application-layer replication.

questions.q: True or false: Trigger-based replication usually has lower overhead and fewer bugs than the database's built-in replication.
questions.explain: It typically has greater overheads and is more prone to bugs and limitations; flexibility is the reason to use it.

questions.q: Besides triggers, how can data changes be made available to application code, according to the chapter?
options: By tools such as Oracle GoldenGate that read the database log
By asking clients to log their own writes into a separate table
By running followers that never apply changes but only store them
By increasing the failover timeout so that changes arrive later
optionExplain: Right: tools like Oracle GoldenGate read the database log and hand changes to an application.
The chapter does not describe client-side logging.
Followers that skip changes would not be replicas.
Timeouts do not expose changes.
questions.explain: Log-reading tools are an alternative to triggers.
questions.rule: Triggers are one way, log readers another.
questions.teaches: Some tools, such as Oracle GoldenGate, can make data changes available to an application by reading the database log.

questions.q: A small team asks whether to use triggers for replication between two PostgreSQL servers with identical schemas. What is a fair answer?
options: Triggers are best because they run application code and therefore avoid built-in limitations
Triggers are required whenever followers are asynchronous so that changes are tracked
Prefer built-in replication unless you need the flexibility, since triggers add overhead and bugs
Triggers avoid replication lag completely because the application copies changes at once
optionExplain: The overhead and bug risk remain.
Asynchronous replication does not require triggers.
Right: with identical schemas and no special needs, built-in replication is simpler and less error-prone.
Triggers do not remove lag.
questions.explain: The question has no need for subset or cross-database replication, so the flexibility is not needed.
questions.rule: Pay for flexibility only if you need it.
questions.teaches: Trigger-based replication typically has greater overheads than other replication methods and is more prone to bugs and limitations than the database's built-in replication.

questions.q: A site with 95% reads and 5% writes needs more read capacity. What is the usual leader-based answer?
options: Add a second leader for each reader so that every reader has a local writer
Add followers and spread the read queries across them, keeping writes on the leader
Move all reads to the leader so that they see the newest data
Stop replicating so that the leader has fewer jobs to do
optionExplain: The question is about reads, which do not need extra leaders.
Right: followers can answer reads, so adding followers adds read capacity.
That would overload the leader instead of relieving it.
Replication is what provides the read replicas.
questions.explain: Reads can go to any replica, writes only to the leader. The card next explains the catch.

questions.q: In a read-scaling architecture you can increase read capacity by adding more ____.
questions.explain: Each follower adds a node that can answer reads.

questions.q: A news site has one leader and gets ten times more page views each day. Writes remain few. What should it do?
options: Make every follower synchronous so that readers see current data on all of them
Send all page views to the leader for consistency of what readers see
Split writes across several followers so that the leader has less to do
Add asynchronous followers and spread reads over them
optionExplain: Synchronous followers would let a single failure stop all writes.
The leader would carry the whole read load.
Followers do not accept writes.
Right: reads grow, so asynchronous followers take them over without making writes fragile.
questions.explain: Reads are the growing part of the load and the usual tool is asynchronous followers.

questions.q: True or false: If every follower in a read-scaling setup were synchronous, adding more followers would make a write stall more likely.
questions.explain: The leader waits for every synchronous follower, so the more nodes there are, the likelier it is that one is down and blocks writes.
