questions.q: What can happen if a client reads from an asynchronous follower and from the leader at the same moment?
options: The two can return different results for the same query
Both return the same result because replication is always fast enough to keep them equal
The follower returns an error whenever the leader is busy writing
The leader returns older data than the follower because the follower is faster
optionExplain: Right: the follower may not have applied every write, so results can differ.
Fast is not guaranteed, so the results can differ.
Followers return results, possibly stale, not errors.
The leader always has the newest writes.
questions.explain: This apparent inconsistency is the price of reading from followers that have not applied every write yet.
questions.rule: Followers can disagree with the leader.
questions.teaches: If you run the same query on the leader and a follower at the same time, you may get different results, because not all writes have been reflected in the follower.

questions.q: A bank wants every balance read to show the latest transfer. Is read scaling with async followers a good fit?
options: Yes, because asynchronous followers are current at all times
Yes, because balance reads are rare, so lag seldom matters
Not for those reads, since followers may lag behind and the reads need the leader
Yes, because the leader copies each write at once, so no lag arises
optionExplain: Asynchronous followers can lag, so they are not always current.
Rarity does not remove the staleness of an individual read.
Right: where the freshest value is required, a lagging follower is the wrong source.
Copying is not instant in asynchronous replication.
questions.explain: Where the freshest value is required, reading from a lagging follower is the wrong tool.
questions.rule: Stale reads rule out follower reads.
questions.teaches: Running the same query on the leader and on a follower at the same time may give different results, because not all writes are reflected in the follower yet; this temporary effect is called eventual consistency.

questions.q: You stop writing to a database with asynchronous followers and wait. What happens to the followers?
options: They stay different from the leader permanently, because lag is never made up
They become leaders of their own data, because nothing else is writing
They eventually catch up and become consistent with the leader, since the lag is temporary
They discard their data to avoid disagreement with the leader
optionExplain: The difference is a temporary state, not a permanent one.
Nothing promotes followers when writes stop.
Right: with no new writes, the followers eventually catch up and match the leader.
They keep their data and apply the remaining log.
questions.explain: The inconsistency is temporary if writes stop. The card next names the effect.

questions.q: The delay between a write on the leader and its reflection on a follower is called replication ____.
questions.explain: Lag measures how far behind a follower is.

questions.q: A follower is 3 minutes behind during a traffic peak. A user views a page twice and sees different data. Which term describes the situation?
options: Eventual consistency, because the follower is temporarily behind but will converge later
Split brain between two leaders, because the two views disagree
A timeout of the failover detector, because the follower is slow
Statement-based divergence, because the follower evaluated a function differently
optionExplain: Right: the follower is temporarily behind and will converge, which is eventual consistency.
Only one leader is involved here.
Failover is not occurring in this scenario.
The cause is lag, not nondeterministic statements.
questions.explain: The data is temporarily out of date and will converge later, so it is eventual consistency.

questions.q: True or false: Eventual consistency tells you a follower will be no more than a few seconds behind the leader.
questions.explain: The term is deliberately vague; there is no limit on how far a replica can fall behind.

questions.q: According to the chapter, which databases show eventual consistency?
options: Only NoSQL databases, since the term became a battle cry of NoSQL projects
Only databases with leaderless replication, since they accept writes anywhere
Only databases that use synchronous replication, since they wait for followers
Also asynchronously replicated relational databases, not only NoSQL ones
optionExplain: The footnote corrects this idea; relational databases show it too.
Leader-based databases show it too whenever followers lag.
Synchronous followers are current, so they do not show it.
Right: followers of an asynchronous relational database behave the same way.
questions.explain: Eventual consistency became a battle cry of NoSQL projects, but it follows from asynchronous replication, which relational databases also use.
questions.teaches: Not only NoSQL databases are eventually consistent: followers in an asynchronously replicated relational database have the same characteristics.

questions.q: A team claims their follower is eventually consistent, so users will not notice. What should they test?
options: Whether the follower is ever perfectly in sync with the leader
How the application behaves if lag grows to minutes
Whether the word eventually appears in the database documentation
Whether the leader can read its own replication log
optionExplain: The question is about behaviour under lag, not whether lag is ever zero.
Right: normal lag may be invisible, but large lag becomes a real problem, so test that case.
Documentation wording does not test behaviour.
Reading its own log is not the issue.
questions.explain: Small lags hide the effect, so the test is the bad case.
questions.rule: Test the application at large lag.
questions.teaches: In normal operation lag may not be noticeable, but when the system operates near capacity or the network has a problem, the lag can easily increase to several seconds or even minutes.

questions.q: A user posts a comment, reloads, and the comment is missing for ten seconds. What guarantee was violated?
options: Read-after-write consistency, which lets a user see updates they submitted themselves
Consistent prefix reads, since the comment and the page it belongs to were seen out of order
Monotonic reads, since the user saw the comment appear and then vanish on a later read
Quorum consistency, since too few replicas may have acknowledged the comment before the reload
optionExplain: Right: the user does not see their own submitted comment, which read-after-write consistency forbids.
Prefix reads concern the order of causally related writes, and here there is only one write.
Monotonic reads concern seeing newer data and then older data; the user never saw the comment.
Quorums belong to leaderless databases, while this scenario is about a user and their own write.
questions.explain: The write went to the leader but the read hit a stale follower. The card next names the guarantee.

questions.q: True or false: Read-after-write consistency guarantees that a user sees the updates submitted by other users right away.
questions.explain: It only promises that a user sees their own updates; other users' updates may appear later.

questions.q: A user edits their bio and refreshes. The page shows the old bio. Which reading explains this?
options: The follower rejected the edit as invalid, so the leader kept the old bio on the page
The leader failed over while the edit was in flight, and the new leader never received it
The edit went to the leader but the read came from a follower that is behind
Two leaders accepted conflicting edits of the bio, and the older one replaced the newer one
optionExplain: Followers do not take client writes, so they never reject an edit.
Nothing in the scenario says a failover happened, and the edit would not be shown as old.
Right: the write went to the leader but the read hit a follower that had not yet received it.
The scenario has one leader and ordinary replication lag, not two writable leaders.
questions.explain: Writes go to the leader and reads to a lagging follower, creating the illusion of a lost write.
questions.rule: Leader write, follower read, stale view.

questions.q: Which promises does read-after-write consistency make to a user who has submitted data?
options: After reloading, the user sees the updates they submitted themselves
The user is reassured that their own input was saved
Other users see the update at once
Reads never return stale data about anyone else
optionExplain: Right: that is the core promise.
Right: that reassurance is its purpose.
The guarantee makes no promise about other users.
Stale data about others remains possible.
questions.explain: The promise protects each user's own input only; others' updates may arrive later.

questions.q: Why is the guarantee limited to the user's own writes, according to the chapter?
options: Users are not allowed to see other users' data at all, so there is nothing else to guarantee
It reassures users that their own input was saved without requiring everything to be current
Followers never hold other users' data, so the guarantee can only cover a user's own records
The leader hides other users' data from readers until all followers have received it
optionExplain: Users do see others' data, just possibly later than it was written.
Right: users notice when their own input vanishes, so the promise covers exactly that and nothing more.
Followers hold copies of all the data, including other users' records.
The leader does not hide data; staleness comes from followers lagging.
questions.explain: The user knows what they wrote and will worry if it vanishes, while others' updates arriving late go unnoticed.
questions.rule: Match the guarantee to what the user can notice.
questions.teaches: It reassures the user that their own input has been saved correctly, while other users' updates may not be visible until some later time.

questions.q: A ticketing app shows a buyer their order right after payment, from a lagging replica. Others' orders may lag. Which fix targets the problem?
options: Make every user see every order instantly after it is placed, whichever replica serves them
Send all reads to the slowest replica so that every user sees the same view of orders
Stop showing orders after payment, so that the stale list can no longer confuse the buyer
Make the buyer's own reads reflect their latest write, without demanding more than that
optionExplain: That is a much stronger guarantee than the problem needs and would be costly.
The slowest replica is the stalest, so the buyer would be least likely to see their order.
Hiding orders removes the symptom but not the missing record the buyer expects to see.
Right: read-your-writes removes the visible bug without demanding that everyone see everything at once.
questions.explain: The user-visible bug is own writes missing, which read-after-write addresses.
questions.teaches: The client can remember the timestamp of its most recent write, and the system then ensures that the replica serving that user's reads reflects updates at least up to that timestamp; otherwise another replica serves the read or the query waits until the replica catches up.

questions.q: A social network lets only the owner edit a profile. How can it give owners read-after-write consistency cheaply?
options: Read every profile from the slowest follower, so that all readers are served the same view
Cache every profile in the browser for good, so the owner always sees what they last saw
Make all followers synchronous, so that every read is current wherever it is served
Read the owner's own profile from the leader and other profiles from followers
optionExplain: The slowest follower is the stalest, so owners would be the most likely to miss their edit.
A permanently cached copy would not show later edits from other devices.
All-synchronous followers make any single outage stop writes.
Right: ownership tells you which profile may have changed, so only those reads need the leader.
questions.explain: The editing rule tells you which reads need the leader. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Use known ownership as a signal.

questions.q: True or false: Reading everything a user might have modified from the leader works well even when most data in the application is editable by the user.
questions.explain: Most reads would hit the leader, which negates the benefit of read scaling.
questions.rule: The rule works when little is editable.

questions.q: In a recipe app, users edit only their own recipes but browse all. Where do their reads go?
options: All recipes from the leader, since the leader always holds the newest copy
Own recipes to the leader and everyone else's recipes to followers, since only own ones can be fresh
All recipes from a random follower, since followers carry the same recipes as the leader
Own recipes from a follower and everyone else's from the leader, since owners rarely reload
optionExplain: That would send all browsing to the leader and negate the benefit of read scaling.
Right: only the user's own recipes might have been edited by them, so only those need the leader.
The owner could miss their own edit if a lagging follower served the page.
The roles are reversed: it protects strangers' reads and leaves the owner exposed.
questions.explain: The editing rule is an easy proxy for potentially modified data.

questions.q: Sort each application into where this leader-routing rule works well or poorly.

items.t: Profiles editable only by their owner
A blog where only authors edit posts
A shared whiteboard where anyone edits any item
A wiki where every page is editable by every reader
Customer records changed only by their account owner
A task board where all members edit all cards

questions.explain: The rule works when you can tell what a user might have modified; when nearly anything could be edited by the reader, most reads go to the leader.

questions.q: If most things are potentially editable by the user, what other criteria might decide to read from the leader?
options: The size of the data requested, since large pages are likelier to have been edited
The brand of the user's device, since devices differ in how they cache replies
Time since the last update, or the lag of each follower
The day of the week, since weekends have different traffic patterns
optionExplain: Size says nothing about whether this user changed the data recently.
Device brand is unrelated to replication state.
Right: both time since the last update and each follower's lag tell you whether a follower may be stale.
Weekday does not indicate whether a follower is behind.
questions.explain: You can track the time of the last update, and for one minute after it read from the leader; or you can monitor follower lag and avoid followers more than one minute behind.
questions.rule: Use update time or lag as the signal.
questions.teaches: You could track the time of the last update and, for one minute after it, make all reads from the leader, or prevent queries on any follower that is more than one minute behind.

questions.q: A forum lets everyone edit their posts and others' wikis. Which approach keeps most reads on followers and still gives authors their edits?
options: Send a user's reads to the leader for a short window after their last write
Send every read to the leader, so that no user can see stale data again
Stop users from reloading for a minute after posting, so that they do not notice the lag
Let each follower read its own local disk more quickly, so that it catches up before reads
optionExplain: Right: a short leader-read window per user keeps most reads on followers and covers the lag period.
Sending all reads to the leader would negate the benefit of read scaling.
Blocking reloads hides the symptom without giving the user the data.
A follower's disk cannot hold writes that have not been replicated to it yet.
questions.explain: A time window keeps most reads on followers.
questions.rule: Bound leader reads with a window.
questions.teaches: Another criterion is to monitor the replication lag on followers and prevent queries on any follower that is more than one minute behind the leader.

questions.q: A replica is behind a client's last write. What can the system do to preserve read-after-write consistency?
options: Return an empty result so that the client retries later against another replica
Serve the read from another replica, or wait until the replica catches up
Serve the read anyway and rely on the client to notice that its write is missing
Delete the client's write from the leader so that the replicas appear consistent
optionExplain: An empty result would look like data loss to the user.
Right: either find a replica that has caught up to the client's write or wait for this one.
Serving the read anyway breaks the guarantee the system is trying to give.
Deleting the write would make the problem worse.
questions.explain: The client carries a marker of its last write. The card next explains how.
questions.rule: Replicas behind the marker must not answer.

questions.q: A client can remember the ____ of its most recent write so replicas can be checked against it.
questions.explain: The replica must reflect updates at least until that point.

questions.q: A client wrote at log position 9,120. Replica R1 has applied up to 9,100 and R2 up to 9,140. Where may it read?
options: From R1 immediately, since it is only twenty positions behind the client's write
From neither, since two replicas disagree about the latest position and cannot be used
From whichever answers first, since the faster replica is probably the fresher one
From R2 right away, or from R1 once it has applied the log up to position 9,120
optionExplain: R1 has not applied the client's write yet, however small the gap.
Replicas differing in position is normal; one of them is sufficiently up to date.
The first to answer may be the stale one; speed says nothing about freshness.
Right: R2 has applied the client's write, and R1 may serve once it reaches position 9,120.
questions.explain: The replica must have applied at least the client's last write.

questions.q: True or false: If the timestamp used is the actual system clock of different machines, clock synchronization becomes critical.
questions.explain: Unsynchronized clocks could mark a replica as caught up when it is not, so a logical timestamp such as a log position is safer.

questions.q: What is an example of a logical timestamp mentioned in the chapter?
options: The log sequence number, which orders writes without needing synchronized clocks
The wall-clock time on the client, which marks when each write was made
The user ID, which is attached to every write from that user
The hostname of the replica, which tells which replica applied the write
optionExplain: Right: the log sequence number orders writes without relying on synchronized clocks.
A wall-clock time is the other option the chapter names, and it needs synchronized clocks.
A user ID does not order writes.
A hostname does not order writes.
questions.explain: A logical timestamp indicates the ordering of writes, such as the log sequence number.
questions.rule: Logical timestamps need no synchronized clocks.
questions.teaches: The timestamp could be a logical timestamp (something that indicates ordering of writes, such as the log sequence number) or the actual system clock.

questions.q: A mobile client wrote an order and then reads its order history. Replicas span two datacenters. What extra consideration applies to the read?
options: Nothing special, since replicas in every datacenter hold identical data at all times
The read can only be served by the client's own device, which keeps the last write
A request served by the leader must be routed to the datacenter that holds the leader
The write must first be repeated in each datacenter before the read can be served
optionExplain: Replicas are not always identical; that is the reason for the guarantee.
Devices do not serve server reads, and the client only remembers a timestamp.
Right: reads that need the leader must be routed to the datacenter that contains the leader.
Repeating writes in every datacenter is not described as part of the approach.
questions.explain: Distribution across datacenters adds complexity because leader-served requests must go where the leader is.
questions.teaches: If your replicas are distributed across multiple datacenters, any request that needs to be served by the leader must be routed to the datacenter that contains the leader.

questions.q: A user enters data on a laptop, then opens the phone app and does not see it. Which guarantee is missing?
options: Monotonic reads, since the data seemed to disappear when the user moved to the phone
Quorum reads, since too few replicas may have been consulted when the phone queried
Cross-device read-after-write consistency, so that data entered on one device shows on another
Synchronous replication, since a synchronous follower would have made the data visible
optionExplain: Monotonic reads concern a sequence of reads going backward, not data missing from another device.
Quorums apply to leaderless databases and are not the guarantee named here.
Right: the user's own data should follow them across devices, which is the cross-device variant.
Replication mode is a mechanism; the user-visible guarantee that is missing is the cross-device one.
questions.explain: It is read-your-writes extended across devices. The card next explains the added complications.
questions.rule: Own writes should follow the user.

questions.q: True or false: Remembering the timestamp of the latest write in the client code on one device is enough for read-after-write consistency across devices.
questions.explain: One device's code cannot know about updates made on another, so the metadata must be centralized.

questions.q: A note app writes on a laptop and reads on a phone, and the two reach different datacenters. If reads need the leader, what must you do?
options: Route requests from all of the user's devices to the same datacenter
Let each device pick the closest datacenter, since proximity gives the fastest reads
Keep a separate copy of the data per device so that each device is always current
Ignore the difference, since network routes from one user never differ between devices
optionExplain: Right: only then can a read that needs the leader reach the datacenter that holds it.
Different datacenters can serve a read that lacks the user's latest write.
Separate copies per device would break consistency between the devices.
The chapter points out that the routes of different devices may be completely different.
questions.explain: Without consistent routing the second device may hit a datacenter that lacks the leader.
questions.rule: Pin a user to one datacenter.

questions.q: Which problems appear once one user works from a desktop and a phone?
options: One device's code does not know about the other device's updates
Devices may be routed to different datacenters
Followers stop applying the log
Writes are rejected at the leader
Last-update metadata must be centralized
optionExplain: Right: each device only knows its own writes.
Right: broadband and cellular routes can differ.
Followers keep applying logs.
The leader still accepts writes.
Right: metadata about the last update has to be shared.
questions.explain: The complications are shared state and routing.
questions.rule: Cross-device needs shared metadata and routing.

questions.q: Why might the desktop and the mobile device be routed to different datacenters, according to the chapter?
options: Mobile devices cannot connect to leaders, so they are served by whichever datacenter is nearest
Desktops are assigned to the leader's datacenter, while mobile devices are assigned to followers
The user has two accounts, one for each device, and each is homed in a different datacenter
They may use different networks, such as home broadband and cellular data
optionExplain: Mobile devices can connect to leaders; the issue is the route taken.
The chapter does not assign device types to roles.
The scenario concerns one user with one account.
Right: broadband and cellular connections may route to completely different datacenters.
questions.explain: Different network routes lead to different datacenters.
questions.teaches: If the user's desktop computer uses the home broadband connection and their mobile device uses the cellular data network, the devices' network routes may be completely different.

questions.q: A photo-sharing app syncs a user's uploads across web, phone and tablet, with replicas in three regions. What is the sound design?
options: Let each device remember its own last write only, since devices cannot see each other
Keep per-user last-write metadata in a shared place and make reads honour it on every device
Serve every device from the nearest region with no checks, since replicas will catch up
Block uploads from a second device until the first has finished syncing everywhere
optionExplain: Each device would not know about uploads from the other devices.
Right: shared last-write metadata lets any device know how fresh a replica must be.
The nearest region may be behind the user's latest upload.
Blocking uploads removes a feature users expect rather than fixing the staleness.
questions.explain: Both pieces are needed: shared metadata and checks on every read.
questions.rule: Shared state for a shared user.
questions.teaches: The remembered write timestamp can be a logical timestamp, such as the log sequence number, or the actual system clock, in which case clock synchronization becomes critical.

questions.q: A user refreshes a page twice. The first view shows a new comment and the second does not. What is a likely cause?
options: The comment was deleted by the leader between the two views, and the delete reached the second follower
The two requests were served by followers with different lag, the second more behind than the first
The leader processed the comment twice, and the second follower dropped the duplicate
The database switched to synchronous replication, which discarded writes it had not confirmed
optionExplain: Nothing in the scenario says a delete happened.
Right: the first request hit a follower with little lag and the second hit one that was further behind.
Double processing would not make the comment vanish for one follower.
A mode change does not remove data that was already visible.
questions.explain: Each request may hit a different follower. The card next explains the anomaly.

questions.q: When a later read is served by a replica that is further behind than the one that served an earlier read, time appears to go ____.
questions.explain: The second query observes the system at an earlier point in time than the first.

questions.q: A chat user sees a friend's message, reloads, and it is gone, then it reappears. What is the likeliest setup?
options: Reads always go to the leader, so each reload shows the leader's current state
Every follower is synchronous, so each reload shows the newest committed state
Only one follower exists, so each reload repeats the same stale answer
Reads are routed at random across followers with different lags
optionExplain: The leader has the newest data, so its reads would not go backward.
Synchronous followers are current, so they would not differ in freshness.
One follower gives consistently stale reads, but not data that vanishes and reappears.
Right: random routing mixes followers with different lag, so a reload can see fresher or staler data.
questions.explain: Fresh then stale then fresh again points to random routing across replicas of different lag.

questions.q: True or false: A read showing nothing, then a read showing the new comment, is the same anomaly as a comment that appears and vanishes.
questions.explain: Seeing data arrive later looks like normal lag. The confusing case is data that appears and then vanishes, because the later read observes an earlier state.
questions.teaches: It would not be so bad if the first query had not returned anything, because the user probably would not know that someone had recently added a comment.

questions.q: In the chapter's example, how likely is the anomaly when a user refreshes a page?
options: Quite likely, if each request is routed to a random server
Not possible, since a refresh always reuses the replica that served the page before
Likely only when the leader fails, because failover changes which replica serves reads
Likely only in leaderless databases, because they have no single ordering of writes
optionExplain: Right: with random routing a refresh can easily reach a follower with more lag than the previous one.
A refresh can be routed anywhere unless routing is deliberately fixed.
Leader failure is not needed; ordinary lag differences are enough.
Followers in a leader-based system cause it as well, as the chapter's example shows.
questions.explain: Random routing across replicas of different lag makes the backward step quite likely.
questions.teaches: This scenario is quite likely if the user refreshes a web page, and each request is routed to a random server.

questions.q: A dashboard shows an order count from random followers: 105, then 103, then 106. What is it?
options: Evidence of a lost order, since the count fell from 105 to 103 before rising again
A leader crash, since the count went down for a moment and then recovered
Backward movement from followers with different lag
A violated unique key, since orders were counted twice and then removed
optionExplain: No order was lost; one follower simply had not received two orders yet.
A crash is not needed to explain different lags on different followers.
Right: the second answer came from a follower further behind, so the user saw time move backward.
Nothing here involves a unique key.
questions.explain: The count dips because a lagging replica answered, not because data changed.
questions.rule: A dip can be staleness, not change.
questions.teaches: In general there is no limit to how far a replica can fall behind, which is why the term "eventually" in eventual consistency is deliberately vague.

questions.q: Which guarantee ensures a user does not read older data after having read newer data?
options: Read-after-write consistency, which makes a user see what they submitted themselves
Eventual consistency, which promises that replicas agree once writes stop
Monotonic reads, which keeps one user's reads from going backward in time
Last write wins, which resolves conflicts by keeping the newest timestamp
optionExplain: Read-after-write is about a user's own submissions, not about regressing reads.
Eventual consistency allows a user to see newer data and then older data.
Right: monotonic reads forbids reading older data after newer data.
Last write wins is a conflict rule and says nothing about what a reader sees.
questions.explain: The name says reads only move forward. The card next places it between two other guarantees.

questions.q: Order these guarantees from weakest to strongest.
items: Eventual consistency
Monotonic reads
Strong consistency
questions.explain: Monotonic reads is stronger than eventual consistency and lesser than strong consistency.

questions.q: A user reads a balance twice and gets $90 then $100, where $100 is the latest. Is monotonic reads violated?
options: No, the second read is newer than the first, so time has not gone backward
Yes, because $100 differs from the $90 that the first read showed to the user
Yes, because the first read was stale, and a stale read always breaks the guarantee
Only if the leader served the second read, since followers cannot serve newer data
optionExplain: Right: the second read is newer than the first, so time did not go backward.
The guarantee forbids older data after newer, not newer after older.
A stale first read is allowed; monotonic reads promises no freshness.
Which node served the read does not decide whether it went backward.
questions.explain: Monotonic reads only forbids going backward.

questions.q: True or false: Monotonic reads guarantees that every read returns the most recent value.
questions.explain: A read may still return an old value; the guarantee is only that one user's reads do not go backward.

questions.q: How does the chapter rank monotonic reads against strong and eventual consistency?
options: Stronger than strong consistency, because it adds a promise about each user
Equal to eventual consistency, because both allow a read to return an old value
Weaker than eventual consistency, because it covers only one user at a time
Weaker than strong consistency, stronger than eventual consistency
optionExplain: Nothing is stronger than strong consistency, and monotonic reads still allows stale values.
It adds a guarantee that eventual consistency lacks, so they are not equal.
Adding a guarantee makes it stronger, not weaker, than eventual consistency.
Right: it rules out one anomaly that eventual consistency allows but promises less than strong consistency.
questions.explain: It adds one guarantee over eventual consistency but promises less than strong consistency.
questions.teaches: Monotonic reads is a lesser guarantee than strong consistency, but a stronger guarantee than eventual consistency.

questions.q: A leaderboard may be a minute stale, but a player should not see their rank get worse and then better. Which guarantee fits?
options: Strong consistency across all players, so that everyone sees the same rank at all times
Monotonic reads for each player, which stops ranks from stepping backward without requiring freshness
Synchronous replication to every follower, so that no follower is ever behind
No guarantee at all, since the leaderboard is allowed to be a minute stale
optionExplain: That is more than needed and costly for a leaderboard that may be a minute old.
Right: it prevents backward steps for one player while allowing staleness.
All-synchronous followers make any single outage stop writes.
Staleness is allowed, but the rank getting worse and then better is still a visible anomaly.
questions.explain: The requirement tolerates staleness but not regress, which is the definition of monotonic reads.
questions.rule: Match the guarantee to the tolerance.
questions.teaches: With an eventually consistent system it is worth asking how the application behaves if replication lag grows to several minutes or hours; if the result is a bad user experience, the system should provide a stronger guarantee.

questions.q: How can a system keep a user from reading older data after newer data, using only routing?
options: Send all of that user's reads to the same replica, so the answers move only forward in time
Send each read to a random replica so that over time every replica gets the same load
Send every read to the slowest replica so that no reader is ever ahead of another
Send each read to a different datacenter so that no single failure affects the reader
optionExplain: Right: a single replica applies the log in order, so its answers only move forward in time.
Random replicas differ in lag, which is the cause of the anomaly.
The slowest replica is the stalest, and it does not address the actual problem of switching.
Different datacenters differ in lag as well.
questions.explain: A single replica applies the log in order. The card next adds details.

questions.q: The replica for a user can be chosen from a ____ of the user ID rather than randomly.
questions.explain: A hash gives a stable choice per user.

questions.q: A system has four replicas and user IDs 1 to 1,000,000. How should it assign replicas for monotonic reads?
options: By the current second, so that the load rotates evenly across the four replicas
By alternating replicas on each request, so that no replica is overloaded
By a hash of the user ID, which gives every user a fixed replica and spreads users evenly
By the length of the user's name, so that each user always lands on the same replica
optionExplain: The second changes, so one user would move between replicas.
Alternating moves a user between replicas, which is what causes regression.
Right: a hash of the user ID is stable per user and spreads users evenly across replicas.
Name length is stable per user but spreads users unevenly; the chapter suggests a hash of the ID.
questions.explain: A hash of the ID spreads users evenly and keeps each on one replica.

questions.q: True or false: If a user's assigned replica fails and the user is rerouted to a replica that is further behind, the user may see older data than before.
questions.explain: Rerouting loses the stable-replica property, so the guarantee can break at that moment.

questions.q: May different users read from different replicas under this scheme?
options: No, all users must share one replica, or else the replicas would drift apart
Yes, the guarantee concerns each user's own sequence of reads
Yes, but only after a failover has changed the cluster's configuration
No, because different replicas would diverge if users were spread across them
optionExplain: One shared replica would remove the read-scaling benefit and is not required.
Right: the guarantee concerns each user's own sequence of reads, so users can use different replicas.
Spreading users across replicas is allowed at all times.
Replicas converge by replication, not by which users read from them.
questions.explain: The guarantee is about one user's own sequence of reads, so users can be spread over replicas.
questions.teaches: Each user always makes their reads from the same replica (different users can read from different replicas).

questions.q: A cache layer routes user requests to any of five application servers, each with its own follower. Users report content flickering. What change fits?
options: Add a sixth server to the pool, so that load is spread more thinly
Make every request wait for the leader, so that every answer is current
Shuffle the servers on every request, so that a stale one cannot be reached twice
Route each user to a fixed server by hashing the user ID
optionExplain: A sixth server does not stabilize which follower serves a user.
That would send all reads to the leader and lose read scaling.
Shuffling makes flicker worse, since each request may reach a different follower.
Right: a fixed path per user gives each user one follower whose answers only move forward.
questions.explain: Flicker means regressing reads; sticky routing removes it.
questions.teaches: Handling replication-lag issues in application code is complex and easy to get wrong, which is why transactions exist: they let the database provide stronger guarantees so the application can be simpler.

questions.q: In a chat, a reply appears on screen before the message it answers. What is the cause?
options: The reply was written first, since the person answering did not wait for the question
The leader reordered both messages on purpose, to apply the shorter one first
The clients typed too quickly, so their messages were stamped with the wrong order
The two messages were replicated with different delays
optionExplain: The reply was written second; the order seen differs from the order written.
A leader applies writes in one order; the reordering happens on the reading side.
Typing speed does not reorder what readers see.
Right: the two messages travelled through followers with different lags, so the reply arrived first.
questions.explain: Causally related writes took paths with different lag. The card next names the guarantee.
questions.rule: Different delays reorder what you see.

questions.q: True or false: In the Mr. Poons and Mrs. Cake example, the observer hears the answer first because the answer travelled through a follower with less lag.
questions.explain: Mrs. Cake's words went through a low-lag follower and Mr. Poons's words through a slower one.

questions.q: A forum shows a post and its reply from different partitions. A reader sees a reply with no post. What describes it?
options: A lost reply, because the database dropped the post that the reply answers
A causality violation caused by uneven replication lag
A deleted post, because the author removed it right after the reply was written
A leader failover, because the new leader never received the post
optionExplain: The post exists; it just has not reached this reader yet.
Right: the cause reaches this reader later than the effect, because the partitions lag differently.
Nothing in the scenario says the author removed it.
No failover is described; ordinary uneven lag explains it.
questions.explain: The post will arrive, but the reader sees the effect first.
questions.rule: Causality can be broken by lag.

questions.q: The observer hears the answer before the question only if the follower carrying the answer has ____ lag than the one carrying the question.
questions.explain: Equal or reversed lags keep the order of the dialogue; the answer must travel on the faster path to overtake the question.
questions.rule: Faster path to the effect reverses the order.

questions.q: Where is the consistent prefix problem particularly likely, according to the chapter?
options: In single-node databases, since only one machine applies writes
In systems with only one follower, since that follower may fall behind
In partitioned (sharded) databases, whose partitions operate and replicate independently
In read-only databases, since stale copies are never refreshed
optionExplain: One node applies writes in a single order, so it cannot reorder them.
A single follower applies the leader's log in order, so the prefix stays consistent.
Right: partitions operate independently, so their lags differ and causal order can be lost.
Read-only data has no writes whose order could be seen wrongly.
questions.explain: Different partitions operate independently, so lag differs between them.
questions.teaches: This is a particular problem in partitioned (sharded) databases.

questions.q: A shop writes an order to one partition and the payment to another. A support tool shows a payment with no order. Which explains it?
options: The partitions replicated at different speeds, so the effect was seen before the cause
The payment was fake, since it is recorded without a matching order
The order was never written, because the shop's code failed before saving it
Support read from the leader of the order partition, which had not yet seen the order
optionExplain: Right: the two partitions replicate at different speeds, so the effect became visible before the cause.
Nothing suggests fraud; the order exists but has not reached this reader yet.
The order was written, and the issue is visibility, not saving.
A leader holds the newest data for its partition, so it would show the order.
questions.explain: The anomaly is not about content but about reading across partitions with different lags.
questions.teaches: The anomaly is a particular problem in partitioned (sharded) databases, because different partitions operate independently and there is no global ordering of writes.

questions.q: Which guarantee ensures readers see a question and its answer in the order they were written?
options: Monotonic reads, which keeps a user from reading older data after newer data
Consistent prefix reads, which shows readers writes in the order they happened
Read-after-write consistency, which lets a user see what they submitted themselves
Eventual consistency, which says replicas agree once the writes stop
optionExplain: Monotonic reads is about one user going backward in time, not about order between writes.
Right: consistent prefix reads makes readers see writes in the order they happened.
Read-after-write concerns a user's own writes, not the order of two users' writes.
Eventual consistency promises convergence but nothing about order along the way.
questions.explain: The name suggests readers see a prefix of the write history. The card next explains.

questions.q: If the database applies writes in one fixed order, reads see a consistent ____.
questions.explain: A prefix of the write history never shows an effect without its cause.

questions.q: A database has one leader and one log. Can a reader see a reply before its question?
options: Yes, because followers are asynchronous and may deliver messages out of order
Yes, because readers are served randomly and may land on a stale follower
Yes, because logical logs do not record the order in which rows were written
No, because the writes apply in one order everywhere, so readers see a prefix of that log
optionExplain: Asynchrony delays delivery but does not change the order of a single log.
A stale follower is behind but still shows a consistent prefix.
Logical logs record writes in order.
Right: all replicas apply one log in one order, so a reader always sees a prefix of it.
questions.explain: A single ordered log prevents the anomaly.

questions.q: Sort each setup into whether it keeps a consistent prefix.

items.t: One log applied in order on every replica
Independent partitions replicating at different speeds
A single partition applying writes in order
Question and answer stored in different partitions, with no global order
Followers all copying one leader's log
Parts of the database in older and newer states

questions.explain: A global order keeps the prefix; independent partitions lose it.

questions.q: Why is there no global ordering of writes in many distributed databases?
options: Different partitions operate independently, so no single order covers all of their writes
Writes are never stored on more than one node, so ordering them is not possible
Clocks always agree across partitions, so ordering is implicit and no log is needed
Only one node exists in each partition, so it cannot agree with the others
optionExplain: Right: each partition orders only its own writes and runs on its own, so no shared order exists.
Writes are stored and replicated; the issue is missing agreement across partitions.
Clocks do not always agree; the chapter warns they cannot be trusted.
Partitions can have several replicas; the issue is the absence of a shared order.
questions.explain: With independent partitions a reader can see some parts in an older state and some in a newer one.
questions.teaches: In many distributed databases, different partitions operate independently, so there is no global ordering of writes.

questions.q: An audit log writes events to partition A and the matching approvals to partition B. Reviewers see approvals first. Which guarantee is missing?
options: Read-after-write consistency, since reviewers should see their own writes first
Monotonic reads, since reviewers saw a later state before an earlier one
Consistent prefix reads across partitions, so dependent writes appear in the order they happened
Last write wins, since the later of the two writes should replace the earlier
optionExplain: Reviewers are not looking at their own writes.
The anomaly is about order between two writes, not about a reader going backward.
Right: dependent writes in different partitions must be seen in the order they happened.
Last write wins is a conflict rule, and these writes do not conflict.
questions.explain: The missing guarantee is ordered visibility of causally related writes.
questions.rule: Dependent writes need an ordered view.
questions.teaches: Simply attaching a timestamp to every write is not enough to order causally dependent events correctly, because clocks cannot be trusted to be sufficiently in sync.

questions.q: A chat app stores each conversation across several partitions. How could it prevent answers appearing before questions?
options: Increase the number of followers in every partition so that replies arrive sooner
Delete old messages so that the partitions have less to copy to their followers
Write all messages of a conversation to the same partition
Move to a bigger database so that the partitions no longer need to be independent
optionExplain: More followers do not create an order between partitions.
Deleting messages does not order the rest.
Right: one partition applies its writes in one order, so related messages keep their order.
A bigger database still has independent partitions if the data is split.
questions.explain: Keeping related writes together gives a single order. The card next shows the catch.

questions.q: One solution is to write causally related data to the same ____.
questions.explain: One partition orders its writes in one log.

questions.q: A comment system keys partitions by article ID. Comments and replies on one article share a partition. What does this guarantee?
options: Replies on that article cannot be seen before their parent comments
Replies on different articles are ordered relative to each other, wherever they are stored
Followers of the partition never lag, so replies can never be late in any way
Writes to the partition become synchronous, so that every follower is current
optionExplain: Right: one partition orders its own writes, so a reply cannot appear before the comment it answers.
Different articles may sit in different partitions, so no order is guaranteed between them.
Followers can still lag; they just apply the partition's log in order.
The replication mode is unchanged by how the data is keyed.
questions.explain: Co-location handles dependencies inside a partition only.

questions.q: True or false: If related writes cannot be grouped in one partition efficiently, explicit causal-dependency tracking is another option.
questions.explain: Some algorithms keep track of causal dependencies, a topic the chapter returns to.
questions.rule: Track dependencies explicitly when grouping fails.

questions.q: Which later topic of the chapter introduces algorithms that track causal dependencies?
options: Setting up new followers, which explains how to replay the log from a position
Statement-based replication, which explains why order matters for statements
Hinted handoff, which explains how writes reach their home nodes after an outage
The happens-before relationship and concurrency, which defines when one operation depends on another
optionExplain: That section is about snapshots and catch-up, not about dependencies.
That section is about the log format, not about tracking causality.
Hinted handoff concerns where writes are stored under a sloppy quorum.
Right: the happens-before section defines when one operation depends on another.
questions.explain: The section on happens-before develops the idea of one operation depending on another.
questions.teaches: There are also algorithms that explicitly keep track of causal dependencies, a topic we will return to in the happens-before relationship and concurrency.

questions.q: A trading app writes orders to partition A and fills to partition B, and orders and fills are unrelated by key. What is the difficulty?
options: Fills never arrive, because the partition for fills has no replicas
Fills may be seen before their orders, and grouping them would need a shared key
Orders are replicated synchronously, so fills always lag behind them
Partition B is read-only, so fills cannot be written until the orders are copied
optionExplain: Fills arrive; the issue is the order in which readers see them.
Right: nothing ties fills to their orders, so they cannot be placed in one partition to keep their order.
The scenario does not mention synchronous replication.
Nothing says partition B is read-only.
questions.explain: Without a shared key the data cannot be co-located.
questions.teaches: To order causally dependent writes correctly, a technique called version vectors can be used.

questions.q: A team ships an app on asynchronous replicas and tests only with small lag. What is the risk?
options: Behaviour under minutes of lag is untested and could be bad
Replication will fail completely once lag exceeds a few seconds, taking the app down
The leader will lose writes at once whenever followers are behind
Followers will refuse reads as soon as they are more than a minute behind
optionExplain: Right: lag is usually small but unbounded, so the bad case may never have been tried.
Replication continues to work under lag; it is the application's behavior that may suffer.
Followers being behind does not make the leader lose writes.
Followers keep answering reads, possibly with stale data.
questions.explain: Lag is usually small but unbounded. The card next gives the test question.

questions.q: True or false: Pretending that replication is synchronous when it is asynchronous is a recipe for problems down the line.
questions.explain: The application may then break when lag grows.

questions.q: A notification app can tolerate a user seeing an old unread count for hours. What follows from the chapter's test?
options: It must use synchronous replication, so that no user ever sees an old unread count
It must read only from the leader, so that the count is always current
Eventual consistency may be fine for it, since large lag causes the users no problem
It needs a distributed transaction, so that the count updates everywhere at once
optionExplain: Synchronous replication would be needless cost for data that tolerates lag.
Leader-only reads would give up the scaling that followers provide.
Right: if hours of lag cause no problem, eventual consistency is acceptable and nothing stronger is needed.
A distributed transaction is far more machinery than a tolerant app requires.
questions.explain: The test asks whether the app tolerates large lag, and here it does.
questions.rule: Tolerant apps need no stronger guarantee.

questions.q: Sort each application into whether it can tolerate hours of replication lag.

items.t: A view counter on an article
A user who just posted a comment and reloads
A weekly recommendations email list
A banking balance shown after a transfer
A trending hashtags page
A shopping cart the shopper just changed

questions.explain: Where users compare against their own recent actions, lag is visible; aggregate or background views tolerate it.
questions.rule: Tie tolerance to what users notice.

questions.q: Why do transactions exist, according to the chapter?
options: To speed up all reads, since transactions let replicas answer queries in parallel
To let the database provide stronger guarantees so the application can be simpler
To remove the need for replication, since a transaction keeps one copy of the data
To make every follower synchronous, since a transaction waits for all replicas
optionExplain: Speed is not the stated purpose of transactions.
Right: the database provides stronger guarantees so application code does not have to.
Transactions do not replace replication.
Transactions are a guarantee, not a replication mode.
questions.explain: Dealing with replication issues in application code is complex, so the database should do the right thing.
questions.rule: Let the database carry the guarantees.
questions.teaches: Transactions exist as a way for a database to provide stronger guarantees so that the application can be simpler.

questions.q: A vendor says eventual consistency is inevitable in a scalable system, so transactions are not needed. How does the book respond?
options: It is correct: scalable systems must give up transactions because they are too slow
It is false: transactions are cheap and every scalable system should use them
It is unrelated: transactions have no bearing on replication lag or consistency
There is some truth, but the claim is overly simplistic
optionExplain: The authors concede only some truth and call the claim overly simplistic.
The authors do not say transactions are cheap or universal.
They link transactions to the guarantees applications need under lag.
Right: the authors grant some truth but call the claim overly simplistic and promise a more nuanced view.
questions.explain: The authors promise a more nuanced view over the rest of the book.
questions.teaches: Many systems abandoned transactions, claiming eventual consistency is inevitable in a scalable system; there is some truth in that, but it is overly simplistic.

questions.q: A client cannot reach the only leader because of a network interruption. What happens to its writes in a single-leader setup?
options: They are accepted by any follower it can reach, which stores them for the leader
They cannot be processed until it can reach the leader
They are queued at the nearest replica and applied later when the leader returns
They are rolled forward on the client's next read from a follower
optionExplain: Followers are read-only for clients, so they refuse writes.
Right: only the leader accepts writes, so writes wait until the client can reach it.
The chapter describes no queueing at replicas.
Reads do not apply writes.
questions.explain: All writes must pass through one node. The card next shows how to relax that.
questions.rule: One leader is a single write path.

questions.q: In a multi-leader configuration, each leader acts as a ____ to the other leaders at the same time.
questions.explain: It forwards its own writes and applies the others' writes.
questions.rule: Each leader also follows the others.

questions.q: A regional office must keep writing even if its link to head office is down. Which design offers that, at a cost?
options: A follower that serves only reads at the office, so that staff can at least view the data
A synchronous follower at head office, so that every write is confirmed at once
A larger leader at head office, so that the link can carry more write traffic
A local node that accepts writes and forwards them later
optionExplain: A read-only follower cannot take writes.
A synchronous follower makes writes wait on the very link that is down.
A bigger leader does not help when the leader cannot be reached.
Right: a local node that accepts writes keeps working without the link, with conflict handling as the cost.
questions.explain: Accepting writes locally avoids dependence on the link, with the cost of conflicts later.

questions.q: Sort each property into single-leader or multi-leader replication.

items.t: Every write must pass through one node
Several nodes accept client writes
Concurrent writes to one record on different nodes can conflict
A network cut to the leader blocks all writes
Each node forwards its writes to all other nodes
Followers are read-only for clients

questions.explain: Multi-leader trades the single write path for conflicts between leaders.
questions.rule: More leaders, more availability, more conflicts.

questions.q: What other names does the chapter give multi-leader replication?
options: Master-master or active/active replication, in which several nodes accept client writes
Active/passive or master-slave replication, which describe one leader and read-only followers
Hot standby or warm standby replication, which describe followers that take over
Dynamo-style or leaderless replication, which describe systems without any designated leader
optionExplain: Right: master-master and active/active mean several nodes accept writes.
Those names describe the single-leader pattern.
Standbys are followers, not leaders.
Leaderless replication has no leaders at all.
questions.explain: Names vary by vendor: master-master and active/active mean several write-accepting nodes.
questions.teaches: A multi-leader configuration is also known as master-master or active/active replication.

questions.q: A company asks whether multi-leader replication fixes slow writes for users on another continent. What is a fair answer?
options: No, followers already accept writes locally, so users never wait for a distant leader
Yes, with no downside, since leaders in different regions agree with each other instantly
It can, by letting a local leader take the writes, but concurrent edits may conflict
No, writes can never leave the single node that holds the leader role
optionExplain: Followers are read-only for clients, so they do not accept writes.
Leaders replicate asynchronously, so they do not agree instantly.
Right: a leader per region takes writes locally, but concurrent edits on different leaders can conflict.
Multi-leader replication changes exactly that.
questions.explain: The benefit of a local write path comes with the cost of conflicts.
questions.teaches: Multi-leader replication has the big downside that the same data may be concurrently modified on different leaders, so write conflicts must be resolved.

questions.q: A single-datacenter application with a primary and replicas wants better availability. Is multi-leader replication usually worthwhile?
options: Yes, since more leaders always improve availability and speed inside a datacenter
Only if reads are slow, since extra leaders help read capacity
Rarely, since the benefits seldom outweigh the extra complexity
Only if replication is synchronous, since that avoids conflicts
optionExplain: Extra leaders add conflicts, so they do not always improve things.
Followers, not leaders, relieve slow reads.
Right: inside one datacenter the benefits seldom outweigh the added complexity.
Synchronous replication does not decide whether multi-leader is worthwhile.
questions.explain: The extra complexity needs a strong reason. The card next lists the reasons.

questions.q: Which situations does the chapter give as reasonable for multi-leader replication?
options: Replicas in several datacenters
Clients that must work while offline
Real-time collaborative editing
A single datacenter with one busy table
Replacing a failed follower
optionExplain: Right: a leader per datacenter.
Right: each device acts as a leader.
Right: local edits replicate asynchronously.
A single datacenter rarely justifies it.
Replacing followers uses snapshots and catch-up.
questions.explain: Three use cases are named: datacenters, offline clients and collaborative editing.

questions.q: A team runs one datacenter and wants to split write load across two nodes. What does the chapter suggest?
options: Think twice: in one datacenter multi-leader rarely pays off, so look at other designs
Adopt multi-leader at once, since two writers share the load
Move to leaderless replication inside the same room, since that has no leader to overload
Add synchronous followers, since they accept a share of the writes
optionExplain: Right: think twice, because in one datacenter the complexity rarely pays off, so consider other designs.
The chapter is cautious about multi-leader inside one datacenter.
Leaderless replication is another approach and not advised here either.
Followers do not accept client writes.
questions.explain: The guidance is cautionary: complexity outweighs benefit in a single datacenter.

questions.q: True or false: A calendar that works offline, a multi-datacenter store and a collaborative editor are all examples where multi-leader replication fits.
questions.explain: Each has local write needs that a single leader would block.

questions.q: How does the chapter describe the relation between offline clients and multi-datacenter operation?
options: They are unrelated problems, since devices are not servers
Offline clients need fewer leaders, because they connect to a single server
Datacenters need offline clients, since replication starts at the edge
The same architecture taken to the extreme, with each device as a datacenter on a very unreliable link
optionExplain: The chapter calls them essentially the same.
Every device is a leader, so there are more leaders, not fewer.
The dependence is the other way: the offline case is the datacenter case taken to the extreme.
Right: essentially the same architecture, taken to the extreme: each device a datacenter with a very unreliable link.
questions.explain: Each device is a datacenter and the connection is extremely unreliable.
questions.rule: Offline is multi-DC at the extreme.
questions.teaches: Offline operation is essentially the same as multi-leader replication between datacenters taken to the extreme: each device is a datacenter and the network connection between them is extremely unreliable.

questions.q: A field app records inspections in remote areas with no signal for days. Which replication shape is natural?
options: A single leader reached over the network for every write, so the data stays consistent
A local database on each device that accepts writes and syncs later
Followers that serve reads only, because the inspectors are mainly viewing records
Synchronous replication to head office, so that nothing is lost
optionExplain: With no signal for days a single remote leader cannot accept writes.
Right: each device accepts writes locally and syncs when it has a connection.
Read-only followers cannot record new inspections.
Synchronous replication would block with no link.
questions.explain: Writes must be accepted without the network, so each device acts as a leader.
questions.teaches: Offline operation is essentially multi-datacenter multi-leader replication taken to the extreme: each device is a "datacenter" and the network connection between them is extremely unreliable.

questions.q: In a single-leader database with replicas in Europe and Asia, the leader is in Europe. What is the cost for writers in Asia?
options: Every write crosses the internet to Europe, adding latency
Their writes go to an Asian follower, so they are quick
Their writes are lost on the way, since long links drop messages
They can only read, since writers must be in the leader's datacenter
optionExplain: Right: every write travels over the internet to the leader's datacenter, adding latency.
Followers do not accept writes.
Writes are not lost by distance; they are only slower.
They can write, only more slowly.
questions.explain: The leader's location sets write latency for everyone. The card next shows the alternative.

questions.q: In a multi-leader setup, a write is processed in the local datacenter and replicated ____ to the others.
questions.explain: Asynchronous copying keeps the writer from waiting on the link.

questions.q: A video app has users in São Paulo and Tokyo, each sending frequent small updates. Which design lowers perceived write delay?
options: One leader in Frankfurt for both regions, so that all writes are ordered in one place
Synchronous replication across regions for each update, so that both regions agree at once
A leader in each region, with updates replicated between regions in the background
A read replica in each region, so that readers of either region are served locally
optionExplain: Both regions would cross oceans for each write.
Waiting for the other region adds delay to each write.
Right: each region writes to a local leader, and updates travel between regions in the background.
Read replicas speed up reads, but they cannot accept writes.
questions.explain: Local acceptance is the source of the improvement.

questions.q: True or false: If an inter-datacenter link slows down, a multi-leader setup with asynchronous replication keeps users' writes as fast as before.
questions.explain: The delay shows up only as replication lag between datacenters, not in the writer's response time.
questions.rule: The link's delay shows up as lag.

questions.q: The chapter says the perceived performance of multi-leader may be better. Why only perceived?
options: Because writes are in fact slower, so the improvement seen is only an impression
The inter-datacenter delay is hidden from users but still exists as replication lag
Because reads become slower, so the total time for a request is unchanged
Because the leaders compete for the same data, which slows the overall system
optionExplain: Writes in the local datacenter are fast.
Right: the delay is hidden from the writer, but other datacenters still see the change later.
Reads are not described as slower.
Competition between leaders is not the reason given.
questions.explain: The work still happens asynchronously, so other datacenters see the write later.
questions.rule: The delay is hidden, not removed.
questions.teaches: The inter-datacenter network delay is hidden from users, which means the perceived performance may be better.

questions.q: A bank wants every branch to see each deposit before the teller confirms it. Does the multi-leader performance argument fit?
options: Yes, because multi-leader replication copies each write to every branch at once
Yes, because all branches share one leader that orders the deposits
Yes, because the hidden link means branches never wait for each other
Not directly, since asynchronous replication means other branches see it later
optionExplain: Replication between datacenters is asynchronous, not instant.
Multi-leader has several leaders, not one shared leader.
The delay is hidden from the writer, but other branches lag behind it.
Right: the gain comes from asynchronous copying, so other branches see the deposit later.
questions.explain: The performance win relies on not waiting, which conflicts with a requirement that all see it first.
questions.rule: Fast local writes mean delayed remote views.
questions.teaches: A single-leader configuration is very sensitive to problems on the inter-datacenter link because writes are made synchronously over it, whereas asynchronous multi-leader replication can usually tolerate a temporary network interruption.

questions.q: A datacenter holding the only leader fails. What must a single-leader setup do before accepting writes elsewhere?
options: Wait for the same datacenter to return, since the data lives there
Ask clients to write to all followers, so that one of them accepts the write
Turn all followers into leaders, so that every datacenter can take writes
Fail over by promoting a follower in another datacenter
optionExplain: Waiting leaves writes blocked for as long as the outage lasts.
Followers do not take client writes.
That would be a multi-leader setup, not single-leader failover.
Right: failover promotes a follower in another datacenter to be the new leader.
questions.explain: Failover is the single-leader recovery step. The card next contrasts the multi-leader path.

questions.q: Match each configuration to how it handles a datacenter outage.
pairs: Fail over by promoting a follower elsewhere
Replication catches up when the datacenter returns
questions.explain: Single-leader needs a role change; multi-leader datacenters stay independent.

questions.q: An airline's booking data is in two datacenters connected over the internet, which drops packets for ten minutes. Which setup keeps both sites writing?
options: A single leader with writes sent over the link, with retries for lost messages
A leader in each datacenter with asynchronous replication between them
Synchronous replication to the other site, so that both stay equal
Read replicas in both sites, so that both can at least show bookings
optionExplain: Writes would fail or stall across the bad link.
Right: each site accepts writes locally, and replication catches up when the link recovers.
Synchronous replication waits on the bad link.
Read replicas cannot accept writes.
questions.explain: Asynchronous multi-leader replication usually tolerates a temporary interruption.
questions.rule: Local leaders ride out link trouble.

questions.q: True or false: In a single-leader setup, a temporary network interruption between datacenters can prevent writes from being processed in the remote datacenter.
questions.explain: Writes are made over the link, so the setup is very sensitive to its problems.

questions.q: Where does traffic between datacenters usually travel, according to the chapter, and why does it matter?
options: Over a private cable that never fails, so it is as reliable as the local network
Over the local network only, because datacenters share their switches
Over the public internet, which may be less reliable than the local network
Over each device's cellular data, because clients carry the writes between sites
optionExplain: The chapter does not describe any link that never fails.
Datacenters are separate sites with their own networks.
Right: it usually crosses the public internet, which may be less reliable than a datacenter's own network.
Cellular data belongs to the offline-client case.
questions.explain: Because the link is less reliable, designs that depend on it for every write suffer.
questions.rule: The link is the weak spot.
questions.teaches: Traffic between datacenters usually goes over the public internet, which may be less reliable than the local network within a datacenter.

questions.q: A retailer's European datacenter is offline for an hour and its stores keep selling. Which later task does multi-leader replication create?
options: Resolving conflicts between the two sides' writes after reconnection
Rebuilding the whole dataset from scratch, since the sides diverged during the outage
Promoting a follower to leader for the first time, since the other side has none
Moving all stores to one leader, since two leaders cannot coexist
optionExplain: Right: both sides accepted writes, so conflicting edits must be resolved after reconnection.
Catch-up replays missing changes; it does not require a rebuild.
Each side already has its own leader.
The design is meant to avoid exactly that.
questions.explain: Independent operation is the advantage, and reconciling is its price.
questions.teaches: Multi-leader replication has a big downside: the same data may be concurrently modified in two different datacenters, and those write conflicts must be resolved.

questions.q: Why might autoincrementing keys cause trouble in a multi-leader setup?
options: Leaders cannot store numbers, so the keys cannot be generated
Two leaders could each assign the same next value to different rows
Followers refuse numeric keys that were generated by another node
The log cannot contain integers, so the keys would be lost in replication
optionExplain: Leaders store numbers like any node.
Right: each leader runs its own counter, so two leaders could give the same key to different rows.
Followers accept them.
Logs can hold integers.
questions.explain: Each leader runs its own counter. The card next lists known trouble spots.

questions.q: Which features does the chapter name as problematic in multi-leader replication?
options: Autoincrementing keys
Triggers
Integrity constraints
Snapshots
Read replicas
optionExplain: Right: independent counters can collide.
Right: triggers fire on each leader.
Right: constraints cannot be checked across leaders at write time.
Snapshots are used to set up followers.
Read replicas are followers.
questions.explain: The chapter lists autoincrementing keys, triggers and integrity constraints.

questions.q: You plan to add a second writable PostgreSQL node using BDR. What should you do first?
options: Assume it behaves like a single node, since the database presents one interface
Turn off all constraints, so that they cannot interfere with replication
Remove the autoincrement column quietly, so that keys cannot collide
Read the documentation and test that it gives the guarantees you assume
optionExplain: It does not behave like one node; that assumption is the pitfall.
Disabling constraints removes safeguards and adds risk.
Silent schema changes cause new bugs.
Right: read the documentation and test that it provides the guarantees you believe it has.
questions.explain: Retrofitted features have surprising interactions, so verify before relying on them.

questions.q: True or false: Multi-leader replication is considered safe and should be preferred whenever more than one datacenter exists.
questions.explain: The chapter calls it dangerous territory to avoid if possible, because of conflicts and pitfalls.

questions.q: Which tools does the chapter name as external multi-leader add-ons?
options: Tungsten Replicator for MySQL, BDR for PostgreSQL, GoldenGate for Oracle
Kafka, RabbitMQ and DRBD, which the chapter lists as users of leader-based replication
Redis, MongoDB and RethinkDB, which the chapter names as other kinds of data stores
Etherpad, Google Docs and CouchDB, which the chapter links to collaborative and offline editing
optionExplain: Right: Tungsten Replicator for MySQL, BDR for PostgreSQL and GoldenGate for Oracle are the external tools named.
Those are examples of leader-based replication.
Those are other databases, not multi-leader add-ons.
Those are editing and offline examples, not add-on tools.
questions.explain: External tools add multi-leader support to databases that were not built for it.
questions.teaches: Multi-leader replication is often implemented with external tools, such as Tungsten Replicator for MySQL, BDR for PostgreSQL, and GoldenGate for Oracle.

questions.q: A team adds a second writable node to a database with a unique-email constraint. Two users register the same email on different nodes. What happens?
options: The second node blocks the registration instantly, since it checks the constraint first
The database merges the two users into one account when the changes arrive
Each node accepts it locally, and the clash appears when changes replicate
The constraint is ignored for good, so duplicate emails are allowed from then on
optionExplain: A local check cannot see a write on another leader that has not arrived.
No merging of accounts is described.
Right: each node checks only its own data, so the clash appears when the changes replicate.
The constraint remains; the violation is found after replication.
questions.explain: Integrity constraints are checked per leader, and conflicts surface only after replication.
questions.rule: Constraints are local to each leader.
questions.teaches: Even if an application checks availability before allowing a booking, a conflict can arise if two bookings are made on two different leaders.

questions.q: A calendar app lets users add meetings on a plane with no connection. How does it work technically?
options: The device sends writes to a leader on landing, losing the meetings entered in flight
The device refuses to save any meeting until it is online again
The device holds a local database that accepts writes and syncs later
The device writes to a follower that forwards the meetings to the leader later
optionExplain: Meetings would be lost, which the design avoids.
Refusing to save would break the requirement.
Right: the device holds a local database that accepts writes itself and syncs later.
Followers are read-only for clients.
questions.explain: The device must accept writes itself. The card next explains the architecture.

questions.q: In an offline-capable calendar, every device has a local database that acts as a ____.
questions.explain: It accepts write requests while offline.

questions.q: A notes app syncs a phone and a laptop. Both edited the same note offline. What is the nature of the sync?
options: Asynchronous multi-leader replication between two leaders
Single-leader replication in which the phone is the leader and the laptop its follower
Synchronous replication in which each device waits for the other to confirm
A read-only mirror in which the laptop only displays what the phone saved
optionExplain: Right: two writable replicas that sync later are two leaders using asynchronous replication.
The laptop also accepted writes, so it is not a follower.
Neither device could wait for the other while offline.
Both devices wrote to the note.
questions.explain: Two writable replicas that sync later are two leaders.

questions.q: True or false: The replication lag between an offline device and the server can be hours or days.
questions.explain: Lag depends on when the device next gets an internet connection.
questions.rule: Offline lag is unbounded by design.
