questions.q: Which database does the chapter name as designed for this mode of operation?
options: Cassandra
PostgreSQL
Kafka
CouchDB
optionExplain: Cassandra is a leaderless Dynamo-style database.
PostgreSQL is named for leader-based replication and add-ons.
Kafka is a message broker with leader-based replication.
Right: CouchDB is named as designed for offline-style multi-leader operation.
questions.explain: Some tools aim to make this configuration easier, and CouchDB is one.
questions.rule: Use tools built for offline sync.
questions.teaches: There are tools that aim to make this kind of multi-leader configuration easier. For example, CouchDB is designed for this mode of operation.

questions.q: A music player lets users build playlists offline on two devices and merges them later. What difficulty can arise on merging?
options: The merge always succeeds without any issues, since each device edited its own copy
Both devices may have changed the same playlist, requiring conflict resolution
The server rejects all device changes made offline, so nothing needs merging
Offline edits are impossible, since a playlist needs the server to be edited
optionExplain: Concurrent edits to the same data can conflict.
Right: both devices may have changed the same playlist, so conflicts must be resolved when they sync.
The design accepts offline changes; that is its purpose.
Offline edits are the premise of the case.
questions.explain: This is the same conflict problem as between datacenters.
questions.teaches: With on-read conflict resolution, as in CouchDB, all conflicting writes are stored and returned together the next time the data is read, and the application may prompt the user or resolve the conflict automatically and write the result back.

questions.q: Two people edit the same document at once and neither waits for the other. What must the system do?
options: Resolve conflicts between their concurrent edits
Ignore one editor entirely, so the other's changes are kept
Lock the document for both editors so that they take turns
Reject all edits until one editor is chosen as the author
optionExplain: Right: concurrent edits require some conflict resolution, since there is no lock to separate them.
Ignoring one editor loses their work.
A lock would make editors wait, which the question rules out.
Rejecting every edit stops the editing altogether.
questions.explain: Without a lock, concurrent edits collide. The card next gives the trade-off.

questions.q: Taking a lock on the document before editing is equivalent to ____-leader replication with transactions on the leader.
questions.explain: The lock serializes editors like a leader processing transactions in turn.

questions.q: A design tool wants users to see each other's cursor moves in real time without waiting for turns. What does the chapter say it needs?
options: A global lock on the whole file, so that only one person moves at a time
Synchronous replication to everyone, so that all cursors are always identical
Very small units of change, no locking, and conflict resolution
A single editor at a time, with the others watching without making changes
optionExplain: A lock forces turn-taking.
Synchronous replication slows each keystroke.
Right: very small units of change, no locking, and conflict resolution, as in multi-leader replication.
One editor at a time defeats the goal.
questions.explain: Fast collaboration means avoiding locks, so it brings the multi-leader challenges.

questions.q: True or false: If editors lock the document before changing it, no editing conflicts can occur.
questions.explain: The lock makes editors take turns, the equivalent of a single leader processing changes in order.
questions.rule: A lock prevents conflicts at the cost of waiting.

questions.q: Which algorithm does the chapter name as behind collaborative editing apps such as Etherpad and Google Docs?
options: Last write wins, which keeps the edit with the highest timestamp and drops the rest
Operational transformation, designed for concurrent editing of an ordered list of items
Hinted handoff, which returns writes held on temporary nodes to their home nodes
Read repair, which fixes stale copies when a client reads from several replicas
optionExplain: Last write wins would silently discard one editor changes, which a document editor cannot accept.
Right: operational transformation resolves concurrent edits to an ordered list such as text.
Hinted handoff belongs to sloppy quorums in leaderless databases, not to document editing.
Read repair belongs to leaderless databases and is not the algorithm named for editors.
questions.explain: Operational transformation resolves conflicts in an ordered list of items, like characters in a text.
questions.teaches: Operational transformation is the conflict resolution algorithm behind collaborative editing applications such as Etherpad and Google Docs.

questions.q: A spreadsheet tool lets users edit different cells at once. A lock on the whole sheet would do what?
options: Make conflicts more likely, since many editors are blocked on the same lock
Speed up concurrent edits, since a single lock removes coordination work
Remove the need for any server, since the lock is held by one user locally
Make editors wait for each other even when editing unrelated cells
optionExplain: Locks remove conflicts at the cost of waiting.
Locks slow concurrent work down.
A server is still needed to hold the lock and the data.
Right: a whole-sheet lock makes editors wait for each other even when their cells are unrelated.
questions.explain: The unit of locking sets how much parallel work is possible; smaller units mean more concurrency and more conflicts.
questions.rule: Lock size trades concurrency for safety.
questions.teaches: Operational transformation is the conflict resolution algorithm behind collaborative editing applications such as Etherpad and Google Docs, designed particularly for concurrent editing of an ordered list of items such as the characters of a text document.

questions.q: Two leaders each accept a different new title for the same page. What happens when they replicate to each other?
options: The later arrival silently wins at both leaders, so nothing needs to be resolved
Each receives a write that conflicts with its own, so a conflict must be resolved
Both leaders reject the incoming write and keep their own title, so each stays as it was
The followers vote on which title is correct, and the majority decides for both leaders
optionExplain: Whichever arrives last would differ at each leader, so the replicas would not agree.
Right: each leader sees a write that clashes with its own, so some conflict resolution is required.
Rejecting the incoming write would leave the two leaders permanently different.
The chapter describes no voting by followers.
questions.explain: Each leader applied its own write first. The card next explains the conflict.
questions.rule: Both writes succeed locally, then clash.

questions.q: True or false: Write conflicts of this kind do not occur in a single-leader database.
questions.explain: A single leader orders all writes, so there is one order and no concurrent leaders.

questions.q: Two clerks in different offices update the same customer phone number at the same moment, each on a local leader. What is this?
options: A stale read from a lagging follower, because one clerk saw the older number
A lost write caused by a failover, because one leader was replaced during the update
A split brain from a failed leader election, because two nodes believed they led
A write conflict detected when the changes replicate
optionExplain: Both writes were accepted on leaders, so no read was stale.
No leader failed in the scenario, so no failover is involved.
Both leaders are legitimate in a multi-leader design; neither is a mistaken second leader.
Right: both writes succeeded locally, and the clash is found when the changes replicate.
questions.explain: Concurrent edits on different leaders produce a conflict at replication time.

questions.q: Title starts as A. Leader 1 sets B then receives C. Leader 2 sets C then receives B. Replicas apply writes in the order they see them. What results?
options: Leader 1 ends with C and leader 2 with B, so the replicas disagree
Both replicas end with B, because the most recent write wins everywhere
Both replicas end with C, because the second title is the one that sticks
Both replicas return to A, because conflicting writes cancel each other out
optionExplain: Right: each leader applies the remote write last, so the two replicas swap titles and disagree.
Leader 2 applies B last, but leader 1 applies C last, so they differ.
Leader 1 applies C last, but leader 2 applies B last, so they differ.
Nothing in the scenario restores the starting title.
questions.explain: Applying writes in arrival order leaves the replicas in different states, which is not acceptable.
questions.rule: Arrival order is not a resolution rule.

questions.q: Every replication scheme must ensure that the data is eventually the ____ in all replicas.
questions.explain: Eventual sameness is required, not instant sameness.
questions.teaches: Every replication scheme must ensure that the data is eventually the same in all replicas, so the database must resolve the conflict in a convergent way.

questions.q: A shared to-do app lets two users on different leaders rename the same task. Which question does the book make you ask?
options: Whether the task is stale on any follower, since lag decides what each user sees
Whether a quorum of nodes can be reached, since writes need acknowledgments
How the system will resolve the clash when the changes replicate
Whether the replication log is physical or logical, since that decides how renames travel
optionExplain: Staleness is a lag topic, not the question when two leaders accept conflicting edits.
Quorums belong to leaderless replication.
Right: concurrent edits on different leaders need a defined rule for resolving the clash.
The log format does not decide what happens to two conflicting renames.
questions.explain: The design must say what happens to concurrent edits of the same record.
questions.teaches: In a single-leader database the second writer either blocks and waits for the first write to complete or is aborted and the user must retry, so such write conflicts do not arise.

questions.q: In a single-leader database, two users update the same record at the same moment. What does the second writer typically experience?
options: Both writes are accepted independently and the clash is found later
The database silently merges the two updates after a short delay
Waiting for the first, or an abort and retry
Both writes are lost and the record returns to its previous state
optionExplain: That is the multi-leader behaviour, not the single-leader one.
Silent merging is not how a single leader treats competing writes.
Right: the second writer either waits for the first or has its transaction aborted so the user can retry.
A single leader keeps one of the writes in order; neither is lost.
questions.explain: A single leader serializes writes. The card next contrasts multi-leader.

questions.q: In multi-leader replication, a conflict is detected ____ at some later point in time.
questions.explain: Both writes already succeeded locally.

questions.q: A user on leader 1 saved a document and closed the app. An hour later leader 2 reports a conflict. Why is asking the user awkward?
options: The user already got success and is gone, so it may be too late to ask
Users are unable to resolve conflicts, because they cannot judge between two versions
Leader 1 refuses any prompts, because only the leader that detects a conflict may ask
Conflicts are never shown to users, because the database always resolves them itself
optionExplain: Right: the user already received success and left, so by the time of detection it may be too late to ask.
Users can resolve conflicts, for instance when versions are returned on read.
Refusing prompts is not described as the cause.
Some designs do show conflicts to users; the problem here is timing.
questions.explain: The write succeeded, the user left, and the conflict surfaced later.

questions.q: True or false: Making conflict detection synchronous in a multi-leader system would remove its main advantage of independent write acceptance.
questions.explain: Waiting for all replicas before success makes each write depend on the others, so you might as well use single-leader.

questions.q: In a single-leader database, what happens to the second of two conflicting writers, according to the chapter?
options: It succeeds and the first write is rolled back, so the later writer wins
It succeeds and both versions are kept, so the conflict is left to later code
It is converted into a read, so the second writer only sees the first value
It blocks and waits, or its transaction aborts so the user retries
optionExplain: Rolling back the first write is not described.
Keeping both is the multi-leader outcome.
Writes are not converted into reads.
Right: the leader serializes the writes, so the second one waits or aborts and the user retries.
questions.explain: This is why the conflict is visible immediately in single-leader systems.
questions.teaches: In a single-leader database, the second writer will either block and wait for the first write to complete, or abort the second write transaction, forcing the user to retry the write.

questions.q: A team wants multi-leader writes but also wants users told immediately when their edit clashes. What is the tension?
options: Users cannot receive notices from a database, because notices are sent only by applications
Immediate notice requires waiting for the other replicas, which removes independent writes
Notices require a quorum of followers to agree, which multi-leader systems lack
Leaders cannot communicate with each other until a conflict has been resolved
optionExplain: Notices are possible; the cost is the wait that makes writes depend on other replicas.
Right: telling users at once means waiting for the other replicas, which removes independent write acceptance.
Quorums are a leaderless concept and not the cause of the tension.
Leaders do replicate to each other; the question is when they find out.
questions.explain: You can have independence or immediate detection, not both.
questions.teaches: A conflict handler that runs on write is called as soon as the database detects a conflict; it typically cannot prompt a user because it runs in a background process and must execute quickly.

questions.q: Which strategy prevents write conflicts without any resolution code?
options: Ensure all writes to a given record go through the same leader
Let each leader apply writes in the order it saw them, which needs no extra code
Pick a random leader for each write, so the load is spread and clashes are rare
Delay every write by one second, so that the other leader has time to send its own
optionExplain: Right: when one leader handles a record, all its writes are ordered and no conflict can occur.
Arrival order differs between leaders and leaves the replicas disagreeing.
Random leaders send writes to the same record to different places, which creates conflicts.
A delay does not remove the clash when the two writes still happen concurrently.
questions.explain: Conflicts need two leaders for one record. The card next shows how to avoid that.

questions.q: When each user is routed to a home datacenter, the setup is essentially ____-leader from that user's point of view.
questions.explain: Though the system has many leaders, each user's data has one.

questions.q: An app keeps each customer's profile on the leader of their nearest datacenter. Customer Mei moves from Tokyo to London. What risk appears?
options: Her profile becomes read-only for good, since her old datacenter no longer owns it
Her old datacenter deletes her data, since it is no longer her nearest one
Writes from her new location may reach a different leader while old writes are still replicating
Nothing changes, since leaders in different datacenters always agree on a profile
optionExplain: Profiles stay writable; the problem is who accepts the writes.
The chapter describes no such deletion.
Right: moving her home leader can let writes from the new and old places reach different leaders concurrently.
Leaders do not agree automatically; that is the reason for conflict handling.
questions.explain: Reassigning the designated leader opens a window for concurrent writes.
questions.rule: Changing the home leader reintroduces conflicts.

questions.q: Sort each scenario into whether conflict avoidance by fixed leader holds or breaks down.

items.t: Each user edits only their own data via their home datacenter
A user's home datacenter fails and traffic is rerouted
A user relocates to another continent
A record is always edited through its owner's leader
Two datacenters take writes for the same record during a failover
Orders are written only at the store that created them

questions.explain: Avoidance holds while the assignment is stable and breaks when it changes.

questions.q: Why does the chapter say avoiding conflicts is frequently recommended?
options: Conflicts never occur in practice, so avoiding them costs nothing
Many multi-leader implementations handle conflicts quite poorly
Resolution code is impossible to write, so avoidance is the only option
Avoidance is always faster than writing resolution code, so teams prefer it
optionExplain: Conflicts do occur whenever two leaders can write the same record.
Right: since many implementations handle conflicts quite poorly, avoiding them is safer.
Resolution code can be written, though it is error-prone.
Speed is not the argument the chapter gives.
questions.explain: Because implementations are poor at conflict handling, avoiding them is safer.
questions.teaches: Since many implementations of multi-leader replication handle conflicts quite poorly, avoiding conflicts is a frequently recommended approach.

questions.q: A document editor lets any team member edit any page from any region. Can conflict avoidance by fixed leader work?
options: Yes, trivially, since every page has a single owner who edits it
Yes, because pages are small enough to be handled by one leader
Only if the pages are replicated synchronously between regions
Poorly, since many users edit the same pages from different places
optionExplain: In shared editing pages do not have one owner.
Size does not decide who writes.
Replication mode does not create a single writer per page.
Right: many users edit the same pages from different places, so no single home leader fits.
questions.explain: Avoidance needs a single writer per record, which shared editing lacks.
questions.rule: Shared data cannot be partitioned by writer.
questions.teaches: To guarantee that there are no editing conflicts the application can obtain a lock on the document before a user edits it, which is equivalent to single-leader replication with transactions on the leader.

questions.q: Leader 1 ends with title C and leader 2 ends with title B, long after all changes replicated. What is wrong?
options: The leaders are in the wrong datacenters, so writes reached them in the wrong order
Replication lag is too small, so the leaders did not have time to talk to each other
The followers are synchronous, so the leaders waited on them and fell out of step
The replicas did not converge on the same value
optionExplain: Location does not decide the final value.
A small lag helps replicas agree faster; it does not cause disagreement.
Follower mode is not the cause of leaders ending on different values.
Right: after all changes replicated, the replicas still hold different values, so they did not converge.
questions.explain: Both replicas applied writes in the order they saw them. The card next gives the principle.

questions.q: Resolving a conflict in a ____ way means all replicas arrive at the same final value when all changes have been replicated.
questions.explain: Convergence is the requirement.

questions.q: Two replicas applied the same two conflicting writes in opposite orders and now differ. Which fix meets the requirement?
options: Let each replica keep what it has, since both values were once correct
A deterministic rule applied the same way on every replica, such as choosing the highest write ID
Restart both replicas, so that they reload their data from disk
Wait longer for the lag to shrink, so that the writes finally arrive in order
optionExplain: Keeping what each has leaves them different.
Right: the same deterministic rule applied everywhere gives every replica the same winner.
A restart does not change the stored state.
Both writes have already arrived; waiting changes nothing.
questions.explain: All replicas must use the same rule on the same inputs to reach the same answer.
questions.rule: Same rule, same inputs, same result.

questions.q: True or false: In a multi-leader configuration there is a natural order of writes that makes one final value more correct than the other.
questions.explain: There is no defined ordering, and neither order is more correct than the other.

questions.q: Which statement about the single-leader case contrasts with multi-leader?
options: Conflicts need a merge function, because writes arrive at several nodes
Replicas may end with different values, because writes arrive at several nodes
The last write in the leader's sequence determines the final value
There is no ordering of writes, because many nodes accept writes
optionExplain: A merge function is needed in multi-leader systems, not with one ordering leader.
With one leader, replicas converge by following its log.
Right: a single leader applies writes in sequence, so the last write sets the final value.
A single leader does order all writes.
questions.explain: The leader applies writes in sequence; if several updates hit one field, the last one wins.
questions.teaches: A single-leader database applies writes in a sequential order: if there are several updates to the same field, the last write determines the final value of the field.

questions.q: A team proposes: each replica keeps whichever write it received first. Does this give convergence?
options: No, replicas that received writes in different orders would keep different values
Yes, because first writes are older and so more trustworthy
Yes, because replicas copy each other's values until they are equal
Yes, since the first write is the true one and later writes are retries
optionExplain: Right: replicas that saw the two writes in different orders would keep different values.
Older does not mean agreed; each replica has a different first write.
Copying is not part of the rule, so nothing makes them equal.
Neither write is the true one without an agreed order.
questions.explain: A rule based on local arrival order cannot make replicas agree.
questions.teaches: One convergent rule is to give each replica a unique ID and let writes that originated at a higher-numbered replica always take precedence over writes from a lower-numbered replica; this also implies data loss.

questions.q: Two replicas must choose between titles B and C. Which method keeps both writes' information?
options: Keep the write with the higher ID, which discards the other write
Record both in a structure and resolve later
Keep the write from the higher-numbered replica, which discards the other write
Keep whichever write arrived first, which discards the other write
optionExplain: The higher ID wins and the other write is lost.
Right: recording the conflict keeps both writes for application code or a user to resolve later.
The higher-numbered replica wins and the other write is lost.
First arrival wins and the other write is lost.
questions.explain: Some methods pick a winner and others keep both. The card next lists them.

questions.q: Match each method to how it settles the conflict.
pairs: Keep all versions for later resolution
questions.explain: Four strategies, with the first two discarding data.

questions.q: Replies are separate rows and are rarely edited concurrently. If some loss is tolerable, which conflict method is acceptable?
options: Leave conflicts unresolved, because rare conflicts can be ignored safely
Merge every field with random text, because that keeps both inputs
Stop replication for that table, because conflicts cannot occur without it
Pick the write with the highest ID, which is simple and converges
optionExplain: Unresolved conflicts leave replicas permanently different.
Random text is not a meaningful merge of two inputs.
Stopping replication gives up its benefits for the whole table.
Right: with rare conflicts and tolerable loss, a highest-ID rule makes all replicas converge.
questions.explain: Simple rules are acceptable when loss is tolerable and conflicts are rare.
questions.rule: Match the method to the loss you can accept.

questions.q: Sort each method into whether it can lose a concurrent write or keeps all information.

items.t: Highest write ID wins
Last write wins using timestamps
Higher-numbered replica takes precedence
Record the conflict for application code to resolve
Keep all versions and prompt the user later
Merge the values alphabetically

questions.explain: Winner-picking discards writes; merging and recording keep information.

questions.q: How does the chapter describe last write wins?
options: Popular, but dangerously prone to data loss
Rare and lossless, because it merges concurrent values
Safe and recommended for all data, because every replica ends with the same value
Used only for numeric fields, because timestamps do not compare for text
optionExplain: Right: popular, but the chapter calls it dangerously prone to data loss.
It is popular and lossy.
The authors warn against it where losing data is not acceptable.
It applies to any value that carries a timestamp.
questions.explain: When timestamps are the write IDs, picking the highest drops the other writes.
questions.teaches: If a timestamp is used, this technique is known as last write wins (LWW). Although this approach is popular, it is dangerously prone to data loss.

questions.q: A to-do app stores tags as a set. Two users add different tags concurrently. Which resolution loses nothing?
options: Keep the set from the later timestamp, which holds the most recent edit
Keep the set from the lower-numbered replica, which wins whenever there is a tie
Take the union of both sets, so every tag that either user added is kept
Discard both sets and ask the users to add their tags again from scratch
optionExplain: The later set drops the tag that the other user added.
The lower replica set drops the tag that the other user added.
Right: the union keeps every tag either user added, so nothing is lost.
Discarding both sets loses every tag, which is worse than losing one.
questions.explain: Merging suits data where combining is meaningful.
questions.teaches: For a shopping cart, a reasonable way to merge concurrent values is to take their union.

questions.q: A conflict handler needs to ask the user which version to keep. At which point can it do so?
options: At write time, inside the background process that runs the conflict handler
During replication lag, while the changes are still travelling between nodes
At read time, when the versions are returned to the application
During failover, when a new leader is being chosen
optionExplain: A write-time handler runs in the background and cannot prompt anyone.
Lag is a delay, not a place to run code.
Right: when conflicting versions are returned on read, the application can prompt the user.
Failover is a different event with no user in the loop.
questions.explain: The two hook points differ in who is available. The card next compares them.

questions.q: Match each item to its description.
pairs: The database calls a handler when it detects the conflict
Conflicting versions are returned for the application to resolve
It runs in the background and must execute quickly
questions.explain: Write-time handlers run automatically; read-time resolution is done by the application.

questions.q: A collaborative address book must let the user decide between two edited phone numbers. Which hook fits?
options: On read, returning both versions to the application
On write, in a quick background handler that picks one of the numbers
On failover, by the controller that chooses the new leader
On snapshot, by the tool that copies data to a new follower
optionExplain: Right: only read-time resolution returns both versions to the application, which can ask the user.
A background handler cannot prompt a user and must run quickly.
Failover is not a place for resolving data conflicts.
Snapshots do not resolve conflicts.
questions.explain: Asking the user requires an interactive point, which exists when the data is read.

questions.q: True or false: If a transaction atomically writes three rows and conflicts with another transaction, the conflict is resolved for the whole transaction as one unit.
questions.explain: Conflict resolution usually applies at the level of an individual row or document, so each write is considered separately.

questions.q: Which database does the chapter name as resolving conflicts on read?
options: Bucardo
Cassandra
PostgreSQL
CouchDB
optionExplain: Bucardo is the on-write example, with a Perl snippet.
Cassandra is leaderless and uses last write wins only.
PostgreSQL is not named as resolving on read.
Right: CouchDB stores all conflicting writes and returns them on the next read.
questions.explain: CouchDB keeps the conflicting versions and the next read returns all of them.
questions.teaches: On read: when a conflict is detected, all the conflicting writes are stored. The next time the data is read, these multiple versions are returned to the application. CouchDB works this way.

questions.q: A team uses a write-time handler written in Perl. It must run in a background process. What constraint follows?
options: It may wait for the user to respond, because the handler runs inside the user's request
It must execute quickly and cannot interact with a user
It can only run on followers, because leaders must stay free for writes
It needs a quorum of nodes to agree before it may run
optionExplain: The handler runs in the background, so no user is waiting to respond.
Right: a background handler cannot prompt a user and must execute quickly.
The handler is invoked when the database detects a conflict, on any node.
Quorums are unrelated to write-time handlers.
questions.explain: Bucardo lets you write a snippet of Perl for this purpose, run when the conflict is detected.
questions.rule: Write-time code is quick and automatic.
questions.teaches: The conflict handler typically cannot prompt a user: it runs in a background process and it must execute quickly.

questions.q: Two copies of a cart disagree: one has an item removed. A rule keeps every item that appears in either copy. What happens to the removed item?
options: It reappears, since the rule cannot tell a removal from an item never added
It stays removed, because the copy that removed it is the more recent one
It is shown twice, because both copies contribute their own entry for it
The cart is emptied, because the two copies disagree and so are discarded
optionExplain: Right: the other copy still lists the item, and a rule that keeps every item brings it back.
The rule keeps any item found in either copy, including the removed one.
A merge by union lists each item once, not twice.
Nothing in the rule discards the whole cart.
questions.explain: The rule cannot tell a removal from an item never added. The card next gives the real case.

questions.q: For some time the conflict resolution logic on Amazon's cart preserved items added to the cart but not items ____ from it.
questions.explain: As a result, customers sometimes saw removed items reappear.

questions.q: A playlist merges concurrent edits by union. A user deletes a song on the phone while the laptop still lists it. What does the user see after sync?
options: The song stays deleted, because the phone changed its list most recently
Both devices are cleared, because the two lists disagree and cannot be kept
The deleted song returns, since the laptop still lists it and the union adds it back
The playlist is locked until the user decides, because a conflict was detected
optionExplain: The union keeps anything present in either list, whichever changed last.
Disagreement does not clear lists under a union merge.
Right: the laptop still lists the song and the union adds it back.
Locking is not part of the described merge.
questions.explain: This is the same failure as in the cart: the removal is not remembered.
questions.rule: Remember removals as well as additions.

questions.q: True or false: If the cart logic also recorded removals explicitly, removed items would stay removed after a conflict is resolved.
questions.explain: A removal that is remembered cannot be undone by the other copy's older view. The chapter later calls such a record a tombstone.

questions.q: Why does the chapter cite this example?
options: It shows leaderless replication is better, because carts are never in conflict there
It is a frequently cited example of surprising effects from a conflict resolution handler
It proves multi-leader replication never works, because large shops abandoned it
It shows carts need synchronous writes, because asynchronous carts lose items
optionExplain: The chapter makes no such comparison.
Right: it is a frequently cited example of surprising effects from a conflict resolution handler.
The chapter says multi-leader is hard, not impossible.
Synchronous writes are not the point of the example.
questions.explain: Custom resolution code is error-prone even at large companies.
questions.teaches: Amazon is a frequently cited example of surprising effects due to a conflict resolution handler.

questions.q: A task tracker merges concurrent edits to a checklist by union. What defect should testers look for?
options: Items disappearing after any edit, because the merge discards one side
Edits being refused, because the merge cannot accept concurrent changes
Tasks being sorted randomly, because the merge does not preserve order
Completed or removed items reappearing after a merge
optionExplain: A union keeps items rather than dropping them.
A union does not refuse edits.
A union does not sort.
Right: a union brings back items that were removed in only one copy.
questions.explain: Any add-and-remove data type merged by union has this risk.
questions.teaches: If an item has been removed in only one of two sibling carts, taking the union of the siblings makes the removed item reappear.

questions.q: Which kind of structure can be edited by many users at once and merge automatically in sensible ways?
options: A write-ahead log, which records each change in order
A timestamp column, which picks the newest value
A secondary index, which speeds up queries
A conflict-free replicated datatype
optionExplain: A log records writes in order but does not merge them.
A timestamp alone picks a winner and discards the rest.
An index speeds queries and has no merge rule.
Right: conflict-free replicated datatypes are built so that concurrent edits merge sensibly.
questions.explain: Some data structures are designed so that concurrent edits merge. The card next names them.

questions.q: Match each approach to its key idea.
pairs: Data structures that merge concurrent edits automatically
Resolves edits to an ordered list such as text
questions.explain: Three approaches with different mechanisms.

questions.q: A team builds a shared collaborative text field. Which technique does the chapter link to Etherpad and Google Docs?
options: Last write wins, which keeps the edit with the biggest timestamp and drops the rest
Operational transformation, built for concurrent edits to an ordered list of items
Hinted handoff, which returns writes held on other nodes to their home nodes
Statement-based replication, which ships the SQL statement text to the followers
optionExplain: Last write wins would discard one editor changes, which a shared text field cannot accept.
Right: operational transformation is the algorithm behind Etherpad and Google Docs.
Hinted handoff belongs to sloppy quorums, not to text editing.
Statement-based replication is a replication log format, not a way to merge edits.
questions.explain: Text is an ordered list of characters, the case OT was designed for.

questions.q: True or false: CRDTs and mergeable persistent data structures both use a three-way merge function.
questions.explain: Mergeable persistent structures use a three-way merge function, whereas CRDTs use two-way merges.

questions.q: Which database does the chapter say implemented some CRDTs?
options: MySQL
Kafka
Riak 2.0
VoltDB
optionExplain: MySQL is named for other things in this chapter, not for CRDTs.
Kafka is a broker with leader-based replication.
Right: some CRDTs have been implemented in Riak 2.0.
VoltDB is named for statement-based replication.
questions.explain: Riak implemented CRDTs for its datatypes.
questions.teaches: Some CRDTs have been implemented in Riak 2.0.

questions.q: A team needs a counter incremented from many devices, where no increment may be lost. What suits the chapter's research?
options: A CRDT counter that merges concurrent increments
Last write wins on a single number, so the counter holds the latest value
A lock held by one device at a time, so increments are serialized
Dropping the older increments, so the counter shows only the newest
optionExplain: Right: counters are among the CRDT types, which merge concurrent increments instead of overwriting them.
Last write wins would lose increments.
A single lock defeats offline use and independent devices.
Dropping increments loses data.
questions.explain: Counters are one of the data types CRDTs cover.
questions.teaches: Mergeable persistent data structures use a three-way merge function, whereas CRDTs use two-way merges.

questions.q: Two leaders each accept a booking for the same room and hour, after each checking the room was free. What is this?
options: No conflict, since each leader checked and found the room free
A conflict, since each check passed locally but the bookings overlap
A stale read of the room list, since one leader saw outdated bookings
A split brain, since two leaders accepted bookings for the same room
optionExplain: A successful local check does not prevent a clash with the other leader's write.
Right: each check passed locally, yet the two bookings overlap, which breaks the application's rule.
Neither leader read stale data; neither had seen the other booking.
Both leaders are legitimate in this design, so it is not split brain.
questions.explain: Each leader could not see the other's booking. The card next generalizes.

questions.q: True or false: A conflict can exist even when no two writes touch the same field.
questions.explain: Two different bookings can overlap in time for one room.

questions.q: A conference app lets two organizers each add a talk at 10:00 in Room 1 on separate leaders. Why does the availability check not help?
options: Availability checks are forbidden on leaders, because they slow writes down
Rooms are always free until a conference starts, so checks give no information
The check ran on a follower, which does not see leader bookings
Each check ran on one leader and could not see the concurrent booking
optionExplain: Checks are allowed; they are just local to one leader.
Rooms are not always free; that is why overlapping bookings matter.
The checks ran on leaders, not on followers.
Right: each check ran on one leader and could not see the booking made concurrently on the other.
questions.explain: The check reads local state only.
questions.rule: Local checks cannot see remote writes.

questions.q: After the two bookings replicate, a leader can detect two ____ for the same room at the same time.
questions.explain: The overlap becomes visible once both writes are present on one leader.

questions.q: Where does the chapter say it will discuss scalable approaches for detecting and resolving conflicts in a replicated system?
options: In Chapter 12, which discusses scalable approaches to detecting and resolving conflicts
In Chapter 1, which sets out the goals of reliable, scalable data systems
In Chapter 3, which covers how storage engines lay out data on disk
Nowhere in the book, since the chapter says the problem has no answer
optionExplain: Right: the chapter points forward to Chapter 12 for scalable approaches.
Chapter 1 sets out the goals of data systems and does not treat conflicts.
Chapter 3 covers storage engines and does not treat conflicts.
The chapter points to a later chapter, so it does not say there is no answer.
questions.explain: The problem is revisited later, with more examples in Chapter 7.
questions.teaches: We will see some more examples of conflicts in Chapter 7, and in Chapter 12 we will discuss scalable approaches for detecting and resolving conflicts in a replicated system.

questions.q: A bank allows two branches to withdraw from one account on separate leaders. Each checks the balance first. What is the conflict?
options: Two writes to the same field, which is the obvious kind of conflict
A stale follower, which returned an out-of-date balance
Withdrawals together exceeding the balance, though each looked fine locally
A timeout, which stopped one branch from completing its withdrawal
optionExplain: The writes may touch different records; the conflict is in the combined effect.
Each branch checked a balance that was fresh on its own leader.
Right: together the withdrawals overdraw the account, although each looked fine on its own leader.
No timeout is involved.
questions.explain: The invariant "balance not negative" is broken by combining two valid local writes.
questions.teaches: Conflict resolution usually applies at the level of an individual row or document, not an entire transaction; each write of an atomic multi-write transaction is considered separately.

questions.q: Four leaders pass each write along a ring, each node forwarding to the next. What is this topology?
options: Star, in which a central node forwards writes to all of the other nodes
Circular, in which each node receives from one node and forwards to the next
All-to-all, in which every leader sends its writes to every other leader
Leaderless, in which any replica accepts writes straight from the clients
optionExplain: A star has a single root forwarding to all the others, not a ring.
Right: each node receives from one node and forwards to one other, which is the circular topology.
All-to-all has direct links between every pair, not a chain.
Leaderless has no leaders at all, while this setup has four.
questions.explain: The shape of the paths defines the topology. The card next names three.

questions.q: Match each topology to its description.
pairs: Every leader sends writes to every other leader
Each node forwards writes to one other node
A root node forwards writes to all others
questions.explain: Each topology fixes who talks to whom.

questions.q: A team has five datacenter leaders. They want each write to reach every leader through the fewest hops. Which topology fits?
options: Circular, in which writes pass from node to node around a ring
A star with one root, which relays every write to the others
Leaderless, in which clients send writes to several replicas
All-to-all, with direct links between every pair
optionExplain: A ring needs several hops to reach the far side.
A star needs two hops via the root.
Leaderless is a different approach and does not answer the topology question.
Right: all-to-all gives direct links, so each write reaches every leader in one hop.
questions.explain: All-to-all gives direct paths between all leaders.

questions.q: True or false: A star topology in this chapter is the same thing as a star schema in a data warehouse.
questions.explain: A star topology describes communication between nodes, whereas a star schema describes the structure of a data model.
questions.rule: Do not confuse the two stars.

questions.q: Which topology does MySQL support by default for multi-leader replication, according to the chapter?
options: Circular
All-to-all
Star
Tree
optionExplain: Right: MySQL by default supports only the circular topology.
All-to-all is the most general topology, not MySQL's default.
A star is another shape that some deployments use.
A tree generalizes the star.
questions.explain: MySQL by default supports only a circular topology.
questions.teaches: MySQL by default supports only a circular topology, in which each node receives writes from one node and forwards those writes plus its own to one other node.

questions.q: A company has one headquarters leader and ten branch leaders. Branches send writes to headquarters, which relays them to everyone. Which topology is it?
options: Circular, in which each node forwards to one other node
All-to-all, in which every pair of leaders is directly connected
Star, which can generalize to a tree
Leaderless, in which any node accepts writes from clients
optionExplain: A ring has no central root.
All-to-all has direct links between branches too.
Right: one root relays writes to all the other nodes, which is a star, and a star generalizes to a tree.
These nodes are leaders.
questions.explain: One designated root forwarding to all the others defines the star.
questions.teaches: MySQL by default supports only a circular topology.

questions.q: In a ring of leaders, how can a node tell that a change has already been processed by it?
options: The change is older than one minute, so it must have travelled around already
The change contains no values, since a changed row is applied only once
The change is tagged with the node's own identifier
The node has a faster clock than the others, so it notices repeats
optionExplain: Age does not show which nodes a change has visited.
Changes carry values; emptiness is not the signal.
Right: each write carries the identifiers of nodes it has passed through, including this node's own.
Clock speed does not record the path.
questions.explain: Each node has a unique ID that travels with the write. The card next shows the rule.

questions.q: When a node receives a data change tagged with its own identifier, it ____ the change.
questions.explain: It knows the change already completed a loop.

questions.q: Leader B receives a change tagged [A, C, B]. What should B do?
options: Ignore it, since its own identifier is in the tag
Forward it to A again, so that A knows the change reached B
Apply it a second time, in case the first application failed
Reject all further changes, because a loop has been detected
optionExplain: Right: B's own identifier is in the tag, so B has already processed this change.
Forwarding would restart the loop.
Applying it again could duplicate its effect.
Only the repeated change should be ignored; others are fine.
questions.explain: The tag shows the change has visited B.

questions.q: True or false: Without node identifiers on writes, a circular topology could pass a write around the ring indefinitely.
questions.explain: Each node forwards what it receives, so nothing stops the loop.

questions.q: Which topologies need this loop protection, according to the chapter?
options: Only all-to-all topologies, because they have the most links
Only two-leader setups, because the two leaders send to each other
None, because every write is delivered directly from the origin
Circular and star topologies, where writes pass through several nodes
optionExplain: All-to-all sends directly, so there is no forwarding to loop.
Two leaders send directly to each other.
Circular and star topologies do forward writes.
Right: forwarding creates the loop risk, and circular and star topologies forward writes.
questions.explain: Forwarding is what creates the loop risk.
questions.teaches: In circular and star topologies, a write may need to pass through several nodes before it reaches all replicas, so each write is tagged with the identifiers of all the nodes it has passed through.

questions.q: A team designs a tree of replicas where parents forward to children and also back up. Which protection is needed?
options: A faster network, so that loops end sooner
Per-write tags of visited node IDs
Synchronous replication, so that each change waits for the others
A longer failover timeout, so that loops are tolerated
optionExplain: Speed does not stop a change from circling.
Right: tags of visited node IDs let a node ignore a change that has come back to it.
Replication mode does not stop forwarding loops.
Timeouts are for failure detection.
questions.explain: Any forwarding structure with cycles needs such tags.
questions.teaches: In circular and star topologies, if just one node fails it can interrupt the flow of replication messages between other nodes; reconfiguring around it usually has to be done manually.

questions.q: In a ring of leaders, one node fails. What happens to replication between the others?
options: It can be interrupted until the topology is reconfigured
It continues unaffected, because the other nodes can pass writes through the failed one
It switches automatically to synchronous mode, so the survivors stay equal
It stops permanently, because a ring cannot be repaired
optionExplain: Right: the failed node was a relay, so the flow is interrupted until the topology is reconfigured.
The failed node cannot relay anything while it is down.
Replication mode does not change by itself.
It can be restored by reconfiguring or by the node returning.
questions.explain: Nodes in a ring depend on each other to relay. The card next compares topologies.
questions.rule: Relays are single points of failure.

questions.q: True or false: In most deployments, working around a failed node in a circular or star topology is done automatically.
questions.explain: The topology could be reconfigured, but in most deployments that must be done manually.

questions.q: A company has six leaders and cannot afford replication to stop if any one fails. Which topology reduces that risk?
options: A single-ring topology, in which each node passes writes to the next
A star with one root, which relays all writes to the others
All-to-all, since writes can take different paths
A chain of leaders, in which each forwards to the next in line
optionExplain: A ring depends on every node staying up.
The root is a single point of failure.
Right: all-to-all offers several paths, so no single node failure cuts off the others.
A chain breaks at the first failed link.
questions.explain: More paths mean no single point of failure.

questions.q: Sort each property into the topology it describes.

items.t: One failed node can interrupt flow between other nodes
Messages can travel along different paths
Reconfiguration around a failure is usually manual
Writes can overtake each other on faster links
Each write may pass through several nodes
Better fault tolerance from dense connections

questions.explain: Sparse topologies are fragile to node failure, while dense ones face ordering issues.

questions.q: What problem does the chapter say all-to-all topologies can have?
options: They cannot survive a node failure, because every node depends on every other
Some replication messages may overtake others
They need synchronous replication, because direct links must be confirmed
They cannot forward writes, because every node sends only its own
optionExplain: They survive failures better than sparse topologies.
Right: some network links are faster than others, so messages can overtake each other.
Replication mode is unrelated.
They do not need to forward writes; the issue is ordering.
questions.explain: Some network links are faster than others, for example due to congestion.
questions.teaches: In all-to-all topologies some network links may be faster than others, with the result that some replication messages may overtake others.

questions.q: A star topology's root leader is rebooted for a patch. What is the effect on the other leaders?
options: They keep replicating through it, because the root caches the writes
They become all-to-all automatically, because the nodes connect directly
They stop accepting writes for good, because their data depends on the root
They cannot exchange writes through it until it returns or the topology is changed
optionExplain: A rebooting root cannot relay while it is down.
No automatic change of topology is described.
The other leaders continue to accept local writes.
Right: the root is the only relay, so the others cannot exchange writes until it returns or the topology changes.
questions.explain: The root is a single point of failure.
questions.rule: Roots and ring nodes are relays.
questions.teaches: In all-to-all topologies some links are faster than others, so replication messages can overtake each other: a leader may receive an update to a row before it receives the insert that created the row.

questions.q: An update to a row reaches a replica before the insert that created the row. What is the problem called in the chapter?
options: A split brain, in which two leaders both believe they are the only leader
A hash collision, in which two keys map to the same node
A lost snapshot, in which a follower cannot find its starting copy
A causality problem from messages overtaking each other
optionExplain: Only one leader wrote each of the two changes.
No hashing is involved in the scenario.
No snapshot is involved.
Right: the update depends on the insert, so receiving it first is a causality problem.
questions.explain: The dependency means order matters. The card next gives the setup.

questions.q: True or false: Attaching a timestamp to every write is sufficient to order dependent writes correctly across leaders.
questions.explain: Clocks cannot be trusted to be sufficiently in sync to order such events correctly.

questions.q: Leader 2 receives an update setting the price of item 99 before the create for item 99. What should a correct system do?
options: Drop the update permanently, because the row it refers to does not exist
Process the create first, then the update
Apply the update to a blank item, so that the price is stored for later
Wait for the clocks of all leaders to agree before applying either change
optionExplain: Dropping the update loses a legitimate change.
Right: the update depends on the create, so the create must be processed first.
A blank item is an invalid state.
Waiting for clocks does not establish which change depends on which.
questions.explain: Order must respect dependency.

questions.q: If leader 3's clock runs behind, the update may carry an ____ timestamp than the insert it depends on.
questions.explain: A lagging clock stamps a later event with an earlier time, which is why timestamps cannot order dependent writes.

questions.q: Which products does the chapter say fall short on ordering or conflict detection?
options: Cassandra and Riak, which the chapter calls leaderless databases
Kafka and RabbitMQ, which the chapter calls leader-based message brokers
PostgreSQL BDR has no causal ordering, and Tungsten Replicator for MySQL does not try to detect conflicts
CouchDB and Etherpad, which the chapter links to offline and collaborative editing
optionExplain: Those are named as Dynamo-style leaderless databases.
Those are named as brokers that use leader-based replication.
Right: BDR lacks causal ordering and Tungsten Replicator does not even try to detect conflicts.
Those are named for offline and collaborative use.
questions.explain: Conflict detection is poorly implemented in many multi-leader systems.
questions.teaches: At the time of writing, PostgreSQL BDR does not provide causal ordering of writes, and Tungsten Replicator for MySQL does not even try to detect conflicts.

questions.q: A team plans a multi-leader product and trusts its documentation's claim of ordering. What does the chapter advise?
options: Read the documentation carefully and test that it provides the guarantees you believe it has
Trust the claim without testing, since vendors document their guarantees precisely
Add a timestamp column, since timestamps order dependent writes
Turn off replication, since multi-leader systems cannot give causal ordering
optionExplain: Right: read the documentation carefully and test that it provides the guarantees you believe it has.
The chapter warns that conflict detection is poorly implemented in many systems.
Timestamps are not enough because clocks cannot be trusted to be in sync.
Replication is the goal, so removing it defeats the purpose.
questions.explain: Check what the system really guarantees.
questions.teaches: It is worth being aware of these issues, carefully reading the documentation, and thoroughly testing your database to ensure that it really does provide the guarantees you believe it to have.

questions.q: A database lets clients send a write to any replica, with no designated leader. What does it give up compared with single-leader?
options: The ability to read, since reads need a node that has the latest data
A single authority that orders writes
All replication, since copying data needs a leader to drive it
The use of the network, since replicas no longer talk to each other
optionExplain: Reads still work in a leaderless database.
Right: with no leader, no node fixes a single order for writes.
Writes are still copied to several replicas.
Clients and replicas still use the network.
questions.explain: Without a leader nobody orders the writes. The card next states the consequences.

questions.q: Databases such as Riak, Cassandra and Voldemort are called ____-style because they were inspired by Amazon's in-house system.
questions.explain: Amazon's Dynamo revived leaderless replication.

questions.q: A team is choosing between a leader-based store and Cassandra for a service that must accept writes during node reboots. Which property of Cassandra helps?
options: It has a leader that is always up, so writes never wait
It forbids reboots, so the problem never arises
It orders all writes globally, so reboots cannot cause conflicts
Any replica can accept writes, so no failover is needed
optionExplain: Cassandra has no leader.
Reboots are permitted and routine.
It does not impose a global order of writes.
Right: any replica can accept writes, so no failover is needed while one node reboots.
questions.explain: Without a leader there is nothing to fail over.

questions.q: True or false: DynamoDB, the AWS hosted product, uses the same leaderless architecture as Amazon's in-house Dynamo system.
questions.explain: Confusingly, DynamoDB uses a completely different architecture based on single-leader replication, and Dynamo is not available outside Amazon.
questions.rule: Do not equate DynamoDB with Dynamo.

questions.q: What does the chapter say about the history of leaderless systems?
options: Some of the earliest replicated systems were leaderless, but the idea was mostly forgotten in the era of relational databases
They were invented by Amazon for its in-house Dynamo system in the 2000s
They were never used before 2007, when open source databases appeared
They replaced relational databases in every large company within a few years
optionExplain: Right: some of the earliest replicated systems were leaderless, but the idea was mostly forgotten for a long time.
Amazon revived the idea; it did not invent it.
Earlier systems used it, according to the chapter.
Relational databases remained dominant for long after.
questions.explain: Dynamo made the architecture fashionable again.
questions.teaches: Some of the earliest replicated data systems were leaderless, but the idea was mostly forgotten during the era of dominance of relational databases.

questions.q: A shop wants one component to decide the order in which cart changes are applied, for all replicas. Does leaderless replication give that?
options: Yes, because the coordinator acts as a hidden leader for all writes
Yes, because Dynamo-style stores attach a global timestamp to every write
No, a coordinator in a leaderless design does not enforce an ordering of writes
Yes, because leaderless replication orders all writes by default
optionExplain: The coordinator forwards writes and does not order them.
Timestamps do not give a single agreed order.
Right: unlike a leader, a coordinator in a leaderless design does not enforce an ordering of writes.
No ordering is provided by default.
questions.explain: The difference from a leader is that no node enforces order.
questions.teaches: Unlike a leader database, the coordinator does not enforce a particular ordering of writes.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: A leaderless database has three replicas and one is rebooting. A write is acknowledged by two. What does the client do?
options: Fails the write and reports an error until all three replicas have responded
Starts a failover to promote one of the replicas to be the new leader
Treats the write as successful, since two of three acknowledgments are enough
Keeps the connection open and retries until the third replica responds
optionExplain: Requiring every replica would make any single reboot stop all writes, which leaderless designs avoid.
There is no leader to replace in a leaderless design, so no failover happens.
Right: the write needs only the required number of acknowledgments, so the reboot does not block it.
Waiting for the rebooting node would stall the client for no benefit; the required count is already met.
questions.explain: The client sends to all replicas and waits for enough replies. The card next explains.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: In a leaderless configuration, failover does not ____.
questions.explain: There is no leader to replace.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: A cluster of three replicas tolerates one missing acknowledgment. One replica is down for an hour. Can writes continue?
options: Yes, as long as the required number of replicas acknowledge each write
No, every write needs all three replicas to acknowledge, so the outage blocks writes
Only after an operator promotes a replica to take over the write role
Only reads continue, while writes wait until the third replica returns
optionExplain: Right: with two live replicas meeting the write requirement, writes continue through the outage.
That would be true only if the configuration demanded every replica, which defeats the purpose.
Promotion is a leader-based step; here no node holds a special write role.
Writes meeting the required count succeed, so they are not held back by one missing node.
questions.explain: The success threshold is below the replica count.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: True or false: A replica that returns after an outage immediately holds all the writes made while it was down.
questions.explain: It missed them, so reads served only by it may return stale values until it is repaired.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: How does the client tell which of several different read responses is newer?
options: By comparing the size of each returned value and keeping the larger one
By choosing the value from the replica with the alphabetically first hostname
By asking the end user which of the returned values is correct
By comparing version numbers attached to the values the replicas return
optionExplain: Size says nothing about recency; a newer value can be shorter.
A hostname is a label for the machine and carries no information about when data was written.
Users are not consulted on every read; the client uses version numbers to decide.
Right: version numbers let the client decide which value is newer.
questions.explain: Version numbers are used to determine which value is newer.
questions.teaches: The client may get different responses from different nodes, and version numbers are used to determine which value is newer.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: A chat service uses leaderless replication. One node fails during a deploy. Compared with a leader-based setup, what operational step is saved?
options: Replication logs no longer have to be written or shipped between nodes
No failover is needed to keep writes flowing when one node goes down
Monitoring of replica health can be dropped because nodes repair themselves
Clients no longer need any knowledge of the replicas they talk to
optionExplain: Leaderless databases still replicate data to several nodes; they only skip the leader role.
Right: with no leader, a failed node simply does not acknowledge, and the others carry on.
Monitoring still matters, for example to see lag and staleness; only the failover step disappears.
Clients still send requests to several replicas and compare their answers, so they know the replicas.
questions.explain: The leaderless design removes the promote-a-leader step.
questions.teaches: In some leaderless implementations a coordinator node sends writes to the replicas on behalf of the client, but unlike a leader it does not enforce a particular ordering of writes.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: A client reads from three replicas and gets version 7 twice and version 6 once. What can it do?
options: Write version 7 back to the replica that returned version 6
Ignore the difference, since two replicas agree and the stale one is harmless
Delete version 7 so that all three replicas return to the older state
Wait for a leader to notice and push the fix to the lagging replica
optionExplain: Right: the client sees the stale replica and writes the newer value to it.
Ignoring the difference leaves a stale replica in place, lowering durability of that value.
Deleting the newer value would lose a legitimate write.
Leaderless databases have no leader to push fixes; the client does the repair itself.
questions.explain: The read reveals which replica is behind. The card next names the technique.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: When a client notices a stale response during a read and writes the newer value back, this is called read ____.
questions.explain: The reader repairs the stale replica.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: A product page key is read thousands of times a day from several replicas. One replica missed a write. How quickly is it likely to be fixed?
options: Only after the stale replica is restarted by an operator who notices it
Not at all, because a missed write cannot be recovered without a leader
Quickly, since the next read that reaches the stale replica repairs it
Only after a nightly job compares replicas and copies the missing writes
optionExplain: A restart is not what triggers repair; reads that see the stale answer do.
Missed writes are recoverable here, because a later read can carry the newer value over.
Right: a frequently read key gets repaired the next time the stale replica answers a read.
A background sweep is a different mechanism, anti-entropy, not the read repair in this scenario.
questions.explain: Frequently read values are repaired fast.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: True or false: A value that is rarely read is repaired as quickly by read repair as a value that is read constantly.
questions.explain: Read repair happens only when the value is read, so rarely read values can stay stale.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: What can happen to a rarely read value if only read repair is used?
options: It is copied automatically by the leader as soon as a replica falls behind
It may be missing from some replicas, which reduces its durability
It is deleted by the database since nobody reads it and it looks unused
It becomes synchronous, so each replica holds it with equal certainty
optionExplain: There is no leader in this design to do any copying.
Right: without reads there is no repair, so some replicas may never receive the value.
Rarely read data is not removed; it simply stays on fewer replicas than intended.
Replication mode is not changed by read frequency; the value just stays unrepaired.
questions.explain: Read repair is only performed when a value is read by the application.
questions.rule: Read repair alone leaves cold data exposed.
questions.teaches: Without an anti-entropy process, values that are rarely read may be missing from some replicas and thus have reduced durability, because read repair is only performed when a value is read.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: An archive stores records read once a year, replicated leaderlessly with read repair only. What risk grows?
options: Reads turning synchronous, which makes each yearly read far slower than before
The leader becoming overloaded by a yearly burst of reads on archived records
Version numbers being reused, so older records overwrite the newer ones
A record missing from some replicas for months, with reduced durability
optionExplain: Read mode stays unchanged; the problem is the long gap between repairs.
There is no leader in a leaderless archive, so none can be overloaded.
Version numbering is not affected by how often a record is read.
Right: records read once a year are repaired only then, so replicas can lag for months.
questions.explain: Cold data has no reads to trigger repair.
questions.teaches: Without an anti-entropy process, values that are rarely read may be missing from some replicas and thus have reduced durability, because read repair is only performed when a value is read by the application.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: Which mechanism repairs replicas even for data nobody reads?
options: Read repair, which fixes replicas whenever the client reads the stale value
A synchronous follower that confirms every write before the client is told
A failover, which promotes a replica that holds the newest copy of the data
A background anti-entropy process that compares replicas and copies missing data
optionExplain: Read repair needs a read; data nobody reads is never touched by it.
A synchronous follower is a leader-based concept and does not repair existing gaps.
Failover applies to leader-based systems and replaces a leader; it does not sync unread data.
Right: only a background process can repair data that no client ever reads.
questions.explain: Read repair depends on reads. The card next adds a background tool.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: True or false: An anti-entropy process copies writes between replicas in the same order as a leader-based replication log.
questions.explain: It does not copy writes in any particular order, and there may be a significant delay.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: A store has both mechanisms. A key was written while a replica was down and is not read by any client. How does the replica get it?
options: Read repair triggers on its own and copies the key to the recovered replica
The background anti-entropy process finds the gap and copies the missing data
The client that originally issued the write resends it once the replica is back
It does not; a replica that missed a write stays behind for good
optionExplain: Read repair runs only as part of a read, and this key is never read.
Right: a background comparison of replicas finds keys that nobody reads and fills the gap.
Clients do not keep and resend old writes after the replica returns.
The background process exists precisely so a missed write is not permanent.
questions.explain: Only the background process covers unread keys.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: Sort each property into read repair or the anti-entropy process.

items.t: Triggered when a client reads a value
Runs constantly in the background
Works well for frequently read values
Copies data that nobody reads
Done by the client that detects the stale response
May copy with a significant delay

questions.explain: Read repair is reactive and client-driven; anti-entropy is a background sweep.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: Which database does the chapter say lacks an anti-entropy process?
options: Cassandra, which the chapter says relies only on read repair
Riak, which the chapter says leaves background repair to the operator
Voldemort, which the chapter says has no anti-entropy process
CouchDB, which the chapter says uses a single leader for repair
optionExplain: The chapter does not describe Cassandra that way.
The chapter does not describe Riak that way.
Right: the chapter notes that without an anti-entropy process, values read rarely have reduced durability, for example in Voldemort.
CouchDB is not mentioned in this context and has no repair leader.
questions.explain: Not all systems implement both mechanisms.
questions.rule: Check which mechanisms your store has.
questions.teaches: Not all systems implement both; for example, Voldemort currently does not have an anti-entropy process.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: Your store only has read repair. A compliance rule needs every replica to hold every record within a day. What follows?
options: Do not rely on read repair alone; look for a background repair mechanism
Read repair suffices, because every record is eventually read by someone
Switch to a single leader, since a leader guarantees all replicas match
Lower the number of replicas so that fewer copies have to be kept in sync
optionExplain: Right: only a background process can guarantee that unread records reach every replica within a day.
Records that are never read are never repaired, so the deadline can be missed.
A leader does not guarantee that asynchronous replicas are in sync within a time limit.
Fewer replicas lowers durability, which works against the compliance goal.
questions.explain: Bounded convergence needs a mechanism that does not depend on reads.
questions.teaches: If a database uses only read repair and no anti-entropy, there is no limit to how old a value might be: a value that is read only rarely may be ancient when returned by a stale replica.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: Three replicas, a write acknowledged by two. A read queries two replicas. Why must it reach a node with the write?
options: Reads always go to the leader, which holds every acknowledged write
The set of nodes written and the set of nodes read must overlap in at least one node
The third replica forwards each write to whichever node later serves a read
Each read triggers a copy of the latest write to the nodes it contacts
optionExplain: There is no leader in this design.
Right: two out of three on each side cannot be disjoint, so at least one node has the latest value.
Forwarding by a third replica is not part of a quorum read or write.
Copying on read is read repair, which is a repair step and not what guarantees the overlap.
questions.explain: Two groups of two out of three cannot be disjoint. The card next generalizes.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: Reads and writes obey the quorum condition when w + r is greater than ____.
questions.explain: n is the number of replicas.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: A database has n = 5. A write needs w = 3 acknowledgments. What is the smallest r that guarantees an up-to-date read?
options: 2, since 3 + 2 = 5 and that equals the number of replicas
1, since a single node can hold the newest value after three acknowledgments
5, since the read must reach every replica to see the value
3, since 3 + 3 = 6 exceeds 5 and the sets must overlap
optionExplain: 3 + 2 equals 5, which is not greater than n, so a read could miss all three write nodes.
One node might be one of the two that did not take the write.
Reading all five is more than the condition needs and hurts availability.
Right: w + r must be greater than n, so r must be at least 3.
questions.explain: The condition is w + r > n, so r must exceed 5 - 3, that is, be at least 3.
questions.rule: Find r from w + r > n.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: With n = 4, which (w, r) pairs satisfy the quorum condition?
optionExplain: 2 + 2 = 4 is not greater than 4.
1 + 3 = 4 is not greater than 4.
questions.explain: Add w and r and compare with n.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: What does the chapter say you can think of r and w as?
options: The minimum number of votes required for the read or write to be valid
The count of leaders that must approve a read or a write before it runs
The maximum size in bytes of each value that can be read or written
The number of datacenters that must hold the data for a request to succeed
optionExplain: Right: the chapter describes r and w as the minimum number of votes needed.
There are no leaders in the leaderless setting being described.
r and w count nodes and not bytes.
They count nodes within the replica set, not datacenters.
questions.explain: Each operation counts successes against a threshold, like a vote.
questions.rule: r and w are vote thresholds.
questions.teaches: You can think of r and w as the minimum number of votes required for the read or write to be valid.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: A team sets n = 6, w = 3, r = 3. Does the quorum condition hold?
options: Yes, because 3 + 3 equals n and so the sets meet at the boundary
Yes, because 3 is a majority of 6 and majorities always overlap
No, 3 + 3 = 6 is not greater than 6, so a read could miss the write
Yes, because an even n guarantees that the halves overlap
optionExplain: Equal is not enough: the read can land on exactly the other three nodes.
Three of six is not a majority, which would need four, so the overlap is not guaranteed.
Right: the condition needs w + r strictly greater than n, and here the sum only equals n.
Parity of n does not create overlap; the sum does.
questions.explain: With w + r = n, the written set and the read set can be completely different.
questions.rule: Equal to n is not enough.
questions.teaches: As long as w + r > n, we expect to get an up-to-date value when reading; with w + r equal to n, the read and write sets could be disjoint.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: A cluster has n = 5 with w = 3 and r = 3. How many nodes can be down while reads and writes still succeed?
options: One, because a second failure would leave too few nodes to form a quorum
Three, because only the last two nodes need to answer a request
Two, because three of five nodes still form a quorum for both reads and writes
Zero, because every node must respond to guarantee that the data is current
optionExplain: Losing two still leaves three, which meets both requirements.
With three down only two remain, below the required three.
Right: with w = r = 3 of 5, any two nodes can be down.
Requiring all five nodes is what w = r = n would mean, not this setting.
questions.explain: The operation needs 3 replies out of 5. The card next gives the general rule.
questions.rule: Tolerated down = n - w (or n - r).
