questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: A common choice sets w = r = (n + 1) / 2, rounded ____.
questions.explain: For n = 5 this gives 3, for n = 3 it gives 2.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: A service uses n = 3 and w = r = 2. One replica crashes. What happens to reads and writes?
options: Both continue, using the two live replicas to meet w and r
Writes stop but reads continue, as reads need fewer nodes
Both stop until a failover chooses a replacement for the crashed replica
Reads stop but writes continue, because writes are queued for later
optionExplain: Right: two live replicas satisfy w = 2 and r = 2, so one crash is tolerated.
Reads and writes need the same two nodes here, so neither alone stops.
There is no failover in this design; quorum arithmetic already allows for one failure.
Writes are not queued; they simply meet their requirement with the live nodes.
questions.explain: Two of three replicas still answer, which meets both thresholds.
questions.rule: One failure is tolerated at n = 3.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: True or false: With n = 3, w = 2 and r = 2, writes still succeed when two of the three replicas have crashed.
questions.explain: Only one replica can answer, which is below w, so the write returns an error.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: For a workload with few writes and many reads, what setting does the chapter suggest, and what is its cost?
options: w = 1 and r = n, which speeds writes but makes every read fail if one node is down
w = r = 1, which is a safe choice because every node always has the latest value
w = n and r = n, which is cheaper because each request touches fewer nodes
w = n and r = 1, which speeds reads but one failed node makes every write fail
optionExplain: That suits a write-heavy workload; the question describes the opposite.
A single node need not have the latest value, so reads may be stale.
Contacting every node is the most expensive option and not cheaper.
Right: with few writes and many reads, cheap reads win, at the cost of writes failing if any node is down.
questions.explain: Moving the threshold onto writes makes reads cheap and writes fragile.
questions.teaches: A workload with few writes and many reads may benefit from setting w = n and r = 1. This makes reads faster, but one failed node causes all database writes to fail.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: A node cannot be reached because its disk is full. Another cannot be reached because of a network break. How does the quorum count them?
options: Only the crashed node, since a full disk still allows reads to succeed
Both as unsuccessful responses, without distinguishing the cause
The full-disk node as a success, since it responded to the connection
Neither, since unreachable nodes are removed from n for the request
optionExplain: The quorum cannot tell why a node failed to respond.
Right: from the client or coordinator, a node that does not respond to the request counts as a failure whatever the cause.
A node that cannot store the write has not acknowledged it.
Nodes are not removed from n; they remain part of the set and simply do not answer.
questions.explain: Only whether the node returned a successful response matters.
questions.rule: Cause is irrelevant to the count.
questions.teaches: We only care whether the node returned a successful response and do not need to distinguish between different kinds of fault.

questions.q: A team lowers r and w so that w + r ≤ n. What is the main risk?
options: Reads are more likely to return stale values, though latency and availability improve
Writes become impossible, since fewer acknowledgments cannot persist the data
The database loses replicas, since smaller quorums delete the extra copies
Clients are rejected, since the database refuses connections under a weak setting
optionExplain: Right: when the sets need not overlap, a read can miss every node that took the write.
Writes become easier, not impossible, since fewer acknowledgments are needed.
Replicas remain; the settings change how many must answer, not how many exist.
Connections are unaffected; only the guarantee on freshness is weakened.
questions.explain: Less overlap means a read may miss the latest write. The card next lists the benefit.

questions.q: True or false: With smaller w and r, the database can keep processing requests when many replicas are unreachable.
questions.explain: It becomes unavailable only when the reachable replicas fall below w or r.
questions.rule: Smaller thresholds are easier to meet.

questions.q: A telemetry store wants very high write availability and tolerates occasionally stale reads. Which setting suits?
options: n = 5, w = 3, r = 3, which needs three nodes for every write
n = 5, w = 5, r = 1, which needs every node for each write
n = 5, w = 1, r = 1, which accepts a write after one acknowledgment
n = 5, w = 4, r = 2, which needs four nodes for each write
optionExplain: Three acknowledgments tolerate fewer failures than one, so write availability is lower.
With w = n any single failure blocks writes, the opposite of the goal.
Right: w = 1 keeps writes available as long as one replica is up, and stale reads are acceptable.
Four acknowledgments make writes even less available than w = 3.
questions.explain: With w = 1 any single node suffices to accept a write.

questions.q: With n = 3, w = 1 and r = 1, the written and read sets can be ____, so a read may miss the write.
questions.explain: Without w + r > n, nothing forces the two sets to share a node.
questions.rule: No overlap guarantee, stale reads possible.

questions.q: Must quorums be majorities, according to the chapter?
options: Yes, a quorum must be a majority of nodes, or reads can miss the write
No, only the read and write sets must overlap in at least one node
Yes, but only for reads, since writes can use any subset of the nodes
No, they need not overlap, because repair will eventually reconcile the values
optionExplain: Majorities are one way to guarantee overlap, but not the only way.
Right: the chapter says quorums need not be majorities; overlap of the read and write sets is what matters.
The overlap condition concerns both the read and the write sets.
Without overlap a read can miss the latest write; repair does not remove that risk at read time.
questions.explain: Other quorum assignments are possible, which allows flexibility in design.
questions.teaches: Quorums are not necessarily majorities; it only matters that the sets of nodes used by the read and write operations overlap in at least one node.

questions.q: A bank balance service uses n = 3, w = 1, r = 1 to stay available. What goes wrong for users?
options: Deposits are rejected, since w = 1 requires acknowledgment from the leader
Reads become slower, since each read now waits for all three replicas
The cluster loses a replica, since weak settings delete the extra copies
A balance read may miss a recent deposit that sits on another replica
optionExplain: w = 1 needs only one acknowledgment from any replica, and no leader exists.
r = 1 makes reads fast, not slow.
Settings never delete replicas; they only change how many must answer.
Right: with w + r not above n, the read and write nodes may not overlap.
questions.explain: The setting favours availability over freshness, which a balance read may not tolerate.
questions.teaches: A workload with few writes and many reads may set w = n and r = 1, which makes reads faster but means that just one failed node causes all database writes to fail.

questions.q: A write succeeded on fewer than w replicas, so the client was told it failed. A later read may:
options: Return the old value, since a failed write is always rolled back
Return the new value, since any stored copy is the latest value
Return an error, since the replicas disagree about the state
Return either the new value or the old one, since the write may exist on some nodes
optionExplain: The chapter says a write that reached fewer than w replicas is not rolled back on the others.
Not every read will find the new copy, since it may sit on only some nodes.
Reads do not fail merely because replicas hold different values; the read returns one.
Right: the failed write is not rolled back, so a read may or may not see it.
questions.explain: A failed write is not undone on the nodes where it landed. The card next lists more cases.

questions.q: Which situations can break the guarantee even when w + r > n?
options: A sloppy quorum placed writes on nodes outside the home n
Two writes happened concurrently
A write happened concurrently with a read
All nodes worked and responded quickly with no concurrency
Reads used r nodes
optionExplain: Right: reads may not overlap the writes.
Right: no clear order.
Right: only some replicas may have it.
That setting gives the expected result.
That is the quorum condition itself.
questions.explain: Several implementation cases weaken the promise.

questions.q: A node holding the newest value dies and is restored from an older replica. What can happen to the quorum condition?
options: The condition is strengthened, since the restored node adds a fresh copy
The count of replicas with the new value may fall below w, so the condition breaks
Nothing changes, since a quorum is defined only by the configured numbers
The new value is copied back automatically from the replica that was restored
optionExplain: A restore from older data takes the newest value away rather than adding it.
Right: restoring from an older replica removes one holder of the new value.
The guarantee depends on how many nodes actually hold the value, not the configured numbers alone.
Nothing copies the value back unless a repair mechanism does so later.
questions.explain: Restoring from stale data lowers the count of replicas with the new value.

questions.q: True or false: When a write is in progress and has reached only some replicas, a concurrent read is guaranteed to return the new value.
questions.explain: It is undetermined whether the read returns the old or the new value, depending on which replicas it reaches.

questions.q: What does the chapter say Dynamo-style databases are generally optimized for?
options: Strict serializable transactions across many different keys
Single-node deployments that never need to replicate
Use cases that can tolerate eventual consistency
The strongest consistency that a distributed store can offer
optionExplain: Dynamo-style stores do not provide strict serializability.
They are designed for replication across several nodes.
Right: the chapter says Dynamo-style databases suit use cases that tolerate eventual consistency.
Strongest consistency is what they trade away for availability and latency.
questions.explain: Quorum parameters tune the probability of stale reads rather than promising freshness.
questions.rule: Know what the store is optimized for.
questions.teaches: Dynamo-style databases are generally optimized for use cases that can tolerate eventual consistency.

questions.q: A team writes: with w + r > n our reads are current, so no stale reads can occur. What is the best correction?
options: Stale reads can still occur in edge cases, such as sloppy quorums or concurrent writes
The statement is correct, since w + r > n guarantees every read is current
The statement holds only when n is an odd number of replicas
It holds only when r = 1, since a single read then reaches the leader
optionExplain: Right: the guarantee has exceptions, so w + r > n is not an absolute promise of freshness.
The chapter lists several edge cases in which stale values are still returned.
Whether n is odd or even does not remove the edge cases.
There is no leader in this design, and r = 1 weakens overlap further.
questions.explain: Treat quorum settings as probabilities, not absolute guarantees.
questions.rule: Do not read quorums as absolute.
questions.teaches: Although quorums appear to guarantee that a read returns the latest written value, in practice it is not so simple.

questions.q: A leaderless store uses w + r > n. Is a user guaranteed to read their own writes?
options: Yes, a quorum read always includes the node that took the user write
Not usually; the lag anomalies can still occur in a quorum system
Yes, but only when the read quorum r is set to exactly one node
Yes, because leaderless replication has no replication lag to cause trouble
optionExplain: The edge cases mean that overlap does not always hold in practice.
Right: the chapter says the lag guarantees such as read-your-writes are not given by quorums alone.
r = 1 makes overlap less likely, not more.
Leaderless systems do have replicas that lag behind one another.
questions.explain: The quorum condition is about overlap, not about user-level guarantees. The card next states the book's view.

questions.q: True or false: In a leaderless database with quorums you usually do get monotonic reads and consistent prefix reads.
questions.explain: Usually you do not get these guarantees, so the anomalies can occur in applications.

questions.q: A user posts a comment to a quorum-based store and refreshes. The comment is missing. What explains it?
options: The leader failed, so the comment was lost during the election
The comment was rolled back by the database because the write failed
A snapshot was taken before the comment and the refresh read from it
Quorum reads do not by themselves guarantee read-your-writes
optionExplain: There is no leader and no election in a leaderless store.
A successful quorum write is not rolled back when a later read misses it.
Snapshots are a transaction concept and are not involved in this scenario.
Right: a quorum store offers no such guarantee unless extra measures are taken.
questions.explain: Missing own writes is possible without extra mechanisms.

questions.q: Sort each guarantee by whether quorums usually provide it.

items.t: Read-your-writes
Monotonic reads
Consistent prefix reads
Eventual convergence of replicas
Tolerating one unavailable node at n = 3, w = r = 2
Reads normally overlapping an acknowledged write when w + r > n

questions.explain: Quorums provide overlap and failure tolerance, not the session guarantees.
questions.rule: Overlap is not a session guarantee.

questions.q: What do stronger guarantees generally require, according to the chapter?
options: Transactions or consensus, which the chapter says are needed for stronger guarantees
More replicas, since each additional copy brings the data closer to current
Larger values of w, which make every write reach each of the replicas
Synchronized clocks, which let every node agree on which write is last
optionExplain: Right: the chapter says guarantees such as read-your-writes need transactions or consensus.
More replicas do not remove the lag anomalies.
Raising w narrows but does not remove the edge cases.
Clocks are unreliable and do not create ordering guarantees by themselves.
questions.explain: The chapter points to later chapters on transactions and consensus.
questions.teaches: Stronger guarantees generally require transactions or consensus. We will return to these topics in Chapter 7 and Chapter 9.

questions.q: A team needs read-your-writes in a Cassandra-style system. What does the chapter imply?
options: Set r = 1, so that every read goes to the node that took the write
Set w = 1, so that each write is acknowledged by the node the user will read
Do not expect it from quorum settings alone; plan for it elsewhere in the system
Add more nodes, since a larger cluster makes stale reads rarer and rarer
optionExplain: r = 1 can return a node that missed the write.
w = 1 means the write may be on only one node, which a read may miss.
Right: the chapter says these guarantees need extra mechanisms beyond quorum settings.
More nodes do not give a guarantee, and may raise lag.
questions.explain: The guarantee must come from application design or a stronger system.
questions.teaches: Even with w + r > n there are edge cases that return stale values; for example, with a sloppy quorum the w writes may land on different nodes than the r reads, so overlap is no longer guaranteed.

questions.q: How can you measure replication lag in a leader-based system?
options: Count the clients that are connected to each follower at one moment
Compare the disk sizes of the leader and the follower to see the gap
Subtract the follower log position from the leader log position
Ask each user whether the data on their screen matches what they wrote
optionExplain: The number of clients says nothing about how far behind a follower is.
Disk size differs for many reasons unrelated to lag.
Right: in leader-based replication both positions are known, and their difference is the lag.
Surveying users is slow and does not give a precise lag measure.
questions.explain: Both nodes number their log entries. The card next explains.

questions.q: In a leader-based system, lag is measured by subtracting the follower's ____ in the replication log from the leader's.
questions.explain: Each node has a position in the log, the number of writes applied locally.

questions.q: Follower F is at position 9,500 and the leader is at 10,000. What is the lag?
options: 500 writes behind the leader, found by subtracting 9,500 from 10,000
9,500 writes behind the leader, as that is the position of the follower
10,000 writes behind the leader, as that is the position of the leader
19,500 writes behind the leader, as that is both positions added up
optionExplain: Right: 10,000 minus 9,500 leaves 500 writes of lag.
9,500 is how far the follower has got, not how far behind it is.
10,000 is how far the leader has got, not the gap.
Adding the two positions has no meaning for lag.
questions.explain: Subtract the follower's position from the leader's.

questions.q: True or false: With read repair as the only mechanism, there is a limit on how old a value on a stale replica can be.
questions.explain: If a value is only infrequently read, a stale replica may return a very old value, so there is no limit.
questions.rule: No read, no repair, no bound.

questions.q: What does the chapter say would be good to include in the standard set of database metrics?
options: Disk temperatures, so that hardware faults can be spotted early
The number of tables, so that schema growth can be watched
The text of each query, so that slow statements can be found
Staleness measurements, so that eventually can be quantified
optionExplain: Hardware metrics are useful but are not the staleness measure.
Table counts do not say how stale the replicas are.
Query text does not say how far a replica is behind.
Right: the chapter says it would be good to include staleness in standard metrics.
questions.explain: Eventual consistency is a deliberately vague guarantee, but for operability it is important to quantify eventual.
questions.teaches: It would be good to include staleness measurements in the standard set of metrics for databases. Eventual consistency is a deliberately vague guarantee, but for operability it is important to be able to quantify eventual.

questions.q: A leaderless cluster with read repair only shows no alerts, yet users report ancient data on rarely used keys. What is the lesson?
options: The alerts are broken, since a stale key always triggers a clear warning
Without staleness metrics, rarely read keys can be stale and nobody notices
The leader is stale, since leaders lag behind followers in this design
Quorums are disabled, since staleness cannot occur when quorums are on
optionExplain: Alerts only report what is measured, and staleness is not measured here.
Right: read repair needs reads, and without a metric the gap stays invisible.
There is no leader in a leaderless cluster.
Quorums can be on and staleness can still occur on rarely read keys.
questions.explain: Monitoring needs a staleness measure, not only health checks.
questions.teaches: Eventual consistency is a deliberately vague guarantee, but for operability it is important to be able to quantify "eventual", so staleness measurements belong in the standard set of database metrics.

questions.q: A client cannot reach the usual n nodes for a key. The database may reject the write or store it elsewhere. What is the second option called?
options: A strict quorum, which accepts writes only on the home nodes of the key
A sloppy quorum, which accepts writes on nodes outside the usual n for the key
Read repair, which fixes stale replicas while serving a client read
Anti-entropy, which compares replicas in the background and copies data
optionExplain: A strict quorum rejects the write when the home nodes cannot be reached.
Right: storing the write on reachable nodes other than the home nodes is a sloppy quorum.
Read repair concerns fixing stale copies, not accepting writes during a cut.
Anti-entropy concerns background comparison, not where a write is stored.
questions.explain: Accepting writes on any reachable nodes is a trade. The card next explains the term.

questions.q: With a sloppy quorum, writes and reads still require w and r successful responses, but they may come from nodes outside the n ____ nodes for the value.
questions.explain: Home nodes are the n designated nodes.

questions.q: A cluster has 20 nodes and n = 3 per key. A partition cuts a client from all three home nodes of key K. What still accepts the write?
options: A strict quorum that insists on the three home nodes of the key
Waiting for the home nodes until the partition heals and then writing
A leader-based failover which promotes another node to take the write
A sloppy quorum that uses other reachable nodes in place of the home nodes
optionExplain: A strict quorum fails here, since none of the three home nodes can be reached.
Waiting means the client stalls instead of the database accepting the write.
There is no leader to fail over in this design.
Right: only a sloppy quorum lets the write land on reachable nodes outside the home set.
questions.explain: The sloppy quorum is designed for exactly this case.
questions.rule: Sloppy quorums accept writes when homes are unreachable.

questions.q: True or false: With a sloppy quorum and w + r > n, a read of r nodes is guaranteed to see the latest write.
questions.explain: The write may be on nodes outside the n home nodes, so the read and write sets may not overlap.

questions.q: Which of these databases enables sloppy quorums by default?
options: Riak, where the chapter says sloppy quorums are enabled by default
Cassandra, where the chapter says sloppy quorums are enabled by default
Voldemort, where the chapter says sloppy quorums are enabled by default
None of them; the chapter says all three turn sloppy quorums off by default
optionExplain: Right: Riak enables them by default, while Cassandra and Voldemort do not.
The chapter says Cassandra and Voldemort leave them disabled.
Voldemort is in the same group as Cassandra on this point.
At least one of them, Riak, has them on by default.
questions.explain: Sloppy quorums are optional in all common Dynamo implementations.
questions.rule: Check the default of your database.
questions.teaches: Sloppy quorums are optional in all common Dynamo implementations. In Riak they are enabled by default, and in Cassandra and Voldemort they are disabled by default.

questions.q: A team enables sloppy quorums and is surprised that a read right after a successful write returns the old value. What explains this?
options: The leader failed, so the acknowledged write was lost before reaching a follower
The snapshot was old, so the read ran against a data version before the write
The write went to nodes outside the home set and has not been handed back yet
Clocks drifted, so the timestamp made the write look older than it was
optionExplain: There is no leader in this design.
Snapshots belong to transactions and are not the cause here.
Right: with a sloppy quorum, w + r > n no longer guarantees overlap with the home nodes.
The cause is where the write was stored, not clocks.
questions.explain: Until the handoff completes, the read may not see the write.
questions.rule: Sloppy quorum is only a durability assurance.
questions.teaches: A sloppy quorum is only an assurance of durability, namely that the data is stored on w nodes somewhere; there is no guarantee that a read of r nodes will see it until the hinted handoff has completed.

questions.q: A node holds a write on behalf of another node during a network cut. What happens when the network is fixed?
options: The temporary node discards the write since the network cut already passed
The temporary node becomes the leader for that key from then on
The temporary node sends the write to the home node it was holding it for
The temporary node keeps the write indefinitely and the home node never gets it
optionExplain: Discarding would lose the write that had been acknowledged.
There are no leaders in leaderless replication.
Right: this step is called hinted handoff, and it moves the writes to the right home.
Keeping it forever would leave the home nodes permanently without the data.
questions.explain: The temporary holder passes it on. The card next names this.

questions.q: Sending writes that a node accepted on behalf of another back to the proper home nodes is called hinted ____.
questions.explain: The temporary holder hands the write off.

questions.q: Node X stored a write for node Y while Y was cut off. Y reconnects. Which comes next?
options: X sends the stored write to Y, which is the node it belongs to
Y deletes its own data and fetches everything again from the node X
X becomes the permanent home node for the key, replacing Y
The client that sent the original write issues it again to Y
optionExplain: Right: X forwards the write on behalf of Y once it is reachable again.
Y does not need to delete anything; it only needs the missing write.
X was only a temporary holder and the home assignment does not change.
The client already got an acknowledgment and does not resend.
questions.explain: The hint says who the write was for.
questions.rule: The hint names the home node.

questions.q: Sort each statement into sloppy quorum or hinted handoff.

items.t: Accepts writes on reachable nodes outside the home set
Sends stored writes back to the home nodes
Increases write availability
Runs after the network interruption is fixed
Means w + r > n no longer guarantees reading the latest value
Completes the placement of writes that were stored elsewhere

questions.explain: Sloppy quorum accepts writes elsewhere during trouble, and hinted handoff cleans up afterwards.

questions.q: Until hinted handoff completes, what can a read of r nodes do?
options: Always see the write, since any node can answer for any key
Delete the write, since a read of a temporary copy removes it
Move the write to the home nodes, since reads trigger the handoff
Miss the write, since it sits on nodes outside the home set
optionExplain: A read of the home nodes cannot see a write held elsewhere.
Reading does not delete anything.
Handoff is triggered by the home node returning, not by a read.
Right: the read nodes may be home nodes that have not received the write yet.
questions.explain: A sloppy quorum is a durability assurance, not a read guarantee.
questions.teaches: There is no guarantee that a read of r nodes will see it until the hinted handoff has completed.

questions.q: A mobile app writes to a Dynamo-style store during a regional outage and its data appears missing for an hour. What is the likeliest cause?
options: The write was rejected, so the app should have received an error message
The write is held on temporary nodes awaiting handoff to the home nodes
The leader crashed during the outage and a new one has not been elected
An index was dropped by the database during the regional disruption
optionExplain: The app got a success, so a rejection is unlikely.
Right: until the network heals, the write is on nodes outside the home set.
There is no leader in this design.
Nothing in the scenario points to an index change.
questions.explain: Data stored elsewhere is not visible to home reads yet.
questions.teaches: A sloppy quorum is not a quorum in the traditional sense; it is only an assurance of durability, that the data is stored on w nodes somewhere, with no guarantee a read of r nodes sees it until hinted handoff completes.

questions.q: In Cassandra's multi-datacenter mode, on whose acknowledgments does a client wait?
options: A quorum within its own local datacenter, without waiting for remote ones
All replicas in all datacenters before the write is reported as complete
Only the farthest datacenter, which acts as the authority for the key
A leader in the first datacenter that forwards the write to the others
optionExplain: Right: the client waits for a quorum in its local datacenter, and remote replicas are updated in the background.
Waiting for every datacenter would make writes slow and fragile across wide-area links.
No datacenter acts as an authority in leaderless replication.
There is no leader, since the design is leaderless.
questions.explain: The client wants to avoid cross-datacenter delay. The card next gives the details.

questions.q: True or false: In Cassandra and Voldemort, the number of replicas n includes nodes in all datacenters.
questions.explain: The configuration says how many of the n replicas live in each datacenter.

questions.q: A client in Frankfurt writes to a Cassandra cluster with replicas in three regions. Which is the usual wait?
options: Acknowledgments from the replicas of all three regions before success
An acknowledgment from one region that the client chooses at random
Acknowledgments from a quorum of the Frankfurt replicas only
No acknowledgments, as the write is sent and forgotten across regions
optionExplain: That would tie the latency to the farthest region.
The client does not pick a region at random; the local datacenter forms the quorum.
Right: the quorum is counted in the client local datacenter, so remote delays do not block it.
The write still needs a quorum; it is not fire-and-forget.
questions.explain: The client sends to all replicas but waits locally.

questions.q: If the link between two datacenters slows down, a local write stays fast because the client waits only for a ____ of nodes in its own datacenter.
questions.explain: The remote datacenter catches up asynchronously, so link delay shows up as lag, not as write latency.

questions.q: How does Riak differ from Cassandra in multi-datacenter operation?
options: Riak uses a single leader in one datacenter for all writes across clusters
Riak keeps client-node communication local to one datacenter and replicates between clusters asynchronously
Riak requires every write to be acknowledged synchronously across datacenters
Riak does not support multiple datacenters and is limited to one cluster
optionExplain: Riak is a leaderless database; it does not use a leader.
Right: Riak uses a local cluster per datacenter with asynchronous cross-datacenter replication.
Synchronous cross-datacenter writes are what Riak avoids.
The chapter describes how Riak supports multiple datacenters.
questions.explain: Riak treats each datacenter as its own cluster with background cross-cluster replication.
questions.teaches: Riak keeps all communication between clients and database nodes local to one datacenter, so n describes the number of replicas within one datacenter.

questions.q: A retailer wants writes in Sydney not to wait for London. Which setting supports that in a Cassandra-style store?
options: Waiting for all replicas in every region so the data is current everywhere
Using a single leader in London that accepts all of the retailer writes
Using synchronous replication to every datacenter before acknowledging
Waiting for a quorum of the Sydney replicas only, with London updated afterwards
optionExplain: Waiting for all replicas makes Sydney writes wait on London.
A London leader would send each Sydney write across the world first.
Synchronous cross-region replication ties latency to the farthest region.
Right: a local quorum keeps Sydney writes fast, with remote regions catching up in the background.
questions.explain: Local quorum is the lever.
questions.teaches: The parameters w and r determine how many nodes the client waits for; reads and writes are normally still sent to all n replicas in parallel.

questions.q: Node 2 receives A then B for key X. Node 3 receives B then A. Each overwrites. What is the final state?
options: Both nodes hold A, since the first value written is the one that is kept
Both nodes hold B, since the second value written is the one that is kept
Both nodes hold both values, since a node keeps whatever it is sent
Node 2 ends holding B and node 3 ends holding A, so the replicas disagree
optionExplain: Node 2 received B last, so it does not hold A.
Node 3 received A last, so it does not hold B.
A plain overwrite replaces the old value; it keeps only one.
Right: each node keeps whichever write arrived last, and the arrival orders differ.
questions.explain: The last arrival differs between nodes. The card next generalizes.

questions.q: True or false: Conflicts can occur in a Dynamo-style database even if strict quorums are used.
questions.explain: Several clients can write the same key concurrently, and the quorum condition does not order them.

questions.q: Node 1 misses client B's write due to a transient outage. It holds A. Others hold B. Which describes the state?
options: Consistent replicas, since a brief outage does not change stored data
Inconsistent replicas that need a rule to converge on one value
A split brain, since two nodes now believe that they hold the true value
A failover in progress, since the missing node is being replaced
optionExplain: The replicas hold different values, so they are not consistent.
Right: one replica holds A and the others B, so they disagree until something reconciles them.
Split brain concerns two leaders, and this design has none.
Leaderless replication has no failover, and the node is still a member.
questions.explain: Missed messages plus differing orders leave replicas apart.

questions.q: If nodes keep overwriting on arrival and no convergence rule is added, replicas may stay permanently ____.
questions.explain: Nothing makes the nodes agree, since the last arrival differs from node to node.

questions.q: Beyond concurrent client writes, where else can conflicts arise in Dynamo-style databases, according to the chapter?
options: During snapshots, when a consistent copy of the database is written to disk
During checkpoint compaction, when old log segments are merged together
During read repair and during hinted handoff, as well as in concurrent client writes
During failover, when a replica is promoted to take over from a leader
optionExplain: Snapshots are not described as a source of conflicts in this chapter.
Compaction is a storage concept and is not the source named here.
Right: the chapter says conflicts can also arise during read repair or hinted handoff.
Failover belongs to leader-based replication, not Dynamo-style databases.
questions.explain: Read repair and hinted handoff move values around and can introduce older values.
questions.teaches: In Dynamo-style databases conflicts can also arise during read repair or hinted handoff.

questions.q: A team writes each user's settings from phone and laptop to a leaderless store. The settings occasionally revert. What is a likely cause?
options: Concurrent writes from the two devices, where arrival order decides which is kept
The leader failed during a write, and a stale follower was promoted
Snapshots of the settings were stale when they were read by the app
Quorums were switched off, so the writes reached only one replica
optionExplain: Right: two devices writing at once is the concurrent write problem, and settings revert when overwritten.
There is no leader in a leaderless store.
Snapshots are not involved in plain key writes here.
Quorums do not decide which of two concurrent writes survives.
questions.explain: Two devices writing the same key are concurrent writers.
questions.teaches: Last write wins forces an arbitrary order on concurrent writes using timestamps and achieves convergence at the cost of durability: only one concurrent write survives and the others are silently discarded even though they were reported successful.

questions.q: Three clients concurrently write different values to one key, and each is told success. Under LWW, how many values survive?
options: All three survive, since every write was reported as successful
One value survives; the others are silently discarded
Two survive, since the database keeps the earliest and the latest
None survive, since concurrent writes cancel each other out
optionExplain: Success was reported to each client, but LWW still drops all except one.
Right: LWW keeps the write with the highest timestamp and discards the others.
LWW does not keep a pair; it keeps exactly one.
One write always has the highest timestamp, so something survives.
questions.explain: LWW keeps one value. The card next gives the cost.

questions.q: Last write wins keeps the write with the ____ timestamp and discards the others.
questions.explain: The biggest timestamp is considered the most recent.

questions.q: A comments service uses LWW. Two users submit edits to the same comment at the same time. What happens to one edit?
options: The two edits are merged, so both users see a combined comment
One edit is queued and applied later, once the first has settled
The users are asked to choose, because LWW needs human input
One edit is silently discarded, though both users were told success
optionExplain: LWW does not merge; it picks one.
LWW has no queue; it decides at once.
LWW does not ask anyone; it follows the timestamp.
Right: the edit with the lower timestamp is dropped even though it was acknowledged.
questions.explain: Both were told success; one survives.

questions.q: True or false: Calling a write the most recent under LWW reflects a real ordering between concurrent writes.
questions.explain: The writes are concurrent, so their order is undefined; LWW forces an arbitrary one with timestamps.

questions.q: Which databases use LWW, according to the chapter?
options: It is the only conflict resolution method in Cassandra and an optional feature in Riak
It is mandatory in Riak and an optional feature in Cassandra
It is used by neither database, since both keep all conflicting values
It is mandatory in both databases and cannot be switched off in either
optionExplain: Right: Cassandra supports only LWW, while Riak offers it as an option.
The roles are the wrong way around: Cassandra is the one limited to LWW.
Both databases use it in some form.
Riak lets you choose other conflict resolution methods.
questions.explain: LWW is the only conflict resolution method Cassandra supports.
questions.teaches: LWW is the only supported conflict resolution method in Cassandra, and an optional feature in Riak.

questions.q: A team reads that LWW achieves eventual convergence. Why is that not the end of the analysis?
options: It prevents convergence, because replicas keep different timestamps forever
It requires a leader, because only a leader can compare timestamps
It achieves convergence at the cost of durability, because concurrent writes are dropped
It requires synchronous replication, because timestamps need a shared order
optionExplain: Replicas do converge under LWW; the issue is what they converge to.
LWW works without a leader, which is why it suits leaderless stores.
Right: converging by discarding writes means acknowledged data can be lost.
It works with asynchronous replication.
questions.explain: Convergence is not the same as keeping all writes.
questions.teaches: LWW achieves the goal of eventual convergence, but at the cost of durability.

questions.q: Which use of a store that only offers LWW is the safest?
options: Updating one shared counter from many clients at the same moment
Editing a shared document in place from several user sessions
Writing each record once under a unique key and treating it as immutable afterwards
Storing a shopping cart that changes whenever the user adds items
optionExplain: Concurrent increments would overwrite each other under LWW.
Concurrent edits to one document key would drop one editor changes.
Right: with a unique key and no updates there are no concurrent writes to lose.
A cart is updated repeatedly, so concurrent updates are likely.
questions.explain: LWW is a problem only when a key sees concurrent writes. The card next states the safe pattern.

questions.q: The only safe way to use a database with LWW is to ensure that a key is written only ____ and thereafter treated as immutable.
questions.explain: Immutable keys cannot see concurrent updates.

questions.q: A team stores sensor readings in Cassandra. Which key design avoids lost updates under LWW?
options: A UUID per reading, so each write goes to a new key
One key per sensor, overwritten with each new reading
One key for the whole fleet, overwritten by whichever sensor writes last
A key based on the hour only, so readings within an hour share a key
optionExplain: Right: unique keys mean no two writes compete, so none is discarded.
Overwriting one key lets readings compete, and the lower timestamp loses.
Many sensors on one key would constantly overwrite one another.
Shared keys within an hour would let readings overwrite each other.
questions.explain: Unique keys make each write independent.

questions.q: Sort each workload into whether LWW is acceptable.

items.t: A cache that can be refilled
Immutable records keyed by UUID
A bank balance updated by many clients
A shared note edited in place
A session store where the last request wins
An inventory count adjusted concurrently

questions.explain: LWW fits disposable or write-once data and fails for mutable shared data.

questions.q: What further problem with LWW does the chapter mention?
options: It cannot use timestamps, so it must rely on arrival order alone
It needs at least three replicas before it can function at all
It never converges, so replicas stay different without a leader
It may even drop writes that are not concurrent, if clocks are skewed
optionExplain: LWW depends on timestamps; that is how it chooses.
The number of replicas is not the problem described.
LWW does converge, which is its selling point.
Right: with skewed clocks a later write can get an earlier timestamp and be dropped.
questions.explain: Clock problems can make an earlier write look later.
questions.rule: Clocks can reorder non-concurrent writes too.
questions.teaches: Moreover, LWW may even drop writes that are not concurrent, as we shall discuss in Timestamps for ordering events.

questions.q: A session cache stores the last page a user visited, refilled on a miss. Is LWW acceptable here?
options: No, since caches always need conflicting values merged by the application
Yes, since losing an occasional write is tolerable when the cache refills on a miss
No, since keys that repeat are exactly what LWW cannot handle at all
Only with a leader, since LWW is unsafe without one for caches
optionExplain: A cache entry can simply be refilled, so merging is not needed.
Right: a cache entry can be recomputed, so a dropped write costs little.
Repeated keys lose writes, but here that loss is tolerable.
LWW does not use or need a leader.
questions.explain: The chapter names caching as a case where lost writes are perhaps acceptable.
questions.teaches: There are some situations, such as caching, in which lost writes are perhaps acceptable.

questions.q: Client B reads a value written by client A, then updates it. What is the relation between the two writes?
options: The two writes are concurrent, because they touch the same key
A happens before B, because B builds on the value that A wrote
B happens before A, because B is the write that the client sees last
The two writes conflict, because both modify the same key
optionExplain: Concurrent means neither knew about the other, and B did know A.
Right: B read A and then updated it, so B depends on A.
The order is set by knowledge of the earlier write, not by when the client looks.
Touching the same key is not a conflict if one write builds on the other.
questions.explain: B read A's result before writing. The card next states the definition.
questions.rule: Knowing about it means after it.

questions.q: Two operations are concurrent if neither ____ before the other.
questions.explain: That is the definition: neither knows about the other.

questions.q: Client X writes key K. Client Y, with no knowledge of X, writes K at about the same time. What do you conclude?
options: X happens before Y, because X was submitted first by a few moments
Y happens before X, because Y overwrote the value that X wrote
The writes are identical, because both target the same key
The writes are concurrent, so they conflict and need resolving
optionExplain: Submission order alone does not make one depend on the other.
Y had no knowledge of X, so it could not build on it.
The same key does not mean the same value.
Right: neither client knew about the other, so neither write depends on the other.
questions.explain: Without awareness in either direction, they are concurrent.

questions.q: True or false: If an increment builds on the value an insert created, the insert and the increment are concurrent.
questions.explain: The increment depends on the insert, so the insert happens before it and the two are ordered, not concurrent.

questions.q: What does the chapter call the relationship where B builds upon A?
options: B is causally dependent on A, since B was written knowing A
B is concurrent with A, since both were applied to a single key
B is eventually consistent with A, since replicas converge over time
B is a replica of A, since B holds the same data as A does
optionExplain: Right: the chapter calls this a causal dependency between the operations.
Concurrent means neither knows of the other, the opposite of this case.
Eventual consistency describes replicas, not the relation between two writes.
A replica is a copy of data on another node, which is a different idea.
questions.explain: Causal dependency is the building block of ordering.
questions.teaches: B's operation builds upon A's operation, so B's operation must have happened later. We also say that B is causally dependent on A.

questions.q: Two editors open the same ticket, each unaware of the other, and both close it with different notes. What should happen?
options: Let the later clock decide silently, since the earlier note is out of date
Reject both notes and ask the editors to open the ticket again
Treat them as concurrent and resolve the conflict by merging or choosing one
Order them by editor name, since that gives a fixed total order
optionExplain: Clocks can be wrong, and silently dropping a note loses information.
Rejecting both throws away two legitimate edits.
Right: neither editor saw the other, so the writes are concurrent and need a conflict rule.
Ordering by name is arbitrary and not based on what was known.
questions.explain: Concurrency is about awareness, and conflicts need explicit handling.
questions.teaches: In the book's insert and increment example the two writes are not concurrent, because the value B increments is the value A inserted, so B is causally dependent on A.

questions.q: Two writes happen an hour apart, but a network outage kept the second client from seeing the first. Are they concurrent?
options: No, because an hour passed between the two writes and that decides it
No, because the clocks of the two clients may differ by a little
Yes, because neither client knew about the other when it wrote
Yes, but only because both writes used the same key
optionExplain: Time apart does not create awareness of the other write.
Clock differences do not decide whether one write knew about the other.
Right: concurrency is about whether either operation knew of the other, not about elapsed time.
Sharing a key is necessary for a conflict, but awareness decides concurrency.
questions.explain: Concurrency depends on knowledge. The card next explains.

questions.q: True or false: Two operations are concurrent only if they overlap in physical time.
questions.explain: They are concurrent if they are unaware of each other, regardless of when they occurred.

questions.q: A writes at noon. B reads A's value at 12:01, then writes. C writes at 12:01 without seeing A or B. Which pair is not concurrent?
options: A and B, since B read the value written by A before writing
A and C, since C wrote without having seen what A wrote
B and C, since neither B nor C saw the write of the other
None of them, since all three wrote to the same key in order
optionExplain: Right: B built on A, so those two are ordered; the other pairs are concurrent.
A and C are concurrent, since C did not see A.
B and C are concurrent, since they did not see each other.
The writes did not all see one another, so some pairs are concurrent.
questions.explain: Only pairs with no awareness are concurrent.

questions.q: Two operations are concurrent if they are ____ of each other, regardless of the physical time at which they occurred.
questions.explain: A client cut off by the network for an hour can still be concurrent with a write made during the outage.

questions.q: The chapter compares this principle to an idea from physics. Which one?
options: Quantum entanglement, where two particles keep affecting each other at any distance
Thermodynamics, where heat flows from hot places to colder ones
The speed of sound, where noise takes time to arrive from far away
The special theory of relativity, where events too far apart for information to travel between them cannot affect each other
optionExplain: Entanglement is not the comparison made.
Thermodynamics is not the comparison made.
Sound speed is not the comparison made.
Right: the chapter compares concurrency to events that information cannot cross in time.
questions.explain: In relativity, information cannot travel faster than light; in computers, network problems can delay information far longer.
questions.teaches: People sometimes make a connection between this principle and the special theory of relativity in physics.

questions.q: Two ledger entries are posted 3 ms apart in two regions that were exchanging updates normally, and one entry was based on the other. Concurrent?
options: Yes, since entries 3 ms apart are close enough in time to be concurrent
No, since one entry was based on the other and so depends on it
Yes, since entries posted in different regions are always concurrent
No, since the clocks of different regions may differ and so cannot be compared
optionExplain: Closeness in time does not decide concurrency; knowledge does.
Right: dependency, not the gap in time, decides that they are not concurrent.
Regions that exchange updates can make one entry depend on another.
Clock difference is not the test; awareness of the earlier write is.
questions.explain: Dependence decides, not distance in time or space.
questions.teaches: Two operations can occur some time apart and still be concurrent, because a slow or interrupted network prevented one from knowing about the other, even though the speed of light would in principle have allowed one to affect the other.

questions.q: A server holds two values for a key: [a] at version 1 and [b] at version 2. A client writes with version 1. What does the server keep?
options: The new value and [b], since [b] was written concurrently with the client write
Only the new value, since a write replaces everything the server holds
Only [a] and [b], since the new write is held until the server sorts it out
Nothing, since conflicting writes are rejected by the server and dropped
optionExplain: Right: version 1 covers [a] only, so [a] is overwritten and [b] is kept as a concurrent value.
The client had not seen [b], so [b] must not be discarded.
The new write is accepted, not held.
The server accepts the write and keeps the concurrent value.
questions.explain: Versions at or below the client's version are replaced; higher ones remain. The card next gives the full rule.

questions.q: When a client writes a key, it must include the ____ number from its prior read.
questions.explain: That tells the server which state the write is based on.

questions.q: The server holds [x] v1 and [y] v2. A client read both and now writes the merged [x, y] with version 2. What remains?
options: The merged value and [y], since version 2 matches the version of [y]
The merged value and [x], since version 2 is newer than the version of [x]
Only the merged value, since the client had seen both and the write supersedes them
Three values, since the server keeps one copy of each version it saw
optionExplain: The client included [y] in the merge, so [y] can go.
The client included [x] in the merge, so [x] can go.
Right: the write carries the highest version, so it overwrites everything the client saw.
Superseded values are removed, not kept.
questions.explain: The server overwrites all values with version at or below the client's.

questions.q: True or false: A write sent without a version number overwrites all existing values for the key.
questions.explain: It is concurrent with every other write, so it overwrites nothing and is returned as one of the values on later reads.

questions.q: Can the value stored be any data structure, such as a cart?
options: No, only plain strings, since the server must read each value to compare
Yes, since the server compares version numbers and does not interpret the values
No, only numbers, since version comparison needs values it can order
Only lists, since the merge step needs items it can combine
optionExplain: Comparison uses version numbers and not the values.
Right: the server just tracks versions, so the client decides what a value contains.
Values are opaque to the server and can be any data.
The client does the merge; the server does not.
questions.explain: Concurrency detection uses only the version bookkeeping.
questions.teaches: Note that the server can determine whether two operations are concurrent by looking at the version numbers; it does not need to interpret the value itself.

questions.q: Client 1 reads cart [milk] v1. Client 2 writes [eggs] with no version. Client 1 writes [milk, flour] with version 1. What does the server hold afterwards?
options: Only [milk, flour], since the later write replaces what the server held
Only [eggs], since the write that came without a version replaces whatever existed
[milk], [eggs] and [milk, flour], since each version is kept for audit
[milk, flour] and [eggs], kept as concurrent values
optionExplain: Client 1 had not seen [eggs], so its write cannot overwrite it.
Client 1 write carries version 1, so it is accepted and does not replace the earlier write.
[milk] was read and superseded by client 1, so it is not kept.
Right: client 1 version covers only its read of [milk], so [eggs] was concurrent and is kept.
questions.explain: The write based on version 1 supersedes [milk] but not the version-less [eggs].
questions.rule: Based-on version decides what is overwritten.
questions.teaches: In the shopping cart example the clients are never fully up to date with the server because another operation is always going on concurrently, yet old versions do get overwritten eventually and no writes are lost.

questions.q: Two sibling carts are [milk, flour, eggs, bacon] and [eggs, milk, ham]. What is a reasonable merge for an add-only cart?
options: Only the common items, milk and eggs, since both carts agree on those
Whichever cart is longer, since it holds more of what the user wanted
Neither cart, since concurrent versions cannot be reconciled
The union of the two carts: milk, flour, eggs, bacon and ham
optionExplain: The intersection would drop items that a user did add.
Length does not tell which items matter, and it would lose items.
Siblings can be reconciled by application code.
Right: for an add-only cart, a union keeps everything anyone added.
questions.explain: The union keeps every addition. The card next shows where it fails.

questions.q: Riak calls concurrent values siblings and clients must ____ them.
questions.explain: Merging is the extra work the algorithm leaves to clients.

questions.q: A to-do list allows adding and completing tasks, and two siblings disagree on a completed task. Why is union risky?
options: Union drops every task, because overlapping entries cancel out
A completed task may reappear as open, since the other sibling still lists it
Union is slow on large lists and so would stall the application
Union requires a leader to decide which list is complete
optionExplain: Union keeps tasks and does not drop them.
Right: union cannot tell a deleted or completed item from one that was never there.
Speed is not the issue here.
No leader is involved in merging siblings.
questions.explain: A removal that exists in only one sibling is undone by the union.

questions.q: True or false: Choosing the sibling with the highest version number or timestamp is a safe way to merge, because no data is lost.
questions.explain: Picking one value is last write wins and implies losing data.

questions.q: What does the chapter say about effort to avoid merging in application code?
options: It is impossible to automate, so every application must write its own merge
It is easy in every case, so the effort is not worth the trouble
There are efforts to design data structures that can merge automatically
Merging is done by the server and so applications need not worry
optionExplain: The chapter says there are efforts to automate merging.
Merging is described as error-prone for application code.
Right: the chapter notes efforts to design data structures that do the merging for you.
The server keeps the siblings; the application merges them.
questions.explain: Riak's datatype support uses CRDTs that merge siblings in sensible ways.
questions.teaches: Merging siblings in application code is complex and error-prone, so there are efforts to design data structures that can perform this merging automatically; Riak's datatype support uses CRDTs.

questions.q: A collaborative tag set allows adding and removing tags. Which design merges siblings correctly?
options: Record removals explicitly so that merging can honour them
Use union only, since adding tags is the common case
Use last write wins, since the later set is the more recent
Use intersection only, since only agreed tags should remain
optionExplain: Right: a removal marker lets the merge tell a removed tag from one never added.
Union would bring back removed tags.
LWW would discard one sibling and lose changes.
Intersection would drop tags that one user added.
questions.explain: Both additions and removals must be represented to merge correctly.
questions.teaches: Riak's datatype support uses CRDTs, a family of data structures that can automatically merge siblings in sensible ways, including preserving deletions.

questions.q: A merge sees an item in one sibling but not the other. How can it know whether the item was deleted?
options: The size of the item, since a deleted item has no size
A deletion marker that carries a version number
The hostname of the sibling, since deletions come from one host
The order of the siblings, since the later one has the deletions
optionExplain: Size cannot distinguish deleted from absent.
Right: a marker with a version records that the item was deleted rather than never added.
A hostname says nothing about deletions.
The order of siblings does not carry deletion information.
questions.explain: Absence is ambiguous. The card next names the marker.

questions.q: A deletion marker kept to show that an item was removed is called a ____.
questions.explain: It marks where the item used to be.

questions.q: A cart sibling removed eggs but another still has them. With a tombstone for eggs at a higher version, what does the merge give?
options: The eggs reappear, since one sibling still lists them
The cart is empty, since the tombstone removes every item
Both versions remain, since the merge keeps every sibling
The eggs stay removed, since the marker has a higher version than the other cart
optionExplain: The marker is what stops the reappearance.
Only the marked item is affected; other items stay.
The merge combines them into one cart.
Right: the deletion marker records the removal at a later version.
questions.explain: The marker records the deletion with a version.

questions.q: True or false: Without tombstones, taking the union of two sibling carts can bring back an item removed in only one of them.
questions.explain: The union keeps any item present in either sibling.

questions.q: Where did the chapter earlier meet tombstones?
options: In log compaction, in the context of hash indexes
In failover, when a new leader is chosen
In read repair, when stale values are fixed
In sloppy quorums, when writes land elsewhere
optionExplain: Right: Chapter 3 used a deletion record in log compaction to discard deleted keys.
Failover was not where the book first used the term.
Read repair is in this chapter, not earlier.
Sloppy quorums are in this chapter, not earlier.
questions.explain: In log-structured storage a deletion is also recorded as a special record.
questions.teaches: We previously saw tombstones in the context of log compaction in Hash Indexes.

questions.q: A distributed set replicates deletions by removing the element outright. Replica B, behind, still holds it and replicates to A. What results?
options: The element stays deleted, since A removed it and B will follow
Both replicas lose the element, since deletion spreads like a write
The element reappears on A, since B still holds it and nothing marks it as deleted
B deletes the element, since it sees that A no longer has it
optionExplain: Without a marker, A cannot reject B copy.
B still has the element, so it is not lost on B.
Right: a plain removal leaves no trace, so the lagging replica brings it back.
B cannot know that A deleted it without a record.
questions.explain: A plain deletion leaves no trace for others to learn from.
questions.teaches: Tombstones were previously seen in the context of log compaction, where a deletion marker records that a key was removed.

questions.q: In a leaderless database several replicas accept writes. What is needed to track causal dependencies?
options: A single global counter kept at a leader for all of the keys
Wall-clock timestamps taken at each replica when it accepts a write
A version number for each replica as well as for each key
A larger read and write quorum so that every write overlaps
optionExplain: A single counter assumes one writer, which leaderless systems lack.
Clock timestamps can be skewed and do not track causality.
Right: with several replicas accepting writes, each replica needs its own counter.
Quorums do not order writes or detect dependencies.
questions.explain: Each replica contributes its own counter. The card next names the structure.

questions.q: The collection of version numbers from all the replicas is called a version ____.
questions.explain: It is a vector with one entry per replica.

questions.q: A client reads a value and its version vector from replica A, then writes back to replica B with that vector. What does the vector allow?
options: B can tell whether the write overwrites or is concurrent with what it holds
B ignores the vector and accepts the write as the latest
B becomes a leader for the key and orders later writes
A deletes its copy because B has the new value now
optionExplain: Right: the vector carries the versions the client had seen.
Ignoring the vector would lose concurrent writes.
No node becomes a leader in a leaderless database.
Nothing tells A to delete data.
questions.explain: The vector encodes what the client had seen.

questions.q: True or false: The version vector structure makes it safe to read from one replica and subsequently write back to another replica.
questions.explain: At worst siblings are created, but no data is lost as long as they are merged correctly.

questions.q: What do vector clocks and version vectors have in common and how do they differ?
options: They are identical in meaning and design, so either name can be used
They are unrelated ideas that have nothing to do with causality
Vector clocks are the right structure for comparing the state of replicas
They are sometimes confused, but version vectors are the right structure for comparing replica state
optionExplain: The chapter says they are not quite the same.
Both relate to tracking causality.
The chapter names version vectors for replicas, not vector clocks.
Right: the chapter says they differ subtly and version vectors suit replica state.
questions.explain: The chapter points to the references for details.
questions.rule: Use version vectors for replica comparison.
questions.teaches: A version vector is sometimes also called a vector clock, even though they are not quite the same; when comparing the state of replicas, version vectors are the right data structure to use.

questions.q: A team uses a single counter per key shared by all replicas. Replicas A and B each accept a write at the same moment. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing goes wrong, since a shared counter orders every write correctly
Both assign the same number, so concurrency cannot be detected
Writes are rejected, since the counter can only be updated by one node
Both replicas become leaders for the key, since the number is equal
optionExplain: A shared counter has no one place to update when replicas accept writes.
Right: the two writes look like they have the same version, hiding the conflict.
Writes are accepted; they just collide in version.
No leader is elected in a leaderless system.
questions.explain: Each replica needs its own counter so independent increments do not collide.
questions.teaches: A version vector is sometimes called a vector clock even though they are not quite the same; when comparing the state of replicas, version vectors are the right data structure to use.

questions.q: Which are purposes of replication named in the summary?
options: High availability
Disconnected operation
Latency
Scalability of reads
Reducing the dataset size
optionExplain: Right: surviving failures.
Right: working offline.
Right: data near users.
Right: more replicas serve reads.
Replication copies, it does not shrink.
questions.explain: The summary lists four purposes. The card next explains each.

questions.q: Match each purpose to its description.
pairs: Keep running when machines or a datacenter fail
Keep working through a network interruption
Handle more reads than one machine can
questions.explain: Each purpose answers a different need.

questions.q: A mobile field app must work in a tunnel without signal. Which purpose of replication is this?
options: Disconnected operation, where the app keeps working without a network
Latency reduction, since the data sits near the user
Scalability, since reads are spread over many copies
High availability of a datacenter, since a second site takes over
optionExplain: Right: the device has its own copy and works offline, then syncs when the signal returns.
Latency is about distance, and the problem here is no connection at all.
Scalability concerns load, not signal.
No datacenter is failing in this scenario.
questions.explain: The need is working without a connection.

questions.q: Sort each goal into whether it is about reads or availability/latency.

items.t: Adding followers to answer read queries
Placing a replica near users in another region
Continuing after a datacenter fails
Working while a device is offline
Spreading read traffic over replicas
Increasing read throughput

questions.explain: Scalability concerns the volume of reads; the other purposes concern availability and latency.

questions.q: What kind of fault does the summary call more insidious than unavailable nodes and network interruptions?
options: Planned maintenance that takes nodes offline for upgrades
Slow followers that fall behind the leader for a long time
Silent data corruption caused by software bugs
Clock changes that make timestamps jump backwards
optionExplain: Maintenance is routine and visible.
Slow followers are a lag problem and not a corruption problem.
Right: the summary calls corruption from bugs more insidious than nodes simply being down.
Clock jumps are not named in this summary.
questions.explain: Replication copies corruption just as faithfully as good data.
questions.rule: Replication does not defend against all faults.
questions.teaches: At a minimum, we need to deal with unavailable nodes and network interruptions (and that is not even considering the more insidious kinds of fault, such as silent data corruption due to software bugs).

questions.q: A team adds a replica in a distant region but gets stale reads. Which purpose did the replica serve, and what did it cost?
options: Availability at no cost, since the extra replica only adds redundancy
Latency, at the cost of staleness from lagging reads
Scalability of writes, since the replica takes some of the write load
Disconnected operation, since the replica works without a network
optionExplain: Replication always has some cost, here staleness.
Right: a nearby replica speeds reads but may lag, so reads can be stale.
A replica does not scale writes; the writes still reach every copy.
The replica is online, so it is not disconnected operation.
questions.explain: Each purpose carries a trade-off.
questions.teaches: Asynchronous replication is widely used despite weakening durability, especially if there are many followers or they are geographically distributed.

questions.q: A team needs the simplest model with no conflict resolution. Which approach fits best?
options: Multi-leader replication, which takes writes at several nodes
Leaderless replication, which takes writes at any replica
All three are equal, since each handles conflicts the same way
Single-leader replication, which orders all writes through one node
optionExplain: Several leaders can conflict and need resolution.
Leaderless replication allows concurrent writes, so it needs conflict handling.
They differ in how conflicts arise and are handled.
Right: with one write path there are no write conflicts to resolve.
questions.explain: Simplicity is the draw of one write path. The card next compares them.

questions.q: Match each approach to its main strength.
pairs: Easy to understand, no conflict resolution
Robust when leaders or links fail, each accepts writes
Robust to node faults, latency spikes, no failover
questions.explain: Each approach buys something and costs something.

questions.q: An app needs writes to continue in two regions through an inter-region outage and can resolve conflicts afterwards. Which suits?
options: Single-leader replication with its leader in one region only
Synchronous replication to all regions before every write completes
No replication at all, so every region keeps its own separate data
Multi-leader or leaderless replication, since both accept writes in each region
optionExplain: Writes in the other region would stop when it cannot reach the leader.
Synchronous replication stalls writes during an inter-region outage.
Without replication the regions would not share data.
Right: both accept local writes during an outage and resolve conflicts afterwards.
questions.explain: Independent write acceptance is needed.

questions.q: True or false: Multi-leader and leaderless replication give the strongest consistency guarantees of the three approaches.
questions.explain: They provide only very weak consistency guarantees in return for robustness.

questions.q: What does the summary say about asynchronous replication when a leader fails and an asynchronously updated follower is promoted?
options: Nothing is lost, since the new leader replays the old log
Recently committed data may be lost
Only reads are lost, since writes were already acknowledged
The old leader wins, since it keeps the full history of writes
optionExplain: Asynchronous followers may have missed writes the old leader acknowledged.
Right: writes the old leader acknowledged but did not send on may be lost.
Acknowledged writes are the ones at risk.
The old leader is replaced after a failover, and its extra writes are usually discarded.
questions.explain: Asynchronous replication can be fast, but the failure case needs attention.
questions.teaches: If a leader fails and you promote an asynchronously updated follower to be the new leader, recently committed data may be lost.

questions.q: A startup chooses leaderless replication because a vendor calls it highly available, but its team wants strict read-your-writes. What should they weigh?
options: Nothing needs weighing, since a highly available vendor product covers it
The approach has a hidden leader that provides read-your-writes
The approach gives only weak guarantees, and read-your-writes needs extra design
Quorums guarantee read-your-writes, so no more design is needed
optionExplain: Availability does not give read-your-writes.
Leaderless replication has no leader.
Right: leaderless replication offers weak guarantees, and the team should check this need.
Quorums do not guarantee read-your-writes.
questions.explain: Availability and strong guarantees pull in opposite directions.
questions.teaches: In a Dynamo-style leaderless database you usually do not get read-your-writes, monotonic reads or consistent prefix reads, and stronger guarantees generally require transactions or consensus.

questions.q: A user posts a comment, refreshes, and does not see it. Which guarantee prevents this?
questions.explain: Each lag anomaly has a matching guarantee. The cards that follow explain them.
options: Monotonic reads, which stop a user seeing older data after newer data
Consistent prefix reads, which keep causally related writes in order
Read-after-write consistency, which shows a user their own submitted writes
Last write wins, which keeps one of several conflicting writes
optionExplain: That concerns reads going backward in time, not a missing own write.
That concerns the order of related writes, such as a question and its answer.
Right: it promises that a user sees the updates they submitted themselves.
That is a conflict rule and not a read guarantee.

questions.q: Consistent prefix reads means users see data in a state that makes ____ sense.
questions.explain: For example a question appears before its reply.

questions.q: After refreshing a page a user sees an earlier snapshot of a discussion than before. Which guarantee is missing?
options: Monotonic reads, which stops a user seeing older data after newer
Consistent prefix reads, which keeps causally related writes in order
Read-after-write consistency, which shows a user their own writes
Last write wins, which picks one of several conflicting writes
optionExplain: Right: seeing an earlier snapshot after a later one is a read that goes backward in time.
Prefix reads address order of causally related writes, not time going backward.
Read-after-write concerns the user own writes.
Last write wins is a conflict rule and not a read guarantee.
questions.explain: Going back in time is the monotonic reads anomaly.

questions.q: Sort each issue into replication lag or concurrent writes.

items.t: A user cannot see what they just submitted
Two leaders accept different titles for one page
A user sees time go backward between reads
Two clients write one key at once in a leaderless store
An answer appears before its question
Siblings must be merged

questions.explain: Lag issues concern what readers see; concurrency issues concern conflicting writes.

questions.q: What does the summary say about how a database can determine whether one operation happened before another?
options: It says this cannot be determined by a database at all
It examined an algorithm for this, and touched on methods for resolving conflicts by merging
It says wall clocks alone are used to decide this order
It says a leader is required to decide which came first
optionExplain: The chapter shows how a database can determine it.
Right: the summary mentions the algorithm for detecting concurrency and merge-based resolution.
Clocks are not trusted for this in the chapter.
The algorithm works without a leader.
questions.explain: The chapter ends by tying concurrency detection to merging.
questions.teaches: We examined an algorithm that a database might use to determine whether one operation happened before another, or whether they happened concurrently, and touched on methods for resolving conflicts by merging together concurrent updates.

questions.q: A team fixes vanishing comments by pinning each user to one replica. Which guarantee is that, and is it enough for read-your-writes?
options: Read-after-write consistency in full, since the user always reads the same replica
Consistent prefix reads, since one replica holds writes in order
Strong consistency, since only one replica is ever read
Monotonic reads, which on its own does not guarantee that users see their own writes
optionExplain: The pinned replica might not have the write yet.
Pinning does not relate to ordering across partitions.
Strong consistency is not provided by reading one lagging replica.
Right: pinning gives monotonic reads only, since the replica may still be behind the write.
questions.explain: Pinning keeps reads from regressing, but the pinned replica may still be behind the user's write.
questions.teaches: Monotonic reads is a lesser guarantee than strong consistency but a stronger guarantee than eventual consistency.

questions.q: A table has outgrown the disks of its server. Read replicas hold full copies, so each replica is also full. What helps?
options: Split the table into pieces and place the pieces on different nodes
Add more replicas so that each copy holds a smaller share of the rows
Send all writes to one replica so the others can free their space
Keep the table whole but compress each replica more than the original
optionExplain: Right: pieces on different nodes spread the data over many disks.
Each replica is a full copy of the same data, so more replicas do not make any copy smaller.
Where writes go does not change how much data each replica must hold.
Compression may buy a little room, but it does not spread the data over more machines.
questions.explain: Spreading different pieces over different nodes is what gives room to grow. The card next names this idea.
questions.rule: Pieces on different nodes, not more copies.

questions.q: Breaking a dataset into pieces so that each record belongs to exactly one piece, placed on different nodes, is called ____ (also known as sharding).
questions.explain: The book calls this partitioning; each record, row or document belongs to exactly one partition.

questions.q: A ticketing site finds one server cannot answer its volume of requests. Which benefit does partitioning give for requests that each touch one partition?
options: Each complex query automatically runs faster because the data is split
Each node can answer the requests for its own partition, so adding nodes raises throughput
Every node holds every record, so any node can answer any request
Each request is copied to every node, so the fastest node answers it first and the others stop work
