optionExplain: Large complex queries can be parallelised, but the book says that gets significantly harder, not automatic.
Right: the nodes work independently on their own partitions, so capacity grows with the number of nodes.
That describes full replication, where every node has all the data, not partitioning.
Sending a request to every node is the opposite of what partitioning does; it is closer to replication.
questions.explain: Single-partition queries are independent of each other, which is why throughput scales with nodes.

questions.q: A data warehouse query scans and aggregates a large share of a dataset spread over 40 partitions. What does the book expect?
options: It runs exactly like a single-partition query, because partitions are independent of each other and share no data
It runs on one chosen node, which fetches all the other partitions first
It can be parallelised across nodes, but this is significantly harder than single-partition queries
It cannot be run at all, because no node holds the whole dataset
optionExplain: Independent partitions help single-partition queries; a query that spans many is a different problem.
That would give up the benefit of spreading the work; the point is to run parts of the query where the data is.
Right: parallel execution across partitions is possible but much harder than a query that stays in one partition.
Databases may support operations that touch multiple partitions at the same time.
questions.explain: Queries that span partitions can use many nodes, but coordinating them is the hard part.
questions.rule: Spanning partitions is possible but harder.

questions.q: True or false: A partitioned database normally stores each record in several partitions, so that it survives the loss of one node.
questions.explain: Each record belongs to exactly one partition. Surviving a node failure comes from replicating each partition on several nodes, which the next idea covers.
questions.rule: Fault tolerance comes from copies of a partition, not from extra partitions.

questions.q: A postmortem reports a network partition between data centres, and a colleague concludes the database is partitioned. How are the two related?
options: Partitioning is the repair applied after a network partition is detected
A network partition happens only in databases that have been split into partitions
They are the same event: a network fault splits the database into the partitions this book describes
They are unrelated: a network partition is a fault, while partitioning is a deliberate split
optionExplain: Partitioning is chosen for scalability in advance; it is not a repair step for network faults.
Network faults can occur in any multi-node system, whether or not its data is partitioned.
The words match, but one is a deliberate design choice and the other is a fault in the network.
Right: the book states that partitioning has nothing to do with network partitions, which are a type of fault.
questions.explain: Partitioning, as used in this chapter, is an intentional way of breaking a large database into smaller ones and has nothing to do with network partitions (netsplits).
questions.rule: Partitioning is a design choice; a network partition is a fault.
questions.teaches: Partitioning, as discussed in this chapter, has nothing to do with network partitions (netsplits), which are a type of fault in the network between nodes.

questions.q: A 4-node cluster splits its data into partitions, each stored on three nodes. Which arrangement is plausible?
options: One node leads every partition and the other three only follow
Each record is cut into three pieces, one piece per copy
Each node leads some partitions and follows others
Each partition lives on one node and copies are kept off the cluster
optionExplain: That is possible, but it would pile all write work on one node; the typical picture spreads leaders around.
Copies hold the same data; a record is not cut up between them.
Right: leaders can be spread over all the nodes, each also following other partitions.
Copies of each partition are stored on several nodes of the cluster for fault tolerance.
questions.explain: Spreading leaders over all nodes is the usual picture. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Every node can lead some partitions and follow others.

questions.q: In a partitioned database with leader-follower replication, each partition's leader is on one node and its ____ are on other nodes.
questions.explain: A partition's followers are placed on other nodes than its leader.

questions.q: Each partition of a file-sync cluster has a leader and two followers. Node 3 fails. Where is the data it led?
options: On the follower nodes that hold copies of those partitions
Only on the routing tier, which caches every record
Moved into other partitions, because records belong to several
Gone until node 3 is repaired, since each record lives on its leader
optionExplain: Right: followers hold copies of the leader's partition, which is why the data survives.
A routing tier forwards requests; it does not hold the data.
Each record belongs to exactly one partition, so it does not move into another.
Without copies that would be true, but combining partitioning with replication is meant to avoid it.
questions.explain: The copies on other nodes keep each partition available when its leader's node fails.
questions.rule: Copies of a partition live on other nodes.

questions.q: Which statement tells partitioning and replication apart?
options: Both split each record into pieces; replication does it on write, partitioning on read
Partitioning gives each record one partition; replication stores copies of the data on several nodes
Both store each record in all pieces; they differ only in which node leads
Partitioning stores copies of the same data on several nodes; replication gives each record to one piece
optionExplain: Neither technique splits individual records into pieces.
Right: partitions divide the data, replicas duplicate it.
Storing each record everywhere is full replication, which does not scale the data size.
This swaps the two definitions.
questions.explain: Partitioning divides the data into disjoint pieces, while replication duplicates pieces on other nodes.

questions.q: True or false: Because each partition is replicated, a single record belongs to the partitions of every node that holds a copy.
questions.explain: A record belongs to exactly one partition. The nodes holding copies store the same partition, not additional ones for that record.
questions.rule: Copies of a partition are not extra partitions.

questions.q: A team already runs leader-follower replication as described for single-node databases and now adds partitioning. What carries over?
options: Only synchronous replication is possible, because each partition is too small for asynchronous followers
The replication scheme must be redesigned, since leaders now depend on the partition boundaries
Replication is no longer needed, because partitions can be rebuilt from the other partitions
Replication ideas apply equally to each partition, and the two choices are mostly independent
optionExplain: Nothing in the chapter ties partitioned databases to a particular replication mode.
The book treats the two choices as mostly independent, so one does not force a redesign of the other.
Other partitions hold different records, so they cannot rebuild a lost partition.
Right: the book says the replication ideas apply equally to partitions, and the choice of partitioning scheme is mostly independent of the choice of replication scheme.
questions.explain: The two choices are mostly independent, which is why the rest of this chapter can ignore replication.
questions.rule: Choose partitioning and replication mostly independently.
questions.teaches: The choice of partitioning scheme is mostly independent of the choice of replication scheme, and everything said about replication applies equally to replication of partitions.

questions.q: A 10-node cluster stores user records, and one node receives most of the requests. How does this affect throughput?
options: Only storage suffers, since requests are cheap compared with data
Throughput stays tenfold, since the data itself is split into ten equal parts across the nodes
Throughput improves, since the idle nodes can rest and recover
The busy node limits the whole cluster, so ten nodes give little more than one
optionExplain: Requests use CPU and disk time on the node that serves them, so a hot node is slow.
Splitting the data does not help if the requests still go to one node.
Idle nodes add no capacity to the busy node's partitions.
Right: the single busy node becomes the bottleneck.
questions.explain: Throughput scales only if load spreads. The card next gives the terms for this.

questions.q: A partition that receives disproportionately high load is called a hot ____.
questions.explain: A hot spot is a partition with disproportionately high load; the unfair spread that causes it is called skew.

questions.q: In a chat service with eight partitions, two hold most messages and take most requests. What describes this?
options: The partitioning is skewed, and those two partitions are hot spots
The partitioning is random, and those two are the cache nodes
The partitioning is balanced, since every partition holds some messages
The partitioning is replicated, and those two are the leaders
optionExplain: Right: unfair spread is skew, and overloaded partitions are hot spots.
Random assignment would tend to spread load evenly, not concentrate it.
Every partition holding some data does not make the load fair.
Replication is about copies of data, not about uneven load.
questions.explain: Skew is the unfair spread, and hot spots are the overloaded partitions it creates.
questions.rule: Skew is the cause; hot spots are the result.

questions.q: A designer assigns each new record to a random node to avoid hot spots. A client then reads one record by its ID. What happens?
options: The client asks one node, which reads the record from the others
The client is refused, since random placement forbids reads by ID
The client cannot tell which node holds it, so all nodes are queried in parallel
The client uses the ID to compute the node, as it would with any scheme based on the key
optionExplain: No node has a way to know where the record is either, without asking.
Reads are possible; they are just expensive.
Right: random placement discards the link between a key and its node.
Computing the node needs a rule based on the key, which random placement does not have.
questions.explain: Evenness bought with randomness costs findability.
questions.rule: Random placement hides where a record lives.

questions.q: True or false: Random assignment is the best scheme because it spreads data evenly and keeps single-record reads cheap.
questions.explain: Random assignment spreads data evenly but makes single-record reads expensive, since every node must be queried. The book looks for better schemes based on the key.
questions.rule: Even spread without findability is a poor deal.

questions.q: A metrics platform finds that every request lands on one partition and nine of its ten nodes idle. What is the bottleneck?
options: The hash function, since it spreads the keys too evenly
The single busy node, because the other nodes cannot share its work
The network between the nodes, since it carries all the load
The replication scheme, since followers slow down the leader
optionExplain: An even spread would help here, not hurt.
Right: in the extreme case of all load on one partition, the one node is the bottleneck.
Nothing in the scenario points to the network; the nodes are idle.
Replication is not the cause; the load is concentrated on one partition.
questions.explain: In the extreme case all the load lands on one partition, nine of ten nodes sit idle and the single busy node is the bottleneck.
questions.rule: At worst a cluster performs like one node.
questions.teaches: In an extreme case all the load could end up on one partition, so 9 out of 10 nodes are idle and the bottleneck is the single busy node.

questions.q: A paper encyclopedia comes in 12 volumes. How can a reader tell from an entry's title which volume holds it?
options: Entries are sorted by length, short titles first
Each volume holds entries by the year they were written
Each volume holds a random sample of titles, listed in an index
Each volume covers a consecutive stretch of the alphabet
optionExplain: Length does not follow from the title the reader knows.
The reader does not know when an entry was written.
Random placement means the reader must check an index, or every volume.
Right: consecutive ranges let the title identify the volume.
questions.explain: Consecutive ranges make location easy. The card next applies this to partitions.

questions.q: In key range partitioning, each partition owns a continuous ____ of keys, from some minimum to some maximum.
questions.explain: A continuous range of keys goes to each partition.
questions.rule: Each partition owns a continuous range.

questions.q: An invoicing app must often fetch all invoices with numbers between 40,000 and 40,500 in one request. Why does key range partitioning suit this?
options: Hashing the invoice numbers puts consecutive invoices next to each other on the same partition
Every partition holds a copy of every invoice in that range
Neighbouring numbers sit together in sorted order, so a few partitions hold the range
The range is split over all nodes so each fetches one invoice
optionExplain: Hashing scatters neighbours instead.
Partitions hold disjoint ranges, not copies of the same invoices.
Right: sorting keeps neighbours together, so the scan stays on few partitions.
Spreading neighbours over all nodes is what range partitioning avoids.
questions.explain: A range scan stays inside one or a few partitions because neighbouring keys are stored together.

questions.q: A surname database is partitioned into 13 equal letter pairs (A-B, C-D and so on). Many surnames start with a few letters. What happens?
options: Some partitions grow much bigger than others, so the boundaries need to adapt to the data
The extra surnames move automatically to the neighbouring partition's index and rebalance it
Range scans become impossible, since the data is uneven
All partitions stay equal, because each holds the same number of letters
optionExplain: Right: equal key ranges do not mean equal amounts of data when keys cluster.
Nothing moves unless boundaries are adjusted by someone or something.
Range scans still work; they are just unevenly priced.
Equal letter counts do not mean equal data when some letters start many more surnames than others.
questions.explain: The ranges of keys are not necessarily evenly spaced, because the data may not be evenly distributed.
questions.rule: Fit boundaries to the data, not to the alphabet.

questions.q: True or false: In key range partitioning the boundaries must be evenly spaced so that each partition holds the same amount of data.
questions.explain: Boundaries need to follow the data. Evenly spaced ranges would give some partitions far more data than others when keys are uneven.

questions.q: A new fleet-tracking database stores vehicle IDs with an uneven distribution. Who can set the partition boundaries under key range partitioning?
options: Neither; the boundaries are fixed by the key type
An administrator can choose them manually, or the database can choose them automatically
Only an administrator, since the database has no way to observe how the keys are distributed
Only the database, since manual boundaries would unbalance the nodes
optionExplain: The key type only fixes the order of keys, not where the boundaries fall.
Right: the book says the boundaries might be chosen manually or by the database itself.
Databases can choose the boundaries automatically, as in the splitting described later.
Manual choice is allowed, and often the only way to start.
questions.explain: Boundaries can be set by an administrator or by the database; the book names Bigtable, HBase, RethinkDB and early MongoDB as users of this scheme.
questions.rule: Boundaries can be manual or automatic.
questions.teaches: The partition boundaries might be chosen manually by an administrator, or the database can choose them automatically.

questions.q: Sensors write readings to a database partitioned by timestamp, one range per day. Which problem would you worry about?
options: Old partitions receive every write because they hold the most data and so are searched first
Each sensor needs a partition of its own
Today's partition receives every write while older partitions sit idle
Writes are spread evenly, so reads become slow
optionExplain: Old partitions receive no new writes, since new readings are timestamped now.
Nothing in the design requires a partition per sensor.
Right: new measurements always carry the latest timestamp.
Evenly spread writes would not be a problem; the issue is the opposite.
questions.explain: Writes follow the clock, so they pile into one partition. The card next shows a fix.
questions.rule: Time-first keys send all writes to now.

questions.q: With one partition per day and a timestamp key, all current writes go to the partition for ____.
questions.explain: Measurements are written as they happen, so they all carry today's timestamp.

questions.q: A ride-booking backend logs trips keyed by pickup time and sees one overloaded partition. Which key change relieves it?
options: Prefix each key with the driver ID so writes from many drivers land on different partitions
Move to one partition per hour instead of one per day
Reverse the timestamp format so recent trips sort first
Make the timestamp finer, down to the millisecond, so that writes arriving together are separated out
optionExplain: Right: leading with an identifier shared by many simultaneous writers spreads the writes.
The current hour is just as hot as the current day.
Reversing the order still keeps all new keys together at one end.
A finer timestamp still sorts by time, and today's range still takes all the new writes.
questions.explain: Only a change in the leading part of the key breaks up the time ordering of new writes.
questions.rule: Lead with a value many writers share.

questions.q: A sensor system now keys by sensor name, then time. A dashboard needs yesterday's readings from 50 sensors. What does the query need?
options: Nothing special, as one partition holds every sensor's data
One range scan over the single partition for yesterday
A hash lookup per timestamp across all sensors
A separate range query for each sensor name
optionExplain: Sensors are spread over partitions by name, so no single partition holds them all.
That is the layout before the change, when time came first.
Hashing does not enter this layout.
Right: each sensor's data is a separate key range.
questions.explain: Spreading writes by sensor name costs the single scan over a time range.
questions.rule: The fix trades away cross-source range scans.

questions.q: True or false: Prefixing the timestamp with the sensor name spreads writes evenly even when only one sensor is writing.
questions.explain: The fix assumes many sensors are active at once. With a single writer, its writes still go to one partition.
questions.rule: The spread comes from many simultaneous writers.

questions.q: A team keeps the timestamp as the first key element and reports on whole calendar months. What benefit do they get?
options: Hot spots disappear, since the timestamps are unique
A range scan fetches all readings from a particular month easily
Writes spread over all partitions, since time varies with each reading
Each sensor's readings stay together, so per-sensor queries are one scan
optionExplain: Unique timestamps do not stop the current time range from taking all writes.
Right: with time first, a month is one range of keys, so it is easy to scan.
The opposite holds: writes pile onto the current partition.
That is the benefit of putting the sensor name first.
questions.explain: Range scans over time are very useful for the timestamp key, for example fetching all readings from a particular month.
questions.rule: Time-first keys still make time-range reads easy.
questions.teaches: Range scans are very useful with a timestamp key, because they let you easily fetch all the readings from a particular month.

questions.q: User IDs are handed out in order, and the newest users are the most active. How could you spread their load over partitions?
options: Give each ID range its own partition, so the newest range has one to itself
Assign each new user to the partition with the lowest ID
Pass each ID through a hash function and partition by the hash value
Keep all active users in the first partition for fast access
optionExplain: Ranges keep newest users together, which concentrates load on the last partition.
Following the lowest ID again keeps new users together.
Right: hashing scatters neighbouring IDs across the partitions.
Concentrating active users is the hot spot you want to avoid.
questions.explain: Hashing breaks up neighbouring keys. The card next shows what it costs.

questions.q: A good hash function takes skewed data and makes it ____ distributed.
questions.explain: The hash values spread uniformly over the range, even when the input strings are very similar.
questions.rule: Hashing evens out skew in the keys.

questions.q: A product catalogue is partitioned by the hash of the SKU. A shopper asks for all SKUs from A100 to A200. What happens?
options: The query goes to every partition, since neighbouring SKUs are scattered
The query goes to two partitions, one for each end of the range
The query goes to one partition, since the SKUs are close in sorted order
The query is rejected, since hashed keys cannot be read at all
optionExplain: Right: adjacent keys no longer share a partition, so the range must be asked of all of them.
The ends of the range hash to unrelated places; the middle keys do too.
That would hold for key range partitioning, not for hash partitioning.
Single-key lookups still work; only the range query is costly.
questions.explain: Sort order is lost under hash partitioning, so ranges scatter.

questions.q: Which workload favours hash partitioning over key range partitioning?
options: Autocomplete lookups that read all names starting with a prefix
Many clients writing sequential IDs, with reads only by exact ID
Exports that stream a continuous slice of the key space
Monthly reports that scan all orders between two dates
optionExplain: Prefix lookups are range reads and want sorted keys.
Right: sequential writes would pile onto one range partition, and exact-ID reads do not need order.
Streaming a continuous slice is a range read.
Date-range scans benefit from sorted keys.
questions.explain: Choose by what the reads need: exact keys can be hashed, ranges cannot.
questions.rule: Hash for exact lookups, ranges for scans.

questions.q: True or false: For partitioning purposes the hash function need not be cryptographically strong.
questions.explain: It only needs to spread keys evenly. Cassandra and MongoDB use MD5 and Voldemort uses the Fowler-Noll-Vo function.
questions.rule: An even spread is the requirement, not secrecy.
questions.teaches: A partitioning hash function need not be cryptographically strong: Cassandra and MongoDB use MD5, and Voldemort uses the Fowler-Noll-Vo function.

questions.q: A developer partitions by the built-in hash of the programming language, and nodes run as separate processes. What risk does the book point out?
options: The built-in hash keeps keys sorted, so range queries become unfair
The built-in hash is too slow to use for any key
The built-in hash always sends similar keys to the same partition
The same key may get a different hash value in different processes
optionExplain: Hash values do not preserve key order.
Speed is not the concern raised; consistency between processes is.
A good hash scatters similar keys; this is not the stated problem.
Right: for example Java's Object.hashCode() and Ruby's Object#hash can differ between processes, so a key could be placed inconsistently.
questions.explain: Built-in hash functions made for hash tables may not suit partitioning because a key can hash differently in different processes.
questions.rule: Use a hash that gives the same value for the same key everywhere.
questions.teaches: Many languages have simple hash functions built in, but they may not be suitable for partitioning: in Java's Object.hashCode() and Ruby's Object#hash the same key may have a different hash value in different processes.

questions.q: A vendor page says its database uses consistent hashing. What might you reasonably question?
options: Whether the database guarantees ACID transactions
Whether the term is used accurately, since it is often applied loosely
Whether the database keeps all of its replicas consistent after every single write
Whether the database sorts keys for range queries
optionExplain: It also does not refer to ACID consistency.
Right: the name suggests more than it says, and database docs often misuse it.
The word consistent does not refer to replica consistency.
Hash-based schemes do not keep keys sorted.
questions.explain: The name is misleading. The card next explains where it comes from.

questions.q: Consistent hashing was defined for evenly distributing load across which kind of system?
options: A single-node database with one B-tree index
A multi-leader replication group spread across several data centres worldwide
An internet-wide system of caches such as a content delivery network
A distributed transaction coordinator
optionExplain: A single node has no partitions to balance.
Replication groups copy data rather than balance partitions.
Right: it was designed for an internet-wide system of caches such as a CDN.
Transaction coordination is a different problem.
questions.explain: Karger and colleagues defined it for caches such as a CDN.

questions.q: True or false: A database that guarantees ACID consistency is for that reason using consistent hashing.
questions.explain: The word consistent in consistent hashing does not refer to ACID consistency or replica consistency. It describes a rebalancing approach.

questions.q: To avoid the confusion, the authors suggest calling it ____ partitioning.
questions.explain: Hash partitioning is the plain description of partitioning by hash of key.

questions.q: A blog says: consistent hashing guarantees that every replica returns the latest write. What is the mistake?
options: It confuses a rebalancing approach with replica consistency
It confuses reads with writes, since only reads are consistent
It confuses caches with databases, since caches never replicate
It confuses hashing with encryption, since consistent means secure
optionExplain: Right: consistent describes a rebalancing approach, not read-after-write guarantees.
The mistake is about the meaning of the word, not about reads and writes.
Caches are where the idea was defined, and the claim is wrong for a different reason.
The word has nothing to do with secrecy.
questions.explain: The word consistent in consistent hashing does not describe replica consistency.
questions.rule: Consistent hashing is not a consistency guarantee.

questions.q: A CDN spans many organisations, and no node can act as a central coordinator. What feature of consistent hashing helps?
options: Every node keeps a full copy of every other node's data
Boundaries are sorted by key name, so every node can compute them without asking any other node
A shared lock service makes every node agree on each key's owner
Random partition boundaries remove the need for central control or distributed consensus
optionExplain: Full copies would defeat the purpose of spreading load.
Sorted boundaries are key range partitioning, not this scheme.
Locking would itself be central control.
Right: random boundaries let each party act without a coordinator.
questions.explain: Karger and colleagues chose random partition boundaries so that no central control or distributed consensus is needed.
questions.rule: Random boundaries remove the need for a coordinator.
questions.teaches: Consistent hashing uses randomly chosen partition boundaries to avoid the need for central control or distributed consensus.

questions.q: A forum wants the posts of each thread kept together and sorted by time, while threads spread over many nodes. What key fits?
options: A key made of thread ID then post time, partitioned by the thread ID
The thread title alone, sorted alphabetically
A random number prefixed to each post, so that posts spread evenly over all nodes
Post time alone, partitioned by ranges of time
optionExplain: Right: the thread ID places the thread, and the time keeps its posts ordered.
Titles do not keep a thread's posts in time order.
A random number keeps neither threads together nor time order.
Time alone would put each day's posts together, across threads.
questions.explain: A two-part key can do both jobs. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: One key part places, another sorts.

questions.q: In a compound primary key, only the ____ part is hashed to determine the partition.
questions.explain: The first part picks the partition; the other columns sort the data inside it.

questions.q: A fitness tracker keys readings by (device_id, reading_time), hashing the device ID. Which query is efficient?
options: Readings of every device with an ID between 10 and 20
All devices' readings between 08:00 and 09:00
The ten devices with the most readings
All readings of device 17 between 08:00 and 09:00
optionExplain: A range of the first column cannot be scanned efficiently once it is hashed.
The time range spans every device, so every partition must be asked.
Counting readings per device is not what the key order supports.
Right: fixing the device ID selects one partition, where readings are sorted by time.
questions.explain: Fix the first column and scan the rest.
questions.rule: Fix the hashed part, scan the sorted part.

questions.q: A query asks for devices with IDs 10 to 20 on that fitness-tracker store. How does it run?
options: It runs on the partition holding the most recent reading
It cannot use a range scan, because the hashed first column scatters those IDs
It runs on the partition holding ID 10, which forwards the rest to the other partitions
It runs as one scan, since the IDs are consecutive
optionExplain: Recency has no role in placing device IDs.
Right: a range of the first column is not searchable efficiently.
No partition forwards queries for other partitions' data in this scheme.
Consecutive IDs hash to unrelated places.
questions.explain: A query cannot search for a range of values within the first column of a compound key.
questions.rule: No ranges on the hashed column.

questions.q: True or false: With a hashed first key part, rows sharing the first value are scattered over partitions by their second column.
questions.explain: Rows with the same first value stay on a single partition, ordered by the other columns.

questions.q: A music app stores each listener's plays under (listener_id, played_at). What does the book say this design gives?
options: A model where every play is stored on its own partition for even load
A model where plays from different listeners are sorted together by time across all partitions
An elegant one-to-many model: one listener's plays come from a single partition, in time order
A model where listener IDs can be scanned as a range
optionExplain: Plays of one listener stay together, not one per partition.
Different listeners may live on different partitions, so there is no global time order.
Right: the concatenated index suits a parent with many children.
Listener IDs sit in the hashed first column and cannot be range scanned.
questions.explain: The concatenated index approach enables an elegant data model for one-to-many relationships, such as one user who posts many updates.
questions.rule: One parent, many children, one partition.
questions.teaches: The concatenated index approach enables an elegant data model for one-to-many relationships, such as the updates posted by a user.

questions.section: Skewed Workloads and Relieving Hot Spots
questions.q: Millions of users comment on one live event whose data is stored under a single key. The key is hashed. What happens to its partition?
options: The requests are queued until the key cools down
The load spreads out, since hashing scatters requests for the key over many partitions
The partition is split into one partition per user
It still receives every request, since one key hashes to the same place
optionExplain: Nothing in hashing queues requests.
Hashing spreads different keys, not repeated requests for one key.
Splitting by user would need a different key per user.
Right: the hash of one key never changes.
questions.explain: Hashing spreads keys, not repeated requests for one key. The card next shows a fix.

questions.section: Skewed Workloads and Relieving Hot Spots
questions.q: True or false: Hashing a key spreads repeated requests for that single key over several partitions.
questions.explain: The same key always has the same hash, so all its requests go to the same partition.
questions.rule: Same key, same hash, same partition.

questions.section: Skewed Workloads and Relieving Hot Spots
questions.q: A ticketing system appends a random two-digit decimal number to one hot event ID. Its writes now spread over ____ different keys.
questions.explain: A two-digit decimal number has 100 values, 00 to 99, giving 100 distinct keys.

questions.section: Skewed Workloads and Relieving Hot Spots
questions.q: After the hot event's writes are spread over 100 keys, what must a read for that event do?
options: Nothing, because the hash restores the original key
Read all 100 keys and combine the data
Read any one key, since all 100 hold the full data
Read the first key, which stores the index of the others
optionExplain: The hash does not undo the random number.
Right: the writes are split, so the data must be gathered.
Each key holds only a share of the writes.
No key is designated as an index in the described technique.
questions.explain: Splitting writes shifts work onto reads.

questions.section: Skewed Workloads and Relieving Hot Spots
questions.q: A team appends a random number to every key in the database, to be safe. What is wrong with this?
options: The keys can no longer be stored on different partitions
A random number makes the hash function return uniform values for every key it sees
Most keys have low write throughput, so reads and bookkeeping pay for nothing
The database cannot store more than 100 keys per partition
optionExplain: Different keys can indeed be placed on different partitions; that is the purpose.
Uniform hashing is a benefit, not a problem.
Right: the technique only makes sense for the small number of hot keys.
Nothing limits partitions to 100 keys.
questions.explain: Only a few keys need splitting, and the rest pay a cost for no benefit.
questions.rule: Split only the keys that are hot.

questions.section: Skewed Workloads and Relieving Hot Spots
questions.q: A team assumes their database detects hot keys and rebalances them automatically. What is the situation the book describes today?
options: Most data systems cannot compensate for heavy skew automatically, so the application must reduce it
Most data systems detect hot keys and split them without being asked
The database always routes hot keys to a dedicated, larger node
Hot keys only arise from poor hash functions, which the database detects and replaces for you over time
optionExplain: Right: the book says most data systems cannot automatically compensate, so it falls to the application.
That may come in the future, but the book says it is not usually available.
The book mentions no dedicated hot-key node.
Even a perfect hash cannot spread a single key.
questions.explain: Most data systems today cannot automatically compensate for a highly skewed workload, so the application is responsible for reducing it.
questions.rule: Skew relief is the application's job today.
questions.teaches: Today, most data systems are not able to automatically compensate for such a highly skewed workload, so it is the responsibility of the application to reduce the skew.

questions.q: A used-car site splits its listings by listing ID, and users filter by colour. Where might the red cars be?
options: In the partition chosen by the colour's first letter
In the partition of the lowest listing ID
In several partitions, since nothing ties colour to listing ID
In one partition, since the colour index gathers all of the matching cars together
optionExplain: Colour does not choose the partition of the listing.
The lowest ID has no special role.
Right: listing IDs are unrelated to colour.
An index finds red cars, but the cars themselves stay where their listing ID put them.
questions.explain: Listings are placed by ID, not colour. The card next shows how the index copes.

questions.q: A document-partitioned secondary index is also called a ____ index.
questions.explain: It is local because each partition indexes only its own documents.

questions.q: A recipe site partitions by recipe ID and indexes recipes by cuisine. A new Thai recipe is added. Which partitions update their index?
options: Every partition, to keep the cuisine counts equal
The partition that holds the first Thai recipe
Two partitions: the recipe's and the one for the letter T
Only the partition that stores the recipe
optionExplain: Other partitions do not index this document, so they have nothing to change.
Where the first Thai recipe lives is irrelevant.
The index is not partitioned by term here.
Right: each partition indexes only its own documents.
questions.explain: Local indexes keep writes within one partition.
questions.rule: A local write touches one partition.

questions.q: On the same recipe site, a user searches for Thai recipes. Where do the matching recipes live?
options: In any partition, so every partition's index must be consulted
In the partition whose ID is numerically closest to the word Thai in the index
In one partition, which holds the Thai index for all
In the partition of the user's last search
optionExplain: Right: the index entries are local, so all partitions must be asked.
Words are not mapped to recipe IDs.
No partition holds a global Thai index in this scheme.
Earlier searches do not decide where recipes are stored.
questions.explain: Reads on a local index touch all partitions unless the document IDs were chosen with care.
questions.rule: Reads on a local index go everywhere.

questions.q: True or false: In a document-partitioned index, adding one document may require updates to the secondary indexes of several partitions.
questions.explain: Only the partition holding the document updates its index. Needing several partitions on a write is the cost of the other approach, term-partitioned indexes.

questions.q: A team on a key-value store builds its own value-to-ID mapping in application code. What does the book warn about?
options: Application code cannot read the partitions that hold the mapping, so it cannot update it either
Race conditions and intermittent write failures can leave the index out of sync with the data
The mapping must be stored in one partition only
The database refuses to hash the keys of a home-grown index
optionExplain: Nothing prevents reading, but consistency is hard to keep.
Right: the index needs great care to stay consistent with the data.
The book does not say the mapping must live in one partition.
The key-value store does not forbid hashing for any key.
questions.explain: A secondary index built by the application can go out of sync because of race conditions and partial write failures.
questions.teaches: If you implement a secondary index yourself in application code, race conditions and intermittent write failures, where some changes were saved but others were not, can easily cause the data to go out of sync.

questions.q: A search must find all red cars across eight partitions, and no partition is known to hold them. How should the query run?
options: Ask every partition and combine the answers
Ask one random partition and retry if it has none
Ask the partition with the most cars
Ask the first partition and trust that it knows the rest
optionExplain: Right: with no clue about location, every partition has to be asked.
Retrying at random may miss cars that live in other partitions.
The largest partition does not hold all matching cars.
A partition does not know about other partitions' documents in this scheme.
questions.explain: With no location clue, the query goes to all. The card next names this.

questions.q: Sending a query to every partition and combining the results is called scatter/____.
questions.explain: Scatter the query out, gather the results back.

questions.q: A concert listing site filters by city and genre together using document-partitioned indexes. Why is a single-partition read hard?
options: Genres are hashed, so each genre ends up in a partition separate from every city's documents
The city index is global, so genre queries are rerouted
Each partition refuses queries with two conditions
Documents matching both conditions are not grouped by either, so they can lie anywhere
optionExplain: Hashing the genre is not part of this scheme.
Local indexes are per partition, not global.
Partitions answer multi-condition queries; the question is where the matches are.
Right: using more than one secondary index in a query makes single-partition service hard.
questions.explain: Two indexes in one query make it hard to arrange for the matches to be together.
questions.rule: Multi-index queries rarely stay in one partition.

questions.q: A query is sent to all 20 partitions in parallel, and one partition is slow. What is the risk?
options: The other partitions retry until the slow one answers
The slow partition's documents are dropped from the results to keep the query on time
The whole query is delayed, because the combined answer waits for the slow partition
The query becomes faster since 19 of 20 have answered
optionExplain: The scenario involves no retrying by other partitions.
Dropping documents would give wrong results; the query waits instead.
Right: this is tail latency amplification.
A combined answer cannot be complete before the slow partition answers.
questions.explain: The slowest partition holds up the combined answer.

questions.q: True or false: Querying the partitions in parallel removes the tail latency problem of scatter/gather.
questions.explain: Even in parallel, scatter/gather is prone to tail latency amplification, because the combined answer waits for the slowest response.

questions.q: A listings site partitions by (city, listing ID) and nearly all searches filter by one city. What does this arrangement allow?
options: City searches must still go to every partition, since the indexes are local to each one
City searches can often be served from a single partition, as vendors recommend
City searches are served from a global index on one node
City searches cannot be indexed, since the city is part of the key
optionExplain: Not if the document IDs are chosen so that matching documents sit together.
Right: structuring partitioning so that common secondary-index queries hit one partition is the vendors' advice.
A global index is a different approach, partitioned by term.
Indexing is possible whatever the key.
questions.explain: Most database vendors recommend that you structure your partitioning scheme so that secondary index queries can be served from a single partition, although that is not always possible.
questions.rule: Shape the key around the common queries.
questions.teaches: Most database vendors recommend that you structure your partitioning scheme so that secondary index queries can be served from a single partition, but that is not always possible.

questions.q: To avoid asking every partition for red cars, where could you keep the index entries for color:red?
options: Together in one index that covers all partitions and is itself split
On the car with the lowest listing ID
Inside the partition of each car, as they are kept now, with no shared index
On the client that issued the most searches
optionExplain: Right: gathering the entries lets a read find all red cars in one place.
A car's ID has nothing to do with where colour entries should live.
Entries kept inside each car's partition are what force the scatter/gather.
A client is not a place to keep a shared index.
questions.explain: Putting all entries for a term together makes reads cheap. The card next shows the cost.
questions.rule: Gather the entries for a term.

questions.q: A global secondary index is partitioned by the ____ being looked up, such as color:red.
questions.explain: That is why it is called term-partitioned.
questions.rule: The term decides the index partition.

questions.q: A job board needs searches by city to be served by one partition. Which design delivers that?
options: A single index stored on one node
A global index partitioned by the city term
A scatter/gather over all job partitions
A local index in each job's partition
optionExplain: One node would become the bottleneck and defeat the purpose of partitioning.
Right: all entries for one city sit in one index partition.
Scatter/gather visits all partitions, not one.
A local index spreads one city's jobs over partitions.
questions.explain: A read goes to the partition of the term.

questions.q: Match each index design or fact with its consequence.
pairs: A write touches one partition and a read scatters to all
A read uses one index partition and a write may touch several
A global index kept on a single node
Likely becomes a bottleneck and defeats partitioning
questions.explain: Local indexes make writes cheap and reads expensive, global indexes the reverse, and an unpartitioned global index defeats the point of partitioning.
questions.rule: Local favours writes, global favours reads.

questions.q: True or false: A global secondary index can be stored on one node, because it is only an index.
questions.explain: A single node would likely become a bottleneck and defeat the purpose of partitioning, so the global index must be partitioned too.
questions.rule: A global index is still partitioned.

questions.q: A used-car site wants queries on asking price between 5,000 and 8,000 from a global index. How should it partition the index?
options: By listing ID, as the cars are
On a single node, to keep price order
By the hash of the term, so price ranges are spread over all partitions
By the term itself, so price ranges sit in few index partitions
optionExplain: That reverts to a local index with scatter/gather.
A single node would be a bottleneck.
Hashing the term evens the load but scatters neighbouring prices.
Right: partitioning by the term itself helps range scans on a numeric property such as price.
questions.explain: Partitioning by the term itself is useful for range scans, while partitioning by hash of the term gives a more even load.
questions.rule: Term for ranges, hash of term for evenness.
questions.teaches: Partitioning by the term itself can be useful for range scans, for example on the asking price of a car, whereas partitioning on a hash of the term gives a more even distribution of load.

questions.q: One write must change index entries on three different nodes. What would you worry about?
options: The write must always be sent to a single node first
The three nodes must hold identical entries
A cross-node transaction is needed, or the index entries may lag
The index cannot be read by anyone until the write is acknowledged by all the nodes
optionExplain: A single entry point does not make three nodes update together.
The entries are different terms, so they are not identical.
Right: keeping all three in step needs a transaction; skipping it means a lag.
The readers could read in between, which is the problem.
questions.explain: Updating several nodes together is costly. The card next shows how databases cope.
questions.rule: Several nodes, no easy atomic update.

questions.q: Updates to global secondary indexes are often ____, so the index may lag behind the write.
questions.explain: Asynchronous means the index entries follow the write rather than changing at the same moment.

questions.q: A seller posts a listing and immediately searches the global category index, but the listing is missing. What explains this?
options: The index update is asynchronous and has not been applied yet
The listing was stored on the wrong partition
The index is local, so it ignores the new listing
The write failed, since the index would otherwise already show the new listing
optionExplain: Right: a read shortly after the write may not see the index change.
The listing's own partition does not decide whether the global index is current.
The scenario involves a global, not a local, index.
A write can succeed while the index entry is still on its way.
questions.explain: A just-made change may not yet be reflected in the index.
questions.rule: Fresh writes may not be in the index yet.

questions.q: A database decides to update its global index synchronously with every write. What does that require?
options: A single index node that takes every write so the index is updated in one place
A distributed transaction across all index partitions that the write affects
A local index in every partition instead
Followers that wait for leader election
optionExplain: A single node would defeat partitioning.
Right: the index changes must commit together across several partitions.
That would change the index design, not make the global index synchronous.
Leader election is unrelated.
questions.explain: An always-current term-partitioned index needs a distributed transaction.

questions.q: True or false: Once a write to a document is acknowledged, a term-partitioned index reflects it at once.
questions.explain: Updates to global indexes are often asynchronous, so the index may lag the write.

questions.q: A team relies on the global secondary indexes of Amazon DynamoDB. What delay does its documentation state?
options: Updated at the same moment as the write, even during faults
Updated within a minute after every write in normal conditions, and even faster during infrastructure faults
Normally within a fraction of a second, but longer delays are possible during infrastructure faults
Updated only when an administrator rebuilds the index
optionExplain: That would need synchronous updates, which the documentation does not claim.
The stated normal delay is a fraction of a second.
Right: the delay is short normally and can grow during faults.
Updates are automatic, not manual.
questions.explain: DynamoDB states that its global secondary indexes are updated within a fraction of a second in normal circumstances, but may see longer propagation delays when the infrastructure has faults.
questions.rule: Plan for longer delays during faults.
questions.teaches: Amazon DynamoDB states that its global secondary indexes are updated within a fraction of a second in normal circumstances, but may experience longer propagation delays in cases of faults in the infrastructure.

questions.q: Which are sensible demands on a rebalancing when a node is added?
options: Every record is copied to the new node first
Load ends up shared fairly between nodes
Reads and writes keep being served while data moves
All writes pause until the move finishes
No more data moves than necessary
optionExplain: Copying everything is far more than necessary.
Right: fairness is the point of the move.
Right: service should continue during the move.
Pausing writes would make the database unavailable for the move's duration.
Right: unnecessary movement costs network and disk I/O.
questions.explain: Fair result, continued service and minimal movement. The card next states them.

questions.q: The process of moving load from one node in the cluster to another is called ____.
questions.explain: Rebalancing moves load to match the cluster's current nodes.

questions.q: A replacement node joins after a failure. Which plan breaks one of the three requirements?
options: Serving reads and writes from the old nodes while the data moves to the new node
Moving only the partitions the new node needs
Ending with each node holding a fair share
Stopping all writes for the hour it takes to copy data to the new node
optionExplain: Serving during the move is what is asked for.
Moving only what is needed is a requirement, not a breach.
A fair result is the goal.
Right: the database should keep accepting reads and writes during rebalancing.
questions.explain: Service must continue during the move.

questions.q: A scheme reshuffles nearly every key when a node joins. Which requirement is most at risk?
options: That reads and writes are accepted, since keys have no addresses while they are being moved
That no more data than necessary moves, which also loads the network and disks
That the cluster ends fair, since reshuffling is random
That the node count stays constant
optionExplain: Reshuffling does not by itself stop service.
Right: excess movement costs time and I/O.
A thorough reshuffle may end up fair, but at a high price.
Adding a node changes the count by definition.
questions.explain: Excessive movement is the cost to avoid.

questions.q: True or false: A rebalancing may refuse writes while data moves, as long as reads keep working.
questions.explain: The database should continue accepting reads and writes while rebalancing happens.
questions.rule: Writes should continue during the move.

questions.q: A team switches from key range to hash partitioning. Do the minimum requirements for rebalancing change?
options: Yes: hash partitioning needs no fairness requirement
Yes: hash partitioning allows service to pause
Yes: key range partitioning needs no limit on data moved
No: they apply whichever partitioning scheme is used
optionExplain: Fairness matters for every scheme.
Service continuity applies to every scheme.
Moving little data matters for every scheme.
Right: the book gives them as expectations regardless of the scheme.
questions.explain: No matter which partitioning scheme is used, rebalancing is usually expected to meet these minimum requirements.
questions.rule: The requirements apply to every scheme.
questions.teaches: No matter which partitioning scheme is used, rebalancing is usually expected to meet these minimum requirements.

questions.q: Keys sit on nodes by hash mod 10. An 11th node joins and the formula becomes hash mod 11. What do you expect?
options: Most keys now map to a different node
No keys move, since the old assignments still work
Half the keys move to the new node
Only keys that hash to 10 move, to the new node
optionExplain: Right: a different divisor changes the result for most keys.
The old formula no longer applies once N is 11.
There is no rule that makes exactly half move.
Only one residue is new, but the remainders of all other keys change too.
questions.explain: A new divisor changes most remainders. The card next calls this a poor approach.

questions.q: With hash mod N, when N changes, most keys must ____ to a different node.
questions.explain: The remainder changes for most keys, so they have to change node.

questions.q: A key's hash is 2024 and 4 nodes (0 to 3) use hash mod 4. A fifth node joins. What happens to the key?
options: It moves from node 0 to node 3
It moves from node 0 to node 1
It moves from node 0 to node 4
It stays on node 0, since 2024 is divisible by 4
optionExplain: 2024 mod 5 is 4, not 3.
2024 mod 5 is 4, not 1.
Right: 2024 mod 4 is 0 and 2024 mod 5 is 4.
The divisor is now 5, so divisibility by 4 no longer decides.
questions.explain: Compute with the new divisor: 2024 divided by 5 leaves 4.

questions.q: An operator adds nodes one at a time to a cluster that uses mod N. What does each addition cost?
options: Only a few keys move, so each addition is cheap for the network and disks
Only the keys on the busiest node move
No keys move, but requests are rerouted
Most keys move, loading the network and disks heavily
optionExplain: That describes schemes that move only what is necessary.
Busyness plays no part in mod N.
The keys themselves change nodes.
Right: mod N makes rebalancing excessively expensive.
questions.explain: Each change in N moves most keys.
questions.rule: Frequent moves make mod N costly.

questions.q: True or false: With hash mod N, adding one node moves only the keys that the new node will own.
questions.explain: Most keys change nodes when N changes, not just those landing on the new node.
questions.rule: Most keys move, not only a few.

questions.q: A key has hash 123456. The cluster grows from 10 to 11 nodes and then to 12. How often does the key move?
options: Once: from node 6 to node 3 only
Twice: from node 6 to node 3, then to node 0
Twice: from node 6 to node 4, then to node 2
Never: 123456 is the same at every size
optionExplain: It also moves to node 0 when N reaches 12.
Right: 123456 mod 10 is 6, mod 11 is 3, and mod 12 is 0.
The remainders are 3 and 0, not 4 and 2.
The hash is the same but the remainder is not.
questions.explain: A single key can move at every change in N, as hash 123456 does on the way from 10 to 12 nodes.
questions.rule: Each growth step can move the same key again.
questions.teaches: A key with hash 123456 is on node 6 with 10 nodes, on node 3 with 11 nodes and on node 0 with 12 nodes.

questions.q: A 10-node cluster will grow over the years. How could its partitions be set up so that adding a node moves little data?
options: Create partitions only when a node joins, one per new node
Create one partition per node and rehash every key into new partitions when nodes join
Create many more partitions than nodes and move whole partitions as nodes join
Keep all data in one partition and replicate it to new nodes
optionExplain: A single new partition for each node leaves the old ones unchanged but unbalanced, and gives no stable key assignment.
Rehashing every key moves most data.
Right: only the assignment of partitions to nodes changes.
One partition replicated everywhere does not spread the data.
questions.explain: Many small partitions are easy to move. The card next explains the trade-off.

questions.q: With a fixed number of partitions, only the assignment of partitions to ____ changes when a node is added.
questions.explain: The partitions and the key assignment to them stay the same.

questions.q: 8 nodes hold 800 partitions, 100 each. A ninth node joins and load is shared evenly. About how many partitions does it get?
options: About 89, taken a few at a time from each existing node
About 8, one from each existing node
About 100, the same number that every node had before the new node joined
About 800, taking over from the oldest node
optionExplain: Right: 800 divided by 9 is about 89.
One partition from each node would leave the new node far below a fair share.
100 each would need 900 partitions.
Taking everything would leave the others empty.
questions.explain: A fair share is the total partitions divided by the new node count.
questions.rule: A fair share is total divided by nodes.

questions.q: A team creates 200 partitions for a 10-node cluster and plans to grow to 300 nodes. What limit do they hit?
options: The partitions become 300 as they split in half
The cluster can grow to 300 nodes, with some nodes holding no partitions
The partition count is the maximum number of nodes, so 200 nodes at most
The partition count grows automatically with each new node, up to 300 partitions
optionExplain: Splitting is not usually implemented in fixed-partition databases.
Nodes with no partitions would hold no data.
Right: the number of partitions configured at the outset is the most nodes you can use.
In this approach the count is not changed afterward.
questions.explain: The number of partitions configured at the outset is the maximum number of nodes you can have.
questions.rule: The count caps the node count.

questions.q: True or false: When a node joins under the fixed-partition approach, keys are reassigned from one partition to another.
questions.explain: Only whole partitions move between nodes. The number of partitions and the assignment of keys to partitions do not change.

questions.q: A cluster mixes two powerful nodes and four weaker ones. How can fixed partitions account for this?
options: Give the weaker nodes copies of the powerful nodes' keys
Rehash the keys with a weighted function
Reduce the partition count to the number of weak nodes
Assign more partitions to the more powerful nodes
optionExplain: Copying keys is replication, not a change in load share.
Keys keep their partitions under this approach.
Fewer partitions would reduce the maximum number of nodes.
Right: more partitions means a greater share of the load.
questions.explain: By assigning more partitions to nodes that are more powerful, you can force those nodes to take a greater share of the load.
questions.rule: Partition counts set each node's share.
questions.teaches: In principle, you can account for mismatched hardware in your cluster by assigning more partitions to nodes that are more powerful, forcing those nodes to take a greater share of the load.

questions.q: A key-range database starts empty and grows to terabytes. How should its partitions come about?
options: Created and divided as the data grows
Created one per row inserted
Defined by hashing each key into a partition
Defined once at the start with fixed boundaries
optionExplain: Right: partitions follow the data as it grows.
One partition per row would produce enormous overhead.
Hash partitioning is a different scheme from key ranges.
Fixed boundaries chosen without knowing the data may leave most partitions empty.
questions.explain: Partitions can grow and divide with the data. The card next shows how.

questions.q: When a partition grows past a configured size, it is ____ into two partitions.
questions.explain: A split puts roughly half of the data on each side.
questions.rule: Over the size limit means split.

questions.q: A log database splits an oversized partition into two halves on the same node. What helps spread the load next?
options: Rehash all the keys in both halves
Move one of the halves to another node
Copy both halves to every node
Merge the two halves back into one
optionExplain: Key ranges are kept; no rehash is needed.
Right: after a split, one half can be transferred to another node to balance load.
Copying to every node is replication, not balancing.
Merging would undo the split.
questions.explain: Splitting makes the pieces movable.

questions.q: A brand-new key-range database on 10 nodes starts receiving writes. What happens before the first split?
options: Writes are spread evenly over all 10 nodes
All writes go to a single node while the others stay idle
Writes wait until the database has first created 10 separate partitions
Writes are hashed to a node, since no ranges exist yet
optionExplain: Without partitions to place, no spread is possible.
Right: an empty database begins with a single partition.
Nothing makes the database wait.
Hashing belongs to another scheme.
questions.explain: With no information about where to draw boundaries, one partition exists at first.

questions.q: True or false: Dynamic partitioning keeps the number of partitions equal to the number of nodes.
questions.explain: The number of partitions follows the size of the dataset. It is independent of the number of nodes.

questions.q: A team must bulk load a new key-range database. How can they avoid the single-node start, and what do they need to know?
options: Load slowly, which needs knowledge of the next merge date
Switch to fixed hash buckets, which needs knowledge of the node count and the key sizes
Add more replicas, which needs knowledge of the follower count
Pre-split: configure initial partitions, which needs knowledge of the key distribution
optionExplain: Slow loading does not end the single-node start.
That changes the partitioning scheme rather than relieving the empty start.
Replicas do not add write capacity for a single partition.
Right: HBase and MongoDB allow an initial set of partitions on an empty database, which requires knowing the key distribution.
questions.explain: HBase and MongoDB allow an initial set of partitions to be configured on an empty database, called pre-splitting; for key-range partitioning it requires knowing the key distribution.
questions.rule: Pre-splitting needs a known key distribution.
questions.teaches: HBase and MongoDB allow an initial set of partitions to be configured on an empty database, called pre-splitting; with key-range partitioning it requires that you already know what the key distribution will look like.

questions.q: A growing dataset makes every partition bigger. Which setup makes partitions smaller again when you add nodes?
options: One partition per row, so adding nodes does not matter
A fixed total number of partitions, chosen once at setup and never changed
A fixed number of partitions per node, so the total grows with the nodes
Partitions that merge whenever a node is added
optionExplain: One partition per row is impractical and ignores node count.
With a fixed total, partitions only grow with the data.
Right: more nodes means more partitions, so each is smaller.
Merging would make partitions larger, not smaller.
questions.explain: Tying partition count to node count ties partition size to data per node. The card next gives the details.

questions.q: In Cassandra's approach, each node has a fixed number of ____.
questions.explain: A fixed number of partitions per node makes the total proportional to the node count.

questions.q: A cluster of 4 nodes has 8 partitions per node. Four more nodes join. How many partitions does it have?
options: 64, with 8 per node on 8 nodes
40, with 4 new ones per new node
36, since each node takes one extra
32, the same as before
optionExplain: Right: 8 nodes with 8 partitions each is 64.
Each new node also has 8, not 4.
Nothing adds one extra per node.
A fixed total of 32 is the other approach.
questions.explain: The total is nodes times partitions per node.
questions.rule: Total equals nodes times partitions per node.

questions.q: The dataset doubles while the number of nodes stays the same. What happens to partition sizes?
options: Each partition is split once and moved to a new node
Each partition halves, since there is more data to share
Each partition stays the same, since the count doubles
Each partition roughly doubles in size
optionExplain: Splits happen when a node joins, not when data grows.
More data per partition is the opposite of halving.
The count is tied to nodes, not to data.
Right: the number of partitions is unchanged, so each holds twice as much.
questions.explain: Size grows with the data while nodes stay unchanged; more nodes bring it back down.
questions.rule: Size grows with data and shrinks with nodes.

questions.q: True or false: In this approach a new node takes entire existing partitions without splitting any of them.
questions.explain: The new node randomly chooses existing partitions to split and takes one half of each.
questions.rule: It takes half of each chosen partition.

questions.q: A blog calls Cassandra-style random-boundary splitting consistent hashing. How does the book regard this?
options: It is the same as hash mod N
It is unrelated, since consistent hashing uses sorted key ranges rather than random boundaries
It corresponds most closely to the original definition of consistent hashing
It is the definition of ACID consistency
optionExplain: Mod N is the way not to do it.
Sorted ranges are key range partitioning.
Right: the original definition used random partition boundaries.
ACID consistency is a different concept.
questions.explain: Picking partition boundaries at random corresponds most closely to the original definition of consistent hashing; newer hash functions achieve a similar effect with lower metadata overhead.
questions.rule: Random boundaries match the original meaning.
questions.teaches: This approach corresponds most closely to the original definition of consistent hashing, and newer hash functions can achieve a similar effect with lower metadata overhead.

questions.q: A node is slow during a traffic spike. The other nodes decide it is dead and automatically move its load away. What do you fear?
options: The extra load makes things worse for the slow node, the others and the network
The moved data is lost for good, since a node that is judged dead cannot hand it over
The other nodes hand the work back, so nothing changes
The slow node recovers at once and needs no help
optionExplain: Right: this can start a cascading failure.
Moving load does not destroy data; the problem is extra load.
Nothing in the scenario hands work back.
A slow node under load gets worse with more work, not better.
questions.explain: Rebalancing is a heavy operation. The card next discusses it.

questions.q: Couchbase, Riak and Voldemort generate a suggested assignment but need an ____ to commit it.
questions.explain: A human commits the suggestion before it takes effect.

questions.q: A payments cluster rebalances automatically and has had sudden latency spikes. Which design change reduces surprises?
options: Add more partitions and let the system pick the moves unprompted, on its own schedule
Generate a suggested assignment and require an operator to commit it
Remove failure detection and rebalance on a timer
Rebalance twice as often so each move is smaller
optionExplain: Unprompted moves are the unpredictable behaviour in question.
Right: a human in the loop is slower but prevents surprises.
A timer is as blind as failure detection and gives no review.
More frequent rebalancing adds more load, not less.
questions.explain: A review step lets an operator choose a quiet moment.

questions.q: Other nodes declare a slow node dead and rebalance away from it. What happens to the slow node?
options: It receives additional load, making its situation worse
It recovers, since it is now excused from work
It is removed from the network, which cools it down
It keeps the same load, since only data moves
optionExplain: Right: moving data and rerouting requests adds load.
Rebalancing adds work, not rest.
The node is not powered off by the move.
The rebalancing itself adds load to it.
questions.explain: Rebalancing puts additional load on the overloaded node, the others and the network.

questions.q: True or false: Fully automatic rebalancing is harmless to running requests, because moving partitions between nodes is cheap.
questions.explain: Rebalancing is an expensive operation: it reroutes requests and moves a large amount of data, and can overload the network or nodes.

questions.q: A team designs a routing layer for a database that does not rebalance automatically. What does the book say this does for the design?
options: It makes routing impossible without an external service
It simplifies the design, as Couchbase's routing does
It makes every request a scatter/gather
It forces every client to keep a full copy of the data
optionExplain: Routing still works; it just changes less often.
Right: the book says Couchbase does not rebalance automatically, which simplifies its design.
Scatter/gather concerns secondary indexes.
Clients need only the assignment, not the data.
questions.explain: Couchbase does not rebalance automatically, which simplifies the design of its routing.
questions.teaches: Couchbase does not rebalance automatically, which simplifies the design.

questions.q: A client wants the value of key foo, but partitions move between nodes. What must someone know?
options: Which replica was added last
The secret key that the hash function uses to protect partitions
Which node currently owns the partition for that key
How many keys the cluster stores
optionExplain: Replica order does not tell where the partition is.
Hash functions for partitioning need no secret.
Right: the request must reach the node that owns the partition now.
The key count does not locate any key.
questions.explain: Someone has to track who owns what. The card next lists the options.

questions.q: Match each routing approach with how it works.
pairs: The node forwards the request if it does not own the partition
A partition-aware load balancer that handles no requests itself
Connects directly to the right node, with no intermediary
questions.explain: The three approaches differ in where the knowledge of partition ownership lives.
questions.rule: Node, tier or client holds the map.

questions.q: A mobile SDK is shipped inside many third-party apps and cannot be updated quickly. Which design keeps partition knowledge out of it?
options: Clients that track partition assignments themselves
Nodes that drop requests for partitions that they do not currently own
Clients that hash keys and guess the node's address
A routing tier that forwards each request to the right node
optionExplain: Slow-to-update clients cannot keep up with changes.
Dropped requests fail instead of being handled.
Guessing addresses would send requests to the wrong nodes.
Right: the tier holds the knowledge, so slow-to-update clients stay simple.
questions.explain: Routing knowledge can sit outside the clients.
questions.rule: Keep the map out of hard-to-update clients.

questions.q: A partition moves to another node, but the routing component is not told. What happens?
options: Clients automatically find the new node
The data is copied back to the old node
The old node forwards all requests to the new owner with no extra cost at all
Requests are sent to the wrong node and are not handled correctly
optionExplain: Without notification, clients keep the old picture.
Data does not move back by itself.
A node that no longer owns the partition cannot answer for it.
Right: all participants must agree on the assignment.
questions.explain: Disagreement leads to misrouted requests.

questions.q: True or false: In the routing-tier approach, the tier also stores and serves the data.
questions.explain: The routing tier handles no requests itself; it only acts as a partition-aware load balancer.

questions.q: A fleet of redundant microservice instances needs callers to find a running instance. Which general problem does it share with partition routing?
options: Service discovery, which is not limited to databases
Rebalancing, which concerns moving partitions
Replica consistency, which concerns copies of data
Skew, which concerns uneven load
optionExplain: Right: partition routing is one instance of service discovery.
Rebalancing moves partitions rather than locates services.
Replica consistency is about keeping copies in agreement.
Skew is about the spread of load.
questions.explain: Finding the address of a node for a request is an instance of service discovery, which applies to any network-accessible software, especially in a redundant, highly available configuration.
questions.teaches: This is an instance of a more general problem called service discovery, which is not limited to just databases.

questions.q: Dozens of routers must agree on which node owns which partition. What is a practical design?
options: Routers vote on the owner for every request
A coordination service holds the authoritative mapping and notifies the routers
All routers share one fixed table written at setup
Each router guesses the owner from the response to the last request that it forwarded
optionExplain: Voting per request is a consensus protocol, which is hard to implement correctly.
Right: one authoritative source with notifications keeps them in step.
A fixed table cannot follow rebalancing.
Guessing from past responses goes stale when partitions move.
questions.explain: One source of truth with notifications keeps routers aligned. The card next names it.

questions.q: ZooKeeper keeps the authoritative ____ of partitions to nodes.
questions.explain: Other actors subscribe to this mapping and are notified of changes.

questions.q: Which statement tells a ZooKeeper-style design apart from gossip?
options: ZooKeeper spreads changes among the nodes; gossip keeps an authoritative copy in an external service
ZooKeeper forbids forwarding; gossip requires clients to know partitions
ZooKeeper keeps the authoritative mapping outside the nodes; gossip spreads changes among the nodes
Both keep the mapping only inside the routing tier
optionExplain: This swaps the two designs.
Gossip lets any node forward requests; clients need not know partitions.
Right: an external service versus peer-to-peer spreading.
Neither design stores the mapping only in the routing tier.
questions.explain: One keeps the truth in an external service, the other spreads it among nodes.

questions.q: A team wants no dependency on an external coordination service. Which cost do they accept with gossip?
options: The loss of request forwarding
A single point of failure in the routing tier
A central mapping that clients must poll
More complexity inside the database nodes
optionExplain: Requests can go to any node, which forwards them.
Gossip uses no central routing tier.
No central mapping exists in this design.
Right: the nodes must spread and absorb the changes.
questions.explain: Gossip puts more complexity in the database nodes but avoids the dependency.
questions.rule: Gossip trades a dependency for node complexity.

questions.q: True or false: Because consensus protocols exist, agreement on partition assignment is easy to implement, so every database builds its own.
questions.explain: Consensus protocols exist but are hard to implement correctly, which is why many systems rely on a separate coordination service.
questions.rule: Consensus is hard to get right.

questions.q: Clients reach a routing tier by name. Its machines change address rarely. How can clients find the addresses?
options: They must ask the routing tier itself for its own current address each time
Often DNS is enough, since addresses change less often than assignments
They must subscribe to ZooKeeper for every address
They must use gossip with every node
optionExplain: Asking the tier requires already knowing where it is.
Right: addresses change more slowly than the assignment, so DNS often suffices.
Subscribing for addresses is heavier than needed.
Gossip serves cluster state, not client addressing.
questions.explain: When using a routing tier or sending requests to a random node, clients still need IP addresses, which change less quickly than the assignment of partitions to nodes, so DNS often suffices.
questions.teaches: Clients still need to find the IP addresses to connect to, which are not as fast-changing as the assignment of partitions to nodes, so it is often sufficient to use DNS for this purpose.

questions.q: An analyst runs a query that joins three big tables, filters, groups and aggregates. How might a partitioned warehouse speed it up?
options: Run it on one single node that holds its own full copy of the whole dataset
Cache the answer under one key and look it up
Break it into stages and run many of them in parallel on different nodes
Send it to every node in turn and keep the first answer
optionExplain: A single node gives up the benefit of partitioning.
A new complex query has no cached key.
Right: parallel stages over partitions use many nodes at once.
Keeping the first answer returns an incomplete result.
