questions.explain: Splitting the work across nodes is the main idea. The card next names it.

questions.q: MPP stands for massively ____ processing.
questions.explain: MPP databases run parts of a query in parallel on many nodes.

questions.q: Which of these queries gains most from parallel execution across partitions?
options: A report that scans two years of sales rows to total revenue by region
A lookup of one order by its order number
A read of one customer record by its ID
A write that sets one product's price
optionExplain: Right: queries that scan large parts of the dataset benefit most.
A single lookup touches one partition.
A single-key read touches one partition.
A single write touches one partition.
questions.explain: Large scans gain most from parallel stages.

questions.q: How does the query support of most NoSQL datastores differ from MPP databases?
options: NoSQL stores run joins and aggregations in parallel, while MPP engines handle only reads and writes of single keys
Both run any query on one node, but MPP engines use more disks
NoSQL stores mostly handle single keys, while MPP engines run joins, grouping and aggregation in parallel
Both handle only single keys, but MPP engines replicate them
optionExplain: This swaps the two.
The point of MPP is parallel work on many nodes.
Right: MPP optimizers handle complex multi-stage queries.
MPP engines are about complex queries, not replication of single keys.
questions.explain: NoSQL datastores offer simple access; MPP engines offer complex analytic queries.

questions.q: True or false: Because partitions work independently, a query that touches every partition is as simple as a single-key lookup.
questions.explain: Large complex queries can be parallelised across nodes, but this gets significantly harder than operating on one partition.

questions.q: A payment updates two accounts stored on different partitions. The first write succeeds and the second fails. What does the book say about this?
options: Writes to several partitions are hard to reason about; later chapters address it
The problem cannot occur, because each account record belongs to exactly one partition
The second write retries on the first partition until it works
The partitions roll back automatically, since they are independent
optionExplain: Right: the summary flags this and defers it.
Each account belongs to one partition, but one operation can touch two.
The scenario involves no such retry.
Independent partitions do not roll each other back.
questions.explain: Operations that write to several partitions can be difficult to reason about, since one partition's write may succeed while another fails; the following chapters address this.
questions.teaches: Operations that need to write to several partitions can be difficult to reason about: what happens if the write to one partition succeeds, but another fails?

questions.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.q: A service writes an order row, then a stock row, and crashes between the two writes. What is the core danger?
options: The database finishes the stock write by itself when it restarts
Every table touched by the service is locked until an operator steps in
Only some of the related changes are stored, and nobody knows which
Nothing is wrong, because each write was stored safely on its own
optionExplain: Databases do not complete a client's missing operations on their own.
Locks are about concurrency, not about a half-finished series of writes.
Right: a partly applied set of changes is the problem transactions address.
Each write may be safe, but the pair together is now inconsistent.
questions.explain: The danger is the half-done state: some writes took effect, others did not, and nobody knows which. The card next shows the remedy.
questions.rule: A crash mid-series leaves a half-done state.

questions.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.q: A transaction either succeeds in full, which is called a ____, or fails and is rolled back.
questions.explain: A successful transaction commits; a failed one aborts (rolls back), and its writes are not kept.
questions.rule: Commit means all of it; abort means none of it.

questions.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.q: A ride app assigns a driver, marks the rider matched, then fails to record the deposit. What should a transaction do?
options: Abort, discard both writes, and retry the whole group later
Commit the first two writes and retry only the deposit later
Keep the first two writes and report the deposit error to the rider
Freeze the database until the deposit write succeeds
optionExplain: Right: abort removes every write of the group, so a retry starts clean.
Committing early makes the partial state permanent and visible.
That keeps the half-done state transactions exist to prevent.
Blocking the database punishes every user and is not what abort does.
questions.explain: A transaction is treated as one operation, so one failed part means the whole group is abandoned and can be retried.
questions.rule: One failed part aborts the whole unit.

questions.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.q: A teammate says transactions stop crashes and network drops from happening. What is wrong with that claim?
options: Nothing; a transaction prevents the crash from occurring at all
The faults still occur; transactions turn them into a retryable abort
Transactions apply only to hardware faults, not to application crashes
Only network drops are prevented; crashes still cause half-done states
optionExplain: Transactions cannot stop a process from crashing; they limit the consequences.
Right: the fault occurs, but the damage is reduced to a simple abort and retry.
The list of faults includes application crashes halfway through operations.
Both kinds of fault still occur; neither is prevented, and both can end in an abort.
questions.explain: Transactions do not make faults vanish. They turn a large class of them into one outcome, an abort, that the application can handle by trying again.
questions.rule: Faults still happen; transactions shrink their effect to an abort.

questions.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.q: True or false: A transaction protects only against mid-series crashes; it does not help when two clients write at once.
questions.explain: The chapter lists concurrent clients overwriting each other and clients reading half-updated data among the problems transactions simplify. Concurrency is a core part of their job.
questions.rule: Transactions cover concurrency problems as well as crashes.
questions.teaches: Transactions also address several clients overwriting each other's changes and a client reading data that is only partly updated, not just crashes.

questions.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.q: A collector adds one number to one record per event. What does the chapter suggest about transactions for it?
options: It needs them, since any production system holding data does
It needs them only if the metrics are replicated to a second site
It cannot use them, because transactions only work with several records
It can probably do without them, as its access is so simple
optionExplain: Valuable data is the vendor argument; the chapter calls such blanket claims hyperbole.
Replication does not change the single-record argument the chapter makes.
Transactions can cover one record; the point is that they add little there.
Right: simple single-record access leaves few error cases for a transaction to remove.
questions.explain: The chapter concludes that an application reading and writing only a single record can probably do without transactions, while complex access patterns gain a lot.
questions.rule: The simpler the access pattern, the less a transaction adds.
questions.teaches: An application with very simple access patterns, such as reading and writing a single record, can probably manage without transactions.

questions.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.q: Why were transactions created in the first place?
options: To simplify programming by letting the database absorb some errors
To control which users may see which rows
To let one database be spread across many machines
To make queries run faster by caching intermediate results in memory
optionExplain: Right: the database takes the burden so that application code can be simpler.
Access control is a separate feature from transactions.
Spreading data over machines is partitioning or replication, a different matter.
Speed is not their aim; the guarantees can even cost performance.
questions.explain: They were made for a purpose: shifting some error handling from every application to the database. The card next gives the details.

questions.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.q: The promises a transaction makes, which let an application ignore certain failures, are called safety ____.
questions.explain: The book names what transactions provide safety guarantees.
questions.rule: Safety guarantees are what you buy with a transaction.

questions.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.q: A team building a file-sync service asks whether it needs transactions. What first step fits the book?
options: Copy the choice of the best-known competitor
Skip them, because sync services must stay highly available
Adopt them everywhere, because file metadata is valuable data and must be protected
List the guarantees and their costs, then compare with the service's needs
optionExplain: A competitor's needs and access patterns may differ from yours.
Availability may argue for weaker guarantees but does not decide it automatically.
Value alone does not decide it; the book calls that kind of blanket claim hyperbole.
Right: the decision depends on concrete guarantees against concrete costs.
questions.explain: The book frames the question as understanding exactly what guarantees transactions give and what they cost before deciding.
questions.rule: Decide from guarantees and costs, not from habit.

questions.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.q: A lead says a database without transactions is broken, because transactions are how databases must work. What is the flaw?
options: The lead is right, but only for non-relational databases
None; transactions are a law of nature that every database must obey in full
Transactions have a purpose, so omitting them can be a deliberate trade
Databases without transactions cannot store any data safely
optionExplain: Relational databases also differ in what they offer; the claim is not restricted that way.
The opening of the chapter denies exactly this.
Right: the book stresses that transactions are not a law of nature.
Some safety properties can be achieved without transactions, so the claim overstates.
questions.explain: Because transactions serve a goal, a system may weaken or drop them for another goal and still be a sensible design.
questions.rule: A missing feature may be a trade, not a defect.

questions.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.q: True or false: According to the chapter, weakening or abandoning transactional guarantees can sometimes buy higher performance or higher availability.
questions.explain: The chapter says that not every application needs transactions and that there can be advantages in weakening or dropping them, for example for performance or availability.
questions.rule: Dropping guarantees can be a performance or availability trade.
questions.teaches: Sometimes there are advantages to weakening transactional guarantees or abandoning them entirely, for example higher performance or higher availability.

questions.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.q: A payments team wants each refund applied exactly once. A colleague insists only transactions can provide such safety. What does the chapter's opening say?
options: Safety is the application's job alone, so transactions are irrelevant here
Some safety needs no transactions, so ask which guarantees are needed
The colleague is right, since safety needs a database transaction
No safety property can be reached without ACID compliance
optionExplain: Transactions do move some safety work to the database, so they are not irrelevant.
Right: the chapter says some safety properties can be achieved without transactions.
That overstates it; the chapter explicitly allows other routes.
The same opening sentence rejects the claim that nothing works without ACID.
questions.explain: The chapter's framing is to ask what safety you need, then see whether transactions are the way to get it.
questions.rule: Name the safety property first, then pick the mechanism.
questions.teaches: Some safety properties can be achieved without transactions.

questions.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.q: Which statement about transactions and large systems is closest to the book's view?
options: Transactions are an outdated idea that newer databases have replaced
Large systems must abandon transactions to stay available
Both 'drop them to scale' and 'serious data needs them' overstate the case
Any application with valuable data must use transactions, whatever the cost
optionExplain: The book describes the old design as still widely used, not as obsolete.
This is the popular NoSQL-era belief that the book rejects.
Right: the book calls both popular positions pure hyperbole.
This is the vendor-side overstatement that the book also rejects.
questions.explain: The book rejects both extremes. The card next shows what it puts in their place.

questions.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.q: What happened to transactions in many databases of the late-2000s NoSQL movement?
options: Many dropped them or redefined the word to mean weaker guarantees
They were moved out of the database and into the client libraries instead
They were extended across data centres as a default feature
They were kept unchanged because customers insisted on them
optionExplain: Right: transactions were the main casualty of that movement.
Client libraries were not the usual replacement; the guarantee simply shrank.
Extending them was not the trend; they were weakened or dropped.
The opposite happened for many of these systems.
questions.explain: The new databases wanted new data models and built-in replication and partitioning, and transactions were the main thing given up.
questions.rule: Many NoSQL systems dropped or redefined transactions.

questions.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.q: A startup CTO says: we expect millions of users, so we must drop transactions. Which reply fits the book?
options: Wait until the user base arrives, then decide at random
Scale alone does not decide it; compare needed guarantees with their costs
Agree, because transactions and scalability are opposed
Disagree, because any serious product needs full transactions whatever they cost
optionExplain: Random choice ignores the trade-offs the chapter sets out to explain.
Right: the choice depends on concrete guarantees and costs.
That is the popular belief the book calls hyperbole.
That is the opposite overstatement.
questions.explain: Neither slogan helps. The book asks you to understand the advantages and limitations of each guarantee in your own situation.
questions.hint: Which claims does the book call hyperbole?
questions.rule: Slogans about scale do not replace analysis.

questions.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.q: Which claims does the book call hyperbole? Select all that apply.
options: Transactions have both advantages and limitations
Many NoSQL databases weakened what they call a transaction
Transactional guarantees are essential for any serious application with valuable data
Any large-scale system must abandon transactions to keep performance and availability
optionExplain: This is the book's own position.
This is a factual remark about the movement, not hyperbole.
Right: this is the vendor-side belief.
Right: this is the popular scalability belief.
questions.explain: The two overstatements are mirror images, one against transactions and one for them. The book's own view sits between.
questions.rule: Spot the two overstatements: always drop, always require.

questions.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.q: True or false: Transaction support in MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server closely resembles that of IBM's 1975 System R.
questions.explain: The chapter says the general idea has stayed almost the same for 40 years, and that today's relational systems are uncannily similar to System R.
questions.rule: Mainstream transaction support descends from System R.
questions.teaches: Most relational databases follow the transaction style introduced in 1975 by IBM System R, the first SQL database, and the general idea has remained virtually the same for about 40 years.

questions.section: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.q: A ticketing company is choosing a database. Which evaluation follows the book's approach?
options: Check that its documentation uses the word transaction somewhere in its feature list
Run it at peak load and see whether it stays available
Choose whichever the largest NoSQL vendors adopted
Study its guarantees in normal operation and in extreme but realistic cases
optionExplain: The word was redefined by some systems, so the label proves little.
Load tests show performance but not which guarantees hold during faults.
Popularity is exactly the slogan-driven reasoning the book warns against.
Right: the book says the details matter in both normal and extreme cases.
questions.explain: To understand trade-offs, the chapter goes into the guarantees transactions provide both in normal operation and in various extreme but realistic circumstances.
questions.rule: Test guarantees under realistic extremes, not just normal runs.
questions.teaches: The guarantees of transactions need to be understood both in normal operation and in various extreme but realistic circumstances.

questions.q: A brochure says a database is fully ACID compliant. What can you safely infer?
options: Little on its own, since ACID implementations differ
That it follows the 1983 definition to the letter
That no committed data can ever be lost, whatever fails
That every transaction behaves as if it ran alone on the database
optionExplain: Right: the label does not pin down the guarantees.
Implementations differ, and the term is now mostly marketing.
Durability has limits; no technique gives absolute guarantees.
That is serializability, which many ACID databases do not provide by default.
questions.explain: ACID is a handy summary, not a precise specification. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Systems that do not meet the ACID criteria are sometimes called ____.
questions.explain: BASE stands for Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency, but the book finds it even vaguer than ACID.

questions.q: Two databases both advertise ACID. Your app is a chat service with many concurrent writers. What is the sound next step?
options: Pick the one with the older ACID claim
Pick the cheaper one, since ACID makes the two of them equivalent
Ask each vendor to confirm the word ACID in writing
Compare how each behaves in the concurrent cases you care about
optionExplain: Age of the claim says nothing about the guarantees.
Equivalence is exactly what the label does not guarantee.
A written label confirms the word, not the behaviour.
Right: only concrete behaviour tells you what you get.
questions.explain: Because one database's ACID differs from another's, the useful comparison is of specific behaviour, not of the label.

questions.q: True or false: A blog says BASE databases are precisely defined, so they differ sharply from ACID ones. The book agrees with this claim.
questions.explain: The book calls BASE even vaguer than ACID; its only sensible definition is not ACID, so it can mean almost anything.
questions.rule: BASE is a negative label, not a specification.

questions.q: What do the letters of BASE stand for?
options: Balanced, Available, Scalable, Eventual consistency
Basically Atomic, Soft state, Eventual serializability
Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency
Backed-up, Asynchronous, Sharded, Eventual consistency
optionExplain: These words describe infrastructure choices, not the acronym.
This mixes ACID terms into the acronym.
Right: this is the expansion the book gives, and it calls the label vague.
This invents a plausible-sounding set of words.
questions.explain: The expansion sounds specific, but the book says it still means little beyond not ACID.
questions.rule: A precise-sounding acronym can still be vague.
questions.teaches: BASE stands for Basically Available, Soft state, and Eventual consistency.

questions.q: Reviewing a vendor's ACID claim, which letter should you question first, because its meaning varies most between databases?
options: Atomicity
Isolation
Consistency
Durability
optionExplain: All-or-nothing on failure is comparatively well understood.
Right: the book notes a lot of ambiguity around the meaning of isolation.
Consistency is overloaded in a different way, being the application's concern.
Durability has limits but a clear meaning: committed data is not forgotten.
questions.explain: Isolation is where databases differ most, as the rest of the chapter shows through the many weak isolation levels.
questions.teaches: There is a lot of ambiguity around the meaning of isolation, so it is the letter on which databases differ most.

questions.q: In ACID, what does atomicity describe?
options: That data survives a power failure once committed
That no two clients are ever allowed to touch the same data at the same moment
What happens when a fault interrupts a group of writes: none remain
That each write is broken into the smallest possible steps
optionExplain: That is durability.
That is closer to isolation.
Right: atomicity is the all-or-nothing outcome after a fault.
Atomic means cannot be broken down, but the ACID meaning concerns faults, not step size.
questions.explain: Atomicity is about the all-or-nothing result of a fault in a group of writes. The card next explains how.
questions.rule: Atomicity: all of it or none of it.

questions.q: ACID atomicity is mainly about what happens after a ____ interrupts a series of writes.
questions.explain: The faults are things like crashes, broken connections or a full disk. Concurrent access is a different letter.

questions.q: A file-sync client uploads a folder as three metadata writes; the disk fills after the second. With atomic transactions, what is stored?
options: The first two, since they succeeded before the fault
Only the third, since the database defers the last write
Whichever writes the client chooses to keep
None of the three writes; the first two are undone
optionExplain: Partial results are exactly what atomicity rules out.
The database does not skip or reorder the group's writes.
The application does not get to keep part of an aborted transaction.
Right: the transaction cannot complete, so all its writes are discarded.
questions.explain: Because the transaction could not commit, the database must discard or undo everything it had written.
questions.rule: An aborted transaction leaves no writes behind.

questions.q: Dana says: atomicity guarantees that another client cannot see half of a transaction's writes. What is wrong with this claim?
options: Visibility is isolation; atomicity only covers undoing writes after a fault
Nothing; this is exactly what atomicity guarantees in ACID transactions
It is durability, because partial work must survive until it is committed
It is consistency, because the application decides what counts as valid data
optionExplain: Right: seeing or not seeing partial work concurrently is isolation.
That is the multi-threaded meaning of atomic, which ACID assigns to the letter I.
Durability concerns surviving crashes after commit.
Consistency is about the application's invariants.
questions.explain: ACID atomicity is not about concurrency. Concurrent access is covered by isolation.
questions.rule: Atomicity is about faults; isolation is about concurrency.

questions.q: True or false: Atomicity applies only when the process crashes; a violated integrity constraint or a full disk partway through is outside its scope.
questions.explain: The faults named include a crash, an interrupted connection, a full disk or a violated integrity constraint. In all of them the transaction is aborted and its earlier writes are undone.
questions.rule: Any fault that stops commit triggers the undo.
questions.teaches: Faults that abort a transaction include a full disk and a violated integrity constraint, not only crashes and interrupted connections.

questions.q: A library says its counter has an atomic increment for threads. How does that word differ from ACID atomicity?
options: For threads it means the increment is split into smaller independent parts
For threads it hides half-finished results; in ACID that is isolation
It means the same; both promise discard-on-fault
For threads it means durability to disk after each increment
optionExplain: Atomic means something that cannot be broken down.
Right: the multi-threaded meaning is about concurrent visibility.
The words overlap but the meanings differ in what is protected.
Thread-level atomicity does not involve disks.
questions.explain: The same word means subtly different things in different branches of computing. In multi-threaded code, atomic means no other thread can see a half-finished operation.
questions.rule: Check which sense of atomic is meant.
questions.teaches: In multi-threaded programming an atomic operation means no other thread can see its half-finished result; in ACID that concern belongs to isolation.

questions.q: A job inserts three rows and fails after two, with no rollback. What is the risk of re-running the whole job?
options: The database refuses all further writes from that client
The two rows already inserted get inserted again
The two inserted rows are replaced with older copies
The retry fails because the table stays locked for good
optionExplain: Databases do not ban a client for a failed job.
Right: repeating a partly applied change duplicates it.
Nothing reverts rows to older copies.
No lock persists after the job has failed.
questions.explain: Without undo, a retry repeats work that already happened. The card next shows how atomicity fixes this.

questions.q: True or false: If a transaction was aborted, the application can be sure it changed nothing in the database.
questions.explain: Aborting means the database discards every write of the transaction, so the state is as before.

questions.q: A metrics batch writes five data points and a summary row; the summary write fails. What should the application do?
options: Retry the whole batch; nothing of the first attempt remains
Delete the five points by hand, then give up on the batch
Skip the summary and keep the five points already stored
Retry only the summary row, since the five points were stored
optionExplain: Right: the abort removed the five points, so the whole batch is safe to run again.
The database already discarded them; manual cleanup is unnecessary.
That leaves a partial result the transaction was meant to prevent.
That would leave the five points missing, since they were undone.
questions.explain: Atomicity guarantees the five points are gone after the abort, so a full retry creates no duplicates.
questions.rule: After an abort, rerun the whole unit.

questions.q: A store without atomicity applies 3 of 5 batch writes before an error. What does re-running all five risk?
options: Nothing, because a store always ignores repeated writes
The three applied writes are rolled back automatically
Repeating changes already applied, risking duplicates
A permanent lock on the three keys
optionExplain: Stores have no built-in memory of which writes a client already sent.
Rollback is what atomicity would provide, and this store lacks it.
Right: without atomicity it is unclear which changes happened, so a full rerun repeats some.
Retries do not leave locks; the risk is repeated data, not blocking.
questions.explain: When partial writes survive, a blind retry can apply the same change twice.
questions.rule: Without atomicity, blind retry is risky.

questions.q: The authors suggest that ____ would have been a better word than atomicity for the ability to abort a transaction and discard its writes.
questions.explain: The defining feature of ACID atomicity is the ability to abort on error and have all writes discarded, so the authors call abortability a better term, though they keep the usual word.
questions.teaches: The authors suggest that abortability would have been a better term than atomicity for the ability to abort a transaction and have all its writes discarded.

questions.q: In a refund service, a debit and a credit are grouped and the credit fails. What does an abort signal to the database designers' philosophy?
options: It lets the application decide which writes to keep
It waits for the credit to succeed, however long that takes to resolve
It keeps the debit and flags the credit for a later retry
It abandons the transaction rather than leave it half-finished
optionExplain: Abort does not leave partial choices to the application.
The philosophy is to abort, not wait indefinitely.
That would keep a half-finished state.
Right: ACID databases prefer abandoning a transaction to leaving it half-finished.
questions.explain: ACID databases follow this philosophy: if the database is in danger of violating a guarantee, it abandons the transaction entirely.
questions.teaches: ACID databases would rather abandon a transaction entirely than let it remain half-finished when atomicity, isolation or durability is in danger.

questions.q: A vendor page says: our system is consistent. What do you need to know before this means anything?
options: Only whether the system uses transactions, which settles the meaning
Nothing more, because consistent has one standard definition in databases
Which sense is meant, since the word has several unrelated uses
How many replicas it keeps, since consistency is about copies only
optionExplain: Even in transactions the ACID sense differs from replica consistency.
That is the false assumption; the word has several senses.
Right: the word is overloaded, so the sense has to be pinned down.
Replicas are one sense among several, not the only one.
questions.explain: The word has at least four meanings in this book. The card next lists them.

questions.q: Match each use of consistency to its meaning.
pairs: Copies of data agree, with possible lag under asynchronous replication
An approach to partitioning, used by some systems for rebalancing
A strong ordering property of reads and writes
The database is in a good state according to the application's rules
questions.explain: Four senses, each in a different part of the book, with unrelated guarantees.

questions.q: A replication guide says reads may be inconsistent for a moment after a write. Which sense of consistency is it using?
options: Replica consistency: copies may lag under asynchronous replication
The CAP sense, which concerns the application's own definition of valid data
ACID consistency: the application's invariants were violated by the write
Consistent hashing: the key moved to another partition during the write
optionExplain: Right: a brief disagreement between copies is replica consistency.
The CAP sense is a strong ordering property, not application validity.
Invariants are the application's rules, not a symptom of replica lag.
Consistent hashing is a method of placing keys on partitions.
questions.explain: Lag between copies after a write is the replica sense, tied to asynchronous replication and eventual consistency.
questions.rule: Lag between copies is replica consistency.

questions.q: A designer says: the database is ACID consistent, so its replicas cannot lag. What is the flaw?
options: ACID consistency covers replicas but only when hashing is consistent
ACID consistency is about the application's valid state, not replicas
None; ACID consistency means all copies are always identical
ACID consistency is a name for eventual consistency in replicated systems
optionExplain: Hashing is a separate sense and plays no role here.
Right: the senses are unrelated, so one cannot imply the other.
That merges two different senses into one.
Eventual consistency is the replica sense and is not what ACID means.
questions.explain: ACID consistency says the application's invariants hold; it makes no promise about how quickly replicas catch up.
questions.rule: ACID consistency says nothing about replica lag.

questions.q: In the CAP theorem, the word consistency is used to mean ____.
questions.explain: CAP's meaning is a fourth, separate use of the word; the book defers linearizability to a later chapter.
questions.teaches: In the CAP theorem the word consistency is used to mean linearizability.

questions.q: A teammate reads that a store uses consistent hashing and expects it to check ACID-style invariants. What is the mix-up?
options: Nothing; hashing and invariants are the same idea under two names
Consistent hashing is the CAP guarantee and is stronger than ACID
Consistent hashing is the same as eventual consistency between replicas
It is a partitioning approach for rebalancing, unrelated to invariants
optionExplain: Hashing and invariants share no idea at all; only the word is shared.
CAP consistency is linearizability, a property of reads and writes, not a hashing technique.
Replica agreement and key placement are different topics that only share a name.
Right: the shared word hides an unrelated meaning; hashing is about placing keys on partitions.
questions.explain: Consistent hashing is an approach to partitioning that some systems use for rebalancing. It shares only a word with ACID consistency.
questions.rule: Shared vocabulary does not mean shared meaning.
questions.teaches: Consistent hashing is an approach to partitioning that some systems use for rebalancing.

questions.q: Which ACID property depends on the application's own definition of correct data?
options: Consistency
Isolation
Durability
Atomicity
optionExplain: Right: only the application knows what valid data means.
Isolation is about concurrent transactions.
Durability is about surviving crashes.
Atomicity is about undoing writes after a fault.
questions.explain: The database can undo, separate and persist writes, but only the application defines good state. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Valid data is defined by the application.

questions.q: Statements about data that must hold at all times, such as balanced debits and credits, are called ____.
questions.explain: The book uses invariants for the application-specific rules that define a good state.

questions.q: A payments app needs each transfer's entries to sum to zero, but a bug records only the debit. What does the database do?
options: It rejects the transaction, because atomicity enforces business rules
It aborts later, once durability detects the imbalance
It repairs the credit entry using isolation
It stores the data, since it cannot know the rule unless told
optionExplain: Atomicity undoes writes after a fault; it does not know your rules.
Durability keeps data after commit; it does not validate it.
Isolation separates transactions; it does not fix data.
Right: the application defines what is valid, and the database only stores it.
questions.explain: A balanced-entries rule is application-specific. Without a declared constraint, the database cannot notice the bug.
questions.rule: The database cannot enforce a rule it does not know.

questions.q: A payments app declares a uniqueness constraint on a key, and a write duplicates the key. What happens?
options: The write succeeds and isolation removes the duplicate later
The write succeeds but durability marks it as suspect
The database can check the constraint and reject the write
The database cannot detect it, since consistency is never checked
optionExplain: Isolation does not clean up data.
Durability does not mark data as suspect.
Right: some invariants can be enforced by the database.
Declared constraints are checked, even if general invariants are not.
questions.explain: The limit of the rule is declared constraints: where the rule is expressed as one the database supports, it is enforced.
questions.rule: Declared constraints are the part the database can enforce.

questions.q: True or false: A remark in the chapter says the C was added to ACID first because it was considered important.
questions.explain: Joe Hellerstein is quoted as saying the C was tossed in to make the acronym work, and that it was not considered important at the time.
questions.rule: The C was added to complete the acronym.
questions.teaches: Joe Hellerstein remarked that the C in ACID was tossed in to make the acronym work, and that it wasn't considered important at the time.

questions.q: Sort each rule by who can enforce it in a typical database.
groups: The database, with a declared constraint
The application, in its transaction logic

items.t: Every order row refers to a customer that exists (foreign key)
No two accounts share the same username (uniqueness)
Debits and credits across all ledger accounts balance
A refund cannot exceed the original payment

questions.explain: The database can check specific kinds of invariants, such as foreign key and uniqueness constraints; in general the application defines what is valid and the database only stores it.
questions.rule: Declared constraints for the simple kinds; application logic for the rest.
questions.teaches: Some specific kinds of invariants can be checked by the database, for example foreign key and uniqueness constraints; in general the application defines what is valid.

questions.q: Two clients each read a counter holding 42, add one, and write the result back at the same moment. What is the likely final value?
optionExplain: 42 would mean neither write took effect.
Right: both wrote 43, so one increment was lost.
That is the value if they ran one after another.
Adding the two read values makes no sense for increments.
questions.explain: Both clients started from 42, so both wrote 43. The card next names this problem.
questions.rule: Concurrent read-add-write can lose an update.

questions.q: What went wrong in the counter example?
options: The database lost power in the middle of the second write operation
One client's write was rejected because the counter was locked forever
Both clients read the same value before either wrote
Each client wrote an older value that the other had already replaced
optionExplain: No fault is involved; this is a timing problem.
Nothing was locked; both writes succeeded.
Right: the second write did not include the first increment.
Both wrote 43, a newer-looking value, not an older one.
questions.explain: Overlapping read-add-write steps let one write overwrite the other's change.
questions.rule: Overlap, not failure, lost the increment.

questions.q: Two support agents each read 10 free licences, subtract one, and save the result at the same moment. What is stored?
options: An error, because two writers cannot be allowed
8, because the database subtracts both
10, because the second write cancels the first
9, although two licences were used
optionExplain: Nothing raises an error here; both writes succeed, which is why the loss goes unnoticed.
8 is what you would get if the two ran one after another; the overlap prevents it.
Neither write cancels the other; the later write simply replaces the earlier one with the same value.
Right: both read 10 and both wrote 9, so one subtraction was lost.
questions.explain: Same pattern as the counter: both read 10 and both wrote 9.
questions.rule: Same read, same write: one change disappears.

questions.q: If the two counter increments had run one after another, the final value would be ____.
questions.explain: Run serially, the second client would read 43 and write 44. The lost update comes only from the overlap.

questions.q: True or false: Two transactions that write entirely different records can still race with each other.
questions.explain: The chapter says there is no problem when clients read and write different parts of the database; the trouble starts when they use the same records.
questions.teaches: Concurrent clients cause no problem when they are reading and writing different parts of the database; concurrency problems arise when they access the same records.

questions.q: A chat message's like count lives in one field and two users like it at once. Which change avoids the loss?
options: Use a built-in increment operation inside the database
Read the count twice and then write the larger result back
Make the like button disabled for one second
Move the like count into a second table
optionExplain: Right: the example assumed the database had no increment operation built in.
Reading twice does not stop another client writing between steps.
Delaying clicks does not remove the race.
A different table still has the same read-then-write pattern.
questions.explain: The counter example is introduced under the assumption that the database has no increment operation built in; a built-in one removes the read step.
questions.rule: A single increment inside the database avoids the race.
questions.teaches: The counter race assumes the database has no increment operation built in; with one, the client need not read the value first.

questions.q: What does serializable isolation guarantee about concurrent transactions?
options: That no transaction ever waits for another to finish
The result equals some run where they went one after another
That each transaction sees the newest data of the others
That they really run strictly one at a time on a single thread
optionExplain: Waiting may well occur in some implementations.
Right: outcomes equal a serial order.
Seeing others' newest data is not the promise.
Execution may overlap; only the outcome must match a serial order.
questions.explain: The promise is about outcomes. The card next gives the precise wording.

questions.q: Isolation is formalized in textbooks as ____.
questions.explain: Each transaction can pretend it is the only one running.
questions.rule: Isolation in the textbook is serializability.

questions.q: Two booking transactions each take the last concert seat. Under serializable isolation, what outcomes are possible?
options: Neither succeeds, since the database cancels both transactions
Only outcomes equal to one transaction running before the other
Both succeed, since each of them saw the seat as free
A mixed outcome with half of each transaction applied
optionExplain: Cancelling both matches no serial order either.
Right: one runs as if first, the other then sees the seat taken.
That would not match any one-after-another order.
Half-applied transactions are not outcomes of any serial run.
questions.explain: Serializability allows only results that some serial order could have produced.

questions.q: True or false: A developer states: serializable isolation means the database literally executes one transaction at a time. The chapter's definition supports this.
questions.explain: Serializability is a promise about the result: it must equal a serial order, though the transactions may in reality overlap. Later sections show it can be achieved with or without real serial execution.
questions.rule: Serializable defines the outcome, not the method.

questions.q: A database offers a level named serializable. The chapter's example is that Oracle 11g's level of that name actually implements what?
options: Snapshot isolation, a weaker guarantee
Literal serial execution on one thread
Two-phase locking, which is stronger
Read committed, which is weaker still
optionExplain: Right: the name serializable does not guarantee serializability.
Serial execution would also be serializable.
Two-phase locking would provide serializability.
Read committed is weaker, but the book names snapshot isolation.
questions.explain: The book gives Oracle as an example of a database that does not truly implement serializable isolation despite the name.
questions.rule: Test behaviour, not the level's name.
questions.teaches: In Oracle 11g the isolation level called serializable actually implements snapshot isolation, which is weaker than serializability.

questions.q: A ride-booking team reads that a level called repeatable read exists. What does the Oracle example suggest they should do?
options: Treat the name as the guarantee, since standards fix the meaning
Assume any name containing read means a weak level
Check what the level actually prevents, not its name
Use only the level the vendor ranks highest in its docs
optionExplain: The book shows names are inconsistent between databases.
Names do not map reliably to strength.
Right: level names and real behaviour can differ.
Documentation rankings do not describe actual anomalies.
questions.explain: Level names are inconsistently implemented, as the Oracle example shows.
questions.rule: Read the behaviour behind a level name.
questions.teaches: Isolation level names are unreliable guides: databases may implement a weaker guarantee under the name serializable.

questions.q: A database tells your app that a transaction has committed. Durability says what about that data?
options: It will be kept forever in its present form without any deletion
It was checked against the application's invariants one more time
It will not be forgotten, even if a crash follows
It is already visible to every other client in the cluster
optionExplain: Durability does not forbid later updates or deletions.
Invariants are the application's concern.
Right: the promise covers loss after commit.
Visibility is an isolation matter.
questions.explain: Durability is about not forgetting committed data. The card next shows how databases deliver that.

questions.q: Put these steps of a durable commit on one node in order.
items: Client sends the transaction
Database writes the data to nonvolatile storage
Database reports the commit as successful
A crash occurs, and the data is still there
questions.explain: The report of success has to come after the write to storage; only then can a later crash leave the data intact.

questions.q: A database acknowledges a ticket sale once the data is in memory, before writing to disk. Which promise is weakened?
options: Durability, since a crash right after could lose the sale
Atomicity, because the sale might be only partly written
Isolation, because other buyers might not see the sale
Consistency, because the sale breaks the venue's capacity rule
optionExplain: Right: acknowledging before the write is complete breaks the order durability needs.
Atomicity is about undoing partial work after faults.
Visibility to others is isolation.
Capacity rules are the application's invariants.
questions.explain: Durability requires waiting until the writes or replications are complete before reporting commit.

questions.q: True or false: Waiting for three copies before acknowledging a commit makes commits faster than waiting for a single copy.
questions.explain: Waiting for more copies to finish means a longer wait; the book says the database must wait for the writes or replications before reporting the commit.
questions.rule: More durability usually costs commit latency.

questions.q: On a single-node database, besides writing to nonvolatile storage, durability usually involves a log that allows what?
options: Copying the data to every replica in the cluster
Recovery if the data structures on disk are corrupted
Faster reads by skipping the main data structures
Running several transactions at the same time without locks
optionExplain: Replication is a separate step.
Right: a write-ahead log or similar supports recovery after corruption.
The log is not a read cache.
Concurrency control is a separate mechanism.
questions.explain: The log lets the database recover when the on-disk structures are damaged, for example after a crash.
questions.rule: A log backs the disk write.
questions.teaches: On a single node durability usually also involves a write-ahead log or similar, which allows recovery if the data structures on disk are corrupted.

questions.q: A file-sync service replicates each change to two data centres before telling the user it is saved. What does durability mean in this system?
options: The change reached the first data centre's memory
The change is hidden from other users until both copies exist there
The change was written once and a backup is planned
The change was copied to some nodes before success was reported
optionExplain: Memory only does not survive a crash.
Visibility is an isolation matter.
Planned backups come after the promise.
Right: in a replicated database durability may mean successfully copied to some number of nodes.
questions.explain: In replicated systems, durability means copying to some number of nodes before reporting commit.
questions.rule: Replicated durability means copies exist before success.
questions.teaches: In a replicated database durability may mean that the data has been successfully copied to some number of nodes.

questions.q: A database keeps three replicas and acknowledges a write after the leader alone has it. What can go wrong?
options: If the leader fails, the write may never have reached a replica
The write is kept on the leader's disk, so no loss can occur
The write is stored only if all replicas are in different rooms
All three replicas always apply the write in the same order
optionExplain: Right: asynchronous replication can lose recent writes.
A disk on a failed leader may be inaccessible.
Room placement does not decide whether the copy was sent.
Order is not the issue when the copies never arrived.
questions.explain: Replication helps with availability but asynchronous copying can lose recent writes. The card next lays out the trade-offs.
questions.rule: Async replication can lose recent writes.

questions.q: Which are weaknesses of the durability methods the chapter compares? Select all that apply.
options: In asynchronously replicated systems, recent writes can be lost when the leader fails
A replicated system loses all its data whenever one node fails
Replicas in different places can never fail together
Data on a failed machine's disk is inaccessible until the machine is fixed or the disk moved
Writing to disk is useless for an in-memory database
optionExplain: Right: the latest writes may exist only on the failed leader.
Replication exists to avoid exactly that.
A correlated fault can take out every replica at once.
Right: the disk survives but cannot serve reads.
The chapter says writing to disk stays relevant for in-memory databases.
questions.explain: Disk-only has an availability gap; async replication has a loss gap.
questions.rule: Each method leaves a different gap.

questions.q: A metrics collector keeps all data in memory on three replicas. A software bug crashes every node on one malformed input. What is lost?
options: Only the data written after the last backup
Only the data on the node that received the input first
Nothing at all, because three replicas cannot fail at the same time
Everything held only in memory, as all replicas failed together
optionExplain: Backups matter only if they exist; here memory-only data has none.
The bug hits every node, not one.
That is the assumption correlated faults break.
Right: a correlated fault defeats replication when data is only in memory.
questions.explain: A bug crashing every node on a particular input is a correlated fault; memory-only data does not survive it.

questions.q: Which design choice best answers a power outage across a whole data centre?
options: Adding a fourth in-memory replica in the same room
Acknowledging writes sooner to reduce the exposure window
Writing data to disk, so it survives a total power loss
Relying on asynchronous replication to the leader's neighbour
optionExplain: A fourth copy loses power too.
Faster acknowledgement increases exposure.
Right: nonvolatile storage keeps data across a total power loss.
A neighbour in the same room fails with it.
questions.explain: Disk writes stay relevant even in replicated or in-memory systems because a correlated fault can knock out all replicas at once.
questions.rule: Disk survives what replicas in one place cannot.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says that writing to disk remains relevant even for in-memory databases.
questions.explain: Because a correlated fault such as a power outage can knock out all replicas, data held only in memory would be lost; a disk write protects against that.
questions.rule: Disk still matters when replicas fail together.
questions.teaches: Writing to disk is still relevant for in-memory databases, because a correlated fault can knock out all replicas and lose data held only in memory.

questions.q: A ride-booking company replicates trip records across three nodes in one rack. What fault does the chapter say can defeat this design?
options: A single node failing while the other two stay up
A correlated fault, such as a power cut, hitting all replicas
A client retrying a request that already succeeded
A transaction aborting because of a violated uniqueness constraint
optionExplain: One failing node is what replication handles.
Right: replicas share the fault when the cause is common.
Retries concern duplicated work, not durability.
Aborts are normal behaviour, not data loss.
questions.explain: Replicas are only independent if their failures are; a shared cause breaks that.
questions.teaches: A correlated fault, such as a power outage or a bug that crashes every node on a particular input, can knock out all replicas at once.

questions.q: A database confirms that fsync succeeded. How much does that prove about the data surviving a sudden power cut?
options: Everything, since fsync is a firm guarantee that the data is physically on disk
That the data is safe but unreadable until the next restart
Less than hoped, since SSDs have been shown to break their guarantees
Only that the data is in the filesystem cache and nothing more
optionExplain: That is the naive assumption the chapter questions.
The concern is loss or corruption, not delay.
Right: even fsync is not guaranteed to work correctly.
A cache is not what fsync is for; the problem is hardware misbehaving.
questions.explain: Hardware can lie about completed writes. The card next lists more cases.
questions.rule: A completed disk write is not proof.

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter list as reasons disk storage may fail to keep data? Select all that apply.
options: Disk firmware can have bugs
Magnetic disks cannot hold data for more than one year
SSDs left unpowered can start losing data within weeks
Data on disk can become corrupted gradually without being noticed
Filesystems always repair themselves after a crash
optionExplain: Right.
The chapter does not say this.
Right: depending on temperature.
Right.
The chapter says subtle interactions with the filesystem can corrupt files after a crash.
questions.explain: The chapter lists several independent routes to loss, from firmware to slow corruption.
questions.rule: Disks fail in many ways besides crashing.

questions.q: A file-sync service finds that a photo on disk has been silently corrupted for months. Replicas and recent backups copied the damage. What restores it?
options: Rewriting the file from the leader's memory
The disk's own error log, which holds the old bytes
The most recent replica, since it is up to date
A historical backup taken before the corruption
optionExplain: Memory contents are not a long-term copy.
Error logs do not keep file contents.
Replicas also copied the corruption.
Right: the chapter says to restore from a historical backup.
questions.explain: If data has been corrupted for some time, replicas and recent backups may also be corrupted, so an older backup is needed.

questions.q: True or false: Replacing SSDs with magnetic drives would remove the risk of drive failure.
questions.explain: Magnetic drives have a lower rate of bad sectors but a higher rate of complete failure than SSDs.
questions.rule: Each drive type has its own failure pattern.

questions.q: A study found that over four years, roughly what share of SSDs developed at least one bad block?
options: Between 30% and 80%
Nearly all of them, over 99%
About 5%
Under 1%
optionExplain: Right: the range is wide but far from negligible.
The range is high but not near-total.
Still far lower than the range given.
The chapter's figure is much higher.
questions.explain: The chapter gives 30% to 80% of SSDs developing at least one bad block in the first four years.
questions.teaches: One study found that between 30% and 80% of SSDs develop at least one bad block during the first four years of operation.

questions.q: A payments team stores ledgers on one SSD with no copies, as SSDs seem reliable. Which chapter point applies?
options: SSDs lose data only if left powered on for several years
SSDs get bad blocks and can misbehave on power loss
SSD failures are always detected immediately
Bad blocks occur only on magnetic drives
optionExplain: The opposite: losing power is the risk.
Right: the evidence argues for redundancy.
Corruption can go undetected for a long time.
The chapter says bad blocks affect many SSDs.
questions.explain: The chapter's evidence is a case for more than one copy and for backups.
questions.rule: A single drive is a single point of failure.
questions.teaches: If an SSD is disconnected from power, it can start losing data within a few weeks, depending on the temperature.

questions.q: Which strategy best reflects the chapter's advice on keeping data safe?
options: Skip backups once the data is replicated to several nodes
Use several techniques together, as none is absolute
Trust the vendor's stated guarantee once it is documented
Pick the single most reliable technique and rely on it fully
optionExplain: Replicas can copy corruption, so backups still matter.
Right: there are only various risk-reduction techniques.
The chapter says to take guarantees with a grain of salt.
Even the best technique has gaps.
questions.explain: The chapter advises layering risk-reduction techniques. The card next gives the list.

questions.q: Order these protections from closest to the data to farthest away.
items: Write to local disk
Replicate to other machines
Keep backups, including historical ones
questions.explain: A local write comes first, replicas next, and backups hold the longest memory of the data.

questions.q: A chat service stores messages on one disk with nightly backups. Which addition best follows the chapter's advice?
options: Also replicate messages to remote machines
Replace the nightly backups with a faster disk
Rely on the disk vendor's reliability statement
Drop the disk write and rely on replicas in memory
optionExplain: Right: adding a layer covers the single-disk gap.
Speed does not remove failure risk.
Guarantees deserve a grain of salt.
Memory-only replicas are exposed to correlated faults.
questions.explain: The techniques are meant to be used together: disk, remote replication and backups.
questions.rule: Add layers, do not swap them.

questions.q: True or false: A team argues that because their data is replicated to five nodes, they no longer need backups. The chapter supports this.
questions.explain: Replicas can copy corrupted data, and a correlated fault can take them all out; backups, including historical ones, are part of the layered approach.

questions.q: How does the chapter suggest treating theoretical guarantees about data safety?
options: As proven once an academic paper states them
As irrelevant, because practice never matches theory
With a healthy grain of salt
As binding once a vendor documents them
optionExplain: Papers state ideals, not real hardware.
Theory is useful, only not absolute.
Right: take any theoretical guarantee with a healthy grain of salt.
Documentation does not make a guarantee true.
questions.explain: The book's advice is to be sceptical of absolute promises and to layer defences.
questions.teaches: It is wise to take any theoretical guarantee with a healthy grain of salt, because there is no technique that provides absolute guarantees.

questions.q: A sync service wants to promise customers their files are safe. How should it word the promise?
options: As a promise that no data is ever corrupted
As a promise of immediate recovery from any disaster
As an absolute guarantee, since replication makes loss impossible
As layered risk reduction that lowers the chance of loss
optionExplain: Corruption can occur silently.
Recovery depends on surviving copies.
Replication does not make loss impossible.
Right: only risk reduction is honest.
questions.explain: Since perfect durability does not exist, honest wording speaks of reducing risk.
questions.teaches: If all hard disks and all backups are destroyed at the same time, there is nothing the database can do; perfect durability does not exist.

questions.q: A checkout writes an order and a stock change. Another user sees the order but not the stock change. Which guarantee was missing?
options: Durability
Atomicity
Isolation
Consistency
optionExplain: Durability concerns loss after commit.
Atomicity concerns faults, not what others see.
Right: the problem is another client seeing a half-done state.
Consistency concerns the application's rules.
questions.explain: Seeing part of a transaction's writes is an isolation failure. The card next sets atomicity beside it.
questions.rule: Half-visible work is an isolation problem.

questions.q: Match each guarantee to the problem it addresses.
pairs: A fault stops a transaction partway through its writes
Another transaction sees or touches a transaction's half-done work
A client wants several records changed together
questions.explain: Atomicity covers the fault; isolation covers the interfering client. Needing several records changed together is why the guarantees matter.

questions.q: Sort each symptom by the guarantee whose absence would explain it.

items.t: A crash leaves an order stored but its invoice missing
A disk filling up halfway leaves some updates applied
A second user reads a balance while a transfer is half done
Two buyers overwrite each other's partly finished updates

questions.explain: Faults that stop a transaction partway point to atomicity; other clients seeing or overwriting half-done work point to isolation.

questions.q: A chat service shows a new message in the list, but the unread counter lags for a second. Which description fits?
options: Another client saw a half-done state, which is an isolation problem
The invariants were broken by bad application logic
A fault left the counter write undone, which is an atomicity problem
The data was lost after commit, which is a durability problem
optionExplain: Right: the counter is just not yet updated when the reader looks.
Invariants come from the application, not this timing gap.
Atomicity would apply if the counter update failed for good.
Nothing was lost after commit.
questions.explain: A reader catching a transaction between two writes is an isolation issue. If the counter write failed for good, atomicity would matter.
questions.rule: A lag that heals is isolation; a gap that persists is atomicity.

questions.q: The chapter says these definitions assume you want to modify several objects at once. Which are examples of an object?
options: Only individual bytes within a record
Rows, documents or records
Only whole database tables
Only complete database servers
optionExplain: Bytes are below the level of objects.
Right: the chapter uses object for rows, documents and records.
Tables are collections of objects, not the unit.
Servers are the machines, not the data objects.
questions.explain: Object is the chapter's neutral word for a row, a document or a record, whatever the data model.
questions.rule: An object is a row, document or record.
questions.teaches: In the chapter an object means a row, a document or a record, and multi-object transactions are needed when several pieces of data must be kept in sync.

questions.q: A file-sync worker crashes between writing a file row and a folder-size row. Which guarantee is needed first?
options: Isolation, to hide the crash from other clients
Durability, to save the second row twice
Consistency, to let the database choose the folder size
Atomicity, to undo the half-done writes
optionExplain: Isolation matters while the transaction runs, but the fault is the first problem.
Durability concerns committed data.
The application defines valid sizes.
Right: the crash left a half-finished transaction that must be undone.
questions.explain: A crash is a fault, so atomicity is first needed; isolation matters for readers while a transaction is in progress.
questions.teaches: Atomicity concerns what the database does after a fault, while isolation concerns what other clients may see while a transaction is running.

questions.q: A mailbox stores a separate unread counter. A new message arrives and a reader sees the message but a count of zero. What caused it?
options: The reader looked between the message insert and the counter update
The message was written to disk but the counter was lost permanently
The counter was rounded down to the nearest ten messages
The reader's query ran on a different version of the database software
optionExplain: Right: a reader caught the pair of writes half done.
A permanent loss would be a different failure.
Nothing about the counter is rounded.
Version differences do not explain the timing gap.
questions.explain: The inconsistency is a timing gap between two writes. The card next shows both guarantees at work.
questions.rule: Between two writes, readers can see a gap.

questions.q: Storing a count beside the data it counts, to avoid a slow query, is a kind of ____.
questions.explain: Denormalization duplicates information for speed and so creates data that must be kept in sync.

questions.q: A ride app keeps a driver's trip count beside the trip rows. How should one completion update both?
options: As two independent writes, since the count is only a convenience
The count first, then the trip row, as separate commits
Only the trip row, and recompute the count whenever it is read
In one transaction, so readers see both changes or neither
optionExplain: Independent writes allow a visible gap and divergence after a failure.
Separate commits still allow a failure between them.
Recomputing drops the optimization, which is a different trade.
Right: a transaction keeps the pair together.
questions.explain: The count is a denormalized copy, so it should change in the same transaction as the trip row.
questions.rule: Change the copy with its source.

questions.q: A developer would keep the message if the counter update fails and fix the count later. What is the risk?
options: No risk, since a counter is always recomputed on the next read
The message is deleted automatically by the failed counter write
The message and counter disagree until someone repairs them
The failed update locks the mailbox until the end of the day
optionExplain: A stored counter is not recomputed on read.
Failures do not delete earlier writes unless a transaction aborts them.
Right: a failed second write leaves the pair out of sync.
No such lock is described.
questions.explain: Atomicity would roll back the message when the counter update fails, avoiding the divergence.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter notes a wrong unread counter is minor, but a wrong account balance in a payment would be serious.
questions.explain: A footnote says an incorrect unread counter is not critical, but one should think of a customer account balance and a payment transaction instead.
questions.rule: Swap the counter for money and the stakes change.
questions.teaches: A footnote asks the reader to think of a customer account balance and a payment transaction instead of an unread counter, since an incorrect counter is not a particularly critical problem.

questions.q: A ticketing site keeps remaining-seat counts beside seat rows. A buyer reserves a seat and the count update fails. What does a transaction do?
options: Keeps the reservation and flags the count as stale
Rolls back the seat reservation, so both stay in step
Splits the reservation into two orders
Retries the count update while holding the seat for ten minutes
optionExplain: That would leave the pair out of sync.
Right: the failed update aborts the whole transaction.
Transactions do not split orders.
Holding the seat is a design choice, not what a transaction does.
questions.explain: Atomicity rolls back the insert if the second write fails, keeping source and copy in step.
questions.teaches: In an atomic transaction, if the update to the derived counter fails, the transaction is aborted and the inserted record is rolled back.

questions.q: In a typical relational database, how are the statements of one transaction identified?
options: They are the statements that touch the same table in a given second
They are the statements flagged by the application in each row
The statements between begin and commit on one connection
They are the statements that share a user name on the server
optionExplain: Timing and tables do not define transactions.
Row flags are not the mechanism.
Right: the connection scopes the transaction.
Users can run many separate transactions.
questions.explain: The common mechanism is the connection plus begin and commit. The card next confirms.
questions.rule: Begin to commit on one connection.

questions.q: On one connection, everything between BEGIN TRANSACTION and ____ is part of the same transaction.
questions.explain: A COMMIT statement ends the grouped operations and asks the database to make them permanent.

questions.q: An app opens one connection, begins a transaction, runs three updates, then the connection is cut before commit. What happens?
options: The three updates are committed anyway as they ran
The first update stays and the last two are discarded
The updates wait indefinitely for the connection to return
The transaction is aborted, so none of the three remain
optionExplain: Without commit they are not committed.
Partial survival would violate atomicity.
The database does not wait for a dead connection.
Right: an interrupted connection aborts the transaction.
questions.explain: Because the transaction is tied to the connection, losing the connection before commit aborts it.
questions.rule: A dropped connection aborts an open transaction.

questions.q: True or false: A cut connection before any reply to COMMIT shows the transaction was aborted.
questions.explain: The server may have committed before the reply was lost, so the client does not know the outcome.
questions.rule: A lost acknowledgement leaves the outcome unknown.

questions.q: How can a transaction manager avoid the problem of being tied to a TCP connection?
options: By using a unique transaction ID not tied to a connection
By committing every statement automatically as soon as it arrives
By running every transaction on the client machine instead
By keeping all clients on one permanent connection forever
optionExplain: Right: an identifier outlives any one connection.
Auto-commit removes multi-statement transactions.
The database still has to keep the data safe.
Permanent connections are not a design the book proposes.
questions.explain: A footnote notes that a transaction manager can use unique transaction identifiers; the book returns to this later.
questions.rule: An identifier can outlive a connection.
questions.teaches: If the connection breaks after a commit request but before the acknowledgement, the client cannot tell whether it committed; a transaction manager using a unique transaction identifier not bound to the TCP connection can solve this.

questions.q: A payments client sends commit, and the reply does not arrive. What should it avoid doing blindly?
options: Logging the uncertain state for later review
Re-running the whole payment, as it may have succeeded
Waiting for the server to report the outcome
Checking whether the payment exists before deciding what to do
optionExplain: Logging does not change the data.
Right: a blind retry could pay twice.
Waiting for the result is safe.
Checking the outcome is safe.
questions.explain: Because the outcome is unknown, a blind retry risks doing the work twice, which later ideas address.
questions.rule: When the outcome is unknown, do not retry blindly.
questions.teaches: A client whose connection breaks after requesting commit may have a transaction that actually committed.

questions.q: A key-value store offers a multi-put that updates five keys in one call. What can you conclude about atomicity?
options: That the store applies the five keys in a transaction
Nothing yet, as the call may succeed for only some keys
That the first key is always applied first and the rest follow
That all five keys are updated or none of them are
optionExplain: The name of the call does not decide it.
Right: a multi-object API does not by itself give transaction semantics.
Order of application is not the question.
That is the unchecked assumption.
questions.explain: A single call is not a transaction unless the database promises all-or-nothing. The card next states this.
questions.rule: One call is not one transaction.

questions.q: True or false: A multi-object API in a key-value store automatically has transaction semantics.
questions.explain: The chapter says the command may succeed for some keys and fail for others, leaving a partially updated database.
questions.rule: A multi-object API is not automatically a transaction.

questions.q: A metrics store has put-many for ten time series. An outage hits after six are written. What can the application assume?
options: Nothing about the other four; a partial update is possible
That the store will finish the call by itself after recovery
That the six were rolled back automatically
That the other four were written in the background
optionExplain: Right: a partial update is possible.
Nothing promises resumption.
Rollback is what a transaction would do, not necessarily this API.
Nothing promises background completion.
questions.explain: Without transaction semantics the command can leave the database partially updated.
questions.rule: Assume a partial result unless promised otherwise.

questions.q: A vendor calls its put-many a transaction because it updates many objects at once. It is one only if a failure ____ all of them.
questions.explain: The test is whether failure undoes all the writes, not how many objects one command reaches.
questions.rule: A transaction is a promise, not a command shape.

questions.q: Which feature would make a multi-put behave like a transaction?
options: A guarantee that the keys are written in sorted order
A guarantee that the call returns within a fixed time
A guarantee that a failed write leaves no new values
A guarantee that all keys are written on the same disk
optionExplain: Order is not atomicity.
Latency is not the issue.
Right: this is the all-or-nothing property.
Placement is not the issue.
questions.explain: All-or-nothing is the missing piece; the chapter says the command may leave a partial result.
questions.teaches: A multi-object API only has transaction semantics if the command cannot succeed for some keys and fail for others.

questions.q: A document store adds a bulk-update command. Which question to its documentation best tests whether it is a transaction?
options: How fast is the command on a large collection?
How many documents can the command update in one call?
Which programming languages can call the command?
What happens to documents already updated if one fails?
optionExplain: Speed is attractive, but a fast command can still leave a partial update.
Size limits tell you about capacity, not about whether a failure undoes earlier updates.
Language support tells you about integration, not about atomicity.
Right: only the outcome after a failure shows whether the command is all-or-nothing.
questions.explain: Ask about failure behaviour; the chapter shows that appearances can mislead.
questions.rule: Ask what happens after a failure.
questions.teaches: Even with a multi-object API, a datastore may leave a partially updated state when some operations fail.

questions.q: A client is writing a 20 KB document when the network fails after 10 KB. What do storage engines almost universally aim to do?
options: Merge the fragment with the old value for the remainder
Block all other writes to the database until a human steps in
Store the 10 KB fragment and mark it for later repair
Avoid storing the fragment: old stays or new is whole
optionExplain: That is the spliced result atomicity prevents.
Engines do not behave this way.
That leaves an unparseable value.
Right: single-object writes are atomic.
questions.explain: Storage engines aim for single-object atomicity and isolation. The card next shows the scope.
questions.rule: A single object is written whole or not at all.

questions.q: True or false: Storage engines almost universally aim to provide atomicity and isolation at the level of one object on one node.
questions.explain: A key-value pair is written whole or not at all, and a concurrent reader does not see it half written.
questions.rule: One object, one node: atomic and isolated.

questions.q: A reader fetches a user profile document while another client is overwriting it. What should a storage engine with single-object isolation show?
options: An error, because reads cannot overlap writes to one object
The complete old version or the complete new version
Whichever fields the reader asked for first, from the newest write
The first half of the new version joined to the old rest
optionExplain: Readers can still be served.
Right: isolation on one object means no half-written view.
Per-field mixing is a partly updated value.
That is the splice isolation prevents.
questions.explain: Single-object isolation means a reader never sees a partly updated value.

questions.q: True or false: Applied to two different keys at once, two updates would still leave each key with one whole value.
questions.explain: The guarantee is per object, so each key is written whole; what is not provided is coordination between the keys.
questions.rule: Per-object guarantees hold independently per object.

questions.q: Which two mechanisms do storage engines typically use for single-object guarantees? Select two.
options: A lock on each object
Writing every change to an archive tape
Sorting writes by client name
A log used for crash recovery
Copying each write to a second node before accepting it
optionExplain: Right: the lock supports isolation by allowing one thread at a time.
Tape is a historical durability method.
Ordering by name does nothing for either guarantee.
Right: the log supports atomicity.
Replication is a different matter.
questions.explain: Atomicity can be implemented using a log for crash recovery, and isolation by a lock on each object that allows one thread at a time.
questions.rule: Log for atomicity, lock for isolation.
questions.teaches: Single-object atomicity can be implemented with a log for crash recovery, and isolation with a lock on each object allowing only one thread to access it at a time.
