questions.q: A chat service stores each conversation as one document and keeps a separate index of conversations per user. Which guarantee covers updating both?
options: A multi-object transaction; per-object locks cover one each
No guarantee is needed because the index is only a copy
The log alone, because the index is rebuilt after a crash
The per-document lock, because the index refers to the document
optionExplain: Right: two objects need grouping.
A stale index causes visible errors.
A log does not coordinate two objects.
A lock on the document does not lock the index.
questions.explain: The document and the index are separate objects, so they need a transaction to move together.
questions.teaches: Per-object atomicity and isolation do not keep two related objects, such as a document and an index entry, in step.

questions.q: A database advertises lightweight transactions that update one counter atomically. What is the book's view of that term?
options: It is irrelevant, since transactions need no definition
It is accurate, since any atomic operation is a transaction
Misleading: a transaction spans several objects
It is accurate, since lightweight means fewer guarantees
optionExplain: The chapter does define the word.
Atomic alone is not the definition.
Right: the term stretches the word transaction.
Fewer guarantees is the point against the label.
questions.explain: The book calls the terminology misleading. The card next gives the reasoning.
questions.rule: Single object is not a transaction.

questions.q: A write that happens only if the value has not been changed by someone else is called ____-and-set.
questions.explain: Compare-and-set avoids lost updates by checking the old value before writing.

questions.q: A feature flag service offers increment-if-unchanged on one key. A salesperson calls it ACID transactions. What is a fair reply?
options: Incorrect, since the operation cannot prevent any lost updates
Useful for one key, but not a multi-object unit
Correct, since marketing terms define the standard
Correct, since any compare operation is a full transaction
optionExplain: It does prevent lost updates on that key.
Right: it helps lost updates but is not a multi-object transaction.
The chapter distrusts marketing terms.
It lacks the grouping across objects.
questions.explain: Single-object operations prevent lost updates on one object, but they do not make the system transactional.
questions.rule: Useful is not the same as transactional.

questions.q: Which operation is a transaction in the usual sense of the word?
options: Customer and invoice rows written together, all or nothing
A compare-and-set that writes only if one counter is unchanged
A write that replaces one key with a new value
An increment of one counter in the database
optionExplain: Right: several operations on several objects as one unit is the usual meaning of transaction.
It protects one counter only, so it is useful but not a multi-object transaction.
Replacing one key touches one object, so there is nothing to group.
An increment touches a single object, however safe it is.
questions.explain: The usual meaning requires multiple operations on multiple objects in one unit of execution.

questions.q: True or false: In ACID terms, an atomic increment would be better called an isolated or serializable increment.
questions.explain: A footnote makes this point and then calls it nitpicky; it shows how atomic changes meaning between settings.
questions.rule: Atomic means different things in different settings.
questions.teaches: Strictly speaking, atomic increment uses atomic in the multi-threaded sense; in the ACID context it should be called an isolated or serializable increment.

questions.q: A team lists what their new store provides: increment, compare-and-set, per-key atomic writes. Can they claim multi-object ACID transactions?
options: No, because transactions cannot exist in key-value stores
Yes, because the operations are all isolated
Yes, because each operation is atomic
No, none of these spans several objects
optionExplain: Key-value stores could add transactions.
Isolation per object is not joint.
Each is atomic, but not jointly.
Right: grouping across objects is missing.
questions.explain: Joint all-or-nothing across objects is the missing piece; the single-object features do not supply it.
questions.teaches: A transaction is usually understood as a mechanism for grouping multiple operations on multiple objects into one unit of execution.

questions.q: Which design needs a multi-object transaction?
options: A cache that replaces one value under one key
A log that appends one line to a single file on one node
A shop updating an order row and a stock row together
A page that reads one record from one table
optionExplain: Replacing one value under one key is a single-object write, which storage engines already make atomic.
Appending one line is one write to one object, so there is nothing to coordinate.
Right: an order and its stock are two objects that must change together.
A read of one record involves no writes to keep in step.
questions.explain: Coordinated changes of related objects are the typical case. The card next lists the patterns.

questions.q: Which situations does the chapter give for needing multi-object writes? Select all that apply.
options: Foreign key references between rows
Storing one counter per user
Reading a single document by key
Denormalized data copied into several documents
Secondary indexes that must follow every value change
optionExplain: Right: references must stay valid.
One counter per user is a single-object update.
A single read needs no coordination.
Right: copies must stay in sync.
Right: each index is another object.
questions.explain: References, copies and indexes are the three cases the chapter gives.

questions.q: A chat service denormalizes a user's display name into each message document. The user renames themselves. What does the design need?
options: A transaction updating all affected documents
A lock on the user's login page
No coordination, since each document is separate
An index on the display name alone
optionExplain: Right: copies must change together.
Locking a login page is unrelated.
Separate documents still must agree.
An index does not update the copies.
questions.explain: Document stores lacking joins encourage denormalization, which makes multi-document updates necessary.

questions.q: A store indexes email. An insert updates the record before the index. What can a reader without isolation see?
options: The index pointing to a record that was never written
A record that appears directly but not via the index
Two records merged into one by the index
The record twice, as the index double-counts it
optionExplain: The index is behind, not ahead.
Right: the record appears in one place but not the other.
Merging is not the failure described.
Double counting is not described.
questions.explain: Indexes are different database objects from a transaction point of view, so without isolation a record can appear in one but not another.

questions.q: True or false: Within a document data model, fields that change together are often inside one document, so no multi-object transaction is needed for them.
questions.explain: A single document counts as a single object; the need arises when denormalized copies live in several documents.
questions.teaches: In a document model the fields that need updating together are often within the same document, which is treated as a single object, so no multi-object transaction is needed for updating a single document.

questions.q: A graph database stores vertices and edges. A new edge connects two vertices that both must exist. What does the chapter's reasoning say?
options: Only the vertices need coordination, not the edge
Graph stores cannot enforce references of any kind
The edge needs no coordination because edges are cheap
Multi-object transactions keep the references valid
optionExplain: The edge references both vertices.
The point is to coordinate, not to forbid.
Cost does not remove the need.
Right: graph references play the foreign-key role.
questions.explain: In a graph model a vertex has edges to other vertices, and these references have to stay valid just like foreign keys.
questions.rule: References need joint updates in any model.
questions.teaches: In a graph-like data model a vertex has edges to other vertices, and multi-object transactions let you ensure that these references remain valid.

questions.q: A distributed store's docs say multi-object transactions are impossible across partitions. How does the book describe the situation?
options: Hard and costly, but nothing fundamentally prevents them
They are easy and only skipped by lazy designers
They are possible only on single-node databases, not on clusters
They are impossible, as the docs claim
optionExplain: Right: difficult, not impossible.
The book says they are difficult.
The book says distributed implementations exist.
The book rejects impossibility.
questions.explain: The book treats the missing transactions as a trade-off. The card next gives its reasons.

questions.q: Which reasons does the chapter give for distributed stores dropping multi-object transactions? Select two.
options: They only work for numeric data
They are difficult to implement across partitions
They can get in the way where very high availability or performance is needed
They cannot be implemented in any database
optionExplain: Not mentioned.
Right.
Right.
The chapter denies this.
questions.explain: The chapter gives difficulty across partitions and conflict with availability or performance demands.

questions.q: A partitioned store lacks transactions, yet an order and invoice must stay in step. What does the team face?
options: Automatic recovery from any partial failure
Nothing, because partitions make orders independent
A forced move to a single machine
Harder error handling and concurrency problems
optionExplain: No store recovers automatically from every partial failure; that was the job atomicity did.
Partitions spread data, but an order and its invoice are still related and must agree.
Nothing forces a move to one machine; the issue is where the guarantees come from.
Right: without transactions the burden of error handling and concurrency moves to the application.
questions.explain: Without atomicity, error handling gets much more complicated, and without isolation concurrency problems appear.
questions.rule: Dropping transactions shifts burden to the app.

questions.q: A designer writes: since no distributed database can support transactions, we should not worry about partial failures. What is the flaw?
options: None; without transactions partial failures cannot happen
Partial failures are fixed by adding partitions
Partial failures remain, and the app must handle them
Partial failures only occur in single-node databases
optionExplain: Partial failures can happen without transactions.
Partitions do not repair failures.
Right: the premise is false, and dropping transactions leaves failures to the app.
They occur in distributed systems as well.
questions.explain: Nothing fundamentally prevents distributed transactions, and without them the application must handle partial failure itself.
questions.rule: No transactions means more app-level handling.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says distributed transactions come with difficult challenges that it discusses in later chapters.
questions.explain: It says transactions in distributed databases open a new set of difficult challenges, covered in the next two chapters.
questions.rule: Distributed transactions are deferred, not dismissed.
questions.teaches: Transactions in distributed databases open a new set of difficult challenges, which the book discusses in the next two chapters.

questions.q: A metrics platform needs very high write throughput across many partitions. According to the chapter's reasoning, what is the honest summary of dropping transactions?
options: A free improvement with no downside
A trade of guarantees for performance
A proof that transactions are incompatible with throughput
A requirement for any system on many machines
optionExplain: There is a downside: complexity returns to the application, which has to handle errors and concurrency itself.
Right: dropping transactions trades guarantees for performance, with the work moving to the application.
The chapter says nothing fundamentally prevents distributed transactions, so incompatibility is not proven.
Nothing requires dropping transactions on many machines; it is a design choice.
questions.explain: The book frames it as a trade-off driven by performance and availability needs.
questions.teaches: Distributed datastores abandoned multi-object transactions because they are difficult to implement across partitions and can get in the way where very high availability or performance is required.

questions.q: A web framework hits a transaction abort and shows the user an error, discarding their input. What did it waste?
options: The lock on the table, which is then never released afterwards
The replica, which stops accepting writes
The chance to retry, which is the point of aborting
The data on disk, which is corrupted by the abort
optionExplain: Locks are released when a transaction aborts, so none remain.
Replicas keep accepting writes; the abort is local to the transaction.
Right: aborts exist so that the work can be retried safely, and the framework threw that chance away.
An abort leaves the data clean; it does not corrupt anything on disk.
questions.explain: The book calls it a shame that ORMs do not retry. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Abort is meant to enable retry.

questions.q: Match each kind of datastore with its attitude to errors.
pairs: Abandons a transaction entirely rather than leave it half done
Best effort: does what it can and does not undo earlier work
Do not retry aborted transactions, so user input is thrown away
questions.explain: ACID favours abort. Leaderless stores favour best effort. Popular ORMs do not retry.
questions.rule: Abort and retry versus best effort.

questions.q: An ORM raises an exception on abort and the app returns a 500 error. What is the better design?
options: Retry forever, whatever the error, until the transaction succeeds
Disable transactions so no aborts occur
Show the error and ask the user to retype
Catch transient aborts and retry before showing an error
optionExplain: Endless retrying, whatever the error, can overload the system or loop on permanent errors.
Disabling transactions removes the atomicity and isolation that prevented the abort's damage.
Asking the user to retype discards their input, which is the waste the chapter criticises.
Right: catching transient aborts and retrying makes use of what aborts are for.
questions.explain: The whole point of aborts is to enable safe retries, so applications should handle them.
questions.rule: Handle aborts by retrying where appropriate.

questions.q: A leaderless store hits an error halfway through a multi-key update. What does best effort imply for the keys already written?
options: They stay written, so the app must recover
They are hidden until the update is retried
They are rewritten from a backup automatically
They are rolled back by the database
optionExplain: Right: best effort does not undo earlier writes, so the application has to detect and repair them.
Nothing hides partial writes from readers in a best-effort store.
No automatic repair from a backup takes place after an error.
Rollback is the ACID approach, not best effort.
questions.explain: Best effort means the database won't undo what it has already done; recovery falls to the application.
questions.rule: Best effort leaves cleanup to you.

questions.q: True or false: Datastores with leaderless replication generally follow the same abort-and-retry philosophy as ACID databases.
questions.explain: They work more on a best-effort basis: the database does what it can and does not undo something it has already done on error, so recovery is the application's responsibility.
questions.teaches: Datastores with leaderless replication work on a best-effort basis: the database does as much as it can and if it runs into an error it does not undo something already done, so recovering is the application's job.

questions.q: A team moves from an ACID database to a best-effort store. What new responsibility lands on their code?
options: Writing the write-ahead log
Spotting and repairing partial results
Granting the store permission to retry
Choosing the isolation level for each query
optionExplain: Logs belong to the storage engine.
Right: recovery is now theirs.
Retry permission is not the issue.
Isolation levels are not the issue.
questions.explain: Without undo, the application has to find and fix partially applied changes.
questions.teaches: Popular ORM frameworks such as Rails ActiveRecord and Django do not retry aborted transactions; the error bubbles up as an exception and the user's input is thrown away.

questions.q: A payment transaction commits, but the confirmation is lost in the network. The client retries. What can happen?
options: The database ignores the second attempt automatically
The payment is made twice without deduplication
The first payment is cancelled by the retry
The retry fails because commits cannot be repeated
optionExplain: Databases do not know the requests are the same.
Right: the transaction succeeded, so retrying repeats it.
A retry is a new transaction.
Nothing prevents a second commit.
questions.explain: A lost confirmation looks like a failure to the client. The card next shows the guard.
questions.rule: A lost reply can double the work.

questions.q: To stop a repeated request from being executed twice, an application needs a mechanism for ____.
questions.explain: Deduplication recognises that two requests are the same and executes only one.

questions.q: A ride app retries a booking request after a timeout. The first request had already committed. What prevents a double booking?
options: A request ID the server uses to spot the repeat
A higher isolation level on the database
A longer timeout on the second request
A faster network connection between client and server
optionExplain: Right: identity of the request is what deduplicates.
Isolation does not know the requests are one.
Longer timeouts do not recognise repeats.
Speed does not remove the ambiguity.
questions.explain: Application-level deduplication is what protects against double execution.

questions.q: A developer says: a retry after any failure is safe, because failed transactions leave no trace. What does this miss?
options: Retries are never needed
Confirmations are delivered in order
A committed transaction may look failed if the reply is lost
Failed transactions leave half-done writes that stay visible
optionExplain: Retries are needed for transient errors.
Delivery order is not the issue.
Right: a lost confirmation looks like a failure.
Aborts leave no trace; the issue is commits that look like failures.
questions.explain: Atomicity protects against partial work after an abort, but the client may not know whether an abort happened.

questions.q: True or false: If the client process crashes while it is retrying, the data it was trying to write can be lost.
questions.explain: The data lived only in the client's memory; the database has no copy of an aborted or never-sent transaction.
questions.rule: Retry state held only in the client is fragile.
questions.teaches: If the client process fails while retrying, any data it was trying to write to the database is lost.

questions.q: A metrics client buffers points in memory and retries sends until acknowledged. What risk remains even with deduplication?
options: The database refusing identical requests permanently
The server executing a deduplicated request twice
The retries being faster than the original request
The client may crash and lose the buffered points
optionExplain: Databases do not permanently refuse identical requests; they just execute them.
Deduplication exists to prevent exactly that double execution.
Speed of retries is not a durability or correctness problem here.
Right: retry state held in a client's memory is lost if the client crashes.
questions.explain: Retry logic held in a process that can crash is not durable; the card's guard does not cover that.
questions.rule: Persist retry state if loss matters.
questions.teaches: Retrying is not perfect: if the client process fails while retrying, any data it was trying to write is lost.

questions.q: A transaction fails because the database is overloaded. A client retries immediately in a loop. What is likely to happen?
options: The retries are cheaper than the original attempts
The database ignores repeated requests
The retries drain the backlog and clear the overload
The extra retries add load and worsen the overload
optionExplain: Retries cost as much as originals.
Databases do not ignore them.
Extra load does not drain a backlog.
Right: retries under overload create a feedback cycle.
questions.explain: Retrying under overload is a classic feedback loop. The card next shows the guard.
questions.rule: Do not retry blindly under overload.

questions.q: Sort each error by whether a retry is worthwhile.

items.t: Deadlock between two transactions
Temporary network interruption
Violation of a uniqueness constraint
Failover to a new leader

questions.explain: Transient errors can clear by themselves. A constraint violation will recur on every retry.

questions.q: A booking service sees constraint violations on a duplicate seat. What should the retry policy do?
options: Retry with exponential backoff until it works
Not retry, and report the conflict
Retry on a different replica
Retry once per second forever
optionExplain: Backoff spaces out attempts but cannot change a permanent error.
Right: the same constraint will reject every retry, so the error should be reported.
Replicas enforce the same constraint, so another replica gives the same answer.
Endless retries waste work against a rule that will not change.
questions.explain: A permanent error will repeat on every attempt.

questions.q: A service retries overload errors with exponential backoff and a cap of five attempts. How does this change the load compared to unlimited immediate retries?
options: It reduces the extra load the retries create
It increases the extra load because attempts are spread out
It has no effect because the cap is too low
It turns the overload into a permanent error
optionExplain: Right: backoff and a cap spread out and limit the retries, damping the feedback cycle.
Spreading attempts out lowers peak load rather than raising it.
A cap of five does limit the extra load, so the effect is real.
Backoff changes timing, not whether an error is transient or permanent.
questions.explain: Limiting retries and using exponential backoff avoids feedback cycles.

questions.q: True or false: Overload-related errors should be handled differently from other errors, where possible.
questions.explain: The chapter advises handling overload-related errors differently, in addition to limiting retries and using exponential backoff.
questions.teaches: Overload-related errors should be handled differently from other errors, if possible.

questions.q: A file-sync client retries uploads after a network error. Which list best matches the chapter's retry rules?
options: Never retry, because retries risk duplicates
Retry only after the user clicks again
Retry transient errors, cap and back off, skip permanent ones
Retry every error instantly until the upload succeeds
optionExplain: Retries are useful for transient errors.
That wastes the benefit of automatic retry.
Right: the four parts of the policy.
That ignores overload and permanence.
questions.explain: The chapter's rules combine classification with limits and backoff.
questions.teaches: Retrying is only worthwhile after transient errors; after a permanent error such as a constraint violation a retry would be pointless.

questions.q: A transaction sends a confirmation email and then aborts. The retry sends another email. What happened?
options: The first email was recalled when the transaction aborted
The email went out despite the abort, and went out again
The email was never sent in either attempt
The second email was suppressed by the database
optionExplain: Aborts reach database writes, not messages sent to a mail server.
Right: the database cannot take back an email that has already left.
The email was sent on the first attempt, before the abort.
The database does not know about emails, so it cannot suppress duplicates.
questions.explain: Rollback affects the database, not other systems. The card next explains the options.
questions.rule: Rollback is local to the database.

questions.q: True or false: A database rollback also undoes an email that the transaction sent.
questions.explain: The email system is outside the database, so the abort does not reach it.
questions.rule: Rollback does not reach other systems.

questions.q: A ride app charges a card inside a transaction, then the transaction aborts. What is true of the charge?
options: It may have happened anyway, outside the database
It is reversed automatically by the database on abort
It is repeated only if the user retries
It is held until the next commit
optionExplain: Right: the card service is outside the database, so the abort cannot undo the charge.
The database can reverse only its own writes, not a charge at an external service.
The charge may be repeated on retry as well, not just when the user retries.
No mechanism holds an external charge until a later commit.
questions.explain: Effects in external systems are outside the transaction's reach.

questions.q: A transaction writes two rows, sends an email, charges a card and posts to a chat channel, then aborts. Sort the effects.

items.t: The first row written in the database
The second row written in the database
The email already sent
The card charge made by an outside service
The chat post already delivered

questions.explain: Atomicity applies to writes in the database, not to messages or charges already sent elsewhere.

questions.q: True or false: Retrying a transaction that sends an email can send the email again on every attempt.
questions.explain: Each attempt that reaches the email step sends one, so retries need protection against duplicates.
questions.teaches: If a transaction has side effects outside of the database, you would not want to send the email again every time you retry the transaction.

questions.q: Which technique does the chapter name for making an order database and a payment service commit or abort together?
options: Compare-and-set
Two-phase locking
Snapshot isolation
Two-phase commit
optionExplain: Compare-and-set is a single-object operation.
Two-phase locking is a concurrency method, a different thing despite the similar name.
Snapshot isolation is an isolation level within one database.
Right: 2PC coordinates several systems.
questions.explain: Two-phase commit can make several different systems either commit or abort together; the book covers it in a later chapter.
questions.teaches: If you want several different systems to either commit or abort together, two-phase commit can help; it is discussed in a later chapter.

questions.q: A balance occasionally comes out wrong in production but does not in the test suite. What is the most likely reason?
options: Production data is larger, so arithmetic overflows
Tests run on a faster disk, which hides rounding
The failure needs unlucky timing between concurrent transactions
The test suite uses a newer version of the language
optionExplain: Overflow would show up consistently, not occasionally.
Disk speed does not explain rounding errors.
Right: concurrency bugs depend on timing.
Versions rarely explain rare wrong balances.
questions.explain: Rare timing makes such bugs hard to reproduce. The card next gives the book's view.
questions.rule: Timing, not logic, hides these bugs.

questions.q: True or false: Concurrency bugs are triggered only when you get unlucky with the timing.
questions.explain: The chapter says they may occur rarely and are usually difficult to reproduce.

questions.q: A ticketing app double-sells one seat about once a week. The team wants to add more tests. What does the chapter suggest?
options: Tests alone cannot show the bug is gone; check the isolation level's guarantees
Disable concurrency in production to be safe
Assume the bug lies in the payment code
More tests will eventually prove it fixed
optionExplain: Right: because the bug depends on timing, only a guarantee, not tests, can rule it out.
Disabling concurrency is impractical for a busy site and not what the chapter proposes.
Nothing in the symptoms points at payments rather than the data access.
More tests may never hit the unlucky timing, so they cannot prove the bug is gone.
questions.explain: Because the failure depends on timing, only a guarantee can protect the application.
questions.rule: Rely on guarantees, not on tests alone.

questions.q: A second team joins and writes new code that updates the same tables. What happens to the difficulty of reasoning about concurrency?
options: It vanishes once the database is replicated
It grows
It stays the same, because each team owns its own tables
It shrinks, because more developers review the code
optionExplain: Replication adds problems of its own.
Right: any code that touches the data adds interleavings.
Shared tables mean shared risk.
Review does not remove interleavings.
questions.explain: In a large application you may not know which other code is using the database.
questions.rule: More code means more possible interleavings.

questions.q: True or false: Concurrency is easier to reason about in a large application, where each developer knows which other code uses the database.
questions.explain: The chapter says concurrency is especially hard in a large application where you may not know which other pieces of code access the database.
questions.rule: Large applications make concurrency harder to reason about.
questions.teaches: Concurrency is very difficult to reason about in a large application where you do not necessarily know which other pieces of code are accessing the database.

questions.q: A metrics team's two-collector test run passed. Which reasons make that a weak check? Select two.
options: Two collectors always behave exactly like one
Rows are locked whenever two collectors run
Passing runs are rounded in the report
The bug depends on timing, so absence in one run proves little
A rare unlucky interleaving may not occur in a small run
optionExplain: Two writers can interleave in ways one cannot.
Locks are not automatic in every setting.
Rounding is unrelated to correctness.
Right.
Right.
questions.explain: Because the bug needs unlucky timing, a small passing run proves little.
questions.rule: A passing run cannot prove the absence of a race.
questions.teaches: Having many concurrent users makes application development much harder than having one user at a time, because any piece of data could unexpectedly change at any time.

questions.q: A manager says: we handle money, so we are safe if we pick an ACID relational database. How does the chapter respond?
options: Correct, because ACID prevents all race conditions
Correct, but only for databases that run on one node
Irrelevant, because money is stored in the application
That misses the point
optionExplain: ACID is a bundle of properties, and isolation inside it is often weak.
Running on one node does not change which race conditions the isolation level allows.
The database still holds the money records and is where the races happen.
Right: many popular ACID databases use weak isolation, so the label does not remove race conditions.
questions.explain: Weak isolation is common even in ACID databases. The card next gives the evidence.

questions.q: Which consequences of weak isolation does the chapter report? Select all that apply.
options: Investigation by financial auditors
Loss of the database's write-ahead log
Corruption of customer data
Slower queries on read-only workloads
Substantial loss of money
optionExplain: Right.
Not mentioned.
Right.
Not mentioned as a consequence.
Right.
questions.explain: The chapter lists money loss, auditor investigations and corrupted customer data as real consequences.
questions.rule: Weak isolation bugs have had real costs.

questions.q: A startup picks the default isolation level of a popular database because it is ACID. What should it do before launch?
options: Learn which race conditions that level allows and test critical paths
Nothing, as ACID databases are safe by default
Switch to a non-ACID database to avoid isolation
Increase the server memory
optionExplain: Right: the default may allow anomalies.
That is the mistake the chapter names.
Non-ACID databases are typically weaker.
Memory does not change isolation.
questions.explain: Understand what the chosen level permits.

questions.q: Which statement about serializable isolation does the chapter make?
options: It is fast, but hard to implement correctly
It is slower only for write-heavy workloads
It is unavailable in all relational databases
It has a performance cost, and many databases choose not to pay it
optionExplain: The stated problem is the performance cost, not difficulty of implementation.
The chapter does not restrict the cost to write-heavy workloads.
Many relational databases do offer a serializable level.
Right: serializable isolation costs performance, which is why many databases skip it.
questions.explain: The performance cost is the reason weak levels dominate.

questions.q: True or false: Weak isolation levels are used in practice even though they are much harder to understand than serializability.
questions.explain: The chapter says weaker levels are much harder to understand and can lead to subtle bugs, but are nevertheless used in practice.
questions.rule: Weak levels persist despite being harder to reason about.
questions.teaches: Weaker levels of isolation are much harder to understand and can lead to subtle bugs, but they are nevertheless used in practice.

questions.q: A bank incident shows duplicated payouts. The CEO says buy a bigger database. What does the chapter suggest to look at first?
options: The speed of the network between data centres
The disk capacity of the database servers
The isolation level in use and which anomalies it permits
The number of replicas of each table
optionExplain: A faster network does not change which interleavings are allowed.
More capacity does not remove race conditions; they come from timing.
Right: duplicated payouts suggest a race the isolation level allows, so check the level first.
More replicas add copies and do not close race windows.
questions.explain: A weak level can permit race conditions, which a bigger database does not fix.
questions.rule: Look at the isolation level first.
questions.teaches: Concurrency bugs caused by weak transaction isolation have led to investigation by financial auditors.

questions.q: How should a developer choose an isolation level, according to the chapter?
options: By picking the level with the most familiar name
By knowing which race conditions each level allows and which it prevents
By picking whatever the framework sets as default
By picking the strongest level without checking costs
optionExplain: Familiar names are a poor guide because the same name can mean different guarantees.
Right: knowing which race conditions each level allows lets you pick on facts.
A framework default may be a weak level that allows the anomalies you care about.
The strongest level may be affordable or not; ignoring costs makes the choice a guess.
questions.explain: The chapter wants a good understanding of the kinds of problems. The card next gives the plan.

questions.q: The kind of concurrency problem that a weak level can allow is called an ____.
questions.explain: An anomaly such as a dirty read or a lost update is what the levels are compared by.

questions.q: A team must decide between two isolation levels for a ride-booking service. What is the first step the chapter implies?
options: Pick the level with the longer name
Run the service under each level for a day
List the race conditions each level allows and see which ones matter
Ask each level's vendor to certify it safe
optionExplain: Name length says nothing about the guarantee.
A day-long trial may miss rare timing failures.
Right: comparing allowed race conditions with what the service can tolerate is the sound first step.
A vendor's certificate is a label, not a statement of behaviour.
questions.explain: The decision depends on which race conditions the application can tolerate.

questions.q: True or false: A guide says an isolation level is safe because its name is serializable. The chapter would accept that reasoning.
questions.explain: The chapter shows that names are inconsistent between databases, so you must check what the level really prevents.

questions.q: How does the chapter describe its own treatment of isolation levels?
options: Limited to the SQL standard's definitions
Fully formal, with proofs for each level
A list of vendor settings for each database
Informal and based on examples
optionExplain: It points out that the standard's definitions are flawed, so it does not stop there.
The chapter says its discussion will be informal.
It explains concepts and is not a configuration guide for each database.
Right: the chapter is informal, uses examples, and refers readers elsewhere for rigour.
questions.explain: The book promises an informal discussion with examples and points to academic work for rigour.
questions.teaches: The discussion of isolation levels in the chapter is informal, using examples; rigorous definitions and analyses are in the academic literature.

questions.q: A payments engineer says: I read the docs, my level is fine. Which question shows whether they really understand the level?
options: Which concurrent interleavings can still corrupt my data at this level?
Has the level been in the product for a long time?
Is the level the default in the dashboard?
How many pages is the vendor's manual?
optionExplain: Right: understanding a level means being able to say what can still go wrong under it.
Age in the product says nothing about which anomalies are possible.
Being the default is a fact about settings, not a guarantee.
Manual length measures reading effort, not understanding.
questions.explain: Understanding a level means knowing which anomalies remain possible.
questions.rule: Ask what can still go wrong.
questions.teaches: Serializable isolation protects against all of these race conditions, while weaker levels leave the developer to handle the others manually.

questions.q: What does the most basic isolation level promise about the data a transaction reads?
options: Only data older than one minute
Only data the transaction wrote itself
Only data that has been committed
Only data on the leader node
optionExplain: Age sounds like a safety margin, but the rule is about commit status, not how old the data is.
A transaction can read other transactions' committed data too; reading only its own writes would make shared data useless.
Right: read committed promises you only ever see data that has been committed.
Replication roles are a separate matter; the guarantee does not depend on which node serves the read.
questions.explain: The most basic level stops transactions from seeing uncommitted data. The card next names it.

questions.q: Read committed guarantees no dirty reads and no dirty ____.
questions.explain: The second promise is that a transaction overwrites only committed data.

questions.q: Transaction A has changed a price but not committed. Transaction B reads the price under read committed. What does B see?
options: The old committed price
A blend of old and new
The new uncommitted price
An error, until A commits
optionExplain: Right: no dirty reads, so B is given the last committed price while A is still uncommitted.
A blend would mean seeing part of A's work; a single price has no halfway state to show.
This is what a dirty read would show; read committed hides uncommitted changes.
Blocking B until A commits is the read-lock approach, which most databases avoid; B simply gets the old value.
questions.explain: Read committed prevents dirty reads, so B continues with the last committed value.
questions.rule: B sees the last committed value.

questions.q: A then commits, and B reads the price again within the same transaction. What does B see under read committed?
options: An error because the value changed
The new committed price
The old price again
The uncommitted price from before
optionExplain: A changed value is not an error; reading committed changes is normal at this level.
Right: once A commits, each new read under read committed sees the latest committed value.
Staying on the old price is snapshot behaviour; read committed does not freeze what a transaction sees.
That price was uncommitted before, but it is committed now and so is visible.
questions.explain: Read committed only promises committed data at the time of each read; it does not freeze what you see.
questions.rule: Read committed does not freeze the view.

questions.q: True or false: Read committed guarantees that the data a transaction reads will not change if it reads the same object twice.
questions.explain: It only promises you see committed data at each read; a second read can return a newer committed value, which is called a nonrepeatable read.
questions.teaches: Under read committed a transaction can read the same object twice and see two different committed values.

questions.q: A ticketing site runs at read committed. Which of these can still happen?
options: A reader sees a seat reserved by an unfinished purchase
A purchase overwrites a seat row another purchase is still writing
A reader sees half of a purchase's seat rows after it commits
A reader sees a seat as free, then a moment later sees it taken
optionExplain: That is a dirty read, which is prevented.
That is a dirty write, which is prevented.
Writes become visible together on commit.
Right: committed changes arrive between reads.
questions.explain: Committed data can change between two reads; only uncommitted data is hidden.
questions.rule: Read committed hides uncommitted data only.
questions.teaches: Read committed applies at the time of each query: each query sees whatever was committed when it runs.

questions.q: A transaction writes a value and later aborts. Another transaction read that value while it was uncommitted. What went wrong?
options: The reader saw data that was never actually committed
The reader was given an older value than expected
The reader's own write was undone by mistake
The database committed the value twice
optionExplain: Right: seeing data that is later rolled back is the definition of a dirty read.
The reader saw a newer, uncommitted value, not an older one.
Reading does not undo anyone's writes; the problem is on the reader's side.
The value was never committed even once, let alone twice.
questions.explain: A dirty read exposes data that may be rolled back. The card next gives the reasons it matters.

questions.q: Reading another transaction's uncommitted write is called a ____ read.
questions.explain: The term dirty read names reading uncommitted data.

questions.q: A mailbox shows a new message but the unread counter, updated by the same transaction, still reads zero. Which anomaly is this?
options: A dirty write of the counter
A phantom caused by an index
A lost update on the message
A dirty read of the message, seen before the counter update
optionExplain: No competing writes occurred.
Phantoms concern search results.
No concurrent update clobbered another.
Right: the reader saw part of an uncommitted transaction.
questions.explain: Seeing some of a transaction's writes before it commits is a dirty read.
questions.rule: Part of a transaction visible = dirty read.

questions.q: A system allows dirty reads, and a transaction that wrote a value aborts. What might a reader that saw the value do next?
options: Read the same value again with no change
Have its own transaction aborted automatically
Act on a value that no longer exists, making wrong decisions
Continue safely because the value was valid at the time
optionExplain: The value was rolled back, so a re-read would not return it.
Aborts do not cascade to readers in this way; the reader keeps running on bad information.
Right: a decision based on rolled-back data is hard to reason about and may be wrong.
Tempting, because the value did exist for a moment, but it was never committed and has now vanished.
questions.explain: The reader's decisions rest on data that never became real.
questions.rule: Dirty reads can lead to decisions on rolled-back data.

questions.q: True or false: Preventing dirty reads also guarantees that a transaction sees all of another transaction's writes or none of them.
questions.explain: Because a transaction's writes become visible only when it commits, and then all at once, others see all or none.
questions.rule: Commit makes writes visible all at once.
questions.teaches: Under read committed, a transaction's writes become visible to others only when it commits, and then all of them become visible at once.

questions.q: A chat app shows a delivery receipt as soon as a transaction writes it, before committing. Which risk is that?
options: The receipt will be slower to display
A receipt may be shown for a message that is then rolled back
The receipt will be shown twice
The message will be sent to the wrong user
optionExplain: Showing it early would make it faster, not slower; the risk is correctness.
Right: showing uncommitted data risks displaying something that is later rolled back.
Duplication is not what exposing uncommitted data causes.
Routing is unrelated to when data becomes visible.
questions.explain: Exposing uncommitted data creates risk if the transaction aborts.
questions.teaches: Seeing the database in a partially updated state is confusing to users and may cause other transactions to take incorrect decisions.

questions.q: Alice and Bob race to buy one car. The listing goes to Bob and the invoice to Alice. What caused this?
options: The invoice table was too slow to update
The car listing was cached by Bob's browser
Their writes to the two objects were interleaved because a later write overwrote an uncommitted one
Alice's payment was not accepted
optionExplain: Slow tables might delay things but cannot give the listing to Bob and the invoice to Alice.
Browser caching affects what a user sees, not which buyer the database records.
Right: when writes to two objects interleave, each object can end up with a different winner.
A failed payment is not part of the story; both writes took effect for different buyers.
questions.explain: Mixed outcomes across two objects are the classic dirty-write damage. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Dirty writes mix up multi-object outcomes.

questions.q: Overwriting a value written by a transaction that has not yet committed is a dirty ____.
questions.explain: A dirty write overwrites uncommitted data.

questions.q: Two agents confirm the same hotel room at once: one updates the room's guest, the other writes the invoice. How does read committed handle it?
options: It lets both writes proceed and keeps the later one
It merges the two guests into one entry
It cancels both and returns an error
It makes the second agent's write to each object wait until the first transaction ends
optionExplain: Keeping the later write is exactly the dirty write that read committed forbids.
Databases do not merge conflicting values into one entry.
Cancelling both is not how read committed behaves; the second writer just waits.
Right: delaying the second write keeps each transaction's updates together.
questions.explain: The delay means one transaction's writes are all applied before the other's begin on the same objects.

questions.q: Read committed delays the second write. What does the waiting writer do when the first transaction aborts?
options: Proceeds, overwriting nothing
Applies the first write's value as well
Fails because the object was locked
Waits forever for the first to commit
optionExplain: Right: when the first transaction aborts, its write is undone and the waiting writer can go ahead.
The aborted write was discarded, so its value cannot be applied.
Locks are released at abort, so the object is no longer locked against it.
The wait ends at commit or abort, so it need not wait forever for a commit.
questions.explain: The wait ends at commit or abort, either way.
questions.rule: Waiting ends on commit or abort.

questions.q: True or false: Read committed prevents the lost counter increment described earlier, where two clients each read 42 and write 43.
questions.explain: In that example the second write happens after the first transaction has committed, so it is not a dirty write. It is still incorrect, but for a different reason.
questions.rule: Not every wrong write is a dirty write.
questions.teaches: The counter race does not involve a dirty write because the second write happens after the first transaction has committed, so read committed does not prevent it.

questions.q: Two dispatchers assign different trips to one driver, each writing a status row and a trip row. What can dirty writes cause?
options: The status row would be read twice
The driver's status could show one trip while the trip row shows another assignment
The status row would be deleted
The trip rows would be merged into one
optionExplain: Double reading is a read anomaly, not a result of overwriting uncommitted writes.
Right: each object can take a different dispatcher's value, so the records disagree.
Dirty writes overwrite values; they do not delete rows.
Rows are not merged; each keeps one writer's value.
questions.explain: With dirty writes, each of the two objects can go to a different winner.
questions.rule: Dirty writes split outcomes across objects.
questions.teaches: Dirty writes can cause a multi-object business action to end up half awarded to one party and half to another.

questions.q: Two transactions each read a counter as 42 and write 43, one after the other. Does read committed stop this?
options: Yes, because it stops the second read
No, because neither write overwrote uncommitted data
No, because the counter is not committed
Yes, because it makes the second write wait
optionExplain: Reads are not blocked by read committed; the problem is that both read 42.
Right: the second write follows a commit, so it is not a dirty write and nothing delays it.
The first write was committed, so this option's premise is wrong.
Waiting applies only while the first transaction is uncommitted; here it has committed.
questions.explain: The race exists even though no dirty write occurred. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Not a dirty write, still a bug.

questions.q: True or false: In the counter example, the second write happens after the first transaction has committed.
questions.explain: That is why it is not a dirty write.

questions.q: Two support agents each read stock 5, subtract one and write 4, in turn, each in its own committed transaction. Which anomaly is this?
options: A lost update; read committed does not prevent it
A phantom that read committed prevents
A dirty write that read committed prevents
A dirty read that read committed prevents
optionExplain: Right: both subtracted from the same starting stock, so one change is lost; read committed does not prevent it.
No search condition is involved; a single stock row is.
It sounds familiar, but the writes were not overwriting uncommitted data.
Nothing uncommitted was read.
questions.explain: The second write ignored the first change; it is a lost update.
questions.rule: Read-modify-write races are not dirty writes.

questions.q: Sort each sequence by whether it is a dirty write.

items.t: B overwrites a value A wrote and has not yet committed
B overwrites a value A wrote and has already committed
B writes a different object than A wrote
A and B both read the same committed value

questions.explain: Dirty means the overwritten value is uncommitted. Later writes after a commit are ordinary, even when they are wrong for another reason.
questions.rule: Dirty requires an uncommitted earlier write.

questions.q: True or false: Read committed makes counter increments safe, because the second write is delayed until the first transaction has committed.
questions.explain: The delay only prevents overwriting uncommitted data. In the counter example the second write comes after the first commit, so nothing delays it.
questions.rule: The delay does not cover read-modify-write races.
questions.teaches: Making counter increments safe is the subject of the later section on preventing lost updates.

questions.q: A metrics service increments a shared counter from many workers at read committed. What happens under heavy load?
options: Every increment is kept, since writes are delayed
All workers see the same value at each moment
Some increments are lost
The database aborts overlapping increments
optionExplain: Delaying writes does not help because the reads that feed them happened earlier.
Read committed does not freeze reads, so workers can see different values at different times.
Right: overlapping read-modify-write cycles lose increments at this level.
Databases do not abort overlapping increments at this level.
questions.explain: Overlapping read-modify-write cycles lose updates unless something else prevents it.
questions.rule: Counters need more than read committed.
questions.teaches: The lost update problem needs its own solutions beyond read committed, which the chapter covers in a later section.

questions.q: How do most databases stop a second transaction from overwriting an uncommitted value?
options: The second writer is told to retry in an hour
The first writer's value is copied to every replica first
The second writer's value is stored in a separate table
The first writer holds a row-level lock until it commits or aborts
optionExplain: Databases do not use a time delay; the wait lasts until the lock is released.
Replication is about copies and does not stop overwrites on the primary object.
No separate table is used to park the second value.
Right: the lock makes the second writer wait until the first commits or aborts.
questions.explain: Locks are the usual mechanism. The card next gives the rule.

questions.q: Put these steps of a locked write in order.
items: Transaction acquires the row lock
Transaction modifies the row
Transaction commits or aborts
Lock is released
questions.explain: The lock is taken before the modification and released only at the end.

questions.q: Two transactions update the same user row. The first holds the lock and is slow. What does the second transaction do?
options: Writes its value immediately
Reads the row to decide
Aborts at once
Waits until the first commits or aborts
optionExplain: Writing at once would be a dirty write.
Reading the row does not give the right to write it.
Aborting immediately is not the default; the second transaction waits for the lock.
Right: only one holder of the lock is allowed, so the second transaction waits.
questions.explain: Only one transaction can hold the lock.

questions.q: True or false: If transactions released their row locks right after writing, dirty writes would be prevented as well.
questions.explain: The lock must be held until commit or abort; releasing early lets a later writer overwrite an uncommitted value.
questions.rule: Hold the lock to the end.

questions.q: Who takes these locks in read committed mode?
options: The client library, before sending queries
The database does so automatically
The application developer, by hand
The operating system on each commit
optionExplain: Client libraries do not hold the database's row locks.
Right: in read committed mode the database takes the locks itself.
Hand-written locks are explicit locking, a separate technique shown later.
The operating system does not manage database row locks.
questions.explain: The locking is done automatically in read committed or stronger levels.
questions.teaches: Row-level locking for read committed is done automatically by the database in read committed mode or stronger isolation levels.

questions.q: A file-sync service has two clients renaming the same file at once. Which mechanism prevents the second rename from overwriting an uncommitted first?
options: A row-level lock on the file's record held until commit
A retry loop in the client
A second copy of the record
A bigger disk
optionExplain: Right: a lock on the record, held until commit, makes the second rename wait.
Retrying in the client does not stop the overwrite.
A second copy does not make writers take turns.
Disk size has no effect on write conflicts.
questions.explain: The same locking applies to any record being modified.
questions.teaches: A lock is acquired per object (row or document), so transactions touching different objects do not block each other.

questions.q: A long write transaction holds a row. How do most databases serve readers of that row?
options: They return an error
They show the uncommitted value
They give readers the old committed value
They make readers wait until the write commits
optionExplain: An error is not how reads of a pending write are handled.
Showing the uncommitted value would be a dirty read.
Right: readers are given the old committed value while the write is pending.
Making readers wait is the read-lock approach, which harms response time.
questions.explain: Readers keep going on the old value. The card next explains why.

questions.q: True or false: Using read locks to prevent dirty reads lets a long write transaction delay many read-only transactions.
questions.explain: A read would have to wait for the lock held by the writer.

questions.q: A reporting query reads account balances while a batch job updates many accounts for an hour. Under the usual implementation, what does the report see?
options: A pause until the batch finishes
The old committed balances for accounts the batch has not yet committed
An error stating the rows are locked
The new balances as the batch writes them
optionExplain: A pause is the read-lock approach, which is avoided because one long write would stall every reader.
Right: the report sees the previous committed balances until each account's update commits.
Rows being written are not reported as errors to readers.
The new balances are uncommitted until the batch commits, so showing them would be a dirty read.
questions.explain: Readers are served the previously committed value.

questions.q: A database switches from versioned reads to read locks. What happens to the response time of read-only queries during a long write?
options: It gets worse
It stays the same
It improves only for old data
It improves, since fewer versions are kept
optionExplain: Right: with read locks, readers wait for the writer, so latency rises during long writes.
Waiting does change response times; they get worse.
No such split by data age exists.
Fewer versions saves space but reads then queue behind the lock.
questions.explain: Read locks tie readers to writers.

questions.q: True or false: Lock waits can spread a slowdown from one part of an application to another, an operability concern.
questions.explain: A slow write can force readers elsewhere to wait.
questions.teaches: Requiring read locks harms the response time of read-only transactions and is bad for operability, since a slowdown in one part of an application can have a knock-on effect on another part.

questions.q: A chat app's export job writes many rows while users read messages. Which two designs avoid user-visible waiting? Select two.
options: Keeping both the old and the new value of each written row
Serving readers the previous committed versions until the export commits
Taking a shared lock for each reader during the export
Pausing all reads until the export ends
Showing partial export rows as they are written
optionExplain: Right.
Right.
That blocks users while the export runs.
That makes every user wait.
That is a dirty read.
questions.explain: Keeping old versions lets readers continue without waiting and without seeing uncommitted data.
questions.rule: Versions beat read locks for latency.
questions.teaches: Remembering an old and a new value for each written object is the mechanism that snapshot isolation generalizes.

questions.q: Which prevents more: read committed or read uncommitted?
options: It depends on the table size
They are the same
Read uncommitted
Read committed
optionExplain: Table size has no bearing on the guarantee.
They differ: only one blocks dirty reads.
The names invite the opposite guess, but uncommitted reads are allowed at the weaker level.
Right: read committed stops dirty reads as well as dirty writes.
questions.explain: Read uncommitted is weaker. The card next explains.

questions.q: Match each level to what it prevents.
questions.explain: Each level adds a guarantee.

questions.q: A team inherits a PostgreSQL service with default settings. Which level are its transactions probably using?
options: Snapshot isolation
Serializable
Read committed
Read uncommitted
optionExplain: Snapshot isolation is offered under another name, repeatable read, and is not the default either.
Serializable is available but is not the default.
Right: PostgreSQL's default is read committed.
Read uncommitted is not the default.
questions.explain: Read committed is the default in PostgreSQL among others.
questions.rule: Read committed is the common default.

questions.q: True or false: A transaction at read uncommitted can read data another transaction wrote and has not committed.
questions.explain: Read uncommitted does not prevent dirty reads.

questions.q: Which mainstream databases use locks for read committed isolation, according to the chapter's footnote?
options: IBM DB2 and SQL Server with read_committed_snapshot=off
MySQL and MemSQL
PostgreSQL and Oracle
Every database listed as default
optionExplain: Right: only those two use locks for read committed; the rest use versions.
These also rely on versioned reads or a different mechanism.
These two use old and new versions, not read locks.
Most databases avoid read locks because they stall readers.
questions.explain: Most databases use versions for reads; only a few use locks.
questions.rule: Most databases version rather than lock.
questions.teaches: At the time of writing, the only mainstream databases that use locks for read committed isolation are IBM DB2 and Microsoft SQL Server in the read_committed_snapshot=off configuration.

questions.q: A developer moves from SQL Server 2012 defaults to PostgreSQL. What can they assume about isolation?
options: Both default to read uncommitted
Both default to serializable
Both default to read committed
They share every anomaly protection
optionExplain: Neither lists read uncommitted as the default.
Neither lists serializable as the default.
Right: both default to read committed, but implementations still differ in details.
Sharing a level name does not mean sharing every guarantee.
questions.explain: Both list read committed as default, but implementations differ.
questions.teaches: Read committed is the default setting in Oracle 11g, PostgreSQL, SQL Server 2012, MemSQL, and many other databases.

questions.q: Alice's two reads straddle a committed $100 transfer, so her total looks $100 short. Does read committed prevent this?
options: Yes, because it hides all uncommitted data from her
No, but only if the transfer is later aborted
No, because each balance she saw was committed when she read it
Yes, because it makes her wait until the transfer finishes
optionExplain: It does hide uncommitted data, but neither balance was uncommitted here.
An abort would change nothing about the committed values she read.
Right: read committed only checks that each value read was committed.
Read committed does not make readers wait for writers; most databases give readers the old value.
questions.explain: Both numbers were committed values, yet together they describe a state that never existed. The card next names the anomaly.
questions.rule: Committed values can still be mismatched in time.

questions.q: The anomaly in which a repeated read returns a different committed value is called a nonrepeatable read or read ____.
questions.explain: Skew here means a timing anomaly between reads.

questions.q: A driver's earnings are read from two tables while a payout moves money between them, and totals mismatch. What is this?
options: Read skew: the reads happened at different moments around the payout
A dirty write: the payout overwrote an uncommitted value
A lost update: the payout hid a change
A phantom: a new row appeared in the totals
optionExplain: Right: the two reads straddled the committed payout, so each was valid but the pair is not.
Dirty writes need two overlapping uncommitted writes; here a reader saw committed values at different moments.
A lost update needs two read-modify-write cycles clashing; this is a reader seeing mismatched values.
A phantom involves a search result changing; here existing rows were read at different times.
questions.explain: The reads straddled a committed transaction.
questions.rule: Reads straddling a commit give skew.

questions.q: Alice reloads the page a few seconds later at read committed. What does she see?
options: An error from the bank
Consistent balances that total $1,000
$1,100 because both updates apply twice
The same $900 until the next day
optionExplain: The bank is not in error; the earlier oddity was a timing effect.
Right: after the transfer finishes, a fresh read shows balances that add up.
Both updates are applied once, so the total stays $1,000.
Nothing preserves the old view; a new read sees current committed data.
questions.explain: In her case the inconsistency is temporary.
questions.rule: Skew in a live view usually heals.

questions.q: True or false: The word skew in read skew has the same meaning as skew in an unbalanced workload with hot spots.
questions.explain: In this chapter skew means a timing anomaly; earlier it meant an unbalanced workload with hot spots.
questions.teaches: The term skew is overloaded: earlier it meant an unbalanced workload with hot spots, while here it means a timing anomaly.

questions.q: A metrics dashboard sums two counters that a job updates together. The sum is briefly off. Is this a dirty read?
options: Yes, because the sum includes uncommitted values
No, because the dashboard only reads
Yes, because dirty reads always cause wrong sums
No, each counter value was committed
optionExplain: Both values had been committed when they were read, so nothing uncommitted was included.
Being read-only does not rule out dirty reads; it simply is not what happened here.
Dirty reads are defined by uncommitted data, not by wrong sums; wrong sums can also come from skew.
Right: each counter value was committed, so this is read skew, not a dirty read.
questions.explain: Read skew uses committed values observed at different moments.
questions.rule: Committed does not mean mutually consistent.
questions.teaches: Read skew is considered acceptable under read committed isolation because the values seen were indeed committed at the time of reading.

questions.q: A backup takes hours while writes continue. If it reads at read committed, what might you restore?
options: A copy where some parts are older and some newer
A copy locked from further restores
A perfect copy as of the moment the backup started
A copy missing only the last hour
optionExplain: Right: a long read at read committed picks up different commits in different parts, baking in inconsistencies.
Nothing locks the copy against restores; the issue is its contents.
A perfect copy as of the start needs a snapshot, which read committed does not give.
The copy is not neatly missing the last hour; parts come from different moments throughout.
questions.explain: Long reads straddle many commits. The card next shows why that is a problem.

questions.q: Which operations does the chapter say cannot tolerate temporary inconsistency? Select all that apply.
options: Reading one user's profile
Appending a log line
Taking a backup
Running periodic integrity checks
Running analytic queries that scan large parts of the database
optionExplain: A short single-object read is fine.
No inconsistency issue.
Right.
Right.
Right.
questions.explain: The chapter lists backups, analytics and integrity checks.

questions.q: A nightly integrity check scans orders and payments while the shop runs. It reports mismatches that vanish on re-run. What is likely?
options: The check itself has a typo
The database has lost data
The payments table is corrupted
The scan saw parts of the database at different times
optionExplain: A typo could cause errors but would not explain mismatches that appear only while the shop is running.
Lost data would not disappear on re-run.
Real corruption would persist on re-run; these mismatches vanish.
Right: scanning while data changes means parts are read at different times, producing false mismatches.
questions.explain: Scans over changing data observe different points in time.

questions.q: A skewed backup is restored after a disaster. What happens to the inconsistencies?
options: They are fixed by replaying the log
They heal on the next reload
They become permanent
They disappear after verification
optionExplain: Replaying a log is a separate recovery step and is not guaranteed to correct a skewed copy.
Reloading a page heals a temporary view, not restored data.
Right: the restored data is the database, so a skewed backup makes the inconsistency permanent.
Verification can detect a problem but does not repair data.
questions.explain: Unlike a transient view, a restore fixes the oddity in place.
questions.rule: A bad backup makes skew permanent.

questions.q: True or false: Analytic queries are common in analytics workloads but also may be part of a periodic integrity check that monitors for data corruption.
questions.explain: The chapter lists integrity checks alongside analytic queries as scans that give nonsensical results when parts are seen at different times.
questions.rule: Both kinds of scan need a stable view.
questions.teaches: Periodic integrity checks that monitor for data corruption are scanning queries that are likely to return nonsensical results if they observe parts of the database at different points in time.

questions.q: A file-sync service copies a user's folder tree while edits continue. The copy contains a file but not its parent folder. Which problem is this?
options: A lost update
The same one as in backups: the copy saw different parts at different times
A dirty write
A deadlock
optionExplain: A lost update needs two read-modify-write cycles; this is one reader seeing a mixed state.
Right: a long copy of changing data sees different parts at different times, as in a backup.
A dirty write needs competing uncommitted writes, not a long read.
A deadlock needs transactions waiting on each other's locks.
questions.explain: Any long copy of changing data faces this.
questions.teaches: Backups on a large database may take hours, during which writes continue to be made.

questions.q: A report starts at 10:00 and runs until 10:30. Another transaction commits a change at 10:10. Under snapshot isolation, does the report see it?
options: Yes, as soon as it commits
Only if the report asks for it
No, it sees only what was committed at 10:00
Yes, but only after the report ends
optionExplain: Seeing changes as they commit is read committed behaviour, not snapshot isolation.
A report cannot ask to see newer data inside a snapshot transaction.
Right: the snapshot was fixed at 10:00, so a change committed at 10:10 stays invisible to the report.
The transaction never sees it, not even at the end; the snapshot does not move.
questions.explain: The snapshot is taken at the start. The card next confirms.

questions.q: Under snapshot isolation, a transaction sees all the data that was ____ in the database at the start of the transaction.
questions.explain: That is the definition of its consistent snapshot.

questions.q: A backup job runs under snapshot isolation for three hours while customers keep ordering. What does the backup contain?
options: Each table at a different time
Only the orders from before midnight
The latest state at the end of the job
The database as it was committed when the job started
optionExplain: Different times for different tables is the skew a snapshot is meant to remove.
Nothing in snapshot isolation limits data to a calendar date.
The latest state at the end would require reading changes that happened after the snapshot.
Right: one snapshot taken at the start gives a single point in time for the whole job.
questions.explain: Snapshot isolation gives one point in time.
questions.rule: One point in time for the whole job.

questions.q: True or false: Under snapshot isolation, rereading an account returns the first value even after another transaction commits a change.
questions.explain: The snapshot does not change inside a transaction, so repeated reads agree. Under read committed the second read would see the new value.
questions.rule: Repeated reads agree under a snapshot.

questions.q: True or false: Snapshot isolation is supported by PostgreSQL, MySQL with the InnoDB storage engine, Oracle, SQL Server and others.
questions.explain: The chapter lists these as examples of popular databases that support it, sometimes under other names.
questions.teaches: Snapshot isolation is supported by PostgreSQL, MySQL with the InnoDB storage engine, Oracle, SQL Server, and others.

questions.q: An analytics team runs a 20-minute revenue report on a live shop database. Which isolation level makes the report easy to reason about?
options: Snapshot isolation
Read committed, as each row is committed
Read uncommitted, as it is fastest
No isolation, as reports are read-only
optionExplain: Right: a snapshot gives a stable view, making a 20-minute report easy to reason about.
With read committed, different parts of the report may reflect different moments.
Read uncommitted may add data that is later rolled back, which makes the report harder to trust.
Reports are read-only, but writes still happen around them and could change what they see.
questions.explain: A frozen snapshot is much easier to understand than changing data.
questions.teaches: It is very hard to reason about the meaning of a query if the data on which it operates is changing at the same time as the query is executing.

questions.q: A long analytics query reads a table that a shop is updating. Under snapshot isolation, how do reads and writes interact?
options: Reads wait for writes
They do not block each other
Writes wait for reads
Both wait for a lock
optionExplain: Reads waiting for writes is the read-lock approach, avoided here.
Right: reads take no locks under snapshot isolation, so they and writes do not block one another.
Writes waiting for reads would stall the shop during long queries, which snapshot isolation avoids.
There is a lock for writers to the same object, but not between readers and writers.
questions.explain: Readers and writers do not block each other. The card next explains.

questions.q: Under snapshot isolation, readers do not block ____.
questions.explain: And writers never block readers.

questions.q: A reporting query runs for an hour under snapshot isolation. A shop writes new orders throughout. What is true?
options: The query reads uncommitted orders
Both proceed without lock contention between them
The query restarts at every order
Orders are held until the query ends
optionExplain: Uncommitted orders are not visible to the query; it reads a committed snapshot.
Right: the query and the order writes run without waiting for each other.
The query keeps its snapshot and does not restart for new orders.
Holding orders until the query ends would make writes wait for readers, which does not happen.
questions.explain: No lock contention.
questions.rule: No contention between read and write.

questions.q: Two transactions at snapshot isolation write the same row. What happens?
options: One waits for the other's write lock
Both proceed freely
Their values are merged
Both abort
optionExplain: Right: write locks still prevent dirty writes, so the second writer waits.
Writers to the same object cannot both proceed freely, or dirty writes would occur.
Values are not merged by the database; one writer waits for the other.
Neither transaction has to abort merely because they overlap; one waits.
questions.explain: Writers still use locks against dirty writes.

questions.q: True or false: Under snapshot isolation, writers hold write locks so a writer can block another writer of the same object.
questions.explain: Implementations use write locks to prevent dirty writes.
questions.teaches: Implementations of snapshot isolation typically use write locks to prevent dirty writes, as in read committed.

questions.q: A chat service's analytics and its message writes share a database. Which property makes snapshot isolation attractive here?
options: Messages are written twice for safety
Analytics see uncommitted messages
Analytics can run without slowing message writes through lock waits
Writers wait for analytics
optionExplain: Writing twice is not part of snapshot isolation.
Reading uncommitted messages is a dirty read, which snapshot isolation avoids.
Right: long analytics reads do not slow message writes through lock waits.
Writers waiting for analytics is exactly what snapshot isolation avoids.
questions.explain: No lock contention between long reads and writes.
questions.rule: Long reads do not stall writers.
questions.teaches: Snapshot isolation lets a database handle long-running read queries on a consistent snapshot while processing writes normally, without lock contention.

questions.q: Two transactions started at different times and read the same row, which a third changed between their starts. What must be kept?
options: Only the newest version, with a note of who read it
A copy of the whole table for each transaction
More than one committed version of that row
Only the oldest version until the last reader finishes
optionExplain: With only the newest version, the earlier transaction would see a state it should not.
Copying whole tables is far more than needed; versions are kept per changed object.
Right: each reader may need a different version.
Keeping only the oldest would give the later transaction stale data.
questions.explain: Different snapshots need different versions at the same time. The card next names the technique.

questions.q: Keeping several committed versions of an object side by side is called multi-version concurrency control, abbreviated ____.
questions.explain: MVCC lets readers use a snapshot without taking locks.
questions.rule: MVCC = several versions of each object.

questions.q: Row versions were committed at times 0, 3 and 7. T1 began at 1, T2 at 5; both still run. Which versions stay?
options: All three: T1 needs the first, T2 the second, new readers the third
Only the first, since it was committed earliest
Only the third, since it is the newest
