The first and the third, since the second was overwritten quickly
optionExplain: Right: running transactions still need their versions.
The first alone would give T2 and newer readers stale prices.
The newest alone would give T1 and T2 data from the future.
The second version is what T2 sees, so it cannot be dropped.
questions.explain: A version is needed as long as some transaction's snapshot may include it.
questions.rule: Keep each version some snapshot needs.

questions.q: True or false: In an MVCC database an update overwrites the value in place, so older transactions see the new value.
questions.explain: MVCC never updates in place for readers' sake: it keeps the old version and creates a new one, so older transactions keep seeing the old value.
questions.rule: Updates create versions; they do not erase them.

questions.q: True or false: A database providing only read committed needs at most two versions of an object.
questions.explain: Those two are the committed version and the overwritten-but-not-yet-committed version. Snapshot isolation needs more because transactions may need different points in time.
questions.rule: Read committed needs two versions; snapshot isolation needs many.
questions.teaches: Read committed alone needs only two versions of an object: the committed one and the overwritten-but-not-yet-committed one.

questions.q: A transaction runs two queries, and between them another transaction commits a change. In an MVCC database, how do the two isolation levels differ?
options: Read committed uses one snapshot for the whole transaction
Read committed uses a new snapshot per query; snapshot isolation uses one for the whole transaction
Both use one snapshot per query
Neither uses snapshots at all
optionExplain: That reverses the two levels.
Right: the snapshot's lifetime is the difference.
That would make snapshot isolation behave like read committed.
Storage engines that support snapshot isolation typically use MVCC for read committed too.
questions.explain: Typically read committed takes a separate snapshot for each query, while snapshot isolation keeps the same snapshot throughout.
questions.rule: Snapshot lifetime separates the two levels.
questions.teaches: Storage engines with MVCC typically give read committed a separate snapshot for each query, while snapshot isolation uses the same snapshot for an entire transaction.

questions.q: In an MVCC database a transaction changes a balance from $500 to $400. What is in the table afterwards?
options: Two identical rows holding $400
One row holding both amounts as a list
One row, with $500 overwritten by $400
Two rows: the $500 version marked as deleted and a new $400 version
optionExplain: Only one version holds the new amount; the other keeps the old one.
Rows do not hold lists of versions.
In-place overwrite would remove the old version that older snapshots need.
Right: the old version is kept but marked.
questions.explain: Updates create new versions and mark old ones deleted. The card next gives the fields used.

questions.q: Match each element of the MVCC design to its role.
pairs: A unique, always-increasing number given to each transaction
The ID of the transaction that inserted the row
The ID of the transaction that requested deletion, empty at first
Later removal of rows no transaction can still access
questions.explain: The first three tag versions; the last frees space.

questions.q: Transaction 31 deletes an order row in an MVCC database. The database sets the row's ____ field to 31 and leaves the row in place.
questions.explain: Deletion is a mark in deleted_by; the row stays until no transaction can need it, and created_by is unchanged.

questions.q: A deleted row is marked by transaction 31. When can the database finally free its space?
options: When no transaction can any longer access the deleted data
When the table is next backed up
When the next transaction ID is issued
As soon as transaction 31 commits
optionExplain: Right: garbage collection waits for that.
Backups are unrelated to cleanup.
Issuing new IDs does not affect which snapshots exist.
Committing is not enough, because older snapshots may still read the row.
questions.explain: A background process removes rows once it is certain nobody can see them.
questions.rule: Free space only when no snapshot needs the row.

questions.q: PostgreSQL transaction IDs are 32-bit integers. What does the chapter say about overflow?
options: They never overflow because they restart at every commit
Overflow forces the database to abort running transactions
They are 64-bit, so overflow is not a concern
They overflow after about 4 billion transactions, and vacuum cleanup prevents harm
optionExplain: IDs are not reset per commit.
The text says cleanup prevents harm, not mass aborts.
The footnote gives 32 bits.
Right: vacuum cleanup keeps the data safe.
questions.explain: A footnote says the limit is about 4 billion, and PostgreSQL's vacuum process ensures overflow does not affect the data.
questions.teaches: Transaction IDs are 32-bit integers, so they overflow after approximately 4 billion transactions, and PostgreSQL's vacuum process ensures overflow does not affect the data.

questions.q: In an MVCC database, transaction 90 changes a driver's status row from available to busy. How many row versions exist?
options: One, because status changes happen in place
Three, one for each field in the row
Two: the old one marked deleted by 90 and a new one created by 90
None until the transaction commits
optionExplain: In-place change would hide the old status from older snapshots.
Versions are per row, not per field.
Right: update means delete plus create.
Versions exist from the write, tagged with the transaction's ID.
questions.explain: Every update leaves two versions until garbage collection removes the old one.
questions.rule: Every update makes a new version.
questions.teaches: By never updating values in place but creating a new version on every change, the database can provide a consistent snapshot while incurring only a small overhead.

questions.q: Transaction 20 starts while transaction 18 is still running. Transaction 18 commits a change a moment later. Does transaction 20 see it?
options: Only if 20 reads the same row twice
No, because 18 was in progress when 20 started
Yes, because it has committed by the time 20 reads
Yes, because 18 has a lower transaction ID
optionExplain: Rereading does not change the rule.
Right: writes of transactions in progress at the start are ignored.
Commit after the snapshot was taken is invisible.
A lower ID does not matter if the transaction was still running at the start.
questions.explain: The snapshot ignores everything that was in progress at the start. The card next gives the full rule list.
questions.rule: In progress at start means invisible.

questions.q: Reader transaction 20 started while transaction 18 was running. Sort the writes it meets.

items.t: Written by transaction 17, which committed before 20 started
Written by transaction 18, which was running when 20 started and commits later
Written by transaction 19, which aborted
Written by transaction 21, which started after 20 began and has committed

questions.explain: Only writes committed before the reader began are visible. Running, aborted and later transactions are ignored.

questions.q: Transaction 12 reads account 2. Transaction 13 deleted the $500 row and created a $400 row, but has not committed. What does 12 see?
options: $400, since it is the newest
Both rows, $500 and $400
$500, since 13's deletion and creation are not visible to 12
Nothing, because the row is being changed
optionExplain: Newest is not visible when its creator is later or uncommitted.
Only one version is visible per object.
Right: later transaction IDs are ignored.
The reader is not blocked.
questions.explain: Transaction 13 has a later ID, so its changes are invisible to 12.

questions.q: Transaction 20 began at time 0. At time 50 it reads a row transaction 25 overwrote at time 10. What does it see?
options: The version written by 25
The average of both versions
An error saying the row was overwritten
The version from before 25's change
optionExplain: 25 started after 20 and is ignored.
No averaging happens.
Reads do not raise such errors.
Right: 25 has a later ID.
questions.explain: A long-running transaction can keep reading values that have long been overwritten for others.
questions.rule: A snapshot ages but stays consistent.

questions.q: True or false: The visibility rules apply to both the creation and the deletion of row versions.
questions.explain: A version is visible if its creator committed before the reader started and it is either not marked deleted or the deleter had not yet committed.
questions.rule: Creation and deletion are both checked.
questions.teaches: An object is visible if the transaction that created it had committed when the reader started, and it is either not marked for deletion or the deleting transaction had not yet committed when the reader started.

questions.q: A chat export starts while bulk import 40 runs, and the import commits a minute later. Are its messages exported?
options: No, because the import was in progress when the export started
Only if the export runs at read committed
Yes, but only the messages written before the export began
Yes, because the import has finished before the export ends
optionExplain: Right: it ignores transactions running at its start.
At read committed the export would see them, but the question concerns a snapshot.
Messages from an in-progress import are not committed at the start.
Finishing later does not matter.
questions.explain: The visibility rules protect the snapshot from transactions still running at the start.
questions.teaches: Any writes made by transactions that were in progress at the start of the reader's transaction are ignored, even if those transactions subsequently commit.

questions.q: A multi-version database has an index on email. A row has three versions with different emails. What must an index lookup do?
options: Return only the newest version
Return only the versions visible to the reader's snapshot
Return all three versions
Refuse the lookup until old versions are removed
optionExplain: An older reader could need an older version.
Right: filtering by visibility.
Older snapshots would see data they should not.
The index must work while old versions still exist.
questions.explain: The index must respect visibility. The card next gives two designs.

questions.q: Which systems use an append-only, copy-on-write B-tree variant? Select all that apply.
options: CouchDB
VoltDB
Datomic
LMDB
Redis
optionExplain: Right.
VoltDB is mentioned for serial execution, not for this tree.
Right.
Right.
Redis is mentioned for serial execution, not for this tree.
questions.explain: These three use a tree that never overwrites pages.

questions.q: An append-only B-tree database updates one record. Which pages does it copy?
options: The whole tree
The changed page and its parent pages up to the root
Only the root
Only the changed page, leaving the parents
optionExplain: That is more than needed.
Right: the path to the root.
The root alone cannot hold the change.
Parents must point at the new child.
questions.explain: Unaffected pages stay immutable and shared.
questions.rule: Copy the path to the root.

questions.q: In an append-only B-tree, a reader holds an old root while a writer commits new data. What does the reader see?
options: A consistent snapshot of the data as of the old root
Only the writer's new data
An error until the writer finishes
A mix of old and new data
optionExplain: Right: the old root never changes.
The old root points only to old pages.
Readers are not blocked.
Pages are immutable, so no mixing.
questions.explain: Each root is a consistent snapshot; no transaction-ID filtering is needed.

questions.q: True or false: An append-only B-tree needs a background process for compaction and garbage collection.
questions.explain: Old pages and old roots accumulate and must be reclaimed.
questions.teaches: With append-only B-trees every write transaction creates a new root and there is no need to filter objects by transaction ID, but a background process for compaction and garbage collection is required.

questions.q: A file-sync service wants cheap snapshot reads of its metadata and tolerates background cleanup. Which index design fits?
options: An in-place tree with read locks on every page
A log with no index at all
A copy-on-write tree where each write makes a new root
A hash index that overwrites entries
optionExplain: Read locks would block readers.
A log without an index makes lookups slow.
Right: roots are snapshots.
Overwriting breaks older snapshots.
questions.explain: Copy-on-write trees give snapshots at the price of cleanup. In practice, details such as PostgreSQL keeping versions on the same page to avoid index updates also shape performance.
questions.teaches: PostgreSQL has optimizations for avoiding index updates if different versions of the same object can fit on the same page.

questions.q: PostgreSQL's level called repeatable read and Oracle's level called serializable are, in practice, which guarantee?
options: Read uncommitted
Full serializability
Read committed
Snapshot isolation
optionExplain: Both are stronger than read uncommitted because they hide uncommitted data.
Oracle's serializable is weaker than the textbook meaning, and PostgreSQL's repeatable read is not serializable either.
Both are stronger than read committed because transactions read from a snapshot.
Right: both implement snapshot isolation under different names.
questions.explain: Names differ across products even when the mechanism is the same. The card next explains why.

questions.q: Sort each database level by whether it is snapshot isolation under a different name or means something else.

items.t: Oracle's serializable
PostgreSQL's repeatable read
MySQL InnoDB's repeatable read
IBM DB2's repeatable read

questions.explain: Oracle, PostgreSQL and MySQL name their snapshot isolation serializable or repeatable read; DB2 uses repeatable read for serializability.

questions.q: A team moves a service from Oracle to PostgreSQL and picks the level named repeatable read. What should they do?
options: Nothing, because the SQL standard fixes the meaning of each name
Check that both databases run on the same operating system
Check only that the level name is spelled the same in both
Check which anomalies each level allows
optionExplain: The standard's definitions are ambiguous and imprecise, so they do not fix behaviour.
The operating system does not decide isolation behaviour.
Spelling matches would hide differences in what the levels allow.
Right: compare behaviour, not names.
questions.explain: Oracle's serializable and PostgreSQL's repeatable read are both snapshot isolation, but the transfer may still hide differences in details.

questions.q: A guide says repeatable read is precisely defined by the SQL standard, so every database offers identical guarantees under it. What is wrong?
options: Repeatable read is defined only by vendors, never by the standard
The standard's definition is ambiguous, and implementations differ widely
Nothing; a standard always produces identical behaviour
Repeatable read always means snapshot isolation
optionExplain: The standard does define it, though the definition is poor.
Right: the standard is flawed and implementations vary.
Standards guarantee compliance claims, not identical behaviour, when the text is ambiguous.
DB2 uses the name for serializability, so it does not always mean snapshot isolation.
questions.explain: The standard is described as ambiguous, imprecise and not implementation-independent. Despite standardization, guarantees differ greatly.
questions.rule: Standardized names can still differ in substance.

questions.q: True or false: IBM DB2 uses the name repeatable read for something other than snapshot isolation.
questions.explain: DB2 uses repeatable read to refer to serializability, which is one more reason the name tells you little.
questions.rule: The same name can mean a stronger guarantee.
questions.teaches: IBM DB2 uses repeatable read to refer to serializability, so the name has at least two very different meanings across products.

questions.q: A vendor page says: we implement repeatable read as the SQL standard requires. How should a careful engineer read this?
options: As weak evidence
As proof the database blocks all concurrent writers
As proof the database offers serializability
As proof the database offers snapshot isolation
optionExplain: Right: the claim is about naming and compliance, not about specific protections.
Blocking writers is a locking approach, unrelated to what the name promises.
DB2 uses the name for serializability, but other databases use it for a weaker level; the name does not tell which.
PostgreSQL and MySQL do offer snapshot isolation under that name, but DB2 does not, so the name alone proves nothing.
questions.explain: A compliance claim does not pin down the guarantee, so ask which anomalies are prevented.
questions.rule: Compliance is weak evidence of behaviour.
questions.teaches: PostgreSQL and MySQL call their snapshot isolation level repeatable read because it meets the requirements of the standard, so that they can claim standards compliance.

questions.q: Two drivers accept a shuttle's last seat at once, each reading 1 seat and writing 0. What was lost?
options: The first driver's read, which was blocked by the second
The seat itself, because the database deleted the row
One acceptance, as both used the same old value
Nothing, because the seat count correctly ends at 0
optionExplain: Reads are not blocked here; both succeeded and used the same stale value.
Rows are not deleted; the damage is a missing change.
Right: two acceptances produced the effect of one.
The count looks right, but it should have gone to -1 or one driver should have been refused.
questions.explain: Both writes were computed from the same read. The card next names this problem.
questions.rule: Two writes from one old read lose a change.

questions.q: When a later write overwrites an earlier one without including its change, we say the later write ____ the earlier one.
questions.explain: Clobbering is the chapter's word for the later write erasing the earlier modification.
questions.rule: A later write can clobber an earlier one.

questions.q: Two moderators edit a post's tag list at once. Each reads the list, appends a tag and saves the whole list. What is likely?
options: One tag is lost, since the second save lacks the first tag
Both tags are lost, because the saves cancel out
The second save fails, because the post is locked for editing
Both tags are kept, because lists merge on save
optionExplain: Right: the second save clobbers the first.
Cancelling out is not how overwriting works; one tag survives.
Nothing locks the post for readers in a read-modify-write cycle.
Lists do not merge automatically when the whole value is written back.
questions.explain: Saving the whole modified value replaces the stored one, so a concurrent change vanishes.
questions.rule: Writing back a whole value overwrites others' changes.

questions.q: The same two moderators now run strictly one after the other. What happens to the tags?
options: One tag is lost, because writing always replaces the list
Both tags are kept, as the second read sees the first
Neither tag is kept, because the saves conflict
Only the second tag is kept, since it is newer
optionExplain: When the second read happens after the first commit, it sees the first tag and keeps it.
Right: the problem comes from the overlap.
Sequential saves do not conflict.
Newer does not erase older when the newer one was built from it.
questions.explain: Lost updates need overlapping read-modify-write cycles; run in sequence, both changes survive.

questions.q: True or false: Setting a field to a fixed value without reading it, such as marking a shuttle full, risks lost updates like an increment.
questions.explain: The lost update arises when the new value is computed from a value read earlier. A write of a fixed value ignores any prior read, so no earlier change is lost through a stale read.
questions.rule: Only values derived from a read can be lost this way.
questions.teaches: Lost updates arise from a read-modify-write cycle, in which the new value depends on an earlier read; a fixed-value write is not exposed in this way.

questions.q: A chat service lets two admins change a channel's settings page, each saving the complete form. Which situation does this resemble?
options: The phantom example: a new row appears in a search
The read skew example: one admin sees mismatched values
The dirty write example: both write to one uncommitted value
The wiki page example: both save the entire content
optionExplain: A phantom concerns search results changing, not whole-form saves.
Read skew concerns one reader seeing mismatched values; here the problem is writes.
No uncommitted value is involved; the first save may already be committed.
Right: whole-value saves clobber each other.
questions.explain: Two users editing the same page and each sending its complete content is a standard lost-update scenario.
questions.rule: Whole-form saves can clobber each other.
questions.teaches: Two users editing a wiki page at the same time, each saving by sending the entire page contents to the server, is a lost update scenario.

questions.q: Which operation hides a read-modify-write cycle?
options: Reading a stored cart, adding an item, and saving it back
Deleting a session record when a user logs out of the site
Inserting a new row with a fresh unique ID for the order
Setting an order's status to shipped when the courier collects it
optionExplain: Right: the new cart depends on the old one.
Deleting is also independent of the old value's contents.
A fresh insert does not derive from any previous value.
Setting a fixed status ignores the old value.
questions.explain: The new state depends on a value that was read. The card next lists the forms.
questions.rule: Look for writes derived from reads.

questions.q: Which situations does the chapter give as read-modify-write cycles? Select all that apply.
options: Incrementing a counter or updating an account balance
Two users saving a wiki page with its full contents
Adding an element to a list inside a JSON document
Appending a row to a log table
Reading the same record twice
optionExplain: Right: the new value depends on the current one.
Right: each save replaces the page with a version built from an earlier read.
Right: the document is parsed, changed and rewritten.
Appending a new row does not depend on a read of an earlier value.
Reading twice involves no write.
questions.explain: The chapter's three forms all compute a write from a read.

questions.q: An app reads a user's saved-events JSON list, adds an event and writes it back. Which risk applies?
options: The database will refuse the write for being too large
The list will be read twice and double-counted
Both additions will be kept, as JSON documents merge
Two simultaneous additions can lose one event
optionExplain: Document size has no bearing on concurrent writes.
Double counting is not the risk of overlapping saves.
Documents do not merge when written whole.
Right: a local change to a complex value is a read-modify-write.
questions.explain: Parse, change, rewrite is exactly the second form.

questions.q: Sort each operation by whether it is a read-modify-write cycle.

items.t: Increase a wallet balance by reading it and writing balance plus 5
Set a user's language field to a chosen value
Add a comment to a thread by reading the comment list and saving the longer list
Insert a new log line with a unique ID

questions.explain: A read-modify-write derives the new value from the old one. Writing a chosen value or adding an independent row does not.
questions.rule: Derived from the old value means exposed.

questions.q: True or false: Treating a document as one object does not by itself make adding to a list inside it safe from lost updates.
questions.explain: A single document write is atomic, but if two clients each read, modify and write back the whole document, one can still clobber the other.
questions.rule: Atomic writes do not cover derived writes.
questions.teaches: Even when a write to a single document is atomic, a read-modify-write cycle on that document can still lose updates.

questions.q: Workers read a sensor's JSON totals, add their count and write it back; totals run low. What to suspect?
options: Disk corruption that removes digits from stored numbers on write
Dirty reads that make totals look larger
Overlapping read-modify-write cycles that lost additions
A bug in the sensors that undercount events
optionExplain: Corruption would not scale with concurrency.
Dirty reads would show wrong values, not systematically missing counts.
Right: lost updates under concurrency.
Sensors may undercount, but low totals that vary with load point to overlapping writes first.
questions.explain: Running low under concurrency is the signature of lost updates.
questions.rule: Missing contributions under load suggest lost updates.
questions.teaches: Lost updates are hard to find by testing because they depend on timing, and a missing contribution may look like a data problem.

questions.q: A client must add 1 to a counter that many clients update. What is usually the best approach?
options: Keep the counter in the client and sync it every hour
Send one database update that adds 1 inside the database
Read the value, add 1 and write it back in the application
Lock the whole table for every increment
optionExplain: Hourly sync loses concurrent changes and delays the true count.
Right: an atomic operation removes the read.
That is the read-modify-write cycle that loses updates.
Table locks work but are far heavier than needed.
questions.explain: The chapter calls atomic operations usually the best solution. The card next shows examples.
questions.rule: Let the database do the arithmetic.

questions.q: The SQL increment value = value + 1 is concurrency-safe because it is an ____ operation.
questions.explain: The database applies the increment without a separate client-side read.
questions.rule: Atomic update removes the read step.

questions.q: Many game servers add points to a player's score after each round. How should they update it?
options: Send scores to one server that overwrites the total each night
Have each server read the score and store the new total
Use an atomic increment so the database adds the points
Store each round in a separate row and never total them
optionExplain: A nightly overwrite is out of date by day and loses changes.
Read, add and store loses points when servers overlap.
Right: a database add is concurrency-safe.
Never totalling avoids the update but removes the feature that was wanted.
questions.explain: Where the change is addition, an atomic increment is the best solution.

questions.q: Which change can an atomic database operation not easily express?
options: Adding one to a shared counter stored in a row
Adding an element to a priority queue
Changing one field inside a stored JSON document
Rewriting a wiki page with arbitrary text edits
optionExplain: Counters are the standard example.
Redis provides atomic operations for such structures.
MongoDB provides atomic local changes to JSON documents.
Right: arbitrary edits need other methods.
questions.explain: The chapter notes that updates to a wiki page involve arbitrary text editing and cannot easily be written as atomic operations.
questions.rule: Arbitrary edits are outside the model.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says it is possible, though complicated, to express the editing of a text document as a stream of atomic mutations.
questions.explain: A footnote says this is possible and points to the section on automatic conflict resolution.
questions.rule: Even arbitrary edits can sometimes be modelled as atomic mutations.
questions.teaches: It is possible, albeit fairly complicated, to express the editing of a text document as a stream of atomic mutations.

questions.q: A chat service tracks unread counts per user. Many workers add or subtract. Which design fits the chapter's advice?
options: Use atomic increments and decrements in the database
Restart the workers when two clash
Round the counts to the nearest ten to reduce conflicts
Read the count in each worker and store the new value
optionExplain: Right: counters are the textbook case.
Restarting does not remove the race either.
Rounding changes the data and does not remove the race.
Overlapping workers would lose updates.
questions.explain: Express the change as an atomic operation.
questions.teaches: Where atomic operations can be used, they are usually the best choice.

questions.q: Which behaviour best describes how many databases make an atomic update safe?
options: They copy the object to a second table and merge the results later on
They hold an exclusive lock from the read until the update is applied
They allow concurrent updates and fix mismatches overnight
They ask the client to confirm each increment twice
optionExplain: No such merge occurs for atomic operations.
Right: the lock keeps others out.
The operation is meant to be correct at once, not repaired later.
Confirmations do not make updates atomic.
questions.explain: The exclusive lock around the read and write prevents interference. The card next gives the name.

questions.q: Locking an object when read, so nobody else reads it until the update is applied, is called cursor ____.
questions.explain: Cursor stability is one way to implement atomic operations.
questions.rule: Cursor stability = lock around read and write.

questions.q: A developer loads a model, adds 1 in Python and saves, although an atomic increment exists. What is the risk?
options: The save will fail when two requests overlap
Concurrent requests can lose increments
None, because the framework converts it into an atomic update
The field will become read-only after the first save
optionExplain: Overlapping saves usually succeed, which is why the loss is silent.
Right: the ORM saved a computed value.
The framework did not translate the Python arithmetic into a database operation.
Fields do not become read-only.
questions.explain: ORM code that reads, changes and saves recreates the unsafe cycle.

questions.q: True or false: A two-request test showed the counter right, so the ORM code is safe. The chapter would support this.
questions.explain: Such bugs depend on timing and are difficult to find by testing; passing a small test does not show the code is safe.
questions.rule: Passing tests do not prove safety.

questions.q: Besides locking, what other way of implementing atomic operations does the chapter mention?
options: Forcing all atomic operations onto a single thread
Delaying them until midnight
Using a distributed vote among all the nodes of the cluster
Running them on a read replica
optionExplain: Right: single-threaded execution avoids interleaving.
Delay would not remove races.
Votes are for consensus, not for atomic increments.
Replicas are for reads and would not serialize writes.
questions.explain: A single thread executes operations one at a time, so none interleave.
questions.teaches: Another option for implementing atomic operations is to force all of them to be executed on a single thread.

questions.q: A team reviews code that increments an inventory count. Which finding is the strongest sign of risk?
options: The code logs each change to a file
The code runs inside a transaction block
The code reads the count, adds in app code, writes back
The code uses one statement that adds to the count in SQL
optionExplain: Logging does not create or remove the race.
A transaction block alone does not prevent lost updates at weak levels.
Right: read-modify-write in the app.
That is the safe form.
questions.explain: A computed write from an earlier read is the sign to look for.
questions.rule: Search for app-side arithmetic on shared values.
questions.teaches: ORM frameworks make it easy to accidentally write code that performs unsafe read-modify-write cycles instead of using atomic operations provided by the database.

questions.q: A move's legality check needs application code before the piece's position is updated. What suitably prevents lost updates?
options: Skip any protection since each player moves slowly
Read the position twice and compare the values
Lock the piece's row first, then check and update
Use the database's atomic increment on the position
optionExplain: Speed of play does not remove overlap; two moves can still collide.
Reading twice does not stop a write between the reads and the final update.
Right: an explicit lock around the cycle.
An increment cannot run game rules, so it does not fit.
questions.explain: Application logic that cannot be a database query needs an explicit lock. The card next shows how.

questions.q: The SQL clause that tells the database to lock all rows a query returns is FOR ____.
questions.explain: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE takes a lock on every row returned.
questions.rule: FOR UPDATE locks the rows read.

questions.q: A ticketing app must check a customer's loyalty tier in code before reducing a coupon's remaining uses. How should it prevent two lost updates?
options: Select the coupon FOR UPDATE, check in code, then update
Update the coupon before checking, then undo if wrong
Let each customer retry until their update sticks
Read the coupon, check in code, then update without locking
optionExplain: Right: lock first, then check and write.
Updating first and undoing later leaves a window where others read wrong data.
Retrying does not stop a lost update; it may repeat it.
Without the lock, two checks can run on the same remaining count.
questions.explain: When the logic is in application code, lock the row for the whole read-modify-write cycle.
questions.rule: Hold the lock across the cycle.

questions.q: Another transaction runs SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the same rows while the first holds the lock. What happens?
options: Both transactions merge their updates
It waits until the first transaction finishes
It reads stale values and proceeds
The database aborts the first transaction at once
optionExplain: The database does not merge competing updates.
Right: the lock forces a wait.
Waiting is the point of the lock; reading stale values would defeat it.
The holder keeps its lock; the newcomer waits.
questions.explain: The second transaction is forced to wait until the first read-modify-write completes.
questions.rule: A held lock makes others wait.

questions.q: True or false: Explicit locking protects the application even when a developer forgets to take the lock in one code path.
questions.explain: The lock only protects code that takes it. If one code path updates the same rows without locking, the race condition returns.
questions.rule: Explicit locks protect only code that uses them.
questions.teaches: It is easy to forget to add a necessary lock somewhere in the code and thus introduce a race condition.

questions.q: A file-sync service lets two clients rename the same folder, and the rename needs a name-validity check in code. Which choice fits the chapter?
options: Use an atomic increment on the folder's version
Make the clients take turns by polling the folder every second
Let both renames run and keep the latter
Lock the folder row FOR UPDATE, check the name, then update
optionExplain: An increment does not run a validity check.
Polling turns a database problem into a client coordination problem.
Keeping the latter is last-write-wins, which silently loses the earlier rename.
Right: explicit locking handles logic outside the database.
questions.explain: When atomic operations cannot express the logic, an explicit lock is the fallback.
questions.rule: Use locks where atomic operations cannot reach.
questions.teaches: Explicit locking requires careful thought about the application logic, since forgetting a lock in one place causes a race condition.

questions.q: A database runs two read-modify-write cycles in parallel and aborts one when it notices a conflict. What is this approach called?
options: Automatic detection of lost updates
An atomic write operation in the database
Explicit locking with SELECT FOR UPDATE
A dirty write that mixes two transactions
optionExplain: Right: the system detects and aborts.
An atomic operation avoids the cycle in the application.
Explicit locking prevents the parallel run in the first place.
A dirty write is an anomaly, not a protection.
questions.explain: The cycles run in parallel and conflicts are caught after the fact. The card next gives the details.

questions.q: Sort each database level by what the chapter says about lost update detection.

items.t: PostgreSQL repeatable read
Oracle serializable
SQL Server snapshot isolation
MySQL InnoDB repeatable read

questions.explain: Three of the four detect lost updates; MySQL InnoDB at repeatable read does not.
questions.rule: Check each database; MySQL InnoDB does not detect.

questions.q: A team on PostgreSQL repeatable read forgot to lock a counter row in one new code path. Two updates collide. What happens?
options: The second update waits forever for the first transaction
Both updates succeed and one of them is silently lost
The database merges both increments into one update
The database detects it and aborts one transaction
optionExplain: Detection aborts one transaction rather than blocking forever.
That is what would happen on MySQL InnoDB repeatable read.
Databases do not merge increments.
Right: detection covers forgotten locks.
questions.explain: Because detection is automatic, it does not depend on the developer remembering the lock.

questions.q: The same code runs on MySQL InnoDB at repeatable read. What happens when two updates collide?
options: The database falls back to table locks to protect it
Both are applied correctly because the level prevents it
A lost update can occur, as it does not detect them
The database aborts one transaction
optionExplain: No fallback exists.
That would need locking or atomic operations.
Right: no detection there.
That is the PostgreSQL behaviour.
questions.explain: MySQL's repeatable read does not detect lost updates.

questions.q: True or false: Some authors argue that a database must prevent lost updates to qualify as providing snapshot isolation.
questions.explain: By that definition MySQL InnoDB's repeatable read would not count as snapshot isolation.
questions.rule: Definitions of snapshot isolation vary on this point.
questions.teaches: Some authors argue that a database must prevent lost updates in order to qualify as providing snapshot isolation, so MySQL does not provide snapshot isolation under that definition.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of relying on lost update detection instead of locking every counter update?
options: It never aborts a transaction, so nothing is retried
It protects code that forgot to use a lock
It makes writes faster than any lock-based approach
It removes the need to retry after a conflict
optionExplain: Detection works by aborting transactions.
Right: protection without developer action.
Speed is not the claimed advantage.
Aborted transactions must be retried.
questions.explain: Automatic detection is less error-prone since it needs no special database features in application code.
questions.teaches: Lost update detection does not require application code to use any special database features, which makes it less error-prone than locks or atomic operations.

questions.q: A store has no transactions. How can a client avoid overwriting a value someone else changed after it read?
options: Read the value again right before writing it back
Write twice to be sure the value sticks in the store
Make the write conditional on the old value
Ask the store to lock every key permanently for you
optionExplain: A re-read still leaves a gap before the write.
Writing twice does not detect a change.
Right: the condition detects the change.
Permanent locks would stop everyone.
questions.explain: The write itself must carry the check. The card next names it.

questions.q: An operation that updates a value only if it still equals what you read is called compare-and-____.
questions.explain: If the value changed, the update has no effect and you retry.

questions.q: Both load a note reading v1. A saves v2 if still v1, then B saves v3 if still v1. What happens to B?
options: B's update is merged with A's
B's update overwrites A's
B's update succeeds and A's is rolled back to v1
B's update does nothing; B must reread and retry
optionExplain: Compare-and-set does not merge.
That would be a lost update.
A's committed change stays.
Right: the condition no longer holds.
questions.explain: The stored text is now 'v2', so B's condition fails and nothing changes.

questions.q: A client uses compare-and-set but does not check whether its update took effect. After a conflict, what does it believe?
options: That its change is saved, though it may not be
That its update failed with an error message
That the value is locked for it
That another client's change was lost in the conflict
optionExplain: Right: silent failure.
The update returns normally with no effect, not an error.
Compare-and-set takes no lock.
The other client's change is what remains.
questions.explain: The application must check whether the update took effect.

questions.q: True or false: A compare-and-set operation was mentioned earlier as a single-object operation that some databases without transactions provide.
questions.explain: Single-object operations like increment and compare-and-set can prevent lost updates when several clients write to the same object.
questions.teaches: Compare-and-set is found in databases that do not provide transactions, as a single-object operation.

questions.q: A feature-flag service stores each flag as one key. Admins toggle flags from different consoles. Which approach avoids silent overwrites?
options: Disable the toggle button while any other admin is online
Write only if the stored value is still what was read
Let the last console to save always win the conflict
Save the flag in each console's local storage only
optionExplain: Disabling blocks legitimate work.
Right: compare-and-set.
Last write wins silently discards the earlier change.
Local copies would diverge.
questions.explain: Conditional writes catch concurrent changes without a heavy lock.
questions.teaches: The purpose of compare-and-set is to avoid lost updates by letting an update happen only if the value has not changed since it was read.

questions.q: A conditional update checks content = 'old' but the database evaluates the check on a snapshot taken before another commit. What can happen?
options: The database blocks until the snapshot is refreshed
The check passes although the content has already changed
The check always fails for safety
The other writer's change is discarded
optionExplain: Conditional updates do not wait for a refresh.
Right: the check sees stale data.
A stale snapshot would make the check pass, not fail.
The other writer's commit stands.
questions.explain: A stale snapshot can validate a check that should fail. The card next states the caveat.
questions.rule: A stale check is no check.

questions.q: True or false: A conditional update whose WHERE clause reads an old snapshot may fail to prevent lost updates.
questions.explain: The condition can be true on the old snapshot even though a concurrent write has changed the value.
questions.rule: Where the condition reads from matters.

questions.q: A team runs UPDATE ... WHERE content = 'old' on a snapshot-isolated database. How should they decide whether it is safe?
options: Check whether the condition is evaluated against current data
Assume it is safe because the clause tests the old value
Run it a thousand times in a test
Wrap it in a retry loop only
optionExplain: Right: depends on the implementation.
That is the assumption the caveat warns about.
Timing bugs may not show up in a test.
Retry does not fix a check that passes wrongly.
questions.explain: The chapter says to check whether the database's compare-and-set is safe before relying on it.

questions.q: If the condition is checked against the latest committed data, a stale compare-and-set update has ____ effect.
questions.explain: Current data shows the change, so the condition fails and the update does nothing; the client then rereads and retries.
questions.rule: Current data makes the check meaningful.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter's wiki compare-and-set carries a comment that its safety depends on the database implementation.
questions.explain: The comment in the example says this may or may not be safe.
questions.teaches: The chapter's wiki compare-and-set statement is marked as possibly unsafe depending on the database implementation, and readers are told to check before relying on it.

questions.q: A ride app uses conditional updates to claim a trip for a driver. Which doubt should the team resolve first?
options: Whether the trip table is indexed on the driver column
Whether the update statement is short
Whether the condition sees the latest committed value
Whether drivers use the same app version
optionExplain: Indexing affects speed, not correctness of the check.
Statement length is irrelevant.
Right: staleness is the risk.
App version is not the cause.
questions.explain: A claim that passes on stale data can double-assign a trip.
questions.teaches: Compare-and-set is only a safe prevention of lost updates if the database does not let its condition read from an old snapshot.

questions.q: A store lets any node accept writes and copies them asynchronously. Why can a lock or a compare-and-set not protect an update there?
options: Replicas refuse conditional writes
Compare-and-set is too slow when many nodes are involved
Locks only work on SSDs
No single up-to-date copy exists for them to guard
optionExplain: Replicas can accept conditional writes; the problem is that concurrent ones diverge.
Speed is not the cause.
Storage type is irrelevant.
Right: they assume a single current copy.
questions.explain: Concurrent writes at different nodes produce different current values. The card next shows what works.

questions.q: Which techniques does the chapter give for avoiding lost updates in multi-leader or leaderless replication? Select all that apply.
options: Use commutative atomic operations such as counter increments
Rely on last write wins
Use SELECT FOR UPDATE on every node
Apply compare-and-set on the nearest replica
Keep conflicting versions as siblings and merge them later
optionExplain: Right: order does not matter for these.
LWW is prone to lost updates.
Locks assume a single copy.
Compare-and-set also assumes a single current copy.
Right: the application or data structure merges.
questions.explain: Siblings with merging and commutative operations both avoid depending on a single current copy.

questions.q: A leaderless shopping-cart store gets two concurrent adds from different devices. Which approach loses neither item?
options: Keep the version with the later timestamp as the winner
Reject the second add as a conflict
Take a lock on the cart across devices
Keep both versions as siblings and merge them
optionExplain: Last write wins discards one add.
Rejecting one add loses an item for the user.
A cross-device lock needs a single copy.
Right: merge the siblings.
questions.explain: Merging siblings preserves both adds.

questions.q: Sort each operation by whether replicas can apply it in any order and converge.

items.t: Increment a counter by 1
Add an element to a set
Overwrite a value with the latest timestamp winning
Replace the whole page text with one editor's version

questions.explain: Increments and set insertions give the same result in any order. Overwrites depend on which one is applied last.

questions.q: True or false: Last write wins is the default conflict resolution method in many replicated databases.
questions.explain: It is prone to lost updates, since it discards concurrent writes.
questions.rule: A common default can lose updates.
questions.teaches: Last write wins conflict resolution is prone to lost updates and is unfortunately the default in many replicated databases.

questions.q: A chat service keeps a read counter per message across three data centres, each accepting writes. Which design is safe from lost updates?
options: One counter per centre overwritten by the latest timestamp
Counters merging increments from all centres
A single replica accepting increments, whatever the latency
A lock held across all three centres
optionExplain: Overwriting by timestamp discards concurrent increments.
Right: commutative merging.
A single accepting replica is single-leader, not the multi-centre design asked for.
A cross-centre lock needs a single copy and is slow.
questions.explain: Riak 2.0 datatypes merge concurrent updates so no updates are lost.
questions.teaches: Riak 2.0 datatypes prevent lost updates across replicas by automatically merging concurrent updates so that none are lost.

questions.q: Two doctors check that at least two are on call, and each then takes themselves off call. Both transactions commit. What is the result?
options: Both doctors remain on call, since the updates cancel
One doctor is on call, since the database rejects the second leave
No doctor is on call, though each check passed
The first doctor's leave is undone by the second
optionExplain: The updates are to different records; they do not cancel.
That would be the result if the transactions ran one after the other.
Right: both saw 2 and both left.
Neither update undoes the other; both are stored.
questions.explain: Each check was true when made, but both were made on the same old state. The card next names the anomaly.
questions.rule: Both checks pass on the same old state.

questions.q: In the on-call example, each transaction checks that ____ or more doctors are on call before taking its own leave.
questions.explain: Both transactions saw 2 and so assumed it was safe for one to leave.

questions.q: Two drivers in a zone each see 2 on duty and go off duty together under snapshot isolation. What is likely?
options: The zone ends with no driver on duty
The zone count becomes 3
The zone keeps one driver, since the second update fails
Both leaves are undone by the database
optionExplain: Right: same pattern.
The count falls, not rises.
Nothing makes the second update fail.
The database sees no conflict to undo.
questions.explain: Both read count 2, both wrote their own row, and the rule was broken.

questions.q: The two doctors' transactions are run strictly one after the other. What happens?
options: The database aborts the second transaction
The second doctor's check finds one doctor on call and the leave is refused
The first leave is undone
Both leaves are granted anyway
optionExplain: The application refuses; the database does not abort.
Right: serial order keeps the rule.
Nothing undoes the first.
With the first leave committed, the second check sees 1.
questions.explain: The anomaly depends on concurrency.
questions.rule: Serial execution would have kept the rule.

questions.q: True or false: In the on-call example both transactions update the same row, so it is a dirty write.
questions.explain: Alice and Bob each update their own record, two different objects. The conflict is not a dirty write or a lost update but write skew.
questions.teaches: The two transactions in the on-call example update two different objects, Alice's and Bob's records, so the anomaly is neither a dirty write nor a lost update.

questions.q: Two withdrawals each check an account's total across two wallets, then take from different wallets. Which anomaly?
options: A phantom caused by an index
A dirty read
A dirty write
Write skew
optionExplain: A phantom would involve a search condition; here the shared check is a sum over existing rows.
No uncommitted data was read.
No uncommitted value was overwritten.
Right: different objects updated on the basis of one shared check.
questions.explain: Both decisions rested on the same total, and each wrote a different wallet.
questions.teaches: Write skew can occur whenever a rule spans several records and concurrent transactions each update a different record on the basis of one shared check.

questions.q: Two transactions read the same objects and then update different ones. Which anomaly is this?
options: Write skew
A dirty read
A lost update
A dirty write
optionExplain: Right: this is the definition.
A dirty read exposes an uncommitted value.
A lost update has both writing the same object.
A dirty write overwrites an uncommitted value.
questions.explain: The shape of reads and writes names the anomaly. The card next states it.

questions.q: Match each pattern of reads and writes to the anomaly.
pairs: Both read an object, then both write that same object based on the read
One overwrites an object the other wrote and has not committed
Both read the same objects, then each updates a different object
questions.explain: The shape of reads and writes tells the anomaly apart.
questions.rule: Shape of reads and writes names the anomaly.

questions.q: Two clerks read the same stock rows and update items A and B, breaking a rule linking them. Which anomaly?
options: A lost update, since both rows were changed
A phantom, since rows exist
A dirty write, since both changed stock
Write skew
optionExplain: Lost updates need the same object.
Phantoms involve a changed search result.
Dirty writes need an uncommitted overwritten value.
Right: different objects.
questions.explain: Different objects, same reads: write skew.

questions.q: In a write skew situation, the two transactions happen to update the same object, and the first committed before the second wrote. Which anomaly results?
options: A phantom
Nothing, since the order was fine
A lost update
A dirty write
optionExplain: No search result changed.
The second write ignored the first, so something was lost.
Right: depends on timing.
The first had committed, so it was not a dirty write.
questions.explain: In the special case where transactions update the same object, you get a dirty write or a lost update depending on timing.
questions.rule: Same object: dirty write or lost update.

questions.q: True or false: Write skew is best thought of as a generalisation of the lost update problem.
questions.explain: It arises when two transactions read the same objects and update some of them; when they update the same object it is a dirty write or lost update.
questions.rule: Lost update is the special case.
questions.teaches: Write skew can be thought of as a generalisation of the lost update problem, in which different transactions may update different objects.

questions.q: Two moderators leave a channel at once after checking the moderator count. Why is this not a lost update?
options: They both read the same record
They update different moderator records, not the same one
The rule is stored in the same table
One write overwrote an uncommitted value
optionExplain: Both read the same objects, but that alone is not the distinction.
Right: different objects.
Table location is irrelevant.
That would be a dirty write.
questions.explain: Different objects updated: write skew.
questions.rule: Different objects is the distinguishing mark.
questions.teaches: Write skew, unlike a lost update, can leave a rule over several records broken even though no single record was ever overwritten.

questions.q: A database detects lost updates automatically. Does that stop the on-call doctors' write skew?
options: No, because it only works on one-node databases
Yes, because it aborts any conflicting pair
No, because the transactions update different records
Yes, because it locks every read row
optionExplain: Node count is not the reason.
It only notices lost updates, not changes to different rows.
Right: detection covers writes to the same object.
Detection does not lock read rows.
questions.explain: Detection looks for overlapping writes to one object. The card next lists defences that fail.
questions.rule: Lost update detection does not see write skew.

questions.q: Which defences does the chapter say do not stop write skew? Select all that apply.
options: Explicitly locking the rows the transaction depends on
True serializable isolation
Automatic lost update detection in snapshot isolation implementations
Atomic single-object operations
A declared uniqueness constraint
optionExplain: Locking can protect against it.
Serializable isolation does prevent it.
Right: not detected in PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, Oracle or SQL Server.
Right: several objects are involved.
A constraint can catch some cases.
questions.explain: Atomic operations work on one object; detection looks for same-object conflicts.

questions.q: A team on PostgreSQL repeatable read argues the on-call bug cannot happen since PostgreSQL detects lost updates. How should you respond?
options: It cannot happen, since detection covers all anomalies
It can happen only after a crash
It can happen only on a replica
It can still happen
optionExplain: Detection covers lost updates only.
Crashes are not the cause.
Replicas are not the cause.
Right: write skew is not detected.
questions.explain: The chapter lists PostgreSQL's repeatable read as not detecting write skew.

questions.q: The doctors app moves to a truly serializable level. What changes?
options: The database prevents the bad outcome, by delaying or aborting one transaction
Both leaves are still granted
Nothing changes, since the bug is in the app
All reads become slower than writes
optionExplain: Right: serializability prevents write skew.
That is the buggy outcome.
Serializable isolation prevents it.
Cost differs, but the bug is prevented.
questions.explain: True serializable isolation automatically prevents write skew.

questions.q: True or false: Among the databases the chapter lists, SQL Server's snapshot isolation level automatically detects write skew.
questions.explain: SQL Server's snapshot isolation detects lost updates but not write skew; the chapter lists it with PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB and Oracle as not detecting write skew.
questions.rule: None of the listed levels detects write skew.
questions.teaches: Write skew is not automatically detected in PostgreSQL's repeatable read, MySQL/InnoDB's repeatable read, Oracle's serializable or SQL Server's snapshot isolation level.

questions.q: Lost update detection and atomic decrements protect each seat counter, but a rule spans two categories. What is needed?
options: A faster server, to shrink the race window
Another mechanism such as serializable isolation or explicit locks
More replicas, to spread the load
Nothing more, since the counter is atomic
optionExplain: Speed only narrows, not removes, the race.
Right: the rule spans objects.
Replicas do not close the race.
Atomic decrements cover single objects.
questions.explain: Rules over several objects need stronger protection.
questions.teaches: Atomic single-object operations cannot protect a rule spanning multiple objects, since the operation sees only one object.

questions.q: A rule says at least one doctor must stay on call. Which database feature most directly enforces rules across several rows?
options: A foreign key on the shift column
A trigger or materialized view implementing the check
A uniqueness constraint on doctor names
A lower isolation level
optionExplain: A foreign key does not count on-call doctors.
Right: possible in some databases.
Uniqueness does not count rows across a set.
Lower isolation makes the problem worse.
questions.explain: Built-in constraints do not usually cover multi-object rules. The card next explains the options.

questions.q: To lock the on-call doctors' rows before updating, the chapter uses SELECT ... ____.
questions.explain: FOR UPDATE tells the database to lock all rows returned.

questions.q: On a database without serializable isolation, how should the doctors app guard the leave transaction?
options: Select the on-call doctors FOR UPDATE, then check and update
Check once in the client, then update
Select the on-call doctors, then update without locking
Update first, then check and undo manually
optionExplain: Right: locking the rows the check depends on forces the second transaction to wait.
A client check can use stale data.
Unlocked reads keep the race.
Undoing manually leaves a bad state visible.
questions.explain: Locking forces the two transactions to take turns on the same rows.
questions.rule: Lock the rows the decision depends on.

questions.q: With the doctors' rows locked FOR UPDATE, Alice's transaction runs first. What does Bob's transaction see after it gets the lock?
options: An empty table
A deadlock error every time
Only one doctor on call
Two doctors on call, as at its start
optionExplain: The table is not empty.
No cycle exists here.
Right: the lock waits for Alice's commit.
That was the stale view.
questions.explain: Bob waits and then sees the committed state.
questions.rule: Locks make the second check see the new state.

questions.q: True or false: Most databases have built-in support for constraints that span several objects.
questions.explain: Most do not, though triggers or materialized views may implement them depending on the database.
questions.teaches: Most databases do not have built-in support for constraints involving multiple objects, but triggers or materialized views may implement them.

questions.q: Without serializable isolation, two transactions each see three surgeons assigned and drop one. What is second-best?
options: Add an index on the assignment table
Run more tests
Use a larger transaction ID
Lock the assignment rows the check depends on before changing any
optionExplain: Indexes do not stop interleaving.
Tests cannot prove absence of a race.
IDs do not matter.
Right: explicit locking.
questions.explain: Locking the rows the decision depends on is the fallback.
questions.rule: Lock what you read to decide.
questions.teaches: If serializable isolation cannot be used, the second-best option is probably to explicitly lock the rows that the transaction depends on.

questions.q: Two users each find no overlapping booking for a room and insert one at once under snapshot isolation. What can happen?
options: The second user sees the first booking in the search
The second insert is rejected automatically
Both inserts are discarded
Both find no overlap and both insert, double-booking the room
optionExplain: Under snapshot isolation the second user's search does not see the first uncommitted insert.
Nothing rejects it without a constraint or serializable isolation.
Neither insert conflicts with the other.
Right: both saw an empty result.
questions.explain: Both searches saw the same empty state. The card next lists the pattern.
questions.rule: Both see no conflict, both write.

questions.q: Match each example to the check it makes before writing.
pairs: Whether an overlapping booking already exists
Whether the name is already taken
Whether the sum of spending items keeps the balance positive
Whether the target position holds no other figure
questions.explain: Each example checks a condition and then writes, which makes it vulnerable.

questions.q: A user may buy while today's purchases are under 4; two simultaneous purchases both see 3 and buy. Which example is it?
options: A dirty read: uncommitted data was read
Preventing double-spending: both checks pass on the same state
Claiming a username: a duplicate unique key
Read skew: one reader saw different moments
optionExplain: Nothing uncommitted was read.
Right: a limit checked by a sum.
A unique key is a different shape of check.
Read skew is about one reader.
questions.explain: The limit is checked against a total; concurrent purchases each stay below it yet exceed it together.

questions.q: Which of these is safe if the database enforces a uniqueness constraint?
options: Two users claiming the same username at once
Two bookings for overlapping times in one room
Two doctors going off call at once, leaving nobody on call
Two spending items that together overdraw an account
optionExplain: Right: the second insert violates uniqueness and aborts.
Overlap is a range condition; a simple unique key does not cover it.
Each doctor-style update touches a different row, no key is duplicated, so a unique constraint cannot catch it.
A total across items is not a uniqueness rule.
questions.explain: A unique constraint turns the username race into an abort of the second transaction.
questions.rule: Uniqueness covers equal keys, not ranges or sums.

questions.q: True or false: In the game example, a lock on one figure also stops two different figures moving to one position.
questions.explain: The lock stops lost updates on one figure but does not stop two different figures being moved to one square; unless a unique constraint applies, write skew remains.
questions.rule: A lock on one object does not guard a rule over a position.
questions.teaches: In the multiplayer game, locking the figure prevents lost updates on it, but players could still move two different figures to the same position, which is write skew unless a unique constraint helps.

questions.q: A seat is reservable if none exists for that seat and time; two riders reserve it at once. What protects it?
options: A retry on timeout
A faster network
Serializable isolation, or a constraint that the database enforces on seat and time
An index on seat and time
optionExplain: Retries repeat the check.
Speed reduces, not removes, the race.
Right: only serialization or a constraint stops it.
Indexes speed lookups but do not stop both inserts.
questions.explain: Absence checks need serializable isolation or a constraint.
questions.teaches: For a double-booking rule, snapshot isolation does not prevent a concurrent conflicting insert; the chapter says serializable isolation is needed again.

questions.q: Two users try to register the same username at the same moment, and the database has a uniqueness constraint. What happens?
options: Both accounts are created with the same name
Both transactions wait forever for each other
The second transaction is aborted for violating the constraint
The first account is replaced by the second
optionExplain: Without the constraint both would succeed; with it, one cannot.
No cycle of waiting arises; one is aborted.
Right: the constraint catches the duplicate.
Replacement is not how uniqueness is enforced.
questions.explain: The database enforces uniqueness regardless of what the transactions saw. The card next states the pattern.
questions.rule: A unique key rejects the second insert.

questions.q: For claiming a username, a simple fix is a ____ constraint.
questions.explain: The second transaction that tries to register the name is aborted.

questions.q: A file-sync folder holds one file per name. Two clients upload the same name at once. What is the simplest fix?
options: A unique constraint on folder and file name
A retry loop on the client
A lock on the whole folder table for each upload
Serializable isolation for the whole app
optionExplain: Right: equal keys are what a unique constraint checks.
Retries would repeat the race.
Far heavier than needed.
Stronger than needed.
questions.explain: The rule is equality of a key, which the database can enforce directly.
questions.rule: Match the rule to the cheapest mechanism.

questions.q: A booking system wants to forbid overlapping times in the same room. Why is a plain unique key on room and start time not enough?
options: Unique keys are checked only after commit
Overlaps involve ranges
Overlaps are only possible on replicas
Unique keys cannot be created on two columns
optionExplain: Unique constraints are checked when writing.
Right: ranges are not equality.
Replicas are not the cause.
Composite unique keys are allowed.
questions.explain: Two bookings can overlap without sharing a start time, so uniqueness on start time does not catch them.

questions.q: True or false: In PostgreSQL, the meeting-room check can be written more elegantly with range types, though they are not widely supported in other databases.
questions.explain: A footnote says that range types allow this but are not widely available elsewhere.
questions.teaches: In PostgreSQL the meeting room booking check can be done more elegantly using range types, but they are not widely supported in other databases.

questions.q: One rule: no two tickets for a seat. Another: at most four tickets per buyer a day. Which fits a unique constraint?
options: Neither, since constraints never help
The four-per-day rule, since it counts rows
Both, since both are rules on tickets
The one-ticket-per-seat rule
optionExplain: Constraints do help with equal keys.
Counting rows is a total, not an equal key.
Only one fits a simple unique key.
Right: equality of a seat key.
questions.explain: Counting limits need serializable isolation or locks; seat uniqueness is a key.
questions.rule: Keys fit constraints; totals do not.
questions.teaches: A unique constraint settles only key equality; rules over totals or ranges, like the double-spending check, still need stronger protection.

questions.q: A service queries how many seats remain, decides to sell one, then inserts a ticket. What makes this fragile under concurrency?
options: The insert changes the result the decision relied on
The query is too slow
The insert uses too much storage
The decision is made in the application
optionExplain: Right: the write alters the premise.
Speed is not the issue.
Storage is not the issue.
Where the decision is made is not the cause.
questions.explain: The write changes the very fact the decision was based on. The card next gives the three steps.

questions.q: Put the three steps of the check-then-write pattern in order.
items: A SELECT checks whether a requirement holds
The application decides how to continue
The application writes and commits
questions.explain: The result of the query drives the decision, and the write follows.

questions.q: A chat app lets a user create a channel if fewer than 10 exist, then inserts it. Which part makes it exposed to write skew?
options: The user clicks a button
The query counts rows
The channel has a name
The insert changes the count the decision relied on
optionExplain: Clicks are irrelevant.
Counting is fine alone.
Names are irrelevant.
Right: write changes the premise.
questions.explain: The decision uses a count that the insert itself changes.
questions.rule: Look for writes that change the checked count.

questions.q: Sort each decision by whether the write changes the result of the query it was based on.
groups: Write does not change the premise

items.t: Allow a doctor to leave if two are on call, then mark the doctor off call
Create a username if none exists, then insert it
Read the site's theme setting, then log a page view
Read a feature flag, then show a banner

questions.explain: The risky decisions are those whose own write changes what the query would return.
questions.rule: Does the write alter the checked result?

questions.q: True or false: The steps can run in reverse: write first, then SELECT, then commit or abort on the result.
questions.explain: The steps may occur in a different order; the same race can arise.
questions.teaches: The check-then-write steps may occur in a different order: first the write, then the SELECT query, and finally a decision to abort or commit based on the query's result.

questions.q: A payments service inserts a tentative spending item, then sums all items and aborts if the sum is negative. Is this still the same pattern?
options: No, since the write comes first
No, since it uses a sum
Yes, with the write first and the check second
No, since it aborts instead of continuing
optionExplain: Order may vary.
A sum is just a search condition over rows.
Right: same shape in a different order.
Aborting is one of the decisions.
questions.explain: Write then check then decide still forms the pattern.
questions.teaches: Checks can be made by a sum or count over matching rows, and the decision can be an abort as well as a continuation.

questions.q: A search for bookings in a slot finds none, then another transaction inserts one. Why could SELECT FOR UPDATE not protect the first?
options: The insert happened too slowly
The search returned no rows
The first transaction had no write privileges
Locks cannot be taken on bookings
optionExplain: Timing speed is irrelevant.
Right: an empty result has no rows to lock.
Privileges are not the issue.
Locks can be taken on existing bookings.
questions.explain: You cannot lock rows that do not exist. The card next names the effect.

questions.q: A write in one transaction that changes the result of a search query in another is called a ____.
questions.explain: Phantom rows appear in later searches.
questions.rule: A phantom changes a search result.

questions.q: A hotel app checks that no reservation exists for room 7 tonight, then inserts one. Two guests do this at once. Which description fits?
options: A dirty write on one reservation row
A dirty read of the reservation
A phantom: each insert changes the other's search result
A lost update on the room row
optionExplain: No uncommitted overwrite occurred.
No uncommitted data was read.
Right: absence checks create phantoms.
No row was read and written back.
questions.explain: Each guest's insert would change the other's search result.

questions.q: Both guests use SELECT FOR UPDATE on the reservation search, which returns no rows. What does the lock protect?
options: Both guests, since the lock covers the search
The first guest only
The room row
Nothing, since there are no rows to lock
optionExplain: The lock attaches to rows, not to the search.
No guest is favoured.
The room row is not in the search result.
Right: empty results hold no locks.
questions.explain: A lock needs an object to attach to.

questions.q: True or false: In the doctors case, SELECT FOR UPDATE on the on-call rows stops write skew, since the written rows were returned.
questions.explain: The rows exist, so they can be locked; the other four examples check for absence and have nothing to lock.
questions.rule: Locking works when the rows exist.
questions.teaches: In the doctors example, the row modified in the write was one of the rows returned by the query, so locking the rows in the query can avoid write skew; in the other four examples there are no rows to lock.

questions.q: A metrics writer creates a time bucket if no row exists. What stops two writers creating the same bucket without serializable isolation?
options: A uniqueness constraint on the bucket's key
SELECT FOR UPDATE on the empty result
A retry on error
A longer timeout
optionExplain: Right: the constraint acts on the insert.
Nothing to lock.
A retry repeats the race.
Timeouts do not change the race.
questions.explain: Where a key can express the rule, a constraint works even without existing rows.
questions.rule: Constraints can guard absence when keys express it.
questions.teaches: A phantom involves a row that does not yet exist, so row locks fail, but a constraint on the key still applies at insert time.

questions.q: A read-only report runs under snapshot isolation while another transaction inserts matching rows. Does the report see the new rows?
options: It depends on how fast the insert is
No, since it reads from its snapshot
Yes, as soon as they commit
Yes, but only at the end of the report
optionExplain: Speed does not matter.
Right: the snapshot is fixed.
That is read committed.
The report never sees them.
questions.explain: A snapshot is frozen. The card next explains where it still falls short.

questions.q: True or false: Snapshot isolation avoids phantoms in read-only queries.
questions.explain: The query sees only rows committed at the snapshot, so later inserts do not appear.

questions.q: Two scheduling transactions each read free slots under snapshot isolation, then book the same one. What is the risk?
options: The second transaction sees the first's booking
Both decide on the same snapshot and book the slot
Both transactions read stale data and abort
Neither transaction commits
optionExplain: It would not see it on its snapshot.
Right: the snapshot hides the first booking.
Neither aborts automatically.
Both commit.
questions.explain: The snapshot hides concurrent inserts, so the decision rests on a stale picture.
questions.rule: Decisions on snapshots can be stale.

questions.q: Sort each use of snapshot isolation by whether phantoms can hurt it.

items.t: A read-only backup
A read-only analytic query
Insert a booking after finding no overlapping one
Insert a username after finding none

questions.explain: Read-only uses rely on a fixed snapshot; decisions that write on an absence check are exposed.
questions.rule: Writes based on reads are exposed.

questions.q: True or false: Snapshot isolation protects a read-write transaction from phantoms in the same way it protects a read-only one.
questions.explain: In read-write transactions, phantoms can lead to write skew, because the decision relies on a snapshot that does not reflect concurrent inserts.
questions.rule: Writes based on a snapshot can be unsafe.
questions.teaches: In read-write transactions, phantoms can lead to particularly tricky cases of write skew, even though snapshot isolation avoids phantoms in read-only queries.

questions.q: A file-sync backup and a file-sync folder-quota check both run under snapshot isolation. Which is exposed to phantom-based write skew?
options: The quota check that inserts a file after counting existing ones
Neither, because both use snapshots
Both equally
The backup that only reads
optionExplain: Right: only decisions that write are exposed.
Snapshots protect only reads.
Only one writes on the check.
Backups only read.
questions.explain: The quota check writes based on a count, so concurrent inserts matter.
questions.rule: Reading is safe; deciding to write is not.
questions.teaches: Snapshot isolation is a good fit for long read-only operations but not for decisions that write on the basis of what was read.

questions.q: A booking app cannot lock bookings that do not exist yet. What can it lock instead?
options: The whole database
The user's session
Pre-created rows, one for each room and time slot
Nothing; locks require existing bookings
optionExplain: Overkill and blocks everyone.
Sessions do not guard rooms.
Right: artificial lock rows.
The idea is to create something to lock.
questions.explain: If there is no object to lock, create one. The card next gives the name.
questions.rule: Create the thing you need to lock.

questions.q: Turning a phantom into a lock conflict on concrete rows is called materializing ____.
questions.explain: The new rows exist only to be locked.

questions.q: A shuttle app wants to stop two riders booking the same seat on the same run. Which materializing-conflicts design fits?
options: A client-side flag
A table of riders locked once a day
A lock on the whole bookings table
A table with a row per seat and run, locked before checking for bookings
optionExplain: Not shared among clients.
Not matched to the seat.
Heavier than needed.
Right: row per seat and run.
questions.explain: A lock row per resource and slot lets transactions wait.
questions.rule: One lock row per contended slot.
