questions.q: A developer adds the lock-row table but forgets to take the lock in one booking code path. What happens on that path?
options: The database blocks every booking
The lock table is dropped
Nothing, since the table protects everything
Double bookings can occur again
optionExplain: Only unlocked paths race.
Nothing is dropped.
Protection depends on every path.
Right: only code that locks is protected.
questions.explain: A forgotten lock reintroduces the race.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter regards materializing conflicts as a first choice, preferred to serializable isolation.
questions.explain: It calls it a last resort because it is hard, error-prone and leaks concurrency control into the data model; serializable isolation is much preferable in most cases.
questions.teaches: Materializing conflicts should be considered a last resort if no alternative is possible, because it is hard and error-prone and lets a concurrency control mechanism leak into the application data model.

questions.q: A ride-booking team has no serializable isolation, no useful constraint and no existing rows to lock. What is their remaining option?
options: Retry failed bookings until one works
Materialize the conflict by creating lock rows for the contended resource and slot
Ask drivers to book slowly
Use a longer timeout
optionExplain: Retries repeat the race.
Right: last resort.
Slowness is not a guarantee.
Timeouts do not stop races.
questions.explain: When nothing else works, artificial lock rows can be made.
questions.rule: When nothing else is available, create the thing to lock.
questions.teaches: The materializing conflicts approach creates rows for all possible combinations ahead of time, for example for the next six months.

questions.q: A team's test suite passes, yet rare concurrency bugs reach production. Why do tests struggle to find them?
options: Tests are only run by one developer at a time
Test databases cannot run more than one transaction at a time
The bugs depend on timing and appear only when requests interleave badly
Concurrency bugs show up only after a database restart
optionExplain: Who runs the tests is irrelevant to whether timing bugs are caught.
Test databases can run concurrent transactions; the trouble is hitting the unlucky timing.
Right: bad interleavings are rare and unpredictable, so a passing run proves little.
Restarts are not what triggers these bugs; interleaving of live requests does.
questions.explain: Timing-dependent bugs hide from ordinary testing. The card next lists the three complaints.

questions.q: Concurrency bugs are hard to test for because they are ____: they occur only if the timing is unlucky.
questions.explain: Problems occur only if you get unlucky with the timing.

questions.q: Which are among the difficulties of relying on weak isolation levels?
options: There are no good tools for detecting race conditions
Level names mean different things in different databases
Safety is hard to judge from application code
Weak levels cannot be used in a large application
Weak levels permit dirty writes in most databases
optionExplain: Static analysis exists in research but is not in practical use.
Repeatable read, for example, varies significantly between implementations.
In a large application you may not know everything happening concurrently.
Size is not the barrier; the barrier is the difficulty of reasoning about safety.
Almost all implementations prevent dirty writes, so this is not a difficulty.
questions.explain: These are the three complaints: confusing names, unclear safety and missing tools.

questions.q: A developer assumes repeatable read behaves identically across database products. What is wrong with that assumption?
options: Its meaning varies significantly between implementations
It is defined differently for each programming language used by the client
It always means the same as read committed in practice
It is only supported by databases that also implement serial execution
optionExplain: Right: the same name can hide different guarantees, so names alone mislead.
The client language does not define the level; the database implementation does.
Read committed and repeatable read differ; they are not interchangeable.
Support for the name is unrelated to serial execution in a database.
questions.explain: Because levels are inconsistently implemented, read the guarantees rather than trusting the label.
questions.rule: The label does not fix the guarantee.

questions.q: True or false: Concern about weak isolation levels is a recent problem that appeared with distributed databases.
questions.explain: The problem has existed since the 1970s, when weak isolation levels were first introduced.
questions.teaches: The difficulty has existed since the 1970s, when weak levels were introduced, and researchers have consistently answered it with one piece of advice: use serializable isolation.

questions.q: A startup hopes to buy a static analysis tool that finds all race conditions. What does the chapter say about such tools?
options: Such tools work only for code written in stored procedures
Static analysis may help in principle
Such tools exist for every database and are routinely used to certify code
Race conditions cannot be analysed at all, so research on the topic has stopped
optionExplain: Stored procedures are not mentioned as a condition for analysis.
Right: the tooling gap is one of the three complaints.
Practical tools of that kind are exactly what is missing today.
Research continues; it simply has not reached practice yet.
questions.explain: No dependable tool exists yet, so the burden stays with developers.
questions.teaches: Static analysis may help in principle, but the research techniques have not yet found their way into practical use.

questions.q: Two transactions run in parallel, and the final data equals what running them one after the other would produce. Which guarantee is this?
options: Durability, which keeps committed data after a crash
Read committed isolation, which allows interleaving but not dirty reads
Atomicity, which makes a transaction all or nothing
Serializable isolation
optionExplain: Durability concerns surviving crashes, not ordering of transactions.
Read committed leaves races such as write skew and lost updates.
Atomicity concerns partial failure, not concurrent interleaving.
Right: parallel execution with the effect of a serial order.
questions.explain: The result matching a serial order is the definition. The card next gives it in full.
questions.rule: Same result as a serial order.

questions.q: Serializable isolation guarantees the result is the same as if transactions had executed one at a ____, serially.
questions.explain: Transactions may run in parallel, but the outcome matches serial execution.

questions.q: A funds-transfer routine is correct when run alone. The database runs many copies concurrently under serializable isolation. What follows?
options: They stay correct
They are correct only for transfers touching a single account row
They are correct only if the transfers run on a single thread
They stay correct only if each transfer also takes an explicit lock
optionExplain: Right: correct-alone transactions stay correct together.
Multi-row transactions are covered, including write skew and phantoms.
Parallel execution is allowed as long as the result matches a serial order.
No extra locks are needed; the database handles the races.
questions.explain: If transactions behave correctly individually, they continue to do so concurrently.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it holds for serializable isolation.

items.t: Concurrent transactions have the effect of some one-at-a-time order
Write skew and phantoms are prevented
Transactions must literally execute on a single thread
A transaction with faulty logic is repaired by the database

questions.explain: Serializable constrains the outcome, not the mechanism, and it assumes each transaction is correct alone.

questions.q: True or false: Under serializable isolation, a transaction that is correct when run alone stays correct when run alongside others.
questions.explain: That is the practical meaning of the guarantee: the database prevents every race condition.
questions.teaches: If transactions behave correctly when run individually, they continue to be correct when run concurrently, so developers need not reason about interleavings.

questions.q: A ride-booking team keeps check-then-write code and moves from snapshot to serializable isolation. What must they add for write skew?
options: SELECT FOR UPDATE on every query in the application
A unique constraint for every business rule
A materialized lock table for every driver and time slot
Nothing extra, since the database prevents the anomaly
optionExplain: Explicit locks are the manual workaround under weaker levels.
Constraints only cover rules expressible as equal keys.
Materializing conflicts is a last resort when serializable isolation is unavailable.
Right: serializable isolation covers write skew and phantoms.
questions.explain: The weak-level workarounds exist because serializable isolation was not in use.
questions.rule: Serializable removes the need for workarounds.
questions.teaches: Choosing serializable isolation removes the need for manual defences such as explicit locks, constraints or materialized conflicts.

questions.q: A team asks why every database does not default to serializable isolation. What is the most relevant factor?
options: Serializable isolation cannot prevent write skew
Serializable isolation needs a special kind of disk
How each implementation performs under load
No database vendor has documented the technique
optionExplain: It does prevent write skew; that is its point.
No special hardware is required.
Right: the implementations have performance costs.
The techniques are well documented and widely used.
questions.explain: The price of each technique explains the hesitation. The card next names the three.

questions.q: Order the techniques by the chapter's presentation, from the simplest idea to the newest.
items: Literally executing transactions in a serial order
Two-phase locking
Serializable snapshot isolation
questions.explain: The chapter covers serial execution, then two-phase locking, then SSI.

questions.q: Match each description to the technique it fits.
pairs: One transaction runs at a time, on a single thread
Readers and writers block each other with locks
Transactions proceed and the database checks at commit
questions.explain: Each description names the defining mechanism of one technique.

questions.q: Which technique is described as the only widely viable choice for several decades?
options: Multi-version read committed
Two-phase locking
Serial execution on a single thread
Serializable snapshot isolation
optionExplain: Read committed is a weak level, not a serializable technique.
Right: 2PL held that position for decades.
Serial execution only became viable around 2007.
SSI was first described in 2008.
questions.explain: Two-phase locking was the standard long before the other two matured.

questions.q: True or false: The three techniques are discussed first for single-node databases, and later generalized to transactions involving multiple nodes.
questions.explain: The chapter says Chapter 9 examines how they can be generalized to distributed systems.
questions.teaches: The chapter discusses the techniques primarily for single-node databases, and a later chapter generalizes them to transactions that involve multiple nodes.

questions.q: A metrics team needs serializable updates on one node, with short transactions and a small in-memory dataset. Which family looks most natural?
options: Serializable snapshot isolation, since it requires no memory
None, since serializability needs several nodes
Serial execution
Two-phase locking, since it avoids all lock overhead
optionExplain: SSI tracks reads and writes, so it has its own bookkeeping.
Serializability applies on a single node as well.
Right: serial execution suits small, fast, in-memory workloads.
2PL adds lock overhead, not removes it.
questions.explain: Short in-memory transactions are the sweet spot for single-threaded execution.
questions.teaches: Which technique fits depends on the workload: short in-memory transactions suit serial execution, contended ones argue against optimistic methods.

questions.q: A database runs exactly one transaction at a time on one thread. Why is its isolation serializable?
options: Each transaction is checked at commit for stale reads
Every transaction reads from a snapshot taken at startup
Locks detect every conflict before it happens
No two transactions overlap
optionExplain: Commit-time checks belong to SSI, not serial execution.
Snapshots are used by SSI and snapshot isolation, not required here.
No locks are needed; nothing overlaps.
Right: with no concurrency there is nothing to conflict.
questions.explain: Removing concurrency sidesteps conflict detection entirely. The card next states the enabling changes.

questions.q: Cheap ____ let many databases keep the whole active dataset in memory, which helped single-threaded execution become feasible.
questions.explain: When all data a transaction needs is in memory, it executes much faster than if it waits on disk.

questions.q: Which developments made single-threaded transaction execution feasible?
options: Disks became fast enough to remove the need for caching
Network latency between clients and servers fell to zero
RAM became cheap enough to hold the active dataset
OLTP transactions are short with few reads and writes
optionExplain: Disk speed is not the stated reason; memory residence is.
Network latency does not vanish; stored procedures avoid network round trips instead.
With data in memory, transactions avoid slow disk waits.
Short transactions release the single thread quickly.
questions.explain: Cheap memory and short OLTP transactions together made the single-thread loop practical.

questions.q: Where should a long-running analytic query run in a system that executes OLTP transactions serially?
options: Outside the serial loop, on a consistent snapshot
Inside the serial loop, split into one transaction per row
On a separate system that stops all writes first
Inside the serial loop, so it sees the latest data
optionExplain: Right: read-only queries use snapshot isolation elsewhere.
Splitting would give an inconsistent view and still occupy the thread.
Stopping writes is not needed with a snapshot.
A long query inside the loop would stall every other transaction.
questions.explain: Analytics are read-only, so a snapshot works without disturbing the loop.
questions.rule: Keep long reads off the single thread.

questions.q: True or false: Designers decided that a single-threaded loop was feasible around 2007, after about 30 years of treating multi-threading as essential for performance.
questions.explain: The change came with cheap RAM and the observation that OLTP transactions are short.
questions.teaches: Database designers decided only around 2007 that a single-threaded transaction loop was feasible, after about 30 years of multi-threaded concurrency being treated as essential.

questions.q: A chat service has small, fast message-posting transactions on in-memory data, but a nightly report scans months of messages. How should it be organised?
options: Report in the serial loop, scheduled on a quiet night
Serial loop for postings, report on a snapshot outside the loop
Postings in a lock-based system, report in the serial loop
Report split into thousands of serial transactions
optionExplain: Even at night, a long query would stall transaction processing for its duration.
Right: OLTP in the loop, analytics on a snapshot.
Mixing the two loses the advantage of single-threaded execution.
Splitting loses a consistent view and keeps the thread busy.
questions.explain: Long read-only work belongs outside the single thread.
questions.teaches: Serial execution is paired with snapshot isolation for read-only analytics, so one slow reader does not stall the loop.

questions.q: A one-at-a-time database receives statements singly, waiting for the application after each. What is the main problem?
options: Results are lost if the client reconnects
The database spends most of its time idle, waiting for the next query
Statements are executed twice, once by the client
Locks accumulate on every row the client touches
optionExplain: Reconnecting is not the issue; round-trip waiting is.
Right: network round trips leave the thread idle.
Nothing is executed twice; the delay is waiting time.
A serial system takes no row locks for this purpose.
questions.explain: Interactive style plus a single thread yields dreadful throughput. The card next gives the fix.

questions.q: In single-threaded systems, the application submits the entire transaction ahead of time as a ____ procedure.
questions.explain: This avoids network round trips during the transaction.
questions.rule: Ship the transaction as a stored procedure.

questions.q: A booking flow has search, itinerary selection, seat booking, passenger details and payment. Why is it a poor fit for one database transaction?
options: Humans are slow
Seat booking requires a different database than search
Itinerary selection always needs more than one hour of CPU time
Payment cannot be recorded inside any transaction
optionExplain: Right: waiting on a person makes long, mostly idle transactions.
One database can serve search and booking.
CPU time is not the issue; human delay is.
Payments can be recorded in transactions; the issue is waiting time.
questions.explain: Most OLTP applications keep transactions short and avoid waiting for users within them.
questions.rule: Do not wait for people inside a transaction.

questions.q: On the web, how are transactions usually kept short in relation to user interaction?
options: The transaction stays open until the browser tab closes
A transaction spans every page of a checkout flow
A transaction is committed within the same HTTP request; a new request starts a new one
One transaction spans the whole user session
optionExplain: Open transactions tied to a tab would pile up idle.
Spanning pages would leave transactions idle between requests.
Right: a transaction does not span multiple requests.
Session-long transactions would hold resources for human-length times.
questions.explain: Per-request transactions keep the human out of the critical path.

questions.q: True or false: Even without humans in the path, transactions kept an interactive client/server style, one statement at a time.
questions.explain: That style remained common, which is why serial systems need stored procedures to avoid network waits.
questions.teaches: Even without humans in the path, transactions continued as interactive client/server exchanges, with queries and results sent back and forth between application and database.

questions.q: A ticketing service moves to a serial-execution database. Its purchase flow reads availability, then decides in client code whether to charge. What must change?
options: The client must hold a lock while it decides
The database must switch to multi-threaded execution
Purchases must wait until the end of the day
The decision logic must move into a stored procedure on the database
optionExplain: Locks held across client decisions bring back long waits.
Going multi-threaded abandons the design.
Delaying work does not address round trips.
Right: ship the whole decision to the database.
questions.explain: The decision belongs in the stored procedure to avoid client round trips.
questions.teaches: Stored procedure transactions in a single-threaded system must contain the full decision logic, since the thread cannot wait for the application between statements.

questions.q: A team fears database-side code because a bug could harm every application using that database. Which complaint about stored procedures is this?
options: Stored procedures cannot read data
Each vendor's language lacks a standard
A database is shared and performance-sensitive
The code cannot be placed in version control at all
optionExplain: Procedures read and write data normally.
The language point is a separate complaint, about vendor lock-in and archaic design.
Right: one instance serves many application servers.
Version control is harder, not impossible, which is another complaint.
questions.explain: A shared database amplifies the effect of one badly written procedure. The card next lists all three.

questions.q: Match each database with the stored procedure language the chapter names for it.
questions.explain: Each vendor has its own language, which is itself one of the complaints.

questions.q: A team can pick the language for its procedures in a serial-execution store. Which choice softens the ecosystem complaint?
options: A general-purpose language such as Java, Clojure or Lua
A language with no libraries so there is less to maintain
A vendor-specific language invented for the database
Plain SQL statements only, with no loops or functions
optionExplain: Right: modern stores adopted existing general-purpose languages.
Missing libraries are the complaint, not a virtue.
A bespoke language repeats the complaint rather than fixing it.
Dropping control flow gives up what procedures were meant to offer.
questions.explain: VoltDB uses Java or Groovy, Datomic uses Java or Clojure and Redis uses Lua.

questions.q: Sort each complaint by whether modern implementations have addressed it.

items.t: Archaic vendor-specific language
Lack of a library ecosystem
Harder to debug and deploy than application code
A bad procedure can hurt every client of a shared database

questions.explain: Adopting general-purpose languages helps with language and libraries, not with operating shared database code.
questions.hint: Ask which problem a better language can fix.
questions.rule: Language is fixable; shared risk remains.

questions.q: True or false: Stored procedures have been part of the SQL standard since 1999 (SQL/PSM).
questions.explain: They have existed in relational databases for some time, yet gained a bad reputation.
questions.teaches: Stored procedures have been part of the SQL standard (SQL/PSM) since 1999, yet each vendor still has its own language.

questions.q: A metrics platform wants to add Redis-style scripts that run inside the store. What operational risk should the team plan for?
options: The script cannot be executed more than once
A heavy script on a shared store can slow every client that depends on it
The script will be copied to every application server
The script will run in the language of each client
optionExplain: Repeated execution is normal for procedures.
Right: a shared instance amplifies one bad script.
Scripts run in the store, not on application servers.
The store, not each client, decides the language.
questions.explain: A single database instance is often shared by many application servers.
questions.teaches: Because one database instance serves many application servers, code that uses a lot of memory or CPU there does more damage than the same code in an application server.

questions.q: Two replicas each run the same transaction code on the same data, but get different results. What is the most likely cause?
options: Serializable isolation is disabled on one replica
The code contains too many statements
The replicas hold the same data in a different order on disk
The code depends on something that differs per node, such as the local clock
optionExplain: A single-threaded system has no isolation setting to differ.
Length of code does not by itself cause divergence.
Disk layout does not change the logical result.
Right: nondeterministic inputs break replication by re-execution.
questions.explain: Different inputs lead to different outputs. The card next states the requirement.

questions.q: VoltDB requires stored procedures to be ____, meaning they produce the same result when run on different nodes.
questions.explain: That lets it replicate by running the same procedure on each replica.

questions.q: A procedure needs the current time to stamp a record, and it replicates by re-execution. How should it obtain the time?
options: Through a special deterministic API supplied by the database
By asking the client to retry until the clocks agree
By reading the local clock on each replica
By generating a random number on each replica
optionExplain: Right: the database provides a value every replica will use.
Retrying does not make independent clocks agree.
Local clocks differ, so replicas would diverge.
Random values differ per node.
questions.explain: A deterministic time API gives all replicas the same value.

questions.q: Which approach does VoltDB use to replicate a transaction's effects?
options: It replays only the transaction's reads
It asks each replica to vote on the final values
It copies the transaction's writes to every node
It executes the same stored procedure on each replica
optionExplain: Replaying reads would not reproduce writes.
Voting is not described for this purpose.
Shipping writes is the traditional approach the chapter contrasts it with.
Right: re-execution instead of write shipping.
questions.explain: VoltDB runs the procedure everywhere instead of copying its writes.
questions.rule: Run the code on every node.

questions.q: True or false: Replication by re-execution needs deterministic procedures, so a procedure reading a random number would be unsuitable.
questions.explain: Random values would differ across nodes, so replicas would end up in different states.
questions.teaches: Any source of nondeterminism, including random numbers, breaks replication by re-execution because each node would compute a different result.

questions.q: A ride-booking store replicates by re-execution. A procedure assigns a ride to a random nearby driver. What is the problem?
options: The assignment would be written twice on one replica
Random choice is slower than a fixed choice
Each replica could pick a different driver, leaving replicas inconsistent
Drivers cannot be selected by stored procedures
optionExplain: Each replica writes once; the writes differ.
Speed is not the issue; correctness across replicas is.
Right: nondeterministic choice causes divergence.
Procedures can select drivers; they just must do it deterministically.
questions.explain: The fix is to derive the choice from inputs all replicas share.
questions.teaches: A procedure that must make a random-looking choice needs a value supplied identically to all replicas, rather than each node generating its own.

questions.q: A serial-execution database has a write-heavy workload and one core is saturated. What is the chapter's suggested way to use more cores?
options: Switch the single thread to run two transactions at once
Partition the data and run one thread per partition
Add more threads that share a single partition
Move the active data from memory back to disk
optionExplain: Two at once is concurrency, which the design avoids.
Right: independent partitions run independently.
Sharing a partition among threads brings back concurrency control.
Disk makes transactions slower, not faster.
questions.explain: Each partition gets its own thread. The card next states the condition.

questions.q: If every transaction touches a single partition, throughput can scale ____ with the number of CPU cores.
questions.explain: Each core gets its own partition.

questions.q: A simple key-value store has one write per transaction on a single key. How well does serial execution with partitioning fit?
options: Poorly, since key-value data cannot be partitioned
Well, but only if all keys sit on a single machine
Well, since each transaction touches one partition and partitions run independently
Poorly, since each write must lock every partition
optionExplain: Simple key-value data is the easy case for partitioning.
Machines can be added; one machine is the limit to avoid.
Right: simple key-value data partitions easily.
Single-key writes touch only one partition.
questions.explain: Single-partition transactions are exactly what partitioning needs.

questions.q: Sort each data shape by whether it suits single-partition transactions.

items.t: Simple key-value data
Per-user data where each transaction touches one user
Data with many secondary indexes
A transaction that updates accounts on different partitions

questions.explain: Secondary indexes and multi-entity writes often span partitions and require coordination.

questions.q: True or false: Partitioning scales serial execution in every case, whatever the application's data structure.
questions.explain: It depends on the data: secondary indexes and transactions spanning partitions need coordination.
questions.teaches: Whether transactions can be single-partition depends on the application's data; data with multiple secondary indexes is likely to need a lot of cross-partition coordination.

questions.q: A file-sync service partitions by user. Most transactions touch one user's files; sharing a folder touches two users. How should the team view sharing?
options: As a reason to stop partitioning by user
As a read-only query that needs no coordination
As a single-partition transaction like any other
As a cross-partition transaction that costs far more than ordinary ones
optionExplain: Most traffic is single-partition, so partitioning still pays.
Sharing writes, so it needs coordination.
Two users may live on different partitions, so it is not single-partition.
Right: touching two partitions needs coordination.
questions.explain: Rare cross-partition work is acceptable; frequent cross-partition work is not.
questions.teaches: Partitioning pays when most transactions stay within one partition; the cost of the occasional cross-partition one is then tolerable.

questions.q: A transaction must change rows held by three different partitions in a serial-execution store. What must the database do?
options: Coordinate the transaction across all three partitions
Run it only on the partition with the most rows
Reject it because transactions cannot span partitions
Run it independently in each partition without coordination
optionExplain: Right: coordination is needed to remain serializable.
Skipping partitions would lose writes.
Cross-partition transactions are possible, with a hard limit on their use.
Uncoordinated runs could expose partial states and break serializability.
questions.explain: The procedure must run in lock-step across the partitions. The card next gives the cost.

questions.q: VoltDB reports roughly ____ cross-partition writes per second.
questions.explain: This is orders of magnitude below its single-partition throughput.

questions.q: A team's workload is 40% cross-partition writes on a serial-execution store. Adding machines is proposed. What does the chapter's reasoning predict?
options: Single-partition transactions become slower and cross-partition faster
The cross-partition rate stays capped
Cross-partition work becomes faster as the number of partitions grows
Throughput doubles with each added machine
optionExplain: Single-partition work is unaffected by this change.
Right: the cross-partition throughput cannot be increased by adding machines.
More partitions increase coordination, not decrease it.
That holds for single-partition work, not cross-partition.
questions.explain: Cross-partition throughput has a hard limit independent of machine count.

questions.q: Which comparison describes cross-partition against single-partition throughput in VoltDB?
options: Cross-partition is higher because it uses all cores
Cross-partition is orders of magnitude lower and does not grow with machines
Cross-partition is lower but grows linearly with machines
Cross-partition is about the same but costs more memory
optionExplain: Coordination makes it slower, not faster.
Right: far lower and capped.
It cannot be increased by adding machines.
The gap is large, not small.
questions.explain: The coordination overhead dominates.

questions.q: True or false: The stored procedure must be performed in lock-step across all partitions a cross-partition transaction touches.
questions.explain: That is how serializability across the whole system is ensured.
questions.teaches: Lock-step execution across partitions is what preserves serializability for the whole system, and it is the source of the extra coordination overhead.

questions.q: A ticketing store partitions by event. A bundle purchase covers tickets for two events. How common can such bundles be before the design suffers?
options: Rare enough that the capped cross-partition rate covers them
None, since cross-partition transactions are forbidden
Common, since cross-partition work is as cheap as single-partition
Any share is fine, since more machines raise the cap
optionExplain: Right: the cap bounds how many bundles can be handled.
They are possible, only limited.
Cross-partition work is vastly slower.
More machines do not raise the cross-partition cap.
questions.explain: The design tolerates a small share of cross-partition transactions.
questions.teaches: Simple key-value data can often be partitioned very easily, but data with multiple secondary indexes is likely to require a lot of cross-partition coordination.

questions.q: One transaction in a serial-execution store takes ten seconds. What happens to the other transactions?
options: They are aborted immediately
They run in parallel on other cores
They all wait
They run on a snapshot of old data
optionExplain: Waiting, not aborting, is the effect.
Parallel cores would mean concurrency, which this design excludes.
Right: only one runs at a time.
Snapshots are used for read-only queries, not for ordinary transactions.
questions.explain: One slow transaction blocks the whole loop. The card next lists the constraints.

questions.q: Which are constraints on using serial execution?
options: The active dataset must fit in memory
The database must run on at least two nodes
Every transaction must use an index-range lock
Transactions must be small and fast
optionExplain: Data outside memory makes a single-threaded transaction very slow.
Serial execution is described for a single thread, not for multiple nodes.
Locks are a different technique, not part of serial execution.
One slow transaction would stall all transaction processing.
questions.explain: Small, fast, in-memory transactions are the core conditions.

questions.q: A reporting-heavy product has transactions that scan millions of rows and a dataset far larger than memory. Is serial execution a fit?
options: Yes, since serial execution is fastest for large scans
Yes, since it avoids all memory use
No, since it cannot ensure serializability
No, since large scans stall the loop and out-of-memory data slows it
optionExplain: Large scans are the worst case for a single thread.
It depends heavily on memory.
It does ensure serializability by definition.
Right: it fails the small-and-fast and in-memory constraints.
questions.explain: Both the size of the transactions and the dataset rule it out.

questions.q: Sort each workload by whether serial execution suits it.

items.t: Short key lookups on an in-memory dataset
Single-partition updates with one core per partition
A mix of transactions where some wait on disk
Heavy writes that mostly span partitions

questions.explain: Slow transactions and heavy cross-partition work break the constraints.
questions.rule: Match the workload to the limits.

questions.q: True or false: Cold data can sit on disk; a transaction needing it is aborted, the data fetched asynchronously, and the transaction restarted.
questions.explain: This approach is known as anti-caching.
questions.teaches: Anti-caching aborts a transaction that needs on-disk data, fetches that data into memory asynchronously while other transactions continue, and restarts the transaction once it is loaded.

questions.q: A chat service finds that 1% of transactions need old messages stored on disk. How can it keep a serial-execution design?
options: Run them concurrently with the others using locks
Let them read from disk inside the loop and accept the stall
Drop old messages from all queries
Abort those transactions, load the data in the background and restart them
optionExplain: Locks bring back the concurrency the design avoids.
A disk wait in the loop stalls everyone.
Removing data changes the product, not the design.
Right: fetch asynchronously, then restart.
questions.explain: Anti-caching keeps the loop fast for the common case.
questions.rule: Fetch in the background and retry.
questions.teaches: The cost of anti-caching is that a transaction needing cold data is aborted and restarted, so it works best when such accesses are rare.

questions.q: Transaction A has read a row. Transaction B wants to write it, under two-phase locking. What happens?
options: B writes immediately, and A keeps its old value
B waits until A commits or aborts
A is aborted so B can write
B writes a new version while A reads the old one
optionExplain: Under 2PL B cannot change the object behind A's back.
Right: a reader blocks a later writer.
Neither side is aborted just for this.
That is snapshot isolation; 2PL does not allow reading an old version.
questions.explain: Readers hold on to their access until they finish. The card next gives the full rule.

questions.q: Under two-phase locking, writers block other writers, and they also block ____.
questions.explain: Readers and writers wait for each other.

questions.q: Transaction A has written a row and has not yet committed. Transaction B wants to read it under 2PL. What happens?
options: B waits until A commits or aborts
B skips the row
B reads A's uncommitted value immediately
B reads the old committed version immediately
optionExplain: Right: reading an old version is not acceptable under 2PL.
Skipping rows would break the query.
That would be a dirty read, which 2PL prevents.
That behaviour belongs to snapshot isolation.
questions.explain: A reader must wait for a writer to finish.

questions.q: Sort each statement by the scheme it describes.

items.t: Writers block readers
Readers and writers wait for each other
Readers never block writers
Reads can see an old version while a write is pending

questions.explain: Blocking is the key difference between the two schemes.

questions.q: True or false: Two-phase locking and two-phase commit are essentially the same technique with different names.
questions.explain: They sound similar but are completely different things; 2PC is discussed in a later chapter.
questions.teaches: Two-phase locking is not two-phase commit; the latter is discussed in Chapter 9, and the two are completely different.

questions.q: A ride-booking team compares 2PL with snapshot isolation for a dispatch board read all day by many viewers while drivers update status. What differs?
options: Both block in exactly the same way
Under 2PL, only updaters wait on other updaters
Under 2PL, viewers and updaters block one another; under snapshot isolation they do not
Under 2PL, viewers see stale data; under snapshot isolation they wait
optionExplain: The mantra of snapshot isolation is non-blocking reads.
Under 2PL readers also block writers.
Right: 2PL blocks in both directions.
The waiting and staleness are reversed in that statement.
questions.explain: Blocking in both directions is the cost of 2PL's protection.
questions.teaches: The stronger protection of 2PL covers lost updates and write skew, at the cost that long readers can hold up writers.

questions.q: Two transactions both want to read the same row under 2PL, and neither writes. Can they proceed together?
options: No, since only one transaction may touch a row at a time
No, since each read needs an exclusive lock
Yes, since several transactions can hold a shared lock at once
Yes, but only after one has upgraded its lock
optionExplain: Multiple readers are allowed when nobody writes.
Reads need only shared locks, not exclusive.
Right: shared locks coexist.
No upgrade is needed to read.
questions.explain: Shared mode lets readers coexist. The card next completes the protocol.

questions.q: Put the lock actions in order for a transaction that reads a row and then updates it.
items: Acquire the lock in shared mode to read
Upgrade the lock to exclusive mode to write
Hold the lock until the transaction commits or aborts
questions.explain: The upgrade works like acquiring an exclusive lock directly, and release happens only at the end.
questions.rule: Shared, upgrade, hold to the end.

questions.q: Transaction A holds a shared lock on a row. Transaction B wants an exclusive lock on it. What happens?
options: B waits until A releases its lock at commit or abort
B and A share the lock until one writes
B gets the lock because shared locks are weaker
B gets the lock and A is aborted
optionExplain: Right: exclusive needs no other holder.
Shared and exclusive cannot coexist.
Exclusive mode may not coexist with any lock.
No abort is triggered just by the request.
questions.explain: An exclusive lock requires that no other transaction holds any lock on the object.

questions.q: Why is the protocol called two-phase locking?
options: Transactions run in two stages, one per replica
Locks are acquired during execution and all released at the end
Locks are first prepared and then committed across nodes
Each lock is taken twice, once for reading and once for writing
optionExplain: Replicas are not part of the name.
Right: acquire then release.
Preparing and committing describes two-phase commit, which is different.
Each lock is not taken twice.
questions.explain: The phases are lock acquisition during execution and release at the end.
questions.rule: Acquire, then release at the end.

questions.q: True or false: A transaction that first reads and then writes an object may upgrade its shared lock to an exclusive lock.
questions.explain: The upgrade works the same as getting an exclusive lock directly.
questions.rule: Upgrade works like a fresh exclusive request.
questions.teaches: Lock upgrades follow the same rules as requesting an exclusive lock directly, so an upgrade must wait while other transactions hold shared locks.

questions.q: A payments transaction reads a balance, then updates it, under 2PL, and others are reading the same row. What may delay the update?
options: The row is locked for writing automatically at the read
The update must wait for the next snapshot
The database must first replicate the lock
Other shared holders must release before the upgrade to exclusive can proceed
optionExplain: The read takes only a shared lock.
2PL does not use snapshots.
Replication of locks is not part of the protocol.
Right: the upgrade waits for other shared holders.
questions.explain: An upgrade is as strict as requesting an exclusive lock.
questions.teaches: Read-then-write patterns can cause two transactions to wait on each other's shared locks, which leads to deadlock.

questions.q: Transaction A waits for a lock held by B, and B waits for a lock held by A. What is this called?
options: A deadlock
A lost update
A dirty write
A phantom
optionExplain: Right: a cycle of waits.
A lost update is overwriting without incorporating changes.
A dirty write overwrites uncommitted data; here two transactions wait on each other.
A phantom changes a search result, not lock waits.
questions.explain: Two transactions each stuck waiting for the other. The card next gives the response.

questions.q: When a database detects a deadlock, it aborts one of the transactions, and the application must ____ it.
questions.explain: The aborted transaction needs to be retried by the application.

questions.q: A deadlock occurs between two orders, and the database aborts one. What should the application do?
options: Switch off locking and rerun both
Ignore the failure, since the data is already updated
Assume the other transaction failed too
Retry the aborted transaction from the start
optionExplain: Disabling locking reopens the races.
An aborted transaction left no changes.
The other transaction was allowed to continue.
Right: retry the aborted transaction.
questions.explain: Aborting is how the database lets the others make progress; the app retries.

questions.q: Compared with lock-based read committed, how often do deadlocks occur under 2PL serializable isolation?
options: Never, since 2PL orders its locks
Equally often, since both use locks
Much more frequently
Much less frequently, since locks are held longer
optionExplain: 2PL does not prevent deadlocks.
2PL holds more locks for longer.
Right: more locks held longer mean more waiting cycles.
Longer holds make cycles more likely, not less.
questions.explain: Deadlocks can happen in both, but occur more often under 2PL.

questions.q: True or false: When a deadlock victim is retried, it starts over and repeats all its work, so frequent deadlocks mean significant wasted effort.
questions.explain: A retried transaction needs to do its work all over again.
questions.teaches: When a transaction is aborted by deadlock and retried, it must redo all its work, so frequent deadlocks waste significant effort.

questions.q: A ticketing service sees many deadlocks after moving from read committed to 2PL serializable. What explains the rise?
options: Retries remove the locks of other transactions
Serializable 2PL takes more locks and holds them to commit
The database now shares locks between unrelated rows
Serializable isolation disables deadlock detection
optionExplain: Retries do not remove other transactions' locks.
Right: more and longer locks mean more cycles.
Locks remain per object or range.
Detection still operates and aborts victims.
questions.explain: Access patterns that held one lock briefly now hold several until the end.
questions.teaches: Because 2PL holds locks until the end of a transaction, a transaction touching many rows can create many lock-wait cycles under contention.

questions.q: A database using 2PL serves most requests quickly, but some take many seconds under heavy contention. What explains the slow tail?
options: Readers never need to wait for writers
Locks are acquired only at commit time
Transactions queue behind others holding locks
The database drops locks after a fixed timeout
optionExplain: Readers do wait for writers under 2PL.
Locks are acquired as objects are accessed.
Right: waits are unbounded and queues form.
Locks are held to the end, not dropped on a short timeout.
questions.explain: Queues of waiting transactions stretch the tail. The card next gives the causes.

questions.q: Under 2PL, latencies can be unstable and very slow at high ____ when there is contention in the workload.
questions.explain: A single slow transaction can bring the rest of the system to a halt.

questions.q: Which are reasons 2PL performs worse than weak isolation?
options: Reduced concurrency, since racy transactions wait for each other
Every transaction reads from a stale snapshot
Locks are released as soon as each statement finishes
The overhead of acquiring and releasing locks
optionExplain: By design, concurrent transactions that might race do not proceed together.
Snapshots belong to snapshot isolation, not 2PL.
2PL holds locks until commit or abort, not until a statement ends.
Lock management costs time on every access.
questions.explain: Lock overhead and, more importantly, lost concurrency slow 2PL.

questions.q: Which workload is 2PL most likely to handle badly?
options: Short transactions spread over unrelated rows
Mostly read-only queries on disjoint data
A single user issuing one transaction at a time
Many transactions contending for the same few rows
optionExplain: Short, disjoint transactions seldom collide.
Disjoint reads rarely wait for one another.
A single user creates no contention.
Right: contention causes queues.
questions.explain: High contention turns locks into queues.

questions.q: True or false: Even if all your transactions are short, a queue may form under 2PL if several transactions want the same object.
questions.explain: A transaction may then wait for several others before it can do anything.
questions.rule: Short does not mean no queue.
questions.teaches: Even with short transactions, a queue can form on a popular object, so one transaction may have to wait for several others to complete.

questions.q: An analytics query that scans a big table runs under 2PL beside an order-entry workload. What risk should the team expect?
options: Its many locks may stall order entry and degrade the whole system
The query will be aborted on its first read
Nothing, since scans take no locks
Order entry will be faster because locks batch writes
optionExplain: Right: a transaction acquiring many locks can halt the rest.
Reads are not aborted by default.
Under 2PL, reads take shared locks.
Locks hold writers back; they do not speed them.
questions.explain: One transaction that accesses lots of data can make others wait.
questions.teaches: Long read-only queries are better run on a consistent snapshot than under 2PL, where they would block writers.

questions.q: One transaction searched room 123 bookings from noon to 1 p.m.; another inserts a booking in that window. What should a serializable lock-based database do?
options: Allow it, but abort the first transaction later
Make the insert wait
Allow it, since the bookings do not yet exist
Block all inserts in the whole database
optionExplain: Aborting later does not prevent the phantom in time.
Right: the new row would match the searched condition.
Not-yet-existing rows are exactly what a predicate lock covers.
Blocking everything is more than the condition requires.
questions.explain: The condition itself must be locked. The card next names the mechanism.

questions.q: A lock that belongs to all objects matching a search condition, rather than to one row, is a ____ lock.
questions.explain: It applies even to objects that do not yet exist but might be added.

questions.q: An insert books room 123 from 12:15 to 12:45. Another transaction holds a shared predicate lock on room 123, noon to 1 p.m. What happens?
options: The insert proceeds because the row is new
The insert waits until the other transaction commits or aborts
The insert proceeds and the lock is widened
The insert is rejected permanently
optionExplain: New rows matching the predicate must wait.
Right: the new value matches the predicate.
Locks are not widened by the insert.
It waits and can proceed later.
questions.explain: A writer checks whether old or new values match any existing predicate lock.

questions.q: What distinguishes a predicate lock from an ordinary row lock?
options: It covers all rows matching a condition, including rows not yet inserted
It is held only until the end of the statement
It covers one row but with higher priority
It covers only rows already in the index
optionExplain: Right: the unit of locking is a condition, not a row.
Locks are held to the end of the transaction.
Priority is not the difference.
Covering absent rows is the point.
questions.explain: Because the lock attaches to a condition, it can guard rows that do not exist.

questions.q: True or false: With predicate locks added, two-phase locking prevents write skew and other races, so its isolation is serializable.
questions.explain: Predicate locks close the phantom gap that row locks leave open.
questions.teaches: Without predicate locks, 2PL on rows alone would leave phantoms, so adding them is what makes the isolation level serializable.

questions.q: Could a predicate lock guard the rule that no two writers create the same time bucket?
options: Yes, but only if the bucket already exists
No, since predicate locks only protect existing rows
Yes, the lock on the bucket condition would block the second creator
No, since predicate locks apply only to updates
optionExplain: Existing rows are not required.
They guard rows not yet inserted.
Right: absence checks are what predicates cover.
They apply to inserts, updates and deletes.
questions.explain: Predicate locks cover the case of checking that something does not exist.
questions.teaches: Predicate locks are applied to inserts, updates and deletes alike, and are checked against both the old and the new value of a changed row.

questions.q: Why is it safe to replace a predicate lock with a lock on a larger set of rows?
options: The database can then skip locking altogether
Larger locks are released earlier than small ones
Larger sets contain fewer objects to check
Any write matching the original predicate also matches the larger set
optionExplain: Locking is still required.
Lock release timing is unrelated.
A larger set holds more objects, not fewer.
Right: the approximation covers at least what the predicate covered.
questions.explain: Widening only adds protection. The card next shows how to do it with an index.

questions.q: Index-range locking is also known as ____ locking.
questions.explain: It is a simplified approximation of predicate locking.

questions.q: A bookings table has an index on room_id. A transaction searches room 123. How can the database protect against phantoms cheaply?
options: Lock the application server's connection
Lock every row in the table in exclusive mode
Take no lock, since the rows may not exist
Attach a shared lock to the index entry for room 123
optionExplain: Connections do not protect rows.
That is much broader than needed.
Without a lock, phantoms would occur.
Right: a writer touching that index entry meets the lock.
questions.explain: Another transaction inserting a booking for room 123 must update the same index part and will wait.

questions.q: Compared with predicate locks, what is the trade-off of index-range locks?
options: More precise and faster, with no downside
Less precise and sometimes over-locking
Equally precise but harder to implement
Cheaper but unsafe against phantoms
optionExplain: They are less precise, not more.
Right: coarser and cheaper.
They are less precise, not equal.
They still protect against phantoms.
questions.explain: They may lock a bigger range than necessary, but the low overhead makes them a good compromise.

questions.q: True or false: If no suitable index exists for a range lock, the database can fall back to a shared lock on the entire table.
questions.explain: This is safe but stops all other transactions writing to the table.
questions.teaches: The whole-table fallback is a safe fallback position but hurts performance because it blocks all other writers to the table.

questions.q: A file-sync search filters by folder, but there is no index on folder. What follows under 2PL?
options: The database may lock the whole table, safe but harmful to write throughput
The search is aborted at once
Phantoms become possible because no index exists
Nothing, since an index is never needed for locking
optionExplain: Right: safe fallback, high cost.
Searches are not aborted for lack of an index.
The fallback keeps protection in place.
Without an index the table lock is used.
questions.explain: An index lets the database lock only a range instead of the table.
questions.teaches: Adding an index on the searched column lets the database attach range locks rather than lock the whole table.

questions.q: A system lets transactions run freely, then checks at commit whether anything went wrong and aborts if so. What is this style called?
options: Serial execution
Pessimistic concurrency control
Optimistic concurrency control
Two-phase locking
optionExplain: Serial execution forbids concurrent work.
Pessimistic control waits before proceeding.
Right: proceed first, check later.
2PL blocks on conflicting access.
questions.explain: Proceeding and checking afterwards defines optimism. The card next compares the two styles.

questions.q: Two-phase locking is a ____ concurrency control mechanism: if anything might go wrong, it waits until the situation is safe.
questions.explain: It follows the mutual-exclusion principle.

questions.q: A workload has high contention on a few hot rows and little spare capacity. Which family is likely to behave worse?
options: Serial execution, since it aborts the most
Optimistic control
Pessimistic control, since it never waits
Neither, since both behave the same under contention
optionExplain: Serial execution does not abort for conflicts.
Right: many aborts add retry load.
Pessimistic control waits when it must.
Contention separates them.
questions.explain: Optimistic control performs badly when many transactions touch the same objects.

questions.q: Sort each technique by whether it is pessimistic or optimistic.

items.t: Two-phase locking
Serial execution on a single thread
Serializable snapshot isolation
Checking for violations when a transaction commits

questions.explain: Locks and serial order wait first; SSI and commit-time checks act first and verify later.

questions.q: True or false: Commutative atomic operations, such as concurrent counter increments with no read in the transaction, reduce contention.
questions.explain: The order of increments does not matter, so they can all apply without conflicting.
questions.teaches: Concurrent increments of a counter commute when the counter is not read in the same transaction, so they can be applied in any order without conflicts.

questions.q: A metrics service updates a per-minute counter from many writers and rarely reads it. Why does optimistic control suit this?
options: Increments commute
Counters cannot be stored in a snapshot
Writers must wait for each other, so aborts are never needed
Optimistic control forbids reading the counter
optionExplain: Right: commutative writes reduce contention.
Counters are stored in snapshots as any data.
Optimistic control does not make them wait.
Reading is allowed; the point is the writes.
questions.explain: Fewer conflicts means fewer aborts under optimistic control.
questions.teaches: Reducing conflicts through commutative operations lets optimistic control perform well on write-heavy counters.

questions.q: A team wants serializability but cannot accept 2PL's blocking or serial execution's one-core limit. Which approach does the chapter call very promising?
options: Read committed with explicit locks everywhere
Repeatable read as implemented by any vendor
Serializable snapshot isolation
Dirty read prevention with longer timeouts
optionExplain: Read committed leaves write skew and lost updates for manual handling.
Repeatable read varies by vendor and often is only snapshot isolation.
Right: SSI is the optimistic route to serializability.
Timeouts do not change which races are possible.
questions.explain: SSI promises full serializability with a small penalty. The card next gives its structure.

questions.q: SSI is based on ____ isolation: all reads in a transaction come from a consistent snapshot of the database.
questions.explain: On top of it, SSI adds an algorithm to detect serialization conflicts.

questions.q: Match each system with its relationship to SSI, according to the chapter.
questions.explain: SSI appears in single-node and distributed databases and has an academic origin.

questions.q: How does SSI differ from earlier optimistic concurrency control techniques?
options: It is based on snapshot isolation
It uses exclusive locks for all reads
It requires application code to detect conflicts
It runs all transactions on a single thread
optionExplain: Right: snapshot reads plus conflict detection.
It does not use locks that block.
The database performs the detection.
It permits concurrent execution.
questions.explain: The main difference is the snapshot basis.

questions.q: True or false: SSI was first described in 2008 and is much older than two-phase locking.
questions.explain: SSI is fairly new compared with other mechanisms, which is why its performance is still being proven.
questions.teaches: SSI is young compared with other concurrency control mechanisms, which is why its real-world performance is still being proven.

questions.q: A ride-booking team wants a serializable default with predictable read latency. What does SSI's design offer them?
options: All transactions run on a single core
Readers and writers do not block each other
Aborts never occur
Readers wait for writers, as in 2PL
optionExplain: That is serial execution.
Right: no blocking between readers and writers.
SSI aborts transactions that fail the check.
That is 2PL behaviour.
questions.explain: Not blocking readers keeps latency more predictable.
questions.teaches: SSI keeps the snapshot-isolation property that writers do not block readers, and vice versa, which makes query latency more predictable.

questions.q: A transaction saw two doctors on call and wrote itself off call. Before commit, the other doctor leaves. What is the problem?
options: Its write was lost by another transaction
Its snapshot was corrupted
It read uncommitted data
The premise behind its decision no longer holds
optionExplain: No other write overwrote its write; its decision rests on stale data.
The snapshot was consistent, only no longer current.
It read committed data, which later changed.
Right: the premise is outdated.
questions.explain: A decision built on stale facts is the problem. The card next states what the database must do.

questions.q: A fact that was true at the beginning of a transaction and drives its decisions is called a ____.
questions.explain: If the premise is no longer true at commit, the writes may be invalid.

questions.q: A snapshot-isolated transaction counted open slots, found three and booked one. Meanwhile another committed bookings. What must a serializable database do?
options: Detect that the count may be outdated and abort the transaction if needed
Let it commit, since the count was correct at the start
Update the count in the transaction silently
Abort every transaction that reads
optionExplain: Right: stale premise, so abort if affected.
The count is no longer valid, so committing risks write skew.
Silent updates change the logic behind its back.
Read-only transactions are safe and need not abort.
questions.explain: The database must detect actions based on an outdated premise.

questions.q: The database cannot see how the application uses a query result. What must it assume?
options: Query results never influence later writes
Only the application can decide to abort
Only changes to rows the transaction later writes matter
Any change in the result may make that transaction's writes invalid
optionExplain: Decisions often rest on query results.
The database must enforce serializability itself.
Dependencies can go through other rows or values.
Right: be safe by assuming a causal dependency.
questions.explain: A causal dependency between reads and writes is assumed.

questions.q: Sort each case by whether the premise rule applies.

items.t: Decided to leave on call after counting two doctors, one has since left
Booked a room after checking no overlapping booking existed
A read-only report running on its snapshot
A transaction that never reads before writing

questions.explain: Only transactions that read and then write can act on an outdated premise.

questions.q: True or false: Under snapshot isolation, a query result may be out of date by commit time, because data may have changed meanwhile.
questions.explain: This is why write skew can occur.
questions.teaches: Under snapshot isolation the query result may no longer be up to date by commit time, so the database must check, at commit, whether the premise has changed.

questions.q: A payments service reads a balance and decides to approve a withdrawal. What is the premise?
options: That the withdrawal will be logged
That the network is reliable
That the balance was high enough at the time of the read
That the user has a password
optionExplain: Logging is not the fact the decision rests on.
Reliability is not the checked fact.
Right: the decision depends on the balance.
Passwords are unrelated to the check.
questions.explain: The premise is the fact the decision relied on.
questions.teaches: If the balance changes before commit, for example through a concurrent withdrawal, the approval may no longer be valid.

questions.q: A transaction reads under MVCC and ignores an uncommitted write by another transaction. When should SSI check whether that matters?
options: Only after the writer aborts
When the reading transaction wants to commit
At the instant the write is ignored
Never, since ignored writes are harmless
optionExplain: Waiting for an abort leaves stale reads undetected.
Right: check at commit.
Aborting at once might be unnecessary.
Ignored writes can matter if they commit later.
questions.explain: The check is deferred to commit. The card next explains why.

questions.q: SSI tracks writes ignored because of MVCC ____ rules, then checks them when the transaction commits.
questions.explain: A write ignored at read time may have taken effect by commit time.

questions.q: Transaction 43 ignored transaction 42's uncommitted write. At 43's commit, 42 has committed. What does SSI do?
options: Commit 43 and abort 42
Commit both without checks
Abort 43
Abort 42, since it committed late
optionExplain: 42 already committed and cannot be undone.
Skipping checks permits write skew.
Right: the ignored write took effect.
42's commit was valid.
questions.explain: 43's premise is no longer true, so it must abort.

questions.q: Why does SSI wait until commit instead of aborting the moment a stale read is detected?
options: Because MVCC forbids early checks
Because aborts cannot be done before commit
Because snapshots expire at commit
The transaction may be read-only, and the writer might abort
optionExplain: Nothing forbids an early check.
Aborts are possible any time.
Snapshots do not expire at commit.
Right: avoid unnecessary aborts.
questions.explain: Read-only transactions are safe, and the ignoring writer may not commit.

questions.q: True or false: By avoiding unnecessary aborts, SSI preserves snapshot isolation's support for long-running reads from a consistent snapshot.
questions.explain: Read-only transactions need not abort, so long reads stay possible.
questions.teaches: Deferring the check preserves long-running read-only queries on a consistent snapshot, which would be hurt by early aborts.

questions.q: A nightly report reads a big snapshot while writers commit. Under SSI, when might it be aborted?
options: Not at all
Whenever a writer is uncommitted
As soon as any writer commits
At the first read it makes
optionExplain: Right: read-only reports are safe.
Uncommitted writers do not trigger aborts for reports.
Writers committing do not abort a read-only report.
Reads do not trigger aborts.
questions.explain: Only read-write transactions with stale premises need aborting.
questions.teaches: Long read-only reports run on a snapshot without locks and are not aborted by SSI.

questions.q: Under SSI, one transaction writes data that another recently read. What does the writer do?
options: Waits until the reader commits
Notifies the reader that its read may be outdated, without waiting
Reads the reader's data to compare
Aborts itself at once
optionExplain: Waiting is 2PL behaviour.
Right: a tripwire, not a lock.
Comparing data is not the mechanism.
Writers are not aborted for this reason alone.
questions.explain: SSI locks act as tripwires. The card next gives the full procedure.

questions.q: In SSI, the record of who read a range acts like a ____ rather than a lock, since it notifies instead of blocking.
questions.explain: The writer finds the record and notifies the readers.

questions.q: Transactions 42 and 43 each read on-call doctors for shift 1234 and each write. 42 commits first. What happens when 43 tries to commit?
options: It commits, since it has not been notified
It aborts
It waits for 42 to commit again
It commits and 42 is rolled back
optionExplain: It was notified, and the conflicting write is committed.
Right: the notified transaction aborts.
42 has already committed.
Committed transactions are not rolled back.
questions.explain: 43's premise was invalidated by 42's committed write.

questions.q: In the same scenario, 42 commits first even though 43's write affected 42's read. Why is 42 allowed to commit?
options: 43 has not committed, so its write has not yet taken effect
Because 42 has a lower transaction ID with automatic priority
Because 43 is read-only
Because notifications are ignored for the first committer
optionExplain: Right: uncommitted writes do not yet count.
Priority is not the reason.
43 writes, so it is not read-only.
The notification is real but its cause had not committed.
questions.explain: Only committed conflicting writes cause aborts.

questions.q: Sort each property by whether it describes SSI tripwires or 2PL locks.

items.t: Does not block other transactions
Notifies transactions that their reads may be outdated
Makes writers wait for readers to finish
Prevents the conflicting write until commit

questions.explain: SSI's records inform rather than block; 2PL's locks make other transactions wait.

questions.q: True or false: Information about what a transaction read can be forgotten once it has finished and all concurrent transactions have finished.
questions.explain: It needs to be kept only for a while.
questions.teaches: Read records need to be kept only until the transaction and all concurrent transactions have finished, after which the database can discard them.

questions.q: A file-sync service has no index on its quota check. How does SSI track reads?
options: It tracks each file separately in memory
It blocks all writes to the table
At the table level
It cannot track them and so becomes unsafe
optionExplain: Per-file tracking needs an index or finer data.
SSI does not block writers.
Right: coarser tracking is the fallback.
It remains safe by tracking at table level.
questions.explain: Without an index the information is tracked at the table level.
questions.teaches: Coarser tracking is faster but may abort more transactions than strictly necessary.

questions.q: Which feature of SSI makes read latency more predictable than under 2PL?
options: All reads take exclusive locks
All reads wait for the next snapshot
Reads are routed to a single thread
Writers do not block readers, and readers do not block writers
optionExplain: Exclusive locks would block others.
SSI reads from the snapshot they started with.
SSI is not single-threaded.
Right: no lock waits for readers.
questions.explain: Without lock waits, latency varies less. The card next compares the techniques.

questions.q: The ____ rate significantly affects the overall performance of SSI.
questions.explain: Long read-write transactions are likely to conflict and abort.

questions.q: Which are advantages of SSI over its alternatives?
options: Transactions do not block waiting for locks held by others
Aborts never happen
Conflict detection can be distributed across machines
Transactions can be long without any penalty
Read-only queries can run on a snapshot without locks
optionExplain: Unlike 2PL, readers and writers do not wait for each other.
SSI aborts transactions that fail its check.
FoundationDB spreads detection, so SSI is not tied to one core.
Long read-write transactions are likely to abort.
Read-only work avoids lock overhead.
questions.explain: Non-blocking, distributable, lock-free reads are SSI's strengths.

questions.q: Which kind of transaction is a poor fit for SSI?
options: A short read-write transaction
A long read-only query
A short read-only query
A read-write transaction that runs for a long time
optionExplain: Short read-write transactions conflict rarely.
Long read-only queries are typically fine.
Short reads are unproblematic.
Right: long read-write work conflicts and aborts.
questions.explain: Long read-write transactions are likely to run into conflicts.

questions.q: True or false: Detailed tracking of transactions gives precise aborts but costs bookkeeping; coarser tracking is faster but may abort more than needed.
questions.explain: This is one of the engineering trade-offs.
questions.teaches: The granularity of read and write tracking trades precision against bookkeeping overhead, and PostgreSQL uses theory to prove some overwritten reads harmless to reduce unnecessary aborts.

questions.q: A ticketing site has mostly read-only browsing and a few short purchases. Which serializable technique matches best, per the chapter?
options: None, since read-heavy loads cannot be serializable
SSI, since reads run lock-free on snapshots and purchases are short
2PL, since readers should block purchases
Serial execution, since reads must run on one thread
optionExplain: SSI is described as appealing for read-heavy workloads.
Right: read-heavy loads suit SSI.
Blocking readers would hurt a read-heavy site.
Reads can run elsewhere on snapshots.
questions.explain: Lock-free reads are very appealing for read-heavy workloads.
questions.teaches: Read-only queries running lock-free on a consistent snapshot are what make SSI attractive for read-heavy workloads.

questions.q: An application updates a record and its denormalized copy without a transaction, and the server crashes between the two writes. What results?
options: The copy goes out of sync with the source
Both writes are automatically rolled back
The database repairs the copy on restart
The crash is hidden from the application
optionExplain: Right: no transaction means partial effects.
Rollback requires a transaction.
Repair requires atomic grouping.
The failure is visible in the data.
questions.explain: Partial failure leaves data inconsistent. The card next summarizes why transactions help.

questions.q: Transactions reduce many errors to a transaction ____, after which the application tries again.
questions.explain: Aborting and retrying is the application's recovery path.

questions.q: A service only ever reads and writes single records by key. Does it need multi-object transactions?
options: Yes, but only on weekends
Yes, since all services require them
Probably not
No, but only if it has no users
optionExplain: Timing of use is irrelevant.
Not every application is susceptible to every problem.
Right: simple access needs less.
User count is irrelevant.
questions.explain: Applications with very simple access patterns can probably manage without transactions.

questions.q: Sort each problem by whether transactions help prevent it.

items.t: Denormalized data going out of sync after a crash
Unexpected concurrency between two clients
A user entering the wrong password
A product manager changing requirements

questions.explain: Transactions address faults and races, not human error or changing requirements.

questions.q: True or false: Transactions are valuable only for relational databases and are not relevant for other data models.
questions.explain: Transactions are a valuable database feature no matter which data model is used.
questions.rule: Transactions apply to any data model.
questions.teaches: The chapter's examples used a relational data model, but transactions are a valuable database feature regardless of the data model.

questions.q: A chat team debates adding transactions to a system where several services touch the same data. What does the chapter suggest?
options: Transactions only matter for read-only workloads
Transactions reduce the number of error cases to think about for complex access patterns
Transactions replace testing
Transactions remove the need to handle any failure
optionExplain: They matter for writes and concurrency.
Right: they cut the error cases.
Testing remains necessary.
Aborts still need retry handling.
questions.explain: Without them, reasoning about interacting accesses becomes very difficult.
questions.teaches: Without transactions, many error scenarios such as crashes, network failures, full disks and concurrency can leave data inconsistent in various ways.

questions.q: A client reads another client's writes before they are committed. Which anomaly is this?
options: A dirty read
A lost update, since a write is affected
A dirty write, since uncommitted data is involved
Read skew, since the values are mismatched
optionExplain: Right: reading uncommitted data is a dirty read.
A lost update is a clobbered read-modify-write cycle.
A dirty write is overwriting uncommitted data, not reading it.
Read skew involves committed values seen at different times.
questions.explain: Reading uncommitted data is a dirty read. The card next lists all the anomalies.

questions.q: A transaction reads something, decides on what it saw, and writes, but the premise is no longer true by then: this is called write ____.
questions.explain: Only serializable isolation prevents this anomaly.

questions.q: A client reads two committed balances at different moments, and the total does not add up. Which anomaly is this?
options: Lost update, since a total was off
Dirty read, since values were mismatched
Dirty write, since two values changed
Read skew
optionExplain: A lost update requires a clobbered read-modify-write.
Dirty reads involve uncommitted data.
Dirty writes need two writers overwriting.
Right: committed values from different moments.
questions.explain: Mismatched committed reads are read skew.

questions.q: Which anomaly is prevented only by serializable isolation?
options: Dirty reads
Dirty writes
Write skew
Read skew
optionExplain: Read committed prevents dirty reads.
Almost all implementations prevent dirty writes.
Right: only serializable prevents write skew.
Snapshot isolation prevents read skew.
questions.explain: Other anomalies are covered by weaker levels, though some by manual locking.

questions.q: True or false: Snapshot isolation prevents straightforward phantom reads, but phantoms in the context of write skew need special treatment, such as index-range locks.
questions.explain: Read-only queries are safe, but decisions on absence need stronger protection.
questions.rule: Phantoms in write skew need more.
questions.teaches: The special treatment for phantoms in write skew, such as index-range locks, is needed because snapshot isolation only prevents straightforward phantom reads.

questions.q: A metrics team sees a total that is off because two writers updated a counter from the same starting value. Which anomaly is this?
options: Lost update
Phantom read
Dirty read
Read skew
optionExplain: Right: one read-modify-write overwrote the other.
No search result changed.
No uncommitted data was read.
No mismatched reads occurred.
questions.explain: Two writers overwrote one another's increments.
questions.teaches: Lost updates are prevented automatically by some snapshot isolation implementations, while others require a manual lock such as SELECT FOR UPDATE.

questions.q: Which protection is the chapter's only complete answer to write skew?
options: Read committed isolation, which blocks dirty reads
Snapshot isolation alone, which gives consistent reads
Serializable isolation
Retrying every transaction after a failure
optionExplain: Read committed leaves write skew possible.
Snapshot isolation still lets write skew happen.
Right: only serializable isolation prevents write skew.
Retrying does not close the race.
questions.explain: Only serializable isolation prevents write skew. The card next maps each anomaly to its defence.

questions.q: Read skew is most commonly prevented with ____ isolation, which lets a transaction read from a consistent snapshot.
questions.explain: It is usually implemented with multi-version concurrency control.

questions.q: A team on snapshot isolation sees lost updates on a counter. What are the chapter's options?
options: Read uncommitted isolation
Disabling MVCC
