Switching the counter to a larger integer type
Atomic updates or explicit locking such as SELECT FOR UPDATE
optionExplain: Weaker isolation worsens the issue.
Disabling MVCC removes the snapshot, not the lost update.
Integer size is unrelated.
Right: manual protection or automatic detection.
questions.explain: Some implementations prevent lost updates automatically; others do not.

questions.q: Sort each defence by whether it requires developer effort.

items.t: Dirty-write prevention in almost all implementations
Read skew prevention by snapshot isolation
Explicit SELECT FOR UPDATE under snapshot isolation
Materialized conflicts when nothing else works

questions.explain: Weak levels leave some anomalies to the application.

questions.q: True or false: Only serializable isolation protects against all the race conditions discussed in the chapter.
questions.explain: Weak levels leave some anomalies for the developer to handle manually.
questions.teaches: Weak isolation levels protect against some anomalies but leave you, the developer, to handle others manually, for example using explicit locking.

questions.q: A ride-booking team has a booking table, snapshot isolation and write skew risk. What does the chapter say is the more complete defence?
options: Reading from a replica
A serializable isolation level
A retry on every read
A longer transaction timeout
optionExplain: Replicas introduce lag, not protection.
Right: only serializable prevents write skew.
Retrying reads does not affect writes.
Timeouts do not close races.
questions.explain: Serializable isolation is the protection that covers write skew.
questions.teaches: For write skew with phantoms, index-range locks under 2PL or SSI provide the needed protection without manual materialized conflicts.

questions.q: A workload has short in-memory transactions and modest write volume. Which technique does the chapter call simple and effective?
options: Materializing conflicts
Executing transactions literally in serial order
Two-phase locking
Read committed with locks
optionExplain: Materialized conflicts are a last resort.
Right: serial order for fast transactions and low throughput.
2PL is the heavier choice.
Read committed is not serializable.
questions.explain: If transactions are fast and throughput low, serial execution is simple and effective.
questions.rule: Fast and low volume suits serial.

questions.q: Order the three serializable techniques from the oldest standard to the newest algorithm.
items: Two-phase locking
Serial execution on a single thread
Serializable snapshot isolation
questions.explain: 2PL held the standard role for decades, serial execution became viable around 2007, and SSI was described in 2008.

questions.q: A read-heavy store with low contention wants serializability and cannot tolerate lock waits. What fits best?
options: 2PL, since lock waits are acceptable
Read committed with explicit locks
SSI, since transactions proceed without blocking and read-only work is lock-free
Serial execution on a single node
optionExplain: The brief rules out lock waits.
That is not serializable by itself.
Right: optimistic with lock-free reads.
A single thread limits the throughput.
questions.explain: SSI fits when contention is low and spare capacity exists.

questions.q: Match each constraint to the technique it belongs to.
pairs: Throughput limited to one CPU core
questions.explain: Each technique's main limit arises from its core mechanism.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter's discussion of serializable techniques focuses on a single machine; transactions across several nodes pose further difficulties.
questions.explain: Distributed transactions are addressed in later chapters.
questions.teaches: The chapter explores ideas and algorithms mostly for one machine; transactions in distributed databases open a new set of difficult challenges for the next chapters.

questions.q: A payments team needs serializability for a small hot set of accounts with high contention. Which technique does the chapter's reasoning disfavour?
options: SSI, since high contention causes many aborts and retries
A single lock around all hot accounts
Two-phase locking with short transactions
Serial execution on a single node
optionExplain: Right: contention hurts optimistic control.
A coarse lock behaves like serial execution.
2PL queues rather than aborts.
Serial execution does not suffer aborts from contention.
questions.explain: Optimistic methods perform badly under high contention.
questions.teaches: Under high contention, pessimistic waiting can beat optimistic aborts, since retries add load to a system near maximum throughput.

questions.q: A memory chip on one server develops a fault. Which outcome do computer designers prefer?
questions.explain: Designers deliberately let a faulty computer crash rather than return wrong results. The card next shows what that choice means for distributed systems.
options: The machine keeps running and returns an occasional wrong value
The machine crashes completely instead of returning wrong results
The machine slows down and retries each operation until it passes
The machine reports success and logs the fault for later review
optionExplain: Staying up sounds helpful, but wrong results are hard to detect and confusing to deal with.
Right: a clean total failure is easier to handle than quietly wrong data.
Retrying sounds careful, but the design goal is a crash, not silent self-repair of results.
Logging is useful, but reporting success on a faulty machine would hand out wrong results.
questions.rule: A single computer is deterministic and either fully works or fully breaks, because designers prefer a crash to a wrong result.

questions.q: When hardware works correctly, the same operation on one computer gives the same result every time, so it is ____.
questions.explain: Determinism is why a healthy single computer is predictable: same input, same output.
questions.rule: A healthy single computer is deterministic.

questions.q: A report script on one healthy machine, with the same input, prints different totals on two runs. Which explanation fits the book?
questions.explain: On one machine with working hardware, a deterministic operation repeating itself is the design. A different result points at the software.
questions.rule: Suspect the software first on a single healthy machine.
options: A software bug, since good software on working hardware repeats itself
Normal physical randomness inside the processor on each run
A network partition between the script and its data
Clock drift between two nodes that disagree on the time
optionExplain: Right: the book blames badly written software, not the machine, for a computer that seems to have a bad day.
Physics is messy, but computers hide that mess and present an idealized, repeatable model.
No network is involved in this setup, so nothing here can partition.
There is only one machine here, so no second clock exists to disagree.

questions.q: True or false: A hardware problem on a single computer usually leaves it half-working but still returning answers.
questions.explain: A hardware problem usually ends in a total failure such as a crash, not a middle state.
questions.rule: Single computers are usually fully working or entirely broken.

questions.q: A colleague says code on five networked servers can rely on the same perfect model a single computer gives. What is wrong?
questions.explain: Computers hide physical messiness behind an idealized model, but that hiding stops at the machine boundary. Across a network, software must confront the real world.
questions.rule: The idealized model ends at the network.
options: With a network there is no choice but to face the messy physical world
Five servers are too few for any perfect model to apply
Servers are built from cheaper parts than a single computer is
The perfect model only ever holds for batch workloads
optionExplain: Right: the idealized model belongs to one computer; across a network the physical reality returns.
Count is not the issue: even two machines joined by a network lose the idealized model.
Part quality is not the point; the network between machines is what removes the guarantee.
The model is about one machine's behaviour, not about whether work is batch or online.

questions.q: A ride-booking app runs on one server and its main board fails. What does the single-computer design lead you to expect?
questions.explain: Hardware faults on one computer usually show up as a crash or failure to boot.
questions.rule: One machine's fault shows up as a crash.
questions.teaches: Typical outcomes of a hardware problem on one computer are a kernel panic, a blue screen of death or a failure to start up: total failures.
options: A degraded server that completes about half of the bookings
A total failure such as a kernel panic or a machine that will not start
A server that books rides but sometimes writes wrong prices
A server whose faults appear only when two bookings overlap
optionExplain: A half-working state is what a network of machines can show, not one healthy-designed computer.
Right: typical hardware faults end in kernel panic, a blue screen or failure to start up.
Wrong results are exactly what designers avoid by letting the machine crash.
Overlap-dependent faults are a concurrency matter, not the usual hardware failure outcome.

questions.q: A chat service runs on three servers. One has a dead disk while two serve users normally. What is this called?
questions.explain: A broken part beside working parts is a partial failure. The card next explains why that is the hard part.
options: A total failure
A deterministic fault
A Byzantine fault
A partial failure
optionExplain: Total failure would mean nothing works, but two servers still serve users.
Deterministic describes repeatable behaviour; this situation is the opposite kind of trouble.
Byzantine faults involve nodes that lie; a dead disk is not lying.
Right: part of the system is broken while the rest still works.
questions.rule: Partial failures are nondeterministic, and that nondeterminism is what makes distributed systems hard to work with.

questions.q: A broken part of a system next to parts that still work is called a ____ failure.
questions.explain: Partial failure is the defining difficulty of distributed systems.
questions.rule: Partial failure means some parts break while others work.

questions.q: A ticketing API call touches two nodes. It failed once, then worked on retry with identical input. What does the book say?
questions.explain: Because the network and partial failures are nondeterministic, the same operation can succeed at one time and fail at another.
questions.rule: Identical calls over a network can have different outcomes.
options: The caller must contain a bug, since identical input gives identical output
The second node is permanently dead and the retry hit a replacement
That is typical: multi-node operations may sometimes work and sometimes fail
The first attempt must have executed fully before the error appeared
optionExplain: That reasoning holds on one computer, but not when a network is involved.
Nothing says the node died; a temporary fault can explain a failure that then clears.
Right: partial failures are nondeterministic, so identical calls can differ.
A failure does not tell you how far the first attempt got, and may not mean it ran at all.

questions.q: Sort each situation by the kind of failure it shows.
questions.explain: Partial failure means part of a multi-node system is broken while the rest works. A standalone machine failing is the total failure of that machine.
questions.rule: A system with working and broken parts is in partial failure.

items.t: One rack is cut off while the rest of the cluster serves users
A single-node database loses power and stops
A call to a remote node works on some tries and fails on others
The kernel of a standalone server panics
One of five replicas stops answering while four respond
A laptop will not start after a hardware fault

questions.q: True or false: When a multi-node operation fails once, repeating it with the same input will fail again, because computers are deterministic.
questions.explain: Determinism describes one healthy computer. With several nodes and a network, outcomes can differ from try to try.
questions.rule: Do not carry single-machine determinism over a network.

questions.q: A metrics collector sends a counter update to another node and hears nothing for five seconds. What can it know?
questions.explain: A reply may be late, lost or absent, so the sender may not know whether the operation happened.
questions.rule: Silence does not tell you whether the operation happened.
questions.teaches: The time a message takes to cross a network is itself nondeterministic, so you may not even know whether an operation succeeded.
options: The update was lost, since replies come back within a few seconds
Nothing certain: delivery time is also unpredictable, so success is unknown
The remote node crashed, because silence is how crashes look
The update succeeded, because no error message came back
optionExplain: No such time limit exists; message travel time is nondeterministic.
Right: it cannot tell whether the update was applied, delayed or lost.
Silence has many causes besides a crash, so it does not prove one.
Missing news is not good news; an error or reply may itself be lost or late.

questions.q: A team runs a three-node service where nodes rarely fail. Which attitude do experienced operators recommend?
questions.explain: Faults will come sooner or later, so the guidance is to be pessimistic and to test. The card next sets out the reasoning.
options: Plan only for the faults seen in the last year of logs
Expect faults, including unlikely ones, and test how the system reacts
Add spare nodes and skip fault tests to save time
Handle faults when the first outage occurs in production
optionExplain: Past logs feel evidence-based, but unlikely faults are exactly the ones that surprise a system.
Right: in distributed systems suspicion and pessimism pay off.
Spare nodes help, but without testing nobody knows how the software reacts.
Waiting is cheap now but costs most when the fault finally arrives unprepared.
questions.rule: Assume faults will occur, build handling into the design, and provoke them in testing.

questions.q: In distributed systems, suspicion, pessimism and ____ pay off.
questions.explain: The book states this as the working attitude for distributed systems.
questions.rule: Suspicion, pessimism and paranoia pay off.

questions.q: Before launching, a ride-booking team wants to know how dispatch behaves when a node loses its network link. What does the book advise?
questions.explain: The book suggests artificially creating faults in testing to see what happens, so behaviour is known in advance.
questions.rule: Cause faults in testing to learn the behavior.
options: Trust the hosting vendor's redundancy and skip the experiment
Review the dispatch code carefully and assume it will cope
Create that situation artificially in a test environment and watch the result
Wait for the first real link failure and study the logs
optionExplain: Redundancy helps but does not tell you how your software reacts to a fault.
Reading code finds some problems, but behavior under real faults is learned by causing them.
Right: provoking faults on purpose shows what the software really does.
That finds out the answer on customers' time instead of in a test environment.

questions.q: Which points belong to the book's advice on faults? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: The advice is broad: design for many faults, build handling in, and make behavior known to operators.
questions.rule: Design for the whole range of faults.
options: Operators should know what behavior to expect in a fault
Assume faults are rare and hope for the best
Plan only for the faults that occur most often
Consider a wide range of faults, even fairly unlikely ones
Make fault handling part of the software design
optionExplain: Right: the people running the system need that knowledge.
The book calls this unwise.
Frequent faults come first in practice, but the advice includes rare ones.
Right: unlikely does not mean never.
Right: it cannot be bolted on after hoping for the best.

questions.q: True or false: In a system with only three nodes, fault handling can wait because most components work correctly most of the time.
questions.explain: Components may work most of the time, but sooner or later some part fails, and the software must then cope.
questions.rule: Small systems still need fault handling.

questions.q: A file-sync service has two servers and a fault happens about once a year. What follows for the design?
questions.explain: Even in small systems, some part will sooner or later be faulty, so the fault handling has to be designed.
questions.teaches: In a small system most components work most of the time, but sooner or later some part will become faulty, and the software must then handle it.
options: Handling can be dropped, because yearly faults cost less than the code
Only an operator runbook is needed, because software cannot handle rare faults
Two servers cannot fail at the same time, so no handling is needed
Handling must still be designed, because the fault will arrive sooner or later
optionExplain: Cost looks sensible, but an unhandled fault can leave the system in an unknown state.
A runbook helps, but the software's own behavior in the fault still has to be designed.
Failures do not need to coincide; one server failing already requires the software to react.
Right: rarity changes how often it happens, not whether the software must handle it.

questions.q: A wireless link flips a few bits at random. How can accurate data still reach the receiver?
questions.explain: Codes let a channel that gets some bits wrong still carry accurate data. The card next shows the general idea.
options: A stronger antenna removes all interference at the source
Error-correcting codes repair a small number of bit errors
The sender transmits each bit once and trusts the channel
The receiver discards any message that contained an error
optionExplain: Better hardware helps, but the question is how accuracy survives when errors still occur.
Right: redundancy in the code lets the receiver fix occasional errors.
Trust would pass the errors straight through to the receiver.
Dropping data does not deliver accurate data; it only avoids using bad data.
questions.rule: A layer on top can hide low-level faults, so the whole can be more reliable than its parts, up to a limit.

questions.q: Match each technology with what it does.
questions.explain: IP is the unreliable base; TCP and error-correcting codes build reliability on top of unreliable channels.
questions.rule: Reliability can be layered on unreliable parts.
pairs: May drop, delay, duplicate or reorder packets
Retransmits lost packets, removes duplicates, restores order
Repair a small number of bit errors in transmitted data

questions.q: A file-sync client downloads over TCP, and two packets swap places on the IP path. What does the application receive?
questions.explain: TCP hides reordering, loss and duplication from the application.
questions.rule: TCP gives ordered, complete streams on top of IP.
options: The data in the order it was sent
The two chunks swapped, followed by a checksum error
The first chunk only, with the second silently dropped
Both chunks twice, once in each order
optionExplain: Right: TCP reassembles packets into their original order.
TCP does the reordering work, so the application is spared from it.
TCP retransmits and reassembles, so nothing is dropped from the stream.
TCP removes duplicates; the application sees each byte once.

questions.q: True or false: A system cannot be more reliable than its least reliable component.
questions.explain: The book calls this an old idea in computing: build a more reliable system from a less reliable base.

questions.q: A developer says TCP makes network delays disappear, so timeouts are unnecessary. What is the flaw?
questions.explain: TCP improves on IP but has a ceiling: it cannot magically make the network faster or bounded.
questions.rule: TCP hides some faults but not delay.
questions.teaches: TCP can hide packet loss, duplication and reordering but it cannot magically remove delays in the network.
options: TCP hides loss, duplication and reordering but cannot remove delays
TCP only hides duplication, never loss or reordering
TCP works only inside one datacenter, never across the internet
TCP removes delays but can introduce data corruption
optionExplain: Right: delays remain visible to the application.
TCP covers all three; the weakness lies elsewhere.
Scope is not the limit; TCP runs across the internet daily.
Corruption is not what the book names as TCP's remaining limit; delay is.

questions.q: A drone sends video over a radio link. Interference swamps the signal. What happens to error-correcting codes?
questions.explain: Reliability from layering is real, but bounded: a heavy enough fault defeats the layer.
questions.rule: There is a limit to the gain.
questions.teaches: Error-correcting codes can repair a small number of single-bit errors, but if interference swamps the signal there is a fundamental limit to how much data gets through.
options: They repair every error given enough extra redundancy
They reach a fundamental limit on how much data gets through
They switch to TCP to retransmit the lost frames
They keep working but only at night, when noise is lower
optionExplain: More redundancy helps, but it cannot beat a channel that is swamped.
Right: codes handle a few errors, not a signal swamped by interference.
Codes and TCP are different mechanisms; codes do not become retransmission.
Nothing in the idea ties them to the time of day.

questions.q: Which workload is typical of a supercomputer?
questions.explain: Supercomputers target computation-heavy scientific jobs. The card next contrasts them with cloud computing.
options: Serving millions of shopping carts around the clock
Weather forecasting on thousands of CPUs
Keeping a chat history synchronized across phones
Storing photos for a social network
optionExplain: Large and demanding, but that is internet-service work with different needs.
Right: computation-heavy science is the classic HPC job.
This is an online service; supercomputers target computation, not live user traffic.
Storage at scale is a cloud service job rather than computation-heavy science.
questions.rule: Internet services sit at the cloud end, so plan for cloud-style faults rather than supercomputer-style reliability.

questions.q: Match each setting with its typical description.
questions.explain: The book describes a spectrum from HPC at one end to cloud at the other.
pairs: Multi-tenant datacenters, commodity machines, metered billing

questions.q: Sort each feature by the setting it typically describes.
questions.explain: HPC means big scientific computation; cloud means multi-tenant commodity machines with elastic, metered resources.
questions.rule: Match the feature to its end of the spectrum.

items.t: Thousands of CPUs simulating molecules
Metered billing per use
On-demand, elastic allocation
A computation-heavy weather forecast
Commodity computers on Ethernet
Shared by many customers in one datacenter

questions.q: A bank runs its own private datacenter for mixed internal applications. Where does it fall on the spectrum?
questions.explain: The book places traditional enterprise datacenters between the two extremes.
questions.rule: Enterprise datacenters are in the middle.
options: Between the two extremes, like a traditional enterprise datacenter
At the HPC end, since the bank owns the hardware
At the cloud end, since many applications share it
Outside the spectrum, because it is not on the internet
optionExplain: Right: such datacenters sit between HPC and cloud.
Owning hardware does not make it a supercomputer for scientific computation.
Sharing alone is not enough: cloud also means commodity, elastic, metered resources.
Internet connection does not decide the position on this spectrum.

questions.q: True or false: Cloud computing is a precisely defined term, so a datacenter either is or is not a cloud.
questions.explain: The book says cloud computing is not very well defined and is only often associated with certain features.

questions.q: A lab moves a simulation with fixed, known communication patterns from a supercomputer to a cloud datacenter. What should it expect about the network?
questions.explain: The network differs: HPC tunes it to known traffic, cloud uses general-purpose IP and Ethernet.
questions.rule: The workload's traffic pattern decides which network suits it.
questions.teaches: Supercomputers often use specialized network topologies such as multi-dimensional meshes and toruses for known communication patterns; large datacenters use IP and Ethernet in Clos topologies.
options: A general IP and Ethernet network instead of one tuned to its patterns
The same multi-dimensional mesh, since networks are standardized
No network at all, since cloud nodes share one memory
A faster network, since cloud providers buy the best hardware
optionExplain: Right: supercomputers use specialized topologies, datacenters use IP and Ethernet.
Meshes and toruses are specialized supercomputer choices, not datacenter defaults.
Cloud nodes communicate over a network and do not share memory.
Commodity parts give lower cost, not necessarily the best performance for a known pattern.

questions.q: A node dies during a weeks-long weather simulation on a supercomputer. What is the common response?
questions.explain: Supercomputers typically stop everything and restart from a checkpoint. The card next explains why that looks like a single computer.
options: Let the surviving nodes carry on and ignore the dead one
Replace the dead node live while the other nodes keep computing
Restart the simulation from its very beginning on spare nodes
Stop the whole workload, repair the node, restart from the last saved state
optionExplain: Plausible for an internet service, but a tightly coupled simulation cannot skip a node.
Live replacement is what fault-tolerant services do, not the usual supercomputer response.
This wastes weeks of work when a saved checkpoint exists.
Right: that is checkpoint-and-restart.
questions.rule: A supercomputer behaves like a single machine: if any part fails, let everything crash.

questions.q: A supercomputer job saves its state to durable storage from time to time; each saved state is called a ____.
questions.explain: Checkpoints let a job restart without redoing everything.

questions.q: A molecular simulation checkpoints on the hour. A node fails at 02:40, and the last checkpoint was at 02:00. Where does the restart begin?
questions.explain: Restarting from the last checkpoint is the standard recovery: everything after it is repeated.
questions.rule: Recovery restarts from the last checkpoint.
options: From the 02:40 state held in the surviving nodes' memory
From the very first checkpoint ever taken by the job
From wherever the failed node's last message was received
From the 02:00 checkpoint after the node is repaired
optionExplain: Surviving nodes' memory is not a consistent saved state of the whole job.
Only the latest checkpoint is needed, so older ones just waste work.
One node's last message does not describe the state of the whole computation.
Right: work since the last checkpoint is lost and redone.

questions.q: True or false: In handling a failed node, a supercomputer resembles a single computer more than it resembles a typical distributed internet service.
questions.explain: It lets partial failure escalate into total failure, as a kernel panic does on one machine.
questions.rule: Escalating to total failure is the single-machine style.

questions.q: An engineer says supercomputers tolerate partial failure well because the job continues on the remaining nodes. What is wrong?
questions.explain: The supercomputer approach is to stop and restart, not to carry on without the failed node.
questions.rule: Supercomputers stop; they do not tolerate.
options: They cannot checkpoint, so they must restart from scratch
They continue, but only after paying a cloud provider for spare nodes
They avoid partial failure by stopping the whole job, not by continuing
They tolerate it, though only for failures of the network
optionExplain: They do checkpoint; that is the mechanism for restarting.
Spare nodes from a provider are not part of the usual picture.
Right: the failure escalates into total failure.
The usual response applies to any failed node, not only network trouble.

questions.q: Which service could adopt stop-everything-and-restart with the least harm?
questions.explain: Online services must serve users at any time, while offline batch jobs tolerate a restart.
questions.rule: Fit the failure policy to whether work is online or offline.
questions.teaches: Offline (batch) jobs such as weather simulations can be stopped and restarted with fairly low impact, whereas online services must serve users with low latency at any time.
options: A live ride-dispatch system with drivers waiting for fares
A nightly batch report that can be rerun from a checkpoint
A checkout API that must answer within milliseconds
A chat service whose users expect messages at any time
optionExplain: Stopping dispatch for repair makes the service unavailable to users.
Right: offline jobs can be stopped and restarted with fairly low impact.
A paused checkout loses sales while the cluster is repaired.
Chat users need the service available at any time, so a full stop is not acceptable.

questions.q: A cluster has 5,000 commodity nodes. Which assumption is reasonable?
questions.explain: In very large systems failure is a constant background condition. The card next shows how services cope.
options: Failures are rare enough that each can be handled by a person
At any moment, something in the cluster is probably broken
If the hardware is good enough, failures stop after burn-in
A failure of any node means the whole service must restart
optionExplain: A person cannot keep up when thousands of parts fail at normal rates.
Right: with that many parts, constant failure somewhere is normal.
Parts keep failing; broken things get fixed and new things break.
That would leave the system recovering all the time instead of serving.
questions.rule: At scale, design the whole to keep working while individual nodes are broken, repaired or replaced.

questions.q: True or false: In a system with thousands of nodes, it is reasonable to assume that something is broken at any given moment.
questions.explain: Over time broken things are fixed and new things break, so some failure is always present.
questions.rule: Large systems always have some failure.

questions.q: A team must upgrade software on 40 nodes of a live service. Which approach matches the book?
questions.explain: Fault tolerance gives a bonus for operations: one node can be restarted while the others serve.
questions.rule: Tolerating node failure enables rolling upgrades.
options: Stop all 40 nodes, upgrade them together, and start them again
Upgrade a single node and wait a week before touching the next
A rolling upgrade, restarting one node at a time while service continues
Upgrade every node at once so they all share the same code version
optionExplain: This makes the service unavailable, which an online service cannot accept.
The point is continuity, not slowness; the rolling pattern does not need a week.
Right: tolerating a node being down lets upgrades proceed without interruption.
All-at-once is simple but exposes every node to the same fault together.

questions.q: A 10,000-node system that gives up on every failure ends up spending much of its time ____ from faults instead of doing useful work.
questions.explain: With something always failing somewhere, giving up each time turns recovery into the main activity.
questions.rule: Giving up on each failure does not scale.

questions.q: A cloud VM is responding slowly. A colleague says the service must wait until it is repaired. What does the book suggest instead?
questions.explain: Because the system tolerates failed nodes, a misbehaving virtual machine can be replaced.
questions.rule: Replace the bad node; do not wait.
options: Wait, because replacing machines breaks the service
Restart the whole cluster so all machines run alike
Ignore it, since slow nodes never matter for correctness
Kill it and request a new one, hoping the new one is faster
optionExplain: The tolerance idea is that replacement does not break the service.
A cluster-wide restart contradicts keeping the service running.
Slow nodes hurt users, and the fix is to replace them, not to ignore them.
Right: in cloud environments a replaced VM is cheap.

questions.q: A file-sync service adds a second region to keep data close to users. What new difficulty does the book name?
questions.explain: Spreading across regions trades lower user latency for communication over slower, less reliable links.
questions.teaches: In a geographically distributed deployment communication most likely goes over the internet, which is slow and unreliable compared with local networks, whereas supercomputers assume their nodes are close together.
options: Nodes in two regions can no longer be replaced independently
Commodity machines cannot be used in more than one region
Supercomputer-style checkpoints become mandatory in each region
Cross-region traffic crosses the internet, which is slower and less reliable than local networks
optionExplain: Nothing in the book ties regions to a loss of replaceability.
Commodity hardware is not restricted by region.
Checkpointing is the supercomputer approach, not a regional requirement.
Right: geographically distributed communication most likely goes over the internet.

questions.q: Two servers in a cluster need data that each holds. In a shared-nothing design, how does server A get B's data?
questions.explain: In shared-nothing designs machines can only ask each other over the network. The card next gives the definition.
options: By sending a request to B over the network
By reading B's memory directly across a shared bus
By mounting B's disk as if it were A's local disk
By waiting until a common clock shows the data is ready
optionExplain: Right: the network is the only path between machines.
Shared memory is exactly what shared-nothing excludes.
Direct disk access is also ruled out, apart from requests to a service.
Clocks do not move data between machines.
questions.rule: In a shared-nothing system the network is the only channel between machines.

questions.q: In a shared-nothing system, the ____ is the only way the machines can communicate.
questions.explain: Everything between machines is a message over the network.
questions.rule: The network is the only link.

questions.q: A chat engineer wants server A to read B's in-memory session table directly. What does shared-nothing allow?
questions.explain: One machine cannot access another's memory or disk except by making requests to a service over the network.
questions.rule: Remote data means a network request.
options: A request to a service on B over the network, which replies
A direct memory read, if both servers are in one rack
A direct read, but only for tables marked read-only
A direct read, provided the network is reliable
optionExplain: Right: access goes through a request over the network.
Rack proximity does not change the rule; each machine has its own memory.
Marking does not create shared memory; the table is still B's own.
Reliability of the network is irrelevant to whether memory is shared.

questions.q: Which statements describe a shared-nothing system? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: Own memory and disk plus communication only by network define shared-nothing.
questions.rule: No shared memory, no shared disk.
options: Each machine has its own memory and disk
All machines share one global clock and memory
Machines communicate only through the network
It requires special hardware to link machines
Machines read each other's memory directly over a bus
optionExplain: Right: nothing is shared.
No shared state is the defining feature.
Right: the network is the only way.
The point is that no special hardware is needed.
Direct reading contradicts the definition.

questions.q: True or false: Shared-nothing is the only possible way to build a distributed system.
questions.explain: The book says it is not the only way, though it has become the dominant approach for internet services.

questions.q: A startup chooses an architecture for a public web service. Which reason does the book give for shared-nothing?
questions.explain: Shared-nothing is comparatively cheap, uses commodity cloud services and achieves reliability through redundancy across datacenters.
questions.teaches: Shared-nothing is dominant for internet services because it is comparatively cheap with no special hardware, can use commoditized cloud services, and can achieve high reliability through redundancy across geographically distributed datacenters.
options: It gives the lowest latency, because machines share memory
It can reach high reliability through redundancy across several datacenters in different places
It removes the need for any failure handling in software
It requires specialized hardware that vendors guarantee
optionExplain: Shared memory is excluded, so this reason is wrong.
Right: redundancy across geographically distributed datacenters is one of its reasons.
Shared-nothing makes failure handling harder, not unnecessary.
The point is the opposite: no special hardware is needed.

questions.q: You send a request across a datacenter network. What does the network promise about delivery?
questions.explain: Such networks give no guarantee on either point. The card next defines them.
options: Delivery, but with an unpredictable delay
A response within one second if the target is alive
Delivery within a fixed time, or a clear error message
Nothing about when it arrives, or whether it arrives
optionExplain: Delivery is also not guaranteed, not only its timing.
No such time bound exists in this kind of network.
A guaranteed error report is also not part of the promise.
Right: delivery and timing are not guaranteed.
questions.rule: An asynchronous packet network guarantees neither when a packet arrives nor that it arrives.

questions.q: An asynchronous packet network gives no guarantee as to when a packet will arrive, or whether it will arrive at ____.
questions.explain: Neither timing nor delivery is guaranteed.
questions.rule: No guarantee on when or whether.

questions.q: A payments service sends a charge request and must decide how long to wait. What can the network tell it about a safe wait time?
questions.explain: Without a guaranteed bound, any chosen wait is an estimate.
questions.rule: No delay bound, so any wait is a guess.
options: The maximum delay of the datacenter, published by the network
A wait of one minute is always safe on a healthy network
Nothing: no upper bound on delay is guaranteed
The wait equals twice the time of the last request
optionExplain: Such a maximum is not provided by this kind of network.
Even healthy networks give no guarantee, and a minute is an invention.
Right: the delay of a packet has no guaranteed limit.
Past delays suggest a guess, but they are not a guarantee.

questions.q: True or false: A datacenter network that is only lightly loaded tonight therefore guarantees delivery times.
questions.explain: Light load makes delays short in practice, but the guarantee depends on the kind of network, which gives none here.
questions.rule: Behaving well is not the same as being guaranteed.

questions.q: A teammate says datacenter cables are short, so a packet is delivered within a millisecond and a hard timeout is safe. What is the flaw?
questions.explain: Typical speed is not a guarantee; the network can still delay or drop a packet.
options: Cable length has no effect on delays of any kind
The network type offers no maximum delay, so the hard timeout can be exceeded
A hard timeout is possible only for requests larger than a packet
Short cables are used only by supercomputers
optionExplain: It has some effect, but queueing and faults dominate, which is not the flaw.
Right: no upper limit is promised on delivery time.
Request size is irrelevant to the guarantee.
Datacenters also have short cables; the flaw is the missing guarantee.

questions.q: A service talks between two datacenters over the internet and, inside each, over Ethernet. What timing guarantee can it count on?
questions.explain: Both the internet and typical internal datacenter networks give no timing guarantees.
questions.rule: Assume no delay bound in practice.
questions.teaches: The internet and most internal datacenter networks (often Ethernet) are asynchronous packet networks.
options: None on either link, because both are asynchronous packet networks
A guarantee inside each datacenter, but none between them
A guarantee between datacenters, but none inside each
A guarantee on both, if packets are small enough
optionExplain: Right: the internet and most internal datacenter networks are of this kind.
Internal datacenter networks, often Ethernet, are also asynchronous packet networks.
The internet is the clearest example of an asynchronous packet network.
Packet size does not create a guarantee.

questions.q: A client gets no reply from a server. Which could explain it? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: Several different things could be behind silence. The card next lists them in a structured way.
options: The server processed it but the reply was lost
The network guaranteed that the server received the request
The client's clock proves the server is dead
The request was lost on the way
The server paused for a long garbage collection
optionExplain: Right: the work was done, only the answer vanished.
No such guarantee exists in this kind of network.
A clock reading proves nothing about the server's state.
Right: a packet may be lost.
Right: a paused node responds later.
questions.rule: A missing response can come from the request, from the node, or from the response on its way back.

questions.q: A remote node may have processed your request while the ____ was lost on the network.
questions.explain: Losing the response looks the same as losing the request.
questions.rule: The response can be lost after the work is done.

questions.q: Sort each cause by where the trouble lies.
questions.explain: Lost and delayed packets are network-side problems; crashes, power-offs and pauses happen at the node.
questions.rule: Locate the trouble: node or network.

items.t: The recipient was powered down
A cable was unplugged so the request never arrived
The recipient was in a long garbage collection pause
A misconfigured switch dropped the reply
The recipient process crashed
An overloaded network delayed the reply

questions.q: A payment request times out. In which listed case has the customer already been charged?
questions.explain: Only a processed request followed by a lost or delayed response leaves work done but unreported.
questions.rule: Silence does not mean nothing happened.
options: The request was lost before reaching the remote node
The remote node had crashed before the request arrived
The remote node processed the request but the response was lost
The request waits in a queue and is not yet delivered
optionExplain: The node never saw it, so no charge occurred.
A crashed node cannot have charged anyone.
Right: the work happened, only the news was lost.
Not yet delivered means not yet processed.

questions.q: True or false: If a client receives no response, the request certainly was not processed.
questions.explain: The node may have processed the request and the response may have been lost or delayed.
questions.rule: No response does not mean not done.

questions.q: A mobile app waits for a reply that arrives very late. Besides the network, where else could overload be the cause?
questions.explain: Delay can sit on the sender's side, in the network, or at the recipient.
questions.rule: A delay may come from any of the machines or links.
questions.teaches: A response can be delayed and delivered later because the network or the sender's own machine is overloaded.
options: Only at the remote node, since a client cannot be overloaded
In the response, which can be lost but never delayed
Nowhere: a late reply always means the remote node crashed
On the app's own machine, which can delay the response
optionExplain: The sender's machine can also be overloaded.
A response can be delayed as well as lost.
A late reply means the node was alive enough to send it.
Right: the response may be delayed because the network or your own machine is overloaded.

questions.q: A client gets no reply to a request. What can it conclude about the cause?
questions.explain: From the sender's side these causes are indistinguishable. The card next states it more exactly.
options: The remote node crashed, since a living node would reply
Nothing certain: several different failures look the same
The request was lost, because replies are rarely lost
The network is partitioned, which is the likeliest cause
optionExplain: Alive nodes can be slow or their replies lost.
Right: the only information is that no response has arrived.
Replies can be lost as easily as requests.
Partitions are one cause among several; silence does not point to one.
questions.rule: Without a response it is impossible to tell why: request lost, node down and response lost look identical.

questions.q: Without a reply, the only information the sender has is that it has not ____ a response yet.
questions.explain: Silence carries no more information than that.
questions.rule: Silence says only that nothing has arrived yet.

questions.q: A ride-booking client sends a booking and hears nothing. Which pair of causes can it not tell apart?
questions.explain: Lost request and lost response are indistinguishable from the sender's side.
questions.rule: Lost request and lost response look the same.
options: The booking request was lost, or the booking was made and the reply was lost
The booking succeeded, or the booking failed with an error message
The client's request had a typo, or it had none
The server has more than 10 cores, or fewer
optionExplain: Right: both look like silence.
An error message would be a response, which would not be silence.
A typo may produce an error reply; that is not silence.
Core counts do not change what the client sees.

questions.q: True or false: In an asynchronous network, a dead remote node and a lost response can be told apart by the sender if it waits long enough.
questions.explain: Waiting longer does not add information; a late response could still arrive, or never.
questions.rule: Waiting does not reveal the cause.

questions.q: A client thinks: the node is only slow, so it is not dead. Why is that conclusion unsafe?
questions.explain: A node that is paused or delayed leaves the same evidence as a node that is dead.
questions.rule: Slow and dead look the same.
questions.teaches: Silence also covers a remote node that has temporarily stopped responding (for example in a long garbage collection pause) and a response that is only delayed, so those cases are indistinguishable from failure too.
options: A temporary pause or delay also leaves no response, so slow and dead look the same
Slow nodes always crash within a minute
Slowness can be measured only with a monotonic clock
A slow node cannot receive requests at all
optionExplain: Right: a temporarily paused node and a failed node are also indistinguishable.
No such rule exists in the book.
Measuring slowness is not the problem; interpreting silence is.
A slow node can receive requests; it just answers late.

questions.q: A file-sync client sends an upload and gets no response. It asks the server in a second request whether the first arrived. What is the limit?
questions.explain: A response is the only way to learn about delivery, and responses share the network's weaknesses.
questions.rule: Evidence of delivery arrives by an unreliable path too.
questions.teaches: The sender cannot tell whether a packet was delivered unless the recipient sends a response, and that response may in turn be lost or delayed.
options: The second answer is always reliable since it is shorter
The second answer can also be lost or delayed, so uncertainty remains
The second request removes the uncertainty about the first
The client cannot send a second request while the first is pending
optionExplain: Length does not make a message immune.
Right: confirmation is another message over the same network.
It only moves the uncertainty to a new message.
Nothing forbids another request; the issue is that its answer is unreliable too.

questions.q: A client times out after three seconds waiting for a reply. What has the timeout established?
questions.explain: A timeout gives a decision, not an explanation. The card next states what remains open.
options: That the remote node did not receive the request
That the remote node has crashed
That the request succeeded but the reply was lost
That the client stopped waiting; nothing certain about the request
optionExplain: Receipt is exactly what is still unknown.
Crashing is one of several possible explanations.
Equally likely or unlikely; the timeout does not say.
Right: the timeout is only a decision to stop waiting.
questions.rule: A timeout ends the wait; it does not reveal what happened to the request.

questions.q: After a timeout, you still do not know whether the remote node got your ____.
questions.explain: The timeout says nothing about receipt.

questions.q: A payment client times out and sends the same charge again. What is the risk?
questions.explain: A retry after a timeout can repeat work that was already done.
questions.rule: A timeout does not make a retry safe.
options: The second request is certainly ignored because it duplicates the first
The first request is certainly cancelled by the retry
The first charge may have been processed, so the customer is charged twice
The client's clock will drift because of the retry
optionExplain: Servers do not ignore duplicates unless designed to.
Sending again does not cancel the first.
Right: the timeout does not say whether the first request ran.
Retries have no effect on clock drift.

questions.q: True or false: A timeout is a sure sign that the remote node is dead.
questions.explain: A timeout only shows that no response arrived in time; the node may be alive and the response lost or late.
questions.rule: Timeout is not proof of death.

questions.q: A developer says a timeout means the request was not processed, so retrying any operation is safe. What is wrong?
questions.explain: A timeout tells nothing about whether the node got the request.
questions.rule: Do not read a timeout as not done.
options: Retries are safe only on odd-numbered attempts
The request may have been processed, so a retry can repeat it
The timeout length decides whether the request ran
Requests are processed only after the client gives up
optionExplain: There is no such rule.
Right: processing and reply loss are possible together.
Length of the wait does not change whether the request ran.
Processing is not triggered by the client's giving up.

questions.q: A ride app times out requesting a driver and shows no drivers. Moments later a driver is assigned. What could have happened?
questions.explain: Giving up on the client side does not remove the request from the network or the queue.
questions.rule: The sender giving up does not unsend the request.
questions.teaches: If a request is still queued somewhere, it may still be delivered to the recipient even though the sender has given up on it.
options: The request was still queued somewhere and was delivered after the app gave up
The timeout caused the request to be cancelled and re-created
The driver node crashed and then restarted instantly with the request
The app's clock moved backward and replayed the request
optionExplain: Right: a request may be delivered later even though the sender gave up.
Timeouts do not cancel requests in the network.
Nothing in the scenario indicates a crash.
Clock movement does not replay network requests.

questions.q: In a study of a medium-sized datacenter, how often did network faults occur?
questions.explain: Faults turned out to be a regular event. The card next draws the lesson.
options: About one per year, nearly all of them whole-datacenter outages
About 12 per month, half hitting one machine and half a rack
About one per day, nearly all of them caused by failing cables
Almost none, because one company controls all of its equipment
optionExplain: Faults that rare would fit the hope that networks are reliable by now, but the study found otherwise.
Right: faults were frequent, even in a controlled environment.
The rate was lower than daily, and misconfiguration, not only cables, is a major cause.
Control by one company does not remove faults; the study found about a dozen a month.
questions.rule: Network faults are surprisingly common, and redundant hardware does not remove human error.

questions.q: Adding redundant networking gear does not reduce outages as much as hoped, because it does not guard against human ____.
questions.explain: Misconfigured switches are a major cause of outages, and spare hardware does not prevent them.
questions.rule: Redundancy does not fix human error.

questions.q: A team buys duplicate switches for every rack and expects almost no network outages. What does the book suggest?
questions.explain: Redundant gear helps against hardware failure but not against human mistakes.
options: Outages will remain, since misconfiguration by people is a major cause
Outages will vanish, since spare switches cover every kind of failure
Outages will increase, because duplicate equipment doubles the failures
Outages will stay, but only for racks in public cloud datacenters
optionExplain: Right: the study found redundancy does not protect against human error.
Spare switches cover hardware failure but not mistakes in configuring them.
The book does not claim redundancy makes things worse, only that it helps less than hoped.
Datacenters of one company also had faults; the cloud is not the only place.

questions.q: Which environment does the book describe as notorious for frequent transient network glitches?
questions.explain: Public clouds have frequent transient glitches; well-managed private networks can be more stable, though nobody is immune.
questions.rule: Environments differ, but none is immune.
options: Public cloud services such as EC2
Well-managed private datacenters, which are very frequently unstable
Supercomputer interconnects built from specialized network parts
Single computers, whose internal buses regularly drop packets
optionExplain: Right: EC2-style clouds are called notorious for transient glitches.
The book says private, well-managed networks can be stabler.
The book does not describe supercomputer networks that way.
A single computer is described as predictable, not as glitchy.

questions.q: True or false: A company that runs its own datacenter network can treat network faults as too rare to design for.
questions.explain: Even controlled datacenters showed regular faults, and nobody is immune.
questions.rule: No environment is exempt from network faults.

questions.q: A metrics pipeline sees packets to one rack delayed by about 90 seconds after a switch software upgrade. Is this plausible?
questions.explain: Software upgrades are one more source of network trouble, with long delays rather than clean failures.
questions.rule: Delays, not only drops, are network faults.
questions.teaches: A problem during a software upgrade of a switch could trigger a network topology reconfiguration during which packets are delayed for more than a minute.
options: No: delays beyond a few milliseconds mean a physical cable cut
Yes: an upgrade problem can trigger a topology reconfiguration that delays packets over a minute
No: switches keep forwarding during upgrades, so delays stay brief
Yes, but only on public cloud networks, never in private datacenters
optionExplain: Delays can come from reconfiguration without any cable being cut.
Right: the book reports exactly such an episode.
The book describes upgrade problems that delayed packets for more than a minute.
The book's example is not limited to public clouds; nobody is immune.

questions.q: A server receives every request, but its replies fail to reach the clients. What kind of fault fits?
questions.explain: One direction can fail without the other. The card next states the point.
options: A fault in the clients' keyboards that garbles each reply
A symmetric outage that drops both directions equally
A clock fault that makes replies look stale and get dropped
An asymmetric fault: one direction works, the other fails
optionExplain: Garbled input would not explain replies that never arrive.
Both directions would be cut, but requests do arrive.
Clocks are not involved in this delivery pattern.
Right: the link works one way only.
questions.rule: A link that works in one direction may fail in the other.

questions.q: True or false: A link that works in one direction is guaranteed to work in the opposite direction.
questions.explain: A network interface may drop all inbound packets while outbound ones succeed.

questions.q: A server's interface drops all inbound packets but sends outbound ones. Its heartbeats still reach the monitor. What does the monitor see?
questions.explain: Outbound health signals can hide an inbound failure.
questions.rule: A heartbeat tests only one direction.
options: A node that looks dead, because no heartbeat arrives
A node that looks slow, because heartbeats arrive late
A node that looks alive, though it receives nothing
A node with the wrong clock, because heartbeats carry timestamps
optionExplain: Heartbeats are outbound, and outbound works in this fault.
Delay is not the symptom; the heartbeats arrive on time.
Right: heartbeats arrive, so it looks healthy while requests never reach it.
Nothing here concerns timestamps; the fault is in packet direction.

questions.q: A node that can receive packets but cannot send any looks ____ to its peers, though it works.
questions.explain: Peers judge by what they hear; a node whose output is lost looks dead.
questions.rule: Reverse the direction, reverse the symptom.

questions.q: An engineer confirmed that node B can send to node C and so concluded that C can send to B. What is wrong?
questions.explain: Check each direction separately.
options: A working path one way proves nothing about the opposite path
B and C must be on different networks for any path to work
Sending to C is impossible if C cannot send to B
The conclusion is right, since links are symmetric by design
optionExplain: Right: the interface can fail in only one direction.
They can be on the same network; the issue is direction.
One-way delivery is possible; that is the fault in question.
The book shows that symmetric behavior cannot be assumed.

questions.q: A node receives requests and processes them normally, but other nodes cannot hear its outgoing replies. What will the others eventually do?
questions.explain: A one-way fault makes a healthy node look dead to its peers.
questions.teaches: Because the other nodes cannot hear its responses, a working node with only outgoing messages dropped is declared dead after a timeout, even though it receives requests normally.
options: Declare it dead after a timeout, though it works perfectly
Keep treating it as healthy, since it still receives data
Ask it to restart, since it has proven it can receive
Switch its role to a read-only replica until it speaks
optionExplain: Right: silence from the node looks like death.
They only see what they hear from it, which is nothing.
Others cannot ask for anything that depends on hearing its reply.
No such automatic step follows from the silence.

questions.q: A runbook says: a partition caused the outage. What might partition refer to?
questions.explain: Context decides between meanings. The card next defines both.
options: Only a section of a hard disk set aside for the operating system
Only a group of servers sharing one power supply in a rack
Only a delay in packet delivery caused by queueing in switches
Either a cut-off part of the network or a shard of stored data
optionExplain: Disk partitions exist, but they are not what this field usually means here.
Shared power is a different grouping, with no special name here.
Delay is a different fault from being cut off.
Right: the same word serves two meanings.
questions.rule: A network partition means part of the network is cut off, and it is a different thing from a shard.

questions.q: When one part of the network is cut off from the rest, that is called a network ____ or netsplit.
questions.explain: A network partition is a cut-off part of the network.
questions.rule: Cut off from the rest means partition.

questions.q: A post-mortem says: nodes in rack 4 could not reach the rest of the cluster. Which term fits best?
questions.explain: The description is about connectivity, which is a network partition.
options: A shard (storage partition)
A noisy neighbor
A garbage collection pause
A network partition (netsplit)
optionExplain: A shard is a subset of stored data, not a connectivity problem.
That concerns shared resource use by another customer.
A pause stops one process, not connectivity of a rack.
Right: one part of the network was cut off from the rest.

questions.q: Match each term with its meaning.
questions.explain: The book keeps these three apart on purpose.
questions.rule: Keep network partitions and shards apart.
pairs: One part of the network is cut off from the rest
A partition of a storage system, covered in Chapter 6
The broader term the book prefers for network trouble

questions.q: True or false: The book uses the term network partition for a subset of a database's data.
questions.explain: A subset of the data is a partition (shard) of a storage system; the book uses network fault for network trouble.
questions.rule: Say network fault and shard to avoid confusion.

questions.q: An on-call note says: the netsplit was rare this year, so we skipped any handling. What does the book say?
questions.explain: Whenever communication happens over a network it may fail, so software must handle it.
questions.rule: If it can fail, handle it.
questions.teaches: Even if network faults are rare in your environment, the possibility means software must be able to handle them, because whenever any communication happens over a network it may fail.
options: Skipping is fine when the netsplit count is below one per year
Handling is needed only when the netsplit affects a shard
Possible faults must still be handled, since any network communication may fail
Skipping is fine when machines are in the same rack
optionExplain: The book gives no such threshold.
Netsplits and shards are different things; handling does not depend on shards.
Right: rarity is not a reason to skip handling.
Same rack does not make communication immune to failure.

questions.q: A small internal tool runs on a stable network. Which handling of network faults is acceptable?
questions.explain: Handling can be modest, but it must be defined and must recover. The card next sets out the full advice.
options: Show users an error while the network is down, and recover afterwards
Ignore faults entirely, because the network is stable on most days
Retry silently forever without ever telling the user or the logs
Crash the tool permanently until an engineer restarts it by hand
optionExplain: Right: handling does not have to mean tolerating.
Stable most days still means faults will happen sometime without a defined reaction.
Endless silent retries are an undefined reaction, not a handled one.
A permanent crash means the tool does not recover once the network returns.
questions.rule: Handle network faults by defining, and testing, what the software does, even if that means only an error message.

questions.q: Deliberately triggering network problems to test a system is the idea behind Chaos ____.
questions.explain: Chaos Monkey is the book's example of testing by causing faults.

questions.q: A team wants confidence in how its booking service reacts to network problems. Which step fits the book?
questions.explain: You find out the reaction by creating the fault, not by waiting for one.
options: Read the network vendor's reliability figures and plan from them
Deliberately trigger network problems and watch how the system responds
Wait for the first customer complaint and reproduce it then
Add logging statements and hope the problems will show up
optionExplain: Vendor numbers say nothing about how your software reacts.
Right: the Chaos Monkey idea.
This tests on customers rather than before them.
Logging helps with diagnosis, but it does not create the situations to test.

questions.q: What if network fault handling is neither defined nor tested, and a fault occurs?
questions.explain: Unanticipated situations lead to unexpected behavior.
options: The system will fail safely, because defaults protect it
Nothing, because the network recovers by itself within seconds
Arbitrarily bad things could happen
Only the affected request fails, and others are unaffected
optionExplain: There is no such default protection; behavior is unpredictable.
Recovery of the network does not repair the software's reaction.
Right: software in an unanticipated situation can do arbitrary unexpected things.
The harm can spread beyond the one request.

questions.q: True or false: Handling network faults means keeping the service fully working throughout the fault.
questions.explain: Handling does not necessarily mean tolerating; an error message can be a valid approach.
questions.rule: Handling is not the same as tolerating.

questions.q: A cluster's network recovers after an outage, but the cluster still serves no requests. What could explain it?
questions.explain: Fault handling can fail in ways that outlast the fault, including deadlock or even data loss.
questions.rule: Bad handling can outlast the fault.
questions.teaches: Without defined and tested handling, a cluster could become deadlocked and permanently unable to serve requests even when the network recovers, or could even delete all of your data.
options: The recovery was incomplete, so the network is still down
The load balancer has deliberately kept the cluster idle
Servers cannot serve any requests until their clocks are reset
Poorly defined fault handling left it deadlocked even after recovery
optionExplain: The scenario states the network has recovered.
Nothing suggests deliberate idling.
Clocks are not related to the scenario.
Right: the book names permanent deadlock after recovery as a possible outcome.

questions.q: Which component must stop sending traffic to a dead server?
questions.explain: Routing around dead nodes needs detection. The card next lists the mechanisms that depend on it.
options: A compiler, which removes the server from the build output
A load balancer, by taking the server out of rotation
The server's operating system, which signals the clients to stop
The monitoring dashboard, which hides the dead server from graphs
optionExplain: A compiler has no role in routing live traffic to servers.
Right: that is its job.
A dead server cannot signal anything to its clients.
Hiding it from graphs does not change where requests go.
questions.rule: Systems need automatic failure detection, but network uncertainty makes it hard to tell whether a node is working.

questions.q: A load balancer takes a dead node out of ____.
questions.explain: Taking it out of rotation means no more requests go to it.

questions.q: A chat service replicates each shard with one leader. The leader hangs. Which automatic action does the system need?
questions.explain: With single-leader replication, a failed leader must be replaced by a follower.
options: Promote one of the followers to be the new leader
Promote the client that sent the last write to be leader
Delete the shard from the follower to avoid disagreements
Pause all writes forever until the old leader returns
optionExplain: Right: failover needs a replacement leader.
Clients are not replicas and cannot hold a leader role.
Deleting data is not a failover step.
Waiting forever contradicts the goal of continuing service.

questions.q: Which tasks depend on automatic detection of faulty nodes? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: Routing and failover both need an answer to is this node working.
options: A load balancer routing around a dead node
A follower being promoted when the leader fails
A spreadsheet formatting numbers as currency
A printer driver choosing a paper size
A compiler checking a file for syntax errors
optionExplain: Right: it needs to know which nodes are dead.
Right: someone has to notice the failure.
No connection to node failures.
No connection to node failures.
This is unrelated to node health.

questions.q: A designer says failure detection is easy: a dead node would announce that it is dead. What is wrong?
questions.explain: Dead nodes are silent, and silence is ambiguous.
questions.rule: Silence is the symptom of a dead node, and it is ambiguous.
options: A crashed node cannot announce anything, and network trouble hides the truth
Dead nodes announce too often and flood the monitoring system
Announcements need a synchronized clock to be believed
Announcements are possible only for load balancers, not databases
optionExplain: Right: the uncertainty of the network makes working versus not hard to tell.
Dead nodes do not send announcements at all.
Clocks are not the main problem here.
The problem applies to both.

questions.q: In a database with single-leader replication, what must happen when the leader is declared failed?
questions.explain: Failover is the detection consumer: when the leader fails, a follower takes over.
questions.teaches: In a distributed database with single-leader replication, if the leader fails, one of the followers needs to be promoted to be the new leader.
options: All followers stop reading until a human restarts the leader
One of the followers is promoted to be the new leader
The leader's disk is cloned onto each follower at once
Clients elect a leader among themselves by majority vote
optionExplain: Stopping everything is not the described response.
Right: that is the standard response.
Cloning is not how the leader role is replaced.
The nodes, not clients, decide who leads.

questions.q: A process on a reachable machine has crashed. What happens when a client opens a new TCP connection to its port?
questions.explain: When the machine is up, its operating system gives immediate feedback. The card next lists such signals.
options: The connection opens, then hangs until the client's timeout expires
The operating system refuses or closes it with an RST or FIN reply
The operating system restarts the process and accepts the connection
The connection succeeds, and the client receives an empty response
optionExplain: A hang is typical for an unreachable machine, but here the OS answers.
Right: nothing listens, and the OS says so.
Operating systems do not restart processes automatically in this way.
A successful connection needs a listening process.
questions.rule: Use explicit feedback about a down node when it is available, but treat it as a bonus, not a guarantee.

questions.q: Match each signal with what it tells you.
questions.explain: These are three forms of explicit feedback the book names.
questions.rule: Explicit feedback comes from the OS, routers and switches.
pairs: The OS found no process listening on the port
A router believes the address cannot be reached
Hardware link failures, such as a powered-down machine

questions.q: Your service runs in a shared datacenter where you cannot reach the switches. Which signal is unavailable?
questions.explain: Switch interfaces are ruled out over the internet or in a shared datacenter.
questions.rule: Some signals need access you may not have.
options: Querying switch management interfaces for link failures
An RST reply from a machine with no listener
A FIN packet from a machine that closed the port
A timeout expiring after no response
optionExplain: Right: that option needs access to the switches.
This comes from the remote operating system and needs no switch access.
Also generated by the remote machine's operating system.
Timeouts need no access to any equipment.

questions.q: Sort each signal by what it needs.
questions.explain: OS-level replies come from the target machine; ICMP and link queries come from routers and switches.
questions.rule: Know where each signal comes from.

items.t: RST reply to a connection attempt
ICMP Destination Unreachable from a router
FIN packet closing a port with no listener
Link-failure query on a switch

questions.q: True or false: When a router replies with Destination Unreachable, it knows the failure state with certainty.
questions.explain: The router has no magic failure detection and is subject to the same limitations as other network participants.

questions.q: A node crashed while handling a client's upload, and the client then receives an RST on reconnecting. What can it know about the upload?
questions.explain: Explicit feedback shows the state now, not what happened to your request earlier.
questions.rule: Feedback does not reveal how far the request got.
questions.teaches: If a node crashed while it was handling your request, you have no way of knowing how much data was actually processed by the remote node.
options: Not how much of the data was actually processed before the crash
That all of the data was processed before the crash
That none of the data was processed, since the process is gone
That the upload can be repeated safely without checking
optionExplain: Right: the feedback says the node is down, not how far it got.
The RST says nothing about completion.
The crash may have come after part of the data was handled.
Repeating may duplicate work already done.

questions.q: A payment gateway's TCP stack acknowledged your packet. What does that prove?
questions.explain: TCP confirms delivery to the machine. The card next explains what confirms handling.
options: That the payment was processed and the customer was charged
That the payment application received the packet and began work
That the gateway's clock agrees with yours within a few seconds
That the packet reached the machine, not that the payment was processed
optionExplain: Processing needs the application to run; the acknowledgment does not show that.
The application may not have read it from the connection yet.
Acknowledgments say nothing about clocks.
Right: the acknowledgment comes from the transport layer.
questions.rule: Only a response from the application itself proves the application handled the request.

questions.q: To be sure a request was successful, you need a positive response from the ____ itself.
questions.explain: Only the program that did the work can confirm it did.
questions.rule: Confirmation must come from the application.

questions.q: A file-sync client sees TCP acknowledge its final chunk. What should it do before marking the file as saved?
questions.explain: Application-level confirmation is what shows the work happened.
questions.rule: Wait for the application's own answer.
options: Mark it saved now, because the network has confirmed delivery
Mark it saved after one more TCP acknowledgment arrives
Mark it saved when the client's local timer expires
Wait for the server application to confirm that the chunk was stored
optionExplain: Delivery to the machine is not storage.
More transport-level acknowledgments still say nothing about the application.
A timer expiring is not evidence of success.
Right: acknowledgment of delivery is not confirmation of storage.

questions.q: What if the application crashes after TCP acknowledged the packet but before processing the request?
questions.explain: The transport layer finished its job; the application never did its own.
questions.rule: The transport layer's job ends at delivery.
options: TCP notices the crash and retransmits the packet to a standby
The client receives an error message from TCP at once
The client sees the acknowledgment, yet the request is never handled
The request is processed later, when the application restarts
optionExplain: TCP retransmits unacknowledged packets; it does not know about the application.
TCP already acknowledged, so it reports no error.
Right: acknowledgment and handling are separate events.
Nothing stores the lost request for the restarted application.

questions.q: True or false: A TCP acknowledgment is enough evidence that the remote application finished processing your request.
questions.explain: Even if TCP acknowledges delivery, the application may have crashed before handling the request.

questions.q: A client handles only explicit error replies and sees none, so it assumes success. What is the weakness?
questions.explain: You may get an error response at some level of the stack, but in general you have to assume you will get no response at all.
questions.teaches: If something has gone wrong you may get an error response at some level of the stack, but in general you have to assume you will get no response at all.
options: Error replies are sent twice, which confuses the client
Often there is no response at all, so silence must be handled too
Explicit errors can come only from the network, not the application
Clients can handle explicit errors only after a timeout
optionExplain: There is no such rule.
Right: in general you must assume you may get no response at all.
Errors can come from various levels of the stack.
Handling an explicit error needs no timeout.

questions.q: A load balancer gets no explicit signal about a backend server. What is the typical way to decide it is dead?
questions.explain: Without signals, silence over time is the criterion. The card next gives the steps.
options: Declare it dead at the very first missing response
Retry a few times, wait for a timeout, then declare it dead
Ask the server's operating system to confirm the failure
Wait until the server announces its own death
optionExplain: One missing response is common even for healthy nodes.
Right: silence over a timeout is the usual criterion.
Unreachable machines cannot answer such a question.
Dead servers cannot announce anything.
questions.rule: Without explicit feedback, retry, wait for the timeout and then declare the node dead.

questions.q: Put the steps in order.
questions.explain: Retries come first, then the timeout, and only then the declaration.
items: Send a request
Retry a few times
Wait for the timeout to elapse
Declare the node dead

questions.q: A client sends a request, retries twice and then waits out the timeout with no reply. What is the next step?
questions.explain: Once the timeout elapses with no response, the node is declared dead.
questions.rule: After the timeout, declare it dead.
options: Send the same request ten more times at once
Wait indefinitely, since the node may still reply
Treat the node as dead and route work elsewhere
Restart the client's operating system to clear its connections
optionExplain: Nothing in the procedure calls for a burst of extra retries.
