Waiting forever is what the timeout exists to avoid.
Right: that completes the usual procedure.
The client's machine is not the suspect.

questions.q: True or false: TCP retries lost packets transparently, but the application may also retry at its own level.
questions.explain: Both layers can retry; the application retry is a separate decision.
questions.rule: Retries can happen in two places.

questions.q: A team says: our node was declared dead, so it must have crashed. What is the flaw?
questions.explain: The declaration is based on missing responses, which have many causes.
questions.rule: Declared dead is not the same as dead.
options: Dead nodes are declared by the nodes themselves, not by others
Nodes can be declared dead only after exactly three retries
A node declared dead is always still running
The declaration came from silence, which a slow or cut-off node can also cause
optionExplain: The declaration is made by others after silence.
The number of retries is not fixed.
It may or may not be running; that is the point.
Right: declaring dead is a judgment, not a proof.

questions.q: A cluster manager runs a script that tells peers when a process is killed while its operating system still runs. What does that save?
questions.explain: Where a crash can be reported explicitly, waiting for a timeout can be skipped.
questions.teaches: If a node process crashed or was killed but its operating system is still running, a script can notify other nodes so that another node can take over quickly without waiting for a timeout to expire; HBase does this.
options: The OS no longer needs to refuse connections to the port
Peers no longer need to retry any requests at all
The process becomes safe from being killed by an operator
Peers need not wait for a timeout before taking over
optionExplain: The OS still behaves as before; the script adds notification.
Retries remain a separate concern.
The script reports the kill; it does not prevent it.
Right: explicit notification lets another node take over quickly.

questions.q: A team shortens its failure-detection timeout from 30 seconds to 1 second. What is the main risk?
questions.explain: Shorter timeouts speed detection but increase false alarms. The card next sets out both sides.
options: Healthy nodes that are briefly slow may be declared dead
Dead nodes will be noticed more slowly than before
Users will wait longer before seeing an error
Clock drift between nodes will increase noticeably
optionExplain: Right: a short timeout misreads slowness as death.
The opposite: a shorter timeout detects faults sooner.
A shorter timeout shortens the wait.
Timeout length has no effect on drift.
questions.rule: Short timeouts detect faults sooner but misjudge slow nodes as dead; long timeouts do the reverse.

questions.q: A timeout that is too ____ risks declaring a node dead when it is only slow.
questions.explain: A short timeout gives a slow node little time to respond.

questions.q: A checkout service must show an error quickly when a backend is down, but its backend occasionally stalls for a second. Which timeout fits the trade-off?
questions.explain: The right length balances detection time against false alarms for the workload.
questions.rule: Match the timeout to the delays you must tolerate.
options: A few seconds, to ride out short stalls and still fail fast
100 milliseconds, to fail as fast as possible
Ten minutes, to be certain the node is really dead
Zero, so that any delay counts as a failure
optionExplain: Right: it balances both costs for this load pattern.
This would treat every second-long stall as a death.
Users would wait ten minutes for an error.
Zero would declare every node dead at once.

questions.q: Sort each consequence by the timeout that causes it.
questions.explain: Short timeouts trade false alarms for speed; long timeouts trade speed for fewer false alarms.
questions.rule: Each timeout length buys one thing and costs another.

items.t: Slow but healthy nodes are declared dead
Users wait longer before seeing an error
Faults are detected sooner
A dead node stays in rotation for longer
More needless takeovers happen
Fewer false alarms occur

questions.q: True or false: The book says a single right timeout value exists that suits every system.
questions.explain: The book says there is unfortunately no simple answer.
questions.rule: There is no one right timeout.

questions.q: A system normally answers within 20 ms, so its team sets a 30 ms timeout. A brief traffic spike doubles round-trip times. What happens?
questions.explain: A low timeout leaves little margin, so transient spikes cause false alarms.
questions.rule: Margin matters more than the average.
questions.teaches: For failure detection it is not sufficient for the system to be fast most of the time: if the timeout is low, it only takes a transient spike in round-trip times to throw the system off-balance.
options: Nothing, because the system is fast most of the time
Many healthy nodes are suspected dead, though they are only slow
The timeout adjusts itself, since timeouts are always adaptive
Only dead nodes are declared dead, which is the intended result
optionExplain: Being fast most of the time is not sufficient for failure detection.
Right: a transient spike is enough to throw a low timeout off-balance.
A fixed timeout does not adapt by itself.
The spike affects healthy nodes too.

questions.q: Node A is alive but slow while sending a customer a receipt. Node B declares A dead and takes over its work. What may result?
questions.explain: Takeover without certainty can duplicate an action. The card next states the danger.
options: The receipt is never sent, since B cancels A's work
The receipt is sent once, because B waits for A
A stops responding permanently after B takes over
The receipt is sent twice, once by each node
optionExplain: B has no way to cancel what A is doing.
B has already decided that A is dead and does not wait.
Nothing forces A to stop; it may carry on.
Right: both nodes may perform the action.
questions.rule: Declaring a live node dead can make its work run twice.

questions.q: If a live node is declared dead and another node takes over, the action may be performed ____.
questions.explain: The original node may still complete its action.

questions.q: A ticketing worker is slow on a big job and a supervisor reassigns it. Which risk follows?
questions.explain: Reassigning work from a live worker means two workers may do it.
questions.rule: A slow worker is not a dead worker.
options: The tickets are lost because both workers abandon them
Tickets are issued with out-of-order timestamps in the log
Two workers may both issue the same tickets
The supervisor learns that the first worker had crashed
optionExplain: Both are not guaranteed to abandon the job.
Order of timestamps is a different issue.
Right: the slow worker may not have stopped.
The worker was only slow, not crashed.

questions.q: What if all actions in the system are safe to repeat (running them twice has the same effect as once)?
questions.explain: The duplication problem exists because actions have effects that do not repeat safely.
options: A premature takeover is worse, since repeats multiply effects
A premature takeover does little harm to results
Takeover becomes impossible, since actions are repeatable
Declaring nodes dead becomes unnecessary
optionExplain: If repeats are harmless, effects do not multiply.
Right: repeated work changes nothing.
Repeatable actions do not forbid takeover.
The system still needs to react to real failures.

questions.q: True or false: When a node is declared dead, it must have stopped working.
questions.explain: Declaration is a judgment from silence; the node may still be alive and mid-action.

questions.q: A payment worker emails a receipt and is declared dead mid-send. Another worker takes over. What does the book warn?
questions.explain: Takeover while the first worker is alive can double side effects like sending email.
questions.teaches: The book's example of a doubled action is sending an email: if the node is alive and in the middle of sending it, and another node takes over, the email may be sent twice.
options: The email may be sent twice
The first worker is erased, so no email is sent
Receipts are sent only when two workers agree
The takeover is rejected by the payment network
optionExplain: Right: the book's own example of a doubled action.
The first worker is not erased.
Agreement is not part of this scenario.
The scenario has no such rejection.

questions.q: A busy cluster declares one overloaded node dead and moves its work to the others. What can follow?
questions.explain: Takeover costs capacity. The card next shows the chain reaction.
options: The cluster recovers quickly, because load is now balanced
Only the removed node is affected, so other nodes stay as before
The others become overloaded and may be declared dead too
The network becomes faster, since there is one node fewer
optionExplain: Moving more load onto already struggling nodes does not balance it.
They now carry its work too.
Right: the extra load can spread the problem.
Extra traffic moves onto the network, not away from it.
questions.rule: False death declarations under overload shift work onto others and can cascade.

questions.q: When a node is declared dead, its responsibilities are moved to other nodes, which adds extra ____ to them.
questions.explain: More work lands on nodes that may already be struggling.

questions.q: A search cluster at 95 percent capacity has one node slow from overload. Which response risks a cascade?
questions.explain: Moving a busy node's load to nodes without spare capacity can spread failure.
options: Reduce incoming traffic while the node recovers
Wait longer before judging it dead
Add new capacity before moving any work
Declare it dead at once and spread its queries over the rest
optionExplain: Reducing traffic lowers the load rather than adding it.
More patience avoids the extra load.
Capacity first avoids overload.
Right: the rest then carry its load at near capacity.

questions.q: What if the system has plenty of spare capacity when a node is wrongly declared dead?
questions.explain: The cascade depends on the others being unable to carry extra load.
options: The cascade still happens, as with any false alarm
All nodes immediately declare each other dead
The node comes back with a fresh clock
The others absorb its work and the harm stays small
optionExplain: The cascade needs overload to propagate.
That is the extreme case under overload.
Nothing in this setup resets a clock.
Right: spare capacity breaks the chain reaction.

questions.q: True or false: A false death declaration only affects the node that was wrongly removed.
questions.explain: Its load moves to other nodes and the network, which can harm them as well.

questions.q: In the extreme case of a cascade, what can the whole cluster end up doing?
questions.explain: In the extreme case all nodes declare each other dead and everything stops working.
questions.rule: Cascades can stop the whole system.
questions.teaches: In the extreme case of a cascading failure, all nodes declare each other dead and everything stops working.
options: Every node restarts together and the cluster returns to normal at once
Every node declares every other dead, and all work stops
Every node elects a new leader and the cluster recovers by itself
Every node pauses until the traffic spike has passed and then resumes
optionExplain: A mass restart is not what the cascade produces; it ends in a standstill.
Right: the book's extreme case.
Elections need healthy, reachable nodes, which the cascade has used up.
Nothing in the cascade waits for traffic to fall; nodes keep suspecting one another.

questions.q: Suppose delivery takes at most d (or is lost) and a healthy node replies within r. How long should a client wait?
questions.explain: Request, handling and response add up. The card next states it.
options: Twice d plus r, since both directions and the handling take time
d plus r, since the response is the only trip that matters
Twice r, since handling happens twice
d alone, since delivery is the only uncertain step
optionExplain: Right: request, handling and response.
The request also needs d.
Handling happens once, not twice.
Handling time and the return trip also count.
questions.rule: With max packet delay d and max handling time r, a timeout of 2d + r detects failure without false alarms.

questions.q: With a maximum packet delay d and a maximum handling time r, a reasonable timeout is 2 d + ____.
questions.explain: Two trips plus one handling time.

questions.q: Packets arrive within 20 ms or are lost, and a healthy node replies within 50 ms. What timeout is exact?
questions.explain: Compute 2d + r with d = 20 and r = 50: 40 + 50 = 90.
questions.rule: Add two trips and one handling.
options: 70 ms
90 ms
140 ms
40 ms
optionExplain: This is 20 + 50: one trip plus handling, forgetting the trip back.
Right: 2 x 20 + 50 = 90 ms.
This counts the handling time twice (40 + 50 + 50), but it happens once.
This is only the two trips (20 + 20) and forgets the handling time.

questions.q: With d = 20 ms and r = 50 ms, the network gets slower so that d becomes 40 ms. What is the new exact timeout?
questions.explain: Only d changes: 80 + 50 = 130.
questions.rule: Plug the new d into 2d + r.
options: 90 ms
100 ms
130 ms
170 ms
optionExplain: That was the old value.
This adds d and r once only.
Right: 2 x 40 + 50 = 130 ms.
This doubles the handling time as well as d.

questions.q: True or false: Most real networks guarantee a maximum packet delay, so 2d + r works for them.
questions.explain: Most systems have neither guarantee: delays are unbounded and servers cannot promise a handling time.
questions.rule: The formula needs guarantees that real systems lack.

questions.q: Why can an ordinary web service not use the formula?
questions.explain: Asynchronous networks have unbounded delay and most servers cannot promise a maximum handling time, so no exact timeout exists.
questions.teaches: Asynchronous networks have unbounded delays, with no upper limit on how long a packet may take, and most server implementations cannot guarantee handling requests within some maximum time.
options: Its network is so fast that no timeout is needed, so the formula is unnecessary
Its servers are too reliable for a timeout, so a formula would never apply
The formula applies only to supercomputers, which have their own networks
Its network has no delay bound and its servers promise no handling time
optionExplain: Speed does not remove the need for a timeout; guarantees are what the formula needs.
Reliable servers still need timeouts to detect the rare fault.
The formula applies wherever the two guarantees hold; the cause is missing guarantees.
Right: both inputs of the formula are missing.

questions.q: What does the book say most often causes the variability of packet delays?
questions.explain: Queues, like traffic jams on roads, cause the variability. The card next locates them.
options: Cable length
Queueing
Packet size
Clock drift
optionExplain: Distance sets a minimum but varies little.
Right: waiting in queues dominates.
Size has a small, steady effect.
Clocks do not delay packets.
questions.rule: Variable packet delay is mostly queueing: at switches, at busy receivers, at paused virtual machines, and at senders.

questions.q: When several nodes send packets to one destination at once, the switch must ____ them and feed them in one by one.
questions.explain: Queueing at the switch is network congestion.

questions.q: Sort each source of waiting by where the queue forms.
questions.explain: Switches queue on the network; receivers, VMs and TCP senders queue on machines.

items.t: Switch queue when several senders target one port
Requests wait because all CPU cores are busy
VM paused while another VM uses the core
Congested link slows the packet's turn
Sender's TCP flow control holds data back
Packet dropped because the switch queue is full

questions.q: A packet reaches its destination, but all CPU cores are busy. Where does it wait?
questions.explain: The waiting happens inside the destination machine.
options: In a queue kept by the operating system until the application is ready
In the switch queue, which waits for the destination to be ready
In a TCP flow control queue at the original sender
In the application, which has already started handling it
optionExplain: Right: the OS queues incoming requests.
The packet has already left the switch.
That queue is before sending, not at the destination.
The application is busy and has not started.

questions.q: True or false: A packet lost because a switch queue is full means the network has failed.
questions.explain: The packet is dropped and must be resent even though the network is functioning fine.
questions.rule: Congestion is not a failure of the network.

questions.q: Round-trip times between two services grow sharply as the shared link nears its maximum capacity. Why?
questions.explain: Utilization is the amplifier: close to the maximum, queues grow fast.
questions.teaches: Queueing delays have an especially wide range when a system is close to its maximum capacity: a system with plenty of spare capacity drains queues easily, while in a highly utilized system long queues build up very quickly.
options: Queueing delays vary most widely near capacity, since queues build up very quickly
Packets travel more slowly along a full link
Busy links change the clock rate of the switch
TCP stops all retransmissions near capacity
optionExplain: Right: spare capacity drains queues easily; a highly utilized system does not.
The speed of a packet on the wire does not change.
Clock rates are not affected by link load.
TCP keeps retransmitting.

questions.q: A live voice call loses one packet. What is the most useful reaction?
questions.explain: In real time, late data has no value. The card next explains the protocol choice.
options: Pause the call until the packet is retransmitted
Replay the previous second of audio to cover the gap
End the call and reconnect automatically
Fill the gap with silence and keep playing
optionExplain: A pause wrecks a live conversation.
Repeating audio is not how the stream is handled.
Reconnecting is far worse than a brief gap.
Right: a retransmitted packet would arrive too late to play.
questions.rule: Choose UDP when delayed data is worthless; choose TCP when every byte must arrive.

questions.q: Unlike TCP, UDP does not perform flow control and does not ____ lost packets.
questions.explain: UDP leaves lost packets lost.

questions.q: A live-score ticker updates every second and a stale score is worthless. Which transport fits?
questions.explain: When only the freshest data matters, losing a packet is better than waiting.
questions.rule: Late data is worthless: use UDP.
options: TCP, so that every update is retransmitted until it arrives
TCP with larger buffers to hide delays
Neither, since only voice traffic can use UDP
UDP, since a lost update is replaced by the next one
optionExplain: Retransmitted old scores arrive late and are useless.
Larger buffers add delay.
UDP is not limited to voice.
Right: delayed data is worthless here.

questions.q: Sort each trait by the protocol it describes.
questions.explain: UDP trades reliability for steadier delay; TCP the reverse.
questions.rule: UDP: steady delay. TCP: reliable delivery.

items.t: Does not retransmit lost packets
Retransmits packets not acknowledged in time
Performs flow control to avoid overload
Avoids sender-side queueing from flow control
Suits a live voice call
Suits transferring an email attachment

questions.q: True or false: With UDP, packets are not delayed by queues.
questions.explain: UDP avoids some sources of variable delay but is still susceptible to switch queues and scheduling delays.
questions.rule: UDP reduces delay variability, not removes it.

questions.q: A video call drops sound for a moment. What does the book call the way this problem is fixed?
questions.explain: When a protocol gives up on reliability, recovery can move up to the people using it.
questions.rule: Recovery can be left to the human layer.
questions.teaches: In a VoIP call over UDP the retry happens at the human layer instead: the listener says Could you repeat that please? The sound just cut out for a moment.
options: The retry happens in UDP, which resends after a timeout
The retry happens in TCP, which resends the missing audio
The retry happens at the human layer: Could you repeat that please?
The retry happens in the switch, which keeps a copy of packets
optionExplain: UDP does not retransmit.
The call is not using TCP.
Right: people ask each other to repeat.
Switches do not keep copies for resending.

questions.q: In a shared public cloud, how should a team choose its network timeouts?
questions.explain: Delays vary and nobody guarantees them, so the practical method is to measure. The card next gives the details.
options: Read the cloud provider's published maximum delay and add a margin
Copy the timeout from a supercomputer manual, which has proven values
Measure round-trip times for a long time on many machines
Use the shortest value the library allows, so failures are caught fast
optionExplain: The cloud makes no such guarantee, so there is no maximum to read.
A different environment with different guarantees; its values do not transfer.
Right: no correct value can be derived, so measure.
Too short a value declares healthy nodes dead during ordinary delay spikes.
questions.rule: With no delay guarantees, set timeouts from measured round-trip times, ideally adjusting them automatically.

questions.q: A failure detector that learns the response time distribution and adjusts timeouts is called a Phi ____ failure detector.
questions.explain: Akka and Cassandra use it.

questions.q: A team moves from a private datacenter to a public cloud with noisy neighbors. How should it set timeouts?
questions.explain: With noisy neighbours the delay distribution is different, so timeouts should be derived from fresh measurements.
options: Keep the old constant, because a timeout belongs to the code, not the platform
Measure delay variation on the new platform and set them from that
Ask the neighbours to reduce their traffic during peak hours of the day
Double all timeouts once and then stop measuring, as the cloud is stable
optionExplain: Timeouts depend on the delays of the environment, which just changed.
Right: the environment determines the right value.
Customers cannot see or control what their neighbours do.
A one-time guess cannot follow delays that vary with neighbours' usage.

questions.q: What if delays slowly rise over a day and the timeout is a fixed constant while another system adjusts from observed data?
questions.explain: Continually measuring response times and jitter lets the adaptive detector keep pace, as the Phi Accrual detector does.
options: Both behave the same, since they use the same failure detection formula
The constant adjusts after a while as it learns the new delay pattern
The adaptive one fails first, because changing its value makes it unstable
The adaptive one follows the rise; the constant starts to raise false alarms
optionExplain: A constant and an adaptive value differ by definition.
A configured constant never changes unless someone changes it.
Tracking conditions is its purpose; it is the constant that misfires.
Right: only the adaptive value tracks the change.

questions.q: True or false: In a public cloud, there is one correct timeout value that can be looked up in the provider's documentation.
questions.explain: There is no correct value; timeouts must be determined experimentally.
questions.rule: Timeouts are measured, not looked up.

questions.q: Why do bursts of MapReduce traffic from other customers matter to your timeouts?
questions.explain: Batch workloads such as MapReduce can easily saturate network links, so a noisy neighbour can make your delays highly variable.
questions.teaches: Batch workloads such as MapReduce can easily saturate network links, so someone near you in a public cloud or multi-tenant datacenter can make your network delays highly variable; this is the noisy neighbor problem.
options: They can saturate shared links and make your delays vary
They make your server clock run faster until their job finishes
They guarantee a fixed share of the link for you, which stabilizes delays
They only matter on supercomputers, since the cloud isolates each customer
optionExplain: Right: a noisy neighbour changes your delays.
Network load does not change clock speed.
Sharing is dynamic; nobody guarantees you a fixed share.
The cloud shares links, switches and CPUs among customers.

questions.q: Why are delayed audio frames and dropped calls very rare on the traditional fixed-line telephone network?
questions.explain: Reservation along the route is the trick. The card next explains it.
options: Telephone cables are made of faster materials than data cables
Each call gets reserved bandwidth along its whole route
Telephone calls use TCP, which retransmits all lost audio
Telephone switches run clocks that are perfectly synchronized
optionExplain: Cable material is not the reason.
Right: reservation removes queueing.
Calls do not use TCP.
Synchronized clocks are not how the guarantee works.
questions.rule: A circuit reserves bandwidth along the whole route, which removes queueing and bounds the delay.

questions.q: A network with a fixed maximum end-to-end latency is said to have a ____ delay.
questions.explain: Bounded means there is an upper limit.

questions.q: A company wants guaranteed latency for a constant-rate audio stream between two offices. Which design does the book's telephone example suggest?
questions.explain: Constant-rate traffic fits a reserved circuit.
options: Reserve a fixed share of bandwidth along the whole route
Send the audio as TCP packets and add a longer timeout
Send each audio packet three times in a row
Let the switches pick the order of packets freely
optionExplain: Right: that is a circuit.
TCP offers no bound on delay.
Duplicates do not bound delay.
Free scheduling is how queueing delays arise.

questions.q: True or false: In a circuit-switched network the reserved space for a call at the next hop is already waiting, so packets do not queue.
questions.explain: Space is reserved in advance at each hop, which removes queueing.

questions.q: A teammate says a telephone network is synchronous because every phone has the same clock time. What is wrong?
questions.explain: In this section synchronous means no queueing and a fixed maximum end-to-end latency, not matching clocks.
questions.rule: Synchronous: bounded delay, not shared clocks.
options: It is synchronous because reserved space removes queueing, giving bounded delay
It is synchronous because every phone shows the same clock time to the second
It is synchronous because only one call is carried at a time on each wire
It is asynchronous because reserved calls can begin at any time without notice
optionExplain: Right: synchronous here means bounded delay.
Clocks are not what the word means in this section.
Many calls share a wire, each in its own reserved slot.
Calls begin at any time, but each one still gets reserved capacity.

questions.q: An ISDN call gets 16 bits per frame in each direction at 4,000 frames per second. How much audio data per second does each side get?
questions.explain: Compute 16 bits x 4,000 per second = 64,000 bits per second, guaranteed.
questions.rule: A circuit guarantees an exact rate.
questions.teaches: An ISDN network runs at a fixed 4,000 frames per second; each call is allocated 16 bits in each frame in each direction, so each side can send exactly 16 bits of audio every 250 microseconds.
options: 16,000 bits
64,000 bits
4,016 bits
250 bits
optionExplain: This multiplies 16 by only 1,000 frames.
Right: 16 x 4,000 = 64,000 bits per second.
This adds the numbers instead of multiplying them.
This confuses the 250-microsecond frame interval with a bit count.

questions.q: While a telephone circuit is established, who else can use its reserved bandwidth?
questions.explain: A circuit is exclusive. The card next contrasts it with TCP.
options: Any packet that finds it idle
Only other calls on the same switch
Only the caller who started the call, and only on one direction
Nobody
optionExplain: That describes dynamic sharing, as TCP does.
Reserved capacity is not shared with other calls.
Both directions are reserved for the call.
Right: it is reserved for that call.
questions.rule: A circuit reserves bandwidth; TCP takes whatever bandwidth is free.

questions.q: Match each item to its description.
questions.explain: Reserved capacity versus opportunistic use.
questions.rule: Circuit reserves; TCP takes what is free.
pairs: Fixed reserved bandwidth that nobody else can use
Packets use whatever bandwidth is available

questions.q: You hand TCP an email of 5 MB. What does TCP try to do?
questions.explain: You can hand TCP a block of any size and it tries to transfer it as fast as available bandwidth allows.
options: Reserve a fixed bandwidth for the whole transfer before it sends
Move it in the shortest time using available bandwidth
Split the email into frames of exactly 16 bits sent every 250 microseconds
Wait for every other connection to go idle before it starts sending
optionExplain: Reservation is how circuits work, not TCP.
Right: TCP adapts to what is free.
Fixed 16-bit slots are the ISDN circuit example.
TCP shares the link and does not wait for idleness.

questions.q: Sort each trait by what it describes.
questions.explain: Circuits reserve and guarantee; TCP shares and adapts.

items.t: Bandwidth fixed for the duration
Packets opportunistically use free bandwidth
Maximum round-trip time can be guaranteed at setup
Uses no bandwidth while idle
Fails to be created if guarantee cannot be met
Accepts a block of any size

questions.q: True or false: A TCP connection reserves bandwidth, so it guarantees a maximum delay.
questions.explain: A TCP connection reserves nothing; its packets use whatever bandwidth is available.

questions.q: An idle TCP connection is kept open for hours. How much bandwidth does it use?
questions.explain: Unlike a circuit, an idle TCP connection costs nothing, which is why packet networks use capacity well.
questions.teaches: Except perhaps for an occasional keepalive packet, if TCP keepalive is enabled, an idle TCP connection does not use any bandwidth.
options: The same as when it is busy, since the connection is open
None, apart from an occasional keepalive packet if enabled
A constant 16 bits every 250 microseconds
Half of the link, held back for future data
optionExplain: That would be circuit behaviour.
Right: idle means no bandwidth, except for keepalives.
That figure is the ISDN example, not TCP.
TCP does not hold bandwidth back.

questions.q: Which workload is best suited to a circuit rather than packet switching?
questions.explain: Circuits suit traffic with a fairly constant rate. The card next explains why the internet uses packets instead.
options: Fetching a web page at a moment nobody can predict in advance
Sending one large file when the link would otherwise be idle for hours
A live audio call needing a constant bit rate
Emailing a short message to a colleague who may read it much later
optionExplain: Bursty and unpredictable, so packets fit it better.
The file wants the fastest possible transfer, not a fixed rate.
Right: constant rate for the length of the call.
A short bursty transfer would waste a reserved circuit.
questions.rule: Packet switching suits bursty traffic, circuits suit constant-rate traffic.

questions.q: Datacenter networks and the internet use packet switching because they are optimized for ____ traffic.
questions.explain: Bursty traffic has no steady bandwidth need.

questions.q: A photo-sharing app uploads photos at irregular times in varying sizes. Which network style suits it?
questions.explain: Irregular transfers of varying size are exactly the bursty traffic packet networks are optimized for.
options: A circuit sized for the largest photo, so every upload fits
Packet switching, which adapts to the bandwidth available
A circuit sized for the smallest photo, so reservations stay cheap
Either style performs the same, because photos are only data to the network
optionExplain: Most of the reserved bandwidth would sit idle between uploads.
Right: bursty and variable-sized.
Larger photos would be slowed unnecessarily by the small allocation.
The styles differ: circuits waste capacity on bursty transfers.

questions.q: What happens if you move a file transfer onto a circuit and guess its bandwidth too high?
questions.explain: A circuit can only be created if its allocation can be guaranteed.
options: The transfer finishes faster, using the spare bandwidth
The circuit is created but shares its extra bandwidth
The file is split into packets automatically
The circuit cannot be set up, since the guarantee cannot be met
optionExplain: The extra is not available; it must be reserved first.
A circuit's bandwidth is not shared.
Circuits do not packetize on their own.
Right: the network refuses a circuit it cannot guarantee.

questions.q: True or false: Using circuits for bursty transfers would make them faster and use capacity better.
questions.explain: Circuits waste network capacity on bursty transfers and make them unnecessarily slow.
questions.rule: Circuits fit constant rates, not bursts.

questions.q: What kind of protocol are Ethernet and IP, and what follows for delay?
questions.explain: Packet switching trades the delay bound for flexible use of capacity.
questions.rule: Packets: flexible, with no delay bound.
questions.teaches: Ethernet and IP are packet-switched protocols, which suffer from queueing and thus unbounded delays; they do not have the concept of a circuit.
options: Circuit-switched, with bounded delay for every connection
Circuit-switched, but with unbounded delays at the switch
Packet-switched, but with bounded delay by design
Packet-switched, with queueing and so unbounded delays
optionExplain: They have no concept of a circuit.
Contradictory: without circuits the delays come from queueing.
Packet switching involves queueing and no bound.
Right: they have no concept of a circuit.

questions.q: Why is sharing a wire dynamically cheaper per byte than giving each user a fixed slot?
questions.explain: Because the wire has a fixed cost, using it more fully lowers the cost per byte. The card next sets out the trade-off.
options: Dynamic sharing runs on cheaper wire, as fixed slots need premium cabling
Dynamic sharing removes the need for switches, which are costly to run
Dynamic sharing makes each packet travel faster, which saves time and money
The wire has a fixed cost, so better use makes each byte cheaper
optionExplain: The wire is the same in both cases.
Switches are what decide who sends next under dynamic sharing.
It causes queueing, so some packets travel slower.
Right: more traffic over the same fixed cost.
questions.rule: Dynamic sharing raises utilization and lowers cost but causes variable delay; static division does the reverse.

questions.q: On the internet, bandwidth is shared ____ , which has the downside of queueing but maximizes utilization of the wire.
questions.explain: Dynamic sharing queues packets but keeps the wire busy.

questions.q: A company wants guaranteed latency for its trading links and is willing to pay. Which resource approach fits?
questions.explain: Latency guarantees are achievable with statically partitioned resources, at the cost of lower utilization and higher expense.
questions.rule: Pay for guarantees with dedicated capacity.
options: Dedicated hardware and exclusive bandwidth allocations
A public cloud's multi-tenant network with dynamic sharing of bandwidth
The cheapest shared link plus a very long timeout to hide delays
A noisy-neighbour strategy that fills spare capacity on a shared link
optionExplain: Right: static partitioning gives guarantees.
Cheap but shared, so delays vary.
A long timeout hides delay but does not guarantee it.
Filling spare capacity raises variability, not guarantees.

questions.q: Sort each consequence by the approach that produces it.
questions.explain: Static buys guarantees with idle capacity; dynamic buys utilization with variability.

items.t: Guaranteed latency
Queueing and variable delay
Lower utilization of the wire
Cheaper per byte sent
Your slot is held even when others are idle
Packets jostle for bandwidth moment by moment

questions.q: True or false: Multi-tenant datacenters with dynamic partitioning give both the best utilization and guaranteed delays.
questions.explain: They give better utilization and lower cost but variable delays; guarantees need static partitioning.
questions.rule: You cannot have both for free.

questions.q: Why is sharing each CPU core dynamically among threads similar to sharing a network wire?
questions.explain: CPUs show the same trade-off as wires: dynamic sharing improves utilization but threads can be paused for varying lengths of time.
questions.teaches: If a CPU core is shared dynamically between threads, one thread sometimes waits in the operating system's run queue and can be paused for varying lengths of time, but the hardware is used better than with a static number of CPU cycles per thread; better utilization is also a motivation for virtual machines.
options: Each thread keeps a private core, so threads never wait for the CPU
Threads need a synchronized clock to take turns on the shared core
A thread may wait in a run queue, so delay varies but hardware is used well
The CPU stops every other thread whenever one thread has to wait
optionExplain: That would be static allocation, with no waiting but poor utilization.
Turn-taking is done by the scheduler and needs no synchronized clocks.
Right: same trade-off.
Dynamic sharing keeps others running; that is how it gains utilization.

questions.q: According to the book, why do networks have variable delays?
questions.explain: Variable delays are the result of choosing cheap, well-used shared resources over expensive guaranteed ones.
options: They result from a cost and benefit trade-off, not a law of nature
They are caused by physics and nothing can ever bound them
They come from poorly written application code that wastes bandwidth
They are caused by disagreeing clocks on the sending machines
optionExplain: Right: better guarantees cost more.
The book says this is not a law of nature.
The cause sits in the network design, not in application code.
Clocks are a separate topic; delay exists with perfect clocks too.
questions.rule: Unbounded delays result from a cost choice, and where guarantees are not offered there is no correct timeout, only measured ones.

questions.q: Variable delays in networks are not a law of nature, but the result of a cost/____ trade-off.
questions.explain: It is a trade-off between cost and benefit.
questions.rule: Variable delay is a cost decision.

questions.q: A public cloud customer asks the provider for a guaranteed maximum packet delay on its shared network. What does the book suggest?
questions.explain: Currently deployed technology in multi-tenant datacenters, public clouds and the internet does not allow guarantees about delays.
options: The provider can guarantee it for free, since guarantees cost nothing extra
The provider must give it by law in every public cloud contract
Such quality of service is not enabled; measure timeouts instead
It is on offer only across the internet and not inside a datacenter
optionExplain: Guarantees reduce utilization, so they cost money.
The book mentions no such requirement.
Right: no guarantee on offer.
Neither place currently offers such guarantees.

questions.q: What if a system used dedicated hardware and exclusive bandwidth for its latency-critical traffic?
questions.explain: Latency guarantees are achievable in some environments when resources are statically partitioned, but it is more expensive.
options: Delays stay unbounded, since every network is the same underneath
Latency guarantees become achievable at the cost of lower utilization
Utilization rises, since fewer users share the hardware and queues empty
Timeouts become impossible to set because delays are then constant
optionExplain: Static partitioning can bound delay, unlike dynamic sharing.
Right: static partitioning trades utilization for guarantees.
Exclusive allocation leaves capacity idle, so utilization falls.
Bounded delay makes timeouts easier, not impossible.

questions.q: True or false: Because delay variation is a cost trade-off, a correct universal timeout value exists for any network.
questions.explain: Where guarantees are not offered there is no correct value for timeouts; they must be determined experimentally.

questions.q: Which techniques can emulate circuit switching on a packet network, according to the book?
questions.explain: With QoS and admission control, packet networks can approximate circuits or give statistically bounded delay.
questions.rule: QoS plus admission control approximates circuits.
questions.teaches: With careful use of quality of service (prioritization and scheduling of packets) and admission control (rate-limiting senders) it is possible to emulate circuit switching on packet networks or provide statistically bounded delay.
options: Quality of service and admission control
Longer timeouts and more retries
Synchronized clocks and monotonic counters
Checksums and error-correcting codes
optionExplain: Right: prioritization/scheduling plus rate-limiting senders.
These affect reaction to delay, not the delay itself.
Clocks do not create bandwidth reservations.
These detect or repair corruption, not delay.

questions.q: Which question asks for a duration rather than a point in time?
questions.explain: An interval such as time spent is a duration; a named date or timestamp is a point in time. The card next sorts more examples.
options: When did the user last sign in, as shown on the profile page?
How long did the user spend on the site?
At what date and time should the reminder email be sent to the user?
What is the timestamp on the user's most recent error in the log file?
optionExplain: This mentions time, but a last sign-in is a moment on the calendar, a point in time.
Right: it measures an interval, the time between arriving and leaving.
Scheduling is about a particular date and time, a point in time rather than an interval.
A timestamp names a moment, so it is a point in time, not a length of time.
questions.rule: Before reading a clock, decide whether you need a duration or a point in time.

questions.q: Sort each question by what it asks for.
questions.explain: Eight examples in the book split evenly between durations and points in time.

items.t: Has this request timed out yet?
When was this article published?
What is the 99th percentile response time?
At what date and time should the reminder email be sent?
How many queries per second in the last five minutes?
What is the timestamp on this log message?

questions.q: A ticketing app must stop a seat hold after 10 minutes. Is this a duration or a point in time?
questions.explain: A hold that ends after ten minutes is measured as elapsed time, which is a duration. Timeouts are durations.
options: A point in time: the app must read the calendar date and compare it to a stored date
Both at once, so the app needs a synchronized clock on every machine involved
Neither, because holds are counted in requests received rather than in time
A duration: ten minutes must elapse since the hold began
optionExplain: Plausible because holds have start times, but expiry after ten minutes is an interval, not a calendar date.
The question needs only one kind of clock; elapsed time does not require machines to agree.
The rule is stated in minutes, so it is about time, not a request count.
Right: the hold is measured as an interval from its start.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly classified?
questions.explain: Durations measure intervals (timeouts, response times, rates); points in time name moments (dates, timestamps, expiry times).
options: Queries per second: duration; log timestamp: point in time
Cache expiry: duration; response time: point in time
Reminder email: duration; time on site: point in time
Timeout: point in time; publication date: duration
optionExplain: Right: a rate is measured over an interval, a timestamp names a moment.
The classes are swapped: response time is an interval, and the book lists expiry among the points in time.
Swapped again: a reminder is sent at a date and time, while time on site is an interval.
Swapped: a timeout is an elapsed interval and a publication date is a calendar moment.

questions.q: True or false: A reminder email scheduled for 9:00 tomorrow is a duration question.
questions.explain: A date and time of day is a point in time.

questions.q: A cache entry is stored with the time it expires. In the book's classification, what kind of question is when does this entry expire?
questions.explain: The book places when does this cache entry expire with the points in time, next to publication dates, reminder times and log timestamps.
questions.teaches: The book lists when does this cache entry expire among the points-in-time questions, together with publication date, reminder time and log timestamps.
options: A duration, because expiry is about how long an entry lasts
Neither, since a cache entry is data and does not involve a clock
A point in time, an event at a particular date and time
Both, since every expiry is measured in whole seconds from creation
optionExplain: Tempting, but the entry stores a moment on the calendar at which it expires.
Expiry needs a clock to decide when the moment has arrived.
Right: the book lists cache expiry with the points in time.
The book classifies it as a point in time; counting in seconds does not change that.

questions.q: Machine A sends a message and machine B receives it. What can be said about the two moments?
questions.explain: The receive moment always follows the send moment, but variable delay means the gap is unknown. The card next shows the consequence for ordering.
options: The receive time equals the send time, as digital messages are instant
The receive time can be earlier if the receiver's clock runs fast
The gap is always one millisecond inside a single datacenter
The receive time is later, by an unknown amount
optionExplain: Messages cross a physical network, so some time always passes.
A clock can read earlier, but the actual moment of receipt is always later than sending.
Delay varies with queues and load, so no fixed figure holds.
Right: delay is real but variable, so the gap is not known.
questions.rule: A message arrives later than it was sent, but by an unknown amount, so cross-machine ordering is uncertain.

questions.q: In a distributed system, communication is not ____ , because it takes time for a message to cross the network.
questions.explain: Delay is what makes ordering hard.

questions.q: Two clients write to two different servers within a millisecond of each other. What makes it hard to say who wrote first?
questions.explain: Each server has its own clock and each message has an unknown delay, so there is no trustworthy common timeline.
options: Variable delay and separate clocks leave their order uncertain
The servers share one memory, which scrambles the order of the writes
TCP reorders the two writes before either server gets to see them
The two writes cancel each other because they arrive so close together
optionExplain: Right: no shared timeline and an unknown delay.
Servers in this book share no memory; they only exchange messages.
TCP orders bytes within one connection, not writes sent to different servers.
Close writes do not cancel; the question is only which came first.

questions.q: True or false: On a single machine, the same ordering uncertainty arises from variable network delay.
questions.explain: The uncertainty comes from message delay between machines; one machine does not have it.

questions.q: A developer reasons: the server logged the request at 12:00:00.100 and the client sent it at 12:00:00.090, so it took exactly 10 ms. What is wrong?
questions.explain: Readings from two different machines can be compared only as far as their clocks agree, and that is exactly what is uncertain.
questions.rule: Do not subtract clocks of different machines.
options: A server cannot log requests with millisecond precision, so the entry is invalid
Requests over a network never complete in as little as ten milliseconds
The two clocks may disagree, so subtracting their readings proves nothing
Logging happens before the request arrives, so the log time comes too early
optionExplain: Logging at that precision is possible; the trouble is accuracy, not precision.
Ten milliseconds is plausible; the flaw is the subtraction across machines.
Right: each machine has its own clock.
A server logs after receipt; the issue is comparing two unsynchronized clocks.

questions.q: A message sent at 100 ms by the sender's clock is stamped 99 ms by the receiver's clock on arrival. What does this show?
questions.explain: The receive time is always later than the send time. When timestamps say otherwise, the two clocks disagree; this can happen even with tightly NTP-synchronized clocks.
questions.teaches: Even with tightly NTP-synchronized clocks, a packet sent at timestamp 100 ms by the sender's clock can arrive at timestamp 99 ms by the recipient's clock, so it looks as though it arrived before it was sent.
options: The network delivered the message faster than the speed of light
The clocks disagree, since the message seems to arrive before it was sent
The sender's clock is the accurate one and the receiver's is wrong
The message was lost and later resent from the receiver's side
optionExplain: That is impossible, so the readings must be wrong.
Right: only the clocks can explain it.
Nothing in the readings shows which clock is the wrong one.
A resend would arrive even later, not earlier.

questions.q: What kind of device keeps time inside most computers?
questions.explain: Computers keep time with a quartz oscillator that runs slightly fast or slow. The card next explains how machines compensate.
options: A shared atomic clock that every machine in the cluster reads
A quartz crystal oscillator
The network switch, which broadcasts the current time to each host
The operating system's scheduler, which counts every task it starts
optionExplain: Machines do not share one clock; each has its own.
Right: a hardware device that is not perfectly accurate.
Switches forward packets and do not supply time.
A scheduler counts tasks, not time, and sits on top of the hardware clock.
questions.rule: Every machine has an imperfect clock of its own; NTP brings clocks closer together.

questions.q: The most commonly used mechanism to synchronize clocks is the Network ____ Protocol.
questions.explain: NTP adjusts a computer's clock based on servers.

questions.q: Two servers in a cluster both start with the same time. A week later they disagree by some milliseconds. Why?
questions.explain: Because the oscillators are not perfectly accurate and differ from each other, clocks that start equal drift apart.
options: NTP deliberately assigns each server a slightly different time
The two servers share a single clock that happens to be inaccurate
The operating system adds a random offset to each clock for security
Their quartz clocks run at slightly different speeds
optionExplain: NTP tries to bring clocks closer together, not apart.
Each server has its own hardware clock.
The book describes no such behaviour; the cause is hardware.
Right: each clock drifts independently.

questions.q: Where do NTP servers in turn get their time?
questions.explain: NTP servers in turn get their time from a more accurate time source, such as a GPS receiver.
questions.rule: NTP chains back to an accurate source.
options: A more accurate source, such as a GPS receiver
The clients that synchronize with them, averaged together
The quartz clock of the busiest client in the network
The nearest network switch, which keeps a master copy of the time
optionExplain: Right: the chain leads back to an accurate source.
That would be circular: the clients rely on the servers.
A single client's quartz is no more accurate than the server's own.
Switches forward packets; they are not time sources.

questions.q: True or false: Once clocks are synchronized with NTP, two machines have identical time.
questions.explain: NTP synchronizes to some degree; differences remain.
questions.rule: NTP reduces differences, not removes them.

questions.q: A team claims that using NTP means timestamps from different machines can be compared exactly. What is the flaw?
questions.explain: NTP allows the computer clock to be adjusted according to a group of servers, but only to some degree; differences remain.
questions.teaches: NTP allows the computer clock to be adjusted according to the time reported by a group of servers, which in turn get their time from a more accurate time source such as a GPS receiver.
options: NTP works only inside one machine and cannot touch other machines
Timestamps from different machines use different calendars, so they never match
NTP synchronizes only to some degree, so comparisons carry error
NTP rewrites timestamps after they are stored, so old values change
optionExplain: NTP is exactly a protocol for synchronizing across machines.
Both use the same calendar and epoch; the issue is clock error.
Right: clocks stay slightly different.
NTP adjusts clocks going forward; it does not edit stored timestamps.

questions.q: Which call returns the current date and time since the epoch?
questions.explain: Calendar time since the epoch comes from the time-of-day clock. The card next defines it.
options: System.nanoTime in Java, which also returns a number of nanoseconds
System.currentTimeMillis in Java
A TCP keepalive counter, which increases while a connection is idle
A CPU temperature sensor, which readings change gradually over the day
optionExplain: The name suggests time, but it is a monotonic clock for durations with an arbitrary origin.
Right: it returns milliseconds since the epoch.
It counts packets, not calendar time.
A sensor measures heat, not the date.
questions.rule: A time-of-day clock gives calendar time since the epoch, comparable across machines only to the accuracy of NTP.

questions.q: Time-of-day clocks count time since the ____ , midnight UTC on January 1, 1970.
questions.explain: The epoch is the reference point.

questions.q: A log service stamps events on many servers and merges them. Which clock type gives timestamps that can be compared across servers?
questions.explain: Only calendar time, kept in step by NTP, is intended to be comparable across machines.
options: The monotonic clock, since its values only ever increase
A boot counter on each machine, which counts seconds since startup
The CPU cycle count of each server, which is a precise hardware number
The time-of-day clock, synchronized with NTP
optionExplain: It is steady but its absolute values differ arbitrarily between machines.
Machines boot at different times, so the values do not line up.
Precise, but unrelated between machines and to the calendar.
Right: it is meant to mean the same everywhere.

questions.q: True or false: Time-of-day clocks are named wall-clock time and count from a calendar reference point.
questions.explain: Wall-clock time is another name for the time-of-day clock.

questions.q: A developer says: currentTimeMillis counts leap seconds, so it is exact to the real UTC second. What is wrong?
questions.explain: The value counts time since the epoch without counting leap seconds, so it is not an exact count of real UTC seconds.
options: It counts seconds since the epoch and does not count leap seconds
It counts whole days only, so it cannot be exact to the second
It uses the local time zone, so it is exact only in one place
It starts at the computer's boot time, so it is exact since startup
optionExplain: Right: leap seconds are not included.
It counts milliseconds, not days.
It uses UTC, not a local zone.
Its origin is the epoch, midnight UTC on January 1, 1970.

questions.q: Older Windows systems moved the time-of-day clock forward in steps of 10 ms. What does that limit?
questions.explain: Resolution is how small a step the clock shows. The book notes coarse steps were a historic problem and are less of one on recent systems.
questions.rule: Resolution limits ordering of close events.
questions.teaches: Time-of-day clocks have historically had quite coarse-grained resolution, such as moving forward in steps of 10 ms on older Windows systems, although this is less of a problem on recent systems.
options: Its epoch, which would have to move forward by 10 ms
Its use of NTP, which cannot synchronize a coarse clock
Its resolution: events within 10 ms cannot be told apart
Its ability to show dates, which require a finer step than 10 ms
optionExplain: The epoch is a fixed reference date.
NTP and resolution are separate matters.
Right: resolution is the smallest visible step.
Dates need no fine steps; coarse steps only blur close events.

questions.q: A service measures a request's duration by subtracting two time-of-day clock readings. What can go wrong?
questions.explain: Forced resets make the time-of-day clock jump, which breaks subtraction. The card next explains why.
options: The subtraction always returns zero because both readings are identical
The clock may jump back between the readings, giving a wrong duration
The clock stops running until the request has completed
The two readings are taken in different time zones and cannot be compared
optionExplain: Readings differ as time passes; the problem is jumps.
Right: resets can move time backward.
The clock keeps running; it can be reset, not paused.
The clock uses UTC, so zones play no part.
questions.rule: Time-of-day clocks can jump, so never use them to measure elapsed time.

questions.q: If the local clock is too far ahead of the NTP server, it may be forcibly reset and appear to jump ____ in time.
questions.explain: Resets can send time backwards.

questions.q: A function times a database query with System.currentTimeMillis before and after. NTP resets the clock backward by 2 seconds during the query. What does the function report?
questions.explain: If the clock jumps back 2 seconds during the query, the end reading is 2 seconds less than it should be, so the duration is too small and possibly negative.
options: The correct duration, because NTP corrects any error it finds
A duration that is two seconds too large, as time is added back
An exception raised by the operating system when the clock changes
A negative or too-small duration
optionExplain: The NTP reset is the cause of the wrong reading.
A backward jump shortens the interval, it does not lengthen it.
Clock changes raise no exception; the code just gets a wrong number.
Right: the end reading is earlier than expected.

questions.q: What if a leap second occurs while a time-of-day clock is used to time an event, and the clock ignores it?
questions.explain: Time-of-day clocks often ignore leap seconds, so an interval spanning one is wrong by about a second.
options: The measured duration is off by about one second
The clock halts until the next leap second arrives
The duration is exact, since leap seconds are too rare to matter
The duration doubles, because the leap second counts twice
optionExplain: Right: the clock does not count the extra second.
Clocks do not halt for leap seconds.
Rare events still break a measurement when they occur.
The extra second is missed, not counted twice.

questions.q: True or false: Time-of-day clocks are the right choice for measuring timeouts because they are synchronized by NTP.
questions.explain: Jumps and ignored leap seconds make them unsuitable for measuring elapsed time.
questions.rule: Use a different clock for durations.

questions.q: Why do the jumps matter less for a log timestamp than for a timeout?
questions.explain: The oddities hurt most when two readings are subtracted. For a calendar timestamp the jump is an accepted risk.
questions.teaches: Time-of-day clocks are unsuitable for measuring elapsed time because of forced resets and the fact that they often ignore leap seconds; they are still the clock that gives calendar timestamps.
options: Logs do not use clocks at all, so jumps cannot affect them
Log timestamps are taken from a monotonic clock, which never jumps
A log needs a calendar time, not an elapsed interval from two readings
A jump never affects any single reading, only the clock's rate
optionExplain: Logs carry timestamps, so they use clocks.
Logs need calendar time, which a monotonic clock cannot give.
Right: jumps break subtraction, not a single reading.
A jump can make a single reading wrong too; it matters less for logs.

questions.q: Which clock is suited to measuring a service's response time?
questions.explain: Durations need a clock that never jumps backward. The card next names it.
options: A monotonic clock
A time-of-day clock, because it is synchronized with NTP
A calendar lookup that is updated once per minute
The clock of the user's phone, which already knows the local time
optionExplain: Right: it only moves forward.
Synchronization helps timestamps, but resets can make it jump back.
Too coarse, and not a clock reading at all.
Phone clocks can be set to anything and are not under the service's control.
questions.rule: Measure durations with a monotonic clock: only the difference between two readings means anything.

questions.q: A monotonic clock is guaranteed to move only ____.
questions.explain: The name comes from that guarantee.

questions.q: A client wants to enforce a 5-second timeout on a request. Which approach is right?
questions.explain: Take the monotonic reading at the start and at the end, and subtract. Only the difference is meaningful.
options: Read the time-of-day clock now and compare against a fixed future time
Compare the monotonic reading with today's calendar date
Read the monotonic clock before and after, and compare the difference to 5 s
Ask the server for its monotonic reading and use that as the deadline
optionExplain: An NTP reset could shift the clock and end the timeout early or late.
The absolute monotonic value has no date meaning.
Right: subtract two readings.
Values on two computers are not comparable.

questions.q: Which statement about the absolute value of a monotonic clock is correct?
questions.explain: The absolute value of a monotonic clock may be time since boot or something similarly arbitrary.
options: It is the number of seconds since January 1, 1970
It is meaningless, perhaps nanoseconds since the computer started
It equals the time reported by the NTP server it follows
It is the same on every machine in a synchronized cluster
optionExplain: That is the time-of-day clock.
Right: only differences matter.
A monotonic clock needs no calendar value from NTP.
Each machine has its own arbitrary origin.

questions.q: True or false: A monotonic clock reading can be used as a timestamp stored in a database for later comparison with other servers.
questions.explain: Its absolute value is meaningless and cannot be compared between computers.

questions.q: Why is a monotonic clock usually fine for timeouts in a distributed system?
questions.explain: Because a timeout only needs elapsed local time, a monotonic clock works without any agreement between nodes.
questions.teaches: In a distributed system, a monotonic clock for measuring elapsed time such as timeouts is usually fine because it does not assume any synchronization between different nodes' clocks and is not sensitive to slight inaccuracies of measurement.
options: It gives timestamps that all nodes can compare with each other
NTP continually corrects it so that it matches the rest of the cluster
It counts leap seconds exactly, which keeps every timeout precise
It assumes no synchronization between nodes and tolerates slight inaccuracy
optionExplain: Its absolute values cannot be compared between computers.
It does not need to match anyone; NTP may only adjust its rate.
Leap seconds are not why it suits timeouts.
Right: timeouts are local durations.

questions.q: What may NTP do to a monotonic clock?
questions.explain: NTP may adjust the frequency at which the monotonic clock moves, but it cannot make it jump.
options: Reset it to the current date when it drifts from the server
Make it jump backward to match the server's value
Speed it up or slow it down slightly, but not make it jump
Replace it with the server's reading at every synchronization
optionExplain: A reset would be a jump, which a monotonic clock does not allow.
Jumping backward is forbidden by definition.
Right: slewing changes the rate only.
Replacement would create jumps in either direction.
questions.rule: NTP can slew a monotonic clock by up to 0.05 percent but cannot make it jump, so differences remain usable.

questions.q: Adjusting the rate at which a clock moves forward is known as ____ the clock.
questions.explain: Slewing changes the rate, not the value.

questions.q: NTP slows a monotonic clock by the maximum default 0.05 percent. A real interval of 600 seconds is measured as how many seconds?
questions.explain: 0.05% x 600 s = 0.3 s, so a slowed clock measures about 599.7 s.
options: About 570 s
About 599.7 s
About 599.97 s
About 630 s
optionExplain: This takes 5 percent instead of 0.05 percent.
Right: 0.05 percent of 600 s is 0.3 s.
This takes 0.005 percent, one decimal place too far.
The clock is slowed, so the measured value is lower, not higher.

questions.q: What if you compare the raw monotonic clock values of two different computers?
questions.explain: Monotonic values are meaningful only as differences on the same computer.
questions.rule: Never compare monotonic values across computers.
options: It shows which machine started first, since smaller values mean earlier
It gives the offset between the two clocks in microseconds
It can be trusted if both machines synchronize with the same NTP server
It is meaningless, since each machine's value has its own arbitrary origin
optionExplain: Boot times and rates differ, and the values are not on one scale.
The difference mixes unrelated origins and says nothing about offset.
NTP does not align the arbitrary origins of monotonic clocks.
Right: no shared reference.

questions.q: True or false: Because a monotonic clock is guaranteed monotonic, it cannot run at a slightly wrong speed.
questions.explain: NTP can slew the rate by up to 0.05 percent; monotonic means no jumps backward, not exact speed.

questions.q: On a server with several CPU sockets, each CPU may have its own timer. What does the book advise about the monotonic guarantee?
questions.explain: Operating systems try to present a monotonic view across CPUs, but it is wise not to rely on it fully.
questions.teaches: On a server with multiple CPU sockets there may be a separate timer per CPU, not necessarily synchronized; operating systems try to present a monotonic view to applications, but it is wise to take the guarantee with a pinch of salt.
options: Take it with a pinch of salt, as per-CPU timers may not be synchronized
Trust it completely, since the operating system hides every discrepancy
Avoid monotonic clocks on multi-socket servers and use time-of-day instead
Disable all but one CPU socket so the timers always agree
optionExplain: Right: the book advises caution.
The OS compensates but does not remove every discrepancy.
Time-of-day clocks can jump, which is worse for durations.
The book suggests no such step.

questions.q: A server clock drifts at 200 ppm and is resynchronized once a day. Roughly how far off can it be before the sync?
questions.explain: Drift multiplies by elapsed time. The card next gives the arithmetic.
options: About 6 milliseconds, since drift is tiny for quartz
About 17 seconds, since a day has 86,400 seconds
About 2 hours, since errors accumulate quickly in cheap hardware
About 1 microsecond, since NTP keeps clocks nearly exact
optionExplain: That is the figure for a 30-second interval; a day is far longer.
Right: 86,400 s x 0.0002 is about 17 s.
Far too large: 200 ppm is two parts in ten thousand.
NTP only corrects at sync time; between syncs the error grows.
questions.rule: Clock drift limits the best possible accuracy: the error grows in proportion to the time since the last sync.

questions.q: Google assumes a clock drift of 200 ____ (parts per million) for its servers.
questions.explain: The unit is parts per million, written ppm.

questions.q: At 200 ppm, a clock is resynchronized every 10 seconds. What is its largest drift error?
questions.explain: Multiply the interval by the drift rate: 10 x 0.0002 = 0.002 s.
options: 2 ms
20 ms, reading ppm as two percent of a second per second
200 ms, reading the 200 as milliseconds per interval
0.2 ms, because short intervals make drift negligible
optionExplain: Off by a factor of ten; 200 ppm is 0.02 percent.
200 is a rate in parts per million, not milliseconds.
Short intervals shrink the error but not by that much: 10 s x 0.0002 is 2 ms.

questions.q: What if the sync interval is doubled from 30 seconds to 60 seconds at 200 ppm?
questions.explain: Error is linear in the interval.
questions.rule: Double the interval, double the error.
options: The worst-case drift doubles, from 6 ms to 12 ms
The worst-case drift stays 6 ms, since NTP corrects it
The worst-case drift halves to 3 ms, since longer intervals average out
The worst-case drift quadruples to 24 ms, since errors compound
optionExplain: Right: drift grows in proportion to elapsed time.
Correction only happens at the sync; the error accumulated before it doubles.
Averaging does not apply; drift accumulates.
The error is linear in time at a constant rate, not squared.

questions.q: True or false: If NTP works perfectly and the network is healthy, quartz drift stops limiting the accuracy of a clock.
questions.explain: Drift limits the best possible accuracy even if everything works correctly, because error builds up between syncs.
questions.rule: Drift limits accuracy even when all works.

questions.q: A rack's cooling fails and the machines run hotter than usual. What is the likely effect on their clocks?
questions.explain: Drift is not a fixed constant, so the sync interval that was safe yesterday may not be today.
questions.teaches: Clock drift varies depending on the temperature of the machine.
options: Nothing changes, since quartz clocks are independent of the environment
Their drift rate may change, since drift depends on temperature
The clocks stop, since quartz oscillators fail when hot
NTP becomes exact, since heat speeds up network messages
optionExplain: The book says drift depends on temperature.
Right: quartz drift varies with machine temperature.
Nothing says they stop; the rate changes.
No such effect is described.

questions.q: What sets a floor on how accurate NTP can be over the internet?
questions.explain: NTP messages cross the same variable network. The card next gives the figures.
options: The color and quality of the network cables used on the path
The age of the hardware in the client computer
The number of applications running on the client machine
The delay and variability of the network path to the server
optionExplain: Cable quality is not what limits a time exchange.
Old hardware may drift more, but it does not set the floor on synchronization accuracy.
Application count affects load, not the network delay NTP has to measure.
Right: the time messages travel is part of the measurement.
questions.rule: NTP accuracy is bounded by the network round-trip delay and its variation, not only by clock quality.

questions.q: In one experiment, the minimum error achievable when synchronizing over the internet was 35 ____.
questions.explain: About 35 ms, with occasional spikes to about a second.
questions.rule: Internet NTP is accurate to tens of ms.

questions.q: Two datacenters synchronize to public NTP servers over the internet. Which timestamp precision is realistic to trust?
questions.explain: Internet NTP gives tens of milliseconds at best.
questions.rule: Expect tens of ms over the internet.
options: Single nanoseconds, since digital clocks count that finely
Exact agreement, since both use the same time standard
Tens of milliseconds, with occasional larger spikes
Several hours, since internet time is only rough
optionExplain: Resolution is not accuracy; the network delay swamps nanoseconds.
A shared standard does not remove the error of reaching it.
Right: network delay limits accuracy.
Only misconfigured servers are off by hours; normal accuracy is far better.

questions.q: What if network congestion makes round-trip delays large and variable?
questions.explain: Noisy delays make the client's estimate worse.
options: NTP error shrinks, since a congested network sends fewer probes
NTP error rises, with spikes around a second, and a client may give up
NTP error stays the same, since it measures and removes the delay
NTP error vanishes, since the client switches to monotonic time
optionExplain: Congestion does not shrink the error; it makes measurements noisier.
Right: delays degrade accuracy.
It cannot fully remove a delay it can only estimate.
A monotonic clock has no calendar time to switch to.

questions.q: True or false: A computer clock that is far from the NTP server is smoothly corrected within seconds, with no visible effect on applications.
questions.explain: The client may refuse to synchronize, or the clock may be forcibly reset; applications see the time jump.

questions.q: A node was accidentally firewalled off from NTP servers a month ago. What is the likely consequence?
questions.explain: Clock errors do not announce themselves; this is why they are dangerous.
questions.rule: A blocked NTP shows up late, if at all.
questions.teaches: If a node is accidentally firewalled off from NTP servers, the misconfiguration may go unnoticed for some time; anecdotal evidence suggests this does happen in practice.
options: The misconfiguration goes unnoticed while the clock drifts away from the others
The node crashes at once, since it cannot reach a time server
The node corrects itself from its peers' clocks over time
The node stops accepting requests until NTP returns
optionExplain: Right: a drifting clock rarely announces itself.
Nothing so dramatic: most things keep working.
No such mechanism exists once NTP traffic is blocked.
It continues serving requests with an increasingly wrong clock.

questions.q: A leap second is added at midnight. What is the effect on the length of that minute?
questions.explain: The calendar can surprise software. The card next lists three such surprises.
options: It stays 60 seconds, since the extra second is hidden
It becomes two minutes, since clocks are reset
It has 61 seconds (or 59 if one is removed)
It disappears from the calendar, since it is skipped
optionExplain: The point is that the extra second is real and upsets software.
Leap seconds adjust by one second, not a minute.
Right: the minute is not 60 seconds long.
The minute exists; it is just one second longer or shorter.
questions.rule: Do not trust a clock blindly: leap seconds, VM pauses and user settings all produce wrong readings.

questions.q: Match each cause with its effect on a clock reading.
questions.explain: Three different sources of clock error.
pairs: VM paused for tens of milliseconds
The clock appears to jump forward
User sets the device clock wrongly
The clock may be wildly in the past or future

questions.q: A mobile game uses the phone's clock to enforce a daily reward limit. What is the risk?
questions.explain: Do not trust clocks on devices you do not control.
questions.rule: Client clocks can be set to anything.
options: The phone's clock will refuse to move forward past midnight
NTP will automatically correct any false clock a player sets
Leap seconds will give each player an extra reward
Players may set the clock to a false date to claim rewards again
optionExplain: Nothing prevents the clock from advancing.
Users can override the setting, so NTP does not protect the game.
Leap seconds are not about rewards.
Right: devices you do not control cannot be trusted.

questions.q: What is smearing?
questions.explain: Smearing spreads the leap second out so no minute has 61 seconds.
options: Servers add a full extra second at midnight and announce it loudly
Clients round every timestamp to the nearest minute
Servers stop their clocks for one second at midnight
NTP servers perform a leap-second adjustment gradually over a day
optionExplain: That is the unsmeared leap second that breaks assumptions.
Rounding timestamps is unrelated to leap seconds.
Stopping the clock is a jump, which is what smearing avoids.
Right: the servers deliberately lie by tiny amounts.

questions.q: True or false: Because leap seconds have crashed many large systems, the book concludes that they cannot be handled safely.
questions.explain: The book uses the crashes to show how easily wrong clock assumptions sneak in, and describes smearing as a way to cope.
questions.rule: Leap seconds are a risk, not an impossibility.

questions.q: Two virtual machines share one CPU core, and each is paused for tens of milliseconds while the other runs. What does a timer in the application see?
questions.explain: A paused VM wakes to a later reading than it expected.
questions.rule: A pause looks like a forward jump.
questions.teaches: In virtual machines the hardware clock is virtualized; when a CPU core is shared, each VM is paused for tens of milliseconds, which to the application looks like the clock suddenly jumping forward.
options: A sudden jump backward, as the clock is restored
A clock that runs slower from then on
A sudden jump forward when it resumes
No change, since the VM's clock stops during the pause
optionExplain: The clock does not go back; it simply reads later.
A pause is a single event, not a change of rate.
Right: time passed while it was paused.
The hardware clock is virtualized and the reading advances.

questions.q: A trading firm must show event times accurate to 100 microseconds. What does that need?
questions.explain: Tight accuracy needs special sources. The card next lists them.
options: GPS receivers, PTP and careful monitoring
The default NTP setup over the public internet
Letting each trader set the clock on a laptop
A faster CPU in each server
optionExplain: Right: precision needs dedicated sources and care.
That reaches tens of milliseconds, not 100 microseconds.
Manual setting is far less accurate.
CPU speed does not give a better time reference.
questions.rule: Accurate clocks are possible with dedicated hardware and careful operation, but they cost significant effort.

questions.q: Very accurate clock synchronization can use GPS receivers and the Precision ____ Protocol.
questions.explain: PTP stands for Precision Time Protocol.
questions.rule: PTP is the Precision Time Protocol.

questions.q: A firm must prove the order of its trades to within a fraction of a millisecond. Which approach does the book's example suggest?
questions.explain: Strict accuracy needs special hardware and monitoring.
options: Plain NTP against a pool of public servers
GPS receivers and PTP, with careful deployment and monitoring
Monotonic clocks on every server
