Timestamps taken from clients' devices
optionExplain: Public NTP is accurate to tens of milliseconds at best.
Right: this is the route the regulation implies.
Monotonic clocks cannot be compared across machines.
Client devices cannot be trusted.

questions.q: What if the firm's NTP daemon is misconfigured or a firewall blocks NTP traffic?
questions.explain: Accuracy depends on continuous, correct operation.
options: Nothing, since GPS alone fixes all errors
The clocks synchronize with each other automatically
Drift error can quickly become large again
The trading stops until the firewall is fixed
optionExplain: If synchronization is broken, the GPS-derived time does not reach the clock.
No such fallback is described.
Right: drift is no longer corrected.
Trading continues with increasingly wrong clocks.

questions.q: True or false: Because 100-microsecond synchronization has been achieved in finance, any company can get the same result cheaply with default settings.
questions.explain: The book says it requires significant effort and expertise.

questions.q: Why does the MiFID II draft want such precise clocks, according to the book?
questions.explain: Regulators need to reconstruct the order of events.
questions.teaches: The MiFID II draft regulation requires clocks synchronized to within 100 microseconds of UTC in order to help debug market anomalies such as flash crashes and to help detect market manipulation.
options: To let traders predict price movements ahead of the market
To reduce network traffic between exchanges
To make stock exchanges run on a single computer
To help debug market anomalies such as flash crashes and detect manipulation
optionExplain: Prediction is not the stated purpose.
Not what the regulation is about.
The regulation does not require that.
Right: events must be ordered reliably.

questions.q: A node's NTP client is misconfigured and its clock slowly drifts. What is the likely visible effect?
questions.explain: Clock problems hide. The card next explains the danger.
options: An immediate crash with a clear error message
Nothing obvious: most things seem to work fine
A loud warning on every request it handles
A refusal to start up after the next reboot
optionExplain: A defective CPU might crash, but a drifting clock rarely does.
Right: that is why clock errors are dangerous.
Software does not warn about clock drift on its own.
A wrong clock does not prevent starting.
questions.rule: Wrong clocks go unnoticed, so monitor offsets and remove nodes whose clocks drift too far.

questions.q: If software relies on an accurately synchronized clock, a bad clock more likely causes silent data ____ than a crash.
questions.explain: Silent data loss is the risk.

questions.q: A team's database depends on synchronized clocks. What should operations do?
questions.explain: Monitoring catches broken clocks early.
options: Monitor the clock offsets between all machines
Check clocks by hand once a year, during an audit
Trust NTP and watch only the CPU and network graphs
Disable NTP so that clocks never jump
optionExplain: Right: that reveals broken clocks before much damage.
Drift can cause damage in days; yearly checks are too slow.
CPU and network graphs do not show clock error.
Without NTP the clocks drift apart faster.

questions.q: What if a node's clock drifts far from the others and nobody monitors it?
questions.explain: Silent errors accumulate.
options: It may silently cause lost or misordered writes before anyone notices
It corrects itself because peers adjust it automatically
It crashes within minutes and is replaced
Other nodes ignore its timestamps from then on
optionExplain: Right: damage accumulates unseen.
No such correction is described.
A drifting clock does not crash a node.
They have no way to know the timestamps are wrong.

questions.q: True or false: A node whose clock has drifted too far from the others should be kept in the cluster to preserve capacity.
questions.explain: The book says such a node should be declared dead and removed, so it cannot cause damage.

questions.q: Why is a clock fault harder to notice than a defective CPU?
questions.explain: A fault that stops work is noticed; one that merely skews results is not.
questions.teaches: If a machine's CPU is defective or its network is misconfigured it most likely will not work at all and will be noticed and fixed quickly, whereas with a defective quartz clock or a misconfigured NTP client most things seem to work fine.
options: CPUs are monitored by NTP, so only clocks are left unwatched
A defective CPU stops the machine from working, but with a bad clock most things seem fine
Clock faults occur only on virtual machines, which are rarely checked
CPUs cannot be misconfigured, so they never fail silently
optionExplain: NTP does not monitor CPUs.
Right: visible failure versus quiet error.
The book does not limit them to virtual machines.
Misconfiguration affects CPUs and networks, but those faults are noisy.

questions.q: Client A writes x = 1 at timestamp 42.004; client B later increments x to 2 at timestamp 42.003. Which value does a last-write-wins replica keep?
questions.explain: LWW follows timestamps even when they are wrong. The card next gives the full example.
options: x = 2, because it truly happened later
Both values, flagged as a conflict for the application
Neither value, with an error returned to both clients
x = 1, because it has the higher timestamp
optionExplain: The replica cannot see that; it sees only the timestamps.
LWW keeps one value and discards the other.
LWW does not report errors; it picks a winner.
Right: LWW compares timestamps only.
questions.rule: LWW trusts timestamps, so a node with a lagging clock can lose writes that really happened later.

questions.q: In last write wins (LWW), the write with the ____ timestamp is kept.
questions.explain: The highest (latest) timestamp wins.

questions.q: Two phones edit a shared note; phone B's clock is 5 seconds slow. B edits after A, yet the sync keeps A's edit. Why?
questions.explain: A lagging clock loses to a faster one.
questions.rule: A slow clock loses its writes.
options: The sync server prefers the phone that connected first
B's edit was lost in the network before reaching the server
B's edit got an earlier timestamp from its slow clock, so LWW dropped it
A's edit used a monotonic clock, which always outranks wall-clock time
optionExplain: LWW ranks by timestamp, not by connection order.
The scenario describes a conflict resolved by timestamp, not a lost packet.
Right: LWW trusted B's slow clock.
The two clock types are not ranked against each other like that.

questions.q: B's increment is dropped at node 2. What does client B see?
questions.explain: LWW discards writes without reporting.
options: An error message saying the write was rejected
No error: the increment is silently lost
A conflict dialog asking which value to keep
An automatic retry that finally applies the increment
optionExplain: Rejection would be visible; LWW drops it silently.
Right: nothing is reported to the application.
LWW resolves the conflict itself, without asking.
No retry occurs because no failure is observed.

questions.q: True or false: LWW works correctly whenever the clock skew between nodes is smaller than 3 ms.
questions.explain: In the book's example the skew is under 3 ms and the writes are still misordered.
questions.rule: Small skew can still misorder writes.

questions.q: A database stamps writes with client-side timestamps instead of server-side ones. What changes for LWW?
questions.explain: Where the timestamp is made does not change that clocks disagree.
questions.rule: Client timestamps do not fix LWW.
questions.teaches: LWW is widely used in multi-leader replication and in leaderless databases such as Cassandra and Riak; some implementations generate timestamps on the client rather than the server, which does not change the fundamental problems.
options: Its fundamental problems remain, since client clocks can be wrong too
The problems disappear, since clients know when they wrote
Writes become atomic across all replicas
The database must reject all concurrent writes
optionExplain: Right: moving the clock does not fix the approach.
Clients' clocks are no more reliable than servers'.
Timestamp source does not change atomicity.
LWW still accepts and then discards some.

questions.q: A node with a lagging clock writes a value after a fast-clock node wrote one. What happens under LWW?
questions.explain: Lagging clocks lose. The card next lists the problems.
options: Its write replaces the old value at once, as it is newer
Both writes are kept side by side for later merging
Its write is dropped until the skew has elapsed
The database stops accepting writes from either node
optionExplain: The lagging timestamp is older, so it loses.
LWW keeps a single winner.
Right: it cannot overwrite the fast clock's value.
Nothing in LWW stops the nodes.
questions.rule: LWW can silently drop data, cannot separate sequential from concurrent writes, and needs tiebreakers for equal timestamps.

questions.q: If two nodes generate writes with the same timestamp, a ____ is needed to decide the winner.
questions.explain: A large random number can serve as one.

questions.q: A database uses LWW with millisecond timestamps. Two nodes write the same key within the same millisecond. What does it need?
questions.explain: Millisecond resolution makes ties possible.
options: Nothing, because the order of simultaneous writes is obvious
A merge of both values into one combined value
A halt of all writes until clocks are resynchronized
An extra tiebreaker value, which can itself violate causality
optionExplain: Equal timestamps have no obvious order.
LWW does not merge; it picks one.
Overkill; a tiebreaker is the usual remedy.
Right: either choice may rank a write wrongly.

questions.q: Which pair of cases can LWW not tell apart?
questions.explain: LWW sees only timestamps, not causality.
options: Writes from node 1 and writes from node 2
Large writes and small writes
Reads and writes
Writes in quick succession and truly concurrent writes
optionExplain: Origin is visible to the database.
Size plays no role in ordering.
They are different operations.
Right: both can show close timestamps.

questions.q: True or false: Adding a random tiebreaker removes every causality violation from LWW.
questions.explain: The book says the tiebreaker approach can itself lead to violations of causality.
questions.rule: A tiebreaker does not restore causality.

questions.q: Which mechanism does the book say is needed to prevent causality violations under LWW?
questions.explain: Version vectors record which writes saw which others.
questions.teaches: Additional causality tracking mechanisms, such as version vectors, are needed to prevent violations of causality with LWW.
options: A more frequent NTP sync to shrink the skew
Longer timestamps with microsecond digits
Additional causality tracking, such as version vectors
More replicas to outvote the lagging node
optionExplain: Smaller skew still leaves ties and misordering.
Finer digits are not more accurate.
Right: track causality directly.
Replica count does not decide timestamp order.

questions.q: What would it take for timestamps to order events across machines reliably?
questions.explain: Error must be below the gaps. The card next states it.
options: A clock source much more accurate than the network delay
A faster CPU in every machine
A bigger log file to store more timestamps
More frequent heartbeat messages between nodes
optionExplain: Right: the error must be smaller than the gaps.
CPU speed does not improve time accuracy.
Storage does not make timestamps accurate.
Heartbeats do not reduce clock error.
questions.rule: Timestamps order events only when clock error is much smaller than the gaps between events.

questions.q: NTP synchronization accuracy is itself limited by the network round-trip ____.
questions.explain: Round-trip time limits it.
questions.rule: NTP is limited by round-trip time.

questions.q: Two events on different servers are 500 microseconds apart; clock error is about 10 ms. Can their timestamps order them?
questions.explain: The error margin exceeds the gap.
questions.rule: A gap smaller than the error cannot be ordered.
options: Yes: timestamps always keep events in order
No: the error is far larger than the gap
Yes, if both servers report UTC
Yes, if the timestamps have microsecond digits
optionExplain: They do not when error exceeds the gap.
Right: the order is ambiguous.
A shared standard does not shrink the error.
Digits give resolution, not accuracy.

questions.q: What if two events are 10 seconds apart and clock error is 10 ms?
questions.explain: Ordering works when the gap is much larger than the error.
options: They cannot be ordered, since any error ruins ordering
The earlier event appears later, since clocks skew
The timestamps order them correctly
Both get identical timestamps
optionExplain: Small error only matters near the gap size.
A 10 ms skew cannot reverse a 10 s gap.
Right: the gap dwarfs the error.
They differ by 10 seconds.

questions.q: True or false: With NTP-synchronized clocks, a packet cannot appear to arrive before it was sent.
questions.explain: Even with tightly synchronized clocks a packet sent at 100 ms on the sender's clock can arrive at 99 ms on the receiver's.

questions.q: Why is it hard to push NTP error below network delay?
questions.explain: The tool is limited by what it must measure.
questions.rule: The measuring path limits the accuracy.
questions.teaches: For correct ordering, you would need the clock source to be significantly more accurate than the thing you are measuring, namely network delay.
options: NTP ignores the network and reads a local oscillator
NTP works only with monotonic clocks
NTP runs only once a day, whatever the delay
NTP learns the time through the same variable network
optionExplain: NTP depends on messages over the network.
NTP adjusts the time-of-day clock.
Frequency is configurable; the delay limit remains.
Right: the limit is circular.

questions.q: What does a logical clock measure?
questions.explain: Counters give order. The card next defines them.
options: Seconds since midnight UTC
The relative order of events
The length of a timeout in microseconds
The temperature drift of a quartz crystal
optionExplain: That is a physical, time-of-day clock.
Right: before or after.
That is a monotonic, physical clock.
Logical clocks do not use crystals at all.
questions.rule: Logical clocks count events to give a safe ordering; physical clocks measure time.

questions.q: Logical clocks are based on incrementing ____ rather than an oscillating quartz crystal.
questions.explain: A counter that increases with events.

questions.q: A collaborative editor must decide which of two edits came after the other that the editor had already seen. Which clock suits?
questions.explain: Ordering needs logical clocks, not wall-clock time.
questions.rule: Use a logical clock for ordering.
options: A logical clock, which tracks the order of events
A time-of-day clock on each user's laptop
A monotonic clock on the server
The CPU cycle count of the server
optionExplain: Right: it captures before and after.
Laptop clocks can disagree, misordering edits.
It gives durations on one machine, not cross-machine order.
Cycle counts cannot be compared across machines.

questions.q: Sort each item by the kind of clock it describes.
questions.explain: Physical clocks measure time; logical clocks measure order.

items.t: Time-of-day clock
Monotonic clock
Counter that increments with each event
Records only whether one event happened before another

questions.q: True or false: A logical clock tells you the calendar date on which an event happened.
questions.explain: Logical clocks do not measure the time of day or elapsed seconds, only the relative ordering of events.

questions.q: A support team wants to know whether a refund request was processed before a customer complaint. Which statement holds for a logical clock?
questions.explain: Logical clocks give order only; clocks that measure actual elapsed time, time-of-day and monotonic, are called physical clocks.
questions.teaches: Time-of-day and monotonic clocks, which measure actual elapsed time, are also known as physical clocks, in contrast to logical clocks, which measure only relative ordering.
options: It can say which came first, but not how many seconds apart they were
It can give the exact seconds between the two events
It can say nothing about order, only about the calendar date
It can only order events that happened on the same machine
optionExplain: Right: order without duration.
It does not measure elapsed seconds.
It is the opposite: order, not date.
Logical clocks are used to order events across machines.

questions.q: A clock reads 10.3894712 seconds past the minute, but its error is plus or minus 100 ms. What do the microsecond digits mean?
questions.explain: Resolution is not accuracy. The card next explains.
options: They are exact, since the clock printed them
They are accurate to within a microsecond
They show the size of the error
They are essentially meaningless
optionExplain: Printed digits say nothing about accuracy.
The error is 100 ms, so not to a microsecond.
The digits are part of the reading, not an error bound.
Right: resolution is not accuracy.
questions.rule: Think of a clock reading as a range of possible times, not a point.

questions.q: A clock reading is more like a range of times within a ____ interval.
questions.explain: A confidence interval.

questions.q: Two timestamps differ by 20 ms, but each is accurate only to within 100 ms. Which event is earlier?
questions.explain: Overlapping intervals cannot be ordered.
options: The one with the smaller timestamp, since numbers decide
The one with the larger timestamp, since it is more recent
Both are simultaneous, since the readings are close
It cannot be told: their intervals overlap
optionExplain: The error is five times the gap.
Same problem in reverse.
Close readings do not mean simultaneous events.
Right: the order is unknown.

questions.q: Spanner's TrueTime API is asked for the current time. What does it return?
questions.explain: Spanner exposes its uncertainty.
options: One exact value to the nanosecond
A single value plus a random jitter term
Two values, the earliest and latest possible time
A counter of transactions so far
optionExplain: Exactness is not available.
It reports a bound, not jitter.
Right: the confidence interval.
That would be a logical clock.

questions.q: True or false: Calling clock_gettime tells you the expected error of the timestamp it returns.
questions.explain: Most systems do not expose this: you do not know whether the interval is five milliseconds or five years.

questions.q: For a clock synchronized to a time server, how can its uncertainty be estimated?
questions.explain: Several error sources add up.
questions.teaches: For a clock synchronized to a server, the uncertainty is, to a first approximation, the expected quartz drift since the last sync plus the NTP server's uncertainty plus the network round-trip time to the server.
options: The quartz drift alone, since the server is exact
Quartz drift since the last sync, plus the server's uncertainty, plus the round-trip time
The round-trip time alone, since drift is negligible
The CPU speed, since faster CPUs keep better time
optionExplain: The server and the network add error too.
Right: the three add up.
Drift between syncs can be large.
CPU speed does not enter the estimate.

questions.q: What makes a single global transaction counter hard in a database spread over datacenters?
questions.explain: Coordination limits throughput. The card next gives the details.
options: Counters cannot count high enough for large databases
Every transaction must coordinate to get its ID
Datacenters have no clocks, so cannot count
Counters always run backwards across regions
optionExplain: Counter size is not the problem.
Right: coordination becomes a bottleneck.
Counting needs no clock.
Nothing like that happens.
questions.rule: A distributed snapshot ID must increase and respect causality, which a simple local counter cannot give without coordination.

questions.q: If transaction B reads a value written by transaction A, then B must have a ____ transaction ID than A.
questions.explain: Higher, so the ID order reflects causality.
questions.rule: B after A means a higher ID.

questions.q: A database hands out blocks of IDs to different nodes so that no node waits. What is the risk?
questions.explain: Block allocation scales but loses causal order.
options: IDs may repeat on different nodes
IDs may run backwards on a single node
IDs may not respect causality across nodes
IDs may become too long to store
optionExplain: Blocks are disjoint, so IDs stay unique.
Within a block IDs rise.
Right: block timescales are longer than reads and writes.
Length is not the issue.

questions.q: A snapshot has ID 100 and a write with ID 105 occurs. What does the snapshot see?
questions.explain: Visibility compares IDs.
options: It sees the write, since writes are always visible
It aborts, since a newer write exists
It sees half of the write, depending on timing
It does not see the write, since its ID is greater
optionExplain: Visibility depends on IDs.
Snapshots do not abort on newer writes.
Writes are all-or-nothing in the snapshot.
Right: later writes are invisible to the snapshot.

questions.q: True or false: On a single-node database, generating monotonically increasing transaction IDs requires distributed coordination.
questions.explain: A simple counter is sufficient on a single node.
questions.rule: One node needs only a counter.

questions.q: Why might synchronized time-of-day clocks look attractive for transaction IDs?
questions.explain: Time offers ordering without coordination if clocks are accurate enough; the catch is their uncertainty. Snapshot isolation is worth the trouble because long read-only jobs such as backups can read a consistent state without locking.
questions.teaches: Snapshot isolation serves databases that must support both small, fast read-write transactions and large, long-running read-only transactions such as backups or analytics, without locking.
options: They are cryptographically unforgeable
They never drift, since NTP corrects them
They are shorter than counters
Later transactions would get higher timestamps with no coordination
optionExplain: Clocks do not provide security.
They drift and the correction is imperfect.
Length is not the reason.
Right: if synchronization were good enough.

questions.q: Time interval A = [10, 12] and interval B = [13, 15] do not overlap. What follows?
questions.explain: Separated intervals are certain. The card next shows how Spanner uses this.
options: B definitely happened after A
A happened after B, since larger ranges win
The order stays unknown, as with any two ranges
They happened at the same moment
optionExplain: Right: A ended before B began.
The range ordering says A is earlier.
Only overlapping ranges leave the order unknown.
They are separated, not simultaneous.
questions.rule: Wait out the confidence interval before committing, so timestamps reflect causality.

questions.q: Spanner waits for the length of the confidence ____ before committing a read-write transaction.
questions.explain: The interval's length.

questions.q: Interval A = [10.3, 10.5] and interval B = [10.4, 10.7]. What can be said about their order?
questions.explain: Check whether one range ends before the other starts.
options: They overlap, so the order is uncertain
B definitely came after A, since 10.7 is larger
A definitely came after B, since it ends first
They are the same instant, since they overlap
optionExplain: Right: B starts before A ends.
B's start is before A's end, so it is not certain.
Ending first does not mean coming later.
Overlap means unknown, not equal.

questions.q: What if the clock uncertainty doubles from 7 ms to 14 ms?
questions.explain: Wait time tracks uncertainty.
options: Commits become faster, because there is more room
Commits wait about twice as long
Commits are unchanged, since the wait is fixed
Commits stop altogether until clocks are reset
optionExplain: A wider interval means more waiting.
Right: the wait equals the interval length.
The wait follows the interval.
They slow down but proceed.

questions.q: True or false: Spanner shortens its commit wait by using larger confidence intervals.
questions.explain: Larger intervals mean longer waits; Google keeps intervals small with GPS or atomic clocks.

questions.q: Why does Google put a GPS receiver or atomic clock in each datacenter?
questions.explain: Better clocks mean shorter waits and higher throughput.
questions.rule: Precise clocks pay for themselves in latency.
questions.teaches: Google deploys a GPS receiver or atomic clock in each datacenter, allowing clocks to be synchronized to within about 7 ms.
options: To encrypt transactions between datacenters
To replace the network between datacenters
To keep clock uncertainty, and so the commit wait, as small as possible
To let datacenters choose their own transaction order
optionExplain: Clocks are not used for encryption here.
Time sources do not carry data.
Right: clocks within about 7 ms.
The point is a shared, tight time bound.

questions.q: A leader checks that its lease is valid and then handles a request. What could make that check misleading?
questions.explain: A valid check is only a snapshot in time. The card next shows two flaws.
options: A request that is too small to need a valid lease
A long pause between the check and the handling
A lease that is renewed too often by the leader
A follower that reads the lease at the same moment
optionExplain: Request size does not change who may lead.
Right: the lease may expire during the pause.
Frequent renewal makes the lease safer, not less.
Followers reading the lease do not invalidate the leader's check.
questions.rule: A check proves the lease was valid at that moment, not when the request is processed.

questions.q: A lease is similar to a lock with a ____.
questions.explain: It expires unless it is renewed.
questions.rule: A lease is a lock with a timeout.

questions.q: A lease expires at 12:00:30 on the lock service's clock. The leader compares that to its own clock, which runs 20 seconds slow. What does the leader believe?
questions.explain: Mixing clocks of two machines creates an error that can extend a leader's belief.
questions.rule: Do not compare clocks across machines.
options: That it holds the lease for about 20 seconds after it has really expired
That the lease expired 20 seconds before it really did
That the lease is valid only if NTP confirms the offset
That it must ask the lock service before every request
optionExplain: Right: the slow clock stretches its belief.
A slow clock reads earlier times, so the leader thinks there is more time left.
The code does not consult NTP when comparing.
The sample code has no such step.

questions.q: The thread freezes for 15 seconds right after the lease check, then continues. What does it do?
questions.explain: The thread acts on information that went stale during the pause.
questions.rule: Stale checks lead to unsafe actions.
options: Processes the request, though another node may already be leader
Notices that 15 seconds passed and drops the request
Renews the lease automatically before processing
Crashes with an error because the lease is stale
optionExplain: Right: nothing tells it that time passed.
The thread has no signal that it was paused.
The renewal happens at the top of the loop, before the pause.
Nothing in the code raises an error.

questions.q: True or false: Switching the lease check to the local monotonic clock removes all danger from the loop.
questions.explain: A pause between the check and the processing can still let the lease expire; that is flaw two.
questions.rule: Monotonic time does not fix pauses.

questions.q: Suppose the system guaranteed the gap between check and action stays under 1 second. How would the 10-second buffer fare?
questions.explain: The 10-second buffer assumes a short gap; a bound turns the assumption into a guarantee.
questions.rule: The loop's safety rests on an unbounded gap.
questions.teaches: The code notices that a lease has expired only at the next iteration of the loop, by which time it may already have done something unsafe by processing the request.
options: It would still fail, since leases cannot be checked in code
It would be ample, since the gap is far shorter than the buffer
It would be useless, since the clocks are in different machines
It would double the risk, since the buffer is longer than the gap
optionExplain: Checks work when the gap is bounded.
Right: the flaw depends on the unbounded gap.
That is flaw one, which a local monotonic clock removes.
A buffer longer than the gap protects.

questions.q: Which of these can freeze a program in the middle of a function?
questions.explain: Several layers can stop code. The card next lists them.
options: A faster network between the servers
A longer variable name in the source
A larger font in the editor
A stop-the-world garbage collection
optionExplain: A faster network does not stop local threads.
Naming has no effect at runtime.
The editor does not affect the running program.
Right: GC can stop all threads.
questions.rule: A process can be paused for an unbounded time at any point by GC, virtualization, scheduling, I/O, paging or signals.

questions.q: Which can pause a thread for a long time? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: The causes sit in the runtime, the OS, the hypervisor and the people operating the machine.
questions.rule: Many layers can pause a process.
options: An extra comment line in the source code
A page fault that loads memory from disk
A SIGSTOP sent by pressing Ctrl-Z in a shell
A stop-the-world garbage collection
A longer lease granted by the lock service
optionExplain: Comments vanish before the program runs.
Right: the thread waits for the disk.
Right: the process gets no CPU until SIGCONT.
Right: it stops all threads of the runtime.
A lease is a lock term; it is not a pause source.

questions.q: A Java service loads a class for the first time during a request, and its disk is a network volume. What may happen?
questions.explain: Disk access can happen where the code shows none.
options: The thread runs faster, since classes load in the background
Nothing, since no file access is visible in the code
The thread pauses for the disk read, subject to network delay
A garbage collection starts, since loading needs memory
optionExplain: The first use waits for the load.
Hidden file access can still block the thread.
Right: lazy class loading is disk access.
Loading does not by itself trigger a collection.

questions.q: What does the book call the CPU time spent in other virtual machines while yours waits?
questions.explain: Steal time is time your VM does not get to run.
options: Drift time
Steal time
Slew time
Lease time
optionExplain: Drift is a clock-rate error.
Right: time stolen by other VMs.
Slewing is a rate adjustment by NTP.
A lease is a lock term.

questions.q: True or false: On a machine with paging enabled, a memory access cannot block a thread.
questions.explain: A page fault can require loading a page from disk, pausing the thread; heavy paging can lead to thrashing.

questions.q: Why is paging often disabled on server machines?
questions.explain: Thrashing can leave a machine doing almost no useful work.
questions.rule: Prefer a clean kill to thrashing.
questions.teaches: Paging is often disabled on server machines because in extreme circumstances the operating system may spend most of its time swapping pages in and out of memory and getting little actual work done, known as thrashing.
options: To avoid thrashing, preferring to kill a process rather than slow everything down
Because servers have unlimited memory and never need to swap
Because paging makes garbage collection run faster
Because paging sends memory pages across the network
optionExplain: Right: one failure is cheaper than a machine swapping constantly.
Memory is finite; the choice is about behavior under pressure.
The book gives no such link.
Paging goes to disk, not across the network.

questions.q: A node resumes after a 20-second pause. What does it know about the pause?
questions.explain: The pause is invisible from inside. The card next states the assumption.
options: That exactly 20 seconds passed, from its internal counter
That it was declared dead, because the others told it
Nothing, until it checks a clock or hears from others
That its lease is still valid, because it never expired locally
optionExplain: Its own counters were paused with it.
Nobody tells it unless it asks.
Right: the pause is invisible from inside.
The lease may have expired while it slept.
questions.rule: A node must assume it can be paused at any point, and others may declare it dead meanwhile.

questions.q: A distributed system has no shared memory, only ____ sent over an unreliable network.
questions.explain: Messages are the only channel.

questions.q: A worker holds a lease and pauses for 40 seconds. What should it assume when it resumes?
questions.explain: After a pause, treat your picture of the world as possibly stale.
options: Nothing has changed, as its own state is intact
It is still the only worker, since leases are exclusive
Others may have declared it dead and taken over
Its clock is exact, since it has only now woken up
optionExplain: Its own state is intact but the world's state is not.
The lease may have expired and been granted to another.
Right: the world kept moving.
A pause does not give it a better time reading.

questions.q: A worker uses a mutex inside its own process to guard a resource shared with other nodes. What does the mutex achieve?
questions.explain: Mutexes live in shared memory, which separate nodes do not have.
options: It excludes every other node, since it is a lock
It works across nodes when the lease is long enough
It becomes a lease automatically after a pause
It orders threads inside that process, but not against other nodes
optionExplain: A local mutex lives in one machine's memory.
Lease length does not extend shared memory.
A mutex has no timeout and no conversion.
Right: it does not span machines.

questions.q: True or false: The tools for making multi-threaded code safe on one machine carry over unchanged to a distributed system.
questions.explain: They do not, because a distributed system has no shared memory, only messages over an unreliable network.

questions.q: The book compares the pause problem to a familiar single-machine problem. What is the lesson from that comparison?
questions.explain: The same uncertainty about timing appears in multi-threaded code.
questions.teaches: The problem is similar to making multi-threaded code on a single machine thread-safe: you cannot assume anything about timing, because arbitrary context switches and parallelism may occur.
options: Timing is exact on one machine, so only the network matters
Pauses happen only on laptops, so servers need no precautions
You cannot assume anything about timing, because context switches may occur at any time
Context switches are rare, so locks are rarely needed
optionExplain: The comparison is about timing uncertainty on one machine.
Servers pause too, for example in GC.
Right: same lesson as thread safety.
Locks are needed because they can occur anywhere.

questions.q: Why must a car's airbag controller not suffer a garbage collection pause?
questions.explain: Where a missed deadline can cause the failure of the whole system, timing guarantees are part of the specification. The card next gives the requirements.
options: A pause would fire the airbag too early, injuring the passengers
Airbag software has no memory to manage, so it never pauses at all
Pauses are harmless whenever the car is not moving, which is most of the time
A late airbag release could be catastrophic
optionExplain: A pause delays the release; it cannot make it happen earlier.
Controllers can pause for many reasons; the point is the harm a delay causes.
The system must meet its deadline at the moment of a crash, not on average.
Right: here the deadline is part of correctness.
questions.rule: Hard real-time means specified deadlines are met in all circumstances, achieved by design and testing across the whole stack.

questions.q: Systems where missing a specified deadline may cause failure of the entire system are called hard ____ systems.
questions.explain: Hard real-time systems.

questions.q: Which of these does a hard real-time system need?
questions.explain: Guarantees need support at all levels of the stack: scheduling, library worst-case times, restricted allocation and heavy testing.
options: A real-time OS that guarantees CPU time at set intervals
Dynamic memory allocation throughout, so the program can use memory freely
Libraries chosen for their good average speed, since averages decide deadlines
A light test plan, since a well-built system rarely misses deadlines in practice
optionExplain: Right: scheduling is the base of the guarantee.
Allocation may be restricted or disallowed, since it can cause unpredictable delays.
Deadlines need documented worst-case execution times, not averages.
An enormous amount of testing and measurement is needed to show the guarantees hold.

questions.q: Which use of real-time matches the embedded-systems meaning?
questions.explain: In embedded systems real-time means carefully designed and tested timing guarantees in all circumstances.
options: A website that pushes updates to browsers as soon as the server can send them
A stream processor tuned for the lowest average latency in its pipeline
A flight controller built and tested to meet timing guarantees in all circumstances
A chat application that feels instant to most of its users most of the time
optionExplain: The looser web use of the word: no hard response-time constraint.
Low average latency is speed, not a guarantee for every case.
Right: a guarantee, not just speed.
Feeling instant is not a deadline that must always be met.

questions.q: True or false: With a real-time garbage collector, the application no longer needs to limit the work it gives the collector.
questions.explain: Real-time collectors exist, but the application must still ensure it does not give the collector too much work.

questions.q: A real-time team asks if it can use ordinary dynamic memory allocation in its control loop. What does the book say?
questions.explain: Real-time systems may restrict or disallow dynamic memory allocation, and library functions must document worst-case execution times.
questions.teaches: In real-time systems dynamic memory allocation may be restricted or disallowed entirely, and library functions must document their worst-case execution times.
options: It is required, because a control loop needs flexible memory to adapt to input
It may be restricted or banned, as it can delay unpredictably
It is fine if the allocator is written in a fast language like C
It is irrelevant to timing, since memory operations are always quick
optionExplain: Flexibility is what such systems give up for predictability.
Right: allocation threatens the deadline.
Speed of the language does not give a worst-case bound.
Allocation can take unpredictable time, which is the problem.

questions.q: Why do most web servers not run on real-time operating systems?
questions.explain: Developing real-time systems is very expensive, so ordinary servers accept pauses and clock instability. The card next elaborates.
options: Real-time operating systems cannot run on server-class hardware at all
Web servers have no response-time goals, so deadlines never come up
Real-time systems are slower than ordinary ones in every respect
The guarantees are not economical or appropriate for server-side processing
optionExplain: They could; the obstacle is cost and restrictions, not hardware.
They have goals, but softer ones that tolerate occasional delays.
They may lose some throughput, but that is not why servers avoid them.
Right: cost and restrictions outweigh the benefits.
questions.rule: Real-time guarantees are costly and can lower throughput, so ordinary servers do without them.

questions.q: Real-time is not the same as high-____.
questions.explain: Real-time systems may have lower throughput.
questions.rule: Real-time is not the same as fast.

questions.q: A startup asks whether to rebuild its checkout API on a real-time stack to avoid GC pauses. What does the book suggest?
questions.explain: For most server-side systems real-time guarantees are not economical or appropriate; techniques such as draining a node before GC reduce the impact.
options: Usually not worth it: accept pauses and reduce their impact
It must do so, because every pause loses sales and real-time prevents pauses
It should drop garbage collection and manage all memory by hand
It should move the API to a supercomputer, which has no pause problems
optionExplain: Right: the server-side norm.
Pauses can be reduced more cheaply, and real time restricts tools heavily.
The book recommends no such step for server software.
Supercomputers target scientific batch work, not online services.

questions.q: What if a high-volume analytics service adopts real-time guarantees?
questions.explain: Real-time systems prioritize timely responses, so their throughput may be lower.
options: Throughput rises, since pauses disappear and servers never wait
Latency becomes unbounded, since nothing in the system is prioritized
Throughput may fall, as timely responses come first
The servers become unnecessary, since the OS does the processing itself
optionExplain: Real-time systems may have lower throughput.
Real-time prioritizes timeliness above all else.
Right: real-time is not the same as high performance.
The servers still do the work; only scheduling changes.

questions.q: True or false: Real-time systems are chosen mainly because they deliver the highest throughput.
questions.explain: They may have lower throughput since they prioritize timely responses.

questions.q: Where are real-time systems most commonly used?
questions.explain: Because of their cost and restrictions, real-time systems are most commonly used in safety-critical embedded devices.
questions.teaches: Because of their cost and restrictions, real-time systems are most commonly used in safety-critical embedded devices, so most server-side data processing systems must suffer pauses and clock instability from operating in a non-real-time environment.
options: In social network back ends that serve millions of users at once
In safety-critical embedded devices
In batch analytics clusters that crunch data overnight
In personal blogs hosted on small virtual machines
optionExplain: These run on ordinary non-real-time servers.
Right: safety justifies the cost.
Batch jobs can tolerate delays, so real time buys them little.
A blog has no deadline whose failure is costly.

questions.q: A node is about to run a long garbage collection. What can the application do to protect clients?
questions.explain: If the runtime can warn of a coming pause, the application can route around the node. The card next gives details.
options: Send it extra requests so the collection finishes sooner
Stop sending it new requests until the collection ends
Ignore the warning and let clients wait out the pause
Restart the entire cluster at once to clear the garbage everywhere
optionExplain: More requests increase the work and the delay clients feel.
Right: treat the pause as a planned outage.
Ignoring it leaves clients with the full delay.
A full restart is far more disruptive than a single node's pause.
questions.rule: Hide GC pauses from clients by draining a node before it collects, or restart it before a full collection is needed.

questions.q: Hiding GC pauses from clients reduces the high ____ of response time.
questions.explain: The slowest responses are the high percentiles.

questions.q: A trading gateway has a runtime that warns of an imminent GC. In what order should it act?
questions.explain: The node is drained of requests, the collection runs while none are in progress, and then the node takes traffic again.
options: Collect first and stop sending requests afterwards, when it is done
Keep taking requests and collect whenever the queue happens to be empty
Shift all traffic away for good and switch the collector off
Stop new requests, finish outstanding ones, collect, then resume
optionExplain: Requests already on their way would be stuck in the pause.
A busy gateway's queue may never empty.
Collection is still needed; the node only needs to be out of rotation briefly.
Right: drain before collecting.

questions.q: A process collects only short-lived objects and is restarted before long-lived objects pile up. What is avoided?
questions.explain: Restarting before enough long-lived objects accumulate avoids the full collection that would pause the process.
options: A full collection of long-lived objects
Any collection at all, since short-lived objects are never freed
The restart itself, since long-lived objects stay for ever anyway
The need for spare capacity, since a restart takes no resources
optionExplain: Right: the restart replaces it.
Short-lived objects are still collected, and cheaply.
The periodic restart is the technique.
Shifting traffic away needs spare capacity on other nodes.

questions.q: True or false: These techniques eliminate garbage collection pauses completely.
questions.explain: They cannot fully prevent GC pauses; they usefully reduce their impact.

questions.q: Restarting one node at a time with traffic shifted away resembles which practice?
questions.explain: Restarting one node at a time with traffic shifted away from it works like the rolling upgrades of Chapter 4.
questions.teaches: Restarting processes periodically before they accumulate enough long-lived objects to need a full GC can be done one node at a time, with traffic shifted away from the node before the planned restart, like a rolling upgrade.
options: A full backup of the database to remote storage
A load test that adds heavy traffic to every node
A rolling upgrade
A cache flush that clears entries on all nodes at once
optionExplain: A backup copies data and does not restart nodes.
A load test adds traffic; here traffic is shifted away.
Right: traffic leaves one node, it restarts, repeat.
A flush clears data on all nodes; this restarts one node at a time.

questions.q: How can a node find out the state of another node?
questions.explain: Because there is no shared memory, a node learns another node's state only by exchanging messages. The card next states the consequences.
options: By reading its memory directly across the network
By consulting a global clock that records every node's state
Only by exchanging messages with it
By watching the network cable for activity on its port
optionExplain: Nodes share no memory; they can only ask over the network.
There is no shared clock or global record of state.
Right: messages are the only channel.
Link activity says little about the node's software state.
questions.rule: A node knows only what messages tell it, and silence is ambiguous.

questions.q: A node in the network cannot know anything for sure; it can only make ____ based on the messages it receives.
questions.explain: It guesses from what arrives and what does not.

questions.q: A monitor sees no heartbeat from a database node. What can it conclude for sure?
questions.explain: Problems in the network cannot reliably be distinguished from problems at a node.
options: The node has crashed, since it stopped sending heartbeats
Nothing for sure: the node or the network may be at fault
The network is down, since heartbeats are tiny and rarely lost
The node is healthy but idle, since no message was reported lost
optionExplain: A lost or delayed heartbeat looks exactly the same.
Right: the two look the same.
Tiny messages can be lost too, and the node may be the problem.
Not hearing a message says nothing about the node's health.

questions.q: Which of these questions does the book call almost philosophical?
questions.explain: The book says discussions of these systems border on the philosophical: what we know, and how sure we can be.
options: Which cloud region is cheapest this month for our traffic?
How many rows fit into a single database page on disk?
Which compiler flags make the build run fastest on the server?
What do we know to be true or false in our system?
optionExplain: A pricing question, not about truth or knowledge.
A storage-layout question.
A tooling question with a measurable answer.
Right: the nature of knowledge in an unreliable system.

questions.q: True or false: A node can learn what data a neighbor stores by reading the neighbor's disk directly.
questions.explain: A node can learn another node's state only by exchanging messages; there is no shared memory or disk.

questions.q: Besides what is true, which further question does the book raise about distributed systems?
questions.explain: Beyond what is true, the book asks whether software should obey the laws we expect from the physical world, such as cause and effect.
questions.rule: The usual physical intuitions may not hold.
questions.teaches: The book asks how sure we can be of our knowledge if the mechanisms for perception and measurement are unreliable, and whether software systems should obey the laws we expect of the physical world, such as cause and effect.
options: Should software obey physical laws such as cause and effect?
Should every node in the cluster run the same operating system?
Should every message between nodes be encrypted in transit?
Should clocks be replaced by calendars in every database?
optionExplain: Right: the book raises it.
A deployment question, not raised in this passage.
A security question the passage does not raise.
Not a question the book raises.

questions.q: What is a system model in the book's sense?
questions.explain: A system model is an abstraction of what an algorithm may assume. The card next explains how it is used.
options: A diagram showing which servers sit in which rack
A list of all the known bugs in the code base
The assumptions about behaviour that the design relies on
A benchmark that measures the peak throughput of the system
optionExplain: An inventory of hardware, not assumptions about behaviour.
Bugs describe defects, not the assumptions a design is built on.
Right: a statement of what may be assumed.
Benchmarks measure; models state what is assumed.
questions.rule: Write down what you assume, then design and prove against those assumptions.

questions.q: Algorithms can be proved to function correctly within a certain system ____.
questions.explain: Proofs are relative to a system model.

questions.q: A team starts designing a lock service. What should it do before writing code?
questions.explain: Designing against stated assumptions gives the algorithm and any proof a target.
options: Pick the fastest hardware available so that timing cannot matter
State which faults and timing behaviour it assumes
Assume nodes never fail, to keep the design simple
Postpone assumptions until after the first production outage
optionExplain: Hardware speed does not define what the design may assume.
Right: define the model first.
A model must match what can actually happen; this assumption is false.
Assumptions drive the design and the proof of it, so they come first.

questions.q: A proof assumes bounded network delay. The real network has unbounded delay. What follows?
questions.explain: A proof is only as good as the match between the model and reality.
options: The proof still holds, since proofs apply to every possible system
The network adjusts its delays to match the assumption in the proof
The algorithm stops running, since it cannot work without bounded delay
The proof no longer covers the real system
optionExplain: A proof holds only inside its model.
Networks do not adapt to proofs.
It keeps running but without the proven guarantee.
Right: model and reality do not match.

questions.q: True or false: Reliable behavior is impossible on a system that provides very few guarantees.
questions.explain: Reliable behavior is achievable even if the underlying system model provides very few guarantees, though it is not straightforward.

questions.q: Where does the book go next to show algorithms with guarantees under particular assumptions?
questions.explain: This chapter lists problems; Chapter 9 shows algorithms that provide particular guarantees under particular assumptions.
questions.teaches: Chapter 9 looks at examples of algorithms and distributed systems that provide particular guarantees under particular assumptions.
options: In Chapter 9, which gives examples of such algorithms
Back in Chapter 1, which covered reliability
In Chapter 4, which covered encoding and evolution
In an appendix on hardware design at the end of the book
optionExplain: Right: the next chapter turns to solutions.
That chapter comes earlier and does not present these algorithms.
Encoding is a different topic.
The book continues with the next chapter, not an appendix.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: A node pauses for one minute in GC and then continues. What does it believe about the time that passed?
questions.explain: From inside, the pause is invisible: the node resumes as if nothing happened. The card next tells the stories.
options: That a whole minute passed, because it counted every second
That it was declared dead, because it heard the verdict directly
That its lease expired, because leases usually last one minute
That hardly any time has passed since it last spoke to the others
optionExplain: Its counters were paused along with everything else.
Nobody has told it anything yet.
It has no knowledge of how long it was away.
Right: it was not running during the pause.
questions.rule: A node may be wrongly declared dead and cannot dispute it, so its self-view is not authoritative.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: A node paused in garbage collection that resumes is surprised to find it was declared ____ by the others.
questions.explain: Declared dead after the others waited, retried and gave up.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: A server's outgoing packets are dropped, so peers hear no replies. What do they decide after the timeout?
questions.explain: Others judge by what they hear. When no replies arrive within the timeout, they declare the node dead.
options: That it is dead, though it receives and processes requests
That it is alive, since it keeps receiving requests from clients
That it should lead, since it is the quietest node in the cluster
That its network is healthy, since inbound traffic still works
optionExplain: Right: silence reads as death.
Peers see only what they hear from it, which is nothing.
Quiet is not a qualification for leading.
Peers cannot observe its inbound health.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: A semi-disconnected node notices that its messages are not acknowledged. What can it do about being declared dead?
questions.explain: Even if it realises that its messages are not acknowledged, the node can do nothing about the others' decision.
options: Override the verdict, since it knows it is alive
Declare all the other nodes dead in return
Nothing: it cannot reverse the others' decision
Restart the cluster from its own copy of the data
optionExplain: Others cannot hear it, so its view carries no weight.
That would not restore its status.
Right: the verdict is theirs.
Nothing gives it the authority to do that.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: True or false: A node that feels healthy can safely ignore the other nodes' verdict that it is dead.
questions.explain: A distributed system cannot rely on a single node's judgment; the others' decision must be respected.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: Why can a distributed system not rely exclusively on a single node?
questions.explain: A system that hangs on one node cannot recover when that node fails, so decisions should involve a quorum.
questions.teaches: A distributed system cannot exclusively rely on a single node, because a node may fail at any time, potentially leaving the system stuck and unable to recover; instead many algorithms rely on a quorum.
options: A single node cannot store any data of its own
A node may fail at any time, leaving the system stuck
A single node is always slower than a cluster of nodes
A single node has no clock that it can consult
optionExplain: Single nodes can store data.
Right: a single point of failure.
Speed is not the reason.
It has a clock; that is not the problem.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: A five-node cluster votes on declaring node 3 dead and four nodes say yes. What happens to node 3?
questions.explain: If a quorum declares a node dead, it must be considered dead and must abide by the decision.
options: It must be treated as dead and step down, even if it feels alive
It stays in charge, since it knows it is alive and the vote is only advice
The vote is void, since node 3 did not agree to its own removal
The cluster waits for node 3 to confirm its death before acting
optionExplain: Right: the quorum decides.
Its own view does not override a quorum.
A majority is enough; the node concerned need not agree.
A dead node cannot confirm anything, so waiting would never end.
questions.rule: Decide by majority vote: a majority declaration binds even the node it concerns.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: Most commonly, a quorum is an absolute ____ of more than half the nodes.
questions.explain: A majority of more than half.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: A cluster has 7 nodes. How many failures can a majority quorum tolerate while still deciding?
questions.explain: Seven nodes need 4 votes for a majority, so 3 can fail.
questions.rule: n nodes tolerate (n - 1) / 2 failures when n is odd.
options: 2: majority quorums tolerate failures of about a third of the nodes
4: up to half of the nodes may fail and a majority still remains
3: four of the seven nodes still form a majority
1: a majority quorum tolerates only a single failure at a time
optionExplain: A third is the figure for some Byzantine protocols, not for simple majorities.
With 4 failed, only 3 remain, which is less than half.
Right: more than half of 7 is 4.
One failure is the figure for 3 nodes, not 7.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: A cluster of 5 splits into groups of 3 and 2 by a network fault. Which side can make decisions?
questions.explain: Only one side can hold more than half of the nodes, so there cannot be two majorities with conflicting decisions.
options: The group of 2, since the smaller group has fewer disagreements
The group of 3, which holds a majority
Both groups, each deciding independently of the other
Neither, because a partitioned network blocks every decision
optionExplain: Fewer nodes cannot form a majority of five.
Right: only one majority can exist.
That would risk conflicting decisions, which a single majority prevents.
The side with more than half can still decide.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: True or false: With a majority quorum, two groups can make conflicting decisions at the same time.
questions.explain: There can only be one majority in the system, so there cannot be two majorities with conflicting decisions.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: A four-node cluster uses a majority quorum. How many failures can it tolerate?
questions.explain: Majority of 4 is 3 votes, so one failure is tolerated: the same as with 3 nodes.
questions.teaches: A majority quorum allows the system to keep working if individual nodes have failed: with three nodes one failure can be tolerated, and with five nodes two failures.
options: 2: half of the nodes can fail and the rest keep a majority
0: an even number of nodes cannot form a majority at all
3: a single surviving node is enough to keep deciding
1: three of the four nodes are needed
optionExplain: If two fail, two remain, which is not more than half.
Three of four is a majority, so one failure is tolerated.
One node of four is far from a majority.
Right: the majority of 4 is 3.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: A former leader was declared dead by the others during a network interruption, then recovered. What is its status?
questions.explain: A node's belief that it is the chosen one does not mean a quorum agrees. The card next explains.
options: It is still the leader, since nobody removed it by name
It becomes leader again once it is back online and reachable
It becomes a second leader alongside the new one, as both are alive
It may have been demoted, with another leader already elected
optionExplain: The group's decision already removed it.
A new election result stands; coming back does not undo it.
The system must prevent that; the old leader is no longer chosen.
Right: its belief is stale.
questions.rule: Being the chosen one is decided by a quorum, not by the node's own belief.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: Which are cases where only one of something is allowed? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: The book names these three.
options: One replica kept in each datacenter
One leader for a database partition
One holder of a lock on a resource
One user registered under a given username
One timestamp printed on each log line
optionExplain: Replica placement is a design choice, not a uniqueness rule in the book.
Right: avoids split brain.
Right: prevents concurrent writes.
Right: usernames must identify users uniquely.
Timestamps are labels, not a thing only one node may hold.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: Two web servers both think they won the race to register the username sam. What went wrong?
questions.explain: Uniqueness requires that a quorum agrees on who won, not that each server believes it did.
options: Usernames cannot be unique in a distributed system at all
The servers' clocks differed slightly, so the faster clock won
Each acted as the chosen one without a quorum agreeing
The network was too fast for the requests to be separated
optionExplain: They can, but uniqueness needs agreement.
Clock differences are not the core problem.
Right: belief is not agreement.
Speed is not the problem; agreement is.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: A self-appointed leader sends instructions to other nodes, and they believe it. What can happen?
questions.explain: If other nodes believe a self-appointed leader, the system as a whole may do something incorrect.
options: Nothing, since the others check with the real leader first
The system as a whole may do something incorrect
The network detects the false leader and corrects it automatically
The others elect it, so its claim becomes valid by their belief
optionExplain: They may not check, and then they act on the false message.
Right: false authority spreads.
Networks do not judge who is leader.
Belief is not election; no quorum chose it.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: True or false: If a node believes it holds the lock, then a quorum of nodes agrees that it does.
questions.explain: A node's belief does not necessarily mean a quorum agrees; it may have been declared dead and replaced.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: What does the book call the problem of having two leaders for one partition?
questions.explain: Only one node may lead each partition, to avoid split brain.
questions.teaches: Only one node is allowed to be the leader for a database partition, to avoid split brain; the same need for uniqueness applies to lock holders and usernames.
options: Clock drift, because two leaders would have clocks that disagree
Thrashing, because two leaders would compete for memory
Slewing, because two leaders would adjust each other's rates
Split brain
optionExplain: Drift is a clock error, not a leadership conflict.
Thrashing is excessive paging, unrelated to leadership.
Slewing is an NTP rate adjustment.
Right: two nodes both acting as leader.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: Client 1 holds a lease, pauses, and its lease expires. Client 2 gets the lease and writes. Client 1 then resumes. What happens?
questions.explain: The paused client wakes with a stale belief and writes anyway. The card next traces the whole story.
options: Client 1 notices the expiry and stops before writing
The storage service rejects client 1 because it checks the lease itself
Client 2's writes are discarded, so only client 1's data remains
Client 1 also writes, believing its lease valid, and the file is corrupted
optionExplain: It has no signal that the lease expired.
In the story, the storage does not check leases.
Both clients' writes proceed and clash.
Right: the old holder is unaware.
questions.rule: A lease check inside the client is not enough, because the client can be paused after checking.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: Put the events of the broken locking story in order.
questions.explain: The expiry happens during the pause; the wake-up comes last.
questions.rule: Expiry during a pause, then a clash.
items: Client 1 obtains a lease from the lock service
Client 1 pauses for too long
The lease expires and client 2 obtains a lease
Client 2 starts writing to the file
Client 1 wakes and also writes, corrupting the file

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: Which design change alone would NOT stop the corruption in this story?
questions.explain: Checks on the client side leave a gap between check and write; only a check at the resource closes it.
questions.rule: The check must be on the resource.
options: Making client 1 check its lease right before each write
Having the storage service check a number sent with each write
Having the storage reject writes from an older lease holder
Making the storage track the newest lease it has seen
optionExplain: Right: a pause after the check still lets the lease expire.
The storage can refuse stale writers; that is fencing.
Rejecting old holders closes the gap.
Tracking the newest lease lets it refuse older ones.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: What if the lease were very long, say a day, and the client's pause lasts a minute?
questions.explain: A lease longer than any pause avoids the bug, but a long lease delays failover when a client really has died.
questions.rule: Longer leases trade away failover speed.
options: The corruption still occurs, since leases never protect anything
The storage rejects client 1 anyway, since its token is stale
No expiry occurs, so this particular corruption does not happen
Client 2 writes twice, since its lease also gets extended
optionExplain: A lease that outlasts the pause does protect here.
The story has no token checks in the storage.
Right: the bug needs the pause to outlast the lease.
Nothing in the story changes client 2's behaviour.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: True or false: The locking bug in this story is purely theoretical and has not happened in real software.
questions.explain: The book says the bug is not theoretical: HBase used to have this problem.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: Why does the book say this is an example of the earlier process-pause problem?
questions.explain: It is the process-pause problem again: the client does not notice that time has passed.
questions.rule: Same root cause: an unnoticed pause.
questions.teaches: The book's locking example is a storage service that wants only one client to access a file at a time because multiple writers would corrupt it, and tries to enforce that by requiring a client to obtain a lease from a lock service before access.
options: The storage service is paused too long, so writes get reordered
The lease holder is paused too long, so its lease expires
The lock service loses its clock, so leases expire early
Client 2 is paused too long, so it writes after client 1
optionExplain: The story is about the client, not the storage.
Right: the same mechanism as before.
The clock of the lock service is not the cause.
Client 2 acts promptly in the story.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: Client 1 holds token 33 and pauses. Client 2 receives token 34 and writes. What should the storage do when client 1 later writes with token 33?
questions.explain: Tokens only grow, so a lower token identifies a stale client. The card next defines fencing.
options: Reject it, since it already processed a higher token
Accept it, because it arrived second and the latest request should win
Accept it and overwrite client 2's data, since client 1 holds a lease
Ask client 1 to renew its lease before accepting the write
optionExplain: Right: older tokens are refused.
Arrival order is not the rule; the token is.
That is the corruption fencing prevents.
The storage checks numbers, not lease status.
questions.rule: Make the resource reject writes whose fencing token is older than one it has already seen.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: A fencing token is a number that ____ every time a lock is granted.
questions.explain: Monotonically increasing.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: A file-sync service wants to stop a stale client from overwriting newer data. The lock service already issues lock numbers. What should the storage do?
questions.explain: The resource enforces the order of the numbers handed out by the lock service.
options: Accept all writes and sort them by arrival time afterwards
Ask each client whether its lock is still valid before writing
Remember the highest number seen and reject lower ones
Delay every write for a fixed time, then apply them together
optionExplain: Arrival order can be wrong after pauses.
A client may be wrong about its own lock.
Right: that is the check fencing needs.
Delays do not identify stale writers.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: A stale client sends a write with token 33 after token 34 was processed. What would happen if the storage did not check tokens?
questions.explain: The token is useless unless the storage compares it with the highest it has seen.
options: The lock service would reject it, since it issued token 34 later
The stale write could clash with the newer one and corrupt data
The write would queue until token 34 expires, then be applied
Nothing would happen, since token 33 is older than 34
optionExplain: The lock service does not see writes to storage.
Right: no check, no protection.
Storage does not queue by token.
Without a check, age has no effect on the write.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: True or false: A client that checks its own lock status before writing is as safe as fencing tokens.
questions.explain: It is not sufficient to rely on clients checking their lock status themselves; the resource must reject old tokens.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: With ZooKeeper as the lock service, what can serve as a fencing token?
questions.explain: Any number that is guaranteed to increase with every grant can serve as the fencing token.
questions.rule: Pick a number that only increases.
questions.teaches: If ZooKeeper is used as a lock service, the transaction ID zxid or the node version cversion can be used as a fencing token, since they are guaranteed to be monotonically increasing.
options: The client's local clock reading at the time of the write
A random number chosen by the client for each request
The size in bytes of the file being written
The transaction ID zxid or the node version cversion
optionExplain: Clocks differ and can go backward.
Random numbers do not increase.
Size has no ordering role.
Right: both increase monotonically.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: Why is a check done by the client alone not enough to protect a storage service?
questions.explain: The check must sit where stale state cannot hide: at the resource. The card next explains.
options: Clients cannot read their own tokens, so they cannot check them
The client may be stale and not know that its lock expired
Clients are always malicious, so they would lie about the check
Clients never talk to the lock service, so they have nothing to check
optionExplain: They can read them; the problem is that their belief may be stale.
Right: it can be paused.
The danger discussed is accident, not malice.
They obtain locks from it.
questions.rule: Make the service protect itself, because it is unwise to assume clients are always well behaved.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: For resources that do not support fencing tokens, you might put the token in the file ____.
questions.explain: A workaround mentioned by the book.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: A storage service has no token support. Which workaround does the book mention?
questions.explain: Even without native support, some kind of check is needed so that requests outside the lock's protection are not processed.
options: Trust the clients to stop writing when their lease ends
Switch off the lock service, since it cannot protect the file
Add more replicas of the file so that writes are spread out
Include the fencing token in the file name
optionExplain: The book warns against assuming clients behave.
That removes protection altogether.
Replicas do not check tokens.
Right: the storage can compare names.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: Why is a server-side token check arguably a good thing, according to the book?
questions.explain: It is unwise for a service to assume its clients are well behaved, so it should protect itself.
options: It protects the service from accidentally abusive clients
It makes every client run faster, since checks are cheap
It removes the need for a lock service, since storage decides alone
It is required by TCP to keep connections ordered
optionExplain: Right: clients are run by people with other priorities.
Checks add a little work; they do not speed anyone up.
The lock service still hands out the tokens.
TCP plays no role in fencing.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: True or false: It is wise for a service to assume that every client will be well behaved.
questions.explain: The book says it is unwise, because clients are often run by people whose priorities differ.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: What kind of mistaken node does fencing stop, and what kind does it not?
questions.explain: Fencing detects and blocks a node acting in error by accident; a node that wants to subvert the system could fake a token.
questions.teaches: Fencing tokens can detect and block a node that is inadvertently acting in error, but a node that deliberately wanted to subvert the guarantees could easily do so by sending messages with a fake fencing token.
options: It stops deliberate liars but not honest mistakes
It stops every kind of faulty node, including malicious ones
It stops inadvertent errors but not a node that sends a fake token
It stops nothing, since a stale node can always send a write
optionExplain: The reverse: a liar can fake a token.
Fencing does not defend against deliberate fakes.
Right: honest mistakes versus deliberate lies.
The storage refuses stale tokens, so it does stop stale nodes.

questions.q: A node that responds is assumed, in the book's model, to be doing what?
questions.explain: The model allows slowness and staleness but not lies. The card next defines the terms.
options: Sending arbitrary responses to test the other nodes
Telling the truth as far as it knows, playing by the protocol
Pretending to have received messages it never saw
Reporting its status according to a global clock
optionExplain: That would be a Byzantine fault.
Right: honest but possibly outdated.
That is a lie, which the model excludes.
Clocks are not part of the honesty assumption.
questions.rule: Assume nodes may be slow, silent or out of date, but not lying, unless you have reason to expect lies.

questions.q: A node that sends arbitrary faulty or corrupted responses, as if lying, has a ____ fault.
questions.explain: Byzantine faults involve lying nodes.

questions.q: A node answers a read request with data from before a long GC pause, honestly reporting what it last knew. Which fault class is this?
questions.explain: Honest but outdated differs from lying.
options: Not Byzantine: it is honest but its state is outdated
Byzantine, because the data is wrong
Byzantine, because the node was paused
A clock fault, because time passed during the pause
optionExplain: Right: stale is not lying.
Wrong data from honest staleness is not lying.
Pausing is not lying.
The issue is stale state, not clocks.

questions.q: Which behavior counts as a Byzantine fault?
questions.explain: Lying about facts is the distinguishing feature.
options: A node claims to have received a message that it never received
A node never responds because its disk failed
A node responds late after a garbage collection pause
A node reports an old value from before a network delay
optionExplain: Right: a lie.
Silence from a fault, not a lie.
Lateness, not lying.
Outdated, not lying.

questions.q: True or false: In this book's system model, a node that responds may send any arbitrary message.
questions.explain: The book assumes nodes are unreliable but honest: if a node responds, it tells the truth to the best of its knowledge.

questions.q: Why can fencing tokens not protect against a malicious node?
questions.explain: Fencing assumes nodes make honest mistakes, so a node that forges its token defeats it.
questions.teaches: Distributed system problems become much harder if there is a risk that nodes may lie, for example by claiming to have received a particular message when in fact they did not; reaching consensus in such an untrusting environment is the Byzantine Generals Problem.
options: Tokens expire too fast to catch it
Tokens are visible only to the lock server, not the storage
It could send messages with a fake fencing token
Malicious nodes cannot take locks in any system
optionExplain: Expiry is not the issue; the lock service issues them in order.
The storage service must see them to check them.
Right: tokens only catch accidents, not deliberate lies.
They can take locks like any other node.

questions.q: In the Two Generals Problem, what makes agreement hard?
questions.explain: Unreliable messengers make agreement hard. The card next adds traitors.
options: One general secretly lies about the plan
The generals cannot count
The camps have different clocks
Messengers may be delayed or lost
optionExplain: That is the Byzantine version.
