Counting is not the problem.
Clocks are not the point.
Right: like packets in a network.
questions.rule: Byzantine fault tolerance means correct operation despite nodes that deviate from the protocol or attackers on the network.

questions.q: In the Byzantine version, some of the generals are ____ who send fake messages.
questions.explain: They try to deceive the loyal generals.

questions.q: A group of partner banks must agree on a shared ledger update, and one bank may submit false data. Which problem is this closest to?
questions.explain: Possible deceit marks the Byzantine version.
options: The Two Generals Problem
A leap second problem
The Byzantine Generals Problem
A garbage collection pause
optionExplain: That one has honest participants and lossy messengers.
That is a clock problem.
Right: some participants may lie.
That is a node-pause problem.

questions.q: How does the Byzantine problem differ from the Two Generals Problem?
questions.explain: The Byzantine version adds deception.
options: It has only two participants
Some participants may deliberately send untrue messages
Messages cannot be lost
It needs a synchronized clock
optionExplain: It has n generals.
Right: traitors.
They can.
Not part of the problem.

questions.q: True or false: The name Byzantine was chosen because the generals of Byzantium were more prone to intrigue than others.
questions.explain: The book says there is no historic evidence of that; the name comes from Byzantine meaning excessively complicated or devious.
questions.rule: The name is a figure of speech.

questions.q: In the Byzantine Generals Problem, is it known in advance who the traitors are?
questions.explain: Unknown traitors make filtering impossible.
questions.rule: Unknown traitors are the hard part.
questions.teaches: Lamport wanted a name that would not offend any readers, and was advised that calling it The Albanian Generals Problem was not such a good idea.
options: No: they try to remain undiscovered
Yes: they are listed before the battle
Yes, but only to the traitors
Only in the Two Generals version
optionExplain: Right: that is why it is hard.
If known, they could be excluded.
The loyal generals do not know.
The Two Generals version has no traitors.

questions.q: Why do flight control systems need to tolerate Byzantine faults?
questions.explain: Corruption plus high stakes. The card next gives both cases.
options: Aircraft nodes are run by competing airlines who may cheat
Flight systems use more nodes than data centers do
Radiation can corrupt memory so a node responds unpredictably, and failure is very costly
Flight control must follow the same laws as web servers
optionExplain: That fits multi-organization systems, not a flight computer.
Node count is not the reason.
Right: arbitrary behavior with fatal consequences.
No such rule exists.
questions.rule: Pay for Byzantine tolerance when nodes can be corrupted or cannot be trusted; in your own datacenter you can usually assume they are not.

questions.q: Match each setting with why Byzantine tolerance may be needed.
questions.explain: Three settings in the book.
pairs: Radiation can corrupt memory or registers
Participants may try to cheat or defraud others
Agreement among mutually untrusting parties with no central authority

questions.q: Several competing companies run nodes of a shared ledger with no trusted operator. What does the book suggest?
questions.explain: Mutual distrust is the trigger.
options: It is not needed, since all nodes follow the same code
Fencing tokens are sufficient
A single leader can be trusted by everyone
Byzantine fault tolerance is relevant, since participants may cheat
optionExplain: Distrust means code may differ in behavior.
Fencing handles honest errors only.
There is no central authority.
Right: mutual distrust.

questions.q: What if all nodes in a datacenter are controlled by your organization and radiation levels are low?
questions.explain: The datacenter case is the book's default.
options: You must still deploy a Byzantine fault-tolerant protocol
You must expect traitors among your own nodes
You should expect memory corruption daily
You can usually safely assume there are no Byzantine faults
optionExplain: The cost outweighs the benefit.
Your own nodes can hopefully be trusted.
Radiation is low enough that it is not a major issue.
Right: the assumption holds.

questions.q: True or false: Protocols for Byzantine fault tolerance are simple, so most server-side data systems use them.
questions.explain: They are quite complicated, and for most server-side data systems the cost makes them impractical.

questions.q: How do web applications handle malicious behavior from browsers, according to the book?
questions.explain: A central authority replaces the need for BFT.
questions.teaches: Web applications must expect arbitrary and malicious behavior from clients under end-user control such as browsers, which is why input validation, sanitization and output escaping prevent SQL injection and cross-site scripting; the server is made the authority rather than using Byzantine fault-tolerant protocols.
options: By running a Byzantine fault-tolerant protocol with every browser
By trusting all inputs since browsers follow the protocol
By making the server the authority on what client behavior is allowed, with input validation and escaping
By synchronizing browser clocks with the server
optionExplain: The book says they typically do not.
Clients under end-user control may behave arbitrarily.
Right: not by BFT protocols.
Clocks do not solve malice.

questions.q: All five nodes of a cluster run the same software, which contains a bug. Would a Byzantine fault-tolerant protocol save you?
questions.explain: The protocol needs a correct supermajority. The card next states the numbers.
options: No: the bug appears on every node, so no correct majority remains
Yes: the protocol outvotes the buggy nodes
Yes, if the nodes use fencing tokens
No, because Byzantine protocols only handle crashes
optionExplain: Right: the protocol needs most nodes to work.
They are all buggy; there is nobody to outvote.
Tokens do not remove shared bugs.
They handle arbitrary behavior, not shared bugs.
questions.rule: Byzantine protocols do not help when all nodes share the same bug or vulnerability; use traditional security mechanisms.

questions.q: Most Byzantine fault-tolerant algorithms require a supermajority of more than ____ of the nodes to function correctly.
questions.explain: More than two-thirds.

questions.q: A team wants to use a Byzantine protocol to guard against a bug in its database server. What would that require?
questions.explain: Independence of implementations is the condition.
options: A single implementation run on more machines
Several independent implementations, hoping the bug appears in at most one
A faster network between the machines
Longer leases for the lock service
optionExplain: The same bug appears on all of them.
Right: independence is the condition.
Network speed does not matter.
Leases do not affect bug tolerance.

questions.q: An attacker compromises one node of a cluster running identical software. What is likely next?
questions.explain: Same software, same vulnerability.
options: The protocol isolates the attacked node automatically
The other nodes outvote the attacker
They can probably compromise all nodes, since the software is the same
The attack stops at the first node
optionExplain: Protocols do not fix a shared vulnerability.
They may all be vulnerable.
Right: a shared weakness.
Same software suggests the same weakness.

questions.q: True or false: Byzantine fault-tolerant protocols are the main protection against attackers in most systems.
questions.explain: Traditional mechanisms such as authentication, access control, encryption and firewalls remain the main protection.

questions.q: A cluster has four nodes and uses a protocol needing more than two-thirds of nodes to work. How many can malfunction?
questions.explain: Compute the fraction that must be correct.
questions.teaches: Most Byzantine fault-tolerant algorithms require a supermajority of more than two-thirds of the nodes to be functioning correctly, so with four nodes at most one may malfunction.
options: 2, because half of the nodes may fail
0, because any malfunction breaks the protocol
3, because one node is enough
1, because 3 of 4 is more than two-thirds
optionExplain: 2 of 4 is only half, less than two-thirds.
One malfunction is tolerated.
One node is not enough.

questions.q: A network packet is corrupted in transit in a way that evades the TCP checksum. What simple protection does the book suggest?
questions.explain: An extra checksum is cheap protection. The card next lists other guards.
options: A longer TCP timeout
A checksum at the application-level protocol
A bigger switch queue
A faster clock
optionExplain: Timeouts do not detect corruption.
Right: a second, independent check.
Queues do not detect corruption.
Clocks do not detect corruption.
questions.rule: Use cheap checks like checksums, input sanity checks and multiple time servers, which catch accidental lies though not deliberate ones.

questions.q: An NTP client configured with several servers checks that a ____ of them agree on a time range.
questions.explain: Outliers are excluded.

questions.q: A public API accepts a text field. Which guard does the book recommend?
questions.explain: Public applications must sanitize inputs.
options: Check that values are in a reasonable range and limit the size of strings
Trust the field, because the API sits behind a firewall
Run a Byzantine protocol with each caller
Encrypt the field before checking it
optionExplain: Right: sanitize inputs.
Even internal services should sanity-check values.
Too costly; simple checks suffice.
Encryption does not validate content.

questions.q: One of five NTP servers reports a time hours off, and the client queries all five. What happens?
questions.explain: Majority agreement protects against one bad server.
options: The wrong server is detected as an outlier and excluded
The client adopts the average of all five
The client stops synchronizing completely
The client trusts the first server it asked
optionExplain: Right: a majority agree on a range.
Averaging would pull the time off.
It continues with the good servers.
It asks them all.

questions.q: True or false: These simple measures amount to full Byzantine fault tolerance.
questions.explain: They are not full Byzantine tolerance, as they would not withstand a determined adversary.

questions.q: An internal service behind a firewall receives values only from your own code. What does the book advise about input checks?
questions.explain: Public services need strict checks; internal ones can relax but not skip.
questions.teaches: Network packets do sometimes get corrupted due to hardware issues or bugs in operating systems, drivers or routers, and usually checksums built into TCP and UDP catch this, but sometimes corruption evades detection.
options: No checks are needed at all
It may get away with less strict checks, but basic sanity checks are still a good idea
The same strict checks as a public service are always required
Checks are only needed for numeric values
optionExplain: Basic sanity checks still help.
Right: relaxed but not absent.
The book says it may do with less.
Not limited to numbers.

questions.q: Which timing model describes systems that behave well most of the time but occasionally exceed delay bounds?
questions.explain: Realistic systems break bounds sometimes. The card next defines the three.
options: Synchronous
Asynchronous
Byzantine
Partially synchronous
optionExplain: The bounds are never exceeded in this model.
No timing assumptions at all.
That describes node behavior, not timing.
Right: mostly synchronous, sometimes not.
questions.rule: Partial synchrony is a realistic model: well behaved most of the time, with occasionally shattered timing assumptions.

questions.q: Match each timing model with its assumption.
questions.explain: Three models.
pairs: Bounded delay, pauses and clock error
Mostly bounded, but bounds sometimes exceeded
No timing assumptions, not even a clock

questions.q: A team designs a lock service for a cloud environment where delays and GC pauses usually stay small but sometimes spike. Which timing model fits?
questions.explain: Usually fine, occasionally not: partial synchrony.
questions.rule: Match the model to the behavior.
options: Synchronous, since delays are usually small
Asynchronous, since spikes occur
Partially synchronous
None, since clouds are untestable
optionExplain: Spikes violate the bounds.
It is too pessimistic for most designs, though safe.
Right: it describes this behavior.
A model fits.

questions.q: Which statement about the synchronous model is correct?
questions.explain: Bounded means a known upper limit.
options: It requires clocks to be exactly equal
It says delay, pauses and drift never exceed fixed bounds, not that clocks are exactly synchronized
It requires zero network delay
It is a realistic model of most practical systems
optionExplain: It does not.
Right: bounded, not perfect.
It does not.
The book says it is not realistic.

questions.q: True or false: In the asynchronous model, an algorithm can use timeouts to detect failures.
questions.explain: The asynchronous model allows no timing assumptions and has no clock, so it cannot use timeouts.

questions.q: When network delays, pauses or clock errors exceed their bounds in a partially synchronous system, how large can they get?
questions.explain: When the bounds break, they break completely.
questions.teaches: Partial synchrony means a system behaves like a synchronous system most of the time, but when timing assumptions are shattered, network delay, pauses and clock error may become arbitrarily large.
options: Arbitrarily large
Only twice the bound
Exactly equal to the bound
Zero
optionExplain: Right: no limit during the violation.
Nothing limits them to twice.
They exceed the bound.
They grow, not vanish.

questions.q: A node crashes, restarts after a few minutes, and keeps its disk contents but loses memory. Which failure model describes it?
questions.explain: Restart with disk intact is crash-recovery. The card next lists the three models.
options: Crash-stop
Byzantine
Crash-recovery
Asynchronous
optionExplain: In crash-stop the node never comes back.
The node is not lying or arbitrary.
Right: it comes back, with stable storage preserved.
That is a timing model.
questions.rule: For real systems, the partially synchronous timing model with crash-recovery faults is generally the most useful.

questions.q: Match each node failure model with its description.
questions.explain: Three node failure models.
pairs: Node fails only by crashing and never returns
Node may crash and return, keeping disk but losing memory
Node may do anything, including deceive

questions.q: A database node crashes, then rejoins the cluster with its committed data still on disk. Which assumption is needed for the algorithm to be correct?
questions.explain: Disk survives, memory does not.
options: The node never returns once it has crashed
The node may report arbitrary data on rejoining
The node keeps all of its memory across the crash
Stable storage survives crashes while in-memory state is lost
optionExplain: That is crash-stop.
That is Byzantine.
Memory is assumed lost.
Right: the crash-recovery model.

questions.q: Sort each statement by the failure model it matches.
questions.explain: Stop means gone; recovery means back with disk.

items.t: The node is gone forever after failing
The node may respond again after an unknown time
In-memory state is lost but disk survives
A failed node never needs to rejoin

questions.q: True or false: In the crash-recovery model, in-memory state is assumed to survive crashes.
questions.explain: Nodes are assumed to have stable storage that is preserved across crashes, while in-memory state is assumed to be lost.

questions.q: Which combination does the book call generally the most useful for modeling real systems?
questions.explain: Realism on both axes.
questions.teaches: For modeling real systems, the partially synchronous model with crash-recovery faults is generally the most useful.
options: Synchronous timing with crash-stop faults
Asynchronous timing with Byzantine faults
Synchronous timing with Byzantine faults
Partially synchronous timing with crash-recovery faults
optionExplain: Both are too optimistic.
Very restrictive and costly.
Unrealistic timing.
Right: realistic on both axes.

questions.q: What does it mean for a sorting algorithm to be correct?
questions.explain: Correctness is a property of results. The card next extends this to distributed algorithms.
options: For any two distinct output elements, the left one is smaller
It runs faster than other sorting algorithms
It uses less memory than other algorithms
It never reads the input twice
optionExplain: Right: a property of the output.
Speed is not correctness.
Memory is not correctness.
Reading is not a correctness property.
questions.rule: An algorithm is correct in a system model if it always satisfies its properties in every situation that model allows.

questions.q: In the fencing token example, the property that no two requests return the same value is called ____.
questions.explain: Uniqueness.

questions.q: A token service returns 7 to request X, which completed before request Y began. Which token value for Y keeps the monotonic sequence property?
questions.explain: Monotonic sequence: if x completed before y began then tx < ty.
options: Any value greater than 7
Any value less than 7
Exactly 7
Any value at all
optionExplain: Right: later requests get larger tokens.
That would break the monotonic sequence.
That would break uniqueness.
The property restricts the value.

questions.q: Which pair of fencing token properties says no duplicates and increasing order?
questions.explain: Three properties, each separate.
options: Availability and uniqueness
Uniqueness and monotonic sequence
Availability and monotonic sequence
Uniqueness and availability
optionExplain: Availability is about responses.
Right.
Availability is about responses.
Availability is not about order.

questions.q: True or false: An algorithm is correct if it satisfies its properties only in the normal case with no failures.
questions.explain: It is correct in a model if it always satisfies its properties in all situations that may occur in that model.
questions.rule: Correct means in all modeled situations.

questions.q: If all nodes crash, or all network delays become infinitely long, what does the book say about any algorithm?
questions.explain: This is why properties are split into kinds, next.
questions.rule: No algorithm can beat total failure.
questions.teaches: If all nodes crash, or all network delays suddenly become infinitely long, then no algorithm will be able to get anything done, which motivates distinguishing safety and liveness properties.
options: A correct algorithm still completes requests
Only Byzantine algorithms can continue
No algorithm will be able to get anything done
The properties become unnecessary
optionExplain: It cannot.
They cannot either.
Right: the model's limits.
They remain; some cannot be guaranteed.

questions.q: Which property is a liveness property?
questions.explain: Look for eventually. The card next defines both kinds.
options: No two requests return the same token
Tokens increase in the order requests complete
A node that requests a token and does not crash eventually receives a response
No token is ever reused
optionExplain: That is safety.
That is safety.
Right: the word eventually gives it away.
That is safety.
questions.rule: A violated safety property has a definite moment and is irreversible; a liveness property can still come true later.

questions.q: Liveness properties often include the word eventually in their definition. Fill in: the word is ____.
questions.explain: Eventually.

questions.q: Sort each property by its kind.
questions.explain: Safety: no bad thing. Liveness: eventually something good.

items.t: No two requests return the same token
A non-crashed requester eventually gets a response
Tokens never decrease over time
Eventual consistency
A violated rule cannot be undone
The system eventually makes progress

questions.q: A duplicate token was returned at 12:00:03. Which kind of property was violated, and what is true of it?
questions.explain: A safety violation can be pinpointed and is permanent.
options: A liveness property, which can still come true later
A safety property, which cannot be undone once violated
A liveness property, which cannot be undone
A safety property, which can still come true later
optionExplain: Liveness has no definite point of violation.
Right: there is a definite moment.
Liveness can still be satisfied.
Safety violations are permanent.

questions.q: True or false: Eventual consistency is a safety property.
questions.explain: The book says eventual consistency is a liveness property.

questions.q: A request has been sent but no response has come yet. Which kind of property is not yet violated, and why?
questions.explain: Waiting is not violation for liveness.
questions.teaches: A liveness property may not hold at some point in time, for example a node may have sent a request but not yet received a response, but there is always hope that it may be satisfied in the future.
options: Liveness: there is still hope the response will arrive
Safety: the response must arrive immediately
Safety: the damage is already done
Neither: unanswered requests violate no property
optionExplain: Right: a liveness property may fail now but hold later.
Safety is not about waiting.
Nothing bad has happened yet.
A liveness property can be hoped for.

questions.q: All the nodes of a cluster have crashed. Which kind of property must still hold?
questions.explain: Safety is unconditional. The card next explains.
options: Liveness: every request must still be answered
Neither: with all nodes down nothing needs to hold
Safety: the algorithm must not return a wrong result
Both, with the same strength
optionExplain: Liveness may carry caveats.
Safety must still hold.
Right: safety holds always.
Only safety is unconditional.
questions.rule: Guarantee safety always; promise liveness only under stated conditions such as a majority being up and the network recovering.

questions.q: Safety properties are required to hold in ____ possible situations of the system model.
questions.explain: In all situations.

questions.q: A request needs a response only if a majority of nodes are up and the network recovers. What kind of property is this?
questions.explain: Liveness can be conditional.
options: A safety property
A Byzantine property
A timing property
A liveness property with caveats
optionExplain: Safety cannot have such caveats.
That is about lying nodes.
The condition is about availability.
Right: conditional promise.

questions.q: The whole network fails for an hour. What must a correct algorithm do during that hour?
questions.explain: Better silent than wrong.
questions.rule: Do not trade safety for response.
options: Return its best guess to keep responding
Break safety temporarily, then repair
Declare itself incorrect and stop
Keep its safety properties, even if it cannot respond
optionExplain: A guess may violate safety.
Violations cannot be undone.
Correctness holds in the model.
Right: refuse rather than be wrong.

questions.q: True or false: The partially synchronous model lets the network stay down forever.
questions.explain: It requires that eventually the system returns to a synchronous state: any period of interruption lasts only a finite duration and is then repaired.

questions.q: Why can liveness caveats mention the network eventually recovering, while safety cannot make such an assumption?
questions.explain: Safety is an unconditional promise.
questions.teaches: The partially synchronous model requires that eventually the system returns to a synchronous state, meaning any period of network interruption lasts only for a finite duration and is then repaired.
options: Safety is weaker than liveness
The network always recovers
Safety must hold even if the network never recovers
Caveats make safety easier
optionExplain: Safety is the strong one.
No guarantee.
Right: unconditional.
Safety has none.

questions.q: A crash-recovery algorithm assumes disk data survives crashes. What can go wrong in practice?
questions.explain: Assumptions can be false. The card next gives an example.
options: The disk data can be corrupted or wiped by hardware error or misconfiguration
The algorithm will detect all such errors automatically
Memory will survive instead
Nothing; disks are perfect
optionExplain: Right: the assumption can fail.
It cannot, if it assumes they never happen.
Memory is assumed lost.
They are not.
questions.rule: An implementation should still handle cases the model calls impossible, even if only by stopping and letting a human clean up.

questions.q: If a node forgets previously stored data, a quorum algorithm suffers from ____ that breaks its correctness.
questions.explain: A node with amnesia breaks the quorum condition.

questions.q: A server has a firmware bug and fails to recognize its drives after a reboot, though they are attached. What assumption breaks?
questions.explain: Stable storage is a model assumption.
options: That the network is synchronous
That stable storage survives crashes
That nodes are honest
That clocks agree
optionExplain: The issue is storage.
Right: the data is effectively gone.
The node is not lying.
Clocks are not involved.

questions.q: What if you invent a model where stable storage mostly survives crashes but may sometimes be lost?
questions.explain: A more realistic model costs reasoning effort.
options: It is easier to reason about than before
It makes all algorithms correct
It matches reality better but is harder to reason about
It removes the need for testing
optionExplain: More possibilities, more complexity.
It does not.
Right: realism versus simplicity.
It does not.

questions.q: True or false: A real implementation should contain no code for cases the theoretical model says cannot happen.
questions.explain: A real implementation may still have to handle the supposedly impossible, even if it only stops and lets a human operator clean up.

questions.q: What does the book mean by joking that handling the impossible case may boil down to printing an error and exiting?
questions.explain: Engineering decides how to respond.
questions.teaches: The book notes that this is arguably the difference between computer science and software engineering: a real implementation may include code that handles a supposedly impossible case, even if that boils down to printing an error message and exiting so a human operator can clean up.
options: Programs should always crash on errors
Operators should never be involved
Theory should be ignored
It may be enough to stop and let a human operator clean up the mess
optionExplain: Not the point.
The opposite.
Not the point.
Right: pragmatic handling.

questions.q: Why are abstract system models helpful?
questions.explain: Models trade realism for tractability. The card next gives the full view.
options: They exactly predict every real fault
They reduce the complexity of real systems to a set of faults we can reason about
They replace the need to test
They make hardware more reliable
optionExplain: They are simplifications.
Right: manageable and systematic.
Testing is still needed.
They reason about; they don't fix.
questions.rule: Use theoretical analysis and empirical testing together; each catches problems the other misses.

questions.q: Theoretical analysis and empirical ____ are equally important.
questions.explain: Both are needed.

questions.q: A team proves its replication protocol correct in a partially synchronous model. What can it still not conclude?
questions.explain: Proofs cover the model, not the implementation.
options: That its implementation will always behave correctly on real machines
That the algorithm is correct inside the model
That the model's properties hold in the model
That the design has been examined systematically
optionExplain: Right: proof of the algorithm is not proof of the code.
The proof gives that.
The proof shows that.
The proof does that.

questions.q: A timing assumption in the model is defeated by unusual circumstances in production. What did the theoretical analysis offer beforehand?
questions.explain: Analysis finds problems early.
options: It may have revealed the problem before it bit in a real system
It guaranteed the problem could not happen
It replaced production monitoring
It forced a Byzantine protocol
optionExplain: Right: analysis can surface hidden problems.
The assumption was defeated.
Not its job.
Not what the book says.

questions.q: True or false: Because models are simplifications, the book concludes that they are worthless.
questions.explain: The book says quite the opposite: they are incredibly helpful for distilling complexity to a manageable set of faults.

questions.q: Which pairing does the book recommend for building confidence in a distributed algorithm?
questions.explain: Each covers the other's gaps.
questions.teaches: Proving an algorithm correct does not mean its implementation on a real system will necessarily always behave correctly, but it is a very good first step because theoretical analysis can uncover problems in an algorithm that might remain hidden for a long time in a real system.
options: Proofs alone, since testing cannot cover everything
Theoretical proofs and empirical testing together
Testing alone, since models are unrealistic
Neither: rely on vendor claims
optionExplain: Both are equally important.
Right: both matter.
Models are still useful.
Not advised.

questions.q: A server's network interface falls to a tiny fraction of its normal speed because of a driver bug, but the server stays up. Why is that awkward?
questions.explain: A limping node sits between dead and healthy. The card next explains.
options: It is dead, so failover happens automatically
It is neither dead nor healthy, so ordinary liveness checks may miss it
It is healthy, since it answers requests
It is Byzantine, since it is lying about its speed
optionExplain: It still responds, only slowly.
Right: it limps.
It is degraded and slows everything that depends on it.
It is not lying; it is slow.
questions.rule: A node that limps without dying can be harder to deal with than one that fails cleanly.

questions.q: A node that is degraded but not dead is described as ____.
questions.explain: Limping.

questions.q: A database node still passes health checks but answers each request after ten seconds. What does the book say about such a node?
questions.explain: Clean failures are simpler.
options: It is easier than a failed node, since it still works
It must be a Byzantine node
It can be harder to deal with than a cleanly failed node
It is a safety violation
optionExplain: The partial failure makes handling harder.
It is not lying.
Right: no clear failure.
This is not about a safety property.

questions.q: A timeout is set very short and a healthy node has a load spike. What happens?
questions.explain: Short timeouts misread delays.
options: It is correctly declared healthy
It is falsely suspected of crashing
It becomes Byzantine
It is declared dead for good
optionExplain: The short timeout fires.
Right: variable delay causes false suspicion.
It does not lie.
Nothing about permanence.

questions.q: True or false: Timeouts can reliably distinguish a network failure from a node failure.
questions.explain: Timeouts cannot distinguish between network and node failures.

questions.q: What does the book give as an example of degradation without death?
questions.explain: The slowdown is the hard part.
questions.teaches: A Gigabit network interface could suddenly drop to 1 Kb/s throughput due to a driver bug; such a node that is limping but not dead can be even more difficult to deal with than a cleanly failed node.
options: A Gigabit network interface dropping to 1 Kb/s due to a driver bug
A hard drive losing a single file
A server running out of coffee
A switch turning off
optionExplain: Right: the book's example.
Not the book's example.
Silly.
That is a clean failure.

questions.q: What do the nodes of a distributed system share?
questions.explain: No shared state. The card next states the consequence.
options: A global variable
A common clock
Nothing beyond the messages they send each other
A shared memory
optionExplain: None exists.
They cannot agree on the time.
Right: no shared state.
None exists.
questions.rule: With no shared state, important decisions need a quorum of nodes to agree.

questions.q: In a distributed system, nodes cannot even agree on what ____ it is.
questions.explain: Not even the time.

questions.q: A cluster must decide which node is leader. Why not let one node decide alone?
questions.explain: Enlist other nodes.
options: A single node cannot send messages
A single node has no clock
A single node cannot be a leader
A single node may fail or be wrong, so a quorum must agree
optionExplain: It can.
It has one.
It can, if agreed.
Right: avoid single-node dependence.

questions.q: Which is a way information can flow between nodes?
questions.explain: The network is the only channel.
options: By reading a global variable
By sharing memory
By consulting common knowledge
By sending messages over the unreliable network
optionExplain: None exists.
None exists.
None exists.
Right: the only way.

questions.q: True or false: Major decisions in a distributed system can be made safely by a single node that is sure of itself.
questions.explain: Major decisions cannot be safely made by a single node; protocols enlist help from other nodes and try to get a quorum to agree.

questions.q: What will the book discuss next about these decisions?
questions.explain: This chapter has been all about problems.
questions.teaches: This chapter has been all about problems and gives a bleak outlook; the next chapter moves on to solutions and algorithms designed to cope with all the problems in distributed systems.
options: More problems, in an appendix
Hardware design
Algorithms that cope with the problems, in the next chapter
Programming languages
optionExplain: The next chapter turns to solutions.
Not the next topic.
Right: solutions follow.
Not the next topic.

questions.q: A team's workload fits comfortably on one modern server. What does the book suggest?
questions.explain: Single machines avoid the whole chapter's problems. The card next gives the full view.
options: Keep it on a single machine if you can
Distribute it anyway for practice
Use Byzantine fault tolerance
Add a quorum of five nodes
optionExplain: Right: avoid the problems of distribution.
Unneeded complexity.
Not needed.
Unneeded complexity.
questions.rule: Use one machine when it suffices; distribute when you need scale, fault tolerance or low latency near users.

questions.q: If you can avoid opening Pandora's box and keep things on a single ____, it is generally worth doing so.
questions.explain: One machine.

questions.q: A startup's service must keep running when one machine fails and must answer quickly to users on three continents. What follows?
questions.explain: Fault tolerance and latency need distribution.
options: A bigger single server will do both
A single node cannot give fault tolerance and low latency near users, so it must distribute
Fault tolerance is optional
Distribution is only for scalability
optionExplain: One server cannot be in three places.
Right: those goals need several nodes.
It is a stated goal.
Fault tolerance and latency are also reasons.

questions.q: What if reliable timing were required for all systems regardless of cost?
questions.explain: Guarantees are bought with lower utilization.
options: Costs would fall
Latency would vary more
Hardware utilization would fall and costs rise
Nothing would change
optionExplain: Guarantees cost resources.
Guarantees reduce variation.
Right: the book's trade-off.
Costs change.

questions.q: True or false: Scalability is the only reason to use a distributed system.
questions.explain: Fault tolerance and low latency, by placing data geographically close to users, are equally important goals.

questions.q: What does the book say about the unreliability of networks, clocks and processes?
questions.explain: Most non-safety-critical systems choose cheap over reliable.
questions.teaches: It is possible to give hard real-time response guarantees and bounded delays in networks, but doing so is very expensive and results in lower utilization of hardware resources; most non-safety-critical systems choose cheap and unreliable over expensive and reliable.
options: It is an unavoidable law of nature
It can be removed for free
It exists only in the cloud
It is not an inevitable law of nature; guarantees are possible but expensive
optionExplain: The book says it is not.
It is expensive.
Not limited to the cloud.
Right: a cost choice.

questions.q: Crashes and races can hit any application. What design spares each application from handling them?
questions.explain: Hiding faults behind one well-tested guarantee scales better than repeating fault handling everywhere. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Build the guarantee once; let applications rely on it.
options: Each team writing its own recovery code for the faults it expects
A faster network, so that faults become too rare to matter
Letting the whole service fail and showing users an error message
A shared abstraction with guarantees, built once and relied on
optionExplain: This feels flexible, but the same hard problems get solved many times, with different bugs each time.
Better hardware lowers the fault rate but does not remove faults, and applications would still need to cope.
This is the simplest handling, but it gives up on tolerating faults instead of hiding them.
Right: one implementation of the guarantee serves every application.

questions.q: By using a ____, an application can pretend there are no crashes, nobody else is accessing the data, and storage is perfectly reliable.
questions.explain: The chapter points back to transactions from Chapter 7 as the model: atomicity, isolation and durability hide crashes, races and disk failures.
questions.rule: A transaction is the model of a hidden-fault abstraction.

questions.q: Five services each need exactly one node acting as scheduler, and every team wrote its own election code. What does the chapter's approach suggest?
questions.explain: Five copies of subtle election code multiply the places a bug can hide; one shared implementation concentrates the effort.
questions.rule: Concentrate hard fault handling in one reusable component.
options: Keep each team's code but agree on one common timeout value
Pin the scheduler to one hand-picked node and skip failover
Use one shared agreement service that every team relies on
Add retries in every service until the election bugs vanish
optionExplain: A common timeout aligns settings, yet five separate implementations of a subtle problem remain.
A fixed node is simple, but when it dies there is no scheduler, so fault tolerance is lost.
Right: implement the hard guarantee once and let the services rely on it.
Retries mask some symptoms, but they do not give a guarantee that exactly one scheduler exists.

questions.q: True or false: Since crashes, races and disk failures still occur, a transaction cannot spare the application from handling them.
questions.explain: The faults do occur, but the abstraction hides their effects, so the application need not handle them. That is the point of the approach.
questions.rule: A hidden fault is still a fault; the guarantee changes what the application sees.

questions.q: Which abstraction does the chapter call one of the most important for distributed systems?
questions.explain: The chapter singles out consensus and warns that reaching it despite network faults and process failures is surprisingly tricky.
questions.rule: Consensus is a core abstraction, and it is harder than it looks.
questions.teaches: Consensus, getting all nodes to agree on something, is one of the most important abstractions for distributed systems, and reliably reaching it despite network faults and process failures is surprisingly tricky.
options: Caching: keeping popular data close to the readers
Sharding: splitting a dataset across many machines
Gossip: passing updates between randomly chosen nodes
Consensus: getting nodes to agree on something
optionExplain: Caching helps speed, but the chapter does not present it as a fault-hiding agreement abstraction.
Sharding spreads data and load; it does not by itself make nodes agree on a value.
Gossip spreads information, but the chapter's key abstraction is a firm agreement among nodes.
Right: once consensus is implemented, applications can use it for purposes such as electing a leader.

questions.q: A single-leader database loses its leader and the remaining nodes must choose a new one. What does a correct consensus implementation prevent?
questions.explain: If two nodes both think they are the leader, both accept writes and the data diverges; agreeing on one leader avoids that.
questions.rule: Agreement on the leader prevents split brain.
questions.teaches: Split brain, two nodes both believing themselves to be the leader, often leads to data loss, and correct consensus implementations help avoid it.
options: Followers applying the leader's log in a different order
A reader seeing a replica that lags slightly behind
A transaction committing on one node but aborting on another
Two nodes both believing they lead, which often loses data
optionExplain: Order of the log is a replication concern, not the problem election by consensus is meant to avoid.
Lag is normal in asynchronous replication and unrelated to who the leader is.
This is the atomic commit problem, a different use of agreement than electing a leader.
Right: this is split brain, and consensus is used to avoid it.

questions.q: A replicated database advertises eventual consistency. Which statement does that promise?
questions.explain: Eventual consistency promises convergence without any bound on how long it takes. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Eventual means convergence, with no time limit.
options: A read always returns the value that was written last
All replicas hold identical data at every moment in time
If writes stop, all replicas end up with one value
Replicas converge within a few seconds of any write
optionExplain: Reading the latest write is a stronger, recency guarantee that eventual consistency does not give.
Replicas routinely differ for a while, which is exactly what the weak guarantee allows.
Right: this is the convergence promise, with no time attached.
No bound on the time to converge is promised, so a few seconds is not part of the guarantee.

questions.q: A better name for eventual consistency may be ____, since all replicas are expected to end up with the same value.
questions.explain: The book suggests convergence because the replicas converge to the same value once writes stop and faults are repaired.

questions.q: A user writes a profile photo and reloads at once, and a different replica serves the read. What does eventual consistency allow?
questions.explain: Eventual consistency says nothing about reads before convergence, so the reader can see stale data or none.
questions.rule: Do not assume a read shows your own write.
options: Only the new photo, because the write has been acknowledged
Only the old photo, until a full minute has passed
An error, because the replicas are disagreeing on the value
The old photo or no photo, since replicas may not yet agree
optionExplain: An acknowledged write still need not be visible on every replica, so this over-reads the promise.
No fixed delay is guaranteed, so a one-minute window is invented.
The database is not required to detect or report the disagreement; it just serves what that replica holds.
Right: before convergence, a read may return anything, including nothing.

questions.q: True or false: Eventual consistency guarantees that a client which writes a value and reads it back right away sees that value.
questions.explain: Reading your own write is not guaranteed, because the read may be routed to a different replica that has not caught up.
questions.rule: Weak guarantees need no assumption about read-after-write.

questions.q: According to the book, which replication method avoids differences between replicas at a given moment?
questions.explain: The book says write requests arrive at different nodes at different times, so the differences appear with every replication method.
questions.rule: Replication lag is not specific to one design.
questions.teaches: Differences between replicas at a given moment occur no matter which replication method is used: single-leader, multi-leader or leaderless.
options: Single-leader, because one node orders all of the writes
Leaderless, because quorums force every replica to agree
None: all three replication methods show them
Multi-leader, because each leader sees the other's writes
optionExplain: A single leader orders writes, yet followers still receive them at different times.
Quorums narrow the gap, but replicas can still differ at a given moment in time.
Right: these inconsistencies occur no matter which replication method is used.
Leaders replicate to each other asynchronously, so a gap remains between them.

questions.q: A chat backlog sits in an eventually consistent store and a fault splits the network for an hour. What can be relied on?
questions.explain: The promise is conditional on repair: once the fault ends and writes stop, replicas converge.
questions.rule: Convergence assumes that faults get repaired.
questions.teaches: Eventual consistency assumes that any faults in the network are also eventually repaired; the inconsistency resolves itself only then.
options: That every reader sees messages in the order they were sent
That reads during the fault return the last acknowledged message
That replicas converge once writes stop and the fault ends
That the store rejects writes it cannot replicate immediately
optionExplain: Order across readers is a separate guarantee, not part of eventual consistency.
During the fault a read may return anything or nothing, so the last message is not promised.
Right: convergence assumes that network faults are also eventually repaired.
Eventually consistent stores keep accepting writes; they do not block on replication.

questions.q: Why might bugs from a weakly consistent database escape testing?
questions.explain: Subtle edge cases only appear when something goes wrong or load is high, which is why they are hard to test for. The card next shows why.
options: The application works well until a fault or high concurrency appears
Test databases never replicate, so there is nothing to find
The bugs depend on clock settings that tests cannot change
Weak guarantees produce errors that the database logs and fixes itself
optionExplain: Right: normal conditions hide the edge cases that faults and heavy concurrency expose.
Test setups may well replicate; the issue is that the troubling timings are rare, not absent.
Clocks can matter elsewhere, but the book's reason is rarity of the triggering conditions.
Nothing is logged or fixed automatically; the application simply receives unexpected values.

questions.q: A database looks superficially like a ____ that you can read and write, but it has much more complicated semantics.
questions.explain: The book compares a database with a variable in a single-threaded program, where reading right after assigning never returns the old value.
questions.rule: A database is not a variable.

questions.q: A shopping cart is tested on one laptop, then shipped on an eventually consistent store. What does the book warn about?
questions.explain: A single laptop hides replication entirely, so the weak guarantee's edge cases stay invisible until production.
questions.rule: Test under faults and concurrency, not just the happy path.
options: The cart will return stale data in every read from the first day
Edge cases may appear only under network faults or heavy concurrency
Eventual consistency makes the cart slower than a strong model
Replicas will never converge because the test never ran concurrently
optionExplain: Stale reads are possible but not constant; the trouble is that they are rare enough to miss.
Right: the application may look fine in testing, with the problem arriving later.
Performance is typically the advantage of the weaker model, not its drawback.
Convergence does not depend on whether tests ran concurrently.

questions.q: True or false: Passing its tests on a weakly consistent database shows that an application does not rely on any guarantee the database lacks.
questions.explain: Passing tests shows little, because the bugs appear only when there is a fault or high concurrency, which tests may never produce.
questions.rule: Absence of failures in tests is not evidence of correctness.

questions.q: According to the book, what is the price of the stronger consistency models that data systems may offer?
questions.explain: The book says systems with stronger guarantees may have worse performance or be less fault-tolerant than systems with weaker guarantees.
questions.rule: Strength has a price in speed or fault tolerance.
questions.teaches: Systems with stronger consistency guarantees may have worse performance or be less fault-tolerant than systems with weaker guarantees, yet they can be appealing because they are easier to use correctly.
options: Worse performance or less fault tolerance
A longer wait before replicas eventually converge
Applications must give up the use of transactions
A requirement that every replica be in the same datacenter
optionExplain: Right: stronger guarantees do not come for free. Remember: Strength has a price in speed or fault tolerance.
Convergence time is a property of the weak model, not a cost of stronger ones.
Strong models do not forbid transactions; they are a separate concern.
Placement is not the stated price; the price is speed and fault tolerance.

questions.q: A payments team weighs a fast weak model against a slower, less available strong one. What does the book let them conclude?
questions.explain: Seeing a few models first puts the reader in a better position to decide which one best fits their needs.
questions.rule: Pick the model by weighing ease of use against cost.
questions.teaches: After seeing a few different consistency models, a reader is better placed to decide which one best fits their needs, because no model is best everywhere.
options: It depends: the strong model is easier to use but costs more
The strong model is better, since correctness always outranks speed
The weak model is better, since stronger guarantees are rarely used
Neither: the book says consistency models do not affect applications
optionExplain: Right: the choice is a trade-off to decide for the needs of the system.
Correctness matters, but the book frames it as a trade-off, not an automatic win for the strong model.
The book does not say strong guarantees are rare; the later sections use them for locks and constraints.
The models do affect applications; the chapter exists to help readers decide which one fits.

questions.q: Two engineers argue about whether stale reads from a replica are an isolation problem. Who is closer to the book?
questions.explain: Isolation is mostly about races between transactions, whereas consistency is mostly about replicas. The card next shows why.
options: Both are one topic, and an isolation level fixes stale replicas
Stale replica reads mainly belong to consistency, not isolation
Isolation covers replicas while consistency covers only transactions
Neither topic covers replicas, only the storage engine does
optionExplain: The hierarchies look similar, but they address different concerns.
Right: consistency is mostly about coordinating replica state under delays and faults.
This swaps the roles of the two; isolation is the concern about concurrent transactions.
Replica state is exactly the subject of distributed consistency, not the storage engine alone.

questions.q: Match each concern with the problem it mainly addresses.
questions.explain: Isolation and consistency are mostly independent: one covers transaction races, the other replica state.
questions.rule: Name the problem before naming the guarantee.
pairs: Coordinating replica state despite delays and faults
All writes take effect or none do

questions.q: Two transactions on one single-node database both read a row and then write based on it. Which concern is this?
questions.explain: One node means no replicas, so the question is how concurrent transactions interleave, which is isolation.
options: Isolation: avoiding races between transactions
Consistency: keeping replicas in step after a delay
Consensus: choosing a leader among several nodes
Convergence: replicas settling on one value
optionExplain: Right: a race between concurrently executing transactions is an isolation problem.
There is only one node, so no replicas need coordinating.
No leader is being chosen; the issue lies in how the two transactions interleave.
Convergence concerns replicas; with a single node there is nothing to converge.

questions.q: A replicated key-value store has no transactions at all but still shows stale reads. Which concern explains the staleness?
questions.explain: Staleness needs only replicas and delay, so it can occur with no transactions.
questions.rule: Replicas alone are enough for a consistency question.
options: Consistency across replicas, which exists without transactions
Isolation, which needs transactions to exist but still applies
Atomicity, because each write is a single object
Durability, because the replicas were not flushed to disk
optionExplain: Right: staleness comes from replica state lagging, so transactions are not required.
Isolation is defined among transactions, and this store has none.
Atomicity is about writes taking effect fully; it does not explain a lagging replica.
Durability concerns surviving crashes, not how current a replica is.

questions.q: True or false: Distributed consistency models and transaction isolation levels are the same hierarchy under two names.
questions.explain: The book notes some similarity and overlap, but calls them mostly independent concerns with different main purposes.
questions.rule: Similar shape does not mean the same subject.
questions.teaches: There is some similarity between consistency models and the hierarchy of isolation levels, but they are mostly independent concerns.

questions.q: A multi-datacenter app sees users read old data after a failover, though every query runs inside a serializable transaction. What follows?
questions.explain: Because the two concerns are mostly independent, strong isolation does not promise fresh replica reads.
questions.rule: Fix a replica problem with a consistency tool, not an isolation tool.
questions.teaches: Serializable isolation does not by itself keep replicas current; strong transaction isolation and strong replica consistency are separate properties to check.
options: The serializable level is broken and must be replaced
Isolation is not enough; replica consistency is separate
Failover must have disabled transactions in the database
Replicas can only be stale if isolation is weak
optionExplain: Serializability can be working as designed while replicas still lag.
Right: isolation concerns races between transactions, not how current a replica is.
Nothing says failover disabled transactions; the problem is replica state.
Staleness comes from replication delay, not from a weak isolation level.

questions.q: What would make a replicated database simplest for application developers to use?
questions.explain: The simplest mental model hides replication completely, as if there were one copy. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Hide the replicas: one copy, atomic operations.
options: Behaving as if there were only one copy of the data
Telling each client which replica is the freshest
Letting each replica process requests on its own schedule
Returning conflicting values and letting clients choose
optionExplain: Right: this is the idea behind linearizability. Remember: Hide the replicas: one copy, atomic operations.
Naming the freshest replica pushes replication details back onto every client.
Independent schedules produce the divergence that confuses developers. The right answer is: Behaving as if there were only one copy of the data.
Clients choosing between conflicting values adds work, not simplicity.

questions.q: In a linearizable system the database behaves as if there were only one ____ of the data.
questions.explain: Linearizability is the illusion of a single copy of the data with atomic operations, even though several replicas exist.

questions.q: A view counter is stored on three replicas and the dashboard is linearizable. What can a developer ignore?
questions.explain: Whichever replica answers, a linearizable system behaves as if the single copy was read.
questions.rule: Replica choice is invisible to a linearizable client.
options: Whether the counter is stored on disk at all
Which replica answered the dashboard request
How many dashboards are open at the same time
Whether the network links between replicas are fast
optionExplain: Storage is still a concern, since the illusion says nothing about durability.
Right: the system acts as if there were one copy, so the choice of replica does not matter.
Concurrent clients still matter; operations are atomic but the clients still run concurrently.
Network speed still affects latency, because maintaining the illusion costs coordination.

questions.q: Client A completes a write of 7 and then tells client B by phone. B reads. In a linearizable database, what does B get?
questions.explain: After a write completes, every client reading afterwards must see that value, even if another channel told them.
questions.rule: Completed writes are visible to all later reads.
options: The value that was there before the write
7, or something written even later
Either the old or the new value, with equal chance
An error, because the replicas do not yet agree
optionExplain: That would show the stale value the guarantee is designed to rule out.
Right: once a write completes, every later read must see it or something newer.
A coin-flip outcome applies only to reads concurrent with the write, not later ones.
A linearizable database does not answer with an error because of replica disagreement; it hides it.

questions.q: True or false: Linearizability is known by several other names, including atomic consistency, strong consistency, immediate consistency and external consistency.
questions.explain: The chapter lists these names for the same guarantee, so seeing them elsewhere means the same idea.
questions.teaches: Linearizability is also known as atomic consistency, strong consistency, immediate consistency or external consistency.

questions.q: A product page must show the same stock number to every shopper the moment an item sells out. Which property fits best?
questions.explain: To give every reader the latest value, the system must act as if there is one copy, which is linearizability.
questions.rule: Same value for everyone, right now: single-copy behaviour.
questions.teaches: Because the database acts as though there is one copy, the application does not need to worry about replication lag at all, and every client has the same view of the data.
options: Linearizability, which makes replicas look like one copy
Eventual consistency, which converges only once the sales stop
Causal consistency, which orders only the causally related events
Snapshot isolation, which reads from a fixed earlier version
optionExplain: Right: a single apparent copy shows every shopper the latest number.
Eventual consistency lets different shoppers see different numbers until sales stop.
Causal consistency only orders events that are causally related, not all reads.
A snapshot deliberately excludes newer writes, so it can show an old number.

questions.q: A write to a key has succeeded. In a system with a recency guarantee, what must the next read of that key return?
questions.explain: Recency means the latest value, never something older. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A completed write cannot be unseen.
options: Any value that some replica still holds
The value that was committed first in the log
The value the reader's own cache holds
The value that was written, or something newer
optionExplain: Letting any replica answer is what a recency guarantee rules out.
The earliest value is the opposite of the most recent one.
A reader's own cache may be stale, which is just what the guarantee excludes.
Right: recency means reads cannot lag behind a completed write.

questions.q: Linearizability is a ____ guarantee: the value read is the most recent, up-to-date value.
questions.explain: The book says in other words that linearizability is a recency guarantee.

questions.q: A password change succeeds, then a later request is served from a cache holding the old hash. What does this violate?
questions.explain: A stale cache returning an older value after a successful write breaks the recency requirement.
options: Durability, since the password change was lost on disk
Atomicity, since the write was applied only in part
Recency, since the read ignored a completed write
Isolation, since two transactions raced for the same row
optionExplain: The write was not lost on disk; the cache simply answered with an older copy.
Nothing says the write was applied partially; the problem is the later read.
Right: the read returned a value older than a write that had already succeeded.
No pair of transactions is described, only a read that ignored a completed write.

questions.q: True or false: Reads are linearizable when every replica is guaranteed to lag by no more than five seconds.
questions.explain: Linearizability is not about staleness within a bound. Any lag lets a read miss a write that has already completed.
questions.rule: No bounded staleness: recency means latest.

questions.q: What gap remains in a system with linearizable reads and writes but no transactions?
questions.explain: It does not group operations together into transactions, so it does not prevent problems such as write skew.
questions.rule: Single-object recency is not multi-object safety.
questions.teaches: Linearizability is a recency guarantee on reads and writes of an individual object; it does not group operations into transactions, so it does not by itself prevent write skew.
options: Reads may return values older than a completed write
Replicas may disagree about the order of writes to a key
Writes may be lost when a node crashes after acknowledging them
Operations are not grouped, so write skew is not prevented
optionExplain: That is what linearizability excludes, so it cannot be the gap.
A single timeline is exactly what linearizability gives, so order is not the gap.
Losing acknowledged writes is a durability issue, which a linearizable system also needs to avoid.
Right: linearizability covers single objects and does not prevent problems such as write skew.

questions.q: A leaderboard is read by many clients. Which design change keeps a read from ever returning a score older than a completed update?
questions.explain: Recency has to be built into the read path; chance and speed do not provide it.
questions.rule: Make the read path respect completed writes.
questions.teaches: A linearizable read must not come from a stale cache or replica, so recency is a property of the read path, not something that more replicas or faster replication can achieve.
options: Add more replicas so that any given request is likely to be fresh
Shorten the replication interval until lag is tiny
Let clients retry a read until they see a higher score
Route every read through a path that sees the latest update
optionExplain: More replicas raise the odds of a stale answer, not lower them.
A smaller lag is still a lag, and a stale read remains possible.
Clients cannot know whether a higher score exists, so retries do not give a guarantee.
Right: the guarantee needs reads that cannot miss the completed write.

questions.q: Alice sees the final score and tells Bob, who then reloads and sees the match still on. Why is this a problem?
questions.explain: Bob's request started after Alice's finished, so an older answer for him breaks the single-copy illusion. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Later requests cannot see older state than earlier ones.
options: Bob should have reloaded using the same phone that Alice used
Score data must not be served from replicas that can lag
Alice's page was served before the final score was announced
Bob's request began after Alice's, so it should be as recent
optionExplain: Using the same phone is irrelevant; the issue is the order of the requests in real time.
Reading from replicas is allowed in general; the issue is that one lags too far.
Alice's result was correct; the stale one is Bob's.
Right: once Alice saw the new state, a later request cannot show an older one.

questions.q: True or false: In the sports example, the stale result would be unremarkable if Alice and Bob had hit reload at the same time.
questions.explain: If both pressed reload simultaneously, neither knows when the server processed each request, so different results would be less surprising.
questions.rule: Simultaneous requests may differ; sequential ones may not.

questions.q: Dev A marks a deploy as done, then Dev B opens the status board and still sees it running. Which statement applies?
questions.explain: Whenever one request provably begins after another ends, the later one must not be older.
questions.rule: Real-time order across clients must be respected.
options: Both reads are allowed since boards are eventually consistent
B must have pressed refresh too early to expect anything
B started after A finished, so a stale result breaks it
A's post was lost in the network, so B saw the correct value
optionExplain: Eventual consistency permits this, but it is exactly what linearizability prohibits.
The timing of B's refresh is the point: it came after A's result was visible.
Right: this is the Alice and Bob situation again, with deploys instead of scores.
Nothing indicates the post was lost; B's replica was lagging.

questions.q: Alice and Bob reload at the same instant; Alice sees the final score, Bob sees the match still on. Is that a violation?
questions.explain: Without a known order between the requests, both outcomes fit a single timeline.
questions.rule: Overlapping requests can be ordered either way.
options: Yes, because Bob received an older result than Alice
Yes, because replicas must answer identically at every moment
Not necessarily, as neither knows which was handled first
No, because linearizability only covers writes, not reads
optionExplain: An older result alone is not a violation; it depends on whether his request began after hers finished.
Replicas may differ at a moment; the guarantee is about the order of non-overlapping requests.
Right: concurrent requests can be processed in either order, so both results can be valid.
The guarantee covers reads and writes on a register, so reads count.

questions.q: The violation was noticed only because of a second channel in the system: Alice's ____ reaching Bob's ears.
questions.explain: Bob noticed the stale result only because Alice told him through a channel the database does not control.
questions.rule: Violations show up when information travels through a second channel.
questions.teaches: The violation was noticed only because there was an additional communication channel (Alice's voice to Bob's ears); without it Bob would simply have refreshed later and seen the final score.

questions.q: A customer's payment is confirmed aloud, yet the clerk's later check shows no payment. What should the team infer?
questions.explain: The same pattern as Alice and Bob: an outside channel exposes that a later read saw older data.
questions.teaches: Linearizability violations can be observed through channels outside the database, such as a person's voice, so any system with another communication path can expose a stale read as a bug.
options: The clerk checked too early to expect any change to appear
The payment confirmation was incorrect and should be retracted
Account stores are not meant to show payments right away
The store is not linearizable; the voice was a second channel
optionExplain: The clerk checked after the confirmation, so the timing was appropriate.
The confirmation was correct; the lagging copy is the problem.
A store that hides recent writes is stale, not designed that way.
Right: a later check should not see older state than the confirmation.

questions.q: A client sends a write at time 10 and its response arrives at time 14. When did the database process the write?
questions.explain: Variable network delay means the client sees only an interval during which processing happened. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A request takes effect somewhere in its interval.
options: Exactly at time 10, when the request was first sent out
Between 10 and 14, at a point the client cannot pin down
Exactly at time 14, when the response arrived back
Before time 10, since the request must have been queued
optionExplain: Network delay means the request needs time to reach the database.
Right: the client only knows the processing happened inside the interval.
The response travels back after processing, so processing is earlier than arrival.
Processing cannot start before the request exists. The right answer is: Between 10 and 14, at a point the client cannot pin down.

questions.q: Match each operation with what it does on a register.
questions.explain: The model has three operations on a register, and each request is drawn as a bar from send to response.
pairs: Returns the current value of register x
Sets register x to value v and returns ok or error
Sets x to new only if x currently equals old
Time from sending a request to receiving its response

questions.q: A read runs from 3 ms to 9 ms. A write finished at 2 ms. In a linearizable store, which value must the read return?
questions.explain: Compare the end of one bar with the start of the next; if one ends before the other begins, the order is fixed.
options: The written value, since the write ended before the read began
Either value, since the read overlaps the network delay
The old value, since the read was sent before the write was seen
The write's value only if the read took under 5 ms
optionExplain: Right: the write ended at 2 ms and the read began at 3 ms, so the read follows the write.
Overlap is with the request's own bar, not with the write's bar.
The write already completed, so the old value is no longer allowed.
How long the read took does not change that it began after the write finished.

questions.q: True or false: A register in this model can only be a key in a key-value store.
questions.explain: In practice a register could be one key in a key-value store, one row in a relational database or one document in a document database.
questions.rule: A register is any individual object.

questions.q: The diagrams assume a global clock, though real systems lack accurate ones. Why does the book accept this?
questions.explain: It is a modelling device for the analysis; the algorithm itself cannot read that clock.
questions.rule: The analyst may assume a global clock; the algorithm may not.
questions.teaches: For analysing a distributed algorithm we may pretend that an accurate global clock exists, as long as the algorithm has no access to it; it sees only an approximation produced by a quartz oscillator and NTP.
options: Because NTP synchronises every machine to an exact shared time
We may pretend an accurate clock exists if algorithms cannot use it
Because the diagrams are only for single-node databases
Because quartz oscillators are accurate enough for ordering
optionExplain: NTP provides only an approximation, which the footnote itself notes.
Right: the algorithm only sees a mangled approximation of real time.
The diagrams show replicated databases; a single node would not need them.
The footnote calls the clock a mangled approximation, not an accurate one.

questions.q: A monitoring tool records only when each request was sent and answered. Which question about a linearizable store can it settle for sure?
questions.explain: Send and response times are enough to establish order only when intervals do not overlap.
questions.rule: Client-side timing fixes order only for non-overlapping requests.
questions.teaches: From the clients' timings alone you can tell that one request must have been processed before another only if the first one's response came before the second one's request was sent.
options: The exact instant at which the database applied each write
Whether non-overlapping requests have a fixed order
Which replica of the database handled each request
How quickly each replica's own clock was drifting
optionExplain: Only the interval is visible, not the exact instant of processing.
Right: if one response arrives before another request is sent, their order is known.
Replica identity is not in the record. The right answer is: Whether non-overlapping requests have a fixed order.
Replica clocks are not part of the recorded information.

questions.q: A write sets a register from 0 to 1. A read begins after the write has completed. What may the read return?
questions.explain: A request that begins after a write ends is ordered after it. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Starts after the write ends: sees the new value.
options: Only 0, the value that was there before
Either 0 or 1, because the system is replicated
Nothing, because it must wait for replicas to agree
Only 1, the value that the write set
optionExplain: The old value is no longer allowed once the write has completed.
Either value is permitted only when the read overlaps the write in time.
Reads do not wait for replicas to agree; they must simply return a permitted value.
Right: the read began after the write finished, so it must see the new value.

questions.q: Match the position of a read to the value it may return while a write sets 0 to 1.
questions.explain: Only overlapping reads have a choice; the other two are ordered by time.
questions.rule: Position in time decides what a read may return.
pairs: Read ends before the write begins
Read begins after the write ends

questions.q: A read ends at 2 s; a write turning a flag on runs from 3 s to 5 s. What must the read return?
questions.explain: Compare the intervals: the read is entirely before the write.
questions.rule: Entirely before the write: old value.
options: Either value, since the write will eventually be applied
The new value, since the write is already on its way
The old value, since it finished before the write began
An error, because the flag changes during the poll
optionExplain: Either value is allowed only for a read overlapping the write.
A write that has not yet begun cannot influence an earlier read.
Right: the read ended before the write began, so it cannot see the write.
Nothing in the model produces an error just because the value changes later.

questions.q: A write runs from 4 s to 8 s and a read from 6 s to 7 s. Which results are valid when linearizable?
questions.explain: An overlapping read cannot be placed before or after the write with certainty, so both are valid.
questions.rule: Overlap means both answers are valid.
options: Only the old value, since the write is incomplete
Only the new value, since B started after 4 s
Either the old or the new value
Neither: B must wait for the write to end
optionExplain: The write may already have taken effect inside its interval, so the new value is also valid.
The write may not yet have taken effect, so the old value is also valid.
Right: B's read overlaps the write, so it could have been processed before or after the write took effect.
Reads do not block; they return a permitted value.

questions.q: If overlapping reads may return old or new and nothing else is required, what problem remains?
questions.explain: Without a further constraint a value could go 0, 1, 0, 1 as seen by successive readers, unlike one real copy.
questions.teaches: If reads concurrent with a write could freely return either value, readers could see a value flip back and forth between old and new several times during a write, which is not what a single copy of the data does.
options: Readers could never see the new value until the write ends
Writers could overwrite one another without any notice
The old value could reappear after the write has finished
Readers could see the value flip between old and new
optionExplain: Overlapping reads are allowed to see the new value, so they are not held back.
Concurrent writers are a separate matter from what reads may see.
After the write finishes, only the new value is allowed, so the old one cannot come back.
Right: this is not how a single copy of the data behaves, so another constraint is needed.

questions.q: True or false: If overlapping reads may return either value, a later read may return the old value after another saw the new.
questions.explain: That would be a flip back, and the next idea adds exactly this constraint: once a read returns the new value, later reads must too.
questions.rule: Overlap freedom is limited by order among the reads.
questions.teaches: A register in which reads concurrent with a write may return either old or new is called a regular register, and it is weaker than a linearizable one because it allows flips.

questions.q: Reader A sees the new value 1 while a write is still running. Reader B then starts a read. What may B return?
questions.explain: A later read cannot show older data than an earlier one that has already finished. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: New value seen once means new value for everyone after.
options: Either 0 or 1, because the write is still running
Only 0, because the write has not finished yet
Neither, because B must wait for the writer's reply
Only 1, because A has already seen it
optionExplain: This is the weak reading of overlapping reads, which allows flip-flopping between old and new.
That would show a value moving backwards after somebody has seen the update.
Reads do not wait for the writer's reply; they return a value that fits one timeline.
Right: a read starting after another has returned 1 cannot go back to 0.

questions.q: In a linearizable system, if one read returns the new value, all ____ reads must also return the new value.
questions.explain: After any one read has returned the new value, all following reads, from the same client or others, must return it too.
questions.rule: No going back after a read has seen the new value.

questions.q: A feature flag changes from off to on. Service X reads on, then service Y starts its own read afterwards. What follows?
questions.explain: The constraint applies across clients, and it does not wait for the writer to learn that its write completed.
questions.rule: Later reads follow earlier reads, whoever makes them.
options: Y may read off, because the update has not been confirmed yet
