Y may read either, because X and Y are different clients
Y must read on, even if the flag update is still being confirmed
Y must read off until the update has been confirmed to its writer
optionExplain: Confirmation to the writer is not required; X already saw on, so a later read cannot see off.
Different clients do not matter, since the constraint covers reads from other clients too.
Right: Y started after X finished, so the flag cannot appear to switch back.
This reverses the rule, forcing the old value after the new one has been seen.

questions.q: True or false: Client A reads the new value from replica 1; afterwards client B reads the old value from replica 2. This is allowed.
questions.explain: B started after A finished and would return an older value than A saw. The system has to rule this out.
questions.rule: Do not let a later read go back in time.

questions.q: In a linearizable system, when does the value of the register change from the old to the new one?
questions.explain: The flip is atomic: before it, reads see the old value; after it, every read sees the new one.
questions.rule: One atomic flip point inside the write.
questions.teaches: In a linearizable system we imagine some point in time, between the start and end of the write, at which the value atomically flips from the old to the new value.
options: Gradually, replica by replica, while the write is running
Only at the moment the writer receives its response
At the moment the first replica applies the write locally
Atomically, at one point between the start and the end of the write
optionExplain: A gradual change is what a replicated system does internally, but the guarantee hides it.
The response may arrive later than the flip, so the writer's reply is not the instant.
A single replica applying the write is an internal event, not the flip point seen by clients.
Right: we imagine a single instant inside the write at which the value flips.

questions.q: Writer C's request is slow to return, but reader A already read 1. Reader B starts afterwards. What must B read?
questions.explain: Visibility follows the flip point, not the writer's acknowledgement.
questions.rule: Reads may reveal a write before its writer is told.
questions.teaches: If one client's read returns the new value, all subsequent reads must also return it even if the write operation has not yet completed.
options: 0, since C has not been told that the write succeeded
Either value, since the write is not complete
An error, until the write is complete for everyone
1, even though C's write operation has not completed yet
optionExplain: The writer's confirmation is not what decides visibility. The right answer is: 1, even though C's write operation has not completed yet.
Either value is allowed only before any read has returned the new one.
The system must still answer reads in a way that fits one timeline.
Right: once A read the new value, later reads must follow, whether or not the write has finished.

questions.q: Which description matches a check that an execution came from a single copy of the data?
questions.explain: Each operation must fit at one instant, and the instants must be consistent with the results. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: One point per operation, moving forward only.
options: Compare every replica's clock with a global clock
Pick a point inside each request's interval so the points form a valid forward sequence
Check that all requests were answered within one round trip
Confirm that the number of writes equals the number of reads
optionExplain: Clocks do not need to be compared; the check uses only request and response times.
Right: this is the intuition behind linearizability. Remember: One point per operation, moving forward only.
Speed of response is not part of the correctness condition.
Counting operations says nothing about their order or results.

questions.q: In a linearizable execution, the line joining the operation markers must move forward in time and may not go ____.
questions.explain: The lines joining the markers may only move forward in time, from left to right, never backward.

questions.q: A reads x=5 at 1 to 2 s, B reads x=3 at 3 to 4 s, and no write overlaps. Is this linearizable?
questions.explain: A later read can return a different value only if some write has taken effect in between.
questions.rule: Every change in value needs a write to explain it.
options: No, unless a write of 3 took effect between the two reads
Yes, because both reads came from the same register
Yes, because the two reads did not overlap in time
No, because a register may only hold one value ever
optionExplain: Right: the second read is later, so the value had to change in between, and no write explains it.
Being the same register does not explain why the value changed back.
Non-overlap fixes the order; it does not make any pair of results valid.
Registers can be overwritten many times; the question is whether a write is available to explain the change.

questions.q: True or false: Reader B overlaps a write of x from 2 to 4, after reader A had already read 4. B may return 2.
questions.explain: A's read finished before B's began, so B may not see an older value than A did. B must read 4.
questions.rule: A finished read sets a floor for later reads.

questions.q: Reader A has already read 4. Reader B starts a read that overlaps the write of 4. Which result is not allowed for B?
questions.explain: Overlap with a write normally allows the old value, but A's earlier read of the new value removes that option.
questions.rule: Overlap is no excuse after a read has seen the new value.
questions.teaches: A read that is concurrent with a compare-and-set update from 2 to 4 may normally return 2, but not if another client has already read 4 before that read started.
options: 4, the value A read earlier
2, the older value, because A already read 4
A later value written by a third client
No result is ruled out, as B overlaps the write
optionExplain: 4 fits the timeline and is allowed. The right answer is: 2, the older value, because A already read 4.
Right: B overlaps the write, but A's earlier read of 4 rules out the old value.
A later value is allowed if another write was processed in the meantime.
Overlap with the write does not free B from the constraint set by A's read.

questions.q: The joined markers must form a valid sequence of register operations. Which rule do the reads in that sequence obey?
questions.explain: A register keeps the last value written, so a read sees whatever the latest write before its marker stored.
questions.rule: Reads return the latest preceding write in the sequence.
questions.teaches: The sequence of markers must also be a valid sequence of reads and writes for a register: every read must return the value set by the most recent write.
options: Each read returns the value that was written first in the sequence
Each read returns the value set by the most recent write before it
Each read returns the average of the recent writes
Each read returns the value from its own client's last write
optionExplain: The first write in the sequence would be overwritten by later ones.
Right: this is what makes the sequence valid for a register.
A register holds one value; averages do not apply.
A client may see other clients' writes; only its own last write would be wrong.

questions.q: Reader B sends a read first, then two writes (0, then 1) are sent. B's read returns 1. Is that acceptable?
questions.explain: A read that was delayed in the network may be processed after the writes. The card next shows why.
options: No, because B sent its request first
Yes, if all three requests overlap in time
No, because a read must return the first value written
Yes, but only if B's read reached the database before the writes
optionExplain: Send order does not decide processing order when requests overlap.
Right: concurrent requests can be processed in any order, so B's read may have arrived late.
No such rule exists for registers; a read sees the most recent write in the sequence.
That condition would make B read the old value, so it cannot explain a read of 1.

questions.q: Requests whose intervals overlap in time are called ____, so they may be processed in either order.
questions.explain: Overlapping requests are concurrent, so any order that gives valid results is acceptable.

questions.q: Request 1 runs 0 to 6 ms and Request 2 runs 5 to 9 ms. The database handled 2 before 1. Why is that acceptable?
questions.explain: Two requests can be ordered either way only if their intervals overlap.
questions.rule: Check overlap before accepting a reordering.
options: The two overlap, so either order fits their intervals
Requests may be reordered whenever they target different clients
Requests with longer intervals are always processed last
The database may process any requests in any order
optionExplain: Right: overlap between 5 and 6 ms leaves the order open.
Clients do not decide this; overlap in time does.
Duration does not set an order; only the intervals' overlap matters.
Non-overlapping requests have a fixed order, so this goes too far.

questions.q: True or false: A request that begins after another request has finished can be processed before it, if the network was slow.
questions.explain: If the second request began after the first one's response, it was necessarily processed after it. Only overlapping requests can be reordered.
questions.rule: Real-time order of non-overlapping requests is fixed.

questions.q: B reads 1 before A gets the ok for writing 1. Does this mean the value was read before it was written?
questions.explain: A response arrives after the operation took effect, so another client can see the value before the writer hears ok.
questions.teaches: A read can return a value before the writer has received its ok response; this does not mean the value was read before it was written, only that the ok was delayed in the network.
options: Yes, so the system is not linearizable
No, the ok response may have been delayed in the network
Yes, but only if the write was a compare-and-set
No, because reads are processed after all writes
optionExplain: The write could have taken effect first; only the response reached A late.
Right: the write took effect inside its interval; only the ok was slow to arrive.
The kind of write does not change the reasoning about timing.
Reads can be processed between writes, so this is not a general rule.

questions.q: A monitoring client sent its read before a deploy marker was written, yet its read shows the marker. What explains this?
questions.explain: The processing order can differ from the sending order when requests overlap.
questions.rule: A late arrival explains an apparent reading of the future.
questions.teaches: A request sent earlier may reach the database after later-sent requests because of network delay, so the database may legitimately process the three concurrent requests in an order different from the sending order.
options: The system is not linearizable, because reads cannot see later writes
The read arrived late, so the database processed it after the marker
The marker was written before the client sent anything
Clients can see the future in distributed databases
optionExplain: Overlapping requests can be processed in any order, so this is not a violation.
Right: if the intervals overlap, the read may have been processed after the write.
That contradicts the statement that the read was sent before the marker was written.
Nothing is seen from the future; the read was simply processed late.

questions.q: Two clients read x as 0, then both try to set it to 1. How can the second one be told it is too late?
questions.explain: The second cas finds that x is no longer 0 and fails with an error. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Compare the current value with the expected one, atomically.
options: Each write is a compare-and-set that expects the value 0
The database delays the second write until later
Each client must send its reads to the same replica
The second client's clock is behind the first one's
optionExplain: Right: after the first succeeds, x is no longer 0, so the second compare fails.
Delay does not tell the client anything has changed.
A shared replica would not stop the second write from overwriting the first.
Clock order does not help; the check relies on the stored value.

questions.q: A compare-and-set sets x to the new value only if x currently equals the ____ value.
questions.explain: cas(x, old, new): if x equals old, it becomes new; otherwise nothing changes and an error is returned.
questions.rule: cas succeeds only if the expected value is still there.

questions.q: Two ticket agents each try cas(seat, free, mine). The first succeeds. What happens to the second agent's request?
questions.explain: The check and the update happen atomically, so only one claimant can win.
questions.rule: Atomic check-and-update lets only one claim win.
options: It succeeds and replaces the first agent's value
It fails with an error, since the seat is no longer free
It waits until the first agent releases the seat
It succeeds only if it was sent after the first one
optionExplain: Replacing would defeat the point of the comparison. The right answer is: It fails with an error, since the seat is no longer free.
Right: the seat holds the first agent's claim, so the comparison fails.
cas does not wait; it compares and answers at once.
Order of sending matters less than the state when the database processes it.

questions.q: True or false: The register model of linearizability guarantees that nobody else changes a value between two reads by the same client.
questions.explain: The model assumes no transaction isolation. Another client may change a value at any time, for example one client may read 1 and then 2.

questions.q: In the book's example, several cas requests arrive for a register that holds 0. Which outcome fits?
questions.explain: The book shows cas requests from B and C succeeding but D's failing, because x was no longer 0 when D's was processed.
questions.rule: cas compares against the value at processing time.
questions.teaches: In the book's example, B's and C's cas requests succeed but D's cas request fails, because by the time the database processes it the value of x is no longer 0.
options: One succeeds; one fails because the value is no longer 0
All succeed, since each saw 0 when it was sent
All fail, since the requests are concurrent
They succeed in the order that they were sent
optionExplain: Right: by the time the later one is processed, the value has changed.
A cas compares at processing time, not at sending time.
Concurrent cas requests can succeed; only those finding the wrong value fail.
Order of sending does not fix the order of processing for overlapping requests.

questions.q: A team wants a linearizable compare-and-set on a leaderless store using quorum reads and writes. What does the book say?
questions.explain: Even a quorum scheme made linearizable for reads and writes cannot implement cas without consensus.
questions.rule: Atomic cas is a consensus-strength operation.
questions.teaches: Only linearizable read and write operations can be implemented with Dynamo-style quorums; a linearizable compare-and-set cannot, because it requires a consensus algorithm.
options: Quorums can give linearizable reads and writes, not cas, which needs consensus
Quorums give a linearizable cas if w + r > n
Quorums give cas only with last-write-wins timestamps
Quorums give cas if the clocks are synchronised
optionExplain: Right: a linearizable compare-and-set requires a consensus algorithm. Remember: Atomic cas is a consensus-strength operation.
w + r > n does not turn a quorum read-write into a cas.
Last-write-wins is the weak point: it is not linearizable.
Clock synchronisation does not give atomic agreement on a value.

questions.q: How could you check that a database behaved as one copy during a test run?
questions.explain: The test needs times as well as results. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Timings plus results can be checked for a valid order.
options: Record all requests and responses with timings and look for a valid order
Compare the sizes of the replicas after the test
Check that every request received an ok response
Count how many reads returned the same value
optionExplain: Right: the arrangement of recorded intervals into a valid sequence is the test.
Sizes may match while reads returned stale values. The right answer is: Record all requests and responses with timings and look for a valid order.
Receiving ok does not tell whether the reads returned the right value.
Counts of equal values say nothing about their timing.

questions.q: To test linearizability you record the ____ of all requests and responses and look for a valid sequential order.
questions.explain: The book describes recording the timings of all requests and responses and checking whether they can be arranged into a valid sequential order.
questions.rule: Record timings, then look for a valid order.

questions.q: A test harness logs only the results of each read and write, with no timestamps. Why is that log unusable for the check?
questions.explain: Linearizability constrains orders by real time, so the recorded timings are part of the evidence.
questions.rule: No timings, no real-time constraint to test.
options: Results are not needed to decide linearizability
Timing decides which operations overlap and so which orders are allowed
Timestamps are only used to find the slowest replica
The check needs the internal state of each replica
optionExplain: Results are essential too; they are what must be explained by the order.
Right: without request and response times, the allowed orders cannot be determined.
Timestamps define the real-time order that the guarantee depends on.
The test uses only what clients see, not the replicas' internals.

questions.q: True or false: If a recorded run passes the check, the system will be linearizable in every later run.
questions.explain: The check examines one recorded execution. Other timings and faults could produce a run that cannot be explained.
questions.rule: A passing test shows the run was explicable, not that the system is always linearizable.

questions.q: A vendor says its single-leader database is linearizable because it has a leader. What does the book add?
questions.explain: A design with a leader suggests linearizability but does not prove it, which is why testing is valuable.
questions.rule: A leader is a hint, not a proof.
questions.teaches: Not every single-leader database is actually linearizable, either by design (for example because it uses snapshot isolation) or due to concurrency bugs.
options: Not every single-leader database is, by design or because of concurrency bugs
Single-leader databases are linearizable only for writes
Leaders make every read stale
Linearizability needs at least three leaders
optionExplain: Right: for example snapshot isolation by design, or concurrency bugs.
Writes via the leader are not the only thing at stake; the problem is reads and bugs.
Reads from the leader can be linearizable; they are not stale by rule.
Multiple leaders make linearizability harder, not required. The right answer is: Not every single-leader database is, by design or because of concurrency bugs.

questions.q: Why would a team run the linearizability check on a sampled test run rather than on all production traffic?
questions.explain: Checking whether many timed operations fit one valid sequence takes a lot of computation, so it is applied selectively.
questions.rule: The check is possible but costly, so scope it.
questions.teaches: Testing whether a system's behavior is linearizable is possible, but it is computationally expensive.
options: The check is computationally expensive on large recorded histories
Production requests carry no timing information to record
Linearizability only applies to test environments
Sampled runs are guaranteed to expose every violation
optionExplain: Right: the book calls the check possible but computationally expensive.
Requests and responses can be timed in production as well, so this is not the reason.
The guarantee applies wherever the system runs, not only in tests.
A sample can miss violations; that is the price of keeping the cost down.

questions.q: A system promises that transactions behave as if run one at a time. Does it also promise that reads are up to date?
questions.explain: Serializability and recency are different guarantees. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Order of transactions is not the same as freshness.
options: No, those are two separate guarantees
Yes, serial order means reads see the latest write
Yes, but only for single-object transactions
No, because transactions never read at all
optionExplain: Right: serial order says nothing about whether a read is recent.
The serial order may differ from the order the transactions actually ran.
Single-object transactions are still not covered by a recency promise.
Transactions do read and write; they simply are not required to be recent.

questions.q: Match each guarantee with what it is about.
questions.explain: Serializability deals with multi-object transactions; linearizability with the recency of one object.
questions.rule: Serializability: transactions. Linearizability: recency of one object.
pairs: Transactions behave as if executed in some serial order
Recency of reads and writes on an individual object
Not prevented by linearizability on its own
The individual object a linearizable system treats as one copy

questions.q: Two doctors each check that someone else is on call and then go off call in separate transactions. Which guarantee would prevent this?
questions.explain: Write skew spans several objects and transactions, which is the territory of serializability.
options: Linearizability, which keeps each object up to date
Serializability, which orders whole transactions
Eventual consistency, which converges later
Sloppy quorums, which accept writes anywhere
optionExplain: Linearizability treats each object separately and does not prevent write skew by itself.
Right: write skew is a transaction anomaly that serializable isolation prevents.
Convergence later does not stop two transactions from violating the rule now.
Sloppy quorums relax guarantees, not tighten them. The right answer is: Serializability, which orders whole transactions.

questions.q: A design review says: reads are fresh, so transactions must be serializable. Which statement exposes the flaw?
questions.explain: Linearizability does not group operations into transactions, so it does not by itself prevent write skew.
questions.rule: Do not infer one guarantee from the other.
options: Fresh reads imply that the database has one replica
Fresh reads on single objects do not stop write skew
Serializability only exists in single-node databases
Transactions cannot be combined with fresh reads
optionExplain: Fresh reads can be provided over many replicas. The right answer is: Fresh reads on single objects do not stop write skew.
Right: recency on individual objects leaves multi-object anomalies open.
Serializability exists in distributed databases as well. The right answer is: Fresh reads on single objects do not stop write skew.
A database can offer both guarantees together. The right answer is: Fresh reads on single objects do not stop write skew.

questions.q: True or false: Under serializability, the serial order that the transactions appear to follow must be the order in which they actually ran.
questions.explain: It is fine for the equivalent serial order to differ from the order in which the transactions were actually run.
questions.rule: Serializability fixes a serial order, not the real-time order.
questions.teaches: Serializability allows the equivalent serial order to differ from the order in which transactions actually ran, which is why it does not by itself give recency.

questions.q: A team uses linearizable storage and also needs to avoid write skew between two objects. What does the book suggest?
questions.explain: Because linearizability is per object, extra steps are needed to protect constraints that span objects.
questions.rule: Add transaction-level measures for multi-object invariants.
questions.teaches: Linearizability does not prevent write skew unless additional measures are taken, such as materializing conflicts.
options: Take additional measures, such as materializing conflicts
Nothing: a linearizable store already prevents write skew
Switch to eventual consistency
Add a second replica to each object
optionExplain: Right: the book mentions materializing conflicts as such a measure.
Linearizability does not prevent write skew on its own.
Eventual consistency is weaker and prevents nothing here. The right answer is: Take additional measures, such as materializing conflicts.
Replicas do not group operations across objects. The right answer is: Take additional measures, such as materializing conflicts.

questions.q: A database gives serializable transactions and up-to-date reads together. What is that combination called?
questions.explain: Combining the two guarantees gives strict serializability. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Serializable plus linearizable is strict serializability.
options: Eventual consistency, which converges once writes stop
Read committed, which hides uncommitted writes
Strict serializability, or strong one-copy serializability
Causal consistency, which keeps related events in order
optionExplain: Eventual consistency is far weaker and promises neither of the two guarantees.
Read committed is a weak isolation level and promises neither recency nor serial order.
Right: both guarantees together carry this name. Remember: Serializable plus linearizable is strict serializability.
Causal consistency orders related events but promises neither serial order nor recency.

questions.q: A database that is both serializable and linearizable is said to offer ____ serializability.
questions.explain: The combination is known as strict serializability or strong one-copy serializability (strong-1SR).

questions.q: A reporting database uses serializable snapshot isolation so that long reads do not block writers. Which guarantee does it give up?
questions.explain: A snapshot deliberately leaves out newer writes, so its reads cannot be the most recent ones.
questions.rule: Snapshot reads are consistent but not necessarily latest.
options: Serializability: snapshots cannot detect conflicts
Durability: snapshots are kept only in memory
Atomicity: snapshots expose half-applied transactions
Linearizability: snapshot reads can miss newer writes
optionExplain: Serializable snapshot isolation does provide serializability, so this gets the design wrong.
Durability has nothing to do with whether the snapshot is current.
Snapshots show consistent states, not half-applied transactions. The right answer is: Linearizability: snapshot reads can miss newer writes.
Right: a snapshot by design excludes writes more recent than the snapshot.

questions.q: True or false: A database with serializable snapshot isolation is therefore also linearizable.
questions.explain: Reads come from a consistent snapshot that leaves out writes more recent than it, so they are not linearizable.

questions.q: Which serializable implementations are typically linearizable as well, according to the book?
questions.explain: Implementations that lock or run transactions in a literal serial order tend to see the latest data.
questions.rule: Locking and serial execution are typically linearizable.
questions.teaches: Implementations of serializability based on two-phase locking or actual serial execution are typically linearizable, unlike serializable snapshot isolation.
options: Serializable snapshot isolation and read committed
Multi-leader replication and last write wins
Two-phase locking and actual serial execution
Sloppy quorums and hinted handoff
optionExplain: Serializable snapshot isolation reads from a snapshot and so is not linearizable.
Multi-leader replication is generally not linearizable, so this pair fails.
Right: lock-based and literally serial designs see the latest data, so they are typically linearizable.
Sloppy quorums rule out linearizability, so they cannot be on the list.

questions.q: An exchange needs transactions that appear serial and reads that are not older than the last committed trade. Which choice fits the book?
questions.explain: Check the implementation behind the isolation label, not just the label.
questions.rule: Look at how serializability is implemented.
questions.teaches: Whether a serializable database is also linearizable depends on its implementation: the same label can come with or without recency, so one has to check how it is built.
options: Snapshot-based serializability, which gives the latest data by design
Eventual consistency with a short lag, which gives strict serializability
Lock-based or serial-execution serializability, which is typically linearizable
Snapshot isolation, which is serializable and linearizable together
optionExplain: Snapshot reads exclude newer writes by design, so the latest data is not given.
A short lag is still a lag, and eventual consistency promises neither guarantee.
Right: these designs are typically linearizable, giving strict serializability.
Snapshot isolation is not serializable in general and is not linearizable either.

questions.q: Several nodes start up together and race for a lock to pick a leader. What must be true of the lock?
questions.explain: A lock is useless unless every node agrees who owns it. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Agreement on the owner is what makes a lock work.
options: It must be held by the node with the fastest clock
All nodes must agree on which node holds it
It must be released after a fixed number of seconds
It must live on the node that starts first
optionExplain: Clock speed does not decide who the lock belongs to.
Right: if nodes can disagree about the owner, there may be two leaders.
Expiry may be useful, but it does not by itself guarantee a single owner.
The first node to start may be the one that fails.

questions.q: If two nodes both believe they are the leader, the situation is called split ____.
questions.explain: Split brain, two nodes both believing they lead, often leads to data loss.

questions.q: One of five scheduler hosts must act at a time, and the owner is stored in a store with stale replicas. What can go wrong?
questions.explain: A stale view of the lock lets two hosts both claim it, which is split brain in a scheduler.
questions.rule: A lock on stale data is not a lock.
options: Two hosts may each read that no one holds the lock
The lock may be acquired more slowly than needed
Five hosts may be too many for one lock to handle
The store may spend too much disk on lock records
optionExplain: Right: stale reads can let two nodes both think the lock is free.
Speed is a secondary concern; correctness is the issue here.
The number of hosts does not cause the problem; staleness does.
Storage cost is a distraction from the real problem.

questions.q: True or false: A lock implemented on an eventually consistent store would still reliably elect a single leader if the store converges within seconds.
questions.explain: Until convergence, different nodes may see different owners, so two may believe they hold the lock.
questions.rule: Eventual convergence is not enough for mutual exclusion.

questions.q: Why do some databases such as Oracle RAC put dedicated network links between their nodes?
questions.explain: When locks are taken for each page access, their speed bounds transaction speed, so a dedicated interconnect helps.
questions.rule: Fine-grained linearizable locks need fast links.
questions.teaches: Oracle RAC uses a lock per disk page, with multiple nodes sharing access to the same disk storage; since these linearizable locks are on the critical path of transaction execution, deployments usually have a dedicated cluster interconnect network.
options: Replication lag needs to be hidden from the clients
Linearizable per-page locks sit on the critical path of transactions
Clock skew between the nodes needs to be removed
Page locks are cheap and are only needed rarely
optionExplain: The network is not there to hide lag from clients.
Right: RAC uses a lock per disk page, and these locks are on the critical path.
A dedicated network does not remove clock skew. The right answer is: Linearizable per-page locks sit on the critical path of transactions.
The locks are frequent, which is why the network is dedicated.

questions.q: A team implements leader election with a correct linearizable lock. What remains to get right, according to the book?
questions.explain: Fencing and other details are needed on top of the linearizable lock.
questions.rule: A correct lock is a foundation, not the whole answer.
questions.teaches: There are still many subtle details in implementing locks and leader election correctly, such as the fencing issue, and libraries like Apache Curator help by providing higher-level recipes on top of ZooKeeper.
options: Nothing: linearizability alone makes locks correct
Subtle details, such as fencing, which libraries help with
Only the choice of a faster clock
Only the number of nodes in the cluster
optionExplain: A linearizable lock is the foundation, not the whole solution.
Right: there are many subtle details, and libraries such as Curator provide recipes.
Clock speed does not address the remaining problems. The right answer is: Subtle details, such as fencing, which libraries help with.
Cluster size is not the remaining issue. The right answer is: Subtle details, such as fencing, which libraries help with.

questions.q: Which kind of service is commonly used to implement distributed locks and leader election?
questions.explain: Coordination services such as ZooKeeper and etcd are built for this purpose. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Use a consensus-based service for locks.
options: A cache with a short time to live for every entry
A message queue that holds the lock requests
A coordination service built on consensus, such as ZooKeeper
A search index of all the nodes in the cluster
optionExplain: Expiring cache entries do not give agreement among nodes about who holds a lock.
A queue orders messages but does not by itself decide a single owner fault-tolerantly.
Right: these services use consensus to give linearizable operations.
An index lists nodes but does not decide who holds the lock.

questions.q: Match each name with its role in coordination.
questions.explain: ZooKeeper and etcd rely on consensus; Curator adds recipes on the client side.
questions.rule: Services give the base; libraries give recipes.
pairs: Coordination service used for locks and leader election
Library with higher-level recipes on top of ZooKeeper

questions.q: A client writes a value to etcd and another reads it from a follower by default. What may the reader get?
questions.explain: Linearizable writes do not make default reads linearizable.
questions.rule: Ask for a linearizable read when you need one.
options: Always the latest value, since all etcd operations are linearizable
An error, because followers refuse reads
The latest value, but only after a long delay
A stale value, because default reads can be served by any replica
optionExplain: The default read is not guaranteed to be the latest.
Followers do serve reads; the issue is their freshness.
No delay is promised; the default read may simply be stale.
Right: writes are linearizable, but reads are not by default.

questions.q: True or false: Everything ZooKeeper and etcd do, including every default read, is linearizable.
questions.explain: Strictly speaking they provide linearizable writes, while reads may be stale by default because any replica can serve them.
questions.rule: Check what the default read gives you.

questions.q: How can a client of etcd or ZooKeeper ask for an up-to-date read?
questions.explain: Both services offer a way to make a read linearizable, at extra cost.
questions.teaches: etcd calls a linearizable read a quorum read, and in ZooKeeper you need to call sync() before the read to make it linearizable.
options: Both require reading from the oldest follower
Both require the client to supply a synchronised timestamp
etcd offers a quorum read, and ZooKeeper needs a sync() call before the read
Both require the client to read twice and compare
optionExplain: Oldest followers are the most likely to be stale.
Timestamps from the client do not give a linearizable read.
Right: these are the options named in the book.
Reading twice may return the same stale value twice, so it does not guarantee freshness.

questions.q: A team stores a feature flag in ZooKeeper and a worker reads it with no extra call. Which risk remains?
questions.explain: The linearizable write does not make a default read linearizable.
questions.rule: Know which operations in a service are linearizable.
questions.teaches: Because ZooKeeper and etcd serve reads from any replica by default, an application that needs the latest value must request a linearizable read rather than assume it.
options: The flag may be changed by two clients at the same moment
The flag may be lost, since ZooKeeper does not store data
The worker may see an old flag value from a lagging replica
The write of the flag may be seen out of order by writers
optionExplain: Concurrent writes are ordered by consensus, so this is not the risk.
ZooKeeper stores data durably, so loss is not the risk here.
Right: writes are linearizable but a default read may be stale.
Writes are linearizable, so writers do not see them out of order.

questions.q: Two shoppers register with the same email address at the same moment, on different replicas. What must the system do?
questions.explain: Exactly one claim may succeed, and every node must agree which. The card next shows why.
options: Accept one registration and return an error to the other
Accept both and merge the accounts later on
Accept the one whose request carries the earlier clock time
Reject both and ask the shoppers to try again
optionExplain: Right: a hard uniqueness rule lets exactly one claim succeed.
Merging accepts a duplicate that the rule forbids, even if it is repaired later.
Clock time on separate machines can be wrong, so it cannot settle who was first.
Rejecting both is safe but unnecessary; one of them can succeed.

questions.q: To enforce uniqueness as data is written, such as a username, you need ____.
questions.explain: The chapter says that if you want to enforce the constraint as the data is written, you need linearizability.
questions.rule: Hard uniqueness at write time needs linearizability.

questions.q: Two devices create report.txt in the same folder at the same moment. Which design lets exactly one create succeed?
questions.explain: The check for the path and its creation must be a single decision made on the up-to-date state.
questions.rule: Check and claim against one agreed state.
options: Each device checks its own replica and then creates
A linearizable check-and-create on the full path
Each replica appends a number to a duplicate name later
Both creates succeed and the newest file wins
optionExplain: Both replicas may see the path as free, so both creates succeed.
Right: the check and create happen against one agreed state.
Renaming later keeps both files, which breaks the rule that only one may exist.
Letting the newest win silently discards one create instead of returning an error.

questions.q: True or false: If each replica checks only its own copy before accepting a username, two concurrent registrations for the same name can both succeed.
questions.explain: Each replica can see the name as free, so both accept it. Only an agreed, up-to-date view prevents this.
questions.rule: Local checks cannot enforce a global rule.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of the same constraint in a file storage service?
questions.explain: The rule has the same shape as usernames: two concurrent creators of one name must not both succeed.
questions.rule: Any must-be-unique key has this shape.
questions.teaches: In a file storage service there cannot be two files with the same path and filename, which is another uniqueness constraint that needs linearizability if enforced as the data is written.
options: No two files may have the same path and filename
Each file must be copied to three replicas
Each file must be smaller than a set size
Each file must be readable by its owner
optionExplain: Right: the book names this alongside usernames as a uniqueness constraint.
Replica counts concern durability, not a rule that needs one agreed answer.
A size limit can be checked on the file itself, with no agreement among nodes.
Permissions concern access, not a conflict between concurrent creators.

questions.q: A ticketing site lets fans claim a handle. Which analogy best captures what claiming a handle needs?
questions.explain: Registering a name behaves like acquiring a lock on it, with all the agreement a linearizable lock needs.
questions.rule: A unique name is a lock on that name.
questions.teaches: When a user registers for a service, you can think of them as acquiring a lock on their chosen username, which is why the operation resembles a linearizable lock.
options: Acquiring a lock on the chosen handle
Appending a note to a shared diary
Voting on the handle among all fans
Reserving a block of numbers in advance
optionExplain: Right: registering is like acquiring a lock on the name, so it must be linearizable.
A diary records events; it does not decide a single winner.
A vote involves many parties and does not describe one claim on one name.
Reserving number blocks is a sequence-number technique, not a claim on a name.

questions.q: Many users try to claim the same name at the same moment. Which operation makes exactly one succeed?
questions.explain: An atomic conditional set decides the winner at once. The card next shows why.
options: A blind overwrite that records the latest claimant
A read of the name followed by a separate write
An append of every claim to a list, resolved at the end
An atomic set that works if the name is unclaimed
optionExplain: Overwriting makes the last claimant win, with no error for anyone.
Read then write leaves a gap, in which another claimant can slip in.
Waiting for resolution at the end delays the answer the user needs now.
Right: the check and the set are one atomic step.

questions.q: A username claim resembles an atomic compare-and-____.
questions.explain: The operation is very similar to an atomic compare-and-set, setting the username to the user's ID provided it is not taken.

questions.q: A seat map stores seat 12A as free. Two travellers press book at once. What should the booking do?
questions.explain: The seat is a key claimed once, so the claim must be conditional on it being free.
questions.rule: Make the claim conditional on the key being unclaimed.
options: Set 12A to the ID of whoever pressed last
Read 12A, then write it if the page shows free
Set 12A to the traveller's ID only if it is still free
Hold the seat for both until they pay
optionExplain: Last press wins would silently overwrite the first booking.
The page can be stale and the gap between read and write lets both through.
Right: conditional set, so only one claim can succeed.
Holding it twice is a double booking, which is the problem to avoid.

questions.q: True or false: With a linearizable register per username, initially null, concurrent claims for the same name can all succeed.
questions.explain: Only one compare-and-set from null to an account ID succeeds. The others find a value other than null.
questions.rule: Only the first conditional set wins.

questions.q: How could you model usernames so that each claim is one compare-and-set?
questions.explain: One register per name gives each name its own compare-and-set, so claims for the same name meet in one place.
questions.rule: One register per name; null means free.
questions.teaches: Imagine a linearizable register with an atomic compare-and-set for every possible username, each initially null (name not taken); a claim sets it from null to the user account ID.
options: One register per user, starting with their list of names
One register for all usernames, holding a list
One register per replica, merged each hour
One linearizable register per username, starting as null
optionExplain: This keys by user, so two users claiming one name would not meet in one place.
One list register forces all claims through a single value, and each claim must rewrite the list.
Per-replica registers merged later cannot decide a winner at once.
Right: a claim sets the register from null to the user's ID.

questions.q: A payments app stops two terminals from using one voucher code. Which approach follows the same pattern?
questions.explain: A key that can be used once is a register with a conditional set.
questions.teaches: If multiple users try to grab the same name concurrently, only one of the compare-and-set operations succeeds, because the others see a value other than null, which is due to linearizability.
options: Each terminal keeps a local list of used codes
Terminals report used codes at the end of the day
The server accepts the first request by clock time
A register per code, set to the terminal ID if unused
optionExplain: Local lists cannot see another terminal's use of the code.
End-of-day reports allow double spending in between. The right answer is: A register per code, set to the terminal ID if unused.
Clock time is unreliable across machines, so it cannot name the first.
Right: one conditional set decides which terminal wins. Remember: One-time keys use conditional sets.

questions.q: Two checkout servers each sell the last unit in stock at the same moment. What went wrong?
questions.explain: Both servers acted on a view in which the unit was still available. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A limit needs a shared, current value.
options: They sold the unit too quickly for the warehouse
They did not agree on one up-to-date stock value
They used an unsuitable currency for the order
They stored the stock level on too many disks
optionExplain: Speed alone is not the problem; stale information is.
Right: both acted on a stale view of the stock level.
Currency is unrelated to who sees the stock level.
Disk count affects durability, not agreement. The right answer is: They did not agree on one up-to-date stock value.

questions.q: Match each constraint with the single value that all nodes must agree on.
questions.explain: The book names balance, stock level and seat occupancy as the single up-to-date values these constraints need.
questions.rule: Find the one value the rule depends on.

questions.q: A ride-sharing app must give each driver only one active ride. Two dispatchers assign rides at the same moment. What do they need?
questions.explain: Like seat occupancy, the driver's assignment is a single value that concurrent writers must not both change.
questions.rule: One scarce resource, one agreed value.
options: One agreed record of the driver's current ride
A faster network between the two dispatchers
A larger number of drivers available in the area
A timestamp on each assignment sent to the driver
optionExplain: Right: the rule limits one value, the driver's assignment, so both dispatchers need the same current view.
Speed reduces the window but does not remove the race.
More drivers do not make two assignments to one driver consistent.
A timestamp on a message does not stop two assignments being accepted.

questions.q: True or false: Linearizability is needed for any rule in an application, including rules that span several unrelated values.
questions.explain: The book ties these rules to a single up-to-date value, and linearizability is a guarantee on individual objects.
questions.rule: Linearizability covers one object at a time.

questions.q: In the seat-booking example, which ordinary business remedy shows the constraint need not be strict?
questions.explain: A flight can be overbooked and the problem repaired afterwards by moving passengers and compensating them.
questions.rule: Some limits can be repaired after the fact.
questions.teaches: In real applications it is sometimes acceptable to treat such constraints loosely; if a flight is overbooked, customers can be moved to a different flight and offered compensation.
options: Asking all customers to arrive three hours early
Rebooking passengers and compensating them
Adding a duplicate seat map to each ticket office
Selling seats only once the flight has departed
optionExplain: Arrival times do not repair an overbooked flight. The right answer is: Rebooking passengers and compensating them.
Right: overbooking is repaired with a different flight and compensation.
Duplicating seat maps would increase the chance of disagreement.
Selling after departure defeats the purpose of booking. The right answer is: Rebooking passengers and compensating them.

questions.q: A metrics service has a cap of 100 alert rules per team. Occasionally a team ends up with 101. What follows from the book's view?
questions.explain: Whether the limit is hard or loose decides whether linearizability is worth its cost.
questions.rule: Ask how bad a violation is and whether it can be repaired.
questions.teaches: Constraints that can be treated loosely, because a violation can be repaired afterwards, may not need linearizability; the book returns to such loosely interpreted constraints in the discussion of timeliness and integrity.
options: Linearizability is required in every case
It depends on whether 101 is harmful or can be repaired
Eventual consistency can never be used here
The cap should be removed since limits cannot be enforced
optionExplain: Requiring it in every case ignores that loose limits are common.
Right: decide by the cost of a violation and whether it can be repaired.
Eventual consistency can be fine when small overshoots are tolerable.
Limits can be enforced; the question is how strictly.

questions.q: Which database rule most directly requires linearizability?
questions.explain: Rules that must decide between concurrent writers need agreement; rules on one record do not. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Uniqueness needs agreement; row-local rules do not.
options: A foreign key from orders to customers
A check that every price is above zero
A default value filled in for a missing field
A uniqueness rule such as one account per email
optionExplain: Foreign keys can be implemented without it, according to the book.
An attribute check looks at the row being written and needs no agreement among nodes.
A default is applied locally and involves no conflict.
Right: concurrent creators of the same value must be decided against one agreed state.

questions.q: Sort each constraint by whether the book says it requires linearizability.
questions.explain: Hard uniqueness constraints require linearizability. Foreign key and attribute constraints can be implemented without it.

items.t: Hard uniqueness constraint
Foreign key constraint
Attribute constraint
Unique username enforced at write time

questions.q: A schema has a unique email column, a foreign key to countries and a not-null name. Which drives the choice of a linearizable store?
questions.explain: Of the three, only uniqueness needs concurrent writers to be decided against one agreed state.
questions.rule: Count which rules compare concurrent writers.
options: The foreign key to the country table
The not-null name column
The unique email column
All three equally
optionExplain: Foreign keys can be implemented without linearizability. The right answer is: The unique email column.
A not-null check looks at one value in one row.
Right: only the uniqueness rule needs a single agreed state.
The three rules differ in what they need, so they do not weigh equally.

questions.q: True or false: A designer says that because foreign keys are constraints, they need linearizability as much as uniqueness does.
questions.explain: The book says foreign key and attribute constraints can be implemented without requiring linearizability.
questions.rule: Not every constraint is a uniqueness constraint.

questions.q: Besides hard uniqueness, how does the book describe the constraints in flight booking that may be treated loosely?
questions.explain: A violation that can be repaired afterwards makes the constraint loose.
questions.teaches: The hard kind of uniqueness constraint is the one you typically find in relational databases, and it is the kind that requires linearizability.
options: They are enforced by the client application only
They are checked once a year by an administrator
They are kept in a separate database from the rest
Violations, like overbooking, can be repaired afterwards
optionExplain: Client-only enforcement is not the book's suggestion. The right answer is: Violations, like overbooking, can be repaired afterwards.
Annual checks are not mentioned. The right answer is: Violations, like overbooking, can be repaired afterwards.
A separate database does not make the rule looser.
Right: a loose reading lets the business fix a violation after it happens.

questions.q: A chat app wants one unique room name and also needs each message to reference an existing room. Which statement fits the book?
questions.explain: Uniqueness is a decision among concurrent writers; a reference check is not.
questions.rule: Split the rules and pay only where needed.
questions.teaches: Other kinds of constraints, such as foreign key or attribute constraints, can be implemented without requiring linearizability, which makes it worth separating them from uniqueness rules in a design.
options: Both rules need linearizability equally
Neither rule needs linearizability at all
The reference needs it; the room name does not
The room name does; the reference may not
optionExplain: Foreign-key-like rules can be implemented without it. The right answer is: The room name does; the reference may not.
The room name must be decided between concurrent creators.
This reverses the roles of the two rules. The right answer is: The room name does; the reference may not.
Right: uniqueness is the hard constraint; the reference is a foreign-key-like rule.

questions.q: A background job is told by a message that a record changed, then reads the record and sees the old version. What happened?
questions.explain: The message arrived before the data was available on the replica that served the read. The card next shows why.
options: The job read the record before the message was sent
The message path was faster than the replication of the data
The record was changed back by another job
The message was delivered twice by the broker
optionExplain: The job acted on the message, so the change had already happened.
Right: two channels raced, and the data channel lost.
Nothing says the record was reverted; the read was simply stale.
Duplicate delivery does not explain an old version being read.

questions.q: A stale read is noticed only because there is an additional communication ____ besides the database.
questions.explain: In the sports example the second channel was Alice's voice; without it Bob would not have noticed.
questions.rule: A second channel reveals the stale read.

questions.q: A chat server saves a message, then notifies the recipient's phone. The phone fetches from a lagging replica and finds nothing. Which paths raced?
questions.explain: The notification path and the data path both carry news of the same write, and the faster one won.
questions.rule: Look for two paths carrying news of one write.
options: The notification and the replication of the saved message
The sender's phone and the recipient's phone
The message text and its attachments
The login request and the logout request
optionExplain: Right: the notification outran the replication. Remember: Look for two paths carrying news of one write.
The phones are endpoints, not the two paths that carried the same news.
Text and attachments are parts of one message and not two channels.
Login and logout are unrelated to this race. The right answer is: The notification and the replication of the saved message.

questions.q: True or false: If nothing learns about a write except by reading the store, a stale read is more likely to go unnoticed.
questions.explain: Without a second channel, a stale reader just sees older data and refreshes later, like Bob would have done.
questions.rule: A stale read hurts when another channel exposes it.

questions.q: If you control the second channel, as with a message queue, what does the book say about alternatives to linearizability?
questions.explain: Owning the second channel lets you pass information along it, but that is extra design work.
questions.rule: Control of the channel enables alternatives.
questions.teaches: Linearizability is not the only way of avoiding the race, but it is the simplest to understand; if you control the additional channel you can use approaches similar to reading your own writes, at the cost of additional complexity.
options: None exist; linearizability is the only option
Other approaches exist, with the cost of additional complexity
Any queue makes linearizability unnecessary
You must replace the queue with a database
optionExplain: The book says linearizability is not the only way, only the simplest to understand.
Right: approaches like reading your own writes can be used, at the price of extra complexity.
A queue alone does not remove the race; it creates one.
Replacing the queue is not suggested. The right answer is: Other approaches exist, with the cost of additional complexity.

questions.q: A payments page redirects the customer to a receipt page, which reads from a replica and shows no payment. Which fix targets the race?
questions.explain: The customer's browser is the second channel; the read must be at least as recent as the payment write.
questions.rule: Make the read at least as recent as the write that triggered it.
questions.teaches: The redirect after a payment is a second communication channel just like Alice's voice, so the read behind it needs a recency guarantee such as reading your own writes.
options: Add a loading spinner to the receipt page while it waits
Read the receipt from the leader, which has the write
Send the customer a confirmation email as well
Cache the receipt page for a longer time
optionExplain: A spinner hides the problem but does not give a recent view.
Right: it gives the reader a view at least as recent as the write the customer just caused.
Another message adds a channel without fixing the lagging read.
Caching longer makes stale data last longer. The right answer is: Read the receipt from the leader, which has the write.

questions.q: A web server saves an upload, then queues a job to process it. The worker reads the upload and finds nothing. Why?
questions.explain: The worker was told about data that its replica did not yet hold. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A message can overtake the data it refers to.
options: The message arrived before the upload had replicated
The queue lost the message on its way
The worker process started before the web server did
Uploads are deleted a moment after the write
optionExplain: Right: the job outran the replication of the data.
If the queue lost the message, the worker would not have started.
Start order of processes is unrelated to the data being missing.
Nothing suggests that the data is deleted. The right answer is: The message arrived before the upload had replicated.

questions.q: Put the steps of the thumbnail pipeline in order.
questions.explain: The photo is written first and the instruction queued afterwards, so the resizer fetches the photo last.
questions.rule: Write the data, then send the message.
items: The user uploads a photo to the web server
The web server writes the photo to file storage
The web server puts a resize instruction on the queue
The resizer takes the instruction from the queue
The resizer fetches the photo from file storage

questions.q: A queue tells a worker to index a document, but a lagging store gives it the old version. What is the lasting effect?
questions.explain: The job completed successfully on stale input, so no step will correct the result.
questions.rule: A job on stale input leaves lasting damage.
options: The index is corrected on the next read of the document
The index and the document stay permanently inconsistent
The queue retries until the index matches
The document is rolled back to match the index
optionExplain: A read of the document does not trigger re-indexing.
Right: nothing makes the worker redo the job, so the old version stays indexed.
The queue believes the job succeeded, so it does not retry.
Documents are not rolled back to match derived data.

questions.q: True or false: With linearizable file storage, the resizer cannot see an older image version than the one the web server wrote.
questions.explain: A linearizable store makes the write visible to every read that starts after it completes, and the instruction is queued only after the write completed.

questions.q: Why does the web server not put the whole photo on the message queue?
questions.explain: Large payloads go to storage and small instructions go through the queue, which creates two channels.
questions.rule: Big data goes to storage, small signals to the queue.
questions.teaches: Most message brokers are designed for small messages, and a photo may be several megabytes, so the photo goes to file storage and only the instruction goes on the queue.
options: Brokers are built for small messages, and photos can be megabytes
Queues cannot carry binary data such as images at all
Photos would then bypass the storage service entirely
Resizers are unable to read instructions from queues
optionExplain: Right: this is the reason given in the book.
Queues can carry bytes; the issue is the size of the messages.
Skipping storage is not the stated problem. The right answer is: Brokers are built for small messages, and photos can be megabytes.
Resizers do read instructions from queues; the photo is the part that is too large.

questions.q: A video platform writes a clip to blob storage and queues a transcoding job. What makes the design sound according to the book?
questions.explain: The same two-channel pattern: the guarantee on the storage side is what protects the pipeline.
questions.rule: Protect two-channel flows with a recency guarantee on the data store.
questions.teaches: If the resizer processes an old version of the image, the full-size and resized images in file storage become permanently inconsistent, so the race produces a lasting error rather than a brief delay.
options: The blob storage is linearizable, so the worker sees the clip
The queue is much faster than the storage
The transcoder retries until it sees any clip
The platform stores the clip in the queue as well
optionExplain: Right: with a recency guarantee, the job cannot race the data.
A faster queue makes the race more likely, not less.
Retrying until it sees any clip could process an old version.
Large clips on queues conflict with how brokers are designed.

questions.q: A queue instruction races the data. Which approach is in the spirit of reading your own writes?
questions.explain: The message can carry freshness information so the reader fetches data at least that recent. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Carry freshness information along the other channel.
options: Delay the instruction by a random time
Send the instruction twice to be safe
Move the whole data into the queue itself
Have the instruction name the version to read
optionExplain: A random delay may still be too short. The right answer is: Have the instruction name the version to read.
Sending twice does not make the data arrive sooner.
Large data on queues is the problem the design avoids.
Right: the reader can then wait or fetch from a fresh replica.

questions.q: True or false: Approaches similar to reading your own writes work when the second channel is people talking, as with Alice and Bob.
questions.explain: You do not control Alice's voice, so only a recency guarantee on the store helps. The alternatives apply to channels you control, such as a message queue.
questions.rule: Control of the channel is what makes alternatives possible.

questions.q: A notification tells a phone about a new order. Which design avoids a linearizable store, in the spirit of reading your own writes?
questions.explain: A version in the message turns a vague stale read into one that waits for the right data.
questions.rule: Use versions in messages to demand freshness.
options: Send the notification before the order is saved
Ask the phone to retry until it sees an order
Put the order version in the notification for the phone to fetch
Keep the only copy of the order on the phone
optionExplain: Sending first guarantees that the data is missing. The right answer is: Put the order version in the notification for the phone to fetch.
Retrying until some order appears may show an older one.
Right: the notification carries the freshness requirement for the read.
Phones would then hold the only copy, losing durability.

questions.q: True or false: Linearizability is the only way to prevent a race between two communication channels.
questions.explain: The book calls it the simplest to understand and says that if you control the second channel, alternatives similar to reading your own writes exist.
questions.rule: Simplest is not the same as only.

questions.q: Approaches similar to reading your own writes avoid the race, at the cost of additional ____ in the application.
questions.explain: The book names additional complexity as the price, because the application must carry the extra information itself.
questions.rule: The price is complexity, not speed.
questions.teaches: Approaches similar to reading your own writes can avoid the race when you control the extra channel, at the cost of additional complexity in the application.

questions.q: Two services share a database and talk through callbacks. The team can edit both services. Which choice fits the book?
questions.explain: Owning both channels opens more options than a store-only fix.
questions.rule: Choose between storage guarantees and channel design.
questions.teaches: Because the team controls both services and so the second channel, it can choose between paying for a linearizable store and designing the channel so that messages carry enough information to read fresh data.
options: Only a linearizable store can work here at all
Neither option is available to the team
Remove the callbacks and poll the database
Pass versions in the callbacks or use a linearizable store
optionExplain: Editing the callbacks gives another way. The right answer is: Pass versions in the callbacks or use a linearizable store.
Both options are open to a team that owns both services.
Polling would still read a possibly stale replica. The right answer is: Pass versions in the callbacks or use a linearizable store.
Right: because they control the callback channel, both options are available.

questions.q: What is the simplest way to make a store behave as if there is one copy?
questions.explain: With only one copy, there is nothing to disagree. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: One copy is simple, not safe.
options: Keep three replicas that update asynchronously
Let each client keep its own cache
Resolve conflicts by timestamp
Keep exactly one copy on a single node
optionExplain: Asynchronous replicas can show different values at the same time.
Client caches multiply the copies. The right answer is: Keep exactly one copy on a single node.
Timestamp conflict resolution applies when several copies exist. The right answer is: Keep exactly one copy on a single node.
Right: but it cannot tolerate faults. Remember: One copy is simple, not safe.

questions.q: With a single copy of the data, if the node holding it fails, the data is lost or ____ until the node comes back.
questions.explain: The data is lost, or at least inaccessible until the node is brought up again.
questions.rule: One node is a single point of failure.

questions.q: A startup keeps its wallet balances on one database node to keep them current. What risk comes with this?
questions.explain: One node cannot have replication problems, but it is one failure from an outage.
options: Two nodes may show different balances
Reads may return stale balances from a follower
That node's failure makes the balances unavailable
Writes may be applied in different orders
optionExplain: With one node there are no other nodes to disagree.
No followers exist in this setup. The right answer is: That node's failure makes the balances unavailable.
Right: a single copy cannot survive the failure of its node.
With one node, writes have one order. The right answer is: That node's failure makes the balances unavailable.

questions.q: True or false: A system with one copy of the data can be linearizable and also survive the loss of the node holding it.
questions.explain: A single copy is easy to keep linearizable, but if its node fails the data is lost or inaccessible.
questions.rule: One copy cannot be fault tolerant.

questions.q: According to the book, what is the most common approach to making a system fault tolerant?
questions.explain: Copies on other nodes keep the data reachable when one node fails, which is why the question becomes which replication methods can be linearizable.
questions.rule: Replicate for fault tolerance; then check the guarantee.
questions.teaches: The most common approach to making a system fault-tolerant is to use replication, so the practical question is which replication methods can be made linearizable.
options: Restarting failed nodes with a supervisor process
Adding a longer timeout to every request
Compressing data so that fewer nodes are needed
Replicating the data onto other nodes
optionExplain: Restarts help the node return, but its data is still unreachable meanwhile.
Timeouts detect failures but do not keep data available.
Compression saves space and has no bearing on tolerating failure.
Right: replication keeps the data available when a node fails.

questions.q: A team reasons: one replica is linearizable, so three replicas must be too. What is wrong?
questions.explain: The guarantee of one copy does not survive replication automatically, and the next sections compare replication methods.
questions.rule: More copies, more work to keep the illusion.
questions.teaches: Replication methods differ in whether they can be linearizable: single-leader potentially, consensus algorithms yes, multi-leader no, leaderless probably not.
options: Three replicas are always slower than one
A single replica is never linearizable
Replicas cannot hold the same data
Replication adds copies that can differ
optionExplain: Speed is a separate matter; the problem is that copies can disagree.
A single copy is trivially linearizable. The right answer is: Replication adds copies that can differ.
Replicas can hold the same data, but not necessarily at the same time.
Right: with several copies, the single-copy illusion has to be maintained.

questions.q: In a single-leader database, which read is most likely to see the latest write?
questions.explain: All writes pass through the leader, so it has the freshest data. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Leader reads have the potential to be fresh.
options: A read served by any asynchronous follower
A read served by the nearest cache
A read served by the leader
A read served by the follower with the lowest load
optionExplain: Asynchronous followers lag behind the leader. The right answer is: A read served by the leader.
A cache may be older than the leader. The right answer is: A read served by the leader.
Right: the leader holds the primary copy that receives all writes.
Load says nothing about how recent a follower's data is.

questions.q: In single-leader replication, reads from the leader or from ____ updated followers have the potential to be linearizable.
questions.explain: A synchronously updated follower is sure to hold each acknowledged write, so it can serve up-to-date reads.

questions.q: A booking system sends all reads to asynchronous followers to spare the leader. What is lost?
questions.explain: Moving reads to lagging copies gives up recency.
options: The ability to accept writes
The copies held by the followers
The order of writes on the leader
The potential for linearizable reads
optionExplain: Writes still go to the leader, so they are not affected.
The followers still hold copies; it is their freshness that suffers.
The leader's order of writes is not changed by where reads go.
Right: asynchronous followers can lag, so reads may be stale.

questions.q: True or false: A database that uses a leader and snapshot isolation is therefore linearizable.
questions.explain: The book says not every single-leader database is linearizable, for example because it uses snapshot isolation by design, or due to concurrency bugs.
questions.rule: A leader is necessary, not sufficient.

questions.q: A single-leader database is split into partitions, each with its own leader. How does the book say this affects linearizability?
questions.explain: Linearizability concerns one object at a time, and an object belongs to one partition.
questions.teaches: Partitioning a single-leader database so that each partition has its own leader does not affect linearizability, because it is a single-object guarantee.
options: It breaks linearizability for every object
It improves linearizability for reads
It does not, because linearizability is a single-object guarantee
It makes linearizability depend on the clock
optionExplain: Per-object guarantees are unaffected; only guarantees across partitions suffer.
Splitting does not add recency. The right answer is: It does not, because linearizability is a single-object guarantee.
Right: each object lives in one partition, so its guarantee is unaffected.
Clocks do not enter into it. The right answer is: It does not, because linearizability is a single-object guarantee.

questions.q: A sharded store has a leader per shard. A transaction updates two objects on different shards. What does the book say?
questions.explain: Single-object recency does not cover a transaction across partitions.
questions.rule: Check what a per-object guarantee leaves open.
questions.teaches: Cross-partition transactions are a different matter from single-object linearizability, and the book returns to them under distributed transactions and consensus.
options: Per-shard leaders make the transaction linearizable
The transaction is safe because each shard is up to date
Cross-partition transactions are a different matter
Transactions across shards cannot be done at all
optionExplain: Per-object guarantees do not add up to a transaction guarantee.
Fresh shards can still disagree on whether to commit.
Right: the per-object guarantee does not cover multi-object operations across partitions.
They are possible, though they need coordination. The right answer is: Cross-partition transactions are a different matter.

questions.q: A leader has been cut off from the network and nobody told it. It still answers reads. What is the risk?
questions.explain: A node that thinks it leads but does not can serve out-of-date data. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Belief in leadership is not leadership.
options: Its answers stay correct as long as its own disk works
Its answers time out, so clients are never misled by them
Its answers are rejected by clients, who detect the problem
Its answers may be stale if another node took over
optionExplain: A working disk says nothing about whether it is still the leader.
It answers normally; clients cannot tell that it is out of date.
Clients have no way of knowing that it has been replaced.
Right: it may be a leader only in its own mind.

questions.q: A node that wrongly believes it is the leader, and keeps serving requests, is called a ____ leader.
questions.explain: The book calls such a node a delusional leader, and serving requests as if it led is likely to break linearizability.
questions.rule: A leader that does not know it has been replaced.

questions.q: A switch fails and the followers elect a new leader. The old leader keeps answering a dashboard. What do dashboard readers risk?
questions.explain: Both leaders accept requests, and the old one is missing what the new one has accepted.
questions.rule: Two believed leaders mean one stale one.
options: Seeing writes that the new leader has not yet accepted
Reading from a follower that rejects every query
Missing writes that the new leader has already accepted
Losing the right to read until a majority agrees
optionExplain: The old leader is behind, not ahead, of the new one.
The old leader is still answering, so queries are not rejected.
Right: the old leader never receives the new leader's writes.
Nothing makes the old leader stop until it learns of the new one.

questions.q: True or false: Sending every read to the leader is enough to guarantee linearizable reads.
questions.explain: The leader must be the real leader, and acknowledged writes must survive failover. A delusional leader or a lost write breaks the guarantee.
questions.rule: Reading from the leader is necessary, not sufficient.

questions.q: With asynchronous replication, what can a failover do to acknowledged writes?
questions.explain: A follower that has not yet received the latest writes becomes the new leader, so those writes vanish.
questions.rule: Asynchronous failover can lose committed writes.
questions.teaches: With asynchronous replication, failover may even lose committed writes, which violates both durability and linearizability.
options: Delay them, which violates only linearizability
Duplicate them, which violates only durability
Reorder them, which violates only isolation
Lose them, breaking durability and linearizability
optionExplain: Lost writes also break durability, so linearizability is not the only casualty.
The risk named is loss, not duplication. The right answer is: Lose them, breaking durability and linearizability.
The risk named is loss, not reordering. The right answer is: Lose them, breaking durability and linearizability.
Right: committed writes can be lost when a follower that missed them is promoted.

questions.q: A cache-warming job reads from whichever node believes it is the leader. When can this mislead it?
questions.explain: The danger comes from a node's belief about its own role, not from the role itself.
questions.rule: A node's belief in its role is not evidence.
questions.teaches: If a delusional leader continues to serve requests, it is likely to violate linearizability.
options: When the real leader serves reads without any failover
When the leader holds the primary copy of the data
When followers keep backup copies on other nodes
A delusional leader keeps serving after losing leadership
optionExplain: A real leader without failover is the case where leader reads can be linearizable.
Holding the primary copy is what makes the leader a good source in normal operation.
Backup copies on followers are the ordinary setup and do not mislead by themselves.
Right: a delusional leader that keeps serving requests is likely to violate linearizability.

questions.q: Which kind of replication can implement linearizable storage safely despite node failures?
