questions.explain: Only consensus-based replication comes with protection for both failure cases. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Consensus protects what plain leader replication leaves open.
options: Replication with several leaders and conflict resolution
Replication with quorums and last write wins
Replication that copies the log to followers asynchronously
Replication run by a consensus algorithm
optionExplain: Several leaders process writes independently, so one copy is not maintained.
Last write wins relies on timestamps, which cannot be trusted to follow real event order.
Asynchronous followers can lag, and a failover may lose acknowledged writes.
Right: consensus protocols include measures against split brain and stale replicas.

questions.q: Consensus protocols contain measures to prevent split ____ and stale replicas.
questions.explain: Split brain, two nodes both believing they lead, and stale replicas are the two failure cases that consensus protocols guard against.

questions.q: A team needs a lock service that must not hand the same lock to two clients when a node fails. Which design fits?
questions.explain: A lock needs one owner agreed by all, even through failures, which consensus supplies.
options: Two primaries that each accept lock requests and merge them later on
A single leader that is promoted manually after a crash
A replicated store run by a consensus algorithm
A leaderless store that reads from any two of three nodes
optionExplain: Two primaries can each grant the lock, and merging afterwards is too late.
A manual promotion makes the service unavailable until a human acts, and it still risks a stale old leader.
Right: agreement among nodes keeps one owner even through failures.
Quorum reads from any two nodes can still return stale values, as the next sections show.

questions.q: True or false: Because consensus algorithms resemble single-leader replication, they offer no protection that single-leader replication lacks.
questions.explain: They resemble it but add measures to prevent split brain and stale replicas, and these details make linearizable storage safe.

questions.q: Which well-known systems implement linearizable storage with consensus algorithms, according to the book?
questions.explain: The book names the coordination services it returns to later.
questions.rule: ZooKeeper and etcd are the standard examples.
questions.teaches: ZooKeeper and etcd use consensus algorithms to implement linearizable storage safely.
options: Cassandra and Riak
Memcached and Redis caches
MySQL replicas and Kafka consumers
ZooKeeper and etcd
optionExplain: Cassandra and Riak are Dynamo-style leaderless systems, which are probably not linearizable.
Caches hold copies and are not described as consensus-based storage.
Replicas and consumers read a log; the book does not call them consensus-based storage.
Right: this is how ZooKeeper and etcd work. Remember: ZooKeeper and etcd are the standard examples.

questions.q: A designer must choose between a leader with manual failover and a consensus-based store for a booking lock. What is the safe choice?
questions.explain: Prefer a design with built-in protection against the two failure cases.
questions.rule: Pick the design whose protections match the failure cases.
questions.teaches: Consensus protocols contain measures to prevent split brain and stale replicas, which plain single-leader replication does not have.
options: The manual leader, because humans will prevent split brain
Either one, since both have a single leader
Neither: no store can be linearizable
The consensus store, which prevents split brain
optionExplain: Human decisions are slow and do not stop an old leader from serving requests.
Both have one leader at a time, but only consensus protects against stale leaders.
Consensus-based stores do implement linearizable storage. The right answer is: The consensus store, which prevents split brain.
Right: the measures against split brain and stale replicas are what make it safe.

questions.q: Two leaders in different datacenters each accept a write to the same key at the same moment. What follows?
questions.explain: Each leader accepts the write independently, so a conflict can arise. The card next shows why.
options: One write is rejected at once by the other leader
The writes conflict and need to be resolved later
The leaders agree on an order before answering
Both writes are applied in the same order everywhere
optionExplain: Leaders do not coordinate before accepting a write in this design.
Right: concurrent writes on separate leaders can conflict. Remember: Independent leaders mean conflicts.
Agreeing before answering is what a consensus-based design does.
Without agreement on order, different nodes may apply the writes in different orders.

questions.q: Multi-leader systems process writes concurrently on several nodes and replicate them ____ to the other nodes.
questions.explain: Concurrent processing and asynchronous replication are why multi-leader systems are generally not linearizable.
questions.rule: Concurrent writes plus asynchronous copying: no single copy.

questions.q: A calendar app lets two offices edit the same event in their local datacenters, which sync later. Which guarantee is lost?
questions.explain: Local acceptance of writes gives availability and speed but gives up the single copy.
questions.rule: Local writes mean no single timeline.
options: A single timeline of all the writes
The ability of each office to keep working
The durability of each office's own writes
The ability to read from the local datacenter
optionExplain: Right: with separate leaders there is no single copy, so linearizability is lost.
Each office can keep working, which is the benefit of this design.
Each write is stored locally, so durability does not depend on the sync.
Local reads still work; they may be stale. The right answer is: A single timeline of all the writes.

questions.q: True or false: After two leaders accept conflicting writes to one key, a later read at either leader can return either write.
questions.explain: After asynchronous replication and conflict resolution, a read at either leader may see either write, which is not the behaviour of one copy.
questions.rule: Conflict resolution comes after the fact.

questions.q: According to the book, what are conflicts in multi-leader systems an artifact of?
questions.explain: A conflict means two copies disagree about what was written; one copy cannot disagree with itself.
questions.rule: Conflicts exist because there is no single copy.
questions.teaches: The conflicting writes of multi-leader systems, which require conflict resolution, are an artifact of the lack of a single copy of the data.
options: The use of too many network links
The lack of a single copy of the data
The presence of clock drift on the leaders
The size of the replication log
optionExplain: The number of links does not create conflicts by itself.
Right: with one copy there would be nothing to conflict.
Clock drift can affect resolution, but the conflicts exist without it.
Log size is unrelated to whether writes conflict. The right answer is: The lack of a single copy of the data.

questions.q: A team must pick replication for a chat service that runs in three regions and wants regional writes to stay fast. What is the trade?
questions.explain: Multi-leader gives local latency and independence at the price of a single timeline.
questions.rule: Local speed costs the single timeline.
questions.teaches: Multi-leader replication is a common choice for multi-datacenter deployments because each datacenter can keep operating on its own, and the price is that the system is not linearizable.
options: Linearizability in exchange for fast local writes
Fast local writes, but no linearizability
Neither: multi-leader systems give both
Strict ordering in exchange for lost writes
optionExplain: This reverses the trade; linearizability costs wide-area round trips.
Right: concurrent writes in each region cannot form a single timeline.
Multi-leader replication gives local speed, not the single-copy illusion.
Lost writes are a failover risk, not what multi-leader trades away.

questions.q: A leaderless store requires w + r > n for its reads and writes. Is it therefore linearizable?
questions.explain: The simple arithmetic leaves room for non-linearizable executions. The card next shows why.
options: Not necessarily, even with strict quorums
Yes, since every read overlaps the last write
Yes, but only with synchronised clocks
No, because quorums cannot overlap
optionExplain: Right: overlapping quorums are not enough with variable network delays.
Overlap alone does not make each read see the latest write at the right moment.
Synchronised clocks do not fix the race that the book describes.
Quorums overlap by construction; the issue lies elsewhere. The right answer is: Not necessarily, even with strict quorums.

questions.q: Leaderless replication is also called ____-style replication.
questions.explain: The book calls leaderless systems with quorum reads and writes Dynamo-style.

questions.q: A vendor's page says its quorum database gives strong consistency. You plan to use it for unique usernames. What is the sound conclusion?
questions.explain: Treat the claim as unproven for hard uniqueness.
questions.rule: Verify before relying on strong consistency claims.
options: Go ahead, since w + r > n gives linearizability here
Do not assume it is linearizable until you check the setup
Use it, but only with a faster network
Avoid quorums, because they never overlap
optionExplain: The arithmetic alone does not prove linearizability. The right answer is: Do not assume it is linearizable until you check the setup.
Right: strong consistency claims depend on the definition and the quorum setup.
A faster network narrows the race but does not remove it.
Quorums do overlap; the problem is something else. The right answer is: Do not assume it is linearizable until you check the setup.

questions.q: True or false: Choosing quorum sizes with w + r > n is enough to guarantee linearizable reads in a leaderless database.
questions.explain: The book says this is not quite true: depending on the exact configuration and definition, quorums can still produce non-linearizable results.
questions.rule: Overlap is necessary at best, not sufficient.

questions.q: Why is last write wins with time-of-day clocks, as in Cassandra, almost certainly not linearizable?
questions.explain: A resolution method that relies on clocks inherits their errors.
questions.rule: Clock skew breaks last write wins as an ordering.
questions.teaches: Last write wins conflict resolution based on time-of-day clocks, as in Cassandra, is almost certainly non-linearizable, because clock timestamps cannot be guaranteed to be consistent with the actual event ordering due to clock skew.
options: Clock skew can make timestamps disagree with real order
Timestamps are too large to be compared across nodes
Writes are stored in a different format on each node
Clients choose the timestamps at random
optionExplain: Right: a later write can get an earlier timestamp.
Size is not the issue; the problem is the accuracy of the clock readings.
Formats are unrelated to ordering. The right answer is: Clock skew can make timestamps disagree with real order.
Clients do not choose timestamps at random. The right answer is: Clock skew can make timestamps disagree with real order.

questions.q: A leaderless store accepts writes on any reachable node, even outside the usual replicas, and hands them back later. What does this do to linearizability?
questions.explain: Writes may sit on nodes that later reads do not contact.
questions.teaches: Sloppy quorums, which accept writes on nodes outside the usual replicas and hand them off later, also ruin any chance of linearizability.
options: It ruins any chance of it
It guarantees it for strict quorums
It has no effect on it
It guarantees it for reads only
optionExplain: Right: sloppy quorums ruin any chance of linearizability. Remember: Sloppy quorums forfeit linearizability.
Sloppy quorums are the opposite of strict quorums. The right answer is: It ruins any chance of it.
Writes landing outside the usual replicas hide from later quorum reads, so this has an effect.
Reads are among the things lost. The right answer is: It ruins any chance of it.

questions.q: A write is in flight. A's two-replica read sees the new value on one; B then reads the others. What may B see?
questions.explain: A quorum pair can miss a write that is still travelling. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A write in flight can be seen by one quorum and missed by the next.
options: The old value from both nodes, which breaks linearizability
The new value, since A has already seen it on one node
An error, since the two quorums disagree
The average of the old and the new value
optionExplain: Right: the write may not yet have reached B's replicas.
A's read does not push the new value onto B's replicas.
Each quorum answers on its own, so there is no error.
Registers hold one value; averages do not exist. The right answer is: The old value from both nodes, which breaks linearizability.

questions.q: In the book's example, the quorum condition w + r > n holds, but the execution is still not ____.
questions.explain: B's request begins after A's completes, yet B returns the older value, so the execution is not linearizable.

questions.q: With n=5, w=3, r=3 and a write in flight, A sees the new value, then B sees the old. Is this possible?
questions.explain: Whatever the numbers, the write reaches replicas at different times.
questions.rule: Larger quorums do not remove the race.
options: It cannot happen, since w + r > n
It is possible, and it breaks linearizability
It is allowed because B is a different client
It is allowed only if the write fails later
optionExplain: The condition holds, and the race still occurs. The right answer is: It is possible, and it breaks linearizability.
Right: the new value reached the replicas at different times.
A different client does not matter; B started after A finished.
Whether the write fails later does not change the order of the reads.

questions.q: True or false: If every replica already held the new value before any read began, two quorum reads would agree on it.
questions.explain: The race needs a write in progress. Once all replicas hold the new value, any quorum returns it.
questions.rule: The problem is timing during the write.

questions.q: Which familiar situation does the book compare the quorum race with?
questions.explain: The pattern is the same: a later request returns older data than an earlier one.
questions.teaches: The nonlinearizable quorum execution is once again the Alice and Bob situation: B's request begins after A's request completes, but B returns the old value while A returns the new one.
options: Alice and Bob checking the football score
A bank transfer between two accounts
Two compilers building one program
A cache that expires after a minute
optionExplain: Right: B starts after A completes but sees older data.
A bank transfer concerns atomicity, not recency order. The right answer is: Alice and Bob checking the football score.
Compilers have nothing to do with read order. The right answer is: Alice and Bob checking the football score.
Expiry is a freshness limit, not the ordering of two reads.

questions.q: A team reads x twice, once from each of two different quorums, and sees 1 then 0. What is the likely explanation?
questions.explain: A 1-then-0 sequence is a symptom of a non-linearizable read path.
questions.rule: Seeing the new value then the old is the signature of the race.
questions.teaches: Because of variable network delays, even strict quorums can show a non-linearizable sequence, so it is safest to assume that a Dynamo-style leaderless system does not provide linearizability.
options: A write was in flight, reaching only some replicas
The clock on the client machine was wrong at that time
The database dropped the write after the first read
Quorums were smaller than the replica count in total
optionExplain: Right: the first quorum overlapped the write, the second did not.
Clocks are not involved in this race. The right answer is: A write was in flight, reaching only some replicas.
A dropped write would not appear in the first read.
Smaller quorums are normal and do not explain a 1-then-0 sequence.

questions.q: How could a leaderless store avoid a later read returning older data than an earlier one?
questions.explain: The reader must make sure the value it returns is on enough nodes before replying. The card next shows why.
options: Let each reader choose the replica with the newest clock
Reduce the number of replicas to one per key
Repair stale replicas before the read returns
Accept writes on any node and merge them later
optionExplain: Newest clock readings are unreliable because of skew. The right answer is: Repair stale replicas before the read returns.
One replica removes fault tolerance, which defeats the point of replication.
Right: synchronous read repair closes the window, at a cost.
Merging later is what makes executions non-linearizable. The right answer is: Repair stale replicas before the read returns.

questions.q: To make quorums linearizable, a reader must perform read ____ synchronously before returning results.
questions.explain: The reader fixes stale replicas before returning, so a later read cannot see older data.

questions.q: A writer sends its update straight to the replicas without looking at their state first. What does the linearizable variant require instead?
questions.explain: Both sides of the protocol take a step to learn the latest state.
options: Sending the write twice to each of the replicas
Waiting for a timeout equal to the average network delay
Writing to the replica with the lowest load
Reading a quorum's latest state before writing
optionExplain: Repeating the write does not tell the writer about the latest state.
A timeout equal to the average delay does not bound the worst delay.
Load does not decide which state is latest. The right answer is: Reading a quorum's latest state before writing.
Right: the writer learns the latest state before it writes.

questions.q: True or false: A database that waits for read repair on quorum reads is therefore linearizable.
questions.explain: Cassandra waits for read repair on quorum reads, but it loses linearizability if there are concurrent writes to the same key, because of last-write-wins resolution.
questions.rule: One protocol step is not the whole guarantee.

questions.q: Why does Riak not perform synchronous read repair, according to the book?
questions.explain: Waiting for repair slows every read, which is the reduced performance that the book mentions.
questions.rule: Speed is the reason many systems skip it.
questions.teaches: Riak does not perform synchronous read repair because of the performance penalty.
options: Because replicas cannot be repaired
Because it prefers last write wins
Because of the performance penalty
Because quorums are strict by design
optionExplain: Replicas can be repaired; the question is when. The right answer is: Because of the performance penalty.
The reason given is cost, not conflict resolution. The right answer is: Because of the performance penalty.
Right: Riak keeps reads fast, so it gives up linearizability.
Strict quorums do not remove the need for repair.

questions.q: A leaderless database waits for read repair on quorum reads, but also uses last write wins. What happens with concurrent writes to one key?
questions.explain: Conflict resolution by timestamp reintroduces the order problem.
questions.rule: Check the whole write path, not just reads.
questions.teaches: Cassandra waits for read repair to complete on quorum reads but loses linearizability if there are multiple concurrent writes to the same key, due to its use of last-write-wins conflict resolution.
options: It stays linearizable, since repair makes replicas agree
It becomes linearizable only for compare-and-set
It loses linearizability, as timestamps can mis-order writes
It rejects the later write with an error
optionExplain: Repair does not fix the order that last write wins chose.
Compare-and-set is not obtained from quorum reads and writes.
Right: this is the Cassandra case in the book.
Last write wins does not reject writes; it picks one.

questions.q: A network cut separates two datacenters. With a single leader in one, what can clients in the other datacenter do?
questions.explain: They cannot reach the leader, so they can only do what a follower can do alone. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Cut off from the leader means no writes and no linearizable reads.
options: Write to their follower and sync it up later on
Make linearizable reads from their follower
Elect themselves leader and continue as before
Read from their follower, possibly stale
optionExplain: Followers accept no writes; those must go to the leader.
A follower cut off from the leader may be behind.
Electing a second leader risks split brain. The right answer is: Read from their follower, possibly stale.
Right: follower reads continue but may be stale. Remember: Cut off from the leader means no writes and no linearizable reads.

questions.q: Match each setup with what happens in the cut-off datacenter.
questions.explain: The datacenter holding the leader is unaffected. Clients elsewhere lose writes and linearizable reads, while multi-leader keeps going.
questions.rule: Where the leader is decides who can work.
pairs: Keeps accepting writes and queues them for later exchange
Cannot write or do linearizable reads

questions.q: An airline runs a single-leader database in Paris and a follower in Tokyo. The link fails. Tokyo agents need to book seats. What results?
questions.explain: The followers must send writes across the broken link.
options: They can book freely, with no effect on Paris at all
They can book, and Paris sees the bookings at once
They cannot book until the link is repaired
They are promoted to leader automatically
optionExplain: Writes need the leader, so they cannot proceed freely.
Paris cannot see anything that never reached it. The right answer is: They cannot book until the link is repaired.
Right: writes must go to the leader in Paris.
Automatic promotion would risk two leaders. The right answer is: They cannot book until the link is repaired.

questions.q: True or false: In a multi-leader setup, writes made in each datacenter during the network cut are lost once the link returns.
questions.explain: The writes are queued up and exchanged when network connectivity is restored.

questions.q: Clients that can reach the leader's datacenter during the cut experience what, according to the book?
questions.explain: Only clients on the far side of the cut lose out.
questions.rule: The problem is limited to the cut-off side.
questions.teaches: If clients can connect directly to the leader datacenter, the network cut is not a problem for them, since the application continues to work normally there.
options: A short delay while a new leader is elected there
Stale reads from the leader
A loss of all the writes made before the cut
No problem; the application works normally there
optionExplain: No election is needed because the leader is still up.
The leader holds the primary copy, not a stale one.
Earlier writes are not lost. The right answer is: No problem; the application works normally there.
Right: for them the leader remains reachable. Remember: The problem is limited to the cut-off side.

questions.q: A region loses its link to the leader. Reads from the nearby follower stay fast, but users see old data. What explains this?
questions.explain: Availability for reads comes with the risk of staleness.
questions.rule: Reads stay up, freshness is lost.
questions.teaches: Clients connected to a follower datacenter can still make reads from the follower during the interruption, but those reads might be stale and so are not linearizable.
options: The follower has been promoted to leader
The client library caches reads for ten minutes
The leader has deleted newer data
Follower reads continue but may not be linearizable
optionExplain: Promotion would also have stopped the stale reads from the old leader.
Nothing in the scenario mentions client caching. The right answer is: Follower reads continue but may not be linearizable.
The leader has not deleted anything. The right answer is: Follower reads continue but may not be linearizable.
Right: reads on the cut-off side can continue but may be stale.

questions.q: Two replicas of a linearizable store lose contact with each other. What must the disconnected replica do with client requests?
questions.explain: A disconnected replica cannot know the latest value, so it cannot answer safely. The card next shows why.
options: Answer from its local copy and sync later
Accept writes and resolve conflicts afterwards
Elect itself as the sole copy
Wait for the network or return an error
optionExplain: Local answers may be stale, which linearizability forbids. The right answer is: Wait for the network or return an error.
Accepting writes independently is the non-linearizable alternative. The right answer is: Wait for the network or return an error.
Electing itself would create two copies. The right answer is: Wait for the network or return an error.
Right: either way it is unavailable until the link is restored.

questions.q: If an application does not require linearizability, each replica can process requests ____ even when disconnected.
questions.explain: Replicas can work on their own, as in multi-leader replication, at the cost of non-linearizable behaviour.

questions.q: A ticketing platform needs globally unique seat claims across two regions. A transatlantic link fails. What should the system do for the cut-off region?
questions.explain: If linearizability is required, availability is the price during a cut.
options: Let both regions sell the same seat and sort it out later
Let the cut-off region sell seats from its local copy
Refuse or delay seat claims there until the link returns
Switch to a different seat map without telling anyone
optionExplain: This gives up the unique claim, which the platform requires.
Local copies could sell the same seat as the other region.
Right: unique claims need agreement, so the cut-off side must wait or fail.
Hidden maps do not give uniqueness. The right answer is: Refuse or delay seat claims there until the link returns.

questions.q: Which service gives up linearizability to stay available during a network cut?
questions.explain: Staying available means processing requests without agreeing with the other replicas.
questions.rule: Availability under a cut means independent replicas.
options: A single-leader database that sends linearizable reads to the leader
A consensus-based lock service that needs a majority
A multi-leader database that queues writes for later exchange
A single node database
optionExplain: This design makes cut-off clients wait, keeping linearizability. The right answer is: A multi-leader database that queues writes for later exchange.
Consensus services stop on the minority side to keep the guarantee.
Right: each datacenter keeps working without agreement. Remember: Availability under a cut means independent replicas.
A single node has no replicas to disagree and keeps the guarantee.

questions.q: True or false: The choice between linearizability and availability arises only in multi-datacenter deployments.
questions.explain: The issue is not specific to multi-datacenter deployments; it can occur on any unreliable network, even within one datacenter.
questions.teaches: The trade-off between linearizability and availability is not specific to multi-datacenter deployments or to a replication method: any linearizable database has this problem on any unreliable network, even within one datacenter.

questions.q: A team replaces a multi-leader database with a linearizable one, hoping the new setup will keep working through network faults. What should they expect?
questions.explain: The move trades availability under network problems for the single-copy illusion.
questions.rule: Expect lower availability under network faults.
questions.teaches: Applications that do not require linearizability can be more tolerant of network problems, because each replica can process requests independently.
options: Availability improves because the data is consistent
The same availability as before
Better availability for writes only
Some replicas become unavailable while disconnected
optionExplain: Consistency does not buy availability; during a cut it costs it.
The multi-leader setup kept working in each datacenter, which this one cannot.
Writes are no exception: they must reach the agreed copy too.
Right: any linearizable database has this problem. Remember: Expect lower availability under network faults.

questions.q: What does the popular CAP insight say about an application that does not need linearizability?
questions.explain: Without the need for one copy, replicas can work on their own during a cut. The card next shows why.
options: It must be restricted to running on a single node
It can be more tolerant of network problems
It cannot make use of replication in any form
It has to give up durability of committed writes
optionExplain: Nothing forces a single node; such systems are built with replication.
Right: each replica can keep processing requests while disconnected.
Replication is exactly how these systems are built, so this is backwards.
Durability is a separate property and is not what gets traded away here.

questions.q: CAP began as a rule of ____, without precise definitions, to start a discussion about trade-offs.
questions.explain: The goal was to start a discussion about trade-offs in databases, so the original statement was loose.
questions.rule: CAP started as a rule of thumb.

questions.q: A chat service stays up in every region during a link failure but shows old messages. Which side of the CAP trade did it choose?
questions.explain: Staying up while disconnected means each side answers on its own, so reads can be stale.
questions.rule: Staying up under a cut costs the single-copy view.
options: Tolerance of network problems over linearizability
Linearizability over tolerance of network problems
Both, because it uses replication
Neither, because it is a messaging service
optionExplain: Right: it keeps working on each side, so it gives up the single-copy view.
A linearizable service would have stopped answering on the cut-off side.
The two pull in opposite directions during a cut, so it cannot have both.
The trade applies to any replicated service, including messaging.

questions.q: True or false: CAP shows that linearizable systems are slower than others even when the network works perfectly.
questions.explain: CAP concerns what happens during a network problem. The slowness of linearizability even without faults is a separate point the book makes later.
questions.rule: CAP is about faults, not everyday speed.

questions.q: According to the book, when was this trade-off named, and how old was the knowledge behind it?
questions.explain: The name is recent, the insight is old.
questions.rule: The name dates from 2000; the trade-off is older.
questions.teaches: The trade-off was named the CAP theorem by Eric Brewer in 2000, although it had been known to designers of distributed databases since the 1970s.
options: Named in 2000, and discovered only after NoSQL appeared
Named in 2000, but known to database designers since the 1970s
Named in 1978, alongside Lamport timestamps
Named in 2014, after the football example
optionExplain: NoSQL grew after CAP, not before it, and the trade-off was known long before.
Right: Brewer named it in 2000, though the trade-off was known earlier.
Lamport's paper is from 1978, but CAP was named later.
2014 is the World Cup final used as an example, not the date of CAP.

questions.q: What culture shift does the book credit CAP with?
questions.explain: Before CAP, many distributed databases aimed at linearizable semantics on a cluster with shared storage.
questions.teaches: Many distributed databases once focused on linearizable semantics on a cluster of machines with shared storage; CAP encouraged shared-nothing designs better suited to large-scale web services, and the explosion of NoSQL technologies since the mid-2000s followed.
options: Moving from relational to graph databases in every company
Moving from shared-storage clusters toward shared-nothing designs and NoSQL
Moving from asynchronous to synchronous replication everywhere
Moving from public clouds back to private datacenters
optionExplain: Graph databases are not what the book credits CAP with.
Right: CAP encouraged engineers to explore a wider design space.
CAP pushed the opposite way, towards designs that tolerate faults.
Hosting choices are not part of the story. The right answer is: Moving from shared-storage clusters toward shared-nothing designs and NoSQL.

questions.q: Why can a team not choose to avoid network partitions?
questions.explain: A fault is not something you can opt out of. The card next shows why.
options: Partitions are found only in systems that are run in the cloud
Partitions exist only in systems with a single leader
Partitions are a design option that most databases do not use
Partitions are faults that happen whether you like it or not
optionExplain: Faults occur on any network, not just in the cloud.
Partitions can affect systems of every replication method. The right answer is: Partitions are faults that happen whether you like it or not.
This treats a fault as a feature, which it is not.
Right: a partition is a kind of fault, not a design option.

questions.q: A better phrasing of CAP is: either ____ or Available when Partitioned.
questions.explain: When a partition occurs, the choice is between consistency (linearizability) and availability.

questions.q: A database is described as AP. During a normal day with a healthy network, what can it do?
questions.explain: When the network works correctly, a system can provide both consistency and total availability.
questions.rule: The choice appears only during a fault.
options: Offer availability only, with no linearizability at all
Offer neither of them until a fault occurs
Offer both, if it is built for that
Offer linearizability only on weekdays
optionExplain: A label describes behaviour during faults, not a permanent limit on healthy days.
Nothing is withheld until a fault occurs. The right answer is: Offer both, if it is built for that.
Right: the trade-off bites only when a network fault occurs.
Days of the week have nothing to do with it.

questions.q: True or false: As a network becomes more reliable, a system that needs linearizability faces the choice between consistency and availability less often.
questions.explain: A more reliable network needs to make this choice less often, but at some point the choice is inevitable.
questions.rule: Reliability reduces the frequency, not the existence, of the choice.

questions.q: What does the book conclude about a more reliable network and the choice?
questions.explain: Reliability changes frequency but not the principle.
questions.rule: A reliable network narrows the choice in time.
questions.teaches: A more reliable network needs to make the choice between linearizability and total availability less often, but at some point the choice is inevitable.
options: The choice disappears once the network is reliable enough
The choice is made more often, because there is more traffic
The choice moves from the network to the application
Less often, but it is inevitable at some point
optionExplain: Faults can never be removed entirely, so the choice does not vanish.
More traffic does not change how often partitions occur.
The choice is the same; only its frequency changes.
Right: reliability reduces how often the choice arises. Remember: A reliable network narrows the choice in time.

questions.q: A vendor labels its product CP. According to the book, how should you treat the label?
questions.explain: Describe the behaviour during a fault directly instead of using the label.
questions.rule: Replace labels with a description of behaviour under a partition.
questions.teaches: The terms CP (consistent but not available under network partitions) and AP (available but not consistent) belong to a classification scheme that has several flaws and is best avoided.
options: Treat it as a precise description of the product's guarantees
Assume it means the product is linearizable on a healthy network only
Assume it means the product never loses data
Avoid relying on it, since the CP and AP scheme has flaws
optionExplain: The labels are loose and the scheme is flawed, so they are not precise.
Nothing in the label ties it to healthy-network behaviour only.
Data loss is a different property and the label does not describe it.
Right: the book says the classification scheme has several flaws and is best avoided.

questions.q: Which statement about CAP's formal definitions does the book make?
questions.explain: The formal availability is idiosyncratic. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: CAP's definitions are narrower than everyday words.
options: Its availability differs from the usual meaning
It defines availability exactly as engineers use the word
It covers every consistency model equally
It covers every fault, including dead nodes
optionExplain: Right: many highly available systems do not meet CAP's availability.
The book says the formalization does not match the usual meaning.
CAP considers only linearizability. The right answer is: Its availability differs from the usual meaning.
CAP considers only network partitions. The right answer is: Its availability differs from the usual meaning.

questions.q: Match each part of the CAP theorem's scope with what it covers.
questions.explain: The theorem covers one consistency model and one kind of fault. Delays and dead nodes are outside it.
pairs: Only network partitions: nodes alive but disconnected

questions.q: A team says their database must be strongly consistent because of CAP. The latency of cross-region reads worries them. Does CAP address latency?
questions.explain: A narrow theorem cannot answer a question that lies outside it.
questions.rule: Use a different result for latency.
options: Yes, it proves latency must be low
No, it says nothing about network delays
Yes, it bounds latency by availability
Yes, it only addresses latency in a single datacenter
optionExplain: CAP makes no claim about latency. The right answer is: No, it says nothing about network delays.
Right: network delays are outside the theorem's scope. Remember: Use a different result for latency.
No bound on latency is part of CAP. The right answer is: No, it says nothing about network delays.
Datacenter count is not what limits its scope. The right answer is: No, it says nothing about network delays.

questions.q: True or false: Many systems that are called highly available also meet CAP's own definition of availability.
questions.explain: The book says many so-called highly available systems do not meet CAP's idiosyncratic definition of availability.
questions.rule: Everyday availability and CAP availability differ.
questions.hint: Think about whose definition of availability the theorem uses.

questions.q: How does the book describe the status of CAP today?
questions.explain: Better-defined results have taken its place for practical reasoning.
questions.rule: CAP is history; use more precise results.
questions.teaches: There are many more interesting impossibility results in distributed systems, and CAP has now been superseded by more precise results, so it is of mostly historical interest today.
options: Superseded by more precise results
The most important result in distributed systems
A theorem that has been disproved in practice
A design pattern recommended for new databases
optionExplain: Right: other impossibility results are more precise. Remember: CAP is history; use more precise results.
The book calls it historically influential but of little practical value.
It is not disproved; its scope is simply narrow.
It is not a design pattern. The right answer is: Superseded by more precise results.

questions.q: A CPU designer is told that multi-core memory is not linearizable because of CAP. What should the book's reader answer?
questions.explain: CAP is about network faults, which the CPU does not face in the same way.
questions.rule: Do not stretch CAP beyond networks.
questions.teaches: It makes no sense to use the CAP theorem to justify the multi-core memory consistency model: within one computer we usually assume reliable communication, and the reason for dropping linearizability there is performance.
options: CAP does not apply inside one computer
CAP applies because the cores form a network of nodes
CAP applies because memory has several replicas
CAP applies once cores exceed four
optionExplain: Right: a single computer is not facing network partitions in the CAP sense.
Cores on one machine are assumed to communicate reliably.
Caches are copies, but the reason for non-linearizability is performance.
The number of cores is irrelevant to the argument.

questions.q: Thread 1 on core A writes an address; thread 2 on core B reads it soon after. What may thread 2 see?
questions.explain: Each core keeps its own cached copy, updated asynchronously. The card next shows why.
options: The new value, since memory is a single copy
An error, since the cores disagree about the address
The new value, but only after waiting for main memory
The old value, as the write may not have arrived
optionExplain: Hardware keeps several copies of the data in caches and buffers.
The hardware does not signal an error for stale reads.
The read does not wait by default; waiting needs a barrier.
Right: caches and store buffers mean that the write may not be visible yet.

questions.q: Every CPU core has its own memory cache and store ____, which delay changes reaching main memory.
questions.explain: The changes are written out to main memory asynchronously, leaving several copies of the data.
questions.rule: Caches and store buffers copy the data.

questions.q: Thread A sets a shared flag, but thread B reads it for a long time without seeing it. Which explanation fits the book?
questions.explain: The hardware itself allows stale reads between cores.
questions.rule: Stale reads can happen inside one computer.
options: The network between the two threads is partitioned
The flag is stored on one replica that has failed
B reads a stale cached copy
The operating system uses last write wins
optionExplain: Threads on one machine do not use a network that could be partitioned.
There are no replicas that fail in the distributed sense.
Right: per-core caches can hold an old value. Remember: Stale reads can happen inside one computer.
Last write wins is a conflict resolution method for replicas.

questions.q: True or false: Using a memory barrier or fence after a write makes other cores see the written value.
questions.explain: The book says a thread on another core is guaranteed to read the written value only if a memory barrier or fence is used.
questions.rule: Barriers restore the needed ordering at a cost.

questions.q: What do you need to guarantee that another core reads a value written by a thread on a different core?
questions.explain: Without such an instruction, visibility is not guaranteed.
questions.teaches: Reading the value written by a thread on another CPU core is guaranteed only if a memory barrier or fence is used.
options: A larger memory cache
A faster clock speed
A second copy of the program
A memory barrier or fence
optionExplain: A larger cache would hold more stale copies. The right answer is: A memory barrier or fence.
Clock speed does not control visibility of writes. The right answer is: A memory barrier or fence.
Copies of the program are unrelated. The right answer is: A memory barrier or fence.
Right: this forces the effects to become visible. Remember: Visibility needs an explicit barrier.

questions.q: A developer claims that a database must be linearizable because RAM is. How does the book answer?
questions.explain: Few systems are linearizable in practice, and memory is not one of them.
questions.rule: Do not assume linearizability from a familiar example.
questions.teaches: Surprisingly few systems are actually linearizable in practice; even the RAM on a modern multi-core CPU is not.
options: RAM is linearizable, so the database must also be
Databases are linearizable but RAM is not
Neither RAM nor databases can be linearizable
Even multi-core RAM is not linearizable
optionExplain: The premise is wrong. The right answer is: Even multi-core RAM is not linearizable.
Databases are not automatically linearizable either. The right answer is: Even multi-core RAM is not linearizable.
Some systems are linearizable, such as consensus-based ones. The right answer is: Even multi-core RAM is not linearizable.
Right: the example shows that fast systems often give the guarantee up.

questions.q: Why do many distributed databases offer weaker guarantees than linearizability?
questions.explain: Linearizable operations need coordination, which takes time. The card next shows why.
options: Mainly because networks never fail in datacenters
Mainly to be faster, not so much for fault tolerance
Mainly because linearizability cannot be implemented
Mainly because applications ask for stale reads
optionExplain: Networks do fail; the claim about performance holds even if they do not.
Right: performance is the main reason. Remember: Speed is the usual reason.
Linearizable storage exists, for example in consensus-based systems. The right answer is: Mainly to be faster, not so much for fault tolerance.
Applications do not generally ask for stale data. The right answer is: Mainly to be faster, not so much for fault tolerance.

questions.q: Linearizability is slow, and this is true all the time, not only during a network ____.
questions.explain: The cost is paid in normal operation as well, which is why performance is the main reason to drop it.
questions.rule: The cost is paid every day.

questions.q: A search service with a healthy network and strict latency goals chooses reads from the nearest replica. Which reasoning matches the book?
questions.explain: No fault is needed to justify weaker guarantees when speed is at stake.
questions.rule: Performance alone can justify weaker reads.
options: It trades linearizability for speed
It cannot use replicas at all in this situation
It must be relying on CAP to justify the choice
It has no way to avoid stale reads of any kind
optionExplain: Right: the cost of coordination is paid every day.
Replicas are used in many fast systems. The right answer is: It trades linearizability for speed.
CAP is about faults, which is not the reason here.
Reading elsewhere or waiting avoids staleness at a cost.

questions.q: True or false: A system with a perfectly reliable network can be linearizable without any loss of speed.
questions.explain: Linearizability is slow even without faults: the response time is at least proportional to the uncertainty of delays in the network.
questions.rule: A reliable network does not make coordination free.

questions.q: What does the book say about the many distributed databases that choose not to provide linearizable guarantees?
questions.explain: Latency is the main motivation.
questions.teaches: Many distributed databases choose not to provide linearizable guarantees primarily to increase performance, not so much for fault tolerance.
options: They do so to avoid conflicts between users
They do so primarily to increase performance
They do so because their clocks are inaccurate
They do so because they have no replicas
optionExplain: Conflicts between users are not the stated reason. The right answer is: They do so primarily to increase performance.
Right: not so much for fault tolerance. Remember: The motive is performance.
Clocks are not the stated reason. The right answer is: They do so primarily to increase performance.
They have replicas; that is why linearizability is at stake.

questions.q: A team plans for rare network faults only, and concludes weak consistency is unnecessary. What does the book add?
questions.explain: Rare faults do not remove the everyday cost of coordination.
questions.teaches: The reason for dropping linearizability in multi-core memory and in many distributed databases is performance, and linearizability is slow all the time, not only during a network fault.
options: They are right: the cost arises only during faults
It costs speed when the network is healthy
They are wrong, because faults are very frequent
They must apply CAP to decide the question
optionExplain: The claim that costs arise only during faults is the mistake.
Right: the cost shows even when the network is healthy.
Frequency of faults is not the argument. The right answer is: It costs speed when the network is healthy.
CAP does not cover this cost. The right answer is: It costs speed when the network is healthy.

questions.q: According to the proof the book cites, what limits the response time of linearizable reads and writes?
questions.explain: Waiting out uncertainty about delays costs time. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Variable delays set a floor on linearizable response time.
options: The uncertainty of network delays
The total number of keys in the database
The size of every stored value in bytes
The speed of the disks in each replica node
optionExplain: Right: response time is at least proportional to that uncertainty.
Key count is not part of the bound. The right answer is: The uncertainty of network delays.
Value size is not part of the bound. The right answer is: The uncertainty of network delays.
Disk speed is not part of the bound. The right answer is: The uncertainty of network delays.

questions.q: Attiya and Welch prove that linearizable response time is at least proportional to the uncertainty of ____ in the network.
questions.explain: With highly variable delays, the response time of linearizable operations is inevitably high.
questions.rule: Uncertain delays mean slow linearizable operations.

questions.q: Cross-continent delays vary from 80 ms to 400 ms. What does the proof imply for linearizable reads?
questions.explain: The wider the uncertainty, the slower a linearizable operation must be.
options: Response times fixed at the 80 ms best case
Times proportional to that uncertainty at least
Response times that depend mainly on disk speed
Response times that shrink as replicas are added
optionExplain: The best case does not set the bound. The right answer is: Times proportional to that uncertainty at least.
Right: variable delays mean the floor is high. Remember: Uncertainty sets the floor.
Disks are not the limit. The right answer is: Times proportional to that uncertainty at least.
More replicas do not shrink a bound set by delays.

questions.q: True or false: A team expects to find a faster algorithm for linearizable reads and writes on a variable-delay network.
questions.explain: The book says a faster algorithm for linearizability does not exist, though weaker consistency models can be much faster.
questions.rule: No algorithm beats the proven bound.

questions.q: Must giving up linearizability for speed mean giving up correctness?
questions.explain: Correctness can be kept by other means; the cost lies in the strongest recency promise.
questions.rule: Weaker consistency is not automatically incorrect.
questions.teaches: In Chapter 12 the book discusses some approaches for avoiding linearizability without sacrificing correctness.
options: No: some approaches avoid linearizability without sacrificing correctness
Yes: any weaker model risks returning wrong results
Yes, unless every read is sent to the leader node
No, because weaker models stay linearizable when the network is healthy
optionExplain: Right: the book says it discusses such approaches in Chapter 12.
Weaker is not the same as wrong; the weaker model's guarantees can still be enough.
Sending every read to the leader brings back the coordination cost, so it is not the way out.
Weaker models are not linearizable on a healthy network; they simply do not promise it.

questions.q: A latency-sensitive trading display shows prices that may be a little stale but kept in causal order. Which statement fits the book?
questions.explain: The bound pushes latency-sensitive designs toward weaker models.
questions.teaches: Weaker consistency models can be much faster than linearizable ones, so the trade-off is important for latency-sensitive systems.
options: Weaker models can be much faster, which matters here
Any weaker model is as slow on variable networks
Weaker models cannot be used where latency matters
The proof applies in the same way to every weaker model
optionExplain: Right: this is the point of the bound. Remember: Latency pressure favours weaker models.
Weaker models can be much faster. The right answer is: Weaker models can be much faster, which matters here.
They are used where latency matters. The right answer is: Weaker models can be much faster, which matters here.
The proof is specific to linearizability. The right answer is: Weaker models can be much faster, which matters here.

questions.q: In single-leader replication, what is the main job of the leader with respect to ordering?
questions.explain: The log fixes the sequence that every follower applies. The card next shows why.
options: To decide the order in which clients connect to it
To rank the followers according to their speed
To order the disk blocks of the whole database
To set the order of writes in the log
optionExplain: Client connection order is not what the log records.
Follower speed is unrelated to the order of writes.
Disk layout is not what the leader orders. The right answer is: To set the order of writes in the log.
Right: followers apply writes in that order. Remember: A leader is an order-giver.

questions.q: Match each earlier context with how it deals with ordering.
questions.explain: Each context handles ordering differently: a leader, a serial equivalent, or timestamps. Without a single leader, concurrency produces conflicts.
pairs: The leader sets the order of writes in the replication log
Transactions behave as if executed in some sequential order
An attempt to decide which of two writes happened later
Conflicts can arise from concurrent operations

questions.q: A team uses a Postgres leader for their orders table and later adds multi-leader writes in a second region. What ordering benefit do they lose?
questions.explain: The leader's job was to determine one order; several leaders break that.
options: The ability to number their orders
The use of a replication log
No single node orders all the writes
The ability to read from followers
optionExplain: Orders can still be numbered, though by different nodes.
Each leader still has a log. The right answer is: No single node orders all the writes.
Right: with several leaders, no single node sequences the writes.
Reads from followers remain possible. The right answer is: No single node orders all the writes.

questions.q: True or false: If there is no single leader, conflicts can occur due to concurrent operations.
questions.explain: Without one node ordering the writes, operations may be concurrent and conflict, as discussed under write conflicts.

questions.q: How can serializability be achieved, according to the recap in this section?
questions.explain: Serial execution or conflict prevention by locking or aborting are the two routes.
questions.rule: Two routes to a serial order.
questions.teaches: Serializability can be achieved by literally executing transactions in a serial order, or by allowing concurrent execution while preventing serialization conflicts by locking or aborting.
options: By running each transaction on a separate node
By delaying all reads until every write is finished
By giving each transaction a random priority value
Serial execution, or concurrency with conflicts prevented
optionExplain: Distributing transactions does not make them serializable. The right answer is: Serial execution, or concurrency with conflicts prevented.
Delaying reads is not described as the method. The right answer is: Serial execution, or concurrency with conflicts prevented.
Random priorities are not the method. The right answer is: Serial execution, or concurrency with conflicts prevented.
Right: both routes are named. Remember: Two routes to a serial order.

questions.q: A metrics pipeline uses timestamps from each server to decide which of two samples is newer. Which recurring theme is this?
questions.explain: Timestamps order events but inherit the errors of the clocks.
questions.rule: Clock ordering is an attempt at order.
questions.teaches: The use of timestamps and clocks in distributed systems is another attempt to introduce order into a disorderly world, and the book also warns that there are deep connections between ordering, linearizability and consensus.
options: A guarantee of linearizability itself
A form of consensus
A proof that the clocks are accurate enough
An attempt to introduce order
optionExplain: Timestamps from different clocks do not give linearizability. The right answer is: An attempt to introduce order.
Consensus is agreement among nodes, not timestamps. The right answer is: An attempt to introduce order.
Clocks are approximate, which is the limitation. The right answer is: An attempt to introduce order.
Right: timestamps and clocks are used to introduce order.

questions.q: A chat reader sees a reply but not the message it answers. What is wrong?
questions.explain: A reply exists only because the message was seen first. The card next shows why.
options: The effect is visible without its cause
The reply was sent too quickly
The reply is longer than the question
The chat has too many participants
optionExplain: Right: a reply is causally after the message it answers.
Speed of sending is not the issue; the order of visibility is.
Length is unrelated to causal order. The right answer is: The effect is visible without its cause.
The number of participants does not create the anomaly.

questions.q: Causality means that a cause comes before its ____.
questions.explain: A message is sent before it is received, and a question comes before the answer: cause before effect.

questions.q: In a ride app, a driver accepts a ride and the rider sees a driver-assigned status. Which view would break causality?
questions.explain: The status is an effect of the acceptance, so the acceptance must be visible too.
options: A driver sees the ride before the rider sees the assignment
A rider sees a driver status while the ride is unassigned
Two riders see the driver status at different seconds
A rider sees the ride request after sending it
optionExplain: Two viewers seeing a cause at different moments does not show an effect without its cause.
Right: the acceptance is the cause and must be visible if its effect is.
Different seconds for two riders do not reorder cause and effect.
Seeing a request after sending it respects the order.

questions.q: True or false: In a system that preserves causality, one reader can see an answer to a question that another reader has not yet seen.
questions.explain: Causality constrains what one observer sees, not when different observers see things. A reader who sees an answer must also see its question.
questions.rule: Observers may lag, but not out of causal order.

questions.q: Why does the book say that ordering keeps coming up in its discussions?
questions.explain: Many anomalies are causality violations, so order is the tool to prevent them.
questions.rule: Order is how causality is preserved.
questions.teaches: There are several reasons why ordering keeps coming up, and one of them is that ordering helps preserve causality.
options: It helps preserve causality
It makes databases faster
It removes the need for replication
It reduces storage use
optionExplain: Right: one of the reasons ordering recurs is that it helps preserve causality.
Order tends to cost speed rather than gain it.
Replication remains necessary for fault tolerance. The right answer is: It helps preserve causality.
Order is unrelated to storage use. The right answer is: It helps preserve causality.

questions.q: Node 1 reads a value and writes a result, node 2 reads that result and writes another. What do these chained operations define?
questions.explain: Each step depends on the one before it, so the chain gives a happens-before order.
questions.rule: Chains of dependency define the causal order.
questions.teaches: Chains of causally dependent operations, where one node reads data and writes something as a result and another node reads that and writes in turn, define the causal order in the system, meaning what happened before what.
options: The causal order of events
A total order by wall-clock time
A quorum of nodes that has voted
A set of concurrent operations
optionExplain: Right: chains of causally dependent operations define the causal order.
Clock time may disagree with the chain. The right answer is: The causal order of events.
A quorum concerns voting, not dependency. The right answer is: The causal order of events.
Dependent operations are the opposite of concurrent ones. The right answer is: The causal order of events.

questions.q: A replica receives an update to a row before the replica has received the creation of that row. What is violated?
questions.explain: An update depends on the creation having happened. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A dependent write must follow what it depends on.
options: Causality: creation must precede the update
Durability: the update was lost on disk
Isolation: two transactions ran in parallel
Atomicity: the update was only half applied
optionExplain: Right: the update depends on the creation. Remember: A dependent write must follow what it depends on.
Nothing was lost; the update simply arrived first. The right answer is: Causality: creation must precede the update.
No two transactions are involved here. The right answer is: Causality: creation must precede the update.
The update itself was whole; it arrived out of order.

questions.q: In a conversation, the person giving the ____ must have seen the question first.
questions.explain: That is why seeing the answer before the question violates our intuition of cause and effect.
questions.rule: An answer depends on its question.

questions.q: In a shared task list, a user deletes a comment and another user's replica shows a reply to the missing comment. Which earlier case matches?
questions.explain: A reply without its parent is the conversation anomaly in a different setting.
options: The lost update to one counter
The answer seen without the question
The write skew between two on-call doctors
The dirty write of two transactions
optionExplain: A lost update concerns two writers overwriting each other.
Right: the reply depends on a comment that the viewer cannot see.
Write skew concerns two transactions reading a shared condition.
A dirty write concerns overwriting uncommitted data. The right answer is: The answer seen without the question.

questions.q: True or false: Two writes by clients unaware of each other violate causality if replicas apply them in different orders.
questions.explain: Writes with no causal link are concurrent, and neither knew about the other. Their order is not a causality matter, though replicas may still need to converge.
questions.rule: Concurrent events are not causally ordered.

questions.q: Why is Bob's stale read after hearing Alice a causality violation?
questions.explain: What Alice said was an effect of the announcement, so Bob should not see a state before it.
questions.rule: Alice's words depended on the score.
questions.teaches: Alice's exclamation is causally dependent on the announcement of the score, so Bob should also be able to see the score after hearing Alice; his stale result is a causality violation.
options: Alice's words depended on the score, which Bob should see
Bob's phone has a slower connection than Alice's phone
Alice and Bob refreshed at exactly the same time
The score was announced before the match had ended
optionExplain: Right: Alice's exclamation is causally dependent on the announcement.
Phone speed is not the issue. The right answer is: Alice's words depended on the score, which Bob should see.
If they had refreshed together, the staleness would be less surprising.
The announcement came after the final whistle by definition.

questions.q: Which of these systems shows the same causality pattern as the football example?
questions.explain: A message about a write arrives before the write is visible.
questions.rule: Look for a message that overtakes its data.
questions.teaches: The same causality pattern appeared again in the cross-channel timing dependency of the image resizing service, where the message queue was faster than the replication inside the file storage service.
options: A resizer told about a photo before the store has it
A cache that expires entries after a minute
A backup job that runs every night at midnight
A load balancer that picks the least busy node
optionExplain: Right: the queue message and the stored photo are two channels.
Expiry is a freshness policy, not a causal dependency.
A nightly job has no dependency on another channel.
Load balancing does not order cause and effect. The right answer is: A resizer told about a photo before the store has it.

questions.q: Operations A and B are concurrent. What does that tell us?
questions.explain: No causal link means neither could have known about the other. The card next shows why.
options: Neither knew about the other
They happened at exactly the same clock time
A depended on the result of B
B must be applied before A everywhere
optionExplain: Right: concurrency means no causal link in either direction.
Concurrent does not mean simultaneous by the clock. The right answer is: Neither knew about the other.
A dependency would make them causally ordered, not concurrent.
A required order would again mean a causal relationship.

questions.q: If A happened before B, then B might have known about A, built upon A, or ____ on A.
questions.explain: A happened-before relationship means that B could have been influenced by A.
questions.rule: Happened before means possibly depended on.

questions.q: Two users edit different paragraphs of a shared document without seeing each other's edits. How are their edits related?
questions.explain: What matters is whether either user could have known about the other's edit.
options: Causally ordered: the first edit caused the second
Concurrent: neither edit knew about the other
Causally ordered: the second edit caused the first
Simultaneous: the edits took place at the same second
optionExplain: No knowledge passed from the first edit to the second.
Right: no one saw the other's edit. Remember: Concurrent is about knowledge.
No knowledge passed in the other direction either. The right answer is: Concurrent: neither edit knew about the other.
Concurrency is about knowledge, not about equal timestamps. The right answer is: Concurrent: neither edit knew about the other.

questions.q: True or false: Two operations an hour apart on the clock cannot be concurrent.
questions.explain: Concurrency means neither could have known about the other. An hour apart on the clock is no guarantee that one knew about the other.
questions.rule: Clock time does not decide concurrency.

questions.q: If A and B are concurrent, what are we sure of, according to the book?
questions.explain: Concurrency is the absence of a causal link.
questions.teaches: If A and B are concurrent, there is no causal link between them; in other words, we are sure that neither knew about the other.
options: Neither knew of the other
A happened before B did
B happened before A did
They touched the same key
optionExplain: Right: there is no causal link between them. Remember: Concurrent means mutually unaware.
Concurrent means no known order, so A is not necessarily first.
For the same reason, B is not necessarily first.
They need not even touch the same key. The right answer is: Neither knew of the other.

questions.q: A replica must decide whether to hold back a write until another write arrives. When is holding back needed?
questions.explain: Causally ordered pairs need order; concurrent pairs do not.
questions.rule: Hold back only for causal predecessors.
questions.teaches: Concurrent operations may be processed in any order, but if one operation happened before another, they must be processed in that order on every replica.
options: When the first happened before the second
When the two writes are concurrent with each other
When the two writes have the same size in bytes
When both writes come from a single client
optionExplain: Right: a causally earlier write must be applied first.
Concurrent writes may be applied in any order. The right answer is: When the first happened before the second.
Size does not decide order. The right answer is: When the first happened before the second.
A single client can issue concurrent writes too, though it usually knows its own earlier ones.

questions.q: A database snapshot contains a reply but not the post it replies to. Is it consistent?
questions.explain: Consistency of a snapshot is about causality, not about age. The card next shows why.
options: No: an answer without its question breaks causality
Yes, since each row was stored correctly
Yes, since snapshots do not show any posts at all
No, since the snapshot is far too old to use
optionExplain: Right: a consistent snapshot has the question if it has the answer.
Each row may be fine, but the combination is not.
Snapshots show whatever data was committed by their time.
Age alone does not make a snapshot inconsistent. The right answer is: No: an answer without its question breaks causality.

questions.q: Read ____, or a non-repeatable read, means reading data in a state that violates causality.
questions.explain: The book says that read skew means reading data in a state that violates causality.
questions.rule: Read skew is a causality violation.

questions.q: A bank snapshot includes a transfer's deposit into account B but not the withdrawal from account A. Which statement fits?
questions.explain: The deposit is an effect of the withdrawal, so a causally consistent snapshot has both or neither.
questions.rule: Both parts of a causal pair, or neither.
options: It is consistent, since both accounts balance in total money
Causality is violated: the effect has no cause
It is consistent, since snapshots may be old
It is invalid, since banks cannot take snapshots
optionExplain: Totals matter less; the cause is missing. The right answer is: Causality is violated: the effect has no cause.
Right: the deposit depends on the withdrawal. Remember: Both parts of a causal pair, or neither.
Old is fine, but half a transfer is not.
Snapshots are allowed; this one is simply inconsistent. The right answer is: Causality is violated: the effect has no cause.

questions.q: True or false: A causally consistent snapshot is the most recent state of the database.
questions.explain: Consistent with causality means no effect without its cause. A snapshot excludes newer writes and may be old.

questions.q: How do the on-call doctors in the write skew example show a causal dependency?
questions.explain: Each transaction acted on a state that the other's action would change.
questions.teaches: In the write skew example, Alice was allowed to go off call because her transaction thought Bob was still on call, and vice versa; the action of going off call is causally dependent on the observation of who is currently on call.
options: Going off call depended on who was on call
Both doctors wrote to the same row at once
The database lost one doctor's update
Each doctor read an older snapshot than the other
optionExplain: Right: the action depended on what each transaction had observed.
They wrote to different rows; the conflict was in their reasoning.
No update was lost. The right answer is: Going off call depended on who was on call.
The point is not the snapshot age but the dependency.

questions.q: Which technique detects write skew by tracking causal dependencies between transactions?
questions.explain: SSI watches what each transaction read and flags a commit when that is out of date.
questions.teaches: Serializable snapshot isolation detects write skew by tracking the causal dependencies between transactions.
options: Serializable snapshot isolation
Read committed with row-level locks
Last write wins resolution
Sloppy quorums with handoff
optionExplain: Right: SSI detects write skew by tracking causal dependencies.
Read committed does not track dependencies between transactions. The right answer is: Serializable snapshot isolation.
Last write wins picks a winner by timestamp. The right answer is: Serializable snapshot isolation.
Sloppy quorums relax guarantees. The right answer is: Serializable snapshot isolation.

questions.q: Which description matches a causally consistent database?
questions.explain: Causal consistency is about dependencies, not recency or sameness. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: See an effect, see its causes.
options: Every read returns the latest write made by anyone
All replicas hold exactly the same data at all times
If you see data, you see the data that causally precedes it
Every transaction runs strictly one after the other
optionExplain: That is the recency guarantee of linearizability. The right answer is: If you see data, you see the data that causally precedes it.
That would be a much stronger promise than causal consistency.
Right: this is the defining property. Remember: See an effect, see its causes.
That describes serializability. The right answer is: If you see data, you see the data that causally precedes it.

questions.q: A system that obeys the ordering imposed by causality is called causally ____.
questions.explain: Causal consistency means the system respects the ordering of cause and effect.

questions.q: A lagging replica shows a comment but not the post it replies to. Is the forum causally consistent?
questions.explain: A lagging replica is fine if it lags consistently.
questions.rule: Lag is allowed; missing causes are not.
options: Yes, since the replica is only lagging behind
Yes, since the comment itself was stored safely
No, since the replica is lagging behind the leader
No: the reader saw an effect without its cause
optionExplain: Lagging is allowed; seeing the comment without the post is not.
Storage alone does not satisfy the dependency. The right answer is: No: the reader saw an effect without its cause.
Lagging itself is not the violation; the missing post is.
Right: the comment depends on the post. Remember: Lag is allowed; missing causes are not.

questions.q: True or false: In a causally consistent system, a reader who sees a comment may be shown the post it replies to only later.
questions.explain: In a causally consistent system, you must be able to see the data that causally precedes what you see, so the post must be visible with the comment.
questions.rule: Causes must be visible together with effects.

questions.q: According to the book, which isolation level provides causal consistency?
questions.explain: A snapshot shows a point in time, so causes come with effects.
questions.teaches: Snapshot isolation provides causal consistency: when you read from the database and see some data, you must also be able to see any data that causally precedes it.
options: Read uncommitted
Eventual consistency
Snapshot isolation
Sloppy quorums
optionExplain: Read uncommitted allows even dirty reads. The right answer is: Snapshot isolation.
Eventual consistency promises only convergence. The right answer is: Snapshot isolation.
Right: snapshot isolation provides causal consistency. Remember: Snapshots respect causality.
Sloppy quorums give up even more. The right answer is: Snapshot isolation.

questions.q: A reader sees a post that causally follows a comment that has since been deleted. What does the book allow?
questions.explain: The exception covers data removed after the fact.
questions.teaches: Snapshot isolation provides causal consistency assuming the data that causally precedes has not been deleted in the meantime.
options: The reader must still see the deleted comment
The post must be hidden from the reader too
The comment may be absent if it was deleted meanwhile
The system loses its causal consistency entirely
optionExplain: A deleted item need not be visible. The right answer is: The comment may be absent if it was deleted meanwhile.
Hiding the post is not required. The right answer is: The comment may be absent if it was deleted meanwhile.
Right: the rule applies if it has not been deleted meanwhile.
Deletion is the exception that the book names. The right answer is: The comment may be absent if it was deleted meanwhile.

questions.q: Can you say which of the sets {a, b} and {b, c} is greater?
questions.explain: Under the subset ordering, neither contains the other. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Incomparable pairs make an order partial.
options: Yes, because {a, b} comes first alphabetically
Yes, because both have two elements
No, because sets cannot contain letters
No, because neither is a subset of the other
optionExplain: Alphabetical order is a different ordering from the subset order.
Equal size makes them tie, not comparable as greater or smaller.
Sets can contain any elements. The right answer is: No, because neither is a subset of the other.
Right: they are incomparable. Remember: Incomparable pairs make an order partial.

questions.q: Natural numbers are ____ ordered: any two of them can be compared.
questions.explain: Of any two numbers, one is greater than the other, so the order is total.
questions.rule: Any two elements comparable: total order.

questions.q: Match each collection with the kind of order described in the book.
questions.explain: Numbers can always be compared. Sets are comparable only when one contains the other.
questions.rule: Check whether every pair can be compared.
pairs: Mathematical sets under the subset relation
Comparable: the first is contained in the second

questions.q: Which statement about a partial order is correct?
questions.explain: Partial means that comparison is defined only for some pairs.
options: No pairs can be compared
All pairs can be compared, but only in one direction
Some pairs can be compared, and some cannot
It is an order that skips some elements
optionExplain: If nothing could be compared, there would be no order.
That describes a total order. The right answer is: Some pairs can be compared, and some cannot.
Right: that is what makes it partial. Remember: Partial: some pairs incomparable.
Elements are not skipped; some pairs are incomparable. The right answer is: Some pairs can be compared, and some cannot.

questions.q: In a partial order of sets, when is one set greater than another?
questions.explain: Comparable sets are nested; others are incomparable.
questions.teaches: In a partial order of sets, one set is greater than another if it contains all the elements of the other; in other cases the sets are incomparable.
options: When it has a greater number of elements
When it was created at a later time
