When it has the same first element
When it holds all elements of the other
optionExplain: More elements alone does not make it a superset.
Creation time is not part of the ordering. The right answer is: When it holds all elements of the other.
A shared first element does not decide the order.
Right: this is the subset relation. Remember: Nested sets are comparable.

questions.q: Two events are concurrent because neither could know about the other. What does this mean for their order?
questions.explain: Causality gives a partial order: related events are ordered, concurrent ones are not.
questions.teaches: Causality defines a partial order: two events are ordered if they are causally related, but they are incomparable if they are concurrent.
options: The earlier one is the greater of the two
They are equal to each other in order
They must be placed in clock order
Incomparable, like sets that are not nested
optionExplain: No event is greater without a causal link. The right answer is: Incomparable, like sets that are not nested.
Concurrent events are not equal; they are unrelated. The right answer is: Incomparable, like sets that are not nested.
Clock order is not defined by causality. The right answer is: Incomparable, like sets that are not nested.
Right: concurrent events are incomparable under causality. Remember: Concurrent equals incomparable.

questions.q: Which description fits the history of a linearizable datastore?
questions.explain: One copy, one timeline. The card next shows why.
options: A timeline that branches and merges
One timeline per replica
A single straight timeline
A set of unordered operations
optionExplain: Branching and merging describes concurrent histories. The right answer is: A single straight timeline.
Separate timelines per replica would not behave as one copy.
Right: all operations are totally ordered. Remember: Linearizable means one timeline.
Unordered operations are not a total order. The right answer is: A single straight timeline.

questions.q: In a linearizable datastore, operations are totally ordered along a single ____.
questions.explain: The system acts on a single copy of the data, along a single timeline, without concurrency.

questions.q: A version history looks like a straight line of commits with no branches. Which model does it match?
questions.explain: A line has no incomparable pairs.
questions.rule: No branches means a total order.
options: A partial order, like causality with concurrency
A set of unrelated events
An eventually consistent store
A total order, like a linearizable store
optionExplain: A partial order would show branches and merges. The right answer is: A total order, like a linearizable store.
Unrelated events would not form a line. The right answer is: A total order, like a linearizable store.
Eventual consistency does not prescribe a line. The right answer is: A total order, like a linearizable store.
Right: every commit comes before or after every other.

questions.q: True or false: In a linearizable store, two operations can be concurrent in the causal sense, with neither ordered before the other.
questions.explain: Every operation takes effect atomically at one point on a single timeline, so any two are ordered.
questions.rule: No concurrency in a linearizable store.

questions.q: How does the book compare a causal history with a familiar tool?
questions.explain: Commits often follow in a line, but concurrent work makes branches and merges.
questions.teaches: Distributed version control systems such as Git have version histories much like the graph of causal dependencies: commits often follow one another in a straight line, but concurrent work creates branches, and merges combine concurrently created commits.
options: With a bank ledger that lists transfers in time order
With a stack of plates that is added to and removed from
With Git, where commits form branches and merges
With a clock whose hands move forward
optionExplain: A ledger is a single line, which resembles a total order.
A stack has no branching. The right answer is: With Git, where commits form branches and merges.
Right: Git histories are like graphs of causal dependencies.
A clock is a total order. The right answer is: With Git, where commits form branches and merges.

questions.q: Several requests are waiting for a linearizable store at the same moment. What does the store guarantee about each?
questions.explain: The store orders waiting requests onto one timeline.
questions.rule: Queues of requests still end up in a single order.
questions.teaches: There might be several requests waiting to be handled, but a linearizable datastore ensures that every request is handled atomically at a single point in time, acting on a single copy of the data, along a single timeline, without any concurrency.
options: It is handled at the same time as the others
It is handled by a different replica each time
It is handled atomically at one point on one copy
It is handled on a separate timeline
optionExplain: Handling at the same time would create concurrency. The right answer is: It is handled atomically at one point on one copy.
Different replicas would break the single-copy illusion. The right answer is: It is handled atomically at one point on one copy.
Right: waiting together does not make them concurrent in the store.
A separate timeline would be a branch. The right answer is: It is handled atomically at one point on one copy.

questions.q: A system is linearizable. What follows about causality?
questions.explain: The single timeline already respects cause and effect. The card next shows why.
options: Causality is preserved without any special handling
Causality must be tracked separately with timestamps
Causality is violated when there are several channels
Causality is preserved only for single-key operations
optionExplain: Right: linearizability implies causality. Remember: Linearizable implies causally consistent.
Timestamps are not needed; the guarantee covers it. The right answer is: Causality is preserved without any special handling.
Several channels are exactly where the guarantee helps. The right answer is: Causality is preserved without any special handling.
The guarantee covers operations across channels. The right answer is: Causality is preserved without any special handling.

questions.q: True or false: Any system that is linearizable will preserve causality correctly.
questions.explain: The book states that linearizability implies causality.

questions.q: A linearizable file store and a queue both tell a worker about an upload. What extra step preserves causality?
questions.explain: The guarantee does the work that timestamps or version vectors would do.
options: Passing timestamps between the components
None: linearizability preserves it automatically
Adding a version vector to every message
Running the worker and the store on one node
optionExplain: Timestamps would be needed without linearizability. The right answer is: None: linearizability preserves it automatically.
Right: the linearizable store guarantees the worker sees the upload.
Version vectors are another way, which this store makes unnecessary.
Co-location is not needed. The right answer is: None: linearizability preserves it automatically.

questions.q: A geographically distributed team makes every store linearizable to preserve causality. What do they risk?
questions.explain: The price is paid in latency and availability.
options: Lost causality across channels
Worse performance and availability
Inconsistent reads on a single key
A weaker guarantee than causal consistency
optionExplain: Causality is preserved. The right answer is: Worse performance and availability.
Right: the cost grows with network delays. Remember: Strength costs performance.
Reads on one key are consistent. The right answer is: Worse performance and availability.
Linearizability is the stronger guarantee. The right answer is: Worse performance and availability.

questions.q: Linearizability ensuring ____ is what makes linearizable systems simple to understand and appealing.
questions.explain: The guarantee spares developers from tracking causal dependencies themselves, which is why the systems are simple to reason about.
questions.teaches: The fact that linearizability ensures causality is what makes linearizable systems simple to understand and appealing, even though it can harm performance and availability.

questions.q: A data system abandons linearizability to gain speed. What is the consequence the book names?
questions.explain: Without the guarantee, developers must handle causality themselves.
questions.teaches: Some distributed data systems have abandoned linearizability, which allows them to achieve better performance but can make them difficult to work with.
options: It can be difficult to work with
It loses durability
It stops using replication
It becomes linearizable at night
optionExplain: Right: abandoning it gives better performance but makes the system harder to work with.
Durability is a separate property. The right answer is: It can be difficult to work with.
Replication remains. The right answer is: It can be difficult to work with.
Nothing like that applies. The right answer is: It can be difficult to work with.

questions.q: Which consistency model is the strongest that does not slow down because of network delays and stays available in network failures?
questions.explain: Causal consistency has the strongest guarantee that can survive a partition. The card next shows why.
options: Linearizability
Strict serializability
Sequential consistency
Causal consistency
optionExplain: Linearizability slows down with network delays. The right answer is: Causal consistency.
It includes linearizability, which has the same cost. The right answer is: Causal consistency.
It adds an order that needs coordination. The right answer is: Causal consistency.
Right: the CAP theorem does not apply to it.

questions.q: True or false: A system can be causally consistent without incurring the performance hit of linearizability.
questions.explain: Linearizability is not the only way to preserve causality, and the CAP theorem does not apply to causal consistency.

questions.q: A collaborative editor must stay usable during network failures but show replies after their questions. Which model fits?
questions.explain: Replies after questions is a causality requirement, and staying usable under failures rules out linearizability.
questions.rule: Match the requirement to the weakest model that satisfies it.
options: Linearizability
Strict serializability
Causal consistency
A single leader with synchronous followers
optionExplain: Linearizability would block on the cut-off side. The right answer is: Causal consistency.
That is stronger still and equally costly. The right answer is: Causal consistency.
Right: causality without coordination across the network. Remember: Match the requirement to the weakest model that satisfies it.
Synchronous followers need the leader to be reachable. The right answer is: Causal consistency.

questions.q: True or false: Moving a comment feed to a causally consistent store can still guarantee that no reply appears before its parent.
questions.explain: Causal consistency keeps causes with their effects, so a reply is shown only together with the comment it answers.

questions.q: Many systems that appear to require linearizability in fact only require ____ consistency, which can be implemented more efficiently.
questions.explain: The research direction rests on this observation: check what the application really requires before paying for the strongest guarantee.
questions.teaches: In many cases, systems that appear to require linearizability in fact only really require causal consistency, which can be implemented more efficiently.

questions.q: What is the status of databases that preserve causality while performing like eventually consistent systems?
questions.explain: The idea is promising, but the research is recent.
questions.rule: A promising direction, not yet mainstream.
questions.teaches: Researchers are exploring new kinds of databases that preserve causality with performance and availability similar to eventually consistent systems, but this research is recent, not much has reached production, and challenges remain.
options: Standard practice in all of the major databases
Proven impossible to build in practice
Obsolete and replaced by linearizable stores
Active research, with little in production
optionExplain: Not much of it has reached production. The right answer is: Active research, with little in production.
They are not proven impossible. The right answer is: Active research, with little in production.
They are not obsolete. The right answer is: Active research, with little in production.
Right: promising but recent. Remember: A promising direction, not yet mainstream.

questions.q: A replica receives a write that depends on an earlier write it has not yet seen. What should it do?
questions.explain: A missing predecessor means that the operation must wait. The card next shows why.
options: Apply it at once and apply the earlier one later
Discard the later write
Ask the client to resend it later
Wait until the earlier write has been processed
optionExplain: Applying out of order shows an effect without its cause.
Discarding loses a valid write. The right answer is: Wait until the earlier write has been processed.
The client does not control the order of processing.
Right: preceding operations must be processed first. Remember: Predecessors first.

questions.q: To decide whether Y depends on X, we ask what the node already ____ when it issued the write Y.
questions.explain: If the node had already seen the value X when it issued Y, then X and Y may be causally related.

questions.q: Replica R gets reply F for post P, but not P. A different reply G has no dependency on P. What should R do?
questions.explain: Concurrent operations can be processed in any order; dependent ones wait.
options: Hold both F and G until P arrives
Process both F and G at once, in any order
Hold F until P arrives, and process G at once
Discard F and then process G
optionExplain: G does not depend on P, so it need not wait.
Processing F now shows a reply without its post.
Right: only the causally dependent operation needs to wait.
Discarding loses the reply. The right answer is: Hold F until P arrives, and process G at once.

questions.q: True or false: Causal consistency needs to track causal dependencies across the entire database, not only for one key.
questions.explain: Detecting concurrent writes to one key is only part of it; the dependencies span all the data a node has read.

questions.q: How is causal tracking related to the detection of concurrent writes in a leaderless store?
questions.explain: Causal consistency must follow dependencies across keys.
questions.rule: A larger scope than a single key.
questions.teaches: Causal consistency needs to track causal dependencies across the entire database, not just for a single key as in detecting concurrent writes; version vectors can be generalized to do this.
options: It is identical in scope and purpose
It applies only to leader-based stores
It replaces the need for version numbers
It goes further, covering the whole database
optionExplain: Detecting concurrent writes was for one key. The right answer is: It goes further, covering the whole database.
Leaderless stores are where the idea started. The right answer is: It goes further, covering the whole database.
Versions are still used. The right answer is: It goes further, covering the whole database.
Right: version vectors can be generalized for this. Remember: A larger scope than a single key.

questions.q: Which mechanism in serializable snapshot isolation resembles causal tracking?
questions.explain: Both need to know which version of the data was read.
questions.rule: Versions read matter in both cases.
questions.teaches: Serializable snapshot isolation also keeps track of which data has been read by which transaction, and at commit it checks whether the version it read is still up to date.
options: Locking every row that a transaction has read
Running all the transactions one after another
Assigning random priorities to transactions
Checking at commit that what was read is still current
optionExplain: Locking is two-phase locking, not SSI. The right answer is: Checking at commit that what was read is still current.
Serial execution is another technique. The right answer is: Checking at commit that what was read is still current.
Random priorities are not used. The right answer is: Checking at commit that what was read is still current.
Right: the database tracks which data was read by which transaction.

questions.q: A client reads hundreds of rows and then writes one. What makes tracking its causal dependencies hard?
questions.explain: Without knowing which reads mattered, the safe choice is to track them all. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Dependencies are fuzzy, tracking is costly.
options: The write takes longer than reading the rows
The rows cannot be read by more than one client
Unclear if the write depends on all the reads or some
The database forgets which rows were read by the client
optionExplain: Duration of the write is a different matter from dependency.
Many clients can read the same rows. The right answer is: Unclear if the write depends on all the reads or some.
Right: tracking everything read means a large overhead. Remember: Dependencies are fuzzy, tracking is costly.
The database could record it, but the cost is the problem.

questions.q: A logical clock generates a sequence of numbers to identify operations, typically using ____ that are incremented for every operation.
questions.explain: Logical clocks do not read the time of day; they count operations.

questions.q: A team wants to order edits across servers, but keeping lists of every record each edit read is too costly. What do they use?
questions.explain: A counter replaces explicit tracking with a cheap label.
options: A full copy of the database attached to every edit
The wall-clock time on each editing laptop
The size of each edit in bytes
A counter-based number attached to every edit
optionExplain: A full copy is the most expensive way to record what was read.
Wall clocks disagree across laptops, so they do not give a dependable order.
Size says nothing about the order. The right answer is: A counter-based number attached to every edit.
Right: a logical clock gives each edit a number.

questions.q: True or false: A timestamp used to order operations must come from a time-of-day clock.
questions.explain: A timestamp can come from a logical clock instead: an algorithm that generates numbers, typically with counters.
questions.rule: Timestamp does not mean time of day.

questions.q: Besides being cheap to produce, what else do sequence numbers offer for ordering?
questions.explain: Unique numbers can always be compared, so any two operations are ordered.
questions.teaches: Sequence numbers or timestamps are compact, only a few bytes in size, and provide a total order: every operation has a unique number, and you can always compare two of them to see which operation happened later.
options: They record who read what
They give a partial order that shows concurrency
They are compact, a few bytes, and give a total order
They make clocks unnecessary in every system
optionExplain: They do not record dependencies. The right answer is: They are compact, a few bytes, and give a total order.
A single number cannot show concurrency. The right answer is: They are compact, a few bytes, and give a total order.
Right: every operation has a unique number and any two can be compared.
They replace time-of-day clocks only for ordering. The right answer is: They are compact, a few bytes, and give a total order.

questions.q: Why is the overhead of explicit dependency tracking large in many applications?
questions.explain: Explicitly tracking everything read costs more than the benefit.
questions.rule: Large read sets make tracking expensive.
questions.teaches: In many applications clients read lots of data before writing, and it is not clear whether the write is causally dependent on all or only some of those prior reads; explicitly tracking all the data read would mean a large overhead.
options: Most writes depend on no earlier reads at all in practice
Reads and writes use different networks in most systems
Clients read much before writing; dependencies are unclear
Databases are unable to store version numbers at all
optionExplain: If writes depended on no reads, tracking would be unnecessary.
The network used is not the point. The right answer is: Clients read much before writing; dependencies are unclear.
Right: tracking all that was read would mean a large overhead.
Databases can store version numbers. The right answer is: Clients read much before writing; dependencies are unclear.

questions.q: Operation A causally happened before B. Which sequence numbers are acceptable in a causally consistent total order?
questions.explain: Cause comes first in the order. The card next shows why.
options: A higher than B
A equal to B
A lower than B
Any numbers, since only clock time matters
optionExplain: A higher number for the cause contradicts causality. The right answer is: A lower than B.
Equal numbers would not be a total order. The right answer is: A lower than B.
Right: a cause must come before its effect. Remember: Causes get lower numbers.
Clock time is not what the consistency requires. The right answer is: A lower than B.

questions.q: In a total order consistent with causality, concurrent operations may be ordered ____.
questions.explain: Only causally related operations are constrained; concurrent ones can go in any order.

questions.q: Messages M1 and M2 are concurrent, and M3 replies to M1. Which numbering is consistent with causality?
questions.explain: Check each cause and effect pair: the effect needs the higher number.
optionExplain: M3 gets 2, a lower number than its cause M1 with 3, so the reply comes before its cause.
M3=1 is lower than M1=2, so the reply comes before its cause.
M3=1 is lower than M1=3, so the reply comes before its cause.
Right: M1 is before its reply M3, and M2 is placed arbitrarily.

questions.q: True or false: A total order consistent with causality imposes exactly the ordering that causality requires and no more.
questions.explain: It captures all causality information but also orders concurrent operations, which is more ordering than strictly required.

questions.q: Why does the book call a total order based on random UUIDs a poor choice?
questions.explain: A total order inconsistent with causality is easy but not useful.
questions.rule: Total is not enough; it must be causal.
questions.teaches: A total order that is inconsistent with causality is easy to create, for example comparing random UUIDs lexicographically, but the UUIDs tell you nothing about which operation actually happened first or whether the operations were concurrent.
options: UUIDs cannot be compared with each other at all
UUIDs are not unique enough to be used
A valid total order that says nothing about what came first
UUIDs are far too large to be stored cheaply
optionExplain: They can be compared lexicographically. The right answer is: A valid total order that says nothing about what came first.
Random UUIDs are unique enough. The right answer is: A valid total order that says nothing about what came first.
Right: it does not respect causality. Remember: Total is not enough; it must be causal.
Size is not the objection. The right answer is: A valid total order that says nothing about what came first.

questions.q: Given only causally consistent sequence numbers 4 and 7, what can you conclude about the operations?
questions.explain: Numbers rule out the reverse dependency only.
questions.rule: A higher number never proves a dependency.
questions.teaches: A causally consistent total order lets you rule out that the higher-numbered operation causally preceded the lower, but it does not tell whether the two operations were concurrent or causally dependent.
options: Operation 7 happened later by the clock
The operations are concurrent
Operation 7 did not causally precede operation 4
Operation 4 caused operation 7
optionExplain: Numbers are not wall-clock times. The right answer is: Operation 7 did not causally precede operation 4.
Numbers cannot show concurrency. The right answer is: Operation 7 did not causally precede operation 4.
Right: if 7 had causally preceded 4, it would have a lower number.
Order does not show that one caused the other.

questions.q: In single-leader replication, who decides the order of writes?
questions.explain: The log is the single source of order. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: The leader's log is the order.
options: Each follower, by the time of arrival
Each client, by the time of sending
A shared clock that all nodes read
The leader, by appending them to the log
optionExplain: Followers apply what the leader has decided. The right answer is: The leader, by appending them to the log.
Clients cannot see each other's sending order. The right answer is: The leader, by appending them to the log.
No shared clock is used. The right answer is: The leader, by appending them to the log.
Right: the log order is the order. Remember: The leader's log is the order.

questions.q: The leader gives each write in the replication log a monotonically ____ sequence number.
questions.explain: The leader increments a counter for each operation, so numbers only go up.

questions.q: A follower applies the leader's log in order but is a minute behind. Is its state causally consistent?
questions.explain: A prefix of a causal order is itself causal.
options: No, since it lags
Only if its clock is synchronised
Yes, even though it lags
Only after it has caught up
optionExplain: Lag is not a causal violation. The right answer is: Yes, even though it lags.
Clocks do not matter here. The right answer is: Yes, even though it lags.
Right: applying in log order keeps causes before effects.
Each prefix of the log is causally consistent. The right answer is: Yes, even though it lags.

questions.q: True or false: A follower that applies writes in the order they appear in the log can show a causality violation if it lags behind.
questions.explain: Even if the follower is behind the leader, its state is always causally consistent, because it applies writes in log order.

questions.q: What can the book say about a lagging follower that applies the log in order?
questions.explain: Causal consistency does not demand recency.
questions.teaches: If a follower applies the writes in the order they appear in the replication log, its state is always causally consistent, even if it is lagging behind the leader.
options: Its state is linearizable
Its state is the latest state
Its state is the same as the leader's
Its state is always causally consistent
optionExplain: Lagging reads can be stale, so they are not linearizable.
It is behind the latest state. The right answer is: Its state is always causally consistent.
It differs from the leader's until it catches up.
Right: lag does not break causality. Remember: Lagging but causal.

questions.q: A multi-leader, leaderless or partitioned database has no single leader. What problem arises?
questions.explain: The single leader was the source of the counter.
questions.rule: No single leader, no single counter.
questions.teaches: If there is not a single leader, because you use multi-leader or leaderless replication or a partitioned database, it is less clear how to generate sequence numbers for operations.
options: It cannot store a sequence number at all
It no longer has any total order
It must use time-of-day clocks
It is less clear how to number operations
optionExplain: Storing a number is not the issue. The right answer is: It is less clear how to number operations.
A total order can still be produced by other generators.
Time-of-day clocks are only one option. The right answer is: It is less clear how to number operations.
Right: there is no single counter. Remember: No single leader, no single counter.

questions.q: Two nodes generate numbers independently so they cannot clash. Which scheme does that?
questions.explain: Disjoint sets cannot clash. The card next shows why.
options: Both nodes issue the next number after the largest they see
Both nodes use the same counter in turn
Both nodes issue random numbers
One node issues odd numbers and the other even numbers
optionExplain: Both could choose the same next number. The right answer is: One node issues odd numbers and the other even numbers.
Taking turns requires coordination. The right answer is: One node issues odd numbers and the other even numbers.
Random numbers can clash. The right answer is: One node issues odd numbers and the other even numbers.
Right: the sets are disjoint. Remember: Disjoint sets guarantee uniqueness.

questions.q: Match each method with how it creates unique sequence numbers.
questions.explain: All four give unique numbers without a central counter.
pairs: Each node generates its own disjoint set of numbers
Each operation gets the physical clock reading
Each node claims a range, such as 1 to 1,000, in advance
Reserved bits in the number identify the node

questions.q: A team gives node A the block 1 to 1,000 and node B the block 1,001 to 2,000. What happens when A runs out?
questions.explain: Nodes allocate a new block when needed.
options: A stops issuing numbers until restarted
A takes numbers from B's block
A claims a new block when running low
A restarts numbering from 1 again
optionExplain: Stopping would halt the service. The right answer is: A claims a new block when running low.
Taking B's numbers risks clashes. The right answer is: A claims a new block when running low.
Right: blocks are allocated again as needed. Remember: Blocks are replenished.
Restarting from 1 repeats numbers. The right answer is: A claims a new block when running low.

questions.q: True or false: Number generators like odd and even counters can be consistent with causality if the nodes issue numbers at the same rate.
questions.explain: Nodes process different numbers of operations per second, so one counter can lag behind the other, and the numbers do not capture the causal order.

questions.q: How can a number guarantee that two different nodes cannot produce the same value?
questions.explain: Bits for the node ID keep each node's numbers separate.
questions.teaches: You can reserve some bits in the binary representation of the sequence number to contain a unique node identifier, which ensures that two different nodes can never generate the same sequence number.
options: Add a random digit at the end
Ask the other node for permission each time
Use the clock's microseconds
Reserve some bits for a unique node identifier
optionExplain: A random digit can clash. The right answer is: Reserve some bits for a unique node identifier.
Asking permission needs coordination. The right answer is: Reserve some bits for a unique node identifier.
Clocks can repeat. The right answer is: Reserve some bits for a unique node identifier.
Right: the node ID makes numbers distinct. Remember: Include the node identifier.

questions.q: Why is it attractive to use one of these three methods instead of a single leader's counter?
questions.explain: No single node is a bottleneck.
questions.rule: They scale; they do not order causally.
questions.teaches: These three options all perform better and are more scalable than pushing all operations through a single leader that increments a counter, and each generates a unique, approximately increasing sequence number for each operation.
options: They give a more exact order
They remove all faults
They need no storage
They perform better and are more scalable
optionExplain: They give a less exact order. The right answer is: They perform better and are more scalable.
They do not remove faults. The right answer is: They perform better and are more scalable.
They still need storage. The right answer is: They perform better and are more scalable.
Right: no single node sequences everything. Remember: They scale; they do not order causally.

questions.q: Node X issues odd numbers and has handled 100 operations; node Y issues even numbers and has handled 10. What problem arises?
questions.explain: Different rates of operations make counters drift apart. The card next shows why.
options: Y's numbers cannot be compared with X's
X's numbers repeat after a short time
Y's numbers eventually become negative values
X's counter runs ahead, so numbers ignore causal order
optionExplain: Odd and even numbers can be compared, and that is the trouble.
Odd numbers do not repeat. The right answer is: X's counter runs ahead, so numbers ignore causal order.
Counters do not go negative. The right answer is: X's counter runs ahead, so numbers ignore causal order.
Right: a causally later operation at Y can get a lower number.

questions.q: With time-of-day timestamps, clock ____ can give a causally later operation a lower timestamp.
questions.explain: Clocks on different nodes disagree, so timestamps do not follow real event order.

questions.q: A holds block 1 to 1,000; B holds 1,001 to 2,000. An operation at B is causally followed by one at A. What is possible?
questions.explain: Blocks are separate ranges, so the later operation can fall in a lower block.
options: The later operation gets a larger number
Both get the same number
The later operation gets a smaller number than the earlier
A refuses to issue numbers
optionExplain: That would be consistent with causality, but it is not guaranteed.
Blocks do not overlap. The right answer is: The later operation gets a smaller number than the earlier.
Right: A's numbers are lower than B's. Remember: Separate ranges ignore causality.
Nothing makes A refuse. The right answer is: The later operation gets a smaller number than the earlier.

questions.q: True or false: With blocks 1 to 1,000 for node 1 and 1,001 to 2,000 for node 2, node 2's numbers exceed node 1's.
questions.explain: Blocks do not overlap, so a causally later operation at node 1 can get a lower number than an earlier one at node 2.
questions.rule: Blocks order by node, not by causality.

questions.q: How can Google's Spanner make timestamps consistent with causality using physical clocks?
questions.explain: Waiting out the uncertainty interval separates the timestamps.
questions.rule: Physical timestamps can be causal if the uncertainty is waited out.
questions.teaches: Google's Spanner estimates the expected clock skew and waits out the uncertainty interval before committing a write, which ensures that a causally later transaction is given a greater timestamp.
options: It uses random numbers instead of clocks
It sends every write through a single leader
It ignores the clocks completely and uses none
It estimates clock uncertainty and waits it out
optionExplain: Random numbers do not help. The right answer is: It estimates clock uncertainty and waits it out.
Spanner does not use a single leader for all writes.
Spanner uses clocks, with an uncertainty estimate. The right answer is: It estimates clock uncertainty and waits it out.
Right: a causally later transaction then gets a greater timestamp.

questions.q: Why can most databases not copy the Spanner approach to physical timestamps?
questions.explain: Without an uncertainty estimate there is nothing to wait out.
questions.teaches: It is possible to make physical clock timestamps consistent with causality, but most clocks cannot provide the required uncertainty metric.
options: Most databases do not use timestamps
Most databases have no clocks at all
Most databases have too many nodes
Most clocks give no uncertainty metric
optionExplain: Many databases use timestamps. The right answer is: Most clocks give no uncertainty metric.
Machines have clocks, but without an error bound. The right answer is: Most clocks give no uncertainty metric.
Node count is not the obstacle. The right answer is: Most clocks give no uncertainty metric.
Right: Spanner depends on a bound for clock error.

questions.q: What are the two parts of a Lamport timestamp?
questions.explain: A counter orders operations; the node ID breaks ties. The card next shows why.
options: A calendar date and a time of day
A counter and a node identifier
A key and a value pair
A hash and a digital signature
optionExplain: Lamport timestamps are not tied to the clock. The right answer is: A counter and a node identifier.
Right: the pair (counter, node ID). Remember: (counter, node ID).
That describes a record. The right answer is: A counter and a node identifier.
That describes authenticated data. The right answer is: A counter and a node identifier.

questions.q: Including the ____ in a Lamport timestamp makes each timestamp unique.
questions.explain: Two nodes may have the same counter value, but the node ID makes the pairs different.
questions.rule: The node ID makes it unique.

questions.q: Which of these two Lamport timestamps is the greater: (5, node 2) or (3, node 9)?
questions.explain: Compare counters first.
options: (5, node 2), because its counter is greater
(3, node 9), because its node ID is greater
They are equal
They cannot be compared
optionExplain: Right: the counter is compared first. Remember: Counter first.
Node ID only matters when counters tie. The right answer is: (5, node 2), because its counter is greater.
They are different pairs. The right answer is: (5, node 2), because its counter is greater.
Lamport timestamps are always comparable. The right answer is: (5, node 2), because its counter is greater.

questions.q: True or false: A Lamport timestamp has a meaningful relationship to the time of day on a physical clock.
questions.explain: A Lamport timestamp bears no relationship to a physical time-of-day clock, yet it provides a total ordering.

questions.q: Who proposed Lamport timestamps, and when?
questions.explain: The method is named after its inventor.
questions.teaches: Lamport timestamps were proposed in 1978 by Leslie Lamport, in what is now one of the most-cited papers in the field of distributed systems.
options: Eric Brewer, in 2000
Leslie Lamport, in 1978
Attiya and Welch, in the 1990s
Fischer, Lynch and Paterson, in 1985
optionExplain: Brewer named CAP. The right answer is: Leslie Lamport, in 1978.
Right: one of the most cited papers in the field.
Attiya and Welch proved the response-time bound. The right answer is: Leslie Lamport, in 1978.
FLP proved the impossibility result. The right answer is: Leslie Lamport, in 1978.

questions.q: Two timestamps have the same counter value, 7. One is from node 1, one from node 3. Which is the greater?
questions.explain: Tie on the counter goes to the greater node ID.
questions.teaches: If the counter values are the same, the timestamp with the greater node ID is the greater timestamp.
options: The one from node 1
The one from node 3
Neither, they tie
The one that arrived first
optionExplain: The smaller node ID loses the tie. The right answer is: The one from node 3.
Right: if the counters are the same, the greater node ID wins.
The node ID breaks the tie. The right answer is: The one from node 3.
Arrival time is not part of the comparison. The right answer is: The one from node 3.

questions.q: Node 1's counter is 1, and it learns of a maximum of 5 from a client. What should node 1 do?
questions.explain: A counter must never be below one that its operation depends on. The card next shows why.
options: Move its counter forward to 5
Keep its counter at the value 1
Reset its counter back to zero
Ignore the client's request
optionExplain: Right: the counter jumps to the maximum seen. Remember: Jump to the max seen.
Keeping 1 could give a later operation a lower number.
Resetting makes order worse. The right answer is: Move its counter forward to 5.
Ignoring the value breaks the rule. The right answer is: Move its counter forward to 5.

questions.q: When a node sees a maximum counter greater than its own, it immediately ____ its own counter to that maximum.
questions.explain: Moving forward ensures later operations get larger timestamps.

questions.q: Put these events in order. Client A, holding counter 5 from node 2, calls node 1, whose counter is 1.
questions.explain: The maximum travels with the request, node 1 jumps to 5, and the next operation gets 6.
items: A receives counter value 5 from node 2
A sends a request to node 1 carrying the maximum 5
Node 1 raises its counter from 1 to 5
Node 1 handles the operation with a counter of 6

questions.q: True or false: Node 1, at counter 1, receives a request carrying maximum 5. Its next operation gets counter value 6.
questions.explain: Node 1 first moves its counter to 5, and then increments it for the next operation, giving 6.

questions.q: In the book's example, which participants carry the maximum counter?
questions.explain: Clients carry the maximum from one node to another.
questions.teaches: In the book's example, client A receives a counter value of 5 from node 2 and then sends that maximum of 5 to node 1; node 1's counter, which was only 1, is moved forward to 5, so its next operation gets 6.
options: Both nodes and clients
Only the server nodes
Only the clients
Only the single leader
optionExplain: Right: the maximum is carried by every node and every client.
Clients also keep and send it. The right answer is: Both nodes and clients.
Nodes keep it too. The right answer is: Both nodes and clients.
There is no leader here. The right answer is: Both nodes and clients.

questions.q: Why does carrying the maximum guarantee consistency with causality?
questions.explain: A later operation has seen the earlier one's counter, so its own is higher.
questions.teaches: As long as the maximum counter value is carried along with every operation, the ordering from the Lamport timestamps is consistent with causality, because every causal dependency results in an increased timestamp.
options: Each dependency raises the timestamp
It makes all clocks agree
It stops concurrent operations
It removes the need for node IDs
optionExplain: Right: a dependent operation always has a higher counter.
Clocks are not synchronised by it. The right answer is: Each dependency raises the timestamp.
Concurrent operations still happen. The right answer is: Each dependency raises the timestamp.
Node IDs are still needed. The right answer is: Each dependency raises the timestamp.

questions.q: Which tool can tell whether two operations are concurrent?
questions.explain: Version vectors keep per-node information. The card next shows why.
options: A Lamport timestamp
A random UUID
A block of sequence numbers
A version vector
optionExplain: Lamport timestamps impose a total order. The right answer is: A version vector.
A UUID says nothing about order. The right answer is: A version vector.
Blocks give no causal information. The right answer is: A version vector.
Right: version vectors show concurrency. Remember: Version vectors detect concurrency.

questions.q: Match each tool with its main property.
questions.explain: Version vectors give richer information, and Lamport timestamps trade it away for compactness.
pairs: Distinguishes concurrent from causally dependent operations
More compact than a version vector
Cannot reveal whether two operations were concurrent

questions.q: A sync tool must detect when two devices changed the same note without seeing each other's change. Which tool fits?
questions.explain: Conflict detection needs to know concurrency.
options: A Lamport timestamp
A time-of-day timestamp
A version vector
A preallocated block
optionExplain: A Lamport timestamp would just order them. The right answer is: A version vector.
A timestamp would pick a winner by clock. The right answer is: A version vector.
Right: it can show that neither change knew of the other.
A block gives no dependency information. The right answer is: A version vector.

questions.q: True or false: A designer says the total order from Lamport timestamps lets them detect which operations were concurrent.
questions.explain: From the total ordering of Lamport timestamps you cannot tell whether two operations are concurrent or causally dependent.

questions.q: What is the advantage of Lamport timestamps over version vectors, according to the book?
questions.explain: A pair of numbers is smaller than a vector with one entry per node.
questions.teaches: The advantage of Lamport timestamps over version vectors is that they are more compact.
options: They detect concurrency
They need no node IDs
They match physical time
They are more compact
optionExplain: Version vectors detect concurrency. The right answer is: They are more compact.
Lamport timestamps include node IDs. The right answer is: They are more compact.
They are logical. The right answer is: They are more compact.
Right: a pair instead of a vector. Remember: Compactness is the benefit.

questions.q: A system needs a cheap total order over millions of operations and does not need to know about concurrency. Which tool?
questions.explain: Match the tool to the requirement.
questions.rule: Cheapest tool that meets the need.
questions.teaches: Because Lamport timestamps are compact and always give a total order, they suit cases that need a causally consistent order and do not need to distinguish concurrent from dependent operations.
options: Version vectors
Two-phase commit
A consensus algorithm
Lamport timestamps
optionExplain: Vectors would be larger than needed. The right answer is: Lamport timestamps.
2PC is for atomic commit. The right answer is: Lamport timestamps.
Consensus is more than needed. The right answer is: Lamport timestamps.
Right: compact and totally ordered. Remember: Cheapest tool that meets the need.

questions.q: Why is comparing Lamport timestamps not enough for a node to decide immediately whether a username is free?
questions.explain: The answer depends on operations the node has not seen. The card next shows why.
options: Lamport timestamps cannot be compared
Usernames have no timestamps
A competing claim may still be on its way
Only the leader has timestamps
optionExplain: They can be compared. The right answer is: A competing claim may still be on its way.
Operations carry timestamps. The right answer is: A competing claim may still be on its way.
Right: a competing claim may still be on its way.
There is no leader here. The right answer is: A competing claim may still be on its way.

questions.q: With Lamport timestamps, the claim with the ____ timestamp wins once all claims have been collected.
questions.explain: The claim that grabbed the name first has the lower timestamp.
questions.rule: Lower timestamp wins after the fact.

questions.q: Node A holds a username claim at timestamp (8, A); B may hold a competing claim. What must A do to be sure?
questions.explain: A has to rule out lower-numbered claims elsewhere.
options: Accept the claim at once
Reject the claim at once
Wait for a fixed ten seconds
Check with every other node what it is doing
optionExplain: Accepting risks a duplicate. The right answer is: Check with every other node what it is doing.
Rejecting is wrong if no competing claim exists. The right answer is: Check with every other node what it is doing.
A fixed wait does not guarantee that all nodes have been heard.
Right: only then can it know no lower timestamp exists.

questions.q: True or false: If one node cannot be reached, a system that checks with all nodes before accepting a username will grind to a halt.
questions.explain: To be sure that no lower timestamp exists, it has to hear from every other node. A failed node blocks it.
questions.rule: Waiting for everyone is not fault tolerant.

questions.q: When does the total order of operations emerge?
questions.explain: Until all operations are known, positions can still change.
questions.rule: The final order needs all operations.
questions.teaches: The total order of operations only emerges after you have collected all of the operations; if another node has generated operations you do not yet know, they may need to be inserted at various positions in the total order.
options: As soon as the first operation arrives
When the clocks are synchronised
Only after all the operations are collected
When the leader is elected
optionExplain: The first operation cannot fix the position of later ones.
Clocks do not finalize the order. The right answer is: Only after all the operations are collected.
Right: unknown operations might need to be inserted at various positions.
There is no leader in this setup. The right answer is: Only after all the operations are collected.

questions.q: A ticketing system gives the seat to the lowest Lamport timestamp. A node must reply to a claim now. What is the problem?
questions.explain: Immediate answers need a finalized order.
questions.rule: Timestamps give an order, not finality.
questions.teaches: Using timestamp ordering to implement a uniqueness constraint cannot tolerate any faults, since a node must check with every other node before it can be sure no lower-timestamped claim exists.
options: Lamport timestamps cannot be assigned to claims
The seat is claimed by the leader
A lower-timestamped claim might still be on its way from another node
The node has no counter
optionExplain: Timestamps can be assigned. The right answer is: A lower-timestamped claim might still be on its way from another node.
No leader awards seats here. The right answer is: A lower-timestamped claim might still be on its way from another node.
Right: the order is not final until all claims are known.
Every node has a counter. The right answer is: A lower-timestamped claim might still be on its way from another node.

questions.q: What does a node need to be sure before it accepts a username claim?
questions.explain: Finality is about nothing coming ahead. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Be sure nothing can come ahead.
options: That its own claim has the highest timestamp
That the username is shorter than ten letters
That nothing can be inserted ahead of it
That its clock is synchronised
optionExplain: A higher timestamp means a later claim. The right answer is: That nothing can be inserted ahead of it.
Length is unrelated. The right answer is: That nothing can be inserted ahead of it.
Right: only then is its claim the first. Remember: Be sure nothing can come ahead.
Clocks are not enough. The right answer is: That nothing can be inserted ahead of it.

questions.q: To implement a uniqueness constraint, a total order is not enough: you also need to know when the order is ____.
questions.explain: Only once the order is final can a claim be declared successful.

questions.q: A node has timestamp (3, A) for a claim and knows that every other node has already reported its claims. What can it do?
questions.explain: If all claims are known, the winner is clear.
options: Wait for more claims to come in later
Reject its own claim as a precaution
Ask the clients to retry their requests
Declare its claim a success if none is lower
optionExplain: No more claims can arrive ahead. The right answer is: Declare its claim a success if none is lower.
Nothing in the facts says to reject. The right answer is: Declare its claim a success if none is lower.
Retries are not needed. The right answer is: Declare its claim a success if none is lower.
Right: the order is final from its point of view.

questions.q: True or false: Having a total order of operations is the same as knowing when the order is final.
questions.explain: A total order can still be extended by operations that you do not know about yet. Finality needs separate knowledge.

questions.q: How does a single CPU core define a total order of operations?
questions.explain: On a single CPU core, order is trivial.
questions.teaches: If a program runs only on a single CPU core, it is easy to define a total ordering of operations: it is simply the order in which they were executed by the CPU.
options: By the clocks of the operations
By a vote of the operations
By the order in which it executed them
By a hash of the operations
optionExplain: Clocks are not needed on one core. The right answer is: By the order in which it executed them.
Operations do not vote. The right answer is: By the order in which it executed them.
Right: the order of execution is the total order.
Hashes do not order. The right answer is: By the order in which it executed them.

questions.q: Why is timestamp ordering less powerful than single-leader replication for uniqueness?
questions.explain: A single leader decides alone, so a failed follower does not block it.
questions.rule: The leader's order is final at once.
questions.teaches: Single-leader replication determines a total order by sequencing all operations on a single CPU core of the leader, but timestamp ordering used for a uniqueness constraint cannot tolerate any faults.
options: Timestamp ordering is slower
Timestamp ordering needs more disk
It cannot tolerate any faults here
Timestamp ordering has no node IDs
optionExplain: Speed is not the point. The right answer is: It cannot tolerate any faults here.
Disk use is not the point. The right answer is: It cannot tolerate any faults here.
Right: it has to hear from every node. Remember: The leader's order is final at once.
It has node IDs. The right answer is: It cannot tolerate any faults here.

questions.q: Which goal does total order broadcast pursue?
questions.explain: The point is agreement on a shared sequence. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: One shared sequence for all nodes.
options: Every node processes messages at the same wall-clock time
Every node processes the same messages in the same order
Every node keeps a different subset of the messages
Every node chooses its own order for local messages
optionExplain: It does not promise the same time of processing.
Right: all nodes agree on one total order. Remember: One shared sequence for all nodes.
All nodes receive all messages. The right answer is: Every node processes the same messages in the same order.
That would be no agreement at all. The right answer is: Every node processes the same messages in the same order.

questions.q: In the distributed systems literature, total order broadcast is also known as ____ broadcast.
questions.explain: The term atomic broadcast is traditional, although it is confusing.
questions.rule: Atomic broadcast is the older name.

questions.q: A chat service's single leader numbers all messages but saturates at peak load, and its failover is slow. Which concept addresses both problems?
questions.explain: Both problems come from relying on one node to order everything.
questions.rule: Replace the single sequencer with a fault-tolerant protocol.
options: Total order broadcast across several nodes
Last write wins with timestamps
A bigger single leader machine
A manual rota for restarting the leader
optionExplain: Right: it targets scaling beyond one leader and handling failover.
Timestamps give an order that does not tolerate faults.
A bigger machine only moves the limit. The right answer is: Total order broadcast across several nodes.
A rota keeps failover manual and slow. The right answer is: Total order broadcast across several nodes.

questions.q: True or false: Timestamp ordering is as powerful as total order broadcast, because both give a total order of operations.
questions.explain: Timestamp ordering cannot be finalized without hearing from every node, so it does not tolerate faults for uniqueness. Total order broadcast is stronger.
questions.rule: Both give order, only one gives finality.

questions.q: Why does the book call the term atomic broadcast confusing?
questions.explain: The word means something else in ACID and in multi-threaded programming.
questions.rule: Prefer the name total order broadcast.
questions.teaches: The term atomic broadcast is traditional but confusing, as it has nothing to do with atomicity in ACID transactions and is only indirectly related to atomic operations or atomic registers; total order multicast is another synonym.
options: It broadcasts to only one node
It has nothing to do with atomicity in ACID transactions
It guarantees that messages are atomic in size
It is identical to atomic registers
optionExplain: It broadcasts to all nodes. The right answer is: It has nothing to do with atomicity in ACID transactions.
Right: it is inconsistent with other uses of the word atomic.
Message size is not the point. The right answer is: It has nothing to do with atomicity in ACID transactions.
It is only indirectly related to atomic registers. The right answer is: It has nothing to do with atomicity in ACID transactions.

questions.q: What are the two challenges that total order broadcast has to meet that a single leader leaves open?
questions.explain: A single leader limits throughput and is a single point of failure.
questions.teaches: With single-leader replication the challenge is how to scale the system if the throughput is greater than a single leader can handle, and how to handle failover if the leader fails; in the literature this problem is known as total order broadcast.
options: Choosing the database schema and indexing the data
Scaling beyond one leader's throughput, and handling failover
Compressing messages and encrypting them
Reducing the clock skew and the number of replicas
optionExplain: Schema and indexing are unrelated. The right answer is: Scaling beyond one leader's throughput, and handling failover.
Right: these are the two named challenges. Remember: Throughput and failover.
Compression and encryption are unrelated. The right answer is: Scaling beyond one leader's throughput, and handling failover.
Clock skew and replica counts are different problems. The right answer is: Scaling beyond one leader's throughput, and handling failover.

questions.q: A message is delivered to node 1 in a total order broadcast. What must also happen?
questions.explain: Delivery to one means delivery to all. The card next shows why.
options: It is deleted on the other nodes
It is delivered to every other node
It is delivered only if it is small
It is delivered at the same moment on all nodes
optionExplain: Deletion is not part of it. The right answer is: It is delivered to every other node.
Right: reliable delivery. Remember: All or none.
Size is not a condition. The right answer is: It is delivered to every other node.
The timing of delivery is not promised. The right answer is: It is delivered to every other node.

questions.q: Match each property to its meaning.
questions.explain: Two properties, both about safety, and nothing about when.
pairs: No messages are lost; delivered to one means delivered to all
Messages are delivered to every node in the same order
Must hold even when a node or the network is faulty

questions.q: Node A delivers messages M1, M2, M3. Node B delivers M2, M1, M3. What has gone wrong?
questions.explain: Same messages, different order.
options: The totally ordered delivery property is broken
The reliable delivery property is broken
Neither property is broken
Both properties are broken
optionExplain: Right: the order differs between nodes. Remember: Check order and completeness separately.
All three messages arrived at both nodes, so nothing was lost.
The order differs, so one property fails. The right answer is: The totally ordered delivery property is broken.
Only the ordering fails. The right answer is: The totally ordered delivery property is broken.

questions.q: True or false: During a network interruption, a correct total order broadcast must keep delivering messages on both sides.
questions.explain: Messages will not be delivered while the network is interrupted. What matters is that they get through later, in the correct order.

questions.q: What does a correct algorithm do about messages during a network interruption?
questions.explain: Safety is never given up for speed.
questions.teaches: Messages will not be delivered while the network is interrupted, but an algorithm can keep retrying so that the messages get through when the network is eventually repaired, and then they must still be delivered in the correct order.
options: Drops them to protect the order
Keeps retrying so they get through once the network is repaired, still in the correct order
Delivers them out of order at once
Switches to timestamp ordering
optionExplain: Dropping violates reliable delivery. The right answer is: Keeps retrying so they get through once the network is repaired, still in the correct order.
Right: delivery waits, order is kept. Remember: Retry, keep the order.
Out-of-order delivery violates the order property. The right answer is: Keeps retrying so they get through once the network is repaired, still in the correct order.
Timestamp ordering does not satisfy the properties. The right answer is: Keeps retrying so they get through once the network is repaired, still in the correct order.

questions.q: A team's pub-sub system delivers all messages to every subscriber but sometimes in different orders. Is it total order broadcast?
questions.explain: A scheme must satisfy both properties.
questions.rule: Both properties, or it is not total order broadcast.
questions.teaches: A correct total order broadcast must satisfy both reliability and ordering properties always, even if a node or the network is faulty.
options: Yes: reliable delivery is enough
No: it has reliable delivery but not totally ordered delivery
Yes: ordering is optional
No: it has neither property
optionExplain: Both properties are required. The right answer is: No: it has reliable delivery but not totally ordered delivery.
Right: the order property is missing. Remember: Both properties, or it is not total order broadcast.
Ordering is a required property. The right answer is: No: it has reliable delivery but not totally ordered delivery.
Reliable delivery is present. The right answer is: No: it has reliable delivery but not totally ordered delivery.

questions.q: Each partition of a database has its own leader that orders its writes. What is missing?
questions.explain: Order is local to each partition. The card next shows why.
options: An ordering of writes across different partitions
An ordering of writes within each partition
A leader for every partition
A copy of the data on followers
optionExplain: Right: each leader orders only its own partition. Remember: Local order only.
Within a partition the order exists. The right answer is: An ordering of writes across different partitions.
Each partition has a leader. The right answer is: An ordering of writes across different partitions.
Followers may well exist. The right answer is: An ordering of writes across different partitions.

questions.q: In a partitioned database with a leader per partition, ordering is often maintained only per ____.
questions.explain: That is why guarantees across partitions are missing.

questions.q: An order-processing system shards orders and customers on different partitions, each with its own leader. Which guarantee is hard to give?
questions.explain: Anything that spans two partitions needs a combined order.
options: Atomic updates to a single order
A snapshot that is consistent across both partitions
Ordering of changes to one customer's address
Durability of each partition's writes
optionExplain: A single order lives in one partition. The right answer is: A snapshot that is consistent across both partitions.
Right: a consistent snapshot needs ordering across partitions. Remember: Cross-partition means extra coordination.
One customer's address lives in one partition. The right answer is: A snapshot that is consistent across both partitions.
Durability is unrelated to cross-partition order. The right answer is: A snapshot that is consistent across both partitions.

questions.q: True or false: A total ordering across all partitions of a sharded database is impossible to achieve.
questions.explain: It is possible, but it requires additional coordination.

questions.q: Which guarantees does the book name as lost when ordering is only per partition?
questions.explain: Guarantees that relate data in different partitions need a combined order.
questions.rule: Cross-partition guarantees need a global order.
questions.teaches: Partitioned databases with a single leader per partition often maintain ordering only per partition, which means they cannot offer consistency guarantees such as consistent snapshots or foreign key references across partitions.
options: Consistent snapshots and foreign key references across partitions
Durability of writes and replication to followers
Compression of logs and index maintenance
Authentication of clients and encryption of traffic
optionExplain: Right: these span partitions. Remember: Cross-partition guarantees need a global order.
Durability and replication are not named. The right answer is: Consistent snapshots and foreign key references across partitions.
Logs and indexes are unrelated. The right answer is: Consistent snapshots and foreign key references across partitions.
Security is unrelated. The right answer is: Consistent snapshots and foreign key references across partitions.

questions.q: A database has a single leader per partition and orders writes only within each partition. Which guarantee is it unable to offer across partitions?
questions.explain: Per-partition ordering cannot give guarantees that span partitions.
questions.teaches: Partitioned databases with a single leader per partition often maintain ordering only per partition, which means they cannot offer consistency guarantees (e.g., consistent snapshots, foreign key references) across partitions.
options: Consistent snapshots spanning several partitions
Order of writes within a single partition
Replication of each partition to followers
Storing records on more than one node
optionExplain: Right: with order kept only per partition, cross-partition guarantees such as consistent snapshots or foreign key references are not offered. Remember: Global order costs coordination.
Order within one partition is exactly what a single leader gives.
Replication to followers is independent of how ordering is scoped.
Partitioning already spreads records over nodes.

questions.q: Three replicas apply the same set of writes but in different orders. What can happen?
questions.explain: Writes do not commute in general. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Same writes, different order, different state.
options: Their states can differ
Their states are always equal
They stop accepting writes
They merge into one replica
optionExplain: Right: order matters for the final state. Remember: Same writes, different order, different state.
Equal states need the same order. The right answer is: Their states can differ.
Nothing stops them accepting writes. The right answer is: Their states can differ.
They do not merge. The right answer is: Their states can differ.

questions.q: Keeping replicas consistent by applying the same writes in the same order is called state machine ____.
questions.explain: The principle is known as state machine replication.

questions.q: Two clients send conflicting writes to x, one setting it to 1 and the other to 2. How does total order broadcast keep replicas consistent?
questions.explain: A shared order gives a shared outcome.
options: It applies only the faster write
It delivers both writes to both replicas in the same order
It lets each replica pick its own order
It stores both values in x
optionExplain: Dropping a write would lose data. The right answer is: It delivers both writes to both replicas in the same order.
Right: both end with the same final value. Remember: Same order, same result.
Different orders give different values. The right answer is: It delivers both writes to both replicas in the same order.
A register holds one value. The right answer is: It delivers both writes to both replicas in the same order.

questions.q: True or false: With total order broadcast, replicas are consistent with each other at every instant, with no replication lag.
questions.explain: They remain consistent aside from any temporary replication lag, because deliveries may arrive at different times.

questions.q: How can total order broadcast implement serializable transactions?
questions.explain: Deterministic code in a shared order gives the same result everywhere.
questions.teaches: Total order broadcast can implement serializable transactions: if every message represents a deterministic transaction to be executed as a stored procedure and every node processes those messages in the same order, the partitions and replicas of the database are kept consistent with each other.
options: Each message is a deterministic transaction run as a stored procedure, processed in the same order everywhere
Each message is a random transaction run on one node only
Each message is a lock request held until the end of time
Each message is a snapshot of the database taken at noon
optionExplain: Right: this keeps partitions and replicas consistent with each other.
Random transactions on one node would not keep replicas consistent.
Holding locks forever blocks everyone. The right answer is: Each message is a deterministic transaction run as a stored procedure, processed in the same order everywhere.
Snapshots are not transactions to be executed. The right answer is: Each message is a deterministic transaction run as a stored procedure, processed in the same order everywhere.

questions.q: Why must the transactions in that scheme be deterministic?
questions.explain: Replay on each node must reach the same state.
questions.teaches: Because every node processes the same messages independently, a non-deterministic transaction could produce different results on different nodes, so the scheme relies on deterministic transactions executed as stored procedures.
options: Different outcomes on different nodes would make replicas diverge
Deterministic code runs faster
Deterministic code needs less memory
Non-deterministic code cannot be written to a log
optionExplain: Right: the same input in the same order must give the same state.
Speed is not the reason. The right answer is: Different outcomes on different nodes would make replicas diverge.
Memory is not the reason. The right answer is: Different outcomes on different nodes would make replicas diverge.
Any code can be logged; the problem is replaying it.

questions.q: A node has delivered messages 1 to 5 in a total order broadcast. A message arrives that claims to belong before message 3. What happens?
questions.explain: Delivered positions are final. The card next shows why.
options: It is inserted before message 3 and the rest are redelivered
It cannot be inserted before message 3
It replaces message 3
It is inserted and the order is announced again
optionExplain: Redelivery would break the fixed order. The right answer is: It cannot be inserted before message 3.
Right: the order is fixed at delivery. Remember: No retroactive insertion.
Replacing would lose message 3. The right answer is: It cannot be inserted before message 3.
Changing the order breaks the guarantee. The right answer is: It cannot be inserted before message 3.

questions.q: In total order broadcast, a node may not ____ insert a message into an earlier position after later messages are delivered.
questions.explain: The order is fixed at the time the messages are delivered.

questions.q: Under timestamp ordering, node X has processed claims up to timestamp 20 when a claim with timestamp 12 appears. What breaks?
questions.explain: That is why timestamps are not final.
options: The claim at 12 should have gone first, so X's earlier decisions may be wrong
Nothing, since 12 is lower than 20
The claim at 12 is ignored by the protocol
X automatically restarts
optionExplain: Right: the late claim is inserted ahead of decisions already made.
A lower timestamp means it goes earlier, which is the issue.
The protocol does not ignore it. The right answer is: The claim at 12 should have gone first, so X's earlier decisions may be wrong.
Nothing restarts automatically. The right answer is: The claim at 12 should have gone first, so X's earlier decisions may be wrong.

questions.q: True or false: Timestamp ordering and total order broadcast are equally strong, since both allow a late message to be inserted earlier.
questions.explain: Total order broadcast does not allow retroactive insertion once later messages are delivered. This fact makes it stronger than timestamp ordering.

questions.q: What does the book say about total order broadcast compared with timestamp ordering?
questions.explain: Delivery order cannot be changed afterwards.
questions.teaches: Because the order is fixed at the time the messages are delivered and a node may not retroactively insert a message into an earlier position, total order broadcast is stronger than timestamp ordering.
options: It is weaker but cheaper
The fixed order makes it stronger
It is equal in strength
It is stronger only on one node
optionExplain: It is stronger and costs more. The right answer is: The fixed order makes it stronger.
Right: the fixed order is the difference. Remember: Stronger because fixed.
The fixed order makes it stronger. The right answer is: The fixed order makes it stronger.
The comparison does not depend on node count. The right answer is: The fixed order makes it stronger.

questions.q: In a name check on total order broadcast, the first delivered claim wins. Why can you answer once your own claim is delivered?
questions.explain: Final order allows an immediate answer.
questions.teaches: Because the order of total order broadcast is final at delivery, a node can decide a uniqueness claim as soon as its own message is delivered back, without asking every other node.
options: Clocks are synchronised across all nodes
No earlier claim can still be inserted ahead of it
The claim has the lowest timestamp
Other nodes have been asked and have agreed
optionExplain: Clocks play no role. The right answer is: No earlier claim can still be inserted ahead of it.
Right: the order is final once delivered. Remember: Delivered means final.
Timestamps are not used. The right answer is: No earlier claim can still be inserted ahead of it.
Nodes are not asked separately. The right answer is: No earlier claim can still be inserted ahead of it.

questions.q: Which everyday structure is most like total order broadcast?
questions.explain: Everyone reads the same sequence. The card next shows why.
options: A cache that evicts old entries
A key-value store with random access
A queue where each node takes a different item
An append-only log that every node reads in order
optionExplain: A cache has no shared order. The right answer is: An append-only log that every node reads in order.
Random access has no sequence. The right answer is: An append-only log that every node reads in order.
Different items for each node would not be the same sequence.
Right: appending is delivering. Remember: Delivery is appending.

questions.q: Delivering a message in total order broadcast is like ____ to a log.
questions.explain: All nodes can then read the log and see the same sequence of messages.

questions.q: Which of these logs gives all nodes the same sequence of writes?
questions.explain: Look for a log everyone shares.
options: A local debug log on each node
A browser history on each client
A replication log fed by total order broadcast
A cache of recent queries
optionExplain: Local logs differ by node. The right answer is: A replication log fed by total order broadcast.
Browser histories are private. The right answer is: A replication log fed by total order broadcast.
Right: all nodes read the same messages in the same order.
A cache is not a log. The right answer is: A replication log fed by total order broadcast.

questions.q: True or false: A write-ahead log, a transaction log and a replication log are all examples of logs, as the book uses the term.
questions.explain: The book names these three as examples when it describes total order broadcast as a log.

questions.q: How can a lock service use the log to provide fencing tokens?
questions.explain: Log position is a monotonically increasing number.
questions.teaches: A lock service can provide fencing tokens by appending every request to acquire the lock as a message to the log and numbering all messages sequentially in the order they appear; the sequence number then serves as a fencing token because it is monotonically increasing.
options: Each client invents its own random token
Each lock holder reads the clock
Each lock holder pings the others
Each lock request is appended and its position in the log serves as a token
optionExplain: Random tokens do not increase. The right answer is: Each lock request is appended and its position in the log serves as a token.
Clocks can go backwards. The right answer is: Each lock request is appended and its position in the log serves as a token.
Pings do not give tokens. The right answer is: Each lock request is appended and its position in the log serves as a token.
Right: the sequence number increases monotonically. Remember: Log position as token.

questions.q: What does ZooKeeper call the sequence number that serves as a fencing token?
questions.explain: The transaction ID names the log position in ZooKeeper.
questions.teaches: In ZooKeeper, the monotonically increasing sequence number that serves as a fencing token is called zxid.
options: epoch
ballot
term
zxid
optionExplain: Epoch is a number for leadership periods in consensus protocols.
Ballot is the Paxos name for the epoch. The right answer is: zxid.
Term is the Raft name for the epoch. The right answer is: zxid.
Right: the transaction ID. Remember: zxid is ZooKeeper's token.

questions.q: Which guarantee does total order broadcast NOT give?
questions.explain: It is asynchronous. The card next shows why.
options: That all recipients see the same order
That no message is lost
That a recipient sees a message by a given time
That the order is fixed once delivered
optionExplain: Same order is promised. The right answer is: That a recipient sees a message by a given time.
Reliable delivery is promised. The right answer is: That a recipient sees a message by a given time.
Right: there is no promise about when. Remember: Order, not timing.
A fixed order is promised. The right answer is: That a recipient sees a message by a given time.

questions.q: Match each guarantee with what it promises.
questions.explain: Order versus recency.
pairs: Reliable delivery in a fixed order, with no promise about when
A read sees the latest value written
One recipient may lag behind the others

questions.q: A log is read by three nodes. One lags a minute behind the others. Which statement is right?
questions.explain: Lag is allowed because delivery is asynchronous.
options: The log violates total order broadcast
The log is linearizable
The log has lost messages
The log still satisfies total order broadcast
optionExplain: Lagging is not a violation of ordering or reliability.
Lagging readers see stale data, so reads are not linearizable.
No messages are lost. The right answer is: The log still satisfies total order broadcast.
Right: lagging is allowed. Remember: Lag is not a violation.

questions.q: True or false: A read from a node that is behind in the broadcast can return a stale value even though the broadcast works correctly.
