questions.explain: Total order broadcast does not promise recency. A read from a lagging node can be stale.

questions.q: If you have total order broadcast, what can you build on top of it?
questions.explain: Order plus a careful read gives recency.
questions.rule: Order can be turned into recency.
questions.teaches: If you have total order broadcast, you can build linearizable storage on top of it, for example ensuring that usernames uniquely identify user accounts.
options: Synchronised clocks
A perfect failure detector
Linearizable storage
A network that never fails
optionExplain: Clocks cannot be built from order alone. The right answer is: Linearizable storage.
A perfect failure detector is not obtained. The right answer is: Linearizable storage.
Right: the book builds linearizable compare-and-set on top of it.
Networks still fail. The right answer is: Linearizable storage.

questions.q: In a formal sense, which problem is easier: a linearizable read-write register or total order broadcast?
questions.explain: Equivalence to consensus makes broadcast the harder problem.
questions.rule: Plain registers are easier than broadcast.
questions.teaches: In a formal sense a linearizable read-write register is an easier problem than total order broadcast, since total order broadcast is equivalent to consensus, which has no deterministic solution in the asynchronous crash-stop model, while a read-write register can be implemented in that model.
options: Total order broadcast, since it only orders messages
They are equally hard
The register, which can be implemented where total order broadcast cannot
Neither can be implemented
optionExplain: It is equivalent to consensus, which is harder. The right answer is: The register, which can be implemented where total order broadcast cannot.
They differ in formal difficulty. The right answer is: The register, which can be implemented where total order broadcast cannot.
Right: total order broadcast is equivalent to consensus. Remember: Plain registers are easier than broadcast.
The register can be implemented. The right answer is: The register, which can be implemented where total order broadcast cannot.

questions.q: Several nodes append claims for the same username to a totally ordered log. How do all nodes agree on the winner?
questions.explain: The shared log order decides the winner. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: The first claim in the log wins.
options: The claim with the earliest wall-clock send time wins
The first claim for that name in the log wins
The claim from the node with the lowest ID wins
Each node picks the claim it received first locally
optionExplain: Send times come from unsynchronised clocks and are not what the log records.
Every node reads the same log, so every node reaches the same verdict.
Node IDs play no part in the log-based procedure.
Local receipt order can differ between nodes, so they could disagree.

questions.q: After appending its claim, a node must wait for the message to be ____ back to it before checking the log.
questions.explain: The node reads the log until its own appended message is delivered back, and only then checks which claim came first.

questions.q: Users A and B claim the name carol. The log holds A's claim at position 7 and B's at 9. What results?
questions.explain: Position in the log decides.
options: A succeeds and B aborts, on every node
B succeeds because its claim is the later and final one
Both succeed and the application merges the two accounts
Each node decides separately, so the outcome can differ by node
optionExplain: Position 7 is first, and all nodes see the same positions, so all agree.
Later claims lose; the first claim for the name wins.
The procedure ensures only one claim is committed. The right answer is: A succeeds and B aborts, on every node.
All nodes read the same log order and therefore reach the same decision.

questions.q: True or false: Your claim is delivered back but another user's claim for the name precedes it. You should still acknowledge success.
questions.explain: If the first message for the name came from another user, the node aborts its own operation instead of acknowledging.
questions.rule: Another user's earlier claim means abort.

questions.q: A node acknowledges a username claim as soon as it is enqueued, without waiting for delivery. What does that resemble?
questions.explain: Skipping the wait loses the ordering guarantee that delivery provides.
questions.rule: Waiting for delivery is what makes the claim safe.
questions.teaches: If you do not wait but acknowledge the write immediately after it has been enqueued, you get something similar to the memory consistency model of multi-core x86 processors, which is neither linearizable nor sequentially consistent.
options: A fully linearizable register, only with lower latency
Like multi-core x86 memory, not linearizable
Strict serializability, with writes ordered by a global clock
Eventual consistency, where conflicts are merged later
optionExplain: Without waiting, the client may be told success before the order is known.
Skipping the wait loses the ordering guarantee that delivery provides.
No clock is involved, and the weaker result is not serializability.
The claims here are not merged; one of them should have lost.

questions.q: A system must make transactions touching several objects serializable, and it already has a total order log. What approach does the book suggest?
questions.explain: Choosing the first of the conflicting writes in log order works for multiple objects too.
questions.rule: The same log trick extends beyond single names.
questions.teaches: A similar approach, choosing the first of the conflicting writes as the winner and aborting later ones, can implement serializable multi-object transactions on top of a log.
options: Give each object its own log and merge the logs by timestamp
Log the transactions; abort later conflicting ones
Let each node commit locally and reconcile conflicts afterwards
Lock every object on every node before appending anything
optionExplain: Separate logs merged by timestamp would lose the single agreed order.
Choosing the first of the conflicting writes in log order works for multiple objects too.
That would allow nodes to disagree about which transaction committed.
The log-based approach does not need to lock everything on every node.

questions.q: A store applies writes from a total order log, but readers use a local copy updated asynchronously. What can a read return?
questions.explain: Order and recency are separate guarantees. The card next shows why.
options: Always the latest value, because the log order is total
A value from a different order than other replicas see
A stale value, though updates still arrive in log order
An error, since reads are not allowed on a log-based store
optionExplain: Total order says nothing about how quickly a replica applies the log.
Every replica applies the same log order, so the order itself does not differ.
The copy lags, so a read can miss the latest write.
Reads are allowed; they just are not guaranteed to be up to date.

questions.q: Log-ordered writes with lagging reads give ____ consistency, which is also called timeline consistency.
questions.explain: That guarantee is slightly weaker than linearizability, because reads may lag behind the latest write.

questions.q: A reader appends a marker message to the log and performs its read once the marker is delivered back. What does the marker define?
questions.explain: A read sequenced through the log is placed in the order.
questions.rule: The marker position is the read time.
options: The set of replicas the read must contact
The timeout after which the read is retried
The version number returned to the client as a cache key
The point in time at which the read happens
optionExplain: The marker does not select replicas; it selects a position in the log.
Position in the log is the point of the marker, not a timer.
Nothing about versioning is involved in sequencing the read.
The marker's log position fixes where the read falls relative to all writes.

questions.q: True or false: A read served from a replica that applies the log asynchronously is linearizable as long as the log itself is totally ordered.
questions.explain: Total ordering of the log does not stop the replica from lagging, so such a read can be stale.

questions.q: A reader can fetch the latest log position in a linearizable way. How does it then make its read linearizable?
questions.explain: That is the idea behind ZooKeeper's sync() operation.
questions.rule: Waiting for a known position removes the lag.
questions.teaches: If the log lets you fetch the position of the latest log message in a linearizable way, you can query that position, wait for all entries up to it to be delivered, and then perform the read; this is the idea behind ZooKeeper's sync() operation.
options: It reads at once and tags the result with that position
It asks a majority of replicas to vote on the read result
It waits for entries up to that position, then reads
It appends the read to the log and discards the earlier position
optionExplain: A tag would not stop the read from being stale.
No voting on read results is needed; waiting for delivery suffices.
That is the idea behind ZooKeeper's sync() operation. Remember: Waiting for a known position removes the lag.
The position is used for waiting, not for being discarded.

questions.q: A design reads only from a replica that is updated synchronously on every write. Which technique from the book does that match?
questions.explain: Chain replication reads from a synchronously updated replica, so it is sure to be up to date.
questions.rule: A synchronous replica cannot lag behind.
questions.teaches: Chain replication makes reads linearizable by reading from a replica that is synchronously updated on writes and is thus sure to be up to date, while quorum reads in etcd work somewhat by sequencing reads through the log.
options: Quorum reads in etcd
Lamport timestamps
Chain replication
Read repair in a leaderless store
optionExplain: Quorum reads in etcd work by sequencing the read through the log.
Lamport timestamps order events but do not make a replica up to date.
Chain replication reads from a synchronously updated replica, so it is sure to be up to date.
Read repair is a leaderless technique for fixing stale replicas, not a synchronous replica.

questions.q: A linearizable counter hands out increasing integers. How could senders use it to give messages one shared order?
questions.explain: A single shared counter orders the messages. The card next shows why.
options: Attach the sender's clock reading and sort by that
Let each node count its own messages and merge the counts
Broadcast messages without numbers and let receivers vote on order
Attach the number to each message, and deliver in number order
optionExplain: Clock readings from different nodes can disagree; the counter is the shared source.
Independent counters collide and give no shared order. The right answer is: Attach the number to each message, and deliver in number order.
Voting would be needed only without a shared counter.
Consecutive numbers from one linearizable source define a shared order.

questions.q: Each sender calls ____-and-get on the linearizable register and attaches the result to its message as a sequence number.
questions.explain: Atomic increment-and-get gives every message a distinct number from one linearizable source.

questions.q: Two senders call increment-and-get on the register at the same moment. What do they receive?
questions.explain: The register gives each caller a unique next value.
options: The same value, with ties broken by node ID
Values from separate local counters that are merged later
Two different consecutive values
Timestamps with the node ID appended to avoid ties
optionExplain: Atomic increment does not hand the same value to two callers.
There is one register, not several local counters. The right answer is: Two different consecutive values.
A linearizable atomic operation hands out each value once.
That is the Lamport scheme, not what the register does.

questions.q: True or false: The sequence numbers from a linearizable increment-and-get register can skip values, as Lamport timestamps can.
questions.explain: The numbers from the register form a sequence with no gaps, unlike Lamport timestamps.

questions.q: A node has delivered message 4 and receives message 6 from the register-based scheme. What should it do?
questions.explain: The numbers have no gaps, so 5 must exist and must come first.
questions.rule: Gap-free numbering lets recipients detect missing messages.
questions.teaches: Because the numbers from the linearizable register have no gaps, a node that delivered message 4 and sees message 6 knows it must wait for message 5; Lamport timestamps lack this, which is the key difference between total order broadcast and timestamp ordering.
options: Deliver message 6 now and insert 5 later
Discard message 6 and ask the sender to renumber it
Assume 5 was lost for good and skip it
Wait for message 5 before delivering message 6
optionExplain: Inserting 5 later would break the fixed delivery order.
Nothing is wrong with 6; renumbering would break the order.
With gap-free numbers a missing 5 means waiting, not skipping.
The numbers have no gaps, so 5 must exist and must come first.

questions.q: Why is keeping the counter in a variable on one node not a complete answer?
questions.explain: The difficulty lies in connection loss and recovering the counter after a crash.
questions.teaches: If nothing failed, a linearizable integer would be easy to keep in a variable on one node; the problem is handling interrupted network connections to that node and restoring the value when it fails, and thinking hard about linearizable sequence number generators inevitably ends in a consensus algorithm.
options: A single variable cannot be incremented atomically
Nodes would receive numbers in a different order from one another
The counter would overflow on any realistic workload
Lost connections and node failure make recovery hard
optionExplain: Atomic increment on a single node is easy; failures are the problem.
The order a single variable hands out is the same for every node.
Overflow is not the concern; fault tolerance is. The right answer is: Lost connections and node failure make recovery hard.
The difficulty lies in connection loss and recovering the counter after a crash.

questions.q: A team can build a fault-tolerant total order broadcast. What else does the book say follows from it?
questions.explain: The problems convert into one another. The card next shows why.
options: A clock synchronised across all nodes to within a millisecond
A linearizable compare-and-set register
A leaderless store without stale reads
An algorithm that tolerates unbounded delay with no timeouts
optionExplain: Ordering a log does not give anyone a synchronised clock.
Total order broadcast and a compare-and-set register are equivalent.
Leaderless quorums are a different mechanism and do not follow.
Tolerating that is the thing the FLP result rules out.

questions.q: Total order broadcast and a linearizable compare-and-set register are both equivalent to ____.
questions.explain: That is the profound result: solve any one of them and you can solve the others.

questions.q: You have solved total order broadcast fault-tolerantly. A colleague wants a fault-tolerant increment-and-get counter. What follows?
questions.explain: Solving one solves the rest.
options: It can be built from it, as they are equivalent
It needs a separate, harder algorithm unrelated to yours
It is impossible, because counters cannot tolerate crashes
It needs synchronised clocks in addition to your solution
optionExplain: Equivalent problems transform into each other. Remember: Transform the solution.
The two are in the same equivalence class. The right answer is: It can be built from it, as they are equivalent.
Equivalence means it is achievable if the other is.
Clocks are not part of the transformation. The right answer is: It can be built from it, as they are equivalent.

questions.q: True or false: If you can solve one of these equivalent problems, you can transform that solution into a solution for the others.
questions.explain: That is what equivalence means here, and the book calls it a profound and surprising insight.

questions.q: Total order broadcast is equivalent to consensus. What does the book say about solving it in the asynchronous crash-stop model?
questions.explain: Consensus has no deterministic solution in that model, and the equivalence carries it over.
questions.teaches: Total order broadcast is equivalent to consensus, which has no deterministic solution in the asynchronous crash-stop model.
options: It is solvable with a deterministic algorithm
It has no deterministic solution there
It is solvable only if every node stays alive
It is solvable but only on a single machine
optionExplain: That would contradict the impossibility result for consensus. The right answer is: It has no deterministic solution there.
Consensus has no deterministic solution in that model, and the equivalence carries it over.
Crash tolerance is exactly what is at stake. The right answer is: It has no deterministic solution there.
A single machine is outside the distributed problem. The right answer is: It has no deterministic solution there.

questions.q: A plain linearizable read-write register gains an atomic compare-and-set operation. How does its difficulty change?
questions.explain: Supporting atomic operations makes the register equivalent to consensus.
questions.teaches: A linearizable read-write register is a formally easier problem that can be implemented in the same asynchronous system model, but supporting atomic operations such as compare-and-set or increment-and-get makes it equivalent to consensus.
options: It stays as easy as before, since compare-and-set is cheap
It becomes equivalent to consensus
It becomes impossible to build with any algorithm
It becomes equivalent to a leaderless quorum read
optionExplain: The atomic operation is what raises the difficulty. The right answer is: It becomes equivalent to consensus.
Supporting atomic operations makes the register equivalent to consensus.
It can be built, with a consensus algorithm. The right answer is: It becomes equivalent to consensus.
Quorum reads are not the equivalence class in question.

questions.q: A transaction spans two partitions; one commits and the other aborts. Which guarantee is violated?
questions.explain: Atomicity needs agreement on the outcome. The card next shows why.
options: Isolation
Atomicity
Durability
Linearizability
optionExplain: Isolation concerns concurrent transactions, not agreement on one outcome.
Atomicity requires all nodes to commit or all to abort.
Durability concerns surviving crashes after commit, not agreement. The right answer is: Atomicity.
Linearizability concerns recency of single objects, not transaction outcome.

questions.q: In atomic commit, nodes must agree that the transaction either commits on all nodes or ____ on all nodes.
questions.explain: If anything goes wrong all nodes abort or roll back; if nothing goes wrong all commit.

questions.q: A transaction spans three partitions and one fails a constraint check. What must the nodes agree on?
questions.explain: All nodes share the single outcome.
options: That all three abort
That the two healthy ones commit and the failing one retries
That the failing node's result is ignored by the others
That each node decides alone using its own timeout
optionExplain: One failure means the whole transaction aborts everywhere. Remember: One shared outcome.
That would leave the transaction partly applied. The right answer is: That all three abort.
Ignoring it would break atomicity. The right answer is: That all three abort.
Independent decisions are what consensus is meant to prevent.

questions.q: True or false: Atomic commit is a particular instance of the consensus problem.
questions.explain: Getting all nodes to agree on the outcome of a transaction is known as the atomic commit problem, an instance of consensus.

questions.q: Why does the book place the consensus discussion late in the chapter?
questions.explain: Replication, transactions, system models, linearizability and total order broadcast are prerequisites.
questions.rule: Consensus builds on the earlier chapters.
questions.teaches: Understanding of consensus only gradually crystallized over decades with many misunderstandings along the way, and many broken systems have been built in the mistaken belief that the problem is easy to solve.
options: Consensus is a minor topic that most systems can ignore
Its subtleties need earlier topics like replication
It depends on clock synchronisation covered in the next chapter
It is an optional extension of two-phase commit
optionExplain: The book calls it one of the most important problems in distributed computing.
Replication, transactions, system models, linearizability and total order broadcast are prerequisites.
The prerequisites listed are earlier topics, not a later chapter.
Consensus is more fundamental than a single protocol. The right answer is: Its subtleties need earlier topics like replication.

questions.q: Two nodes in a single-leader database both believe themselves to be the leader. What outcome does the book describe?
questions.explain: Two leaders accepting writes at once cause divergence.
questions.teaches: If there were two leaders, they would both accept writes and their data would diverge, leading to inconsistency and data loss.
options: Writes are blocked until one of them steps down on its own
Both accept writes and the data diverges
The followers vote and refuse both leaders' writes
Only the older leader's writes are kept, losing nothing
optionExplain: Nothing in split brain forces either to step down.
Two leaders accepting writes at once cause divergence. Remember: Split brain breaks single-leader replication.
Followers do not automatically veto split brain without consensus.
Both leaders' writes are accepted, and data can be lost.

questions.q: A proof says no algorithm can guarantee consensus if a node may crash. Why can real systems still reach it?
questions.explain: Check the assumptions of the model. The card next shows why.
options: Real nodes do not crash, so the proof does not apply
The proof assumes a restrictive model without timeouts
Real networks do not lose or delay messages
The proof only applies to systems with more than ten nodes
optionExplain: Nodes do crash; the book says we must assume they may.
Real systems use timeouts, which the model forbids. Remember: Model matters.
Real networks do lose and delay messages. The right answer is: The proof assumes a restrictive model without timeouts.
The result is not tied to a cluster size.

questions.q: The FLP result is proved in the ____ system model, which allows no clocks or timeouts.
questions.explain: That model assumes a deterministic algorithm that cannot use clocks or timeouts.

questions.q: Which change lets an algorithm escape the FLP impossibility result?
questions.explain: The model must be relaxed.
options: Using timeouts to suspect crashed nodes
Requiring every node, not a majority, to answer each request
Assuming that no node can ever crash during a protocol run
Forbidding the algorithm from retrying any message
optionExplain: Suspicion of crashed nodes makes consensus solvable. Remember: Allow timeouts.
Waiting for all nodes makes crashes block progress, not solve them.
That removes the problem rather than solving it, and nodes can crash.
Dropping retries does not escape the result. The right answer is: Using timeouts to suspect crashed nodes.

questions.q: True or false: FLP shows that distributed systems cannot achieve consensus in practice.
questions.explain: FLP is proved in a restrictive model; the book says distributed systems can usually achieve consensus in practice.

questions.q: Besides timeouts, what even smaller change gets an algorithm around FLP?
questions.explain: Random numbers alone are sufficient to get around the impossibility result.
questions.teaches: Even just allowing the algorithm to use random numbers is sufficient to get around the impossibility result.
options: Letting the algorithm read a perfectly synchronised clock
Letting the algorithm use random numbers
Letting the algorithm run on only a single node
Letting the algorithm skip the termination requirement entirely
optionExplain: A clock helps, but the book singles out something smaller.
Random numbers alone are sufficient to get around the impossibility result.
A single node is not a distributed consensus algorithm.
Dropping termination would make the problem trivial and uninteresting.

questions.q: A colleague says FLP means we should stop building consensus systems. What is the best reply?
questions.explain: The book says exactly this about FLP.
questions.teaches: Although the FLP result about the impossibility of consensus is of great theoretical importance, distributed systems can usually achieve consensus in practice.
options: They are right, and consensus systems are all unsafe
Important in theory, yet consensus works in practice
FLP only applies to systems that do not use a network
FLP has been disproved, so the question is moot
optionExplain: Consensus systems exist and work, with timeouts and suspicion.
The book says exactly this about FLP. Remember: Do not over-read impossibility results.
The result concerns crashes in an asynchronous model, not network use.
The proof stands; its model is just restrictive. The right answer is: Important in theory, yet consensus works in practice.

questions.q: Atomic commit forces an abort if any participant says no. Consensus may choose any proposed value. How are they related?
questions.explain: Different formulation, same difficulty. The card next shows why.
options: They are unrelated problems with different solutions
Atomic commit is strictly harder in every form
Consensus is strictly harder, since it lacks a veto rule
They differ in rules but are reducible to each other
optionExplain: The book says they reduce to each other. The right answer is: They differ in rules but are reducible to each other.
Only the nonblocking form is harder; the ordinary form reduces both ways.
They are mutually reducible, so neither is strictly harder.
Each can be turned into the other despite the different formulations.

questions.q: In atomic commit, a transaction must ____ if any participant needs to abort.
questions.explain: A single no vote forces the whole transaction to abort.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the commit decision in atomic commit?
questions.explain: Every participant must vote yes.
options: Commit if a majority of participants voted to commit
Commit if the first participant to reply voted to commit
Commit only if every participant voted to commit
Commit if the coordinator votes yes, regardless of the rest
optionExplain: A majority is enough for consensus quorums, not for atomic commit.
The first reply alone says nothing about the others.
Atomic commit commits only when all vote yes. Remember: All yes.
The coordinator cannot override a participant's no vote. The right answer is: Commit only if every participant voted to commit.

questions.q: True or false: Nonblocking atomic commit is easier than consensus.
questions.explain: The footnote says nonblocking atomic commit is harder than consensus.

questions.q: How does the book judge two-phase commit when viewed as a consensus algorithm?
questions.explain: The book says exactly that of 2PC.
questions.teaches: Two-phase commit is the most common way of solving atomic commit, and it turns out to be a kind of consensus algorithm, but not a very good one.
options: An excellent consensus algorithm used by ZooKeeper
Not a consensus algorithm in any sense
The only consensus algorithm that tolerates crashes
A consensus algorithm, but not a very good one
optionExplain: ZooKeeper uses Zab, not 2PC. The right answer is: A consensus algorithm, but not a very good one.
It is a kind of consensus algorithm, only a weak one.
It fails to tolerate coordinator crashes. The right answer is: A consensus algorithm, but not a very good one.
The book says exactly that of 2PC. Remember: 2PC is weak consensus.

questions.q: After studying 2PC, which consensus algorithms does the book work toward?
questions.explain: These are the better consensus algorithms the section builds toward.
questions.rule: Learn from 2PC, then move to better algorithms.
questions.teaches: By learning from 2PC the book works toward better consensus algorithms, such as those used in ZooKeeper (Zab) and etcd (Raft).
options: Three-phase commit used in MySQL and Paxos used in Redis
Lamport timestamps used in ZooKeeper and vector clocks in etcd
Two-phase locking used in etcd and Zab in Raft
Zab used in ZooKeeper and Raft used in etcd
optionExplain: Neither pairing is what the book names. The right answer is: Zab used in ZooKeeper and Raft used in etcd.
Those are ordering tools, not the consensus algorithms named.
Two-phase locking is unrelated, and Zab is not part of Raft.
These are the better consensus algorithms the section builds toward.

questions.q: A database crashes while committing. On restart, how does it decide whether the transaction was committed?
questions.explain: The log decides the outcome after a crash. The card next shows why.
options: It asks the client whether the commit was acknowledged
It checks the log for a durable commit record
It compares timestamps on the data pages with the clock
It re-executes the transaction and compares the results
optionExplain: The client's view is not what recovery uses; the log is.
A durable commit record means committed; its absence means roll back.
Recovery does not use page timestamps to decide the outcome.
Re-execution is not how the commit outcome is determined.

questions.q: On one node, the transaction's data is made durable first, and then a ____ record is appended to the log.
questions.explain: If that record is durable when the node restarts, the transaction counts as committed.

questions.q: A crash hits after all of a transaction's data is durable but before the commit record is written. What happens on recovery?
questions.explain: No commit record means roll back.
options: The transaction is rolled back
The transaction is committed, because its data is on disk
The node waits for the client to say which outcome to apply
Half the writes are kept and half are discarded
optionExplain: Without a commit record the transaction is treated as not committed.
Durable data alone does not commit; the commit record does.
Recovery decides from the log without waiting for the client.
Atomicity means all or none of the writes remain.

questions.q: True or false: On a single node the order of durable writes is irrelevant, provided both the data and the commit record eventually reach disk.
questions.explain: Commit depends on the order: data first and then the commit record. Writing them out of order could expose a commit without its data.

questions.q: On a single node, what is the key deciding moment for whether a transaction commits or aborts?
questions.explain: Before then a crash aborts it; after then it is committed even through a crash.
questions.rule: The commit record write is the decision point.
questions.teaches: The key deciding moment is when the disk finishes writing the commit record: before that moment it is still possible to abort due to a crash, but after it the transaction is committed even if the database crashes.
options: When the client sends the commit request
When the disk finishes writing the commit record
When the first data page reaches disk
When the last lock on the transaction is released
optionExplain: The request alone does not decide; durability of the record does.
Before then a crash aborts it; after then it is committed even through a crash.
Data pages reaching disk do not by themselves decide the outcome.
Releasing locks follows the outcome rather than deciding it.

questions.q: Which component actually makes a single-node commit atomic?
questions.explain: A single device decides the commit, which is what is lost across nodes.
questions.teaches: It is a single device, the controller of one particular disk drive attached to one particular node, that makes the commit atomic.
options: The lock manager that serialises concurrent transactions
The controller of that node's one disk drive
The operating system scheduler that orders the writes
The client library that retries unacknowledged commits
optionExplain: Locks provide isolation, not crash atomicity. The right answer is: The controller of that node's one disk drive.
A single device decides the commit, which is what is lost across nodes.
The scheduler does not make the commit record durable atomically.
Retries by the client do not make the on-disk commit atomic.

questions.q: A client sends commit requests to three nodes, and each commits independently. What can go wrong?
questions.explain: Independent commit can split the outcome. The card next shows why.
options: All three commit but in a different order from each other
The client receives three acknowledgments for one transaction
The commit is slower, but all nodes always end in agreement
Some nodes commit while others abort, breaking atomicity
optionExplain: The issue is a split outcome, not ordering of commits.
Duplicate acknowledgments are not the central risk. The right answer is: Some nodes commit while others abort, breaking atomicity.
Agreement is exactly what independent commits cannot promise. The right answer is: Some nodes commit while others abort, breaking atomicity.
Nothing forces the nodes to reach the same outcome.

questions.q: Independent commits risk some nodes committing and others aborting, which violates the ____ guarantee.
questions.explain: Atomicity requires all of a transaction's writes to take effect or none.

questions.q: Node 2 receives its commit request, but node 3 times out waiting for its own. Which failure mode is this?
questions.explain: Match the symptom to the failure mode.
options: A constraint violation detected on only one node
A crash before the commit record was written on one node
A lost commit request that times out
A deadlock between two committing transactions
optionExplain: No constraint is mentioned; a request simply did not arrive.
The node is waiting, not recovering from a crash.
One request is lost while another arrives, splitting the outcome.
Deadlock is not one of the three failure modes.

questions.q: Which of these can make independent commits leave nodes inconsistent?
questions.explain: Conflicts, lost requests and crashes all split the outcome.
options: One node detects a conflict and has to abort
A commit request is lost and the node times out
A node crashes before its commit record is fully written
One node has a faster disk than the others
The client reads the data a moment after commit
optionExplain: Others may still commit, so the outcomes differ.
That node aborts while others receive the request and commit.
It rolls back on recovery while others commit.
Disk speed alone does not split the outcome.
Reading afterwards does not cause a split.

questions.q: One node has committed, and it later turns out another node aborted. Can the commit be taken back?
questions.explain: That is why a node must commit only when sure all others will.
questions.rule: A commit on one node is final.
questions.teaches: Once a transaction has been committed on one node, it cannot be retracted if it later turns out to have aborted on another node, so a node must only commit once it is certain that all other nodes in the transaction are also going to commit.
options: Yes, the first node can roll back when told
Yes, but only if no client has connected since
Yes, the database automatically reverses it after a timeout
No, once committed on one node it cannot be retracted
optionExplain: Commits cannot be retracted, which is the whole difficulty.
There is no such exception; commits are irrevocable. The right answer is: No, once committed on one node it cannot be retracted.
No automatic reversal exists for a committed transaction. The right answer is: No, once committed on one node it cannot be retracted.
That is why a node must commit only when sure all others will.

questions.q: A write updates a row and a term-partitioned index entry that lives on another node. What does atomic commit protect?
questions.explain: Each index is a separate structure and must change together with the data.
questions.rule: Atomicity covers index and data together.
questions.teaches: Atomicity prevents failed transactions from littering the database with half-finished results and half-updated state; each secondary index is a separate data structure, so atomic commit ensures it stays consistent with the primary data.
options: It makes reads of the index faster than reads of the row
It removes the need to update the index at all
It lets the index run ahead of the row, to be reconciled later
It keeps the index consistent with the primary data
optionExplain: Speed is not what atomic commit provides. The right answer is: It keeps the index consistent with the primary data.
The index still needs to be updated; commit makes it atomic.
Atomicity prevents half-updated state, so no reconciliation is expected.
Each index is a separate structure and must change together with the data.

questions.q: A transaction has committed on node A, but node B then fails to commit. Can A take back its commit?
questions.explain: Commits are final. The card next shows why.
options: No, a commit is irrevocable once made
Yes, A rolls back as soon as B reports the failure
Yes, but only if A has not yet answered the client
Yes, the database re-runs the transaction on A afterwards
optionExplain: Retroactive aborts are not allowed after a commit. Remember: Irrevocable.
Rolling back a commit is exactly what is forbidden.
No such exception exists for commits. The right answer is: No, a commit is irrevocable once made.
Re-running does not retract the original commit. The right answer is: No, a commit is irrevocable once made.

questions.q: A later transaction that undoes the effects of a committed one is called a ____ transaction.
questions.explain: The database sees it as an ordinary new transaction.

questions.q: An order was committed and the customer then cancels. How does the database view the refund that undoes it?
questions.explain: Compensation is a new transaction.
options: As an abort of the original transaction
As a separate, new transaction
As a rollback inside the original transaction
As a continuation that the database links to the original
optionExplain: The original stays committed; no abort happens after the commit.
It is a compensating transaction, unrelated at database level.
The original is already finished and cannot be rolled back.
The database treats the two as unconnected. The right answer is: As a separate, new transaction.

questions.q: True or false: The database guarantees cross-transaction correctness between a committed transaction and its compensating transaction.
questions.explain: From the database's point of view the compensating transaction is separate, so any cross-transaction correctness is the application's problem.

questions.q: Why is aborting a transaction after it committed ruled out?
questions.explain: They would have to be reverted as well, and so on.
questions.rule: Others may already depend on committed data.
questions.teaches: If a transaction were allowed to abort after committing, any transactions that read the committed data would be based on data retroactively declared not to have existed, so they would have to be reverted as well.
options: Readers may have relied on the committed data
Disks cannot undo a write after the commit record is stored
The coordinator would run out of transaction IDs
Aborted transactions cannot be logged on more than one node
optionExplain: They would have to be reverted as well, and so on.
Disks could, but the issue is what readers saw.
Transaction IDs have nothing to do with the rule.
Logging is not the obstacle. The right answer is: Readers may have relied on the committed data.

questions.q: Which isolation guarantee relies on the rule that commits are irrevocable?
questions.explain: Once data is committed, other clients may start relying on it.
questions.rule: Committed data is visible and relied on.
questions.teaches: The irrevocability of commit forms the basis of read committed isolation: once data has been committed it becomes visible to other transactions, and other clients may start relying on it.
options: Read committed
Eventual consistency
Linearizability
Total order broadcast
optionExplain: Once data is committed, other clients may start relying on it.
Eventual consistency is a replication property rather than an isolation level.
Linearizability concerns recency of single objects, not irrevocable commits.
Broadcast ordering is a different concept altogether. The right answer is: Read committed.

questions.q: Three database nodes must commit a transaction together. What does a two-phase protocol ask them first?
questions.explain: Phase one asks, phase two acts. The card next shows why.
options: To commit immediately and report any failure afterwards
To send their data to the coordinator for storage
Whether each of them is able to commit
To pick one of the three nodes to decide for the others
optionExplain: Committing first is the one-phase approach that can split outcomes.
The coordinator does not take over the data. The right answer is: Whether each of them is able to commit.
The prepare phase asks before anyone commits. Remember: Prepare first.
The decision belongs to the coordinator, not a participant.

questions.q: In phase 1 of two-phase commit the coordinator sends a ____ request to every participant.
questions.explain: Participants answer whether they are able to commit.

questions.q: Participants A and B answer yes to prepare, while C answers no. What does the coordinator send in phase 2?
questions.explain: A single no aborts everyone.
options: A commit request to A and B only
A new prepare request to C until it says yes
A commit request to all, since two of three agreed
An abort request to all three participants
optionExplain: Committing on two of three would split the outcome.
A no vote is final and leads to abort.
2PC needs every vote to be yes, not a majority.
Any no vote means abort for everyone. Remember: Any no means abort.

questions.q: True or false: In 2PC, a single no answer in phase 1 is enough to make the coordinator abort the transaction on all participants.
questions.explain: Commit requires yes from every participant, so one no leads to an abort request for all.

questions.q: Besides internal use in some databases, how is 2PC made available to applications?
questions.explain: Both interfaces expose 2PC to applications.
questions.teaches: Two-phase commit is used internally in some databases and also made available to applications in the form of XA transactions (supported by the Java Transaction API, for example) or via WS-AtomicTransaction for SOAP web services.
options: As a replication mode of single-leader databases
As a clock synchronisation service for the participants
As XA transactions or WS-AtomicTransaction
As a feature of leaderless quorum reads and writes
optionExplain: 2PC is not a replication mode. The right answer is: As XA transactions or WS-AtomicTransaction.
It is a commit protocol, not a clock service.
Both interfaces expose 2PC to applications. Remember: 2PC reaches applications through standard interfaces.
Quorums do not use 2PC. The right answer is: As XA transactions or WS-AtomicTransaction.

questions.q: In the book's marriage analogy, what corresponds to participants answering yes in phase 1?
questions.explain: The minister asks individually, like a prepare request.
questions.rule: The analogy maps votes to I do.
questions.teaches: Like a marriage ceremony, the minister (coordinator) asks bride and groom individually whether each wants to marry (prepare), and after both say I do pronounces them married (commit); if either does not say yes, the ceremony is aborted.
options: The minister pronouncing them husband and wife
The guests applauding after the ceremony
Each partner saying I do when the minister asks
The partners signing the certificate afterwards
optionExplain: That corresponds to the commit decision in phase 2.
Guests are the broadcast of the outcome, not the votes.
The minister asks individually, like a prepare request. Remember: The analogy maps votes to I do.
The signing is not part of the analogy. The right answer is: Each partner saying I do when the minister asks.

questions.q: A document says a system uses a two-phase protocol. A teammate takes it to mean serializable isolation. What should you check?
questions.explain: Name similarity hides a difference in purpose. The card next shows why.
options: Whether the protocol uses more than two nodes
Whether the system stores data on disk or in memory
Whether it means commit or locking
Whether the protocol is implemented as a library
optionExplain: Node count does not separate the two protocols. The right answer is: Whether it means commit or locking.
Storage medium does not separate them. The right answer is: Whether it means commit or locking.
The two names cover different problems. Remember: Commit versus locking.
Packaging does not separate the two concepts. The right answer is: Whether it means commit or locking.

questions.q: Two-phase ____ provides serializable isolation, whereas two-phase commit provides atomic commit.
questions.explain: They solve different problems despite the similar names.

questions.q: A distributed database must make all nodes of a transaction commit or all abort. Which protocol does it need?
questions.explain: Match the protocol to the problem.
options: Two-phase locking
Snapshot isolation by itself
Lamport timestamps on each write
Two-phase commit
optionExplain: Locking provides isolation, not agreement on the outcome. The right answer is: Two-phase commit.
Isolation does not make commit atomic across nodes. The right answer is: Two-phase commit.
Timestamps order events but do not decide commit or abort.
Atomic commit across nodes is what 2PC provides. Remember: Atomic commit needs 2PC.

questions.q: True or false: The coordinator in 2PC must be a separate service on its own machine.
questions.explain: It is often a library inside the application process, though it can also be a separate process or service.

questions.q: Where is the 2PC coordinator often implemented?
questions.explain: For example embedded in a Java EE container.
questions.teaches: The coordinator is often implemented as a library within the same application process that requests the transaction (for example embedded in a Java EE container), but it can also be a separate process or service.
options: As a standby replica of one of the database nodes
As a firmware feature of the disk controller
As a library in the application process
As a service run by the cloud provider's DNS layer
optionExplain: It is not a replica of a participant. The right answer is: As a library in the application process.
Disk controllers play no part in 2PC. The right answer is: As a library in the application process.
For example embedded in a Java EE container. Remember: Coordinator placement affects failure behaviour.
DNS has no role in the coordinator. The right answer is: As a library in the application process.

questions.q: Which nodes are participants in a 2PC transaction?
questions.explain: The transaction begins with ordinary reads and writes on multiple nodes.
questions.rule: Participants are the data nodes involved.
questions.teaches: A 2PC transaction begins with the application reading and writing data on multiple database nodes as normal; these database nodes are called participants in the transaction.
options: The nodes that vote to elect the coordinator
The replicas that only store the coordinator's log
The database nodes the application used
The client machines that issue the transaction requests
optionExplain: 2PC does not elect its coordinator. The right answer is: The database nodes the application used.
Those are not the data nodes taking part. The right answer is: The database nodes the application used.
The transaction begins with ordinary reads and writes on multiple nodes.
Clients are not participants. The right answer is: The database nodes the application used.

questions.q: A participant replies yes to a prepare request. What has it done?
questions.explain: Yes means a binding promise. The card next shows why.
options: Committed the transaction and made its writes visible
Promised to commit if it is later asked
Told the coordinator to proceed regardless of other votes
Reserved the right to abort later if a better option appears
optionExplain: Commit only happens when the coordinator's phase 2 request arrives.
It surrenders the right to abort but has not yet committed.
The coordinator still waits for all the votes. The right answer is: Promised to commit if it is later asked.
Voting yes gives up the right to abort. The right answer is: Promised to commit if it is later asked.

questions.q: By voting yes, a participant surrenders its right to ____ the transaction on its own.
questions.explain: It must commit if the coordinator later says so.

questions.q: Before replying yes to prepare, what must a participant do?
questions.explain: Make commit certain before promising.
options: Write its data to disk and check conflicts
Wait for the coordinator to announce the final decision
Release its locks so that other transactions can proceed
Send its changes to every other participant for review
optionExplain: Only then can it promise to commit under all circumstances.
That comes after voting, not before. The right answer is: Write its data to disk and check conflicts.
Locks must be held until the outcome is known.
Participants do not exchange changes in 2PC. The right answer is: Write its data to disk and check conflicts.

questions.q: True or false: After voting yes, a participant that crashes may refuse to commit on recovery if its disk has run out of space.
questions.explain: It already wrote all transaction data to disk before voting, so such an excuse is not acceptable.

questions.q: Why must a participant write all data to disk before voting yes?
questions.explain: The promise must hold under all circumstances.
questions.teaches: A participant must make sure it can definitely commit under all circumstances, including writing all transaction data to disk, because a crash, a power failure, or running out of disk space is not an acceptable excuse for refusing to commit later.
options: The coordinator needs to read that data to compute its decision
No excuse such as a crash or full disk is acceptable
Other participants copy that data to stay in sync
Disk writes are the only way to send votes over the network
optionExplain: The coordinator never reads participant data. The right answer is: No excuse such as a crash or full disk is acceptable.
The promise must hold under all circumstances. Remember: The promise must survive crashes.
Participants do not copy each other's data. The right answer is: No excuse such as a crash or full disk is acceptable.
Votes travel over the network, not through disk writes.

questions.q: In the book's analogy, a partner says I do and then faints before the pronouncement. What is the status?
questions.explain: Saying I do cannot be retracted.
questions.teaches: If you faint after saying I do and do not hear the minister's pronouncement, the transaction was still committed; when you recover you can query the minister for the status of your global transaction ID, or wait for the minister's next retry of the commit request.
options: The marriage is aborted because they did not hear the pronouncement
It is committed; they can ask the minister later
The marriage is undecided until the partner wakes up and agrees again
The marriage goes ahead only if the guests also vote
optionExplain: Fainting does not undo the yes. The right answer is: It is committed; they can ask the minister later.
Saying I do cannot be retracted. Remember: A yes cannot be retracted.
The yes already given is binding. The right answer is: It is committed; they can ask the minister later.
Guests have no vote in the analogy. The right answer is: It is committed; they can ask the minister later.

questions.q: A coordinator holds all yes votes. In which order should it log the decision and send commit requests?
questions.explain: Persist the decision before it leaves. The card next shows why.
options: Log it to disk first and then send
Send first and log once the replies arrive
Send to half of the nodes, log, then send to the rest
Log only if a participant asks for the decision
optionExplain: A crash after sending but before logging would lose the decision.
Logging late risks forgetting a decision that others already acted on.
Splitting the sends around the log adds risk without benefit.
The decision must be durable regardless of requests. The right answer is: Log it to disk first and then send.

questions.q: The moment the coordinator's decision is written to its transaction log is called the ____ point.
questions.explain: From that moment the outcome is fixed.

questions.q: The coordinator's commit request to participant B times out. What must it do?
questions.explain: The decision must reach everyone.
options: Abort the transaction on all participants
Retry until the request succeeds
Ask all participants to vote again
Leave B in doubt and move on to other work
optionExplain: A commit decision cannot be switched to abort. The right answer is: Retry until the request succeeds.
The decision is final and must be enforced however many retries it takes.
The votes are already in and the decision is made.
The coordinator must keep going until B has the decision.

questions.q: True or false: If the decision was commit, the coordinator may switch to abort after too many failed retries.
questions.explain: There is no going back: a commit decision must be enforced no matter how many retries it takes.

questions.q: A participant that voted yes crashes before the commit request arrives. What happens when it recovers?
questions.explain: The coordinator's retries eventually reach it.
questions.rule: A yes vote binds across a crash.
questions.teaches: If a participant has crashed in the meantime, the transaction will be committed when it recovers, since the participant voted yes and so cannot refuse to commit when it recovers.
options: It commits, since it voted yes
It aborts the transaction because it lost contact
It holds a new vote with the other participants
It waits indefinitely for the client to retry
optionExplain: The coordinator's retries eventually reach it. Remember: A yes vote binds across a crash.
Having voted yes it cannot abort on its own.
No fresh vote takes place in 2PC. The right answer is: It commits, since it voted yes.
The coordinator, not the client, delivers the decision. The right answer is: It commits, since it voted yes.

questions.q: A prepare request to one participant fails or times out. What does the coordinator do?
questions.explain: A missing prepare answer means the transaction aborts.
questions.teaches: If any prepare request fails or times out, the coordinator sends an abort request for that transaction ID to all participants; the transaction ID was requested from the coordinator at the start and is globally unique.
options: Sends an abort for that transaction to all
Commits on the remaining participants and retries the failed one
Waits forever for the missing reply before deciding
Asks the failed participant's neighbour to answer for it
optionExplain: A missing prepare answer means the transaction aborts. Remember: A failed prepare means abort.
Committing without the failed vote would break atomicity. The right answer is: Sends an abort for that transaction to all.
The coordinator aborts on failure or timeout of a prepare.
No participant can vote on another's behalf. The right answer is: Sends an abort for that transaction to all.

questions.q: In 2PC, after which two events can nobody back out any longer?
questions.explain: Two promises make 2PC atomic. The card next shows why.
options: A yes vote and the coordinator's decision
The prepare request and the participant's disk write
The coordinator's timeout and the participant's reply
The commit request and the acknowledgment
optionExplain: Those two promises ensure atomicity. Remember: Yes vote and decision.
Those steps lead up to the promises but are not themselves the points of no return.
Timeouts do not bind anyone. The right answer is: A yes vote and the coordinator's decision.
These carry out the decision after the points of no return.

questions.q: After a participant votes yes, the ____ may still choose to abort.
questions.explain: The yes only promises that the participant can commit if asked.

questions.q: Participant B voted yes and then crashed, and the coordinator logged commit. What must happen to B when it recovers?
questions.explain: Both promises bind B.
options: It aborts, because it crashed
It commits the transaction
It votes again and may change its answer
It waits to see whether the other participants committed
optionExplain: Crashing does not release the promise. The right answer is: It commits the transaction.
Its yes vote was a promise, and the decision is irrevocable.
A yes vote cannot be re-voted. The right answer is: It commits the transaction.
B does not need the others; the decision is already made.

questions.q: True or false: Before a participant votes yes, it is still free to abort the transaction.
questions.explain: The first point of no return is the yes vote, so earlier the participant keeps the right to abort.

questions.q: How do the two points of no return appear in a single-node atomic commit?
questions.explain: On one node, the vote and the decision coincide.
questions.rule: One node merges the two events.
questions.teaches: Single-node atomic commit lumps the two points of no return into one event: writing the commit record to the transaction log.
options: They merge into one event, the commit record write
They are two separate disk flushes on different machines
They do not exist, since there is no failure to handle
They are replaced by a vote among the node's threads
optionExplain: On one node, the vote and the decision coincide.
A single node has only one log write. The right answer is: They merge into one event, the commit record write.
Crashes still need handling on a single node. The right answer is: They merge into one event, the commit record write.
No voting occurs inside a single node's commit. The right answer is: They merge into one event, the commit record write.

questions.q: Where does the commit point of 2PC reduce to a regular single-node atomic commit?
questions.explain: The decision is made durable like any single-node commit.
questions.rule: The coordinator's log is the decision.
questions.teaches: The commit point of 2PC comes down to a regular single-node atomic commit on the coordinator.
options: On the coordinator, when it logs its decision
On each participant, when it receives the prepare request
On the client, when it receives the acknowledgement
On the network, when all packets have been delivered
optionExplain: The decision is made durable like any single-node commit.
Participants make a promise there, not the final decision.
The client has no durable role. The right answer is: On the coordinator, when it logs its decision.
The network is not a commit device. The right answer is: On the coordinator, when it logs its decision.

questions.q: Database 1 voted yes, then lost contact with the coordinator, while database 2 already committed. What should database 1 do?
questions.explain: Only the coordinator knows the outcome. The card next shows why.
options: Abort after a timeout
Commit after a timeout because most participants probably did
Keep waiting for the coordinator
Ask the client which outcome to apply
optionExplain: Aborting would contradict database 2, which committed. The right answer is: Keep waiting for the coordinator.
Another participant may have aborted, so a guess is unsafe.
Guessing either way could leave it inconsistent with database 2.
The client does not know the coordinator's decision. The right answer is: Keep waiting for the coordinator.

questions.q: A participant that voted yes and has not heard the outcome is said to be in ____.
questions.explain: It is also called uncertain.

questions.q: The coordinator committed and told database 2 but crashed before telling database 1. Why is a timeout abort unsafe on database 1?
questions.explain: A unilateral decision breaks atomicity.
options: The timeout is too short to detect a crash reliably
Abort requests can only be sent by the coordinator's replica
Database 1's locks would then be released too early
Database 2 committed, so database 1 would disagree
optionExplain: Even a long timeout would not make the abort safe.
Any participant can abort; the issue is consistency. The right answer is: Database 2 committed, so database 1 would disagree.
Lock timing is not what makes the abort unsafe.
The two would disagree on the outcome. Remember: Abort would disagree.

questions.q: True or false: A participant that has not yet received any prepare request can safely abort if the coordinator fails.
questions.explain: Before voting yes it has not promised anything, so it may still abort on its own.

questions.q: How does a restarted coordinator resolve in-doubt transactions?
questions.explain: Its log holds the decisions it recorded before crashing.
questions.teaches: When the coordinator recovers, it determines the status of all in-doubt transactions by reading its transaction log, and any transaction without a commit record in the log is aborted.
options: It asks each participant to vote again from scratch
It commits every transaction it finds, to be safe
It reads its log and aborts those without a commit
It waits for a client to resubmit each transaction
optionExplain: The earlier votes and the logged decision are used instead.
Committing blindly could contradict a decision to abort. The right answer is: It reads its log and aborts those without a commit.
Its log holds the decisions it recorded before crashing.
Clients do not drive the recovery. The right answer is: It reads its log and aborts those without a commit.

questions.q: Could in-doubt participants resolve the problem by asking each other how they voted?
questions.explain: 2PC does not define such communication.
questions.teaches: In principle the participants could communicate among themselves to find out how each participant voted and come to some agreement, but that is not part of the 2PC protocol.
options: No, participants are not able to communicate with each other at all
Yes, and 2PC requires it after every coordinator crash
In principle yes, but that is not part of the 2PC protocol
Yes, and it removes the blocking problem completely
optionExplain: Nothing prevents it physically; the protocol just does not use it.
2PC does not require it. The right answer is: In principle yes, but that is not part of the 2PC protocol.
2PC does not define such communication. Remember: 2PC relies on the coordinator alone.
The protocol as defined does not use it, so blocking remains.

questions.q: Why is 2PC called a blocking atomic commit protocol?
questions.explain: Blocking means stuck waiting. The card next shows why.
options: It blocks all reads on every participant at all times
It forbids participants from voting no
It locks the coordinator while the participants vote
It can get stuck waiting for the coordinator
optionExplain: It blocks in-doubt participants, not all reads always. The right answer is: It can get stuck waiting for the coordinator.
Participants are free to vote no in phase 1.
The blocking concerns participants waiting, not the coordinator. The right answer is: It can get stuck waiting for the coordinator.
In-doubt participants can do nothing until then. Remember: Stuck on the coordinator.

questions.q: Three-phase commit assumes a network with ____ delay, which most real systems do not provide.
questions.explain: It also assumes bounded response times.

questions.q: A team swaps 2PC for 3PC on a network with occasional multi-minute delays. What risk remains?
questions.explain: Unbounded delay defeats 3PC.
options: None, since 3PC is nonblocking and therefore always safe
Only a small slowdown from the extra phase
Atomicity may fail because delay is unbounded
The coordinator's log will no longer be needed
optionExplain: Being nonblocking does not help if its assumptions fail.
The risk is lost atomicity, not just speed. The right answer is: Atomicity may fail because delay is unbounded.
3PC depends on bounded delays and response times. Remember: Delay breaks 3PC.
The risk concerns correctness, not logging. The right answer is: Atomicity may fail because delay is unbounded.

questions.q: True or false: In practice, three-phase commit guarantees atomicity even with unbounded network delay and process pauses.
questions.explain: In systems with unbounded delay and pauses it cannot guarantee atomicity, which is why 2PC is still used.

questions.q: What does nonblocking atomic commit require, according to the book?
questions.explain: Only then can it avoid getting stuck.
questions.teaches: In general, nonblocking atomic commit requires a perfect failure detector, a reliable mechanism for telling whether a node has crashed or not.
options: A synchronised wall clock on every participant
A coordinator that is replicated on three machines
A majority quorum on each participant's disk
A perfect failure detector
optionExplain: A clock is not the stated requirement. The right answer is: A perfect failure detector.
Replication alone does not give a failure detector. The right answer is: A perfect failure detector.
Quorum disks are not the stated requirement. The right answer is: A perfect failure detector.
Only then can it avoid getting stuck. Remember: Nonblocking needs reliable failure detection.

questions.q: Timeouts cannot detect crashes reliably when delay is unbounded. What follows for real systems?
questions.explain: No practical nonblocking alternative works under unbounded delay.
questions.teaches: In a network with unbounded delay a timeout is not a reliable failure detector, since a request may time out due to a network problem even if no node has crashed; for this reason 2PC continues to be used despite the known problem with coordinator failure.
options: Atomic commit is abandoned in every distributed database
Timeouts are replaced by perfect failure detectors
Participants decide on their own after a timeout
2PC stays in use despite its blocking problem
optionExplain: 2PC is still implemented in many systems. The right answer is: 2PC stays in use despite its blocking problem.
Perfect detectors are not available in such networks. The right answer is: 2PC stays in use despite its blocking problem.
Unilateral decisions would break atomicity. The right answer is: 2PC stays in use despite its blocking problem.
No practical nonblocking alternative works under unbounded delay. Remember: Practice keeps 2PC.

questions.q: A team hears that distributed transactions kill performance. Where does much of the 2PC cost come from?
questions.explain: The cost is forced writes and round trips. The card next shows why.
options: Compressing all data before sending it to the coordinator
Re-reading every row twice before the commit begins
Extra disk forcing and extra network round trips
Encrypting each message with a new key for every phase
optionExplain: Compression is not what drives the cost. The right answer is: Extra disk forcing and extra network round trips.
Double reads are not part of the protocol. The right answer is: Extra disk forcing and extra network round trips.
Both are needed for crash recovery and for the two phases.
Encryption is not the stated cost. The right answer is: Extra disk forcing and extra network round trips.

questions.q: Much of the cost of 2PC comes from additional disk forcing, called ____, and extra network round trips.
questions.explain: The forced writes are needed for crash recovery.

questions.q: A latency-sensitive service needs consistency across two databases. What is a fair reading of the book's view?
questions.explain: Weigh the guarantee against the cost.
options: Dismiss distributed transactions outright as unusable in practice
Use them everywhere, since the cost is negligible in practice
Use two-phase locking instead, since it also gives atomic commit
Weigh the guarantee against the performance and operational cost
optionExplain: The book says not to dismiss them outright. The right answer is: Weigh the guarantee against the performance and operational cost.
The book describes real performance and operational costs. The right answer is: Weigh the guarantee against the performance and operational cost.
Two-phase locking gives isolation, not atomic commit. The right answer is: Weigh the guarantee against the performance and operational cost.
The book urges examining distributed transactions rather than dismissing them.

questions.q: True or false: The book advises dismissing distributed transactions outright, since they offer no useful safety guarantee.
questions.explain: They are seen as providing an important safety guarantee that would be hard to achieve otherwise, so the book examines them rather than dismissing them.

questions.q: How much slower are distributed transactions in MySQL reported to be than single-node transactions?
questions.explain: That is a heavy penalty and explains why people advise against them.
questions.rule: The penalty can be an order of magnitude.
questions.teaches: Distributed transactions in MySQL are reported to be over 10 times slower than single-node transactions, so it is not surprising when people advise against using them.
options: About 20 percent slower
About twice as slow, no more
Over 10 times slower
No slower, only the memory use rises
optionExplain: The report is of a much larger penalty than that.
The reported slowdown is far above two times. The right answer is: Over 10 times slower.
That is a heavy penalty and explains why people advise against them.
There is a reported performance penalty. The right answer is: Over 10 times slower.

questions.q: What have many cloud services chosen to do about distributed transactions?
questions.explain: The problems they engender outweigh the guarantee for these services.
questions.rule: Operational cost can push services away.
questions.teaches: Many cloud services choose not to implement distributed transactions due to the operational problems they engender.
options: Implement them as the default for every write
Implement them only for read-only queries
Not implement them at all
Replace them with two-phase locking across regions
optionExplain: They have mostly avoided them. The right answer is: Not implement them at all.
Read-only queries do not need atomic commit. The right answer is: Not implement them at all.
The problems they engender outweigh the guarantee for these services.
Two-phase locking is not a substitute for atomic commit.

questions.q: Which distributed transaction is usually easier: among nodes of one database product, or across two vendors' products?
questions.explain: Control over both sides helps. The card next shows why.
options: Across two vendors, since they can negotiate a protocol freely
They are equally hard, since both use 2PC
Neither is possible without a shared clock
Among the nodes of one database product
optionExplain: Different vendors must follow a shared standard instead. The right answer is: Among the nodes of one database product.
Control over the participants makes a large difference. The right answer is: Among the nodes of one database product.
No shared clock is required for 2PC. The right answer is: Among the nodes of one database product.
One vendor controls every participant. Remember: Same vendor is easier.

questions.q: A transaction that spans a database and a message broker is called a ____ distributed transaction.
questions.explain: The participants are different technologies.

questions.q: A transaction involves a PostgreSQL database and an ActiveMQ message broker. Which kind is it?
questions.explain: Count the technologies.
options: Database-internal
Single-node
Heterogeneous
Replicated only
optionExplain: Internal ones involve nodes of the same database software.
Two separate systems are involved. The right answer is: Heterogeneous.
The participants are different technologies. Remember: Two technologies.
Replication is not the issue here. The right answer is: Heterogeneous.

questions.q: True or false: Database-internal distributed transactions must stay compatible with other systems, so they cannot use specialised optimizations.
questions.explain: They do not have to be compatible with any other system, so they can apply optimizations specific to their technology.

questions.q: Why can database-internal distributed transactions often work quite well?
questions.explain: They can apply optimizations specific to their own technology.
questions.rule: Control of both ends allows tuning.
questions.teaches: Database-internal transactions do not have to be compatible with any other system, so they can use any protocol and apply optimizations specific to that particular technology.
options: They never fail, since all nodes run identical software
They skip the prepare phase entirely
They run in a single process with shared memory
They need not match other systems
optionExplain: Failures still occur; control helps, but does not remove them.
They still need atomic commit among nodes. The right answer is: They need not match other systems.
They span several nodes of a distributed database. The right answer is: They need not match other systems.
They can apply optimizations specific to their own technology.

questions.q: Which examples does the book give of database-internal distributed transaction support?
questions.explain: Both support internal transactions among their own nodes.
questions.teaches: VoltDB and MySQL Cluster's NDB storage engine are examples of distributed databases, using replication and partitioning in their standard configuration, that support internal transactions among the nodes of that database.
options: ActiveMQ together with PostgreSQL, as one transaction
Kafka together with Oracle, as one transaction
IBM MQ together with DB2, as one transaction
VoltDB and MySQL Cluster's NDB storage engine
optionExplain: That pairing is a heterogeneous combination. The right answer is: VoltDB and MySQL Cluster's NDB storage engine.
That pairing mixes different technologies. The right answer is: VoltDB and MySQL Cluster's NDB storage engine.
That pairing also mixes different technologies. The right answer is: VoltDB and MySQL Cluster's NDB storage engine.
Both support internal transactions among their own nodes. Remember: Internal means one product.

questions.q: A consumer writes to a database and then crashes before acknowledging the message. What problem results?
questions.explain: Acknowledgment and write must succeed together. The card next shows why.
options: The database write is rolled back automatically
The broker deletes the message anyway after a delay
The message is delivered to a second broker
The message is redelivered and processed again
optionExplain: Nothing links the write to the missing acknowledgment. The right answer is: The message is redelivered and processed again.
An unacknowledged message is not simply deleted. The right answer is: The message is redelivered and processed again.
Brokers do not forward unacknowledged messages like that. The right answer is: The message is redelivered and processed again.
The database write already happened, so reprocessing duplicates it.

questions.q: Committing the acknowledgment and the database writes together gives effectively ____ processing of the message.
questions.explain: Retries are allowed, yet the effects occur once.

questions.q: Message delivery succeeds but the database transaction fails. In the atomic scheme, what happens to the acknowledgment?
questions.explain: One transaction, one outcome.
options: It is committed, and the database write is retried later
It is held until an administrator approves it
It is aborted along with the database writes
It is sent to the database as a replacement write
optionExplain: That would lose the effects of the message. The right answer is: It is aborted along with the database writes.
Nothing in the scheme asks for manual approval. The right answer is: It is aborted along with the database writes.
Both are part of one transaction, so both abort.
An acknowledgment is not a database write. The right answer is: It is aborted along with the database writes.

questions.q: True or false: Atomic commit across a broker and a database requires both to be the same technology.
questions.explain: It works across unrelated technologies on different machines, provided they use the same atomic commit protocol.

questions.q: Processing a message sends an email through a server that does not support 2PC. What can happen on retry?
questions.explain: The email is outside the transaction and cannot be rolled back.
questions.rule: Side effects outside the transaction can repeat.
questions.teaches: If a side effect of processing a message is to send an email and the email server does not support two-phase commit, the email could be sent two or more times if message processing fails and is retried.
options: The email is automatically recalled on abort
The email is queued until the transaction commits
The email is sent exactly once regardless of retries
The email may be sent two or more times
optionExplain: Without 2PC support the email cannot be undone. The right answer is: The email may be sent two or more times.
A server without 2PC support cannot do that. The right answer is: The email may be sent two or more times.
That guarantee needs the email to join the transaction.
The email is outside the transaction and cannot be rolled back.

questions.q: Processing aborts after the database write was made. What happens to that write and the message?
questions.explain: The abort discards side effects of the partial transaction.
questions.teaches: The abort discards any side effects of the partially completed transaction, so the processing step can safely be retried as if nothing had happened, and the message is effectively processed exactly once.
options: The write stays and the message is deleted
The write stays and the message is processed again on top
Both stay until the next successful retry overwrites them
The write is discarded; the message is redelivered
optionExplain: That would lose the message's processing. The right answer is: The write is discarded; the message is redelivered.
Duplicate effects are what the scheme prevents. The right answer is: The write is discarded; the message is redelivered.
The abort removes them rather than leaving them. The right answer is: The write is discarded; the message is redelivered.
The abort discards side effects of the partial transaction.
