questions.q: A transaction spans a relational database and a message broker from different vendors. What must they share for 2PC?
questions.explain: A common standard connects unlike systems. The card next shows why.
options: The same storage engine and file format
Support for the same atomic commit standard
A shared clock accurate to one millisecond
The same query language for all participants
optionExplain: Different vendors will not share storage engines. The right answer is: Support for the same atomic commit standard.
XA lets unlike systems join one 2PC. Remember: Same commit standard.
2PC does not need synchronised clocks. The right answer is: Support for the same atomic commit standard.
The language of queries is not what is needed.

questions.q: XA is not a network protocol but a ____ API for interfacing with a transaction coordinator.
questions.explain: Bindings exist for other languages as well.

questions.q: A Java application wants its database and message broker in one XA transaction. Which API does it use?
questions.explain: XA appears as JTA in Java.
options: The Java Transaction API (JTA)
A custom TCP protocol defined by the coordinator
JDBC alone, with no transaction manager
A REST endpoint exposed by each database
optionExplain: JTA is how XA transactions are used in Java EE applications.
XA is an API, not a network protocol. The right answer is: The Java Transaction API (JTA).
JDBC drivers call XA but a coordinator is still needed.
XA does not use REST endpoints. The right answer is: The Java Transaction API (JTA).

questions.q: True or false: XA is a network protocol that the participating databases speak to each other.
questions.explain: XA is a C API for interfacing with a transaction coordinator, and the drivers call it; it is not a network protocol.

questions.q: Does the XA standard say how the transaction coordinator must be implemented?
questions.explain: The standard leaves the coordinator's implementation open.
questions.teaches: The XA standard does not specify how the coordinator should be implemented; in practice it is often a library loaded into the same process as the application, keeping track of participants and using a log on the local disk to record each commit or abort decision.
options: Yes, it must be a separate replicated service
No; often it is a library in the application
Yes, it must run inside the database server
Yes, it must be stored in a distributed hash table
optionExplain: The standard does not mandate that. The right answer is: No; often it is a library in the application.
The standard leaves the coordinator's implementation open. Remember: The standard leaves implementation open.
The coordinator is not inside the database. The right answer is: No; often it is a library in the application.
No such requirement exists. The right answer is: No; often it is a library in the application.

questions.q: Can a database server contact the XA coordinator directly to ask about an in-doubt transaction?
questions.explain: The server only sees the driver's callbacks.
questions.rule: The driver is the only path.
questions.teaches: The database server cannot contact the coordinator directly, since all communication must go via its client library.
options: Yes, through a dedicated coordinator port
No, only via its client library
Yes, by broadcasting to all application servers
Yes, but only after the administrator unlocks it
optionExplain: No such direct channel exists. The right answer is: No, only via its client library.
The server only sees the driver's callbacks. Remember: The driver is the only path.
Servers do not broadcast to find coordinators. The right answer is: No, only via its client library.
Direct contact is not available at all. The right answer is: No, only via its client library.

questions.q: A participant is in doubt after a coordinator crash. What happens to other transactions that want the same rows?
questions.explain: Locks outlive the coordinator's crash. The card next shows why.
options: They overwrite the rows, since no commit has happened
They block until the doubt is resolved
They are redirected to a replica of the rows
They proceed after a short timeout
optionExplain: Exclusive locks prevent that. The right answer is: They block until the doubt is resolved.
The in-doubt transaction cannot release its locks. Remember: Others block.
Replicas of locked rows are not used this way.
The lock stays until the outcome is known. The right answer is: They block until the doubt is resolved.

questions.q: An in-doubt transaction cannot release its ____ until it learns whether to commit or abort.
questions.explain: Row-level exclusive locks prevent dirty writes.

questions.q: The coordinator is down and an in-doubt transaction holds locks on order rows. A new transaction updates them. What happens?
questions.explain: Blocked on the locks.
options: It waits for the locks to be released
It steals the locks, since the owner is unreachable
It runs on a copy of the rows and merges later
It aborts at once and reports a constraint violation
optionExplain: Locks cannot be taken over. Remember: It waits.
Stealing locks would break the promises of 2PC. The right answer is: It waits for the locks to be released.
The database does not fork the rows. The right answer is: It waits for the locks to be released.
It blocks rather than aborting by default. The right answer is: It waits for the locks to be released.

questions.q: True or false: Other transactions can ignore an in-doubt transaction and carry on with their own work on the same rows.
questions.explain: If they want to access the same data they are blocked, which can make large parts of an application unavailable.

questions.q: A coordinator takes 20 minutes to start up again. How long are the in-doubt locks held, and what if its log is lost?
questions.explain: Locks last as long as the doubt does.
questions.teaches: If the coordinator has crashed and takes 20 minutes to start up again, the locks will be held for 20 minutes; if the coordinator's log is entirely lost, the locks will be held forever, or at least until an administrator manually resolves the situation.
options: A few seconds, as locks expire by timeout
About 20 minutes; forever if the log is lost
20 minutes, and a lost log releases them at once
Until the next database backup runs
optionExplain: Locks do not expire by themselves. The right answer is: About 20 minutes; forever if the log is lost.
Locks last as long as the doubt does. Remember: Lock time equals doubt time.
A lost log leaves them held, not released. The right answer is: About 20 minutes; forever if the log is lost.
Backups play no role. The right answer is: About 20 minutes; forever if the log is lost.

questions.q: A database uses two-phase locking for serializable isolation. What additional locks might an in-doubt transaction hold?
questions.explain: Serializable isolation with 2PL takes shared locks on rows read.
questions.teaches: If you want serializable isolation, a database using two-phase locking would also have to take a shared lock on any rows read by the transaction, and depending on the database, other transactions may even be blocked from reading the locked rows.
options: Table-wide locks on every table in the database
Shared locks on the rows it read
No further locks, as shared locks release early
Locks on the coordinator's log file
optionExplain: 2PL locks rows read and written, not whole databases.
Serializable isolation with 2PL takes shared locks on rows read.
Under 2PL shared locks are held until the end.
Log files are not what 2PL locks. The right answer is: Shared locks on the rows it read.

questions.q: A coordinator's log was corrupted by a bug, leaving transactions in doubt. What is the way out?
questions.explain: Only a human can decide. The card next shows why.
options: Restart the database servers to clear the locks
An administrator decides by hand
Wait for the participants to time out and abort
Let each participant choose its own outcome
optionExplain: A restart does not clear in-doubt transactions. The right answer is: An administrator decides by hand.
No automatic resolution is possible without the log. Remember: Manual resolution.
Timing out would risk breaking atomicity. The right answer is: An administrator decides by hand.
Independent choices risk inconsistency. The right answer is: An administrator decides by hand.

questions.q: A transaction whose coordinator cannot decide the outcome is called an ____ in-doubt transaction.
questions.explain: It cannot be resolved automatically.

questions.q: An administrator finds that participant A already committed an orphaned transaction while B is still in doubt. What should B get?
questions.explain: Match the participant that has decided.
options: Commit, to match A
Abort, to be safe
Whichever outcome B prefers
Neither, until a new vote is held
optionExplain: The same outcome must be applied to all participants.
That would contradict A's commit. The right answer is: Commit, to match A.
The outcome must be uniform. The right answer is: Commit, to match A.
No new vote exists to run. The right answer is: Commit, to match A.

questions.q: True or false: Rebooting the database servers clears orphaned in-doubt transactions and releases their locks.
questions.explain: They survive restarts, so locks stay in place until someone resolves the transaction.

questions.q: Why does a restart not release the locks of an in-doubt transaction?
questions.explain: Releasing the locks could let others see a possibly wrong state.
questions.teaches: A correct implementation of 2PC must preserve the locks of an in-doubt transaction even across restarts, since otherwise it would risk violating the atomicity guarantee.
options: Locks are stored on the client and survive server restarts
Correct 2PC must keep them to protect atomicity
The coordinator holds a master copy that is reloaded
The operating system restores the locks from swap
optionExplain: Locks are held by the database. The right answer is: Correct 2PC must keep them to protect atomicity.
Releasing the locks could let others see a possibly wrong state.
That is not why the restart fails. The right answer is: Correct 2PC must keep them to protect atomicity.
The reason is protocol correctness, not the OS. The right answer is: Correct 2PC must keep them to protect atomicity.

questions.q: What are heuristic decisions in XA implementations?
questions.explain: They are an emergency escape hatch for catastrophes.
questions.rule: A last resort that sacrifices atomicity.
questions.teaches: Many XA implementations have an emergency escape hatch called heuristic decisions, allowing a participant to unilaterally decide to abort or commit an in-doubt transaction; heuristic here is a euphemism for probably breaking atomicity, intended only for catastrophic situations and not for regular use.
options: A faster path used for ordinary commits
A one-sided decision that may break atomicity
A vote among the participants to pick the outcome
A coordinator setting that retries prepare requests
optionExplain: They are not meant for regular use. The right answer is: A one-sided decision that may break atomicity.
They are an emergency escape hatch for catastrophes. Remember: A last resort that sacrifices atomicity.
They are made by one participant alone. The right answer is: A one-sided decision that may break atomicity.
They concern in-doubt participants deciding alone. The right answer is: A one-sided decision that may break atomicity.

questions.q: A 2PC commit needs every participant to respond. What does that do to failures in the system?
questions.explain: All must respond. The card next shows why.
options: It hides them, since the coordinator retries until success
It amplifies them: one broken part fails all
It spreads them evenly over all participants
It removes them, because votes are written to disk
optionExplain: Retries do not help when a participant is down.
That runs counter to building fault-tolerant systems. Remember: Failure amplification.
The transaction simply fails. The right answer is: It amplifies them: one broken part fails all.
Disk writes do not prevent failures. The right answer is: It amplifies them: one broken part fails all.

questions.q: Because XA must work with many data systems, it is necessarily a lowest common ____.
questions.explain: It cannot assume features that only some systems have.

questions.q: The coordinator runs on a single machine and is not replicated. What risk does that create?
questions.explain: Treat the coordinator like a database.
options: A single point of failure
Slower commits, but no extra risk
A risk only for read-only transactions
A risk that disappears once participants have voted
optionExplain: Its failure leaves transactions in doubt. Remember: Replicate it.
The bigger issue is blocking on locks. The right answer is: A single point of failure.
The danger is for prepared write transactions. The right answer is: A single point of failure.
Voting yes is exactly what leaves them stuck. The right answer is: A single point of failure.

questions.q: True or false: Database-internal distributed transactions suffer all the same limitations as XA.
questions.explain: Their limitations are not so great; for example a distributed version of SSI is possible, though failure amplification remains.

questions.q: What happens to statelessness when the coordinator is part of the application server?
questions.explain: They are as important as the databases themselves.
questions.teaches: When the coordinator is part of the application server, its logs become a crucial part of the durable system state, as important as the databases themselves, because they are needed to recover in-doubt transactions after a crash; such application servers are no longer stateless.
options: Nothing changes, as logs can be discarded after each request
They are no longer stateless
The servers become faster, since they hold the data locally
The servers can be added and removed at will, as before
optionExplain: The logs are needed to recover in-doubt transactions. The right answer is: They are no longer stateless.
They are as important as the databases themselves. Remember: Logs make servers stateful.
The change is about operational burden, not speed. The right answer is: They are no longer stateless.
Adding and removing is no longer free. The right answer is: They are no longer stateless.

questions.q: What can XA not do across different data systems?
questions.explain: Both would need a standard way to share lock or conflict information.
questions.teaches: XA cannot detect deadlocks across different systems, since that would require a standardized protocol for exchanging information on the locks each transaction waits for, and it does not work with serializable snapshot isolation, since that would require a protocol for identifying conflicts across different systems.
options: Commit a transaction across two nodes
Detect cross-system deadlocks
Write a coordinator log to local disk
Send a prepare request to a participant
optionExplain: Committing across systems is what XA is for. The right answer is: Detect cross-system deadlocks.
Both would need a standard way to share lock or conflict information.
Logging locally is part of normal operation. The right answer is: Detect cross-system deadlocks.
That is its core function. The right answer is: Detect cross-system deadlocks.

questions.q: Customers 1 and 2 both try to buy the last seat, and each serving node proposes its customer's ID. What does consensus do?
questions.explain: One proposed value is decided. The card next shows why.
options: Decides on both IDs and splits the seat between them
Decides on a new ID generated by the algorithm itself
Decides on whichever customer's node has the lowest address
Decides on exactly one of the proposed IDs
optionExplain: A single seat cannot be shared by incompatible operations.
The decided value must have been proposed by some node.
Nothing in the definition favours a node address. The right answer is: Decides on exactly one of the proposed IDs.
One incompatible operation wins and the other loses. Remember: Pick one proposal.

questions.q: In the formal model, nodes ____ values and the consensus algorithm decides on one of them.
questions.explain: The decided value is one of the proposals.

questions.q: Three nodes propose customer IDs 4, 9 and 15 for the last seat. Which outcome is a valid decision?
questions.explain: A decision is one proposed value.
options: ID 20, the next unused customer ID
IDs 4 and 9 together as joint owners
ID 9, since some node proposed it
No value at all, for as long as the nodes disagree
optionExplain: Nobody proposed 20. The right answer is: ID 9, since some node proposed it.
Only one value is decided. The right answer is: ID 9, since some node proposed it.
Any proposed value may be decided. Remember: Pick a proposal.
The algorithm has to decide on one of the proposals.

questions.q: True or false: A consensus algorithm may decide on a value that none of the nodes proposed.
questions.explain: The decided value must be one that some node proposed; otherwise trivial solutions such as always deciding null would pass.

questions.q: The book lists last seat on a plane and the same theater seat. What other racing operation does consensus settle?
questions.explain: Consensus picks one winner among incompatible operations.
questions.rule: Consensus picks the winner of a race.
questions.teaches: If several people concurrently try to book the last seat on an airplane or the same seat in a theater, or to register an account with the same username, a consensus algorithm could determine which of these mutually incompatible operations should be the winner.
options: Reading a cached page from a nearby server
Compressing a log file in the background
Copying an immutable file to a second replica
Registering an account with the same username
optionExplain: A read does not compete with another for a unique outcome.
Compression involves no race for a unique outcome. The right answer is: Registering an account with the same username.
Copying does not pit incompatible operations against each other.
Consensus picks one winner among incompatible operations. Remember: Consensus picks the winner of a race.

questions.q: What is the variant of consensus defined by these four properties called?
questions.explain: It is equivalent to regular consensus in asynchronous systems with unreliable failure detectors.
questions.teaches: This particular variant of consensus is called uniform consensus, which is equivalent to regular consensus in asynchronous systems with unreliable failure detectors.
options: Byzantine consensus
Nonblocking consensus
Optimistic consensus
Uniform consensus
optionExplain: Byzantine consensus concerns misbehaving nodes, a different matter. The right answer is: Uniform consensus.
Nonblocking is a property of atomic commit protocols. The right answer is: Uniform consensus.
No such variant is named in the book. The right answer is: Uniform consensus.
It is equivalent to regular consensus in asynchronous systems with unreliable failure detectors.

questions.q: An algorithm decides null whatever was proposed. Which property does it violate?
questions.explain: Validity rules out trivial answers. The card next shows why.
options: Uniform agreement
Validity
Integrity
Termination
optionExplain: All nodes decide the same, so agreement is satisfied.
Null was not proposed by any node. Remember: Validity.
Each node decides once, so integrity is satisfied. The right answer is: Validity.
It decides promptly, so termination is satisfied. The right answer is: Validity.

questions.q: The ____ property says that no node decides twice.
questions.explain: Once decided, a node cannot change its mind.

questions.q: For one instance, node A decides X and node B decides Y. Which property is broken?
questions.explain: Different decisions break agreement.
options: Uniform agreement
Integrity, the no-double-decision rule
Validity, the proposed-value rule
Termination, the progress rule
optionExplain: Two nodes decided differently. Remember: Agreement.
Neither node decided twice. The right answer is: Uniform agreement.
Both values could have been proposed. The right answer is: Uniform agreement.
Both nodes did decide, so progress was made. The right answer is: Uniform agreement.

questions.q: True or false: Validity is the property that guarantees every node that does not crash eventually decides a value.
questions.explain: That is termination. Validity only requires that a decided value was proposed by some node.

questions.q: Which idea do agreement and integrity capture together?
questions.explain: They define the core idea of consensus.
questions.teaches: The uniform agreement and integrity properties define the core idea of consensus: everyone decides on the same outcome, and once you have decided, you cannot change your mind; validity exists mostly to rule out trivial solutions.
options: Every node proposes at least one value
A shared outcome that is final
The leader decides before any follower does
Decisions are made within a fixed time limit
optionExplain: Proposing is not what they require. The right answer is: A shared outcome that is final.
They define the core idea of consensus. Remember: Same outcome, no reversal.
Nothing is said about a leader. The right answer is: A shared outcome that is final.
They say nothing about timing. The right answer is: A shared outcome that is final.

questions.q: If you do not care about fault tolerance, how hard is satisfying the first three properties?
questions.explain: A single decision-maker satisfies them trivially.
questions.rule: Without fault tolerance a dictator works.
questions.teaches: If you do not care about fault tolerance, satisfying the first three properties is easy: you can hardcode one node to be the dictator and let that node make all of the decisions.
options: Almost as hard as the full problem, since all four interlock
Easy: hardcode one dictator node
Impossible without a synchronised clock on every node
Possible only with a majority vote on every decision
optionExplain: Without fault tolerance the first three are easy. The right answer is: Easy: hardcode one dictator node.
A single decision-maker satisfies them trivially. Remember: Without fault tolerance a dictator works.
No clock is needed for the first three. The right answer is: Easy: hardcode one dictator node.
A dictator needs no vote. The right answer is: Easy: hardcode one dictator node.

questions.q: A consensus algorithm sits idle forever once one node fails. Which property does it violate?
questions.explain: Progress is the missing piece. The card next shows why.
options: Validity
Integrity
Uniform agreement
Termination
optionExplain: Validity concerns which values may be decided. The right answer is: Termination.
Integrity concerns deciding twice. The right answer is: Termination.
Agreement concerns differing decisions. The right answer is: Termination.
Nodes that did not crash must still decide. Remember: Termination.

questions.q: Termination is a ____ property, whereas agreement, integrity and validity are safety properties.
questions.explain: Liveness says something good eventually happens.

questions.q: A design hardcodes one dictator node, and the dictator crashes. Which property fails?
questions.explain: A dictator is a single point of failure.
options: Validity
Integrity
Termination
Uniform agreement
optionExplain: No invalid value is decided. The right answer is: Termination.
No node decides twice. The right answer is: Termination.
The other nodes cannot reach a decision. Remember: Termination fails.
No two nodes decide differently. The right answer is: Termination.

questions.q: True or false: An algorithm that must wait for a crashed node to recover can still satisfy termination in this model.
questions.explain: A crashed node never comes back in this model, so waiting for it means the others never decide.
questions.rule: Waiting for a crash to heal fails.

questions.q: Does two-phase commit meet the termination requirement?
questions.explain: Any algorithm that waits for recovery fails termination.
questions.teaches: In this system model, any algorithm that has to wait for a node to recover is not able to satisfy the termination property; in particular, 2PC does not meet the requirements for termination.
options: Yes, since participants vote within a timeout
Yes, since the log lets the coordinator recover
Yes, as long as at least one participant votes yes
No, it waits for the coordinator
optionExplain: Voting quickly does not help if the coordinator is gone for good.
Recovery is exactly what the model denies. The right answer is: No, it waits for the coordinator.
A single yes does not let the others decide.
Any algorithm that waits for recovery fails termination. Remember: 2PC fails termination.

questions.q: How does the book suggest picturing a node crash in the consensus model?
questions.explain: The node must be assumed gone for good.
questions.rule: A crash is permanent in this model.
questions.teaches: The system model of consensus assumes that when a node crashes it suddenly disappears and never comes back; picture an earthquake and a datacenter destroyed by a landslide, with your node buried under 30 feet of mud.
options: A short reboot after which the node rejoins at once
A slow network link that eventually delivers messages
A node that sends contradictory messages to its peers
A datacenter lost to a landslide
optionExplain: In this model it never rejoins. The right answer is: A datacenter lost to a landslide.
That is a delay, not a crash. The right answer is: A datacenter lost to a landslide.
That is a Byzantine fault, not a crash. The right answer is: A datacenter lost to a landslide.
The node must be assumed gone for good. Remember: A crash is permanent in this model.

questions.q: At least how many of five nodes must work for a consensus algorithm to ensure termination?
questions.explain: Majority means more than half. The card next shows why.
options: Two, since two nodes can agree
Three, a majority
Four, since at most one may fail
All five, since every node votes
optionExplain: Two of five is not a majority. The right answer is: Three, a majority.
More than half must work. Remember: Three of five.
A majority needs only three of five. The right answer is: Three, a majority.
Consensus tolerates minority failures. The right answer is: Three, a majority.

questions.q: Termination requires at least a ____ of nodes to be functioning correctly.
questions.explain: That majority can form a quorum.

questions.q: A seven-node cluster has three nodes down. Can termination still be assured?
questions.explain: Count the working nodes against half.
options: Yes, four of seven is a majority
No, because any failure stops a consensus system
No, because an even number is required
Yes, but only if the three failed nodes rejoin first
optionExplain: More than half are still working. Remember: Four of seven.
A minority of failures is tolerated. The right answer is: Yes, four of seven is a majority.
Seven is fine; four of seven is a majority.
Rejoining is not required for a majority. The right answer is: Yes, four of seven is a majority.

questions.q: True or false: Consensus algorithms need every node to be working in order to ensure termination.
questions.explain: They need only a majority of nodes working correctly.

questions.q: A majority of nodes fails or the network is severely disrupted. What happens to the safety properties in most implementations?
questions.explain: An outage stops requests but cannot corrupt decisions.
questions.teaches: Most consensus implementations ensure that the safety properties (agreement, integrity and validity) are always met even if a majority of nodes fail or there is a severe network problem, so a large-scale outage can stop the system from processing requests but cannot corrupt the consensus system by causing it to make invalid decisions.
options: They lapse until a majority returns
They still hold; the system may stop
They hold only for decisions made before the failure
They are replaced by eventual consistency
optionExplain: Most implementations keep safety even then. The right answer is: They still hold; the system may stop.
An outage stops requests but cannot corrupt decisions. Remember: Safety survives loss of progress.
They hold for all decisions. The right answer is: They still hold; the system may stop.
Safety is not downgraded in this way. The right answer is: They still hold; the system may stop.

questions.q: Three of five nodes are alive but unreachable from the other two because of a network fault. How does that count for termination?
questions.explain: Termination assumes fewer than half are crashed or unreachable.
questions.rule: Unreachable is as bad as crashed.
questions.teaches: The termination property is subject to the assumption that fewer than half of the nodes are crashed or unreachable.
options: Only crashed nodes count, so progress is unaffected
Both count against the majority
Unreachable nodes count in favour, as they still hold data
The two reachable nodes can decide alone
optionExplain: Unreachable nodes cannot help form a quorum either. The right answer is: Both count against the majority.
Termination assumes fewer than half are crashed or unreachable.
Unreachable nodes cannot vote. The right answer is: Both count against the majority.
Two of five is not a majority. The right answer is: Both count against the majority.

questions.q: A node sends contradictory votes to different peers. Which assumption of most consensus algorithms does it violate?
questions.explain: Standard consensus trusts nodes to follow the protocol. The card next shows why.
options: That the network has bounded delay
That the cluster has an odd number of nodes
That every node proposes a value
That nodes follow the protocol
optionExplain: Delay is a separate assumption. The right answer is: That nodes follow the protocol.
Cluster size is a separate matter. The right answer is: That nodes follow the protocol.
Proposing is not the point here. The right answer is: That nodes follow the protocol.
Contradictory messages are Byzantine behaviour. Remember: No Byzantine faults.

questions.q: Most consensus algorithms assume there are no ____ faults.
questions.explain: Such faults are nodes that do not follow the protocol.

questions.q: A cluster of trusted servers that can only crash needs consensus. Is Byzantine tolerance required?
questions.explain: Match the fault model to the threat.
options: Yes, since every consensus algorithm must tolerate lies
Yes, otherwise a crash would corrupt decisions
No; standard crash-tolerant consensus fits
No, since consensus cannot be made fault tolerant at all
optionExplain: Most algorithms assume no Byzantine faults. The right answer is: No; standard crash-tolerant consensus fits.
Crashes are handled by ordinary consensus. The right answer is: No; standard crash-tolerant consensus fits.
Byzantine tolerance matters when nodes may misbehave. Remember: Crash faults only.
Consensus is fault tolerant to crashes. The right answer is: No; standard crash-tolerant consensus fits.

questions.q: True or false: Standard consensus algorithms keep their guarantees even when a node sends contradictory messages to different nodes.
questions.explain: Most assume no Byzantine faults, so such a node may break the safety properties.

questions.q: Byzantine-robust consensus is possible as long as what fraction of the nodes is faulty?
questions.explain: That is the known bound.
questions.rule: Byzantine tolerance needs a bigger honest margin.
questions.teaches: It is possible to make consensus robust against Byzantine faults as long as fewer than one-third of the nodes are Byzantine-faulty, but the book does not have space to discuss those algorithms in detail.
options: Fewer than one-half
Fewer than two-thirds
Any number, if at least one node is correct
Fewer than one-third
optionExplain: A bare majority is enough only for crash faults.
That is too many for Byzantine tolerance. The right answer is: Fewer than one-third.
A single correct node is not enough. The right answer is: Fewer than one-third.
That is the known bound. Remember: Byzantine tolerance needs a bigger honest margin.

questions.q: What can a Byzantine node do to a standard consensus protocol, per the book?
questions.explain: That is the example the book gives.
questions.teaches: If a node does not correctly follow the protocol, for example if it sends contradictory messages to different nodes, it may break the safety properties of the protocol.
options: Slow the protocol but never affect the decisions
Make the cluster elect two leaders in one epoch
Force the cluster to lose its majority
Send contradictory messages and break safety
optionExplain: Safety can actually be broken. The right answer is: Send contradictory messages and break safety.
That is not the example given. The right answer is: Send contradictory messages and break safety.
That is a failure scenario, not a Byzantine behaviour.
That is the example the book gives. Remember: Misbehaviour threatens safety.

questions.q: Raft decides the order of operations in a replicated log. In this chapter's terms, what kind of algorithm is it?
questions.explain: A sequence of decisions is a broadcast. The card next shows why.
options: A two-phase commit variant for transactions
A clock synchronisation algorithm for nodes
A total order broadcast algorithm
A leaderless quorum protocol for key-value stores
optionExplain: Raft is not a commit protocol. The right answer is: A total order broadcast algorithm.
Raft does not synchronise clocks. The right answer is: A total order broadcast algorithm.
It decides a sequence of values. Remember: Raft is broadcast.
Raft uses a leader. The right answer is: A total order broadcast algorithm.

questions.q: Total order broadcast is equivalent to repeated ____ of consensus, one per delivered message.
questions.explain: In each round nodes propose the next message and decide on one.

questions.q: In each round nodes propose the next message and decide on one of them. What does repeating this build?
questions.explain: One decision per slot builds a log.
options: A set of unordered messages with no duplicates
A vector clock for every node
A snapshot of all replicas at one instant
A total order of delivered messages
optionExplain: Each round fixes a position, so order exists. The right answer is: A total order of delivered messages.
No clocks are built this way. The right answer is: A total order of delivered messages.
That is not what the rounds build. The right answer is: A total order of delivered messages.
Each decision fixes the next message in the order.

questions.q: True or false: Viewstamped Replication, Paxos, Raft and Zab are identical algorithms that differ only in name.
questions.explain: There are quite a few similarities, but the algorithms are not the same.

questions.q: What is Paxos's optimisation of deciding a whole sequence directly called?
questions.explain: It decides a sequence rather than one value.
questions.teaches: Viewstamped Replication, Raft and Zab implement total order broadcast directly, because that is more efficient than doing repeated rounds of one-value-at-a-time consensus; in the case of Paxos, this optimization is known as Multi-Paxos.
options: Paxos-Lite
Paxos-Prime
Multi-Paxos
Paxos-Plus
optionExplain: No such name is used in the book. The right answer is: Multi-Paxos.
No such hybrid is described. The right answer is: Multi-Paxos.
It decides a sequence rather than one value. Remember: Multi-Paxos is the sequence variant.
No such hybrid is described. The right answer is: Multi-Paxos.

questions.q: A consensus-based broadcast loses a message that was sent. Which consensus property does the book tie to that guarantee?
questions.explain: Termination ensures that messages are not lost.
questions.rule: Each property backs one broadcast guarantee.
questions.teaches: Repeated rounds of consensus give the guarantees of total order broadcast, because agreement means same messages in same order, integrity means no duplicates, validity means no corrupted or fabricated messages, and termination means no lost messages.
options: Uniform agreement, the same-order rule
Integrity, the no-duplicates rule
Termination
Validity, the no-fabrication rule
optionExplain: Agreement ensures all nodes deliver the same messages in the same order.
Integrity ensures that messages are not duplicated. The right answer is: Termination.
Termination ensures that messages are not lost. Remember: Each property backs one broadcast guarantee.
Validity ensures messages are not corrupted or fabricated out of thin air.

questions.q: An operations team manually picks the leader and reconfigures the system after a failure. In consensus terms, what is that?
questions.explain: Humans are the tie-breaker. The card next shows why.
options: A fault-tolerant consensus algorithm
A quorum-based election with majority votes
Dictatorial consensus, no termination
A leaderless protocol with read repair
optionExplain: Human intervention defeats termination. The right answer is: Dictatorial consensus, no termination.
No quorum vote takes place. The right answer is: Dictatorial consensus, no termination.
Progress waits on humans. Remember: Dictator.
A single leader is used. The right answer is: Dictatorial consensus, no termination.

questions.q: A manually chosen leader fails the ____ property of consensus because progress needs human intervention.
questions.explain: The system cannot make progress by itself.

questions.q: The leader fails at 3 a.m. and nobody is on call, so writes stop until morning. Which property failed?
questions.explain: Waiting on a human is a liveness failure.
options: Integrity
Validity
Uniform agreement
Termination
optionExplain: No node decided twice. The right answer is: Termination.
Decisions were not invalid. The right answer is: Termination.
No two nodes decided differently. The right answer is: Termination.
The system could not progress without a human. Remember: Termination.

questions.q: True or false: A manually configured leader cannot work well in practice.
questions.explain: Such a system can work well in practice; it just does not satisfy the termination property of consensus.

questions.q: What do some databases do to get closer to fault-tolerant total order broadcast?
questions.explain: That brings the system closer to solving consensus.
questions.teaches: Some databases perform automatic leader election and failover, promoting a follower to be the new leader if the old leader fails, which brings us closer to fault-tolerant total order broadcast and thus to solving consensus.
options: Let followers accept writes independently and merge later
Replace the log with a synchronised clock
Elect a leader automatically
Require operators to approve every write
optionExplain: That is multi-leader replication. The right answer is: Elect a leader automatically.
Clocks do not give total order broadcast. The right answer is: Elect a leader automatically.
That brings the system closer to solving consensus. Remember: Automatic failover approaches consensus.
That adds humans, not fault tolerance. The right answer is: Elect a leader automatically.

questions.q: A script now promotes a follower automatically after failure. What new problem must it solve?
questions.explain: Otherwise the database becomes inconsistent.
questions.rule: Automation needs agreement on who leads.
questions.teaches: All nodes need to agree who the leader is; otherwise two different nodes could each believe themselves to be the leader, and consequently get the database into an inconsistent state.
options: Compressing the replication log before failover
Making followers read from the old leader
Agreeing on a single leader
Removing the need for any leader at all
optionExplain: Compression is not the new problem. The right answer is: Agreeing on a single leader.
That would not solve agreement. The right answer is: Agreeing on a single leader.
Otherwise the database becomes inconsistent. Remember: Automation needs agreement on who leads.
A leader is still used. The right answer is: Agreeing on a single leader.

questions.q: Consensus needs a leader, and electing a leader needs consensus. What is the problem?
questions.explain: The circle is logical, not physical. The card next shows why.
options: There are too few nodes to hold a vote
The leader cannot be told about its election
Votes are always lost in transit
It is circular: a leader is needed first
optionExplain: The circle does not depend on cluster size. The right answer is: It is circular: a leader is needed first.
Notification is not the problem. The right answer is: It is circular: a leader is needed first.
Lost votes are not the cause of the circle.
To elect a leader you first need a leader.

questions.q: In order to solve consensus, we must first solve ____, which is the conundrum of electing a leader.
questions.explain: That is the circle the chapter describes.

questions.q: A design says: use a leader to run the vote that picks the leader. What is wrong with it?
questions.explain: Spot the hidden assumption.
options: A leader cannot run votes over a network
Votes must be run by every node at once
It assumes a leader already exists
It needs a synchronised clock on each node
optionExplain: Leaders can run votes; the issue is where the first one comes from.
Not every node runs the vote. The right answer is: It assumes a leader already exists.
The leader needed for the vote is the thing being elected.
Clocks do not break the circle. The right answer is: It assumes a leader already exists.

questions.q: True or false: Single-leader replication needs no agreement on who the leader is, so no consensus is ever involved.
questions.explain: All nodes need to agree on the leader, otherwise two nodes could each believe they lead; that agreement needs consensus.

questions.q: How do the consensus protocols discussed escape the circle?
questions.explain: A weaker promise about the leader breaks the loop.
questions.rule: A weaker leader promise breaks the circle.
questions.teaches: All of the consensus protocols discussed internally use a leader in some form or another, but they do not guarantee that the leader is unique; they make a weaker guarantee instead.
options: They avoid leaders altogether
They guarantee exactly one leader at all times
They ask a human to pick the first leader
They use a non-unique leader internally
optionExplain: They all use a leader in some form. The right answer is: They use a non-unique leader internally.
They make no such guarantee. The right answer is: They use a non-unique leader internally.
A human would remove termination. The right answer is: They use a non-unique leader internally.
A weaker promise about the leader breaks the loop.

questions.q: A node believes it has been elected leader. Why can it not trust that belief?
questions.explain: A node cannot necessarily trust its own judgment.
questions.rule: Truth is defined by the majority.
questions.teaches: A node cannot necessarily trust its own judgment: just because a node thinks that it is the leader does not mean the other nodes accept it as their leader; the truth is defined by the majority.
options: Its own clock is always wrong
Beliefs are not stored on disk
Elections cannot complete without the old leader's vote
The other nodes may not accept it as their leader
optionExplain: The problem is acceptance, not its clock. The right answer is: The other nodes may not accept it as their leader.
Storage is not the issue. The right answer is: The other nodes may not accept it as their leader.
The old leader's vote is not required. The right answer is: The other nodes may not accept it as their leader.
A node cannot necessarily trust its own judgment. Remember: Truth is defined by the majority.

questions.q: Two nodes each believe they lead, in epochs 7 and 9. Whose decisions prevail?
questions.explain: Higher epochs outrank lower ones. The card next shows why.
options: The leader of epoch 7, since it was elected first
Whichever leader contacted more nodes
The leader of epoch 9
Both, and the clients pick one of them
optionExplain: A newer epoch outranks an older one. The right answer is: The leader of epoch 9.
Epoch numbers decide, not message counts. The right answer is: The leader of epoch 9.
The higher epoch number prevails. Remember: Epoch 9.
Conflicts are resolved by epoch number. The right answer is: The leader of epoch 9.

questions.q: Within each ____, the leader is unique, even though leaders in different ones may overlap in time.
questions.explain: Epoch numbers are totally ordered and increase monotonically.

questions.q: A leader from epoch 4 wakes after a long pause, and an election has since produced epoch 5. What happens to its proposals?
questions.explain: Stale leaders lose.
options: They win, since epoch 4 was elected first
They are merged with the epoch 5 proposals
They are accepted until a majority objects
They lose to the epoch 5 leader
optionExplain: Older epochs do not outrank newer ones. The right answer is: They lose to the epoch 5 leader.
Conflicts are resolved, not merged. The right answer is: They lose to the epoch 5 leader.
A higher epoch overrides it. The right answer is: They lose to the epoch 5 leader.
The higher epoch prevails. Remember: Newer epoch wins.

questions.q: True or false: Consensus protocols guarantee that exactly one leader exists at any moment in time.
questions.explain: They only guarantee that the leader is unique within each epoch; two leaders from different epochs can coexist briefly.

questions.q: What is the epoch number called in Raft?
questions.explain: Raft calls it the term number.
questions.teaches: The epoch number is called the ballot number in Paxos, the view number in Viewstamped Replication, and the term number in Raft.
options: Ballot number
View number
Term number
Fencing token
optionExplain: That is Paxos's name. The right answer is: Term number.
That is Viewstamped Replication's name. The right answer is: Term number.
Raft calls it the term number. Remember: Same idea, different names.
A fencing token belongs to lock services. The right answer is: Term number.

questions.q: What must a leader do before it is allowed to decide anything?
questions.explain: That check protects against a conflicting decision.
questions.teaches: Before a leader is allowed to decide anything, it must first check that there is not some other leader with a higher epoch number which might take a conflicting decision.
options: Wait until its clock passes the previous leader's lease
Broadcast its decision first and retract if challenged
Check for a higher-epoch leader
Ask the client to confirm the leader's identity
optionExplain: Leases are not the mechanism described. The right answer is: Check for a higher-epoch leader.
Deciding must come after the check. The right answer is: Check for a higher-epoch leader.
That check protects against a conflicting decision. Remember: Check before deciding.
Clients play no part. The right answer is: Check for a higher-epoch leader.

questions.q: Why must the quorum voting on a proposal overlap the quorum that elected the leader?
questions.explain: Overlap carries knowledge of the election. The card next shows why.
options: So the leader can vote twice
So at least one voter knows of the latest election
So fewer messages are needed overall
So the election can be skipped for later proposals
optionExplain: Double voting is not the purpose. The right answer is: So at least one voter knows of the latest election.
That voter would reveal any higher epoch. Remember: Shared voter.
Overlap does not reduce messages. The right answer is: So at least one voter knows of the latest election.
The election still happens. The right answer is: So at least one voter knows of the latest election.

questions.q: A node votes in favor of a proposal only if it is not aware of any other leader with a higher ____.
questions.explain: That check is the node's contribution to safety.

questions.q: How many rounds of voting are involved in electing a leader and then deciding one value?
questions.explain: Election vote, then proposal vote.
options: Two: election and proposal votes
One, since the leader decides alone after election
Three: nominate, elect and then confirm
None, if the old leader approves the new one
optionExplain: Both rounds use quorums that overlap. Remember: Two rounds.
The leader still needs a quorum for each proposal.
The book describes two rounds. The right answer is: Two: election and proposal votes.
Approval by a quorum is needed. The right answer is: Two: election and proposal votes.

questions.q: True or false: The quorum that elects a leader and the quorum that approves its proposal may be completely disjoint.
questions.explain: They must overlap, so that at least one voter on the proposal also took part in the latest election.

questions.q: A leader's proposal vote reveals no higher epoch. What can the leader conclude?
questions.explain: The overlap would have exposed one.
questions.teaches: If the vote on a proposal does not reveal any higher-numbered epoch, the current leader can conclude that no leader election with a higher epoch number has happened, and therefore be sure that it still holds the leadership and can safely decide the proposed value.
options: That it is the only leader the cluster has ever had
No newer election; it still leads
That it can now skip future votes
That its epoch number must be incremented
optionExplain: Only recent epochs matter. The right answer is: No newer election; it still leads.
The overlap would have exposed one. Remember: Overlap makes silence meaningful.
Each decision needs its own vote. The right answer is: No newer election; it still leads.
The epoch is unchanged until a new election. The right answer is: No newer election; it still leads.

questions.q: What does the quorum for a leader's proposal typically consist of?
questions.explain: Quorums are typically but not always majorities.
questions.rule: A quorum is usually a majority.
questions.teaches: The quorum typically, but not always, consists of a majority of nodes.
options: Every node in the cluster, without exception
A majority of nodes, though not always
A single node chosen by the leader
Only the nodes that voted in the previous round
optionExplain: That is the rule for 2PC, not consensus. The right answer is: A majority of nodes, though not always.
Quorums are typically but not always majorities. Remember: A quorum is usually a majority.
One node cannot protect against a higher epoch. The right answer is: A majority of nodes, though not always.
The quorum is not defined by the previous voters.

questions.q: Which difference lets consensus keep working when one node fails, unlike 2PC?
questions.explain: Majority beats unanimity for availability. The card next shows why.
options: It needs only a majority of votes
It uses a faster network protocol than 2PC
It avoids writing anything to disk
It lets participants decide alone after a timeout
optionExplain: A minority failing cannot block the vote. Remember: Majority.
Speed is not the difference. The right answer is: It needs only a majority of votes.
Consensus writes to disk too. The right answer is: It needs only a majority of votes.
Unilateral decisions would break safety. The right answer is: It needs only a majority of votes.

questions.q: In 2PC a ____ vote is required from every participant, whereas consensus needs only a majority.
questions.explain: One missing yes blocks a 2PC commit.

questions.q: One of five voters is down. Which can still decide: 2PC or majority consensus?
questions.explain: Count the required votes.
options: 2PC, since four yes votes are enough
Majority consensus; 2PC needs all five
Neither, as one failure stops both
Both, since neither needs the failed voter
optionExplain: 2PC needs a yes from every participant. The right answer is: Majority consensus; 2PC needs all five.
Four of five voters are a majority. Remember: Consensus continues.
Consensus tolerates a minority of failures. The right answer is: Majority consensus; 2PC needs all five.
2PC does need every participant. The right answer is: Majority consensus; 2PC needs all five.

questions.q: True or false: In 2PC the coordinator is elected by the participants, as the leader is in consensus.
questions.explain: In 2PC the coordinator is not elected, which is one of the differences from fault-tolerant consensus.

questions.q: What do consensus algorithms define, beyond voting, to keep safety after a leader change?
questions.explain: It ensures the safety properties are always met.
questions.rule: Recovery is part of the algorithm.
questions.teaches: Consensus algorithms define a recovery process by which nodes can get into a consistent state after a new leader is elected, ensuring that the safety properties are always met.
options: A recovery process for consistency
A clock synchronisation step among all nodes
A manual approval by the operator
A second coordinator that mirrors the first
optionExplain: It ensures the safety properties are always met. Remember: Recovery is part of the algorithm.
No clock step is involved. The right answer is: A recovery process for consistency.
Humans are not part of it. The right answer is: A recovery process for consistency.
That would not provide recovery. The right answer is: A recovery process for consistency.

questions.q: Since consensus algorithms provide total order broadcast, what else can they implement fault-tolerantly?
questions.explain: Total order broadcast can implement them.
questions.teaches: Consensus algorithms provide total order broadcast, and therefore they can also implement linearizable atomic operations in a fault-tolerant way.
options: Linearizable atomic operations
Eventual consistency without any ordering
Version vectors for concurrent writes
Last-write-wins conflict resolution
optionExplain: Total order broadcast can implement them. Remember: Broadcast gives atomic operations.
That needs no consensus. The right answer is: Linearizable atomic operations.
Version vectors do not need consensus. The right answer is: Linearizable atomic operations.
That needs no consensus either. The right answer is: Linearizable atomic operations.

questions.q: A three-node consensus system loses one node. Can it keep deciding?
questions.explain: Two of three is a majority. The card next shows why.
options: Yes, two of three is a majority
No, all three are needed
Yes, but only after the failed node returns
No, an even number of nodes is required
optionExplain: A strict majority is still present. Remember: Yes.
Consensus tolerates minority failures. The right answer is: Yes, two of three is a majority.
It does not wait for the failed node. The right answer is: Yes, two of three is a majority.
Three is fine for tolerating one failure. The right answer is: Yes, two of three is a majority.

questions.q: Consensus systems require a strict ____ of nodes to operate.
questions.explain: More than half must be reachable.

questions.q: A network failure splits a five-node cluster into groups of two and three. Which group can make progress?
questions.explain: Only a majority can proceed.
options: The group of two, since it is smaller and faster
The group of three, a majority
Both, each deciding independently
Neither, until the network heals
optionExplain: Two of five is not a majority. The right answer is: The group of three, a majority.
Only the majority side proceeds. Remember: Three.
That would risk divergent decisions. The right answer is: The group of three, a majority.
The majority side continues. The right answer is: The group of three, a majority.

questions.q: True or false: Voting on proposals before they are decided is a form of asynchronous replication.
questions.explain: It is a kind of synchronous replication, which is why consensus can be slower than asynchronous setups.

questions.q: What do many people accept by choosing asynchronous replication over consensus voting?
questions.explain: They trade that risk for better performance.
questions.rule: Speed is bought with durability risk.
questions.teaches: With asynchronous replication some committed data can potentially be lost on failover, but many people choose to accept this risk for the sake of better performance.
options: Some committed data can be lost on failover
Replicas can never agree on any value
The leader is no longer unique in any epoch
Reads become unavailable permanently
optionExplain: They trade that risk for better performance. Remember: Speed is bought with durability risk.
Replicas can still converge. The right answer is: Some committed data can be lost on failover.
That is a different matter. The right answer is: Some committed data can be lost on failover.
Reads remain available. The right answer is: Some committed data can be lost on failover.

questions.q: How many nodes does a consensus system need to tolerate two failures?
questions.explain: Three of five is a majority.
questions.teaches: A consensus system needs a minimum of three nodes in order to tolerate one failure, since the remaining two of three form a majority, or a minimum of five nodes to tolerate two failures, since the remaining three of five form a majority.
options: Five; three remain a majority
Four, since two can fail and two remain
Three, since each failure needs one spare
Six, since an even number splits evenly
optionExplain: Three of five is a majority. Remember: Tolerating f failures needs 2f+1 nodes.
Two of four is not a strict majority. The right answer is: Five; three remain a majority.
Three tolerates only one failure. The right answer is: Five; three remain a majority.
Even numbers do not help. The right answer is: Five; three remain a majority.

questions.q: A consensus cluster spans continents, and a node's timeout fires after a brief network hiccup. What is the likely effect?
questions.explain: Safe but slow. The card next shows why.
options: A needless election, not unsafe
Corrupted decisions across the cluster
A permanent split into two clusters
Automatic removal of the suspected node
optionExplain: False suspicion does not break the safety properties. Remember: Needless election.
Safety is not harmed by false suspicion. The right answer is: A needless election, not unsafe.
The cluster does not split permanently. The right answer is: A needless election, not unsafe.
Membership is fixed in most algorithms. The right answer is: A needless election, not unsafe.

questions.q: Most consensus algorithms assume a ____ set of nodes that participate in voting.
questions.explain: Adding or removing nodes needs extensions.

questions.q: An operator wants to grow a running cluster from three to five nodes. What does the book say about this?
questions.explain: Membership change is the delicate part.
options: It is trivial because consensus ignores membership
Extensions exist but are less understood
It is forbidden by the safety properties
It needs a perfect failure detector first
optionExplain: Most algorithms assume fixed membership. The right answer is: Extensions exist but are less understood.
Static membership is the better understood case. Remember: Extensions exist.
Extensions allow it. The right answer is: Extensions exist but are less understood.
That is a requirement for nonblocking commit. The right answer is: Extensions exist but are less understood.

questions.q: True or false: False suspicion of the leader can corrupt the safety properties of consensus.
questions.explain: It does not harm the safety properties; it only causes frequent elections and poor performance.

questions.q: One network link is consistently unreliable while the rest works. What can happen to Raft?
questions.explain: The system effectively never makes progress.
questions.rule: One bad link can stall a cluster.
questions.teaches: Raft has been shown to have unpleasant edge cases: if the entire network works correctly except for one consistently unreliable link, leadership can continually bounce between two nodes or the current leader can be continually forced to resign, so the system effectively never makes progress.
options: Leadership keeps bouncing
It decides two values for the same slot
It silently drops to asynchronous replication
It ejects the faulty link from the cluster
optionExplain: The system effectively never makes progress. Remember: One bad link can stall a cluster.
Safety is not broken. The right answer is: Leadership keeps bouncing.
No such fallback exists. The right answer is: Leadership keeps bouncing.
It has no such mechanism. The right answer is: Leadership keeps bouncing.

questions.q: Why are frequent leader elections especially likely in geographically distributed systems?
questions.explain: Timeouts misfire when delays vary widely.
questions.teaches: Consensus systems generally rely on timeouts to detect failed nodes; in environments with highly variable network delays, especially geographically distributed systems, a node often falsely believes the leader to have failed due to a transient network issue.
options: Variable delays cause false suspicion
Distant nodes vote more slowly by design
Epoch numbers wrap around over long distances
Clocks drift faster in remote datacenters
optionExplain: Timeouts misfire when delays vary widely. Remember: Variable delay defeats timeouts.
Voting speed is not the reason. The right answer is: Variable delays cause false suspicion.
Epoch numbers do not wrap. The right answer is: Variable delays cause false suspicion.
Clock drift is not the cause. The right answer is: Variable delays cause false suspicion.

questions.q: Why do ZooKeeper and etcd implement a consensus algorithm even though they look like key-value stores?
questions.explain: Consensus serves coordination. The card next shows why.
options: To store all of an application's data with high throughput
To replace the application's own caches entirely
To avoid needing any disk writes for durability
To keep small shared state consistent
optionExplain: They are not suited as a general-purpose database. The right answer is: To keep small shared state consistent.
That is not their role. The right answer is: To keep small shared state consistent.
They still write to disk for durability. The right answer is: To keep small shared state consistent.
Total order broadcast keeps the replicas of the data identical.

questions.q: ZooKeeper and etcd are designed to hold small amounts of data that fit entirely in ____.
questions.explain: They still write to disk for durability.

questions.q: Which data suits ZooKeeper better: which node leads partition 7, or a request counter updated a million times a second?
questions.explain: Match data to the tool.
options: The request counter updated a million times a second
Both equally, since both are small values
Which node leads partition 7
Neither, since it cannot store any values
optionExplain: Rapidly changing runtime state is not what it is meant for.
Rate of change matters, not just size. The right answer is: Which node leads partition 7.
Slow-changing facts suit it. Remember: Slow-changing facts.
It stores small values well. The right answer is: Which node leads partition 7.

questions.q: True or false: ZooKeeper is well suited as a general-purpose database for all of an application's data.
questions.explain: It holds small amounts of data that fit in memory, so you would not want to store all your application's data there.

questions.q: An application grows to thousands of nodes. How does ZooKeeper avoid inefficient majority votes among all of them?
questions.explain: Many clients are served while the voters stay few.
questions.teaches: ZooKeeper runs on a fixed number of nodes, usually three or five, and performs its majority votes among those nodes while supporting a potentially large number of clients, thus outsourcing some of the work of coordinating nodes (consensus, operation ordering and failure detection) to an external service.
options: It votes among all client nodes in parallel
It replaces voting with a human decision
It lets each client keep a private copy of the decisions
It votes among a fixed few nodes, usually three or five
optionExplain: That would be terribly inefficient. The right answer is: It votes among a fixed few nodes, usually three or five.
Humans are not involved. The right answer is: It votes among a fixed few nodes, usually three or five.
Clients do not decide for themselves. The right answer is: It votes among a fixed few nodes, usually three or five.
Many clients are served while the voters stay few.

questions.q: Application state that changes millions of times per second must be replicated. What does the book point to?
questions.explain: ZooKeeper is not intended for such state.
questions.teaches: ZooKeeper is not intended for storing the runtime state of the application, which may change thousands or even millions of times per second; if application state needs to be replicated from one node to another, other tools such as Apache BookKeeper can be used.
options: Storing it in ZooKeeper nodes
Using ephemeral nodes for each update
Moving it into DNS records
Tools like Apache BookKeeper
optionExplain: That is not what it is intended for. The right answer is: Tools like Apache BookKeeper.
Ephemeral nodes are for session-bound data. The right answer is: Tools like Apache BookKeeper.
DNS is not a replication tool for application state.
ZooKeeper is not intended for such state. Remember: Fast-changing state needs another tool.

questions.q: Several nodes race to take the same lock. How can a coordination service ensure only one wins?
questions.explain: Atomic operations pick one winner. The card next shows why.
options: Give the lock to the node with the fastest clock
Use an atomic compare-and-set
Let every node hold it and sort out the conflict later
Ask each node to vote and take the average
optionExplain: Clocks do not decide the winner. The right answer is: Use an atomic compare-and-set.
Only one concurrent compare-and-set can succeed. Remember: Compare-and-set.
That defeats the lock. The right answer is: Use an atomic compare-and-set.
Votes are not averaged. The right answer is: Use an atomic compare-and-set.

questions.q: A distributed lock is usually implemented as a ____, which has an expiry time so that it is released if the client fails.
questions.explain: Expiry ensures eventual release.

questions.q: A client pauses, its lock expires, and a new holder starts. How can the resource reject the old client's stale write?
questions.explain: A fencing token orders lock holders.
options: Refuse the lower fencing token
Check that the old client's clock is still running
Trust the client to know it has lost the lock
Ask the old client to confirm it released the lock
optionExplain: Tokens increase with each acquisition. Remember: Refuse the old token.
Clocks can mislead after a pause. The right answer is: Refuse the lower fencing token.
A paused client may not know. The right answer is: Refuse the lower fencing token.
It cannot confirm while paused. The right answer is: Refuse the lower fencing token.

questions.q: True or false: A distributed lock with no expiry is safe, because the holder releases it when it is done.
questions.explain: A failed holder would never release it, which is why a lock is usually a lease with an expiry time.

questions.q: What does the consensus protocol guarantee for these compare-and-set operations?
questions.explain: The guarantee holds even when a node fails mid-operation.
questions.rule: Consensus makes the lock operations atomic.
questions.teaches: The consensus protocol guarantees that the compare-and-set operation will be atomic and linearizable, even if a node fails or the network is interrupted at any point.
options: They are fast, with no waiting for any other node
They stay atomic despite failures
They may be reordered, but only within one node
They are eventually consistent across replicas
optionExplain: Consensus requires voting, so they are not free. The right answer is: They stay atomic despite failures.
The guarantee holds even when a node fails mid-operation.
They are linearizable, not reordered. The right answer is: They stay atomic despite failures.
Linearizable is stronger than eventual. The right answer is: They stay atomic despite failures.

questions.q: Why does a resource protected by a lock or lease need a fencing token at all?
questions.explain: A paused holder may act after its lease has expired.
questions.teaches: When some resource is protected by a lock or lease, you need a fencing token to prevent clients from conflicting with each other in the case of a process pause; the token is a number that monotonically increases every time the lock is acquired.
options: To encrypt requests to the resource
To stop conflicts after a pause
To count how many clients are connected
To speed up lock acquisition
optionExplain: Tokens are not for encryption. The right answer is: To stop conflicts after a pause.
A paused holder may act after its lease has expired.
Counting clients is not their purpose. The right answer is: To stop conflicts after a pause.
Tokens do not make acquisition faster. The right answer is: To stop conflicts after a pause.

questions.q: A client holding a lock dies. How can a coordination service free the lock automatically?
questions.explain: Sessions tie locks to liveness. The card next shows why.
options: An operator must delete the lock by hand
The lock moves to the next client in alphabetical order
The session times out and its ephemeral nodes disappear
The server asks the dead client to release it
optionExplain: Automatic release avoids that. The right answer is: The session times out and its ephemeral nodes disappear.
Locks are not reassigned that way. The right answer is: The session times out and its ephemeral nodes disappear.
Locks can be tied to the session. Remember: Ephemeral nodes.
A dead client cannot respond. The right answer is: The session times out and its ephemeral nodes disappear.

questions.q: Locks held by a session can be released automatically when it times out, using what ZooKeeper calls ____ nodes.
questions.explain: They disappear when the session dies.

questions.q: A client wants to know when another client joins the cluster. What spares it from frequent polling?
questions.explain: Watches replace polling.
options: Reading the value in a tight loop
Asking the other client to send a message
Restarting its own session each second
Subscribing to change notifications
optionExplain: That is the polling it wants to avoid. The right answer is: Subscribing to change notifications.
That requires a direct channel. The right answer is: Subscribing to change notifications.
Restarts do not provide notifications. The right answer is: Subscribing to change notifications.
Watches push changes to the client. Remember: Subscribe.

questions.q: True or false: A ZooKeeper session ends the moment a single heartbeat is missed.
questions.explain: The session is declared dead only if heartbeats cease for longer than the session timeout.

questions.q: Of these ZooKeeper features, which really requires consensus?
questions.explain: Only they really require consensus.
questions.teaches: Of these features, only the linearizable atomic operations really require consensus, but it is the combination of the features that makes systems like ZooKeeper so useful for distributed coordination.
options: Failure detection through heartbeats
Change notifications to watchers
The linearizable atomic operations
Ephemeral nodes released on timeout
optionExplain: Heartbeats do not need consensus. The right answer is: The linearizable atomic operations.
Notifications do not need consensus. The right answer is: The linearizable atomic operations.
Only they really require consensus. Remember: Only atomic operations need consensus.
Timeouts do not need consensus. The right answer is: The linearizable atomic operations.

questions.q: A client's connection to ZooKeeper is briefly interrupted, or one ZooKeeper server fails. What happens to the session?
questions.explain: Short interruptions and server failures do not kill it.
questions.teaches: Even if the connection is temporarily interrupted, or a ZooKeeper node fails, the session remains active; it is declared dead only if the heartbeats cease for a duration longer than the session timeout.
options: It ends at once and the locks are freed
It moves to a different cluster automatically
It remains active
It becomes read-only for the rest of its life
optionExplain: Only a heartbeat gap beyond the timeout ends it.
The session stays in the same service. The right answer is: It remains active.
Short interruptions and server failures do not kill it.
No such mode exists. The right answer is: It remains active.

questions.q: A new node joins a cluster that owns partitions. What must happen to keep the load balanced?
questions.explain: Join triggers rebalancing. The card next shows why.
options: Some partitions move from existing nodes to the new one
Nothing, since the new node serves requests from caches
All partitions are re-created from scratch
The oldest node is shut down to make room
optionExplain: Rebalancing spreads work onto the new node. Remember: Move partitions.
A new node needs partitions to share the load.
Moving some partitions is enough. The right answer is: Some partitions move from existing nodes to the new one.
No node needs to be removed. The right answer is: Some partitions move from existing nodes to the new one.

questions.q: As nodes are removed or fail, other nodes need to take over the failed nodes' ____.
questions.explain: Their partitions must be reassigned.

questions.q: Five instances run and one must be primary; if it fails another must take over. Which feature set fits?
questions.explain: Claim, expire, notify.
options: Eventual consistency and read repair
Atomic claim plus ephemeral node
Last-write-wins with synchronised clocks
A cron job that restarts the primary hourly
optionExplain: Those do not give a single primary. The right answer is: Atomic claim plus ephemeral node.
The claim picks one, expiry frees it, notifications wake the rest.
That can leave two primaries. The right answer is: Atomic claim plus ephemeral node.
That does not fail over automatically. The right answer is: Atomic claim plus ephemeral node.

questions.q: True or false: If done correctly, this approach lets the application recover automatically from faults without human intervention.
questions.explain: That is the benefit, though doing it correctly is not easy.

questions.q: What does the book say about libraries such as Apache Curator for this kind of work?
questions.explain: Still better than implementing consensus from scratch.
questions.rule: Libraries help but do not remove difficulty.
questions.teaches: Despite libraries such as Apache Curator that provide higher-level tools on top of the ZooKeeper client API, doing this is not easy, but it is still much better than attempting to implement the necessary consensus algorithms from scratch, which has a poor success record.
options: Higher-level tools, still not easy
They make the work trivial and error-free
They replace the need for ZooKeeper itself
They are slower than hand-written consensus
optionExplain: Still better than implementing consensus from scratch. Remember: Libraries help but do not remove difficulty.
The book says it is not easy. The right answer is: Higher-level tools, still not easy.
They sit on top of the ZooKeeper client API.
Hand-written consensus has a poor success record. The right answer is: Higher-level tools, still not easy.

questions.q: Besides single-leader databases, where else is picking one leader from several instances useful?
questions.explain: They also need one active leader and a fast takeover.
questions.teaches: Choosing one instance as leader or primary, with another taking over if it fails, is useful for single-leader databases but also for job schedulers and similar stateful systems.
options: Job schedulers and similar stateful systems
Stateless web caches with identical content
Immutable file servers with no writes
DNS resolvers using time-to-live caching
optionExplain: They also need one active leader and a fast takeover.
Stateless caches need no leader. The right answer is: Job schedulers and similar stateful systems.
No leader is needed without writes. The right answer is: Job schedulers and similar stateful systems.
Resolvers do not need a leader. The right answer is: Job schedulers and similar stateful systems.

questions.q: A service restarts on a new virtual machine with a new IP address. How do other services find it?
questions.explain: Register on startup, look up later. The card next shows why.
options: Other services scan the network for a matching name
It registers its endpoint in a service registry
The old IP address is reused by the new machine
Operators update every client's config by hand
optionExplain: Scanning is not how registries work. The right answer is: It registers its endpoint in a service registry.
Others then look it up there. Remember: Service registry.
Addresses change as machines come and go. The right answer is: It registers its endpoint in a service registry.
A registry avoids that. The right answer is: It registers its endpoint in a service registry.

questions.q: DNS is the traditional way to look up an IP address, and its reads are not ____.
questions.explain: They go through several layers of caches.

questions.q: A DNS answer is a few seconds stale. Is that usually considered a problem?
questions.explain: Availability beats recency for lookups.
options: Usually no; availability matters more
Yes, it makes all lookups unsafe
Yes, unless DNS is made linearizable
No, because DNS runs a consensus algorithm
optionExplain: DNS is valued for staying reachable. Remember: Staleness tolerated.
Stale results are usually tolerated. The right answer is: Usually no; availability matters more.
DNS reads are not linearizable and that is accepted.
DNS does not run consensus. The right answer is: Usually no; availability matters more.

questions.q: True or false: Service discovery requires consensus in the same way that leader election does.
questions.explain: It is less clear that service discovery needs consensus, and DNS shows it can work without; leader election does require it.

questions.q: What do read-only caching replicas in some consensus systems do?
questions.explain: They do not take part in voting.
questions.rule: Replicas that do not vote can serve cheap reads.
questions.teaches: Some consensus systems support read-only caching replicas that asynchronously receive the log of all decisions of the consensus algorithm but do not actively participate in voting, so they can serve read requests that do not need to be linearizable.
options: Vote on proposals but never serve reads
Follow the log; serve non-linearizable reads
Serve linearizable reads by joining each vote
Replace the leader when it fails
optionExplain: They do not vote. The right answer is: Follow the log; serve non-linearizable reads.
They do not take part in voting. Remember: Replicas that do not vote can serve cheap reads.
They skip voting. The right answer is: Follow the log; serve non-linearizable reads.
They are not candidates. The right answer is: Follow the log; serve non-linearizable reads.

questions.q: A consensus system already knows who the leader is. How can that help other services?
