questions.explain: Leader election needs consensus, so the knowledge already exists.
questions.teaches: Although service discovery does not require consensus, leader election does, so if your consensus system already knows who the leader is, it can make sense to also use that information to help other services discover who the leader is.
options: It can replace their DNS entirely
It can help them discover the leader
It can let each of them vote on the leader again
It cannot, since the leader is a secret
optionExplain: DNS still serves other lookups. The right answer is: It can help them discover the leader.
Leader election needs consensus, so the knowledge already exists.
Services do not vote. The right answer is: It can help them discover the leader.
The information can be shared. The right answer is: It can help them discover the leader.

questions.q: Network delay is unbounded, so failure detection is unreliable. What does a membership service add?
questions.explain: Agree on the view even if imperfect. The card next shows why.
options: A perfect failure detector that is never wrong
A bound on network delay across the cluster
Automatic repair of crashed nodes
Agreement among nodes on who is alive
optionExplain: Detection remains unreliable. The right answer is: Agreement among nodes on who is alive.
It does not bound delay. The right answer is: Agreement among nodes on who is alive.
It decides membership, not repairs. The right answer is: Agreement among nodes on who is alive.
Consensus turns uncertain suspicion into a shared view. Remember: Shared view.

questions.q: A membership service determines which nodes are currently active and ____ members of a cluster.
questions.explain: It gives a shared view of membership.

questions.q: Consensus declares node 4 dead although it is actually alive. Is the membership service still useful?
questions.explain: Shared views are valuable.
options: No, any wrong declaration makes it useless
No, unless the declaration is revoked within a second
Yes; a shared view still matters
Yes, because the declaration is always correct
optionExplain: A shared view is still valuable. The right answer is: Yes; a shared view still matters.
No such revocation is needed. The right answer is: Yes; a shared view still matters.
All nodes act on the same view. Remember: Still useful.
It can be incorrect. The right answer is: Yes; a shared view still matters.

questions.q: True or false: A membership service can reliably tell whether another node has failed.
questions.explain: Reliable failure detection is not possible with unbounded delays; the service only gives agreement on a view.

questions.q: Roughly when did research into membership services begin, and what was it used for?
questions.explain: ZooKeeper and friends are part of that long history.
questions.teaches: ZooKeeper and friends can be seen as part of a long history of research into membership services, which goes back to the 1980s and has been important for building highly reliable systems, for example for air traffic control.
options: In the 2010s, for cloud web caches
In the 1960s, for early database indexes
In the 1990s, for browser session handling
In the 1980s, for air traffic control
optionExplain: The history goes back much further. The right answer is: In the 1980s, for air traffic control.
That is not the stated history. The right answer is: In the 1980s, for air traffic control.
That is not the stated history. The right answer is: In the 1980s, for air traffic control.
ZooKeeper and friends are part of that long history.

questions.q: Nodes pick the lowest-numbered current member as leader but hold different views of the member list. What happens?
questions.explain: Divergent views of membership break it.
questions.teaches: Choosing a leader could mean simply choosing the lowest-numbered among the current members, but this approach would not work if different nodes have divergent opinions on who the current members are.
options: It still works, since every node ends up with the lowest ID
It works, but only with a synchronised clock
It works, since leaders are chosen by epoch number
It fails: nodes pick different leaders
optionExplain: The lowest ID depends on the view. The right answer is: It fails: nodes pick different leaders.
Clocks do not fix divergent views. The right answer is: It fails: nodes pick different leaders.
That is a different mechanism. The right answer is: It fails: nodes pick different leaders.
Divergent views of membership break it. Remember: Leader choice needs agreed membership.

questions.q: A team must build a lock service, a unique-username check and a cluster membership list. How many separate hard problems is that?
questions.explain: Equivalent problems share one core. The card next shows why.
options: Three unrelated problems with three solutions
Two: locks and usernames match but membership is different
None, since each is easy on a single node
One: all reduce to consensus
optionExplain: They are equivalent, not unrelated. The right answer is: One: all reduce to consensus.
Membership is equivalent too. The right answer is: One: all reduce to consensus.
Easy on one node, but not when tolerating its failure.
They are equivalent to each other. Remember: One core problem.

questions.q: Uniqueness constraints, locks and total order broadcast are all ____ to consensus.
questions.explain: A solution to one can be transformed into the others.

questions.q: Match each problem to the decision it must make.
questions.explain: Each problem asks the system to decide one thing irrevocably, which is the shape of consensus.
pairs: Which of several conflicting records is allowed
The order in which to deliver messages
Whether to commit or abort a transaction
Whether to set the value given its current state

questions.q: True or false: Atomic commit and total order broadcast are equivalent, since a solution to one can be transformed into a solution to the other.
questions.explain: Both appear in the list of problems that are equivalent to consensus.

questions.q: In the list of equivalent problems, what do locks and leases decide?
questions.explain: The lock picks a single winner.
questions.teaches: When several clients are racing to grab a lock or lease, the lock decides which one successfully acquired it.
options: Which client holds the oldest session
Which node has the fastest network link
Which key in the store has the largest value
Which racing client gets the lock
optionExplain: Age of session is not the decision. The right answer is: Which racing client gets the lock.
Speed is not the decision. The right answer is: Which racing client gets the lock.
That is not the decision. The right answer is: Which racing client gets the lock.
The lock picks a single winner. Remember: Locks pick one winner.

questions.q: In the list of equivalent problems, what does a membership or coordination service decide?
questions.explain: It decides given a failure detector such as timeouts.
questions.teaches: Given a failure detector such as timeouts, a membership or coordination service must decide which nodes are alive, and which should be considered dead because their sessions timed out.
options: Which node stores the largest partition
Which clients may read stale data
Which transaction has the highest ID
Which nodes are alive or dead
optionExplain: Partition size is not the decision. The right answer is: Which nodes are alive or dead.
Reading policy is not the decision. The right answer is: Which nodes are alive or dead.
Transaction IDs are not the decision. The right answer is: Which nodes are alive or dead.
It decides given a failure detector such as timeouts.

questions.q: Why can a single-leader database settle a uniqueness conflict with no voting at all?
questions.explain: One decider means no vote. The card next shows why.
options: Every follower independently checks the conflict
A quorum of clients approves the winning record
The leader alone decides
The clocks of the followers pick the earlier record
optionExplain: Followers do not decide. The right answer is: The leader alone decides.
Clients do not vote. The right answer is: The leader alone decides.
All decision power is vested in one node. Remember: The leader decides.
Clocks are not the mechanism. The right answer is: The leader alone decides.

questions.q: In a single-leader database, all the power to make ____ is vested in the leader.
questions.explain: That is why it needs no vote per operation.

questions.q: A single-leader database's leader becomes unreachable because of a network interruption. What can the system do?
questions.explain: A single decider is a single point of failure.
options: Continue normally, using any follower
Fall back to last-write-wins on every follower
Elect a new leader instantly, with no coordination
Make no progress until it is back
optionExplain: Followers cannot decide on their own. The right answer is: Make no progress until it is back.
That would give up the guarantees. The right answer is: Make no progress until it is back.
Replacing the leader needs agreement. The right answer is: Make no progress until it is back.
Decisions were vested in that one node. Remember: Stuck.

questions.q: True or false: A single-leader database avoids all need for consensus, including when its leader fails.
questions.explain: When the leader fails or is unreachable, the system must wait, fail over manually, or use a consensus algorithm.

questions.q: Which guarantees does a single-leader database provide because the leader decides everything?
questions.explain: All follow from one decision-maker.
questions.teaches: Because all the power to make decisions is vested in the leader, a single-leader database is able to provide linearizable operations, uniqueness constraints, a totally ordered replication log, and more.
options: Leaderless quorum reads and tunable consistency
Causal consistency without any ordering
Linearizability, uniqueness and an ordered log
Eventual consistency across several leaders
optionExplain: Those belong to leaderless systems. The right answer is: Linearizability, uniqueness and an ordered log.
It does not give up ordering. The right answer is: Linearizability, uniqueness and an ordered log.
All follow from one decision-maker. Remember: One leader gives strong guarantees.
That describes multi-leader systems. The right answer is: Linearizability, uniqueness and an ordered log.

questions.q: On a single node with no failures, how hard are the problems equivalent to consensus?
questions.explain: The hardness comes from tolerating failures.
questions.teaches: All of these problems are straightforward if you only have a single node, or if you are willing to assign the decision-making capability to a single node.
options: Still as hard, since the proofs apply to one node too
Impossible, since one node cannot be linearizable
Straightforward, since one node can decide everything
Hard only for locks and not for the rest
optionExplain: A single node has nothing to agree with. The right answer is: Straightforward, since one node can decide everything.
A single node can be linearizable. The right answer is: Straightforward, since one node can decide everything.
The hardness comes from tolerating failures. Remember: Failures are the difficulty.
All of them are easy on one node. The right answer is: Straightforward, since one node can decide everything.

questions.q: A leader crashes and may not return. Which approach avoids blocking forever without human help?
questions.explain: Only automatic election removes humans and waiting. The card next shows why.
options: Automatic election with consensus
Waiting for the leader to recover
Having an operator promote another node
Letting every follower accept writes
optionExplain: It needs no human and no recovery. Remember: Automatic election.
That may block forever. The right answer is: Automatic election with consensus.
That depends on a human. The right answer is: Automatic election with consensus.
That risks split brain. The right answer is: Automatic election with consensus.

questions.q: Waiting for a failed leader fails the ____ property, since the system can be blocked forever if the leader does not recover.
questions.explain: Progress must not depend on one node returning.

questions.q: A runbook says a human operator promotes a new primary database after a failure. Which option is that?
questions.explain: Who decides identifies the option.
options: Waiting for recovery
Manual failover
Automatic election
Leaderless replication
optionExplain: The old leader is not awaited. The right answer is: Manual failover.
Humans choose the new leader. Remember: Manual.
No algorithm picks the leader. The right answer is: Manual failover.
A single leader is still used. The right answer is: Manual failover.

questions.q: True or false: Waiting for the failed leader to recover fully solves consensus.
questions.explain: It does not satisfy the termination property, because if the leader never recovers the system can block forever.

questions.q: Which of the three options do many XA/JTA transaction coordinators choose?
questions.explain: Participants stay blocked until the coordinator returns.
questions.teaches: Many XA/JTA transaction coordinators choose to wait for the leader to recover and accept that the system is blocked in the meantime.
options: Wait for the leader to recover
Manually fail over to a standby
Elect a new coordinator with consensus
Let participants decide on their own
optionExplain: Participants stay blocked until the coordinator returns. Remember: Many coordinators wait.
That is the choice of many relational databases. The right answer is: Wait for the leader to recover.
That is not their usual choice. The right answer is: Wait for the leader to recover.
That would break atomicity. The right answer is: Wait for the leader to recover.

questions.q: Many relational databases use manual failover. How does the book describe it?
questions.explain: A human outside the system makes the decision.
questions.teaches: Manual failover is a kind of consensus by act of God: the human operator, outside of the computer system, makes the decision, and the speed of failover is limited by the speed at which humans can act, which is generally slower than computers.
options: Consensus by act of God, limited by human speed
A fault-tolerant consensus algorithm in the formal sense
The fastest way to elect a leader
A form of leaderless replication
optionExplain: A human outside the system makes the decision. Remember: Manual failover relies on humans.
It lacks termination. The right answer is: Consensus by act of God, limited by human speed.
Humans are generally slower than computers. The right answer is: Consensus by act of God, limited by human speed.
It still uses a single leader. The right answer is: Consensus by act of God, limited by human speed.

questions.q: A database uses one leader and claims it needs no consensus. What is the catch?
questions.explain: Consensus moves, not vanishes. The card next shows why.
options: Followers must vote on every single write
The leader cannot be replaced once chosen
Writes become eventually consistent
Consensus is still needed for leadership
optionExplain: The leader decides writes alone. The right answer is: Consensus is still needed for leadership.
Leaders can be replaced. The right answer is: Consensus is still needed for leadership.
Linearizable operations are still possible. The right answer is: Consensus is still needed for leadership.
Leadership itself needs agreement. Remember: Leadership needs it.

questions.q: Having a leader only kicks the ____ down the road, since consensus is still required for leadership changes.
questions.explain: It happens less often, not never.

questions.q: Compared with running consensus on every write, how often does a single-leader database run it?
questions.explain: Consensus is rarer, not gone.
options: As often as on each write
Never, as the leader decides alone
Only for leadership changes
Only when clients ask for strong reads
optionExplain: That is the cost the leader avoids. The right answer is: Only for leadership changes.
Leadership changes still need it. The right answer is: Only for leadership changes.
That is less frequent than every write. Remember: Leadership changes.
Client requests do not trigger it. The right answer is: Only for leadership changes.

questions.q: True or false: A single-leader database needs no consensus at all.
questions.explain: It still requires consensus to maintain its leadership and for leadership changes.

questions.q: What role do tools like ZooKeeper play, according to the summary?
questions.explain: Applications can use them instead of building their own.
questions.teaches: Tools like ZooKeeper play an important role in providing an outsourced consensus, failure detection and membership service that applications can use; it is not easy to use, but much better than developing your own algorithms that can withstand all the problems of Chapter 8.
options: They replace the need for any leader election
They guarantee that no node ever fails
They act only as a cache in front of a database
Outsourced consensus and failure detection
optionExplain: They support leader election. The right answer is: Outsourced consensus and failure detection.
They cannot stop failures. The right answer is: Outsourced consensus and failure detection.
They are not just a cache. The right answer is: Outsourced consensus and failure detection.
Applications can use them instead of building their own.

questions.q: When choosing an algorithm to elect a leader automatically, what does the book advise?
questions.explain: Home-made algorithms tend to fail under bad networks.
questions.teaches: Using an algorithm to automatically choose a new leader requires a consensus algorithm, and it is advisable to use a proven algorithm that correctly handles adverse network conditions.
options: Write your own, tailored to your workload
Pick the simplest algorithm, ignoring network faults
Use timestamps from synchronised clocks
Use a proven algorithm
optionExplain: That has a poor success record. The right answer is: Use a proven algorithm.
Network faults are the main danger. The right answer is: Use a proven algorithm.
Clocks are not a safe election mechanism. The right answer is: Use a proven algorithm.
Home-made algorithms tend to fail under bad networks. Remember: Prefer proven algorithms.

questions.q: Which replication styles typically do not use global consensus?
questions.explain: Without a global decider, no global consensus. The card next shows why.
options: Single-leader with automatic failover
Leaderless and multi-leader
Chain replication with a fixed head
Replication using total order broadcast
optionExplain: Automatic election needs consensus. The right answer is: Leaderless and multi-leader.
They have no single global decision-maker. Remember: Leaderless and multi-leader.
A fixed head still needs a way to change.
That is equivalent to consensus. The right answer is: Leaderless and multi-leader.

questions.q: Leaderless and multi-leader replication typically do not use ____ consensus.
questions.explain: Consensus across different leaders is missing.

questions.q: An app can tolerate partitions and merge conflicting edits later. Does it need consensus?
questions.explain: Tolerating conflicts removes the need.
options: Not necessarily; merge branches
Yes, for every write it accepts
Yes, otherwise it cannot tolerate partitions
Only if it uses a quorum of five nodes
optionExplain: It can cope without linearizability. Remember: Not necessarily.
Merging replaces the need to decide up front. The right answer is: Not necessarily; merge branches.
Partition tolerance is possible without consensus. The right answer is: Not necessarily; merge branches.
Quorum size is unrelated. The right answer is: Not necessarily; merge branches.

questions.q: True or false: Maybe we can cope without linearizability by working with data that has branching and merging version histories.
questions.explain: That is the suggestion made for systems that do not use global consensus.

questions.q: What causes the write conflicts seen in leaderless and multi-leader systems?
questions.explain: Nobody decides a single order.
questions.rule: Conflicts are the price of no consensus.
questions.teaches: The conflicts that occur in leaderless and multi-leader systems are a consequence of not having consensus across different leaders, but maybe that is okay.
options: Too few replicas in the cluster
No consensus across leaders
Followers that apply writes too slowly
Clients retrying writes after errors
optionExplain: Replica count is not the cause. The right answer is: No consensus across leaders.
Nobody decides a single order. Remember: Conflicts are the price of no consensus.
Lag does not create conflicts. The right answer is: No consensus across leaders.
Retries are not the cause. The right answer is: No consensus across leaders.

questions.q: A design needs a fault-tolerant lock service. What does the book advise?
questions.explain: Locks are reducible to consensus.
questions.rule: Fault-tolerant consensus tasks belong in a proven service.
questions.teaches: If you find yourself wanting to do one of those things that is reducible to consensus, and you want it to be fault-tolerant, then it is advisable to use something like ZooKeeper.
options: Build a custom protocol on top of clocks
Use something like ZooKeeper
Use last-write-wins replication
Skip fault tolerance, since it costs too much
optionExplain: Clock-based designs are fragile. The right answer is: Use something like ZooKeeper.
Locks are reducible to consensus. Remember: Fault-tolerant consensus tasks belong in a proven service.
That cannot provide mutual exclusion. The right answer is: Use something like ZooKeeper.
The requirement was fault tolerance. The right answer is: Use something like ZooKeeper.

questions.q: A paper proves something impossible under unrealistic assumptions. How should a practitioner use it?
questions.explain: Theory is a guide, not a verdict. The card next shows why.
options: Ignore it, since the assumptions are unrealistic
Treat the result as binding on every real system
As a guide, after checking its assumptions
Wait until the paper is rewritten for real systems
optionExplain: The book finds such papers valuable. The right answer is: As a guide, after checking its assumptions.
Real systems differ from the model. The right answer is: As a guide, after checking its assumptions.
Theory informs practice when its model is understood. Remember: Use with care.
That is not the advice. The right answer is: As a guide, after checking its assumptions.

questions.q: Theoretical results help us reason about what can and cannot be ____.
questions.explain: They also expose counterintuitive flaws.

questions.q: Which is the better use of an FLP-style impossibility proof when designing a system?
questions.explain: Know the model.
options: Conclude that consensus cannot be built at all
Skip the proof, since it is only academic
Apply it unchanged to every possible system
Note its model and relax assumptions
optionExplain: Practical systems relax the model. The right answer is: Note its model and relax assumptions.
It reveals what cannot be done. The right answer is: Note its model and relax assumptions.
Models differ across systems. The right answer is: Note its model and relax assumptions.
Timeouts relax the model. Remember: Check assumptions.

questions.q: True or false: Theoretical papers are useless for practical work because their assumptions are sometimes unrealistic.
questions.explain: The book calls them incredibly valuable for informing practical work, even when assumptions are unrealistic.

questions.q: Which chapter of Part II covered the failure models of distributed systems?
questions.explain: Part II covered failure models there.
questions.teaches: Part II covered replication (Chapter 5), partitioning (Chapter 6), transactions (Chapter 7), distributed system failure models (Chapter 8), and finally consistency and consensus (Chapter 9).
options: Chapter 6
Chapter 7
Chapter 8
Chapter 5
optionExplain: Chapter 6 covered partitioning. The right answer is: Chapter 8.
Chapter 7 covered transactions. The right answer is: Chapter 8.
Part II covered failure models there. Remember: Part II sets the foundation.
Chapter 5 covered replication. The right answer is: Chapter 8.

questions.q: What does Part III turn to after this foundation of theory?
questions.explain: It shows how to build powerful applications.
questions.teaches: Having laid a firm foundation of theory, Part III turns once again to more practical systems and discusses how to build powerful applications from heterogeneous building blocks.
options: More proofs about replication and consensus
Hardware design for faster disks
More practical, heterogeneous systems
A single-node database engine
optionExplain: It turns to practical systems. The right answer is: More practical, heterogeneous systems.
Hardware is not the subject. The right answer is: More practical, heterogeneous systems.
It shows how to build powerful applications. Remember: Theory feeds into practice.
It stays with distributed systems. The right answer is: More practical, heterogeneous systems.

questions.q: A nightly job recomputes a recommendation list from a whole day of purchases. Which measure matters most for it?
options: Response time of each individual request to the job
Availability: whether a client can reach the job at any moment
Throughput: how long it takes to crunch an input of that size
Number of simultaneous users the job can serve at once
optionExplain: response time is how a waiting user judges a service, but this job has no requests to answer.
availability matters when clients call in, and a job with no clients has nothing to be reachable for.
Right: no user waits for the job, so the time to get through the whole dataset is what counts.
serving many users is a service concern; a batch job serves nobody while it runs.
questions.explain: A job with a big fixed input and nobody waiting is judged by how fast it gets through the data. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Batch jobs are judged by throughput.

questions.q: A batch processing job is usually judged by its ____, the time it takes to crunch an input dataset of a certain size.
questions.explain: Throughput is the primary measure for batch jobs, while response time is the primary measure for services.

questions.q: A bank app shows a customer's balance when they tap a button. Which type of system is this, and what comes first?
options: A service, where response time and availability matter most
A batch system, where throughput over the whole day of data matters most
A stream system, where the cost of storing past events matters most
An offline system, where a scheduled run once a day is the natural fit
optionExplain: Right: a person is waiting after the tap, so a fast reply and being reachable decide quality.
batch fits big inputs with no one waiting, but here a customer waits on one lookup.
streams react to events, yet a balance lookup is a request that needs an answer back.
a daily run would show yesterday's balance and leave the tapping customer with no reply.
questions.explain: A request from a waiting client and a quick answer define a service.
questions.rule: A person waiting means a service.

questions.q: True or false: A log-crunching job that takes twenty minutes fails its performance goal, because users wait too long for it.
questions.explain: Nobody waits on a batch job, and batch jobs often run for minutes to days. Throughput on the input is the yardstick, not a waiting user's patience.
questions.rule: Use the yardstick that belongs to the type.

questions.q: Why can a stream job produce results sooner than the equivalent batch system?
options: It uses a faster programming language than the batch tools do
It skips the output step and answers each client directly
It reads a smaller input file than a batch job would read
It acts on events soon after they happen, not on fixed input
optionExplain: the speed gain comes from when work starts, not from which language the job is written in.
a stream job still produces output and, like batch, does not answer requests from clients.
stream input is not a smaller file; it is a flow of events processed as they arrive.
Right: that is how streams reach lower latency than a batch job over a fixed dataset.
questions.explain: A batch job operates on a fixed set of input data, while a stream job operates on events shortly after they happen, which allows lower latency.
questions.rule: Streams are faster to react because they start on events as they arrive.
questions.teaches: A stream job operates on events shortly after they happen, whereas a batch job operates on a fixed set of input data, which lets streams reach lower latency.

questions.q: A finance team wants a monthly cost report built from a full ledger. The job runs for hours. Which description fits?
options: A service that must answer within a fraction of a second
A scheduled batch job that nobody waits on
A stream job that must react to every ledger entry on arrival
A failed design, because jobs that run for hours cannot be reliable
optionExplain: a report over the whole ledger cannot be produced in a fraction of a second, and nobody is waiting on a reply.
Right: batch jobs commonly run from minutes to several days and are scheduled periodically.
a monthly report needs the finished month, not a reaction per event.
long runs are normal for batch jobs and are not a design failure.
questions.explain: A large, fixed input with no one waiting suits a periodic batch job, whatever the run time.
questions.rule: Hours of run time is normal for batch.
questions.teaches: Batch jobs often run from a few minutes to several days, and are usually scheduled to run periodically, for example once a day.

questions.q: MapReduce was published in 2004. Compared with earlier parallel systems for data warehouses, it was mainly notable for what?
options: A richer, higher-level query language than the warehouse systems offered
A much larger scale of processing on commodity hardware
Being the first system ever to process data in batches
Needing special storage appliances with custom hardware
optionExplain: it was lower-level than the warehouse systems, which already had query languages.
Right: it was a lower-level model, and its advance was the scale it reached on ordinary machines.
the chapter notes that batch processing is a very old form of computing.
the point was using commodity machines, not special hardware.
questions.explain: The step forward was scale on commodity hardware, not a nicer programming model. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Which of these implemented MapReduce, according to the chapter? Select all that apply.
options: Hadoop
CouchDB
MongoDB
Lucene
GNU sort
optionExplain: Right: the chapter names Hadoop as an open source implementation.
Right: the chapter lists CouchDB among the systems that implemented it.
Right: the chapter lists MongoDB as another implementation.
Lucene is a full-text search library; it comes up later as something batch jobs build indexes for.
GNU sort is a Unix utility used in the log example, not a MapReduce implementation.
questions.explain: Hadoop, CouchDB and MongoDB are the three systems the chapter names as implementing MapReduce.
questions.rule: Hadoop is the main running example.

questions.q: A teammate says: skip chapter 10, MapReduce is declining anyway. What does the author suggest instead?
options: Skip it, because declining tools teach nothing about current ones
Learn only its Java code, since nothing else about it carries over
Learn it as the one algorithm behind all modern scalable systems
Still learn it: it shows why and how batch processing is useful
optionExplain: the author argues the opposite and treats it as a clear picture of batch processing.
the chapter values the ideas, not the Java classes.
the chapter calls such a claim over-enthusiastic, not a reason to study it.
Right: the author says it is worth understanding despite its declining importance.
questions.explain: The author says that MapReduce is declining, yet still worth understanding for what it shows about batch processing.

questions.q: True or false: MapReduce is a high-level model that spares programmers from writing low-level code.
questions.explain: The chapter calls it a fairly low-level programming model compared with the parallel processing systems built for data warehouses.

questions.q: Which older machines does the chapter say MapReduce bears an uncanny resemblance to?
options: IBM card-sorting machines of the 1940s and 1950s
The Unix pipe tools designed in the 1970s
The disk arrays used in modern storage appliances
The first programmable digital computers
optionExplain: Right: the author points to those machines as the older cousin of the model.
the Unix link comes up for the philosophy, but the chapter's resemblance remark is about card sorting.
no such comparison is made; shared-disk storage is contrasted with HDFS later on.
the chapter says punch card machines came long before programmable digital computers.
questions.explain: The author remarks that MapReduce resembles IBM card-sorting machines, which shows how old the batch idea is.
questions.rule: The batch idea predates digital computers.
questions.teaches: MapReduce bears an uncanny resemblance to the electromechanical IBM card-sorting machines widely used for business data processing in the 1940s and 1950s.

questions.q: A manager calls batch processing a fad of the big-data era. Which fact from the chapter best answers this?
options: MapReduce was published in 2004, so batch processing began then
Hadoop is open source, so batch processing must be a recent hobby
Punch-card machines in the 1890 US Census did batch processing
Unix pipes were invented in 1964, the start of all batch work
optionExplain: 2004 is the date of the paper, not the start of batch processing.
being open source says nothing about the age of the idea.
Right: the census machines computed aggregate statistics from large inputs long before digital computers.
pipes are a later landmark; the chapter dates batch processing to punch card machines.
questions.explain: The chapter dates batch processing back to tabulating machines used in the 1890 US Census.
questions.teaches: Punch-card tabulating machines such as the Hollerith machines of the 1890 US Census implemented a semi-mechanized form of batch processing.

questions.q: You open a web server log for the first time. What do you need before you can analyse its lines?
options: A database that holds the log lines as rows
A sorted copy of the file
The server's source code
The definition of the log format
optionExplain: the log works as a plain text file; nothing needs a database.
sorting helps counting later, but it does not reveal what the fields mean.
the format is documented separately; you do not read the server's code to interpret a line.
Right: without it you cannot tell which piece of a line is the address, the URL or the status.
questions.explain: A line is only data until you know the format that produced it. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Splitting an nginx access log line by whitespace, the requested URL is field number ____.
questions.explain: In the default format the request is the method GET, then the URL, then the protocol, so after the address, two hyphens, the time and a zone, the URL falls in field 7.
questions.rule: In the nginx default format, $7 is the URL.

questions.q: Using the card's format, what does this line record?
options: An anonymous visitor sent a GET to /api/orders and received 500 bytes
Alice sent a POST to /api/orders and the response status was 500
Alice received status 212 after posting to /api/orders
A visitor at 198.51.100.4 asked for /api/orders with status 404
optionExplain: alice's name sits in the user field, and 500 is the status, not a byte count.
Right: the user field names alice, the request is a POST to /api/orders and the status field holds 500.
212 is the size of the response body; the status comes just before it.
the first field is the address, but the status in this line is 500.
questions.explain: Match each position to its meaning in the format: address, user, time, request, status, bytes.

questions.q: True or false: Running awk with the program {print $9} on the line shown prints 212, the number of bytes sent.
questions.explain: Field 9 is the status, 500. The byte count 212 is field 10, because the quoted request splits into three whitespace-separated fields.
questions.rule: Count every whitespace-separated field, including the three from the request.

questions.q: In the user field of the sample line, a ____ stands in when the user was not authenticated.
questions.explain: The line shows the third field as a hyphen because the request came from an unauthenticated user.
questions.rule: A hyphen marks a field with no value.
questions.teaches: When the user was not authenticated, the $remote_user field in the log line is set to a hyphen.

questions.q: Your team's new log lines separate fields with pipe characters instead of spaces. What must change in a whitespace-based analysis?
options: Nothing, since all text logs split the same way
The way lines are separated, because pipes now end each record
How lines are split into fields, to suit the pipe encoding
The log must be converted to a database table first
optionExplain: tools commonly split on whitespace or tabs, but CSV, pipe-separated and other encodings are also used.
lines remain the records; the pipes only separate fields inside a line.
Right: record boundaries stay lines, but the field parsing must follow the new encoding.
a text file with a different field separator needs different parsing, not a database.
questions.explain: Fields are found by a parsing rule; change the encoding and the rule has to change.
questions.teaches: Unix tools commonly split a line into fields by whitespace or tab characters, but CSV, pipe-separated and other encodings are also used.

questions.q: You must list the five most requested URLs from a huge log using only basic command-line tools. Which plan works?
options: Extract the URL, sort, count repeats, sort by count, keep five
Sort by count first, then extract the URL field, then keep five lines
Keep the first five lines of the log, then count the URLs in them
Extract the URL field, keep five lines, then sort the five by count
optionExplain: Right: grouping equal URLs first makes counting easy, and ranking the counts gives the top five.
counts only exist after equal lines have been grouped and counted, so ranking cannot come first.
the first five lines are the oldest requests, not the most popular ones.
cutting before counting throws away nearly all of the data you need.
questions.explain: Counting needs equal items grouped together, and ranking needs the counts, so the order of stages matters. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Put the stages of the top-pages pipeline in the order they run.
items: Read the log file
Print only the URL field of each line
Sort the URLs alphabetically
Count each run of equal lines
Sort by count, largest first
Keep the first five lines
questions.explain: Each stage feeds the next: sorting makes equal URLs adjacent, uniq counts the runs, and the second sort ranks the counts before head cuts to five.
questions.rule: Each stage's output is the next stage's input.

questions.q: Your manager wants the five busiest client addresses instead of the five busiest pages. What do you change?
options: Only the extraction stage: print the first field, the address
The counting stage, so it counts addresses instead of URLs
The final stage, so it keeps the top addresses instead of lines
All stages, because a different key needs a different pipeline
optionExplain: Right: everything after extraction counts and ranks whatever key it is given.
the counting stage counts any repeated line; it has no idea whether lines are URLs or addresses.
the last stage keeps lines; the key is chosen before it ever runs.
the stages after extraction are independent of which field was picked.
questions.explain: Only the extraction stage knows which field is the key; the counting and ranking stages work on any lines.
questions.rule: To change the question, change the extraction stage.

questions.q: What does this command print?
options: 2 /b, then 3 /a
3 /a, then 1 /c
3 /a, then 2 /b
1 /c, then 2 /b
optionExplain: the second sort is reversed numerically, so the largest count comes first.
b appears twice and c once, so b ranks above c in the top two.
Right: sorting groups the lines, the count gives a:3, b:2, c:1, and head keeps the top two.
ascending order would put the smallest counts first, but the sort is reversed.
questions.explain: Sorting groups equal lines, uniq -c counts them, and sort -r -n ranks by count with the largest first.
questions.rule: Trace each stage on a small input.
questions.code:
printf '/a
/b
/a
/c
/a
/b
' | sort | uniq -c | sort -r -n | head -n 2

questions.q: True or false: A short chain of standard Unix tools can get through gigabytes of log files in a matter of seconds.
questions.explain: The author calls such a chain incredibly powerful, and adds that surprisingly many analyses can be done in minutes with awk, sed, grep, sort, uniq and xargs, and perform surprisingly well.
questions.rule: Simple tools can be fast enough for large logs.
questions.teaches: A chain of Unix commands will process gigabytes of log files in a matter of seconds, and surprisingly many analyses can be done with awk, sed, grep, sort, uniq and xargs.

questions.q: Your team wants the top pages again, but without image files. Where in the pipeline does that filter belong?
options: In the final stage, by dropping image lines from the top five
In the extraction stage, so images do not get counted
In the counting stage, by telling it to ignore image URLs
In a new pipeline run on each image file separately
optionExplain: dropping them after the cut would leave fewer than five pages and miss other pages.
Right: the author omits CSS files by changing the awk argument, filtering before the counting.
the counting stage only counts adjacent equal lines and has no notion of file types.
a second run gives a different report; the filter belongs inside the one chain.
questions.explain: Filter in the first stage, where each line is looked at, so later stages only see what you want to count.
questions.teaches: The author omits CSS files from the report by changing the awk argument to a pattern that skips URLs ending in .css, so filtering happens in the extraction stage.

questions.q: True or false: The uniq command counts how many times a line appears anywhere in the file, whatever the order.
questions.explain: It only compares neighbouring lines, so equal lines that are far apart are counted as separate runs. The card next shows why.

questions.q: The uniq command filters out repeated lines by checking whether two ____ lines are the same.
questions.explain: The check is between two adjacent lines, which is why sorting must come first.

questions.q: What does this command print?
options: Two lines, 3 b and 2 a, as after sorting
Two lines, 2 a and 3 b, in sorted order
One line holding 5, the total number of lines
Five lines, each starting with the count 1
optionExplain: that is the result you would get after sorting, which has not happened here.
uniq does not sort, so it cannot gather the repeats into totals.
uniq -c prints a count per run, not a single total of the input.
Right: no two neighbouring lines are equal, so each run has length one.
questions.explain: With no sort in front, equal lines are not neighbours, and uniq -c reports five runs of length one.
questions.rule: Without sorting, every run has length one.
questions.code:
printf 'b
a
b
a
b
' | uniq -c

questions.q: To count HTTP status codes you print field 9 with awk, run a command, then run uniq -c. Which command goes in the middle?
options: head -n 5
sort -r -n
sort
awk '{print $1}'
optionExplain: head cuts the input to five lines before any counting, which loses most of the codes.
ranking by a leading number needs counts that exist only after uniq has run.
Right: sorting puts equal status codes in a row, so uniq -c counts each code once.
this would replace the status codes with client addresses and count the wrong thing.
questions.explain: uniq needs equal lines side by side, so the blank must group the codes, and sort does that.

questions.q: True or false: In the pipeline, the second sort compares the number that uniq -c wrote at the start of each line.
questions.explain: The second sort uses its numeric option on the number at the start of each line, and the reverse option puts the largest count first.
questions.rule: uniq -c prepends the count; the second sort ranks by it.
questions.teaches: The second sort in the pipeline sorts by the number (-n) at the start of each line, which is the number of times the URL was requested, in reverse (-r) order with the largest first.

questions.q: A help desk exports ticket tags, one per line. For which files does uniq -c give one correct count per tag?
options: bug, bug, bug, billing, billing
bug, billing, bug, billing, bug
billing, billing, bug, bug, bug, login
login, bug, login
optionExplain: Right: equal tags are already in runs, so each run is a full count.
the tags alternate, so every run has length one and the counts are wrong.
Right: equal tags are neighbours, so each run is the whole count for its tag.
login is split into two runs by bug, so it would be counted twice as 1.
questions.explain: uniq -c gives a correct count per value only when equal values are already neighbours.
questions.rule: Check adjacency before trusting a count.
questions.teaches: Sorting makes equal keys adjacent, so combining them is easy without keeping a lot of state in memory.

questions.q: A script must count requests per URL in a single pass over a log. Which data structure fits best?
options: A hash table mapping each URL to a counter
A list of all lines that is sorted at the end
A single number that counts every line in the file
A stack that holds the most recent URL only
optionExplain: Right: each line looks up its URL and adds one, with no sorting required.
that is the pipeline's approach with sorting, not a one-pass counter.
one number counts lines in total and cannot tell URLs apart.
a stack of recent items forgets older URLs, so it cannot count per URL.
questions.explain: A map from key to counter lets each line update its own count directly. The card next shows why.

questions.q: The program keeps a ____ table that maps each URL to the number of times it has been seen.
questions.explain: The hash table gives each URL its own counter, and the counters start at zero.
questions.rule: One counter per URL in a hash table.

questions.q: A new URL list is counted with this snippet. What does it print?
optionExplain: a repeated URL increments the existing counter instead of being stored once.
the dictionary holds counts per URL, not the original list.
the counts follow the data: /a occurs three times and /b once.
Right: the dictionary counts each URL: /a three times, /b once.
questions.explain: Each repeat of a key adds to the same counter, so the table ends with one entry per distinct URL.

questions.q: How does the execution flow of the hash-table program differ from the Unix pipeline?
options: The program sorts the log first; the pipeline keeps a table in memory
The program keeps a table of counts; the pipeline sorts repeats
Both keep a hash table, but only the pipeline writes it to disk
Both sort the entire log, but the program does it inside one process
optionExplain: the roles are reversed: the pipeline sorts, the program uses the table.
Right: that is the difference between aggregating in a table and sorting the repeats.
the pipeline has no hash table at all, so there is nothing for it to write.
the program never sorts the raw log; it sorts only the table at the end.
questions.explain: The pipeline relies on sorting a list where repeats stay repeated, while the program has a table of counts.
questions.hint: Which one needs memory that grows with the number of distinct URLs?

questions.q: True or false: The author says choosing between the pipeline and the program is partly taste, though they behave differently on large files.
questions.explain: Both are readable enough that preference plays a part; the real difference is how each behaves once the log is large, which the next ideas explain.
questions.rule: Taste on style, execution flow on scale.
questions.teaches: Which of the two you prefer is partly a matter of taste, but there is a big difference in execution flow that becomes apparent on a large file.

questions.q: A site has 300,000 distinct URLs, and each table entry (URL plus counter) takes about 100 bytes. Can the in-memory approach run on a laptop?
options: No: a hash table of that size can only live on a dedicated server
Yes: about 30 MB, far below the roughly 1 GB for mid-sized sites
No: the table must hold every log line, which is millions of entries
Yes, but only because the log lines themselves are sorted already
optionExplain: 30 MB is small; the author says even a laptop is fine for a small working set.
Right: 300,000 times 100 bytes is 30 MB, well within what a laptop holds.
the table holds one entry per distinct URL, not per log line.
the program does not need sorted input; the table is what makes it work.
questions.explain: The table's size follows the distinct keys: 300,000 entries at 100 bytes each is about 30 MB.
questions.rule: Estimate size from distinct keys times entry size.
questions.teaches: For most small to mid-sized websites, you can probably fit all distinct URLs and a counter for each in about 1 GB of memory.

questions.q: Counting requests per URL, which change makes an in-memory table need much more memory?
options: A hundred times more requests for the same URLs
A hundred times faster arrival of requests
A hundred times more days of logs with the same URLs
A hundred times more distinct URLs in the log
optionExplain: repeat requests only bump existing counters; they add no entries.
speed does not change how many distinct URLs the table must hold.
more days of the same URLs still means the same number of entries.
Right: the table has one entry per distinct URL, so more distinct URLs means more entries.
questions.explain: The table grows with distinct keys, and each repeat only changes an existing counter. The card next shows why.

questions.q: The amount of memory a job needs random access to is called its ____ set.
questions.explain: The working set is the memory the job needs random access to; for URL counting it depends on distinct URLs.
questions.rule: Working set: memory needed for random access.

questions.q: A log has 5 billion lines but only 20,000 distinct URLs. What decides whether a counting table fits in memory?
options: The 20,000 distinct URLs and the size of each entry
The 5 billion lines, since every line must be kept in the table
The average length of every log line in the file
The speed of the disk the log file is read from
optionExplain: Right: each distinct URL has one entry and one counter, whatever the line count.
lines update counters; they are not stored individually.
only the URL and the counter are stored, not whole lines.
disk speed affects the reading time, not the table size.
questions.explain: Working set = distinct keys times entry size, so 20,000 entries is a small table.

questions.q: A colleague says: the log doubled to 10 GB, so the counting table will need twice the memory. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, since memory scales with the input size
Doubling the log halves the memory, as repeats are merged
Memory follows distinct URLs; repeats add no entries
The table will need ten times the memory, not twice
optionExplain: for counting, the table scales with distinct keys, which may stay the same.
memory does not shrink; it stays equal when the distinct URLs stay equal.
Right: repeat requests only increment counters in existing entries.
no fixed multiple applies, since memory follows distinct keys, not file size.
questions.explain: The working set is set by the number of distinct keys; a bigger file with the same keys changes nothing.
questions.rule: Do not equate input size with working set.

questions.q: True or false: A job with a small working set can use an in-memory hash table even on a laptop, however long the log is.
questions.explain: If the working set is small enough, the in-memory table works fine even on a laptop, because the table does not grow with repeated entries.
questions.rule: Small working set: memory is enough.
questions.teaches: If the working set is small enough, an in-memory hash table works fine, even on a laptop.

questions.q: A bank counts failed logins per customer from 5 billion events across 80 million customers. What is the main risk for a table?
options: The 5 billion events, because each needs its own entry
The number of days the events cover, as old events pile up
The speed of failed logins, which can overflow the table
80 million customers may push the working set past memory
optionExplain: events update counters; the table holds one entry per customer.
days do not add entries unless new customers appear.
speed does not change how many entries the table needs.
Right: one counter per customer is 80 million entries, which may outgrow memory.
questions.explain: Distinct customers set the table size; if that exceeds memory, another approach is needed.
questions.rule: Check the distinct keys before choosing the method.
questions.teaches: If the job's working set is larger than the available memory, the sorting approach has the advantage that it can make efficient use of disks.

questions.q: A job's working set is bigger than memory. Which approach copes by using disks efficiently?
options: Keep the table in memory and look keys up on disk when absent
Sort chunks in memory, spill sorted segments to disk, merge them
Count only the first million entries and skip the rest
Compress every URL until the whole table fits in memory
optionExplain: random lookups on disk are slow, which is why this does not scale well.
Right: sorted chunks merged in order use sequential disk access, which suits disks.
skipping data gives wrong results; the job needs every record.
compression may help a little, but it gives no guarantee that the table will fit.
questions.explain: Mergesort works on chunks and merges sorted runs, and sequential access performs well on disks. The card next shows why.

questions.q: In the sort-based approach, chunks are sorted in memory, written as segment files, and then segments are ____ into a larger sorted file.
questions.explain: Merging sorted segments produces a larger sorted file, as in SSTables and LSM-trees.

questions.q: You must count requests per URL with 2 TB of distinct URL strings on a machine with 64 GB of RAM. Which fits?
options: A single in-memory hash table sized to the full set of URLs
A table that holds only the last hour of requests
The sort-based pipeline that spills to disk and merges
Counting with uniq alone, without sorting any of the input
optionExplain: 2 TB of distinct strings cannot fit in 64 GB, so the table would fail.
dropping older requests changes the question and gives incomplete counts.
Right: the working set is far above memory, so sorting with disk segments suits.
uniq counts neighbours only, so unsorted input gives wrong counts.
questions.explain: A working set far above memory rules out the table; chunked sorting and merging works at any size.
questions.rule: Working set above memory means sort.

questions.q: True or false: If a sort job's data doubles beyond memory, the merge step switches from sequential to random disk access.
questions.explain: Mergesort keeps sequential access patterns, which is why it performs well on disks even when the data far exceeds memory.

questions.q: Does the GNU sort utility need special options to handle a file bigger than memory?
options: No: it spills to disk and uses several cores by itself
Yes: you must split the file into pieces that each fit in memory
Yes: it stops with an error unless a larger swap file is configured
No, but it uses one CPU core only, so it is slow
optionExplain: Right: that is how GNU sort in Coreutils is described.
the utility handles larger-than-memory datasets itself by spilling to disk.
the chapter says it scales to large datasets without running out of memory.
the chapter says it automatically parallelizes across multiple cores.
questions.explain: GNU sort handles larger-than-memory input automatically and uses several cores.
questions.rule: The tool does the chunking for you.
questions.teaches: The sort utility in GNU Coreutils automatically handles larger-than-memory datasets by spilling to disk, and automatically parallelizes sorting across multiple CPU cores.

questions.q: A team pipes a 500 GB log through sort on one server with enough cores. What will probably limit the speed?
options: The rate at which the input file can be read from disk
The amount of RAM, since sort aborts when memory is full
The number of CPU cores, since sort uses only one
The length of the pipeline, since each stage doubles the time
optionExplain: Right: with sorting parallelized and spilling automatic, reading the input is the likely bottleneck.
sort spills to disk when memory is full instead of aborting.
sort parallelizes across cores, so cores are rarely the limit.
stages run as a stream, so they do not multiply the running time.
questions.explain: With spilling and parallel sort handled by the tool, reading input off the disk is the likely limit.
questions.rule: The disk read rate is the likely bottleneck.
questions.teaches: With GNU sort the simple chain of commands scales to large datasets without running out of memory, and the bottleneck is likely to be the rate at which the input file can be read from disk.

questions.q: Early Unix authors wrote that a program's output should be ready to serve as what?
options: A report meant for a person reading it on screen
A fixed-column file that databases can bulk-load later
Input to another, as yet unknown, program
A prompt that asks the user how to continue next
optionExplain: readable decoration clutters output; the rule says to avoid extraneous information.
fixed columnar and binary formats are on the list to avoid.
Right: they expected output to become the input of programs not yet written.
the rule says not to insist on interactive input.
questions.explain: Output is designed as the future input of another program, so it stays plain and uncluttered. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Match each rule of the Unix philosophy to its gist.
pairs: Build afresh rather than adding features to old programs
Do not clutter output with extraneous information
Throw away clumsy parts and rebuild them
Detour to build tools, even if you discard some later
questions.explain: The four rules are focus, composable output, early trials and a preference for building tools.
questions.rule: Focus, composable output, early trials, tools.

questions.q: A report tool prints a cheerful banner and a progress bar before its data, so later programs choke. Which rule is broken?
options: Each program must do one thing well, and the banner adds a second thing
Output must stay free of extra information, so it can feed other programs
Programs must be tried early, and the banner delays the first trial
Tools must be preferred to unskilled help, and the banner is unskilled
optionExplain: doing one thing well is about scope, not about the extra text in the output.
Right: the banner clutters output that another program will read.
the early-trial rule concerns how soon software is built and tested.
that rule concerns building tools to lighten work, not output format.
questions.explain: The second rule asks for output that is ready to be input, without decorations.

questions.q: A teammate adds charting and email sending to a log-counting tool so it can work alone. What does the philosophy advise?
options: Accept it, since a tool that works alone is easier to reuse
Accept it, as long as the new features are optional and documented
Reject it only if the tool becomes slower than before
Keep the counter focused and build separate tools to connect to it
optionExplain: the philosophy favours small parts joined together over one tool doing everything.
the rule advises against adding features to old programs, documented or not.
speed is not the test; the test is whether the program does one thing well.
Right: the first rule says to build afresh instead of complicating old programs.
questions.explain: To do a new job, build a new tool instead of piling features on an existing one.

questions.q: True or false: The author says the Unix philosophy sounds like the Agile and DevOps movements of today.
questions.explain: Automation, rapid prototyping, incremental iteration, friendliness to experimentation and breaking projects into manageable chunks echo Agile and DevOps, and surprisingly little has changed in four decades.
questions.rule: Unix ideas echo Agile and DevOps.
questions.teaches: The Unix approach of automation, rapid prototyping, incremental iteration, experimentation and breaking projects into chunks sounds remarkably like the Agile and DevOps movements.

questions.q: The sort tool is arguably better than most languages' standard sort, yet barely useful alone. What does that show?
options: A focused tool should grow more features until it can work alone
A tool that is barely useful alone has been designed badly
A focused tool gains its power by joining other tools
Programming languages should drop their own sort functions
optionExplain: the philosophy goes the other way: keep tools small and compose them.
being weak alone is the expected price of doing one thing well.
Right: sort becomes powerful in combination with tools such as uniq.
the chapter says language libraries lack features like spilling to disk, but it does not tell anyone to drop them.
questions.explain: Sort does one thing very well, and it is combined with uniq and others to become a data processing job.
questions.rule: Focused tools gain power when composed.
questions.teaches: The sort tool is arguably a better sorting implementation than most programming languages' standard libraries, which do not spill to disk or use multiple threads.

questions.q: In Unix, what single interface lets very different things be plugged into the same tools?
options: The file: an ordered sequence of bytes
The database table: rows with named columns
The API call: a request with a typed reply
The message queue: records with a fixed header
optionExplain: Right: disks, pipes, devices and sockets can all be presented as sequences of bytes.
tables belong to databases, not to the common interface across Unix programs.
typed calls need each side to know the other's definitions; Unix tools do not.
queues need agreed headers; the Unix interface has no such structure.
questions.explain: Unix keeps the interface minimal: a file is just an ordered sequence of bytes. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: The file is the common interface.

questions.q: In Unix, the uniform interface is a file or, more precisely, a file ____.
questions.explain: A file descriptor refers to a sequence of bytes, whether it is a disk file, a pipe or a socket.

questions.q: Which of these can a Unix program read through the same file interface? Select all that apply.
options: A file on the filesystem
The stdout of another process
A TCP connection socket
A function call inside another program's memory
A record inside a database's own storage engine
optionExplain: Right: an ordinary file is the original case of the interface.
Right: a communication channel to another process is also a byte sequence.
Right: a socket for a TCP connection is presented through the same interface.
a function call passes values within one program; it is not a byte sequence shared between programs.
a database's internal storage is reached through its own interface, not as a plain byte sequence.
questions.explain: Files, channels, devices and sockets all look like byte sequences.
questions.rule: Many different things share the file interface.

questions.q: True or false: Unix tools can be joined only if all of them were written by the same team.
questions.explain: Many of the programs are written by different groups of people, yet they join together flexibly because they share the uniform interface.
questions.rule: A shared interface removes the need for one author.

questions.q: Which foundation of the web does the author give as another example of a uniform interface?
options: HTML and CSS, which fix how every page must look
Browsers, which hide the differences between servers
DNS, which turns names into numeric addresses
URLs and HTTP, which let you link to any resource from any site
optionExplain: styling is not the interface; the point is addressability across sites.
the browser relies on the uniform interface; it is not the interface itself.
DNS is not mentioned as the example; the author names URLs and HTTP.
Right: a URL identifies a resource and can be linked from anywhere.
questions.explain: URLs identify things and HTTP fetches them, so a link works across unrelated organizations.
questions.rule: A common address scheme is a uniform interface.
questions.teaches: URLs and HTTP, the foundations of the web, are another uniform interface: a URL identifies a resource, and you can link to any URL from any other website.

questions.q: Before the web, one bulletin board could refer to another only by phone number and modem settings. What was missing?
options: A faster modem that connects without manual dialling
A uniform way to address content inside another system
A larger archive on each board to avoid references
A common file format for the messages on all boards
optionExplain: the problem was addressing, not speed; even a faster modem leaves the reference format unsolved.
Right: you could not link directly to content inside another bulletin board.
more storage would not let one board point into another.
a message format helps reading, but linking to content needed a shared address scheme.
questions.explain: The boards each had their own phone number and settings, so there was no shared way to link to content.
questions.rule: Uniform addressing makes cross-system links possible.
questions.teaches: In the bulletin board era a reference to another system was a phone number and modem settings; the user had to hang up and dial, and could not link directly to content inside another system.

questions.q: Several command-line tools process the same file one record at a time. What do they need to agree on?
options: A schema that names every field of the file
What character ends a record
A common database to hold intermediate counts
The same programming language for all of the tools
optionExplain: they share no schema; records are just lines of text.
Right: without a shared record separator, each tool would cut the stream differently.
the tools exchange bytes through pipes, not through a shared database.
the tools are written in many languages; only the data convention is shared.
questions.explain: Tools need only a shared record separator to cut the stream into the same records. The card next shows why.

questions.q: In the log example, the tools treat the file as records separated by the ____ character.
questions.explain: They use the newline character, written \n and ASCII 0x0A, to separate the records.

questions.q: You write a tool for an existing pipeline. How should it treat its input to fit with sort and uniq?
options: As one long record, read from beginning to end
As a binary stream, with a length header per record
As rows in a table, with typed columns in a schema
As lines of text, with one record on each line
optionExplain: sort and uniq expect many records separated by newlines, not one block.
binary formats are discouraged in the philosophy, and these tools do not read headers.
the pipeline tools have no schema or typed columns.
Right: line-per-record text is what sort and uniq expect.
questions.explain: Newline-separated text records are the shared format of the tools.

questions.q: Sort these facts about Unix text tools into the settled convention and the looser part.

items.t: Records are separated by the newline character
awk, sort, uniq and head all treat input as lines
Fields may be split by whitespace, tabs, commas or pipes
xargs has half a dozen options for how to parse input
Output of one tool is read as the next tool's lines

questions.explain: Record splitting is the settled convention; how a record is cut into fields is much more varied.
questions.hint: Look at how many options a tool needs to parse its input.

questions.q: Which ASCII character does the author say would arguably have been a better record separator than newline?
options: The record separator character, 0x1E
The tab character, 0x09
The null character, 0x00
The comma character, 0x2C, as used in CSV files
optionExplain: Right: it is intended for this purpose, so it would arguably fit better.
tab commonly splits fields, but the author names a different character.
the null character is not the one the author names.
the comma is used by CSV for fields, not named here as a record separator.
questions.explain: Newline is an arbitrary choice; ASCII has a dedicated record separator that was meant for the job.
questions.rule: Newline is a convention, not the only choice.
questions.teaches: The choice of the newline character is arbitrary: the ASCII record separator 0x1E would arguably have been a better choice, since it is intended for this purpose.

questions.q: Which fact shows that field parsing is looser than record splitting among Unix tools?
options: The sort tool needs a schema file before it can sort any lines
Every tool uses a different character to end a record, so none can be combined
Even a tool as simple as xargs has half a dozen options for parsing its input
Tools refuse to read files that contain commas
optionExplain: sort needs no schema file; it just orders lines.
records are cut at newlines by almost all of the tools.
Right: many options exist because the input format is not fixed.
CSV is one of the encodings in use, so commas do not stop tools.
questions.explain: A simple tool still needs about six options to say how its input is cut into fields, which shows the looseness.
questions.rule: Field parsing is configured, not standardized.
questions.teaches: Even a fairly simple tool like xargs has half a dozen command-line options for specifying how its input should be parsed.

questions.q: What does the author call the result of products that cannot easily exchange data with each other?
options: Normalization of data
Denormalization of data
Federation of data
Balkanization of data
optionExplain: normalization is a schema-design idea about reducing duplicate values, not about isolation.
denormalization copies data into records, which is a different topic.
federation suggests systems working together, the opposite of the author's point.
Right: isolated pools of data resemble a region broken into separate parts.
questions.explain: A lack of integration leaves data in separate, unconnected pools. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: No shared interface, no easy integration.

questions.q: The lack of integration between systems leads to ____ of data.
questions.explain: The author uses the word Balkanization for data that is split into isolated parts.
questions.rule: Poor integration splits data into pools.

questions.q: A company runs two document databases from different vendors, both with the same data model. Moving data takes weeks. What does this show?
options: A shared data model guarantees an easy move between products
Even a shared data model does not guarantee easy data movement
Document databases cannot ever be moved between vendors
The weeks are caused by the amount of data and nothing else
optionExplain: the author says the opposite: the same model does not make export and import easy.
Right: the author says databases with the same model often make export and import hard.
the chapter does not say it is impossible, only that it is often hard.
the author blames the lack of integration, not just volume.
questions.explain: Models can match while the interfaces do not, and then data movement is hard.
questions.rule: Same model, hard move: no common interface.

questions.q: True or false: Unix-style composition is the norm for programs today, and special cases like databases are the exception.
questions.explain: The author says today it is an exception, not the norm, to have programs that work together as smoothly as Unix tools.

questions.q: Besides unreadable syntax, what does the chapter name as one cost of the plain-text interface of Unix?
options: It cannot represent files that contain more than text
It stops tools from reading input that arrives over a network connection or a pipe
Field positions like the seventh one are hard to read, unlike named fields
It makes sorting slower than a database index would be
optionExplain: files are sequences of bytes and can hold more than text; text is only a convention.
the limits on network connections are about stdin and stdout, not about text.
Right: the log example fetches the URL as field seven; a named field would read better.
the chapter makes no such claim about sorting speed.
questions.explain: The interface mostly works but is not beautiful: an ideal world would name the URL field instead of numbering it.
questions.rule: Plain text trades readability for compatibility.
questions.teaches: The text interface mostly works but is not beautiful: {print $7} is not very readable, and in an ideal world it could be {print $request_url}.

questions.q: Orders, support tickets and web logs sit in three systems with three formats. What cost does this show?
options: Joining the datasets is hard until someone writes converters between them
Each system will lose data unless all three are moved into one shared database
The three systems will be faster because each is specialised
Only the logs can be analysed, since they are plain text
optionExplain: Right: isolated pools of data in different formats resist being combined.
nothing says data is lost; the cost is the difficulty of combining it.
specialisation may help each system but does not remove the integration cost.
the issue here is the lack of integration, not which files are analysable.
questions.explain: Separate systems with separate formats leave data in pools that need custom work to join.
questions.rule: Integration cost grows with each separate format.
questions.teaches: Bringing data from various parts of an organization together in one place is valuable, because it enables joins across datasets that were previously disparate.

questions.q: A data tool is easiest to reuse in many pipelines when it does what about its input and output?
options: Reads from stdin and writes to stdout, leaving the wiring to the shell
Opens fixed file paths that are written into its source code
Asks the user for the path of the file on each run
Writes to a log folder and reports only the file name
optionExplain: Right: the caller can then connect it to a file, a pipe or the screen.
fixed paths tie it to one arrangement and make reuse hard.
that insists on interactive input, which the philosophy advises against.
files named inside the program cannot be re-wired by the caller.
questions.explain: A program that uses standard streams can be placed anywhere in a chain. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Logic in the program, wiring in the shell.

questions.q: Pipes attach the stdout of one process to the ____ of another process.
questions.explain: Pipes connect one process's standard output to another's standard input, using a small in-memory buffer.

questions.q: You write a tool that turns IP addresses into country codes. How do you make it usable in the log pipeline?
options: Make it read the log file by name and write a new file
Make it open a network connection to the log server
Read addresses from stdin and write country codes to stdout
Make it ask the user which column holds the address
optionExplain: naming its own files makes the tool impossible to re-wire from the shell.
a program that opens its own connections does its own wiring.
Right: then it can be plugged into the pipeline like any system tool.
interactive input breaks the pipe, since nobody is there to answer.
questions.explain: A tool that uses stdin and stdout can be joined with others by whoever builds the pipeline.
questions.rule: Make your tool a good citizen: stdin in, stdout out.

questions.q: True or false: The sort program behaves differently when its input comes from a program you wrote than when it comes from a system program.
questions.explain: Sort does not care whether it communicates with another part of the operating system or with your program; it reads stdin.
questions.rule: The program is blind to its neighbours.
questions.hint: Think about what a program on the end of a pipe can actually see.

questions.q: Which three names does the author give for the idea of separating wiring from logic?
options: Strong typing, early binding and tight coupling
Loose coupling, late binding and inversion of control
Load balancing, sharding and replication
Serialization, compression and encryption
optionExplain: these are close to the opposite of what the author describes.
Right: the book offers these as other names for the same idea.
these are distributed-systems terms from other chapters, not names for wiring.
these deal with data encoding, not with wiring.
questions.explain: The wiring is left to the user of the program, so the program itself is only loosely coupled and its binding is late.
questions.rule: Loose coupling, late binding, inversion of control.
questions.teaches: Separating the wiring of input and output from the program logic is a form of loose coupling, late binding, or inversion of control.

questions.q: A team's job code reads from a hard-coded warehouse path and writes to a hard-coded report path. What is the main cost?
options: It will be slower than a job that reads from standard input
It cannot read any file larger than the available memory
It will lose data, as hard-coded paths drop records
It can be reused elsewhere only by editing its code, not by re-wiring
optionExplain: speed is not the point; the point is how easily the job can be re-wired.
memory use is unrelated to whether the paths are hard-coded.
hard-coded paths do not lose records; they reduce reuse.
Right: separation of logic and wiring is what makes a tool reusable by others.
questions.explain: The code mixes what to do with where to read and write, so each new arrangement needs a code change.
questions.teaches: MapReduce jobs also separate logic from wiring (the configuration of input and output directories), so one team can write a job that does one thing well while other teams decide where and when to run it.

questions.q: Which job is awkward to do with pipes alone?
options: Sorting the output of a program and counting the lines
Sending one file through two programs, one after the other
Feeding a program's output into a remote network connection
Showing the output of a program on the screen
optionExplain: this is the standard pipeline and works well.
