chains of programs are what pipes do best.
Right: a pipe cannot reach a network connection directly; another tool is needed.
that is the default; no special wiring is needed.
questions.explain: Pipes connect processes on one machine; reaching a network connection needs another tool. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Pipes do not reach network connections.

questions.q: A program that opens its own files, starts a subprocess or opens a network connection does its own ____ of inputs and outputs.
questions.explain: Such a program wires its own I/O, which reduces the flexibility of wiring it up in a shell.
questions.rule: Self-opened I/O is wired by the program.

questions.q: A tool merges two sorted input files into one sorted output. Why is it awkward with pipes?
options: It needs two inputs, but a program has only one stdin
It needs sorted data, which a pipe cannot carry
It writes output, and pipes can only read input
It uses more memory than a pipe buffer can hold
optionExplain: Right: multiple inputs are possible but tricky with stdin and stdout.
pipes carry any bytes, including sorted data, so that is not the obstacle.
a pipe has a writing end and a reading end.
the pipe buffer is small by design, and the tool still works with it.
questions.explain: One stdin and one stdout fit single-stream programs; a two-input tool needs another way.
questions.rule: Multiple inputs strain the pipe model.

questions.q: True or false: If a program opens its own network connection, a shell user can still re-wire it freely with pipes.
questions.explain: That I/O is wired by the program itself, so the flexibility of wiring inputs and outputs in a shell is reduced.

questions.q: How does the chapter say you can send a program's output over a network connection?
options: Pipe it straight into the connection with the shell
Write it to a file and mail the file
Run the program on the remote machine instead
Use a separate tool such as netcat or curl
optionExplain: the chapter says you cannot pipe output into a network connection directly.
that is not the workaround the chapter names.
the chapter does not describe moving the program.
Right: those tools bridge between pipes and network connections.
questions.explain: Because pipes do not reach network connections, a separate tool such as netcat or curl acts as the bridge.
questions.rule: Use a bridging tool for network I/O.
questions.teaches: You can pipe a program's output into a network connection only by using a separate tool, such as netcat or curl.

questions.q: Which operating system design fits more strictly the idea that everything is a file, including a TCP connection?
options: BSD sockets, which treat each connection as a file
Plan 9 and Inferno, which show a TCP connection as a file
Unix as it started, with sockets as ordinary files
Hadoop, which shows a connection as a distributed file
optionExplain: BSD sockets deviated from the everything-is-a-file convention, so they do not fit.
Right: the research systems treat connections as files at /net/tcp.
Unix started out trying to represent everything as files, but sockets later deviated.
Hadoop is a data system, not an operating system.
questions.explain: Plan 9 and Inferno are more consistent: they present a TCP connection as a file in /net/tcp.
questions.rule: Some systems keep the file idea further than Unix did.
questions.teaches: Unix started out trying to represent everything as files, but the BSD sockets API deviated; Plan 9 and Inferno represent a TCP connection as a file in /net/tcp.

questions.q: You are debugging a long pipeline of text tools. What helps most?
options: Running it only once, in a production environment
Stopping at a stage and looking at its output
Letting each stage overwrite the original input file
Hiding the stages inside one compiled program
optionExplain: one run in production gives no chance to look at stages.
Right: you can end a pipeline at any point and inspect the result.
overwriting loses the original, so a mistake becomes irreversible.
a single program removes the points where you could inspect data.
questions.explain: Seeing each stage's output tells you which stage went wrong. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Because Unix commands treat their input files as ____, you can run them as often as you want without damaging the input.
questions.explain: Immutable inputs make reruns harmless.

questions.q: A three-stage pipeline's second stage takes an hour, and you keep changing the third. What should you do?
options: Rerun the whole pipeline after each change to the third stage
Merge the second and third stages into one command
Let the third stage overwrite the second stage's input
Write the second stage's output to a file and feed the third from it
optionExplain: this repeats the hour-long stage every time for no gain.
merging removes the point where you can save and restart.
overwriting inputs destroys the thing that makes reruns safe.
Right: then only the third stage reruns when you change it.
questions.explain: Saving an intermediate file lets you restart the later stage without rerunning earlier ones.
questions.rule: Save intermediate output when stages are slow.

questions.q: True or false: Unix tools are useful for experimentation because they are sophisticated and well optimized, like a relational query optimizer.
questions.explain: The author calls them blunt, simple tools compared with a query optimizer; their transparency and immutable inputs make them useful.
questions.rule: Simplicity and transparency make them good for experiments.

questions.q: What does the author name as the biggest limitation of Unix tools?
options: They run only on a single machine
They cannot process more than a megabyte of data
They change their input files as they work
They cannot be combined with programs of your own
optionExplain: Right: that is where tools like Hadoop come in.
the chapter shows they handle gigabytes in seconds.
the opposite: inputs are normally treated as immutable.
you can write your own programs and join them with system tools.
questions.explain: Everything the pipeline does happens on one machine, which is why distributed tools are needed.
questions.rule: The Unix limit is the single machine.
questions.teaches: The biggest limitation of Unix tools is that they run only on a single machine, and that is where tools like Hadoop come in.

questions.q: A data team replaces a pipeline with a script that updates the source table in place. What is lost?
options: The ability to use more than one programming language
The ability to run the job on more than one machine
The ability to rerun with changes without damaging the input
The ability to sort the data before it is updated
optionExplain: the choice of language is unrelated to whether inputs are changed.
distribution is a separate issue; the cost here is lost safety.
Right: in-place updates make experiments irreversible, so reruns could corrupt the data.
sorting is still possible; the loss is that reruns could now corrupt the data.
questions.explain: When inputs stay unchanged, reruns are safe; in-place updates remove that safety.
questions.rule: Do not change inputs; derive outputs.
questions.teaches: With read-only inputs, any previous output is completely replaced by the new output and there are no other side effects, so you can rerun a command as often as you like without messing up the state of your system.

questions.q: A single MapReduce job is comparable to what in the Unix world?
options: A shell script that edits files in place as it goes
The whole Unix kernel, which manages all processes
An interactive terminal session with a human user
A single Unix process with inputs and outputs
optionExplain: MapReduce jobs do not modify their input; in-place edits are the opposite.
a job is one unit of work, not the system that runs all work.
jobs run without a human responding to prompts.
Right: it takes inputs, produces outputs and has no other side effects.
questions.explain: The author compares one job with one Unix process: inputs in, outputs out, no other effects. The card next shows why.

questions.q: In Hadoop's implementation of MapReduce, jobs read and write files on a distributed filesystem called ____.
questions.explain: HDFS plays the role that stdin and stdout play for Unix tools.
questions.rule: HDFS holds job input and output.

questions.q: A team must clean 40 TB of raw event files without any risk to the raw data. Which property of a MapReduce job helps?
options: It edits the raw files in place so no extra storage is needed
It does not modify its input and writes results to new output files
It sends each cleaned record straight to a remote database
It asks an operator to confirm each step as it runs
optionExplain: in-place edits would put the raw data at risk; MapReduce avoids them.
Right: raw data stays untouched while cleaned copies are written elsewhere.
side effects other than its output are what the model avoids.
jobs run without an operator; nobody is prompted.
questions.explain: Unchanged inputs and fresh output files mean a bad run cannot damage the raw data.
questions.rule: Derive new outputs; do not edit inputs.

questions.q: True or false: A MapReduce job normally updates its input files in place as it processes them.
questions.explain: Running a job normally does not modify the input and has no side effects other than producing the output.

questions.q: How does the chapter say MapReduce output files are written?
options: In random order, with parts rewritten as results improve
In parallel by every task into one shared file
Once, in a sequential fashion, without modifying written parts
By appending to the input files, one record at a time
optionExplain: random updates to existing parts are what the model avoids.
each task writes its own output; the model does not use one shared file.
Right: output files are written once and sequentially.
outputs are separate files; input files are not modified.
questions.explain: Writing once and sequentially goes with unchanged inputs: nothing already written is ever modified.
questions.teaches: MapReduce output files are written once, in a sequential fashion, not modifying any existing part of a file once it has been written.

questions.q: A startup wants its Unix-style batch job to run on thousands of cheap machines. What changes and what stays the same?
options: Data moves to a distributed filesystem; the unchanged-input discipline stays
Nothing changes, since pipes can join processes across machines
Everything changes, as unchanged inputs do not scale up
The job must edit shared files in place to avoid copying data
optionExplain: Right: files on HDFS replace stdin and stdout, and the discipline carries over.
pipes cannot reach other machines, which is why the filesystem is needed.
the discipline carries over; it is what makes retries safe at scale.
in-place edits are not how MapReduce works; it writes new outputs.
questions.explain: The discipline of immutable input and new output stays; the exchange medium becomes a distributed filesystem.
questions.teaches: HDFS is an open source reimplementation of the Google File System (GFS), and other distributed filesystems such as GlusterFS and the Quantcast File System exist too.

questions.q: A cluster stores huge files on its own commodity machines, joined by a normal datacenter network. Which principle is this?
options: Shared nothing
Shared disk
Shared memory
Shared secrets
optionExplain: Right: each machine uses its own disks, and no special shared hardware is needed.
shared-disk systems use a central storage appliance with special hardware.
shared memory would let machines reach the same RAM, which is unrelated to disk files.
that is a security idea and unrelated to how storage is organized.
questions.explain: The commodity machine plus ordinary network design is called shared nothing. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: No special hardware is the shared-nothing mark.

questions.q: NAS and SAN storage use the ____-disk approach, with a centralized storage appliance.
questions.explain: Shared-disk storage is built on a central storage appliance, while HDFS uses shared nothing.

questions.q: A company adds capacity by buying a rack of ordinary servers with disks and joining them to its datacenter network. Which design?
options: Shared disk, as in a SAN with Fibre Channel
A tape library with robotic loading arms
Shared nothing, the way HDFS grows
A single large machine with the biggest disk made
optionExplain: a SAN is a central appliance with special network gear, not a rack of ordinary servers.
the chapter does not mention tape; the design is about disks on ordinary servers.
Right: ordinary machines on an ordinary network add capacity.
that is one machine; the design spreads data across many.
questions.explain: Capacity grows by adding ordinary machines, which is the shared-nothing approach.

questions.q: Sort these features into shared disk (NAS or SAN) or shared nothing (HDFS).

items.t: Centralized storage appliance
Custom hardware and Fibre Channel networking
Only a conventional datacenter network
Computers with their own attached disks
Special network infrastructure

questions.explain: NAS and SAN rely on a central appliance with special gear; HDFS relies on ordinary machines and a conventional network.
questions.rule: Appliance and special gear: shared disk.

questions.q: Why was HDFS able to reach tens of thousands of machines and hundreds of petabytes at lower cost than a storage appliance?
options: It stores one copy of each block on the fastest disk
It uses commodity hardware and open source software
It replaces the datacenter network with a faster one
It limits files to a few megabytes so lookups are quick
optionExplain: HDFS replicates blocks, so it does not rely on one copy.
Right: ordinary parts and free software cost far less per unit of capacity.
HDFS runs on a conventional datacenter network, so it does not need that switch.
the chapter says input files are typically hundreds of megabytes.
questions.explain: Commodity hardware and open source software make large capacity much cheaper than a dedicated appliance.
questions.teaches: The biggest HDFS deployments run on tens of thousands of machines with a combined storage capacity of hundreds of petabytes, at a much lower cost than the equivalent capacity on a dedicated storage appliance.

questions.q: A team stores data in Amazon S3 and reads it from compute machines. Which statement matches the chapter's view of this service?
options: It is a shared-disk SAN that depends on Fibre Channel
It is a MapReduce engine that runs the team's code
It is a relational database that enforces a schema
It is similar in many ways to a distributed filesystem like HDFS
optionExplain: object stores are not described as SANs; they are similar to distributed filesystems.
object stores store data; the engine is a separate thing.
the chapter lists S3 among storage services, not databases.
Right: the chapter says object stores are similar in many ways.
questions.explain: S3 and similar object stores resemble HDFS as storage, though they usually separate storage from computation.
questions.teaches: With HDFS, computing tasks can be scheduled to run on the machine that stores a copy of a particular file, whereas object stores usually keep storage and computation separate; and besides HDFS there are other distributed filesystems such as GlusterFS and QFS.

questions.q: In HDFS, which component tracks which file blocks are stored on which machine?
options: Each mapper, as it reads its input file
A tracker kept on the client that wrote the file
The NameNode, a central server
The reducers, once they have merged the output
optionExplain: mappers read blocks; they do not keep the global map.
the map is kept centrally, not by the writing client.
Right: it holds the map of blocks to machines.
reducers work on key-value pairs and do not track block locations.
questions.explain: The NameNode knows where every block lives. The card next shows why.

questions.q: HDFS runs a ____ process on each machine, exposing a network service so other nodes can access its files.
questions.explain: The daemon serves the files stored on its own machine to the other nodes.
questions.rule: A daemon runs on every machine.

questions.q: A client wants to read a large file in HDFS. What must it learn first?
options: Which machines hold the file's blocks, which the NameNode knows
Which reducer will process the file when it arrives
Which join algorithm will later be used on the file when it is read
Which partition of the file is hot in the cluster
optionExplain: Right: the NameNode keeps the map from file blocks to the machines that store them.
reducers belong to MapReduce processing, not to locating blocks.
join choice is a processing matter, not a lookup of storage.
skew concerns processing later on; locating the blocks has to come first.
questions.explain: The NameNode tracks the blocks, so the client asks it where to find them.
questions.rule: Ask the NameNode where blocks live.

questions.q: True or false: HDFS keeps every file on the single machine that runs the NameNode.
questions.explain: The NameNode only tracks which blocks are on which machine; the file blocks live on the disks of the machines running the daemon.

questions.q: What does the chapter assume about the machines that make HDFS work?
options: Each machine has a special storage card from the vendor
Each machine is dedicated to storage and does no computing
Only a few big dedicated machines hold all of the disks in the cluster
Every general-purpose machine in the datacenter has some disks attached
optionExplain: the shared-nothing design avoids special hardware on the machines, so no card is needed.
the chapter pictures the same machines also running tasks.
the design spreads the data over the disks of many machines, not a few big ones.
Right: the daemon design assumes disks on each general-purpose machine.
questions.explain: HDFS uses the disks that ordinary machines already have, rather than a separate storage tier.
questions.rule: HDFS uses the disks of ordinary machines.
questions.teaches: The HDFS design assumes that every general-purpose machine in a datacenter has some disks attached.

questions.q: A photo-sharing site wants one logical volume out of the spare disks of 2,000 web servers. Which HDFS idea applies?
options: A single shared Fibre Channel appliance for all servers
A daemon per machine plus a central map of where blocks are stored
Copying the entire volume onto every web server
A central server that stores all of the data itself
optionExplain: that is the shared-disk design with a central appliance, which HDFS avoids.
Right: this is how HDFS builds one big filesystem from many disks.
that wastes space and is not how HDFS spreads blocks.
the NameNode stores the map, not the data.
questions.explain: A daemon on each machine serves local disks, and a NameNode-style server knows where each block is. HDFS also replicates blocks on several machines to tolerate failures.
questions.teaches: In order to tolerate machine and disk failures, HDFS replicates file blocks on multiple machines.

questions.q: A distributed filesystem must survive a machine failure without losing data. What is the basic move?
options: Compress each block so that the disk stops failing
Store redundant data on other machines
Sort the blocks so the failed disk is found sooner
Keep all blocks on the machine with the best disk
optionExplain: compression makes blocks smaller, but a failed disk still takes its blocks with it.
Right: extra copies, or coded pieces, let lost data be recovered.
sorting changes the order of the blocks, but it does not recover any lost data.
a single location is still lost if that machine fails.
questions.explain: Redundancy on other machines is what lets lost blocks be recovered. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Erasure coding schemes such as ____ codes recover lost data with lower storage overhead than full replication.
questions.explain: Reed-Solomon codes are the example the chapter gives of an erasure coding scheme.
questions.rule: Erasure coding saves space compared with full copies.

questions.q: A cold archive of rarely read data costs too much to keep as three full copies. What does the chapter's approach suggest?
options: Keep a single copy on the biggest and most reliable disk
Replace the filesystem with a central storage appliance
Add a write-ahead log to every block of the archive
Use an erasure coding scheme to cut the storage overhead
optionExplain: one copy cannot survive a disk or machine failure.
the chapter contrasts HDFS with appliances because of cost and special hardware.
a log protects writes in a database, not blocks against disk failure.
Right: erasure coding recovers lost data with less overhead than full copies.
questions.explain: Erasure coding gives similar protection for less space, which suits data that is rarely read.
questions.rule: Choose redundancy by what it costs.

questions.q: True or false: RAID and HDFS-style replication both spread redundancy across machines joined by a conventional datacenter network.
questions.explain: RAID provides redundancy across several disks attached to the same machine; in a distributed filesystem, file access and replication happen over a conventional datacenter network without special hardware.
questions.rule: RAID: one machine. HDFS: many machines.

questions.q: What do you lose when erasure coding is used, according to the chapter?
options: The advantage of running a task on the machine that holds the data
The ability to recover from a lost disk
The ability to store files larger than one disk
The ability to use any distributed filesystem, whatever its block size
optionExplain: Right: data from several machines must be combined to reconstitute the file.
recovery from loss is the point of erasure coding.
file size is not the issue; locality is.
the choice of filesystem is not affected by whether erasure coding is used.
questions.explain: With erasure coding, no single machine holds a whole copy of a block, so local reads lose their advantage.
questions.teaches: If erasure coding is used, the locality advantage is lost, because the data from several machines must be combined in order to reconstitute the original file.

questions.q: A video team has network bandwidth as its bottleneck and wants tasks to read their blocks from local disk. Which choice fits better?
options: Erasure coding, so that fewer bytes cross the network
A central appliance, so every read crosses the network
Full copies of blocks, so a machine can hold a whole local copy
Compressed blocks only, so tasks need no original copy
optionExplain: the block must be reassembled from several machines, which uses the network.
that sends more bytes over the network, which is the bottleneck in this case.
Right: a task can be scheduled on a machine that stores a copy of the file.
compression does not place a copy of the block on the machine that runs the task.
questions.explain: Whole local copies allow tasks to read from local disk; coded pieces force reads from several machines.
questions.rule: Copies keep locality; coding saves space.
questions.teaches: Reading from a local disk has a performance advantage if network bandwidth is a bottleneck.

questions.q: In a MapReduce job, which of these steps do you not have to write yourself?
options: The code that extracts a key and value from each record
The code that processes the values collected for each key
Both the mapper and the reducer, since the framework does it all
The sort of the key-value pairs by key
optionExplain: that is the mapper, which you write yourself.
that is the reducer, which you write yourself.
the job is defined by your two callbacks, so the framework cannot write them for you.
Right: the framework sorts the mapper output before the reducer sees it.
questions.explain: Two steps are your custom code and the sort step is implicit in the framework. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: You write map and reduce; the framework sorts.

questions.q: Put the four steps of a MapReduce job in order.
items: Read the input files and break them into records
Call the mapper to extract a key and value from each record
Sort all the key-value pairs by key
Call the reducer to go over the sorted pairs
questions.explain: Records come first, then keys and values, then sorting, then the reduce call that sees equal keys side by side.

questions.q: You want the number of orders per customer from an orders file. What does the mapper emit?
options: The order total as the key, once per order record
The customer ID as the key, once per order record
One line with the total number of order records
The customer ID as the key, once per customer in the file
optionExplain: grouping on totals would count orders with equal totals, not per customer.
Right: sorting then puts each customer's orders together for counting.
the mapper sees one record at a time and cannot see the total.
the mapper runs per order record, so it cannot see customers as a whole.
questions.explain: The key decides what is grouped, so for per-customer counts the key is the customer ID.
questions.rule: The key is what you group by.

questions.q: True or false: In a MapReduce job the programmer writes the mapper, the sort and the reducer.
questions.explain: Steps two and four are custom code; the sort step is implicit, because the mapper output is always sorted before it reaches the reducer.

questions.q: Which part of a MapReduce job breaks the input files into records?
options: The mapper, which splits each file into lines
The reducer, once the sort is finished
The input format parser
The scheduler, when it assigns tasks
optionExplain: the mapper receives records already formed; it does not form them.
the reducer works after the records have been mapped and sorted.
Right: step one is handled by the input format parser.
the scheduler assigns tasks; it does not parse records.
questions.explain: Breaking files into records is handled by the input format parser, so the mapper starts with ready-made records.
questions.rule: A parser produces records for the mapper.
questions.teaches: Step 1, breaking files into records, is handled by the input format parser; steps 2 (map) and 4 (reduce) are where you write custom code.

questions.q: A job counts page views. The mapper emits the URL as key and leaves the value empty. Why is an empty value enough?
options: Counting only needs to see how many times each key appears
The reducer looks up the value in a database
The framework fills the value with a timestamp so the records stay in order
Empty values are required for any sorted data
optionExplain: Right: the reducer counts the records that share a key, like uniq -c.
the reducer works on the values it is given and does not query a database here.
the framework does not invent values; the mapper decides what it emits.
values can carry data; they are empty here only because the count needs none.
questions.explain: In the log example the mapper extracts the URL as key and leaves the value empty, because the reducer only counts how often the key occurs.
questions.rule: Emit only what the reducer needs.
questions.teaches: In the log example the mapper is awk, which extracts the URL ($7) as the key and leaves the value empty; the reducer is uniq -c.

questions.q: A mapper is called for each input record. What may it remember from one record to the next?
options: Nothing: each record is handled independently
The running total of all the records seen so far
The last key it emitted, to avoid repeating it
The records of the same key seen on earlier calls
optionExplain: Right: the mapper keeps no state between records.
a running total is state across records, which the mapper does not keep.
that would also be state carried between records.
grouping by key is the job of the sort and the reducer.
questions.explain: A mapper call sees one record, emits pairs, and forgets everything. The card next shows why.

questions.q: The reducer is called with a key and an ____ over the collection of values that belong to that key.
questions.explain: The reducer gets an iterator over the values and can produce any number of output records.
questions.rule: Reducer input: a key and an iterator.

questions.q: What does a word-count job with the mapper and reducer shown in the card output for the single line a b a?
options: a with 1, b with 1, and a with 1
a with 3, since there are three words
a with 2, and b with 1
b with 1 only, since it appears once
optionExplain: the reducer sums the counts per key, so a appears once with 2.
three is the number of words, not the number of times a occurs.
Right: the mapper emits a, b, a with 1 each, and the reducer sums per word.
a appears twice, so it is not dropped.
questions.explain: The mapper emits one pair per word; sorting groups equal words; the reducer sums each group.
questions.rule: Map emits, sort groups, reduce sums.

questions.q: A mapper needs to drop records whose country field is empty. Is that allowed?
options: No: it must emit one pair for each record it receives
Yes: it may emit no pairs for a record
No: only the reducer is allowed to discard records
Yes, but only after it has seen the whole file
optionExplain: the rule allows a mapper to emit any number of pairs per record, including zero.
Right: the mapper may generate any number of pairs, including none.
the mapper can emit nothing; dropping is not limited to the reducer.
the mapper handles one record at a time and cannot wait for a whole file.
questions.explain: A mapper may emit any number of pairs per input record, so filtering is a natural job for it.
questions.rule: Zero or more outputs per record.

questions.q: True or false: A mapper can compute a running total over all records by keeping a counter between calls.
questions.explain: The mapper keeps no state from one input record to the next, so each record is handled independently.

questions.q: In the chapter's view, what is the role of the mapper compared with the role of the reducer?
options: The mapper sorts the data; the reducer writes the output files
The mapper reads the output of the reducer to fix its mistakes
The mapper and the reducer do the same job on different machines, to share the load evenly
The mapper puts data into a form suitable for sorting; the reducer processes the sorted data
optionExplain: sorting is done by the framework between them.
data flows from mapper to reducer, not back.
they have different roles: one prepares, one processes.
Right: that is how the chapter sums up the two roles.
questions.explain: Mappers prepare data for sorting; reducers process the sorted data.
questions.teaches: Viewed this way, the role of the mapper is to prepare the data by putting it into a form that is suitable for sorting, and the role of the reducer is to process the data that has been sorted.

questions.q: A job to find each user's first purchase date needs memory across records. Where does that logic belong?
options: In the mapper, using a variable that persists between records
In the input format parser, which sees the whole file
In the reducer, with the user ID as the key
In a second sort, run after the reducer has finished
optionExplain: a mapper keeps no state between records, so a variable cannot persist.
the parser breaks files into records and holds no logic of this kind.
Right: the reducer sees all of a key's values together.
the sort is implicit and not where you write the logic.
questions.explain: Anything that depends on several records of one user belongs in the reducer for that user.
questions.rule: Cross-record logic goes in the reducer.
questions.teaches: The reducer function is called once per key with an iterator over all the values for that key, so it sees all the records for a key in one go.

questions.q: A MapReduce job counts page views per URL. What do you need to rank URLs by number of views?
options: A second job that reads the first job's output
A larger reducer that sorts the counts itself in memory
A mapper that remembers the highest count so far
Nothing more, since the first job already ranks the URLs
optionExplain: Right: ranking by count needs a second round of sorting.
a reducer sees one key at a time, so it cannot rank all URLs.
mappers keep no state between records, so they cannot track the highest count.
the first job's output is sorted by URL, not by count.
questions.explain: The first job groups by URL; ranking by count is a new sort over its output. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A new sort key means a new job.

questions.q: In a MapReduce job the sort between the map and reduce steps is ____, so you do not have to write it.
questions.explain: The mapper output is always sorted before it is given to the reducer.

questions.q: You need page views per URL, then the top ten URLs. How many MapReduce jobs does that take?
options: One: the reducer ranks the URLs while it counts them
Three: one for each of mapping, sorting and reducing
Zero: Hadoop provides ranking as a built-in step
Two: one to count per URL, one to rank the counts
optionExplain: a reducer sees one URL at a time and cannot rank all of them.
each job already contains map, sort and reduce.
the framework sorts by key only; ranking needs a job.
Right: the ranking is a second round of sorting.
questions.explain: Counting and ranking need two different sort keys, which means two jobs.
questions.rule: Two sort keys mean two jobs.

questions.q: True or false: One MapReduce job can find the most popular URLs, because its reducer can hold all counts and rank them.
questions.explain: A single job can determine page views per URL but not the most popular URLs, since that requires a second round of sorting.

questions.q: How do the two jobs find each other in Hadoop MapReduce?
options: By a call from the first job to start the second job once it exits
By directory name: the second job reads the directory the first writes
By an index that the NameNode keeps for each job
By a shared memory area between the two jobs
optionExplain: the framework has no workflow support; jobs are independent.
Right: chaining is done implicitly by directory name.
the NameNode tracks the location of blocks, and says nothing about job dependencies.
jobs write to the distributed filesystem, not to shared memory.
questions.explain: The first job writes its output to a designated directory and the second reads that same directory as input.
questions.teaches: Hadoop MapReduce has no particular support for workflows, so chaining is done implicitly by directory name: the first job writes to a designated directory and the second reads it as its input.

questions.q: A team computes revenue per country, then wants the countries ranked by revenue. What is the plan?
options: One job with country as key that also ranks the results
First job groups by country; second job ranks the totals
One job with revenue as key that also sums per country
Two jobs that both group by country with the same code
optionExplain: ranking all the countries needs a second round of sorting, which is a second job.
Right: the second sort is a second job.
revenue as key groups equal revenues, not countries.
the second job needs to sort on revenue, not on country.
questions.explain: Group by country first, then sort the totals; that is two groupings and two jobs.
questions.rule: Map the question to the number of sorts.
questions.teaches: Viewed this way, the output of the first job becomes the input of the second job.

questions.q: In Hadoop MapReduce, what mainly determines how many map tasks a job has?
options: The number of keys the mapper will emit
The number of machines that the scheduler finds free
The number given by the job author in the settings
The number of blocks in the input files
optionExplain: keys are known only after mapping; they cannot decide the task count.
free machines affect where tasks run, not how many exist.
the author configures the number of reduce tasks, not map tasks.
Right: each file or file block is a partition for its own map task.
questions.explain: Map tasks follow the input blocks; reduce tasks are configured by the job author. The card next shows why.

questions.q: In HDFS each input file or file ____ is treated as a separate partition for its own map task.
questions.explain: Partitioning by file block gives each map task its own slice of the input.

questions.q: An input directory holds 400 files, each one block. Roughly how many map tasks does the job have?
options: About 400, one for each block
One, since the job reads a single directory
As many as the job author sets in the configuration
As many as the distinct keys in the input
optionExplain: Right: each block is a partition that gets its own map task.
the directory is split into per-block partitions, each with its own map task.
the author sets the number of reduce tasks, not map tasks.
keys are only produced later, by the mappers.
questions.explain: 400 one-block files give 400 partitions and so about 400 map tasks.

questions.q: True or false: The job author sets the number of map tasks, as the number of reduce tasks.
questions.explain: The number of map tasks is determined by the number of input file blocks, whereas the number of reduce tasks is configured by the job author.
questions.rule: Map: by blocks. Reduce: by author.

questions.q: How large is a typical input file in this setting, according to the chapter?
options: A few kilobytes
Tens of gigabytes
Hundreds of megabytes
Exactly one record
optionExplain: the chapter describes large files, not tiny ones.
that is larger than the files the chapter describes.
Right: typical input files are hundreds of megabytes in size.
files hold many records, and a typical file is far larger than that.
questions.explain: Large inputs are cut into big blocks, so each map task handles a substantial slice.
questions.teaches: Each input file is typically hundreds of megabytes in size.

questions.q: A team splits its input into thousands of tiny files instead of a few big ones. What does that do to the job?
options: It reduces the number of map tasks to one per directory
It lowers the number of reduce tasks automatically
It has no effect on tasks, since only key counts matter
It creates many tiny map tasks
optionExplain: the partition unit is the file or block, not the directory.
reduce tasks are set by the author, not by input layout.
the layout of the input directly sets the map task count.
Right: each file or block is a partition with its own map task.
questions.explain: Many tiny inputs mean many small map tasks, because tasks follow files and blocks.
questions.teaches: The MapReduce scheduler tries to run each mapper on one of the machines that stores a replica of its input file.

questions.q: A mapper needs 500 MB of input stored on several machines. Where does MapReduce prefer to run it?
options: On the machine with the most free disk space
On a machine that stores a replica of that input
On a random machine, then copy the input to it
On the NameNode, which knows where every block is
optionExplain: free disk space is unrelated to where the input is.
Right: that avoids copying the input over the network.
copying a large input is what the scheduler tries to avoid.
the NameNode keeps metadata and does not run the mappers.
questions.explain: Running next to a replica avoids moving the big input across the network. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Running a task on the machine that stores its input is known as putting the computation near the ____.
questions.explain: This principle reduces network load and increases locality.

questions.q: A 2 GB dataset sits on three machines, and the job code is 5 MB. What should the scheduler move?
options: The 2 GB of data to the machine that holds the code
Both code and data to a new, empty machine
The 5 MB of code to a machine holding a replica
Neither, and run the code over the network
optionExplain: moving the big data is exactly what locality avoids.
this moves the large data as well, for no benefit, which defeats the locality principle.
Right: moving code is cheaper than moving data.
a remote read is still network traffic for all of the input.
questions.explain: Small code goes to the large data, which keeps network traffic low.

questions.q: True or false: The scheduler runs a mapper beside its input replica even when that machine has no spare RAM or CPU.
questions.explain: The scheduler tries to do so only if the machine has enough spare RAM and CPU resources to run the map task.

questions.q: What must the framework do before a map task can start on its machine?
options: Copy the application code, such as JAR files, to that machine
Copy the input file from HDFS to the NameNode
Wait until all reducers have started their work
Sort the input file so the mapper can read it in order
optionExplain: Right: the code is usually not yet present on the machine.
the input stays on the machine that holds its replica; only the code is moved.
mappers run first; reducers fetch their output later.
the sort comes after the map step, not before it.
questions.explain: The code is usually not there yet, so the framework ships it to the machine.
questions.teaches: In most cases the application code is not yet present on the machine assigned to run a map task, so the framework first copies the code (for example JAR files) to that machine.

questions.q: A team runs compute in one cluster and stores data in a separate object store. What do they lose compared with HDFS?
options: The chance to run tasks on the machine that holds the data
The ability to store data as files
The ability to run any code at all
Any form of fault tolerance for the stored data
optionExplain: Right: storage and computation are separate, so locality is lost.
object stores store data too; the loss is about locality.
code can still run; it simply runs apart from the data.
fault tolerance comes from other mechanisms and is separate from the question of locality.
questions.explain: Locality needs compute on the storage machines; separate storage removes that option.
questions.teaches: Reading from a local disk has a performance advantage if network bandwidth is a bottleneck.

questions.q: Mappers on different machines emit pairs for the same key. How do all of them reach one reducer?
options: Each mapper sends its pairs to the first reducer
The reducers ask every mapper at random for pairs
The framework hashes the key to choose the reduce task
A central server merges all pairs before the reduce step
optionExplain: that would overload one reducer and ignore the partitioning.
random fetching would not keep equal keys together.
Right: equal keys have equal hashes, so they go to the same reducer.
no central server merges everything; reducers fetch their own partitions.
questions.explain: A hash of the key picks the reducer, the same way for every mapper. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Same key, same hash, same reducer.

questions.q: The number of reduce tasks is configured by the job ____.
questions.explain: The reduce count is the author's choice and can differ from the number of map tasks.
questions.rule: Reduce tasks are configured by the author.

questions.q: A job has 12 map tasks and the author sets 5 reduce tasks. What decides which of the 5 gets the key apple?
options: The map task that first emitted apple
A hash of the key apple
The order in which the reducers started
The size of the file the key came from
optionExplain: if each mapper chose its own reducer, equal keys would be split.
Right: the hash maps the key to one of the 5 reduce tasks.
start order does not keep equal keys together.
file size is not used to pick a reducer.
questions.explain: The same hash function sends apple to the same reducer from every mapper.
questions.rule: The key's hash picks the reducer.

questions.q: True or false: With 3 reducers and 40 map tasks, all pairs of one key still go to one of the 3 reducers.
questions.explain: The number of reduce tasks is configured by the author and can differ from the number of map tasks; the key hash still picks one reducer per key.
questions.rule: Equal keys go to one reducer, whatever the count.

questions.q: Which earlier idea about partitioning does the chapter point to for hashing by key?
options: Write-ahead logs, from the chapter on storage
Quorum reads, from the chapter on replication
Two-phase commit, from the chapter on transactions
Partitioning by hash of key, from the chapter on partitioning
optionExplain: logs concern durability of writes in a database, and have nothing to do with partitioning.
quorums concern how many replicas must agree, and not the partitioning of keys.
two-phase commit concerns atomic commits across nodes, and not the choice of reducer.
Right: the chapter refers back to partitioning by hash of key.
questions.explain: Choosing a reducer by key hash is the same idea as partitioning a database by hash of key.
questions.rule: Reduce partitions work like hash partitions.
questions.teaches: To choose the reducer the framework uses a hash of the key, as in partitioning by hash of key from the chapter on partitioning.

questions.q: One reducer is overloaded because one key has 60 percent of all records. Does hashing the key help?
options: Yes: the hash splits that key evenly across all reducers
Yes: more map tasks make the hash spread each key out
No: all records of that key still land on one reducer
No: the framework ignores the hash for frequent keys
optionExplain: equal keys have equal hashes, so they stay together.
map task count does not change where a key goes.
Right: hashing balances keys, not the number of records per key.
the framework applies the hash to every key alike.
questions.explain: A hot key stays whole by design; spreading it needs a special technique, not plain hashing.
questions.rule: Hash partitioning cannot split one key.
questions.teaches: Collecting all the activity related to a very popular key in a single reducer leads to skew, so a MapReduce job is only complete when the slowest reducer has completed.

questions.q: A job's key-value pairs are too many to sort on a single machine. What does MapReduce do?
options: Sort in stages: each mapper sorts its own output and reducers merge
Send all the pairs to the one machine with the most RAM and sort them there
Skip the sort and let reducers search for equal keys
Sort each pair as it arrives at a central server
optionExplain: Right: partial sorted files are merged into the final order.
that machine would be a bottleneck and the data may not fit.
without sorting, equal keys would not be adjacent for the reducer.
a central server would have the same size problem.
questions.explain: Sorted pieces from mappers are merged by reducers; no machine has to sort everything. The card next shows why.

questions.q: The process of partitioning by reducer, sorting, and copying data partitions from mappers to reducers is known as the ____.
questions.explain: The chapter calls it a confusing term, as unlike shuffling cards there is no randomness.

questions.q: Put these events of the shuffle in the order they happen.
items: A map task partitions its output by reducer using the key hash
Each partition is written to a sorted file on the mapper's local disk
The mapper finishes and the scheduler notifies the reducers
Reducers download the sorted files for their partition
Each reducer merges the files, keeping the sort order
questions.explain: The sorting happens on the map side first; reducers pull the sorted files and then merge them.
questions.rule: Partition and sort at the mapper, then pull and merge.

questions.q: True or false: In the shuffle, the key-value pairs are randomly assigned to reducers, like cards in a shuffled deck.
questions.explain: The partitioning is based on the hash of the key, which is deterministic; the chapter calls the name confusing because there is no randomness in MapReduce.

questions.q: What does a reducer do with the sorted files it fetches from different mappers?
options: It sorts them again from scratch in memory
It discards all but the first mapper's file and rereads the input instead
It writes them back to the mappers' disks
It merges them together while preserving the sort order
optionExplain: the files are already sorted, so merging suffices.
all files are needed to see every value for a key.
reducers read the files and do not write them back.
Right: records with the same key from different mappers become adjacent.
questions.explain: Merging preserves the order, so equal keys from different mappers end up next to each other.
questions.rule: Reducers merge; they do not re-sort.
questions.teaches: The reduce task takes the files from the mappers and merges them together, preserving the sort order, so records with the same key produced by different mappers are adjacent in the merged reducer input.

questions.q: A reducer starts before every mapper has finished. Can it begin fetching immediately?
options: No: it must wait for all mappers to finish first
It can fetch from each mapper that has finished its sorted files
Yes, and it can read the unfinished mappers' partial files
No: reducers only start when the sort is complete everywhere
optionExplain: reducers may start downloading from finished mappers earlier.
Right: the scheduler notifies reducers as each mapper finishes.
the files are fetched after a mapper finishes writing its sorted output.
the sort is staged; reducers download as mappers finish.
questions.explain: The scheduler notifies reducers per mapper, so downloads overlap with the map phase.
questions.rule: Fetching can start as mappers finish.
questions.teaches: Whenever a mapper finishes reading its input file and writing its sorted output files, the MapReduce scheduler notifies the reducers that they can start fetching the output files from that mapper.

questions.q: Two MapReduce jobs must run one after the other, the second using the first's results. How does Hadoop connect them?
options: Through a pipe that connects the two running jobs
Through a directory in HDFS that one writes and the other reads
Through a workflow engine that is part of Hadoop MapReduce
Through a shared hash table in the memory of the cluster
optionExplain: jobs are not connected by a pipe; they are independent.
Right: the chain is made implicitly by directory name.
the framework has no particular support for workflows.
jobs exchange data through files on the distributed filesystem.
questions.explain: The framework sees two independent jobs; the chain is a directory name both agree on. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Chained MapReduce jobs resemble commands that write their output to a ____ file for the next command to read.
questions.explain: Chained jobs are like commands whose output goes to a temporary file, not like a pipe with a small buffer.
questions.rule: Chained jobs: temporary files, not pipes.

questions.q: Job A writes to /out/clicks and job B reads /out/clicks. What does the framework know about their relation?
options: That B depends on A, so it starts B when A finishes
That A and B form one workflow with one shared plan
That B may start while A is still running
Nothing: they are two independent jobs
optionExplain: the framework does not understand this dependency; it sees two independent jobs.
the framework has no notion of a workflow here.
the framework does not manage this at all; a scheduler does.
Right: the dependency exists only in the directory names.
questions.explain: From the framework's view A and B are independent; a scheduler outside has to order them.

questions.q: True or false: Chained MapReduce jobs pass data through a small in-memory buffer, like a Unix pipe.
questions.explain: Chained jobs write full output to the distributed filesystem and the next job reads it, more like a sequence of commands using temporary files.
questions.rule: Chained jobs write files, not pipes.

questions.q: What question does the chapter postpone about this design?
options: Its advantages and disadvantages, under materialization of intermediate state
Whether workflow tools can run without a filesystem
Whether Hadoop's workflows can be written in Java instead of in a scripting language
Whether Unix pipes can ever carry MapReduce output between two jobs on a cluster
optionExplain: Right: a later section discusses the trade-offs of writing intermediate state to files.
the chapter does not raise that question; its postponed discussion is about the cost of files.
the programming language is not the question that the chapter postpones.
the later section is about files versus streaming of intermediate data.
questions.explain: Writing everything out to files has benefits and costs, which are examined when materialization is discussed.
questions.teaches: The chapter discusses the advantages and disadvantages of passing data between jobs through files in the section on materialization of intermediate state.

questions.q: A nightly ETL has five stages, each writing a folder that the next reads. What is the main thing keeping them in order?
options: Hadoop itself, which tracks the dependencies between jobs
The NameNode, which orders jobs by the folder they write to
An outside scheduler or the folder names, since the jobs are independent
The reducers, which start the next job when they finish
optionExplain: the chapter says it has no particular support for workflows.
the NameNode tracks the location of blocks, and does not order or launch any jobs.
Right: the framework does not know the stages belong together.
reducers write outputs; they do not launch jobs.
questions.explain: Independent jobs need something external to order them; the next idea looks at such schedulers.
questions.rule: Order comes from outside the framework.
questions.teaches: One job in a workflow can only start when the prior jobs that produce its input directories have completed successfully.

questions.q: A batch job crashes halfway through. What happens to its partial output in MapReduce?
options: It is kept so the next job can use what exists
It is merged into the output of the next run
It is sent to the reducers for a second attempt
It is discarded, since output is valid only after success
optionExplain: using partial output would feed incomplete data downstream.
the partial results are discarded when the job fails, and are not merged into any later run.
reducers do not take over partial output; a failed job simply produces nothing.
Right: partial output of a failed job is thrown away.
questions.explain: Only a successfully completed job produces valid output. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Output is valid only after success.

questions.q: Workflow schedulers for Hadoop include Oozie, Azkaban, Luigi, ____ and Pinball.
questions.explain: Airflow is the fourth scheduler in the chapter's list.

questions.q: Job C reads the outputs of jobs A and B. When may C start?
options: As soon as A or B has written its first file
After both A and B have completed successfully
At the same time as A and B, to save time
Right after A finishes, even if B has failed
optionExplain: partial output is not yet valid, so a job reading it could see incomplete data.
Right: its input directories must be complete and valid.
C needs their complete outputs to be present.
B's missing output would make C's input incomplete.
questions.explain: A job can start only when the jobs producing its inputs have all completed successfully.

questions.q: True or false: A Hadoop job may start while the jobs producing its input are still running, since data arrives incrementally.
questions.explain: Because a batch job's output is valid only after success, a job can start only when the prior jobs have completed successfully.

questions.q: How large can workflows get, according to the chapter?
options: Fewer than five jobs, because of the limits of Hadoop
Hundreds of thousands of jobs per recommendation list
50 to 100 MapReduce jobs are common when building recommendation systems
Exactly one job per team in an organization, regardless of the products it builds
optionExplain: the chapter cites far larger workflows, so a limit of five jobs is not accurate.
the figure given is 50 to 100 jobs.
Right: workflows of 50 to 100 MapReduce jobs are common for recommendation systems.
the chapter says different teams may run many jobs that read each other's output.
questions.explain: Recommendation-system workflows commonly chain 50 to 100 jobs, which is why tool support matters.
questions.teaches: Workflows consisting of 50 to 100 MapReduce jobs are common when building recommendation systems, and many teams in a large organization may run jobs that read each other's output.

questions.q: A company has three teams whose nightly jobs read each other's outputs. What is the main reason to adopt a scheduler?
options: To manage dependencies and maintain a large collection of jobs
To make each individual job run faster on the cluster
To avoid writing any output files to HDFS
To let jobs share state in memory across the teams
optionExplain: Right: schedulers have management features for large collections of jobs.
scheduling dependencies does not speed up a single job.
output still goes to the distributed filesystem, as for every other MapReduce job.
jobs stay independent from each other, and they share only files in the filesystem.
questions.explain: With many jobs and teams, dependencies and management become the problem a scheduler solves.
questions.teaches: Higher-level tools such as Pig, Hive, Cascading, Crunch and FlumeJava also set up workflows of multiple MapReduce stages that are automatically wired together appropriately.

questions.q: Which task is a poor fit for a full scan of all the data?
options: Fetching the profile of one user by ID
Averaging order totals across all 80 million customers
Counting page views for every URL in a year of logs
Grouping all activity events by the user who made them
optionExplain: Right: an index finds a single record far faster than a scan.
aggregating over many records is what scans are good for, especially in parallel.
counting over a whole log needs every record, so a full scan is reasonable.
grouping touches every event, so scanning all of them is expected.
questions.explain: Scans pay off when you need a large share of the records; for one record an index wins. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Scan for aggregates, index for lookups.

questions.q: When a MapReduce job reads the entire content of its input files, a database would call this a full ____ scan.
questions.explain: Reading all the input is a full table scan, which is costly for a few records but reasonable for large aggregates.
questions.rule: MapReduce has no indexes: it scans.

questions.q: A retailer wants the average age of buyers for every product in a year of data. Is a full scan sensible?
options: No: any query without an index lookup is a poor design
No: a scan cannot be spread over several machines
Yes: it needs a large share of all records, and scans parallelize
Yes, but only if each product has its own file
optionExplain: an index only helps when few records are wanted, which is not the case here.
the chapter says processing can be parallelized across machines.
Right: analytic aggregates over many records suit a parallel scan.
the layout of the files is not what makes a scan reasonable.
questions.explain: Aggregating over many records makes reading everything reasonable, and parallelism helps.

questions.q: True or false: In batch processing a join looks up the data of one particular user, as an index would.
questions.explain: A batch join resolves all occurrences of an association, processing the data of all users at once; one user would be served better by an index.
questions.rule: Batch join: all records at once.

questions.q: Does denormalization remove the need for joins?
options: Yes: a denormalized dataset needs no join at all
Not entirely: it reduces the need for joins but generally cannot remove it
No: it makes joins more frequent because data is duplicated
Yes, but only for graph data and document references that point to other records
optionExplain: the chapter says it only reduces the need.
Right: the chapter says denormalization generally does not remove joins entirely.
denormalization reduces the need for joins, not increases it.
the chapter does not limit its claim to those models.
questions.explain: Copying data into records helps, yet some associations still need a join.
questions.rule: Denormalization reduces joins but does not remove them.
questions.teaches: Denormalization can reduce the need for joins but generally not remove it entirely.

questions.q: The joins in this chapter match records that share an identical value in some field. What are they called?
options: Range joins, which match records by a less-than test
Outer joins, which keep records with no match
Graph joins, which follow edges until a result converges
Equi-joins, the most common type of join
optionExplain: the chapter says it does not cover such general joins.
the chapter does not discuss this type.
the transitive closure example comes later and is not what is meant here.
Right: records are associated by equal values in a field such as an ID.
questions.explain: The chapter's joins are equi-joins; some databases support more general conditions, which it does not cover.
questions.rule: Equal field values define an equi-join.
questions.teaches: The joins in the book are generally equi-joins, in which a record is associated with other records that have an identical value in a particular field such as an ID.

questions.q: A batch job must look up a user profile for each of two billion events. What limits a per-event remote lookup?
options: The sorting of the events by user ID
The number of columns in the user table
The round-trip time to the database server
The size of the output file written at the end
optionExplain: no sorting is involved in a per-event lookup.
column count does not limit lookup throughput.
Right: each lookup waits for a network round trip, which caps throughput.
output size is not the limit on the lookup design.
questions.explain: A remote database call per record makes round trips the bottleneck. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Which problems does the chapter name for querying a remote user database once per event? Select all that apply.
options: Throughput is limited by round-trip time
A local cache may help only as far as the data distribution allows
Many parallel queries can overwhelm the database
The remote database cannot return a date of birth
Events must be sorted before any lookup can start
optionExplain: Right: every lookup waits for a network round trip.
Right: its effectiveness depends on the distribution of the data.
Right: a large number of parallel queries could easily overwhelm it.
it can; the problem is performance, not capability.
no sort is needed for per-event lookups.
questions.explain: Round-trip limits, cache dependence on data distribution and overload of the database are the three named problems.

questions.q: A job makes 5 billion remote lookups at 1 millisecond each. Roughly how long does one thread need?
options: About 58 days, which is far too long
About 83 minutes, which is acceptable
About 5 seconds, since lookups run in memory
About 58 hours, which a cluster can absorb
optionExplain: Right: 5 billion times 1 millisecond is 5 million seconds, about 58 days.
that would be 5 million milliseconds, but the unit conversion gives far more.
a remote lookup is not an in-memory operation, so the calculation does not hold.
5 million seconds is 58 days, not hours.
questions.explain: At one millisecond per remote lookup, 5 billion lookups need 5 million seconds, which is about 58 days on one thread.

questions.q: True or false: The main objection to per-event lookups is that the user database might change during the job.
questions.explain: Change during the job is one problem, but the main objection is performance: round trips limit throughput and parallel queries can overload the database.

questions.q: Besides speed, what other property does a remote lookup take away from a batch job?
options: Fault tolerance, since the remote database cannot be retried
Parallelism, since the database serves one query at a time
Security, since the lookups are sent in plain text
Determinism, since the remote data might change between reads
optionExplain: the chapter's point is that the contents may change, not that retries are impossible.
the chapter says many parallel queries can overwhelm the database.
the chapter makes no claim about security here.
Right: the job becomes nondeterministic, because remote data can change between reads.
questions.explain: A job that reads live data may produce different results on two runs.
questions.rule: Remote reads make results depend on when you ask.
questions.teaches: Querying a remote database would make the batch job nondeterministic, because the data in the remote database might change.

questions.q: A fraud job must compare 300 million card transactions with a customer risk table. What does the chapter's reasoning favour?
options: A remote call to the risk service for each transaction
A copy of the risk table placed next to the transactions
A cache with the 10,000 most frequent customers only
An index on the transactions, queried by customer ID
optionExplain: that repeats the per-record network lookup the chapter warns against.
Right: the job then reads both sides locally.
a cache helps only as far as the data distribution allows.
an index serves lookups of few records, not a pass over everything.
questions.explain: Computation should be local to a machine; copy the small side of the join to where the big side lives.
questions.rule: Bring the data to the computation.
questions.teaches: In order to achieve good throughput in a batch process, the computation must be, as much as possible, local to one machine.

questions.q: A batch job must join log files with database data. What is a better plan than querying per record?
options: Cache every query result in the memory of the database server
Copy the database content into the same filesystem as the logs
Move the log files into the database and run a normal query
Lower the number of events by sampling a few of them
optionExplain: the database would still be asked for each record the cache has not yet seen.
Right: both inputs are then local files for the job.
the chapter's approach moves the database content, not the large logs.
sampling changes the answer, and does not solve the join.
questions.explain: Put both sides in the filesystem, and let the batch job bring related records together. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Bring both inputs to one place.

questions.q: The user database copy is placed in the same ____ filesystem as the activity events.
questions.explain: Both datasets sit in the distributed filesystem, as sets of files.

questions.q: A shop wants to join 3 TB of click logs with its 50 GB product catalogue stored in a database. What do you do first?
options: Query the catalogue database for each click
Delete the catalogue and keep only the logs
Index the click logs by product with a database
Export the catalogue into files beside the click logs
optionExplain: that repeats the per-record lookup problem.
the join needs the catalogue data.
indexing the huge logs is the reverse of the chapter's plan.
Right: then the join runs on local files in the batch framework.
questions.explain: Export the smaller reference data and place it next to the big log so the join is local.

questions.q: True or false: Copying the user database into HDFS makes the job depend on the live database for every record, as before.
questions.explain: Once the copy is in the filesystem, the job reads only files and never queries the live database during the join.
questions.rule: A copy removes the live dependency.

questions.q: How does the chapter suggest getting the copy of the user database?
options: Extract it from a database backup with an ETL process
Query the live database record by record at night
Rebuild it from the events in the activity log
Ask every user to upload their profile again
optionExplain: Right: ETL from a backup avoids loading the live database.
that is the per-record lookup the approach avoids.
the events do not hold the full user profile.
the chapter proposes no such step.
questions.explain: An ETL process can extract the user data from a backup, which spares the production database.
questions.rule: Use an ETL extract of the data.
questions.teaches: The copy of the user database can be extracted from a database backup using an ETL process.

questions.q: Reports run on a 6 TB event log joined with a profile table that changes hourly. What do reports built on the copy show?
options: Profiles as they are now, updated while the job runs
Profiles that contradict each other inside one report
Profiles as they were when the copy was taken
Profiles from the live database, with a delay of a second
optionExplain: the copy does not follow the live database.
one copy gives the job one consistent view during the run.
Right: a copy is a snapshot, and later changes are not seen.
the job reads only the copy, so there is no live read at all.
questions.explain: A copy gives a consistent view, but only of the moment it was taken, which is a gain for repeatable results.
questions.rule: A copy fixes the data for the run.
questions.teaches: The input data of a batch job is a fixed snapshot, such as a set of log files at some point in time or a snapshot of a database's contents, so a job has a known, fixed size.

questions.q: Two datasets must be joined on user ID in MapReduce. What do the mappers of both datasets emit?
options: The record as the key, with the user ID as the value
The date of birth as the key, with the event as the value
A random number as the key, with the record as the value
The user ID as the key, with the record as the value
optionExplain: keys decide where records meet, so the record as key would not group by user.
this would group by birth date, not by user.
random keys scatter related records to different reducers.
Right: equal keys then reach the same reducer and sit next to each other.
questions.explain: The shared key is the user ID; the shuffle then brings matching records together. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Emit the join key from every input.

questions.q: This join is called a sort-merge join because the mapper output is sorted by key and the reducers ____ the sorted lists from both sides.
questions.explain: The reducers merge together the sorted lists of records from both sides of the join.

questions.q: Join orders (order ID, customer ID) with customers (customer ID, city) to count orders per city. What is the mapper key for both?
options: The order ID
The customer ID
The city
The order total
optionExplain: customers have no order ID, so they could not be matched.
Right: both datasets share it, so matching rows meet in one reducer call.
orders have no city field before the join.
totals do not link orders to customers.
questions.explain: The customer ID is the only field both inputs share, so it is the join key.
questions.rule: Join on the field both sides share.

questions.q: In one reducer call for user 7, the profile record arrives first, then three events. How many output pairs does the reducer emit?
options: One: the profile combined into a single record
Four: three events and one profile record
Three: one for each event, using the stored profile
None: output is created by the mappers
optionExplain: the reducer emits one result per event, not one per user.
the profile is data to join with, not a result row.
Right: the reducer joins the stored birth date with every event.
the reducer performs the join and emits the results.
questions.explain: The reducer stores the date of birth in a local variable and emits a pair for each event.

questions.q: True or false: In the sort-merge join the reducer keeps only one user record in memory at any one time.
questions.explain: Since the reducer processes all the records for a user ID in one go, it holds that user's record and streams the events, with no network requests.
questions.rule: Low memory and no network calls.
questions.teaches: Since the reducer processes all the records for a particular user ID in one go, it only needs to keep one user record in memory at any one time, and it never needs to make any requests over the network.

questions.q: A team joins support tickets with product records on product ID. Which cost grows with the size of both inputs?
options: The sorting, copying and merging between mappers and reducers
The memory used by each reducer for the whole product table
The number of network requests to a product database
The time to write the mapper code for each new record
optionExplain: Right: the data of both sides goes through the whole shuffle.
a reducer holds only one key's records at a time.
the join makes no network requests to a database.
the code does not change with data size.
questions.explain: The reduce-side join needs no assumptions, at the price of sorting and moving all the data.
questions.rule: Reduce-side joins cost a full shuffle.
questions.teaches: The reduce-side approach has the advantage of needing no assumptions about the input data, but the sorting, copying to reducers and merging of reducer inputs can be quite expensive.

questions.q: In a join reducer, the user's profile must come before that user's events. What guarantees this?
options: A sort order that places the profile record first within the key
The mapper reading the user file before the events file
The reducer asking the NameNode which record is first
The events being sorted by user name instead of ID
optionExplain: Right: the framework can arrange values inside each key.
mappers run in parallel and the shuffle merges their outputs, so reading order does not carry over.
the NameNode tracks blocks and does not order records.
the order inside a key is not set by the name of the user.
questions.explain: A secondary sort puts the profile first among the values for each key. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Control the order within a key.

questions.q: The technique of arranging values within a key so that a given record comes first is known as a ____ sort.
questions.explain: A secondary sort lets the reducer see the user database record first.
questions.rule: Secondary sort orders values inside a key.

questions.q: A reducer must emit each order line with the order header's customer name. Which arrangement helps?
options: The lines first, then the header record last
Lines and header sorted into a random order
The header record first, then the lines for that order
Each line sent to its own separate reducer
optionExplain: the reducer would have to hold all the lines until the header arrives.
random order forces the reducer to buffer records.
Right: the reducer remembers the name and streams the lines.
that separates the lines from the header they need.
questions.explain: With the header first, the reducer stores one value and processes the lines one by one.

questions.q: True or false: A secondary sort sends the user record and the user's events to different reducers.
questions.explain: A secondary sort only orders the values within a key; the user record and its events still reach the same reducer.
questions.rule: Order within a key, not across reducers.

questions.q: The join outputs pairs of viewed URL and viewer age. What can later jobs do with them?
options: Recover the full user profile of every viewer
Work out the distribution of viewer ages for each URL
Re-run the join without the user database copy
Decide which reducer receives each user's events
optionExplain: only the age and URL are in the pairs, not the profile.
Right: the pairs feed further jobs that group by URL and by age group.
the user data is needed for the join, so the join cannot be rerun without it.
the reducer choice is made earlier, by the key hash, not by later jobs.
questions.explain: The output pairs are input to subsequent jobs, which can compute age distributions for each URL.
questions.teaches: Subsequent MapReduce jobs could then calculate the distribution of viewer ages for each URL, and cluster by age group.

questions.q: A reducer for a bank account must see the opening balance, then the day's transactions in time order. Which tool fits?
options: A second MapReduce job that sorts the balances alone
A random partition of transactions across all reducers, followed by a final sort of every balance
A broadcast of every transaction to all reducers
A secondary sort with the balance record first and transactions by time
optionExplain: that would separate the balance from the transactions.
this scatters the transactions of one account.
the chapter uses broadcast for small inputs in map-side joins, not here.
Right: this is the same pattern as the profile and its events.
questions.explain: A reference record first, then events in time order, is a secondary sort.
questions.teaches: The secondary sort lets the reducer keep the date of birth in a local variable and then iterate over the activity events with the same user ID, outputting pairs of viewed URL and viewer age in years.

questions.q: Mappers emit pairs, and equal keys reach the same reducer call. What does the key behave like?
options: A password that protects the value from other tasks
A timestamp that orders the values in time
A destination address for the value
A summary of what the value contains
optionExplain: keys do not protect anything; they route.
ordering by time is the job of a secondary sort.
Right: all values with the same key are delivered to the same place.
a key need not summarise the value; it only routes.
questions.explain: The key decides which reducer call the value is delivered to. The card next shows why.

questions.q: When a mapper emits a key-value pair, the ____ acts like the destination address to which the value should be delivered.
questions.explain: The key is an arbitrary string, yet it behaves as an address.

questions.q: You want each customer's complaints and orders to meet in one place. What should both mappers use as the key?
options: The customer ID
The complaint or order text itself
The date of the record
A fresh random number per record
optionExplain: Right: all records with the same customer ID reach one reducer call.
the text differs per record, so related ones would not meet.
records of one customer on different dates would be sent to different places.
random keys scatter the related records to different reducers.
questions.explain: Choose the key so that the records that must be processed together share it.

questions.q: How does a MapReduce job differ from a typical application that fetches related data from a database?
options: It queries the database more often, once for every key
It reads related data from the same machine without a network
It stores related data inside the mapper's memory and looks the key up there
Data is routed to the code by keys, instead of the code querying inside its logic
optionExplain: the job makes no queries to a database during the join.
records move between machines in the shuffle.
mappers keep no state between records.
Right: network communication is separated from the application logic.
questions.explain: In MapReduce the framework moves the data, so application code does not make requests deep inside its logic.
questions.rule: The framework handles the data movement.
questions.hint: Who is responsible for getting the data to the right machine?
