questions.q: True or false: When a task crashes during the job, the framework transparently retries it without affecting the application logic.
questions.explain: Since MapReduce handles all network communication, it shields the application code from partial failures such as the crash of another node.
questions.teaches: Since MapReduce handles all network communication, it shields the application code from partial failures, such as the crash of another node, by transparently retrying failed tasks without affecting the application logic.

questions.q: A developer separates routing from computation in a feed service. Which MapReduce idea matches?
options: The reducer decides the destination of each record itself
Keys set the destination, and the reducer holds the computation
The framework decides the computation for each key
Mappers hold the computation and reducers the routing
optionExplain: the key decides destinations; the reducer works after delivery.
Right: this is the separation of routing from logic.
the user code defines the computation.
this reverses the roles of mappers and reducers.
questions.explain: Keys do the routing, and the reducer code is the computation; the two are separated.
questions.rule: Routing by key, logic in code.
questions.teaches: This separation contrasts with the typical use of databases, where a request to fetch data from a database often occurs somewhere deep inside a piece of application code.

questions.q: To compute the total spend per customer in MapReduce, what do you use as the mapper's key?
options: The spend amount
The customer ID
The order date
The name of the reducer
optionExplain: keying by amount groups equal amounts, not customers.
Right: grouping is done by making the grouping field the key.
keying by date groups orders by day, not customer.
keys are data fields, not names of tasks.
questions.explain: Grouping uses the grouping field as the key, so each customer's orders meet in one reducer call. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Match each SQL-style aggregation to what the reducer does.
pairs: Count the records in the group
Add up one field across the group
Pick the k best records by a ranking function
questions.explain: These are the three examples of aggregation within a group that the chapter lists.
questions.rule: Count, sum and top k within a group.

questions.q: Find the three most expensive orders per customer from an orders file. What does the reducer receive and do?
options: One order at a time, and it keeps the cheapest of each
All orders of all customers, and it ranks them together
The customer name only, and it looks the orders up
All orders for one customer, and it keeps the top three by price
optionExplain: the reducer receives all values for a key, not one order.
a reducer sees one key's values per call.
the reducer needs the order values, which arrive with the key.
Right: the reducer picks the top k within the group.
questions.explain: After the shuffle, one reducer call holds a customer's orders and can rank them.
questions.rule: Group, then rank within the group.

questions.q: True or false: Grouping with MapReduce needs a different mechanism from joining, because the framework treats the two as unrelated.
questions.explain: Grouping and joining look quite similar on MapReduce: both rely on partitioning and sorting to bring related records to the same reducer.

questions.q: What does the chapter call the collating of all activity events for a particular user session?
options: Sessionization
Normalization
Serialization
Materialization
optionExplain: Right: events for a session are gathered by a key such as a session cookie.
normalization is a schema design idea.
serialization turns data into bytes, which is unrelated to gathering a session.
materialization writes out intermediate state, which is unrelated to gathering a session.
questions.explain: Gathering a user's events together, to see the sequence of actions, is sessionization.
questions.teaches: Collating all the activity events for a particular user session, to find the sequence of actions, is called sessionization.

questions.q: A streaming service wants watch minutes per country from a viewing log. Which design is right?
options: Mapper emits minutes as key and country as value; reducer counts
Mapper sums minutes in memory across all records
Mapper emits country as key and minutes as value; reducer sums
Reducer joins each viewing record with a country table
optionExplain: keying by minutes groups equal minutes, not countries.
mappers keep no state between records.
Right: grouping by country and summing within the group.
no join is needed: the log already holds the country.
questions.explain: Make the grouping field the key and sum the values in each group.
questions.rule: Group by key, aggregate in the reducer.
questions.teaches: Grouping and joining look quite similar when implemented on top of MapReduce, since both bring records with the same key to the same reducer.

questions.q: A user's page views are spread over logs from five web servers. What do you group by to rebuild their session?
options: The server that handled the request
The URL of the page requested
The time of day of the request
A user ID or session cookie
optionExplain: that splits one user's events across servers, the opposite of what you want.
that groups by page, not by user.
time of day mixes the events of many users.
Right: it identifies one user's events wherever they were logged.
questions.explain: An identifier of the user or session keys all their events together. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Collating all the activity events of one user session to find the sequence of actions is called ____.
questions.explain: Sessionization groups events by a session identifier.

questions.q: A shop wants the click sequence of each visitor. Which key should the mapper emit?
options: The product ID of the clicked item
The session cookie of the visitor
The IP address of the web server
The HTTP status of the response
optionExplain: that groups clicks by product, not by visitor.
Right: it brings each visitor's events to one reducer.
server addresses split visitors across servers.
status codes group unrelated visitors together.
questions.explain: The key must identify the visitor so that the reducer sees the whole sequence.

questions.q: True or false: After sessionization by user ID, all events of user A reach one reducer call, even if they were logged on five servers.
questions.explain: All events with the same key are delivered to the same destination, which is one call to the reducer.

questions.q: What example use of sessionization does the chapter give?
options: Choosing which disks to replicate in a cluster
Finding the shortest path between two web pages
Testing whether a new website version leads to more purchases (A/B testing)
Counting the bytes written by each reducer
optionExplain: replication placement is unrelated to sessions.
that is a graph algorithm, not sessionization.
Right: sessions show what users did after seeing each version.
byte counts are not about user sessions.
questions.explain: Sequences of actions per user let you compare purchase rates between versions of a site.
questions.teaches: Sessionization can be used to work out whether users shown a new version of a website are more likely to make a purchase than those shown the old version (A/B testing), or to calculate whether a marketing activity is worthwhile.

questions.q: A job joins a click log with a customer table. In star schema terms, which is the fact table?
options: The click log, the table of events
The customer table, since it holds the descriptions
Both, as every join result is a fact table
Neither, since batch jobs do not use star schemas
optionExplain: Right: the log of events is the fact table.
descriptive tables such as users are the dimensions.
the join result is not what defines the fact table.
the chapter explicitly relates the example to a star schema.
questions.explain: In the example, events are the fact table and the user database is a dimension.
questions.rule: Events are facts; descriptions are dimensions.
questions.teaches: In the activity example, the log of events is the fact table of a star schema, and the user database is one of the dimensions.

questions.q: A job groups posts by author. One author has 50 million posts and others have a few hundred. What is the risk?
options: One reducer gets far more records than the others
The mappers will run out of keys to emit
The sort will stop working for large keys
The output will contain duplicate records
optionExplain: Right: all posts of that author go to a single reducer.
mappers emit as many keys as the data holds.
the sort works; the problem is the load on one reducer.
duplicates are not the risk here.
questions.explain: Equal keys go to one reducer, so a very frequent key overloads it. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Disproportionately active database records are known as linchpin objects or ____ keys.
questions.explain: Hot keys cause skew, also called hot spots, in the reducers.

questions.q: In a ride-hailing log, one city has 100 times more trips than any other. You group by city. What do you expect?
options: All reducers finish at the same time
The reducer for that city finishes first
The reducer for that city runs far longer than the others
The smaller cities are merged into one reducer
optionExplain: equal finishing needs similar group sizes.
a larger group takes longer, not shorter.
Right: its group is much larger.
keys stay separate; only hashing decides where they land.
questions.explain: The biggest group takes the longest, so the job waits for it.

questions.q: True or false: Skew is harmless because later jobs can start as soon as most of the reducers are done.
questions.explain: A MapReduce job is complete only when all its mappers and reducers have completed, so later jobs must wait for the slowest reducer.
questions.rule: The slowest reducer sets the pace.

questions.q: Why must later jobs wait for the slowest reducer?
options: The slowest reducer holds the lock on the whole filesystem
A job is complete only when all mappers and reducers have completed
Reducers share one output file that is closed at the end
The NameNode refuses to hand out new blocks until it ends
optionExplain: no such lock is described anywhere in the chapter.
Right: so the downstream job's input is not valid until then.
each reducer writes its own output file.
the NameNode is not involved in this wait.
questions.explain: The job's output is valid only after every task is done, so one slow reducer delays everything after it.
questions.rule: The job ends when the last task ends.
questions.teaches: Since a MapReduce job is only complete when all of its mappers and reducers have completed, any subsequent jobs must wait for the slowest reducer to complete before they can start.

questions.q: A video site groups views by video ID. One video has half of all views. How does the job's duration compare to an even case?
options: It is about the same, since reducers work in parallel
It is shorter, since popular videos have fewer distinct keys
It cannot finish, since one reducer cannot hold that key
It lasts longer, since one reducer processes half of all views
optionExplain: parallelism does not help the one reducer that holds the hot key.
fewer keys do not shorten the hot reducer's work.
the reducer streams the values; it can finish, only late.
Right: the hot key's reducer sets the finishing time.
questions.explain: The hot key's reducer handles half the data, so the job takes about as long as that one reducer.
questions.rule: A hot key sets the job's finishing time.
questions.teaches: Collecting all the activity related to a celebrity, for example replies to something they posted, in a single reducer can lead to significant skew.

questions.q: A join has one very hot key. Which change spreads its load over several reducers?
options: Send all its records to the reducer with the most memory
Drop the records of the hot key from the join
Send its records to randomly chosen reducers, and copy the other side to each
Sort the hot key's records twice in one reducer and join them against a single copy
optionExplain: that keeps the single bottleneck, since that reducer still gets every record.
dropping records gives an incomplete join result.
Right: random choice spreads the load and replication keeps the join complete.
extra sorting in the same reducer does not spread the work.
questions.explain: Spreading the hot side requires the other side to be available at every reducer that gets a share. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Spread one side, replicate the other.

questions.q: The skewed join in Pig starts with a ____ job to determine which keys are hot.
questions.explain: A sampling job finds the hot keys before the actual join runs.
questions.rule: Sample first to find hot keys.

questions.q: Hot key K of join input A is spread over 6 reducers. What happens to input B's records for K?
options: They are copied to all 6 reducers
They are split into 6 random pieces
They stay on one reducer chosen by a hash
They are discarded after the sampling job
optionExplain: Right: every reducer holding a share of A's K needs B's K records.
splitting B too would break the match with A's records.
then five of the six reducers would have nothing to join with.
B's records are needed for the join result.
questions.explain: A's hot-key records are scattered randomly, so B's matching records must be at each receiving reducer.
questions.rule: Replicate the other side to every reducer.

questions.q: True or false: In a skewed join the framework picks the reducer for a hot key by hashing the key, as for other keys.
questions.explain: For hot keys the mappers choose among several reducers at random, in contrast to conventional MapReduce, which chooses a reducer deterministically from a hash of the key.
questions.rule: Hot keys use random choice, not the hash.

questions.q: How does the sharded join method in Crunch differ from Pig's skewed join?
options: It avoids replicating the other join input
It sends the hot keys to a single reducer
It samples the data twice instead of once
It needs the hot keys to be specified explicitly instead of using a sampling job
optionExplain: the technique is similar, so it also replicates.
spreading over several reducers is the point of both.
Crunch does not use a sampling job.
Right: the technique is similar but the hot keys are given by hand.
questions.explain: Both spread hot keys; Crunch is told which keys are hot, and Pig finds them by sampling.
questions.teaches: The sharded join method in Crunch is similar to Pig's skewed join, but it requires the hot keys to be specified explicitly rather than using a sampling job.

questions.q: In which known setting is the same randomization idea used to relieve a hot spot?
options: A Unix pipe, where randomization orders the lines
A partitioned database, where randomization spreads a hot key
A B-tree, where randomization balances the pages
A write-ahead log, where randomization hides writes
optionExplain: pipes keep lines in order and do not randomize.
Right: the chapter points back to the chapter on partitioning.
B-trees were not described this way.
logs are about durability, not hot spots.
questions.explain: Random placement to relieve a hot spot appears in both MapReduce joins and partitioned databases.
questions.teaches: This technique is very similar to one discussed for skewed workloads in partitioned databases, using randomization to alleviate hot spots.

questions.q: Which technique does Hive use for hot keys in a skewed join?
options: A sampling job to find hot keys, followed by random reducers to spread their records
Hot keys named in table metadata, stored in separate files and joined map-side
Hashing of the key into a larger number of reducers
Dropping hot keys from the data before joining, and rejoining them in a second job
optionExplain: that is the Pig method, not the Hive one.
Right: this is Hive's explicit approach.
plain hashing keeps a hot key on one reducer.
dropping the hot keys would lose results from the join.
questions.explain: Hive relies on explicit metadata and a map-side join for the hot keys. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Hive: explicit hot keys, map-side join.

questions.q: Match each system to how it learns about hot keys in a skewed join.
pairs: Runs a sampling job to find them
Hot keys are specified explicitly by the user
Hot keys are given in the table metadata
questions.explain: Pig samples; Crunch and Hive are told, and Hive stores the hot keys in separate files.

questions.q: A bank knows its three giant corporate customers cause skew. Which method suits stable, known hot keys?
options: Pig's: sample the data every time to find them
A single reducer for each of the 3 customers
Hashing each customer ID across all reducers, so that no key goes to only one
Hive's: list them in metadata and store them in separate files
optionExplain: sampling is unnecessary when they are already known.
this recreates the bottleneck, as one reducer handles each giant key.
hashing keeps equal keys together on one reducer.
Right: known hot keys can be declared up front.
questions.explain: When hot keys are stable and known, declaring them avoids the cost of sampling.
questions.rule: Known hot keys can be declared.

questions.q: Which join does Hive use for the records of hot keys?
options: A map-side join over the metadata file
A reduce-side join with randomly chosen reducers
A broadcast of all records to all reducers
An index lookup in the user database for each record
optionExplain: Right: the hot-key records sit in separate files and are joined in the mappers.
that is the Pig style, which relies on random reducers.
broadcast is a map-side technique, used here for hot keys only.
batch jobs do not use indexes in this design.
questions.explain: Hive moves the hot keys to a map-side join, so no reducer is overloaded by them.
questions.hint: Where does the join logic run for the hot-key files?

questions.q: True or false: A reduce-side join needs no assumptions about the properties or structure of the input data.
questions.explain: Whatever the input looks like, the mappers can prepare it for joining; the price is the sorting, copying and merging.
questions.teaches: The reduce-side approach has the advantage that you do not need to make any assumptions about the input data: whatever its properties and structure, the mappers can prepare the data to be ready for joining.

questions.q: Hive joins the hot-key files in the mappers. Which parts of an ordinary reduce-side join does this skip?
options: The reading of the input files from the filesystem
The extraction of the join key from each record
The reducers and the sorting
The writing of the joined output to the filesystem
optionExplain: the mappers still read their file blocks.
the join still needs the key to match records.
Right: a map-side join is a cut-down job with no reducers and no sorting.
each mapper writes one output file.
questions.explain: A map-side join needs no reducers and no sort, which is why it is cheaper for the hot keys.
questions.teaches: A map-side join uses a cut-down MapReduce job in which there are no reducers and no sorting; each mapper reads one input file block and writes one output file.

questions.q: You count events per user, and one user has a billion events. How can you avoid one overloaded reducer?
options: Sort the events of that user twice in the same reducer
Hash the user ID with a stronger hash function
Send the user's events to the mappers instead, and count them there without a shuffle
Count in two stages: partial counts at random reducers, then combine
optionExplain: extra sorting does not spread the load.
a stronger hash still sends one key to one reducer.
mappers cannot combine records across tasks.
Right: each first-stage reducer sees only part of the hot key.
questions.explain: Partial aggregation at random reducers spreads the work, and a second job merges the partials. The card next shows why.

questions.q: In two-stage grouping, the first stage sends records to a ____ reducer, so each reducer groups only a subset of the hot key's records.
questions.explain: Random assignment spreads the hot key's records across reducers.

questions.q: Put the steps of two-stage grouping for a hot key in order.
items: Mappers send the hot key's records to random reducers
Each first-stage reducer outputs a compact aggregated value for its subset
A second MapReduce job reads those partial values
The second job combines them into one value per key
questions.explain: The first stage shrinks the hot key into a few partial values; the second job merges them.

questions.q: True or false: Two-stage grouping lets you compute any aggregation of a hot key without combining partial results.
questions.explain: The second stage exists to combine the values of all first-stage reducers into a single value per key.

questions.q: How does two-stage grouping compare to the skewed join in how records are sent to reducers?
options: Both send each hot key to one reducer chosen by hash
Both use randomness to spread a hot key over several reducers
Neither uses randomness, since both use sampling
Only the join replicates data to every reducer
optionExplain: that is conventional MapReduce, which they replace.
Right: random reducers relieve the hot spot in both.
random choice is central to both.
the grouping example does not need replication, but both use random reducers.
questions.explain: Both techniques apply randomization to spread a hot key, though grouping needs no replication of a second input.
questions.teaches: Grouping in two stages sends records to a random reducer in the first stage, whereas conventional MapReduce chooses a reducer deterministically based on a hash of the key.

questions.q: A news site counts clicks per article; one article has most of the clicks. Which plan fits?
options: One job where the hot article goes to one reducer
One job where each mapper keeps its own counter for the article and a single reducer adds them
A first job with random reducers for partial counts, then a job to add them
A join between the clicks and a table of articles
optionExplain: that recreates the hot spot on one reducer.
mappers keep no state between records.
Right: it is the two-stage plan, which spreads the work.
no join is needed to count clicks per article.
questions.explain: Partial counts from random reducers are added up by the second job.
questions.teaches: The second MapReduce job combines the values from all of the first-stage reducers into a single value per key.

questions.q: Compared with a reduce-side join, what does a map-side join give up to be cheaper?
options: Freedom from assumptions about the input data
The ability to read files from the distributed filesystem
The ability to produce any output files at all
The use of keys to match records from the two inputs
optionExplain: Right: it skips sorting and shuffling by relying on a known layout.
it still reads input file blocks as usual.
each mapper writes one output file.
matching on a key is still how joins work.
questions.explain: Cheaper joins come from assuming the data is sized, sorted or partitioned in a useful way. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Sort these features into reduce-side or map-side joins.

items.t: Makes no assumptions about the input
Has no reducers and no sorting
Sorts and copies all data to reducers
Each mapper reads one block and writes one file
Mappers only prepare keys and values for joining

questions.explain: The reduce-side join does the work in reducers after a full shuffle; the map-side join is a map-only job.

questions.q: Two huge, unsorted, unpartitioned datasets must be joined once. Which join suits them?
options: A reduce-side join that sorts and merges both inputs
A map-side join, since mappers are faster
A map-side merge join for these inputs
A broadcast hash join for these inputs
optionExplain: Right: it makes no assumptions, so it works on any input.
without the right layout, a map-side join cannot match the records.
a merge join needs both inputs sorted and partitioned the same way.
a broadcast needs one side small enough for memory.
questions.explain: Without any known layout, the general reduce-side join is the safe choice.

questions.q: True or false: A map-side join runs with reducers but skips the sort that a reduce-side join needs.
questions.explain: A map-side join is a cut-down job with no reducers and no sorting at all.

questions.q: Why can the reduce-side join be slow?
options: Mappers cannot run in parallel on the same files, so the input must be split
Reducers must query the NameNode for every record
Data may be written to disk several times as it passes through the stages
The join key must be recomputed for every reducer call, which costs extra time
optionExplain: mappers run in parallel on separate blocks.
reducers read sorted files from mappers, not from the NameNode.
Right: the sorting, copying and merging are expensive.
keys are extracted once by the mappers.
questions.explain: Depending on available memory buffers, data is written to disk several times during sorting and merging.
questions.rule: The shuffle is the expensive part.
questions.teaches: Depending on the available memory buffers, data may be written to disk several times as it passes through the stages of MapReduce.

questions.q: A team joins a fresh 50 GB dataset daily with a dimension table it knows to be tiny. What should it check first?
options: Whether reducers can be added, to speed up the sort
Whether the tiny table fits in memory, which allows a map-side join
Whether the join key has hot spots on the tiny side
Whether the table can be written to a write-ahead log, which ensures it is durable
optionExplain: a map-side join removes the need for reducers and sorting.
Right: a small enough side permits a broadcast hash join.
hot keys concern big frequent groups, not a tiny table.
logs are unrelated to joining, which is about matching records on a key.
questions.explain: Knowing a table is small is exactly the kind of assumption that lets a map-side join work.
questions.rule: Look for assumptions you can use.
questions.teaches: The simplest way of performing a map-side join applies where a large dataset is joined with a small dataset that is small enough to be loaded entirely into memory in each of the mappers.

questions.q: A huge click log is joined with a small country table that fits in memory. What is the cheapest plan?
options: Send both inputs to reducers and sort-merge them
Query a remote database for the country of each click while the job runs
Split the table so each mapper gets only a few countries
Load the table into a hash table in each mapper and look up each click
optionExplain: that works but sorts the large input for no need.
per-record remote queries are slow, which is the problem this join avoids.
the mapper needs all countries, since any click may match any one.
Right: no sorting or reducers are needed.
questions.explain: A small side in memory turns the join into a hash lookup per record. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Small side in a hash table.

questions.q: In a broadcast hash join, the word broadcast reflects that each mapper reads the ____ of the small input.
questions.explain: Each mapper for a partition of the large input reads the entire small input.
questions.rule: Broadcast: every mapper reads the whole small side.

questions.q: Using the card's code, what does this yield for an event of user 2 on /home, with users loaded as in the card?
options: An error, as the table has no entry
optionExplain: 36 would come from the birth year 1990 of user 1.
the mapper yields the URL and the age, not the user ID.
Right: the join looks up user 2's birth year 1985 and returns 2026 minus 1985.
user 2 is in the table, so the lookup succeeds.
questions.explain: 2026 minus 1985 is 41, and the mapper yields the URL with the age.
questions.rule: Look up the key, compute the result.

questions.q: A 4 TB order log has 4,000 file blocks; the product table is 200 MB. How many map tasks run, and what does each load?
options: About 4,000 map tasks, each loading all 200 MB of products
One map task that loads 200 MB and reads all 4 TB
About 4,000 map tasks, each loading 200 MB divided by 4,000
About 200 map tasks, one per megabyte of products
optionExplain: Right: one map task per block, each broadcasting the small table in.
that would give up parallelism; there is a task for each block.
each mapper needs the entire small input, not a slice.
the tasks follow the blocks of the large input.
questions.explain: Each map task takes one block of the large input and loads the whole small table.
questions.rule: One task per large block; whole small side each.

questions.q: True or false: The small input must be split among the mappers, so that each mapper holds a different part of it.
questions.explain: Each mapper loads the small input entirely, so every mapper holds the whole of it; this is the broadcast.
questions.rule: Broadcast means every mapper gets all.

questions.q: Which tools support this join under other names, such as replicated join or MapJoin?
options: Only Hadoop MapReduce with hand-written Java code
Only relational databases with a query planner
Unix tools such as sort and uniq
Pig and Hive, and also Cascading, Crunch and Impala
optionExplain: several higher-level tools name it, so a hand-written job is not required.
the chapter lists batch tools and Impala.
those tools do not implement this join.
Right: the broadcast hash join is widely supported.
questions.explain: Pig calls it a replicated join, Hive calls it MapJoin, and it also appears in Cascading, Crunch and Impala.
questions.rule: Many tools support it under different names.
questions.teaches: The broadcast hash join is supported by Pig (as a replicated join), Hive (as MapJoin), Cascading and Crunch, and is also used in data warehouse query engines such as Impala.

questions.q: A mapper has 2 GB of RAM and the lookup table is 50 GB. What follows for a broadcast hash join?
options: It works if the table is sorted before it is loaded
It is not possible as it stands, because the table does not fit in memory
It works because mappers can hold a table of any size in their memory
It works if only reducers load the table
optionExplain: sorting does not change the amount of memory needed.
Right: the small input must be small enough to load in each mapper.
memory is limited in each mapper.
a map-side join has no reducers.
questions.explain: The method needs the whole small input in memory in each mapper; a read-only index on disk is a way around.
questions.teaches: Instead of loading the small join input into an in-memory hash table, an alternative is to store it in a read-only index on the local disk.

questions.q: A lookup table is a bit too big for a mapper's memory. What keeps lookups fast without loading it into memory?
options: Sending each lookup to a remote database server
A read-only index on the local disk, helped by the page cache
Sorting the table and reading it from the start per lookup
Compressing the table until the lookups stop
optionExplain: network round trips are the problem we avoid.
Right: frequently used parts stay in the operating system's cache.
scanning per lookup would be very slow.
compression does not by itself replace the need for an index.
questions.explain: The page cache keeps the hot parts of the index in memory automatically. The card next shows why.

questions.q: The frequently used parts of the read-only index remain in the operating system's page ____.
questions.explain: The page cache gives nearly in-memory speed.
questions.rule: Page cache keeps hot parts in RAM.

questions.q: A 3 GB table must be joined with a log on mappers with 2 GB of free RAM. What do you do?
options: Give up map-side joins and sort everything in reducers
Load half the table and ignore records for the rest
Query the product database for each record
Build a read-only index of the table on each mapper's local disk
optionExplain: the index approach still allows a map-side join.
ignoring records would give incomplete results.
that brings back per-record network lookups.
Right: the page cache keeps the hot part fast.
questions.explain: A disk-based index relaxes the requirement that the small side fit in RAM.

questions.q: True or false: A disk-based index makes every lookup a slow random disk read, much slower than a memory hash table.
questions.explain: The frequently used parts remain in the page cache, so random-access lookups are almost as fast as an in-memory hash table.

questions.q: Why is the index read-only?
options: The small input is a fixed dataset that mappers only read
Because the page cache cannot hold writable pages
Because the index has to be sorted by the reducers
Because HDFS forbids any local disk writes
optionExplain: Right: nothing writes to it during the join.
the chapter gives no such reason.
a map-side join has no reducers.
local disk writes are common in MapReduce, for example mapper output.
questions.explain: The input to the join is fixed for the run, so a read-only structure is simple and fast.
questions.teaches: Read-only data structures are simple, since the files are written once by a batch job and are then immutable, so they do not need a write-ahead log.

questions.q: A lookup structure of 500 GB with uniformly random access is used by mappers with 8 GB RAM. What is the risk?
options: The index becomes writable, loses consistency and gives different answers to mappers
The mappers will run out of file descriptors
The page cache cannot hold the hot parts, so most lookups go to disk
The cache will be bigger than the index
optionExplain: the index remains read-only, since the input to the join is fixed.
file descriptors are not the issue when the cache cannot hold the index.
Right: caching works when usage is concentrated.
the index is far bigger than memory.
questions.explain: Uniformly random access over 500 GB leaves no hot subset for the page cache to keep, so most lookups would read from disk.
questions.rule: Caches help skewed access, not uniform access.
questions.teaches: With the frequently used parts of the index in the page cache, this approach provides random-access lookups almost as fast as an in-memory hash table, but without actually requiring the dataset to fit in memory.

questions.q: Two datasets are both partitioned by user ID the same way. How can mappers exploit this?
options: Each mapper reads all partitions of both inputs
Each mapper sorts the partitions and joins at reducers
Each mapper joins records at random with the other input
Each mapper joins one partition of each input independently
optionExplain: that wastes the partitioning, since only one partition of each input can match.
a map-side join has no reducers.
random matching would miss many pairs.
Right: matching records are in the same numbered partition.
questions.explain: Matching partitions contain all the records that can match, so each pair is joined on its own. The card next shows why.

questions.q: In Hive, a partitioned hash join is known as a ____ map join.
questions.explain: Hive calls partitioned hash joins bucketed map joins.
questions.rule: Partitioned hash join = bucketed map join in Hive.

questions.q: Events and users are both partitioned by user ID modulo 8 into 8 files each. Which pair does mapper 5 read?
options: Event partition 5 and all user partitions
Event partition 5 and user partition 5
Event partition 5 and user partition 8
All event partitions and user partition 5
optionExplain: reading all user partitions removes the benefit.
Right: matching partitions hold the records that can match.
partition numbers must match for the join.
that would join events of other partitions with the wrong users.
questions.explain: With the same partitioning, partition k of one side only matches partition k of the other.

questions.q: True or false: A partitioned hash join works even if one input has 10 partitions and the other has 12.
questions.explain: Both inputs must have the same number of partitions, with records assigned by the same key and the same hash function.

questions.q: When is it reasonable to assume that both inputs are partitioned the same way?
options: Yes, since MapReduce partitions all datasets alike
When the datasets are stored in the same directory
When they come from earlier MapReduce jobs that already did that grouping
When both are smaller than the memory available to each of the mappers
optionExplain: the assumption holds only when it was arranged.
directories say nothing about how the data inside was partitioned.
Right: such jobs may have produced the partitioning.
size is unrelated to whether partitioning was done in the same way.
questions.explain: Outputs of earlier jobs that grouped by the same key and function can satisfy the assumption.
questions.rule: Earlier jobs may create the layout.
questions.teaches: If the inputs are generated by prior MapReduce jobs that already perform this grouping, then the assumption that both are partitioned in the same way can be reasonable.

questions.q: A team repartitions its orders by customer ID into 64 files daily. Customers are also in 64 files. What can they now do?
options: A partitioned hash join per file pair, if the hash function is the same
A broadcast of all customers to all mappers
A reduce-side join without sorting, which shuffles the files in random order
A join with a remote database for each order
optionExplain: Right: same count, key and function allow it.
the partitioning offers a cheaper way.
the reduce-side join needs sorting, which the partitioned join avoids.
the chapter rules out per-record lookups.
questions.explain: Matching partitions on the same key with the same hash function make a partitioned hash join possible.
questions.teaches: If the partitioning is done correctly, all the records you might want to join are in the same numbered partition, so it is sufficient for each mapper to read only one partition from each of the input datasets.

questions.q: Two inputs are partitioned the same way and sorted by the same key. How can a mapper join them?
options: Read both in key order and match equal keys, like a reducer's merge
Load the entire smaller input into a hash table and probe it for every record
Send the records to reducers chosen by random numbers
Query a remote index for each of the keys
optionExplain: Right: sorted inputs can be merged in one pass.
that is the broadcast or partitioned hash join.
no reducers are needed here, since a map-side join does all of the work.
per-record queries are what we avoid.
questions.explain: Both inputs are in order, so a single merging pass matches the records. The card next shows why.

questions.q: A map-side merge join reads both input files incrementally, in order of ascending ____.
questions.explain: Reading both in key order lets the mapper match records with the same key.

questions.q: Two daily datasets are written sorted by customer ID in the same 32 partitions. Do they need to fit in memory to be joined?
options: Yes: a mapper must load each partition into memory
Yes: the smaller input must be broadcast
No: a merge join reads both incrementally in key order
No: because mappers sort the data in memory first
optionExplain: that is true of hash joins, not merge joins.
no broadcast is needed here, since both inputs are split the same way.
Right: memory size is not a constraint for a merge.
the sorting was done before, not by the mapper.
questions.explain: A merge join only needs the current records of each input in memory.
questions.rule: Merge needs no memory for whole inputs.

questions.q: True or false: A map-side merge join works on any two inputs, because the mapper sorts them first.
questions.explain: It requires inputs that are partitioned in the same way and already sorted by the same key.

questions.q: If a map-side merge join is possible, what does that probably mean about earlier jobs?
options: They wrote their output in random order
They brought the inputs into partitioned and sorted form
They replicated the data to all mappers so each one could look it up
They deleted the input files after use
optionExplain: random order would rule out a merge join.
Right: the layout was prepared on purpose.
replication of the small input is the broadcast approach, not a merge join.
the files are the inputs for the merge join.
questions.explain: Prior jobs most likely did the partitioning and sorting, perhaps in their reduce stage.
questions.rule: Someone paid for the sort earlier.
questions.teaches: If a map-side merge join is possible, it probably means that prior MapReduce jobs brought the input datasets into this partitioned and sorted form in the first place.

questions.q: A team could do the merge in the reduce stage of the previous job, but chooses a separate map-only job. When is that sensible?
options: When the previous job has no reducers to run
When the join must run on a single machine because the datasets are small
When the inputs do not fit on the disks
When the sorted, partitioned datasets are also needed for other purposes
optionExplain: the previous job did produce the layout.
the map-side approach still runs in parallel.
disk size is not what decides this.
Right: then the layout is reused.
questions.explain: A separate join job keeps the sorted, partitioned data available for other uses.
questions.teaches: It may still be appropriate to perform the merge join in a separate map-only job, for example if the partitioned and sorted datasets are also needed for other purposes besides this particular join.

questions.q: The output of a reduce-side join is partitioned and sorted by what?
options: The timestamp of each record
The size of each record in bytes
The join key
The order of the mappers' start times
optionExplain: timestamps are not what the shuffle sorts by in the join.
size is unrelated to the sort order.
Right: the reducers receive and process records by the join key.
start times do not define the output order.
questions.explain: Reducers write output grouped and sorted by the key they were given. The card next shows why.

questions.q: The output of a map-side join is partitioned and sorted in the same way as the ____ input.
questions.explain: One map task starts for each file block of the large input.
questions.rule: Map-side output follows the large input.

questions.q: Job B needs its input sorted by customer ID. Job A joins on customer ID using a reduce-side join. Does B get that layout?
options: Yes: reduce-side output is partitioned and sorted by the join key
No: reduce-side output is in random order
No: only map-side joins sort their output, since reducers write in arrival order
Yes, but only if the join used a broadcast
optionExplain: Right: customer ID is the join key.
it is sorted by the join key.
map-side joins keep the large input's layout.
a broadcast join belongs to the map-side family.
questions.explain: The reduce-side join's output is partitioned and sorted by its join key.
questions.rule: Join key determines the output order.

questions.q: True or false: The output of a broadcast hash join is partitioned and sorted by the join key.
questions.explain: The output of a map-side join is partitioned and sorted in the same way as the large input, not by the join key.
questions.rule: Map-side output follows the large input.

questions.q: Why do map-side joins preserve the layout of the large input?
options: They sort the large input by the join key first
They send the large input to reducers in order
They copy the large input to the NameNode
One map task starts for each file block of the large input
optionExplain: map-side joins do no sorting, so they cannot produce a sorted output.
no reducers are used in a map-side join, so nothing is sent to them.
the NameNode does not process data.
Right: each output file corresponds to an input block.
questions.explain: Tasks follow the large input's file blocks, so each output file lines up with its input block.
questions.teaches: With a map-side join, one map task is started for each file block of the join's large input, regardless of whether a partitioned or a broadcast join is used.

questions.q: Two joins in a row use the same key. Which first join leaves the data partitioned and sorted by that key?
options: A broadcast join, whose output is partitioned like the small input
A reduce-side join, whose output is partitioned and sorted by join key
Any join, since layout is not preserved by any join
A third job that rewrites the files in random order
optionExplain: output follows the large input, not the small one.
Right: its output has the layout the next job needs.
the layouts are described for both types.
random order destroys the layout that the next job needs.
questions.explain: Look at the layout each join produces before picking one.
questions.rule: Plan joins by the layout they leave.
questions.teaches: Knowing about the physical layout of datasets becomes important when optimizing join strategies.

questions.q: To use a partitioned hash join on two datasets, what must you know about them besides their format?
options: The names of the programmers who wrote them
The number of partitions and the keys they are partitioned by
The date on which the NameNode was started and the workflow was last run
The total number of files in the filesystem
optionExplain: authors do not affect the join.
Right: the join works only if these match.
the NameNode's start date is not relevant.
a global count tells nothing about these datasets.
questions.explain: Partition count and partitioning key tell you whether partitions line up. The card next shows why.

questions.q: In the Hadoop ecosystem, metadata about the partitioning of datasets is often kept in HCatalog and the Hive ____.
questions.explain: HCatalog and the Hive metastore hold such metadata.
questions.rule: Partitioning metadata lives in the metastore.

questions.q: A colleague offers a dataset in /data/clicks in Avro format. What else do you ask before planning a merge join?
options: Which programming language wrote the file?
Which editor or tool was used to create the directory, and by whom?
How many programmers use the dataset?
Is it sorted, and by which key, and into how many partitions?
optionExplain: language is irrelevant to the join.
the tools used to create a directory are irrelevant to its layout.
the number of users says nothing about the layout of the data.
Right: the merge join depends on sorting and partitioning.
questions.explain: Format and directory are not enough; the join also needs sorting, partitioning and partition count.
questions.rule: Ask about layout, not just format.

questions.q: True or false: Knowing the encoding format and the directory of a dataset is enough to choose the best join strategy.
questions.explain: You must also know the number of partitions and the keys by which the data is partitioned and sorted.

questions.q: Which systems does the chapter name as keeping this partitioning metadata?
options: HCatalog and the Hive metastore
The NameNode and the DataNode
The MapReduce scheduler and Oozie
Avro and Parquet
optionExplain: Right: they maintain metadata about the partitioning of datasets.
the NameNode maps blocks, not dataset partitioning.
schedulers order jobs and do not hold dataset metadata.
these are file formats, not systems that keep partitioning metadata.
questions.explain: Layout metadata is kept in catalog services, not by the filesystem or scheduler.
questions.teaches: In the Hadoop ecosystem, metadata about the partitioning of datasets is often maintained in HCatalog and the Hive metastore.

questions.q: A team inherits ten datasets with no layout metadata. What is the safest join?
options: A merge join, as most datasets are sorted
A partitioned hash join, as partitions are common
A reduce-side join, which needs no assumptions
A broadcast of the largest dataset
optionExplain: an unchecked assumption could give wrong results.
without metadata the match is unknown.
Right: it works whatever the layout.
the largest dataset is the wrong one to broadcast.
questions.explain: Unknown layout means no assumptions are safe, so the general join is the fallback.
questions.teaches: The reduce-side approach has the advantage that you do not need to make any assumptions about the input data.

questions.q: A nightly job scans all of a year's logs and builds a recommendation structure. Which workload does it most resemble?
options: Transaction processing, which looks up records by key for a user
Neither, since batch jobs read only small inputs from disk
Transaction processing, because the job runs every night
Analytics, which also scans large portions of the data
optionExplain: OLTP reads a few records by key, using indexes, and presents them to a person waiting.
large scans are the typical pattern of a batch process.
the schedule does not decide the type; the access pattern does.
Right: it reads large parts of its input, unlike a lookup by key.
questions.explain: Batch jobs scan big parts of their input, as analytic queries do. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Sort these properties into OLTP queries or analytic queries.

items.t: Look up a few records by key
Scan over a large number of records
Use indexes to locate records quickly
Perform groupings and aggregations
Present records to a user, for example on a web page
Output is often a report, such as a metric over time

questions.explain: OLTP touches few records through indexes; analytics scans many and aggregates, often to produce a report.

questions.q: A job reads a week of sensor data and writes a lookup file for a mobile app. How is its output best described?
options: A chart of the change in a metric over time for an analyst
A data structure for another system, not a report for a manager
A top-10 list for a business decision by a manager
A set of transactions to be committed to a database
optionExplain: a report is one possible output, but this job writes a lookup file.
Right: batch output is often some other kind of structure.
this describes analytic reports, not a file for an app.
transaction processing is a different workload from this scan.
questions.explain: The consumer is an app, so the output is a data structure and not a report.

questions.q: True or false: A MapReduce workflow is the same as an analytic SQL query, so its output is a report.
questions.explain: A workflow of MapReduce jobs is not the same as an analytic SQL query, and its output is often not a report but some other kind of structure.
questions.rule: Batch output is not always a report.

questions.q: Who is the consumer of an analytic report, according to the chapter?
options: A web page that serves a user's request in real time
Another batch job that does not show the data to anyone
Often an analyst or a manager who makes business decisions
A database engine that stores the report as an index
optionExplain: that describes OLTP, where results are presented to users.
that describes batch output, not the typical report reader.
Right: reports serve people deciding on the business.
a report is a summary for a person, not an index.
questions.explain: Reports go to people who make decisions; batch outputs often go to other systems.
questions.teaches: The consumer of an analytic report, such as a graph of a metric over time, the top 10 items by a ranking or a breakdown into subcategories, is often an analyst or a manager who needs to make business decisions.

questions.q: A bank job scans every account and writes fraud scores for the card system. Is this OLTP, analytics or neither?
options: Closer to analytics in its scan, but its output feeds a system
OLTP, because the card system will read single records later
Plain analytics, because it reads the full data and nothing else
A transaction, because it updates every account's score
optionExplain: Right: it scans a lot, and the output is not a report.
the job itself scans everything; the later lookups are done by another system.
the output is a file used by a system, not a report for a person.
it writes new output files, not transactions on the accounts.
questions.explain: Scanning makes it analytics-like; the system-facing output sets it apart from a report.
questions.rule: Judge the scan and the output separately.
questions.teaches: Batch processing is closer to analytics than to transaction processing, in that a batch process typically scans over large portions of an input dataset.

questions.q: A batch job must build a keyword index for 100 million fixed documents. How does it spread the work?
options: Mappers partition the documents; each reducer builds the index for one partition
Each mapper builds the whole index and reducers pick the best
A single reducer builds the index while mappers wait for it
Mappers write documents to a database that builds the index and serves queries
optionExplain: Right: each reducer owns one slice of the index.
building the whole index in every mapper multiplies the work.
a single reducer gives up the parallelism of the cluster.
the index files are built by reducers and written to the filesystem.
questions.explain: Document-partitioned indexes are built in parallel, one partition per reducer. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Match each part of a full-text index to its role.
pairs: Document IDs that contain a keyword
Part of the index built by one reducer
questions.explain: A keyword is looked up in the term dictionary, which leads to the postings list of documents.

questions.q: A legal firm indexes 2 million contracts once a quarter. Which batch design fits?
options: Query a remote index service for each contract, one by one
Let each mapper write straight into a production search server
Partition the contracts, build each partition's index in a reducer, write files
Sort the contracts by size and write them out as one big index file
optionExplain: per-record remote calls are slow compared to a bulk job.
writing from tasks to an external system has side effects.
Right: a fixed set indexes well in a batch job.
sorting by size does not produce a keyword index.
questions.explain: A fixed set of documents is indexed in bulk and the index files go to the filesystem.
questions.rule: Fixed document set: build in bulk.

questions.q: True or false: Because indexes are queried by many users, the index files must be updated in place by every reducer as documents arrive.
questions.explain: Querying by keyword is read-only, so the index files are immutable once they have been created.

questions.q: How many MapReduce jobs did Google's original search index workflow use?
options: A single job with one mapper and one reducer
A workflow of 5 to 10 jobs
A workflow of about 5,000 jobs chained by name
No MapReduce, only hand-written servers
optionExplain: indexing was a multi-job workflow, not a single job.
Right: the original indexing was a workflow of several jobs.
the chapter says 5 to 10, not thousands.
MapReduce was originally used for index building.
questions.explain: Google's original use of MapReduce was to build the indexes for its search engine, in a workflow of 5 to 10 jobs.
questions.teaches: Google's original use of MapReduce was to build indexes for its search engine, implemented as a workflow of 5 to 10 MapReduce jobs, though Google later moved away from MapReduce for this purpose.

questions.q: A team wants to index logs for Lucene or Solr with Hadoop. What does the chapter say about this?
options: MapReduce cannot be used for Lucene or Solr indexes
Only Spark can build indexes for Lucene and Solr
It works only if the index is written by a single reducer
MapReduce remains a good way of building indexes for Lucene and Solr
optionExplain: the chapter says Hadoop MapReduce remains a good way.
Spark is not named for this purpose in the chapter.
the chapter's design has one reducer per index partition.
Right: even now, it is a good way to build them.
questions.explain: Hadoop MapReduce is still a good way of building Lucene or Solr indexes, even though Google moved away.
questions.rule: Old tools can still fit a job.
questions.teaches: Even today, Hadoop MapReduce remains a good way of building indexes for Lucene/Solr.

questions.q: Only 0.1 percent of 50 million documents changed overnight. What is the main drawback of rebuilding the full index?
options: It loses the old index while the job is running
It cannot run on documents that have changed
It repeats nearly all the work for a few changes
It needs a database transaction for each document
optionExplain: the old files stay until the new ones replace them wholesale.
a rebuild runs on any set of documents.
Right: the whole set is processed again.
rebuilds are done in bulk, not by transactions.
questions.explain: A full rebuild is expensive when only a few documents have changed. The card next shows why.

questions.q: With the rebuild approach, the process is easy to reason about: documents in, ____ out.
questions.explain: Documents go in and indexes come out, with no hidden state.

questions.q: A news archive changes about 5 documents a week out of 3 billion. Which approach fits better?
options: Incremental updates with new segment files
A full rebuild every night, replacing all index files
A full rebuild every minute to stay current
No indexing, with a scan of all documents per search
optionExplain: Right: very few changes make a full rebuild wasteful.
that repeats the work of 3 billion documents for 5 changes.
this multiplies the cost of rebuilding.
scanning everything for every query would be very slow.
questions.explain: With few changes, writing new segments and merging them in the background saves work.

questions.q: True or false: If Lucene adds new segment files for changed documents, old segment files are merged and compacted asynchronously in the background.
questions.explain: Lucene writes out new segment files and asynchronously merges and compacts segment files in the background.

questions.q: Where does the chapter say it covers incremental processing in more detail?
options: In the earlier chapter on encoding formats
In the appendix on Unix commands
In the same section, with a worked example
In the next chapter, on stream processing
optionExplain: formats are not the topic of incremental processing.
the chapter points forward, not to an appendix.
the chapter defers the details of incremental processing to a later chapter.
Right: incremental processing comes up again there.
questions.explain: Incremental processing is picked up in the following chapter.
questions.teaches: We will see more on incremental processing in Chapter 11, on stream processing.

questions.q: A retailer rebuilds its product search index each night, taking 2 hours. Management asks for new products to show up in minutes. What changes?
options: Run the full rebuild on twice as many machines
Move to incremental index updates, since a full rebuild is too slow
Rebuild the index every ten minutes for the whole catalogue
Stop indexing and let users browse categories only
optionExplain: even halved, the rebuild takes about an hour.
Right: minutes of latency cannot come from a 2-hour rebuild.
a 2-hour rebuild cannot be run every ten minutes.
removing search does not satisfy the requirement.
questions.explain: A rebuild that takes hours cannot show changes in minutes, so updates must be incremental.
questions.teaches: A full rebuild is computationally expensive if only a small number of documents have changed, but it has the advantage that the indexing process is very easy to reason about.

questions.q: A recommendation job finishes overnight. How does the web app usually get its results?
options: By running the batch job again for each page view
From a database that can be queried by user ID
By reading the Hadoop input files at request time
By asking the NameNode for the latest recommendations
optionExplain: batch jobs run for minutes to days, not per page view.
Right: the output is a lookup table of suggestions.
the web app is separate from the Hadoop infrastructure.
the NameNode tracks blocks, not recommendations.
questions.explain: The job's output is a database keyed by user ID or product ID. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Batch output feeds a lookup database.

questions.q: Match each batch-built system to an example.
pairs: Related products queried by product ID
questions.explain: The chapter lists classifiers such as spam filters and recommendation systems such as friend suggestions.
questions.rule: Classifiers and recommenders come from batch jobs.

questions.q: A music app wants to show related artists on each artist page. Which output shape fits?
options: A report of the top-10 artists for the management team
A log of every play event, appended at request time
A full copy of all artists, sent to each web server on every request
A lookup keyed by artist ID that returns a list of related artists
optionExplain: that is a report for people, not a lookup for the app.
this does not give the app related artists by key.
copying everything per request would be very slow.
Right: queried by key from the web app.
questions.explain: The app asks by artist ID and gets back a ready list.

questions.q: True or false: The web application that serves user requests normally runs inside the Hadoop infrastructure that built the data.
questions.explain: The database is queried by the web application that handles user requests, which is usually separate from the Hadoop infrastructure.

questions.q: Which question does the chapter raise after describing these outputs?
options: How does the output of the batch job get into a database that the web app can query?
How can the web app run MapReduce jobs on its own to answer each request?
How can the database be made to compute the recommendations?
How can classifiers be replaced by joins?
optionExplain: Right: the chapter asks how the results get there.
the web app is separate from Hadoop.
the batch job computes them, so the database does not need to.
that is not asked in the chapter.
questions.explain: The outputs have to be moved into a serving database, which leads to the next idea.
questions.rule: The gap between building and serving.
questions.teaches: The chapter asks how the output from the batch process gets back into a database where the web application can query it.

questions.q: A bank scores 80 million customers for fraud every night. Cards are swiped all day. What suits the swipes?
options: Re-run the scoring job for each swipe
Read the whole score file on each swipe
Look up the customer's precomputed score by customer ID
Skip scoring and approve every swipe until the next batch run finishes
optionExplain: a batch job cannot run for each swipe.
scanning the file per swipe is too slow.
Right: the job produced a score for each key in advance.
this drops the use of the batch output.
questions.explain: Precomputed scores can be served by lookup, though they are as fresh as the last run.
questions.teaches: The output of those batch jobs is often some kind of database, for example one queried by user ID to obtain suggested friends, or by product ID to get related products.

questions.q: A reducer writes each output record straight to a production database. What goes wrong first at scale?
options: The reducer output becomes unsorted by key
The NameNode loses track of the job's blocks
The mapper loses its input records
The database is overwhelmed and its query speed drops
optionExplain: ordering of output is unrelated to the database writes.
the NameNode is not involved in external writes.
records read are unaffected by where the reducers write.
Right: tasks write at batch speed, far above what the database expects.
questions.explain: Batch tasks produce writes at a rate that production databases are not built for. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Which are reasons the chapter gives against writing to an external database from tasks? Select all that apply.
options: A network request per record is far slower than normal batch throughput
Parallel tasks can overwhelm the database and hurt its query performance
Side effects cannot be hidden, so partial results may be visible
Databases refuse connections from machines with a firewall
Mappers cannot compute a key to write
optionExplain: Right: it is orders of magnitude slower than normal batch throughput.
Right: many tasks write at once.
Right: an external system shows writes immediately.
the chapter assumes the firewall allows access.
mappers extract keys; that is not the problem.
questions.explain: Speed, overload and visible side effects are the three reasons.

questions.q: A team's job has 500 reducers writing 20 million rows into an orders database used by the shop. What should the plan be?
options: Keep the direct writes but add more reducers
Write files to the output directory and bulk-load them after the job
Keep the direct writes but retry failed rows until each one succeeds
Switch off the shop's queries until the job ends
optionExplain: more reducers write faster and make the overload worse.
Right: the live database is protected from the job's write rate.
retries add load and hide partial results.
this treats the symptom and makes the shop unavailable.
questions.explain: Produce files first, then load them in bulk, so the job has no external side effects.

questions.q: True or false: If a MapReduce job fails after writing to an external database, the framework discards those writes.
questions.explain: Writing to an external system from inside a job produces externally visible side effects that cannot be hidden, so partial results may be seen.
questions.rule: External writes escape the discard rule.

questions.q: What does MapReduce guarantee about job output when it writes only to its own output files?
options: Each task writes as many times as it was retried
Output is visible as soon as one record is written
A clean all-or-nothing result: every task counted once, or no output if the job fails
Output is guaranteed only for the first task that finishes in each partition
optionExplain: retried attempts are discarded, not kept.
output becomes valid only after the job succeeds.
Right: tasks may be retried, yet the result is as if each ran once.
the guarantee covers all tasks of the job.
questions.explain: If the job succeeds, the output is that of running every task exactly once, even if some failed and were retried.
questions.teaches: Normally MapReduce provides a clean all-or-nothing guarantee for job output: if a job succeeds, the result is the output of running every task exactly once, even if some tasks failed and had to be retried, and if the entire job fails, no output is produced.

questions.q: A job sends an email for each record to customers from inside its reducers. The reducer attempt fails and is retried. What is the consequence?
options: Some customers may get the email twice
The framework removes the duplicate emails
No email is ever sent, since the job failed
Each customer receives exactly one email
optionExplain: Right: side effects of a failed attempt cannot be hidden.
it cannot undo external side effects.
the earlier attempt already sent some emails.
retrying an attempt repeats its external side effects.
questions.explain: Task attempts, retries and speculative execution can repeat external side effects.
questions.teaches: Writing to an external system from inside a job means you have to worry about results from partially completed jobs being visible to other systems, and about the complexities of Hadoop task attempts and speculative execution.

questions.q: A batch job must produce a lookup database for a web app. Which delivery method does the chapter favour?
options: Write the database files to the output directory, then bulk-load them
Send each record to the live server as it is computed
Keep the results in the memory of the reducers
Email the files to the team that runs the app
optionExplain: Right: the job has no side effects on live servers.
record-by-record writes are what the chapter warns against.
reducer memory disappears when the job ends.
the files go to the distributed filesystem and are then loaded in bulk.
questions.explain: Build the database as files, then load it in one go. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Key-value stores such as Voldemort and ElephantDB can load database files built in MapReduce, and HBase supports bulk ____.
questions.explain: HBase bulk loading is one of the options named in the chapter.
questions.rule: Build in MapReduce, bulk-load in the store.

questions.q: Put the delivery of batch-built lookup data in order.
items: The job writes the database files to its output directory
The files are loaded in bulk into the read-only servers
The servers switch over to the new data files
The web app queries the new data by key
questions.explain: The job produces files first; only then are they loaded, so the live servers see no writes from the job.
questions.rule: Build files, load in bulk, then serve.

questions.q: Why is building index files a good use of MapReduce?
options: MapReduce can update records in place faster than the database can
It avoids the need for any disk writes
Extracting a key with a mapper and sorting by it is already much of the work
It makes the database writable by the web app
optionExplain: MapReduce writes new files, not in-place updates.
MapReduce is eager to write data to disk.
Right: that is the core of building an index.
most of these stores are read-only.
questions.explain: Mapper extracts the key, sorting orders by key: that is much of what building an index needs.
questions.rule: Map and sort already build most of an index.
questions.hint: Which two MapReduce steps produce an ordered key structure?

questions.q: Why do these read-only stores not need a write-ahead log?
options: They keep all data in memory, so crashes cannot lose any
The files are written once by a batch job and are then immutable
They use B-trees, which are crash-proof
They write records twice to different servers
optionExplain: the data is on disk in files.
Right: there are no incremental writes to protect.
B-trees need a log to be made reliable.
that is replication, which is not what removes the need for a log.
questions.explain: A WAL protects incremental writes; files written once by a batch job need no such protection.
questions.teaches: Because most of these key-value stores are read-only, the data structures are quite simple; for example, they do not require a write-ahead log (WAL).

questions.q: A social app's friend suggestions are built daily by Spark and queried at 50,000 requests per second. What does the batch-built file design deliver?
options: Fresh suggestions that update at every click
Writes from the app into the suggestion files
A job that produces no output files and keeps its results in memory
Fast reads from immutable files, but suggestions as fresh as the last run
optionExplain: files are replaced by the next run; they do not update per click.
the files are read-only for the serving servers.
the job's product is the files.
Right: the data changes only when a new set is loaded.
questions.explain: Read-only batch-built data is easy to serve but stale by up to one run.
questions.teaches: Various key-value stores support building database files in MapReduce jobs, including Voldemort, Terrapin, ElephantDB and HBase bulk loading.

questions.q: A server must load a new set of data files while still answering queries. What is the safe order?
options: Delete the old files, then copy in the new ones
Overwrite the old files in place as new data arrives
Copy the new files, then switch to them in one step
Stop the server, copy the files, then restart it
optionExplain: queries would fail during the copy.
readers would see a mixture of old and new data.
Right: queries keep using the old files until the switch.
this causes downtime that the switch avoids.
questions.explain: The old data stays in use until the new data is complete. The card next shows why.

questions.q: When copying finishes, Voldemort ____ switches over to querying the new files.
questions.explain: The switch happens in one step, so queries never see a mixture.

questions.q: The new files turn out to be bad one hour after the switch. What can the server do?
options: Switch back to the old files, which are still there and immutable
Repair the new files in place while serving them
Rebuild the old files from the new ones by reversing the last job
Stop serving until the batch job is rewritten
optionExplain: Right: nothing was overwritten, so the old data is still intact.
in-place repairs risk inconsistency while serving.
there is no need, as they still exist.
the old files let it carry on.
questions.explain: Because the old files are immutable and still there, switching back is quick.
questions.rule: Keep the old files; switch back if needed.

questions.q: True or false: If the copy of new files to the server fails halfway, queries keep being served from the old files.
questions.explain: The server only switches when the copy is complete, so until then queries use the old files.
questions.rule: No switch before the copy completes.

questions.q: What makes the switch back possible if anything goes wrong in the process?
options: The new files hold a copy of the old data
The batch job can undo its output
The web app holds a cache of the old data
The old files are still there and immutable
optionExplain: the new files are separate from the old ones.
the job's output is simply replaced.
the chapter does not rely on such a cache.
Right: nothing has changed them, so they are exactly as before.
questions.explain: Immutable old files can be switched back to at any time.
questions.teaches: If anything goes wrong in this process, the server can easily switch back to the old files, since they are still there and immutable.

questions.q: A configuration service reads a rules file. Admins edit it in place. Compared with the batch-built file approach, what is lost?
options: The ability to read the file at all
A clean old version to switch back to when an edit is bad
The ability to run on more than one machine
The need for any disk space
optionExplain: reading still works, so this is not what is lost.
Right: in-place edits destroy the previous state.
this is unrelated to in-place editing.
editing in place uses disk too.
questions.explain: Immutable versions provide an undo; in-place edits do not.
questions.teaches: Databases with read-write transactions do not have this property: if you deploy buggy code that writes bad data to the database, then rolling back the code will do nothing to fix the data in the database.

questions.q: A deployed job has a bug that corrupts its output. What fixes it fastest in the batch design?
options: Write a script that edits each wrong record in place
Roll back the code and rerun the job on the same input
Restore the input data from the last backup
Wait for the next release and ignore the wrong output
optionExplain: this is how read-write databases are repaired.
Right: the input is intact, so output will be correct again.
the input was never changed by the job.
wrong output could be used meanwhile.
questions.explain: With immutable input, a rerun of the fixed code replaces the bad output. The card next shows why.

questions.q: The ability to recover from buggy code is called human fault ____.
questions.explain: Human fault tolerance means being able to recover from human mistakes such as bugs.

questions.q: Yesterday's job output went to /out/v41; today's buggy job wrote /out/v42. What is the quickest recovery?
options: Edit the files in /out/v42 by hand
Delete the input data and start again from a fresh copy of the source
Move the job to a larger cluster
Point consumers back at /out/v41 while the bug is fixed
optionExplain: hand edits are slow and error-prone.
the input is needed to rerun.
more machines do not repair wrong output.
Right: old output is kept in a different directory.
questions.explain: Keeping old output in a separate directory lets you switch back.
questions.rule: Keep old versions to switch back.

questions.q: True or false: Rolling back buggy application code also repairs the bad data it already wrote into a read-write database.
questions.explain: Rolling back the code does nothing to fix the data in the database, whereas a batch job simply recomputes its output from its intact input.

questions.q: How does the chapter link easier rollback to feature development?
options: Features ship faster when mistakes can be undone
Features can be released without testing
Features can only be added once a month
Features are written by the framework
optionExplain: Right: minimizing irreversibility benefits Agile development.
the point is about recoverability, not skipping tests.
no such constraint is described anywhere in the chapter.
developers still write the code; the framework does not.
questions.explain: If mistakes can be undone, teams can move faster.
questions.teaches: As a consequence of the ease of rolling back, feature development can proceed more quickly than in an environment where mistakes could mean irreversible damage; this principle of minimizing irreversibility is beneficial for Agile software development.

questions.q: A shop sends discount emails from a nightly job's output. A bug picked the wrong customers. What can rerunning NOT undo?
options: The wrong customer list the job wrote
The bug in the job's code
The emails that were already sent
The old output in the previous directory
optionExplain: the list is derived data and is replaced by a rerun.
a code fix is a separate action.
Right: side effects outside the data cannot be rerun away.
old output is kept separately, so it is not removed.
questions.explain: Our reading: human fault tolerance covers derived data; actions taken on it in the real world remain.
questions.rule: Derived data can be redone; real-world effects cannot.
questions.teaches: By treating inputs as immutable and avoiding side effects such as writing to external databases, batch jobs not only achieve good performance but also become much easier to maintain.

questions.q: A reduce task crashes because a machine lost power. What does MapReduce do?
options: Fails the job at once without trying again
Skips the task and carries on with the others
Asks the programmer to repair the partial output
Reruns it on the same input, possibly on another machine
optionExplain: the framework retries failed tasks automatically.
skipping would leave the output incomplete.
partial output is discarded, not repaired.
Right: the input is unchanged, so a retry gives the same result.
questions.explain: Rerunning on unchanged input is safe, so the framework does it automatically. The card next shows why.

questions.q: If a task keeps crashing because of a bug, the job eventually ____ after a few attempts.
questions.explain: Repeated crashes from a bug end with a failed job, whereas transient faults are tolerated.
questions.rule: Bugs fail the job; transient faults are retried.

questions.q: A task fails once from a network blip and succeeds on the second attempt. What does the final output show?
options: Records duplicated by the failed attempt
The same result as if no fault had occurred
Missing records from the failed attempt
A message for the programmer to merge two outputs
optionExplain: the output of failed attempts is discarded.
Right: failed output is discarded, and the retry reads the same input.
the retry produces the full output.
no merging by hand is needed.
