questions.explain: The framework can guarantee that the final output is the same as if no faults occurred.
questions.rule: Final output equals the fault-free result.

questions.q: True or false: Automatic retries stay safe even if a task increments a counter in an external database each time it runs.
questions.explain: Retries are safe only because inputs are immutable and outputs of failed tasks are discarded; an external counter would be incremented again.

questions.q: If several attempts for the same partition succeed, how many make their output visible?
options: All of them, merged by key
None, until the job is rerun
Only one of them
Exactly two, for comparison
optionExplain: only one output per partition is kept.
a successful attempt's output is kept.
Right: the framework picks one and discards the others.
no comparison between attempts is described in the chapter.
questions.explain: Only one attempt's output becomes visible.
questions.teaches: If several tasks for a partition succeed, only one of them actually makes its output visible.

questions.q: A task writes a log line to an external audit service for every record. A retry occurs. What is the issue?
options: The audit service sees duplicate lines
The framework removes the audit lines of the failed attempt
The audit service refuses all later lines
The retry reads different input
optionExplain: Right: external effects are not discarded.
it can only discard its own files.
nothing suggests the service refuses them.
the input is unchanged, so a retry does not read different data.
questions.explain: External writes escape the framework's cleanup.
questions.teaches: Callback functions such as mappers and reducers are assumed to be stateless and to have no externally visible side effects besides their designated output, which lets the framework retry tasks safely and discard the output of failed tasks.

questions.q: Many teams want to read the output files of one job. What property of the batch design supports this?
options: The output files are immutable, so any job can read them safely
The output is held in memory by the producing job
Every consumer must ask the producer for permission to read
Each consumer receives a private edited copy
optionExplain: Right: readers cannot disturb each other.
output is written to files, not held in memory.
files are shared by directory, with no per-read request.
the same files are used as input for different jobs.
questions.explain: Immutable files are safe to share among many jobs. The card next shows why.

questions.q: MapReduce jobs, like Unix tools, separate logic from ____, which means configuring the input and output directories.
questions.explain: Separating logic from wiring enables reuse of code across teams.

questions.q: A team wants to check each night whether its job's output looks sane compared with last night's. What does the design allow?
options: A change to the main job so it writes into the monitoring database
A lock on last night's output so nobody reads it
A monitoring job that reads both outputs and measures discrepancies
An edit to last night's output to match tonight's
optionExplain: side effects in the main job are what the design avoids.
locking is unnecessary for immutable files.
Right: the same files can feed monitoring jobs.
outputs are not edited; they are replaced by new runs.
questions.explain: A monitoring job compares output with the previous run's output.

questions.q: True or false: In MapReduce, the team that writes a job must also decide where and when it runs and where it reads and writes.
questions.explain: Logic is separate from wiring, so one team can write a job while other teams decide where and when to run it.

questions.q: What does the chapter say this separation provides?
options: Faster hardware for every job in the cluster
A separation of concerns and potential reuse of code
A guarantee that no job can fail
A single owner for all of the datasets
optionExplain: no hardware change is involved in separating logic from wiring.
Right: teams can specialise in jobs that each do one thing well.
failures still occur and are retried.
the point is the opposite: many teams.
questions.explain: Teams can focus on jobs that do one thing well while others place and schedule them.
questions.teaches: MapReduce jobs separate logic from wiring (configuring the input and output directories), which provides a separation of concerns and enables potential reuse of code.

questions.q: Team A writes a job that cleans addresses. Teams B and C want it on their own data. What makes this easy?
options: They copy the job's code and edit the paths inside it
They ask team A to run the job for each of them
They merge their data into team A's directory
They point the job at their own input and output directories
optionExplain: the design avoids hard-coded wiring, so edits to paths are not needed.
the job can be run by anyone.
this is unnecessary since directories are configurable.
Right: the wiring is configurable, so no code copy is needed.
questions.explain: A job that does not hard-code paths can be run on any directories.
questions.teaches: The same set of files can be used as input for various different jobs, including monitoring jobs that evaluate whether a job's output has the expected characteristics, for example by comparing it to the output from the previous run.

questions.q: Compared with plain text logs, what does a schema-based file format save a batch job?
options: All disk writes during the job
The need for any sorting by key before a join or a grouping
Low-value parsing, since fields have names and types
The need for a distributed filesystem
optionExplain: files are still written to disk.
sorting by key is separate from the format.
Right: the format describes its own structure.
the format is stored in the filesystem.
questions.explain: A schema lets jobs read fields by name instead of parsing text by position. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Two structured file formats often used on Hadoop are Parquet and ____.
questions.explain: Avro and Parquet provide schema-based encoding.

questions.q: A team's jobs pass data as space-separated text, and a new column breaks downstream jobs. What would help?
options: A schema-based format with named, typed fields
A longer separator character between columns
A rule that nobody may add columns again
A switch to a monolithic database
optionExplain: Right: schema evolution handles added fields.
the problem is the lack of schema, not the separator.
this blocks change instead of managing it.
this is a bigger change than needed.
questions.explain: Avro and Parquet allow schema evolution, so added fields do not break readers.

questions.q: True or false: On Hadoop, jobs must still parse untyped text by field position, as Unix tools do.
questions.explain: Hadoop jobs often use structured file formats such as Avro and Parquet, removing some of that parsing.

questions.q: What does the chapter say Avro and Parquet allow their schemas to do over time?
options: Stay fixed once the first file is written
Be replaced by plain text with no loss of types
Be read only by the program that wrote them
Evolve as the data changes over time
optionExplain: schemas can evolve; that is part of their value.
plain text has no schema at all.
any program with the schema can read them.
Right: they allow evolution of their schemas over time.
questions.explain: Schema-based formats let their schemas change over time without breaking readers.
questions.teaches: Avro and Parquet provide efficient schema-based encoding and allow evolution of their schemas over time.

questions.q: A pipeline extracts a field by position. A colleague wants it to use a field name. What does this resemble?
options: An optimization the author warns against
The author's ideal: a named field, not a position
A feature that Unix tools already have for all files
A way to make sort faster
optionExplain: the author wishes for names, so this is not something to warn against.
Right: named fields read better than positions, as the author notes.
plain text has no field names.
names concern readability and not the speed of sorting.
questions.explain: Structured formats offer named, typed fields, closer to the author's ideal.
questions.teaches: The text interface is not beautiful: the log analysis used {print $7}, whereas ideally it could have been {print $request_url}.

questions.q: Which came first: parallel join algorithms in databases, or MapReduce?
options: MapReduce, which then inspired the databases that followed
The database algorithms, more than a decade earlier
Neither, as both appeared in the same year, 2004
The Unix tools, which implemented parallel joins in 1978
optionExplain: the databases had them first, so they were not inspired by MapReduce.
Right: MPP databases implemented them first.
the chapter says the databases came more than a decade before.
the Unix tools run on one machine and are not parallel joins in a cluster.
questions.explain: MPP databases had parallel joins more than a decade before the MapReduce paper. The card next shows why.

questions.q: MPP stands for massively ____ processing.
questions.explain: MPP databases run analytic SQL queries in parallel on a cluster.

questions.q: A colleague says sort-merge joins were invented for Hadoop. What is the best reply?
options: True: no database had any parallel join before MapReduce
True, but only for joins on text files
False: they were first invented in Unix pipes
They were already implemented in MPP databases long before
optionExplain: MPP databases had them more than a decade before.
the algorithms are not limited to text files.
Unix pipes do not implement distributed joins.
Right: the sort-merge and hash join algorithms predate MapReduce by more than a decade.
questions.explain: The processing and parallel join algorithms were already implemented in MPP databases.

questions.q: True or false: MPP databases and the MapReduce-plus-filesystem combination are both mainly systems for running analytic SQL queries.
questions.explain: MPP databases focus on parallel analytic SQL queries, while MapReduce plus a distributed filesystem is much more like a general-purpose operating system running arbitrary programs.

questions.q: Which database systems does the chapter name as pioneers of MPP?
options: The Gamma database machine, Teradata and Tandem NonStop SQL
MongoDB, CouchDB and Redis, the document stores
Voldemort, Terrapin and ElephantDB, the key-value stores
Hive, Pig and Cascading, the MapReduce tools
optionExplain: Right: these were pioneers in this area.
the chapter names MongoDB and CouchDB as MapReduce implementers, not MPP pioneers.
these are key-value stores that load batch-built files.
these are higher-level tools on top of MapReduce.
questions.explain: Gamma, Teradata and Tandem NonStop SQL pioneered MPP databases.
questions.teaches: The Gamma database machine, Teradata and Tandem NonStop SQL were pioneers in massively parallel processing databases.

questions.q: A vendor says its new engine is the first to join huge tables across a cluster. How should you judge this?
options: Accept it, as no earlier system could join tables in parallel
Reject it, as parallel joins cannot work across a cluster of machines
Check what it adds beyond MPP databases, which already did parallel joins
Accept it only if it is written in Java
optionExplain: MPP databases did so more than a decade before MapReduce.
they do work on clusters, as MPP databases showed long before MapReduce.
Right: the algorithm is old; the platform may be new.
the language says nothing about whether the idea is new.
questions.explain: Many such ideas are old; novelty lies in what the platform adds.
questions.teaches: Hadoop is somewhat like a distributed version of Unix, where HDFS is the filesystem and MapReduce is a quirky implementation of a Unix process that happens to always run the sort utility between the map phase and the reduce phase.

questions.q: An organization wants to bring data from many departments together quickly. Which approach does the chapter favour?
options: Design one perfect schema before any data is collected
Load only data whose queries are known in advance
Keep each department's data in its own database
Dump the data in raw form and work out how to use it later
optionExplain: the author says speed of availability is often more valuable than such a schema.
the point is not to need to know in advance.
this keeps data in separate pools that cannot be joined.
Right: availability beats an ideal model chosen up front.
questions.explain: Raw collection makes data available quickly, even if it is awkward to use at first. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Match each kind of system to how it treats incoming data.
pairs: Needs careful up-front modeling before import
Stores any byte sequence in any model or encoding
Brings data from many parts of an organization together
questions.explain: Databases insist on a model first; a filesystem accepts any bytes; a warehouse centralises data for joins.

questions.q: A retailer receives sensor logs, images and order records and has not yet decided how to analyse them. What should it do first?
options: Convert all of it to one relational schema before storing
Store everything as raw files and model it when the analysis is clear
Store only the order records, which have a schema
Wait until the analysis is fully designed and the schema is agreed on
optionExplain: it feels safe, but up-front modeling delays collection, the opposite of what is wanted.
Right: no up-front schema is needed to start collecting.
this leaves out data that could be joined later.
waiting for a perfect design only delays collection further.
questions.explain: A filesystem takes any byte sequence, so the data can be collected now.

questions.q: True or false: The author argues that careful up-front modeling gives better data, so it should precede collection.
questions.explain: From a purist's view modeling gives better-quality data, but in practice making data available quickly, even in a raw form, is often more valuable.
questions.rule: Speed of availability often beats an ideal model.

questions.q: What name is sometimes given to collecting data in its raw form and worrying about schema design later?
options: A data cube, or materialized view
A star schema, or snowflake
A data lake, or enterprise data hub
A column store, or row store
optionExplain: cubes and views are aggregation structures.
these are warehouse schema designs and have nothing to do with raw collection.
Right: these are the names the chapter mentions.
these describe storage layouts, not the practice of collecting raw data.
questions.explain: Raw collection into one place is known as a data lake or an enterprise data hub.
questions.rule: Data lake: raw data in one place.
questions.teaches: Collecting data in its raw form and worrying about schema design later is sometimes known as a data lake or an enterprise data hub.

questions.q: Two teams disagree for months on a common schema for card and loan data. What does the chapter's view suggest?
options: Land both in raw form in one place, so that joining can begin
Wait for the teams to agree a schema before any copying
Have each team keep its data and answer queries by hand
Drop the loan data to keep the schema simple
optionExplain: Right: careful schema design slows central collection.
waiting is the slowing effect the author warns against.
that keeps the data in separate pools and prevents the join the bank needs.
dropping data loses the join the bank needs.
questions.explain: Bringing the data into one place enables joins across datasets, and modeling can follow.
questions.rule: Do not let modeling block collection.
questions.teaches: Simply bringing data from various parts of a large organization together in one place is valuable, because it enables joins across datasets that were previously disparate.

questions.q: When data is stored raw, which party bears the burden of interpreting it?
options: The consumer, who reads it with a schema of their own
The producer, who must publish a clean schema first
The filesystem, which converts every format on write
The scheduler, which orders jobs by data type
optionExplain: Right: interpretation is left to those who use the data.
that is the opposite of schema-on-read.
a filesystem stores bytes and does not interpret them.
schedulers order jobs and do not interpret data.
questions.explain: Schema-on-read means the consumer decides how to interpret the data. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Leaving the interpretation of raw data to the consumer is called the schema-on-____ approach.
questions.explain: Schema-on-read means the schema is applied when the data is read.

questions.q: A sales team and a fraud team both read the same raw transaction dump, but with different needs. What benefit does the raw form give?
options: Both teams are forced to use the same standard format
The producer decides for each team what the data means
Each team can derive the view that suits its own purpose
Neither team needs to understand the data
optionExplain: that is the schema-on-write way, where the producer standardizes first.
interpretation is left to the consumers.
Right: different views onto the same raw data are possible.
consumers must understand the data, since they apply their own interpretation.
questions.explain: With raw data, each consumer applies its own interpretation.

questions.q: True or false: Under schema-on-read, the producer of a dataset must bring it into a standardized format before sharing.
questions.explain: Indiscriminate dumping shifts the burden: interpretation becomes the consumer's problem rather than the producer's.

questions.q: What has the principle that raw data is better been named?
options: The lake principle
The sushi principle
The cube principle
The hub principle
optionExplain: the chapter uses data lake for the storage, not this name for the principle.
Right: raw data is better, like raw fish.
cubes relate to precomputed aggregation, not to the raw data principle.
hub is part of enterprise data hub, a different name.
questions.explain: The sushi principle says raw data is better, because it allows many different transformations.
questions.teaches: The idea that simply dumping data in its raw form allows for several different transformations has been dubbed the sushi principle: raw data is better.

questions.q: A producer team insists on publishing only perfectly cleaned data, and the dataset arrives months late. Which downside of up-front standardization does this show?
options: It forces consumers to interpret the data themselves
It prevents the data from ever being joined with data from another source
It makes the data impossible to store in a filesystem
It slows availability, and consumers with other needs may still find it unsuited
optionExplain: that is the schema-on-read burden, not this situation.
cleaned data can be joined too, so this does not describe the downside.
the filesystem stores any format, so cleaned data can be stored.
Right: standardizing for everyone delays and may not fit.
questions.explain: Standardizing slows collection and may not satisfy every consumer's view.
questions.teaches: There may not even be one ideal data model, but rather different views onto the data that are suitable for different purposes.

questions.q: Hadoop is often used for ETL. What is its role in the chapter's picture?
options: Replace the warehouse and store only reports
Serve single-record lookups to the web app directly
Clean and transform raw dumped data before it enters a warehouse
Collect data only from other Hadoop clusters and never from outside systems
optionExplain: the warehouse is the destination for analytics.
that is the role of a serving database.
Right: jobs prepare the relational form.
the data comes from transaction processing systems.
questions.explain: Raw data lands in the filesystem and batch jobs shape it for the warehouse. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Put the ETL steps with Hadoop in order.
items: Transaction systems dump data in raw form to the distributed filesystem
MapReduce jobs clean up the raw data
The jobs transform the data into a relational form
The result is imported into an MPP data warehouse
questions.explain: The raw copy comes first, then cleaning and transforming, then loading the warehouse for analytics.

questions.q: A shop's checkout, stock and support systems each produce their own log formats. Analysts want one warehouse. What is the plan?
options: Dump all logs raw, run batch jobs to normalize them, then load the warehouse
Make every system emit one agreed format before collection and reject the rest
Load each log type into its own warehouse table as it is
Skip the warehouse and give analysts the raw files
optionExplain: Right: modeling happens after collection, in a separate and decoupled step.
this slows collection, which the raw approach avoids.
unmodeled data would be hard for analysts to use.
the pipeline ends in a relational warehouse.
questions.explain: Raw dumps decouple collection from modeling; the jobs bridge the two.

questions.q: True or false: Using Hadoop for ETL means no data modeling happens at all.
questions.explain: Data modeling still happens, but in a separate step, decoupled from the data collection.

questions.q: What makes the decoupling of collection and modeling possible?
options: The warehouse accepts any record without a schema
MapReduce converts files to tables on write
Transaction systems store data in a common format
A distributed filesystem supports data encoded in any format
optionExplain: the warehouse needs a relational form.
the conversion is done by jobs later.
they need not share a format.
Right: raw dumps need no format agreement.
questions.explain: Because the filesystem accepts any encoding, collection does not need agreement on a format.
questions.teaches: The decoupling of data collection from data modeling is possible because a distributed filesystem supports data encoded in any format.

questions.q: An insurer wants claims data in a warehouse by next week from three legacy systems it barely knows. What helps?
options: Model all three systems fully first, then copy
Copy the raw data into the filesystem now and model it step by step
Wait until the legacy systems are replaced and a clean model can be designed
Ask analysts to query the legacy systems directly
optionExplain: this delays the start of collection.
Right: collection can start before the modeling.
waiting does not deliver data next week.
direct queries of operational systems create load and no joins.
questions.explain: The raw copy gives analysts a place to start and a base for later modeling.
questions.teaches: Hadoop has often been used for implementing ETL processes: data from transaction processing systems is dumped into the distributed filesystem in some raw form, and then MapReduce jobs clean it up, transform it into a relational form and import it into an MPP data warehouse.

questions.q: Which job is a poor fit for SQL alone?
options: Counting orders per customer
Feature engineering for a machine learning model
Joining orders with customers on an ID
Finding the top 10 products by revenue
optionExplain: this is a typical GROUP BY aggregation.
Right: such processing is specific to the application and needs code.
joins are standard SQL, so they need no more general model.
this is also easily expressed as a SQL query.
questions.explain: Application-specific processing needs code, not just queries. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Which kinds of processing does the chapter say may need a more general model than SQL? Select all that apply.
options: Machine learning and recommendation systems
Full-text search indexes with relevance ranking
Image analysis
Counting rows with GROUP BY
Joining two tables on an ID
optionExplain: Right: such processing is application-specific and needs code.
Right: ranking models need code, not only queries.
Right: it is not a natural SQL query.
this is a standard SQL aggregation.
this is a standard SQL join, so it is no problem for SQL.
questions.explain: Machine learning, ranked search and image analysis are the chapter's examples.

questions.q: A bank builds a fraud risk estimation function used inside its pipeline. Which approach does the chapter suggest?
options: Only SQL queries, which can express any risk function
An MPP database with a fixed query language
A spreadsheet that holds each customer's inputs
A general processing model that lets the team run its own code
optionExplain: not all processing can be expressed as SQL.
the monolithic design limits what you can run.
this does not scale to large datasets.
Right: risk estimation functions are application-specific.
questions.explain: Risk estimation is application-specific, so it needs a model that runs arbitrary code.

questions.q: True or false: MapReduce prevented anyone from building a SQL engine, since it supports only custom code.
questions.explain: The Hive project built a SQL query execution engine on top of HDFS and MapReduce, while other batch processes can be written that are not expressed as SQL.

questions.q: What did people find about MapReduce for some kinds of processing after a while?
options: It was too limiting and performed too badly, so other models were built on Hadoop
It was too slow only for SQL queries, which it never ran, so other models were built
It was faster than every other model for all tasks
It was dropped at once and never used again
optionExplain: Right: this led to more processing models.
Hive ran SQL queries on top of it, so SQL was possible.
people found it too limiting for some tasks.
the chapter says its importance is declining, not that it vanished.
questions.explain: People found it too limiting and too slow for some processing, so more models were developed.
questions.teaches: People found that MapReduce was too limiting and performed too badly for some types of processing, so various other processing models were developed on top of Hadoop.

questions.q: A team can add a new processing model to an open platform but not to a closed monolithic database. What does this show?
options: A monolithic database is always slower than Hadoop
An open platform cannot run SQL queries
Openness made a range of approaches feasible that a monolith would not allow
Open platforms need no scheduler for jobs
optionExplain: monolithic databases can perform very well on their intended queries.
Hive runs SQL queries on Hadoop, so SQL is possible there.
Right: the Hadoop platform could host many models.
open platforms still need schedulers, so that claim does not follow.
questions.explain: Due to the openness of the Hadoop platform, a whole range of approaches was feasible.
questions.teaches: Due to the openness of the Hadoop platform, it was feasible to implement a whole range of approaches, which would not have been possible within the confines of a monolithic MPP database.

questions.q: Several teams want to run different processing models on the same large files. What does the shared-cluster approach offer?
options: Each model gets its own private copy in a special format
They must all use MapReduce for compatibility
They must agree on a single schema first
They all use the same files on the distributed filesystem
optionExplain: the shared approach avoids such copies.
several models run on the cluster.
the filesystem takes any format, so no schema agreement is needed.
Right: no copying into specialised systems.
questions.explain: One filesystem and one cluster serve many models. The card next shows why.

questions.q: The Hadoop ecosystem includes the random-access OLTP database HBase and the MPP-style analytic database ____.
questions.explain: HBase and Impala both use HDFS for storage but neither uses MapReduce.
questions.rule: HBase and Impala live in the ecosystem.

questions.q: A firm wants SQL analytics, graph processing and machine learning over the same 2 PB. Which design follows the chapter?
options: Three separate systems, each importing a copy of the data
One shared cluster where each tool reads the same files
One monolithic database that does all three
Three clusters that exchange data over the network each day
optionExplain: this multiplies data movement and copies of the data.
Right: no repeated imports are needed.
a monolith limits the range of models.
this moves data around for no reason.
questions.explain: The data stays put, so each tool can use it at once.
questions.rule: Run models where the data is.

questions.q: True or false: HBase and Impala depend on MapReduce for processing, so they cannot coexist with other models.
questions.explain: Neither HBase nor Impala uses MapReduce, but both use HDFS for storage, and they can be integrated in the same system.

questions.q: Which benefit of not moving data around does the chapter name?
options: It removes the need for any replication
It guarantees that no job ever fails, as the cluster has spare machines
It makes it easier to experiment with new processing models
It makes the sort step unnecessary
optionExplain: replication is still used, so this benefit is not claimed.
failures still happen, and they are retried by the framework.
Right: data is already in place.
sorting is a separate matter, unrelated to where the data lives.
questions.explain: With the data in place, trying a new model costs less.
questions.teaches: Not having to move data around makes it a lot easier to derive value from the data and to experiment with new processing models.

questions.q: A team must run an OLTP store and an analytic engine over files that live in one place. What does the Hadoop ecosystem show?
options: Both can coexist and use HDFS for storage
They cannot coexist, since they differ too much
Both must use MapReduce to run
Both must copy the data into a private format
optionExplain: Right: HBase and Impala are an example.
they differ but are integrated in the same system.
neither of them uses MapReduce for its processing.
they use the shared storage and do not need private copies.
questions.explain: Very different access approaches can share one filesystem.
questions.teaches: HBase and Impala are very different approaches to accessing and processing data, but they can nevertheless coexist and be integrated in the same system.

questions.q: A node crashes while an MPP database is running a query. What do most MPP databases do?
options: Abort the whole query and let it be rerun
Continue the query with the lost partition ignored
Recompute only the lost task on another node
Pause the query until the node is repaired
optionExplain: Right: short queries are cheap to retry.
ignoring a partition gives a wrong answer.
that is how MapReduce reacts, not how MPP databases react.
most MPP databases abort rather than pause.
questions.explain: For queries of seconds or minutes, aborting and retrying is acceptable. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: MPP: abort and retry the query.

questions.q: Sort these design choices into MPP databases or MapReduce.

items.t: Abort the whole query when a node crashes
Retry only the failed task
Keep as much data as possible in memory
Write data to disk eagerly
Aimed at queries lasting seconds or minutes
Aimed at large jobs likely to see a task failure

questions.explain: MPP optimizes for short queries; MapReduce is built for long jobs where failures are likely.
questions.rule: Short and in memory versus long and on disk.

questions.q: A job processes 40 TB over 12 hours on 2,000 machines. Which recovery style fits?
options: Abort and rerun the entire job on any failure
Ignore failed machines and accept partial output
Task-level retry, since restarting the whole job would waste hours
Replace the cluster with one very reliable machine that never terminates tasks
optionExplain: that wastes the work done so far.
partial output is not valid, so ignoring a node gives wrong results.
Right: one failure is likely over 12 hours.
no machine is reliable enough, and it is not scalable.
questions.explain: For large jobs, recovering one task is cheaper than restarting everything.
questions.rule: Large jobs need small recovery units.

questions.q: True or false: Task-level recovery makes fault-free processing faster, which is why MapReduce uses it.
questions.explain: Recovery at the granularity of a task introduces overheads that make fault-free processing slower; it is a reasonable trade-off only if the rate of task failures is high enough.
questions.rule: Recovery overhead is paid even without faults.

questions.q: What other reason does the chapter give for MapReduce writing data to disk so eagerly?
options: Disk writes are always faster than memory
It assumes the dataset will be too big to fit in memory anyway
Memory is not available on machines in the cluster for use by jobs
Hash joins need data on disk to work
optionExplain: memory is faster than disk, so that cannot be the reason.
Right: the dataset is expected to exceed memory.
machines have memory; it is just not enough for the data.
hash joins keep data in memory.
questions.explain: Large datasets are expected not to fit in memory, so spilling to disk is the default.
questions.rule: Disk is the default for big data.
questions.teaches: MapReduce writes data to disk eagerly partly for fault tolerance, and partly on the assumption that the dataset will be too big to fit in memory anyway.

questions.q: In a cluster where machine failures are rare, most jobs see none. What follows for MapReduce's design?
options: Task-level recovery becomes faster than any alternative
Jobs need no output files at all
Queries should be aborted on any failure
The overhead of task-level fault tolerance is hard to justify
optionExplain: it still adds overhead in fault-free runs.
outputs are still written to the filesystem in every case.
that depends on job length, not only on failure rate.
Right: the design pays costs for a fault that rarely occurs.
questions.explain: If failures are rare, the cost of recovery is paid for little benefit; the chapter then asks what the real environment looks like.
questions.teaches: In most clusters, machine failures do occur, but they are not very frequent, probably rare enough that most jobs will not experience a machine failure.

questions.q: Why does MapReduce at Google face frequent unexpected task termination?
options: The hardware in the datacenters is especially unreliable
The network drops most of the messages between mappers
Low-priority tasks can be preempted for higher-priority ones
Programmers write buggy code that crashes tasks
optionExplain: the chapter says the cause is not unreliable hardware.
this is not the explanation given.
Right: batch tasks share machines with production services.
preemption is not caused by bugs.
questions.explain: Preemption by higher-priority tasks makes termination frequent. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Because MapReduce jobs run at low priority, they pick up the ____ under the table.
questions.explain: Batch jobs use the computing resources that remain after high-priority processes take what they need.

questions.q: Using the card's code, with a 5 percent hourly risk and 100 tasks of 10 minutes each, what is printed?
options: 0.57, more than a 50 percent chance of at least one termination
0.05, the same as for one task of an hour
0.01, since each task runs only 10 minutes and the odds are small
1.0, since some task will always be terminated
optionExplain: Right: the chance that none is terminated is about 43 percent.
100 tasks together are far more exposed than one task.
the risk compounds over 100 tasks.
the risk is high but not certain.
questions.explain: The chance of at least one of 100 tasks being terminated within 10 minutes each is about 57 percent.
questions.code:
p_hour = 0.05
per_10_min = 1 - (1 - p_hour) ** (1 / 6)
at_least_one = 1 - (1 - per_10_min) ** 100
print(round(at_least_one, 2))

questions.q: At a 5 percent hourly preemption risk, which job is most likely to lose at least one task?
options: A job with 5 tasks of 5 minutes each
A job with 1 task of 1 minute
A job with 20 tasks of 2 minutes each
A job with 500 tasks of 30 minutes each
optionExplain: few short tasks give a small risk.
a single short task has a very small risk.
20 short tasks have a lower risk than 500 longer tasks.
Right: more tasks and longer tasks both raise the risk.
questions.explain: Total task-time exposure decides the risk, and 500 half-hour tasks have by far the most.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says MapReduce tolerates task termination because the hardware in Google datacenters is particularly unreliable.
questions.explain: It is not because the hardware is particularly unreliable but because the freedom to arbitrarily terminate processes enables better resource utilization.

questions.q: A cloud team wants high machine utilization by mixing production and batch work. What does Google's design suggest?
options: Give batch tasks the highest priority so they never stop
Let batch tasks run at low priority and be preempted when needed
Run batch on separate machines to avoid any preemption
Disallow containers to simplify resource accounting
optionExplain: that would hurt production services, which batch work must not disturb.
Right: overcommitting low-priority resources raises utilization.
that is the segregated design with lower utilization.
containers enforce resource allocation and are still needed.
questions.explain: Preemptible batch work fills machines with idle capacity, but it must tolerate termination.
questions.teaches: Priority also determines the pricing of computing resources: teams must pay for the resources they use, and higher-priority processes cost more.

questions.q: In an open source cluster where tasks are rarely terminated, how do MapReduce's design decisions look?
options: They make more sense, since failures are now rare
They make less sense, as the recovery overhead buys little
They are unchanged, because design is independent of environment
They are improved by adding preemption everywhere
optionExplain: rare termination reduces the value of recovery.
Right: the design assumed frequent termination.
the chapter ties design to environment.
the chapter does not recommend that.
questions.explain: Without frequent preemption, task-level recovery costs more than it saves. The card next shows why.

questions.q: MapReduce tolerates frequent task termination because the freedom to terminate processes enables better resource ____.
questions.explain: The reason is better resource utilization, not unreliable hardware.

questions.q: A company runs batch jobs on a Kubernetes cluster that rarely preempts tasks. What should it ask about MapReduce?
options: Whether to make tasks less reliable to match what runs at Google
Whether to remove the shuffle from the job
Whether to give up the distributed filesystem
Whether paying for task-level recovery is worth it with few terminations
optionExplain: reliability is not reduced to match an environment.
the shuffle is unrelated to preemption.
the filesystem is not what depends on preemption.
Right: the cost may not buy much.
questions.explain: Where termination is rare, MapReduce's overheads are harder to justify.
questions.rule: Match the design to the environment.

questions.q: True or false: MapReduce's design decisions make as much sense in clusters where tasks are rarely terminated.
questions.explain: In an environment where tasks are not so often terminated, the design decisions of MapReduce make less sense, because their recovery costs buy little.

questions.q: Which kind of preemption does YARN's CapacityScheduler support?
options: Preemption for balancing the resource allocation of different queues
General priority-based preemption, as at Google
Preemption of production services by batch jobs
No preemption of any kind at all
optionExplain: Right: this is what it supports.
general priority preemption is not supported in YARN, Mesos or Kubernetes.
batch jobs are the ones that get preempted, not production services.
it supports a limited form for queue balancing.
questions.explain: YARN supports queue-balancing preemption, while general priority preemption is unsupported in YARN, Mesos or Kubernetes.
questions.teaches: YARN's CapacityScheduler supports preemption for balancing the resource allocation of different queues, but general priority preemption is not supported in YARN, Mesos, or Kubernetes at the time of writing.

questions.q: A startup copies a design from a large company without asking why it was built that way. What is the lesson?
options: Large companies' designs always work for small teams
Designs matter less than programming languages
The design may rest on conditions the startup does not share
Fault tolerance is never needed in small clusters
optionExplain: MapReduce shows the opposite, since its design depends on its environment.
the lesson is about conditions, not about programming languages.
Right: like MapReduce's reliance on preemption.
the lesson is to check the conditions, not to drop fault tolerance.
questions.explain: Ask what conditions justify a design before copying it.
questions.teaches: Batch jobs effectively pick up the scraps under the table, using any computing resources that remain after the high-priority processes have taken what they need.

questions.q: The chapter calls MapReduce a simple abstraction. In what sense?
options: Easy to use, since joins are built in
Simple because it hides all performance concerns
Simple because it has only one machine to manage
Simple to understand, not easy to use
optionExplain: the chapter says you would implement join algorithms from scratch.
performance problems remain in the execution model.
tempting because it sounds easy, but MapReduce runs across many machines.
Right: its behaviour is clear, though complex jobs are laborious to write.
questions.explain: The abstraction is clear to understand, but hand-writing complex jobs is hard. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Simple to understand, not to use.

questions.q: Higher-level tools built on MapReduce include Pig, Hive, Cascading and ____.
questions.explain: Crunch is the fourth of the higher-level programming models the chapter names.

questions.q: A team must write a join of two big datasets and has only the raw MapReduce APIs. What does the chapter predict?
options: It will call a built-in join function and be done in a minute
It will implement the join algorithm from scratch, which is laborious
It will find the job runs faster than any other tool
It will have no way to run on a cluster at all
optionExplain: built-in joins belong to higher-level tools.
Right: raw MapReduce offers no ready-made join.
other tools are sometimes orders of magnitude faster.
tempting as a joke, but MapReduce does run on clusters and was built for that.
questions.explain: Raw MapReduce APIs leave joins to you, and higher-level tools were created for that reason.

questions.q: True or false: A higher-level language on top of MapReduce removes the performance limits of the MapReduce execution model.
questions.explain: Problems with the execution model itself are not fixed by adding another level of abstraction and show up as poor performance for some kinds of processing.

questions.q: In what way does the chapter call MapReduce very robust?
options: It runs faster than every alternative on all kinds of data
It does not need to retry any of its tasks after a termination
It finishes huge jobs despite frequent task terminations on shared machines
It requires dedicated reliable machines for every task
optionExplain: other tools are sometimes orders of magnitude faster.
it relies on retries to survive terminations.
Right: robustness is its strength, albeit slowly.
tempting for robustness, but it tolerates unreliable shared machines instead.
questions.explain: MapReduce can process almost arbitrarily large quantities of data in a hostile environment and still get the job done.
questions.teaches: MapReduce can process almost arbitrarily large quantities of data on an unreliable multi-tenant system with frequent task terminations and will still get the job done, albeit slowly.

questions.q: A startup's analytics jobs run in a stable, single-tenant cluster with rare failures. What does the chapter suggest it weigh?
options: Whether other tools that are far faster for its kind of processing fit better
Keep MapReduce, since it is the only robust choice and its speed is fine
Drop all abstractions and write raw MapReduce for every one of its jobs
Use stream processing for every batch job
optionExplain: Right: the robustness of MapReduce may not be needed.
other engines are described as alternatives.
tempting for simplicity, but raw APIs are laborious and joins must be hand-written.
tempting, but streams are described as another way of speeding up batch processing, not a replacement for each job.
questions.explain: Its robustness matters most in harsh environments; elsewhere speed may count more.
questions.rule: Match the tool to the environment.
questions.teaches: Stream processing, the subject of the next chapter, can be regarded as another way of speeding up batch processing.

questions.q: A MapReduce job writes its full output to files for the next job. What is this called?
options: Materialization of intermediate state
Streaming the output through a pipe
Partitioning by the hash of the key
Sessionization of the activity events
optionExplain: Right: eagerly computing a result and writing it out.
pipes pass data incrementally through a small buffer.
that decides which reducer gets a pair.
that is grouping a user's events.
questions.explain: Writing intermediate state to files is called materialization. The card next shows why.

questions.q: A Unix pipe passes data through a small in-memory ____ instead of writing the whole stream to disk.
questions.explain: Pipes stream output to input incrementally using a small in-memory buffer.

questions.q: Team A's output is read by 12 teams by name; team B's only by its own next stage. Which can skip materializing?
options: Team A's, since many jobs read it
Both, because all output can be passed in memory
Team B's, since it is only temporary intermediate state
Neither, because every job output must be a file
optionExplain: many readers are exactly why a named, published dataset is worth writing out.
published data must be durable and reusable.
Right: only one consumer needs it, so naming and publishing add nothing.
nothing requires every intermediate stage to be materialized.
questions.explain: Published datasets benefit from files; private intermediate state does not.

questions.q: True or false: In a Unix pipe, the whole output of one command is written to disk before the next command starts reading.
questions.explain: Pipes stream the output to the input incrementally using only a small in-memory buffer, so the intermediate state is not fully materialized.

questions.q: From which earlier topic does the chapter borrow the term materialization?
options: Materialized paths in a tree of documents
Materialized views, which eagerly compute a result and write it out
Normalization in relational schema design, which removes duplicated data
Compaction in log-structured storage
optionExplain: the chapter links it to views.
Right: the term means computing eagerly rather than on demand.
normalization is a schema design concept and has no link to eager computation.
compaction is also unrelated to this term.
questions.explain: A materialized view stores a precomputed query result, and materialization of intermediate state is the same eager idea.
questions.teaches: Materialization is the same idea as in materialized views: to eagerly compute the result of some operation and write it out, rather than computing it on demand when requested.

questions.q: A reporting dataset must be found by name by many teams and reused as input to several jobs. What does that favour?
options: A pipe between the producer and each consumer
A temporary file deleted after each run
A copy kept only in the producer's memory
A named, materialized dataset in a well-known location
optionExplain: a pipe ties jobs together and cannot be named and reused.
consumers need the dataset to stay available.
memory does not outlive the job.
Right: publishing allows loose coupling between producers and consumers.
questions.explain: Publishing to a well-known location lets jobs avoid knowing who produces or consumes their data.
questions.rule: Publish widely used data as named files.
questions.teaches: Publishing data to a well-known location in the distributed filesystem allows loose coupling so that jobs don't need to know who is producing their input or consuming their output.

questions.q: In a workflow of chained MapReduce jobs, what does the second job wait for?
options: The first record written by the first job
The first reducer that finishes
All tasks of the preceding jobs to complete
The cluster scheduler to rewrite the mappers
optionExplain: a job cannot start on partial output.
one finished reducer does not complete the job.
Right: output is valid only after every task finishes.
mappers are not rewritten between jobs.
questions.explain: Straggler tasks delay the start of the next job. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Next job waits for every task.

questions.q: Which are downsides of full materialization named in the chapter? Select all that apply.
options: A job must wait for all tasks of the previous jobs
Mappers often read back what a reducer wrote
Replicating temporary files over several nodes is overkill
Intermediate files can never be read by other jobs
Materialized files cannot survive a machine failure
optionExplain: Right: stragglers slow the whole workflow, so this is a named cost.
Right: such mappers are redundant, so this is a named cost.
Right: the replication wastes effort for temporary data.
published files can be read by others, which is an advantage.
they are durable, which is a benefit.
questions.explain: Waiting, redundant mappers and over-replication are the three costs.

questions.q: A five-stage MapReduce pipeline has a stage-2 straggler ten times slower than its peers. What happens to stage 3?
options: It waits for the straggler to finish before starting
It starts on the output of the finished tasks
It starts at once and reads the straggler's output later
It splits the straggler's work among its own mappers
optionExplain: Right: a job starts only after all preceding tasks complete.
partial output is not valid input.
the framework does not pipeline between jobs.
the framework does not reassign work this way.
questions.explain: A single slow task delays the whole workflow because jobs run strictly in sequence.

questions.q: True or false: Unix pipes start the consuming process only after the producing process has exited.
questions.explain: Processes connected by a pipe are started at the same time, with output being consumed as soon as it is produced.

questions.q: Under what condition could the mapper code be folded into the previous reducer?
options: When the mapper runs on a different cluster
When the previous job was written in Java and the next in the same language
When the output is replicated three times
When the reducer output is partitioned and sorted the way mapper output would be
optionExplain: tempting, but where the mapper runs does not decide whether it is redundant.
the programming language is not the condition.
tempting, but the replication factor is unrelated to chaining reducers directly.
Right: then the reducers could be chained directly.
questions.explain: If reducer output already has the layout that the mapper would create, the mapper adds nothing.
questions.teaches: In many cases the mapper code could be part of the previous reducer: if the reducer output was partitioned and sorted in the same way as mapper output, then reducers could be chained together directly, without interleaving with mapper stages.

questions.q: A team's three-stage workflow writes 5 TB of temporary files replicated three times to HDFS, read once by the next stage. Which cost is this?
options: Waiting for stragglers
Over-replication of temporary data
Redundant mappers
Hot keys in the first stage
optionExplain: waiting is a different cost, about job start times.
Right: replicating files that only one job reads is overkill.
this concerns re-reading just-written data in a mapper.
hot keys cause skew, which is a different issue.
questions.explain: Temporary data used once does not need the durability that replication across nodes buys.
questions.rule: Replication is overkill for temporary data.
questions.teaches: Storing intermediate state in a distributed filesystem means those files are replicated across several nodes, which is often overkill for such temporary data.

questions.q: Spark, Tez and Flink treat a multi-stage computation how?
options: As separate jobs linked only by directory names
As one job, instead of a chain of independent jobs
As a single SQL query in a database
As a stream of events processed forever
optionExplain: that is how chained MapReduce jobs work.
Right: they handle the entire workflow as a single job.
they are execution engines, not SQL databases.
stream processing is the next chapter's topic.
questions.explain: A whole workflow is one job in a dataflow engine. The card next shows why.

questions.q: In a dataflow engine, the user-defined functions that replace strict map and reduce roles are called ____.
questions.explain: Operators can be assembled more flexibly than alternating mappers and reducers.

questions.q: Match each way of connecting operators to the join or step that uses it.
pairs: Partition the same way, skip sorting
Send one output to all partitions
questions.explain: Sorting is needed for sort-merge, but a hash table randomizes order anyway, and a broadcast sends the small input everywhere.
questions.rule: Choose the connection to match the join.

questions.q: True or false: In a dataflow engine, functions must still strictly alternate between a map role and a reduce role.
questions.explain: Unlike in MapReduce, the operators need not take the strict roles of alternating map and reduce but can be assembled in more flexible ways.

questions.q: Why can partitioned hash joins skip the sort when partitioning inputs the same way?
options: Partitioned inputs are already sorted by definition, once split by key hash
A hash table sorts records by key while it builds
The scheduler sorts the inputs in the background
Building the hash table randomizes the order, so order is irrelevant
optionExplain: tempting, but partitioning does not imply any order within a partition.
a hash table does not sort.
tempting, but the chapter describes no background sorting of inputs.
Right: only the partitioning matters, as the order is irrelevant to a hash table.
questions.explain: Order does not matter to a hash join, so the engine can save the sorting cost.
questions.rule: Skip the sort when order is irrelevant.
questions.teaches: For partitioned hash joins, the partitioning of records is important but the order is irrelevant, because building the hash table randomizes the order anyway, so the sort can be skipped.

questions.q: A team's 8-stage ETL runs as eight chained MapReduce jobs. What does moving it to a dataflow engine change?
options: The engine sees all eight stages as one job and can optimize across them
Nothing: dataflow engines also run each stage as an independent job
The ETL must be rewritten, since operators cannot do map and reduce work
The ETL can no longer partition inputs
optionExplain: Right: it models the whole flow of data.
they handle the entire workflow as one job.
the same processing can be implemented on dataflow engines.
tempting, but partitioning is still used to parallelize the work.
questions.explain: Handling the whole workflow as one job lets the engine decide where to sort, to keep data and to run tasks.
questions.rule: One job gives the engine a view of the whole workflow.
questions.teaches: You can use dataflow engines to implement the same computations as MapReduce workflows, and they usually execute significantly faster due to the optimizations.

questions.q: Compared with chained MapReduce jobs, where does a dataflow engine perform the expensive sort?
options: Between every pair of operators, as MapReduce does
Nowhere, since dataflow engines cannot sort
Only where it is actually required
Only before the first operator
optionExplain: that is the MapReduce default the engines avoid.
they can repartition and sort by key where needed.
Right: it does not sort by default between every stage.
sorting is placed where an operator needs it.
questions.explain: Sorting is a choice of the workflow, not a fixed step. The card next shows why.

questions.q: In a dataflow engine, intermediate state between operators can be kept in memory or written to ____ disk instead of HDFS.
questions.explain: Local disk or memory needs less I/O than replicated HDFS files.

questions.q: A workflow's consumer operator can run on the same machine as the operator that produces its input. What can the data use?
options: A write to HDFS with three replicas
A remote database that both operators query
A pipe that both operators open by name
A shared memory buffer instead of a network copy
optionExplain: the engine avoids this for intermediate state.
tempting, but no database is involved in exchanging intermediate state.
this is the Unix mechanism, not the engine's optimization.
Right: co-located operators can exchange data in memory.
questions.explain: The scheduler can place a consumer next to its producer so they exchange data through shared memory.

questions.q: True or false: Dataflow engines start every operator only after the entire preceding stage has finished.
questions.explain: Operators can start executing as soon as their input is ready; there is no need to wait for the entire preceding stage to finish before the next one starts.
questions.rule: Operators start when input is ready.

questions.q: How do dataflow engines reduce JVM startup overhead compared with MapReduce?
options: They run every operator inside one single JVM
They reuse existing JVM processes to run new operators
They avoid the JVM and run native code only
They start a new JVM per record
optionExplain: they reuse processes, not run everything in one.
Right: MapReduce launches a new JVM for each task.
the engines run on the JVM.
that would be far slower than MapReduce.
questions.explain: Reusing JVM processes avoids the startup cost that MapReduce pays for each task.
questions.rule: Reuse processes to avoid startup costs.
questions.teaches: Existing JVM processes can be reused to run new operators, reducing startup overheads compared with MapReduce, which launches a new JVM for each task.

questions.q: A team's Hive workflows run on MapReduce. What does the chapter say about moving them to Tez or Spark?
options: It needs a full rewrite of every query in Java
It is impossible, since Hive works only on MapReduce
It can be a simple configuration change, with no code modified
It requires the data to be moved out of HDFS
optionExplain: Pig, Hive and Cascading workflows switch without modifying code.
Hive can use Tez or Spark.
Right: operators generalize map and reduce, so the code can run on either.
dataflow engines still read inputs from HDFS.
questions.explain: Because operators are a generalization of map and reduce, the same code can run on either engine.
questions.teaches: Workflows implemented in Pig, Hive or Cascading can be switched from MapReduce to Tez or Spark with a simple configuration change, without modifying code.

questions.q: A Spark machine fails and its intermediate data is lost. What does the engine do?
options: Recomputes the lost data from earlier stages or the original input
Reads the lost data back from replicas stored on HDFS, as MapReduce would
Asks the user to rerun the job from the beginning
Drops the lost partitions and goes on
optionExplain: Right: other data is still available.
intermediate state is not written to HDFS.
tempting, but the engine recovers by itself without a manual rerun.
dropping partitions would change the result.
questions.explain: Recomputation from ancestors replaces durable intermediate files. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Spark uses the resilient distributed ____ abstraction, known as an RDD, to track the ancestry of data.
questions.explain: An RDD is a resilient distributed dataset that records how data was computed.

questions.q: Which two things must the framework track to recompute a lost partition?
options: The input partitions used and the operators applied
The names of the users who ran the job and when
The number of replicas and their disk locations
The size of the output and its checksum
optionExplain: Right: that is how the partition can be rebuilt.
who ran the job does not allow recomputation.
intermediate state is not replicated like HDFS files.
a size cannot recreate the data.
questions.explain: To rebuild data, record its inputs and the operators applied to them.

questions.q: True or false: Flink recovers from faults by writing all intermediate state to HDFS, as MapReduce does.
questions.explain: Spark, Flink and Tez avoid writing intermediate state to HDFS; Flink checkpoints operator state to resume an operator that hit a fault.

questions.q: How does Flink let an operator that ran into a fault resume?
options: It replicates operator state to three HDFS nodes
It restarts the operator from zero with no state
It checkpoints operator state
It uses the RDD abstraction, as in Spark
optionExplain: this is how MapReduce handles durability.
tempting, but checkpoints exist so an operator does not start over.
Right: the state can be restored from a checkpoint.
tempting, but RDDs are Spark's mechanism and not what Flink uses.
questions.explain: Flink saves operator state at checkpoints and resumes from the latest one.
questions.teaches: Flink checkpoints operator state, allowing it to resume running an operator that ran into a fault during its execution.

questions.q: A Spark node holding a stage's output is lost, but the stage's input survives elsewhere. What is the cheapest recovery?
options: Rerun the entire job from the original files
Recompute only the lost partitions from that input
Write all partitions to HDFS and then continue
Skip the lost partitions and report partial results
optionExplain: the nearest available ancestor is enough.
Right: the ancestry says how to rebuild them.
that adds the cost the engine avoids.
tempting, but skipping lost partitions changes the result of the job.
questions.explain: Recompute from the nearest ancestor that is still available.
questions.teaches: Intermediate state is recomputed from a prior intermediary stage if possible, or otherwise from the original input data, which is normally on HDFS.

questions.q: A recomputed partition differs from the lost original that downstream operators already used. What is the usual remedy?
options: Ignore the difference, since the sizes of the old and new data match
Keep the old data on the downstream side only
Roll back to the beginning of the previous day
Kill the downstream operators too and run them again on the new data
optionExplain: tempting, but contradictory data cannot be ignored by downstream operators.
mixing old and new gives inconsistent results.
the remedy is to rerun the downstream operators.
Right: this avoids contradictions between old and new data.
questions.explain: If recomputed data differs, everything built on the old data must be redone. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Which causes of nondeterminism does the chapter name? Select all that apply.
options: Iteration order over a hash table
Use of random numbers in probabilistic algorithms
Use of the system clock
Reading input from an immutable file
Sorting a list with a fixed comparison
optionExplain: Right: many languages guarantee no particular order.
Right: random numbers differ between runs.
Right: the time differs between runs, so output can differ.
an immutable file gives the same input each time.
a fixed comparison gives a repeatable result.
questions.explain: Hash table order, random numbers and clocks or external data break determinism.

questions.q: A Spark job uses random sampling in one operator. How do you make recovery reliable?
options: Use the system clock as the seed on each run
Remove the sampling and use every record
Generate the pseudorandom numbers from a fixed seed
Let each task choose its own random seed
optionExplain: tempting, but the clock differs between runs and breaks repeatability.
it changes the job instead of fixing the cause.
Right: the same seed repeats the same sequence.
tempting, but different seeds give different samples on each rerun.
questions.explain: A fixed seed makes a pseudorandom sequence repeatable.

questions.q: True or false: Reading the current time inside an operator keeps it deterministic, since every machine has a clock.
questions.explain: Any use of the system clock or of external data sources is nondeterministic; such causes need to be removed to recover reliably from faults.

questions.q: What do nondeterministic operators force on the recovery when some output was already sent downstream?
options: A cascading rerun of the downstream operators on the new data
A rerun of the whole cluster
A switch to a different scheduler
Nothing, since downstream operators ignore changes
optionExplain: Right: this is the cost of nondeterminism.
only downstream operators need to be rerun.
tempting, but scheduling is not the issue; the rerun is about data.
tempting, but downstream operators would see contradictory data.
questions.explain: Nondeterminism spreads reruns through the dependent operators.
questions.teaches: With nondeterministic operators, the solution is normally to kill the downstream operators as well, and run them again on the new data, which causes cascading faults.

questions.q: A report operator adds the current date to each row. After a node failure the operator is recomputed a day later. What is the issue?
options: The rows are sorted in a different order and the report columns shift
The rows are lost and cannot be rebuilt
The date is the same, so no problem arises
The recomputed rows have a different date, contradicting what was sent downstream
optionExplain: the problem is the changing value.
tempting, but they are not lost for good because they can be recomputed.
tempting, but the date has changed by the time of recomputation.
Right: the clock is an external, changing input.
questions.explain: The clock reads a different value, so recomputed data differs from what was already sent.
questions.teaches: It is easy for nondeterministic behavior to accidentally creep in, for example from hash-table order, random numbers, the system clock or external data sources.

questions.q: An intermediate result is tiny compared with the input but took hours of CPU to produce. What is cheaper after a failure?
options: Recomputing it from the source data
Reading it back from materialized files
Skipping it and using an approximation
Recomputing it with a different seed
optionExplain: tempting, but recomputation costs the hours of CPU work again.
Right: recomputing it would repeat hours of CPU work.
tempting, but approximations change the result of the job.
a different seed gives different results.
questions.explain: Small data and heavy computation favour materializing. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Recomputation is not the best choice in every case: if the computation is very ____-intensive, materializing is probably cheaper.
questions.explain: Very CPU-intensive computations are costly to redo after a fault.

questions.q: A stage reduces 10 TB of logs to a 20 MB summary using a cheap filter. Which recovery is cheaper?
options: Recompute it from the 10 TB each time
Materialize the 20 MB summary, since it is tiny
Store the full 10 TB again as intermediate state
Skip recovery and rely on the final output
optionExplain: this repeats a big scan for a tiny result.
Right: writing a tiny result costs little.
that is the reverse of a small materialization.
the final output needs the summary.
questions.explain: A small result is cheap to write and expensive to recompute from large input.

questions.q: True or false: Recomputing lost data is cheaper than materializing it, whatever the data size and computation cost.
questions.explain: If the intermediate data is much smaller than the source data, or the computation is very CPU-intensive, it is probably cheaper to materialize.

questions.q: Which two factors does the chapter name as pointing toward materializing?
options: Intermediate data larger than the source, and a cheap computation
Deterministic operators, and a fast network between machines
A small cluster, and a high number of replicas
Intermediate data much smaller than the source, and very CPU-intensive computation
optionExplain: tempting, but a larger intermediate result and cheap work favour recomputing.
tempting, but determinism helps recomputation and does not point to materializing.
the size of the cluster is not named.
Right: both make recomputation costly, so they point to materializing.
questions.explain: Cheap-to-store data and costly-to-recompute work favour writing it down.
questions.teaches: If the intermediate data is much smaller than the source data, or if the computation is very CPU-intensive, it is probably cheaper to materialize the intermediate data to files than to recompute it.

questions.q: A rendering stage takes 4 hours of GPU work and outputs 5 MB. After a node failure, which choice fits the chapter?
options: Materialize its output once, so a failure does not repeat 4 hours
Recompute it when needed, since recomputation is the default
Replicate the 4 hours of work over three machines
Drop the stage and approximate its output
optionExplain: Right: small output and expensive work point to materializing.
the chapter says it is not always the right answer.
replication of the computation is not the suggestion.
tempting, but approximation changes the result of the job.
questions.explain: Heavy work with a small result is the case where writing it down wins.
questions.teaches: Recovering from faults by recomputing data is not always the right answer.

questions.q: Why can a sort operator not emit its first output record before reading all its input?
options: Sorting always needs a second pass over the disk
The framework forbids early output from a sort
The last input record might be the lowest key and so come first
The first record is always the largest one, so it must be held back
optionExplain: the reason is about the last record, not disk passes.
the reason is logical, not a framework rule.
Right: so output has to wait for the whole input.
nothing says the first record is the largest.
questions.explain: Until all input is read, the smallest key may still arrive. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A sort must see everything first.

questions.q: Flink is built around ____ execution: incrementally passing the output of an operator to other operators.
questions.explain: Pipelined execution does not wait for the input to be complete.

questions.q: A workflow filters records, sorts them, then formats them. Which operators can stream?
options: All three operators, including the sort
Only the sort, since the others need all the data
None of them, since they depend on one another
The filter and the formatting; the sort waits for its input
optionExplain: a sort cannot emit before seeing all of its input.
the filter and formatter can process records as they arrive.
operators can be pipelined where they do not block.
Right: only the sort blocks, since filter and format stream records.
questions.explain: Filter and format stream; the sort accumulates state until its input ends.

questions.q: True or false: A dataflow engine can start emitting a sorted result from the first input record it reads.
questions.explain: A sorting operation inevitably needs to consume its entire input before it can produce any output.

questions.q: When a dataflow job completes, where does its output usually go?
options: Into the memory of the engine only
Back to the distributed filesystem, as a durable result
To a stream that never ends and is read by users
Into each operator's local state on disk
optionExplain: memory does not outlive the job.
Right: users find and use it there.
that is stream processing, in the next chapter.
that state disappears after the job.
questions.explain: Final outputs, like inputs, are materialized datasets on HDFS.
questions.rule: Inputs and outputs stay on HDFS.
questions.teaches: When a job completes, its output needs to go somewhere durable so that users can find and use it, most likely the distributed filesystem again; with a dataflow engine, only the intermediate state is no longer written there.

questions.q: Compared with MapReduce, what does a dataflow engine save for a workflow of ten stages?
options: Writing the final output, which now stays in memory and is never saved
Reading the original input, which is now generated
Writing every intermediate result to the filesystem, though inputs and final output stay there
All sorting, since no operator needs sorted data
optionExplain: the final output is written to the filesystem.
the input still comes from the filesystem.
Right: the improvement is in intermediate state.
operators that need sorting still sort.
questions.explain: Inputs and outputs are still materialized on HDFS; the intermediate writes are what go away.
questions.rule: Savings are in the intermediate state.
questions.teaches: Like with MapReduce, the inputs are immutable and the output is completely replaced; the improvement over MapReduce is that you save yourself writing all the intermediate state to the filesystem as well.

questions.q: A Spark job's operators form a directed acyclic graph. Is that graph processing?
options: No: the DAG is the data flow, while the data is relational-style tuples
Yes: any job whose operators form a DAG is a graph algorithm by definition
Yes, because Spark stores every table as a graph
No, because DAGs are only used in databases
optionExplain: Right: graph processing needs the data itself to be a graph.
tempting because of the shared word, but the DAG describes operators and not the data.
tempting but Spark data typically consists of tuples.
tempting but dataflow engines do use DAGs for their operators.
questions.explain: A DAG of operators and a graph as data are different things. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Operator DAG is not graph data.

questions.q: One of the most famous graph analysis algorithms, which estimates page popularity from incoming links, is ____.
questions.explain: PageRank feeds the ordering of web search results.

questions.q: A team wants to rank users in a social network by how many well-ranked users follow them. What kind of workload is it?
options: Offline analysis of an entire graph, repeating until the ranks settle
An OLTP query that finds a few vertices matching some criteria, with low latency
A single pass over flat log lines with one reducer call
A key-value lookup of one precomputed row
optionExplain: Right: ranking over all vertices is a whole-graph batch task.
tempting, but ranking needs every vertex and not a few of them.
tempting, but ranks depend on neighbours' ranks over repeated rounds.
tempting, but nothing has been precomputed yet.
questions.explain: Ranking systems need whole-graph offline processing, which is the batch graph use.

questions.q: True or false: In graph processing the data is relational-style tuples, and the graph is only the operator layout.
questions.explain: That describes dataflow engines; in graph processing the data itself has the form of a graph.
questions.rule: Graph data differs from DAG operators.

questions.q: What was the transitive closure example used earlier in the book to show a repeated edge traversal?
options: Counting page views per URL in an access log, grouped by key in a reducer
Joining user activity events with a profile table
Listing all locations in North America by repeatedly following within-edges
Sorting a list of words with the sort command
optionExplain: tempting, but that is a grouping and not a traversal.
tempting, but that is a join between two datasets.
Right: it followed which location is within which other.
tempting, but that is not an edge traversal.
questions.explain: Following edges until none remain is a transitive closure.
questions.teaches: This kind of repeated edge-following algorithm is called a transitive closure, as in the list of locations in North America from Chapter 2.

questions.q: A colleague says, 'Flink jobs are graph processing, since the job is a graph.' What should you check?
options: Whether the job runs on more than ten machines
Whether the data being processed is itself a graph
Whether the job uses a sort-merge join anywhere
Whether the job writes results to HDFS
optionExplain: tempting, but cluster size does not define graph processing.
Right: the operator graph says nothing about the data's shape.
tempting, but the join algorithm is unrelated to data shape.
tempting, but the output location is unrelated to data shape.
questions.explain: The data shape decides whether it is graph processing.
questions.rule: Check the data, not the job.
questions.teaches: Graph processing and the DAG of a dataflow engine are an unfortunate naming confusion: they refer to different things.

questions.q: Why can plain MapReduce not express a repeat-until-done graph algorithm by itself?
options: It cannot read files that contain graphs
It can only run on one machine at a time
It forbids jobs that run more than a minute
It performs only a single pass over the data
optionExplain: tempting, but a graph can be stored as lists of vertices and edges.
tempting, but MapReduce is distributed and runs across many machines.
tempting, but no such limit exists.
Right: looping needs something outside the job.
questions.explain: A job is one pass, so repetition comes from an external scheduler. The card next shows why.

questions.q: In the iterative style, an external ____ runs one batch step, checks the completion condition, and runs another round if needed.
questions.explain: The scheduler drives the repetition outside the MapReduce job.
questions.rule: A scheduler loops the batch jobs.

questions.q: Only 1 percent of vertices changed in the last round. How much input does the next MapReduce round read?
options: Only the 1 percent of vertices that changed
Only the vertices adjacent to the changed ones, found through the edge lists
The entire input dataset, and it writes a completely new output
Nothing, as the earlier output is reused in place
optionExplain: tempting, but the framework does not track changes between rounds.
tempting, but that needs knowledge the framework lacks.
Right: MapReduce has no notion of what changed.
tempting, but each round rewrites the whole output.
questions.explain: MapReduce reads everything again each round, whatever changed.

questions.q: True or false: A scheduler stops the iterations only when the algorithm has exactly zero edges left to follow.
questions.explain: The condition can also be that the change compared with the last iteration is below some threshold.
questions.rule: A threshold also ends the loop.

questions.q: Which two kinds of completion condition does the chapter give for an iterative job?
options: No more edges to follow, or the change from last time being below a threshold
