A fixed time limit, or a maximum number of reducers allowed in the job
The scheduler restarting, or the input file growing
All mappers finishing, or the output being sorted
optionExplain: Right: either signals the algorithm is done.
tempting, but neither is given as a completion condition.
tempting, but neither of these signals that the algorithm has finished.
tempting, but those happen in every round.
questions.explain: Convergence is checked after each round by the scheduler.
questions.teaches: The scheduler checks completion based on a condition such as no more edges to follow, or a change compared with the last iteration below some threshold.

questions.q: A PageRank job needs 30 rounds on a graph where most ranks settle after 3. How does MapReduce behave?
options: It stops processing settled vertices after round 3
It processes only the changing vertices after round 3
It caches settled ranks in memory between rounds
It reprocesses the entire graph in all 30 rounds
optionExplain: tempting, but the framework has no such notion.
tempting, but each round reads the entire input.
tempting, but state is not kept in memory across jobs.
Right: it cannot skip the settled parts.
questions.explain: Settled parts are still read and rewritten in every round.
questions.teaches: MapReduce will always read the entire input dataset and produce a completely new output dataset, even if only a small part of the graph has changed.

questions.q: In the Pregel model, how does one vertex send information to another?
options: By reading the other vertex's memory directly
By sending a message, typically along an edge
By writing a file that the other vertex opens
By querying a shared database for its row
optionExplain: tempting, but vertices communicate only by messages.
Right: vertices pass messages and do not query each other.
tempting, but that is how MapReduce jobs communicate.
tempting, but no shared database is involved.
questions.explain: Message passing along edges is the communication primitive. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Pregel is the common name for the bulk ____ parallel model of computation.
questions.explain: BSP stands for bulk synchronous parallel.

questions.q: In round 7, a region of the graph receives no messages. What does Pregel do for those vertices?
options: It reprocesses them using the state stored on disk
No work, because the function is called only with incoming messages
It calls their functions with empty message lists, to be safe, in every round
It restarts the whole round for those vertices
optionExplain: tempting, but the state is in memory and no processing is needed.
Right: nothing arrived, so nothing needs processing.
tempting, but the work is avoided where no messages flow.
tempting, but rounds are not restarted for idle regions.
questions.explain: Idle parts of the graph cost nothing.

questions.q: True or false: In Pregel a vertex must read its whole state from disk at the start of every iteration.
questions.explain: A vertex remembers its state in memory from one iteration to the next, so only new incoming messages need processing.

questions.q: How does Pregel differ from the actor model, even though each vertex resembles an actor?
options: Pregel vertices share memory and actors do not
Pregel messages can be delivered in any order and at any time, as with actors
Pregel keeps no state between rounds, unlike actors
Vertex state and messages are durable, and delivery happens in fixed rounds
optionExplain: tempting, but vertices pass messages and share nothing.
tempting, but delivery follows fixed rounds.
tempting, but vertices keep state in memory.
Right: actors normally have no such guarantees.
questions.explain: Fixed rounds and durability set Pregel apart from actors.
questions.teaches: At every iteration the framework delivers all messages sent in the previous iteration, a timing guarantee that actors normally lack.

questions.q: Why do Pregel jobs spend less time waiting on communication than they would if vertices could query each other?
options: Messages can be batched, so the only waiting is between iterations
Vertices can query each other's memory with no network at all
The scheduler skips the barrier between iterations
Vertices send each message as a separate network packet
optionExplain: Right: that is the benefit of message-only communication.
tempting, but they cannot query each other.
tempting, but a barrier does exist between iterations.
tempting, but messages are batched to reduce waiting.
questions.explain: Batching messages reduces waiting, leaving only the wait between rounds.
questions.teaches: The prior iteration must completely finish, and all its messages be copied over the network, before the next can start; that is the only waiting.

questions.q: What does a Pregel implementation guarantee about each message despite an unreliable network?
options: It is processed at most once, so lost messages are skipped
It is processed at least once, so duplicates are possible and the vertex must cope
It is processed exactly once at the destination vertex in the next iteration
It is processed in the same iteration it was sent
optionExplain: tempting, but the guarantee is exactly once.
tempting, but duplicates are hidden from the vertex.
Right: the framework hides drops and duplicates.
tempting, but delivery is in the following iteration.
questions.explain: Exactly-once processing is guaranteed one iteration later. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Pregel saves vertex state by periodically ____ it to durable storage at the end of an iteration.
questions.explain: Writing the full state of all vertices is the checkpoint.

questions.q: A node fails in iteration 12; the last checkpoint was after iteration 10. What is the simplest recovery?
options: Continue from iteration 12 using the surviving nodes
Restart the computation from the original input files
Replay only iteration 11 on the failed node
Roll the whole graph back to iteration 10's checkpoint and rerun
optionExplain: tempting, but the lost state cannot be rebuilt that way.
tempting, but a checkpoint is a closer point.
tempting, but the simplest recovery rolls back everything.
Right: memory state was lost, so restart from the last durable copy.
questions.explain: Simplest recovery restores all vertices to the last checkpoint.

questions.q: True or false: After a failure, Pregel can recover only a lost partition and cannot roll back the entire graph.
questions.explain: The simplest solution rolls back the entire graph computation; partition-only recovery needs a deterministic algorithm and logged messages.
questions.rule: Full rollback is the simple option.

questions.q: What two conditions allow Pregel to recover only the partition that was lost?
options: The graph fits in memory and has no cycles
The algorithm is deterministic and messages are logged
The checkpoint is replicated and the clock is synchronized
The messages are encrypted and the vertices are sorted
optionExplain: tempting, but neither condition enables selective recovery.
Right: the same messages can then be replayed to rebuild the partition.
tempting, but neither is the stated condition.
tempting, but these are unrelated to recovery.
questions.explain: Determinism plus logged messages permits selective recovery.
questions.teaches: With a deterministic algorithm and logged messages it is possible to selectively recover only the partition that was lost, as discussed for dataflow engines.

questions.q: A Pregel job takes checkpoints every iteration, and checkpoints are slow. What is the trade being made?
options: Faster normal runs, in return for losing all state on failure
Slower recovery, in return for exactly-once delivery
Slower normal runs in return for a recent point to roll back to
Faster recovery, in return for dropping messages
optionExplain: tempting, but the state is saved on purpose.
tempting, but exactly-once is a separate guarantee.
Right: writing full state costs time but limits redone work.
tempting, but no messages are dropped.
questions.explain: Frequent checkpoints cost time in normal runs but cut the work redone after a failure.
questions.teaches: Like MapReduce, the framework transparently recovers from faults in order to simplify the programming model for algorithms on top of Pregel.

questions.q: How is a graph often partitioned across machines in Pregel-style systems in practice?
options: By an arbitrarily assigned vertex ID, with no attempt to group related vertices
By grouping vertices that exchange the most messages onto the same machine in advance
By placing each connected component on a single machine
By sorting vertices alphabetically by their names
optionExplain: Right: optimal partitioning is hard, so arbitrary IDs are used instead.
tempting, but finding that grouping is hard and rarely done.
tempting, but nothing in the chapter says so.
tempting, but the chapter mentions vertex IDs.
questions.explain: Arbitrary ID-based partitioning ignores which vertices talk to which. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Because a vertex function deals with only one vertex at a time, the approach is sometimes called thinking like a ____.
questions.explain: The one-vertex-at-a-time view lets the framework partition arbitrarily.

questions.q: A graph of 8 GB must be ranked on a team's server with 64 GB of memory. What does the chapter suggest first?
options: A single-machine algorithm, which will quite likely beat a distributed job
A Pregel cluster, since graph jobs always need many machines to hold the vertices
A MapReduce loop with a scheduler, for better fault tolerance
A key-value store, with one lookup per edge
optionExplain: Right: the graph fits in memory on one computer.
tempting, but network overhead can make a cluster slower.
tempting, but that rewrites the whole graph each round.
tempting, but the chapter does not suggest this.
questions.explain: If the graph fits in memory, one machine can win.

questions.q: True or false: In graph jobs the messages between nodes are usually much smaller than the original graph.
questions.explain: The intermediate state, meaning the messages sent between nodes, is often bigger than the original graph.

questions.q: What option does the chapter give for a graph too big for memory but small enough for one computer's disks?
options: A cluster with one vertex per machine, so messages never wait for each other
A MapReduce workflow with a sort-merge join
Single-machine processing with a framework such as GraphChi
A Pregel job with checkpoints every round
optionExplain: tempting, but this is the costliest layout.
tempting, but it is not suggested for this case.
Right: it works on graphs held on disk.
tempting, but a cluster is needed only if one machine cannot hold the graph.
questions.explain: A disk-based single-machine tool still avoids the network cost.
questions.teaches: If the graph fits on the disks of a single computer, single-machine processing using a framework such as GraphChi is a viable option.

questions.q: A graph is 40 TB and no single computer can hold it. What does the chapter say about the approach?
options: Single-machine processing is still the best option
A distributed approach such as Pregel is unavoidable
Graph processing is impossible at this size
A plain MapReduce job beats Pregel in this case
optionExplain: tempting, but the graph does not fit.
Right: no one machine can hold the data.
tempting, but distributed approaches such as Pregel exist for this case.
tempting, but that is not claimed.
questions.explain: Only when the graph is too big for one machine is a cluster unavoidable.
questions.teaches: Efficiently parallelizing graph algorithms is an area of ongoing research.

questions.q: Which building blocks do the dataflow APIs of Spark and Flink generally use to express a computation?
options: Graph-style ones: vertices, edges and messages
Stream-style ones: unbounded logs and offsets
File-style ones: open, read, seek and close, as in a filesystem API
Relational-style ones: join, group by key, filter and aggregate
optionExplain: tempting, but those belong to the Pregel model.
tempting, but that is the next chapter's topic.
tempting, but those are low-level filesystem calls.
Right: these map onto the join and grouping algorithms.
questions.explain: Relational-style blocks sit on top of the join and grouping algorithms. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Besides requiring less code, high-level interfaces allow ____ use, writing analysis code incrementally in a shell.
questions.explain: Interactive use helps when exploring a dataset.

questions.q: An analyst wants to try five ways of cleaning a new dataset and look at results after each. Which style fits best?
options: A hand-written MapReduce job rebuilt for every try
A nightly scheduled workflow with fixed stages
A high-level API in a shell, run incrementally
A Pregel job with checkpoints after each try
optionExplain: tempting for control, but it is laborious for each experiment.
tempting for reliability, but feedback comes only once a day.
Right: interactive use suits exploration, since results come back quickly.
tempting for durability, but the data is not a graph.
questions.explain: Exploration needs quick iteration, which interactive shells provide.

questions.q: True or false: High-level batch APIs have no relation to the Unix philosophy, since they run on clusters.
questions.explain: Interactive, incremental use of these interfaces is reminiscent of the Unix philosophy.

questions.q: Which high-level APIs and languages does the chapter name as popular because hand-written MapReduce is laborious?
options: Hive, Pig, Cascading and Crunch
Giraph, GraphX and Gelly
Voldemort, Terrapin and ElephantDB
Teradata, Gamma and NonStop SQL
optionExplain: Right: these were built on top of MapReduce.
tempting, but these are Pregel-style graph processing APIs.
tempting, but these are key-value stores for batch output.
tempting, but these are MPP databases.
questions.explain: These languages ease writing jobs and could move to Tez without rewriting.
questions.teaches: With the emergence of Tez, these high-level languages gained the benefit of moving to the new dataflow engine without rewriting job code.

questions.q: A team's Hive scripts must move from MapReduce to Tez. What does the chapter say about the effort?
options: Every script must be rewritten as Java callbacks
The data must first be converted to a graph
The scripts must be limited to a single stage
The job code need not be rewritten
optionExplain: tempting, but that is the laborious approach the languages avoid.
tempting, but the engine change has no effect on data shape.
tempting, but dataflow engines handle multi-stage workflows.
Right: high-level languages can move to the new engine.
questions.explain: Declarative or high-level code is decoupled from the engine beneath it.
questions.teaches: Spark and Flink also include their own high-level dataflow APIs, often taking inspiration from FlumeJava.

questions.q: When joins are specified declaratively, who decides between a sort-merge join and a broadcast hash join?
options: The programmer, by naming the algorithm in code
The query optimizer, from the properties of the join inputs
The mapper, by checking the size of each record as it reads the input
The filesystem, when it replicates the blocks
optionExplain: tempting, but that is the non-declarative way.
Right: the application states only which joins it needs.
tempting, but mappers do not choose algorithms.
tempting, but the filesystem does not plan joins.
questions.explain: A declarative join leaves the how to the optimizer. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Hive, Spark and Flink have cost-based query ____ that can choose join algorithms and change the order of joins.
questions.explain: Reordering joins can minimize the amount of intermediate state.

questions.q: A query joins three tables. What else can a cost-based optimizer do besides choosing each join algorithm?
options: Change the contents of the tables to make joins cheaper
Change the order of the joins to minimize intermediate state
Convert the three tables into a single graph
Move the output into an external key-value store
optionExplain: tempting, but the data is left as it is.
Right: the order changes how much data is carried forward.
tempting, but that is a different data model.
tempting, but that is a batch output pattern and not an optimization.
questions.explain: Join order is part of what the optimizer controls.

questions.q: True or false: A declarative join forces the programmer to understand and remember every join algorithm in the chapter.
questions.explain: It is nice not to have to remember the join algorithms, which is possible when joins are specified declaratively.

questions.q: Where had the declarative idea been met earlier in the book?
options: In the replication chapter, with leader election
In the partitioning chapter, with hash ranges
In the storage chapter, with SSTables only
In query languages for data, in the data models chapter
optionExplain: tempting, but that is not about query languages.
tempting, but that is about splitting data.
tempting, but column storage is the related link later.
Right: the application states what it wants, not how.
questions.explain: Declarative query languages were covered in the data models chapter.
questions.teaches: The idea of declarative specification, where the application states what is needed and the system decides how, was previously met in Query Languages for Data.

questions.q: A team hand-codes a sort-merge join, but one input turns out to be tiny. What would a declarative join have done?
options: Let the optimizer see the small input and pick a broadcast hash join
Failed, because declarative joins cannot take small inputs
Still run a sort-merge join, since declarative joins have one algorithm
Copied the tiny input into every reducer by hand
optionExplain: Right: it analyzes the properties of the inputs.
tempting, but nothing prevents small inputs.
tempting, but several algorithms exist behind the declaration.
tempting, but the framework handles that on its own.
questions.explain: Letting the framework see the inputs lets it pick a cheaper join.
questions.teaches: The framework can analyze the properties of the join inputs and automatically decide which of the join algorithms would be most suitable for the task at hand.

questions.q: What is the advantage of MapReduce's callback style over SQL?
options: The optimizer can inspect every callback and reorder it
Callbacks are always faster than declarative operators
A mapper or reducer can call arbitrary code and existing libraries
Callbacks avoid the need for any distributed filesystem
optionExplain: tempting, but callbacks are opaque to optimizers.
tempting, but arbitrary code costs CPU overhead on every record.
Right: the function is free to do anything to produce output.
tempting, but MapReduce relies on one.
questions.explain: Arbitrary code reaches the whole ecosystem of libraries. The card next shows why.

questions.q: A mapper or reducer is a user-defined function called as a ____ for each record or group of records.
questions.explain: MapReduce is built around the idea of function callbacks.

questions.q: A job must run image analysis on every photo in a dataset. Which style does the chapter's reasoning favour?
options: Pure SQL, since declarative queries cover all processing
A graph algorithm, since photos are linked by edges
A stream processor, as photos arrive over time
Callbacks, which can use an existing image analysis library
optionExplain: tempting, but SQL does not run arbitrary library code well.
tempting, but the data is not a graph.
tempting, but the chapter's reasoning concerns arbitrary code.
Right: the library ecosystem is available to callbacks.
questions.explain: Existing libraries are reached through callbacks.

questions.q: True or false: MPP databases integrate user-defined functions smoothly with package managers such as npm and Maven.
questions.explain: Database user-defined functions are often cumbersome to use and not well integrated with package managers and dependency management systems.

questions.q: What has long distinguished batch systems of MapReduce heritage from MPP databases, according to the chapter?
options: Their ability to run SQL on a cluster
The freedom to easily run arbitrary code
Their reliance on a shared-nothing design
Their use of a cost-based query optimizer
optionExplain: tempting, but MPP databases also do that.
Right: databases offer it only through awkward user-defined functions.
tempting, but both families use shared-nothing hardware.
tempting, but both can have one.
questions.explain: Arbitrary code is the long-standing differentiator.
questions.teaches: The freedom to easily run arbitrary code has long distinguished batch processing systems of MapReduce heritage from MPP databases.

questions.q: A team needs both library-based text parsing and optimizer-chosen joins in one job. What do dataflow engines offer?
options: Only callbacks, so the joins must be hand-coded
Only declarative operators, so parsing must move elsewhere
Callbacks for the parsing and declarative operators for the joins
Neither, as the two styles cannot share a job
optionExplain: tempting, but declarative operators exist in the same APIs.
tempting, but callbacks remain available alongside declarative operators.
Right: they mix both styles in one job.
tempting, but the engines combine them.
questions.explain: Dataflow engines add declarative features while keeping arbitrary code.
questions.teaches: Having the extensibility of running arbitrary code and reading data in arbitrary formats retains the batch frameworks' flexibility advantage.

questions.q: Why can a declarative filter allow the engine to read fewer bytes from disk than a callback?
options: The optimizer can read only the required columns from a column-oriented layout
The optimizer compresses the callback into a smaller file before it is run
The callback is run on the disk controller itself
The filter is applied after copying all the data to one machine
optionExplain: Right: it knows which fields are used.
tempting, but compression of the callback is not the issue.
tempting, but callbacks run in the job's tasks.
tempting, but that would read more, not less.
questions.explain: Declarative operators reveal which columns are needed. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Hive, Spark DataFrames and Impala use ____ execution, iterating over data in a tight inner loop that is friendly to CPU caches.
questions.explain: Vectorized execution also avoids function calls.

questions.q: A callback only selects two fields from 100-field records. What cost does it carry at billions of records?
options: A function call per record, which adds significant CPU overhead
A full sort of the records before the selection
A network copy of every field of every record to the reducer
A rebuild of the graph from its vertices
optionExplain: Right: an opaque callback is invoked for every record.
tempting, but selection needs no sorting.
tempting, but the cost described is the per-record call.
tempting, but the data is not a graph.
questions.explain: A simple callback still pays the per-record function-call overhead.

questions.q: True or false: Spark generates native machine code for its tight inner loops, while Impala generates JVM bytecode.
questions.explain: It is the other way around: Spark generates JVM bytecode and Impala uses LLVM to generate native code.

questions.q: What does Impala use to generate native code for its inner loops?
options: JVM bytecode, as Spark does
The Unix awk interpreter
LLVM
A MapReduce mapper per record
optionExplain: tempting, but that is how Spark generates its loops.
tempting, but awk plays no role in these loops.
Right: Impala uses LLVM, whereas Spark generates JVM bytecode.
tempting, but that would add the call overhead being avoided.
questions.explain: Impala compiles with LLVM; Spark emits JVM bytecode.
questions.teaches: Spark generates JVM bytecode and Impala uses LLVM to generate native code for these inner loops.

questions.q: What happens to the gap between batch frameworks and MPP databases as declarative features are added?
options: The gap widens, as callbacks become the only supported style for new jobs
Batch frameworks begin to look more like MPP databases and can approach comparable performance
The gap closes because arbitrary code is removed from the batch frameworks
The gap is unchanged, as optimizers are irrelevant
optionExplain: tempting, but declarative features are being added.
Right: while keeping their flexibility advantage.
tempting, but arbitrary code remains possible.
tempting, but optimizers exploit the declarative parts.
questions.explain: Declarative parts give performance close to MPP databases; arbitrary code keeps flexibility.
questions.teaches: By incorporating declarative aspects and optimizers that take advantage of them, batch frameworks can achieve comparable performance to MPP databases.

questions.q: Which tool implements machine learning algorithms inside a relational MPP database rather than on a batch engine?
options: Mahout, running on MapReduce
GraphChi, running on one machine
Hive, running on Tez
MADlib, running inside Apache HAWQ
optionExplain: tempting, but Mahout runs on MapReduce, Spark and Flink.
tempting, but GraphChi is for single-machine graph processing.
tempting, but Hive is a query language and not a machine learning library.
Right: it brings similar functionality into the database.
questions.explain: MADlib lives in an MPP database; Mahout lives on batch engines. The card next shows why.

questions.q: The spatial algorithm that searches for items close to a given item in a multi-dimensional space is k-nearest ____.
questions.explain: It is a kind of similarity search.

questions.q: A team wants a recommendation system on an existing Spark cluster and prefers not to write the algorithms. What fits?
options: MADlib, which runs on Spark clusters
Pregel, which recommends items out of the box
A reusable library such as Mahout, which runs on Spark
A Unix pipeline of awk and sort commands
optionExplain: tempting, but MADlib runs inside an MPP database.
tempting, but Pregel is a graph model and not a recommender.
Right: it implements machine learning algorithms on several engines.
tempting, but it does not scale to this case.
questions.explain: Mahout offers recommendation algorithms on MapReduce, Spark and Flink.

questions.q: True or false: Approximate search matters in genome analysis because algorithms need to find strings that are exactly identical.
questions.explain: Genome analysis needs to find strings that are similar but not identical, which is why approximate search is important.

questions.q: What does the chapter conclude about batch engines and MPP databases as each gains the other's features?
options: They begin to look more alike, as systems for storing and processing data
They split further, because their goals differ and each keeps its own strengths
Batch engines replace MPP databases entirely
MPP databases drop SQL in favour of callbacks
optionExplain: Right: built-in functions and programmability bring them together.
tempting, but the trend described is convergence.
tempting, but no replacement is claimed.
tempting, but nothing says SQL is dropped.
questions.explain: Both are, in the end, systems for storing and processing data.
questions.teaches: As batch systems gain built-in functionality and high-level declarative operators, and MPP databases become more programmable and flexible, the two begin to look more alike.

questions.q: Traditionally, which domain did MPP databases serve, and what does the chapter say it is among many?
options: Genome analysis, the only domain for batch work
Graph ranking, the only domain for which batch work is used today
Log shipping, the only domain for batch work
Business intelligence and reporting, one of many batch domains
optionExplain: tempting, but genome analysis is one of many domains.
tempting, but ranking is another example.
tempting, but this is not described.
Right: batch processing now reaches further.
questions.explain: Business reporting is only one domain in which batch processing is used.
questions.rule: BI is one domain among many.
questions.teaches: Batch processing engines are being used for distributed execution of algorithms from an increasingly wide range of domains.

questions.q: In MapReduce, what determines how mappers are partitioned?
options: The hash of the join key
The blocks of the input files
The number of reducers configured
The order of keys after sorting
optionExplain: tempting, but that decides reducer partitions.
Right: mappers are partitioned according to input file blocks.
tempting, but that sets the reducer side.
tempting, but sorting happens after mapping.
questions.explain: Input blocks decide the mapper partitions. The card next shows why.

questions.q: Post-MapReduce dataflow engines try to avoid ____ unless it is required, but otherwise partition in a broadly similar way.
questions.explain: MapReduce sorts between every map and reduce stage.

questions.q: A MapReduce job and a Spark job both lose a worker. Which one must typically recompute more data?
options: The MapReduce job, since it writes less to disk
The Spark job, since it keeps more in memory and materializes less
Both equally, since they keep the same state
Neither, as both replicate all state three times across the nodes
optionExplain: tempting, but it writes to disk frequently.
Right: less durable state means more recomputation.
tempting, but they differ in materialization.
tempting, but dataflow engines avoid that replication.
questions.explain: Less materialization means more to recompute after a failure.

questions.q: True or false: Writing to disk often makes MapReduce quicker in the failure-free case, at the cost of harder recovery.
questions.explain: Frequent writes make recovery of a single task easy but slow down execution when nothing fails.

questions.q: What reduces the amount of data that must be recomputed after a node fails in a dataflow engine?
options: A faster network between nodes
A larger number of reducers
A sort before each operator
Deterministic operators
optionExplain: tempting, but speed does not change the amount to recompute.
tempting, but reducer count is a partitioning choice.
tempting, but sorting is avoided unless required.
Right: they produce the same output when rerun.
questions.explain: Repeatable outputs keep downstream operators from being redone.
questions.teaches: Deterministic operators reduce the amount of data that needs to be recomputed.

questions.q: A team must pick between an engine that recovers a failed task cheaply and one that runs faster when nothing fails. What is the trade?
options: Heavy materialization eases recovery but slows normal runs; light does the opposite
Heavy materialization speeds both recovery and normal runs
Light materialization makes recovery free, since nothing was ever written down
Recovery and speed are unrelated to materialization
optionExplain: Right: recovery cost versus failure-free speed.
tempting, but it slows the failure-free case.
tempting, but more must be recomputed.
tempting, but the degree of materialization affects both recovery and speed.
questions.explain: Materialization trades normal-run speed against recovery cost.
questions.teaches: The purpose of repartitioning, sorting and merging is to bring all the related data, such as records with the same key, together in the same place.

questions.q: What assumption about callbacks such as mappers and reducers lets a batch framework retry tasks safely?
options: They run only once and are never rerun
They write results to an external database as they go
They are stateless and have no side effects besides their designated output
They share memory with every other task so state survives a retry
optionExplain: tempting, but retries are exactly what is allowed.
tempting, but external writes would repeat on a retry.
Right: a retry then repeats only harmless work.
tempting, but shared state would make retries unsafe.
questions.explain: Statelessness makes retries safe. The card next shows why.

questions.q: If several tasks for a partition succeed, only ____ of them actually makes its output visible.
questions.explain: The framework discards extra outputs.

questions.q: A reducer task crashes and is retried on another machine. What happens to the crashed task's output?
options: It is merged with the retry's output
It is published, and the retry is ignored
It is kept alongside as a second copy
It is discarded, and only the retry's output is used
optionExplain: tempting, but partial output would corrupt the result.
tempting, but failed output is discarded.
tempting, but only one output becomes visible.
Right: failed tasks leave nothing visible.
questions.explain: Failed output is thrown away, so the final result is unaffected.

questions.q: True or false: A batch job's final output can differ depending on how many tasks had to be retried.
questions.explain: The framework can guarantee that the final output is the same as if no faults had occurred.

questions.q: How do the batch semantics compare with online services that write to databases as a side effect of requests?
options: They are weaker, since failures change the output
They are much stronger than what online services usually have
They are the same, as both retry on failure
They are unrelated, as online services need no guarantees
optionExplain: tempting, but the output matches a fault-free run.
Right: faults are hidden from the job's code.
tempting, but online side effects can repeat.
tempting, but online services do need them.
questions.explain: Online services with side effects must handle repeated writes themselves.
questions.teaches: These reliable semantics are much stronger than what you usually have in online services that handle user requests and that write to databases as a side effect of processing a request.

questions.q: A mapper also sends an email for each record it reads. What goes wrong when tasks are retried?
options: Nothing, as the framework also retracts sent emails
The job fails, as mappers may not read records that are inside a retry
Emails are sent again, since the side effect is visible outside the output
The emails are sent only once, as retries are not visible
optionExplain: tempting, but the framework cannot undo external effects.
tempting, but reading records is allowed and is what mappers do.
Right: the restriction forbids such side effects.
tempting, but the side effect happens on each attempt.
questions.explain: Only the designated output is protected; outside effects repeat on each attempt.
questions.teaches: Your code in a batch job does not need to implement fault-tolerance mechanisms, because the framework guarantees the final output is as if no faults had occurred.

questions.q: What does it mean that the input of a batch job is bounded?
options: It has a known, fixed size, so the job can tell when it is done
It is stored on a single machine
It is sorted by key before the job starts, with all records in order
It cannot be read more than once
optionExplain: Right: it can be cut off at a point in time.
tempting, but bounded refers to size and not location.
tempting, but order is not the point.
tempting, but the input is immutable and can be reread.
questions.explain: A bounded input has an end. The card next shows why.

questions.q: A batch job produces output that is ____ from its input, without modifying the input.
questions.explain: The output is derived from the input.

questions.q: A job reads the log files collected up to midnight and writes a daily report. Is its input bounded?
options: Yes, because the set of files at that point in time has a fixed size
No, because logs are written continuously
No, because the report is written in text rather than in a binary format
Yes, because the report is smaller than the input
optionExplain: Right: the snapshot has a known end.
tempting, but the job reads a snapshot, not the live stream.
tempting, but the format is unrelated to boundedness.
tempting, but the size of the output is unrelated.
questions.explain: A snapshot of files at one moment is bounded.

questions.q: True or false: A batch job may modify its input files in place as it processes them.
questions.explain: A batch job reads input and produces output without modifying the input; the output is derived from it.

questions.q: Which two examples of bounded input does the chapter give?
options: A live feed of user clicks, and a message queue that keeps receiving records
A stream of sensor readings, and a topic of events in a log that keeps growing
A set of log files at some point in time, and a snapshot of a database's contents
A running counter, and a heartbeat signal
optionExplain: tempting, but both of these keep growing and never reach an end.
tempting, but both of these are unbounded and have no end.
Right: both have a known, fixed size, so a job can finish.
tempting, but both of these continue forever with no end.
questions.explain: Files at a point in time and database snapshots are bounded.
questions.teaches: Examples of bounded input are a set of log files at some point in time, or a snapshot of a database's contents.

questions.q: A team's data arrives continuously with no end. What does the chapter suggest regarding batch processing?
options: Batch jobs handle it by waiting for the input to end before they start
The unbounded case is the subject of the next chapter, on streams
Batch jobs handle it by ignoring new records
Batch jobs handle it by sorting records first
optionExplain: tempting, but unbounded input has no end.
Right: batch assumes a known, fixed size.
tempting, but ignoring new records discards data.
tempting, but sorting needs the whole input.
questions.explain: Unbounded data needs a different model than a finishing batch job.
questions.teaches: Because the input is bounded, a job knows when it has finished reading it; stream processing, covered next, handles data that is not bounded.

questions.q: A store's sales events keep arriving with no final end. Why does a batch job process them in daily slices?
options: A distributed filesystem cannot hold more than one day of records, so older records must be deleted first
Batch jobs run faster when each run covers a short period, so the slices reduce the total work
The job needs to know when its input is finished, and endless data never finishes
Sales events can only be encoded in a file format once per day, so a daily boundary is required
optionExplain: Storage size is not the issue; the slicing comes from the job needing a finite input to finish.
Short runs do not reduce total work; they only change how soon results appear.
Right: a batch job must know where its input ends, so endless data is artificially divided into slices.
Events can be encoded at any time; the daily boundary comes from the job design, not from the encoding.
questions.explain: A batch job needs a known end to its input, so unbounded data is cut into slices. The card next shows how streams avoid the cut.
questions.rule: Batch needs an end to its input.

questions.q: Input that has no known end and keeps arriving over time is called ____ input.
questions.explain: Batch jobs assume bounded input of known, finite size. A stream is data made available incrementally over time and never has to end.

questions.q: A ride-booking app wants driver earnings to update within seconds of a trip, not after a nightly job. What change addresses this?
options: Process each trip event as it happens, instead of waiting for a time slice to end
Run the nightly job on a much larger cluster, so each night's run finishes in minutes
Sort the night's trips by driver first, so that the output can begin before all input is read
Write trips into a relational table, so the nightly job can read them faster
optionExplain: Right: removing the slices removes the wait for the slice to finish.
A faster job still runs once per night, so earnings still lag until the next run.
Sorting needs the whole input first, so it cannot start output early; this is the very problem.
A faster read helps the job finish sooner but does not remove the daily slice boundary.
questions.explain: Delay comes from waiting for the slice to end, not from slow processing. Handling events as they arrive removes the wait.
questions.rule: Remove the slice to remove the wait.

questions.q: True or false: A user acts at 10:05; the hourly batch job, run at each hour's end, can show it before 11:00.
questions.explain: The job only reads that hour's data once the hour has ended. If the slice shrinks to a second, the delay shrinks to about a second, and with continuous processing it nearly disappears.
questions.rule: Delay is about the length of the slice.

questions.q: Why can the sort at the heart of MapReduce not start emitting output before it has read all of its input?
options: The sort writes to a single output file, which can only be opened once all records exist
The input files are immutable, so partial results would change when the files are later replaced
Output keys must be assigned from a counter that is only known after the last record
The last record read might have the lowest key, so it would have to be output first
optionExplain: Output files are not the obstacle; the ordering depends on seeing every key.
Immutability of the input is not the reason; the order of the output is.
Keys come from the records, not from a counter assigned after reading.
Right: any later record might sort first, so output cannot begin until the input has ended.
questions.explain: Sorting needs to see every record, because any one of them could belong first. That is why it needs bounded input.
questions.teaches: MapReduce's sort must read its entire input before producing output, because the last record read could be the one with the lowest key and so the first one out.

questions.q: A team reads 'stream' in the chapter and thinks it means a message queue product. Which use of the word fits the chapter's general meaning?
options: A database table that has been exported to a single file overnight
Audio delivered over the internet while it is still being played
A set of records that is complete before anyone reads it
A report that is produced once at the end of each month
optionExplain: An exported file is bounded and complete, the opposite of a stream.
Right: data made available incrementally over time, as with audio and video, is a stream.
A complete set that is read afterwards is bounded data, not a stream.
A monthly report is the output of a slice, not data arriving incrementally.
questions.explain: The chapter uses stream broadly: stdin and stdout of Unix, lazy lists, file APIs, TCP connections, and audio and video over the internet all qualify.
questions.rule: A stream is data made available over time.
questions.teaches: The word stream is used broadly: Unix stdin and stdout, lazy lists, file APIs such as FileInputStream, TCP connections, and audio and video over the internet are all streams.

questions.q: In a streaming system, what do you expect one 'event' to contain?
options: A running summary of everything the system has seen up to the present moment
Details of something that happened, usually with a timestamp
A request for another service to carry out an action and return a result
A pointer to a database row that the consumer must go and read
optionExplain: A running summary is derived state, not a single event.
Right: an event is a small record of something that happened, often timestamped.
A request to act is closer to an RPC call than to a record of something that happened.
An event is self-contained, so it does not need a pointer to be understood.
questions.explain: An event records something that happened. The card next defines it with producers, consumers and topics.

questions.q: In streaming terms, related events are grouped into a ____.
questions.explain: Related events are grouped into a topic or stream, in the way a filename identifies a set of related records in a filesystem.

questions.q: A fitness app records a CPU temperature reading from a watch every minute. How does the chapter describe such a reading?
options: As a topic, because a series of readings is grouped under one watch
As a producer, because it is the source of the data entering the system
As a consumer, because the app receives the data and stores it
As an event: a periodic measurement from a sensor
optionExplain: A topic is the group that readings belong to, not a single reading.
The watch or app that sends readings acts as the producer; the reading itself is the event.
A consumer is whatever processes events, not the data itself.
Right: events can come from user actions or from machines, such as a periodic sensor measurement.
questions.explain: The chapter's examples of events include user actions, such as viewing a page, and machine readings, such as temperature or CPU metrics.
questions.rule: Events can come from people or machines.

questions.q: True or false: An engineer says the producer creates a separate event for each consumer. This matches the chapter.
questions.explain: The chapter says an event is generated once by a producer and then potentially processed by multiple consumers.

questions.q: Where does an event usually carry its timestamp from, according to the chapter?
options: A time-of-day clock, recording when it happened
A monotonic clock, recording the elapsed time since the process started
The message broker's counter, assigned in arrival order
The consumer's clock, recorded at the moment it reads the event
optionExplain: Right: events usually contain a timestamp from a time-of-day clock.
Monotonic clocks measure elapsed time and have no meaning as dates, so they do not fit this role.
A broker counter such as an offset exists, but it is separate from the event's own timestamp.
A consumer-side clock would give processing time, which the chapter later contrasts with when the event occurred.
questions.explain: The timestamp records when the event happened according to a time-of-day clock, as discussed in the earlier chapter on clocks.
questions.teaches: An event usually contains a timestamp from a time-of-day clock indicating when it happened, rather than a monotonic clock.

questions.q: A web server log is processed with Unix tools in an earlier chapter. In streaming terms, what is each log line?
options: A topic, because every line concerns the same web server
A consumer, because it is read by the processing tool
An event, much like a record read from a file
A trigger, because writing it causes other work to start
optionExplain: The whole log, taken as a group, would be nearer to a topic than any single line.
The tool processing the lines would be the consumer, not the lines.
Right: each line of the web server log is an event, the same thing as a record.
Triggers are database features, not log records.
questions.explain: The chapter points out that in its earlier web log example each line of the log is an event, and a record in the batch world becomes an event in the streaming world.
questions.rule: Record in batch, event in streams.
questions.teaches: In the earlier Unix-tools batch example, each line of the web server log is already an event, so a record and an event are essentially the same thing.

questions.q: Many consumers check a database every second for new events. What is the main cost of polling this often?
options: Each poll deletes the events it reads, so other consumers lose them
The database must be encoded in a different format for every consumer
Polling forces all the consumers to read the events in a single shared order
Most requests find nothing new
optionExplain: Polling reads; it does not delete, and deletion is a feature of some brokers.
Encoding is unrelated to how often the consumers poll.
Polling does not impose a shared order on consumers.
Right: the more often you poll, the smaller the share of requests that return new events.
questions.explain: The cost of polling is wasted requests. The card next explains how notification avoids that.

questions.q: As polling becomes more frequent, the percentage of requests that return new events goes ____.
questions.explain: The more often you poll, the lower the percentage of requests that return new events, so the overhead per useful result grows.

questions.q: A search index must reflect new products within a second. The team polls the product table 50 times a second. What does the chapter suggest?
options: Let the consumer be notified when new events appear instead of polling
Poll at a higher rate, so each poll finds more new rows
Poll less often, so each poll finds more new rows, and accept a longer delay
Copy the whole table to the index once a day instead
optionExplain: Right: notification avoids the wasted requests of frequent polling.
Polling still faster raises overhead even more, since most polls find nothing new.
Less frequent polling does batch the work, but it gives up the one-second requirement.
A daily copy is a batch process and misses the delay target by a wide margin.
questions.explain: With a tight delay target, polling creates mostly empty requests. A notification mechanism lets work happen only when events exist.

questions.q: True or false: if consumers poll a datastore less often, the share of their requests that return new events rises.
questions.explain: Each poll then covers a longer interval, so it is more likely to find something new. The price is a longer delay before events are seen, which is why daily batch jobs poll once.
questions.rule: Less polling means fuller polls and more delay.

questions.q: Relational databases have triggers that react to a row being inserted. How does the chapter judge triggers as a notification tool?
options: The standard way to deliver events to many consumers at once with low delay
Very limited in capability, and an afterthought in database design
Fully equivalent to a message broker, so no specialised tool is required
Too slow for notification because they are evaluated once a day
optionExplain: Triggers react to changes, but they cannot do what a dedicated delivery tool does for many consumers.
Right: the chapter calls them very limited and somewhat of an afterthought.
Specialised tools were developed precisely because triggers fall short.
Triggers run when the change happens; the problem is their limited ability, not schedule.
questions.explain: Databases have traditionally not supported notification well, which is why specialised event-delivery tools were developed.
questions.rule: Triggers are limited, so specialised tools exist.
questions.teaches: Relational database triggers can react to a change such as a row insert, but they are very limited and were somewhat of an afterthought, which is why specialised notification tools were developed.

questions.q: A nightly job compares yesterday's invoices with the ledger. Someone suggests replacing its once-a-day file read with a notification system. What is a fair view?
options: It is needed, because polling once a day is the most expensive way to read data
It is required, because a file can never be read by more than one job
It would add little, since one daily poll returns plenty of new data
It would be wrong, because notification systems cannot hold more than a day of data
optionExplain: Polling once a day has very little overhead compared with polling every second.
A file written once can be read by many jobs; the chapter says so about batch processing.
Right: one poll a day finds a full day of new data, so the polling overhead the card describes does not arise.
Capacity of a notification system is not the issue; the daily job has no polling overhead to remove.
questions.explain: Our reading: polling overhead only bites when you poll often to get low delay. A daily job polls once, so notification buys nothing for it.
questions.rule: Low delay is what makes polling costly.
questions.teaches: In batch processing a file is written once and can then be read by multiple jobs, so a daily job polling a file or datastore is essentially what a batch process does.

questions.q: A producer sends 1,000 messages a second to a consumer that handles 600. What could the messaging system do?
options: Drop some messages, hold the extra in a queue, or block the producer
Speed up the consumer's processor until it keeps pace with the producer
Reorder messages so that the slowest ones are always handled first
Convert the messages to a smaller format so that they take less time
optionExplain: Right: the system can drop, buffer or apply backpressure.
A messaging system cannot make the consumer's hardware faster.
Reordering messages does not change how many the consumer can handle per second.
Encoding does not close a gap of this size between the producer and consumer rates.
questions.explain: The gap has to be absorbed somewhere. The card next names the three ways.

questions.q: Match each response to a fast producer with what it does.
pairs: Messages the consumer cannot handle are discarded
Extra messages wait in a queue
The producer is blocked from sending more
questions.explain: The three options differ in where the excess goes: discarded, stored, or held back at the source.

questions.q: A TCP connection has a small fixed-size buffer, and the receiver stops reading. What happens to the sender?
options: It silently discards the newest messages so the buffer never fills
It grows the buffer on disk until the receiver recovers
It is blocked until the receiver takes data out of the buffer
It starts delivering the same messages to a second receiver
optionExplain: Dropping is a different option; TCP does not discard on the sender's side here.
Growing a queue on disk is buffering, which brokers may do but TCP does not.
Right: this is backpressure, as in Unix pipes and TCP.
TCP connects exactly one sender with one receiver, so there is no second receiver.
questions.explain: Pipes and TCP block the sender once the small buffer is full, so the sender slows to the receiver's pace.

questions.q: Sort each behaviour into backpressure or not backpressure.

items.t: A Unix pipe makes the writer wait when its small buffer is full
A TCP sender is blocked until the receiver takes data out of the buffer
A broker lets its queue grow and writes the backlog to disk
A system discards the newest messages when the consumer is busy

questions.explain: Backpressure means blocking the producer. Growing a queue is buffering, and discarding messages is dropping.

questions.q: When a queue no longer fits in memory and messages are written to disk, what does the chapter say to ask?
options: Whether the producer should be told to resend all messages in order
Which consumer should be removed so that the queue can shrink
How the messages can be compressed into a single batch for the disk
How the disk access affects the performance of the messaging system
optionExplain: Resending is not part of the question the chapter raises.
Removing a consumer would make the backlog worse, not better.
Batching onto disk is not what the chapter asks about here.
Right: the chapter asks what the disk access does to performance.
questions.explain: The chapter asks whether the system crashes when the queue exceeds memory or writes to disk, and if so how disk access affects performance.
questions.rule: Queue growth has a performance cost.
questions.teaches: If messages are buffered, one should ask whether the system crashes when the queue no longer fits in memory or writes to disk, and how the disk access affects performance.

questions.q: A messaging tool blocks a web shop's checkout whenever the order consumer is slow. Which option does the tool use?
options: Buffering, which stores the extra orders in a queue
Backpressure, which blocks the producer from sending more
Dropping, which discards orders the consumer cannot handle
Fan-out, which delivers each order to every consumer
optionExplain: Buffering would let the checkout continue while orders wait.
Right: blocking the sender while the consumer is slow is what backpressure means.
Dropping would not block checkout; it would lose orders.
Fan-out is about delivering to several consumers, not about slow ones.
questions.explain: Backpressure protects the consumer by slowing the producer, which in a shop means the sender, here checkout, waits.
questions.rule: Backpressure moves the cost to the producer.
questions.teaches: Backpressure, also known as flow control, protects a slow consumer by blocking the producer, so the cost of a slow consumer shifts to the producer's side.

questions.q: A system sends a temperature reading every second and also counts completed purchases. Which can better tolerate occasional lost messages?
options: The purchase counter, since counters correct themselves over time
The temperature readings, since the next one arrives soon
Both equally, since any lost message is replaced by the next one
Neither, since losing any message always breaks a stream system
optionExplain: A lost purchase is never replaced, so the count stays too low.
Right: a missing periodic reading is soon replaced by an updated value.
Only periodic values are refreshed by a later message; counts are not.
Systems differ; the application decides whether some loss is acceptable.
questions.explain: How tolerant an application is of loss depends on what it does with the messages. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Loss tolerance depends on the use.

questions.q: True or false: If you can afford to sometimes lose messages, you can probably get higher throughput and lower latency on the same hardware.
questions.explain: Durability needs disk writes and/or replication, which cost time. Giving up some of it saves that cost.

questions.q: A game sends frame-rate samples to a dashboard and in-app purchases to a revenue counter. Where is message loss most costly?
options: The revenue counter, since every lost message makes the total incorrect
The frame-rate samples, since each missing sample leaves a permanent gap
Both are equally costly, because both come from the same app
Neither, because the next message always corrects any earlier loss
optionExplain: Right: when counting, each lost message means an incorrect counter.
A later sample soon replaces a missing frame-rate value.
They differ: a periodic value is superseded, a count is not.
A later message corrects a periodic value, but it cannot restore a lost increment.
questions.explain: Periodic readings are replaced by the next one; counts are cumulative. So loss costs more when counting.

questions.q: A metrics pipeline silently drops a large share of messages during an outage. What is a risk the chapter warns about?
options: The remaining messages will be delivered twice to make up the difference
All consumers will stop and the producer will be blocked
It may not be immediately apparent that the metrics are incorrect
The metrics will be exactly right, since averages hide missing points
optionExplain: Duplicate delivery is a different effect, tied to retries and acknowledgments.
Blocking the producer is backpressure, not what silent dropping does.
Right: the chapter warns that if many messages are dropped, the error may go unnoticed.
Averages computed from fewer points are still wrong, and may look plausible.
questions.explain: Silent loss looks like a lower number, not like an error. Large drops need to be monitored.
questions.teaches: If a large number of messages are dropped, it may not be immediately apparent that the metrics are incorrect.

questions.q: As with databases, message durability may require writing to disk and/or ____, which has a cost.
questions.explain: The chapter ties message durability to the same ideas as database durability, and notes that it costs throughput and latency.
questions.teaches: As with databases, message durability may require writing to disk and/or replication, which has a cost.

questions.q: A click counter for an ad campaign receives clicks over a fire-and-forget channel. What does the chapter's reasoning say?
options: It is fine, since occasional loss is acceptable for all kinds of events
It is fine as long as the dashboard shows averages instead of totals
It is impossible, since counters cannot be built on a message stream
It risks wrong counts, since a lost message skews the counter
optionExplain: Loss is acceptable only for data like periodic readings that are quickly replaced.
Averages computed from lost data are still skewed; they do not solve it.
Counting on a stream is possible, but it needs reliable delivery.
Right: when counting events, each lost message makes the counter wrong.
questions.explain: The StatsD example shows this: its counter metrics are only correct if all messages are received, so using UDP makes the metrics at best approximate.
questions.teaches: The StatsD protocol's counter metrics are only correct if all messages are received, so sending them over unreliable UDP makes the metrics at best approximate.

questions.q: A producer sends events straight to a consumer over the network, with no broker. What is the main weakness?
options: The consumer cannot ever receive events in the order they were produced
The producer must wait for every other producer before it can send
A consumer that is offline may miss messages sent meanwhile
The messages must be stored in a relational table before delivery
optionExplain: Direct channels can preserve order; order is not their main weakness.
Producers send independently; they do not wait for each other.
Right: a consumer that is unreachable misses the messages sent meanwhile.
Direct messaging has no database in the middle.
questions.explain: Without an intermediary, nobody holds messages for an absent consumer. The card next shows examples and limits.
questions.rule: No middle node, no holding place.

questions.q: Match each direct messaging example to how it works.
pairs: Used for stock market feeds where low latency matters
A brokerless library implementing publish/subscribe over TCP or IP multicast
A callback URL registered so a service makes a request on each event
questions.explain: All four skip a central broker. They differ in transport and in how they register interest.

questions.q: A payments service calls a URL that a partner registered whenever a refund is issued. What is this pattern called?
options: A webhook
A tombstone
A consumer offset
A hopping window
optionExplain: Right: a callback URL registered with a service, called when an event happens, is a webhook.
A tombstone marks a deletion in a compacted log.
An offset is a position in a log.
A hopping window is a type of time window for aggregation.
questions.explain: Webhooks make a direct HTTP or RPC request to the consumer when an event occurs.
questions.rule: A webhook pushes to a registered URL.

questions.q: True or false: when a producer with direct retries crashes, the messages it was retrying are still delivered after restart.
questions.explain: The retry buffer is lost when the producer crashes, so the approach may break down. That is why direct messaging tolerates only a limited set of faults.
questions.rule: A crashing producer loses its retry buffer.

questions.q: UDP is unreliable. How can a UDP multicast feed still recover from lost packets?
options: The network layer repairs the loss on its own, so the application needs no extra code
The consumer replays the log from an earlier offset that the broker has kept for it
The consumer asks the database for a snapshot of the latest values and carries on
Protocols above TCP/UDP recover them, but producers must remember what they sent
optionExplain: UDP itself does not repair loss; that is the point of the application-level protocol.
Brokers and offsets are not part of direct messaging.
A database snapshot is not how UDP multicast feeds recover.
Right: recovery happens at the application level, and the producer must keep what it sent.
questions.explain: The chapter notes that UDP is unreliable but application-level protocols can recover lost packets, as long as the producer retains what it sent.
questions.rule: Recovery needs the producer to remember.
questions.teaches: Application-level protocols can recover packets lost on unreliable UDP, but the producer must remember the packets it has sent so it can retransmit them on demand.

questions.q: A team wants metrics from many servers to reach one collector, and exact counts matter. Which direct option would the chapter suggest caution about?
options: Reliable TCP between each pair, because TCP never blocks the sender
Unreliable UDP, since counter metrics are only correct if all messages arrive
A message broker, because brokers cannot hold messages for clients that are offline
A webhook, because webhooks cannot carry any event data
optionExplain: TCP does apply backpressure and blocks the sender when its buffer fills; it is not the main concern for counts.
Right: StatsD-style UDP makes counters at best approximate.
Brokers hold messages for clients that come and go; that is their purpose.
A webhook carries a request when an event occurs and can carry its data.
questions.explain: UDP gives low overhead but no delivery guarantee, so exact counting needs more than a bare UDP channel.
questions.rule: Exact counts and UDP do not mix.
questions.teaches: Because StatsD uses unreliable UDP, its counter metrics are only correct if all messages are received, so they are at best approximate.

questions.q: What does putting a broker between producers and consumers mainly change?
options: Every consumer must now process messages in exactly the same instant
Clients can come and go, since the broker holds messages and takes over durability
Producers must keep their own copy of every message until the consumer has processed it
Messages can only be read once and must be read in the producer's absence
optionExplain: Brokers decouple timing; consumers do not process in lockstep.
Right: centralising data in the broker makes it easier to tolerate clients that connect, disconnect or crash.
Producers hand off messages; the broker takes over responsibility.
Brokers do not require the producer to be absent when messages are read.
questions.explain: A broker is a server that stores the messages in between. The card next explains what that changes.

questions.q: A message broker is also known as a message ____.
questions.explain: A message broker (also known as a message queue) is a kind of database optimised for handling message streams.
questions.rule: A broker is a database for messages.

questions.q: A mobile game's server must hand scores to a leaderboard service that restarts nightly. Where does the broker help most?
options: It lets the game server wait until the leaderboard has finished processing each score
It guarantees the leaderboard processes each score within a millisecond of sending
It removes the need for the leaderboard to ever store scores itself
It holds the scores while the leaderboard is down
optionExplain: The producer only waits for the broker to buffer the message, not for processing.
Delivery happens at an undetermined future time, often fast but not guaranteed to be within a millisecond.
A consumer still keeps its own state, such as the leaderboard; the broker only transports messages.
Right: the broker buffers messages for a consumer that is temporarily offline.
questions.explain: The broker makes the restart harmless to the producer, because messages wait there until the consumer returns.

questions.q: True or false: after a producer receives the broker's confirmation, the consumer has already processed the message.
questions.explain: The producer normally waits only for the broker to confirm it has buffered the message. Delivery to consumers happens at some undetermined future point.

questions.q: How do message brokers generally treat slow consumers, according to the chapter?
options: They generally allow unbounded queues, depending on setup
They always drop messages, because queues cannot be allowed to grow
They always apply backpressure to the producer, as TCP does
They remove the consumer permanently from the topic
optionExplain: Right: brokers generally allow unbounded queueing, as opposed to dropping or backpressure.
Dropping is one of the three options, but brokers generally choose queueing.
Backpressure is what pipes and TCP use; brokers generally queue instead.
The chapter does not say slow consumers are removed.
questions.explain: Among the three options for fast producers, brokers usually pick buffering, which makes consumers asynchronous.
questions.teaches: Faced with slow consumers, message brokers generally allow unbounded queueing rather than dropping messages or applying backpressure, though configuration can change this.

questions.q: A broker keeps messages only in memory. After the broker server crashes, which statement fits the chapter?
options: No broker can ever lose a message, because the broker is a database
The messages are safe because the producer has been told that they were buffered by the broker
It depends on configuration: some brokers keep messages only in memory, others write to disk
The consumer can rebuild the lost messages from its offset
optionExplain: A broker is a kind of database but memory-only operation can lose messages when it crashes.
Buffer confirmation does not help when the buffer is only in memory and the broker dies.
Right: some brokers keep messages only in memory, and others, depending on configuration, write them to disk.
Offsets belong to log-based brokers and do not recreate lost memory contents.
questions.explain: Durability moves to the broker, so it matters whether the broker writes to disk, replicates, or only keeps memory.
questions.rule: Check what the broker does on a crash.
questions.teaches: Some message brokers only keep messages in memory, while others, depending on configuration, write them to disk so they are not lost in a broker crash.

questions.q: A team wants to keep three years of order history in a traditional message broker. What is the problem?
options: Brokers cannot accept messages from more than one producer at a time
Brokers encrypt every message so that it cannot be read again later
Brokers only accept messages written in a binary format
Most brokers delete messages once delivered
optionExplain: Brokers allow multiple producers to send to the same topic.
Encryption is not the reason; deletion on delivery is.
Encoding format is not what limits long-term storage.
Right: most brokers automatically delete delivered messages.
questions.explain: Databases keep data until it is deleted, but most message brokers do not. The card next lists the differences.

questions.q: Sort each trait into database or traditional message broker.
questions.explain: Databases are built to store and query; traditional brokers are built to pass messages on and notify.
questions.rule: Store and query versus deliver and notify.

items.t: Keeps data until it is explicitly deleted
Deletes a message once it is successfully delivered
Query results are a point-in-time snapshot
Notifies clients when new messages arrive

questions.q: An analyst wants to learn whether a customer's balance changed after she first read it. Which system behaviour supports being told about the change?
options: A message broker, which notifies clients when new data arrives
A database query, which updates its earlier result automatically
A database secondary index, which signals clients that data changed
A snapshot, which refreshes itself every time a write occurs
optionExplain: Right: brokers notify clients when data changes, by delivering new messages.
A query result is a snapshot; the client is not told it is outdated unless it repeats the query or polls.
Indexes help find data; they do not notify clients.
A point-in-time snapshot does not refresh itself.
questions.explain: A query result goes stale silently. A broker pushes new messages, which is how clients learn something changed.

questions.q: True or false: if a broker must buffer many messages because consumers are slow, its throughput may degrade.
questions.explain: Brokers quickly delete messages, so they assume a small working set. Buffering a lot, perhaps spilling to disk, slows each message down.

questions.q: Which assumption about queue length do most brokers make, and why?
options: That queues are long, because they keep every message until it is explicitly deleted
That queues are short, because they delete messages as soon as they are delivered
That queues are unbounded, because they apply backpressure to every producer
That queues are empty, because producers wait for consumers to finish each message
optionExplain: Keeping messages until deleted is how databases behave, not most brokers.
Right: since they delete quickly, brokers assume a fairly small working set.
Brokers generally allow unbounded queueing, but that is not the assumption behind their performance.
Producers wait only for the broker's confirmation of buffering, so queues are not empty by design.
questions.explain: Quick deletion implies short queues, so performance is tuned for that case.
questions.teaches: Because most brokers assume a fairly small working set, if they must buffer many messages because consumers are slow, each message takes longer to process and overall throughput may degrade.

questions.q: A broker supports XA two-phase commit, so a colleague calls it a database. What is the chapter's view?
options: It must now keep every delivered message forever, as a database does, with no deletion
It can now answer arbitrary queries about earlier messages
It becomes similar to a database, yet important practical differences remain
It is identical, so the four differences no longer apply
optionExplain: Support for XA does not change the delete-after-delivery default.
Brokers do not support arbitrary queries over the messages they hold.
Right: two-phase commit support makes it similar, but the practical differences remain.
The differences in storage, queue assumptions, search and notification still apply.
questions.explain: XA and JTA support brings brokers closer to databases in transaction behaviour, but not in retention or querying.
questions.rule: Transactions alone do not make it a database.
questions.teaches: Some message brokers can participate in two-phase commit protocols using XA or JTA, which makes them similar in nature to databases while practical differences remain.

questions.q: Two services both need every order message. A third group of workers should share the heavy processing of orders. Which delivery patterns fit?
options: Fan-out for the two services, load balancing among the workers
Load balancing for the two services, fan-out among the workers
Load balancing for everyone, so that each message goes to one consumer
Fan-out for everyone, so that every worker repeats all processing
optionExplain: Right: services needing every message get fan-out, and workers sharing work get load balancing.
That would give each service only part of the orders and make the workers duplicate each other.
Then each service would miss messages that went elsewhere.
Then the workers would not share the load but each do all of it.
questions.explain: The two patterns answer different needs: everyone needs everything, or the work is shared. The card next defines both.
questions.rule: Share the work, or share the data.

questions.q: Sort each statement by the pattern it describes.
questions.explain: Load balancing divides the stream among consumers; fan-out copies it to all of them.

items.t: Each message goes to one of the consumers
Each message goes to every consumer
Consumers share the work of processing the stream
Consumers each see the whole stream independently

questions.q: A video platform must resize each uploaded video, which takes minutes. Many resizer machines read the same upload topic. Which pattern should they use?
options: Fan-out, so that every resizer resizes every upload for resilience
Fan-out, so that each resizer sees each upload and chooses whether to act
Load balancing, so each upload goes to one resizer and the work is shared
Neither, because only one consumer can read a topic at a time
optionExplain: Then every machine would repeat the same expensive work.
Choosing among all uploads needs coordination the broker already provides with load balancing.
Right: expensive messages are best shared among consumers so that more machines mean more throughput.
Multiple consumers can read one topic; that is what these patterns are for.
questions.explain: Load balancing is useful when messages are expensive to process, so you add consumers to parallelise.
questions.rule: Expensive messages call for load balancing.

questions.q: True or false: with pure fan-out to one group of five consumers, adding a sixth consumer makes each message processed faster.
questions.explain: In fan-out every consumer handles every message, so a new consumer repeats the work instead of sharing it. Sharing needs load balancing.
questions.rule: Fan-out copies; it does not share work.

questions.q: Two separate groups of consumers each subscribe to a topic. Within each group, which node receives a given message?
options: All nodes in both groups receive it, so each node does the same work as every other
Only one node across both groups receives it, so the second group sees nothing
No node receives it until the groups agree, which needs a merge step between them
One node per group receives it, so each group together receives every message
optionExplain: That would be pure fan-out, with no sharing of work inside a group.
That would be pure load balancing across everyone, so the second group would miss messages.
Groups do not need to agree before delivery; the broker handles each group separately.
Right: this is the combination of fan-out across groups and load balancing within a group.
questions.explain: Each group gets the full stream (fan-out), and each node in the group gets a share (load balancing).
questions.rule: Fan out to groups, balance within.
questions.teaches: The two patterns can be combined: two separate groups of consumers may each subscribe to a topic, each group receiving all messages, with only one node in each group receiving each message.

questions.q: In AMQP, how would you implement load balancing, and what does JMS call the equivalent?
options: Several clients bind separate exchanges; JMS calls it a topic subscription
Several clients consume from one queue; JMS calls it a shared subscription
One client consumes all messages; JMS calls it a durable queue
Each client reads a separate partition; JMS calls it a consumer group
optionExplain: Exchange bindings and topic subscriptions provide fan-out in AMQP and JMS.
Right: multiple clients on one queue share the messages, called a shared subscription in JMS.
A single client consuming everything gives no sharing of work.
Partitions belong to log-based brokers, not to AMQP queues.
questions.explain: The chapter maps patterns to standards: load balancing is several clients on one queue (AMQP) or a shared subscription (JMS); fan-out is exchange bindings (AMQP) or topic subscriptions (JMS).
questions.rule: Know the standards' names for each pattern.
questions.teaches: In AMQP, load balancing is multiple clients consuming from the same queue (a shared subscription in JMS), while fan-out is exchange bindings in AMQP and topic subscriptions in JMS.

questions.q: A broker delivers a message and the consumer crashes before finishing. How can the broker make sure the message is not lost?
