options: Delete it immediately on delivery and trust the consumer to process it before crashing
Keep it until the consumer acknowledges it, and redeliver it if none arrives
Send it to every consumer so that at least one of them is bound to finish it
Ask the producer to wait until the consumer is back before sending the next message
optionExplain: Deleting on delivery would lose the message when the consumer crashes.
Right: acknowledgments plus redelivery protect against crashes mid-processing.
Sending to all is fan-out and does not guarantee anything about completion.
Producers do not wait for consumers in a broker setup; the broker holds messages.
questions.explain: The broker has to wait for proof that the work finished. The card next names this acknowledgment.

questions.q: A broker removes a message from the queue only after the client sends an ____.
questions.explain: A client must explicitly tell the broker when it has finished processing so the broker can remove the message.

questions.q: A consumer sends an email for a queued job, then its network drops before the acknowledgment arrives. What does the broker do?
options: Assume it was not processed and redeliver the job to another consumer
Mark the job as done, because the consumer started working on it
Delete the job, because the connection closing means the work is finished
Pause the queue until the original consumer reconnects and confirms
optionExplain: Right: with no acknowledgment, the broker assumes the job was not processed and redelivers.
Starting work is not completion; only the acknowledgment counts.
A closed connection without an ack is treated as not processed.
The chapter describes redelivery to another consumer, not pausing the queue.
questions.explain: The email may be sent twice. This is the case where the work was done but the ack was lost.
questions.rule: A lost ack can cause a duplicate.

questions.q: True or false: a broker that redelivers after a missing acknowledgment cannot cause a message to be processed twice.
questions.explain: If the message was fully processed but the acknowledgment was lost in the network, redelivery processes it again. Handling this case requires an atomic commit protocol.

questions.q: What does the chapter say is needed to handle the case where a message was processed but the acknowledgment was lost?
options: A longer timeout, so the acknowledgment has more time to arrive
A second broker that holds a copy of every acknowledgment
An atomic commit protocol, as in distributed transactions
Deleting the message at the moment of delivery
optionExplain: A longer timeout reduces but does not remove the case; the acknowledgment may be lost for good.
Another broker has the same lost-message problem and does not fix atomicity.
Right: this case needs an atomic commit protocol, discussed in distributed transactions.
Deleting on delivery loses the message when the consumer crashes.
questions.explain: The chapter points back to distributed transactions: processing and acknowledgment must happen atomically.
questions.teaches: If a message was fully processed but its acknowledgment was lost in the network, handling this case requires an atomic commit protocol.

questions.q: A team uses a queue for invoice generation and notices that some invoices are generated twice after network blips. Which explanation matches the chapter?
options: Fan-out, which delivers every message to all consumers by design
Backpressure, which blocks producers and makes them resend messages
Log compaction, which keeps duplicates of the same key
Redelivery after a lost acknowledgment
optionExplain: Fan-out is a deliberate pattern; it does not depend on network blips.
Backpressure blocks the producer, but does not resend messages.
Log compaction removes duplicates rather than creating them.
Right: a lost acknowledgment makes the broker redeliver a message that was in fact processed.
questions.explain: Network blips can drop acknowledgments, so the broker redelivers; invoice generation must be safe to repeat or be made atomic.
questions.teaches: Because a broker redelivers when an acknowledgment is lost, a processed message can be delivered again, so consumers whose actions are not safe to repeat may act twice.

questions.q: Two consumers share a queue and one crashes mid-message, so its message goes to the other. What happens to processing order?
options: The order is always preserved because the broker numbers every message
All later messages wait until the crashed consumer returns, so the order holds
The redelivered message can be processed after later messages
Only the messages after the crash are reordered, and the reordering stops at once
optionExplain: Numbering does not prevent a redelivered message from being processed late.
Load-balanced consumers do not wait for each other.
Right: a redelivered message can arrive after messages that were sent later.
The pretest scenario shows reordering already, but no mechanism makes it stop at once.
questions.explain: Redelivery puts an old message behind newer ones. The card next walks through the sequence.

questions.q: Put the events of the chapter's example in order.
items: Consumer 2 starts processing m3 and consumer 1 starts processing m4
Consumer 2 crashes before acknowledging m3
The broker redelivers m3 to consumer 1
Consumer 1 processes m4, m3, m5 in that order
questions.explain: m3 goes out first, but because it is redelivered later, consumer 1 ends up handling it after m4.

questions.q: Bank transfers are processed by several consumers on one shared queue: first open account, then deposit. A crash redelivers open account. What can go wrong?
options: The deposit may be processed before the account exists
The deposit is lost forever, because redelivery removes later messages
The account is opened twice, which cancels out the deposit
Nothing, because brokers keep dependent messages together
optionExplain: Right: causal dependencies make reordering a problem.
Redelivery does not remove later messages; it only changes the order.
Opening twice is a separate issue; the reordering issue concerns the sequence.
A load-balancing broker does not know about dependencies between messages.
questions.explain: Messages that depend on each other, such as open then deposit, need to be seen in order.

questions.q: True or false: giving each consumer its own queue avoids redelivery reordering, at the cost of giving up load balancing.
questions.explain: With one consumer per queue, a redelivered message can only go back to the same consumer, but the queue's work is no longer shared.

questions.q: Do the JMS and AMQP standards, which require brokers to try to preserve order, remove this reordering?
options: Yes, because the standards forbid redelivery of messages that were already sent
Yes, because the standards require a single consumer per queue
No, because the standards allow brokers to drop the older message
No, because load balancing with redelivery inevitably leads to reordering
optionExplain: Redelivery is part of how acknowledgments work; the standards do not forbid it.
The standards allow several consumers on a queue, which is load balancing.
Dropping is not what the chapter attributes to the standards.
Right: even brokers that preserve order otherwise cannot avoid it in this combination.
questions.explain: Order preservation by the broker cannot overcome redelivery to a different consumer.
questions.teaches: Even if the broker tries to preserve message order, as both the JMS and AMQP standards require, load balancing with redelivery inevitably leads to messages being reordered.

questions.q: A team ingests independent page-view counts, where each message adds one to a counter. Is redelivery reordering a concern for its design?
options: Yes, because any reordering of any messages invalidates every total
Not for ordering, since the messages are independent of each other
Yes, because counters require the strictest ordering of all workloads
Not at all, because redelivery never happens for counters
optionExplain: Independent increments give the same total in any order.
Right: reordering is not a problem for completely independent messages.
Order matters when there are causal dependencies, which independent increments lack.
Redelivery can still happen; the point here is that its reordering is harmless.
questions.explain: Our reading: the order of independent adds does not change the sum, but a redelivery could still double-count unless duplicates are handled.
questions.teaches: Message reordering is not a problem if messages are completely independent of each other, but it can matter if there are causal dependencies between them.

questions.q: A new analytics consumer is added to an AMQP-style broker today. Which messages will it normally receive?
options: Every message since the topic was created, because the broker keeps its full history for new readers
The latest message for each key, because the broker keeps one current value per key for late joiners
Only messages sent after it registered, because earlier ones were deleted when delivered
Only messages that other consumers failed to acknowledge, because those are the ones kept
optionExplain: Keeping full history is how files and databases behave, not how this style of broker works.
Keeping one value per key is log compaction, which a traditional broker does not do.
Right: earlier messages are gone, so a new consumer only sees what is sent after it registers.
Unacknowledged messages are redelivered to existing consumers, which is a different mechanism.
questions.explain: A transient broker keeps nothing for latecomers. The card next shows what this costs.

questions.q: True or false: In an AMQP or JMS-style broker, receiving a message is destructive when the acknowledgment causes it to be deleted.
questions.explain: Once the message is acknowledged and deleted, running the same consumer again will not give the same result.

questions.q: A team wants to rerun a fraud score over last week's payments. Why does a traditional broker make that hard?
options: The broker would send each event to every consumer at once, so the two runs would overlap and clash
The broker would refuse a second consumer, because each topic accepts only one registered reader
The broker would reorder the events on the second run, so the scores could never be compared
The first run's acknowledgments delete the events, so a second run would find nothing to read
optionExplain: Delivery to every consumer is fan-out, which is not what prevents repeated runs.
Brokers allow several consumers per topic, so refusing a second one is not the issue.
Reordering can happen with redelivery, but it is not why the second run has no input.
Right: destructive reads leave nothing for a second run.
questions.explain: Rerunning needs the input to still exist, which is true of a read-only file but not of deleted messages.

questions.q: Match each system to how it treats data once it has been read.
pairs: Read-only, so jobs can be run repeatedly
Deletes the message after the acknowledgment
Keeps data until someone explicitly deletes it
questions.explain: The first three show the transient versus durable mindsets; the log-based broker is the hybrid built to join them.

questions.q: A broker durably writes every message to disk before acknowledging it. Does that change the transient mindset?
options: No: such brokers still delete messages soon after delivery
Yes: a message written to disk can never be deleted by any acknowledgment from a consumer
Yes: durability makes the broker behave like a filesystem that keeps data for a new reader
No: disk writes are only used for the broker's index, never for messages in the queue
optionExplain: Right: durability against a crash is different from keeping messages after delivery.
Acknowledgments still trigger deletion, even for messages that were written to disk first.
Writing to disk for safety does not give later readers access to earlier messages.
Disk writes are used for messages in brokers that choose durability; they are not limited to an index.
questions.explain: Surviving a broker crash and surviving delivery are separate properties.
questions.teaches: Even message brokers that durably write messages to disk quickly delete them again after they have been delivered to consumers, because they are built around a transient messaging mindset.

questions.q: Two tools are attached six months after launch: one to a database, one to a traditional broker. What does the broker tool see?
options: All messages from launch, while the first tool sees only rows written after it was attached
Only messages sent after it was registered
The same history as the first tool, because both systems retain data for the same period
Nothing at all, because brokers cannot deliver to a consumer attached after launch
optionExplain: This reverses the two systems: the database keeps history and the transient broker does not.
Right: a database lets a new client read data written arbitrarily far in the past; a transient broker does not.
The two systems differ in retention, which is the contrast the chapter draws.
Brokers can deliver to late-joining consumers, but only messages sent after registration.
questions.explain: With files and databases you can add a new client at any time and read older data, as long as it was not overwritten or deleted.
questions.teaches: With files and databases you can add a new client at any time and it can read data written arbitrarily far in the past, as long as it has not been overwritten or deleted by the application.

questions.q: Why can a log-based broker promise a total order for messages within one partition?
options: The broker sorts every message by its timestamp before it delivers it to a consumer in that partition
Each message is acknowledged separately, so the broker knows the order in which they were processed
The partition is append-only, so each message gets the next sequence number
All partitions of a topic share one sequence number, so any two messages can be compared
optionExplain: Ordering comes from the position in the log, not from sorting by timestamp.
Log-based brokers avoid per-message acknowledgments; order comes from the log's structure.
Right: appending to the end and numbering in sequence gives a total order in that partition.
There is no ordering guarantee across partitions, so numbers are not shared across them.
questions.explain: The log structure itself gives the order. The card next describes it.

questions.q: Within each partition, the broker assigns every message a monotonically increasing sequence number called an ____.
questions.explain: The offset marks the message's position in its partition; because the partition is append-only, offsets give a total order there.

questions.q: Two events are appended to different partitions of the same topic. What can a consumer rely on about their relative order?
options: Nothing: ordering is guaranteed only within a partition, not across partitions
The one with the smaller offset came first, since offsets are comparable across the topic as a whole
The one written to the lower-numbered partition came first, since partitions are filled in numerical order
They arrive in the order produced, since a topic keeps its partitions in step with one another
optionExplain: Right: there is no ordering guarantee across different partitions.
Offsets are assigned per partition, so offsets from different partitions are not comparable.
Partition numbers do not encode time; each partition is filled independently.
Partitions are read and written independently, so a topic does not keep them in step.
questions.explain: Each partition is its own log, readable and writable independently of the others.

questions.q: True or false: splitting a topic into partitions hosted on separate machines lets the log reach higher throughput than a single disk can provide.
questions.explain: Each partition is a separate log that can be read and written independently, so the load spreads over machines.

questions.q: These brokers write all messages to disk. How can they still reach millions of messages per second?
options: By keeping the newest messages only in memory, and they write older messages to disk later
By skipping the disk for messages that are acknowledged quickly, and they replicate only the slow ones
By partitioning across multiple machines, and they get fault tolerance by replicating messages
By dropping duplicate messages, and they recover the dropped ones from the producers
optionExplain: The chapter says these brokers write all messages to disk, not only the old ones.
Every message is written to disk; fast acknowledgments do not skip it.
Right: throughput comes from partitioning over machines, fault tolerance from replication.
Dropping duplicates is not how the throughput is reached.
questions.explain: Disk writes are cheap when sequential, and spreading partitions across machines multiplies the throughput.
questions.rule: Partition for speed, replicate for safety.
questions.teaches: Even though these brokers write all messages to disk, they reach throughput of millions of messages per second by partitioning across multiple machines, and fault tolerance by replicating messages.

questions.q: A team evaluates Google Cloud Pub/Sub and asks whether it exposes a log abstraction like Kafka. What does the chapter say?
options: It is a traditional broker with no relation to logs, so it deletes every message after delivery
It exposes the same log abstraction as Kafka, with offsets and partitions visible to the consumer
It only supports direct messaging, so producers must deliver the messages to consumers themselves
It is architecturally similar but exposes a JMS-style API rather than a log abstraction
optionExplain: It is described as architecturally similar to log-based brokers, so the relation exists.
Its API differs: it exposes a JMS-style API rather than a log abstraction.
It is a broker, not a brokerless direct messaging library.
Right: the chapter calls it architecturally similar but with a JMS-style API.
questions.explain: What the system does underneath and what API it presents can differ, so check both.
questions.teaches: Google Cloud Pub/Sub is architecturally similar to log-based message brokers but exposes a JMS-style API rather than a log abstraction.

questions.q: A topic has four partitions. Ten consumer nodes in one group read it with partition-level load balancing. How many nodes can have work?
options: Ten, because the broker splits individual messages among all of the nodes
Four, because each partition is given to only one node of the group
Eight, because each partition can be shared by two nodes at a time
Two, because a topic supports only a pair of consumers per group
optionExplain: Splitting single messages is how AMQP-style load balancing works, not partition assignment.
Right: messages in the same partition are delivered to the same node, so at most four nodes have work.
A partition goes to one node of the group, not two.
There is no such pair limit; the limit is the number of partitions.
questions.explain: The partition is the unit of assignment. The card next gives the costs.

questions.q: True or false: In a log-based broker, a consumer reading a message removes it from the log, so other consumers cannot read it.
questions.explain: Reading does not delete, so several consumers can read the same log independently. That is why fan-out is trivial.

questions.q: A topic has eight partitions, and one message in partition 3 takes ten minutes to process. What happens to later messages in partition 3?
options: They are moved to another partition automatically so that they can be processed in parallel
They wait behind it, and other partitions continue unaffected, as in head-of-line blocking
They are skipped by the consumer and processed only when the slow message finishes
They are delivered to all other consumers, which also wait on the slow message
optionExplain: The broker does not move messages between partitions to avoid delays.
Right: a single slow message holds up processing of the later messages in its partition.
Skipping would break the order that partition-level reading preserves.
Other consumers have their own partitions and are not held up.
questions.explain: The consumer reads its partition sequentially, so one slow message blocks the rest of that partition.
questions.rule: One slow message blocks its partition.

questions.q: A team has expensive messages, wants per-message parallelism, and does not care about order. Which broker style does the chapter prefer?
options: The JMS/AMQP style, which can hand individual messages to any free consumer
The log-based style, which assigns each message to a partition by its position in the log
The log-based style, with more partitions than the expected number of consumers
Neither, because only direct messaging supports expensive messages
optionExplain: Right: when messages are expensive and order matters little, the JMS/AMQP style is preferable.
Log-based brokers assign partitions, not messages, so a slow message blocks its partition.
More partitions raise the cap, but a slow message still blocks the messages behind it.
Direct messaging has its own limits; brokers are not ruled out for expensive messages.
questions.explain: The chapter prefers per-message distribution for expensive messages where order is not important, and the log for high throughput with fast messages and important order.
questions.rule: Match the broker to the workload.

questions.q: Within one log partition, single-threaded processing is preferable, and parallelism can be increased by using more ____.
questions.explain: Ways to share one partition exist, such as even and odd offsets or a thread pool, but they complicate offset management.
questions.teaches: Two consumers could share a partition by reading all messages and handling even or odd offsets, or by using a thread pool, but that complicates offset management; single-threaded processing is preferable and parallelism is increased by using more partitions.

questions.q: A topic with 8 partitions is read by 8 nodes that cannot keep up with 5x the traffic. What helps?
options: Adding more nodes helps without limit, because the broker will split single messages among them
Removing old segments will free consumers, because the consumer offset then moves forward
Adding more nodes will not help beyond 8, so the topic needs more partitions to add parallelism
Switching to fan-out will help, because every node then shares the topic's load
optionExplain: Splitting single messages is not how partition-based balancing works.
Deleting old segments risks missing messages and does not speed up processing.
Right: the number of nodes sharing a topic is at most its number of partitions.
Fan-out gives every node every message, which multiplies work instead of sharing it.
questions.explain: With partition-level balancing, a ninth node would have no partition to read.
questions.teaches: The number of nodes sharing the work of consuming a topic can be at most the number of log partitions in that topic, because messages within the same partition are delivered to the same node.

questions.q: An image-resizing job queue: each job takes minutes, order is irrelevant, and jobs are not reread. Which broker style fits?
options: The log-based style, which hands whole partitions to workers and keeps the jobs for later rereading
The log-based style, because only logs can parallelise work over many machines
Neither, because the jobs are too long to be held by any broker
The AMQP/JMS style, which hands single jobs to free workers and deletes them when acknowledged
optionExplain: A partition would be held up behind a slow job, and rereading is not needed here.
AMQP/JMS-style brokers parallelise work by giving individual messages to different consumers.
Brokers handle long jobs; it is the style that matters.
Right: expensive messages, no ordering needs and no rereading suit per-message acknowledgment.
questions.explain: Match the broker to the cost and order needs of the messages. The card next lists the criteria.

questions.q: Sort each requirement by the broker style that suits it better.

items.t: Messages are expensive and parallelism per message is wanted
Order of processing is not important
Messages are fast and throughput is high
Message order is important
Old messages must be reread later

questions.explain: Per-message handling suits costly, unordered work; the partitioned log suits fast ordered streams and rereading.

questions.q: A fraud team consumes card payments, needs each customer's payments in order, and wants to rebuild a risk table from old events. What suits?
options: The AMQP/JMS style, since individual messages are handed to the first free consumer
The AMQP/JMS style, since consumers can then redeliver messages in any order they like
The log-based style, since order matters and old messages can be reread
Either style equally, since the broker does not affect order or rereading
optionExplain: Handing messages to free consumers gives up order and deletes messages on acknowledgment.
Redelivery with load balancing is what reorders messages.
Right: ordering plus rereading are the log-based strengths.
The two styles differ on both order and rereading.
questions.explain: The requirements point to partition-level order and retained messages.

questions.q: True or false: the log-based style suits jobs that take minutes each, since a slow job only delays its own consumer.
questions.explain: A slow message holds up all later messages in its partition, and at most as many workers as partitions can share the topic.

questions.q: How does the chapter describe the AMQP/JMS style as appropriate use, in its summary?
options: As an asynchronous form of RPC, for example in a task queue where exact order does not matter
As the best way to store a complete history, since the broker keeps all acknowledged messages
As the way to rebuild a search index, since the broker lets a new consumer start from offset 0
As a replacement for databases, since brokers support secondary indexes and arbitrary queries
optionExplain: Right: the summary names asynchronous RPC and task queues, where order is unimportant and there is no need to reread.
The AMQP/JMS style deletes acknowledged messages, so it is not a history store.
Starting from offset 0 is a log feature.
Brokers do not support arbitrary queries over the messages they hold.
questions.explain: The summary sets the AMQP/JMS style apart from the log: tasks, not history.
questions.rule: Task queues use the AMQP/JMS style.
questions.teaches: The chapter's summary calls the AMQP/JMS style appropriate as an asynchronous form of RPC, for example in a task queue where the exact order of message processing is not important and old messages need not be read again.

questions.q: A search index, a cache and an analytics store must each read every event of one flow. Which broker style does the chapter favour?
options: The AMQP/JMS style, since each of the three stores can be given a share of the messages
The AMQP/JMS style, since acknowledged messages remain available for the later stores to read
Direct messaging, since three consumers cannot share a broker
The log-based style, which suits streams that generate derived state or output streams
optionExplain: Sharing messages would give each store only part of the data; they all need everything.
Acknowledged messages are deleted in that style, so later stores would miss them.
A broker can serve many consumers; direct messaging does not remove that need.
Right: the summary calls the log-based approach especially appropriate for deriving state or streams.
questions.explain: Feeding several derived systems calls for fan-out of a durable stream.
questions.teaches: The chapter's summary says the log-based approach is especially appropriate for stream processing systems that consume input streams and generate derived state or derived output streams.

questions.q: A broker must resume a consumer after it crashes. In a log, what does it need to remember?
options: A list of every message the consumer has acknowledged, so that any gaps can be found
The consumer's offset, since everything before it is processed and everything after it is not
A copy of each message the consumer was holding, so the messages can be replayed from the copy
The time the consumer last responded, so that messages from before it can be skipped
optionExplain: That is the per-message acknowledgment bookkeeping that logs avoid.
Right: one offset per partition says exactly what has been processed.
The log already holds every message, so no extra copy is needed.
Time of last response cannot tell which messages are done; the offset can.
questions.explain: Sequential reading turns progress into a single number. The card next explains the trade-off.

questions.q: A log-based broker only needs to periodically record each consumer's ____, not acknowledge each message.
questions.explain: All messages below the consumer's offset are processed, so no per-message tracking is needed.

questions.q: A consumer processed up to offset 1,040 but only 1,000 was recorded before it crashed. Where does its replacement start?
options: At 1,040, because the broker can see which messages were processed in memory
At 1,000, so the messages from 1,000 to 1,040 are processed a second time
At 1,000, so the messages from 1,000 to 1,040 are skipped as if processed
At offset 0, so the whole partition is processed again from the beginning
optionExplain: The broker only has the recorded offset, not the dead consumer's memory.
Right: the new node starts at the last recorded offset, so unrecorded work is repeated.
Skipping would lose messages; the design repeats instead.
Restarting from 0 is not needed when an offset has been recorded.
questions.explain: Recording offsets only periodically makes the broker's job cheap but allows repeats.
questions.rule: Recorded offset sets the restart point.

questions.q: True or false: if a consumer node fails, another node in the consumer group takes over its partitions and starts at the last recorded offset.
questions.explain: That is how the group recovers. The messages after the recorded offset are processed again if they had already been handled.
questions.rule: Takeover starts at the recorded offset.

questions.q: How does the chapter relate a consumer offset to database replication?
options: It is like a version vector in multi-leader replication: it detects writes that happened at the same time
It is like a quorum in leaderless replication: it counts the replicas that have acknowledged the write
It is like a tombstone in a log-structured engine: it marks that a key has been deleted
It is like the log sequence number in single-leader replication: broker as leader, consumer as follower
optionExplain: Version vectors detect concurrent writes; offsets measure sequential progress.
Quorums count acknowledgments across replicas; offsets locate a position.
Tombstones mark that a key was deleted; offsets mark a position.
Right: a follower uses the log sequence number to resume replication without skipping writes, and consumers use offsets the same way.
questions.explain: The same principle lets a follower reconnect to a leader and carry on.
questions.rule: Offsets work like log sequence numbers.
questions.teaches: A consumer offset is very similar to the log sequence number in single-leader database replication, which lets a disconnected follower reconnect to the leader and resume without skipping writes; the broker behaves like a leader and the consumer like a follower.

questions.q: A team runs consumers for a payment topic. A node processes 500 messages, crashes, and the successor repeats some. Which design lesson follows?
options: Side effects of processing should be safe to repeat
Offsets must be recorded after every single message, because periodic recording always causes data loss
The topic should be switched to fan-out, because fan-out prevents any repeated processing
The broker should delete messages on delivery, because deletion guarantees each is handled once
optionExplain: Right: reprocessing is possible, so effects need handling; the chapter returns to this later with idempotence and transactions.
Recording after each message would add the bookkeeping that logs avoid, and it does not remove duplicates entirely.
Fan-out sends messages to every consumer and would multiply the repeats.
Deletion on delivery would lose messages when the consumer crashes.
questions.explain: The chapter says it discusses ways of dealing with the second processing later.
questions.teaches: If a consumer had processed messages but not yet recorded their offset, those messages are processed a second time upon restart, and the chapter later discusses ways of dealing with this issue.

questions.q: A log-based broker does not delete anything from a partition. What eventually happens?
options: The oldest messages are rewritten in place, since a log must always overwrite its oldest records
Consumers slow down together, since reading a larger log takes proportionally longer for them
The disk fills up, which is why the log is divided into segments that can be deleted or archived
Producers are blocked forever, since the broker applies backpressure as soon as one segment is full
optionExplain: Overwriting happens as an effect of deleting segments, but it is not what a log does by itself.
Reading the log sequentially does not get slower in proportion to its size.
Right: unlimited appending exhausts disk space, so old segments are removed or archived.
Backpressure on a full segment is not how the log works; it frees space by dropping old segments.
questions.explain: Space has to come from somewhere. The card next explains the segment approach and the numbers.

questions.q: Because a log discards its oldest segments when it is full, it behaves like a circular buffer, also called a ____ buffer.
questions.explain: The log acts as a bounded-size buffer: when it fills, new data overwrites old.
questions.rule: A bounded log is a ring buffer.

questions.q: A broker has a 12 TB disk array writing at 300 MB/s at full speed. About how long until it starts discarding the oldest data?
options: About 22 hours, since doubling the capacity doubles the time and the write rate does not matter
About 5 hours, since doubling the write rate halves the time and the capacity does not matter
About 40 hours, since writing at full speed is not possible for the whole array at once
About 11 hours, since capacity and write rate both double, so the ratio is unchanged
optionExplain: Both the capacity and the rate doubled, so the time stays the same.
Both doubled, so the effect on the time cancels.
The calculation assumes the full write rate, giving about 11 hours.
Right: 12 TB divided by 300 MB/s is 40,000 seconds, about 11 hours; the ratio stays the same when you scale both.
questions.explain: The chapter notes that the ratio remains the same even if you use many hard drives and machines.
questions.rule: Capacity over write rate gives retention.

questions.q: True or false: a consumer whose saved offset points into a deleted segment will miss some messages when it resumes.
questions.explain: The log keeps only a bounded amount of history, so messages in discarded segments are no longer available to a consumer that fell too far behind.
questions.rule: Retention bounds how far a consumer can lag.

questions.q: How does the throughput of a log change as the amount of retained history grows?
options: It stays more or less constant, since every message is written to disk anyway
It drops steadily, since the log must scan more history for each new message
It rises, since larger logs can batch more messages into each write
It falls sharply once the queue outgrows memory, since writing begins to spill to disk
optionExplain: Right: because every message goes to disk regardless, retention does not change throughput much.
Appending does not scan history, so more history does not slow writes.
Larger retained history does not itself allow more batching.
That describes in-memory-first brokers, the contrast the chapter draws.
questions.explain: Systems that keep messages in memory by default and spill to disk only when queues grow are fast when queues are short and slow when they grow.
questions.rule: Log throughput does not depend on retention.
questions.teaches: The throughput of a log remains more or less constant regardless of how long messages are retained, since every message is written to disk anyway, unlike brokers that keep messages in memory and only write to disk when the queue grows.

questions.q: A pipeline writes 20 MB/s to a 6 TB log. Is the retention more or less than the 11 hours at full speed?
options: The same 11 hours, since the log capacity is always a fixed number of hours
Much more: about 83 hours at that rate, in line with logs that hold days of messages
Much less: about 1 hour, since slow writes make a log discard messages sooner
More, but only for one drive, since several drives cannot be added to extend retention
optionExplain: Retention is not fixed; it depends on the write rate.
Right: 6 TB divided by 20 MB/s is 300,000 seconds, about 83 hours, which is several days of retention.
A slower write rate fills the disk more slowly, so history lasts longer.
The chapter says the ratio holds with many drives, so adding drives extends capacity and retention in proportion.
questions.explain: Deployments rarely use the full write bandwidth, which is why several days or weeks can be kept.
questions.teaches: In practice, deployments rarely use the full write bandwidth of the disk, so a log can typically keep a buffer of several days' or even weeks' worth of messages.

questions.q: A log has ten consumers, and one falls far behind. What is the effect on the other nine?
options: They slow down to the pace of the slowest, so that the log can discard old segments safely
They are paused until the slow one catches up, so that all nine stay at the same offset
None: only the slow consumer is affected, and it may start missing messages
They lose the same messages, since the log drops old messages for every consumer at once
optionExplain: Consumers read independently, so none waits for another.
Offsets are separate for each consumer; no pause is needed.
Right: a lagging consumer affects only itself in a log.
The messages a lagging consumer needs may be gone for it, while others at the head read as normal.
questions.explain: The log decouples its readers. The card next details the consequences.
questions.rule: Consumers are isolated in a log.

questions.q: True or false: In a log, one consumer that falls far behind disrupts the service for the other consumers.
questions.explain: Only the lagging consumer is affected, because consumers read the log independently. The log is a buffer with a large but fixed size, so a consumer that falls off the end misses messages.
questions.rule: A log buffers, up to a limit.

questions.q: To get early warning that a consumer may soon miss messages, monitor how far it is behind the ____ of the log.
questions.explain: Because the buffer is large, there is enough time for a human operator to fix the slow consumer before it starts missing messages.

questions.q: True or false: when a consumer lags, a log-based broker applies backpressure and blocks producers until the consumer catches up.
questions.explain: The log is a buffer with a large but fixed size. It does not block producers; if a consumer falls behind what is retained, the broker in effect drops the old messages for that consumer.

questions.q: A developer runs an experimental consumer on the production log, then shuts it down. What remains afterwards?
options: Only its consumer offset, and the other consumers are not disrupted
A queue of messages for it, which keeps accumulating and takes memory from other consumers
A lock on the partitions it read, which stops other consumers from reading them
A copy of the log it consumed, which must be deleted before production resumes
optionExplain: Right: when a consumer stops, the only thing left is its offset.
That is the problem with traditional brokers, where queues of dead consumers must be deleted.
Consumers do not lock a log; reading is non-destructive.
The consumer holds no copy; it reads the shared log.
questions.explain: This makes experimenting on production data low-risk, in contrast to traditional brokers.
questions.rule: A stopped consumer costs nothing but its offset.
questions.teaches: You can experimentally consume a production log for development, testing or debugging without worrying much about disrupting production services, and a stopped consumer leaves only its consumer offset.

questions.q: In a team's old broker, queues of shut-down consumers kept growing. How does a log treat a shut-down consumer?
options: It still accumulates messages in a private queue, so the queue must be deleted by hand
It keeps every message pinned on disk, so the log can never reclaim any segment
It stops using resources, because nothing accumulates for it beyond its stored offset
It blocks the producers, because the log waits for the dead consumer to catch up
optionExplain: That describes the old system, where leftover queues take memory from active consumers.
Segments are deleted by age or size, regardless of any consumer.
Right: unlike traditional brokers, a log needs no cleanup of queues for consumers that are gone.
Producers are not blocked by consumers in a log.
questions.explain: In traditional brokers you need to delete queues of consumers that have been shut down, otherwise they take memory away from active consumers.
questions.teaches: In traditional message brokers you need to delete the queues of consumers that have been shut down, otherwise they keep accumulating messages and take memory away from consumers that are still active.

questions.q: A bug corrupted yesterday's derived totals. How can a log-based pipeline recover?
options: Ask each producer to resend yesterday's events, since the log kept nothing after delivery
Wait for the log to compact itself, since compaction rebuilds all derived totals automatically
Delete the topic and start again, since a log can only be rebuilt from the very first message
Rerun a fixed consumer from yesterday's offset, writing output elsewhere
optionExplain: The log retains the events, so producers need not resend them.
Compaction does not recompute totals; it only drops overwritten keys.
The consumer can start from any retained offset; deleting the topic would destroy the input.
Right: the offset is under the consumer's control, so reprocessing is just reading again.
questions.explain: Reading a log does not consume it. The card next describes how replay works.

questions.q: In a log-based broker, consuming messages is more like reading from a ____, a read-only operation that does not change the log.
questions.explain: The log is unchanged by reading; only the consumer's offset moves forward.
questions.rule: Reading a log is like reading a file.

questions.q: A team wants to test a new algorithm on yesterday's clicks without touching production results. What does the chapter suggest?
options: Switch the production consumer to the new code and watch the results, since the offset can be reset later
Start a copy of the consumer with yesterday's offsets and write its output to a different location
Copy the clicks into a relational table and run the algorithm there, since logs cannot be reread
Ask the producers to pause for a day so that the consumer can catch up on the backlog
optionExplain: Changing production in place would risk the live results; a copy avoids that.
Right: a separate consumer with an earlier offset and a separate output leaves production untouched.
Logs can be reread, so copying to a table is not needed.
Pausing producers is unnecessary because replay reads the retained log.
questions.explain: The chapter says you can repeat this any number of times, varying the processing code.

questions.q: True or false: replaying from a log can reach back past the log's retention, because the consumer controls its own offset.
questions.explain: The consumer controls the offset, but only retained messages can be read. Our reading: replay shares the retention limit that applies to slow consumers.

questions.q: Which feature of batch jobs does this replay ability bring to log-based messaging?
options: Output is made visible only after the whole job has completed, so partial results never appear
Derived data is separated from input data through a repeatable transformation process
Input is sorted by key before any processing starts, which makes joins easier
Jobs always process a fixed day of data, which makes their results easy to compare
optionExplain: Making output visible only on completion is not possible for an endless stream.
Right: the log is the input and the derived output is repeatable from it, as in batch.
Sorting is a batch step that needs bounded input.
Replay is not limited to fixed-day slices.
questions.explain: That makes the log a good tool for integrating dataflows, with easier recovery from errors and bugs.
questions.teaches: Replaying makes log-based messaging more like batch processing, where derived data is clearly separated from input data through a repeatable transformation, which allows more experimentation and easier recovery from errors and bugs, and makes a log a good tool for integrating dataflows within an organisation.

questions.q: A stream job restarts after a crash and must see exactly the messages it saw before, in the same order. Which log property provides this?
options: Reading is non-destructive and the consumer controls its offset
Each message is deleted once delivered, so only the unprocessed messages remain for the restart
The broker assigns messages to whichever consumer is free, so the restart picks up the next ones
The broker keeps one current value per key, so the restart sees only the latest versions
optionExplain: Right: non-destructive reads plus a movable offset let a restarted task replay the same messages in the same order.
Deleting on delivery is the AMQP style, which cannot replay.
Handing messages to free consumers is load balancing, which can reorder messages.
One value per key is compaction, which removes older versions rather than replaying everything.
questions.explain: Fault tolerance based on idempotence assumes that restarting a failed task replays the same messages in the same order.
questions.rule: Replay gives restarts the same input.
questions.teaches: Relying on idempotence for fault tolerance requires that restarting a failed task replay the same messages in the same order, which a log-based message broker does.

questions.q: A follower database ends up with exactly the same data as its leader. Which view of replication explains this?
options: The follower reads the leader's current tables repeatedly, and copies whichever rows differ
The leader emits a stream of write events, and the follower applies them in the same order
Each client sends its writes to both databases, and the two apply them in whatever order arrives
The follower rebuilds its data nightly from a backup, and applies the day's changes in bulk
optionExplain: Comparing tables is not how replication logs work; they ship the changes.
Right: a replication log is a stream of write events applied in order.
Writes sent by clients to two places can arrive in different orders and diverge.
A nightly rebuild is a batch process, not the stream of events the chapter describes.
questions.explain: Replication already works by streaming the writes. The card next states the principle.
questions.rule: A replication log is a stream.

questions.q: The principle that replicas which process the same events in the same order reach the same state is called state machine ____.
questions.explain: If each event is a write and processing is deterministic, every replica ends in the same final state.
questions.rule: Same events, same order, same state.

questions.q: Three replicas apply the same stock changes in the same order, but one ends in a different state. What may explain it?
options: The leader did not number the changes, which the principle requires for every replica
Processing a change on that replica was not deterministic
The change list was too short, because replicas need a minimum number of events to agree
One replica applied the events too quickly, because speed alone can change a final state
optionExplain: Ordering is already given in the stem; numbering is not what differs.
Right: the principle assumes processing an event is a deterministic operation.
No minimum number of events is part of the principle.
Speed does not change the result when processing is deterministic.
questions.explain: Deterministic processing is what lets identical input always give identical state.

questions.q: True or false: if two replicas apply the same writes in different orders, they are guaranteed to end up in the same state.
questions.explain: The principle needs the same events in the same order. Different orders can leave different final values, as the next ideas show.

questions.q: Where does the chapter say it came across state machine replication before?
options: In the discussion of hash joins, in the chapter on batch processing and MapReduce
In the discussion of Bloom filters, in the chapter on storage engines
In the discussion of schema evolution, in the chapter on encoding
In the discussion of total order broadcast, in the chapter on consensus
optionExplain: Hash joins deal with combining datasets, not replicated state.
Bloom filters are an optimisation for set membership.
Schema evolution concerns compatible encodings, not replicas.
Right: it appeared with total order broadcast.
questions.explain: Total order broadcast delivers the same messages in the same order to every node, which is what state machine replication needs.
questions.rule: Total order broadcast supplies the order.
questions.teaches: The state machine replication principle was introduced in the discussion of total order broadcast: if every event is a write and every replica processes the same events in the same order, the replicas end in the same state.

questions.q: Two game servers replay one move log, and each move calls a random-number function. What risk follows?
options: The servers may end up in different states
The log will be read twice, because random numbers force a retry of each move
The moves will be reordered, because random numbers change the offsets in the log
Nothing, because identical logs always yield identical states in every case
optionExplain: Right: replicas stay identical only when processing an event is deterministic.
Randomness inside processing does not trigger a retry of the log.
Offsets are fixed by position in the log, whatever the processing does.
The principle holds only if processing is deterministic.
questions.explain: Determinism is a requirement of the principle, so processing steps like random numbers or clocks need care.
questions.teaches: Events in a replication log describe the data changes that occurred, and the state machine replication principle assumes that processing an event is a deterministic operation.

questions.q: An item's price changes in the main database. Which other places may also need the new price?
options: Only the cache, since search indexes and warehouses are always rebuilt from scratch
Only the search index, since caches and warehouses read the database at query time
The cache, the search index and the data warehouse, since each keeps its own copy
None of them, since a database update propagates itself to every system that depends on it
optionExplain: Warehouses and search indexes also hold copies and need to follow changes.
Caches and warehouses hold their own data, not live views of the database.
Right: each system holds its own copy in its own representation, so each must be updated.
Updates do not spread automatically between independent systems.
questions.explain: Different systems optimise the same data for different jobs, so each must be kept up to date. The card next gives the usual methods.

questions.q: Match each way of keeping systems in sync to its description.
pairs: Take a full copy, transform it and bulk-load it
Application code writes to each system explicitly
Reflect changes only after the next dump runs
questions.explain: ETL and dumps are batch methods. Dual writes are done in application code, one system after another.

questions.q: A shop updates its product database, then its search index, then clears its cache, all in one request handler. Which approach is this?
options: ETL, since the data is transformed on its way to the other systems
Change data capture, since the changes are copied out of the database
Event sourcing, since each step records an immutable event
Dual writes, since application code explicitly writes to each system
optionExplain: ETL takes a full copy and bulk-loads it; here the application writes directly.
CDC would observe the database's changes rather than have the application write each one.
Event sourcing stores an event log as the source of truth, which this does not.
Right: writing to each system in turn from the application is dual writing.
questions.explain: The chapter's example of dual writes is exactly this: write the database, update the index, invalidate the cache.
questions.rule: Dual writes: the application does the syncing.

questions.q: A warehouse is usually kept in sync by ETL, which takes a full ____ of the database, transforms it and bulk-loads it.
questions.explain: The chapter says this is often done by taking a full copy, which is a batch process, so periodic dumps can be too slow.
questions.teaches: Data warehouses are usually synchronised by ETL processes that take a full copy of a database, transform it and bulk-load it into the warehouse, which is a batch process.

questions.q: A team's nightly ETL keeps its warehouse one day behind. They need the warehouse within seconds. What does the chapter's reasoning point toward?
options: A mechanism that streams each change
A larger nightly job, since batch jobs can be tuned to run once per second
More dual writes, since writing twice is always more reliable than writing once
A smaller warehouse, since less stored data shortens the delay by itself
optionExplain: Right: when full dumps are too slow, you need a way to carry changes continuously.
A batch job's delay comes from its slice, not from its size.
Dual writes have their own serious problems, which the next ideas show.
Warehouse size is not what delays each change.
questions.explain: The next ideas show dual writes fail, and that change streams solve it.
questions.teaches: If periodic full database dumps are too slow, an alternative that is sometimes used is dual writes, in which application code explicitly writes to each of the systems, though it has serious problems.

questions.q: Two clients update one item, each writing the database then the search index. Can the systems end with different values?
options: Yes, but only if one of the writes fails, because otherwise both systems agree
Yes, if the writes reach the two systems in opposite orders, with no error at all
No, because writing the database first always makes the index follow the same order
No, because both systems keep the larger value of the two
optionExplain: No failure is needed; the disagreement arises from timing.
Right: interleaved requests can reach the systems in different orders, which leaves them permanently different.
Writing in the same sequence per client does not fix the order across clients.
Neither system chooses a value by size; each keeps the last write it saw.
questions.explain: Concurrent writers can be ordered differently by two systems. The card next walks through the sequence.

questions.q: Put the dual-write race in order, starting with the first write to the database.
items: Client 1 sets X to A in the database
Client 2 sets X to B in the database
Client 2 sets X to B in the search index
Client 1 sets X to A in the search index
questions.explain: The database ends at B and the search index ends at A, so they disagree permanently.

questions.q: Two staff set a price (10 and 12) at once, each writing database then cache. The database ends at 12. What could the cache hold?
options: 12, since the cache always follows the database's final value
11, since the cache averages the writes it receives
10, if the cache received the writes in the opposite order
Empty, since concurrent writes are ignored by a cache
optionExplain: There is no link that forces the cache to follow the database's order.
Neither system averages values; each keeps the last write it sees.
Right: reversed arrival order leaves the cache with the first writer's value while the database has the second's.
Concurrent writes are applied in whatever order they arrive, not ignored.
questions.explain: Because the systems order the two writes independently, they can disagree.

questions.q: True or false: if both systems are replicated databases, each with its own leader, the dual-write race cannot occur because each leader orders its writes.
questions.explain: Each leader orders only its own writes. With two systems, neither follows the other, so they can order concurrent writes differently.

questions.q: Why does nobody notice the inconsistency created by the race?
options: There is no concurrency detection
Both systems log a warning, but the warnings are rarely read by operators
The search index repairs itself on the next read, which hides the difference
The database undoes the later write as soon as it detects the difference
optionExplain: Right: unless a mechanism such as version vectors detects concurrency, overwrites go unnoticed.
No warning is produced; nothing in either system sees a problem.
Nothing repairs the index; the difference is permanent.
The database has no knowledge of the index's content.
questions.explain: Version vectors were introduced earlier to detect concurrent writes.
questions.teaches: Unless you have an additional concurrency detection mechanism, such as the version vectors discussed earlier, you will not even notice that concurrent writes occurred; one value will simply silently overwrite another.

questions.q: A chat app writes each message to a store and a search index. Two people post at once. Which symptom might result?
options: The main chat view loses both messages because concurrent writes cancel each other out
Both stores refuse the second write, which the user sees as an error message
Search shows one message as latest while the main view shows the other, with no error
The search index slows down, because ordering conflicts force it to rebuild every night
optionExplain: Concurrent writes do not cancel out; each lands in some order.
The systems accept both writes, so there is no refusal.
Right: the two stores can order the writes differently, which gives permanently inconsistent views without an error.
Nothing forces a rebuild; the inconsistency stays.
questions.explain: The race arises from unordered concurrent writers, not from the type of data.
questions.rule: Same race in any pair of stores.
questions.teaches: In the dual-write race, no error occurs and each system is internally consistent; the two systems are simply permanently inconsistent with each other.

questions.q: An application writes to a database, then to a search index, and the second write fails. What is the situation afterwards?
options: The systems stay consistent, since the index catches up from the database at the next read
Both writes are rolled back automatically, since an application's writes are always atomic together
The index holds the new value, since the failed write was already stored before the error
The systems are inconsistent, and making both succeed or both fail is an atomic commit problem
optionExplain: Nothing makes the index fetch from the database by itself.
Separate systems do not roll back together without a protocol such as atomic commit.
A failed write leaves the index unchanged.
Right: one write succeeded and the other did not, and making both atomic is costly.
questions.explain: Two independent writes can partly fail. The card next names the problem.

questions.q: Ensuring that two writes either both succeed or both fail is called the ____ commit problem.
questions.explain: Atomic commit is expensive to solve, which is why dual writes are unattractive.
questions.rule: Both or neither is atomic commit.

questions.q: A shop's order service writes to the orders database and then publishes to a shipping system. It crashes between the two. What state results?
options: The order is rolled back, because a crash cancels every earlier write in the same request
The order exists but shipping never hears of it
Shipping receives the order twice, because a crash makes the service resend everything
Both systems hold the order, because the two writes are always applied together
optionExplain: A crash does not undo the earlier write to a separate system.
Right: a crash between two independent writes leaves one done and one not.
Nothing in the stem causes a resend.
The writes are separate, so nothing makes them atomic.
questions.explain: This is the same partial-failure problem as a failed second write.
questions.rule: A crash between writes splits systems.

questions.q: True or false: if the search index followed a database that is the only leader, the leader would set the write order.
questions.explain: Followers apply the leader's order, so state machine replication works. Neither system following the other is what lets conflicts arise.
questions.teaches: If there is only one leader (for example the database) and the search index is a follower of it, that leader determines the order of writes, so state machine replication works.

questions.q: Why does the chapter say conflicts can occur between a database and a search index even if each is a replicated system?
options: Replicated systems never agree on a leader, so every write is repeated until one agrees
The database may have a leader and so may the index, but neither follows the other
Search indexes are not allowed to be replicated, so their writes have no order
The database applies writes in parallel, so no order can be given to the index
optionExplain: The issue is the absence of one shared leader, not endless repetition.
Right: two systems each with their own leader have no shared order, as in multi-leader replication.
Search indexes can be replicated; the point is that the leaders are independent.
A database leader does give an order; the index just does not follow it.
questions.explain: Independent leaders are the multi-leader situation, where conflicts can occur.
questions.teaches: In the dual-write setup the database may have a leader and the search index may have a leader, but neither follows the other, so conflicts can occur, as in multi-leader replication.

questions.q: A search index must match the order of changes in the main database. What arrangement gives this?
options: The index consumes the database's changes as a stream, applied in the same order
The application writes to the index after each database write, with retries on failure
The index scans the whole database every hour and replaces its old content
Each client picks whichever system to update first, and the other follows
optionExplain: Right: applying the same changes in the same order lets the index match the database.
That is dual writing, which can reorder and partly fail.
Hourly scans are batch and leave the index stale between scans.
Letting clients choose is exactly what leads to inconsistent orders.
questions.explain: A stream of changes gives one order for everyone. The card next names it.

questions.q: The process of observing all data changes written to a database and extracting them in a replicable form is called change data ____.
questions.explain: Change data capture, or CDC, makes changes available as a stream, ideally right as they are written.

questions.q: A retailer wants its recommendations cache to match its orders database within seconds, in the same write order. What does the chapter recommend?
options: Make the web app write to both stores and retry any failure it sees
Rebuild the cache from a full copy every night and serve stale data between
Capture the order database's changes as a stream for the cache to consume
Add a trigger to every page that refreshes the cache when the page loads
optionExplain: That is dual writing, which brings races and partial failures.
A nightly rebuild is a batch process and is too slow for seconds.
Right: derived data systems become consumers of the system of record's change stream.
Page-load refreshes are polling and do not give a single ordered stream.
questions.explain: The cache becomes a follower of the database via the change stream.
questions.rule: Derived systems consume the change stream.

questions.q: True or false: a derived system that applies a database's changes in a different order is still guaranteed to match the database.
questions.explain: CDC works because the log of changes is applied in the same order as it was written. A different order can leave different final values.
questions.teaches: If the log of changes is applied in the same order, you can expect the data in the search index to match the data in the database; the search index and other derived data systems are just consumers of the change stream.

questions.q: Why is a log-based message broker well suited to carry change events from a database?
options: It deletes each change once it is read, which keeps the broker small as the database grows
It assigns each change to the least busy consumer, which balances the load among search nodes
It stores only the latest change per row, which hides earlier versions from every reader
It preserves message order, avoiding the reordering that load-balanced redelivery can cause
optionExplain: Deleting on read would remove changes that other derived systems still need.
Handing changes to the least busy consumer would spread them and break order.
Keeping only the latest per key is log compaction, a separate option.
Right: order preservation is the property CDC needs, and logs keep it within a partition.
questions.explain: Log-based brokers keep order and let several consumers read independently.
questions.teaches: A log-based message broker is well suited to transporting change events from the source database, since it preserves the ordering of messages and so avoids the reordering issue of load-balanced redelivery.

questions.q: Which approach to extracting a database's changes is more robust, according to the chapter?
options: Adding a trigger to every table that writes to a changelog table
Asking the application to write each change to a log file as well
Parsing the database's replication log
Reading the whole database at intervals and comparing it with the previous copy
optionExplain: Triggers are described as fragile with significant performance overhead.
Application-level logging is a form of dual writing and has the same ordering problems.
Right: log parsing is described as more robust, though it has challenges.
Comparing full copies is a batch approach and not described as robust or fast.
questions.explain: The replication log already has the changes in order. The card next compares the options.

questions.q: Match each CDC tool to the database it reads from.
pairs: PostgreSQL, via an API that decodes the write-ahead log
questions.explain: Most tools read the database's own log; only the format differs.

questions.q: A team adds triggers to 40 tables for CDC; writes slow down and triggers break. Which statement fits the chapter?
options: Triggers tend to be fragile and add significant performance overhead
Triggers are the most robust way to do CDC, and slowdowns are caused by the index
Triggers never see updates, so the index is missing some of them
Triggers can only be used on one table at a time, so forty is too many
optionExplain: Right: the chapter says triggers tend to be fragile and have significant overhead.
The chapter calls log parsing, not triggers, the more robust approach.
Triggers can observe changes; they are fragile, not blind.
Registering triggers on many tables is possible; the issue is fragility and cost.
questions.explain: The symptoms match the chapter's description of trigger-based CDC.

questions.q: True or false: parsing a database's replication log avoids all challenges, including those caused by changes to the schema.
questions.explain: Parsing the replication log can be more robust than triggers, but handling schema changes is one of its challenges.
questions.teaches: Parsing the replication log can be a more robust approach than triggers, although it comes with challenges such as handling schema changes.

questions.q: LinkedIn's Databus, Facebook's Wormhole and Yahoo's Sherpa all use the CDC idea. What does that say about the technique?
options: It is limited to relational databases, as the three use only relational stores
It requires a trigger on every table, as all three use triggers
It was abandoned after these systems, as newer tools replaced it
It is used at large scale, so it is not only a theoretical option
optionExplain: The chapter does not limit CDC to relational databases; it lists a MongoDB tool too.
The chapter does not say they use triggers.
The chapter describes growing interest in CDC, not abandonment.
Right: the chapter lists these as large-scale uses of CDC.
questions.explain: Examples show the idea in production at companies with very large data.
questions.teaches: LinkedIn's Databus, Facebook's Wormhole and Yahoo!'s Sherpa use change data capture at large scale, and tools exist for PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB and Oracle.

questions.q: A new consumer of a database's change stream is very slow. What is the effect on the database that is the source?
options: The database slows to the pace of this consumer, because it waits for each change to be applied
Little or none, because the database commits without waiting for consumers
The database drops writes it cannot send, because its change stream has no buffering
The database stops accepting writes, because a slow consumer fills its transaction log
optionExplain: Waiting for each consumer would make the source depend on the slowest one.
Right: asynchronous CDC means commits do not wait for consumers.
Dropping writes would be a data loss that CDC is designed to avoid.
The source keeps accepting writes while the consumer lags.
questions.explain: The source commits first and consumers follow. The card next names the price.

questions.q: True or false: Change data capture is usually asynchronous: the system of record does not wait for changes to be applied to consumers before committing.
questions.explain: Like message brokers, CDC decouples the source from its consumers.

questions.q: A user renames themselves, then searches at once, but the index shows the old name. Which cause does the chapter point to?
options: A dual-write race between two clients, which wrote the name in opposite orders
Replication lag in an asynchronous change stream from database to index
Log compaction, which removed the newest change from the log
A synchronous commit protocol, which waited too long on the index
optionExplain: A race needs two concurrent writers; here one user made one change.
Right: the index is a follower consuming changes asynchronously, so it may be behind.
Compaction keeps the latest value, so it would not remove the newest change.
CDC is asynchronous, so there is no synchronous wait.
questions.explain: The issue is replication lag, discussed earlier in the book.

questions.q: Because CDC is asynchronous, all the issues of replication ____ apply to it.
questions.explain: Consumers apply changes after the commit, so a derived system can be behind, and a reader may not see their own write there.
questions.teaches: Because change data capture is usually asynchronous, all the issues of replication lag apply, including a user not seeing their own write in a derived system.

questions.q: A team wants a derived read view to show a user's write immediately and considers a transaction covering both writes. What is the chapter's view?
options: It is free with asynchronous consumers, because they apply every write at once
It is impossible, because event logs cannot take part in transactions
It is unnecessary, because replication lag always disappears within a second
It requires a transaction across the event log and the read view
optionExplain: Asynchronous consumers apply writes later, which is the problem.
The chapter describes transactions, or the linearizable storage approach, as options.
Lag is not bounded; nothing guarantees it disappears.
Right: synchronous update of the view needs an atomic unit across log and view.
questions.explain: The chapter offers synchronous updates in a transaction as one answer to reading your own writes.
questions.teaches: To make a read view update synchronously with appending the event to the log, you need a transaction combining the writes into an atomic unit, either by keeping the log and view in one storage system or by a distributed transaction.

questions.q: A new search index is built from a change log that only holds the last week of changes. What else does it need?
options: A full snapshot of the database at a known log position
Nothing more, since the last week's changes cover every item in the database
A second change log from the previous week, since two weeks cover every item
A copy of the search index from another system, since indexes can be merged with new ones
optionExplain: Right: items not recently updated would be missing without a snapshot.
Items not touched this week never appear in the last week's changes.
Another week of log would still miss items that have not changed in longer.
Merging an unrelated index would not reflect the database's content.
questions.explain: A short log tail does not hold the full data. The card next shows the fix.

questions.q: True or false: The snapshot used to start a new derived system must correspond to a known position or offset in the change log.
questions.explain: That position tells you where to start applying the changes after the snapshot has been processed.

questions.q: Support wants a new customer-search index built from a CDC stream. The stream keeps only 3 days. Which plan works?
options: Start reading the stream today and wait three days for it to cover every customer
Copy the latest week of the stream to the index and hope that every customer appears in it
Take a consistent snapshot noting the log position, load it, then apply changes after it
Load the snapshot first and apply the whole 3 days from the oldest change available
optionExplain: Customers not updated in three days would still be missing.
Customers without recent changes would not appear.
Right: the snapshot and its log position give a consistent starting point.
Without the snapshot's exact position, replaying from the oldest change may skip or repeat changes.
questions.explain: The snapshot supplies the content and the position supplies the ordering handoff.

questions.q: True or false: if a snapshot is taken without recording the log position, the consumer can still tell exactly where to begin applying changes.
questions.explain: Without a known position it would not know which changes the snapshot already includes, so it might skip some or apply some twice.

questions.q: Keeping every change forever would need too much ____ space, and replaying the log would take too long.
questions.explain: Truncation is the reason a snapshot is needed in the first place.
questions.teaches: If you have the log of all changes ever made you can reconstruct the entire state of the database by replaying it, but keeping all changes forever would require too much disk space and replaying it would take too long.

questions.q: A team compares building a new index by replaying a full change log with building it from a snapshot. When is the snapshot unnecessary?
options: When the index is small, because small indexes never miss any items
When the database is read-only, because snapshots are only for writes
When the log holds only recent changes, because those cover every item
When the whole history is available
optionExplain: Size does not decide it; missing items does.
A read-only database still needs a way to populate a new index.
A log of recent changes is exactly the case that needs a snapshot.
Right: the full log history contains every change, so replay alone rebuilds the state.
questions.explain: Our reading: the snapshot only substitutes for log history that was truncated.
questions.rule: Snapshot stands in for the lost history.
questions.teaches: Some CDC tools integrate the snapshot facility, while others leave it as a manual operation.

questions.q: A change log stores every update to every row. How can its size be bounded while still letting a new consumer rebuild the database?
options: Keep only the latest update for each key, and discard overwritten ones
Keep only the first update for each key, and discard everything written later
Keep a random sample of updates, and discard the others to save disk space
Keep updates for a fixed number of days, and discard the older updates entirely
optionExplain: Right: keeping the latest value per key preserves a full copy of the current data.
The first update is outdated once a key is overwritten.
A sample would lose keys and cannot rebuild the whole database.
A time cutoff loses keys that have not changed recently.
questions.explain: Only the latest value per key matters for rebuilding current state. The card next shows the mechanism.

questions.q: In a compacted log, a special null value that marks a deleted key is called a ____.
questions.explain: A tombstone causes the key to be removed during compaction.

questions.q: A topic keyed by user ID holds full profiles. After 10 million updates for 100,000 users, how many records remain after compaction?
options: About 10 million, one record for every update ever made
About 100,000, one latest record per user
About 5 million, half of the updates are removed by compaction
About 1,000, only the busiest users keep a record
optionExplain: That is the size of the uncompacted log, with one record for every update ever made.
Right: the compacted size depends on the number of keys, not on the number of writes.
Compaction removes all overwritten values, not a fraction.
Every key with a current value keeps its latest record.
questions.explain: The disk space depends only on the current contents of the database.

questions.q: True or false: a consumer starting at offset 0 of a log-compacted topic is guaranteed to see the most recent value for every key.
questions.explain: The compacted log keeps at least the latest value of each key, and maybe some older values, so no new snapshot of the source is needed.
questions.teaches: The log is guaranteed to contain the most recent value for every key in the database, and maybe some older values, so starting a consumer at offset 0 of a log-compacted topic gives a full copy without a new snapshot.

questions.q: Which broker feature does the chapter say allows a message broker to be used for durable storage, not only transient messaging?
options: Acknowledgments, as used by AMQP and JMS brokers
Backpressure, as used by Unix pipes and TCP
Log compaction, as supported by Apache Kafka
Fan-out, as provided by topic subscriptions
