options: More scheduling and coordination overhead for each block
Longer delay before any result becomes visible, since small blocks wait for large ones
Loss of fault tolerance, since small blocks cannot be retried
Loss of ordering, since blocks of different sizes are processed in parallel
optionExplain: Right: smaller batches mean more overhead.
Larger batches, not smaller, mean longer delay.
Small blocks can be retried just as well.
Block size does not affect ordering.
questions.explain: Batch size is a trade-off. The card next gives both ends.

questions.q: Name the framework the chapter says uses microbatching: ____ Streaming.
questions.explain: Spark Streaming breaks the stream into small blocks and treats each block like a miniature batch job.

questions.q: A microbatching job has one-second batches and must report five-minute totals. What must it do?
options: Increase the batch size to five minutes, since a batch is the only window it can have
Ignore the five-minute requirement, since microbatching supports only one-second windows
Switch to event-time windows automatically, since microbatching uses event timestamps
Carry state from one microbatch to the next
optionExplain: A five-minute batch would delay all results by minutes.
Larger windows are possible with extra state.
Microbatching windows use processing time, not event timestamps.
Right: larger windows need explicit state carried across batches.
questions.explain: The implicit tumbling window equals the batch size, based on processing time.

questions.q: True or false: microbatching windows are based on the event timestamps rather than the processing time.
questions.explain: Microbatching implicitly provides a tumbling window equal to the batch size, windowed by processing time, not event timestamps.

questions.q: Why is one second a typical batch size, according to the chapter?
options: It is the fastest rate at which brokers can deliver messages to consumers
It is the length of a TCP timeout, which determines when batches close
It is the result of a performance compromise between overhead and delay
It is required by the AMQP standard for acknowledgments
optionExplain: Brokers can deliver faster than that.
TCP timeouts are unrelated.
Right: smaller batches cost overhead and larger ones delay results.
AMQP does not set a batch size.
questions.explain: The compromise point depends on overhead per batch.
questions.teaches: Microbatch size is typically around one second, as the result of a performance compromise: smaller batches incur greater scheduling and coordination overhead, while larger batches mean a longer delay before the results of the stream processor become visible.

questions.q: An alerting team needs results within 50 milliseconds. Is one-second microbatching a fit?
options: Probably not, since microbatches of about a second add that much delay before results appear
Yes, since smaller delay is always achieved by larger batches
Yes, since microbatching removes all delay by processing events as they arrive
Only if the batch size is raised to one minute, since larger batches reduce latency
optionExplain: Right: the typical batch size sets a floor on delay.
Larger batches increase delay.
Microbatching processes in blocks, not event by event.
A larger batch adds delay.
questions.explain: Our reading: microbatching has a built-in delay of about its batch size.
questions.teaches: Microbatching also implicitly provides a tumbling window equal to the batch size, windowed by processing time rather than event timestamps.

questions.q: A stream operator crashes. It saved its state to durable storage a minute earlier. What does recovery do?
options: Restart from the very first event ever processed and recompute all state
Keep the output made since then and continue from the crash point with empty state
Ask a human operator to choose which of the events to process again
Restore the saved state and discard any output made after it was saved
optionExplain: Restarting from the beginning is what the chapter says may not be viable for long-running jobs.
Keeping later output while losing state would produce duplicates and wrong results.
Recovery is automatic.
Right: that is checkpointing.
questions.explain: Checkpoints make restarts fast. The card next explains.

questions.q: Checkpoints in a stream are triggered by ____ in the message stream, similar to the boundaries between microbatches.
questions.explain: Barriers mark checkpoint positions without forcing a particular window size.

questions.q: A Flink job takes a checkpoint at 10:00 and crashes at 10:03. What happens to the output it wrote between 10:00 and 10:03?
options: It is kept and the job resumes from 10:03 with no state
It is discarded, and processing resumes from the 10:00 checkpoint
It is kept and also produced again after the restart, so downstream sees two copies
It is merged with the output of a fresh job started at 10:03
optionExplain: Resuming at the crash point without state would be wrong.
Right: the output after the last checkpoint is discarded.
Duplicate output would violate exactly-once semantics within the framework.
A fresh job does not know the state.
questions.explain: Restart from the checkpoint and discard output generated after it.

questions.q: Sort each property into microbatching or checkpointing.

items.t: Used by Spark Streaming
Gives an implicit tumbling window equal to the batch size
Used by Apache Flink
Triggered by barriers in the message stream
Does not force a particular window size

questions.explain: Both give recovery boundaries, but checkpoints do not impose window sizes.

questions.q: Where does Flink write its periodic snapshots of operator state, according to the chapter?
options: To the producers' local memory, which is quick to read back
To durable storage such as HDFS
To the topic's first partition, which holds all operator states
To the search index, which keeps a copy of each operator state
optionExplain: Producer memory is not durable.
Right: Flink periodically captures snapshots of operator state and writes them to durable storage such as HDFS.
Operator state is not stored in a topic partition in this description.
Search indexes are not used for operator state.
questions.explain: Durable storage lets a replacement node restore state.
questions.teaches: Flink periodically captures snapshots of operator state and writes them to durable storage such as HDFS.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares checkpointing with microbatching?
options: Both force windows equal to their block size, so window size equals checkpoint interval
Both rely on event time windows, so late events are never a problem
Both need the whole stream to finish, so output waits for completion
Both give batch-like recovery boundaries, but checkpoints do not tie windows to the boundary size
optionExplain: Only microbatching ties windows to batch size.
Microbatching uses processing time windows.
Neither can wait for a stream to finish.
Right: checkpoint barriers are like microbatch boundaries without forcing a window size.
questions.explain: Barriers are logical markers in the stream.
questions.teaches: Checkpoints are triggered by barriers in the message stream, similar to the boundaries between microbatches, but without forcing a particular window size.

questions.q: A checkpointed job sends an email for each large order. It crashes, restores a checkpoint and replays. What may customers get?
options: A duplicate email, because the framework cannot take back an email already sent
No email at all, because restoring a checkpoint cancels every email sent before it
The same single email, because checkpointing makes every side effect happen once
A corrupted email, because the replay mixes old and new order data
optionExplain: Right: the email left the framework and cannot be discarded.
Emails already sent are not recalled by a checkpoint restore.
Checkpointing covers state inside the framework only.
Replay does not mix orders; the issue is repetition.
questions.explain: External effects are outside the framework's control. The card next explains.

questions.q: Match each output to whether the framework can discard it after a failed batch.
pairs: Row written to an external database
Cannot be taken back by the framework
questions.explain: Only what stays within the framework is under its control.

questions.q: A microbatch job writes totals to an external database. A batch fails after writing half its rows and is rerun. What is the risk?
options: The database refuses writes from reruns, so no row is applied twice
The database discards the half batch automatically, since it is part of the framework
Rows written by the failed attempt may be applied again, so some effects happen twice
The rerun skips the rows written earlier, since the framework tracks external writes
optionExplain: Databases do not know the batch failed.
The database is outside the framework.
Right: the framework cannot discard external writes, so a rerun repeats them.
The framework does not track external writes.
questions.explain: Restarting a failed task causes external side effects to happen again.

questions.q: True or false: if a job only writes to its own internal state and nothing outside the framework, microbatching or checkpointing gives exactly-once semantics for it.
questions.explain: Within the confines of the framework, the two approaches provide the same exactly-once semantics as batch processing.

questions.q: Which of these external actions does the chapter list as leaving the framework's control?
options: Reading from a partition, advancing an offset, and writing to local state
Sorting records, partitioning by key, and merging sorted runs
Rounding a timestamp, computing a sum, and filtering a record
Writing to a database, sending messages to an external broker, and sending emails
optionExplain: These are internal actions within the processing framework and log.
These are batch processing steps.
These are internal computations.
Right: these actions leave the framework.
questions.explain: Anything whose output the framework cannot discard counts.
questions.teaches: As soon as output leaves the stream processor, for example by writing to a database, sending messages to an external message broker, or sending emails, the framework is no longer able to discard the output of a failed batch.

questions.q: A team uses a framework with exactly-once semantics and still sees duplicate charges to a payment gateway. Which is the most likely cause?
options: The gateway call is an external side effect that repeats when a failed task restarts
The framework breaks its guarantee for any state it keeps, so charges are doubled
The framework dropped the first copy of each event, so the retry doubled up
The payment gateway ignores retries, so it always charges once per request
optionExplain: Right: external effects fall outside the guarantee.
The guarantee covers the framework's own state.
Dropping an event would lose charges, not duplicate them.
A gateway that ignored retries would not cause duplicates.
questions.explain: Our reading: the fix is idempotent requests or an atomic commit across both steps.
questions.teaches: Within the confines of the stream processing framework, microbatching and checkpointing provide the same exactly-once semantics as batch processing, but as soon as output leaves the processor they are not sufficient alone.

questions.q: A stream processor handles an event: it updates state, sends a message downstream and advances its input offset. Which outcome is acceptable for exactly-once?
options: Any two of the three happen, as long as the third is retried later
All three happen, or none of them happen
Only the offset moves, since the other two can be inferred later
The message is sent first, then the other two happen whenever convenient
optionExplain: A mix leaves state, output and offset out of sync.
Right: effects must be atomic together.
Without the state and the message, the event's work would be lost.
Unordered effects can leave them out of sync after a failure.
questions.explain: Out-of-sync effects cause duplicates or losses. The card next explains.

questions.q: In a log-based broker, acknowledging input includes moving the consumer ____ forward.
questions.explain: That step must also be part of the atomic unit.
questions.rule: Offset advance is an effect too.

questions.q: A processor writes a result to its output topic and advances its input offset in two separate steps and crashes between them. What can happen?
options: The result is lost, because the offset was already advanced before the write
Nothing, since the two steps are always combined by the broker
On restart the event is processed again, so the result is written twice
The output topic is compacted, which removes the duplicate result
optionExplain: Here the write happened first; the offset move was lost.
Separate steps are not combined unless a transaction does it.
Right: the offset did not move, so the event is replayed.
Compaction is by key and is not a guarantee against duplicates.
questions.explain: Atomic commit prevents this half-done state.

questions.q: True or false: the exactly-once approach in Google Cloud Dataflow and VoltDB provides transactions across heterogeneous technologies, like XA.
questions.explain: These implementations keep the transactions internal by managing both state changes and messaging within the stream processing framework.

questions.q: How can the overhead of the transaction protocol be reduced, according to the chapter?
options: By amortising it over several input messages processed in a single transaction
By running every message in its own transaction, so each is small
By skipping the acknowledgment of input, so there is less to commit
By moving state to an external database, so the framework has no state
optionExplain: Right: batching several messages per transaction spreads the cost.
One transaction per message increases overhead per message.
Skipping acknowledgments breaks the all-or-nothing rule.
External state would take the effects outside the framework.
questions.explain: A transaction covering many messages pays the protocol cost once.
questions.teaches: The overhead of the transaction protocol can be amortised by processing several input messages within a single transaction.

questions.q: Why does the chapter say atomic commit can be efficient in these systems although XA has problems?
options: They use XA more cleverly, with extra locks across all the participating databases
They drop durability, so commits are cheap but results may be lost
They work in a restricted environment and keep both state changes and messaging inside the framework
They run the transaction at the consumer, which can then reject events
optionExplain: The implementations do not rely on XA across databases.
Durability is not dropped.
Right: restricting scope avoids the heterogeneity that makes XA costly.
Consumers cannot reject events.
questions.explain: Chapter 9 covered the problems with traditional distributed transactions such as XA.
questions.teaches: Unlike XA, these implementations do not attempt to provide transactions across heterogeneous technologies, but instead keep them internal by managing both state changes and messaging within the stream processing framework.

questions.q: Which of these writes to a key-value store is safe to repeat after a crash without changing the final result?
options: Adding 1 to the counter stored in the key
Appending a new line to the value stored in the key
Doubling the number stored in the key
Setting the key to the fixed value 42
optionExplain: Repeating an increment adds twice.
Repeating an append adds the line twice.
Repeating a doubling multiplies twice.
Right: writing the same value again overwrites it with an identical value.
questions.explain: Safe repeats are idempotent. The card next defines the term.
questions.rule: Set is safe; increment is not.

questions.q: An operation that has the same effect whether performed once or many times is called ____.
questions.explain: Setting a key to a fixed value is idempotent; incrementing a counter is not.
questions.rule: Same effect once or many times.

questions.q: A job increments a view counter in an external database for each Kafka message. After a crash, a message is replayed. How can the job avoid counting twice?
options: Increment the counter twice, so replays and originals always add up evenly
Store the offset of the last applied message with the counter, and skip messages at or below it
Delete the counter before replaying, so the replay starts from zero for every message
Ask the producer to stop sending messages until the job is back
optionExplain: Doubling increments would distort the count.
Right: the stored offset tells you whether an update has already been applied.
Deleting the counter would lose the earlier count.
Producers do not wait for jobs.
questions.explain: The metadata turns a non-idempotent increment into an idempotent update.

questions.q: True or false: setting a key to a fixed value is idempotent, because writing the same value again overwrites it with an identical value.
questions.explain: Repeating the write leaves the same final state.

questions.q: What property of Kafka messages makes the offset trick work?
options: Every message is deleted when acknowledged, so duplicates cannot exist
Every message has a persistent, monotonically increasing offset
Every message carries a random identifier that changes on each replay
Every message is delivered to all consumers, so offsets are shared
optionExplain: Kafka does not delete on acknowledgment.
Right: a persistent, increasing offset lets you compare positions.
A changing identifier would not identify repeats.
Sharing offsets across consumers does not identify repeats.
questions.explain: You can compare a message's offset to the last applied offset.
questions.teaches: Every Kafka message has a persistent, monotonically increasing offset, so when writing a value to an external database you can include the offset of the message that triggered the last write and thus tell whether an update has already been applied.

questions.q: A team compares a distributed transaction with idempotent writes for exactly-once output. What does the chapter say about idempotence?
options: It can be an effective way of achieving exactly-once semantics with only a small overhead
It is much more expensive than a transaction, since every write needs a lock
It cannot be combined with log-based brokers, since offsets change on restart
It is only possible when all writes are increments, since overwrites cannot be repeated
optionExplain: Right: despite caveats, idempotent operations are effective at small overhead.
Idempotence does not require locks on each write.
A log-based broker is what makes replay the same.
Overwrites are the typical idempotent operation.
questions.explain: Trident in Storm uses a similar idea.
questions.teaches: Despite all the caveats, idempotent operations can be an effective way of achieving exactly-once semantics with only a small overhead, and the state handling in Storm's Trident is based on a similar idea.

questions.q: A retried task reads the same messages but computes its result with the current time. Why is the retry unsafe?
options: The retry reads messages in the wrong order, so the offsets no longer match
The retry runs on a second node, and a second node may never write a value
Processing is not deterministic, so the retry may write a different value from the original
The broker deletes the messages after the first attempt, so none are left to read
optionExplain: The messages are the same in the stem; the nondeterminism comes from the time.
Another node can write; the issue is concurrency with a live node.
Right: determinism is one of the assumptions.
A log-based broker keeps messages, so the retry can read them.
questions.explain: A retry must repeat the original computation. The card next lists the assumptions.
questions.rule: Retries must compute the same thing.

questions.q: Sort each item into an assumption of idempotent recovery or not.

items.t: A restarted task replays the same messages in the same order
Processing is deterministic
No other node concurrently updates the same value
Every write is an increment
Every message is deleted after delivery

questions.explain: The assumptions guarantee that a retry repeats the original attempt.
questions.rule: Same input, same logic, one writer.

questions.q: A team's processing reads a log-based topic, is deterministic, and writes values to a store. A node thought dead is actually alive and still writing. What is needed?
options: More partitions, so the live node has less to write
A tumbling window, so its writes expire at the window end
A tombstone for the node, so the store removes its writes
Fencing, to prevent interference from the node thought to be dead
optionExplain: More partitions do not stop a node from writing.
Windows are about aggregation and do not control writers.
Tombstones mark deleted keys, not dead nodes.
Right: fencing stops a presumed-dead node from interfering.
questions.explain: Concurrent updates break the third assumption.

questions.q: True or false: if two nodes may write the same value at once, idempotent retries still guarantee exactly-once results.
questions.explain: One assumption is that no other node may concurrently update the same value.

questions.q: Which broker property satisfies the replay assumption, according to the chapter?
options: A traditional broker redelivers messages to any free consumer
Direct messaging resends lost packets from the producer's memory
A log-based message broker replays the same messages in the same order
A webhook calls the consumer again with a new message
optionExplain: Redelivery to any consumer can reorder messages.
Direct messaging may lose its retry buffer.
Right: the chapter says a log-based broker does this.
A webhook retry does not replay the original sequence.
questions.explain: A log has stable offsets and order.
questions.teaches: Relying on idempotence implies that restarting a failed task must replay the same messages in the same order, as a log-based message broker does.

questions.q: A team replaces its log-based broker with a load-balanced queue and keeps idempotent writes. Which assumption is now at risk?
options: Replaying the same messages in the same order
Deterministic processing, since queue brokers randomise message content
Single writer per value, since queue brokers write directly to the store
Offsets, since queue brokers stop numbering messages entirely
optionExplain: Right: load-balanced redelivery can reorder messages, breaking the replay assumption.
Message content is not randomised by a queue.
Brokers do not write to the store; consumers do.
The assumption at risk is about order; offsets are a feature of logs.
questions.explain: Our reading: an earlier idea showed that redelivery with load balancing reorders messages.
questions.teaches: When failing over from one processing node to another, fencing may be required to prevent interference from a node that is thought to be dead but is actually alive.

questions.q: A stream job keeps a five-minute running count in memory. The node crashes. What is a cheap way to recover the count?
options: Restore the count from a nightly backup of the whole datacentre
Ask users to resubmit their requests from the last hour
Accept the loss, because counts in stream jobs never need recovery
Replay the last five minutes of input events to recompute it
optionExplain: A nightly backup would be far too stale.
Users cannot be asked to resubmit events.
Loss of counts would give wrong output.
Right: a short window is fast to rebuild from the input.
questions.explain: Short windows are quick to rebuild from the log. The card next lists options.

questions.q: Match each framework to how it protects operator state.
pairs: Periodic snapshots of operator state written to durable storage such as HDFS
State changes sent to a dedicated Kafka topic with log compaction
Each input message processed redundantly on several nodes
questions.explain: Different frameworks make different choices about where state is replicated.
questions.rule: Snapshot, changelog topic, or redundant processing.

questions.q: A job keeps a local copy of a user table, kept up to date by CDC from a compacted topic. Its node dies. How can the replacement get the table?
options: Query the remote user database for every event the replacement receives
Rebuild it by reading the log-compacted change stream from the beginning
Start with an empty table and fill it as users happen to appear in events
Ask the old node to write the table to disk after it has crashed
optionExplain: Per-event remote queries are slow and may overload the database.
Right: the compacted stream holds the latest value of every key.
An empty table would produce wrong joins until it filled.
A crashed node cannot write anything.
questions.explain: A local replica maintained by CDC can be rebuilt from the compacted stream.

questions.q: True or false: if state is kept in a remote datastore, each message needs a network query, which can be slow.
questions.explain: The chapter notes that having to query a remote database for each individual message can be slow.
questions.rule: Remote state costs a round trip.

questions.q: Which framework approach rebuilds operator state by sending state changes to a Kafka topic with log compaction?
options: Flink, by writing HDFS snapshots on every message
Samza and Kafka Streams, in a manner similar to change data capture
Spark Streaming, by running a global sort on all state
VoltDB, by writing its transaction log to an email server
optionExplain: Flink snapshots periodically, not on every message.
Right: they replicate state changes to a dedicated compacted topic, like CDC.
Spark Streaming does not use a global sort for state.
VoltDB uses redundant processing, not email.
questions.explain: State changes are treated like CDC events.
questions.teaches: Samza and Kafka Streams replicate state changes by sending them to a dedicated Kafka topic with log compaction, similar to change data capture.

questions.q: A job needs to recover a one-hour windowed aggregate and has plenty of input log retained. Which approach matches the chapter's reasoning?
options: Replicating the aggregate to a remote database after each event is required
Redundant processing on three nodes is required, since replay is never allowed
The aggregate must be recomputed from the very first event ever recorded
Replaying the window's events may be fast enough
optionExplain: Replicating after each event is one option, not a requirement.
Redundant processing is VoltDB's choice, not a requirement.
Only the window's events are needed for a windowed aggregate.
Right: for short windows, replaying the corresponding input may be fast enough.
questions.explain: The trade-offs depend on the infrastructure.
questions.teaches: If the state consists of aggregations over a fairly short window, it may be fast enough to simply replay the input events corresponding to that window.

questions.q: A team moves from slow spinning disks to a fast datacentre network. How might this affect the choice between local and remote state?
options: Remote state may become more attractive
Local state always becomes better, since network speed has no effect on stream jobs
Remote state always becomes worse, since networks cannot carry state queries
The choice no longer matters, since fast networks remove all state recovery costs
optionExplain: Right: relative speeds decide the trade-off.
Network speed matters for remote queries, so it is relevant.
Fast networks make remote queries cheaper, not worse.
Recovery costs still exist.
questions.explain: Relative costs of disk and network drive the answer. The card next explains.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says there is a universally ideal trade-off between local and remote state for all situations.
questions.explain: It says there is no universally ideal trade-off for all situations, and the merits may shift as storage and networking technologies evolve.

questions.q: A processor on a cluster with very low network latency and slow local disks must hold join state. Which direction does the chapter's reasoning favour?
options: Insist on local disk state, since local data is always faster than remote data
Avoid state altogether, since state cannot be used in stream joins
Consider remote state, since network delay may be lower than local disk latency
Use only memory, since neither disks nor networks are suitable
optionExplain: The premise that local is always faster fails in this setup.
Joins require state.
Right: when the network is faster than disk, remote state can win.
Memory-only state loses data on failure.
questions.explain: The merits depend on the infrastructure.

questions.q: Sort each factor by whether it favours local state or remote state, given the chapter's discussion.

items.t: Network delay is higher than local disk latency
Querying a remote database per message is slow
Network delay is lower than local disk latency
Network bandwidth is comparable to disk bandwidth

questions.explain: The decision follows the relative performance of network and disk, which the chapter says may change.

questions.q: What does the chapter say may happen to this trade-off over time?
options: Local state will always win, since disks improve faster than networks
Remote state will always win, since cloud providers offer bigger networks
The trade-off will disappear, since stream jobs will not hold state
The merits of local versus remote state may shift as storage and networking technologies evolve
optionExplain: The chapter does not predict a permanent winner.
The chapter does not predict a permanent winner.
State remains needed for aggregations and joins.
Right: the best choice can change with technology.
questions.explain: Treat the choice as provisional.
questions.teaches: The merits of local versus remote state may also shift as storage and networking technologies evolve.

questions.q: A designer copies a published stream architecture that keeps state locally, without measuring their own infrastructure. What is the chapter's caution?
options: The best choice depends on the performance of the underlying infrastructure, so it may not transfer
Published architectures are always optimal, so measuring is wasted effort
Local state is unsafe, so no published design can use it
Remote state is required for correctness, so the design is wrong
optionExplain: Right: all the trade-offs depend on the infrastructure.
There is no universally ideal trade-off.
Local state is used by several frameworks.
Neither option is required for correctness.
questions.explain: Our reading: copy ideas but check the assumptions against your own network and disks.
questions.teaches: All of the state-recovery trade-offs depend on the performance characteristics of the underlying infrastructure.

questions.q: In the chapter's comparison with batch processing, what do message brokers and event logs correspond to?
options: A sort-merge join, which pairs records by key
A filesystem, which holds the inputs and outputs of jobs
A cache, which holds the latest value of every key
A data warehouse, which holds nightly extracts
optionExplain: Joins are a processing step, not storage.
Right: brokers and event logs serve as the streaming equivalent of a filesystem.
Caches hold derived data and are not the transport for streams.
Warehouses are fed by ETL and are not the streaming transport.
questions.explain: Both hold the data that jobs read and write. The card next fills in the mapping.

questions.q: Match each batch concept to its streaming counterpart.
pairs: Replay a log from an earlier offset
questions.explain: The streaming world renames familiar batch ideas.

questions.q: A team wants to rerun last week's processing with a changed algorithm and compare the outputs. Which streaming component makes this possible?
options: An AMQP-style broker, whose messages are deleted once acknowledged
A direct UDP feed, whose messages vanish after being sent
A log-based broker, whose messages are retained and can be reread
A webhook, whose events are pushed once to a single URL
optionExplain: Deleted messages cannot be reread.
A UDP feed leaves no copy of the data.
Right: a retained log is like a file that can be reread.
A webhook pushes an event once and keeps nothing.
questions.explain: Retention is what makes rereading possible.

questions.q: True or false: a sort-based batch step, such as a sort-merge join, has a direct counterpart in streaming, with no change needed.
questions.explain: Sorting does not make sense with an unbounded dataset, so sort-merge joins cannot be used on streams.

questions.q: According to the summary, which kind of broker is especially appropriate for stream processing systems that derive state or derived output streams?
options: The log-based approach, which has similarities to replication logs and log-structured storage engines
The AMQP/JMS style, since it deletes messages and so keeps the system small
Direct messaging, since it avoids a central broker
Any broker, since all three behave identically for derived data
optionExplain: Right: the summary says the log-based approach is especially appropriate.
Deleting messages prevents the replay needed for derived data.
Direct messaging can lose messages and has no retention.
The three differ in retention and ordering.
questions.explain: The log connects back to replication logs from Chapter 5 and log-structured storage from Chapter 3.
questions.teaches: The log-based approach has similarities to the replication logs found in databases and log-structured storage engines, and is especially appropriate for stream processing systems that consume input streams and generate derived state or derived output streams.

questions.q: A data team knows only batch processing. Which sentence best explains stream processing to them, using the chapter's framing?
options: It is batch processing with a faster cluster, so the daily jobs finish in seconds
It is a database feature that replaces batch processing altogether
It is batch processing done continuously on unbounded streams rather than a fixed-size input
It is batch processing without input or output files, using only memory
optionExplain: A faster cluster still processes slices, not a continuous flow.
Streams and batch coexist; one does not replace the other.
Right: this is the summary's framing.
Streams still read and write via brokers and logs.
questions.explain: The chapter's summary describes it exactly this way.
questions.rule: Stream processing is continuous batch-like processing.
questions.teaches: In some ways stream processing is very much like batch processing, but done continuously on unbounded streams rather than on a fixed-size input.

questions.q: A company wants a search index, a cache and an analytics store to follow its main database. Which approach does the chapter's summary recommend?
options: Have the application write to all four systems whenever data changes
Dump the whole database into the three systems once a week
Make the three systems poll the database tables every second
Have each derived system consume the database's log of changes and apply them
optionExplain: That is dual writing, with its race conditions and partial failures.
Weekly dumps leave the copies stale.
Heavy polling is costly and does not give a single ordered stream.
Right: a change log lets all derived systems follow one source of truth.
questions.explain: Consuming a changelog integrates systems. The card next ties the earlier ideas together.

questions.q: Sort each technique by how it captures a database's changelog.

items.t: Parse the replication log of an existing mutable database
The application does not need to know that capture is happening
The application writes immutable events to an event log
Events record user intent at the application level

questions.explain: CDC extracts the changelog from outside; event sourcing makes it the primary record.

questions.q: A team wants to add a new recommendation view over its existing data without disturbing production. What does the summary suggest?
options: Add the new view to the production database and migrate the existing tables in place
Start a new consumer from the beginning of the change log and build the view from scratch
Ask the producers to resend all historical events from their own archives
Stop the production system until the new view has caught up on the backlog
optionExplain: In-place migration disturbs production.
Right: a fresh view can be built by consuming the log from the beginning.
Producers do not keep archives for this purpose.
Stopping production is unnecessary.
questions.explain: A retained changelog can feed any number of new views.

questions.q: True or false: log compaction can allow a stream to retain a full copy of the contents of a database.
questions.explain: The compacted log keeps the latest value for every key, so reading it from the start yields a full copy.

questions.q: Which sources of streams does the summary list?
options: Only database writes captured by triggers on the main tables
User activity events, sensors providing periodic readings, and data feeds such as market data in finance
Only log files copied from web servers once a day
Only messages from actor frameworks inside a single process
optionExplain: Triggers are one way to capture database writes, but they are not the only source.
Right: these are naturally represented as streams.
Daily copies are batch inputs.
Actor frameworks are discussed as a contrast, not as the sources.
questions.explain: Database writes are an additional source.
questions.teaches: User activity events, sensors providing periodic readings, and data feeds such as market data in finance are naturally represented as streams.

questions.q: A company already has an event-sourced order service and a mutable customer database. How can both feed the same set of derived views?
options: Treat both as sources of change streams: event sourcing explicitly, and CDC implicitly
Convert the event-sourced service to mutable tables first, since views need tables
Use CDC for the order service and event sourcing for the database, which reverses their roles
Feed the views from only the database, since event logs cannot feed views
optionExplain: Right: both give a changelog that derived systems can consume.
No conversion is needed; the event log is already a stream.
That reverses their natural roles; CDC suits mutable databases.
Event logs can feed views, which is a main point of event sourcing.
questions.explain: The summary calls the changelog available either implicitly through CDC or explicitly through event sourcing.
questions.teaches: Representing databases as streams opens up powerful opportunities for integrating systems, and you can build fresh views onto existing data by starting from scratch and consuming the log of changes from the beginning all the way to the present.

questions.q: A team wants to keep a search index consistent with its database as the data changes. Which purpose of stream processing is this?
options: Complex event processing
Stream analytics
Maintaining a materialised view
Search on streams
optionExplain: CEP looks for patterns of events.
Analytics computes aggregates over windows.
Right: derived data kept up to date is a materialised view.
Stream search matches stored queries against arriving documents.
questions.explain: The goal is a maintained copy of data. The card next maps purposes to needs.

questions.q: Match each purpose to a typical need.
pairs: Find a specific sequence of events
Compute a rolling average over a window
Keep a cache up to date with a database
questions.explain: The three purposes differ in what the output represents: a pattern, a statistic, or a copy of state.

questions.q: A utility wants to be alerted when a meter reports three abnormal readings in a row. Which purpose fits best?
options: Stream analytics, since it computes a rolling average of meter readings
Materialised view maintenance, since it copies meter data to a dashboard
Search on streams, since it matches full-text queries against meter messages
Complex event processing, since it searches for a pattern of events
optionExplain: A rolling average is statistical, not a pattern of three events.
A dashboard copy keeps state but does not detect a sequence.
Readings are not text documents.
Right: a specific sequence of events is CEP.
questions.explain: Sequences of events call for CEP.

questions.q: True or false: a framework built mainly for short analytics windows is a natural choice for a materialised view that needs events from the beginning of time.
questions.explain: View maintenance requires events to be kept forever, which runs counter to the assumptions of some analytics-oriented frameworks.

questions.q: Which three purposes does the summary list for stream processing?
options: Sorting large files, joining datasets by key, and writing search indexes in batch
Replacing databases, avoiding transactions, and removing the need for backups
Searching for event patterns, computing windowed aggregations, and keeping derived data systems up to date
Compressing data, encrypting data, and archiving data to tape
optionExplain: Those are batch tasks.
Streams do not replace these database concerns.
Right: these are CEP, stream analytics and materialised views.
Those are unrelated to the chapter's list.
questions.explain: The summary lists them in one sentence.
questions.teaches: The summary lists the purposes of stream processing as searching for event patterns (complex event processing), computing windowed aggregations (stream analytics), and keeping derived data systems up to date (materialised views).

questions.q: A team wants to know whether tonight's checkout latency is unusually high compared with the same hour last week. Which purpose is this?
options: Stream analytics, since it compares current statistics with earlier intervals
Complex event processing, since it finds specific sequences of checkout events
Materialised view maintenance, since it keeps a copy of the checkout table
Search on streams, since it matches a saved query against new events
optionExplain: Right: comparison with previous intervals is analytics.
No specific sequence of events is being searched.
No derived table is being maintained.
No saved query is matched against documents.
questions.explain: The chapter names this comparison with last week as an analytics example.
questions.teaches: Stream analytics tends to be less interested in finding specific event sequences and more oriented toward aggregations and statistical metrics over a large number of events.

questions.q: Both join inputs are changelogs of database tables, and the output must be a continually updated join result. Which join is this?
options: A stream-stream join
A stream-table join
A sort-merge join
A table-table join
optionExplain: Stream-stream joins pair activity events within a window.
Stream-table joins enrich events with table data.
Sort-merge joins need bounded input.
Right: two changelogs joined into a materialised view.
questions.explain: The input types give the answer. The card next summarises all three.

questions.q: Sort each description into the join it fits.

items.t: Both inputs are streams of activity events
Searches for related events within a window of time
Both inputs are database changelogs
Result is a stream of changes to a materialised view

questions.explain: Stream-stream pairs events in a window; table-table maintains a view from changelogs.

questions.q: A team wants to match each login with another login by the same user within 30 minutes to detect account sharing. Which join is this?
options: A stream-table join, enriching each login with a user profile
A stream-stream join within a window, with both inputs being the same stream
A table-table join, joining a logins table with a users table
A sort-merge join, run at the end of each day
optionExplain: No profile lookup is involved.
Right: related events within a time window, in a self-join.
No tables are being joined into a view.
A daily sort-merge job would not produce timely matches.
questions.explain: The summary's own example is two actions by the same user within 30 minutes.
questions.rule: Same stream both sides is a self-join.

questions.q: True or false: in a stream-table join, the table input is an ordinary static snapshot that does not change while the processor runs.
questions.explain: The table input is a database changelog that keeps a local copy of the database up to date.

questions.q: What is a self-join in the summary's wording?
options: A join between a table and its own backup, to detect corrupted rows
A stream-stream join where the two inputs are the same stream, to find related events within it
A join where a consumer reads its own writes, to confirm that they arrived
A join between two windows of one stream, always of equal length
optionExplain: Backup comparison is not a stream join type.
Right: the two join inputs may be the same stream.
Reading your own writes is a different concept.
The self-join does not require windows of equal length.
questions.explain: Related events within one stream are found by joining the stream with itself.
questions.teaches: In a stream-stream join the two join inputs may in fact be the same stream (a self-join) if you want to find related events within that one stream.

questions.q: A team adds product details to each click event and also keeps an up-to-date table of product prices joined with product stock. Which joins do they use?
options: A stream-stream join for the clicks, and a stream-table join for the price and stock view
Two table-table joins, since all data eventually becomes tables
A sort-merge join for each, since sorting is always available
A stream-table join for the clicks, and a table-table join for the price and stock view
optionExplain: Clicks enriched from a table are not a join of two event streams.
Clicks are events, not a table changelog.
Sorting does not work on unbounded input.
Right: events with table data is stream-table; two changelogs is table-table.
questions.explain: Match each pair of inputs to its join.
questions.teaches: In a table-table join both input streams are database changelogs, and every change on one side is joined with the latest state of the other side.

questions.q: A stream job has run for a year and one task fails. Why can the whole output not be discarded, as in a batch job?
options: The job is long-running and produces output continuously
The output is stored in a format that cannot be deleted, so only repairs are possible
The job has no state, so nothing can be recovered after a failure
The broker deletes the output after reading it, so it cannot be discarded
optionExplain: Right: the whole output is too big and continuous to throw away.
Output can be deleted; the issue is that discarding everything is impractical.
Stream jobs have state; that is part of the recovery problem.
Output stored elsewhere is not deleted by the broker after reading.
questions.explain: Granularity is the point. The card next lists the techniques.

questions.q: Match each recovery technique to how it works.
pairs: Treat small blocks of the stream as miniature batch jobs
Restore the latest snapshot of state and discard later output
Make outputs, state changes and input acknowledgments commit together
Make repeated writes have the same effect as one
questions.explain: The four techniques all make retries safe, in different ways.

questions.q: A job's only side effect is writing totals to an external database, and each message has an increasing offset. Which technique is the cheapest fit?
options: Microbatching alone, since it discards external writes on failure
Checkpointing alone, since it undoes writes in the external database
Idempotent writes, storing the offset with each value written
Dropping exactly-once, since external writes cannot be protected
optionExplain: Microbatching cannot discard writes that leave the framework.
Checkpointing cannot undo external writes.
Right: idempotent writes protect external effects at small overhead.
External writes can be protected by idempotence or transactions.
questions.explain: External effects need transactions or idempotence.

questions.q: True or false: transactions that are efficient in Google Cloud Dataflow and VoltDB can span any mix of heterogeneous technologies.
questions.explain: They keep the transactions internal to the framework, managing state changes and messaging within it.

questions.q: Which sentence from the summary describes why a finer-grained mechanism is needed?
options: Since a stream process is short-lived, we can restart it from the beginning each time
Since a stream process writes only to files, we can delete the files after a failure
Since a stream process is deterministic, we never need to recover it
Since a stream process is long-running and produces output continuously, we cannot discard all output
optionExplain: Stream jobs are not short-lived.
Stream jobs are not limited to files.
Determinism is an assumption of some techniques, not a reason to skip recovery.
Right: this is the summary's reasoning.
questions.explain: Finer-grained recovery is the conclusion.
questions.teaches: As with batch processing, we need to discard the partial output of any failed tasks, but since a stream process is long-running and produces output continuously, we cannot simply discard all output, so a finer-grained recovery mechanism is used.

questions.q: A company sends push notifications from a stream job on a framework with checkpointing. Duplicates arrive after a crash. Which fix fits best?
options: Add idempotence or an atomic commit around the notification step
Increase the checkpoint interval, since longer intervals prevent duplicates
Switch to a larger window, since windows remove duplicate notifications
Disable replay, since replay causes duplicates in every system
optionExplain: Right: the notification is an external effect that checkpointing cannot undo.
Longer intervals mean more output may be repeated after restore.
Windows group events and do not deduplicate effects.
Disabling replay would lose messages.
questions.explain: Our reading: external effects need their own guard.
questions.teaches: Within the confines of the framework, microbatching and checkpointing provide the same exactly-once semantics as batch processing, but effects outside it need further measures.

questions.q: A stream processor counts events per minute while consumers sometimes fall behind. What two distinctions must its designers handle?
options: Fan-out versus load balancing, and what to do with acknowledgments
Event time versus processing time, and what to do with straggler events
Tumbling versus session windows, and what to do with sort keys
Event sourcing versus CDC, and what to do with snapshots
optionExplain: Those are broker delivery patterns.
Right: these are the time difficulties the summary names.
Window types matter, but they do not solve lag and lateness by themselves.
Those concern how databases feed streams.
questions.explain: Lag and late events are the core time problems. The card next states them.

questions.q: Match each time term to its meaning.
pairs: When the processor handles the event
An event that arrives after its window was thought complete
Estimated difference between device clock and server clock
questions.explain: These four terms cover the time difficulties of the chapter.

questions.q: An app buffers events offline for days, then uploads them. The team windows by server receive time. What goes wrong?
options: The events are lost, since servers drop all events older than a minute
The windows grow without limit, since receive time never advances
Old events land in new windows
The events are processed twice, since offline buffering duplicates them
optionExplain: Events are not automatically dropped by age.
Receive time advances normally.
Right: receive time reflects arrival, not occurrence.
Buffering does not duplicate events.
questions.explain: Event timestamps (with clock correction) are needed instead.

questions.q: True or false: batch processing avoids all the time-reasoning issues of stream processing.
questions.explain: Batch processing suffers from exactly the same issues, though they are more noticeable in streaming.
questions.rule: Batch has the same time issues.

questions.q: Which option does the chapter give for events that arrive after a window was declared complete?
options: Ignore them and monitor drops, or publish a correction and possibly retract the earlier output
Insert them into the next window so the totals stay balanced overall
Reject the entire window and recompute it from the input stream's first event
Hold the window open indefinitely so no event is ever a straggler
optionExplain: Right: these are the two options.
Moving them to the wrong window distorts both windows.
Recomputing from the first event is not suggested.
Holding windows open forever means no results.
questions.explain: The choice depends on accuracy needs.
questions.teaches: Handling straggler events means choosing between ignoring them while tracking the number of dropped events as a metric, or publishing a correction and possibly retracting the earlier output.

questions.q: A metrics dashboard counts requests per minute by processing time. After a redeploy, it shows a spike followed by a flat line. What is the likely cause?
options: A real traffic surge followed by an outage of all users
Stragglers dropped by the window, since they are always discarded
A backlog processed all at once after the restart
A hopping window that doubled the counts for a minute
optionExplain: The stem's pattern matches the backlog artefact, not a real surge.
Dropped stragglers would reduce counts, not cause a spike.
Right: processing-time windows bunch backlog events.
Hopping windows overlap but do not create spikes this way.
questions.explain: The chapter's own example is a rate measured by processing time looking like a sudden anomalous spike during backlog processing.
questions.teaches: Confusing event time and processing time leads to bad data, such as a false spike in the request rate while a backlog is processed after a redeploy.

questions.q: True or false: nightly ETL copies keep a data warehouse as current as the OLTP database it was loaded from.
questions.explain: ETL is a batch process: a full copy is transformed and bulk-loaded, so the warehouse trails the database until the next load.
questions.rule: Batch loads lag behind the source.

questions.q: True or false: applying captured changes to a search index in the database's write order makes the index match the database.
questions.explain: Applying the changes in the same order makes the search index match the database, much as a follower replays a leader's log.
questions.rule: Same order gives the same state.

questions.q: True or false: parsing the replication log is more robust than triggers, though it has its own challenges such as schema changes.
questions.explain: Triggers tend to be fragile and add overhead; log parsing is sturdier but must handle schema changes.
questions.rule: Log parsing beats triggers, with caveats.

questions.q: True or false: because CDC is asynchronous, a derived system may briefly show data behind the database.
questions.explain: The system of record commits without waiting for consumers, so all the issues of replication lag apply to derived systems.

questions.q: True or false: a compacted log grows with the number of writes ever made to the database.
questions.explain: Compaction keeps only the latest update per key, so the log size depends on the current contents, not on the number of writes.

questions.q: True or false: in VoltDB the exported stream is a table that transactions can insert into but that cannot be queried.
questions.explain: The stream is the log of tuples that committed transactions wrote to it, in commit order.

questions.q: True or false: A well-built general-purpose database can efficiently serve every way an organisation uses its data.
questions.explain: The author argues that every piece of software, even a general-purpose database, is designed for a particular usage pattern. The card next shows why one tool rarely covers every use.
questions.rule: No tool is good at everything.

questions.q: According to the chapter, why does one piece of software trying to do everything tend to turn out poorly?
questions.explain: The chapter says it is hard enough to get one code path robust and performing well. Trying to do everything in one piece of software almost guarantees the implementation will be poor.
questions.rule: Breadth costs quality in a single implementation.
options: Vendors deliberately weaken some features so that customers are pushed to buy a second product to finish the job.
Getting even one code path robust and fast is hard, so a do-everything product is bound to be weak.
Open-source projects lack the review needed to ship more than one storage approach in a single release.
Hardware limits prevent one machine from running both reads and writes at the same time without conflict.
optionExplain: Plausible cynicism, but the chapter gives an engineering reason, not a commercial one.
It matches the chapter: the difficulty of getting one approach right is the reason.
Review quality is not the argument; the chapter is about the difficulty of each approach.
Nothing in the chapter blames hardware; the point is software design trade-offs.

questions.q: A shop keeps orders in one relational database. It now wants typo-tolerant product search and heavy nightly sales analysis. What does the chapter suggest?
questions.explain: Search and analytics are different access patterns from order processing. The chapter expects the application to combine several tools, which then raises the question of how data reaches each of them.
questions.rule: New access pattern, new tool, plus a plan for feeding it.
options: Tune the order database harder until it serves all three uses well, since a good database is general-purpose by design.
Move every table to the search engine, because search handles reads better than any other tool.
Ask the vendor whether the database can do all three and rely on its answer when it says yes.
Expect to add specialised tools for search and analytics, and plan how each one gets its data.
optionExplain: This trusts the general-purpose label, which the chapter says hides a particular usage pattern.
It replaces one single tool with another and ignores that search indexes are poor systems of record.
Vendors are reluctant to describe workloads where they fit badly, so the answer alone settles little.
It follows the chapter: different uses of the data call for different tools, plus an integration plan.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it reflects the chapter's view of tool choice.
questions.explain: The chapter ties tool choice to circumstances and notes that one piece of software cannot suit every use. It also warns that vendors are reluctant to describe the workloads where their software is a poor fit.
questions.rule: Match tool to workload; do not trust a universal claim.

items.t: The right tool depends on the circumstances of use
A general-purpose database is designed with a particular usage pattern in mind
Complex applications often use the same data in several different ways
One well-chosen database should eventually replace every specialised tool
Mapping products to the circumstances where they fit is the first challenge
Vendors can be relied on to list the workloads that suit them badly

questions.q: True or false: Adding a second specialised tool for a new access pattern removes the need to think about keeping the tools consistent.
questions.explain: The opposite holds: combining tools creates the integration problem. The data now exists in more than one place and the copies must be kept in step.
questions.rule: Every added tool adds an integration task.

questions.q: You read a database brochure that lists strengths but no unsuitable workloads. How does the chapter suggest you proceed?
questions.explain: Vendors are understandably reluctant to describe workloads for which their software is poorly suited. The chapter hopes the earlier chapters have given you questions to ask so you can understand the trade-offs yourself.
questions.rule: Infer the weak spots from trade-offs when the brochure is silent.
questions.teaches: Vendors are reluctant to say which workloads their software is poorly suited for, so the reader must use trade-off questions to read between the lines.
options: Use earlier trade-off questions to read between the lines and work out where the product would fit badly.
Treat the missing weaknesses as proof there are none, since a vendor would be sure to list any real limit it has.
Choose the product with the longest feature list, since more features reduce the chance of a poor fit.
Wait until a competitor publishes a comparison, because only outsiders can judge the fit.
optionExplain: Vendors are reluctant to name poor-fit workloads, so the reader must infer them from knowledge of trade-offs.
This assumes honesty by omission; the chapter says vendors are understandably reluctant to mention limits.
Feature count does not map to circumstances; breadth is exactly what the chapter says harms quality.
The chapter hopes readers can use the earlier chapters' questions themselves instead of waiting.

questions.q: True or false: Since databases can build indexes, a system of record and a search index can usually be one system.
questions.explain: The chapter says search indexes are generally not very suitable as a durable system of record. The card next shows why applications keep several copies.
questions.rule: Search index and system of record are different jobs.

questions.q: Why does the chapter say many applications need to combine a database with a separate search tool?
questions.explain: More sophisticated search facilities need specialist information retrieval tools. Search indexes are generally not very suitable as a durable system of record, so the two tools are combined.
questions.rule: Specialist search plus a durable record means two systems.
options: Databases cannot store text at all, so a search index is the only place where full documents can be kept at all.
Search tools guarantee stronger transactions than databases, so they are used to confirm every write.
Sophisticated search needs specialist tools, and search indexes are generally poor as a durable record.
A search index replicates faster than a database, so combining the two roughly doubles the overall write throughput.
optionExplain: Databases store text fine; the issue is sophisticated search and the index's role as a record.
The chapter says nothing of the sort; the index is not the authority.
Both halves are from the chapter: the specialist need and the weak durability role.
Throughput is not the argument; the argument is about fitness for different jobs.

questions.q: A small internal tool needs basic keyword search over its own records. What does the chapter say about adding a search engine?
questions.explain: A database's built-in full-text indexing can be sufficient for simple applications. More sophisticated search facilities require specialist information retrieval tools.
questions.rule: Start with what the database already offers.
questions.teaches: Some databases, such as PostgreSQL, include a full-text indexing feature, which can be sufficient for simple applications.
options: A separate search engine is mandatory, because databases cannot index text for keyword queries at all.
Any use of search forces the database to be demoted from being the system of record to being a mere cache.
Some databases, such as PostgreSQL, ship full-text indexing that can be enough for simple applications.
Search engines should be avoided entirely, because the chapter says copies are never worth the cost.
optionExplain: The chapter names PostgreSQL's built-in full-text feature, so this is false.
Nothing in the chapter demotes the database; the index is what is not a record.
The chapter says built-in full-text features can suffice for simple needs.
The chapter says more sophisticated facilities need specialist tools, so copies are sometimes needed.

questions.q: An online bookshop stores books and orders in one database. Which of its needs add another representation of that data to keep in step?
questions.explain: The chapter lists analytics copies, caches or denormalised objects, and machine learning or recommendation systems as derived representations. An index inside the same database is handled by the database.
questions.rule: Count every derived system outside the database.
options: A paper backup of the supplier list kept in the warehouse
A recommendation model trained on purchase history
A cache of denormalised product pages
A second index on the order id column inside the same database
optionExplain: A paper list is not a derived representation of the application's data stream.
The model is derived from the orders, so it is another copy to keep current.
A cache of objects derived from the original data is one of the chapter's listed representations.
The database maintains its own indexes itself; this is not a separate system needing integration.

questions.q: True or false: A few extra systems keep integration easy now, yet the problem may still grow harder as representations are added.
questions.explain: As the number of different representations increases, the integration problem becomes harder. A small number of copies today does not show that the problem stays small.
questions.rule: Difficulty grows with the number of representations.

questions.q: A firm keeps shipments in a database and sends changes to a route planner and a notifier. Which statement fits the chapter?
questions.explain: Notifications sent on changes appear in the chapter's list of things derived from the data. With several consumers, you need to be explicit about where data is written first and which representations come from which sources.
questions.rule: Name the source and the derived copies.
questions.teaches: When copies are kept to serve different access patterns, you need to be clear about where data is written first and which representations are derived from which sources.
options: Both are derived uses of one dataset, so the firm should be clear where data is written first and what derives from it.
The route planner should be treated as a second system of record so that both sources of truth stay equal.
Notifications are not derived data because they are sent once and not stored, so they need no tracing back to the source at all.
The firm should accept that the two services will hold different versions of the data and treat that as perfectly normal.
optionExplain: It applies the chapter's advice about inputs, outputs and derivation.
Making each copy an equal source of truth is the muddle the chapter wants to avoid.
The chapter lists notifications triggered by changes among the integration targets.
The goal is consistency with the record, not tolerating arbitrary differences.

questions.q: True or false: An engineer saying 99 percent of people do not need a technology is mainly measuring how many people need it.
questions.explain: The author reads such statements as saying more about the speaker's experience. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Such claims reveal the speaker's range of experience.

questions.q: The author reads claims such as 99 percent of people only need X as saying more about the speaker's ____.
questions.explain: The author says such statements say more about the experience of the speaker than about the actual usefulness of a technology.
questions.rule: Experience is narrower than the range of needs.

questions.q: A colleague says nobody needs a graph database, since they have not used one. Which response matches the author's reasoning?
questions.explain: The author says that such statements tell you about the speaker's experience. The sound response is to look at what your own application needs rather than at a popularity claim.
questions.rule: Test claims against your own circumstances.
options: Agree, since a colleague's years of practice are a reliable sample of all the problems engineers face.
Adopt a graph database anyway, because unusual tools are more likely to be central to some team's real needs.
Ask each colleague to vote and follow the majority, because popularity measures usefulness.
Their view reflects the problems they have met; check your own data's needs before dismissing it.
optionExplain: One person's practice is exactly the narrow sample the author warns about.
That swings the other way; the chapter asks for fit to circumstances, not novelty.
Counting opinions repeats the problem of experience-based claims.
It treats the sentence as evidence about the speaker and sends the question back to your needs.

questions.q: Which of these two claims is the kind the author warns about?
questions.explain: The warning is against universal statements about what people need, drawn from personal experience. Claims bounded by one's own data or by a named circumstance do not make that mistake.
questions.rule: Beware universal claims from narrow experience.
options: Our users rarely need fuzzy matching, based on our query logs for the last year.
Almost every user needs only basic keyword search, so specialist retrieval is pointless.
Fuzzy matching is a central requirement for our product, since our users often misspell names.
Some applications use specialist retrieval tools because their queries go beyond what simple keyword matching can do.
optionExplain: This is evidence from the speaker's own data about their own case, not a claim about everyone.
A sweeping claim about all users based on narrow experience is the type described.
This states a need grounded in the product's own circumstances.
This acknowledges variety of needs instead of dismissing them.

questions.q: A conference speaker declares that nobody needs event logs. Give two questions you would ask before accepting this.
questions.rule: Ask what the claim rests on.
questions.teaches: The need for data integration often only becomes apparent when you zoom out and consider the dataflows across an entire organization.
questions.a: What range of applications has the speaker actually worked on, since the statement may reflect only their experience? Is there a requirement elsewhere in an organisation, for example keeping derived data in step, that depends on it? The need often only appears when you zoom out to dataflows across the whole organisation.

questions.q: True or false: If a search index is updated only by applying changes captured from the database, the index is derived from the database.
questions.explain: When the captured change stream is the only input to the index, nothing else can put data there. The card next shows the full pattern.
questions.rule: One input path means a derived copy.

questions.q: Applying captured database changes to the search index in the same ____ keeps the index consistent with the record.
questions.explain: The pattern is to capture changes and apply them to the index in the same order as the database made them.

questions.q: A recipe site stores recipes in one database and keeps a cache of rendered pages. How should the cache be kept current under this pattern?
questions.explain: The cache becomes entirely derived only if captured changes are its sole source. Any second route in can make it contradict the database.
questions.rule: Keep a single route into each derived copy.
options: Let the web server write each edit to the database and to the cache at the same moment
Rebuild each cache page whenever any visitor requests it, ignoring the database order of edits
Let editors fix cached pages by hand when they notice stale content, then sync later
Update it only from the recipe database's captured changes, applied in commit order
optionExplain: That is a second input path to the cache and invites the conflicts the chapter describes.
This avoids ordering rather than following it, and gives no derivation from the record.
Hand edits are an extra source of input, so the cache stops being entirely derived.
The cache then has one input path and is derived from the record.

questions.q: Put the steps of keeping a search index in step with the database in order.
questions.explain: Writes land in the record first, changes are captured and applied in order, and reads later use the derived index.
items: A user's update is written to the system of record
The change is captured from the database
The captured change is applied to the search index
Queries for keywords are answered from the index

questions.q: A design sends database changes to the index through CDC, but admins also edit the index by hand. What is the flaw?
questions.explain: If CDC is the only way of updating the index, you can be confident it is derived from the system of record. A manual path breaks that sole-input property.
questions.rule: Sole input path, or no guarantee.
options: CDC cannot be combined with any other process, so the index must be rebuilt every night anyway
Hand edits are a second input, so the index is no longer entirely derived and can drift from the record
Hand edits are slower than CDC, so the index lags behind the database by a constant amount
The database must lock the index during edits, which stops all reads of the system of record
optionExplain: CDC works fine with other processes; the issue is the extra writer to the index.
Once there are two inputs, the guarantee of being derived and consistent is lost.
Speed is not the problem; having a second source of truth is.
Nothing in the chapter requires such locking; the problem is the second input path.

questions.q: A CDC pipeline has a bug that drops some changes before they reach the index. What does the chapter's guarantee say about this?
questions.explain: Being the only way to update the index makes it derived, hence consistent with the record, barring software bugs. A bug in the pipeline is outside that guarantee.
questions.rule: Sole input path assumes the pipeline code is correct.
questions.teaches: The confidence that a CDC-fed index is consistent with the system of record applies barring bugs in the software.
options: The guarantee is unconditional, so the missing changes will reappear in the index when the next change arrives
The guarantee covers bugs too, because the sole-input rule makes the pipeline itself reliable by definition
It holds only barring bugs in the software, so the index can still drift despite CDC being the sole input
The guarantee fails only when the database is down, not when the pipeline code is wrong
optionExplain: The chapter attaches a bug caveat; missing changes do not heal by themselves.
A single input path does not make the code that moves data correct.
The chapter adds the qualification barring bugs in the software.
The caveat named in the chapter is about software bugs, not just outages.

questions.q: True or false: If two stores each receive concurrent conflicting writes directly from clients, they may end up permanently different.
questions.explain: Without one party deciding the order, each store may order the writes its own way. The card next shows the example.
questions.rule: Nobody in charge of order means divergence.

questions.q: Why can a database and a search index disagree for good after two clients write to both?
questions.explain: The two stores process writes independently, so each may choose its own order. That lets the stores make contradictory decisions and stay inconsistent.
options: Neither is in charge of write order, so each may order the conflicting writes differently
The index always rejects the second write it receives because search tools cannot handle updates
The database retries failed writes forever while the index gives up after one attempt each
Network latency makes one write arrive later, and later writes are discarded by both systems
optionExplain: That is the cause given: no single party decides the ordering.
Indexes accept updates; the issue is order, not rejection.
The chapter's scenario involves no retry difference.
Neither system discards later writes; they apply them in different orders.

questions.q: A service writes each edit to a document database and to a cache, from two threads. What risk does the chapter predict?
questions.explain: The same shape applies: a primary store and a derived copy both written directly. With two editors, they may apply the edits in different orders.
questions.rule: Two direct writers per item risk lasting disagreement.
options: Two users editing one item may leave the cache and database with different final values
The cache will hold the older value until its expiry time, then match the database again
The database will reject one of the edits, since it never accepts changes from two threads
Reads will slow down because the cache has to lock the database before every lookup
optionExplain: Different processing orders at the two stores can produce contradictory results.
Expiry might hide the difference, but the chapter says the inconsistency can be permanent.
The chapter's problem is not rejection; both stores accept the writes.
No locking relationship is involved; ordering is the issue.

questions.q: True or false: If only one client ever writes a given item, the ordering problem with direct dual writes cannot arise for that item.
questions.explain: The problem comes from two clients with conflicting writes at the same time. With one writer there is no concurrent conflict to order differently.
questions.rule: The risk comes from concurrent conflicting writers.

questions.q: If one system decides the order of every write, a second store can derive its state by processing the writes in the same ____.
questions.explain: A single decider of order lets a derived copy replay the same sequence and reach the same state.
questions.rule: Same writes, same order, same result.

questions.q: A colleague says: the index and database disagree, but waiting a few minutes will fix it. Why is that wrong here?
questions.explain: Each store settled on a different final value. Nothing in the setup makes either one the authority, so time alone does not reconcile them.
questions.rule: Lasting disagreement needs repair, not patience.
options: Search indexes cannot be changed after creation, so the colleague's wait would never end
The database will overwrite the index after a timeout, which makes any waiting unnecessary
Contradictory orderings can leave them permanently inconsistent; waiting does not reconcile
Waiting works only if both systems run in the same datacenter, which they do not here
optionExplain: Indexes can be updated; the disagreement comes from ordering, not immutability.
No timeout-based overwrite is part of the described setup.
The chapter says they may become permanently inconsistent.
Datacenter placement is not the point; permanent inconsistency is.

questions.q: Which change addresses the dual-write problem, according to the chapter?
questions.explain: If it is possible to send all user input through one system that fixes the order, other representations are derived by processing the same ordered writes.
questions.rule: One system decides the order; the rest follow.
