questions.teaches: Funnelling all user input through a single system that decides an ordering for all writes makes it much easier to derive other representations by processing them in the same order.
options: Add a faster network so both stores receive each write at exactly the same instant
Funnel all user input through one system that decides the order, then derive copies from it
Make the search index the primary store so writes reach it first and the database second
Retry every write twice at both stores so any missed write is applied again later
optionExplain: Speed cannot guarantee identical order; the problem is the lack of one decider.
Funnelling input through one ordering system makes derivation straightforward.
Swapping which store is first leaves two independent writers.
Repeating writes does not choose an order; duplicates can add trouble.

questions.q: True or false: To keep derived systems consistent, choosing change data capture over event sourcing matters more than deciding on a total order of writes.
questions.explain: The chapter says the choice between CDC and an event sourcing log is less important than the principle of deciding on a total order. The card next explains why.

questions.q: The approach of processing the same writes in the same order in every replica is called state machine ____.
questions.explain: The chapter ties funnelling writes through one ordering system to state machine replication, as seen with total order broadcast.
questions.rule: Same inputs, same order, same state.

questions.q: An airline wants its booking database, a seat-map cache and an email service to agree. What should it settle first?
questions.explain: Each copy derives from the stream of booking changes. Agreement about the order of that stream matters before any tooling choice.
questions.rule: Settle the order, then pick the tool.
options: Which message broker brand is used, because the tool choice fixes the consistency of the copies
How often each copy polls the others, because polling more often makes the order irrelevant
Which team owns the cache, since ownership is the only source of conflicts between copies
Which single system decides the order of booking changes that all three then process
optionExplain: The chapter says the tool choice is less important than deciding on a total order.
Faster polling does not create agreement about the order of writes.
Ownership does not decide the order of writes; a single ordered stream does.
A total order is the principle that makes derivation easy.

questions.q: One team uses CDC and another uses event sourcing, and each claims a total order. How do the two relate?
questions.explain: The chapter says that whether you use CDC or an event sourcing log is less important than simply deciding on a total order.
options: Only event sourcing supplies an order, because CDC reads from a database that is unordered
Only CDC supplies an order, because event sourcing records events with no relation to time
Either can supply the ordered log; what counts is that one total order exists
Neither supplies an order, so total order broadcast must be added to either approach
optionExplain: CDC reads the database's own ordered change log; both can supply an order.
Event sourcing logs are ordered by definition in the chapter.
The chapter treats the two as alternatives for the same principle.
Total order broadcast is the underlying idea, not an add-on to each approach.

questions.q: A system adds a second service that also writes to the derived views directly, bypassing the ordered log. What is the likely effect?
questions.explain: A write that skips the ordering system reintroduces the situation where no single party decides order. That is the situation the principle exists to avoid.
options: The views no longer follow a single order, so contradictions between them become possible again
Nothing changes, because consistency depends on the log technology rather than on who writes
The log becomes faster, since the second service takes load off the single ordering system
The views become immune to conflicts, since two writers cross-check each other's entries
optionExplain: A second path undermines the total order that kept the views consistent.
The chapter says the order is the principle, not the technology.
Speed is not what the order protects; a bypass breaks consistency.
Two uncoordinated writers are the source of the earlier dual-write problem.

questions.q: True or false: A view that a second service also writes directly, bypassing the log, can still be relied on to follow the log.
questions.explain: The bypass creates a second writer with no shared order, which reintroduces the contradictions the principle exists to avoid.
questions.rule: Every writer must go through the order.

questions.q: A friend asks why deciding a total order of writes is likened to something from earlier chapters. Which link does the chapter make?
questions.explain: Funnelling all input through one ordering system applies the state machine replication approach from the total order broadcast discussion.
questions.rule: Log-based ordering is state machine replication.
questions.teaches: Funnelling writes through a single ordering system is an application of state machine replication, the approach seen with total order broadcast.
options: Two-phase commit, which orders writes by asking every node to vote on each
State machine replication, which relates to total order broadcast
Quorum reads, which order writes by comparing version numbers from several replicas
Hash partitioning, which orders writes by spreading keys evenly across nodes
optionExplain: Two-phase commit is the contrast case (atomic commit), not the link made here.
The chapter names state machine replication and total order broadcast.
Quorum reads are from replication; they are not what the chapter links here.
Partitioning spreads keys; it does not decide a total order.

questions.q: True or false: If an update from an event log is idempotent, running it twice has the same effect as running it once.
questions.explain: That is what idempotent means: same effect however many times it runs. The card next explains how this helps recovery.

questions.q: What does it mean for a derived-data update to be idempotent?
questions.explain: An idempotent operation has the same effect no matter whether it is executed once or multiple times. That makes a retry harmless.
options: It always completes in the same amount of time on every replica that runs it
It can only be executed by the node that currently holds the leader role in the cluster
It is written to the log before being applied to the derived view in the same transaction
It has the same effect whether it is applied once or several times
optionExplain: Idempotence is about effect, not duration.
Leadership is unrelated to repeatability.
That describes write-ahead ordering, not idempotence.
This is the definition used in the chapter.

questions.q: A job derives a leaderboard from a log of match results. It crashes halfway. What makes rerunning it safe?
questions.explain: Replaying the same log through a deterministic function gives the same output, and idempotent updates do no harm when repeated. Recovery is a rerun.
questions.rule: Deterministic plus idempotent equals safe rerun.
options: The job is deterministic and idempotent, so replaying the same results gives the same board
The log is deleted after each read, so the job cannot read the same result twice
The leaderboard is stored on the job's local disk, which survives every kind of crash intact
Each match result is processed by two jobs at once, so the second always covers the first
optionExplain: Deterministic, idempotent derivation allows safe replay.
Deleting reads would make recovery harder, not easier.
Local storage does not make a replay safe; the properties of the derivation do.
Running twice is only safe because of idempotence, not because of coverage.

questions.q: An update that has the same effect whether it is executed once or several times is called ____.
questions.explain: Idempotence is what makes a retry after a fault safe.

questions.q: A job inserts one row per click, keyed by event id, and is retried after a fault. What happens to a duplicate?
questions.explain: A repeat with the same key has no further effect. Operation identifiers are one way to make a non-idempotent step idempotent.
options: The duplicate row is stored, doubling the count, because retries always create new rows
The job halts permanently, because the database cannot cope with a repeated key at all
Both rows merge into a new row with a new id, so the original id is lost
The unique key makes the second insert have no further effect, so the row count stays correct
optionExplain: With a unique key on the event id the repeat can be recognised.
Rejecting a duplicate is the intended effect, not a permanent halt.
Nothing merges rows into a new id here.
Keyed on the event id, repeats do not add rows.

questions.q: True or false: A derived-data job that adds one to a counter for each event is idempotent, so retrying it after a crash is safe.
questions.explain: Adding one per event changes the total each time it runs, so a repeat counts the event twice. An idempotent version would need to record which events were applied.
questions.rule: Increments are not idempotent on their own.

questions.q: A team drops idempotence because the log guarantees order. What does the chapter's reasoning suggest?
questions.explain: A deterministic derivation gives the same result for the same events, but a retry may apply an update twice. Idempotence makes that harmless.
questions.rule: Keep both properties for easy recovery.
questions.teaches: Updating a derived data system from an event log can often be made deterministic and idempotent, which is what makes recovery from faults quite easy.
options: Nothing is lost, since an ordered log never delivers anything more than once
It is fine, since idempotence only helps when the log is partitioned across several nodes
Order is not enough; retries can repeat an update, so make it idempotent
It is fine, since deterministic functions can never produce the same effect twice
optionExplain: Faults and retries can repeat work; order does not prevent that.
Retries matter in any setting, not only partitioned ones.
Ordered logs and idempotent updates together make recovery easy.
Deterministic means same input gives the same output, which says nothing about repeats.

questions.q: True or false: Distributed transactions and log-based derived data pursue a similar goal by different means.
questions.explain: Both aim to keep several systems consistent with each other, one with locks and atomic commit, one with a log. The card next sets them side by side.

questions.q: Match each concern to how a distributed transaction handles it versus how a log-based system does.
questions.explain: Transactions use locks and atomic commit. Log-based systems order with a log and get exactly-once effect through deterministic retry and idempotence.
questions.rule: Locks and commit versus log and idempotence.
pairs: A log that fixes the order

questions.q: After a customer edits a profile, the page reloads from a derived read copy that is updated asynchronously. What might the customer see?
questions.explain: Transaction systems usually provide linearizability and so reading your own writes. Asynchronously updated derived data does not by default.
questions.rule: Async copies can lag behind your write.
options: Their new profile always, because derived data systems are linearizable by design
Their old profile, since derived data often lacks the timing guarantee of reading your own writes
An error page, because asynchronous systems reject reads that follow a write quickly
A merged profile, because derived systems combine old and new versions before answering
optionExplain: Transactions usually provide linearizability; derived data does not by default.
Asynchronously derived data does not by default offer read-your-own-writes.
Nothing rejects the read; it may simply return stale data.
The chapter describes no merging; the issue is timing.

questions.q: Which feature belongs to log-based derived data rather than to a distributed transaction?
questions.explain: The log supplies the order and deterministic retry with idempotence supplies safe repetition. Locks and atomic commit belong to transactions.
questions.rule: Know which mechanism belongs to which approach.
options: Holding locks on every participant until the commit decision arrives
Retrying deterministically with idempotent operations
Running an atomic commit protocol across the participating systems
Providing linearizability so a writer waits until all readers can see the write
optionExplain: Locking for mutual exclusion is the transaction mechanism.
Log-based systems rely on deterministic retry and idempotence.
Atomic commit is what distributed transactions use for exactly-once effect.
Linearizability is typically provided by transaction systems.

questions.q: A team replaces a distributed transaction with an asynchronous log. Which guarantee will they most likely have to give up by default?
questions.explain: The biggest difference is linearizability and the guarantees it implies, such as reading your own writes. Derived data is often updated asynchronously.
questions.rule: Expect to lose timing guarantees by default.
options: The guarantee that each update eventually takes effect once the pipeline is running
The ability to order writes, because logs cannot decide a sequence of events
The ability to recover from faults, because retries are not possible without locks
The timing guarantee that a reader sees a write right after it is committed
optionExplain: Eventual effect is what log-based systems aim for, so it is not given up.
Logs are used precisely to order writes.
Log-based systems retry with idempotence; recovery remains possible.
Linearizability and read-your-own-writes are not provided by default.

questions.q: True or false: A colleague says log-based derived data and distributed transactions use the same mechanism, locks, to decide the order of writes.
questions.explain: Distributed transactions use locks for mutual exclusion, while change data capture and event sourcing use a log to fix the order.

questions.q: A bank wants a receipt to appear instantly after a transfer. Which approach gives that by default, according to the chapter's comparison?
questions.explain: Timeliness for readers is something transactions usually give by default. Log-based pipelines can add it only with extra work, as the chapter later discusses.
questions.rule: Need instant visibility: expect extra work with logs.
questions.teaches: Transaction systems usually provide linearizability, which implies guarantees such as reading your own writes, whereas asynchronously derived systems do not by default.
options: A transaction system that is typically linearizable
An asynchronous log pipeline, since log-based systems always update every copy immediately
A derived search index, since indexes answer queries faster than the record they copy
An offline cache on the device, since local copies are always updated before the server
optionExplain: Transaction systems usually provide linearizability by default.
Log pipelines are usually asynchronous, with no default timing guarantee.
Speed of lookup is unrelated to how soon a write becomes visible.
A local cache has the opposite problem of staleness without explicit work.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, distributed transactions have been used successfully in no environment at all.
questions.explain: The author says that within limited environments willing to pay the cost, they have been used successfully. The card next shows his actual position.
questions.rule: His criticism is aimed at XA's limits, not at every use.

questions.q: According to the author, what makes XA a poor basis for general integration?
questions.explain: The author says XA has poor fault tolerance and performance characteristics, which severely limit its usefulness.
options: It cannot make two databases commit together, so it fails at its single main job
It is available only for relational databases, which excludes every other kind of store
Its poor fault tolerance and performance characteristics severely limit its usefulness
It depends on logs rather than locks, which makes recovery after a crash impossible
optionExplain: XA is designed to do exactly that; his complaint is about cost and resilience.
He does not make a coverage argument.
These are the two reasons he gives.
XA is on the transaction side, and the author favours the log side.

questions.q: A team must keep a billing database and a reporting store in step, and no better protocol exists. What would the author most likely suggest?
questions.explain: He prefers log-based derived data but wants good guidance for coping with weaker timing guarantees.
questions.rule: Prefer logs, but offer guidance for the weaker guarantees.
options: Run XA across both stores, since he calls it the most promising approach for heterogeneous systems
Tell users that eventual consistency is inevitable and leave them to deal with it themselves
Derive the reporting store from the billing database's log, and plan for the timing guarantees it lacks
Merge both workloads into one database so that no integration is needed at all
optionExplain: He calls log-based derived data the most promising one, not XA.
He explicitly says that is not a productive thing to tell everyone.
He favours log-based derived data and says guidance is needed on eventual consistency.
Merging does not address the chapter's premise that no one tool fits every use.

questions.q: The author says XA has poor fault tolerance and ____ characteristics, which severely limit its usefulness.
questions.explain: These two shortcomings are why he turns to log-based derived data for integration.

questions.q: Suppose a widely adopted, well-performing distributed transaction protocol appeared. How would the author's argument likely change?
questions.explain: He says that in the absence of widespread support for a good distributed transaction protocol, log-based derived data is the most promising approach.
questions.rule: The conclusion depends on the stated condition.
options: The case for log-based derived data would weaken, since it rested on that gap
Nothing, since he considers logs superior to transactions in every setting and every workload
He would then argue logs are unsafe, since transactions would be the only way to order writes
He would call XA the best choice, since it would by then have solved its performance problems
optionExplain: His claim was framed as holding in the absence of widespread support for a good protocol.
His claim is conditional on the absence of a good, widely supported protocol.
He does not argue logs are unsafe; his claim concerns practicality.
XA's limits are his reason for looking elsewhere, and a new protocol is a different thing.

questions.q: True or false: A summary says the author holds that eventual consistency is inevitable and users should cope. The summary is accurate.
questions.explain: He says he does not think it is productive to tell everyone that, at least not without good guidance on how to deal with it.
questions.rule: He rejects a bare suck-it-up stance.

questions.q: A colleague claims a better distributed transaction protocol would solve this, and asks if the author agrees. What did he say?
questions.explain: He believes a better protocol might be possible, but adoption and integration with existing tools would be challenging and unlikely to happen soon.
questions.rule: A good protocol is not the same as a deployed one.
questions.teaches: A better distributed transaction protocol may be possible, but getting it widely adopted and integrated with existing tools would be challenging and unlikely to happen soon.
options: It is impossible in principle, because atomic commit cannot be made faster than two-phase commit
It already exists and is widely deployed, so the choice between the two approaches is settled
It is possible and imminent, so readers should wait before choosing log-based approaches
Possible in principle, but adoption would be hard and slow
optionExplain: He says it might be possible; his doubt is about adoption.
He says the opposite: such a protocol is not widely supported today.
He calls wide adoption unlikely to happen soon.
The author makes this point about adoption.

questions.q: True or false: Events in two different partitions of a partitioned log have a well-defined relative order.
questions.explain: Each partition has its own order, so the order between partitions is ambiguous. The card next explains the scale limits.

questions.q: Why does a totally ordered log usually need all events to pass through a single leader node?
questions.explain: Constructing a totally ordered log needs one node that decides the ordering for all events.
options: Followers cannot store events unless the leader has first compressed them into batches
One node must decide the order of all events
Leaders are the only nodes allowed to talk to clients over a network connection
The log can only be read by one node at a time, so readers queue behind the leader
optionExplain: Compression is not the reason; deciding order is.
A single deciding node is what creates one total order.
Client access is not the constraint described.
Reads are not the constraint; deciding the order is.

questions.q: A messaging service outgrows one machine and splits its event log across eight partitions. What has it lost?
questions.explain: The throughput of one machine was the limit, so the log is partitioned and the order across partitions becomes ambiguous.
questions.rule: Scale by partitioning costs cross-partition order.
options: The ability to order events inside each partition, since partitioning removes all ordering
The ability to store events durably, since partitions have no replicas of their own
The need for a leader, since each partition now decides its order by majority vote
A defined order between events in different partitions
optionExplain: Order inside a partition is preserved; it is between partitions that it is lost.
Partitioning does not remove durability.
Each partition still has a leader that decides its order.
Within a partition order holds; across partitions it is ambiguous.

questions.q: Which setup yields an undefined order between events from two places?
questions.explain: With multiple datacenters you typically have a separate leader in each, because network delays make synchronous coordination inefficient. Events from different datacenters have no defined order.
questions.rule: Leader per site means undefined order across sites.
options: One datacenter with one leader, where all events pass through the leader in sequence
Two datacenters with a leader each, since cross-datacenter coordination is slow
A single-leader database whose followers copy the leader's log in the same order
A small application whose events are all handled by one machine and one log
optionExplain: A single leader gives a total order.
The chapter says separate leaders per datacenter imply undefined ordering between them.
Followers replay the leader's order; no ambiguity arises.
Small systems can construct a totally ordered log.

questions.q: In formal terms, deciding on a total order of events is known as total order ____.
questions.explain: Total order broadcast is equivalent to consensus, which is why scaling it is hard.

questions.q: True or false: Scaling a system by adding more machines makes a totally ordered log easier to maintain.
questions.explain: More machines usually means partitioning or multiple leaders, both of which make the order across them ambiguous.

questions.q: A friend suggests a consensus algorithm to order events across many nodes. What does the chapter say about doing this at scale?
questions.explain: Deciding a total order of events is known as total order broadcast, which is equivalent to consensus. Designing consensus algorithms that scale beyond one node and work well across locations is still open research.
questions.rule: Consensus ordering has a single-node throughput limit.
questions.teaches: Total order broadcast is equivalent to consensus, and most consensus algorithms assume one node can handle the whole stream, so scaling beyond that remains an open research problem.
options: Consensus algorithms split ordering work across any number of nodes, so the problem is solved
Consensus is unrelated to total order broadcast, so it cannot help with ordering at all
Most consensus algorithms assume one node handles the stream; scaling past it is open research
Consensus works only inside one datacenter and has no known problems there at any scale
optionExplain: The chapter says they do not provide a mechanism for nodes to share the work.
The chapter says total order broadcast is equivalent to consensus.
The chapter equates total order broadcast with consensus and calls the scale problem open.
The chapter's concern is throughput beyond a single node, as well as geography.

questions.q: True or false: Two events produced by two different microservices with independent state have a defined order relative to each other.
questions.explain: With no durable state shared between services, there is no defined order between their events. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Independent state means no shared order.

questions.q: When two events originate in different services with independent durable state, there is no ____ order for those events.
questions.explain: Each service keeps its durable state as an independent unit, so nothing fixes an order between events from different services.

questions.q: Order these cases from easiest to hardest to give a defined order, according to the chapter's reasoning.
questions.explain: Routing all updates of one object to one partition gives a total order easily; one leader orders its own events; different datacenters or offline clients lack a defined order.
questions.rule: Shared leader means order; separate state means none.
questions.teaches: When there are multiple updates of the same object, they can be totally ordered by routing all updates for that object ID to the same log partition.
items: Updates to one object routed to one log partition
Events from one datacenter's leader
Events from two different datacenters
Events from a client acting offline and a server

questions.q: A shop has an orders service and a stock service, each with its own database. What is true of their events?
questions.explain: When two events originate in different services with no shared durable state, there is no defined order for those events.
questions.rule: No shared state, no shared order.
options: There is no defined order between events that originate in different services
The orders service's event always comes first, because orders cause stock changes
Both are stored in one shared log, so their order is always the log's order
Their order is set by the larger timestamp, which every service agrees on exactly
optionExplain: Independent services share no durable state to fix an order.
The chapter says no order is defined between them, even if one is intuitive.
Services keep independent durable state in the design described.
Clock timestamps are not a defined shared order here.

questions.q: True or false: Two concurrent events with no causal link between them can be ordered arbitrarily without causing a serious problem.
questions.explain: Where there is no causal link the lack of a total order is not a big problem, since concurrent events can be ordered arbitrarily.
questions.rule: Order matters when events are related.

questions.q: A note-taking app edits on phones offline, then syncs. Which statement fits the chapter?
questions.explain: Client-side state updated immediately and offline use means clients and servers are very likely to see events in different orders.
questions.rule: Offline clients lack the server's order.
options: The server always sees the edits in the same order as the phone, since both read one log
Edits to different notes are always causally linked, so all of them need a total order
The phone and the server may see edits in different orders, so ordering cannot be assumed from the server
The app can avoid all ordering questions because phones cannot keep any state locally
optionExplain: Offline operation breaks that assumption.
Unrelated edits have no causal link, and concurrent ones can be ordered arbitrarily.
Clients acting offline are likely to see events in a different order from servers.
Offline operation relies on client-side state, which is the point.
questions.teaches: Applications that update client-side state immediately on user input, without waiting for the server, and keep working offline are very likely to see events in a different order from the servers.

questions.q: True or false: If friendship status and messages are stored in separate places, a notification service could process a message before an earlier unfriend event.
questions.explain: Without a captured causal dependency the two events may be handled in either order. The card next gives the example.
questions.rule: Separate stores can lose cause and effect.

questions.q: In the chapter's social network example, what does the notification service effectively perform?
questions.explain: Notifications are effectively a join between the messages and the friend list, which relates to the timing issues of joins.
options: A merge of two replicas of the friend list held in different datacenters
A join between the messages and the friend list
A compaction of old messages into a smaller summary
An election of a leader to decide which message is delivered first
optionExplain: There is one friend list; the issue is its relation to messages.
Notifications are effectively a join of messages and friend status.
Compaction is unrelated to the example.
No leader election takes place in the example.

questions.q: A forum user blocks another user and then posts a rude comment. The two events go to different services. What could go wrong?
questions.explain: The block must be processed before the comment for the rule to hold. If the dependency is not captured, the comment may be handled first.
options: The comment could be shown twice to everyone, because blocks duplicate all later events
The block could be undone automatically, because later events override earlier ones
The forum would stop accepting comments, because blocks and comments cannot coexist in one system
The comment could be shown to the blocked user because the block was not seen first
optionExplain: Duplication is not the failure in the example.
That is not what the example describes.
The failure is wrong delivery, not a halt.
The causal dependency between block and comment may be lost.

questions.q: In the social network example, the notification service is effectively performing a ____ between messages and the friend list.
questions.explain: A join combines two datasets, and the result depends on the timing of the events on each side.

questions.q: If both the unfriend and the message events were put through one totally ordered log partition, what would happen to the notification?
questions.explain: In one ordered stream the unfriend event precedes the message, so the notification step sees the correct state. Capturing the dependency is what matters.
options: The unfriend would be processed first, so the ex-partner would not be notified
The ex-partner would still be notified, because logs ignore the content of events
Nobody would be notified, because logs drop messages that follow friend changes
The ex-partner would be notified twice, once from each event, because logs deliver both
optionExplain: One ordered stream preserves the order in which they occurred.
An ordered log preserves the order of the events.
No dropping occurs in an ordered log.
Delivery count is not affected by ordering in this way.

questions.q: True or false: Capturing the causal dependency between an unfriend event and a later message would stop the ex-partner from being notified.
questions.explain: If the notification step knows the unfriend came first, it can use the updated friend list and skip the ex-partner.
questions.rule: Capture the dependency, avoid the wrong effect.

questions.q: A team blames a slow network for the wrong notification and expects it to fix itself. What does the example suggest instead?
questions.explain: The two events were both handled correctly in isolation; the failure came from processing them in the wrong relative order.
questions.rule: Wrong order of related events is not a speed problem.
options: The bug comes from too few notification servers, so adding capacity will remove it
The bug comes from using friend lists at all, so lists should be removed from the design
The wrong notification came from lost ordering between related events, not from slowness
The bug comes from users sending messages too quickly, so a rate limit would remove it
optionExplain: Capacity does not restore a lost causal order.
The example does not argue against friend lists.
The cause is an uncaptured causal dependency between events.
Rate limiting would not restore the order of the two events.

questions.q: A payments app records a refund in one system and sends a receipt from another. Which concern from the chapter applies?
questions.explain: As with the unfriend example, an external action (a notification or receipt) can depend on the order of related events kept elsewhere.
questions.teaches: The notification case is a timing issue of joins: a join between two data sources can depend on the order of events, so related events in separate places need their order recorded.
options: Receipts are always sent first because they are cheaper to process than refunds
The receipt may run before the refund, so capture the causal order
Refunds and receipts can never be related, so no ordering is needed
Only the refund system needs a total order, because receipts have no effect outside the app
optionExplain: Processing cost does not decide order.
Same shape: related events in different places, with an external effect.
They are related; that is why the order matters.
A receipt is an external effect, which is where wrong order shows.

questions.q: True or false: Conflict resolution algorithms can undo the effect of a notification that was already sent to the wrong person.
questions.explain: They help with state, but not when actions have external side effects such as sending a notification. The card next lists the starting points.
questions.rule: You cannot unsend an external action.

questions.q: What is one thing logical timestamps give you, according to the chapter?
questions.explain: Logical timestamps provide total ordering without coordination. Recipients must still cope with events delivered out of order and extra metadata must travel with them.
questions.rule: Order without coordination, at the price of metadata.
options: A guarantee that every event is delivered in order to every recipient
A way to avoid passing any metadata between systems
A means of undoing external side effects after they happen
A total ordering without needing coordination
optionExplain: The chapter says recipients still have to handle out-of-order delivery.
They require additional metadata to be passed around.
Timestamps do not undo external effects.
That is their advantage when total order broadcast is not feasible.

questions.q: An online shop wants to know what price and stock status a customer saw when they bought an item. Which starting point fits?
questions.explain: Logging an event for the state the user saw, with a unique identifier, lets later events reference it to record the dependency.
questions.rule: Reference the event that informed the decision.
options: Log what the customer saw as an event with an id that the purchase references
Use logical timestamps alone, because they record the screen contents shown to each user
Rely on conflict resolution, because it reconstructs what the customer saw after the fact
Route all customers to one server, because a single server remembers everything shown
optionExplain: That is the second starting point.
Timestamps order events; they do not record what a user saw.
Conflict resolution handles out-of-order events, not recorded views.
That does not record what was shown and does not scale.

questions.q: Match each starting point to what it offers or lacks.
questions.explain: Each tool addresses part of the problem; none removes the need to think about dependencies.
questions.rule: Know what each tool does and does not cover.
pairs: Total order without coordination, but needs metadata
Records the state the user saw before deciding
Fixes state but not external side effects

questions.q: A team relies only on conflict resolution to fix out-of-order events. What kind of mistake will remain?
questions.explain: State can be corrected after the fact, but a sent notification cannot be reordered. External side effects remain the gap.
questions.rule: State can be repaired; outside actions cannot.
options: Wrong values in the stored state, because conflict resolution cannot touch stored data
Lost events in the log, because conflict resolution deletes the oldest events
Wrong timestamps on messages, because it cannot read the timestamps of events
Actions with external side effects, such as a notification already sent
optionExplain: It is useful for maintaining state, so stored state is its strength.
It does not delete events as described in the chapter.
Timestamps are not what the weakness concerns.
Conflict resolution helps maintain state but not these actions.

questions.q: True or false: A conflict resolution algorithm can repair state that was updated in the wrong order, but cannot reverse a notification already sent.
questions.explain: State can be corrected afterwards, whereas an action with external side effects cannot be undone by reordering.

questions.q: A chat system sends push alerts for new messages. Which choice best handles the ex-partner style problem for alerts?
questions.explain: Because the effect is outside the system, the dependency has to be respected before acting. Reordering later is no help.
questions.rule: For external effects, get the order right first.
questions.teaches: Logical timestamps still require recipients to handle events delivered out of order and require additional metadata to be passed around.
options: Send the alert and fix it with conflict resolution later, because conflict resolution reverses alerts
Skip ordering because the state is eventually correct, so alerts do not matter
Capture the dependency so the alert step sees the block event first
Delay all alerts by a fixed minute, because a delay always restores the right order
optionExplain: It does not help with external side effects.
Eventually correct state does not undo a sent alert.
External effects need the order right in advance.
A fixed delay does not guarantee the dependency is captured.

questions.q: True or false: Stream processors handle unbounded datasets, while batch inputs have a known finite size.
questions.explain: The chapter gives bounded versus unbounded input as the main difference. The card next adds how engines blur it.

questions.q: Which pair names the outputs the chapter gives for batch and stream processes?
questions.explain: Outputs of batch and stream processes are derived datasets such as search indexes, materialized views, recommendations to show users and aggregate metrics.
options: Source tables and raw event logs
Search indexes and materialized views
Hardware sensors and network switches
Transaction locks and commit records
optionExplain: Those are inputs, not derived outputs.
Derived datasets such as these are named.
Hardware is not an output of processing.
Locks and commit records belong to databases, not derived data.

questions.q: A nightly job recomputes a recommendation table from a full day of purchases. Which kind of input does it process?
questions.explain: Batch inputs are of known, finite size. A day's purchases collected before the run fits that description.
options: An unbounded stream that never ends, so it is stream processing
A finite dataset of known size, so it is batch processing
A message queue with no end, so it is stream processing with microbatches
A live feed of exchange rates, so it is a join with an unbounded input
optionExplain: A day of purchases is a closed dataset.
Fixed, bounded input is the batch case.
Microbatches are a stream engine technique; this input is finite.
The job described reads a fixed file of purchases.

questions.q: How do Spark and Flink illustrate the blurring of batch and stream processing?
questions.explain: Spark breaks the stream into microbatches over its batch engine, whereas Apache Flink performs batch processing on top of a stream processing engine.
questions.rule: Know which engine builds on which.
options: Both only do batch processing, but they use different names for the same operations
Both only do stream processing, so batch jobs must be written for another tool
Spark does batch processing on a stream engine, while Flink does stream processing on a batch engine
Spark runs streams as microbatches on a batch engine; Flink runs batches on a stream engine
optionExplain: Each supports both styles, built on opposite foundations.
Flink also runs batch jobs, and Spark handles batch natively.
This reverses their designs.
Each emulates one style on top of the other.

questions.q: Stream processors operate on ____ datasets, whereas batch inputs are of a known, finite size.
questions.explain: Bounded versus unbounded input is the fundamental difference the chapter names.

questions.q: True or false: Because one style of processing can be emulated on the other, performance will be the same whichever you use.
questions.explain: In principle either can emulate the other, but performance characteristics vary. For example, microbatching may perform poorly on hopping or sliding windows.
questions.rule: Emulation is possible; equal speed is not guaranteed.

questions.q: A team builds a stream job on top of a microbatching engine, with hopping windows over the last hour. What does the chapter warn about?
questions.explain: In principle one type can be emulated on the other, but performance varies; microbatching may perform poorly on hopping or sliding windows.
questions.rule: Check the fit of the engine to the window type.
questions.teaches: Microbatching may perform poorly on hopping or sliding windows, one example of how performance characteristics vary when one style of processing is emulated on the other.
options: Microbatching may perform poorly on hopping or sliding windows
Microbatching cannot produce any output until the stream has fully ended
Microbatching always loses events when windows overlap in time
Microbatching works for windows but fails for aggregations and joins on the same data
optionExplain: The chapter gives this as an example of performance differing.
Microbatching produces output per batch; the stated problem is windows.
The chapter says only that performance may be poor.
The chapter does not make this claim.

questions.q: True or false: A batch function whose output depends only on its input, with no side effects, suits fault tolerance.
questions.explain: Deterministic, pure functions can be rerun with the same result. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Same input, same output, rerun safely.

questions.q: Which description of batch processing matches the chapter's functional flavour?
questions.explain: The chapter describes batch processing as encouraging deterministic, pure functions with no side effects other than explicit outputs, treating inputs as immutable and outputs as append-only.
options: Functions that update their inputs in place so no extra storage is needed
Functions that depend on the time they are run, so results vary between runs
Deterministic functions with immutable inputs and append-only outputs
Functions that write to several external services as side effects at the same time
optionExplain: The flavour treats inputs as immutable.
Determinism is the point; results should not vary.
Correct. The chapter describes batch processing as encouraging deterministic, pure functions with no side effects other than explicit outputs, treating inputs as immutable and outputs as append-only.
Side effects other than explicit outputs are avoided.

questions.q: Stream processing is similar to batch processing but extends operators to allow managed, fault-tolerant ____.
questions.explain: Stream operators may keep state, such as for aggregations and joins, and the framework manages it to survive faults.
questions.rule: Streams add managed state to the functional picture.
questions.teaches: Stream processing extends the functional operator model to allow managed, fault-tolerant state.

questions.q: A team writes a job that overwrites its input files to save space. What does the functional principle suggest?
questions.explain: Pure functions over immutable inputs allow recovery by recomputation. Destroying the input removes that option.
questions.rule: Never destroy what you derive from.
options: Keep overwriting, since overwriting makes the job faster and rerunning is rarely needed
Encrypt the inputs first, since encryption makes a job deterministic
Write to new append-only outputs and leave inputs untouched
Run the job twice at once, since two copies make overwriting safe
optionExplain: Rerunning is the reason for the principle.
Encryption does not make a function pure.
Immutable inputs and append-only outputs keep derivation repeatable.
Two copies do not give repeatable results.

questions.q: True or false: A batch job that overwrites its own input file can be rerun safely after a crash.
questions.explain: Once the input has been overwritten the original data is gone, so a rerun would not start from the same input.
questions.rule: Never destroy the input you derive from.

questions.q: A colleague says a job is functional because it is deterministic, even though it sends an email on every run. What is missing?
questions.explain: Output must depend only on the input and have no side effects other than explicit outputs. An email on each run is such a side effect.
options: It has a side effect beyond its output, breaking purity
Determinism requires randomness, so a deterministic job cannot be functional
Emails are an append-only output, so the job already meets the principle
The job should run slower, since functional jobs must be single threaded
optionExplain: No side effects other than explicit outputs are allowed in the principle.
Determinism means same input gives same output.
An email is an external side effect, not an explicit data output.
The principle does not address speed or threads.

questions.q: A team maintains a machine learning model and a cache from the same event log. Which framing does the chapter encourage?
questions.explain: No matter whether derived data is a search index, a statistical model or a cache, it helps to think of data pipelines that derive one from another.
questions.rule: One mental model for all derived data.
options: Treat the model as a database and the cache as an application, with separate rules for each
Update the cache by hand and the model by batch, since the two cannot share a pipeline
Avoid deriving the model from events, since models can only be built from files
Treat both as pipelines pushing state changes through functional code
optionExplain: The chapter uses one pipeline view for all derived data.
Both can be derived by pipelines from the same events.
Nothing in the chapter forbids deriving models from event logs.
The principle applies whether the derived data is an index, a model or a cache.
questions.teaches: Thinking in terms of data pipelines means pushing state changes in one system through functional application code and applying the effects to derived systems.

questions.q: True or false: A distributed transaction tends to spread a failure of one participant to the others.
questions.explain: Distributed transactions abort if any one participant fails, which amplifies failures. The card next contrasts this with asynchronous derivation.

questions.q: Why does the chapter say distributed transactions amplify failures?
questions.explain: Distributed transactions abort if any one participant fails, so they tend to amplify failures by spreading them to the rest of the system.
questions.rule: All must succeed, so one failure hurts all.
options: They require every participant to run on the same hardware as the coordinator
They abort if any one participant fails, spreading the failure to the rest
They store a second copy of every record, which doubles the chance of a crash
They delay commits until all clients are idle, which makes outages last longer
optionExplain: Hardware co-location is not the reason.
Correct. Distributed transactions abort if any one participant fails, so they tend to amplify failures by spreading them to the rest of the system.
Storage duplication is not the argument.
The reason is abort propagation, not waiting for idle clients.

questions.q: A reporting store is fed from an order log. The reporting store goes down for an hour. What happens under asynchronous derivation?
questions.explain: The log buffers events, so a slow or failed consumer does not affect the producer or other consumers, and it can catch up later.
questions.rule: Logs let consumers fail without harming others.
options: Orders stop, because the log refuses new events while any reader is down
Orders continue but the missed hour is lost, because the store cannot read old events
Orders continue, but every other derived system also goes offline until the store returns
Orders continue to be accepted and the reporting store catches up from the log after recovery
optionExplain: Logs keep accepting events while readers are down.
The store reads the buffered events after recovery.
A fault in one consumer does not stop others.
The fault is contained locally.

questions.q: Which setup would likely amplify the outage of a search index into the main database?
questions.explain: A distributed transaction ties the fates of the participants. The log and queue designs decouple them.
questions.rule: Coupling spreads failure; buffering contains it.
options: The index is fed from the database's log and may lag behind it during an outage
Both are updated in one distributed transaction, so index failure aborts writes
The index is rebuilt overnight from a snapshot of the database
The index is fed by a queue that holds changes while the index is unreachable
optionExplain: This is the contained, asynchronous setup.
An aborting participant spreads failure to the rest.
A rebuilt index does not block database writes.
The queue buffers changes and decouples the two.

questions.q: Distributed transactions abort if any one participant fails, so they tend to ____ failures.
questions.explain: The abort spreads a local failure to the rest of the system.

questions.q: A term-partitioned secondary index must update several partitions for each write. How does the chapter say this is best done?
questions.explain: A partitioned system with secondary indexes either sends writes to multiple partitions (term-partitioned index) or reads to all partitions (document-partitioned index). Such cross-partition communication is most reliable and scalable if the index is maintained asynchronously.
questions.teaches: Secondary indexes often cross partition boundaries, and maintaining them asynchronously makes the cross-partition communication most reliable and scalable.
options: Synchronously in one distributed transaction, so every write reaches all partitions together
By sending reads to every partition instead, since write routing is always unreliable
Asynchronously, because cross-partition communication is then most reliable and scalable
By avoiding secondary indexes entirely, since partitioned systems cannot support them
optionExplain: That is the approach the chapter says is less robust.
That describes the document-partitioned case, not term-partitioned.
Asynchronous index maintenance is the recommended route.
The chapter does not say they cannot be supported.

questions.q: True or false: In an asynchronous log-based system, a crash of one consumer forces the producer to stop accepting new events.
questions.explain: The log buffers events for the failed consumer, so the producer and other consumers carry on.

questions.q: A system keeps one table and its own index inside one database, updated in the same transaction. Does the chapter's argument say to change this?
questions.explain: The chapter notes that a relational database updates secondary indexes synchronously in the same transaction. The robustness argument concerns systems spanning components.
questions.rule: Scope the argument to cross-system derivation.
options: No, synchronous index maintenance inside a single database is a normal case that works well
Yes, every index should be rebuilt asynchronously, whatever the system
Yes, because transactions inside one database also amplify failures to other applications
No, because indexes inside a database are never derived data at all
optionExplain: The argument is about derived data across systems.
The point concerns systems that cross boundaries.
The amplification concern is about distributed transactions.
The chapter treats an index as a derived dataset.
questions.teaches: A relational database updates its secondary indexes synchronously within the same transaction as the write to the table being indexed, which works well inside a single database.

questions.q: True or false: Without reprocessing, schema evolution is mostly limited to simple changes such as adding an optional field.
questions.explain: The chapter says this holds for both schema-on-write and schema-on-read. The card next shows what reprocessing adds.

questions.q: Which job does the chapter give to batch processing when maintaining derived data?
questions.explain: Stream processing reflects changes with low delay, whereas batch processing reprocesses accumulated historical data to derive new views.
questions.rule: Stream for freshness, batch for reprocessing.
options: Reprocessing large amounts of accumulated historical data to derive new views
Reflecting each new input change in views with the lowest possible delay
Making sure every user sees their own writes immediately
Deciding the total order of concurrent writes across datacenters
optionExplain: Batch is suited to bulk historical reprocessing.
That is the job of stream processing.
Read-your-writes is a timing guarantee unrelated to batch.
Ordering is a role of the log, not of reprocessing.

questions.q: True or false: The limit on schema evolution without reprocessing applies in a schema-on-write context but not in a schema-on-read one.
questions.explain: The chapter says it applies to both. Even schema-on-read data still needs reprocessing for a restructuring.
questions.rule: Both styles hit the same limit.
questions.teaches: The limit on schema evolution without reprocessing holds in both a schema-on-write and a schema-on-read context.

questions.q: A music app wants to change its listening-history data from one table per user to a graph of artists and listeners. What does reprocessing offer?
questions.explain: Reprocessing existing data lets you derive a completely different model for new requirements.
questions.rule: New model means new derived view.
options: A way to add the graph by editing each record in place as users log in
A guarantee that the old table design can be kept forever without change
Rerun new code over all the history to derive the graph as a new view beside the old one
A rule that data models cannot change once a system is in production
optionExplain: That is a slow in-place change, not reprocessing.
Reprocessing is about changing, not keeping.
Reprocessing can restructure a dataset into a completely different model.
The chapter says reprocessing makes change possible.

questions.q: Stream processing reflects changes with low delay, whereas ____ processing reprocesses accumulated historical data to derive new views.
questions.explain: Batch is the tool for bulk reprocessing of history.
questions.rule: Stream for freshness; batch for history.

questions.q: A reviewer says: our schema evolution only supports optional fields, so we cannot ever restructure the data. What is overlooked?
questions.explain: Without reprocessing, evolution is limited to simple changes in either schema-on-write or schema-on-read context. With reprocessing it is possible to restructure completely.
options: Optional fields can be turned into mandatory fields by renaming them in code
Reprocessing the stored data can rebuild it into a different model
Schema-on-read systems never need reprocessing to change structure
Schema-on-write systems can restructure data freely without any reprocessing
optionExplain: Renaming does not restructure data into a different model.
Reprocessing removes the limit to simple changes.
The chapter says the limit applies to schema-on-read as well.
The limit applies to both schema-on-write and schema-on-read.

questions.q: A company wants to start deriving a new fraud score from three years of past transactions. Which mechanism fits?
questions.explain: Batch processing derives a new view from accumulated history and stream processing then reflects new changes with low delay.
questions.rule: Backfill with batch, keep fresh with stream.
options: Stream processing alone, since historical data cannot be reprocessed after it has been read once
A distributed transaction across all past records to compute the score atomically
Manually scoring each customer when they next appear, since reprocessing is not supported
Batch reprocessing of the stored history to compute the new view, then stream processing to keep it fresh
optionExplain: Retained history can be replayed or reprocessed.
Nothing here needs atomic commit across history.
Reprocessing is the supported mechanism for a new view.
Batch derives the view from history; stream keeps it current.
questions.teaches: Reprocessing existing data is a good mechanism for maintaining a system and evolving it to support new features and changed requirements.

questions.q: True or false: When restructuring a dataset, the safest approach is a sudden switch from the old schema to the new one.
questions.explain: The chapter favours gradual migration with both views kept side by side. The card next shows how.

questions.q: What does the railway analogy illustrate?
questions.explain: Adding a third rail made tracks work for both gauges, so the conversion could proceed over years while both old and new trains kept running.
questions.rule: Let old and new coexist during change.
options: Standardising to one gauge overnight is cheap, so computing migrations should copy it
Different gauges prove that no standard should ever be chosen for a network
Converting to dual gauge lets old and new trains run together while the change happens gradually
Rail networks need two sets of tracks, which doubles the cost of data pipelines
optionExplain: The chapter says the gradual conversion was expensive but workable.
A standard was chosen in 1846.
A third rail allowed gradual conversion with both kinds of train.
The analogy concerns coexistence of old and new, not cost doubling.

questions.q: According to the chapter's story, what keeps nonstandard railway gauges in use today?
questions.explain: The conversion could be done gradually but is expensive, so some systems, such as BART in the San Francisco Bay Area, still use a nonstandard gauge.
questions.rule: Gradual change still has a cost.
questions.teaches: Converting tracks to a standard gauge by adding a third rail was an expensive undertaking, which is why nonstandard gauges such as BART's still exist.
options: The standard was never decided, so each region kept its own
Trains of both gauges cannot share any track, so conversion is impossible
Standard gauge track wears out faster, so some lines avoided changing
Converting track by adding a third rail is an expensive undertaking
optionExplain: A single standard gauge was decided in 1846.
The third-rail method let trains of both gauges run.
Wear is not mentioned.
The BART example shows the expense kept a different gauge.

questions.q: A shop wants to move its product pages to a new data structure with little risk. What does the chapter suggest?
questions.explain: Maintaining the old and new views side by side lets you test with a few users and increase the proportion over time.
questions.rule: Ramp the share; keep the fallback.
options: Serve a small share from the new structure and raise it step by step
Switch everyone on a Sunday night and keep a backup of the old structure on tape
Convert the old structure in place, record by record, with no copy to fall back to
Ask customers to choose a version themselves and remove the other after a week
optionExplain: That is the gradual migration pattern.
That is a sudden switch, not a gradual one.
No fallback view remains if something goes wrong.
That is not described as the pattern, and it removes the old view too early.

questions.q: Put the stages of a gradual migration between two derived views in order.
questions.explain: The old view stays until the new one has proved itself with an increasing share of users.
questions.rule: Ramp up, then retire the old view.
items: Derive the new view beside the old one
Route a small share of users to the new view
Raise the share as problems are found and fixed
Drop the old view

questions.q: The new view shows a bug when 5 percent of users are routed to it. What does the pattern let you do?
questions.explain: Because you always have a working system to go back to, a failed step is easily reversed.
questions.rule: Keep the old view until the new one proves itself.
options: Delete the old view immediately, so that the bug cannot be blamed on it
Route those users back to the old view, which is still working, and fix the bug
Let all users keep using the new view while a patch is written
Rebuild the old view from scratch, since it can no longer be trusted
optionExplain: The old view is the safety net.
Every stage is reversible.
Reversibility is the point of the pattern.
The old view was untouched and still works.

questions.q: True or false: In a gradual migration, a bug found in the new view can be handled by routing users back to the old view.
questions.explain: The old view is still running, so every stage is easily reversible.
questions.rule: Keep the old view until the new one is proven.

questions.q: A database team has only enough disk for one copy of the data. How should they view the gradual migration pattern?
questions.explain: The pattern relies on two independently derived views existing together, which costs space and processing. That cost is the limit on the pattern.
options: As costly, since two views must coexist for a while, so it may not fit tight limits
As free, since a derived view takes no space beyond the original data
As unnecessary, since a single copy can be migrated and rolled back by itself
As required, since all migrations must keep three views for safety
optionExplain: The pattern needs both views present during the change.
A derived view is stored data and takes space.
Without a second view there is nothing to roll back to.
The pattern needs two views, not three.
questions.teaches: By reducing the risk of irreversible damage you can be more confident about going ahead, and so move faster to improve your system.

questions.q: True or false: In the lambda architecture, the stream processor's quick update is later replaced by a corrected version from the batch processor.
questions.explain: The stream path gives a fast approximate view and the batch path corrects it. The card next gives the full design.
questions.rule: Fast and approximate first, slow and exact later.

questions.q: The lambda architecture records incoming data as ____ events appended to an ever-growing dataset.
questions.explain: Like event sourcing, the design stores events that are never changed, and derives views from them.

questions.q: What reasoning led to running both a batch and a stream system in the lambda architecture?
questions.explain: The reasoning was that batch processing is simpler and thus less prone to bugs, while stream processors were thought less reliable and harder to make fault-tolerant. The stream path could also use fast approximate algorithms while the batch path used slower exact ones.
questions.rule: Lambda trades two systems for reliability and accuracy.
questions.teaches: Lambda assumed that batch processing is simpler and less bug-prone while stream processors are less reliable, and that the stream path can use fast approximate algorithms where the batch path uses slower exact ones.
options: Stream processors cannot read events, so the batch system must be used to ingest all of the data
Batch is simpler and less prone to bugs, and streams can use fast approximate algorithms
Batch processors are faster than stream processors, so the batch system gives the live answers
Two systems cost less to operate than one, because each can then be run at lower capacity
optionExplain: Plausible if you think of streams as outputs only, but stream processors consume events and update the view quickly.
The batch path was seen as the reliable one and the stream path as the quick one.
A natural mix-up of speed and scale, but the batch path gives the later, corrected answers.
It sounds efficient, yet the next idea lists the extra effort of two systems as a problem.

questions.q: A site shows live page-view counts within seconds from a stream job, and a nightly job recomputes exact counts. Which design is this?
questions.explain: The stream path quickly produces an approximate update, and the batch path later consumes the same events to produce a corrected view.
questions.rule: Two paths over one set of events.
options: A single-leader log, where one writer appends entries that many followers copy in order
A federated database, where one query interface reaches several storage engines at read time
A distributed transaction, where every view is updated together in one atomic step
The lambda architecture, with a fast approximate path and a corrective batch path
optionExplain: Tempting because a log is involved, but this describes replication of one dataset, not two processing systems producing one view.
Tempting because several systems are involved, but federation unifies reads and has no correction step.
Tempting because the views are meant to agree, but lambda runs two independent paths rather than one atomic update.
Both paths read the same events and the batch result corrects the stream view, which is the lambda design.

questions.q: Which feature separates the lambda architecture from event sourcing on its own?
questions.explain: Both record immutable events and derive views. Lambda adds the pairing of a batch system with a separate stream system.
questions.rule: Lambda's mark is the pair of parallel systems.
options: Lambda stores its events as immutable records, while event sourcing changes them in place afterwards
Lambda has no read-optimised views at all, while event sourcing always derives views from its events
Two processing systems run in parallel to produce and then correct one view
Lambda needs one database for everything, while event sourcing spreads data over a cluster of systems
optionExplain: Reasonable if you think of the two as opposites, but both rely on immutable events.
Plausible because lambda sounds like pure processing, but it derives read-optimised views from events too.
Both start from immutable events; only lambda adds the parallel batch and stream pair.
It sounds right if you confuse the single log with a single store, but lambda is the one that runs two systems.

questions.q: True or false: In the lambda architecture the stream path is expected to give exact results while the batch path gives quick approximate ones.
questions.explain: It is the other way round: the stream path gives a quick approximate update, and the batch path later produces the corrected version.
questions.rule: Stream: fast and approximate. Batch: slow and corrective.

questions.q: A team has a stream job and wants exact answers later without a second system. What does the lambda design ask of them?
questions.explain: Lambda runs a batch system such as Hadoop MapReduce and a separate stream-processing system such as Storm in parallel.
options: A single system that can switch between exact and approximate algorithms depending on load
A second, separate batch system running in parallel over the same events
A distributed transaction that links the stream output and the batch output into one atomic step
A smaller dataset, since lambda discards events older than one day to keep batch runs short
optionExplain: Sounds like the answer to their wish, but that is the unified approach discussed later, not lambda.
Lambda proposes running two different systems, such as Hadoop MapReduce and Storm, in parallel.
Plausible because the two outputs must agree, but lambda merges separate outputs and uses no transaction.
It would shorten batch runs, but lambda keeps an always-growing dataset of immutable events.
questions.teaches: The lambda proposal names a batch processing system such as Hadoop MapReduce and a separate stream-processing system such as Storm.

questions.q: True or false: In the lambda architecture the same processing logic must be maintained in both a batch and a stream framework.
questions.explain: This duplicated logic is the first practical problem the author lists. The card next lists the other two.
questions.rule: Two systems often mean two codebases.

questions.q: Why must the outputs of the two lambda pipelines be merged?
questions.explain: Since the stream pipeline and the batch pipeline produce separate outputs, they need to be merged in order to respond to user requests.
options: The stream output is encrypted in transit and only the batch system holds the key to read it
The batch output always contains every stream result, so extra records must be trimmed off
Merging is the step that turns the recorded events into immutable events for later reuse
The pipelines produce separate outputs, and a request needs one answer
optionExplain: Sounds like a technical reason, but encryption plays no part in the chapter's explanation.
Plausible if batch is seen as a superset, but nothing says that, and the merge is about combining outputs.
Mixes up cause and effect: the events are immutable from the moment they are recorded.
Separate outputs have to be combined to respond to user requests.

questions.q: A team's view needs joins and sessionization, beyond a sum over fixed windows. How does this affect a lambda merge?
questions.explain: The merge is fairly easy for a simple aggregation over a tumbling window, but significantly harder if the view uses joins, sessionization or non time-series output.
options: It becomes significantly harder than for a simple tumbling window aggregation
It becomes trivial, because joins already combine the outputs of both pipelines automatically
It is unaffected, because the merge depends only on how many events the pipelines have read
It disappears, because sessionization removes the need for the stream pipeline altogether
optionExplain: Joins, sessionization and non time-series output make the merge harder.
Tempting because a join sounds like a merge, but the chapter says complex operations make merging harder.
Plausible if merging is thought of as bookkeeping, but the kind of computation matters.
Sounds neat, but the stream pipeline still runs and its output still has to be merged.

questions.q: The lambda architecture needs the same ____ maintained in both a batch and a stream processing framework.
questions.explain: Keeping the same computation in two frameworks is significant additional effort.
questions.rule: Two frameworks, one logic, double effort.

questions.q: A team adopts a library that runs one computation in either batch or streaming mode. What problem does the author say remains?
questions.explain: Libraries such as Summingbird provide an abstraction for computations that can run in either context, but the operational complexity of two systems remains.
questions.rule: One abstraction does not make two systems one.
questions.teaches: Libraries such as Summingbird provide an abstraction for computations that can run in a batch or streaming context, but the operational complexity of debugging, tuning and maintaining two systems remains.
options: The library cannot express aggregations, so every computation would need rewriting by hand
The library forces events to become mutable, which breaks the guarantees of the batch pipeline
The operational complexity of debugging, tuning and maintaining two different systems
The library removes approximate results from the stream path but leaves the batch path unchanged
optionExplain: Reasonable worry about libraries, but the library is described as giving an abstraction for computations.
Sounds like a typical trade-off, but nothing like it is said and events stay immutable.
A shared abstraction helps the logic but not the operating of two systems.
Plausible because the paths differ in accuracy, but the problem stated is operational, not about results.

questions.q: True or false: A reviewer says that running the batch layer on hourly increments keeps it as simple as before. The author agrees.
questions.explain: He says incrementalising adds complexity, such as stragglers and windows that cross batch boundaries, making the batch layer more like the streaming layer.

questions.q: A small team chooses between lambda and one system doing both jobs. Which of the author's points weighs most for a small team?
questions.explain: The author's first point is the effort of maintaining logic in both frameworks. For a small team this cost is likely to dominate (our reading).
questions.rule: Match the cost to the team's capacity.
options: Lambda gives up immutable events, which a small team cannot do without in practice
Lambda cannot be paired with any stream processor, so the team would have to write its own
Keeping the same logic running in two frameworks is significant added effort
Lambda's merge step is always trivial, so a small team gains nothing from avoiding it
optionExplain: Seems a costly loss, but lambda is built on immutable events.
Would be decisive if true, but lambda uses a separate stream system such as Storm.
A small team feels duplicated effort most; this is our reading of how his points apply.
Plausible for simple aggregations, but the merge gets hard for complex views.
questions.teaches: Incrementalizing a batch computation adds complexity and makes the batch layer more akin to the streaming layer, which runs counter to the goal of keeping it as simple as possible.

questions.q: True or false: When historical events are replayed through a stream processor, windowing by processing time still gives meaningful results.
questions.explain: Processing time is meaningless when reprocessing historical events, so windows must use event time. The card next lists the features.

questions.q: What does exactly-once semantics mean for a stream processor in this chapter?
questions.explain: Exactly-once means the output is the same as if no faults had occurred, even if faults did occur. Like batch processing, this requires discarding the partial output of any failed tasks.
questions.rule: Faults must leave no visible trace in the output.
options: The output is the same as if no faults had occurred, even when faults did occur
Each message reaches the processor a single time, even across restarts and retries
The processor never fails during its lifetime, so no fault tolerance is needed
Each event is stored once in the log and deleted as soon as the processor has seen it
optionExplain: Correct. Exactly-once means the output is the same as if no faults had occurred, even if faults did occur.
Intuitive from the name, but the definition is about the effect on output, not the delivery count.
The word once suggests this, yet faults can occur and the output must still be right.
Sounds like tidy storage, but storage and deletion are not part of the definition.

questions.q: A team wants one pipeline to process live clicks and also rerun last year's clicks. What must the system support first?
questions.explain: To unify the two, the system must replay historical events through the same engine that handles recent ones, as log-based brokers and some stream processors reading from HDFS can.
questions.rule: Same engine for new and old events.
options: A separate batch engine with a different programming model for the old data
Windows based on the time each event was processed by the engine
A guarantee that old events are never altered after the replay has finished
Replay of historical events through the same engine as the live stream
optionExplain: Sounds like the standard answer, but that is the lambda design this avoids.
Tempting because engines know it, but processing time is meaningless for replayed events.
Immutability helps, but it is not one of the features listed.
Replay is the first of the three required features.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether the chapter lists it as needed to unify batch and stream processing.
questions.explain: Replay, exactly-once output and event-time windows are the three features. Running two parallel engines is the lambda design.

items.t: Replaying historical events through the same engine
Exactly-once semantics for stream processors
Windowing by event time instead of processing time
Running two engines in parallel and merging their outputs
Using a distributed transaction across all derived views
Keeping the batch layer free of any incremental processing

questions.q: A system replays old events but windows them by processing time. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: A replay compresses past events into the present, so processing time windows would group events by when they were replayed.
questions.rule: Window by when it happened, not when it was processed.
options: Windows follow event times accurately, because the two clocks agree during a replay
Windows reflect when the replay runs, not when events happened, so results are meaningless
The replay fails to start, because every engine rejects processing-time windows on old data
Output becomes exactly-once, because processing time removes duplicate events from the replay
optionExplain: Plausible if you assume clocks agree, but the replay runs long after the events occurred.
A replay compresses the past into the present, so processing-time windows group events wrongly.
Sounds like a safety check, but the result is quietly wrong rather than a startup failure.
Mixes two features: window choice has no bearing on exactly-once.

questions.q: True or false: A system that replays historical events through the engine handling the live stream removes the need for a separate batch system.
questions.explain: Replay through one engine, together with exactly-once output and event-time windows, is what lets one system do both jobs.

questions.q: Which tool does the chapter name for expressing event-time computations that can run on different engines?
