questions.explain: Apache Beam provides an API for expressing such computations, which can then be run using Apache Flink or Google Cloud Dataflow.
questions.teaches: Apache Beam provides an API for expressing event-time windowed computations that can be run using Apache Flink or Google Cloud Dataflow.
options: Summingbird, which can run on Hadoop MapReduce or Storm
PostgreSQL, which can run on Flink or Google Cloud Dataflow
HDFS, which can run on Flink or Google Cloud Dataflow
Apache Beam, which can run on Apache Flink or Google Cloud Dataflow
optionExplain: Plausible because it also spans two engines, but it is cited in the lambda discussion.
A familiar name from the chapter, but it appears only in the foreign data wrapper example.
HDFS can supply replayed input, but it is a filesystem and not an API for computations.
Beam is the example the chapter gives.

questions.q: True or false: Unix pipes and files are sequences of bytes, whereas relational databases offer SQL and transactions.
questions.explain: The two systems took very different philosophies about abstraction. The card next compares them.

questions.q: Which description fits the relational approach in the chapter?
questions.explain: Relational databases wanted to give application programmers a high-level abstraction that hides the complexities of data structures on disk, concurrency, crash recovery and so on.
options: A thin wrapper around hardware resources that exposes sequences of bytes to programmers
A high-level abstraction that hides disk structures, concurrency and crash recovery
A set of small tools composed by a shell language into larger programs and workflows
A federation of separate engines that share no common model but offer one front door
optionExplain: Sounds like a database to someone who thinks of storage, but it is the Unix view.
That is how relational databases are described.
Plausible for data processing, but this is again the Unix tradition.
Sounds modern and relevant, but federation is a later topic and not the relational philosophy.

questions.q: What practical difference between a filesystem and a database does the chapter give?
questions.explain: The chapter says that many filesystems do not cope very well with a directory containing 10 million small files, whereas a database containing 10 million small records is completely normal.
questions.rule: Abstractions differ in what they scale to.
questions.teaches: Many filesystems do not cope well with a directory containing 10 million small files, whereas a database containing 10 million small records is completely normal.
options: Ten million small files strain many filesystems, but ten million records are normal for a database
Filesystems cannot hold small files at all, and databases can hold nothing but small records
Databases cannot store anything above a megabyte, but filesystems have no size limit of any kind
Filesystems need SQL to list a directory, while databases are read through pipes between tools
optionExplain: This is the example given.
A rough reading of the example, but the point is about handling very many small items.
Sounds like a typical limit, but none is stated.
This swaps the philosophies: pipes belong to Unix and SQL to databases.

questions.q: A developer chains small programs that read and write plain text streams. Which philosophy does this fit?
questions.explain: Unix developed pipes and files that are sequences of bytes, with small programs composed through them.
options: Relational, with a declarative query planned by an optimiser across indexes and join methods
Federated, with one query interface placed over several different storage engines
Unix, with pipes carrying byte streams between small tools
Lambda, with a batch path and a stream path both reading from one growing event set
optionExplain: Tempting because data is being processed, but this is the high-level approach.
Federation is a later topic and involves a query interface, not chained tools.
Pipes and sequences of bytes are the Unix approach.
Plausible because streams are involved, but lambda is about processing paths, not tool composition.

questions.q: In what sense does the chapter call each system simpler?
questions.explain: Unix is simpler in the sense that it is a fairly thin wrapper around hardware resources. A relational database is simpler for the query author, who need not understand the implementation details.
questions.rule: Simple for the implementer or simple for the user.
options: Unix thinly wraps hardware, while a short SQL query uses powerful infrastructure
Unix is simpler to learn, and a relational database is simpler to implement internally
Both are simple because they expose the same few operations on top of different hardware
A relational database is simpler because it avoids indexes and join methods entirely
optionExplain: Each is simple in a different sense.
Natural contrast, but it is not the sense in which the chapter uses the word.
Plausible, but they expose very different abstractions.
Sounds like a simplification, but it uses indexes and joins behind the query.

questions.q: Unix developed pipes and files that are sequences of bytes, whereas databases developed SQL and ____.
questions.explain: SQL and transactions are the relational counterparts to pipes and byte files.
questions.rule: Unix: pipes. Databases: SQL and transactions.

questions.q: True or false: The author says the tension between the Unix and relational philosophies has been settled in favour of relational databases.
questions.explain: He says the tension has lasted for decades and still is not resolved.

questions.q: A founder says the NoSQL movement was only a fashion. How does the author interpret it?
questions.explain: The author would interpret the NoSQL movement as wanting to apply a Unix-esque approach of low-level abstractions to the domain of distributed OLTP data storage.
questions.rule: NoSQL read as Unix-style low-level abstractions.
options: As a revival of relational ideas under a new name, with SQL kept as the main interface
As a rejection of storing data on disk in favour of keeping all data in memory
As an attempt to bring the Unix-style low-level approach to distributed OLTP storage
As proof that low-level interfaces never work for storing data at scale
optionExplain: The name suggests a link to SQL, but he ties NoSQL to Unix, not to relational ideas.
Plausible for some products, but he makes no such claim.
Correct. The author would interpret the NoSQL movement as wanting to apply a Unix-esque approach of low-level abstractions to the domain of distributed OLTP data storage.
Sounds like a verdict, but he says the tension between the philosophies is still unresolved.
questions.teaches: The author would interpret the NoSQL movement as wanting to apply a Unix-esque approach of low-level abstractions to the domain of distributed OLTP data storage.

questions.q: True or false: Setting up a new follower replica and building a new index involve a similar process.
questions.explain: Both take a snapshot, then catch up on later changes. The card next lays out the steps.

questions.q: Put the steps of CREATE INDEX in order, assuming writes continue during the build.
questions.explain: The database builds from a snapshot, then replays writes that arrived during the build, then maintains the index as part of normal operation.
items: Scan a consistent snapshot of the table
Pick out and sort the indexed values
Write out the index
Process the backlog of writes made since the snapshot
Keep the index up to date for new writes

questions.q: A team must add a new search index to a live service while writes continue. What does the CREATE INDEX analogy suggest?
questions.explain: The analogy is snapshot, then backlog, then continuous maintenance, which also describes bootstrapping CDC.
options: Stop all writes until the index is finished, then restart the service from a clean state
Build from a snapshot, apply the changes made since, then keep applying new changes
Build the index from the newest writes only and leave the older data out of it
Wait for a full copy of the table in a new cluster before indexing any rows at all
optionExplain: Safe but costly; the analogy assumes writes carry on during the build.
That mirrors CREATE INDEX and CDC bootstrapping.
Fast, but an index needs the existing data as well as the new writes.
A way to isolate the work, but it is not what the analogy describes.

questions.q: Which two tasks does the chapter compare to building a new index?
questions.explain: The process is remarkably similar to setting up a new follower replica and to bootstrapping change data capture in a streaming system.
options: Running two-phase commit and electing a new leader after a failure of the old one
Compacting a log and rotating the encryption keys that protect data at rest
Resolving write conflicts and merging the states of replicas after a network partition
Setting up a new follower replica and bootstrapping change data capture
optionExplain: Both are consensus-related and familiar, but neither is in the comparison.
Both are routine maintenance, but neither appears in the comparison.
Both are multi-leader topics, but not the ones compared here.
Correct. The process is remarkably similar to setting up a new follower replica and to bootstrapping change data capture in a streaming system.

questions.q: True or false: If the table is locked during index creation, there is no backlog of writes to process afterwards.
questions.explain: The backlog exists only when writes continue during the build. Locking the table avoids it at the cost of blocking writes.

questions.q: How does the chapter relate a snapshot of state to a log of all changes?
questions.explain: The existing data may be a snapshot of state rather than a log of all changes that ever happened, but the two are closely related.
questions.rule: State and changes are two views of one thing.
questions.teaches: The existing data may be a snapshot of the state rather than a log of all changes that ever happened, but the two are closely related.
options: They are unrelated, since one is data and the other is code that must be run to see anything
They are identical, since any snapshot contains every change that was ever made to the data
They are closely related, since a snapshot is a state and a log records the changes behind it
They conflict, so a system must choose one form and discard the other for its derived data
optionExplain: Tempting because they look different, but both are forms of the same data.
A snapshot of state does not contain the history of changes.
The chapter says the two are closely related.
The chapter does not present them as rivals.

questions.q: True or false: In the author's picture, batch and stream processors play a role like triggers and materialized view maintenance in a database.
questions.explain: They keep derived data in step with the source, just as database internals do. The card next draws the full analogy.
questions.rule: Processors are index maintenance, writ large.

questions.q: Match each database feature to its counterpart in the organisation-wide dataflow.
questions.explain: The processors do the work that database subsystems do for indexes and views, but across separate products.
pairs: Triggers, stored procedures and materialized view maintenance
Index types such as B-tree or spatial
Derived data systems such as search indexes or caches
The subsystem that keeps indexes up to date
A batch, stream or ETL process that moves data between forms

questions.q: A warehouse load job, a search indexer and a cache refresher are run by three teams. How does the chapter frame them?
questions.explain: Whenever a batch, stream or ETL process transports data from one place and form to another it acts like the database subsystem that keeps indexes or materialized views up to date.
questions.rule: Each job maintains one kind of index.
options: As parts of one huge database, each keeping a derived structure current
As three unrelated tools, since separate teams own and operate them independently
As backups of one another, since all three copy the same source data into new places
As replicas of one table, since all three read the same events from the same source
optionExplain: That is the picture of the dataflow as one huge database.
Plausible given the org chart, but the chapter sees them as one dataflow despite separate ownership.
They share a source, but each produces a different derived structure, not a backup.
Sounds right because the input is shared, but replicas hold the same data and these hold different derived data.

questions.q: How does the author's picture differ from index maintenance inside a single database product?
questions.explain: Instead of being features of a single integrated database product, they are provided by various pieces of software, running on different machines, administered by different teams.
options: The indexes live in memory only, so they cannot be recovered after a restart of the machine
The facilities come from different software on different machines run by different teams
The system of record is removed, so every derived copy is treated as equally authoritative
A single schema must now be shared by every team that maintains a piece of the dataflow
optionExplain: A plausible worry for derived data, but storage location is not the difference he draws.
That is the difference he describes.
Sounds radical, but the system of record stays in the design.
Sounds like a coordination need, but nothing in the passage requires it.

questions.q: True or false: If no single data model suits every access pattern, the organisation will need to compose several specialised systems into a cohesive whole.
questions.explain: The premise leads to the author's question of how different tools can be composed, which the next ideas take up.

questions.q: A manager calls the ETL job plumbing outside the database. How does the author's view differ?
questions.explain: He sees any batch, stream or ETL process that moves data from one place and form to another as acting like the database subsystem that keeps indexes or materialized views up to date.
questions.rule: Moving data between forms is index maintenance.
questions.teaches: Batch, stream and ETL processes that transport data from one place and form to another act like the subsystem that keeps indexes or materialized views up to date.
options: He agrees: ETL jobs are plumbing outside the data system and need no design attention
He wants ETL jobs replaced by triggers inside the source database in every circumstance
He treats ETL jobs as databases themselves, since they store the moved data permanently
The ETL job does what the subsystem that keeps an index or view up to date does
optionExplain: A common view, but he explicitly counts such processes in the picture.
Triggers are named as a comparison, not as a replacement.
Sounds close, but they derive data rather than serve as stores.
That is the analogy; he includes ETL jobs.

questions.q: True or false: A federated database solves the problem of keeping writes to several storage systems in sync.
questions.explain: It unifies read-only querying, but does not have a good answer for synchronising writes. The card next explains.

questions.q: A federated database is also called a ____.
questions.explain: The chapter uses federated database and polystore as names for a unified query interface over many engines.

questions.q: An analyst wants one SQL query joining tables in a relational database with a collection in a document store. Which approach fits?
questions.explain: Federation provides a unified query interface so that users who want to combine data from disparate places can do so through it.
options: A federated interface that maps both stores into one query language
A distributed transaction that spans both stores so the query runs as one atomic step
An unbundled pipeline that rewrites both stores whenever a read comes in from a client
A lambda architecture with a batch path and a stream path producing the joined result
optionExplain: A unified query interface over underlying engines.
Sounds thorough, but transactions address writes, not read queries across stores.
Unbundling carries changes between stores; it is not a query interface.
Plausible for joins over time, but lambda is about processing paths, not query interfaces.

questions.q: Which statement describes a limit of federation rather than of unbundling?
questions.explain: Federation addresses read-only querying across several systems but does not have a good answer to synchronising writes.
options: It cannot be combined with a relational query language, which limits its use to simple lookups
It forces applications to stop using the underlying engines directly once the interface exists
It depends on a shared log with idempotent consumers, which most teams find hard to build
It has no good answer for synchronising writes across the systems
optionExplain: Plausible for a mixed system, but it follows the relational tradition.
Sounds like a cost, but applications can still access the engines directly.
A fair description of unbundling, which is the other approach.
That is the gap the author notes.

questions.q: True or false: Mapping one data model into another for federated reads is described by the author as ultimately a manageable problem.
questions.explain: He says it takes some thought but is manageable, and calls keeping writes in sync the harder engineering problem.

questions.q: A team calls PostgreSQL's foreign data wrapper an example of what pattern?
questions.explain: PostgreSQL's foreign data wrapper feature fits the federated pattern. Applications needing a specialised data model can still use the underlying engines directly.
questions.rule: Foreign data wrapper: a federated example.
questions.teaches: Applications that need a specialised data model or query interface can still access the underlying storage engines directly while the federated interface serves users who combine data from many places.
options: An unbundled database, with a log that feeds derived stores
A lambda architecture, with parallel batch and stream systems over one set of events
A federated database, with one interface over other stores
Total order broadcast, with one leader that orders every event
optionExplain: Close in spirit because both compose systems, but this is the write-side approach.
A different pairing of two systems, but unrelated to wrappers.
That is the example the chapter gives.
Related to logs and ordering, not to query interfaces.

questions.q: True or false: Unbundling a database follows the Unix tradition of small tools that do one thing well and communicate through a uniform low-level API.
questions.explain: The author draws this parallel with pipes and the shell. The card next explains the approach.

questions.q: Which problem does the unbundled approach target, as opposed to federation?
questions.explain: Federation addresses read-only querying, while unbundling addresses making sure all data changes end up in all the right places.
questions.rule: Federate for reads; unbundle for writes.
options: Querying several engines through one language that hides which engine holds the data
Synchronising writes across different storage systems
Hiding disk structures, concurrency and recovery behind SQL and transactions
Choosing how many partitions a log needs so that throughput scales with the load
optionExplain: That is what federation does.
That is the problem federation leaves open.
That is the relational abstraction, not unbundling.
A tuning issue that follows once logs are used, but not the problem unbundling targets.

questions.q: A team uses change data capture to feed a search index and a cache from one database. How does the chapter describe this?
questions.explain: Making it easier to plug storage systems together, for example through CDC and event logs, is like unbundling a database's index-maintenance features.
questions.rule: CDC feeding derived stores is unbundling.
options: It federates three databases behind a single query interface for the applications
It unbundles the index-maintenance features of a database
It runs a distributed transaction across all three stores to keep them identical
It merges the cache and index into the primary database to avoid any copies
optionExplain: Several systems are involved, but no unified query interface is.
CDC and logs let writes reach disparate systems.
Tempting for consistency, but the approach is chosen to avoid that.
The point is to keep them as separate specialised systems.

questions.q: Match each Unix element to its counterpart in the unbundled-database picture.
questions.explain: The author maps Unix composition onto data systems: small systems, a uniform log interface, and a missing composing language.
questions.rule: Unix composition mapped to data systems.
pairs: Small tools doing one thing well
Pipes as a uniform low-level API
The shell as a higher-level language
A declarative way to compose the systems (not yet available)

questions.q: Changes flow through an event log. What must a new derived store do to join the system?
questions.explain: Because changes flow through a log, a new consumer can subscribe and derive its store, like a new index being built.
options: Be written to directly by every application that produces data for the system
Join a distributed transaction with every other store before accepting any data
Replace the system of record as the first place where new writes are accepted
Subscribe to the log and apply its changes
optionExplain: Direct writers bring back the dual-write ordering problem.
Safe sounding, but the unbundled approach exists to avoid that.
Tempting for simplicity, but the record stays where it is.
A consumer of the log can build a derived store.

questions.q: True or false: A team says federation already solves synchronising writes across storage systems, so unbundling is unnecessary.
questions.explain: Federation covers read-only querying and has no good answer to synchronising writes, which is the gap unbundling addresses.

questions.q: Which statement about reads and writes across systems does the author make?
questions.explain: Federated read-only querying requires mapping one data model into another, which is manageable. Keeping the writes in sync is the harder problem, so he focuses on it.
questions.rule: Writes across systems are the hard part.
questions.teaches: The author considers the mapping of one data model into another in federated reads manageable, and keeping writes to several storage systems in sync the harder engineering problem, so he focuses on it.
options: Federated reads are manageable, but keeping writes in sync is the harder engineering problem
Writes across systems are easy, and the mapping of data models for reads is the hard part
Both are equally easy once the systems share a log, so no new approach is needed
Both are impossible without a distributed transaction spanning every store involved
optionExplain: He says so and focuses on writes.
A natural guess, but he says the opposite.
Sounds reassuring, but he treats the write side as the hard part.
Plausible traditionally, but he argues against that approach.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, distributed transactions are the right way to synchronise writes across storage systems from different groups.
questions.explain: He calls this traditional approach the wrong solution across heterogeneous systems. The card next explains why a log is simpler.

questions.q: What does the author call a much simpler abstraction, and so more feasible across heterogeneous systems?
questions.explain: An ordered log of events with idempotent consumers is a much simpler abstraction, and thus much more feasible to implement across heterogeneous systems.
questions.rule: Across technologies: ordered log, idempotent consumers.
options: A two-phase commit protocol that every storage system is required to implement
A shared relational schema that every team agrees to use for all of its data
An ordered log of events with idempotent consumers
A synchronous remote procedure call from each system to every other system
optionExplain: Familiar and strict, but this is the traditional approach he considers the wrong solution.
Would simplify integration, but the author's abstraction is the log, not a schema.
That is his answer to cross-technology integration.
Simple to picture, but synchronous calls spread failures and are not what he proposes.

questions.q: The author says distributed transactions are used within some stream processors to achieve ____ semantics.
questions.explain: Inside a single stream processing system, transactions can deliver exactly-once processing, and the author says this can work quite well.
questions.rule: Scope matters: inside one system, transactions are feasible.
questions.teaches: Distributed transactions are used within some stream processors to achieve exactly-once semantics, and this can work quite well.

questions.q: A stream processor writes results to two stores run by other teams. Which approach does the author favour?
questions.explain: Across systems built by different groups, an ordered log with idempotent consumers is a much simpler abstraction than a distributed transaction.
questions.rule: Log plus idempotent consumers across team boundaries.
options: A distributed transaction spanning the processor, the key-value store and the search index
Direct writes from the processor to each store, with no log in between them
An ordered log with idempotent consumers feeding both stores
A rewrite of both stores so that they share one codebase and one commit protocol
optionExplain: Familiar and strict, but a poor fit when each system was built by a different group.
Simple to build, but it brings back the dual-write ordering problem.
A simple abstraction that works across heterogeneous systems.
Would give a protocol but is unrealistic across teams and misses the author's point.

questions.q: True or false: The author argues that transactions cannot work inside a stream processor, since they are too expensive.
questions.explain: He notes that distributed transactions are used within some stream processors to achieve exactly-once semantics, and that this can work quite well.
questions.rule: Transactions inside one system can be fine.

questions.q: Two vendors' services must stay in step, and a colleague wants to wait for a transaction standard. What would the author reply?
questions.explain: A log with idempotent consumers does not depend on a standard transaction protocol, which is why the author calls it much more feasible across heterogeneous systems.
questions.rule: Do not wait for a standard; use a log.
options: An ordered event log with idempotent consumers is feasible now without waiting for such a protocol
Waiting is wise, because only a standard transaction protocol can keep two services consistent
Choose one vendor's service and drop the other, because integration across vendors cannot be done
Let both services write to each other directly and accept occasional disagreement as normal
optionExplain: He argues a log is simpler and more feasible.
Reasonable caution, but he thinks a log gives a practical alternative today.
A drastic response that conflicts with the chapter's premise that tools must be composed.
Easy to build, but it gives up the ordering the log provides.
questions.teaches: Where systems are written by different groups of people, the lack of a standardised transaction protocol makes integration much harder.

questions.q: True or false: In log-based integration a slow consumer forces the producer and the other consumers to slow down as well.
questions.explain: The log buffers messages, so the producer and other consumers run unaffected. The card next gives both levels of coupling.

questions.q: What happens to a consumer that fails and is later repaired, in a log-based system?
questions.explain: If a consumer runs slow or fails, the event log can buffer messages. The faulty consumer can catch up when it is fixed, so it does not miss any data.
questions.rule: The log lets consumers catch up.
options: It restarts from the newest message, since older messages were dropped while it was down
It asks the producer to resend everything, since only the producer holds the data
It triggers an abort in every other consumer so that all of them restart together
It catches up from the log and does not miss any data
optionExplain: A plausible way logs might work, but the log keeps messages for it.
Sounds natural, but the log, not the producer, holds the buffered messages.
That is how synchronous transactions spread failures, not how a log behaves.
The log buffered the messages it missed.

questions.q: Sort each benefit of log-based integration by the level at which it appears.
questions.explain: Robustness to outages and slow components concerns the running system. Independent development and specialisation concern the people and teams.

items.t: A failed consumer does not stop the producer
Slow consumers are absorbed by buffered messages
Teams ship their component without waiting for others
Each team focuses on one thing behind a defined interface

questions.q: A synchronous request that must succeed replaces the log between two components. What happens when the second one slows down?
questions.explain: Synchronous interaction ties the caller to the callee's health, which is how local faults escalate into large-scale failures.
options: Nothing, since a synchronous request ignores the second component's speed
The first component is slowed or blocked as well, so a local problem spreads
The first component speeds up, since it no longer waits for a buffered message
The second component's backlog grows without affecting anyone, as in a log
optionExplain: A natural guess that confuses synchronous with independent.
Synchronous interaction tends to escalate local faults.
Sounds plausible because a buffer adds delay, but without it the caller waits on the slow callee.
That describes the log setup, not a synchronous call.

questions.q: True or false: Because the log buffers messages, a consumer that failed for an hour will have missed the data produced during that hour.
questions.explain: The log buffers the messages, and the consumer catches up when it is fixed, so it misses nothing.
questions.rule: Buffered logs let consumers catch up.

questions.q: What does the author say event logs offer as an interface between teams' systems?
questions.explain: Event logs provide an interface powerful enough to capture fairly strong consistency properties (due to durability and ordering of events), but general enough to be applicable to almost any kind of data.
questions.teaches: Event logs are powerful enough to capture fairly strong consistency properties, thanks to the durability and ordering of events, but general enough to be applicable to almost any kind of data.
options: A way to avoid ever agreeing on a data format, since any record may be stored
Complete freedom from ordering concerns, since consumers can always reorder events locally
A specialised interface tuned for relational data, which is what most teams use
Strong enough for fairly strong consistency, general enough for most data
optionExplain: Appealing for independent teams, but the interface still needs defined events.
Sounds convenient, but ordering is exactly what makes the log powerful.
Contradicts the point that the interface is general.
He credits durability and ordering of events for this.

questions.q: True or false: If unbundling becomes the way of the future, it will replace databases in their current form.
questions.explain: The author says it will not: databases are still needed as much as ever. The card next explains the roles that remain.
questions.rule: Unbundling composes databases; it does not retire them.

questions.q: What is the goal of unbundling, according to the author?
questions.explain: The goal of unbundling is not to compete with individual databases on performance for particular workloads; it is to combine several different databases to achieve good performance for a much wider range of workloads. It is about breadth, not depth.
options: Depth, so that each database wins every benchmark on its own workload
Breadth, so that combined databases serve a wider range of workloads
Uniformity, so that one data model replaces the many models in use today
Cost saving, so that fewer machines are needed than with a single large database
optionExplain: Sounds like a sensible aim, but he says the goal is not to compete on performance for particular workloads.
He says it is about breadth, not depth.
Contradicts the premise that no single model suits all access patterns.
A common hope, but it is not the stated aim.

questions.q: A startup's whole workload fits one well-known database that already does what they need. What does the author advise?
questions.explain: If there is a single technology that does everything you need, you are most likely best off simply using that product.
options: Split it across several tools anyway, because composed systems are more modern and flexible
Build a custom log-based pipeline first, so that later growth is already covered
Use that product instead of building a composed system from lower-level parts
Wait until every team agrees on a single standard before choosing any product at all
optionExplain: Appealing as a trend, but the chapter calls unneeded complexity a cost.
Sounds like planning ahead, but it is the premature optimisation he warns against.
A single technology that does everything you need is usually best.
A cautious path that the chapter does not suggest.

questions.q: Which roles does the author say databases keep in an unbundled world?
questions.explain: Databases remain required for state in stream processors and for serving query results. They do not become the log or the sole write path.
options: Replacing the event log as the source of ordered changes
Maintaining state inside stream processors
Serving queries on the output of batch and stream processors
Acting as the only place where every application writes new data
optionExplain: The log remains the ordering mechanism in this design.
Stream processors need databases for their state.
Derived outputs are served from databases.
Plausible from habit, but writes may enter through a log instead.

questions.q: True or false: If one existing product satisfies all your requirements, the author advises composing your own system from lower-level components anyway.
questions.explain: He advises using the single product, since unbundling only pays when nothing satisfies all your requirements.
questions.rule: Use the single product if it fits.

questions.q: Why might a single integrated product perform better than a set of composed tools, according to the author?
questions.explain: A single integrated software product may be able to achieve better and more predictable performance on the kinds of workloads for which it is designed, compared to a system consisting of several tools composed with application code.
questions.teaches: A single integrated software product may achieve better and more predictable performance on the workloads it is designed for than a system of several tools composed with application code.
options: It may achieve better and more predictable performance on the workloads it was designed for
It always has more features than the composed tools, so its queries finish faster
It avoids storing data on disk, so there is less to read at query time
It removes the need for any indexes, so writes are cheaper than in composed systems
optionExplain: He cites this advantage of integrated software.
Feature count is not the claim.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
A mistaken simplification; the claim is about workload fit.

questions.q: True or false: The author says a declarative tool equivalent to the Unix shell for composing storage systems is already widely available.
questions.explain: He says one major part is missing: such a high-level language. The card next gives his example.
questions.rule: The shell for data systems is still a wish.

questions.q: The author imagines declaring mysql | elasticsearch, by analogy with Unix ____.
questions.explain: The analogy is to Unix pipes, which connect one program's output to another's input.

questions.q: A team currently writes custom code to copy every product change into a search cluster. What would the author's wished-for tool do for them?
questions.explain: It would take all the documents in the database and index them in the search cluster, then continually capture all changes and apply them automatically, without custom code.
questions.rule: Initial copy plus continuous apply, declared once.
options: Index all existing documents, then capture and apply every later change automatically
Replace the product database with the search cluster so that no copy is needed
Run a distributed transaction between the database and the cluster on each change
Show the team a report of differences each night so that they can fix them by hand
optionExplain: That is the unbundled equivalent of CREATE INDEX.
Solves the copy problem by removing the second system, which is not his aim.
Familiar, but not what the declarative pipe would do.
Helpful, but the wish is for automatic, continuous synchronisation.

questions.q: Which line best sums up the relation between CREATE INDEX and the wished-for pipe?
questions.explain: The declaration would be the unbundled equivalent of CREATE INDEX: it builds the index and keeps it updated, but across separate systems.
options: The pipe would replace CREATE INDEX inside relational databases from now on
The pipe is a kind of federated query that reads from both systems at once
The pipe would be the unbundled equivalent of CREATE INDEX across separate systems
The pipe is a lambda pipeline that runs batch and stream paths for the index
optionExplain: Sounds ambitious, but databases keep their own indexing.
Federation is the read-side approach; the pipe is about writes.
That is how the author describes it.
A different idea: lambda is about two processing paths.

questions.q: True or false: The author hopes declaring a link from a database to a search cluster would also apply later changes to the index.
questions.explain: He wants the declaration to index all existing documents and then continually capture and apply changes.

questions.q: What does the author suggest for caches, using the same idea?
questions.explain: A materialized view is essentially a precomputed cache, so you could imagine creating a cache by declaratively specifying materialized views for complex queries, including recursive queries on graphs and application logic. Differential dataflow is early-stage research in this area.
questions.rule: Declare the view; let the system maintain the cache.
questions.teaches: Differential dataflow is interesting early-stage research toward declaratively specified materialized views for complex queries, including recursive graph queries and application logic.
options: Drop caches entirely, since materialized views make precomputed results unnecessary
Declare caches as materialized views, even for recursive queries and logic
Fill caches by polling the database more often so that they stay close to current
Keep caches separate from any declared pipeline, so that they cannot affect the data
optionExplain: A confusion: a materialized view is itself a precomputed cache.
He ties caches to materialized views as precomputed caches.
Polling is what the chapter wants to move away from.
Opposite of the proposal, which would derive caches declaratively.

questions.q: True or false: The author calls the database inside-out approach a grand new architecture.
questions.explain: He says calling it a new architecture is too grandiose and sees it as a design pattern. The card next tells the idea.

questions.q: What property of spreadsheets does the author want data systems to share?
questions.explain: In a spreadsheet, whenever any input to a formula changes, the result is automatically recalculated. The author wants this at data system level.
questions.rule: Change an input, derived results follow.
options: Every cell can be edited by several users at the same time without any conflicts
All formulas are stored in a relational schema that can be queried with SQL
Calculations run on a cluster so that very large sheets can be computed in parallel
When an input changes, dependent results are recalculated automatically
optionExplain: Sounds like a collaboration feature that spreadsheets offer, but it is not the property he cites.
Plausible for a data system, but it is not the point of the comparison.
Scale is something data systems must add; it is not the spreadsheet property.
That is the spreadsheet behaviour he highlights.

questions.q: True or false: The author says most data systems still have something to learn from features that VisiCalc already had in 1979.
questions.explain: VisiCalc recalculated dependent cells automatically when inputs changed, and the author thinks most data systems still lag in this.
questions.teaches: The author says most data systems still have something to learn from features that VisiCalc already had in 1979.

questions.q: A database record changes. Under the spreadsheet analogy, what should happen to its search entry and a cached total?
questions.explain: When a record in a database changes, any index for that record and any cached views or aggregations that depend on it should be automatically refreshed.
questions.rule: Dependent data refreshes on its own.
options: Both stay as they are until a nightly job recomputes them from scratch for everyone
Both are recalculated by whichever user next reads them from the application screen
Both are refreshed automatically, without the application managing the refresh
Both are deleted so that stale data cannot be read until they are rebuilt later
optionExplain: Common in practice, but the aim is automatic refresh when the input changes.
Shifts the burden onto every reader instead of the system.
That is the behaviour the analogy asks for.
Avoids staleness by removing results, which is not recalculation.

questions.q: The term unbundling in this context was proposed by Jay ____.
questions.explain: The chapter credits Jay Kreps with the term and calls the approach an amalgamation of other people's ideas.

questions.q: True or false: The author presents the database inside-out approach as his own original invention.
questions.explain: He says the ideas are an amalgamation of other people's ideas and that the term unbundling was proposed by Jay Kreps.

questions.q: What must a data system do that a spreadsheet does not, according to the author?
questions.explain: Today's data systems need to be fault-tolerant, scalable and store data durably, and they need to integrate disparate technologies written by different groups over time.
options: Be fault-tolerant, scalable and durable, and integrate technologies from different groups
Recalculate results when an input changes, which spreadsheets are unable to do at all
Be written in one language so that formulas can be evaluated everywhere in the system
Avoid derived data entirely, since spreadsheets cannot keep the results of their formulas
optionExplain: Those are the extra demands he lists.
Spreadsheets already recalculate; that is why they are the analogy.
He calls it unrealistic to expect all software to be built with one language.
Derived data is the whole point of the comparison.
questions.teaches: It is unrealistic to expect all software to be developed using one particular language, framework or tool.

questions.q: True or false: A machine learning model can be seen as a dataset derived from training data by applying functions.
questions.explain: Feature extraction and statistical analysis turn training data into a model, so the model is a derived dataset. The card next lists more examples.

questions.q: The derivation function for a secondary index is so common that you invoke it in many databases by saying CREATE ____.
questions.explain: Because the function is standard, databases offer it as a core feature.

questions.q: A team's cache stores each product page in the exact form the interface shows it. The page layout changes. What follows?
questions.explain: A cache often holds an aggregation in the form shown in the UI, so populating it needs knowledge of the fields the UI references. Changes in the UI may require changing the definition and rebuilding it.
options: Nothing, since a cache is derived data and derived data always adapts to its source on its own
The rule for filling the cache must be updated and the cache rebuilt to match the new fields
Only the source table needs updating, since the cache is a copy and follows whatever the table says
The cache must be dropped for good, since a cache cannot be rebuilt once the interface has changed
optionExplain: Convenient if true, but the derivation function encodes which fields the interface uses.
Changes in the UI may require updating how the cache is populated and rebuilding it.
A copy would, but this cache is an aggregation shaped for the screen.
Rebuilding is exactly what the chapter says may be needed.

questions.q: Sort each derivation by whether the chapter treats it as standard enough to be built into databases.
questions.explain: Secondary indexes and basic linguistic features for common languages are built in; domain-specific search tuning, feature engineering and screen-shaped caches need application knowledge.
questions.rule: Standard is built in; specific is custom.
groups: Built in as a core feature

items.t: A secondary index over a column
Basic full-text indexing for common languages
Sophisticated full-text features for a specific domain
Feature engineering for a machine learning model
A cache shaped for a particular screen

questions.q: True or false: As derivations become more application-specific, the built-in support of databases covers them better.
questions.explain: The chapter says custom code is needed for non-standard derivations and that this is where many databases struggle.

questions.q: What does the author say about feature engineering for machine learning?
questions.explain: In machine learning, feature engineering is notoriously application-specific, and often has to incorporate detailed knowledge about the user interaction and deployment of an application.
questions.teaches: Feature engineering in machine learning is notoriously application-specific and often has to incorporate detailed knowledge about the user interaction and deployment of an application.
options: It is a standard step that databases can run for any model as a built-in operator
It is best left entirely to automatic tools, since human knowledge adds little to feature design
It matters only for training data, not for the data a model is applied to later
It is notoriously application-specific and often needs detailed knowledge of user interaction and deployment
optionExplain: Appealing if models are treated like indexes, but the chapter says the opposite.
The chapter stresses application knowledge instead.
The chapter treats both the model and its outputs as derived data.
He says so in discussing derivation functions.

questions.q: True or false: The author thinks databases make a good deployment environment for arbitrary application code.
questions.explain: He says in practice they have turned out to be poorly suited. The card next lists why.
questions.rule: Databases are for state, not for hosting code.

questions.q: Which requirement does the author say databases fit poorly when used to run application code?
questions.explain: Databases do not fit well with the requirements of modern application development, such as dependency and package management, version control, rolling upgrades, evolvability, monitoring, metrics, calls to network services and integration with external systems.
options: Rolling upgrades and version control for the code
Writing data durably so that it survives a crash of the machine
Enforcing uniqueness constraints on stored records
Answering declarative queries over large tables with indexes
optionExplain: These are among the modern development needs he lists.
Durability is what databases do well.
Constraints are a database strength.
Query answering is what databases are built for.

questions.q: The functional programming joke quoted in the chapter is: We believe in the separation of Church and ____.
questions.explain: Church refers to the mathematician Alonzo Church, whose lambda calculus has no mutable state.
questions.rule: Church and state: code and data apart.
questions.teaches: The functional programming joke refers to Alonzo Church, whose lambda calculus, an early form of computation, has no mutable state.

questions.q: A web shop uses stateless application servers behind a load balancer. Why is this convenient, according to the chapter?
questions.explain: In a stateless service any user request can be routed to any application server, and the server forgets everything about the request once it has sent the response.
questions.rule: Stateless servers are easy to scale.
options: Servers keep each user's cart in memory, so repeated requests are answered faster
The database can be removed, since stateless servers have no need for stored state
Each server keeps a copy of the whole database, so that a request never waits on a network call
Any request can go to any server, so servers can be added or removed at will
optionExplain: That would be a stateful design, the opposite of what is described.
The state still has to go somewhere, typically a database.
Not the described setup; state is held in the database.
Correct. In a stateless service any user request can be routed to any application server, and the server forgets everything about the request once it has sent the response.

questions.q: True or false: A speaker says stateless services have no state at all, so no component stores data. The chapter agrees.
questions.explain: The services are stateless, but the state has to go somewhere, typically a database.
questions.rule: Stateless services push state into a database.

questions.q: A team wants to move business rules into stored procedures so they run next to the data. How does the author's reasoning cut against this?
questions.explain: Deployment and cluster management tools are designed specifically for running application code. By focusing on doing one thing well, they do it much better than a database that provides execution of user-defined functions as one of its many features.
questions.rule: Let each system do one thing well.
questions.teaches: Deployment and cluster management tools such as Mesos, YARN, Docker and Kubernetes focus on running application code and so do it much better than a database offering user-defined functions as one of many features.
options: Stored procedures cannot read the data they are placed next to, so they must fetch it first
Rules inside a database cannot be changed after deployment, which blocks any later improvement
Tools built to run code do that job better than a database offering code execution as one of many features
Databases refuse to run any code at all, so the plan could not be carried out
optionExplain: They can read it, so the objection would fail.
Changeability is not the stated objection; the tooling is.
Specialisation: doing one thing well.
Databases do support stored procedures, but poorly suited for this purpose.

questions.q: True or false: In a typical web application, the database notifies the application when a value it has read changes.
questions.explain: Databases are passive: the application must poll to find out about changes. The card next explains the model.

questions.q: To find out whether the content of a database has changed, often the only option is to ____, that is, repeat the query periodically.
questions.explain: Polling is the passive approach databases inherited from the variable-in-memory model.

questions.q: A dashboard checks an orders table every five seconds to see whether anything is new. What does the chapter call this?
questions.explain: Without a change subscription, your only option is often to poll.
options: Subscribing, since the dashboard receives updates from the database as they happen
Polling, the passive approach where the reader must repeat the query to learn about changes
The observer pattern, since the dashboard watches the table for changes
Dual writing, since the dashboard and the table both hold the same information
optionExplain: A subscription would push changes to the dashboard.
Repeating the query is polling.
The observer pattern would notify the watcher; here it asks again and again.
Dual writing means two systems written by the application.

questions.q: True or false: If a database offered a feed of changes, an application could learn of updates without repeating its query.
questions.explain: That is what subscribing to changes means, and the chapter says it is only beginning to emerge as a feature.

questions.q: True or false: Most languages build in the observer pattern, so passive variables are not an issue. The chapter agrees.
questions.explain: You can implement notifications with the observer pattern in your own code, but most languages do not have it as a built-in feature.
questions.rule: Observer is available, not built in.

questions.q: Where does the chapter say subscribing to changes in databases stands today?
questions.explain: Subscribing to changes is only just beginning to emerge as a feature, as the chapter's reference to API support for change streams shows.
questions.teaches: Subscribing to changes of a database is only just beginning to emerge as a feature, through API support for change streams.
options: It is a mature feature offered by almost every database in current use
It is only beginning to emerge as a feature
It is impossible in principle for any storage system that keeps data on disk
It is available only in databases that give up durability for speed
optionExplain: Would make polling rare, but the chapter says otherwise.
The chapter points to API support for change streams as an emerging feature.
Disk storage is not the barrier.
Plausible trade-off, but not claimed in the chapter.

questions.q: True or false: Views derived from one event log must process events in the same order to stay consistent with each other.
questions.explain: The order of state changes is often important for derived data. The card next gives the two demands.

questions.q: What makes losing a single message serious for derived data?
questions.explain: Fault tolerance is key for derived data: losing just a single message causes the derived dataset to go permanently out of sync with its data source.
questions.rule: One lost message corrupts a derived copy.
options: The broker stops accepting messages until the lost one is replaced by the sender
The sender is charged for the lost message, which makes loss expensive for the team
The remaining messages are delivered twice, which doubles all later results
The derived dataset goes permanently out of sync with its source
optionExplain: Brokers do not behave like that, and the harm is to the derived copy.
Cost to a sender is not the concern.
A lost message does not cause duplicates.
A missing change is never applied unless something repairs it.

questions.q: A team feeds a search index and a cache from a broker that redelivers unacknowledged messages out of order. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: Derived views that process events in different orders may no longer agree. Many message brokers do not have the order-keeping property when redelivering unacknowledged messages.
questions.rule: Choose a broker that preserves order on redelivery.
options: The two views may apply events in different orders and stop agreeing with each other
The broker deletes the messages once redelivered, so the views never see them again
The views become identical to each other, since redelivery equalises their state
The messages are applied in order but twice, so counts double and the views stay equal
optionExplain: Many brokers do not preserve order when redelivering, which breaks derived-data consistency.
Redelivery does not delete them; the issue is the order.
Redelivery in varying order would instead cause divergence.
Duplicates are a separate problem, and the scenario describes disorder.

questions.q: Match each demand to what it protects against.
questions.explain: Order, loss and dual writes are the three hazards the chapter names for derived data.
questions.rule: Order, no loss, no dual writes.
pairs: Views disagreeing because events were applied in different orders
A lost message leaving the derived data permanently stale
Two systems being written separately and ordering conflicts

questions.q: True or false: Using actor systems that keep actor state and messages in memory by default is a safe way to maintain derived data.
questions.explain: If the machine running an actor crashes, state and messages are lost, so the derived dataset can go out of sync.
questions.rule: In-memory messaging is not fault tolerant enough.

questions.q: How do the demands of stable ordering and fault tolerance compare in cost with distributed transactions, according to the author?
questions.explain: Stable message ordering and fault-tolerant message processing are quite stringent demands, but they are much less expensive and more operationally robust than distributed transactions. Modern stream processors provide them at scale.
questions.rule: Order and reliability beat transactions on cost.
questions.teaches: Modern stream processors can provide stable ordering and fault-tolerant processing at scale and let application code run as stream operators, composed like Unix tools chained by pipes.
options: They cost more than distributed transactions but give stronger timing guarantees to every reader
They cost about the same as distributed transactions, so the choice is a matter of taste
They are stringent but much less expensive and more operationally robust than distributed transactions
They cannot be provided at scale, so only small systems can maintain derived data this way
optionExplain: Reasonable since they sound strict, but he says the opposite about cost.
He draws a clear preference based on cost and robustness.
He says modern stream processors can provide them at scale.
He says modern stream processors provide them at scale.

questions.q: True or false: Stream operators communicate through synchronous request and response, like microservices.
questions.explain: Stream operators use one-directional asynchronous message streams. The card next compares the two.
questions.rule: One-way async versus request and response.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of a service-oriented architecture over a monolith, according to the chapter?
questions.explain: The advantage is primarily organisational scalability through loose coupling: different teams can work on different services, which reduces coordination effort, as long as services can be deployed and updated independently.
options: Lower latency, because services avoid network hops that a monolith must make
Stronger consistency, because each service enforces its own global transaction
Organisational scalability through loose coupling between independently deployed services
Smaller storage costs, because services share one database for all their data
optionExplain: Services add network calls, so this reverses the truth.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
Different teams can work on services without much coordination.
Services usually keep independent state.

questions.q: Service A calls service B per order and waits for the reply. B then publishes a stream that A subscribes to. What changes?
questions.explain: Composing stream operators uses one-directional, asynchronous message streams rather than synchronous request/response interactions.
options: The link becomes a one-directional asynchronous stream instead of a synchronous request
A and B become one deployable unit, since a subscription requires shared code
B must now wait for A to confirm every update before it can publish the next
A can no longer read B's data, since only the publisher may query its own data
optionExplain: That is the difference between services and stream operators.
Subscription does not merge deployment.
That would be synchronous again.
A reads from its own local copy built from the stream.

questions.q: Stream operators communicate through one-directional, ____ message streams rather than synchronous request/response interactions.
questions.explain: The communication mechanism is the main difference from services that call each other synchronously.

questions.q: True or false: Moving from synchronous requests between services to asynchronous streams can improve fault tolerance.
questions.explain: The chapter lists better fault tolerance among the advantages of message-passing dataflow, since a failed service no longer blocks its callers.

questions.q: Which statement fits the author's comparison of dataflow systems with microservices?
questions.explain: Dataflow systems of stream operators have many characteristics in common with microservices, including loose coupling, but the underlying communication mechanism is very different.
questions.teaches: Besides the advantages of message-passing dataflow such as better fault tolerance, dataflow systems can also achieve better performance than services that call each other synchronously.
options: They are incompatible, since loose coupling is only available with synchronous requests
They are identical, since asynchronous streams are only another name for REST
They differ only in that dataflow requires a single team to own every operator
Both loosely couple parts, but they communicate differently
optionExplain: The chapter links both to loose coupling.
REST is synchronous request and response.
Independent deployment is shared by both.
Both give independence; the mechanism is what differs.

questions.q: True or false: Subscribing to a stream of exchange rates can make a purchase faster than querying a rate service on every sale.
questions.explain: The purchase code queries a local database instead of making a network request. The card next shows the approach.

questions.q: In the dataflow approach, the purchase code queries a ____ database instead of making a synchronous network request.
questions.explain: The rate is already stored locally from the stream of updates.

questions.q: A delivery app must show estimated fees that depend on a fuel price updated hourly by another team. Which design matches the dataflow approach?
questions.explain: The dataflow approach subscribes to a stream of updates ahead of time and records the current value in a local database, so no network request is needed at processing time.
options: Call the fuel price service for each estimate and wait for its reply every time
Subscribe to the price stream and keep the latest value in a local table
Ask the other team to write fuel prices directly into the app's database tables
Hard-code a price into the app and update it with every release
optionExplain: That is the microservices approach.
Subscribe ahead of time and query locally.
Creates a shared writer to the app's data, which is not the stream approach.
Avoids the call but loses freshness.

questions.q: True or false: If the exchange-rate service is down, a purchase service using the dataflow approach can still convert currencies using its local rates.
questions.explain: The local database already holds the most recent rate, so the dataflow approach is more robust to the failure of another service.

questions.q: Why does the chapter say a cache in the microservices style ends up like the dataflow approach?
questions.explain: A service could cache the rate locally, but to keep the cache fresh it would need to poll for updated exchange rates or subscribe to a stream of changes, which is exactly what happens in the dataflow approach.
questions.rule: A fresh cache is a subscription in disguise.
questions.teaches: A microservice could avoid the synchronous request by caching the exchange rate locally, but to keep the cache fresh it would need to poll or subscribe to a stream of changes, which is exactly the dataflow approach.
options: A cache never needs updating, since exchange rates change too slowly to matter
A cache removes the need for any rate service, since rates can be guessed from earlier values
A cache makes calls synchronous, since every read waits for the service to confirm it
Keeping the cache fresh needs polling or a subscription to changes, which is what dataflow does
optionExplain: Cache freshness is the issue.
The cache still depends on updates from the source.
Caches avoid that wait; the problem is staleness.
That is the point of the footnote.

questions.q: True or false: If purchase events are reprocessed a year later using today's exchange rate, the output will match the original output.
questions.explain: The rate has changed, so you need the rate at the original time of purchase. The card next explains.

questions.q: What must you obtain to reconstruct the original output of a purchase when reprocessing it later?
questions.explain: If the purchase events are reprocessed at a later point in time, the exchange rate will have changed. To reconstruct the original output, you obtain the historical rate at the original time of purchase.
questions.rule: Use the value as it was then.
options: The latest exchange rate at the time the reprocessing runs
The historical exchange rate at the original time of purchase
An average of all rates since the purchase happened
A copy of the purchase event stored in a second database
optionExplain: Tempting as the easy value, but it is not what was used originally.
The join is time-dependent.
Plausible as a fair compromise, but it would not reproduce the original.
The event is not the missing piece; the rate is.

questions.q: A loyalty scheme changes its points rate yearly and recomputes last year's tiers from old purchases. Which rate should it use?
questions.explain: A time-dependent join needs the value at the original time, otherwise reprocessing gives a different result from the first run.
questions.rule: Keep a history of changing reference data.
options: This year's rate for every purchase, since it is the rate in force now
The average of last year's and this year's rate, as a fair middle value
The rate that applied at the time of each purchase, kept as history
Whichever rate is lowest, to avoid awarding too many points
optionExplain: Easy to fetch, but gives different tiers from the original run.
Not a faithful reconstruction of either year.
Historical values reproduce the original output.
A policy choice that does not reproduce the original output.

questions.q: To reconstruct the original output when reprocessing a purchase, you need the ____ exchange rate at the original time of purchase.
questions.explain: Reprocessing with today's rate would give a different result from the first run.
questions.rule: Use the value as of the event time.

questions.q: True or false: The time dependence of the join exists whether the handler queries a rate service or subscribes to a stream of rate updates.
questions.explain: Either way, the rate changes over time, so reprocessing needs the historical value.
questions.rule: The problem is in the join, not the transport.

questions.q: How does the author describe the state of time-dependent joins?
questions.explain: There are still many open questions, for example around issues like time-dependent joins, but he believes building applications around dataflow ideas is a very promising direction.
questions.rule: Open questions remain, but the direction is promising.
questions.teaches: The author lists time-dependent joins among the open questions in building applications around dataflow, while still calling the direction very promising.
options: As one of the open questions that remain in building applications around dataflow
As a solved problem that stream processors handle automatically for every join
As a reason to abandon dataflow in favour of synchronous service calls
As a problem that affects only batch processing and never stream processing
optionExplain: He says there are still many open questions, for example time-dependent joins.
Would remove the concern, but he lists it as open.
He still calls dataflow a very promising direction.
It arises in stream joins when events are reprocessed.

questions.q: True or false: The write path is the part of a data journey done only when someone asks to see the data.
questions.explain: That describes the read path. The write path is precomputed eagerly as data arrives. The card next defines both.
questions.rule: Write path eager; read path on demand.

questions.q: Which pair matches the write path and the read path to eager and lazy evaluation?
questions.explain: The write path is precomputed, done eagerly as soon as the data comes in; the read path happens only when someone asks. This is like eager and lazy evaluation in functional programming.
options: Write path is like eager evaluation; read path is like lazy evaluation
Write path is like lazy evaluation; read path is like eager evaluation
Both paths are like eager evaluation, since both must complete before an answer
Both paths are like lazy evaluation, since both wait for a request
optionExplain: Precomputing resembles eager evaluation; on-demand work resembles lazy.
Tempting if you think writing is slow, but it reverses the analogy.
Mistakes finishing a task for doing it ahead of time.
Only the read path waits for a request.

questions.q: A weather site precomputes tomorrow's forecast map for every city overnight, and visitors fetch the image. Where is the work done?
questions.explain: Work done as soon as data arrives, regardless of whether anyone has asked to see it, is the write path.
options: Mostly on the read path, since visitors are the ones who trigger the image to be shown
Equally on both paths, since the visitor and the overnight job each handle half
Mostly on the write path, since the result is prepared before anyone asks
On neither path, since a static image is not derived from any dataset
optionExplain: Showing it is the read path, but the heavy work was done before they asked.
The heavy computing happens in advance, not half and half.
Eagerly precomputed work belongs to the write path.
The map is derived from forecast data, so it is a derived dataset.

questions.q: The derived dataset is the place where the write path and the ____ path meet.
questions.explain: It represents a trade-off between work at write time and work at read time.
questions.rule: Write path and read path meet in the derived dataset.

questions.q: True or false: Moving work from the read path to the write path makes reads cheaper but writes more expensive.
questions.explain: A derived dataset is a trade-off between work at write time and at read time, so precomputing more shifts cost to writes.

questions.q: True or false: A colleague says the derived dataset is part of the read path only, because users query it. The chapter agrees.
questions.explain: The derived dataset is where the write path and the read path meet.
questions.rule: The derived dataset is the meeting point.

questions.q: Which earlier example in the book does the chapter say was about shifting the write and read path boundary?
questions.explain: Shifting the boundary between work done on the write path and the read path was the topic of the Twitter example in Describing Load, where it might be drawn differently for celebrities compared to ordinary users.
questions.rule: Twitter's timelines are a boundary choice.
questions.teaches: The Twitter example at the beginning of the book was about shifting the boundary between the write path and read path, drawn differently for celebrities compared to ordinary users.
options: The two-phase commit example in the transactions chapter about coordinators
The Twitter example in Describing Load at the beginning of the book
The column storage example in the chapter on storage engines
The Raft example in the chapter on consensus about leader election
optionExplain: Not tied to the read and write path boundary.
It said the boundary may differ for celebrities versus ordinary users.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
Unrelated to the read and write path boundary.

questions.q: True or false: Having no search index means less work on the write path but much more work on the read path.
questions.explain: Without an index there is nothing to update at write time, but every query must scan all documents. The card next lays out the options.
questions.rule: No index: cheap writes, costly reads.

questions.q: Why is precomputing the answers to all possible search queries impractical?
questions.explain: The set of possible search queries is infinite, so precomputing all possible search results would require infinite time and storage space.
questions.rule: Unbounded query space rules out full precomputation.
options: Search engines cannot store results, so precomputed answers would be lost on restart
Users change their queries too quickly, so results are stale before they are read
Precomputed answers would be slower to return than a scan of all documents
The set of possible queries is infinite, so it would need infinite time and space
optionExplain: Storage is possible; the issue is the number of queries.
Staleness is a concern but not the stated reason.
Reads would be fast; the cost would be on the write side.
Correct. The set of possible search queries is infinite, so precomputing all possible search results would require infinite time and storage space.

questions.q: A help centre has 200 articles. Searches are rare and the articles change often. Which boundary suits best?
questions.explain: Scanning without an index is possible on a small number of documents, which keeps the write path cheap.
options: A cache of precomputed results for every possible query a visitor might type
A full index plus a materialized view per article, rebuilt on every edit
No index, scanning the 200 articles on each query
A distributed index across many nodes, to keep up with expected growth
optionExplain: Impossible and wasteful for an unbounded set of queries.
Too much write work for a small, rarely searched set.
With few documents, scanning is acceptable and writes stay cheap.
Premature for 200 articles that are rarely searched.

questions.q: Match each approach to where it puts the work.
questions.explain: Each option shifts the boundary: scanning leaves everything to the read path, an index shares the work, and a cache precomputes the popular answers.
questions.rule: Index, cache and view move the boundary.
pairs: Almost all work on the read path
Extra write-path work to serve popular reads quickly

questions.q: True or false: If new documents appear that match a cached common query, the cache or materialized view must be updated.
questions.explain: A cache of common queries is also a materialized view and has to be updated when new documents should be included in its results.

questions.q: How does the chapter relate the cache of common search queries to a materialized view?
questions.explain: Precomputing results for a fixed set of the most common queries would generally be called a cache, although we could also call it a materialized view, as it must be updated when new documents appear.
questions.rule: Cache of results equals materialized view.
questions.teaches: Precomputing results for only the most common queries would generally be called a cache, though it could equally be called a materialized view since it must be updated when new documents affect those queries.
options: They are the same thing under two names, since it needs updating when new documents match
A cache is read-only, while a materialized view accepts writes from users directly
A cache holds raw documents, while a materialized view holds only indexes
A materialized view is always larger than the index, while a cache is smaller than it
optionExplain: It says we could call it a cache or a materialized view.
Neither takes direct writes in this context.
Both hold precomputed query results here.
Size is not how the chapter relates them.

questions.q: True or false: Traditionally, web browsers were stateless clients that could do useful things only with an internet connection.
questions.explain: Almost the only thing you could do offline was scroll a page already loaded. The card next describes the shift.

questions.q: What do offline-first applications do?
questions.explain: Offline-first applications do as much as possible using a local database on the same device, without requiring an internet connection, and sync with remote servers in the background.
options: Wait for a server reply to every action so that data is never shown stale
Work mostly from a local database on the device and sync with servers in the background
Refuse to work without a connection to keep the user from seeing old data
Store data only on servers and push screenshots of it to the device
optionExplain: That is the stateless client model.
Correct. Offline-first applications do as much as possible using a local database on the same device, without requiring an internet connection, and sync with remote servers in the background.
The opposite of offline-first.
Offline-first keeps state on the device.

questions.q: Match each layer of a client app to what it is in the author's picture.
questions.explain: The chapter treats the device's state as a cache, the model as a replica and the screen as a view derived from it.
questions.rule: Screen, model, server: view, replica, source.
pairs: A materialized view onto model objects
A local replica of state in a remote datacenter
A cache of state on the server

questions.q: True or false: With state on the device, a user interface no longer has to wait for synchronous network requests.
questions.explain: Most interactions can use the local state, which matters on slow and unreliable cellular connections.

questions.q: Which problem with mobile networks makes offline-first especially useful, according to the chapter?
questions.explain: Since mobile devices often have slow and unreliable cellular internet connections, it is a big advantage for users if their interface does not wait for synchronous network requests and if apps mostly work offline.
questions.teaches: Single-page JavaScript apps and mobile apps can store a lot of state on the device, so most user interactions do not need a round-trip to the server.
options: Mobile devices have too little storage to ever hold data from a server
Mobile networks forbid synchronous requests for security reasons
Mobile networks always deliver messages in the wrong order
Mobile devices often have slow and unreliable cellular connections
optionExplain: Devices can store a lot of state.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
Not stated and not true as a rule.
That is why it is an advantage for apps to mostly work offline.

questions.q: True or false: RSS feed subscription is a basic form of polling.
questions.explain: A feed reader repeatedly asks whether there is anything new. The card next explains the shift to pushing.
