questions.q: Which technologies let a server push messages to a web browser, according to the chapter?
questions.explain: Server-sent events (the EventSource API) and WebSockets provide communication channels by which a browser can keep an open TCP connection to a server, and the server can actively push messages.
options: Server-sent events and WebSockets
RSS and plain HTTP request and response
Post/Redirect/Get and TCP sequence numbers
Two-phase commit and XA transactions
optionExplain: Both keep an open TCP connection so the server can push.
These involve the client asking, not the server pushing.
These relate to avoiding duplicate form submissions.
These are atomic commit mechanisms for databases.

questions.q: A live auction page must show new bids within a second. Which design fits the chapter?
questions.explain: Pushing state changes to client devices reduces the staleness of the client-side state.
options: Have the page reload itself once a minute to fetch the latest bids
Ask users to press refresh when they suspect a new bid has arrived
Store bids on the device and sync them at the end of the auction
Keep a WebSocket open so the server pushes each new bid to the page
optionExplain: That is polling and leaves state stale for a minute.
Leaves staleness to the user.
Delays updates until after the auction has finished.
Pushing extends the write path to the end user.

questions.q: Pushing state changes all the way to client devices extends the ____ path to the end user.
questions.explain: The client still needs a read path for its initial state, but afterwards it relies on a stream of changes.

questions.q: True or false: A designer says a phone offline for an hour must reload all its data on reconnecting. The chapter agrees.
questions.explain: The consumer-offset technique lets a device resume from the last message it saw without missing messages.

questions.q: How does the chapter apply the idea of consumer offsets to end-user devices?
questions.explain: Consumers of log-based message brokers can reconnect after failing and not miss messages that arrived while disconnected. The same technique works for individual users, where each device is a small subscriber to a small stream of events.
questions.rule: A device is a subscriber with its own offset.
questions.teaches: The consumer offsets technique of log-based message brokers lets a reconnecting device continue without missing messages, treating each device as a small subscriber to a small stream of events.
options: Each device must stay connected all the time or it loses its place permanently
Each device must ask the server for a full snapshot every time it reconnects
Each device subscribes to a small event stream and can reconnect without losing messages
Each device shares one offset with all other devices of the same user
optionExplain: The offset technique exists to avoid this.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
Same technique as for log-based brokers.
Each device is its own subscriber.

questions.q: True or false: Instant messaging and online games already use an end-to-end real-time architecture.
questions.explain: These applications send changes from one user to another with low delay. The card next asks why not all applications do.
questions.rule: Real-time apps already work end to end.

questions.q: Tools such as Elm, React, Flux and Redux manage client-side state by subscribing to a stream of ____.
questions.explain: The streams carry user input or server responses and are structured like event sourcing.
questions.rule: Client state is an event stream.

questions.q: A shared whiteboard app needs one user's drawing to appear on another user's screen within a second. Which design fits?
questions.explain: State changes can flow through an end-to-end write path from one device to the user interface of a person observing the state on another device, with low delay.
questions.rule: Push the change end to end.
options: The second device asks the server for new drawing data when its user clicks reload
A change flows from one device through the server to the other device's pipeline
Both devices write to each other directly and settle their differences later
The server stores each drawing and shows it when the second user logs in next time
optionExplain: That is polling on demand.
That is the end-to-end write path.
Direct writes bring back ordering problems.
Delivers changes late, not within a second.

questions.q: A team wants to give every screen in its app live updates. What obstacle does the chapter expect?
questions.explain: The assumption of stateless clients and request/response interactions is very deeply ingrained in our databases, libraries, frameworks and protocols.
options: Browsers cannot hold TCP connections open for longer than a few seconds
Its tools assume stateless clients and request/response
Event logs cannot represent user input in any usable form
Users will refuse to use applications that update themselves
optionExplain: Server-sent events and WebSockets keep connections open.
That assumption is deeply ingrained.
Client frameworks already structure input as events.
Not a point in the chapter.

questions.q: True or false: The author says that most datastores already let a request return a stream of responses over time.
questions.explain: Many datastores support read and write requests that return one response, but far fewer let you subscribe to changes.

questions.q: What does the author hope designers will keep in mind?
questions.explain: If you are designing data systems, he hopes you will keep in mind the option of subscribing to changes, not just querying the current state.
questions.rule: Offer subscriptions as well as queries.
questions.teaches: The author thinks the advantages of more responsive user interfaces and better offline support would make it worth moving from request/response interaction to publish/subscribe dataflow.
options: The option of avoiding all state on the device so the server stays the single source
The option of replacing every query with a polling loop for simplicity
The option of giving up durability to make live updates faster
The option of subscribing to changes, not only querying the current state
optionExplain: The opposite of the offline-first argument.
Polling is what he wants to move beyond.
Durability is not traded off in the passage.
That is his closing request for this section.

questions.q: True or false: A one-off read request can be seen as a join between a stream of read events and a database.
questions.explain: The read passes through the join operator and is then forgotten. The card next describes it.
questions.rule: Reads as events make queries joins.

questions.q: In this design, what does a subscribe request correspond to?
questions.explain: A one-off read request just passes the request through the join operator and then immediately forgets it; a subscribe request is a persistent join with past and future events on the other side of the join.
questions.rule: Subscribe: a join that stays open.
options: A persistent join with past and future events on the other side
A one-off read that is forgotten immediately after the answer
A write that is appended to the log and applied exactly once
A copartitioning step that places the data on a new partition
optionExplain: Unlike a one-off read, it stays in place.
That is the one-off read.
A write is a different kind of event.
Copartitioning is about routing, not about the lifetime of a request.

questions.q: A read for user 7 must reach the node holding user 7's data. What does the chapter liken this routing to?
questions.explain: The read event needs to be sent to the database partition holding the data, just like batch and stream processors need to copartition inputs on the same key when joining.
questions.rule: Route reads by key like a join.
options: Two-phase commit coordinators asking every participant to vote
Leader election choosing a node to decide the order of writes
Batch and stream processors copartitioning inputs on the same key when joining
Quorum reads asking a majority of replicas for the latest version
optionExplain: That is a different protocol.
Leader election is about ordering, not routing reads.
Routing reads to the right partition is like copartitioned joins.
Quorum reads are a replication technique.

questions.q: When reads and writes are both events routed to one stream operator, the operator performs a stream-____ join.
questions.explain: The stream of read queries is joined with the database, which acts as the table.

questions.q: True or false: In this design, a stream processor could answer a read event by emitting the result to an output stream.
questions.explain: The processor handles both read and write events and responds to reads by emitting results.

questions.q: What does the author say about the correspondence between serving requests and performing joins?
questions.explain: This correspondence between serving requests and performing joins is quite fundamental.
questions.rule: Serving a request is performing a join.
questions.teaches: Some stream processing frameworks let outside clients query the state a processor maintains for aggregations and joins, turning the stream processor itself into a kind of simple database.
options: It is accidental and has no use in design
It applies only to batch processing and never to stream processing
It is quite fundamental
It was disproved by research on stream processing
optionExplain: He calls it fundamental.
It is presented in a stream-table join context.
He cites it as a deep link.
He cites research supporting it.

questions.q: True or false: Recording the results of read queries makes it possible to reconstruct what a user saw before making a decision.
questions.explain: That is the benefit for tracking causal dependencies. The card next gives the shop example.
questions.rule: Log reads to know what was seen.

questions.q: What cost does the chapter attach to writing read events to durable storage?
questions.explain: Writing read events to durable storage enables better tracking of causal dependencies, but it incurs additional storage and I/O cost.
options: Additional storage and I/O cost
A loss of ordering among write events in the main log
A need to use distributed transactions for every read
A guarantee that the reads can never be repeated
optionExplain: Durable logging adds both.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.

questions.q: A travel site wants to analyse whether showing a delay warning changes bookings. What should it record?
questions.explain: To analyse the connection between what was shown and what was bought, you need to record the result of the user's query.
questions.rule: Record the view that led to the decision.
options: Only the final booking, since the decision is all that matters for analysis
Only the write path events, since reads do not change any stored data
Only an average of warnings across all customers each day
The warning each customer was shown, as an event that later bookings can refer to
optionExplain: Without the view, the cause is invisible.
Reads leave no trace there, which is the gap.
Averages lose the per-decision link.
That reconstructs what the user saw.

questions.q: Recording read events helps track causal dependencies and data ____ across a system.
questions.explain: Provenance is where data came from and what influenced a result.

questions.q: True or false: If a system already logs read requests for operational purposes, using the log as the source of requests is a large change.
questions.explain: The author says it is not such a great change in that case.

questions.q: True or false: A colleague claims the overhead of logging reads is a solved problem. The chapter agrees.
questions.explain: Optimising such systems to reduce the overhead is still an open research problem.

questions.q: A bank wants to explain later why an officer approved a loan after seeing a risk screen. What does this idea suggest?
questions.explain: Recording the result of the query allows you to reconstruct what the user saw before they made a decision, at the price of additional storage and I/O.
questions.rule: Log what was shown when decisions must be explainable.
questions.teaches: Logging read events also helps track data provenance across a system, not only causal dependencies.
options: Record the screen's contents as a durable event, accepting extra storage and I/O
Keep only the approval itself, because a decision cannot depend on what was displayed before it
Store the screen contents only in the officer's browser, which avoids all central storage cost
Ask the officer to describe the screen from memory, which is as reliable as a log
optionExplain: Logging what was seen reconstructs the decision's context.
Appealing for its small cost, but the decision may depend on the screen.
Cheap, but not durable or reliable for tracking provenance across a system.
A memory is not a record; the point is to reconstruct what the user saw.

questions.q: True or false: For a query that touches only one partition, sending it through a stream is probably overkill.
questions.explain: The benefit appears only when data from several partitions must be combined. The card next gives examples.
questions.rule: Single-partition queries do not need streams.

questions.q: Which example does the chapter give of a multi-partition computation?
questions.explain: Storm's distributed RPC computed the number of people who have seen a URL on Twitter, the union of the follower sets of everyone who tweeted that URL. Users are partitioned, so results must be combined from many partitions.
options: Renaming a column in a single table on one machine
Compressing a single log segment on disk
Computing a checksum of one packet on a network link
Counting people who have seen a URL by uniting follower sets
optionExplain: Involves one machine, not several partitions.
A local operation.
Not a partitioned data problem.
The follower sets are spread over partitions.

questions.q: A bank scores card payments using reputation data on IP, email and billing address, each in a partitioned database. Which approach fits?
questions.explain: To assess the risk of a purchase you examine scores for the IP address, email address, billing address and so on. Each reputation database is partitioned, so collecting scores requires a sequence of joins with differently partitioned datasets.
options: One distributed transaction locking all three reputation databases for each payment
A sequence of joins of the purchase event with the differently partitioned reputation datasets
A single copy of all reputation data kept on the payment server
A nightly batch that scores all payments the following morning
optionExplain: Heavy and unneeded for read-only lookups.
That is the fraud-prevention example.
Ignores that each dataset is partitioned.
Too late for fraud prevention.

questions.q: Storm's distributed ____ feature supports sending queries through a stream and combining results from several partitions.
questions.explain: It was used to compute the number of people who have seen a URL on Twitter.

questions.q: True or false: If an MPP database already provides multi-partition joins, it is probably simpler to use it than build them with a stream processor.
questions.explain: The chapter says exactly this, and treats queries as streams as an option for applications at the limits of off-the-shelf solutions.
questions.rule: Prefer the product if it exists.

questions.q: Why would a team consider treating queries as streams despite the extra effort?
questions.explain: Treating queries as streams provides an option for implementing large-scale applications that run against the limits of conventional off-the-shelf solutions.
questions.rule: An option for the extremes of scale.
questions.teaches: Storm's distributed RPC feature supports treating queries as streams, for example to compute the number of people who have seen a URL on Twitter by combining results from many partitions.
options: It guarantees that every query runs faster than on a single-node database
It removes the need for partitioning, since streams hide the location of data
It lets large applications run complex queries off-the-shelf tools cannot
It removes the need to log any events, since queries are executed immediately
optionExplain: The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
Partitioning remains; routing deals with it.
The chapter gives it as an option at the limits.
Events are central to the design.

questions.q: True or false: With a stateless service that only reads data, fixing a bug and restarting the service returns everything to normal.
questions.explain: A stateless read-only service holds nothing that a bug can corrupt for good. The card next contrasts it with stateful systems.

questions.q: Why can a mistake in a stateful system be more serious than one in a stateless service?
questions.explain: Stateful systems such as databases are designed to remember things forever, more or less, so if something goes wrong the effects also potentially last forever, which requires more careful thought.
options: Databases remember things for a very long time, so the effects of an error can last as long
Stateful systems run on slower hardware, so every error takes longer to find and repair
Stateless services never fail, so only stateful systems can have bugs worth fixing
Databases refuse to restart after a crash, so any bug requires a rebuild from backups
optionExplain: Stateful systems are designed to remember, so wrong data persists.
Hardware speed is not the argument, and error detection is not its point.
Stateless services can fail too; the difference is what a bug leaves behind.
They do restart; the problem is that the bad data stays in them.

questions.q: Tests pass at low load with no faults, and a team plans to ship on a weak isolation level. What does the chapter warn?
questions.explain: Often simple solutions appear to work correctly when concurrency is low and there are no faults, but turn out to have many subtle bugs in more demanding circumstances.
options: Simple solutions work at low concurrency without faults, then show subtle bugs
Weak isolation levels are always correct provided that tests pass at low concurrency
Weak isolation levels cannot be used with stateful systems at all
Tests are unnecessary because databases verify their own isolation guarantees
optionExplain: That is the author's observation.
Tests at low concurrency are exactly what can mislead.
The chapter says they are confusing, not unusable.
The chapter notes it is very difficult to determine whether it is safe at a level.

questions.q: A system that remembers things is called ____, and mistakes in it can have effects that last.
questions.explain: Stateful systems such as databases are designed to remember things, so wrong data persists.

questions.q: True or false: If an application uses a database whose claimed guarantees are accurate, the application is then guaranteed to use those guarantees correctly.
questions.explain: Even if infrastructure products were free from problems, application code would still need to use their features correctly, which is error-prone when configuration is hard to understand.
questions.rule: Correct products do not guarantee correct use.

questions.q: What did Kyle Kingsbury's Jepsen experiments highlight, according to the chapter?
questions.explain: Jepsen experiments have highlighted the stark discrepancies between some products' claimed safety guarantees and their actual behavior in the presence of network problems and crashes.
questions.teaches: Kyle Kingsbury's Jepsen experiments have highlighted stark discrepancies between some products' claimed safety guarantees and their actual behaviour in the presence of network problems and crashes.
options: That every database performs equally well when the network is partitioned
That weak isolation levels are safe to use whenever a product advertises them
Claimed guarantees that differ from behaviour under network problems and crashes
That stateless services are less reliable than databases under crashes
optionExplain: The finding was discrepancies, not equality.
The finding was that claims did not always hold.
That is the finding the author cites.
Not what the experiments showed.

questions.q: True or false: Serializability and atomic commit typically work only within a single datacenter.
questions.explain: This rules out geographically distributed architectures. The card next lists the costs.
questions.rule: Strong guarantees are tied to one site.

questions.q: What does the author say about applications that can tolerate occasional unpredictable corruption or loss?
questions.explain: If your application can tolerate occasionally corrupting or losing data in unpredictable ways, life is a lot simpler, and you might be able to get away with simply crossing your fingers.
options: They must still use serializable transactions, because corruption is never acceptable
Life is a lot simpler and they might get away with hoping for the best
They cannot exist, because every application depends on perfectly correct data
They should use atomic commit across datacenters to catch the rare cases
optionExplain: The author says they can avoid the machinery.
No strong machinery is needed.
The author grants such applications exist.
Atomic commit is what stronger assurance would require.

questions.q: A global chat service wants atomic commit for every message across datacenters on three continents. What limitation does the chapter point to?
questions.explain: Serializability and atomic commit typically only work in a single datacenter (ruling out geographically distributed architectures) and they limit the scale and fault-tolerance properties you can achieve.
options: Atomic commit cannot protect any data at all outside of one process
Serializability forbids more than one user per datacenter
Atomic commit requires that no message is ever sent twice
They typically work only in one datacenter, ruling out geographic distribution
optionExplain: Overstated; it works within a datacenter.
Unrelated to the limitation.
That is not the stated limitation.
Hence the cost for the global design.

questions.q: Serializability and atomic commit typically work only within a single ____.
questions.explain: That limits geographically distributed architectures.
questions.rule: Strong transactions are bound to one site.

questions.q: True or false: The author says the traditional transaction approach is going away and should be replaced entirely by dataflow methods.
questions.explain: He says it is not going away, but it is not the last word in making applications correct and resilient to faults.
questions.rule: Transactions stay, but are not the end.

questions.q: What does the author set out to do in the rest of this part of the chapter?
questions.explain: While the traditional transaction approach is not going away, the author will suggest some ways of thinking about correctness in the context of dataflow architectures.
questions.teaches: The author wants to suggest ways of thinking about correctness in the context of dataflow architectures, working toward a middle ground between distributed transactions and asynchronous log-based systems.
options: Prove that dataflow architectures always give weaker guarantees than transactions
Argue for dropping correctness goals in favour of performance
Suggest ways of thinking about correctness in the context of dataflow architectures
Argue that all applications should use atomic commit across datacenters
optionExplain: He argues for a middle ground, not a proof.
Opposite of his aim.
That is his stated aim.
Opposite of the point just made about cost.

questions.q: True or false: Serializable transactions protect against an application bug that deletes data from the database.
questions.explain: A transaction guarantees isolation of what the application asks for, not that the request is right. The card next explains.

questions.q: Why does the author favour immutable and append-only data in this context?
questions.explain: Because it is easier to recover from mistakes if you remove the ability of faulty code to destroy good data.
options: It is easier to recover from mistakes when faulty code cannot destroy good data
It makes the application free of bugs, since there is nothing left that code could break
It makes serializable transactions unnecessary for every kind of application
It makes reads faster than any mutable design for all workloads
optionExplain: Removing the ability to destroy data limits damage.
Immutability limits harm but does not prevent bugs.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
Not the stated reason.

questions.q: A deploy contains a bug that overwrites customer addresses with blanks. The database runs at the strictest isolation level. What happens?
questions.explain: If an application has a bug that causes it to write incorrect data, or delete data from a database, serializable transactions are not going to save you.
options: The database detects the bad writes and aborts them as violations of isolation
The transactions execute correctly and the blanks are stored, so isolation does not help
The database rolls back to the last good state on its own
The blanks are rejected because serializable transactions validate address formats
optionExplain: Isolation concerns concurrency, not the meaning of the data.
The database faithfully applies what the code asks for.
No such automatic repair exists.
Serializability does not validate content.

questions.q: Making data immutable and ____-only makes it easier to recover from faulty code.
questions.explain: Append-only data cannot be destroyed by a bug in the writer.

questions.q: True or false: With immutable, append-only storage, a team that ships a buggy writer can still recover the earlier good data.
questions.explain: The bad data adds new records but does not destroy old ones, so earlier state remains available for repair.

questions.q: The chapter says immutability is not a cure-all. What kind of problem does it introduce next?
questions.explain: Immutability is not a cure-all by itself, so the chapter looks next at a more subtle example of data corruption, using exactly-once execution of an operation.
questions.teaches: The author calls exactly-once execution a more subtle example of data corruption, which immutability alone does not prevent.
options: A shortage of disk space that always forces old data to be deleted
A loss of ordering among events in an append-only log
A requirement for every user to authenticate before reading
Processing the same operation twice
optionExplain: The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
It leads into exactly-once execution.

questions.q: True or false: Processing a message twice is a form of data corruption.
questions.explain: A customer charged twice or a counter incremented twice is wrong data. The card next explains how to avoid it.

questions.q: What does exactly-once mean in this chapter?
questions.explain: Exactly-once means arranging the computation such that the final effect is the same as if no faults had occurred, even if the operation actually was retried due to some fault.
questions.rule: Same effect as a fault-free run.
options: The final effect is the same as if no faults had occurred, even if the operation was retried
The message is delivered exactly one time to the processor even after failures
The operation is never retried, so no fault can cause a repeat
The message is dropped on failure so that it can never be processed twice
optionExplain: The definition concerns effect, not delivery.
Delivery count is not the definition.
Retrying is exactly what the arrangement allows.
That trades duplicates for data loss.

questions.q: A system credits loyalty points by adding 10 each time, and a retry could add them twice. Which change makes this safe?
questions.explain: Taking an operation that is not naturally idempotent and making it idempotent may need additional metadata such as the set of operation IDs that have updated a value.
options: Run the award in a faster thread so the retry arrives before the timeout
Remove the retry logic and accept that failed awards are lost
Encrypt the award message so it cannot be read twice
Record the id of each award and skip an award whose id was already applied
optionExplain: Speed cannot guarantee that no retry occurs.
Trading duplicates for lost data.
Encryption does not prevent a repeat.
Extra metadata (operation ids) turns an increment into an idempotent operation.

questions.q: Sort each operation by whether it is idempotent without extra work.
questions.explain: Setting a value or a flag has the same result however often it runs. Adding, appending and charging change the total each time, so they need operation ids or similar.
questions.rule: Setting is idempotent; adding is not.

items.t: Set the delivery address to a given value
Mark an order as shipped
Add 5 to a counter
Append a line to an invoice
Charge a card for 20 pounds

questions.q: True or false: When a node fails over to another, making an operation idempotent can still require fencing.
questions.explain: The chapter says you may need to ensure fencing when failing over from one node to another, so two nodes do not both act.

questions.q: A team plans to make a payment handler idempotent. Besides operation ids, what else does the chapter mention it may need?
questions.explain: Making a non-idempotent operation idempotent requires some effort and care: you may need to maintain additional metadata and ensure fencing when failing over from one node to another.
questions.teaches: Making a non-idempotent operation idempotent may require additional metadata and ensuring fencing when failing over from one node to another.
options: A faster network between the payment handler and the database
An additional copy of each payment kept on paper
Fencing when failing over from one node to another
A rule that only one payment may happen per day
optionExplain: The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
Named alongside operation ids.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.

questions.q: True or false: TCP suppresses duplicate packets even when the client opens a brand-new connection.
questions.explain: TCP duplicate suppression works only within the context of a single connection. The card next shows what that means for retries.

questions.q: What does a client not know when its connection times out right after sending COMMIT?
questions.explain: If the client suffers a network interruption and timeout after sending the COMMIT but before hearing back, it does not know whether the transaction has been committed or aborted.
questions.rule: A timeout leaves the outcome unknown.
options: Whether the database server is still running and reachable
Whether the transaction was committed or aborted
Which client sent the COMMIT statement to the database
Whether the SQL it sent was written correctly
optionExplain: It may suspect that, but the key unknown is the transaction outcome.
The outcome message may never have arrived.
The client knows what it sent.
Not the issue.

questions.q: A terminal adds 5 units to stock in a transaction. The link drops after COMMIT and the clerk reruns it. What is the risk?
questions.explain: The retry arrives outside the scope of TCP duplicate suppression, and an increment is not idempotent, so both runs can take effect.
questions.rule: Retry after timeout can double an increment.
options: The rerun is rejected automatically, because TCP remembers the first transaction across connections
The database rolls back the first transaction when the second one begins on a new connection
Stock rises by 5 only, because a transaction applied twice has the same effect as once
The rerun is not recognised as a duplicate, so stock may rise by 10 instead of 5
optionExplain: TCP's memory is per connection.
A committed transaction is not rolled back by a retry.
Only an idempotent operation has that property.
The new connection is outside duplicate suppression.

questions.q: TCP numbers packets with ____ numbers to put them in order and to detect loss and duplicates.
questions.explain: This works only within the context of a single TCP connection.

questions.q: Both runs of the script in the card commit. Account 7 starts at 100. What is its balance afterwards?
questions.explain: Nothing identifies the second run as a duplicate, so both commit and each adds 25.
questions.rule: A non-idempotent retry doubles the effect.
optionExplain: Correct only if the retry were suppressed as a duplicate, which nothing here does.
Each committed run adds 25, so two runs add 50.
Would hold if the second run cancelled the first, but both commit.
Would need three runs.

questions.q: True or false: A textbook calls this transfer a correct, standard example of atomicity, so a bank can use it as written. The chapter agrees.
questions.explain: The chapter says it is actually not correct, since a retried transfer could move twice the amount, and real banks do not work like this.
questions.rule: Atomic is not the same as idempotent.

questions.q: A mobile client sends a withdrawal of 50 and loses the connection before the reply. It reconnects and resends. Which risk applies?
questions.explain: Once the client reconnects and retries, the request is outside the scope of TCP duplicate suppression, so a non-idempotent operation could run twice.
questions.teaches: Two-phase commit protocols break the one-to-one mapping between a TCP connection and a transaction, since a coordinator must be able to reconnect to a database and tell it whether to commit or abort an in-doubt transaction.
options: The first connection's duplicate suppression silently drops the retried request
The database cannot accept the retry until the first one has timed out on the server
The reconnect makes the withdrawal idempotent because TCP numbers packets
The server may treat the retry as a separate request and withdraw twice
optionExplain: That works only within one connection.
No such rule exists.
TCP numbers packets, not requests across connections.
Duplicate suppression of the first connection does not cover the new one.

questions.q: True or false: If duplicates are suppressed between a database client and server, no duplicate request can reach the database.
questions.explain: A user can resubmit a form from the browser, which creates a new request and a new transaction. The card next explains.

questions.q: From the database's point of view, what is a user's manual retry of a form after a timeout?
questions.explain: From the web server's point of view the retry is a separate request, and from the database's point of view it is a separate transaction.
questions.rule: A retry looks like new work.
options: A separate transaction
A continuation of the first transaction
A duplicate packet to be dropped by TCP
A rollback of the first transaction
optionExplain: It has no link to the first attempt.
Nothing joins them.
It is a new request, not a repeated packet.
Nothing is rolled back.

questions.q: A checkout page errors after the connection drops mid-submit, and the user submits again. Which tool avoids the warning but not the duplicate?
questions.explain: The Post/Redirect/Get pattern avoids the warning message in normal operation, but it does not help if the POST request times out.
options: Two-phase commit, which stops all duplicates from the browser
TCP sequence numbers, which stop the browser resubmitting
Post/Redirect/Get, which does not help if the POST times out
Serializable isolation, which stops the same payment being made twice
optionExplain: It repairs only the database hop.
They work within one connection only.
It prevents the browser warning in normal operation only.
It does not identify a repeat as a duplicate.

questions.q: The Post/Redirect/Get pattern avoids the resubmit warning but does not help if the POST request times ____.
questions.explain: A timed-out POST leaves the user unsure whether it arrived, and a retry creates a separate request.

questions.q: True or false: Two-phase commit lets a coordinator resolve an in-doubt transaction but does not by itself stop a user's resubmission.
questions.explain: The chapter asks whether this is sufficient and answers no: the network between the user device and application server remains.

questions.q: Which statement best sums up the lesson of the browser retry example?
questions.explain: Even if we can suppress duplicate transactions between the database client and server, we still need to worry about the network between the end-user device and the application server.
questions.teaches: Web browsers warn Are you sure you want to submit this form again, and a user who wanted the operation to happen says yes, which turns a failed attempt into a second request.
options: Duplicates arise only inside the database, so the database should deduplicate
Duplicates are harmless, since users rarely retry a form
Duplicates can arise at any hop, so a solution must cover the whole path from user to database
Duplicates can be avoided by making the browser warning stricter
optionExplain: The example shows they arise before the database.
The example shows users do retry.
The usual deduplication mechanisms do not help here.
A warning does not identify a duplicate request.

questions.q: True or false: A uniqueness constraint on a request id in the database can stop a retried request from taking effect twice.
questions.explain: The second insert of the same id fails and aborts the transaction. The card next shows the whole design.

questions.q: Which two ways does the chapter suggest for creating an operation id on the client?
questions.explain: You could generate a unique identifier for an operation, such as a UUID, and include it as a hidden form field, or calculate a hash of all the relevant form fields to derive the operation ID.
options: A UUID in a hidden form field, or a hash of all the relevant form fields
The time of the click, or a counter kept on the application server
The user's password, or the IP address of the browser
The row number of the table, or the name of the database
optionExplain: Both make two submissions carry the same id.
Both change between retries.
Neither identifies one operation.
Neither exists before the operation reaches the database.

questions.q: Generate the operation id on the ____ and pass it all the way to the database.
questions.explain: Generating it at the client side means every retry of the same user action carries the same id.
questions.rule: The id starts at the client.
questions.teaches: The operation id should be generated at the client, such as in a hidden form field, and passed all the way through to the database, because the end-to-end flow of the request must be considered.

questions.q: An API client generates a new random id on every attempt of a call. What does that do to retry protection?
questions.explain: The request id must stay the same across attempts of one operation. A new id per attempt makes a retry indistinguishable from a new operation.
questions.rule: Reuse the id on every retry (our reading).
options: It strengthens it, since fresh ids make duplicates easier to spot
It does not matter, since the database deduplicates by amount
It matters only for read requests, since writes are always unique
It defeats it, since a retry looks like a different operation
optionExplain: Fresh ids make duplicates invisible.
The database deduplicates by id.
Writes are exactly where duplicates hurt.
The protection depends on the retry carrying the same id.

questions.q: A booking form must keep one id across a user's repeated submits. When should that id be generated?
questions.explain: An id created with the form and carried through each submit is the same for every retry of that operation.
questions.rule: Create the id once, at the client.
options: When the server receives each submit, so that every request gets a fresh id
When the form page is created, stored in a hidden field and sent with every submit
When the database commits, so that the id matches the stored row
When the user clicks the submit button, using the current time
optionExplain: A fresh id per request makes each look like a new operation.
Then every resubmit carries the same id.
Too late to protect against the duplicate.
Each click gives a different value.

questions.q: A payment with transfer id t-100 is submitted twice. The table has a UNIQUE constraint on that id. What does the second attempt do?
questions.explain: Example uses a uniqueness constraint: if a transaction attempts to insert an ID that already exists, the INSERT fails and the transaction is aborted.
questions.rule: Duplicate id: insert fails, no effect.
options: Both attempts commit and the balance changes twice
The second attempt silently overwrites the first row with new values
The second attempt waits until the first row is deleted
The insert fails and the transaction aborts, so the balance changes only once
optionExplain: That would happen without the constraint.
A unique constraint rejects rather than overwrites.
It does not wait; it fails.
The constraint stops the repeat.

questions.q: True or false: If a second attempt carrying the same transfer id reaches the database, the uniqueness constraint makes its insert fail.
questions.explain: The insert fails and the transaction aborts, so the operation does not take effect twice.

questions.q: A developer looks for an existing row with the transfer id and inserts one if none exists, with no uniqueness constraint. What is the flaw?
questions.explain: Relational databases can generally maintain a uniqueness constraint correctly, even at weak isolation levels, whereas an application-level check-then-insert may fail under nonserializable isolation.
questions.rule: Let the constraint do the checking.
options: The SELECT locks the whole table, so all other transfers wait
Under nonserializable isolation, two concurrent requests can both pass the check and both insert
The insert cannot store a text id, since only numbers can be unique
The check makes the operation idempotent only at the strictest isolation level, which no database offers
optionExplain: The flaw is a race, not a lock.
A check-then-insert may fail without serializability.
Text ids can be unique.
Serializable isolation exists; the issue is weak isolation.

questions.q: Besides blocking duplicates, what else can the table of transfer ids be seen as?
questions.explain: Besides suppressing duplicate requests, the requests table acts as a kind of event log, hinting in the direction of event sourcing.
questions.rule: A request table is an event log.
questions.teaches: Besides suppressing duplicate requests, the requests table acts as a kind of event log, hinting in the direction of event sourcing.
options: A second system of record that should replace the accounts table
A cache of balances that must be refreshed after every transfer
A lock table that serialises all transfers one at a time
A kind of event log, pointing toward event sourcing
optionExplain: It records requests, not balances.
It holds requests, not balances.
It is a record of requests, not a lock manager.
Each row records a request.

questions.q: True or false: According to the end-to-end argument, a communication system alone can completely implement duplicate suppression.
questions.explain: The argument says the function can be completely and correctly implemented only with the help of the endpoint applications. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Only the endpoints can finish the job.

questions.q: The end-to-end argument was articulated by Saltzer, Reed and Clark in ____.
questions.explain: It is a long-standing principle from networking and systems design.

questions.q: A team uses a stream processor that advertises exactly-once processing and still sees a customer charged twice after a browser retry. What explains this?
questions.explain: Some stream processors provide exactly-once semantics at the message processing level, but that is not enough to prevent a user from submitting a duplicate request if the first one times out.
questions.rule: Each layer's guarantee has a scope.
options: The stream processor must have a bug, since an exactly-once guarantee covers every duplicate
The guarantee covers message processing, not a duplicate request submitted by the user before it
Exactly-once only applies to reads, so charging needs a different technology
The customer's browser disabled TCP duplicate suppression for security
optionExplain: The guarantee has a defined scope; the retry happened outside it.
Lower layers cannot cover the whole path.
It applies to processing, not only reads.
Browsers do not do that, and TCP is not the layer at issue.

questions.q: Sort each mechanism by whether it alone can rule out a user's duplicate submission.
questions.explain: Each lower layer protects its own hop. Only an identifier carried across all the hops can identify the repeat.
questions.rule: Only an end-to-end id covers the whole path.
groups: Can, when passed end to end

items.t: TCP duplicate suppression
Database transactions
Stream processor exactly-once semantics
A transaction identifier from the client to the database

questions.q: True or false: An identifier passed from the client to the database lets a system recognise a duplicate that no single lower layer can.
questions.explain: This is the end-to-end solution the chapter describes.
questions.rule: Carry the identifier end to end.

questions.q: What does the authors' statement allow about an incomplete version of the function offered by the communication system?
questions.explain: The quoted argument adds that sometimes an incomplete version of the function provided by the communication system itself may be useful as a performance enhancement.
questions.rule: Lower layers help, but do not finish the job.
questions.teaches: Sometimes an incomplete version of the function provided by the communication system itself may be useful as a performance enhancement, even though it cannot complete the function.
options: It should be avoided because it weakens the end-to-end guarantee
It makes the end-to-end solution unnecessary once it is turned on
It may still be useful as a performance enhancement
It is the only practical way to implement the function in real systems
optionExplain: The authors say it may be useful.
They say the function cannot be completed there.
The statement says so in parentheses.
The function needs the endpoints.

questions.q: True or false: TLS between a client and a server protects against a compromise of the server itself.
questions.explain: TLS protects against network attackers but not against a compromised server. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Transport security stops at the endpoint.

questions.q: Which corruption can Ethernet, TCP and TLS checksums not detect?
questions.explain: Network checksums can detect corruption of packets in the network, but they cannot detect corruption due to bugs in the software at the sending and receiving ends, or corruption on the disks where the data is stored.
questions.rule: Network checksums cover the network only.
options: Bugs at the ends, or corruption on the disks
A bit flipped on the wire between two switches in the network
A packet lost completely while travelling across the network
A packet delivered twice by a misbehaving router
optionExplain: They check packets in transit only.
These checksums are designed for exactly that.
That is a loss, handled by retransmission, not a checksum failure.
A duplicate is handled by sequence numbers, not checksums.

questions.q: A photo service uploads files over TLS and stores them on disks. Years later some files are damaged on disk. What would have detected this?
questions.explain: If you want to catch all possible sources of data corruption, you also need end-to-end checksums.
questions.rule: Check at the endpoints and storage.
options: A checksum computed by the client or application and verified when the file is read back
The TLS checksum, which is verified again every time the file is served
The Ethernet checksum, which is stored with the file on disk
The TCP sequence numbers, which are recorded with each stored file
optionExplain: An end-to-end checksum covers the disks too.
TLS verifies packets in transit only.
Ethernet checksums are not kept with stored files.
They order packets, not stored data.

questions.q: Match each protection to what it does not defend against.
questions.explain: Each protects one segment. Only end-to-end encryption, authentication and checksums cover all segments.
pairs: Software bugs at the ends and corrupted disks

questions.q: True or false: Dropping low-level reliability features such as TCP's ordering would leave end-to-end correctness unaffected.
questions.explain: The chapter says HTTP requests would often get mangled without TCP putting packets in the right order. Low-level features reduce the probability of problems at higher levels.

questions.q: What does the home WiFi password example show about encryption?
questions.explain: The password on your home WiFi network protects against people snooping your WiFi traffic, but not against attackers elsewhere on the internet.
questions.teaches: Only end-to-end encryption and authentication can protect against both network attackers and compromises of the server, which hop-level protections such as WiFi passwords and TLS cannot.
options: It protects every message all the way to the final recipient on the internet
It protects against compromised servers because it is a strong password
It protects the local link but not against attackers elsewhere on the internet
It is unnecessary once TLS is used, because TLS makes the WiFi link private for good
optionExplain: It covers only the WiFi link.
Password strength is not the point.
Encryption at one hop does not cover the rest of the path.
TLS and WiFi encryption protect different segments.

questions.q: True or false: The author thinks transactions, which reduce many failures to commit or abort, are enough of an abstraction for fault tolerance.
questions.explain: He calls it a huge simplification but fears it is not enough. The card next sets out the reasons.
questions.rule: Commit-or-abort is not the whole answer.

questions.q: What does a transaction collapse a wide range of possible issues into?
questions.explain: Transactions take a wide range of possible issues (concurrent writes, constraint violations, crashes, network interruptions, disk failures) and collapse them down to two possible outcomes: commit or abort.
options: A single outcome: the write always succeeds
Two possible outcomes: commit or abort
Three outcomes: commit, abort or retry later
No outcome at all until the next checkpoint
optionExplain: Transactions can abort.
That simplification is its strength.
Only two are named.
A transaction has a definite outcome.

questions.q: The author thinks it is worth exploring fault-tolerance ____ that make it easy to provide application-specific end-to-end correctness properties.
questions.explain: He wants such abstractions to keep good performance and good operational characteristics at large scale.
questions.teaches: The author wants fault-tolerance abstractions that make it easy to provide application-specific end-to-end correctness properties while keeping good performance and operational characteristics in a large-scale distributed environment.

questions.q: A team avoids distributed transactions because they are costly and writes its own retry logic across three systems. How does the author view that choice?
questions.explain: When we refuse to use distributed transactions because they are too expensive, we end up having to reimplement fault-tolerance mechanisms in application code, and the author suspects most application-level mechanisms do not work correctly.
options: He is confident that hand-written retry logic will be correct, since teams know their own systems
He says it is fine, since lost data is always noticed and fixed within a day
He says it is wrong, because only distributed transactions can ever be correct
He suspects most such application-level mechanisms do not work correctly, risking lost or corrupted data
optionExplain: The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
He warns of lost or corrupted data.
He does not say that; he looks for better abstractions.
Reasoning about concurrency and partial failure is difficult and counterintuitive.

questions.q: True or false: As low-level mechanisms such as TCP improve, the remaining high-level faults become more common.
questions.explain: Low-level mechanisms work quite well, so the remaining higher-level faults occur fairly rarely.
questions.rule: Fewer low-level faults leave rarer high-level ones.

questions.q: Why does the author fear that application-level fault tolerance is often wrong?
questions.explain: As numerous examples throughout this book have shown, reasoning about concurrency and partial failure is difficult and counterintuitive, so he suspects that most application-level mechanisms do not work correctly.
questions.rule: Partial failure is hard to reason about.
options: Application developers do not have access to the source code of the databases
Modern hardware has become too unreliable for any software to cope
Concurrency and partial failure are hard to reason about and counterintuitive
Transactions are free of cost, so there is no excuse for avoiding them
optionExplain: Not his argument.
He says low-level mechanisms work quite well.
That is his stated reason.
He says they are expensive.
questions.teaches: Reasoning about concurrency and partial failure is difficult and counterintuitive, as numerous examples throughout the book have shown.

questions.q: True or false: Ensuring that a room has no overlapping bookings is a constraint similar to uniqueness.
questions.explain: Two bookings for the same slot conflict just as two users with one username do. The card next lists the family of constraints.

questions.q: Which of these is given as a uniqueness requirement?
questions.explain: A username or email must uniquely identify a user, a file storage service cannot have more than one file with the same name, and two people cannot book the same seat on a flight or in a theater.
options: Two people cannot book the same seat on a flight
An account balance cannot exceed a bank's total deposits
A file must be at most one gigabyte in size
A message must reach every subscriber within a second
optionExplain: A seat identifies one booking.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
Not a uniqueness requirement.

questions.q: A coworking space must stop two members booking one desk for the same hour. Which existing idea helps most?
questions.explain: Techniques that enforce uniqueness can often be used for constraints such as no overlapping bookings of a meeting room.
options: Rely on members to check the calendar first, since social checking is reliable
Treat the desk-and-hour pair as something that must be unique, using the same techniques
Allow all bookings and delete the older ones if two clash
Use a separate queue for each desk, with no uniqueness idea at all
optionExplain: Nothing in the chapter supports this.
Overlapping bookings are in the same family.
Silently deleting is a compensating step, not enforcement.
Ignores the common structure.

questions.q: Sort each requirement by whether the chapter lists it as a uniqueness constraint or as a similar constraint.
questions.explain: Names and seats are uniqueness. Balances, stock and overlaps are similar constraints that techniques for uniqueness can often serve.

items.t: A username must identify one user
No two files with the same name in a folder
One person per flight seat
Account balance never negative
Never sell more than the warehouse stock
No overlapping meeting room bookings

questions.q: True or false: A balance that must stay non-negative is a constraint that the same techniques as uniqueness can often handle.
questions.explain: The chapter lists it with stock levels and bookings as similar kinds of constraint.

questions.q: Why does the chapter focus on uniqueness constraints in the discussion of constraints?
questions.explain: In particular, the chapter focuses on uniqueness constraints, such as the one relied on for the request id, because techniques that enforce uniqueness can often be used for similar constraints.
questions.teaches: The uniqueness constraint relied on for the request id in the earlier example is one of several uniqueness requirements; others include usernames, file names and seat bookings.
options: Uniqueness is the only constraint databases are able to enforce
Uniqueness constraints never need coordination, which makes them easiest
Uniqueness constraints are specific to relational databases
The earlier request-id mechanism relied on one, and its techniques carry over
optionExplain: Other constraints exist.
The next idea shows they need consensus.
They appear in many kinds of systems.
It builds on the earlier example.

questions.q: True or false: Asynchronous multi-master replication is suitable for enforcing a uniqueness constraint.
questions.explain: Different masters might concurrently accept conflicting writes, breaking uniqueness. The card next explains.

questions.q: What is the most common way of reaching the consensus needed for uniqueness?
questions.explain: The most common way of achieving this consensus is to make a single node the leader, and put it in charge of making all the decisions.
options: Make a single node the leader and put it in charge of all the decisions
Let every node accept the first request it sees and reconcile differences later
Ask clients to retry until two nodes happen to agree on the same value
Store every request in a file and sort them once a day
optionExplain: A leader decides which conflicting operation is accepted.
That is the multi-master approach the chapter rules out.
Not a mechanism for deciding.
That is batch resolution, not immediate enforcement.

questions.q: A signup service has too many requests for one node to handle all username checks. What does the chapter propose?
questions.explain: Uniqueness checking can be scaled out by partitioning based on the value that needs to be unique. If you need usernames to be unique, partition by hash of username.
questions.rule: Partition on the value that must be unique.
options: Let each node accept names independently and merge lists nightly
Partition by signup time, so older requests are checked on a different node
Add a second leader for each region and let them both accept names
Partition by the hash of the username, so one partition decides each name
optionExplain: Independent acceptance breaks uniqueness.
Two requests for one name could land on different nodes.
Two deciders per value can both accept the same name.
Uniqueness checking scales out by partitioning on the unique value.

questions.q: Uniqueness checking can be scaled out by ____ based on the value that needs to be unique.
questions.explain: For usernames you would partition by the hash of the username.

questions.q: True or false: To reject a write that would violate a uniqueness constraint immediately, synchronous coordination is unavoidable.
questions.explain: The chapter says so, citing that asynchronous multi-master replication is ruled out.

questions.q: What is the drawback of the single-leader approach to uniqueness, according to the chapter?
questions.explain: That works fine as long as you don't mind funnelling all requests through a single node (even if the client is on the other side of the world), and as long as that node doesn't fail.
questions.rule: One decider is a bottleneck and a single point of failure.
questions.teaches: A single leader enforcing uniqueness means funnelling all requests through one node, even for a client on the other side of the world, and tolerating its failure brings back the consensus problem.
options: It cannot enforce uniqueness at all, because a leader sees only its own requests
It needs every client to be in the same datacenter as every other client
All requests funnel through one node, even for a distant client, and that node must not fail
It makes duplicates more likely, since a single node has to merge copies
optionExplain: The leader sees them all.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
Those are the two caveats given.
A single decider reduces duplicates.

questions.q: True or false: In the log-based username design, requests for the same username are appended to the same log partition.
questions.explain: Partitioning by the hash of the username puts conflicting requests in one ordered sequence. The card next gives the algorithm.

questions.q: Put the steps of claiming a username with a partitioned log in order.
questions.explain: The log fixes the order, one processor decides, and the client watches the output stream for the result.
questions.rule: Append, read in order, decide, answer.
items: The request is appended to the partition chosen by the hash of the username
A stream processor reads the requests in order
The processor checks its local database of taken names
The processor emits a success or rejection message
The client reads the answer from the output stream

questions.q: Two users request the same username almost at once. How does the log-based design decide?
questions.explain: Because the log is partitioned by username and the processor reads sequentially, it can decide unambiguously and deterministically which of several conflicting operations came first.
options: Both are accepted and the system later asks one user to pick another name
Accept the first request in the partition and reject the later one
Both are rejected, because a conflict cannot be resolved without a leader election
The user with the larger user id wins, because ids are compared first
optionExplain: That is a looser approach, not this design.
Sequential processing makes the decision unambiguous.
The processor decides without an election.
Order of arrival in the log decides.

questions.q: True or false: Adding more log partitions lets this design handle a higher throughput of username requests.
questions.explain: Each partition can be processed independently, so the design scales by increasing the number of partitions.

questions.q: What does the client in this design do after sending its request?
questions.explain: The client that requested the username watches the output stream and waits for a success or rejection message corresponding to its request.
questions.rule: Results come back on an output stream.
questions.teaches: The username algorithm is basically the same as implementing linearizable storage using total order broadcast, and it scales to a large request throughput by increasing the number of partitions.
options: It polls the log partition until its own request disappears
It watches an output stream for a success or rejection message matching its request
It waits for a database lock to be released by the stream processor
It assumes success unless the server closes the connection
optionExplain: Requests do not disappear.
That is how it learns the result.
No lock is involved.
It waits for an explicit answer.

questions.q: True or false: The log-based approach to uniqueness works only for uniqueness constraints and no other kind.
questions.explain: The chapter says it works for many other kinds of constraints. The card next states the principle.

questions.q: What is the fundamental principle of the approach?
questions.explain: Its fundamental principle is that any writes that may conflict are routed to the same partition and processed sequentially.
options: Writes that may conflict are applied everywhere at once with a distributed lock
Writes that may conflict are spread across all partitions to share load
Writes that may conflict are merged by the client before being sent
Writes that may conflict are routed to the same partition and processed sequentially
optionExplain: A lock is not the mechanism.
That separates them.
The processor decides, not the client.
That is the principle given.

questions.q: A booking system must prevent two guests from reserving the same room on overlapping nights. How should the booking requests be partitioned?
questions.explain: Conflicting writes (same room, overlapping dates) should be routed to the same partition and processed one after another.
questions.rule: Partition by the thing that conflicts.
options: By room, so all requests that could clash for a room reach the same partition
By guest, so each guest's requests are processed together
By arrival time, so the oldest requests are always on one partition
Randomly, so load is balanced and no partition becomes hot
optionExplain: Conflicting writes go to one partition.
Two guests competing for a room could reach different partitions.
Conflicts could be split across partitions.
Random placement separates conflicts.

questions.q: Any writes that may ____ are routed to the same partition and processed sequentially.
questions.explain: The definition of a conflict may depend on the application.
questions.rule: Conflicting writes meet in one partition.

questions.q: True or false: A colleague says the stream processor can only compare values for equality, so stock limits are out of reach. The chapter agrees.
questions.explain: The definition of a conflict may depend on the application, and the stream processor can use arbitrary logic to validate a request.

questions.q: Which earlier system does the chapter compare to this idea?
questions.explain: This idea is similar to the approach pioneered by Bayou in the 1990s.
questions.teaches: The idea of routing potentially conflicting writes to one place and validating them with application logic is similar to the approach pioneered by Bayou in the 1990s.
options: Dynamo, introduced in the 2000s
Paxos, proposed in the 1980s
Bayou, pioneered in the 1990s
Hadoop, released in the 2000s
optionExplain: Not named in this context.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
The chapter names it.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.

questions.q: True or false: Applying a transfer across three partitions with atomic commit forces it into a total order with other transactions on them.
questions.explain: That cross-partition coordination means partitions can no longer be processed independently, so throughput is likely to suffer. The card next shows an alternative.

questions.q: Put the stages of the transfer in order.
questions.explain: A single logged request is the starting point. Debit and credit instructions are derived from it, and the request id lets each final stage ignore repeats.
items: The client appends the request, with a unique id, to a log partition
A stream processor reads the request log
It emits a debit instruction and a credit instruction carrying the request id
Further processors deduplicate by request id and apply the changes

questions.q: A ticket resale site moves a ticket from seller to buyer and must not credit the buyer twice after a crash. What should it do?
questions.explain: Directly sending credit and debit instructions would need an atomic commit to ensure that either both or neither happen. Logging one request and deriving the rest avoids it.
options: Write the buyer's credit and the seller's debit directly from the client in separate calls
Lock the seller and buyer partitions until both updates are confirmed by the client
Log the transfer request with an id, derive two instructions from it and deduplicate by id
Apply the credit first and the debit later, trusting the debit to arrive eventually
optionExplain: A client sending both directly would need an atomic commit to be safe.
That is the coordination the pattern avoids.
Same structure as the money transfer.
A crash between them could leave one without the other.

questions.q: Match each partition key to what it keeps together.
questions.explain: Each stage is partitioned by the key that stage needs, so no single partition has to coordinate with the others.
questions.rule: Each stage has its own partition key.
pairs: The log of incoming transfer requests

questions.q: True or false: If the client sent credit and debit instructions directly to their partitions, atomic commit would be needed for both-or-neither.
questions.explain: That is why steps 1 and 2 exist: a single durably logged request replaces a multi-partition atomic write.
questions.rule: One logged message replaces a distributed atomic write.

questions.q: Why is it enough that the request either appears in the log or does not, without any multi-partition commit?
questions.explain: We first durably log the request as a single message, and then derive the credit and debit instructions from that first message. Single-object writes are atomic in almost all data systems.
questions.teaches: Single-object writes are atomic in almost all data systems, so a request logged as one message either appears in the log or does not, without any multi-partition atomic commit.
options: Single-object writes are atomic in almost all data systems
Logs never lose a message, so atomicity is guaranteed by hardware
Each partition independently decides whether to accept the request
Requests are replayed until they appear in all three partitions at once
optionExplain: Appending one message is such a write.
The point is the atomicity of a single write.
The request goes to one partition only.
That would need coordination.

questions.q: True or false: If the processor deriving debit and credit instructions crashes and resumes from a checkpoint, it may emit duplicate instructions.
questions.explain: It never skips a request but may repeat some. The card next shows why duplicates are harmless here.

questions.q: Why are duplicate debit and credit instructions harmless in this design?
questions.explain: Since the processor is deterministic, it will just produce the same instructions again, and the processors in step 3 can easily deduplicate them using the end-to-end request ID.
options: The database rejects any instruction that arrives more than once from any source
The client resends the request until it has seen two confirmations
Duplicates are applied twice, but the total is divided by two afterwards
The processor is deterministic and the next stage deduplicates by the request id
optionExplain: Rejection is done by the deduplicating stage using the id.
Not part of the design.
Nothing like that happens.
Both properties together make repeats safe.

questions.q: The chapter says the idea of several differently partitioned stages is similar to what was discussed under multi-____ data processing.
questions.explain: That earlier section treated queries across partitions as streams.
questions.teaches: The idea of using multiple differently partitioned stages is similar to what was discussed under multi-partition data processing, and to concurrency control in stream processing.

questions.q: A bank wants to ensure a payer cannot be overdrawn by a transfer. Where should the check be placed in the log-based design?
questions.explain: To ensure that the payer account is not overdrawn, you can have a stream processor, partitioned by payer account number, that maintains balances and validates transactions. Only valid transactions are then placed in the request log.
options: In the credit stage, after the money has already been taken from the payer
In a processor partitioned by payer account that keeps balances, before requests enter the log
In the client, using the balance it last saw on its own screen
In every payee partition, by asking the payer partition for its balance
optionExplain: Too late to stop the overdraft.
Only valid transactions enter the request log.
A stale balance is not a reliable check.
That adds the cross-partition coordination the design avoids.

questions.q: True or false: Without deduplication by request id in step 3, a crash and replay in step 2 could apply a transfer twice.
questions.explain: The request id is what turns the repeated instructions into a single effect.
questions.rule: The request id makes replay safe.

questions.q: What has this design achieved compared with a traditional atomic commit across three partitions?
questions.explain: By breaking down the multi-partition transaction into two differently partitioned stages and using the end-to-end request ID, we have achieved the same correctness property even in the presence of faults, and without using an atomic commit protocol.
options: Weaker correctness but better speed, since some transfers may be applied only to one account
The same speed but weaker durability, since the log may lose some requests
Stronger correctness because the log can undo any transfer afterwards
The same correctness, that every request is applied exactly once to both accounts, without an atomic commit protocol
optionExplain: The design keeps the same property.
Requests are durably logged.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
That is the stated result.
questions.teaches: By breaking down the multi-partition transaction into two differently partitioned stages and using the end-to-end request ID, the same correctness property is achieved even in the presence of faults, and without an atomic commit protocol.

questions.q: True or false: A stale read caused by replication lag is a violation of integrity.
questions.explain: It is a violation of timeliness, and it resolves by waiting and trying again. The card next defines both.
questions.rule: Stale is timeliness, corrupt is integrity.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
questions.explain: Timeliness is about freshness and can be repaired by waiting. Integrity is about correctness and needs explicit repair.
pairs: Users observe the system in an up-to-date state
No data loss, and no contradictory or false data

questions.q: A search index is missing some documents that are in the database for good, because a bug skipped them. Which property is violated?
questions.explain: A derived view must correctly reflect the underlying data. An index in which some records are missing is not very useful, and waiting will not repair it.
questions.rule: Permanent mismatch is an integrity violation.
options: Timeliness, since the index is behind the database
Integrity, since waiting will not fix an index that misrepresents the data
Neither, since the index is only a derived copy of the data
Both equally, since every inconsistency is a mix of the two
optionExplain: It would be timeliness only if it caught up by itself.
A permanent mismatch with the source is an integrity failure.
A derived dataset must be correct.
Their causes and repair differ.

questions.q: Sort each situation by which property is violated.
questions.explain: Lagging but later correct data breaks timeliness. Lost or contradictory data that persists breaks integrity.

items.t: A user reads stale data from a lagging replica
A credit card statement lacks yesterday's purchase for now
A payment is charged but never paid to the merchant
An index silently lacks some records

questions.q: True or false: Waiting and trying again will fix a violation of integrity in most cases.
questions.explain: It will not fix database corruption in most cases. Explicit checking and repair is needed.

questions.q: Which sense of consistency does the CAP theorem use, according to the chapter?
questions.explain: The CAP theorem uses consistency in the sense of linearizability, which is a strong way of achieving timeliness. In ACID, consistency is usually understood as some kind of application-specific notion of integrity.
questions.teaches: The CAP theorem uses consistency to mean linearizability, a strong way of achieving timeliness, whereas consistency in ACID is usually understood as application-specific integrity, with atomicity and durability as tools for preserving it.
options: Application-specific integrity, which is what ACID consistency means
Eventual convergence of replicas after writes stop
Linearizability, which is a strong way of achieving timeliness
Absence of corruption on disk
optionExplain: That is the ACID sense.
A weaker idea than linearizability.
That is the sense used.
Integrity, not the CAP sense.

questions.q: True or false: On a credit card statement, a purchase made in the last 24 hours not yet appearing is a serious integrity failure.
questions.explain: That is a normal lag, a timeliness issue. The card next gives the failures that would be integrity problems.
questions.rule: Lag is tolerable; wrong sums are not.

questions.q: Which statement does the author make about the relative importance of the two properties?
questions.explain: I am going to assert that in most applications, integrity is much more important than timeliness. Violations of timeliness can be annoying and confusing, but violations of integrity can be catastrophic.
options: In most applications integrity is much more important than timeliness
Timeliness matters more, since users notice stale data before any corruption
They are equally important in every application
Neither matters once transactions are used
optionExplain: He asserts this.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
He singles out integrity.
Both matter; transactions provide them together.

questions.q: Which problem on a bank statement would the author treat as the more serious?
questions.explain: It would be very bad if a transaction was charged to you but not paid to the merchant (disappearing money). Such problems would be violations of the integrity of the system.
options: A charge that was taken from the customer but never paid to the merchant
A purchase from this morning that has not yet appeared
A pending transaction shown in a different order than it happened
A balance that updates a few minutes late after a deposit
optionExplain: Disappearing money is an integrity failure.
Normal lag; a timeliness issue.
Annoying but not corruption.
A timeliness delay.

questions.q: Violations of integrity can be catastrophic, whereas violations of timeliness are annoying and ____.
questions.explain: The author says violations of timeliness can be annoying and confusing.
questions.rule: Timeliness failures annoy; integrity failures wreck.

questions.q: True or false: A banking system that reconciles transactions asynchronously, with some lag, can still be considered sound if integrity is preserved.
questions.explain: Banks reconcile and settle asynchronously, and timeliness is not very important there.
questions.rule: Lag is fine when integrity holds.
