questions.q: Why does the author find it normal that a recent transaction is missing from a statement?
questions.explain: On your credit card statement, it is not surprising if a transaction that you made within the last 24 hours does not yet appear. We know that banks reconcile and settle transactions asynchronously.
questions.teaches: Banks reconcile and settle transactions asynchronously, so timeliness is not very important on a credit card statement, though the statement must still sum correctly.
options: Banks never process transactions on the same day they happen
Statements are produced by a different system that has no access to recent data
Banks reconcile and settle transactions asynchronously, so a certain lag is expected
Customers prefer to see purchases only after they have been double checked
optionExplain: He speaks of a certain lag, not a fixed delay.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
That is the stated reason.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.

questions.q: True or false: In a log-based design, a sender does not wait for consumers to process its message.
questions.explain: Consumers of a log are asynchronous by design. The card next explains how a client can still wait for an outcome.

questions.q: What does waiting on the output stream achieve in the username example?
questions.explain: The waiting only has the purpose of synchronously informing the sender whether or not the uniqueness check succeeded, but this notification can be decoupled from the effects of processing the message.
questions.rule: Waiting informs; it does not enforce.
options: It makes the uniqueness check itself correct
It synchronously tells the sender whether the uniqueness check succeeded
It delays the processor until the client has acknowledged the result
It locks the username so no other client can see it
optionExplain: The check is correct whether or not anyone waits.
That is the only purpose of waiting.
The processor does not wait for the client.
No lock is involved.

questions.q: A signup page shows a rejection only after the stream processor replies. If the user closes the tab first, what happens to the claim?
questions.explain: The correctness of the uniqueness check does not depend on whether the sender of the message waits for the outcome.
options: The claim is cancelled, since a request is only valid while the client is waiting
The name is held in limbo until the user comes back and confirms
The processor stops, since it cannot proceed without a connected client
The check still runs and the name is claimed or rejected, as correctness does not depend on the user waiting
optionExplain: Waiting is not part of validity.
No such confirmation exists in the design.
It does not depend on the client.
The enforcement is independent of the waiting.

questions.q: The notification of the outcome can be ____ from the effects of processing the message.
questions.explain: The check is enforced asynchronously whether or not the sender waits for the reply.
questions.rule: Decouple the answer from the enforcement.

questions.q: True or false: Transactions are typically linearizable, so a writer waits until commit and afterwards its writes are visible to all readers.
questions.explain: This is a convenient property of transactions that unbundled stages do not provide by default.

questions.q: How does the author reconcile asynchronous consumers with a client that needs an answer?
questions.explain: It is possible for a client to wait for a message to appear on an output stream. This is what was done in the uniqueness example.
questions.teaches: Because consumers of a log are asynchronous by design, a client that needs an answer can wait for a message to appear on an output stream, which is how the username example informs the sender.
options: The client polls every partition of the log until it finds its request
The consumer blocks until the client sends an acknowledgement
The client can wait for a message to appear on an output stream
The client uses a distributed transaction that spans the consumers
optionExplain: Not the mechanism described.
Consumers do not block on clients.
That is what the username example does.
Avoids the coordination the design is built to avoid.

questions.q: True or false: ACID transactions usually provide both timeliness and integrity guarantees.
questions.explain: For example linearizability for timeliness and atomic commit for integrity. The card next shows how dataflow systems differ.

questions.q: What is central to streaming systems, according to the chapter?
questions.explain: When processing event streams asynchronously, there is no guarantee of timeliness, unless you explicitly build consumers that wait for a message to arrive before returning. But integrity is in fact central to streaming systems.
options: Integrity, since there is no timeliness guarantee unless consumers are built to wait
Timeliness, since streams are always up to date for every reader
Linearizability, since logs order every event globally
Atomic commit, since stream processors rely on it for every operation
optionExplain: Integrity is central; timeliness is optional.
Streams are asynchronous, so not by default.
Linearizability is a transaction property, not provided by default.
The point is to avoid it.

questions.q: A team's pipeline sometimes loses an event and sometimes applies one twice. Which property is at risk?
questions.explain: If an event is lost, or if an event takes effect twice, the integrity of a data system could be violated.
options: Timeliness, because events arrive later than users would like
Integrity, because a lost or doubled event can corrupt data
Linearizability, because users read stale values
Availability, because the pipeline stops accepting new events
optionExplain: Delay is a timeliness issue; loss and duplication are integrity.
That is the risk the chapter names.
Staleness is timeliness.
The scenario is about wrong data, not availability.

questions.q: Exactly-once or effectively-once semantics is a mechanism for preserving ____.
questions.explain: A lost event or an event taking effect twice could violate integrity.

questions.q: True or false: Fault-tolerant message delivery and duplicate suppression are important for maintaining integrity in the face of faults.
questions.explain: That is why exactly-once or effectively-once semantics is called a mechanism for preserving integrity.

questions.q: Which statement about stream processing and timeliness is accurate?
questions.explain: When processing event streams asynchronously, there is no guarantee of timeliness, unless you explicitly build consumers that wait for a message to arrive before returning.
questions.teaches: Exactly-once or effectively-once semantics is a mechanism for preserving integrity, and reliable stream processing can preserve integrity without distributed transactions and atomic commit.
options: Stream processing is linearizable by default, so every read sees the latest write
Stream processing cannot be made timely by any technique
Stream processing guarantees timeliness but not integrity
There is no timeliness guarantee unless you explicitly build consumers that wait for a message
optionExplain: That is not the case.
Consumers that wait can provide it.
The reverse emphasis holds.
That is the chapter's wording.

questions.q: True or false: Reliable stream processing can preserve integrity without distributed transactions and atomic commit.
questions.explain: It does so through a combination of mechanisms. The card next lists them.
questions.rule: Integrity without atomic commit is possible.

questions.q: Put these mechanisms in the order the chapter lists them.
questions.explain: The chapter lists the single message, the deterministic derivation, the request id and finally immutability with reprocessing.
questions.rule: Single message, derivation, request id, immutability.
items: Represent the write as a single message
Derive other state updates deterministically from that message
Pass a client-generated request id through all levels
Make messages immutable and allow reprocessing

questions.q: A team's pipeline writes a purchase to three tables in one go and then retries after a failure. Which mechanism would make the write safer?
questions.explain: Representing the content of the write operation as a single message can easily be written atomically, and all other state updates are derived from it deterministically.
options: Write one purchase message and derive the table updates from it deterministically
Write to the three tables in parallel and compare them afterwards
Lock all three tables until a human checks the result
Retry the whole write until it succeeds on all three tables at once
optionExplain: That is mechanism one with mechanism two.
Comparing afterwards does not preserve integrity during the write.
Not one of the mechanisms.
Retrying a non-idempotent write can duplicate it.

questions.q: Match each mechanism to the problem it addresses.
questions.explain: Each mechanism addresses one failure mode: partial writes, non-reproducible derivations, duplicates and unrecoverable bugs.
pairs: Writing several places can be left half-done
Recovering from a bug in processing code

questions.q: True or false: If a bug is found in the derivation code, immutable messages let the derived data be reprocessed after the fix.
questions.explain: Making messages immutable and allowing derived data to be reprocessed makes it easier to recover from bugs.

questions.q: Which comparison with older techniques does the chapter draw for the deterministic derivation functions?
questions.explain: Deriving all other state updates from that single message using deterministic derivation functions is similar to stored procedures.
questions.teaches: Deterministic derivation functions applied to a single message are similar to stored procedures, which also relate to actual serial execution.
options: They are similar to two-phase commit coordinators
They are similar to leader election protocols
They are similar to quorum reads
They are similar to stored procedures
optionExplain: The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
The chapter makes this comparison.

questions.q: True or false: Many airlines deliberately violate the one-person-per-seat constraint by overbooking.
questions.explain: They expect some passengers to miss flights and have compensation processes ready. The card next lists more examples.

questions.q: What is a change that corrects a mistake, such as apologising and asking a user to choose another username, called?
questions.explain: This kind of change to correct a mistake is called a compensating transaction.
options: A distributed transaction
A materialized view
A compensating transaction
A total order broadcast
optionExplain: That spans several systems.
That is a precomputed query result.
The chapter uses this name.
That orders events.

questions.q: A small shop sells 12 items online when it has only 10 in stock. Following the chapter, how can it handle this?
questions.explain: If customers order more items than you have in your warehouse, you can order in more stock, apologize to customers for the delay and offer them a discount.
options: Cancel every order of that item and refund all customers immediately
Order more stock, apologise for the delay and perhaps offer a discount
Stop selling online altogether, since stock limits cannot be enforced
Ask customers to choose which of them gets the item by themselves
optionExplain: More drastic than the chapter's approach.
The same process is needed if a forklift damages stock.
The chapter shows the limit can be handled loosely.
Not the described process.

questions.q: Sending an apology and asking the person to choose another name is called a ____ transaction.
questions.explain: A change that corrects a mistake is called a compensating transaction.

questions.q: True or false: A bank that lets an account be overdrawn has no way to limit its risk. The chapter agrees.
questions.explain: It can charge an overdraft fee, ask for repayment, and limit total withdrawals per day, which bounds the risk to the bank.

questions.q: Why does the chapter say the apology workflow for oversold stock is not new work?
questions.explain: This is the same as what you would have to do if, say, a forklift truck ran over some of the items in your warehouse, so the apology workflow already needs to be part of your business processes.
questions.teaches: The apology workflow for oversold stock is the same one needed if a forklift truck ran over some of the items in the warehouse, so it is already part of the business process and a linearizable stock constraint may be unnecessary.
options: Customers expect to receive apologies from every online shop
It matches what you do when a forklift ruins stock, so the process exists
Apologies are required by law for every order delay
Stock is never oversold in practice, so no workflow is needed
optionExplain: Not the reason.
Same recovery process for a different cause.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
It is oversold in the example.

questions.q: True or false: Whether the cost of an apology is acceptable is a business decision, according to the author.
questions.explain: If the apology is affordable, strict pre-checking may be unnecessarily restrictive. The card next explains.

questions.q: What does the author say about checking all constraints before writing when apologies are affordable?
questions.explain: If the cost of the apology is acceptable, the traditional model of checking all constraints before even writing the data is unnecessarily restrictive, and a linearizable constraint is not needed.
options: It is essential, because any temporary violation can destroy integrity
It is impossible, because writes cannot be validated before they are stored
It is required only for relational databases
It is unnecessarily restrictive, and a linearizable constraint is not needed
optionExplain: He says integrity is kept, and timeliness of enforcement is relaxed.
Validation before the write is possible; it is just not required here.
Not his distinction.
He draws that conclusion.

questions.q: Sort each action by whether an after-the-fact fix is possible, according to the chapter.
questions.explain: A refund, a follow-up email or an apology fixes many mistakes. Cash already paid out cannot be directly recovered, and an email cannot be unsent.
questions.rule: Check first before the costly-to-reverse step.
groups: Hard or impossible to take back

items.t: A customer charged twice by mistake
An email with a wrong detail
A seat sold twice
Cash paid out by an ATM
A message that has been sent and read

questions.q: True or false: A system that writes optimistically and checks afterwards should still validate before doing something expensive to recover from.
questions.explain: Validation before costly actions is not ruled out. You need not validate before writing the data.

questions.q: What do loosely checked applications still require?
questions.explain: These applications do require integrity: you would not want to lose a reservation or have money disappear due to mismatched credits and debits. But they don't require timeliness on the enforcement of the constraint.
questions.teaches: Checking a constraint after the fact is similar to the conflict resolution approaches discussed under handling write conflicts.
options: Integrity, such as not losing a reservation or having money vanish
Timeliness of enforcement, since stale checks lead to violations
Linearizable constraints on every item
Synchronous coordination for all writes
optionExplain: They need integrity but not timeliness of enforcement.
That is what they can relax.
Not needed.
That is what they avoid.

questions.q: True or false: A coordination-avoiding system could run in several datacenters in a multi-leader setup, replicating asynchronously.
questions.explain: Each datacenter can keep operating independently. The card next explains the integrity it still keeps.

questions.q: What kind of guarantees does such a system have?
questions.explain: Such a system would have weak timeliness guarantees, since it could not be linearizable without introducing coordination, but it can still have strong integrity guarantees.
options: Strong timeliness but weak integrity
Strong timeliness and strong integrity
Weak timeliness but strong integrity
Weak timeliness and weak integrity
optionExplain: The reverse.
Strong timeliness would need coordination.
It cannot be linearizable without coordination, but it can preserve integrity.
Integrity remains strong.

questions.q: An online marketplace runs in three regions and wants each to keep working during a link failure between regions. Which design fits?
questions.explain: Any one datacenter can continue operating independently from the others, because no synchronous cross-region coordination is required.
options: Use a distributed transaction across all regions for every sale
Send all writes to a single region and make the others read-only
Replicate asynchronously, apologise for rare conflicts and keep integrity
Block writes in a region whenever it cannot reach the others
optionExplain: Needs coordination and halts during failures.
Does not let each region operate independently.
Coordination-avoiding design.
Gives up availability.

questions.q: Match each coordination choice to its cost.
questions.explain: More coordination reduces apologies for inconsistencies but increases apologies for outages. You look for the sweet spot.
pairs: More availability problems and slower operation
Neither too many inconsistencies nor too many availability problems

questions.q: True or false: In a coordination-avoiding system, serializable transactions can no longer be used anywhere.
questions.explain: They remain useful for maintaining derived state, run at a small scope where they work well. Heterogeneous XA transactions are not required.
questions.rule: Transactions at small scope still help.

questions.q: How does the chapter describe the number of apologies you can achieve?
questions.explain: Coordination and constraints reduce the number of apologies due to inconsistencies, but also reduce performance and availability, and so increase the number of apologies due to outages. You cannot reduce the number of apologies to zero, but you can find the best trade-off.
questions.teaches: Coordination and constraints reduce the apologies due to inconsistencies but reduce performance and availability, increasing the apologies due to outages, so you look for the sweet spot with neither too many inconsistencies nor too many availability problems.
options: Not to zero, but to the best trade-off between inconsistency and unavailability
It can be reduced to zero by adding enough coordination
It does not matter, since apologies cost nothing
It is minimised by never using coordination at all
optionExplain: That is the sweet spot idea.
Coordination causes outage apologies.
Costs vary, as seen earlier.
Too many inconsistencies result.

questions.q: True or false: A traditional system model treats each fault as either possible or impossible, rather than as more or less likely.
questions.explain: The binary approach is convenient, but the card explains that reality is a matter of probabilities.

questions.q: In reality, whether a fault needs attention is more a question of ____ than a yes-or-no assumption.
questions.explain: Some faults are more likely and others less likely, and the question is whether they happen often enough to be met in practice.

questions.q: A team assumes memory is not corrupted, but its app runs on millions of phones. What fits the pattern?
questions.explain: The pattern is to weigh how often a violation happens. At fleet scale, rare faults do occur and deserve some attention.
options: Keep the assumption, because bit-flips are rare on modern hardware and the model stays simpler
Replace all phones with servers that use only error-correcting memory in every data centre
Disable all caching so that no value stays in memory for long enough to be corrupted
Treat bit-flips as rare but possible and plan some checking
optionExplain: Rarity lowers the odds but a large fleet still meets them.
That is a drastic hardware change the card does not suggest.
Memory is still used while processing, so this removes nothing.
Rare is not impossible, and scale makes rare events occur.

questions.q: Sort each assumption by whether the card's example system model allows it to happen.
questions.explain: The model lets crashes, power loss and network delay or loss happen, while assuming durable fsync, intact memory and a correct CPU.
questions.rule: Models split faults into can and cannot.

items.t: A process crashes
The network drops a message
A machine loses power suddenly
Data written after fsync is not lost
Data in memory is not corrupted
The CPU multiplication instruction returns the right result

questions.q: True or false: Because random bit-flips are rare on modern hardware, they can be treated as beyond the realm of possibility.
questions.explain: They are rare but not impossible, so they deserve some attention.

questions.q: What makes very unlikely faults show up in a real product, according to the author?
questions.explain: Some crash reports could only be explained by random bit-flips in device memory, which shows that with enough devices very unlikely events happen.
questions.teaches: If you have enough devices running your software, even very unlikely things do happen.
options: Unlikely faults become more probable the longer the same software stays unchanged in production
With enough devices running the software, even very unlikely things happen
Hardware makers hide the true failure rates, so the published figures are unreliable
Crash reports are written by clients, so they exaggerate how often memory is corrupted
optionExplain: Age is not the reason given.
Large numbers make rare events routine.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
The reports could only be explained by bit-flips.

questions.q: True or false: A network or filesystem checksum will detect data corruption caused by a bug in the database software.
questions.explain: Checksums catch low-level damage, but a bug produces wrong data that is correctly checksummed afterwards.
questions.rule: Checksums do not catch logic bugs.

questions.q: ACID consistency only makes sense if the transaction is free from ____.
questions.explain: If the application uses the database incorrectly, the integrity of the database cannot be guaranteed.

questions.q: An app stores orders but declares no foreign key or uniqueness constraint, relying on its own code. What is the risk?
questions.explain: Constraints are the database's way of preserving integrity; skipping them lets application bugs corrupt data unnoticed.
questions.rule: Declare the constraints you rely on.
options: The database will automatically add the missing constraints once it notices repeated mistakes
Storage checksums will detect the invalid rows, because they compare every row to its replicas
Nothing, because ACID consistency guarantees that the data always matches the business rules
Bugs in the app can write bad rows the database would have rejected
optionExplain: Databases do not infer constraints from usage patterns.
Checksums see bytes, not business rules.
Consistency depends on the application using the database correctly.
The database cannot reject what it was never told about.

questions.q: Match each integrity problem to where the card places it.
questions.explain: The author saw MySQL fail on a uniqueness constraint and PostgreSQL show write skew, and notes that many applications do not use constraints at all.

questions.q: True or false: Application code needs more attention to bugs than database code because it usually receives much less review and testing.
questions.explain: Most applications do not receive anywhere near the review and testing that database code does.

questions.q: What does the author conclude about the period between a bug appearing and being fixed?
questions.explain: Bugs are rare and eventually found and fixed, but there is still a period during which they can corrupt data.
questions.rule: A bug's window can still corrupt data.
questions.teaches: Although bugs are rare and they eventually get found and fixed, there is still a period during which such bugs can corrupt data.
options: Fixed bugs leave no trace, so data written earlier can be trusted once the fix ships
Even rare, eventually fixed bugs can corrupt data during that window
Mature databases are free of such windows because years of testing remove every bug
Only less mature storage technology is affected, so established databases need no checks
optionExplain: Corrupted data stays corrupted after the code is repaired.
The harm happens before the fix.
Even battle-tested databases are cited as having bugs.
The author's examples come from well-regarded databases.

questions.q: True or false: Checking the integrity of data is known as auditing.
questions.explain: The card uses auditing for exactly this activity.

questions.q: HDFS and Amazon S3 run background processes that read back files and ____ them to other replicas.
questions.explain: This catches silent corruption on one disk.

questions.q: A company has taken nightly backups for years without restoring one. What does the pattern advise?
questions.explain: Otherwise you may only find out that a backup is broken when it is too late and data has been lost.
options: Add a second backup system, since two untested copies are twice as likely to work
Compare the backup file sizes each night, which confirms the contents are intact
Restore from a backup now and then to prove it works
Keep trusting the backups, because a broken backup would have raised an error at write time
optionExplain: More untested copies do not prove that any works.
Equal size says little about the content.
An untested backup may be broken.
Silent corruption raises no error.

questions.q: Put the auditing loop of a large storage system in order.
questions.explain: The loop reads, compares, detects and repairs, which is how corruption is found sooner rather than later.
items: A background process reads back a stored file
It compares the file with its other replicas
A mismatch reveals silent corruption
The system repairs the file or moves it from the bad disk

questions.q: True or false: If a storage system does not read back its data, silent corruption on a disk would be noticed quickly.
questions.explain: You have to actually read data and check it to know it is still there.

questions.q: What reason does the author give for auditability being highly important in finance?
questions.explain: Auditing is not just for financial applications, but it is highly important in finance because everyone recognises the need to detect and fix problems.
questions.teaches: Auditability is highly important in finance precisely because everyone knows that mistakes happen, and we all recognize the need to be able to detect and fix problems.
options: Mistakes happen, and we need to be able to detect and fix them
Financial regulators require every company to run HDFS or S3 for storing their ledgers
Financial data is the only kind that can be corrupted by hardware or software faults
Banks cannot afford any storage lag, so audits must complete before each transaction commits
optionExplain: Mistakes are expected, so detection matters.
No such rule is mentioned.
Auditing is not just for financial applications.
Timeliness of audits is not the stated reason.

questions.q: True or false: The author hopes future systems will check their own integrity continually instead of relying on blind trust.
questions.explain: He hopes for more self-validating or self-auditing systems.

questions.q: The author describes the approach of continually auditing yourself as trust, but ____.
questions.explain: Trusting is reasonable, as long as verification backs it up.

questions.q: A team moves from a mature SQL database to a weaker-consistency store, but keeps its old, check-free habits. What does the author say?
questions.explain: Audit mechanisms had not been developed, yet applications kept relying on blind trust even as the technology got riskier.
options: The blind trust is now more dangerous and checks are needed
Nothing changes, because the application code decides integrity, not the store underneath
The team is safe if the new store is popular, since many users would have found problems
Audits become unnecessary, because weaker guarantees mean the team already expects errors
optionExplain: The technology guarantees less, so trust is riskier.
The store's guarantees matter to how much can go wrong.
Popularity does not replace verification.
Expecting errors without checking for them leaves them unnoticed.

questions.q: The author hopes for self-validating or ____ systems that continually check their own integrity.
questions.explain: Such systems would not rely on blind trust.

questions.q: True or false: Under the author's argument, a strong transaction mechanism by itself makes auditing unnecessary.
questions.explain: Blindly trusting a transaction mechanism is exactly the attitude the author criticises.
questions.rule: Do not rest on one mechanism.

questions.q: Why were audit mechanisms not seen as worth the investment in the ACID era?
questions.explain: Because the trusted technology worked well enough most of the time, nobody thought auditing mechanisms were worth building.
questions.teaches: Since the technology we trusted worked well enough most of the time, auditing mechanisms were not deemed worth the investment.
options: Auditing was too expensive to run on the disks and networks available at the time
ACID transactions provided a built-in audit trail that already satisfied every regulator
The technology worked well enough most of the time
Developers believed failures to be so frequent that checking could not keep up with them
optionExplain: Cost of hardware is not given as the reason.
No such audit trail is claimed.
Success bred complacency.
The belief was the opposite: failures seemed rare.

questions.q: True or false: A transaction log of inserts, updates and deletes shows why the application made those changes.
questions.explain: The log shows the mutations, but the application logic that decided on them is transient and cannot be reproduced.

questions.q: In event sourcing, user input is represented as a single ____ event.
questions.explain: State updates are derived from that event, which is never changed.

questions.q: An auditor suspects a materialised view is wrong. In an event-sourced system, how can she check it?
questions.explain: For derived state, we can rerun the processors that derived it from the event log and check whether we get the same result.
options: Read the view again several times to see whether the values change between reads
Rerun the derivation on the event log and compare the result
Ask the developers which tables the original transaction touched when it ran
Delete the view and trust the next write to correct whatever was wrong in it
optionExplain: Repeated reads do not test correctness against the source.
Deterministic derivation reproduces the expected state.
That is the unclear picture the card describes.
Deleting hides the evidence rather than checking it.

questions.q: Sort each check by what it verifies in an event-sourced system.
questions.explain: Hashes guard the event storage, whereas rerunning or duplicating the processors checks the derived state.
questions.rule: Hash the log, rederive the state.

items.t: Compare hashes of stored events
Rerun the stream processors and compare outputs
Run a redundant derivation in parallel
Detect that event storage was corrupted

questions.q: True or false: If the derivation code is not deterministic, rerunning it on the same event log is a reliable way to check derived state.
questions.explain: Checking by rederivation relies on getting the same result from the same log and the same code version.

questions.q: What diagnostic ability does a deterministic, well-defined dataflow give beyond integrity checks?
questions.explain: It is valuable to reproduce the exact circumstances that led to an unexpected event, a kind of time-travel debugging capability.
questions.teaches: It is valuable to have the diagnostic capability to reproduce the exact circumstances that led to the unexpected event, a kind of time-travel debugging capability.
options: Predicting every future bug before it occurs, by analysing the event log statistically
Removing the need for logs, since state can be reconstructed from the final tables alone
Making all processing synchronous so that errors are reported to the user at once
Reproducing the exact circumstances of an unexpected event, like time travel
optionExplain: Nothing about prediction is claimed.
The log is what makes replay possible.
Determinism is not about synchrony.
The same inputs replay the same behaviour.

questions.q: True or false: The more systems an integrity check covers, the fewer chances corruption has to go unnoticed.
questions.explain: A check across the whole path implicitly includes every stage inside it.

questions.q: If an entire derived data pipeline is checked end to end, disks, networks, services and ____ along the path are implicitly included.
questions.explain: That covers hardware and software alike.
questions.rule: End to end includes everything on the path.

questions.q: A team checks each service's output against its own input checksum but does not compare the final report to the source. What is missing?
questions.explain: Only a check spanning source to final output includes every stage between them.
options: Faster hardware, because per-service checks only fail when the machines are overloaded
More per-service checks, because each added check makes an end-to-end check redundant
An end-to-end check from source data to final report
A weaker consistency model, so that stages no longer depend on one another's results
optionExplain: Speed does not decide whether the checks cover the whole path.
Local checks leave gaps between the stages.
Stage checks can miss corruption between stages.
Consistency level is unrelated to check coverage.

questions.q: Match each checking idea to its role in the card.
questions.explain: Like automated testing, continuous checking finds bugs quickly and lets you change a system with less fear.
pairs: Find bugs quickly before a change does damage
Raise confidence so changes can move faster
Corruption found only after downstream damage

questions.q: True or false: Finding corruption late, after it has caused downstream damage, makes the source easier to track down.
questions.explain: Late discovery is harder and more expensive to trace.

questions.q: How does continuous end-to-end checking help a team evolve its application?
questions.explain: Having continuous checks gives confidence, which allows you to move faster; if you are not afraid of making changes, you can evolve the application.
questions.teaches: If you are not afraid of making changes, you can much better evolve an application to meet changing requirements.
options: Being unafraid of changes lets it meet changing requirements
It freezes the schema so that no change can ever alter results seen by the audit
It moves all processing into one database so that checking becomes trivial for operators
It guarantees that no bug will ever be shipped, so releases need no further testing
optionExplain: Safety encourages change.
The card does not say changes are blocked.
Nothing in the card centralises processing.
Checks raise the chance of finding bugs quickly, not a guarantee.

questions.q: True or false: Signing a transaction log with a hardware security module proves that the right transactions went into the log.
questions.explain: Signing makes the log tamper-proof afterwards, but it does not show that the right transactions were recorded in the first place.

questions.q: Merkle trees are trees of ____ that can efficiently prove a record appears in a dataset.
questions.explain: Each node is a hash of its children.

questions.q: A bank wants replicas run by rival firms to check each other. Which part of distributed ledgers fits?
questions.explain: Distributed ledgers host replicas with mutually untrusting organisations, which continually check one another and agree by consensus.
options: A single trusted operator signs the log once a day and publishes the hash for everybody
Replicas continually check each other and agree by consensus
Proof of work, which the author finds a good way to keep throughput high
A separate audit table in the main database, written by the application at commit time
optionExplain: That does not let untrusting parties check each other continuously.
That is how the ledger replicas work.
The author calls proof of work extraordinarily wasteful.
That is the approach whose integrity is hard to guarantee.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether the author is positive or skeptical about it.
questions.explain: He likes the integrity checking and Merkle trees but doubts Byzantine fault tolerance and finds proof of work wasteful.
questions.rule: Take the integrity ideas, leave the waste.

items.t: The integrity-checking aspects of ledgers
Merkle trees in certificate transparency
Byzantine fault tolerance aspects
Proof of work such as Bitcoin mining

questions.q: True or false: The author expects blockchain-style auditing to be adopted for data systems without any further work on scalability.
questions.explain: Some work is needed to make them as scalable as systems without cryptographic auditing.

questions.q: Outside the hype of cryptocurrencies, where do Merkle trees already protect people?
questions.explain: Certificate transparency is a security technology that relies on Merkle trees to check the validity of TLS and SSL certificates.
questions.teaches: Certificate transparency is a security technology that relies on Merkle trees to check the validity of TLS/SSL certificates.
options: In hardware security modules, which sign each transaction log entry
In consensus protocols, which order transactions between untrusting replicas
In TCP checksums, which catch most corruption on the network
In certificate transparency, which checks TLS and SSL certificates
optionExplain: Signing was a separate technique in the card.
Consensus agrees on order, not hash proofs.
TCP checksums are not Merkle trees.
That is the author's named example.

questions.q: True or false: The author argues that engineers may focus on the technology and leave its consequences to others.
questions.explain: He says it is not sufficient to ignore consequences, because the ethical responsibility is the engineers' as well.

questions.q: The author says a technology is not good or bad in itself; what matters is how it is ____.
questions.explain: That is true of a search engine as much as of a weapon like a gun.

questions.q: A product manager says a tracking feature is only a neutral technology, so its effects are not the team's concern. How does the author respond?
questions.explain: A technology is judged by how it is used and how it affects people, so engineers cannot ignore consequences.
options: Engineers must weigh the consequences of what they build
The manager is right as long as the feature was built to specification and passed testing
Only the users who choose to enable the feature carry any responsibility for its effects
The effects are unpredictable, so thinking about them in advance is a waste of the team's time
optionExplain: Neutrality of the tool does not remove responsibility.
Passing tests says nothing about consequences for people.
The author places responsibility on the engineers building it.
He says engineers have a responsibility to consider consequences carefully.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether the author asserts it or rejects it.
questions.explain: He asserts dignity and engineers' responsibility, and rejects the view that technology is inherently good or bad or that consequences can be ignored.

items.t: Human dignity is paramount
Engineers must decide what kind of world they want
Technology is good or bad in itself
Ignoring consequences is sufficient for engineers

questions.q: True or false: On the author's view, data about people can be handled like any other abstract data, without special respect.
questions.explain: Many datasets are about people, and such data must be treated with humanity and respect.

questions.q: What does the author say about codes of ethics for software engineers?
questions.explain: Guidelines such as the ACM code exist, but are rarely discussed, applied and enforced, so engineers and managers can be cavalier about privacy and consequences.
questions.teaches: Guidelines such as the ACM code of ethics are rarely discussed, applied and enforced in practice, so engineers and product managers sometimes take a very cavalier attitude to privacy and potential negative consequences.
options: They do not exist, so each company must write its own from scratch before shipping
They are strictly enforced, which is why engineers rarely cause harm to users
They apply only to hardware engineers, since software has no direct effect on people
They exist but are rarely discussed, applied or enforced
optionExplain: He names the ACM code as an existing guideline.
He says the opposite about enforcement.
The guidelines cited are for software engineers.
The gap lies in practice, not in the existence of guidelines.

questions.q: True or false: Predicting the spread of a disease has the same direct effect on individual lives as predicting loan default.
questions.explain: Predictions about individuals directly affect their lives, whereas predicting the weather or a disease does not target a person.

questions.q: Being systematically excluded from key parts of society by algorithms has been called algorithmic ____.
questions.explain: It describes a large constraint on an individual's freedom.

questions.q: A lender's model labels an applicant risky, and several landlords and insurers also reject her. Which part of the argument fits?
questions.explain: A label of risk can lead to many no decisions, which add up to exclusion from jobs, insurance and other key parts of society.
options: Each organisation acted independently, so no single decision harmed the applicant
The label must be accurate, because organisations only reject applicants who are truly risky
Repeated no decisions can add up to systematic exclusion
The applicant can appeal each rejection to a court that presumes her innocent
optionExplain: The argument is about the accumulated effect of many decisions.
A person may be labelled risky accurately or falsely.
A risk label spreads across organisations.
Automated exclusion lacks proof of guilt and has little chance of appeal.

questions.q: Match each cost to how the organisation sees it.
questions.explain: Because the cost of a bad loan or hire is higher than that of a missed opportunity, organisations lean toward caution.

questions.q: True or false: Because organisations bear a low cost for a missed opportunity, they will tend to say no when in doubt.
questions.explain: From their point of view a bad loan or hire costs much more than a missed opportunity.

questions.q: How does automated exclusion differ from the presumption of innocence in the justice system?
questions.explain: In countries that respect human rights, the justice system presumes innocence, but automated systems can arbitrarily exclude a person without any proof of guilt and with little chance of appeal.
questions.rule: Automation skips the presumption of innocence.
questions.teaches: Automated systems can systematically and arbitrarily exclude a person from participating in society without any proof of guilt, and with little chance of appeal.
options: It requires stronger proof than a court, since algorithms are more accurate than judges
It can exclude people without proof of guilt and with little chance of appeal
It applies only after a criminal conviction, so innocent people are not affected
It always gives the person a hearing, because the algorithm must explain each decision
optionExplain: The author makes no such claim about stronger proof.
No proof is needed, and appeal is hard.
The labelled person may be falsely labelled.
Opacity and little chance of appeal are the concern.

questions.q: True or false: A system trained on biased data is likely to learn and amplify that bias.
questions.explain: If there is a systematic bias in the input, the system will most likely amplify it in its output.

questions.q: Predictive analytics systems ____ from the past, so a discriminatory past is codified.
questions.explain: If the past is discriminatory, the system codifies that discrimination.

questions.q: A hiring model is not given ethnicity, but uses postal code and learns from past decisions. What is the concern?
questions.explain: In racially segregated neighbourhoods a postal code or IP address is a strong predictor of race, so bias in past data can persist.
options: None, because removing the protected trait from the inputs makes the output impartial
Postal code can proxy for race, so past bias returns
The model is slower, since postal codes are harder to process than other inputs
The model will refuse to learn, as correlated features always cancel each other out
optionExplain: Correlated features can stand in for the removed trait.
A correlated feature carries the protected trait.
The concern is fairness, not speed.
Correlated features do not cancel; they can carry the bias.

questions.q: Put the author's argument about bias in order.
questions.explain: Bias in the data is learned, amplified and hidden in opaque patterns, so humans must supply the moral imagination.
items: Past decisions contain bias
A system infers its rules from that data
The learned pattern is opaque but amplifies the bias
Moral imagination from humans is needed for a better future

questions.q: True or false: Belief that a fair output can come from biased input data is satirised as machine learning being like money laundering for bias.
questions.explain: The author quotes that satire to criticise the idea that biased data can produce impartial output.
questions.rule: Biased data is not cleaned by a model.

questions.q: What role does the author want data and models to play?
questions.explain: If we want the future to be better than the past, moral imagination is required and only humans provide it; data and models should be tools, not masters.
questions.teaches: Data and models should be our tools, not our masters.
options: Final judges, because they are free from human prejudice and fatigue
Hidden inputs, so that users cannot challenge the decisions that rely on them
Replacements for anti-discrimination laws, which have become too slow to apply
Our tools, not our masters
optionExplain: He rejects blind faith in data-driven decisions.
He wants accountability and transparency, not hiding.
Those laws prohibit treating people differently by protected traits.
People decide; models assist.

questions.q: True or false: When a human makes a mistake, the affected person can appeal, whereas responsibility for an algorithm's mistake is unclear.
questions.explain: The author contrasts accountable humans with the open question of who answers for an algorithm.

questions.q: Machine-learning scoring algorithms typically use a much wider range of inputs and are much more ____ than a classic credit score.
questions.explain: This makes it harder to see how a decision came about.

questions.q: A court asks a company to explain why its model refused a loan to a particular person. What problem does the author predict?
questions.explain: He asks whether you can explain to the judge how the algorithm made its decision, which opacity makes hard.
options: The company may be unable to explain how the algorithm decided
The court will accept the model's accuracy statistics as a full explanation for each case
The company will be exempt, because machine-learning decisions are not covered by judicial review
The person will automatically be able to correct the data, as with every credit record
optionExplain: Opaque patterns resist explanation.
Aggregate accuracy does not explain an individual decision.
He asks whether the company can explain to the judge, not whether review applies.
Correction is hard, and for erroneous data recourse is almost impossible.

questions.q: Match each scoring approach to the question it answers.
questions.explain: A credit score summarises your own past, while predictive analytics draws parallels to other people's behaviour.
pairs: How did you behave in the past?
Who is similar to you, and how did people like you behave?
Can leave the person with little recourse if the data is wrong

questions.q: True or false: A traditional credit score is based on relevant facts about a person's actual borrowing history.
questions.explain: That grounding in relevant facts is one reason a bad score, although harmful, is easier to understand and challenge.

questions.q: What problem arises when predictive analytics judges someone by people similar to them?
questions.explain: Drawing parallels to others' behaviour implies stereotyping people, for example by where they live, and recourse is almost impossible if the data is wrong.
questions.teaches: Drawing parallels to others' behaviour implies stereotyping people, for example based on where they live, which is a close proxy for race and socioeconomic class.
options: Slower decisions, because comparing each person with millions of others takes time
Excessive privacy, since the person's own data is no longer used in the calculation
Stereotyping, which can put people in the wrong bucket
Perfect fairness, because everyone in a group is treated identically by the model
optionExplain: The author's concern is stereotyping, not speed.
The person's data remains part of the input.
Similarity is a proxy that can misplace individuals.
Identical treatment of a group can still be unfair to individuals in it.

questions.q: True or false: A prediction system whose overall probability distribution is correct can still be wrong for individual cases.
questions.explain: Averages and distributions say little about the outcome for one particular person.

questions.q: From an average and a probability distribution you cannot say much about how long one particular ____ will live.
questions.explain: Life expectancy of 80 does not make 80 the age of death.

questions.q: A hospital's model says patients like Sam have a 30% readmission risk. Which reading respects the author's point?
questions.explain: The output is probabilistic and may well be wrong in individual cases.
options: Sam will be readmitted in 30% of his days, so staff should plan for that share of time
The model is wrong for Sam, since his actual outcome cannot be exactly 30%
Sam may or may not be readmitted, as 30% describes similar patients
Sam is certain to be readmitted, because the model was trained on thousands of cases
optionExplain: Probability of readmission is not a share of days.
A single outcome cannot match a probability, but that does not make it wrong.
A probability describes a group, not one outcome.
A large training set does not turn a probability into certainty.

questions.q: Sort each use of analytics by whether the author presents it as helpful or harmful.
questions.explain: The same ability to reveal people's circumstances can focus aid or enable predatory selling.

items.t: Focusing aid on people who most need it
Finding vulnerable people to sell high-cost loans
Selling worthless college degrees to vulnerable people
Revealing financial and social characteristics to direct support

questions.q: True or false: The author thinks a blind belief in the supremacy of data for decisions is harmless if the data set is large.
questions.explain: He calls such belief delusional and positively dangerous.

questions.q: What does the author say society must learn to do as data-driven decisions spread?
questions.explain: We will need to figure out how to make algorithms accountable and transparent, how to avoid reinforcing existing biases, and how to fix them when they inevitably make mistakes.
questions.teaches: We will need to figure out how to make algorithms accountable and transparent, how to avoid reinforcing existing biases, and how to fix them when they inevitably make mistakes.
options: Make algorithms accountable and transparent, avoid reinforcing bias, and fix mistakes
Replace human judgement entirely, because mistakes will become rarer as data grows
Keep model details secret so that people cannot game the decisions made about them
Collect more personal data, so that every individual case becomes accurately predicted
optionExplain: He lists these three needs.
He calls blind belief in data dangerous.
He wants transparency, not secrecy.
More data does not remove individual error.

questions.q: True or false: A recommendation system that gets very good at predicting taste may show people only views they already agree with.
questions.explain: That is how echo chambers form.

questions.q: The approach of thinking about the entire system, including the people who interact with it, is known as ____ thinking.
questions.explain: It helps predict many consequences of a data analysis system.

questions.q: An employer screens by credit score; a candidate with a sudden hardship misses bills and is rejected. What follows?
questions.explain: Joblessness pushes toward poverty, which further worsens scores, making it harder to find employment.
options: A correction, because the candidate's score will rise again as soon as she is rejected
Nothing further, since a single rejection does not alter the information the score uses
Fairer hiring over time, because rejected candidates are replaced by better ones
A spiral: lower score, less work, deeper poverty and a lower score again
optionExplain: Rejection worsens her situation, which lowers the score.
Her finances are affected by the lost job, which changes the score.
The spiral harms the same person with an unfairly self-reinforcing effect.
The output feeds back into the input.

questions.q: Match each system to the harm the author links with it.
questions.explain: Recommenders can narrow views, and credit-score hiring can trap people in self-reinforcing hardship.

questions.q: True or false: The author says feedback loops can be foreseen by analysing the software alone.
questions.explain: We cannot always predict them, though thinking about the entire system, including people, can predict many consequences.
questions.rule: Software alone is not the system.

questions.q: What questions does systems thinking ask about a data analysis system?
questions.explain: We can try to understand how a system responds to different behaviours, structures or characteristics, and whether it reinforces and amplifies existing differences between people.
questions.rule: Ask whether the system amplifies inequality.
questions.teaches: Systems thinking asks whether a data analysis system reinforces and amplifies existing differences between people, such as making the rich richer or the poor poorer, or tries to combat injustice.
options: Does it process data faster than rival systems built by other companies in the industry?
Does it amplify differences between people or combat injustice?
Does it store data in the cheapest format available that satisfies the compression rules?
Does it avoid all unintended consequences by relying on a more precise mathematical model?
optionExplain: The questions concern effects on people.
These questions test for reinforcing effects.
Storage cost is not what the author asks.
He warns of unintended consequences even with the best intentions.

questions.q: True or false: When a user explicitly enters data because they want it stored, the system performs a service for that user.
questions.explain: The user is then the customer and the system does what the user asks.

questions.q: In an advertising-funded service, the ____ are the actual customers.
questions.explain: The users' interests take second place.
questions.rule: Advertisers pay, so they are customers.

questions.q: A free app logs every tap, keeps it for years and builds profiles sold to marketers. Which relationship does this resemble?
questions.explain: Tracking data becomes more detailed, analysis further-reaching and retention longer, to build profiles for marketing purposes.
options: A plain service where the user is the customer and logging only follows what they asked for
A neutral research study, since the profiles are compiled from the behaviour of consenting volunteers
An A/B test of the interface, whose logs are deleted as soon as the new design is chosen
One where advertisers are the customer and the user's interests come second
optionExplain: The tracking is far beyond what the user requested.
The card describes marketing profiles, not neutral research.
Long retention for profiling is not an A/B test.
The tracking serves the funders.

questions.q: Sort each tracking use by whether it mainly benefits the user or the advertiser.
questions.explain: Features such as ranking and recommendations help users, while profiling and engagement maximising serve advertisers.

items.t: Ranking search results by clicks
Recommending items others also liked
Detailed long-term profiles for marketing
Coaxing users to engage as much as possible

questions.q: True or false: On the author's view, every form of behavioural tracking works against the users' interests.
questions.explain: Tracking clicks, recommendations and A/B tests help users, but tracking often does not stop there.

questions.q: What does the author call the relationship between an ad-funded company and the people it tracks?
questions.explain: The tracking of the user serves the advertisers who fund the service, which he describes as surveillance.
questions.teaches: The user is given a free service and is coaxed into engaging with it as much as possible, and the tracking serves the needs of the advertisers who fund the service.
options: A fair value exchange, since the user receives a free service for their attention
Surveillance, a word with more sinister connotations
A partnership, because both parties benefit equally from the data collected
A licence agreement, in which users sell their data at a price they have negotiated
optionExplain: He says there is no fair value exchange.
He picks the stronger word on purpose.
He describes the interests as conflicting.
He says there is no negotiation.

questions.q: True or false: The author says all data collection qualifies as surveillance.
questions.explain: He says not all of it does, but that examining it as such helps us understand the relationship.
questions.rule: Not all, but a useful lens.

questions.q: As a thought experiment, replace the word data with ____ and see whether common phrases still sound good.
questions.explain: The experiment is meant to expose connotations.

questions.q: A health insurer ties coverage to wearing a fitness tracker. Which point does this illustrate?
questions.explain: When surveillance determines things that hold sway over important aspects of life such as insurance or employment, it appears less benign.
questions.rule: High stakes remove the benign look.
options: Tracking is benign whenever the purpose is better personalised recommendations
Government agencies and corporations differ so greatly that corporate tracking is harmless
Surveillance that sways important aspects of life stops looking benign
Wearables cannot reveal anything beyond step counts, so the privacy risk is small
optionExplain: Purpose seems benign only when stakes are low.
He says the difference is just who collects the data.
Insurance coverage is one of those aspects.
Motion sensors can reveal what you are typing.

questions.q: Match each device to the reason the author gives for concern.
questions.explain: Each shows a way ordinary devices become surveillance tools.
pairs: Can be used to work out what you type
Smart toys with cloud speech recognition
Add microphones, often with poor security

questions.q: True or false: On the author's view, a person with nothing to hide has no reason to worry about surveillance.
questions.explain: That position assumes you are in line with existing power structures and need not fear persecution, which not everyone is.
questions.rule: Nothing to hide is a privilege.

questions.q: Why does the author say we throw ourselves into a world of total surveillance?
questions.explain: Even the most repressive regimes could only dream of such tracking, yet we enthusiastically accept it, and the difference is that corporations rather than government agencies collect it.
questions.teaches: We apparently voluntarily, even enthusiastically, throw ourselves into this world of total surveillance, and the difference is that the data is collected by corporations rather than government agencies.
options: The data is collected by corporations rather than government agencies
Governments have required citizens to carry tracking devices for the benefit of public safety
Users understand exactly what is collected and consider the trade-off to be fair to them
Total surveillance has been shown to be the only way to provide useful online services
optionExplain: That difference is the one he highlights.
He says we choose it apparently voluntarily.
He argues users have little knowledge of what is collected.
He does not claim that tracking is necessary.

questions.q: True or false: Most privacy policies do more to obscure than to illuminate what happens to a user's data.
questions.explain: That is why the author says users cannot give meaningful consent.

questions.q: Data from one user also reveals things about people who are not users and have not agreed to any ____.
questions.explain: Those people never consented to anything.

questions.q: A messaging app is the only way a community arranges events, so leaving costs people social access. What does the author say about opting out?
questions.explain: If a service is regarded by most people as essential for basic social participation, it is not reasonable to expect them to opt out.
questions.rule: Essential services are de facto mandatory.
options: Opting out is not a free choice, because use is de facto mandatory
Opting out is free, since anyone who dislikes the tracking can leave
Opting out is irrelevant, because only government services are ever mandatory in practice
Opting out is possible for everyone equally, provided the person reads the privacy policy first
optionExplain: Network effects make leaving costly.
Leaving has a social cost when the service is essential.
He describes private services that become de facto mandatory.
Only the privileged have the time, knowledge and means to opt out.

questions.q: Sort each point by whether it supports or answers the consent argument.
questions.explain: Agreement and value are what the argument offers, and opacity and asymmetry are why the author rejects it.

items.t: Users agreed to the terms of service
The service is valuable to its users
Users cannot understand derived datasets
The service sets the terms with no negotiation

questions.q: True or false: Under the author's argument, users who read a privacy policy carefully give meaningful consent.
questions.explain: Even careful reading cannot reveal how derived datasets combine behaviour and external sources, so consent still lacks understanding.

questions.q: Who can actually afford to decline a service because of its tracking?
questions.explain: Declining is only an option for the small number of people with the time and knowledge to understand the policy and who can afford to miss opportunities; for others surveillance is inescapable.
questions.teaches: For people in a less privileged position there is no meaningful freedom of choice, and surveillance becomes inescapable.
options: Everyone, because declining always costs the same for every person
Mostly people in less privileged positions, who have fewer relationships to lose
Only the privileged, with time and knowledge and a tolerance for missing opportunities
Nobody, because all online services are designed to be technically impossible to quit
optionExplain: He says the cost falls unevenly.
He says the less privileged have no meaningful freedom of choice.
Choice is a luxury.
He says a privileged few can decline.

questions.q: True or false: Having privacy means keeping everything secret.
questions.explain: Privacy means having the freedom to choose what to reveal, what to make public and what to keep secret.

questions.q: The right to privacy is a decision ____, letting each person choose between secrecy and transparency.
questions.explain: It is an important aspect of freedom and autonomy.

questions.q: A person posts holiday photos publicly but wants her illness kept private, yet an ad network targets people with that illness. What happened?
questions.explain: Even if users cannot be reidentified, they have lost agency over disclosure of intimate information; the company exercises the privacy right to maximise profit.
options: Nothing happened, because posting any photo means that she has given up her privacy completely
The decision about disclosure moved from her to the company
Her privacy was fully protected, because the ad network never learned her name
Her privacy settings stopped the advertiser, since only the platform itself could use the data
optionExplain: Privacy is about choosing what to reveal, case by case.
The company exercised the privacy right for profit.
Even without reidentification the disclosure was not her choice.
Settings do not limit the service's own use.

questions.q: Match each claim to the author's verdict.
questions.explain: He argues that sharing by choice is exercising privacy, and surveillance moves the decision to companies.
pairs: Privacy is dead because people share online
Surveillance erodes privacy rights into nothing
Rather, rights are transferred to the collector

questions.q: True or false: Privacy settings that restrict what other users see also limit what the service itself can do with the data.
questions.explain: The service still has unfettered access and may use the data in any way its privacy policy permits.
questions.rule: Settings do not bind the service.

questions.q: What makes the transfer of privacy rights to corporations historically unprecedented?
questions.explain: Surveillance used to be expensive and manual, and trust relationships such as with a doctor are governed by ethical, legal and regulatory constraints, whereas internet services amass data at scale without meaningful consent.
questions.teaches: Surveillance has always existed, but it used to be expensive and manual, not scalable and automated.
options: Surveillance and trust relationships never existed before the internet was created
Doctors and attorneys now collect more data than companies do, with few legal limits
Data protection laws once made it impossible to collect any personal information at all
Automated surveillance at huge scale without meaningful consent or strict governance
optionExplain: He says both have always existed.
He says their use of data is strictly governed.
The chapter does not say this; the correct option gives the claim it actually makes.
Scale, automation and missing constraints.

questions.q: True or false: The author argues that behavioural data is worthless waste, so analysing it is a form of recycling.
questions.explain: He says the more correct view is the other way round: for ad-funded services it is the core asset.

questions.q: Behavioural data is sometimes called data ____, suggesting it is worthless waste.
questions.explain: The author argues this view is mistaken.

questions.q: A start-up with a million active users but no revenue is valued highly. What does this show, in the author's view?
questions.explain: Startups are valued by their user numbers, in other words by their surveillance capabilities, which supports the claim that personal data is a valuable asset.
options: Investors believe the product's source code is the real asset, whatever the user numbers
User numbers are irrelevant, since only audited profit can support any valuation
Valuation by eyeballs reflects surveillance capability and the value of the data
Startups hold personal data of no value, so the valuation is a pure accounting error
optionExplain: The valuation is tied to users, not code.
He cites valuation by eyeballs as evidence.
Users' data is the asset.
He argues that personal data is valuable.

questions.q: Sort each party by whether it wants personal data for commercial or political reasons.
questions.explain: Companies and brokers want the data to monetise it, and governments and future regimes want the power it brings.

items.t: Advertisers
Data brokers
Governments compelling disclosure
A regime that later takes over the country

questions.q: True or false: When a company that has collected personal data goes bankrupt, that data is among the assets that get sold.
questions.explain: This is one of the ways data ends up with parties the user never chose.

questions.q: Why does the author say we should consider all possible future governments when collecting data?
questions.explain: There is no guarantee every future government will respect human rights, so it is poor civic hygiene to install technologies that could facilitate a police state.
questions.rule: Plan for the worst future regime.
questions.teaches: There is no guarantee that every government elected in future will respect human rights and civil liberties.
options: No guarantee that every future government will respect human rights
Present governments are certain to abuse any data they collect from companies
Future governments will pay companies to hand over data without any legal compulsion
Data collected today is automatically deleted when a new government takes office
optionExplain: Today's politics may not last.
He does not claim certainty about today's governments.
The concern is compulsion and abuse, not payment.
He wants us to avoid creating a dataset that survives.

questions.q: True or false: The author says the Industrial Revolution brought benefits only, with no major problems.
questions.explain: It brought growth and better living standards, but also pollution, poor housing and child labour.

questions.q: In Bruce Schneier's words, protecting privacy is the environmental ____ of the information age.
questions.explain: Data is described as the pollution problem.

questions.q: A company argues that new rules on data would raise its costs. How does the analogy answer this?
questions.explain: The cost of doing business increased when factories could no longer dump waste, but society as a whole benefited hugely.
options: The company is right, because rules that raise costs have never improved society overall
Safeguards raised factories' costs too, but society gained hugely
Costs do not matter, since data collection is free for every business that uses it
The rules are pointless, because factories in the past improved without any regulation
optionExplain: The analogy says the opposite.
Costs rose, but few want to go back.
The analogy concedes that costs increased.
It took a long time to establish safeguards, which then helped.

questions.q: Match each industrial-era harm to the safeguard that eventually addressed it.
questions.explain: Each harm was eventually met by a safeguard that is now taken for granted.

questions.q: True or false: In the analogy, data that stays around after collection is compared to pollution that festers.
questions.explain: Schneier says almost all computers produce information that stays around, festering.

questions.q: How does Schneier expect future generations to judge us?
questions.explain: Our grandchildren will look back at these early decades of the information age and judge us on how we addressed the challenge of data collection and misuse.
questions.rule: History will judge our handling of data.
questions.teaches: Our grandchildren will look back at us during these early decades of the information age and judge us on how we addressed the challenge of data collection and misuse.
options: By how many users our services attracted during these early decades
By how quickly we digitised every industry that existed before the internet
By how well we ignored the problem so that innovation could proceed unhindered
By how we addressed data collection and misuse
optionExplain: He talks about judging how we handled misuse.
Speed of adoption is not the criterion.
He says our grandchildren will wonder how we ignored it, as we wonder about pollution.
As we judge early industrial pollution.

questions.q: True or false: The author claims data protection law is effective in the internet context.
questions.explain: He says it is doubtful, because its rules run counter to the Big Data philosophy.

questions.q: The 1995 directive requires personal data to be collected for specified, explicit and ____ purposes.
questions.explain: It also requires data to be adequate, relevant and not excessive.

questions.q: A firm collects clicks for one feature, then mines them later for an unplanned purpose. How does this relate to the directive?
questions.explain: Exploration means using data for unforeseen purposes, which is the opposite of the specified and explicit purposes for which consent was given.
options: It conflicts with specified and explicit purposes
It complies, because any use of data counts as specified once the data exists
It is required, because the directive demands that all collected data be combined
It is irrelevant, since the directive only applies to paper records held by governments
optionExplain: Exploration means unforeseen purposes.
The purposes must be specified at collection.
The directive limits further processing.
It covers personal data held by organisations.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it supports regulation or the case against over-regulation.
questions.explain: Both sides have valid points, which is why the author says balancing them is difficult.

items.t: Data protection law could preserve individual rights
Privacy risks of sharing medical data are clear
Better diagnostics could prevent many deaths
Regulation can hinder innovation

questions.q: True or false: The author thinks all opposition from data-collecting companies to regulation is unjustified.
questions.explain: To some extent the opposition is justified, for example for medical data where over-regulation may prevent breakthroughs.

questions.q: What is the philosophy of Big Data that clashes with purpose limitation?
questions.explain: Big Data's philosophy is to maximise data collection, combine it with other datasets and experiment and explore, which runs counter to the directive's rules.
questions.rule: Big Data explores; the law limits purpose.
questions.teaches: The philosophy of Big Data is to maximize data collection, to combine it with other datasets, to experiment and to explore in order to generate new insights.
options: Collect the minimum data and delete it at the end of each session
Ask each user for fresh consent before every individual query on the data
Store data only in the user's own device, where companies cannot combine it
Maximise collection, combine datasets and explore for new insights
optionExplain: That is the opposite of Big Data.
Big Data does not require that.
Combining data is part of the philosophy.
Collect widely, then look for uses.

questions.q: True or false: The author thinks ubiquitous surveillance is inevitable and we cannot stop it.
questions.explain: He says it is not inevitable and that we are still able to stop it.

questions.q: The author says personal data should be ____ as soon as it is no longer needed, rather than retained forever.
questions.explain: This runs counter to immutability, but he says that issue can be solved.

questions.q: A company promises in its policy that staff will not read private messages. Which approach does the author favour instead?
questions.explain: A promising approach is to enforce access control through cryptographic protocols rather than merely by policy.
options: Rely on the policy, since a written promise is the strongest guard that exists
Store the messages forever, so that auditors can verify later who read them
Enforce access with cryptographic protocols, not policy alone
Let advertisers audit access, since they are the actual customers of the service
optionExplain: He prefers cryptography over mere policy.
He wants unneeded data purged.
Technical enforcement does not rely on promises.
That would reinforce the problem of interests.

questions.q: Put the author's proposals in the order he introduces them.
questions.explain: The culture shift and self-regulation come first, then education, and then the practical steps like purging.
items: Stop treating users as metrics to be optimised
Self-regulate data collection and processing
Educate end users about how their data is used
Purge data that is no longer needed

questions.q: True or false: Under the author's comparison, an individual's right to control their data needs no protection to survive.
questions.explain: Like a national park it will be destroyed if not explicitly protected and cared for.

questions.q: Why is the national park comparison apt for personal data control?
questions.explain: If we do not explicitly protect and care for our right to control our data, it will be destroyed in a tragedy of the commons and we will all be worse off.
questions.teaches: Our individual right to control our data is like the natural environment of a national park: if we do not explicitly protect and care for it, it will be destroyed.
options: Both can be owned by a single company that sells entry tickets to visitors
Unprotected shared goods get destroyed, a tragedy of the commons
Both are best managed by leaving them untouched and unmonitored for many years
Both are too large for any individual to affect, so action is pointless
optionExplain: The comparison concerns protection, not ownership.
Everyone loses if no one protects the commons.
He says they need explicit care.
He says we are still able to act.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter begins from the observation that one single tool can efficiently serve all use cases.
questions.explain: No single tool can, so applications must compose several pieces of software.

questions.q: Certain systems are designated as systems of ____, and other data is derived from them through transformations.
questions.explain: Indexes, materialised views and models are derived.
questions.rule: System of record plus derived data.

questions.q: A team wants to change the structure of a search index built from its event log. What does the chapter suggest?
questions.explain: If you want to change a processing step, rerun the new transformation on the whole input dataset to rederive the output.
options: Edit the existing index in place and hope the changes match the log's contents
Rerun the new transformation code over the whole input
