Stop all writes until every consumer has switched to the new structure
Treat the index as the system of record and discard the log it came from
optionExplain: Rederiving is safer than in-place edits.
Derive the new index again from the source.
The chapter prefers loose coupling that avoids stopping.
The log is the source of truth.

questions.q: Match each chapter idea to the benefit it brings.
questions.explain: Each idea contributes a different advantage to the overall design.
pairs: UIs that update and work offline

questions.q: True or false: Making derivations asynchronous and loosely coupled prevents a problem in one area from spreading to unrelated parts.
questions.explain: This increases the robustness and fault tolerance of the system as a whole.

questions.q: How are these dataflow processes related to what databases already do?
questions.explain: These processes are quite similar to what databases already do internally, so dataflow applications are recast as unbundled database components composed loosely.
questions.teaches: These processes are quite similar to what databases already do internally, so the idea of dataflow applications is recast as unbundling the components of a database.
options: They are entirely unlike database internals, which cannot be reproduced outside one product
They replace databases completely, so that no storage engine remains in the system
They apply only to batch jobs, because databases can never process event streams
They are similar to what databases do internally, so databases can be unbundled
optionExplain: The author draws a similarity.
Components are composed, not removed.
Event streams are part of the design.
The author recasts dataflow this way.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter concludes that strong integrity guarantees require traditional distributed transactions.
questions.explain: They can be implemented scalably with asynchronous event processing, idempotent operations and asynchronous constraint checks.

questions.q: Operations are made idempotent by using end-to-end operation ____.
questions.explain: A unique id lets duplicates be recognised.

questions.q: A booking service must stay available across regions. Which choice follows the chapter's conclusion?
questions.explain: Checking constraints asynchronously avoids most coordination while maintaining integrity, even across geographies and faults.
options: Check constraints asynchronously and apologise when one is violated
Run a distributed transaction across all regions for every booking request
Skip constraint checks entirely, since integrity matters less than speed for users
Block every client until all replicas confirm that the constraint has been satisfied
optionExplain: Avoid coordination and accept occasional apologies.
That is the traditional approach the chapter calls less scalable.
The chapter keeps integrity, loosening only timeliness.
That coordination is what the design avoids.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it belongs to the technical or the ethical part of the conclusion.
questions.explain: The first half is about preserving integrity at scale; the second is about harms from the use of data.

items.t: Idempotent operations with end-to-end ids
Asynchronous constraint checking
Discrimination and exploitation
Normalised surveillance

questions.q: True or false: On the chapter's account, audits are used to verify the integrity of data and detect corruption.
questions.explain: The chapter closes its technical part by talking about audits.

questions.q: What final responsibility does the author assign to engineers?
questions.explain: As software and data have such a large impact, engineers carry a responsibility to work toward the kind of world that treats people with humanity and respect.
questions.teaches: Because software and data have such a large impact on the world, engineers carry a responsibility to work toward a world that treats people with humanity and respect.
options: To maximise the data collected so that models improve as quickly as possible
To leave ethical choices to regulators while concentrating on the technology
To work toward a world that treats people with humanity and respect
To ensure users agree to the terms so the company is protected from liability
optionExplain: That is contrary to his argument.
He says engineers carry responsibility.
That is the closing wish.
Legal protection is not his concern here.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Partitioning a dataset across machines is mainly a way to make a system survive hardware faults.
questions.explain: Partitioning mainly spreads data and load so that no single machine holds everything; surviving machine loss comes from replication. The card next shows how the book sorts techniques by goal.
questions.rule: Partitioning is for scale; copies are for fault tolerance.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Letting old and new code versions run side by side during a rolling upgrade mainly serves the goal of ____.
questions.explain: Rolling upgrades allow small, frequent releases without downtime, which makes a system easier to change. Compatible encodings are what make running two versions at once safe.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A team splits its customer table over eight machines because it no longer fits on one. Which goal does this serve, and what does it tax?
options: Reliability; reads of a secondary index become cheaper because copies are nearby
Maintainability; every query becomes a lookup inside one single partition only
Scalability; writes that span several partitions become harder to reason about
Scalability; replication lag disappears because each partition has one single owner
optionExplain: Copies near the reader come from replication, and partitioning does not give them.
Many queries now touch several partitions, so they get harder, not simpler.
Splitting data spreads storage and load, which is scale. The price is that one write can succeed on one partition and fail on another.
Lag belongs to replication between copies, and partitioning alone does not remove it.
questions.explain: Partitioning serves scale. The book notes that operations writing to several partitions are hard to reason about, because part of the work may succeed while another part fails.
questions.rule: Name the goal served and the goal taxed.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each technique to the goal it mainly serves.
pairs: Promoting a follower after the leader dies
Schemas that old and new code can both read
questions.explain: Failover keeps the service working after a fault, extra read replicas raise capacity, and compatible schemas make change safe.
questions.rule: Match the technique to the goal it buys.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Adding asynchronous followers to serve reads raises read capacity without any cost to how fresh a read can be.
questions.explain: Asynchronous followers can lag behind the leader, so a read from one may return older data. Read capacity is bought with weaker freshness, which is exactly the cost the card tells you to name.
questions.rule: Every gain has a cost elsewhere.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: According to the book, how easy is it to make an application reliable, scalable and maintainable all at once?
options: There is no easy fix; certain patterns recur, but each application needs its own judgement
A standard architecture exists that delivers all three if its steps are followed closely
Only maintainability is hard, because reliability and scale follow once enough hardware is bought
It becomes easy once a distributed database with automatic failover has been chosen for storage
optionExplain: The book states there is no easy fix, and that patterns recur across applications.
No such standard architecture is offered; the book denies a generic one-size-fits-all design.
More hardware does not remove faults or complexity, and the book treats all three goals as hard.
Failover helps reliability only, and does nothing for scale or for ease of change.
questions.explain: The authors say there is unfortunately no easy fix for making applications reliable, scalable or maintainable, though certain patterns and techniques keep reappearing.
questions.teaches: The book says there is no easy fix for reliability, scalability or maintainability; there are only patterns and techniques that keep reappearing across applications.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A startup ships well-designed software but has no monitoring, runbooks or on-call rota. According to the book, what is the likely outcome?
options: Reliability will hold anyway, because well-designed software restores itself after any fault
Only scalability suffers, since operations teams mainly handle growing load and rarely deal with faults
Nothing changes, because automation can replace the human setup and checking of operations
It may still fail to run reliably, since good software cannot run reliably with bad operations
optionExplain: Software cannot fix every fault by itself; people still watch health and restore service.
Operations teams also monitor health and restore service after faults, not only manage load.
Automation is itself set up by humans, who must make sure it keeps working.
The book cites the view that good operations can work around poor software, but good software cannot run reliably under poor operations.
questions.explain: Operations is part of maintainability, and the book says it is up to humans to set up automation and check that it works.
questions.teaches: The book cites the suggestion that good operations can often work around the limitations of bad or incomplete software, but good software cannot run reliably with bad operations.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: A system built from unreliable parts can still give applications strong guarantees, if the likely faults are planned for.
questions.explain: That is the book's premise: reliable systems are built from unreliable parts by tolerating their faults. The card next shows how the layers fit.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A ____ is one component deviating from its specification, whereas a failure is the whole system ceasing to provide the service.
questions.explain: Chapter 1 separates the two: the aim is to stop a fault from turning into a failure.
questions.rule: Fault is a part; failure is the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Three nodes must pick one lock holder after the old holder froze in a long garbage-collection pause. What does the book support?
options: Let each node check its own clock and claim the lock whenever its lease still appears to be valid at that moment
Decide by quorum vote, and let the protected resource reject stale holders by their token numbers
Trust the frozen holder, since it knows best whether it still holds the lock after waking
Rely on TCP acknowledgments as proof that the old holder has really stopped doing work
optionExplain: A node's clock and its own view can be wrong, which is why the lease check fails after a pause.
A quorum decides, and fencing tokens let the resource refuse writes from a holder whose grant has been superseded.
A paused node does not know it was paused, so it cannot judge its own state.
An acknowledgment shows delivery, not that the other side has stopped or finished processing.
questions.explain: A paused node cannot tell it was paused, so safety must come from a quorum decision and from the resource checking increasing token numbers.
questions.rule: Decide by quorum; let the resource check tokens.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reviewer writes: our transactions are atomic, so after a timeout we can retry blindly. What is wrong with that reasoning?
options: Atomicity covers only reads, so a crash can still leave writes half applied afterwards
Atomic transactions forbid retries, so a failed transaction must be abandoned for good and reported to the user
A timeout cannot show whether the first attempt committed, so the retry may repeat work already done
Retries are safe only on replicated databases, because a single node cannot abort cleanly
optionExplain: Atomicity covers writes; it is the guarantee against half-applied writes.
Atomicity is what makes retry attractive: an aborted attempt leaves nothing behind.
Atomicity is about all-or-nothing, but a timeout hides the outcome. If the first attempt committed, the retry runs the work twice.
A single node aborts cleanly; replication is not needed for atomic retry.
questions.explain: The timeout leaves the outcome unknown. A committed first attempt followed by a retry repeats the work, so duplicates must also be handled above the database.
questions.rule: Atomic abort is safe to retry; an unknown outcome is not.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Order these layers from the base that everything rests on to the top that applications use.
items: Unreliable networks, clocks and processes
Replication and quorums that tolerate node loss
Consensus, which lets nodes agree on one decision
Guarantees such as linearizability and transactions
questions.explain: Each layer is built on the one below: faulty parts, then replication and quorum voting, then consensus, then the guarantees that application code relies on.
questions.rule: Guarantees rest on consensus, which rests on tolerating faulty parts.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A team keeps three replicas, nightly backups and write-ahead logs, then declares data loss impossible. What does the book's durability discussion say?
options: Replication across three nodes is enough on its own, because correlated faults cannot hit all the replicas at once
Writing to disk is obsolete once replication exists, since replicas are more durable than any disk
Backups are redundant when replication is synchronous, so they can be dropped to cut cost
No single technique gives absolute guarantees, so disks, replicas and backups should be combined
optionExplain: A power outage or a crash-causing bug can take out every replica at once, which is a correlated fault.
A fault that hits every node at once still loses data held only in memory, so disks stay relevant.
A corrupted record may be copied to replicas, and then only an older backup can restore it.
Perfect durability does not exist, so several partial protections are layered.
questions.explain: The book says nothing is perfect: disks, replicas and backups each fail in some ways, so no one technique can provide absolute guarantees.
questions.rule: Layer risk reductions; trust no single one.
questions.teaches: In practice no single technique gives absolute durability; writing to disk, replicating to remote machines and keeping backups are risk-reduction techniques that can and should be used together.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Because relational databases can store any data, one data model and storage engine is the best choice for every application.
questions.explain: The book argues the opposite: different models and engines suit different uses, and one model can imitate another only awkwardly. The card next shows how to choose.
questions.rule: Fit the tool to the workload.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Analytic queries that scan millions of records are usually limited by disk ____, whereas OLTP lookups are limited by seek time.
questions.explain: OLTP queries touch few records found through an index, so seek time dominates; analytic scans read enormous amounts, so bandwidth dominates.
questions.rule: OLTP is seek-bound; analytics is bandwidth-bound.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A social app stores friendships where anyone may link to anyone, and its queries follow chains of friends. Which model fits the book's reasoning?
options: A document model, because each profile is self-contained and links between profiles are rare
A column-oriented warehouse, because queries touch many rows but only a few columns
A hierarchical tree, because friendships nest like folders under a single parent
A graph model, because anything may be related to anything else
optionExplain: That reasoning fits the opposite case; here the links are the heart of the data.
A warehouse suits scans over many rows, while this workload follows links.
The hierarchical model failed for many-to-many relationships, and friendships are many-to-many.
Graph databases target data where anything is potentially related to everything.
questions.explain: The book says document stores suit data with rare links between documents, while graph databases target data where anything is potentially related to everything.
questions.rule: Many connections point to a graph.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each workload or design to the storage choice that fits it.
pairs: Fetch one customer by id, thousands of times a second
Total sales by month over billions of rows
Very high write volume, appended and merged in the background
Pages overwritten in place, protected by a write-ahead log
questions.explain: Key lookups need an index, scans need columns, append-heavy writes suit log-structured files, and in-place page updates describe B-trees.
questions.rule: Read the access pattern, then pick the structure.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A colleague says graph data cannot be stored in a relational database, so a graph store is mandatory. What is the flaw?
options: Graph databases are relational databases renamed, so choosing between them makes no difference
Relational systems store graphs so efficiently that a graph store is not worth considering
One model can be emulated in another, though awkwardly, so the question is fit, not possibility
Documents can hold graphs without any cost, which makes a relational database unnecessary for this kind of data
optionExplain: The models differ in what they make easy; they are not the same thing.
Emulation works but is awkward, so it is not a reason to rule graph stores out.
The book says graph data can be represented relationally, but the result is often awkward.
Documents handle rare links well, and many-to-many links strain them.
questions.explain: The book says one model can be emulated in terms of another, but the result is often awkward, which is why there are different systems for different purposes.
questions.rule: Possible is not the same as fitting.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Analysts scan five of one hundred columns across a billion rows. Which change does the book's reasoning favour, and why?
options: Column-oriented storage, which reads only the needed columns and encodes them compactly
A bigger B-tree index, so each scan jumps straight to the rows it needs
An in-memory hash index, so each row is found directly by its key
More write-ahead log space, so scans see a consistent copy of each page
optionExplain: A scan wants to read little data from disk, and columns let it skip the ninety-five it does not need.
Indexes help when few rows are fetched; a scan of every row gains little from them.
A hash index finds single keys and does nothing for scans over many rows.
The log protects against crashes during writes and does not reduce the data a scan reads.
questions.explain: When queries scan many rows, indexes matter less and the amount read from disk matters most, which column-oriented storage reduces.
questions.teaches: For queries that scan many rows, indexes are much less relevant; what matters is encoding data very compactly to minimise what is read from disk, which column-oriented storage helps achieve.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: A node that is leader for one partition cannot also be a follower for another partition.
questions.explain: In the book's design a node can hold some partitions as leader and others as follower. The card next shows how the two techniques combine.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A secondary index kept in the same partition as the records it indexes is called a ____ index.
questions.explain: A local index is stored beside the records it covers, so a write updates one partition, but a read must ask all partitions.
questions.rule: Local index: cheap writes, scattered reads.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A sensor service uses key-range partitioning on timestamp keys and mostly writes current readings. Which problem should it expect?
options: All new writes land in the partition holding the latest time range, creating a hot spot
Every range query must contact all partitions, because the keys are stored in unordered form
Secondary indexes become impossible, because ranges of timestamps cannot be indexed at all
Rebalancing becomes impossible, because a key range cannot be split once it has been made
optionExplain: Timestamps increase, so every write targets the newest range, which one partition owns.
Range queries are cheap under key-range partitioning because keys are sorted.
Secondary indexes can be partitioned locally or globally, whatever the primary key.
Key ranges can be split when a partition grows too big.
questions.explain: Key-range partitioning keeps keys sorted, which helps range scans, but keys that are close together in order are hit together, as with timestamps.
questions.rule: Sorted keys invite hot spots at the newest end.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each partitioning choice to its main consequence.
pairs: A write updates one partition; reads scatter to all
A read hits one partition; a write updates several
Spreads load evenly but range queries become inefficient
Efficient range queries but a risk of hot spots
questions.explain: The two index types and the two partitioning schemes each trade write cost against read cost or ordering against balance.
questions.rule: Each scheme moves cost from one place to another.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A design review says partitioning alone gives fault tolerance, because data is spread over many machines. What is missing?
options: Partitioning forbids copies, so replication would have to be switched off for the design to hold
Spreading data across machines increases the chance of faults, so partitioning is harmful to reliability
Each record still has a single copy, so a lost node loses its partitions unless they are also replicated
Fault tolerance needs a global secondary index, which partitioning alone does not create
optionExplain: The book explicitly combines the two, and partitions are normally replicated.
More machines do raise fault odds, but the cure is copies, not abandoning partitioning.
Partitioning splits data without duplicating it; the book combines it with replication so copies of each partition live on several nodes.
Secondary indexes affect queries, not whether data survives a node loss.
questions.explain: Partitioning is usually combined with replication so copies of each partition are stored on multiple nodes.
questions.rule: Partitioning for scale, replicas for survival.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: One celebrity's user id receives millions of writes, and the table is hashed by user id. What does the book say about fixing this?
options: Hashing already spreads identical keys evenly, so the load is balanced across the partitions
The database detects the hot key itself and automatically moves its writes across several partitions to balance the load
Switching to key-range partitioning places the single hot key on several partitions
Hashing cannot help; the application can add a random number to the hot key, but reads must then combine the split keys
optionExplain: Two identical keys hash to the same value, so they land on the same partition.
The book says most data systems cannot compensate for such skew automatically.
A single key belongs to one range and therefore to one partition under key ranges as well.
A hash of the same key is the same, so a single hot key stays on one partition unless the application splits it.
questions.explain: Skew on one key is the application's job to reduce. Splitting the key spreads writes, at the price of extra read work and bookkeeping about which keys are split.
questions.rule: A hot key must be split by the application.
questions.teaches: Because hashing the same key gives the same hash, the application must split a known hot key, for example by adding a random number to it, and then reads must read all the split keys and combine them.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Linearizability and serializability are two names for the same guarantee.
questions.explain: They are different: linearizability concerns recency of reads and writes on one object, and serializability concerns transactions. The card next lays out the ladders.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Under ____ consistency, replicas only promise to converge on the same value once writes stop.
questions.explain: Eventual consistency is the weakest rung: it says nothing about what a reader sees before convergence.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A user posts a comment, refreshes and sees nothing, then refreshes again and sees it. Which guarantee short of linearizability targets this?
options: Consistent prefix reads, so a reply never appears before the question it answers
Monotonic reads, so a later read never shows an older state than an earlier read
Eventual consistency, so replicas converge once writes stop arriving
Read-after-write consistency, so users see their own submitted writes
optionExplain: That concerns order across several writes, such as a question and its answer.
The user first saw nothing and then the comment, so reads did not go backward.
Convergence says nothing about when; it would not prevent this view.
The user did not see their own write at first, which is exactly what read-after-write consistency rules out.
questions.explain: The guarantee that users always see data they submitted themselves is read-after-write consistency. Monotonic reads and consistent prefix reads cover other anomalies.
questions.rule: Match the anomaly to the weakest guarantee that stops it.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each anomaly to the guarantee that prevents it.
pairs: A transaction reads data another has not committed
A read sees part of another transaction's changes
Two doctors each go off call after checking the other is on
An answer appears before the question it answers
questions.explain: Dirty reads need read committed; read skew needs a snapshot; write skew needs serializability; ordering of related writes needs consistent prefix reads.
questions.rule: Each rung stops a named anomaly.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A linearizable database spans two datacenters and the link between them is cut. What must an isolated datacenter do?
options: Keep serving normally, since linearizability needs no contact between the replicas
Stop answering affected clients, or keep answering and give up linearizability
Serve reads from its local replica, which stays linearizable because it holds a full copy
Switch to serializable isolation, which restores single-copy behaviour across the cut
optionExplain: Linearizability needs replicas to coordinate so reads see the latest write.
With the link cut, a replica cannot know it has the latest value. It can wait, losing availability, or answer and risk breaking linearizability.
A local copy may miss writes accepted on the other side.
Serializability is a different guarantee and does not give single-copy behaviour.
questions.explain: This is the trade-off behind the CAP theorem: when the network fails a linearizable system must give up availability on the cut-off side, or give up linearizability.
questions.rule: Linearizable or available when the network is cut.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A team says: our database offers serializable transactions, so its reads are guaranteed to be linearizable. What is the flaw?
options: Serializability orders transactions but gives no recency guarantee; snapshot-based serializable systems can read slightly old data
Serializable transactions are slower than linearizable reads, so they can only be used in single-node systems
Linearizability concerns several objects at once, so a guarantee about a single object cannot be derived from serializability in any system
Serializability forbids reads that overlap a write, so linearizable reads would have to wait for every commit
optionExplain: Serializable snapshot isolation reads from a consistent snapshot that leaves out newer writes, so its reads are not linearizable.
Speed is not the point; the guarantees differ in kind.
Linearizability applies to a single object, and serializability to transactions over several.
Some serializable systems do allow overlapping reads; they just read from a snapshot.
questions.explain: Implementations based on two-phase locking or serial execution are typically linearizable, but serializable snapshot isolation is not, because it deliberately reads from a snapshot.
questions.rule: Serializable does not mean up to date.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A collaborative notes app spans continents and must stay usable when the network between regions is cut. Which model fits best?
options: Linearizability, which stays available during a network cut by serving the latest value from any replica that is still reachable
Serializable isolation, which keeps single-object reads recent without any cross-region contact
Causal consistency, the strongest model that avoids network-delay slowdown and stays available in network failures
Eventual consistency, the strongest model that remains available during network failures
optionExplain: A replica cut off from the others cannot know it holds the latest value, so linearizability gives up availability.
Serializability needs coordination about conflicting transactions and does not remove it.
Causal consistency keeps cause before effect without cross-node coordination on each operation.
Causal consistency is stronger than eventual consistency and also stays available.
questions.explain: The book says many systems that seem to need linearizability only need causal consistency, and causal consistency avoids the cost of CAP.
questions.rule: Ask whether causal consistency is enough.
questions.teaches: Causal consistency is the strongest possible consistency model that does not slow down due to network delays and remains available in the face of network failures, and many systems that appear to need linearizability only need causal consistency.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Enforcing a username uniqueness constraint across several nodes is the same kind of problem as electing a leader.
questions.explain: Both need the nodes to agree on one irrevocable decision. The card next shows how many jobs reduce to this problem.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Atomic commit, locks and total order broadcast are all equivalent to the problem of ____.
questions.explain: If you can solve one of them you can turn the solution into a solution for the others.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Two nodes may each accept the last seat on a flight at the same instant. How does the card classify keeping exactly one booking?
options: As a replication-lag problem, curable by reading from the leader after every write
As a consensus problem, because the nodes must agree on one winner
As a throughput problem, solved by adding replicas to absorb the load
As a clock problem, solved by trusting the earliest timestamp each node records
optionExplain: Lag makes reads stale; here two writes compete and one must be refused.
Deciding which of several competing requests wins is the uniqueness-constraint case of consensus.
More replicas add more nodes that could accept the seat, which makes agreement harder.
Clocks drift and nodes cannot compare timestamps they have not yet seen.
questions.explain: A seat, like a username, can go to only one claimant, so nodes must agree on a single winner.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which of these does the book list as problems reducible to consensus?
options: A linearizable compare-and-set register
Merging sibling values after concurrent writes
Deciding the delivery order of messages to all nodes
Compacting old segments of a log
Running read repair on a stale replica
Deciding which client gets a lock
optionExplain: The register must decide atomically whether a write wins; this is on the book's list.
Merging siblings resolves conflicts afterwards and needs no agreement among nodes.
Total order broadcast makes nodes decide one delivery order; it is listed.
Compaction is local housekeeping and needs no decision across nodes.
Read repair copies newer data to a stale replica without a collective decision.
Locks and leases decide among racing clients; this is on the list.
questions.explain: Compare-and-set registers, total order broadcast and locks each require nodes to decide one outcome; merging, compaction and read repair do not.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A shopping cart replicates across regions without a leader and accepts conflicting edits. According to the card, what does it give up?
options: Fault tolerance, since without a leader no node can accept any write
Availability, since every write must wait for a majority of regions to answer
Global agreement on one winner, so concurrent edits can conflict and need merging
Durability, since each write is acknowledged by only one single node
optionExplain: Leaderless systems accept writes on several nodes, which helps fault tolerance.
Waiting for a majority of regions is what consensus does, which this design avoids.
Leaderless systems avoid global consensus, so concurrent writes can conflict and must be merged.
Leaderless writes go to several nodes, not one.
questions.explain: Leaderless and multi-leader systems avoid global consensus, so they cope with branching version histories and merging instead.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A database operator manually promotes a follower after the leader dies. How does the book describe this way of choosing a leader?
options: A kind of consensus decided by a human outside the system, limited by how fast humans can act
A true consensus algorithm, since the operator and the replicas vote and then agree on the result
A violation of safety, because only an algorithm may promote a follower to leader
A form of leaderless replication, since no node chooses itself as the new leader
optionExplain: A person outside the computer system makes the decision, so it is slow but it does produce a single choice.
No vote takes place; the operator decides alone from outside.
Manual failover is common and is not described as unsafe in itself.
The system still has a single leader after failover, so it is not leaderless.
questions.explain: When a single leader fails, there are three options: wait for recovery, choose by human action, or use a consensus algorithm.
questions.rule: Leader failure needs a decision from somewhere.
questions.teaches: When a single leader fails a system can wait for it to recover (and may block forever), have humans choose a new leader manually (consensus by act of God), or use a consensus algorithm to choose one automatically.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Writing the same update separately to a database and to a search index from application code keeps the two consistent.
questions.explain: Concurrent writes can reach the two stores in different orders, or one write can fail, leaving them different. The card next shows the log-based alternative.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A consumer of a log-based broker records how far it has read as an ____ in the log.
questions.explain: The offset marks the last message processed, so the consumer can resume or replay from a chosen point.
questions.rule: Offsets track progress through a log.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: An app updates its database and its cache separately, and under concurrent updates the two end up different for good. What does the book prefer?
options: Write to the cache first and the database second, so the cache stays authoritative
Add a retry loop around both writes, so the copies converge once requests slow down
Treat the database as the system of record and update the cache from its ordered change log
Let each client pick which store to write first, then repair any differences between the stores in a nightly job
optionExplain: Changing the order of two direct writes does not stop concurrent clients from interleaving them.
Retrying does not fix interleaved writes that left permanently different values.
A single ordered log gives every consumer the same sequence of changes, so the copies cannot disagree for good.
Different clients choosing different orders makes the race worse and relies on repairs.
questions.explain: The book proposes that all writes go through one system of record, with other stores derived by consuming its change log in order.
questions.rule: One writer path, many derived views.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each property into the kind of message broker it describes.

items.t: Deletes a message once a consumer acknowledges it
Keeps messages on disk so consumers can read them again
Assigns individual messages to any free consumer
Gives all messages of a partition to one consumer, in order
Suits a task queue where order of processing is unimportant
Consumers keep their place as an offset

questions.explain: An AMQP/JMS-style broker hands out and deletes individual messages; a log-based broker keeps an ordered, replayable log per partition.
questions.rule: Queue to hand out work; log to share history.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A designer says one global ordered log makes causality safe even though each service keeps its own database. What is the flaw?
options: Ordered logs are slower than databases, so causality is lost whenever throughput rises beyond what a single log handles
A log orders only reads, so writes from the services can still arrive in any order
Causality needs wall-clock timestamps, which a log cannot supply to the services
Services with separate databases share no log, so there is no common order and causal links can be lost
optionExplain: The log's speed is not the issue; the lack of a shared log is.
A log orders the writes appended to it, which is its main purpose.
Logical order from a log does not depend on wall-clock timestamps.
A shared order exists only where events pass through the same log; separate services have no such order.
questions.explain: The book notes that when services each have their own database, there is no shared order of events, so causal dependencies can be lost.
questions.rule: Causal order needs a shared order.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A new team wants a full copy of a database's contents from its change stream, years after the data was first written. What makes that possible?
options: Log compaction, which keeps the latest record per key so the stream can rebuild a view from the start
A longer retention window, since a log must keep every single change forever in order to be a complete copy
Consumer offsets, which store the database contents inside each consumer's own position
Dual writes, which copy each update to a second store as it happens
optionExplain: Compaction discards older values for a key while keeping the latest, so the log stays a full copy of the contents.
Keeping every change forever is not needed once compaction keeps the latest value per key.
An offset is only a position and holds no data.
Dual writes are the racy approach the log replaces.
questions.explain: A compacted change stream holds the current value of every key, so a new derived view can start at the beginning of the log and catch up.
questions.rule: A compacted log can rebuild any view.
questions.teaches: Log compaction allows a change stream to retain a full copy of a database's contents, so a fresh derived view can be built by consuming the log from the beginning to the present.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: A stream processing job reads its input to the end and then finishes.
questions.explain: A stream is unbounded: there may always be more events to come, so the job does not complete. The card next shows what else follows from that.
questions.rule: Unbounded input means a job that never finishes.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The input of a batch job is ____, meaning it has a fixed, known size, while a stream's input is unbounded.
questions.explain: The defining difference is that batch input is bounded and stream input is unbounded.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A fraud team must flag a card used in two countries within ten minutes, and also recompute last year's scores after a model change. Which pairing fits?
options: Flag with a nightly batch job, and recompute scores by sampling the live stream
Do both with a batch job, since streams cannot be replayed
Flag with a stream job, and recompute scores by replaying stored events through the new logic
Do both with a stream job, since stored events cannot be reprocessed
optionExplain: A nightly job is too slow for ten minutes, and sampling the live stream cannot recompute last year.
Log-based brokers can replay messages, and ten-minute detection needs continuous processing.
Flagging within minutes needs continuous processing, while recomputing history is a reprocessing of stored events.
Stored events can be reprocessed; that is how derived views are rebuilt.
questions.explain: Fresh events call for stream processing, and rederiving old output means replaying stored events through the new code, as in unified batch and stream systems.
questions.rule: Fresh needs streams; history needs replay.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each property into the kind of job it describes.

items.t: Input has a known, fixed size
Input never ends
Recovers by rerunning a failed task and discarding its partial output
Recovers with checkpoints or microbatches while running continuously
Knows when it has finished reading its input
Must handle late events that arrive after a window was thought complete

questions.explain: Boundedness explains the rest: a finite input allows rerun-and-discard recovery, while an endless one needs finer recovery and window handling.
questions.rule: Boundedness drives recovery and time handling.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A colleague says the lambda architecture is best because two systems, each simple, are simpler than one. What does the book say is wrong?
options: Maintaining the logic twice, merging two outputs and incrementalising batch runs add effort and complexity
Batch systems cannot process historical data, so the batch half does nothing useful
Stream processors already give exact results from the first event, so the batch half only repeats work that is already done
The two systems must share one disk, which the architecture cannot provide on clusters
optionExplain: The book credits the lambda idea of deriving views from immutable events, but lists practical costs of running two systems.
Batch processing is exactly what reprocesses historical data.
In the lambda design the stream layer gives quick approximate results.
The architecture does not require a shared disk; the cost is duplicated logic and merging.
questions.explain: The book names three problems: logic maintained twice, merging separate outputs, and reprocessing cost pushing the batch side towards incremental runs.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A team's dashboard shows quick approximate counts that a nightly job later replaces with exact ones. What reasoning lies behind that split?
options: Stream processors are faster at exact results, so the nightly job exists only to check them for mistakes later
Batch is thought simpler and less bug-prone, so it supplies the corrected view while the stream gives speed
Batch jobs run on live events, so they correct the dashboard as each event arrives
Approximate answers are wrong, so the stream layer must be discarded each night
optionExplain: The stream layer is the one giving approximate results here.
The design pairs a fast approximate stream layer with a slower, simpler batch layer that later corrects it.
Batch jobs read bounded input, not live events.
Approximate results are kept until the batch result replaces them.
questions.explain: In the lambda design the stream layer gives quick approximate updates and the batch layer later produces a corrected version of the same view.
questions.teaches: In the lambda architecture the stream processor quickly produces an approximate update and the batch processor later consumes the same events to produce a corrected version, on the reasoning that batch is simpler and less prone to bugs.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: In most applications a short delay before an update becomes visible is worse than permanently missing or contradictory data.
questions.explain: A delay fixes itself by waiting; corrupted or lost data does not. The card next shows how the author separates the two.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The author uses the term ____ for the absence of corruption, data loss and contradictory data.
questions.explain: The author splits consistency into timeliness (up-to-date views) and integrity (no corruption, loss or contradiction).
questions.rule: Integrity: not corrupted, lost or contradictory.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A hotel site sells rooms in two regions that sync asynchronously, and the last room is sold twice. What does the book's approach suggest?
options: Reject all bookings until both regions agree on every room, since any oversell is unacceptable
Delete the second booking silently, since a guest cannot object to what they never saw
Disable asynchronous sync, since timeliness matters more than integrity in most applications that sell rooms
Accept bookings optimistically, check afterwards, and compensate the second guest if the apology is cheap
optionExplain: That coordination would reduce availability and may cause more apologies for outages.
Hiding the change loses a booking silently, which harms integrity.
The author argues the opposite: integrity matters more than timeliness.
A compensating apology is often cheaper than coordinating every booking, as long as no confirmed booking is lost.
questions.explain: The author notes that many businesses already overbook and compensate, and that whether the apology cost is acceptable is a business decision.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each problem into a timeliness problem or an integrity problem.

items.t: A transaction made an hour ago does not yet show on the statement
The statement balance differs from the sum of its transactions
A guest is charged but the merchant is never paid
A user's own profile edit is missing after a refresh
An index lacks records that exist in the database
A reader sees a replica that is a few seconds behind

questions.explain: Delays that disappear on their own are timeliness; permanent errors in sums, lost money or missing index entries are integrity.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A payment is retried after a timeout, and the retry crosses browser, server and database. Without a unique operation id, what can happen?
options: TCP removes the duplicate, because it suppresses repeats across every hop
Any hop can repeat the request, so the payment may be applied twice
The database detects the repeat through its transaction, so the payment is applied once
The second request is dropped, since retries carry the same timestamp as the original
optionExplain: TCP suppresses duplicates only within a single connection.
Each hop can retry independently, and no single layer sees the whole chain, so only an id carried end to end can identify a duplicate.
The two attempts may arrive in separate transactions, which the database cannot link.
Timestamps are not a reliable duplicate marker; a client-generated operation id is.
questions.explain: A client-generated operation id passed through all levels allows end-to-end duplicate suppression and idempotence.
questions.rule: Carry one id end to end.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A ticket company considers a global lock on every seat sale across continents. According to the book, what trade-off does that coordination create?
options: It reduces apologies for oversold seats but can add apologies for outages, so aim for a balanced sweet spot
It removes apologies altogether, since a global lock guarantees that no seat can ever be oversold
It adds apologies for oversold seats while removing all outage apologies from the system
It has no effect on availability, because locks are held only during the very short sale itself
optionExplain: Coordination cuts inconsistencies but can cut availability, so the number of apologies has two sources.
Apologies cannot be reduced to zero: outages and failures still happen.
Locking cannot add oversells; the effect on outages runs in the opposite direction.
Cross-continent locks wait on slow or cut links, which hurts availability.
questions.explain: Coordination and constraints reduce inconsistency apologies but can lower performance and availability, which raises outage apologies.
questions.rule: Balance inconsistency apologies against outage apologies.
questions.teaches: Coordination reduces the apologies owed for inconsistencies but can reduce performance and availability and so increase the apologies owed for outages; the aim is the sweet spot with neither too many inconsistencies nor too many availability problems.

questions.q: In the diagram, a client writes a record through the API. Put the steps in the order the arrows show.
items: The request enters through the API to application code
Application code sends the write to the primary database
Other application code captures the changes to data
The cache is invalidated or updated and the search index gets updates
questions.explain: The diagram shows the write going to the primary database first; a separate piece of application code then captures the change and pushes it on to the cache and the full-text index.
questions.rule: Application code keeps caches and indexes in sync with the main database.

media.alt: Diagram of a combined data system inside a dashed boundary. A client calls through an API into application code. Application code reads an in-memory cache, sends cache misses and writes to a primary database, sends search requests to a full-text index, and sends asynchronous tasks to a message queue. Other application code captures changes from the primary database, then invalidates or updates the cache and applies updates to the search index. The queue feeds further application code that sends email to the outside world.

questions.q: In the diagram, a user requests the home timeline. Which work does that read perform?
options: It reads only that user's own prepared list of tweets
It finds the accounts the user follows and merges their tweets
It copies the new tweet into each follower's list
It scans the all-tweets list for the followed senders
optionExplain: Right: in the diagram each recipient has a ready list, and the read arrow points at it alone.
This describes approach 1, where reads do the lookup and merge; the diagram moves that work to post time.
Copying into follower lists happens when a tweet is posted, shown on the left, not on a read.
Scanning the global list is how reads work in approach 1; here the reads go to per-recipient lists.
questions.explain: In the diagram the home-timeline read arrows go to each recipient's own list, so a read is cheap. The heavy copying happens at post time.
questions.rule: Fan-out on write moves work from reads to posts.

media.alt: Fan-out pipeline: a user posts a tweet at 4.6k writes per second into an All tweets list. Arrows fan out from it to separate timeline lists for recipients 1, 2 and 3, labelled up to 31M followers per user and 345k writes per second. At the right, users get their home timeline from their own list, labelled 300k reads per second.

questions.q: True or false: In the diagram, the mean line sits above the median line because a few very slow requests pull the mean upward.
questions.explain: A few tall bars reach the 95th and 99th percentile levels. They raise the mean but barely change the median, which is the middle of the sorted times.
questions.rule: Outliers pull the mean up; the median is not moved by them.

media.alt: Bar chart of response time for about 100 requests along the horizontal axis, most bars short and a few tall. Dotted horizontal lines mark the median (p50) at the lowest level, the mean (average) slightly above it, then the 95th percentile and the 99th percentile near the top. Only a few bars reach above the 95th line.

questions.q: In the diagram, backend 6 speeds up from 487 ms to 90 ms and nothing else changes. How long does the end-user request take now?
options: About 90 ms, because the changed call now sets the pace
About 143 ms, set by the slowest of the seven calls
About 723 ms, because the seven call times add together
About 103 ms, the average of the seven call times
optionExplain: The changed call is now fast, so it no longer sets the pace; the request waits for the slowest call.
Right: the calls run in parallel, so the request ends when the slowest, now backend 4 at 143 ms, returns.
Adding times fits calls made one after another; the diagram shows them in parallel.
An average hides the wait: the user cannot be served until the slowest call returns.
questions.explain: The end-user request in the diagram lasts until the slowest parallel call finishes. After the change that is 143 ms.
questions.rule: A request that fans out waits for its slowest call.

media.alt: A web application sends one request each to seven backends, each with its own database. Response times shown are 92, 76, 103, 143, 86, 487 and 133 ms. At top left, a bar for the end-user request spans from the start to the end of the longest bar, 487 ms.

questions.q: In the diagram's relational schema, Bill adds a third job. What changes in the tables?
options: His users row gains a third job column holding the title
A row is added to the regions table pointing at his user_id
A row is added to the positions table carrying his user_id 251
The industries table gains a row, one for each new organization
optionExplain: Columns hold one-per-user facts; a repeating job cannot be a new column for each person.
The regions table lists places and holds no user_id, so it records nothing about jobs.
Right: each job is a row in positions with user_id 251 as a foreign key to the users table.
The industries table lists industry names; organizations are stored in the positions rows.
questions.explain: One-to-many data lives in separate tables with a foreign key. Each job is a new positions row whose user_id is 251.
questions.rule: Repeating items become rows in a child table with a foreign key.

media.alt: A LinkedIn profile for Bill Gates on the left and, on the right, its relational tables. The users table row 251 has region_id us:91 and industry_id 131 pointing to the regions and industries tables. The positions, education and contact_info tables each have several rows carrying user_id 251, one row per job, school or contact.

questions.q: In the diagram, going from the Idaho box up to the North America box crosses ____ within edges.
questions.explain: Idaho is within United States, and United States is within North America, so two within edges are crossed.
questions.rule: Graph queries follow chains of edges of varying length.

media.alt: Graph of boxes with properties. Lucy and Alain, type person, are linked by married. Lucy is born_in Idaho (state) and lives_in London (city). Alain lives_in London and is born_in Beaune. Within arrows chain Idaho to United States to North America, London to England to United Kingdom to Europe, and Beaune to Cote-d'Or to Burgundy to France to Europe.

questions.q: In the diagram, which row is new after rule 2 is applied the second time?
options: usa with North America
idaho with United States
namerica with North America
idaho with North America
optionExplain: This row was already added the first time rule 2 was applied.
This row is shaded in the middle table, so it came from the first application.
Rule 1 created this row, and it appears in the first table.
Right: the second pass joins idaho's parent usa with usa's new North America row.
questions.explain: The third table gains only idaho with North America. It is derived from within(idaho, usa) and the row usa with North America from the first pass.
questions.rule: Rules are applied repeatedly until no new facts appear.

media.alt: Three tables named within_recursive with columns Location and Name. After rule 1 there are three rows: namerica North America, usa United States, idaho Idaho. After rule 2 once, usa North America and idaho United States are added. After rule 2 twice, idaho North America is added. Dashed lines link rows between tables.

questions.q: In the diagram, a new record for key 42 is appended at the end of the file. What happens to the hash map and the file?
options: Both map offsets are recomputed because the file grew, so key 123456 also receives a new offset.
Only the entry for key 42 changes to the new record's offset; the old record stays in the file.
Only the entry for key 42 changes, and the old record at offset 64 is erased in place.
The map gains a second entry for key 42, so offset 64 and the new offset both remain.
questions.explain: The map keeps one offset per key and is updated to the newest record. The file is only appended to, so the old record stays until compaction removes it.
optionExplain: Tempting because the file grew, but appending does not move earlier records, so other offsets stay valid.
Right: one map entry per key points to the newest record, and old records are left alone in the log.
Tempting as an update in place, but a log-structured file is append-only and never overwrites old bytes.
Plausible as keeping history, but a hash map holds a single value per key, which is the latest offset.
questions.rule: A hash index points each key at its newest record; old records wait for compaction.

media.alt: Diagram: an in-memory hash map with two rows, key 123456 at byte offset 0 and key 42 at byte offset 64, each with an arrow down to a log-structured file on disk drawn as one box per byte. The file holds the text of two records, one per key: JSON documents for London and San Francisco, each ending in a newline. Arrows land on the first byte of each record.

questions.q: In the diagram, yawn: 511 occurs only in segment 1 and scratch: 252 only in segment 2. What does the merged segment do with them?
options: It drops both entries, because keys that are not repeated across segments count as stale data.
It keeps only scratch, because merging prefers whatever the newer segment contributes to the result.
It keeps both, because only older values of a repeated key are thrown away during a merge.
It keeps both but marks them as deletion markers until the next compaction decides their fate.
questions.explain: Merging discards only values superseded by a newer value for the same key. A key found in a single segment has no newer value, so its entry survives.
optionExplain: Plausible if merging were pruning by age, but it only removes duplicates, not unique keys.
Tempting because newer wins for repeated keys, but yawn has no newer competitor, so it stays too.
Right: an entry is dropped only when a more recent value for the same key exists.
Confuses merging with deletion; deletion markers are a separate mechanism written by delete requests.
questions.rule: Merging keeps the latest value of every key and discards only superseded ones.

media.alt: Diagram: data file segment 1 (mew 1078 up to 1082, purr 2103 to 2108, yawn 511) and data file segment 2 (purr 2109 to 2114, mew 1083 to 1087, scratch 252) both feed arrows into a compaction and merging process. It outputs merged segments 1 and 2: yawn: 511, scratch: 252, mew: 1087, purr: 2114.

questions.q: In the diagram, which lookups would start scanning the segment at offset 102134, the handbag entry?
options: hammer
handbag
handkerchief
handsome
handstand
questions.explain: Keys are sorted, so a lookup starts at the nearest index entry at or before the key. Handbag and handkerchief fall from handbag up to before handsome; hammer starts at hammock and the others at handsome.
optionExplain: Hammer sorts between hammock and handbag, so its scan starts at the hammock offset instead.
Right: handbag has its own index entry, so scanning starts exactly there.
Right: handkerchief sorts after handbag and before handsome, so the handbag entry is the nearest earlier one.
Handsome has its own index entry at 104667, so its scan starts there rather than at handbag.
Handstand sorts after handsome, so its nearest earlier index entry is handsome, not handbag.
questions.rule: With a sparse index, start at the nearest earlier indexed key and scan forward.

media.alt: Diagram: a sparse in-memory index with rows hammock 100491, handbag 102134, handsome 104667 and hangout 106812, with arrows into a sorted segment file (SSTable) on disk. Between handbag and handsome lies a shaded compressible block of sorted entries from handbag to handprinted; handsome starts the next block.

questions.q: In the diagram, key 334 is added to a leaf with no spare space. What changes in the parent page?
options: Nothing changes, because the full leaf grows longer to hold the extra key.
Key 334 becomes a boundary key, replacing 333 so that the lower range starts there.
The parent page itself is split first, so the leaf can keep its current layout.
A new boundary key 337 appears, with one reference to each of the two halves.
questions.explain: The leaf is split into two pages and the parent records the new boundary key between them. The parent had spare space, so it does not need to split.
optionExplain: Pages have a fixed size, so a full leaf cannot grow; it has to be split instead.
Boundary keys come from the split point of the leaf, not from the key being inserted.
The parent only splits when it too runs out of room; here the diagram shows it has spare space.
Right: the split adds a boundary key and a second child reference to the parent page.
questions.rule: A full page splits in two and the parent gains a boundary key.

media.alt: Diagram in two parts: a parent page with keys 310, 333, 345 and spare space, whose child leaf holds keys 333, 335, 337, 340, 342 with no room. After adding key 334, the leaf is split into two leaves, 333 to 335 and 337 to 342, and the parent gains boundary key 337 pointing to both.

questions.q: True or false: In the diagram, the business analyst's query goes to the Sales DB, Inventory DB and Geo DB directly.
questions.explain: The analyst's query arrow points only to the data warehouse. The OLTP databases are copied into it by extract, transform and load steps, so analytic queries do not disturb them.
questions.rule: Analysts query the warehouse, not the live OLTP databases.

media.alt: Diagram: three users (customer, warehouse worker, truck driver) each use an OLTP system (ecommerce site with Sales DB, stock-keeping app with Inventory DB, vehicle route planner with Geo DB). Each database goes through extract, a transform box and load into one data warehouse; a business analyst sends a query arrow to the warehouse only.

questions.section: Stars and Snowflakes: Schemas for Analytics
questions.q: In the diagram, the first fact_sales row has product_sk 31, store_sk 3, and NULL promotion and customer. What does it record?
options: One Fish food sold in Palo Alto on 2 January 2014, with no promotion and no known customer.
One Bananas sold in Seattle on 2 January 2014, with the promotion and customer not yet looked up.
One Fish food sold in San Francisco to a named customer who used a direct mail promotion.
A new Fish food product added to the product table, still waiting for store and customer values.
questions.explain: Each fact row is one event; its sk columns point to dimension rows. Product 31 is Fish food, store 3 is Palo Alto, and a NULL means no promotion or customer applies.
optionExplain: Right: follow product_sk to Fish food, store_sk to Palo Alto, date_key to 2 January; NULLs mean none.
Bananas is product 30 and Seattle is store 1, so this reads the wrong dimension rows.
San Francisco is store 2, and a NULL customer means no customer is recorded for the sale.
Fact rows record sales events; products are added to dim_product, not as fact rows.
questions.rule: Each fact row is one event whose key columns point to dimension rows.

media.alt: Diagram of a star schema: a central fact_sales table (date_key, product_sk, store_sk, promotion_sk, customer_sk, quantity, net_price, discount_price) with arrows from its key columns to dim_product, dim_store, dim_date, dim_customer and dim_promotion tables. The first fact row is date 140102, product 31 (Fish food), store 3 (Palo Alto), NULL promotion, NULL customer, quantity 1, price 2.49.

questions.q: In the diagram, product_sk 69 has run-length encoding 0, 4, 12, 2 over 18 rows. Where does 69 occur?
options: In the first 4 rows and the last 2 rows, with 12 other values in between.
In 4 rows, then 12 rows, then 2 rows, so 69 fills 18 rows in total.
In row 4 and row 12 only, because the numbers give row positions of each match.
In the middle 12 rows, framed by 4 non-matching rows and 2 more rows after.
questions.explain: Run lengths alternate zeros and ones, starting with zeros: 0 zeros, 4 ones, 12 zeros, 2 ones. So 69 fills the first 4 and last 2 of the 18 rows.
optionExplain: Right: runs alternate zeros then ones, so 0 zeros, 4 ones, 12 zeros, 2 ones.
Treats every run as a match, but runs alternate between rows without the value and rows with it.
The numbers are run lengths, not row positions, so they do not name individual rows.
Reads the first run as a run of ones; runs start with zeros, so the 12 are zeros, not matches.
questions.rule: Run-length encoding alternates runs of zeros and ones, starting with zeros.

media.alt: Diagram: a product_sk column of 18 values (69 69 69 69 74 31 31 31 31 29 30 30 31 31 31 68 69 69). Below, one row of 18 zero or one boxes per distinct value (29, 30, 31, 68, 69, 74), with ones where that value occurs, then run-length encodings such as 31 as 5, 4, 3, 3 and 69 as 0, 4, 12, 2.

questions.section: Aggregation: Data Cubes and Materialized Views
questions.q: In the diagram, which cell answers the bottom-left query, total net_price for product_sk 32 over all dates?
options: The 149.60 cell in the first row, since it belongs to product 32.
The 40710.53 cell in the right-hand total column for date 140101.
The 14967.09 cell in the bottom total row, under the product 32 column.
The 132.18 cell in the second row, because it is the latest value for product 32.
questions.explain: The cube precomputes sums along each dimension. Summing down the product 32 column over all dates gives the bottom-row total, so the query reads one cell.
optionExplain: That cell is only product 32 on one date, not the sum over all dates.
That total is for a single date across all products, which answers a different query.
Right: the bottom row holds per-product totals summed over all dates.
That is one date's value for product 32; cells are not latest values and are not summed alone.
questions.rule: A cube stores sums along dimensions, so a matching total is one lookup.

media.alt: Diagram of a grid: rows are date_key (140101 to 140104), columns are product_sk (32 to 35), each cell holds a sum of net_price, for example 149.60 for 140101 and product 32. A right column totals each date (140101 is 40710.53) and a bottom row totals each product (32 is 14967.09). Three SQL SUM queries point at a cell, the right total and the bottom total.

questions.q: In the MessagePack breakdown, what does each of the three fields still carry that Thrift and Protocol Buffers replace with a number?
questions.explain: MessagePack stores every field name as text with a length byte, which is why it saves little over JSON (66 bytes here).
questions.rule: Binary JSON encodings keep field names in the data.

media.alt: MessagePack encoding of the example record, 66 bytes. A hex byte sequence is shown, then a breakdown: an object marker with 3 entries, then the strings userName, favoriteNumber and interests each with a length byte and the field name spelled in characters, followed by values: Martin, 1337 as uint16 (05 39), and an array of 2 strings, daydreaming and hacking.

options: A numeric field tag stored beside the type byte
The field name spelled out as characters after a length byte
A schema version number stored at the start of the object
A pointer to a shared dictionary of field names
optionExplain: Field tags belong to Thrift and Protocol Buffers; the MessagePack breakdown shows names instead of tags.
The diagram shows userName, favoriteNumber and interests spelled out as bytes after length markers, which is the cost of keeping names.
No version number appears in the byte sequence; the object marker only gives the entry count of 3.
There is no dictionary in the diagram; each name is written in full inside the record itself.

questions.q: In the Thrift BinaryProtocol breakdown, order the parts of the first field (the string Martin) from first byte to last.
questions.explain: Each field starts with a type byte and a field tag, and a string then carries its length before its characters.
questions.rule: A tagged field is type, tag, then value.

media.alt: Thrift BinaryProtocol encoding of the example record, 59 bytes. The breakdown lists each field as a type byte, a two-byte field tag (1, 2, 3), then the value: string Martin with a four-byte length 6, an i64 holding 1337 in eight bytes, and a list of 2 strings, daydreaming and hacking, each with a four-byte length. A final zero byte ends the struct.

items: Type byte (string)
Field tag 1
Length 6
The characters of Martin

questions.q: In the CompactProtocol diagram, how are field tag and type stored compared with BinaryProtocol?
questions.explain: CompactProtocol packs the tag and type into a single byte, one reason the record shrinks from 59 to 34 bytes.
questions.rule: CompactProtocol saves space by packing small values together.

media.alt: Thrift CompactProtocol encoding of the example record, 34 bytes. Each field starts with one byte whose bit pattern packs the field tag (shown as an increment from the previous one) beside the type. Martin has a one-byte length 6. The number 1337 is packed into two bytes by a variable-length integer with a sign bit. The list header byte holds 2 items and item type string. Strings carry one-byte lengths, and a zero byte ends the struct.

options: Both share one byte, with the tag shown as an increment
The type is dropped, and only a two-byte field tag is kept
Tag and type each keep a full byte but the lengths shrink
Tags are removed and fields are found by their order
optionExplain: Correct: the diagram shows a byte whose bits hold the tag increment and the type side by side.
The type is still present; in fact the type nibble such as 8 for string appears in each header byte.
This describes BinaryProtocol more closely, which uses a type byte plus a two-byte tag, and so is larger.
Ordering without tags is the Avro approach; here tag increments are still encoded in every header byte.

questions.q: In the schema diagram, match each field to what the Avro reader does with it.
questions.explain: Avro resolves by field name: writer-only fields are ignored, reader-only fields take their default, and position does not matter.
questions.rule: Avro schema resolution matches fields by name.

media.alt: Two tables side by side, writer's schema and reader's schema for a Person record, each with datatype and field name columns. Writer: string userName, union of null and long favoriteNumber, array of string interests, string photoURL. Reader: long userID, union of null and int favoriteNumber, string userName, array of string interests. Arrows join userName, favoriteNumber and interests across the two tables even though their row positions differ. photoURL and userID have no arrow.

questions.q: In the diagram, the stored record loses photoURL. Which step causes the loss?
questions.explain: The old code decodes into a model object with no photoURL field, then encodes from that object, so the field is never written back.
questions.rule: Unknown fields vanish if code round-trips through a model object that lacks them.

media.alt: Data loss with an old application. A database holds a JSON record with userName, favoriteNumber, interests and photoURL, written by newer code. Old Java Person class code, which has no photoURL field, reads and decodes it into a model object, calls setFavoriteNumber(42), then re-encodes it to JSON and writes it back. The stored record now lacks photoURL, which the diagram labels as lost.

options: The database discards unknown keys when it receives a write
The new code wrote photoURL in a format old code cannot parse
The setFavoriteNumber call replaces the whole stored document
Decoding into a model object that has no photoURL field, then re-encoding it
optionExplain: The database stores whatever it is given; the loss happens before the write, inside the application.
The record decodes fine in the diagram, since the other fields survive; only the unknown one is dropped.
The setter only changes the favoriteNumber field of the object; it does not touch other fields.
Correct: the old Person class cannot hold photoURL, so the re-encoded JSON omits it.

questions.q: In the diagram, a user writes to partition 4. Which nodes receive that write through replication streams?
questions.explain: Partition 4's leader is on node 4; its followers are on nodes 2 and 3, so those receive the replication streams.
questions.rule: Each partition has its own leader and followers, spread over different nodes.

media.alt: Four nodes, each holding three partition replicas. Node 1 holds partition 1 leader and partition 2 and 3 followers; node 2 holds partition 2 follower, 3 leader, 4 follower; node 3 holds partition 1 follower, 2 leader, 4 follower; node 4 holds partition 1 and 3 followers and partition 4 leader. Arrows show replication streams from each leader to its followers. A user writes to partition 4 at node 4.

options: Nodes 1 and 3, as the nodes holding follower copies
Nodes 1, 2 and 3, since every other node copies each write
Nodes 2 and 3, which hold followers of partition 4
Node 4 only, because the leader keeps all copies
optionExplain: Node 1 holds no copy of partition 4; its replicas are partitions 1, 2 and 3.
Replication goes only to the followers of that partition, not to every other node in the cluster.
Correct: nodes 2 and 3 each hold a partition 4 follower, so the arrows from node 4 end there.
Node 4 is the leader, but followers on other nodes exist so the data survives node failure.

questions.q: True or false: In the diagram, a query for every reading from 17:08:10 to 17:08:15 can be answered by a single partition.
questions.explain: Hashing scatters neighbouring timestamps across p0, p2, p3, p6 and p7, so a range query must reach several partitions.
questions.rule: Hash partitioning loses key order, so range queries spread out.

media.alt: Six consecutive one-second timestamps, 17:08:10 to 17:08:15, each hashed with the first two bytes of MD5 to a number between 0 and 65,535, drawn against eight equal partitions p0 to p7. Values 7,372, 18,805, 50,537, 31,579, 62,253 and 24,510 land in p0, p2, p6, p3, p7 and p2 respectively, so neighbouring timestamps end up in scattered partitions.

questions.q: In the diagram, why must the red-car query contact both partitions?
questions.explain: Each partition indexes only its own documents, so red cars may sit in any partition.
questions.rule: A document-partitioned index covers only the documents in its own partition.

media.alt: Two partitions, each with a primary key index of car records (id to colour, make, location) and its own secondary indexes on colour and make, covering only its own cars. Partition 0 lists colour:red as 191 and 306; partition 1 lists colour:red as 768. A user asking for a red car sends a scatter/gather read to both partitions.

options: Colour entries are split by colour, so red appears in each
The primary key index cannot be searched by colour at all
Each partition indexes only its own cars, so red ones can be anywhere
Both partitions must confirm a result before it is returned
optionExplain: Splitting by colour describes a term-partitioned index, not this local one where each partition lists all its colours.
The primary index is separate; the secondary index on colour exists in each partition and can be searched there.
Correct: partition 0 holds red cars 191 and 306, partition 1 holds 768, so both must be asked.
There is no confirmation step; the results are gathered and combined from both partitions.

questions.q: In the diagram, car 768 is stored on partition 1. What follows for a write that adds or changes this car?
questions.explain: Its colour:red entry lives in partition 0, so the write may touch an index partition other than the one holding the car.
questions.rule: A term-partitioned index makes reads cheap but a single write may touch several partitions.

media.alt: Two partitions with primary key indexes of car records and secondary indexes partitioned by term. Partition 0 holds colour:black, colour:red, make:Audi, make:Dodge, make:Ford; partition 1 holds colour:silver, colour:yellow, make:Honda, make:Volvo. Colour:red in partition 0 lists 191, 306 and 768, though 768 is stored in partition 1. Dashed arrows show records pointing to index entries in the other partition. A red-car query goes to partition 0 only.

options: The write may also update index entries held on another partition
The write stays on partition 1 because index and data are kept together
The write must be copied to every partition to keep indexes aligned
The write is slower only because partition 1 holds two colours
optionExplain: Correct: the red entry for 768 sits in partition 0, so updating the index reaches across partitions.
That describes the document-partitioned index; in this diagram the red entry is on a different partition.
