Only the partitions holding the affected terms are touched, not all of them, so a full copy is not needed.
The cost comes from the index entry living elsewhere, not from how many colours one partition holds.

questions.q: In the diagram, adding node 4 moves ____ partitions in total.
questions.explain: Four partitions (p4, p9, p14, p19) move, one from each old node, and the rest stay put.
questions.rule: With many fixed partitions, a new node steals a few whole partitions.

media.alt: Before and after rebalancing. Four nodes (0 to 3) hold partitions p0 to p19, five each. After a fifth node is added, nodes 0 to 3 keep four partitions each and node 4 holds p4, p9, p14 and p19. Dashed lines mark partitions staying on the same node; four solid arrows show those partitions migrating, one from each old node, to node 4.

questions.q: In the three routing panels, match each approach to where the partition knowledge lives.
questions.explain: The hatched fill marks the knowledge: in the nodes in panel 1, a separate routing tier in panel 2, and the client in panel 3.
questions.rule: The three routing approaches differ in who knows the partition assignment.

media.alt: Three numbered panels showing a client getting key foo, stored on node 2. In 1, the client contacts node 0 at random, which holds partition knowledge and forwards to node 2. In 2, the client asks a routing tier that holds the knowledge and sends the request to node 2. In 3, the client holds the knowledge and connects directly to node 2. A hatched fill marks where that knowledge lives.

pairs: Client contacts any node at random, which forwards
Client sends all requests to a routing tier
Knowledge held by the routing tier
Client connects directly to the owning node

questions.q: In the diagram, which pair of simultaneous machine failures still leaves every stored document available on some machine?
options: Partition 1, Replica 1 and Partition 1, Replica 2
Partition 2, Replica 1 and Partition 2, Replica 2
Partition 1, Replica 2 and Partition 2, Replica 1
Any two machines, because each document sits on two machines so one copy always remains
questions.explain: Each partition holds different documents, and each has two replicas. Losing both replicas of one partition loses its documents; losing one replica from each partition loses nothing.
optionExplain: Both replicas of partition 1 would be gone, so keys 136, 211 and 377 vanish.
Both replicas of partition 2 would be gone, so keys 629, 696 and 858 vanish.
Each partition keeps one surviving replica, so every document is still stored somewhere.
This ignores that the two copies of a document live in the same partition, so losing both machines loses it.
questions.rule: Replicas protect a partition only while at least one of its own copies survives.

media.alt: Four boxes in two columns. The left column is Partition 1 with Replica 1 above Replica 2; the right is Partition 2 with Replica 1 above Replica 2. Partition 1 boxes each hold three documents keyed 136, 211 and 377; Partition 2 boxes hold 629, 696 and 858. A dashed double-headed arrow labelled copy of the same data joins the two replicas of each partition.

questions.q: In the diagram, put these events in the order they happen, earliest first.
items: User 1234 sends the update to the leader
The leader sends the data change to follower 1 and follower 2
Follower 1 sends ok to the leader
The leader sends ok to user 1234
Follower 2 sends its ok to the leader
questions.explain: The leader waits only for the synchronous follower, follower 1, before telling the user. Follower 2 is asynchronous, so its confirmation arrives after the user has already been told.
questions.rule: With one synchronous follower, the user's ok does not wait for the asynchronous ones.

media.alt: Timeline with time running left to right and lanes for user 1234, leader, follower 1 and follower 2. The user sends an update to the leader, which sends a data change to both followers and waits. Follower 1 replies ok, and then the leader sends ok to the user. Follower 2's ok reaches the leader later, after the user already has its ok.

questions.q: In the diagram, user 1234 reads no results for a comment it inserted moments ago. Which sequence explains it?
options: The leader rejected the insert, so no copy of the comment exists on any node
The select reached follower 2 before the leader's copy of the insert arrived there
The select went to the leader, which had not yet applied the insert it acknowledged
Follower 1 overwrote the comment with older data shortly before the select arrived
questions.explain: The insert was acknowledged by the leader, but the copy to follower 2 was still in transit when the read arrived. The user's own write is invisible to that read.
optionExplain: The user received insert ok, so the leader accepted the write and has the comment.
Replication to follower 2 lags, so a read there precedes the insert; this is the stale read shown.
A leader applies a write before acknowledging it, so reading the leader would find the comment.
Followers only apply the leader's changes in order; nothing here overwrites a newer value with an older one.
questions.rule: A read from a lagging follower can miss the user's own acknowledged write.

media.alt: Timeline with lanes for user 1234, leader, follower 1 and follower 2. The user sends an insert of a comment to the leader and gets insert ok. The leader sends the insert to both followers, but the copy to follower 2 travels slowly. The user's select for that comment goes to follower 2 and returns no results before the insert arrives there.

questions.q: True or false: In the diagram, user 2345's second query returns nothing because the comment was deleted from follower 1 after the first query.
questions.explain: Nothing is deleted. The second query went to follower 2, which had not yet received the insert, while the first went to follower 1, which had.
questions.rule: Reads from replicas with different lag can make data seem to vanish.

media.alt: Timeline with lanes for user 1234, leader, follower 1, follower 2 and user 2345. User 1234 inserts a comment on the leader, which sends the insert to both followers; the copy reaching follower 2 arrives late. User 2345 first runs a select against follower 1 and gets 1 result, then runs the same select against follower 2 and gets no results.

questions.q: In the diagram, why does the observer hear the answer before the question?
options: Mrs. Cake spoke before Mr. Poons had finished asking, so the answer really came first
Partition 2's leader accepted the answer before it knew the question had been written anywhere
The observer read from a leader in one partition and a follower in the other partition
The question reached the observer through a lagging follower, after the answer arrived by a faster one
questions.explain: The two partitions replicate independently. The follower relaying the question lagged more than the follower relaying the answer, so the effect is seen before its cause.
optionExplain: The diagram shows Mrs. Cake answering only after she heard the question.
Leaders do not need to see the other partition's data; the lag is in the followers.
Both copies the observer sees come from followers, not from a leader.
Different lag in two independent partitions reorders what the observer sees.
questions.rule: Independent partitions have no shared order, so lag can reverse cause and effect.

media.alt: Timeline with lanes for Mr. Poons, partition 1 leader, partition 1 follower, Mrs. Cake, partition 2 leader, partition 2 follower and an observer. Mr. Poons's question goes to the partition 1 leader and to Mrs. Cake, whose answer goes to the partition 2 leader. The answer reaches the observer through partition 2's follower first; the question arrives later through partition 1's follower.

questions.q: In the diagram, which claim about the two writes is wrong?
options: Leader 1 refuses user 1's write because it detects the conflict before replying ok
Both users receive ok before either leader has seen the other user's change
Each leader notices the conflict only when the other leader's change arrives
Without resolution, leader 1 would hold title B while leader 2 holds title C
questions.explain: Each write succeeds locally and is acknowledged. The conflict appears only later, asynchronously, when the leaders exchange their changes.
optionExplain: Both users get ok, so the conflict is not detected at write time; this claim is false.
This is true: each user is acknowledged by their own leader first.
This is true: the conflict messages appear after the change arrives from the other leader.
This is true: each leader applied its own write, so their titles differ until resolved.
questions.rule: In multi-leader replication, conflicts are detected after both writes are acknowledged.

media.alt: Timeline with lanes for user 1, leader 1, leader 2 and user 2. A page with id 123 starts with title A. User 1 sets the title to B on leader 1 and user 2 sets it to C on leader 2; each gets ok. The leaders then send each other the change messages (old A, new B and old A, new C), and each reports a conflict on receiving the other's.

questions.q: True or false: In the diagram, client B's update does not depend on client A's insert, because they are sent to different leaders.
questions.explain: B increments the value that A inserted, so the update depends on the insert even though the two clients used different leaders. Leader 2 receives them in the wrong order.
questions.rule: A dependency between writes does not disappear because they enter at different leaders.

media.alt: Timeline with client A, leaders 1, 2 and 3, and client B. Client A inserts key x with value 1 on leader 1 and gets ok; leader 1 sends the insert to leaders 2 and 3. Client B updates x to value plus one on leader 3, which sends update value 2 to leaders 1 and 2. At leader 2 a shaded box marks the update arriving before the insert.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: In the diagram, which step brings replica 3 back up to date after it was offline?
options: User 2345 writes the version 7 value to replica 3 after seeing its old version 6 in a read
Replica 3 pulls the newer value from replica 1 when it comes back online
The original write by user 1234 is retried automatically against replica 3
A leader replays its log to replica 3 once the node is reachable
questions.explain: The reader noticed replica 3's stale version 6 in the responses and wrote the newer value back to it. That is read repair.
optionExplain: The reader compares versions and writes the newer value back; this is read repair.
A background process pulling data would be anti-entropy, which the diagram does not show.
The diagram shows no retry by user 1234; their write to replica 3 was lost.
A leaderless database has no leader or log replay, and none appears in the diagram.
questions.rule: A client that sees a stale response during a read can write the newer value back.

media.alt: Timeline with user 1234, replicas 1, 2 and 3, and user 2345. User 1234 sets a profile picture; replicas 1 and 2 answer ok, while replica 3 is marked node offline and the write to it is lost. User 2345 then reads all three: replicas 1 and 2 return me-new.jpg version 7, replica 3 returns me-old.jpg version 6. User 2345 then sends a set with version 7 to replica 3, which answers ok.

questions.section: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
questions.q: In the diagram, the replicas written and the replicas read overlap at replica number ____.
questions.explain: Writes succeeded on replicas 1, 2 and 3, and reads succeeded on replicas 3, 4 and 5. Since w + r > n, the two sets must share a node, here replica 3.
questions.rule: When w + r > n, a read set always overlaps a successful write set.

media.alt: Five replicas in a row with n = 5. A writer above reaches replicas 1, 2 and 3 (w = 3 successful writes, outlined) while the arrows to replicas 4 and 5 are crossed out. A reader below fails to reach replicas 1 and 2 (crossed out) but reads replicas 3, 4 and 5 (r = 3 successful reads, outlined). The two outlines overlap at replica 3.

questions.q: In the diagram, node 2 holds B and node 3 holds A. What accounts for the difference?
options: Client B's write was lost on node 3 because node 3 was marked unresponsive
The nodes received the two writes in opposite orders and each kept the last to arrive
Node 2 is the only one that checks which client wrote first and keeps that value
Client A's write failed on node 2, so only B's value could be stored there
questions.explain: Node 2 received A then B and node 3 received B then A. Each simply overwrote on arrival, so replicas permanently disagree.
optionExplain: The unresponsive node in the diagram is node 1, not node 3.
Different arrival order combined with overwrite-on-arrival leaves each node with a different value.
Nothing in the diagram shows any node comparing writers; each overwrites on arrival.
Node 2 acknowledged A first; its write to node 2 did arrive before B.
questions.rule: Overwriting on arrival makes replicas depend on message order.

media.alt: Timeline with client A, nodes 1, 2 and 3, and client B. Client A sends set X = A and client B sends set X = B to all three nodes, but node 1 is marked unresponsive and B's write to it is lost. Node 2 receives A then B; node 3 receives B then A. A later get X by client B returns A from node 1, B from node 2 and A from node 3.

questions.q: In the diagram, client 1 writes [milk, flour] with version 1, yet the reply still lists [eggs]. Why?
options: The server merges every incoming write with all values it already holds
The write overwrote only values up to version 1, and [eggs] was stored afterward as version 2
Client 2's write was acknowledged first and so always wins over client 1
The server kept [eggs] because it is shorter than [milk, flour] and so cannot be dropped
questions.explain: Version 1 tells the server which state the client had seen. Only values at or below that version are overwritten; [eggs], written later at version 2, is a concurrent sibling.
optionExplain: The server does not merge; merging is left to clients, as the reply with two values shows.
The version sent says what the client knew, so later values survive as siblings.
No such precedence exists; the later write does not win by being acknowledged earlier.
Value size plays no role; only the version number sent decides what is overwritten.
questions.rule: A write overwrites only the values its version number says the client had seen.

media.alt: Timeline with client 1, a database and client 2 building a shopping cart. Client 1 sets cart [milk], then [milk, flour] with version 1, then [milk, flour, eggs, bacon] with version 3. Client 2 sets [eggs] with no version, then [eggs, milk, ham] with version 2. Each reply gives a version number and the values held; from the second write onward replies list two values.

questions.q: In the diagram, user 2's first query shows the new email, but the second query returns 0 unread. What order of events explains this?
questions.explain: User 2's queries ran in the gap after the insert and before the counter update, so the two copies of the truth disagreed. Isolation would have hidden the half-finished transaction.
questions.rule: Without isolation, a reader can run between the writes of one transaction and see an inconsistent state.

media.alt: Timeline with User 1, Database and User 2. User 1 inserts an email for recipient 2 and gets ok. User 2 then selects the email (returns Hello, true) and next selects the unread count, which returns 0. Only afterwards does User 1 send the update that adds 1 to the unread counter, and it gets ok.

options: Both of user 1's writes were applied before user 2 ran either of its queries.
User 1's insert was rolled back after user 2's first query had already read it.
User 2's second query ran after the insert but before the counter update was applied.
User 2's second query ran first, so it read the counter before the email existed.
optionExplain: If both writes had finished first, user 2 would see the email and a counter of one.
A rollback would be an atomicity story, but the diagram shows the update arriving later with ok.
Correct: the query slotted between the two writes, so it saw the new email but the old counter.
The email query comes first in the diagram, so the counter was not read before the email.

questions.q: In the diagram, user 2 sends one more get x shortly before user 1 commits. The value returned is ____.
questions.explain: Until user 1 commits, other transactions keep seeing the old committed value 2, even though x = 3 has been written. The new value appears only after the commit.
questions.rule: Under read committed, uncommitted writes stay invisible to other transactions until commit.

media.alt: Timeline with User 1, Database and User 2. User 1 sets x = 3, then y = 3, each acknowledged ok, then commits. User 2 runs get x three times: the first two, made before the commit, return 2, and the third, made after the commit, returns 3.

questions.q: In the diagram, Alice's and Bob's writes interleave and both transactions commit. What final state do the listing and the invoice end in?
questions.explain: Each object keeps whichever write came last, and the last write to the listing is Bob's while the last to the invoice is Alice's. The sale is split between two customers.
questions.rule: Interleaved uncommitted writes to several objects can leave them pointing at different winners.

media.alt: Timeline with Alice, Listings, Invoices and Bob. Alice sets the listing buyer to Alice, then the invoice recipient to Alice. Bob updates the listing buyer to Bob between her two writes, then sets the invoice recipient to Bob. Annotations say the listing ends with buyer Bob and the invoice with recipient Alice.

options: The listing names Bob but the invoice goes to Alice.
The listing names Alice and the invoice also goes to Alice.
The listing names Alice but the invoice goes to Bob.
The listing and the invoice both name Bob, the later transaction.
optionExplain: Correct: Bob's listing write came after Alice's, while Alice's invoice write came after Bob's.
That would need Alice's listing write to come last, but Bob overwrote it in the diagram.
This swaps the winners; the diagram's annotations show the opposite pairing.
Bob's invoice write was overwritten by Alice's later one, so the invoice does not name Bob.

questions.q: In the diagram, put these steps in the order they happen, so that Alice's total of her two balances comes to 900.
questions.explain: Alice reads account 1 before the transfer touches it and account 2 after the transfer has changed it, so she combines an old and a new value. That is read skew.
questions.rule: A reader that straddles a transaction's writes can see one object before the change and another after it.

media.alt: Timeline with Alice, Account 1, Account 2 and a Transfer. Both balances start at 500. Alice reads account 1 and gets 500. The transfer then adds 100 to account 1 (now 600), subtracts 100 from account 2 (now 400) and commits. Alice reads account 2 and gets 400.

items: Alice reads account 1 and gets 500
The transfer adds 100 to account 1, making it 600
The transfer subtracts 100 from account 2, making it 400
Alice reads account 2 and gets 400

questions.q: In the diagram, transaction 12 reads account 2 and gets 500, although a row with balance 400 exists. Which reason fits the visibility rules?
questions.explain: The 400 row was created by transaction 13, which started after transaction 12, so its writes are ignored. The 500 row's deletion by 13 is ignored for the same reason.
questions.rule: A transaction ignores writes from transactions that started after it did, whether or not they have committed.

media.alt: Transaction 12 reads two accounts while transaction 13 transfers 100 between them. Account 1 rows show created by 3 with balance 500, then a row deleted by 13 and a new row created by 13 with 600. Account 2 shows 500 deleted by 13 and a new 400 row created by 13. Transaction 12 reads 500 from both accounts.

options: Transaction 12 always reads the oldest version of every row, whatever the transaction IDs say.
The 400 row was deleted by transaction 12 itself before its read reached the table.
Transaction 12 is waiting on a lock held by transaction 13 and was handed the last value.
The 400 row was created by transaction 13, which has a later ID, so transaction 12 ignores it.
optionExplain: Readers pick the newest version that is visible to them, not simply the oldest one.
The row's deleted-by and created-by fields name transaction 13, not transaction 12.
Snapshot reads do not take locks; readers are not blocked by writers in this design.
Correct: the later transaction ID makes both of 13's changes invisible to transaction 12.

questions.q: In the diagram, Alice and Bob update different doctor rows. Why does the database let both transactions commit?
questions.explain: The two writes touch different rows, so there is no write conflict, and each check saw a valid snapshot showing two doctors. Only together do they break the rule.
questions.rule: Write skew slips through because conflict checks look at the same row, not at a rule spanning several rows.

media.alt: Two columns of pseudo-code for Alice and Bob. Each begins a transaction, counts doctors with on_call true for shift 1234 (result 2), and if the count is at least 2 sets their own on_call to false, then commits. The doctors table starts with Alice and Bob true, Carol false, and ends with all three false.

options: Bob's check read Alice's uncommitted change, a dirty read that the database tolerates.
The two writes touch different rows, so no conflict exists, and each check saw a valid snapshot.
Alice's update overwrote Bob's earlier uncommitted write to the same row, a dirty write.
Both transactions changed the same row and the database applied each change in turn.
optionExplain: Both counts return 2, so Bob did not see Alice's uncommitted update.
Correct: no row is shared, so row-level conflict detection has nothing to flag.
Alice writes her own row and Bob writes his, so there is no overwrite of an uncommitted write.
The updates are on rows named Alice and Bob, so no single row is changed twice.

questions.q: In the diagram, how does the stored procedure version differ from the interactive transaction for the application?
questions.explain: In the stored procedure case the whole check-and-update logic runs inside the database after one call, so the application does not wait on network hops between statements.
questions.rule: Shipping the whole transaction as one call removes the round trips between statements.

media.alt: Two timelines. Interactive transaction: Application sends a select count query across a network hop to query processor and storage, gets 2, evaluates an if in its own code, then sends a separate update and gets ok. Stored procedure: Application sends one call to run the procedure, whose select, if and update run inside the database, and gets one ok.

options: It sends the select first, then decides in its own code, then sends the update.
It uses a faster query processor, but still makes two separate requests to it.
It makes a single call and the select, if and update all run inside the database.
It skips the if check, so the update always runs without reading the count.
optionExplain: That describes the interactive version in the top half of the diagram.
The diagram shows one request in the stored case, not two to a faster processor.
Correct: one network hop in, one ok back, with all steps executed next to the data.
The if check is still present inside the procedure; only where it runs has changed.

questions.q: True or false: In the diagram, the index-range table records transactions 42 and 43 as readers of key 1234, so a write by either can flag the other's read.
questions.explain: Both transactions are listed as readers of the range, so each one's update can notify the other that its read may be outdated. The record only warns, it does not block.
questions.rule: SSI tracks readers per index range and uses writes as tripwires that notify rather than block.

media.alt: Same timeline of transactions 42 and 43 as the previous figure, each reading doctors for shift 1234, then updating, 42 committing first and 43 aborted. A table of index-range locks lists key range 1234 as read by transaction 42 and read by transaction 43, with a note that 42's update affects 43's read.

questions.q: In the diagram, the client sees no reply in all three cases. In which case did the service actually process the request?
questions.explain: Only in case (c) does the request arrive and get handled, with the response lost on the way back. The client sees the same silence as in the others.
questions.rule: A missing response does not show whether the work was done, since a lost response hides success.

media.alt: Three timelines with Client, Network and Service, each ending in question marks as the client waits. (a) The request is lost in the network, shown as an X. (b) The request reaches a service marked node unresponsive and is lost. (c) The service replies ok, but the response is lost in the network.

options: Case (a) only, where the request is lost in the network.
Case (c) only, where the response is lost in the network.
Case (b) only, where the node was unresponsive at that time.
Cases (a) and (b), since both involve the request reaching the node.
optionExplain: In case (a) the request never arrives, so there was nothing to process.
Correct: the service handled the request and replied ok, but the reply never made it back.
In case (b) the request is dropped at an unresponsive node, so it was not handled.
Case (a) loses the request before it reaches the node, so it cannot count as arriving.

questions.q: In the diagram, node 2 receives x = 1 stamped 42.004 and x = 2 stamped 42.003. Under last write wins, what does node 2 keep?
questions.explain: Last write wins keeps the highest timestamp, so node 2 keeps x = 1 and silently drops x = 2, although B's increment was causally later. Node 3's clock ran behind node 1's.
questions.rule: Timestamps from unsynchronized clocks can reverse the real order and cause the newer write to be dropped.

media.alt: Timeline with Client A, Nodes 1, 2, 3 and Client B, each node showing clock readings. Client A sets x = 1 on node 1 (clock 42.004). Client B then increments x on node 3 (clock 42.003). Node 1's write is replicated with ts 42.004, node 3's x = 2 with ts 42.003, and both arrive at node 2.

options: x = 2, because B's increment happened after A's write in real time.
x = 2, because its lower timestamp marks it as the more recent write.
Both values, because node 2 stores every version it receives.
x = 1, because it carries the higher timestamp, so B's write is discarded.
optionExplain: Last write wins compares timestamps, not the real order of events.
A lower timestamp means an earlier time, so it loses the comparison.
Last write wins keeps a single value per key rather than storing every version.
Correct: 42.004 beats 42.003, so the causally later increment is lost without any error.

questions.section: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority
questions.q: In the diagram, suppose client 1's write with token 33 reached storage before client 2's write with token 34. What would storage do?
questions.explain: Storage rejects only a token lower than one it has already processed. Token 33 arrives first and is the highest seen, so it is accepted; 34 is higher still and is accepted too.
questions.rule: The resource accepts writes whose token is at least as high as any it has processed, and rejects lower ones.

media.alt: Same lock service timeline, now with fencing tokens. Client 1 gets lease with token 33 and pauses in GC. Client 2 gets token 34 and writes data with token 34, which storage accepts. Client 1 wakes and writes with token 33, and storage rejects it as an old token.

options: Accept 33 first, then accept 34, since each token is higher than any already processed.
Reject 33, because the lease behind token 33 had already expired when it arrived.
Accept 33 and then reject 34, because the first writer to arrive holds the file.
Reject both writes and ask the lock service which lease is currently valid.
optionExplain: Correct: tokens are checked against the highest seen, and both arrive in increasing order.
Storage does not know about expiry; it compares token numbers, which is why it stays safe.
Arrival order is not what decides; a higher token is accepted over a lower earlier one.
Storage decides alone from the tokens, without calling back to the lock service.

questions.q: In the diagram, why must client A's third read return 1 while B's reads may return either 0 or 1?
options: A's third read starts after the write returned ok, so no write is in progress to excuse an old value
A's earlier reads returned 0 and 1 in turn, so its next read continues the pattern and ends on 1
A is the client closest to the database, so its reads always see newer data than B's reads do
B's reads are later in time than A's third read, so they are allowed to lag behind the write
optionExplain: Correct: the arrow from the write's ok to A's read shows the read begins once the write is complete.
Reads do not follow a pattern; the value depends on timing against the write, not on earlier results.
Distance from the database plays no part in the model; only the order of request start and finish times counts.
B's reads begin before the write finishes, so they overlap it and are not later than A's third read.
questions.explain: A's third read begins after write C has returned ok, so the write is no longer in progress. B's reads overlap the write, so either value is allowed.
questions.rule: A read that starts after a write completes must see the new value; an overlapping read may see either.

media.alt: Timeline for clients A, B and C on a register x. C has one long bar, write(x, 1), ending with ok. A makes three reads: the first, before the write, returns 0; the second, overlapping the write, returns 0 or 1; the third starts after the write ends, with an arrow from the write's end, and returns 1. B makes two reads, both overlapping the write, each labelled returns 0 or 1.

questions.q: True or false: In the diagram, B's first read returning 0 is allowed, since it ended before A's read that returned 1 began.
questions.explain: B's first read overlaps the write and finishes before A's second read starts, so no earlier read had shown 1 yet. Returning 0 breaks no recency rule.
questions.rule: A read may return the old value unless a read of the new value finished before it began.

media.alt: Timeline for clients A, B and C on register x, with C's long write(x, 1) ending in ok. A reads three times, returning 0, then 1, then 1. B reads twice: the first returns 0 and ends before A's second read begins; the second returns 1. An arrow runs from A's second read, which returned 1, to B's second read, which starts after A's second read ended.

questions.q: In the diagram, D's cas(x, 0, 3) returns error. What explains the error?
options: D's own earlier write of 0 was lost, so the register held no value when the cas ran
The cas reached the database before A's write of 1, and requests that arrive early are rejected
A cas cannot run while other clients are reading, so the database refuses it with an error
By the time it took effect, x had been changed to 2, so x no longer equalled the expected 0
optionExplain: D's write(x, 0) returned ok and took effect first; the later writes simply replaced that value.
The marker for the cas lies after A's write and B's cas on the database line, not before them.
The model does not block cas during reads; other clients may change values at any time.
Correct: the database line shows x=1 and x=2 before the marker for D's cas, so the expected 0 no longer matched.
questions.explain: A compare-and-set succeeds only if x equals the expected value when it takes effect. By then writes by A and B had changed x from 0 to 1 and then 2, so the cas fails.
questions.rule: A cas fails when the register no longer holds the expected old value at the point it takes effect.

media.alt: Timeline for clients A, B, C, D and a Database line with marker points x=0, x=1, x=2, x=4. Operations: D write(x,0) ok; A write(x,1) ok; B read returns 1; C reads 1 then 2; B cas(x,1,2) ok; C cas(x,2,4) ok; D cas(x,0,3) returns error; A read returns 4. Grey lines join each operation to a database marker. B's last read, shaded with a warning sign, starts after A's read of 4 ended and returns 2.

questions.q: In the diagram, what has failed during the network interruption?
options: Each application can no longer reach the database inside its own datacenter
Only the replication connection between the databases, while clients, applications and local databases keep working
The clients of Datacenter 2 can no longer reach any application at all
One of the two databases has crashed and must be replaced before service resumes
optionExplain: The arrows from each application to its local DB are intact; only the link between the datacenters is marked broken.
Correct: the break mark sits on the replication connection, and the client arrows remain unbroken.
Client arrows to Datacenter 2's application are drawn unbroken, so those clients can still reach it.
No database is shown failed; the fault is in the network between them, which is a partition, not a crash.
questions.explain: Only the replication link between the two databases is cut; each datacenter's application, database and clients still work. The choice is whether they may keep serving requests without the other side.
questions.rule: A network partition can cut off replication while every node and client stays healthy.

media.alt: Two boxes, Datacenter 1 on the left and Datacenter 2 on the right, each holding an Application with an arrow to its DB. A curved replication connection between the two DBs is broken by a mark labelled network interruption (network partition). Below, client figures send arrows to the application in their own datacenter: four on the left, three on the right.

questions.q: In the diagram, order these timestamps from smallest to largest under Lamport timestamp ordering.
questions.explain: Timestamps compare by counter first; when counters tie, the greater node ID wins. So (6, 1) comes before (6, 2).
questions.rule: Compare the counter first and break ties with the node ID.

media.alt: Timeline with Client A, Node 1, Node 2, Client B. A writes with max = 0 to Node 1 (counter c = 1) and receives (1, 1). B writes to Node 2 four times with max = 0, 1, 2, 3, counters c = 1 to 4, replies (1, 2), (2, 2), (3, 2), (4, 2). A writes max = 1 to Node 2 (c = 5), gets (5, 2); then writes max = 5 to Node 1 (c = 6), gets (6, 1). B writes max = 4 to Node 2 (c = 6), gets (6, 2).

questions.q: In the diagram, until when does Database 1 hold the locks shown by the grey bar?
options: Until it answers yes to the prepare request, since the vote ends its work
Until the coordinator finishes sending write data to both databases
Until the commit request of phase 2 has been processed and acknowledged
Until phase 1 ends, as soon as both databases have voted yes
optionExplain: The grey bar continues past the yes vote, because the outcome is still unknown at that point.
Write data is only the start of the transaction; the grey bar extends far beyond that step.
Correct: the bar ends only after the commit round trip in phase 2.
Phase 1 ends at the votes, but the bar still runs through all of phase 2 afterwards.
questions.explain: The grey bar for each database runs from its write data until the commit has been processed, so locks are held through both phases.
questions.rule: A participant holds its transaction locks until the commit or abort has been carried out.

media.alt: Timeline with Coordinator, Database 1 and Database 2. Coordinator sends write data to each database, each replying ok. In phase 1 it sends prepare to both and each replies yes. In phase 2 it sends commit to both and each replies ok. A grey bar on each database, running from its write data until after commit is processed, marks locks held by the transaction.

questions.q: In the diagram, database 1 voted yes but hears nothing more from the coordinator. Why can it not commit on its own?
options: It does not know the decision, and another participant may have voted no, which makes the outcome abort
The crash destroyed the coordinator's signature, so any commit by database 1 would be rejected as forged
A yes vote can only be followed by a commit after database 1 sends a second prepare to itself
Database 2 holds the locks on the shared rows, so database 1 is physically blocked from committing
optionExplain: Correct: the participant only knows its own vote, not whether all others voted yes.
Two-phase commit uses no signatures; the issue is missing knowledge of the decision, not authentication.
No second prepare exists in the protocol; the yes vote is already the participant's promise to commit if told.
Locks are held per database for its own rows; database 2's locks do not stop database 1 committing.
questions.explain: Database 1 never learned the decision. If any participant had voted no, the outcome would be abort, so a unilateral commit could contradict it.
questions.rule: A participant that voted yes must wait for the coordinator's decision; guessing either way can break atomicity.

media.alt: Timeline with Coordinator, Database 1 and Database 2. Coordinator sends write data (both ok), then prepare in phase 1 (both reply yes). In phase 2 the coordinator crashes, shown by an explosion and a grey crashed bar. The commit request reaches Database 2, which replies ok; the commit to Database 1 never arrives, and its line is labelled stuck in prepared state.

questions.q: If the job in the diagram had 5 map tasks and 3 reduce tasks, each reduce task would fetch ____ sorted files.
questions.explain: Every map task writes one sorted file per reduce task, so each reducer fetches one file from each of the 5 mappers and merges them.
questions.rule: Each reducer fetches one sorted partition from every map task.

media.alt: Three map tasks on the left, each with an input file (m1, m2, m3 from the HDFS input directory), a Mapper and three sorted output files named by map and reduce number, such as m1,r1 m1,r2 m1,r3. Arrows carry each file to the reduce task with its r number. Each of three reduce tasks gets three files, merges them, runs a Reducer and writes r1, r2 or r3 to the HDFS output directory.

questions.q: In the diagram, a new activity event for user 106 is added. Where do it and the profile record for 106 go?
options: Both go to reducer partition 1, because 106 is an even-numbered user ID
The event goes to partition 1 and the profile to partition 2, as they come from different mappers
Both go to reducer partition 2, because newly added records are sent to the last partition
They go to whichever partitions are least busy, since the user ID does not decide placement
optionExplain: Correct: the key decides the partition, so the event and profile of user 106 meet in partition 1.
Placement follows the key, not the source dataset, otherwise the join could never bring the records together.
New records get no special treatment; the user ID alone determines the partition.
Load does not choose the partition; if it did, matching records could be separated and the join would fail.
questions.explain: The reducer partition is chosen by the key, here the user ID, so records of one user from both datasets meet in the same partition. 106 is even, so partition 1.
questions.rule: The join key decides the reducer, so all records for one key from both inputs arrive together.

media.alt: Two mapper pipelines feed two reducer partitions. The user activity mapper reads events (user 104 loaded /x, user 173 loaded /y, user 104 loaded /z) and emits 104 with url /x, 104 with url /z, 173 with url /y. The user database mapper reads records of users 103 and 104 and emits 104 with dob 1989 and 103 with dob 1947. Reducer partition 1 (even-numbered user IDs) receives the 104 records and outputs url and dob pairs; partition 2 (odd-numbered IDs) takes 173 and 103.

questions.q: In diagram (b), a third consumer joins the fan-out setup and would receive ____ of the messages m1 to m4.
questions.explain: In fan-out every message is delivered to every consumer, so a new consumer would see all four messages, not a share of them.
questions.rule: Fan-out gives every message to every consumer; load balancing splits the messages among them.

media.alt: Two timelines, (a) load balancing and (b) fan-out, with lanes Producer 1, Producer 2, Broker, Consumer 1 and Consumer 2. In both, producers send messages m1 to m5 to the broker. In (a) m1 and m3 go to Consumer 2 while m2 and m4 go to Consumer 1. In (b) every message m1 to m4 goes to both consumers.

questions.q: In the diagram, which statements about the topic B partitions and the consumer group hold?
options: Each partition of topic B is read by exactly one client of the consumer group.
The two clients take turns reading single messages from the same partition.
Each client records a separate offset for every partition it reads.
Numbering in partition 2 continues from the last number of partition 1.
questions.explain: The group splits topic B by whole partitions, and each client tracks one offset per partition it reads. Message numbers restart in each partition.
optionExplain: Correct: the picture shows partitions 0 and 1 going to one client and partition 2 to the other.
Wrong: partitions are assigned whole, not shared message by message, within a group.
Correct: client one lists offsets B.0 and B.1 while client two lists B.2.
Wrong: every partition is numbered from 1 independently, so offsets only order messages within a partition.
questions.rule: A log is split into partitions; each partition is read in order by one consumer of a group, which tracks its offset.

media.alt: Two topics drawn as rows of numbered boxes. Topic A has partition 0 (1 to 10) and partition 1 (1 to 8); topic B has partition 0 (1 to 4), partition 1 (1 to 7) and partition 2 (1 to 12). Two producer clients append at dashed empty slots at partition ends. A consumer group has two clients: one reads B partitions 0 and 1 with offsets B.0 = 4 and B.1 = 5, the other reads B partition 2 with offset B.2 = 9.

questions.q: In the diagram, suppose one leader had ordered both writes and the search index followed it. What final value would the index hold?
options: A, because the first request to arrive at the index is the one that wins
B, because the search index would apply the writes in the database's order
A, because each client's own write is applied last for that client
Either, because the order of two concurrent writes cannot be fixed
questions.explain: The database applied A then B. If the index followed that same order it would also end at B, and the two would agree.
optionExplain: A first-arrival-wins rule is not what happens here; the index would follow the leader's order instead.
Correct: following a single ordering of writes keeps both systems equal, ending at B.
There is no per-client last-write rule in the picture; the order is set by the system of record.
A single leader does fix an order for concurrent writes, which is what removes the disagreement.
questions.rule: A single ordering of writes, followed by every system, prevents the dual-write disagreement.

media.alt: Timeline with lanes Client 1, Database, Search index and Client 2. Client 1 sends set X = A and Client 2 sends set X = B to each store, each getting ok. The database receives A first and then B, ending with final value X = B. The search index receives B first and then A, ending with final value X = A.

questions.q: True or false: in the diagram, once the search index and the data warehouse consume the log, both hold X = B.
questions.explain: Both consumers apply the logged changes in order, X = A and then X = B, so each ends with B.
questions.rule: Consumers that apply the captured change log in order end up matching the system of record.

media.alt: Diagram: Client 1 sets X = A and Client 2 sets X = B on a system of record database. Change data capture appends these changes to a log of data changes shown as boxes with X = A then X = B. Two log consumers, a search index and a data warehouse, each read the log and apply the changes in order.

questions.q: In the diagram, a teammate says the spike after the restart means real traffic grew. What does the diagram show instead?
options: Traffic really grew, and the restart exposed it
The web server sent requests faster while the processor was down
The actual request rate stayed at 10 while the processor worked through its backlog
The processor lost requests during the restart and later counted them twice
questions.explain: The actual request rate line is flat. The measured rate dips to 0 during the restart and spikes when the backlog is processed, an artifact of windowing by processing time.
optionExplain: The flat actual-rate panel contradicts a real traffic increase.
The web server row shows steady request boxes; only the processor's handling changed.
Correct: the true rate is flat and the spike is the backlog being processed in a short span.
Nothing in the picture shows loss or double counting; the delayed events are processed late.
questions.rule: Windowing by processing time turns delays into false dips and spikes.

media.alt: Four stacked panels over time. A web server row of request boxes feeds a stream processor row, which has a grey restarting gap followed by a dense burst of boxes. The processing-time rate graph falls from 10 to 0 during the restart then jumps above 10 and decays. The actual request rate line stays flat at 10 throughout.
